10606-hamlet-a-study-with-the-text-of-th:
George MacDonald published this study of Hamlet in 1885, with the text of the Folio of 1623. He dedicates it to his relative Alexander Stewart MacColl, to whom he owed his true grasp of the great soliloquy. MacDonald's son later called the commentary the most important reading of the play ever written. He praised intuitive grasp over learned analysis alone.

MacDonald gives Hamlet and Shakespeare their due, reading the prince's delay, madness, and moral struggle through the Folio text. The study is for mature youth and adults, rich in quotation and reflection. Readers get a deep, Victorian-era reading of Shakespeare's greatest tragedy.
11032-wilson-s-tales-of-the-borders-and-:
Volume twenty-three of Wilson's Tales of the Borders and of Scotland gathers historical, traditional, and imaginative stories, revised by Alexander Leighton. Contents include the Lawyer's Tales, with Lord Kames's Puzzle over the curious case of Napier versus Napier, the Orphan, the Brownie of the West Bow, gleanings of the Covenant.

Other tales follow Tibby Fowler, the Cradle of Logie, the death of the Chevalier de la Beaute, the Pelican, the Widow's ae Son, twin brothers, a girl forger, and two red slippers. Leighton and John Mackay Wilson write of law courts, covenants, and border villages with local colour. The volume suits readers of Scottish short fiction and of the border country itself.
15457-the-great-round-world-and-what-is-:
This April 15, 1897 number of The Great Round World is a weekly newspaper for boys and girls, published in New York at five cents a copy. Its editors argue that parents should watch the quality of children's reading, so that school lessons on current questions take root. Teachers are offered a special trial rate of one dollar a year.

The paper itself, in magazine form, reports political and scientific news in a bright yet simple manner, made for young readers. That mix of news and clarity was its claim: the finest children's newspaper of its kind, in its own proud words. The issue shows late Victorian faith in informed youth, with the week's world boiled down to short pieces a schoolchild could grasp and discuss.
18745-the-great-round-world-and-what-is-:
This June 9, 1898 issue, volume 2 number 23, is the weekly newspaper for boys and girls called The Great Round World, published at New York. Single copies cost five cents, with a year of 52 numbers for a dollar and a half. Copies sold at stores from Wanamaker's in Philadelphia to Whitaker and Ray in San Francisco, and bound volumes could be had for a small fee.

Ads in the issue tout a three-dollar talking machine for children, patriotic songs at ten cents, and a premium catalogue for a two-cent stamp. The paper mixed news of the world with matter meant for young readers each Thursday. The issue is a charming relic of children's journalism of 1898.
24706-james-cutbush-an-american-chemist-:
Edgar F. Smith, provost of the University of Pennsylvania, wrote this life of James Cutbush, an American chemist who lived from 1788 to 1823. Smith printed it at Philadelphia in 1919, dedicating it to his fellow chemists, with the motto urging readers to preserve the memory of deserving men, lest others likewise deserve.

Smith argues that anything touching the growth of chemical science in America must interest chemists, and he shows how Cutbush and his generation wrought for the young nation. His short biography rescues a forgotten pioneer from obscurity. Readers of science history will find it a careful, affectionate portrait.
30894-the-works-of-robert-louis-stevenso:
Held here is volume twenty-three of the Swanston Edition of Robert Louis Stevenson's works, printed in London in 1912. The edition ran to twenty-five volumes, with two thousand and sixty copies printed and two thousand for sale. This volume holds Stevenson's letters, edited by Sidney Colvin, in parts one through six, with thanks to Methuen for leave to use them.

Part one covers student days at Edinburgh, travels, and excursions, with letters to his father Thomas Stevenson, his mother, Alison Cunningham, Charles Baxter, and Mrs. Churchill Babington, among others. Later parts carry the young writer onward through work and travel. Readers get Stevenson's early voice at its freshest: eager, funny, and full of plans for the books to come.
36345-letters-of-david-ricardo-to-thomas:
Letters of David Ricardo to Thomas Robert Malthus, 1810 to 1823, was shaped by James Bonar and printed at Oxford by the Clarendon Press in 1887. Eighty eight letters fill the book, with an outline of subjects, a chronicle, and an index. The letters print for the first time from the manuscripts.

In his preface Bonar says Colonel Malthus kindly lent the manuscripts for the purpose. Ricardo kin made search for Malthus answering letters, but without success. The set covers the whole span of the friendship of the two men. What is of purely private interest, a very small part, has as a rule been left out. Ricardo hand is clear and good, the editor notes, and the earlier letters have no envelopes. Money thought fans get two great minds at close, friendly war.
42479-la-ronge-journal-1823:
La Ronge Journal, 1823, is the manuscript journal of George Nelson, a fur trader. Nelson drafted the work in June 1823 as a study of native belief. He meant to revise and publish it later, but no printed edition came in his lifetime.

The journal treats the religion and myth of the Cree and Northern Ojibwa peoples. A full scholarly edition at last appeared in 1988, edited by Brown and Brightman. Their book, The Orders of the Dreamed, adds deep study of the shaking lodge rite and of medicines. Nelson's earlier journals of 1802 to 1804 are also in print, as My First Years in the Fur Trade. This edition gives a lightly edited text in three parts, made to keep the work in wide reach.
44343-the-journal-of-negro-history-volum:
Journal of Negro History, volume eight, for 1923, is a year of the scholarly journal edited by Carter Woodson. The Association for the Study of Negro Life and History published it at Lancaster and Washington. Woodson name stands as editor on the title page of the volume. Contents of the January number open with an article by Jackson.

That article treats the educational efforts of the Freedmen Bureau and the freedmen aid societies in South Carolina. Its span is 1862 to 1872, the years of emancipation and reconstruction in that state. Woodson founded the journal in 1916 to make Black history a field of record rather than of rumour. Volume eight shows the work in its stride: documents, monographs, and reviews building the archive on which the whole later study of the subject stands.
46672-holinshed-s-chronicles-vol-3-of-6-:
Holinshed's Chronicles tell England's story year by year, and this slice opens with the reign of Henry the Sixth in 1422. Death had bereft the world of that noble prince King Henry the Fifth. His only son Prince Henry, aged nine months or thereabouts, was proclaimed king of England and France on the thirtieth day of August. Trumpets sounded at the crowning of an infant.

The custody of the young prince was given to Thomas Duke of Exeter and Henry Beauford, Bishop of Winchester. The Duke of Bedford was made regent of France, and the Duke of Gloucester protector of England. Gloucester called wise and grave counsellors to him for the government of the realm at home and the wars abroad. Valiant captains were appointed. The chronicle's old spelling and side notes carry the reader into the reign.
4899-life-and-death-of-john-of-barneveld:
This complete volume gathers John Lothrop Motley's life and death of John of Barneveld from 1609 to 1623, the advocate's full arc in one place. It opens with Barneveld founding the commonwealth's institutions, holding the Union of Utrecht, and compromising between civil and church officials, while Maurice serves as stadholder under the States-General.

Embassies to France, England, and Venice, the Arminius appointment at Leyden, and the Cleves succession all unfold across the span, ending in the advocate's fall. Motley presents a statesman whose patience built a republic and whose enemies finally destroyed him. The complete form lets readers follow one man's fate alongside his country's.
5297-tales-and-novels-of-j-de-la-fontain:
La Fontaine's twenty-third volume gathers The River Scamander, The Confidant Without Knowing It, or The Strategem, and The Clyster, opening with a pretty tale of love. The author notes that love laughs at what he has sworn and prevails over men, gods, and all, who show full obedience to the urchin.

In future, La Fontaine promises expressions not so warm when celebrating love's flame, though the tales that follow keep their heat. Readers get three stories in which love's stratagems, confidants, and rivers carry the comedy, told in verse that balances gallantry with irony.
5926-the-history-of-don-quixote-volume-2:
Pastoral love and a famous wedding fill chapters nineteen and twenty of this Don Quixote portion. Chapter nineteen relates the adventure of the enamoured shepherd, with other truly droll incidents, after Quixote falls in with priests or students and peasants mounted on beasts beyond Don Diego's village. Chapter twenty gives an account of the wedding of Camacho the Rich, a feast of pageantry, music, and competing loves.

Cervantes gives his pastoral comedy at its richest, as shepherds' sighs meet a rich man's wedding and a poor lover's wit. The chapters favor song, debate, and spectacle over swordplay, letting love's economics take the stage. This part suits readers following volume two, since Camacho's wedding becomes a test of Quixote's ideals about merit and money.
64518-short-stories-early-october-1923: Short Stories was a pulp magazine of popular fiction, and this entry holds its early October 1923 issue. The opening pages of the hosted copy are given over to the ads of the day, the matter a reader flipped past to reach the tales. One full page pushes a hollow gramophone needle, the Tone Pen, said to play 80 to 100 records where a plain needle played one. Readers of pulp history get the wrapper of a 1923 fiction magazine, ads and all.
68028-the-yale-literary-magazine-vol-lxx:
The Yale Literary Magazine for January 1923 is volume eighty-eight, number four of the student magazine conducted by the students of Yale University. The editors published it in New Haven at thirty-five cents a copy, printed at the Van Dyck Press. Its front pages list trade discounts at local shops, from tailors and jewelers to the Yale University Press.

The magazine is among the oldest college literary monthlies in America, and this number carries the verse, fiction, and essays of its student writers. One essay argues, with some edge, that nearly everyone has befriended the Christian through inertia, dishonesty of mind, or fear of disapproval. Such undergraduate numbers preserve the tone of a campus at a fixed date better than any later history can.
68029-the-yale-literary-magazine-vol-lxx:
The Yale Literary Magazine, volume 88, number 5, for February 1923, conducted by the students of Yale University and sold at thirty-five cents. The editors include Maxwell Evarts Foster and Francis Otto Matthiessen.

The front pages carry the college world in advertisements: Brooks Brothers clothing, the Yale Co-op boasting nineteen hundred five members, and trade slips at New Haven shops. The contents list a leader by Winfield Shiras, five sonnets, a story called Girl Friends, and an essay on the artistry of art. The leader opens on a campus wrapped in polemics, with controversies over Christianity, chapel, and whether Yale can make great men. Undergraduates get their monthly mirror.
68030-the-yale-literary-magazine-vol-lxx:
Students at Yale ran the magazine whose March 1923 issue forms the hosted text. The issue, volume eighty-eight, number six, was sold for thirty-five cents and printed in New Haven. Editors named on the masthead include Maxwell Evarts Foster, Russell Wheeler Davenport, and Francis Otto Matthiessen.

Inside, a lead essay reflects on campus life at Yale, with places like Mory's and the Bowl named as shared ground. Russell W Davenport adds a drama for two voices and an essay on the modern age, and Foster adds five sonnets. A piece on the soul of a button, book reviews, and an editor's table round out the issue for student readers.
70190-the-yale-literary-magazine-vol-lxx:
Volume eighty-nine, number three of The Yale Literary Magazine is dated December 1923. The magazine, conducted by the students of Yale University, was printed at New Haven. A Latin motto on the title page praises Yale's name and fame. The opening pages given here are the magazine's advertiser, aimed at student readers.

Local shops pitch goods for the young writer: lounging robes, pipes, lamps, theme tablets, pencils, and a portable typewriter. A bookshop on High Street presents itself as a friendly club for finding the right book. A notice offers Harvard and Princeton art studies for three dollars and fifty cents. Student literary magazines like this one trained college writers for a century, and their ads preserve the look of campus life in 1923.
78290-the-bookman-anthology-of-essays-19:
The Bookman Anthology of Essays gathers prose pieces drawn from books by their authors, edited by John Farrar. It was published in New York by George H Doran Company in 1923. It forms one part of The Bookman Books, a series of volumes on literary subjects. Companion volumes in the series include The Bookman Anthology of Verse from 1922 and a guide called The Business of Writing.

The index of authors lists more than twenty names, among them Heywood Broun, Floyd Dell, Zona Gale, and Hugh Walpole. Broun contributes Mr Dempsey's Five-Foot Shelf, taken from his book Pieces of Hate. Aline Kilmer writes on works of reference, and Oliver Herford offers a comic piece called The Hundredth Amendment. John Erskine writes on fame, while Alexander Woollcott writes on O Henry as a playwright. Kenneth Macgowan treats religion and the theatre.
a-general-history-and-collection-of-voya: Volume twelve of Robert Kerr's voyages opens the era of George the Third's southern discoveries. Its book treats voyages ordered by the king and performed by Byron, Wallis, Carteret, and others. These southern hemisphere voyages advanced geography on scientific principles. Kerr presents them as the third part of his systematic history.
achad-egyptian-revival-1923:
Achad turned his new key on Egypt and the tarot in his second major book of 1923. The Egyptian Revival reads the ever-coming son, a figure of the new age, in the light of the cards. Charles Stansfeld Jones writes here as Frater Achad, Crowley's breakaway student.

Egyptian gods and signs are matched to the tarot trumps by his revised scheme of the Tree. The son who ever comes stands for the god of each new age, crowned and conquering. The book carries the project of Q B L into myth and image. It is the middle panel of his Kabbalah trilogy.
aeneas-tacticus-asclepiodotus-onasander-:
A 1923 Loeb volume binds three Greek works on military science together. The Illinois Greek Club translated Aeneas Tacticus, Asclepiodotus, and Onasander into English. Greek text faces the translation in the Loeb manner throughout.

Aeneas, writing around 350 BCE, teaches how to hold a city under siege. Passwords, gates, signals, and spies fill his practical chapters. Asclepiodotus offers a drill book of formations and commands for infantry. Onasander advises generals on character, strategy, and choosing the moment of battle. Together the three founded the literature of ancient military technology. Officers and historians still read them for Greek warfare's working details.
akeley-in-brightest-africa-1923:
Carl Akeley went to Africa to kill gorillas for museums and stayed to save them. In Brightest Africa, printed in 1923, is his classic of the hunt and the wild. Akeley was the great taxidermist of his age and a sculptor of animal groups.

He tells of elephants, lions, and the mountain gorillas of the high volcanoes. His gorilla work showed the beast as shy and grand, not the fiend of old tales. The book helped turn hunters into guards of the great ape in time. Akeley's prose is as clean and bright as his museum glass.
anderson-constitutions-1723:
James Anderson wrote The Constitutions of the Free-Masons in 1723. The Grand Lodge of England had been formed six years past. Anderson gave the new body its laws and its tale of the past. The book is the root text of the craft as a world guild.

A long tale traces Masonry from Adam through kings and saints to London. The Charges then lay down the faith, morals, and peace each Mason owes. Rules for lodges, ranks, and meets fill the last part. The book fixed the shape of the craft for the age to come.
anderson-horses-men-1923:
Horses and Men, published in 1923, gathers Anderson's later stories of the American Midwest. Horses run through the book as measures of human worth: creatures of grace beside men cramped by money, shame, or longing.

'The Man Who Became a Woman' tells of a young horse-hand's frightening, tender awakening at a county fair. Other stories follow grooms, trainers, and small-town dreamers in Anderson's halting, musical prose. The racing world gave him some of his finest material. The collection confirms his gift for lives that official America overlooked, told from inside their own confusion and hope.
anderson-many-marriages-1923:
Sherwood Anderson published Many Marriages in 1923, the most outspoken of his novels. Anderson had been through divorces of his own and wrote obsessively about the gap between respectable marriage and inner desire. The book shocked some readers and was banned in places for its frankness.

John Webster, a washing-machine manufacturer in a Wisconsin town, walks through his house at midnight and confesses everything to his daughter. He tells her of his dead wife, his erotic discontent, and his plan to begin life again with his secretary. The confession takes the whole novel, part sermon and part breakdown. Anderson's plain, groping style tries to say what his characters cannot. Many Marriages remains his most daring treatment of marriage.
arxiv-2412-00023:
Humam Kourani, Alessandro Berti, Daniel Schuster, and Wil van der Aalst benchmarked language models in twenty twenty-four on business process modeling — drawing the formal diagrams organizations use to document workflows. The team built an automation framework, a benchmark of twenty diverse business processes, and an analysis of how models might improve their own outputs.

Sixteen state-of-the-art models from major vendors were evaluated. Performance varied widely, models from similar families trended together, and quality correlated positively with how efficiently a model handled errors. Among self-improvement strategies — self-evaluation, input optimization, output optimization — the last showed the most promise, especially for models that started weak. The results give practitioners a map for using language models in process management and point toward more automated modeling pipelines.
arxiv-2412-00423:
Stefan Meisenbacher and co-authors study day ahead wind power forecasts in a 2024 paper. Grid operators need those forecasts to plan backup actions as wind replaces older plants. Turbines are sometimes shut down in irregular grid interventions, and those gaps can distort forecasts that learn from past output.

The team compare three deep learning methods that use past output plus weather forecasts. They test them on data with regular and with irregular shutdowns. The paper maps where shutdowns hurt accuracy and which designs cope best. Reliable forecasts would let wind farms take a larger role in keeping the grid stable.
arxiv-2412-00523:
Sumit Banik and co-authors link two puzzles in particle physics inside a model with two Higgs fields, in a 2024 paper. Detectors have hinted at extra scalar particles near ninety-five and one hundred fifty-two giga electron volts, seen through decays into photon pairs. Tiny electric asymmetries in matter, called dipole moments, test the same model.

Within the model, one coupling drives both the photon decays and the asymmetries when it mixes real and complex parts. The team maps where the photon hints can be explained while the electron's measured asymmetry stays within bounds. Neutron and proton asymmetries add further checks. The study shows how collider hints and tabletop precision tests constrain each other.
arxiv-2412-00623:
Building a 3D scene from a single image is guesswork, since many shapes fit the same picture. Generative models suit the task, but they usually demand 3D training data that barely exists. Chensheng Peng and co-authors present in 2024 a way to train a 3D diffusion model with only 2D supervision. Their trick decouples the two sides of training: the noisy samples being cleaned up live in 3D, while the supervision signal stays in 2D.

A deterministic image-to-3D model plays teacher, producing imperfect 3D guesses that become the noisy inputs the diffusion model learns to refine. Tested on object and scene datasets with two different Gaussian-splat teachers, the student consistently beat its teachers. The authors argue the approach makes 3D generative modeling scalable and sharper without any full 3D ground truth.
arxiv-2412-00823:
American colleges must publish how many sexual assaults are reported on campus each year, but the published number mixes two unknowns: how many assaults happened, and what share victims reported. Casey Bradshaw and David Blei untangle the two with a hierarchical Bayesian model in a 2024 paper.

National crime statistics supply prior beliefs that break the tie between a quiet campus and a silent one. A Hamiltonian Monte Carlo sampler then estimates, school by school, both the reporting rate and the true incidence behind the 2014 to 2019 disclosures. Reporting rates rose across the period for the overall college population, the authors find, but the depth of underreporting varies widely between schools. That spread, they warn, should change how each campus reads its own crime statistics.
arxiv-2412-01223:
Ruichen Wang and co-authors wrote this 2024 paper on a plug-in that steadies diffusion models when they fill in masked parts of pictures. Diffusion inpainting looks gorgeous but often drifts from the text prompt inside the masked patch and ignores how users actually draw masks. PainterNet slots into existing models to fix both habits.

Local prompt input lets users describe the patch itself, while attention control points and a new attention loss pin the focus of the model onto the right words and places. The mask generator was rebuilt to imitate real user scribbles, and the team released a matching training set, PainterData, plus a benchmark, PainterBench. Across quality and text-consistency metrics, local and global, the plug-in beat current state-of-the-art inpainting systems.
arxiv-2412-01323:
Satoru Takano and co-authors published a 2024 paper describing a ground-based detector for very slow gravitational waves. Gravitational waves are faint ripples in space caused by huge events far away. Most detectors on Earth listen for fast ripples. Slow ones, down to a thousandth of a cycle per second, are much harder to catch from the ground.

Their device, called TOBA, uses a bar hung so it can twist gently, like a slow pendulum. That loose twist lets it respond to slow ripples despite sitting on Earth. The paper reviews earlier small test versions of the device. It also describes the work now under way toward a full-size version ten meters across. A working detector of this kind would open a new low band of waves for study, adding to what current observatories can hear.
arxiv-2412-01623:
Dottorini and co-authors study the ultraviolet slope of distant galaxies in a 2024 paper, using spectra from the James Webb telescope. The slope, called beta, tells how blue a galaxy's light is, which hints at its age, dust, and metal content.

More than seven hundred galaxies from several Webb programs, all seen as they were in the early universe, form the sample. Brighter galaxies tended to be redder, as past work found, but that trend flattened at the greatest distances. The slope also grew bluer with distance in a steady way. Fifty one galaxies were bluer than even dust free young star models predict. The team compares those odd cases with redder peers to hunt for the cause.
arxiv-2412-01923:
Paolo Arnaudo and Benjamin Withers compute exact response functions in 2024 for a holographic model of a superconductor. Their setting pairs a quantum field theory with a charged black hole in a curved space, a duality used to study strong interactions. At low temperature the math hinges on a special differential equation family.

Using new results from a related theory, they solve the connection problem in a controlled double limit where frequency and temperature fall together. From the response function they extract the critical temperature for the holographic superconductor. They also derive dispersion formulas for gapped and gapless low-temperature modes. The exact results match numerical work precisely.
arxiv-2412-02523:
Cameron Franc, Nathan Heisz, and Hannah Nardone count how often primes behave tamely for hypergeometric series, in a 2024 paper. Such series are built from factorials with adjustable parameters, and for each prime one can ask whether the series stays bounded in the p-adic sense. The share of good primes, the density, turns out to encode deep facts about the series' symmetries.

For series whose parameters are rational numbers, the authors extend an exact density formula from the simplest family to a broader one. The density equals one exactly when the symmetry group is finite, matching a classic classification. For parameters from a quadratic number field, they prove a lower bound on the density unconditionally. If the p-adic digits of such numbers are normally distributed, the bound becomes exact. Examples reaching the ceiling of one-half all come, so far, from imaginary quadratic fields.
arxiv-2412-02723:
Daniel Seal and co-authors extend in 2024 a generative diffusion frame to rain nowcasting over South America from satellite data. Extreme rain grows more common, and fast short-range forecasts help officials act in time. Satellite rain data feed forecasts up to four hours ahead.

Tweaks to the base frame suit rain data better than the stock form. A new loss joins three error and image quality scores in one aim. Scores for weak, moderate, and heavy rain beat four rival models in the tests. Forecasts stay sharp and stable to two hours on a heavy rain case, with slow decay after.
arxiv-2412-02823:
Wang, McCoy, and Steinert-Threlkeld tested a simplicity bias in language models in this paper from twenty twenty-four. People learn simple concepts more easily than tangled ones. The authors asked whether large language models show the same tilt when learning from examples in the prompt. They built concept tasks with known logical structure.

Each concept could be scored by its Boolean complexity, a count of the logical steps it needs. Model success tracked that score closely across tasks. Concepts with low complexity were learned well, while tangled ones tripped the models. The pattern mirrors findings in human concept learning. The authors suggest that in-context learning shares a bias for simple rules with human learners.
arxiv-2412-03023:
Cebajel Tanan and co-authors built a free web tool that inspects an internet address and reports how risky it looks. Cybercrime has grown with digital life, and internet protocol addresses are a key clue in threat intelligence, yet the authors found no single free, open tool that checks them fully. Their tool reports where an address is located, whether it appears on blocklists, and whether it hides behind a VPN, a proxy, the Tor network, or a bot. It also scans ports and gathers domain details such as name servers and registrar.

To make the verdict trustworthy, the tool combines results from several reliable public sources into one confidence score. A local database caches past results, so repeat checks return fast with fewer outside calls. The tool accepts both domain names and IPv4 addresses. The authors offer it as a one-stop analyser for analysts who track online threats.
arxiv-2412-03123:
Xiaojun Xu, Jinghan Jia, Yuanshun Yao, Yang Liu, and Hang Li hide multi-bit watermarks in rewritten text in a 2024 paper. Owners of AI-written text need marks that survive editing. Their trick uses two fine-tuned paraphrasing models that subtly phrase things differently.

To encode a bit at each sentence, the writer picks one paraphraser or the other. A trained classifier then reads the bits back from the wording style alone. Detection accuracy topped 99.99 percent even with small paraphraser models, while meaning stayed intact. The marks held up under word swaps and full re-paraphrasing by attackers, and human judges found the text natural.
arxiv-2412-03223:
Chanyeol Choi and co-authors describe Linq-Embed-Mistral, a text retrieval model whose strength comes mainly from careful data work. The 2024 model builds on the E5-mistral and Mistral-7B models. The team refines, filters, and mines hard negative cases, with each step tailored to its task. Synthetic training sets made by large language models join real benchmark data in the mix.

Tasks of the same kind are ordered together during training to steady learning and improve stability. The finished model averaged 68.2 across 56 datasets on a broad benchmark, as of late May 2024. On retrieval tasks alone it ranked first, with a score of 60.2. A light evaluation path at four-bit precision speeds up checking without losing accuracy, the team adds.
arxiv-2412-03323:
Aryan Bhardwaj and co-authors build a fiber setup in a 2024 paper that makes linked pairs of photons across a comb of colors. Photon pairs that are born together share timing ties, a resource for quantum communication and sensing. Their source mixes light waves inside a highly nonlinear fiber, a process called four-wave mixing, and needs no bulk optics.

Timing tests confirmed the photons were truly correlated, not random. The source reached a high rate of paired counts, with true pairs standing well above chance matches. To grasp the physics, the team also simulated a general mixing event between a color comb and a steady pump laser. Their model of the fiber's nonlinear flow matched the lab results. A compact, tunable pair source of this kind suits quantum network tests.
arxiv-2412-03923:
Yuhito Shibaike and co-authors predict the glow of a disk that may circle a young planet in a paper from 2024. The planet candidate, AB Aurigae b, still pulls in gas from its birth disk. Such planets should host small disks of their own that shine in thermal light.

Telescope searches at millimeter waves have not seen that shine. The team modeled how dust evolves in the disk and forecast its brightness. Across wide settings, the forecast stayed below past detection limits. That fits the non-detection without ruling the planet out. Some settings imply a heavier planet with faster gas intake. The case study gives hunters a guide for other growing planets.
arxiv-2412-04023:
Olger Siebinga models the sidewalk salsa, the awkward shuffle when two walkers dodge the same way, twice. Everyone knows the dance; no model had explained how it starts. His frame treats each pedestrian as holding a firm plan plus a fuzzy guess about the other's plan.

Risk is the referee: each walker steers to keep collision risk under a private threshold. In simulation, a perfectly matched pair falls into the salsa on cue. Offset starts or mismatched thresholds produce lifelike passes instead. A built-in bias about which side others favor, a stand-in for local custom, also feeds the dance. Robot designers get a mechanism to design against.
arxiv-2412-04123:
Oriel Humes and Josef Hanus wrote a 2024 paper on the spin and shape of asteroid Pompeja. The main belt rock shows odd swings in the color slope of its light over time. Those swings may come from patches on its surface that rotate in and out of view.

Dense light curves exist for just two passes, and the spin period sits close to a full Earth day, which makes ground views hard. The team pulled a dense light curve from a space telescope archive, covering about 22 full spins in 2021. They measured the spin as seen from Earth and its light swing. The curve then refined shape and pole models, yielding two pole solutions.
arxiv-2412-04523:
Aidin Rasti wrote this software study in 2024 on a daily headache for open-source teams: users post plain questions in the issue tracker, where bug reports should go. On big projects, the flood of off-topic posts buries real bugs and eats staff time. Reading and tagging each post by hand does not scale. Rasti set out to tag them by machine.

The first step scrubbed post text, stripping logs, error dumps, and code traces that add noise. A trained classifier then sorted posts into question or not. On a set of more than 102,000 records, the method tagged questions with accuracy above eighty-one percent. Rasti says the tool can free maintainers for real fixes and point users to proper help boards.
arxiv-2412-04623:
Kaihua Chen, Deva Ramanan, and Tarasha Khurana taught video models in 2024 to outline whole objects even where they are hidden. People know a thing is still there when it slips behind cover. Most vision tools trace only what can be seen. Past amodal tools worked on still frames or stiff goods and broke down at deep cover. Time in video can fill those gaps.

Their method treats the task as guided generation. A video model takes the seen-part masks and rough depth maps and grows the full shape. A second stage paints the hidden part in. On four test sets, the method beat the field by a wide edge in the hidden zones. It held up from stiff to soft goods.
arxiv-2412-04823:
Anar Dosi published this paper in 2024. It builds a complex analytic geometry for the quantum plane, a deformed space from quantum algebra. The starting point is Manin's quantum q-plane, studied here when the deformation parameter is not on the unit circle. Dosi first works out how the algebra can act on Banach spaces. He then stretches its smooth envelope into a sheaf of Fréchet algebras over the spectrum.

The resulting ringed space splits into two pieces: one copy of the complex plane with a q-flavored topology, and one with a disk topology. Modulo its radical, the sheaf turns out commutative. That fact unlocks a functional calculus and a spectral mapping property, phrased through the noncommutative Harte spectrum. The paper serves specialists weaving algebra, geometry, and operator theory into one fabric.
arxiv-2412-04923:
Antonello Ceravola and co-authors present an operating system where scientists work inside living graphs in a 2024 paper. HyperGraphOS treats models as customizable graphs that are at once drawings on a screen and data structures underneath, editable by hand or by code. It runs in a web browser, asking nothing more exotic of its users.

Model-based engineering, graph modeling, data containers, and computing tools share one workspace. Domain-specific languages steer navigation through the graphs, generate code, invite AI assistance, and organize processes. Trials crossed unlike territories: steering virtual avatars, planning robot tasks with large language models, and meta-modeling for feature-based code generation. In each, the authors report gains in flexibility, data handling, computation, and document management. The pitch is a single bench where a project's knowledge, files, and models stay connected instead of scattered.
arxiv-2412-05423:
A large international team reports two mini-Neptune planets locked in a resonant rhythm around the star TOI-1803, in a paper published in two thousand twenty-four. Resonant planets circle their star in periods that form a simple ratio, a clue to how the system formed and migrated.

Three facilities joined forces for the discovery and characterization. The space telescope TESS spotted the planets' transits, dips in starlight as the planets crossed the star. The HARPS-N spectrograph measured the star's wobble to weigh the planets. The CHEOPS space telescope added precise transit timing and shapes. Combining the three views pins down sizes, masses, and orbits far better than any one instrument could. Mini-Neptunes, bigger than Earth but smaller than Neptune, are among the most common planets known. A resonant pair like this is a natural laboratory for testing how such worlds assemble.
arxiv-2412-05623:
Yajun Wang and co-authors tackle signal design for a future wireless network that mixes several ideas at once. Base stations spread across an area serve users jointly, with no cell borders. Smart surfaces that reflect radio waves help steer the signals. The goal is to set all the transmissions together so total data speed is as high as possible.

The design problem is large and tangled, since the best settings for the stations and the surface depend on each other. The team splits it into two halves solved in turns, one using a consensus method for the stations, the other fast gradient methods for the surface. The model also accounts for how the surface responds across wide channels. Simulations showed clear gains in data speed over earlier methods. The authors say the approach can raise capacity while keeping computing costs in check.
arxiv-2412-05823:
Yongzhe Jia and co-authors present DapperFL in 2024, a federated learning frame for edge devices. Devices train a shared model without sending private data away. Edge fleets differ wildly in power, and local data domains shift. Both traits drag standard federated methods down.

A fusion pruning module trims each local model with knowledge pooled from all domains. The pruned models stay compact and personal while resisting domain shift. A second module adds regularization drawn from the pruned model, which steadies learning across domains. A custom aggregation step then merges models of unlike shapes. Tests on a real testbed show gains over prior federated frames under mixed conditions.
arxiv-2412-05923:
Fresh telescope data on a nearby pulsar tightens what we know about matter inside neutron stars, and a 2024 paper by Len Brandes and Wolfram Weise folds it into their ongoing analysis. The NICER telescope measured the mass and size of the pulsar PSR J0437-4751, and the team added those numbers to their Bayesian study.

Radii for typical neutron stars shrank by about two to three hundred meters, landing near twelve kilometers. Central densities rose a little but stayed below five times the density of normal nuclear matter. The new data also strengthened the case that a certain pressure measure turns negative inside heavy stars. The paper is an update, showing how one new object refines the whole picture.
arxiv-2412-06023:
Anya Nordskova and Michel Van den Bergh prove, in a 2024 math paper, results about twist moves on K3 surfaces, a rich class of geometric shapes. Each special object on the surface defines a twist of its derived category, an algebraic shadow of the shape. The team shows that the group spanned by all such twists, on a surface with the simplest label structure, is free: no hidden relations tie the moves together.

They give a recipe for the free generators and settle when the group needs finitely many. That recipe in turn classifies the special objects themselves. The results then verify the first three-dimensional case of a standing conjecture. A braid group acts transitively on the full exceptional collections of a class of Fano shapes.
arxiv-2412-06123:
Khrystik bounds the length of a finite-dimensional algebra, a measure of how many generator products suffice to build everything. Given a generating set, its length is the smallest word length whose products span the whole algebra. The algebra's length is the worst case over generating sets. Such bounds connect generation cost to intrinsic invariants.

The paper shows the length never exceeds the larger of half the dimension and one less than the biggest minimal-polynomial degree among elements. Both quantities are computable from the algebra's basic data. As an application, the length of the group algebra of the dihedral group of twice an odd number of elements equals exactly that odd number. The general bound and the sharp family together anchor the theory. Length joins dimension and polynomial degree as a basic algebraic statistic.
arxiv-2412-06723:
Ashutosh Marwah and Frédéric Dupuis prove a universal chain rule for a smoothed measure of entropy used in quantum information, in a 2024 paper. A chain rule splits the uncertainty of a whole system into the uncertainties of its parts, added step by step. The standard rule fails for the smooth min-entropy, a quantity central to quantum cryptography.

The authors prove the rule for a close variant of that entropy, equal to the usual one up to a constant, for any number of parts. A dual result follows for the matching max-entropy. Their proof leans on entropy triangle inequalities. As a bonus, they prove a relaxed entropy accumulation theorem that drops the usual demand that the state be built step by step.
arxiv-2412-06823:
Brian Ye, Zhuonan Hao, Priya Shah, and Mohammad Khalid Jawed build a soft robot that moves objects by squeezing waves in this 2024 paper. The motion, called peristalsis, is the same wave motion guts use to push food along. Soft robots suit fragile and oddly shaped loads, yet this transport style had seen little use. Their system stacks donut shaped air modules that inflate in sequence.

Live pressure feedback keeps the modules in sync as they grip and pass an object along. The design needs no intricate sensing or heavy control logic. Modules can be swapped, so the system is scalable and easy to repair. Tests showed it handled objects of varied shapes and materials, balancing firm grip with gentle handling. The authors present the system as a low cost path to safe handling of delicate goods.
arxiv-2412-07123:
Nhat Nghiem proposed a frame in 2024 for estimating the amplitudes of a quantum state with single-qubit measures only. The usual route measures all qubits to gather outcomes. Restricting measures to one qubit at a time seems limiting, yet the author shows it can suffice.

Outcomes from measures in varied bases form a system of nonlinear equations. Solving that system classically yields estimates of each amplitude, with real and imaginary parts. The paper then counts how many measures are needed for set accuracy goals. Bounds are given for single amplitudes, for total variation, and for average error, each scaling in a stated way with qubit count.
arxiv-2412-07523:
Ryo Tazaki and a large team image a planet-forming disk from its edge with the James Webb Space Telescope. The disk, HH 30, wraps a young star and shows its structure edge-on. Their 2024 set joins new near- and mid-infrared images with older images from the Hubble Space Telescope and a ground array, ALMA. The stack gives the finest view of this disk yet obtained.

The images show two bright fans split by a dark lane, plus a spiral, a tail, a cone-shaped outflow, and a tight jet. Large dust grains sit mixed through the full height of the disk. Fine dust, by the ALMA reading, lies flat in the midplane. A knot in the jet was caught moving for the first time, by matching two mid-infrared images. The tilt of the disk differs a bit by the kind of reading used.
arxiv-2412-07623:
Christopher Vairogs and Bin Yan speed up quantum state fidelity checks in a 2024 paper. Verifying that a prepared quantum state matches its target is foundational. Direct estimation already beats full tomography on cost. Its price still grows linearly with the state space size.

Their protocol cuts overall cost to a square-root scaling. Measurement counts and inter-party communication also drop sharply. Amplitude estimation supplies the quantum speedup ingredient. Classical shadow methods supply cheap state sketches. Combined, they estimate fidelity for generic states efficiently. Trust between distant quantum devices is a natural use. Certification of quantum hardware outputs becomes cheaper. The authors stress the protocol works beyond special state families. Generic states were the hard case addressed. Quantum network verification is the motivating setting.
arxiv-2412-07723:
Bartuska and co-authors present a 2024 paper on nested integration, a hard computing problem in applied math. A nested integral feeds one integral into another through a curved function, which makes it costly in high dimensions. Such problems arise in experiment design, finance risk, and uncertainty studies. Plain Monte Carlo sampling can be too slow for them.

The authors build a multilevel estimator that mixes fixed and randomized quasi-random sampling. Each level pairs a sample count with a set accuracy for the inner integral. Their error bounds show less bias and spread than standard methods. Number tests confirm the gains, above all when the inner integral can only be evaluated roughly.
arxiv-2412-07823:
Jimin An and co-authors shrink the data burden for hip exoskeletons in a 2024 paper. Estimating a wearer's hip joint moment from sensors takes deep learning. Such models usually demand long lab sessions across many tasks. Their strategy clusters movement tasks by biomechanical features. It then keeps only a minimal representative set for training.

A network trained on the slim set matched full-set accuracy across subjects. Its error stayed near zero point three newton-meters per kilogram. It also clearly beat training on cyclic tasks alone. Readers who build wearable robots get a way to collect far less data. They keep control quality while cutting cost and time.
arxiv-2412-07923:
Sagi Shaier, Mario Sanz-Guerrero, and Katharina von der Wense ask a playful question with a serious edge: do language models answer better when a question is repeated? Their 2024 study tests five recent models, from a small commercial one to open-source systems. Each model read passages and answered questions that appeared once, three times, or five times in the prompt. Three reading data sets were used to check the pattern.

Accuracy rose by up to six percent with repetition in some setups. Yet across all models and settings, the gain never reached statistical significance. The authors read this as a caution: a trick that sometimes helps is not a reliable method. The work adds to the craft of prompt design, where folklore often outruns proof.
arxiv-2412-08523:
Gauhar Abbas and Neelam Singh, two authors named in the head byline, study a particle physics model in 2024. The catalog lists only Abbas, but the head names both authors. Their model tiers the values that give particles mass, and a new version curbs unwanted flavor effects.

With those effects curbed, new physics could sit at a scale current colliders can reach. The model predicts clear signals for the next runs of large colliders. One light particle in it can explain a bump near ninety-five GeV seen by two detectors. It also offers a dark matter candidate that interacts only with neutrinos.
arxiv-2412-08623:
Galaxy surveys measure how galaxies cluster and how their gravity bends light, but the ordinary matter in and around galaxies, called baryons, distorts those signals on small scales. Matteo Zennaro and co-authors propose a cheap fix. Models of the galaxy and matter cross spectrum usually track dark matter only. The authors argue that the baryonic effect on that cross spectrum can be borrowed from the effect on the matter spectrum alone, through a simple square root correction.

They test the idea on the FLAMINGO simulations, which include full gas physics. In mock analyses, ignoring baryons biased the galaxy properties, and ignoring them everywhere biased the cosmology too. With their correction, the model matched every physics variant to within one percent on the scales their bias model covers. Fitted values landed on the truth within the errors. The team offers the method for the coming generation of sky surveys.
arxiv-2412-08823:
El Alaoui and co-authors track a quantum symmetry through noise in a 2024 paper. Two faces of a quantum state are linked: its Wigner function, a portrait with negative dips that flag non classical behavior, and a skew information measure of coherence. States rich in one tend to be rich in the other. The team use that link to read parity symmetry in superpositions of spin coherent states.

The study covers the simplest spin and general spin alike, under a Gaussian noise channel. Whether parity asymmetry survives noise tells engineers if the state's quantum character is usable or already lost. Spin ensembles serve sensors and memories, so the survival test has practical stakes.
arxiv-2412-08923:
The classical Alexandrov-Fenchel and Minkowski inequalities bound the geometry of convex bodies, and geometers keep extending them. Kwok-Kun Kwong and Yong Wei derive new sharp weighted versions for smooth closed hypersurfaces in Euclidean, spherical, and hyperbolic spaces. The weights are convex, non-decreasing positive functions, and beyond that they are arbitrary.

Each choice of weight function yields its own inequality, so the results form a broad family rather than a single statement. The authors work under various convexity assumptions on the hypersurface. They present the family as a flexible extension of the classical theory of space forms, ready to be specialized to whatever weight a problem supplies.
arxiv-2412-09023:
Rishabh Sabharwal and three co-authors add a light attention module, STEAM, to convolutional networks for image tasks. Their work appeared in twenty twenty-four. Attention helps networks focus, but most designs add heavy cost in parameters and computing.

STEAM models both channel and spatial focus at once with a fixed, tiny parameter count. It borrows relational tools from graph transformers, a first for this pairing. A guided pooling step sharpens the spatial side cheaply. On standard image sorting tests, it lifted a leading network's accuracy by two points with barely more computing. Against top rival modules it won on accuracy while using three times fewer operations. Detection and segmentation tests round out the case.
arxiv-2412-09423:
Manuel Hagelüken, Marco Huber and Marco Roth predict the excited-state properties of molecules with a quantum neural network that needs very little training data in 2024. Excited states govern how molecules absorb light, but computing them costs far more than ground states.

Their model reads the ground state and predicts transition energies and dipole moments across molecular shapes. A symmetry-aware quantum circuit keeps the parameter count growing only linearly with the number of orbitals, and a tunable measurement reduces how much must be measured. On hydrogen and lithium hydride test cases, the method often beat classical models by up to a hundredfold in error. The design runs on today's noisy quantum hardware.
arxiv-2412-09623:
Weiqi Li and eight co-authors wrote a 2024 paper on OmniDrag, a method for controlling motion in omnidirectional videos generated from a single image. Virtual reality needs immersive 360 degree video that creators can direct. Text prompts alone give loose control and often produce content errors.

Drag based motion control works for flat video, but spherical motion breaks it, causing distortion. OmniDrag is presented as the first method to offer both scene level and object level motion control for this format. It builds on pretrained video diffusion models, adding an omnidirectional control module tuned together with the temporal layers. A new spherical motion estimator extracts control signals faithfully and lets users guide movement on the sphere.
arxiv-2412-09723:
Xu and five co-authors presented this system in twenty twenty-four for teams of agents that map a place together. Each agent must track its own motion and help build one shared, sharp 3D model. Older methods give sparse maps, while dense ones run too slowly. Their system, MAC-Ego3D, builds the model from soft blobs called Gaussian splats.

Each agent builds a local map and keeps nearby splats in agreement. A second process then aligns the local maps into one global model, working in parallel. The shared format lets agents render views quickly and match their maps with ease. On test sets the system ran about fifteen times faster than rivals. It also cut motion errors sharply and raised image quality by wide margins.
arxiv-2412-09823:
Xuefang Xu and co-authors report a deep sky survey of regions where massive stars are forming, in a 2024 paper. They used a thirty-meter radio telescope in Spain to listen across a band of millimeter waves. Wide, sensitive scans like this catch many molecules at once without prior bias about which to seek.

The team observed fifty such regions in the Milky Way. They identified twenty-seven kinds of molecules, sixteen of them complex organic ones. For each line they measured peak strength, total power, and line width. Lines from kin molecules rose and fell together in width, a hint they come from the same gas. The dataset gives a base for tracing how molecules evolve in massive star-forming cores.
arxiv-2412-10323:
Yen-Hua Chen and co-authors report a passing lens that briefly blurred a pulsar's twinkle pattern in a 2024 paper. Pulsars shimmer as their radio waves cross thin gas screens in space, drawing arcs that stay stable for years. Sometimes a second screen drifts across and warps the arcs for days or months.

Using phase retrieval to separate the two screens, the team measured the second lens's arc curve and drift for pulsar B1737+13. Fitting the yearly swing gave a likely distance and tilt for the main screen. They checked the method on a pulsar with a known answer and recovered it. The passing lens spans only about one to three times the Earth-Sun distance, a size compatible with an extreme scattering event, though proof stays open.
arxiv-2412-10923:
Binita Maity and co-authors keep clustering fair even when outliers pollute data in a 2024 paper. Fair k-means promises every point a center among its nearest neighbors. Outliers break that promise's math, since wild points demand centers of their own.

A linear program first flags which points count as outliers. Those points leave the dataset before the fair clustering runs. A rounding algorithm then places centers under the fairness rule. This is the first treatment of fair clustering with outliers for k-means. Honest fairness must survive messy, real-world data, not just clean sets.
arxiv-2412-11323:
Some random processes spread so unevenly that noise reaches parts of the state space only indirectly — hypoelliptic diffusions, with smooth polynomial drift and degenerate, additive noise. Juraj Földes and David Herzog develop in 2024 an inductive procedure for how such a process behaves in the first instant after it starts.

The procedure yields two rescaled views of the process. One is pathwise, in the spirit of the law of the iterated logarithm; the other is distributional. Each view leads to a control problem. The authors solve these in nontrivial examples with tools from geometric control theory. The control answers then give a practical test for when a boundary point is regular for the diffusion. That question decides how solutions of related equations behave at the edges.
arxiv-2412-11623:
Yalun Zhang and Longwen Zhou show how pair ties bend phase shifts in one way quasi grids of bosons, in a 2024 paper. One way grids host odd edge and phase acts that draw much work. How pair ties and one way hops mix in such grids was the open ask.

Pair ties stretch a lone freeze line to a mid phase band. Bound pairs roam free in part while lone states stay froze there. At open ends, bound pairs crowd the edge in skin acts. Hop terms steer which edge the pairs crowd to in tests. A frame sorts the glow, place, and phase shifts in step.
arxiv-2412-11723:
Two mathematicians, I. Panin and A. Stavrova, settle a special case of the Grothendieck-Serre conjecture in a 2024 paper. The work concerns reductive group schemes over a discrete valuation ring of mixed characteristic, a setting that mixes prime and zero characteristic behavior.

The authors prove that the conjecture holds for any reductive group scheme over such a ring, whenever the algebra involved is geometrically regular and local. They also prove a version of a known geometric presentation lemma in the same setting. The constant case is one step in a long program, and closing it in mixed characteristic removes a case that earlier approaches had left open.
arxiv-2412-11823:
Md Iftekhar Islam Tashik and co-authors review work on question answering systems for the Bangla language, published in 2024. Such systems let a computer answer questions posed in natural language. Bangla systems have grown in recent years, but they still lag behind those for larger languages.

The review covers seven prior studies in depth. It traces how each gathered data, prepared it, built a model, and tested the results. Methods include attention-based sequence models, context-based systems, and deep learning that draws on prior knowledge. The authors stress shared limits: too little well-labeled data, few good reading test sets, and trouble with word meaning in context. Those limits hold back both accuracy and real-world use.
arxiv-2412-11923:
Sepideh Mamooler and three co-authors present PICLe in this 2024 paper, a method for named entity detection when labeled examples are scarce. Language models can learn a task from a few examples shown in the prompt, a style called in-context learning. The catch is that results swing with the choice of examples. The team's study of this swing produced a surprise: examples with partly wrong entity labels worked about as well as fully correct ones.

PICLe builds on that finding. A model first labels many examples on its own, with no human help. Those noisy examples are clustered, and sets are sampled from each cluster to make separate predictions. A self check then picks the final set of entity mentions. On five biomedical data sets, PICLe beat standard in-context learning in low resource settings. It did so with zero human annotation.
arxiv-2412-12323:
Lokesh Kumar Sharma, Suresh Parekh, and Anil Kumar Yadav used both statistics and deep learning to test a modified theory of gravity in a 2024 paper. Their theory changes how gravity works at the cosmic scale, and they ask whether it can explain why the universe expands faster over time. They use a stated form of the theory plus a flexible curve for the expansion rate. Two very different fitting methods are set side by side.

One method is the classic sampling approach used across cosmology. The other is a mixed neural network run inside a framework that needs no explicit likelihood. The network method matched the classic results while proving faster to train, the authors report. Their fitted universe shifts from slowing expansion to speeding expansion at a set point in the past. The work is offered as proof that learning based fitting can serve cosmology well.
arxiv-2412-12423:
Nikola Zubić and Davide Scaramuzza introduce Graph-Generating State Space Models in a 2024 paper, a new take on the sequence models used in vision and time series work. Standard state space models process data along a fixed one-dimensional path, which limits how they capture links between distant parts of an input. Even flexible scanning variants follow preset paths.

Their framework instead builds a graph from the data itself, linking features by their relationships with a minimum spanning tree method, and passes information along that graph. Tested on eleven datasets, from ImageNet classification to optical flow and eye tracking, the models set new best results on every task. They also used fewer parameters than rivals on some tasks.
arxiv-2412-12523:
Bhaskar and Pyne give in 2024 algorithms to compute stable outcomes in a classic model of election positioning. In the model, voters sit along a line by ideology, and each candidate picks a spot to win the most votes. Each voter backs the nearest candidate, which sets up a game.

Past work studied whether stable pure outcomes exist and what they look like, but not how to compute them. The authors give three algorithms that cover continuous and discrete voter spreads and candidate spots. Each returns an exact stable outcome, or one as close as desired, when one exists. The work may spur computing work on the model's many extensions.
arxiv-2412-12923:
Johannes Martin and five co-authors test a learning method for cosmic ray paths in a 2024 paper. Charged particles from space move through strong magnetic turbulence, and modeling that motion matters for solar and cosmic ray studies. Running full simulations for each path is costly. A generative model might produce realistic paths far faster.

They trained a diffusion model on paths from a detailed turbulence simulation. The generated paths matched the real ones closely on speed changes, spread, and curvature, at fixed particle energies. They also compared two simpler synthetic turbulence models. The authors close by discussing what still blocks a ready-to-use transport model built this way.
arxiv-2412-13023:
Lennert De Smet and co-authors propose a 2024 model class that joins neural sequence learning with strict logic rules. Deep sequence models such as transformers excel at tasks like language and control. Yet they cannot promise that set constraints will hold, which blocks trusted use. Older neurosymbolic tools can enforce rules but grow too slow on long sequences.

Relational neurosymbolic Markov models are built to do both jobs at once, and they provably satisfy relational logic constraints. Inference and learning stay end-to-end trainable by mixing Bayesian inference, automated reasoning, and gradient estimates. Tests show the models solve tasks past the reach of current neurosymbolic systems while keeping their guarantees. Constraints can also be swapped at test time, and the models stay easier to read than black-box rivals.
arxiv-2412-13123: Eliezer Batista, Felipe Lopes Castro and Mykola Khrypchenko introduce partial actions of groups on strict monoidal categories in their 2024 arXiv paper. Partial group actions are already studied for algebras, where key constructions include globalization, a subalgebra of partial invariants, and the partial smash product. The authors propose versions of these constructions adapted to monoidal categories, extending the theory of partial symmetry into a categorical setting where objects combine under a tensor-like operation.
arxiv-2412-13223:
Sai Advaith Maddipatla and co-authors tackle a hard problem in protein science: proteins move and flex, and a single still structure hides that motion. X-ray experiments record electron density maps that quietly contain signs of the many shapes a protein takes. Fitting a whole set of shapes to those maps is an ill-posed task with no single right answer.

The team guides an existing shape-making model with the measured maps, using a method that lets the generated shapes differ from one another rather than copying a single pattern. In their tests, the method recovers complex cases where a protein's backbone truly switches between distinct forms seen in single crystal data. The work points toward richer, more honest pictures of protein motion drawn straight from lab measurements.
arxiv-2412-13623:
Arne Gevaert and Yvan Saeys bind all score-tale crafts in one frame in a 2024 paper. Such crafts tell why a black-box tool made its call, each by a split of the score among the marks it read.

New crafts breed fast, and the pick of one has been a guess. The pair shows most known crafts are one kind: cut a mark out, weigh the shift. A sole build then breeds each such craft's split, and each craft's split is one of a sole clan of game counts. With that tie in hand they set rules a craft can be sworn to keep, and the terms on which the oath holds. The frame also speeds old crafts' sums. The authors cast it as a base for a science of such tales.
arxiv-2412-14023:
Christian Kirkham and co-authors present calibration methods for global 21-cm cosmology in a 2024 paper. Such experiments hunt a faint signal from the cosmic dawn, buried under bright galactic foregrounds. A well-calibrated instrument is essential, or system flaws will bias the faint result.

Three methods use a noise wave frame to model a low-noise amplifier. One weights calibrators to dodge singularities and normalize noise. A second fits polynomials while sampling their order. The third is set out in the full text. Care with calibrator noise is a theme throughout. The work helps teams build trust in a signal that is easy to fake by accident.
arxiv-2412-14123:
Guillaume Astruc and three co-authors present a 2024 paper on one model for all kinds of Earth observation data. Satellite data vary in sharpness, scale, and sensing type, and most models demand one fixed input form. Their model, AnySat, learns from the mix in a self-taught way.

To train it, the team built GeoPlex, a bundle of five data sets from 11 sensors. One model trained on all of them at once. Tuned for tasks from land cover maps to flood and fire scar outlines, it matched or beat specialist tools on the bundle and on six outside data sets.
arxiv-2412-14323:
Lisa Wang, Adam Meyers, John Ortega, and Rodolfo Zevallos study a quirk of Chinese nouns that makes machine translation into English go wrong. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-four.

Some Chinese nouns act as traits of a next noun, and the mark that shows the link is often left out. That gap breeds doubt in English. The team took news heads from a Chinese text bank and put the lost mark back by hand. That gave a set tuned to the flaw. They used it to fine-tune open translation models. The fix lifts how this key mark is handled. It adds a sharp tool to the broad ways past work gave for this pair of tongues.
arxiv-2412-14623:
Kim, Kwon, Lee, and Kim present FRIDAY in twenty twenty-four, a training method for deepfake detectors. Detectors work well on their training data but fail on new synthesis methods. Studies show they often key on facial identity instead of faking artifacts. That habit causes poor results on new data sets.

FRIDAY uses a face recognizer to push identity out of the detector. The recognizer is trained first, then frozen during detector training. Both models receive the same images, and a loss term penalizes alike feature embeddings. That forces the detector to build features distinct from identity features. Experiments show large gains on both in domain and cross domain data. The authors present the method as a fix for a hidden bias in detection.
arxiv-2412-14823:
Théo Brugeat studies how an axion could sway neutron-antineutron swings in a 2024 paper. Matter beat antimatter in the early universe, so baryon number must break somewhere. Neutrons flipping into antineutrons would prove that break without endangering protons.

The study allows the most general couplings between the swing and dark matter candidates. A Rabi resonance appears, where the axion field can amplify the oscillation. That effect is still unconstrained for axion-like particles, the analysis finds. For the classic QCD axion, its Goldstone nature rules out most scenarios. A tabletop-scale swing hunt thus reaches into deep cosmology.
arxiv-2412-14923:
Jakob Glas and Matthew Hase-Liu study rough spots in a space of curves in a 2024 mathematics paper. The space collects all maps of a set degree from smooth curves onto a smooth surface of low degree. Geometers need to know how bad the space's own kinks can get.

For map degree large next to the curve's genus, the authors prove the kinks are at worst terminal. That class of kink is mild enough for many uses in geometry. Their path runs through jet schemes, which record how curves sit to high order. For those, they build a form of the circle method, a classic counting tool from number theory. The work ties two far-apart fields in a new way.
arxiv-2412-15023:
Riccardo Fosco Gramaccioni and co-authors present FolAI in a 2024 paper, a system that generates sound effects for video. Foley artists rebuild everyday sounds, footsteps, doors, crashes, to match what happens on screen, a slow manual craft. Teaching a computer to do it means solving two problems at once: the sound must fit the action in meaning, and land at the right moments.

FolAI splits the job in two stages. First it reads the video's motion and draws a smooth control signal that captures how intense and rhythmic the action is over time. Then a diffusion model composes the sound, guided by that timing scaffold and by semantic cues about what should be heard. The authors argue that separating when from what keeps generated effects locked to the picture, a step toward automated sound design that still respects a creator's intent.
arxiv-2412-15123:
The ATLAS Collaboration reports the first clear observation of a rare event in proton collisions, in work from 2024. The event makes three heavy force-carrying particles at once, in a machine run at high energy. Data came from the ATLAS detector at the Large Hadron Collider.

The team sifted records of particle decays that end in light charged particles, with some events also showing particle jets. The three-particle rate they gauged matched forecasts from the standard theory of particles. The signal stood at well over the bar for a firm claim. A related two-plus-one event also showed strong evidence. The team used the results to bound new physics that would change how these particles interact.
arxiv-2412-15323:
Marcus Stålhammar and Lukas Rødland wrote a 2024 paper on the topology of exceptional points. Exceptional points are special spectral degeneracies in non-Hermitian systems, where eigenvalues and eigenvectors merge at once. Multifold versions bring several states together at a single point. Their topology was recently described with resultant winding numbers and doubling theorems, but a deeper mathematical account was missing.

The authors rebuild the classification using similarity relations, covering both local and non-local symmetries. They read the resultant vector through three lenses: the tenfold way of topological matter, the Mayer-Vietoris sequence, and vector bundle theory. The scheme also predicts new bulk Fermi arcs guarded by a Z2 invariant from non-local symmetry. The work aims to serve experiments in both classical and quantum physics.
arxiv-2412-15423:
Bhupendra Acharya and Thorsten Holz offer a 2024 study of a fast-growing fraud called pig butchering. In this scam, criminals build trust with a victim over weeks or months, often through a fake romance or friendship. Once trust is high, they lure the victim into putting large sums into fake investments, then vanish with the money.

The authors gather evidence from several angles at once. They read victims' own stories posted on social media, search public abuse report databases, and study cases told in news outlets. Data was collected across most of 2024. Joining these views shows how the scams recruit, groom, and drain their targets. The work gives platforms, banks, and police a clearer map of a fraud that thrives on patience.
arxiv-2412-15823:
A Civit-Bertran and co-authors simulate a core density collapse event in the Large Helical Device plasma in three dimensions, published in 2024. Such collapses are sudden drops of the dense core in this stellarator. A new non-linear magnetohydrodynamics model, extended with heat flow along field lines, was built into an existing code and checked against the older model.

The test case was a super dense core discharge with a steep pressure gradient and strong shift of the magnetic axis, a setup prone to instability. In the runs, high-order ballooning modes on the weak-field side destabilized the plasma first. Pressure and density profiles then collapsed, the magnetic field turned stochastic, and the action shifted to low-order core modes during relaxation. The model reproduces the event's preliminary character.
arxiv-2412-16023:
Ricard Ravell Rodríguez and Simon Morelli identify the best Gaussian probe states for estimating an unknown phase, in a paper from twenty twenty-four. The setting is phase estimation in a continuous-variable system with homodyne detection. A catch drives the work: the optimal probe depends strongly on the phase value being estimated. Prior knowledge therefore changes what should be sent in.

For large prior uncertainty, the optimal pure single-mode Gaussian probes sit close to coherent states. As estimates sharpen, putting more energy into squeezing the probe pays off. Surprisingly, the optimum then jumps abruptly to a squeezed vacuum state. That state maximizes the Fisher information for the task. The authors also apply their results to repeated measurements. They compare strategies for adapting the probe as knowledge from earlier rounds accumulates.
arxiv-2412-16123:
Javier Jiménez-López, Paul Newman, and Katarzyna Wichmann scope in 2024 what the future Electron-Ion Collider could learn about the proton's inner structure. Their target is the longitudinal structure function, a quantity that separates how the proton responds to different photon polarizations and that probes its gluon content.

The team simulates a Rosenbluth separation, varying sample sizes, error budgets, and beam energy setups. With enough energy settings and tight control of systematics, the collider should measure the function with unmatched precision even at modest luminosity. The reach complements older fixed-target and HERA data, and in the best cases rivals them as a direct gluon probe.
arxiv-2412-16223:
Ronen Brilleslijper and Oliver Fabert lift a branch of geometry from curves to surfaces in this 2024 paper. Symplectic topology studies rigid features of the spaces where mechanics lives. Its classic paths are geodesics, the straightest curves on a surface. The natural two-dimensional heirs of geodesics are harmonic maps from surfaces, and the paper builds the matching theory.

The authors define the surface version of symplectic manifolds and of Hamilton's equations, landing on equations that behave like their one-dimensional parents. Two rigidity theorems anchor the work: a non-squeezing result, which says some shapes cannot be deformed into others, and a cuplength result for a class of systems on cotangent bundles. The second proof needs a surface version of Floer curves, and the paper supplies the analytic groundwork, including the compactness arguments such proofs stand on.
arxiv-2412-16423:
Shogo Watanabe wrote this 2024 technical report on a small language model built for Japanese medicine. Big models are heavy and costly, and Japanese clinical text has its own dense vocabulary of diseases, drugs, and tests. His model, NCVC-slm-1, holds only one billion parameters and trained on carefully filtered, high-quality Japanese text enriched with medical content.

A specialized tokenizer, built on a morphological analyzer for Japanese, helps the small model read clinical phrasing well. Fine-tuned, it topped six of eight tasks on the JMED-LLM benchmark against larger rivals, and it can both generate and understand medical text. Watanabe presents the result as proof that small, focused models can carry real clinical workloads.
arxiv-2412-16723:
Yu-Fan Lin, Bo-Cheng Qiu, Chia-Ming Lee, and Chih-Chung Hsu present in a 2024 paper a two stage model to find bleeding in gut images. Exact spotting of bleeding helps diagnose ulcers and bowel cancer early. Joint models that class and outline at once can let the two tasks fight each other.

Stage one sorts each image as bleeding or not, which shields stage two from mixed labels. Stage two then grounds the bleed area in the images flagged as bleeding. Weight averaging and test time flips add toughness against domain shift and sloppy labels. The method took second place in a public challenge on capsule endoscopy data. Gains were clearest on series with steady visual patterns, the team report.
arxiv-2412-17023:
Marcin Osial and co-authors improve the craft of merging several fine-tuned models into one that does all their jobs. Model merging avoids retraining on every task's data, but merged models often blur each task's features — a representation bias that drags performance down. Their 2024 paper proposes IntervMerge, which corrects the blur with small task-specific interventions inside the shared model.

A lighter variant, mini-interventions, adjusts only part of the representation, trimming the extra parameters further. Across experiments, the method beat state-of-the-art merging approaches while adding fewer parameters than they do. The appeal is frugality: one model to ship, many skills inside. Machine learning practitioners get a cheaper path from a zoo of specialists to a single generalist.
arxiv-2412-17623:
Shiyuan Qu and co-authors speed up hard planning problems in 2024 with an unsupervised learning trick. The problems, called mixed-integer programs, mix whole-number and continuous choices and can take solvers very long. Their method trains an autoencoder on past optimal answers for a family of like problems. The trained network's settings then yield new cutting constraints.

Added to a fresh problem, those constraints shrink the search space around good answers. Off-the-shelf solvers then finish much faster at like quality. The team tested the idea on a batch process scheduling problem. Results showed clear cost savings. The code is shared openly for others to try.
arxiv-2412-18023:
Rebecca Ramnauth, Drazen Brscic, and Brian Scassellati build, in a 2024 paper, robots that can hold small talk, not just task talk. Small talk is a social handshake: it builds ease and trust. A robot that does it well feels more warm and its chats run smooth. The team tests how far today's large language models can drive such talk. Gaps show, and they add a fix: a loop that grades the model's lines on its own and steers them to small-talk norms. No human needs to mark each line by hand.

Tests ran in two fields, text chats and live human-robot chats. The steered lines read more true, warm, and smooth. The path fits social robots at large.
arxiv-2412-18323:
Tom Lyche and two co-authors build leaner spline tools for smooth shapes over triangle meshes, in a 2024 math paper. Splines are patchwork curves used to model smooth surfaces in design and simulation. The full cubic spline space on a split triangle mesh is rich but heavy. The team carve out subspaces that keep cubic power while using far fewer control values. Some versions need data only at mesh corners and edges, and one needs corners alone.

The leanest space uses just six values per mesh corner. Each patch can be built on its own from local data, in a macro-element style. A local basis handles the tricky split geometry behind the scenes. The authors say the savings suit large models where each degree of freedom costs time.
arxiv-2412-18423:
Surfaces that sit smoothly inside four-dimensional spaces are a classic topic in topology, and building them takes deep tools. Arunima Ray, writing alone in a 2024 survey article, explains the two main ways mathematicians build such flat surfaces. Both ways rest on a famous disc embedding theorem of Freedman and Quinn.
