One way reshapes a given map by hand, while the other leans on surgery theory. Ray sketches proofs of two landmark results to show the methods at work. The first builds a flat torus for a wide class of homology classes. The second shows that a broad family of knots can bound a flat disc, which makes them topologically slice.
arxiv-2412-18523:
Yushi Hamaguchi and Dai Taguchi bound the flaw of a stock scheme for chance-based rules with a past. The work came out in 2024. In these rules, the now rests on the whole past. The Euler-Maruyama scheme is the stock way to run them on a screen.

The team studies weak match. They ask how close the scheme's spread of ends is to the true spread. They gauge the gap with the Levy-Prokhorov gauge on path space. With mild terms on the weights in the rules, they prove a firm bound on the flaw. In some cases the bound is sharp, in both the shape gauge and its rate. They use the find on ten models from many fields. For each one, they pull out a flaw bound. The proof rests on a broad link trick for chance gauges.
arxiv-2412-18723:
Arya Bangun and co-authors speed 3D MRI rebuilds with a diffusion model kept on a tight rein, in a study from 2024. MRI gives fine views of flesh and leaf, but full scans are slow. Fast scans take sparse raw reads, and the rebuild must guess the rest sans smear or noise.

Past fast builds worked slice by slice, in 2D. This one builds the whole block at once. A diffusion model, taught what true scans look like, guides the guess, while a firm math step keeps the guess true to the reads. Tests ran on clinic scans and plant scans, with mixed sparse plans and fresh or stale teach sets. The team reports gains over past builds in faith and clean form. Block-true builds may cut scan waits in wards and labs.
arxiv-2412-18923:
Dohyun Kim and Woojoo Shim study how crowds of moving frames settle into agreement when each drifts by its own rotation. Their setting is the Kuramoto model lifted to Stiefel manifolds, where each agent's state is a whole orthonormal frame rather than a single angle. Without interaction each frame rides its own natural flow; coupling pulls every agent toward the crowd's average.

When all natural motions match, the system is a tidy gradient flow. The authors tackle the unruly case where they differ, using orbital stability analysis to prove convergence. Consensus on manifolds underlies synchronization problems from power grids to coordinated robots carrying rigid orientations through space.
arxiv-2412-19023:
Lu-Qi Zhang, Yao Ma, and Yong-Liang Ma published a physics paper in 2024 on nuclear matter in an extended effective theory of the strong force. Their theory adds a dilatonic scalar meson to the chiral frame. Applied to nuclear matter, it reproduces known behavior near saturation density. Against older Walecka-type models, it improves the fit for symmetry energy and stiffness without extra free knobs.

Predicted neutron star structures fall inside limits set by a major gravitational wave event and two pulsar measures. The top star mass can reach about three solar masses with a purely hadronic core. The authors note that the theory's symmetry patterns strongly shape star structure.
arxiv-2412-19123:
Kaixing Yang and co-workers generated group dances from music with focus to how the dancers hang jointly in a 2024 paper. Solo dance making is well studied, but group choreography often comes out incoherent, dancers drifting out of sync and looking unnatural jointly. Their setup, CoheDancers, decomposes coherence into three targets: synchronization with the music and each other. Naturalness of movement, and fluidity across time, then assigns a plan to each.

Cycle consistency training ties dance back to music to impose synchronization; an autoregressive fix plan counteracts exposure bias for fluidity; hostile training polishes naturalness. The team also built what they describe as the most diverse and comprehensive open data set yet for group dance making. The result targets games and virtual shows, where a troupe must move as one.
arxiv-2412-19223:
Lovepreet Singh and Tiwari study additive maps on division rings, in a math paper from twenty twenty-four. They test a key identity for one such map. Two generalized polynomials frame the map's value, and their product equals a third such form. Both of those outer polynomials are not zero. Their main result sorts what can happen in this setup.

They then use that result on a special case. It mixes a map with powers and inverses of its input. On a non-commutative division ring whose characteristic is not two, the outcome is stark. The only maps that meet the identity are zero maps. That holds when the two exponents are not both one. The work thus turns a broad identity result into a sharp vanishing result.
arxiv-2412-19723:
Qiushi Sun and co-authors flip the way training data for computer-using agents is made. Such agents learn from step-by-step records of tasks done on real screens, but collecting those records needs people or scripted tasks, which are costly and narrow. Their system, OS-Genesis, lets an agent wander an interface first, clicking and exploring, and only afterward writes the task that the wandering accomplished.

A reward model then grades the records and keeps the good ones. Agents trained on this reversed data did markedly better on hard live benchmarks than agents trained on older synthetic sets. The authors also report the data was more varied and closer to real use.
arxiv-2412-19923:
Alexeev and a large international collaboration present a 2024 measurement from the COMPASS experiment on how muons can knock a lone neutral pion out of a proton target. The process is called hard exclusive muoproduction: the muon strikes, a single pion leaves, and the target stays whole. Its cross section, the rate gauge for the event, is the paper's core output. Such clean events probe the inner layout of the proton, since no messy spray hides the exchange.

COMPASS fires high-energy muon beams at fixed targets to catch rare events of this kind. Rates for the lone-pion channel feed models of the proton's part structure. Each hard channel adds a line to that map. Particle teams share such rates so rival models can be tested on the same numbers.
arxiv-2501-00023:
Krystian Polczyński and co-authors study a pendulum pushed by a magnet whose pull changes phase with the pendulum's own position. Such a system swings between order and chaos. The team models a real bench setup, where a magnetic torque term carries the position-dependent phase, then checks the model against experiment.

Bifurcation analysis maps the rich behavior: steady periodic swings, period-doubling routes, and chaotic motion, often coexisting for the same settings. Simulations and bench results agree closely, which backs the model. The work also shows how touchy the energy exchange is to the magnetic coupling. Nonlinear dynamics readers get a small system with a full zoo of behaviors, captured both in math and in metal.
arxiv-2501-00723:
Four authors led by Sriram Muralidhar measure the body fuel cost of holding forces that rise and fall with time. Muscles burn fuel to make force even when no joint moves, a case past cost models treat thinly. Each test person spent five hours in lab trials, pushing in wave forms with set means, swings, speeds, and rise-fall splits. Fuel burn was read as they pushed at a range of joint loads.

A clean sum of two power curves fit the burn well across the whole grid. Cost rose with load at a 1.36 power and with load swing rate at a 2.5 power. One twist stood out: easing a load off cost near four times more fuel than piling it on. Move plans and robot aids can use the fit for live cost reads.
arxiv-2501-00823:
Zhenyu Guo and Wenguang Chen design a modular Transformer that separates knowledge from reasoning. Standard Transformers mix both jobs in one block, which hurts how interpretable and flexible they are. Their design routes knowledge through a broad cross-attention step to a shared knowledge base used by all layers, with layer-specific changes for retrieval.

A derivation in math shows that the feed-forward network in a standard Transformer is a special case of this cross-attention. That result recasts feed-forward layers as implicit knowledge retrieval, supporting the modular design. The authors frame the work as a base for models that interact more openly with external knowledge stores.
arxiv-2501-00923:
Ruifeng Yuan and Lei Wu wrote a 2025 paper on optimizing the shape of bodies moving through gases of any thinness. Gas flow around a body ranges from thick continuum air to the free-molecular regime of near-vacuum. One optimization method that works across that whole span did not exist.

Their adjoint method rests on the kinetic BGK equation with diffuse reflection at the surface. A body-fitted mesh hugs the interface. Continuous and discrete adjoint analysis together yield how drag changes with each bump of the boundary. Multiscale solvers keep the sensitivity accurate in every regime. A quasi-Newton optimizer then walks the shape downhill. One subtlety: discretizing molecular velocities makes sensitivities oscillate, cured by careful boundary parameterization. Airfoil drag tests reached their optima in about a dozen iterations and minutes of computing.
arxiv-2501-01123:
Junya Ono and Hiromi Wakaki improve emotion detection in conversations in a 2025 paper. Knowing who feels what in a dialogue helps chatbots and analysts, but models tend to blur the turns together, marking speakers and order only with crude tokens. Their method, TED, writes turn information directly into the attention mechanism.

Each turn gets a priority from its position and its speaker, and attention scores are adjusted by those dialogue features. Multi-head attention then runs over turn-level vectors. On four standard benchmarks the method performed strongly overall, and it set a new best score on IEMOCAP, a data set with long conversations. The authors argue explicit turn structure beats implicit hints.
arxiv-2501-01223:
Amil Bhagat, Milind Jain, and Subramanyam introduced conditional consistency models for image translation in a 2025 paper. Consistency models rival diffusion models while needing only one generation step, but multi-domain translation was barely tried with them. Tasks range from crossing between image types to rescuing dark photos.

Task-specific guiding inputs steer the cleaning process, so outputs keep the structure and context of the source image. Ten data sets tested the approach across domains. Translated images came out sharp and faithful in the reported checks. The authors say one-step generation can serve translation and enhancement, not just fresh creation. Code is public for builders who want to test the claim.
arxiv-2501-01623:
Joshua Angrist and colleagues developed in 2025 new instrumental variable methods for trials where treatment is taken over time and many patients do not follow their assigned plan. Their case is a trial of revascularization for ischemic heart disease, where some assigned to invasive care stayed untreated and some controls crossed over to treatment.

Simple comparisons then mix up the effect of the assignment with the effect of the care itself. The new methods target patients who comply at each follow-up point, called dynamic compliers. For those patients, the gains in quality of life from revascularization were larger and lasted longer than older intent-to-treat or per-protocol estimates had shown.
arxiv-2501-01823:
Sandipan Manna, Sthitadhi Roy, and Sreejith study the projected ensemble in a quantum system with many conserved charges that have local support. Their 2025 paper extends work on deep thermalization in isolated quantum many-body systems.

Past research focused on reduced density matrices of local subsystems, in settings of thermalization, integrability, and localization. New experiments can measure the full distribution of quantum states, which led to the projected ensemble: pure states of a subsystem obtained by measuring its complement. Earlier work covered chaotic circuits, Hamiltonian evolution, and global charges. Their system is a strongly disordered quantum spin chain with many local charges.
arxiv-2501-02423:
Xingwu Sun and co-authors map the scaling laws of training language models in low-precision floating point. Cutting number precision slashes training and serving costs, and production shops already train this way. Old scaling laws, though, were fit to integer quantization and miss how floats divide their bits. Their 2025 study varies each ingredient in turn.

What gets quantized, how many bits go to exponent versus mantissa, and how coarsely scale factors are shared all move the final loss. Exponent bits buy slightly more quality than mantissa bits, and the team tabulates the best split at each total width. A unified law then predicts loss across the whole design space. Model trainers get a recipe card for cheap precision without the usual trial and error.
arxiv-2501-02723:
Konrad Deka and co-authors settle a long open question from the math of symbolic dynamics, posed by Rufus Bowen as his Problem 32. The question asks whether systems with the specification property can be sorted by a tidy list of concrete traits. Such systems model shifting symbol streams with strong mixing rules.

The authors build a family of systems with the property and show that telling two of them apart up to conjugacy is too hard for any such tidy list. In short, no clean invariant set can finish the sorting job. Along the way they answer two linked questions on pointed systems. One concerns Cantor systems, the other systems on the Hilbert cube. Their gauge of the problem's hardness gives future work a firm map of what classification can and cannot do.
arxiv-2501-02923:
Nicolás M González reports, for the Pierre Auger Collaboration in 2025, on the hunt for ultra-high-energy photons and neutrinos. The Pierre Auger Observatory is the world's largest cosmic ray detector, and the same showers it records can betray these neutral messengers from extreme events or even dark matter decay.

The searches blend three detector types that watch air showers from above, at ground level, and underground. So far no photon or neutrino candidate has turned up. That silence yields the tightest limits yet on how many such particles can be streaming above set energy levels, from both diffuse glow and steady point sources. The limits squeeze models of cosmic accelerators and dark matter, and the team also hunts in step with gravitational wave alerts.
arxiv-2501-03323:
Matt Cusack and six co-authors simulate how gas clouds break into pieces in starburst settings, the violent star-forming regions found at the center of our galaxy and in young galaxies far away. Such places bathe clouds in strong radiation and cosmic rays, unlike the calm solar neighborhood. Most past simulations ignored those harsh conditions. The team ran detailed fluid simulations with both factors raised to starburst levels.

The harsh setting changed how clouds fragment. On the large scale, clouds broke into fewer but heavier cores. Inside those cores, though, fragmentation ran stronger, producing richer clusters of star systems. The final mass mix tilted toward heavier systems at both levels. The authors credit faster gas feeding onto growing systems for the shift. Their picture ties the extreme environment directly to the kinds of stars a cloud produces.
arxiv-2501-03423:
Nikita Belenkov and co-authors present a systematization of knowledge review of cross-chain bridge hacks in 2023, published in 2025. Blockchain technology enables secure, decentralized transactions, but separate chains cannot naturally move assets between each other. Cross-chain bridges emerged as vital web3 infrastructure to solve that problem and support interoperability.

Despite sophisticated designs and security measures, bridges remain vulnerable to various attacks, and the industry saw a surge of them in 2023 with large losses. The review catalogs that year's bridge hacks, their methods, and their consequences in detail. For builders and auditors, a systematized record of real attacks is the raw material for stronger future designs.
arxiv-2501-03523:
Achintya Sarkar and co-authors warped voice features for keyword spotting in two thousand twenty-five. Keyword spotters listen for trigger words on devices. Speakers vary in vocal tract length, shifting their sounds. Warping features can normalize those differences. The team built three spotting methods around warping. A neural network scored the warped features.

One method trains on many warp factors at random. At test time it averages scores across warps. A second scores plain features against the same network. A third stacks warps into one large feature set. Tests used an English voice command dataset. Warped methods improved spotting accuracy. The gains help assistants serve diverse voices fairly.
arxiv-2501-03723:
Buldgen and co-authors use two fading elements in the Sun's outer layers to probe how material circulates just beneath them. Lithium and beryllium burn at different depths, so their surviving amounts record how strongly and how deeply mixing reaches below the convective envelope. The team folds fresh abundance measurements into solar models and checks the results against the envelope's depth, its helium content, sound-speed maps, and neutrino output.

A mixing law that fades with density, with an index between 3 and 6, reproduces the data, needing an efficiency near 6000 square centimetres per second at the envelope's base. The extra mixing slightly worsens the match to neutrino fluxes. The authors also report that the magnetic Tayler instability, a proposed driver tied to spin transport inside the Sun, cannot explain the observed depletion in its current form.
arxiv-2501-04223:
Kotochigova, Gupta, and Blinov cast plain motes as mail bits tween ion tool banks in this twenty twenty-five paper. Ion banks hold fine math bits, yet banks must link to grow large. Light links tween banks run slow, which caps the tool's growth pace.

Inside, a tweezer beam ferries one plain mote bit from bank to bank. At each bank the mote ties with one ion bit in a gate act. That tie then links the two banks through the mote's own state. Beam push leaves ions calm, and trap hum leaves the mote calm. Pace marks top light links by near a hundred-fold in their counts.
arxiv-2501-04423:
César Godinho and co-authors recheck a test of quantum theory in atoms in a 2025 paper. Helium-like ions, atoms stripped down to two electrons, give clean lines whose energies can test quantum electrodynamics in strong fields. Past checks used rival statistical styles and reached clashing verdicts on whether the measures drift from theory.

The authors use Bayesian statistics, which assigns odds to each claim. They model any drift from theory as a power of the nuclear charge, across elements from boron to uranium. With current data, they find no firm drift from theory. Recent experiments have shrunk the room for the drifts claimed in older work. The paper also states how precise future measures must be to settle the question.
arxiv-2501-04523:
Toby Rodel and a large team of co-authors announce an eclipsing pair with a tiny late M dwarf. Their 2025 paper presents NGTS-EB-7, found by a ground survey. M dwarfs are the galaxy's commonest stars, yet their sizes stay poorly pinned. Eclipsing pairs let astronomers measure radii directly.

The small star circles an evolved G-type primary on a long, eccentric orbit. Its radius looks inflated against model predictions, a trend seen in earlier M dwarfs. Magnetic activity is the suspected cause. Whether the swelling reaches the latest, fully convective dwarfs was unclear. Long periods mean weak tides, so the pair tests models cleanly. Each such system sharpens the yardstick for the smallest stars.
arxiv-2501-04623:
Amritanshu Pandey, Mads Almassalkhi, and Sam Chevalier review the heavy optimization machinery the future power grid will need, in a 2025 paper. Running a grid laced with solar, wind, batteries, and flexible demand means solving huge optimization problems, fast and often. These solvers hedge risk, size up local resources, and trim cost, emissions, and outage odds.

The review sorts recent progress in transmission and distribution optimization into two camps. Physics-based methods, built on the grid's equations, still lead the science. Data-driven methods, especially ones fenced in by physics, are rising where the classic solvers choke. The authors also map the field's open gaps, gathered from the literature and from experts, to steer the next round of work.
arxiv-2501-05323:
Hesham Moussa and co-authors view distributed AI through a networking lens in this 2025 paper. Big models usually train and answer from one central cloud. That design raises privacy worries, storage costs, energy demands, and a single point of failure.

Spreading learning across many machines avoids those traps but adds moving parts. The authors propose a framework that treats data and model pieces as a network problem. Their survey maps how training and inference can be split, moved, and coordinated. Edge devices and private data stand to gain most. The paper aims to give system builders a shared map of a scattered field.
arxiv-2501-05423:
Jerry Chongyi Hu, Mohammed Shahid Modi, and Boleslaw Szymanski read the mood of Chinese social media through the COVID-19 outbreak, in a 2025 study. Weibo, the country's main microblogging site, carries fast public reaction to crises. Sentiment there bends toward more than a simple good or bad, though.

An open language model, Llama 3 with eight billion weights, sorted posts into positive, negative, sarcastic, and neutral piles. Posts spanned the calm before the virus, the outbreak, and the first control phase. Tracking those piles over time shows how events and state actions moved public feeling. Sarcasm, often missed by blunt tools, gets its own lane. The work fills a gap in crisis sentiment study for Chinese platforms.
arxiv-2501-05623:
Gonzalo Constante-Flores and Can Li propose an approximation for power grid optimization in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. The AC optimal power flow problem is central to running grids, but it is nonconvex and hard to solve at scale. Common simplifications rest on assumptions that may not hold in modern grids.

Their method rewrites the problem with quadratic constraints, then convexifies the hard terms around a warm-start voltage point. The result is an inner convex approximation that keeps the grid equations' sparse structure. It does not assume high reactance ratios or near-nominal voltages. Tests on library cases up to thirty thousand buses beat other relaxations and a linear model. Case studies cover reactive power dispatch and solar hosting capacity.
arxiv-2501-05723:
Maia Stiber and co-authors taught robots to notice mistakes from human reactions in two thousand twenty-five. People flinch, frown, and speak when robots err. Those signals arrive faster than formal reports. Their system reads face and voice cues live. Error context sharpens the detection further. Feedback from users feeds the same loop.

Twenty-eight people worked with the proactive system. A reactive baseline waited for explicit complaints. The new system caught errors more reliably. It also caught them sooner in the task. Users rated the experience more favorably. Trust survives mistakes that get caught quickly. Service robots gain a social early-warning sense.
arxiv-2501-05923:
Frans Öhrström and four co-authors study cyber threats to battery energy storage systems in a 2025 paper. Big batteries help balance the power grid, soaking up surplus power and feeding it back at peaks. They are often run from the cloud, though, which opens a path for attackers whose success could shake the whole grid.

The team builds a reference model of a cloud-controlled balancing setup with remote battery sites. They then stage a series of simulated attacks against the model. The runs map the system's attack surface and show how intrusions could threaten the safety and stability of the grid. The authors offer the model as a base for hardening real systems.
arxiv-2501-06123:
Robert M Corless asks why computer simulations of chaotic systems can be trusted at all. Chaotic systems amplify tiny errors, so a computed path soon strays from the true one. His 2025 paper reviews backward error analysis, which asks a different question: what nearby problem did the computer solve exactly?

Three tools are compared: checking leftovers from the equations, studying modified equations, and shadowing, where a true path stays near the computed one. Each helps explain why simulations still capture true behavior. Numerical methods can also fake chaos or hide it, and the paper weighs those risks. One puzzle stays open: why the long-run statistics of computed orbits so often come out right.
arxiv-2501-06223:
Yiqin Zhang, Meiling Chen, and Zhengjie Zhang build a small module that learns how to window a CT scan for a neural network, and can explain its choices. Windowing, choosing which brightness range to display, has always shaped CT reading. Prior fusion methods improved networks but were opaque and domain-bound. Writing in twenty twenty-five, the team's plug-and-play module grows out of a tanh activation shape and the physics of CT itself. Its design is domain-invariant, so clinicians can watch its preferences in intuitive terms rather than trusting a black box.

Across several open data sets, the module lifted segmentation scores substantially on hard targets. Gains ranged from modest to several-fold, the authors report. Interpretability is pitched as a trust feature for medical deployment, not a decoration. The module drops into mainstream architectures unchanged.
arxiv-2501-06323:
A workshop report by Josephine Paton describes redoing the model of Fermilab's Booster Neutrino Beam, whose first flux figures date to a 2009 MiniBooNE paper. The old code can no longer run, yet the Short-Baseline Neutrino Program needs fresh flux numbers for its running near and far detectors. The new framework, G4BNB, tracks each particle's full ancestry so hadron production errors can be handled with more precision.

It also adds neutral mesons from proton-beryllium collisions, opening studies of exotic scenarios beyond the Standard Model. Paton presents the update as core infrastructure, since flux accuracy caps what the detectors can claim.
arxiv-2501-06423:
Xiaoxin Yin (2025) introduces AlgoPilot, a system that synthesizes working programs without any human-written code to learn from. Program synthesis usually leans on human specifications, examples, or earlier algorithms. AlgoPilot instead trains with reinforcement learning, guided by a trajectory language model. That model was itself trained on the behavior traces of random Python functions. It acts as a soft constraint, favoring action sequences that look like plausible algorithms.

Using sorting as the test case, the system produced behavior traces that can be read as classical algorithms, including bubble sort, despite starting with no algorithmic knowledge. Yin presents this as a new paradigm for algorithm discovery. Reusable program logic emerges from scratch rather than being copied from human examples. He offers it as groundwork for more autonomous program synthesis.
arxiv-2501-06623:
Andrew Haverly presents a bold climate proposal in a 2025 paper: use a buried nuclear explosion to speed carbon capture. Crushed basalt rock reacts with carbon dioxide and locks it away, a process called enhanced rock weathering, but natural rates are slow. Haverly argues for detonating a device under a remote basalt seabed to pulverize vast rock volumes at once.

Placement under the seabed aims to confine debris, radiation, and energy while the fresh rock surfaces weather fast. The analysis sets out the parameters needed for efficient capture with minimal side effects, and it claims a yield on the order of gigatons is required for global impact. Safety, ecosystem, political, and cost questions are each examined. The paper invites study, not action.
arxiv-2501-06823:
Yiqing Zhang, Xiaozhong Liu, and Fabricio Murai predict clinical trial outcomes with a lightweight attention model in a 2025 paper. Trials are the gold test of a drug, but they cost years and fortunes, so a good forecast of success is valuable. A forecast must take in several kinds of data at once: the drug molecule, the target disease, and who may enroll.

Older deep models often need lab-made data or hand-built interaction designs, which import human bias. Their model, MEXA-CTP, instead assigns a specialist module, a mode expert, to each data kind. Cross-attention lets the experts consult each other and fuse what they know. The design is deliberately lean. The team trains it to sort trials into likely success and failure from public data alone.
arxiv-2501-06923:
Alankrita Bhatt, Or Ordentlich, and Oron Sabag study how a bookmaker should set payouts for bets placed over time, in a paper from twenty twenty-five. In online betting, the bookmaker can change the offered payoffs again and again before an event happens. Each change can depend on the bets placed so far. The authors ask how the house can guard its worst-case return across all gambler behavior and both outcomes.

They shape the task as a formal game and solve it in full for events with two outcomes. Their best plan rests on a new tool they call bi-balancing trees. The plan makes the house lose the same amount on every decisive betting path, where a gambler stakes all funds on one outcome each round.
arxiv-2501-07123:
Nour Makke and Sanjay Chawla use machine learning to find a formula for a key function in particle physics in a 2025 paper. Fragmentation functions describe how energetic particles produce hadrons, and they cannot be computed from theory. Standard practice fits data with a guessed formula shape and tunes its values.

Their method, symbolic regression, learns the formula shape itself straight from measured hadron counts. The learned function looks like a classic string based formula from earlier models and fits the data well. The authors propose it as a candidate for global fits and as a template for like studies in the strong force field.
arxiv-2501-07323:
Wave math in closed seas needs schemes that keep energy honest, and Shashkin and co-authors build such a scheme for shallow water, in work from twenty twenty-five. Their grid is staggered and can bend across blocks, which suits round basins. Past work had done the same on straight grids alone.

Two join tricks are paired at block edges, which softens stiffness and damps fake still waves. Spin terms are built to add no net energy. Tests on a spinning sphere, a stand-in for air and sea flow, beat the older packed-grid method on wave truth. The scheme aims at weather and ocean codes that run on bent grids.
arxiv-2501-07423:
Muhammad Umair Danish and co-authors test how well machine learning can forecast energy use in student housing across the seasons. Use in such homes swings with the weather, holidays, and the odd habits of students, which makes sharp forecasts hard.

The team compare plain deep learning models with newer ones, from transformers to mixed designs. No one model won in all seasons. Two of their own designs coped well with sharp summer swings in use. The authors argue for picking a model by season, or building one that adapts, rather than trusting a single model all year round.
arxiv-2501-07523:
Philhoon Oh, Jinwoo Shin, and James Thorne present a method to make retrieval based language models care less about passage order, in a 2025 paper. Such models add outside text to answer questions, but they often fail when the key passage sits in the middle of the input, a flaw known as lost in the middle.

Their framework fuses the stored keys and values for passages in parallel, so the output stays the same no matter the order of the passages. Tests on three open question tasks showed that invariance in practice. The method also held up better when useless passages were mixed in than past approaches for such pipelines.
arxiv-2501-07623:
Darby Kramer and co-authors propose a new way to probe how the universe's first stars reionized the gas around them, in a 2025 paper. Two faint imprints on the cosmic microwave background carry news of that era. One, the kinetic Sunyaev-Zel'dovich effect, is fairly strong but tangles with other signals. The other, patchy screening, is weaker but can be read from a cleaner channel of the same light.

The team suggests cross-matching a map of the screening signal with the square of the other signal's map. Using simulations, they show this combined signal is sensitive in a special way to the first half of reionization and to the clumping pattern of the ionized gas. Forecasts for coming surveys say one planned telescope array would catch only a hint of it. A more ambitious one would detect it firmly, at up to fourteen times the noise level.
arxiv-2501-07723:
Mohammadreza Sediqin and Shlomo Engelson Argamon chop text into its smallest argument pieces with a deliberately simple tool. Discourse parsing starts by finding elemental discourse units, the clause-like spans that carry single points. Their segmenter, ESURF, reads only word and character n-gram features and lets a random forest vote on each boundary.

Despite having no deep network and no syntax tree, the method beat rival segmenters on standard tests. Plugged into a leading discourse parser, it lifted the whole pipeline's accuracy. The authors draw a moral for the field: surface patterns carry more discourse signal than assumed, and lean feature-based tools can train faster and cheaper than the fashionable heavy machinery.
arxiv-2501-07823:
Amit Kumar, Abhijit Majumder, Chathuranga Sirimanna, and Yasuki Tachibana wrote this paper in two thousand twenty-five. It looks at how wide a jet grows across its path as a hard quark splits and showers inside matter.

The authors redo the case of a lone gluon shed by a quark, using wave packets rather than point paths. That gives the quantum blur in the quark size at the split, which is then fed into a shower simulation. The showers come out much wider than the old antenna size suggests, with no clear link to the parton's virtuality. They also tie a key jet quenching factor to a gluon spread law, and show that factor fades as virtuality rises.
arxiv-2501-08223:
Sebastian Ober, Samuel Power, Tom Diethe, and Henry Moss fix a flaw in a popular rule for picking big batches of training cases, in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. The rule, BatchBALD, mixes two kinds of doubt: what the model lacks and what noise adds. That mix can steer picks badly.

Their fix scores cases by forecast odds alone, which carry only the model's own doubt. The new score both picks better and runs faster to compute. Faster scoring opens larger batches than the old rule allowed. Readers who teach models by query get a cleaner, quicker batch picker.
arxiv-2501-08323:
Utsav Dewan tackles a classic convergence problem on curved spaces in a 2025 paper. The problem asks how smooth starting data must be for wave solutions to return to it point by point. In flat space it carries the name of Carleson. Dewan moves the question to Damek-Ricci spaces with round-symmetric starts.

Three wave equations are treated, for fractional, Boussinesq, and beam dynamics. Two versions of the Laplace operator are covered for each. The paper maps the local behavior of the related maximal functions in full. That mapping yields a sharp smoothness bound for pointwise return. The bound holds up to the endpoint value stated in the text. A general transfer principle for wave multipliers aids the proof. The results extend a celebrated flat-space theory to a rich curved setting.
arxiv-2501-08623:
Andrew Frey and Ratul Mahanta work out, in a 2025 paper, the low-energy rules for a string theory setup with a warped internal space. Knowing those rules helps judge which effective field theories could ever arise from a complete theory of quantum gravity. Their case pairs a compactified shape of the kind called Calabi-Yau with a special kind of flux passing through it.

Starting from the full ten-dimensional equations of motion, the pair derive the metric on the Kähler moduli space of the theory. That step completes a derivation left open in past work. They also give the first derivation of an effective action for flat directions in the complex structure moduli space, which generally mix with the axiodilaton. Worked examples in toroidal compactifications show the rules in use. The authors outline applications to precision string phenomenology and to the tadpole conjecture.
arxiv-2501-08823:
Jeffrey Shallit, a solo author, presents a note from twenty twenty-five on a number array first set out by Wesley Ivan Hurt and Ali Sada. The top row lists the whole numbers in order. Each next row is made by taking the entry with that row's index and jumping it that many spots to the right. Sada also tracked the first number each jump passes over.

Shallit shows the array and that sequence tie deep to the golden ratio. The link runs through the Zeckendorf form, which writes a number as a sum of non-near Fibonacci numbers. He then tours kin sequences that grow from the same play. The note is short and proof based.
arxiv-2501-09223:
Tong Xiao and Jingbo Zhu wrote Foundations of Large Language Models as a grounding text, not a tour of every new trick. Their 2025 book walks through the core ideas behind the systems that now write, answer, and reason in plain language. Six chapters carry the load.

The chapters take up pre-training, generative models, prompting, alignment, inference, and reasoning, in that order. Each treats its topic at the level of first principles, so readers build the mental frame before meeting the flood of variants. The authors aim the book at college students and at professionals in language technology and nearby fields. It can also serve, they note, as a reference for anyone who wants to understand what these models are before judging what they do.
arxiv-2501-09523:
Paulo Firmino and Laurentiu Leustean wrote this mathematics paper, published in two thousand twenty-five, on how fast a common iterative method settles down. The method, a broad form of the Krasnoselskii-Mann iteration, is used to find fixed points of maps that never stretch distances.

The authors use proof mining, a logic-based method that pulls hard numbers out of proofs that seem to give none. They work in uniformly convex spaces, a class of spaces with a strong roundness property. Their outcome is a rate: a bound on how soon the steps of the iteration stop changing much. For special choices of the method's settings, the rate comes out quadratic, which is fast. The paper adds hard guarantees to a method often used with only soft promises.
arxiv-2501-09623:
Marta Milewska, Remco van der Hofstad, and Bert Zwart model disease spread on networks that change as the disease moves in a 2025 paper. In the classic SIR setup, people are susceptible, infected, then recovered. Real contact networks rewire over time, which older models freeze.

The authors study graphs whose edges keep evolving while the epidemic runs. Starting from a small infected share, they show the outbreak near a typical person matches spread on a local limit graph. That limit is what one sees by zooming into one node's neighborhood. The team builds the needed theory of dynamic local convergence. One lesson stands out: the convergence must take a specific strong form for the match to hold.
arxiv-2501-10223:
José Barrientos and co-authors construct spinning spacetimes filled with a free scalar field, in both four and five dimensions. The scalar field presses back on the geometry, so these solutions describe how a rotating black hole's spacetime responds to the field living on it. Their method adapts a decades-old integrability result to ordinary spherical coordinates, simplifying the machinery considerably.

With it they re-derive a known 4D solution more transparently and find a new 5D one carrying two independent spins. They also build a 4D charged, rotating solution with an extra NUT charge, whose scalar varies with angle as well as radius. The authors frame the set as a unified account of recently proposed static solutions with scalar hair, extended into rotation and higher dimensions.
arxiv-2501-10423:
Davide Cacciarelli and co-authors measure how wind and sun truly move British power prices in this 2025 paper. Simple regressions can confuse cause with coincidence in market data. The team used a double machine learning method built for causal claims. They fed it UK wholesale prices and generation data from 2018 to 2024.

Wind showed a U-shaped effect. At low output each extra unit cut prices sharply, the effect faded at mid levels, then strengthened again. Solar pressed prices down hard at low output but weakened fast as output rose. Both effects grew stronger over the study years. The authors offer the findings as firmer ground for energy policy.
arxiv-2501-10523:
Jing Dong, Berk Görgülü, and Vahid Sarhangian wrote this research paper, published in 2025. It tackles scheduling in service queues where waiting itself makes service slower, a pattern seen in health care when patients who wait longer need more care.

The paper studies systems with several customer classes and several servers, where each class suffers differently from waiting. Finding the best order to serve people is hard. The authors build a simulation-based method that learns near-best policies. It shapes the policy with classifiers, compares outcomes by a pairing trick, and samples the states that matter most. In tests, the learned policies beat standard benchmarks. A case study on scheduling rehab admissions shows the approach in action, and the results expose a trade-off between quick wins now and avoiding costly pile-ups later.
arxiv-2501-10623:
Anna Ordog leads a team of fifteen authors who made the first Faraday rotation maps of diffuse Galactic emission that span each scale of size. Faraday rotation traces the magnetic field in the ionized gas that lies between us and the source of light. Single dishes see the broad forms, while interferometers see the fine grain, and on its own each one falls short.

The team merged survey data from a single antenna, from GMIMS, with polarization data from the Canadian Galactic Plane Survey made by aperture synthesis, once space-based filtering was done. The merged maps reach a sharpness of three arcminutes and still keep their feel for large scales. Rotation measures were fit pixel by pixel across four frequency channels. The result sits well next to maps of brightness used to study the magnetic field of the Galaxy.
arxiv-2501-10723:
Istvan Kovacs and Luka Sinkovec complete a classification problem in group theory about when cyclic groups have a strong isomorphism property. Their paper came out in 2025. The property concerns whether two networks built on the group must be identical whenever their connection sets can be matched by a group automorphism.

Building on earlier work by two other researchers, they settle the question for all values of the parameter from three upward. For the directed version, the cyclic group qualifies exactly when its order avoids divisibility by eight and by squares of small odd primes. For the undirected version with a larger parameter, the same conditions hold apart from three small exceptional orders. Classifications like this one close long-standing gaps in the theory of Cayley graphs, networks built directly from groups.
arxiv-2501-10823:
Tabea Bacher, Marina Garrote-López, Christiane Görgen, and Marius Neubert reported on making a math data resource FAIR in 2025. FAIR data are findable, accessible, interoperable, and reusable. Their test case was an early web library of small phylogenetic trees, built in the early two thousands.

The team followed a three-part plan. They wrote software that lets users reproduce the database results. They built a friendlier web site with links to theory papers, code pieces, and stored outputs. All through the work, they documented each step to draw lessons for like projects. Their paper covers that third part, while the software and the site live at public addresses given in the text.
arxiv-2501-11523:
Ignacio Ceresa Dussel, Julián Fernández Bonder, Nicolas Saintier, and Ariel Salort wrote this math paper in two thousand twenty-five. It proves that a paired system of fractional Lane-Emden equations, of Hamiltonian type, has solutions.

Each equation uses a fractional Laplacian, a nonlocal spread of the classic one, and each unknown feeds the other's rate through a shared potential. Both unknowns must vanish outside a fixed region. The proof leans on a flexible method that traces back to work by De Figueiredo and Felmer. It joins fractional Sobolev spaces with tools for self-adjoint operators. The same path can serve other nonlocal operators, the authors note.
arxiv-2501-11623:
Seorin Kim and four co-authors test large language models on historical handwriting in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. Archives hold vast handwritten records in tables, and traditional recognition tools often struggle with them. The team pitted two leading models against four conventional systems.

Documents were fed line by line or as whole scans. On character error and match scores, the language models beat every traditional tool. Human judges then rated the whole-scan outputs to check what the scores miss. Two-shot prompting worked best: one model led on line images, the other on whole scans. The authors present this as early evidence that general models now out-transcribe specialist software on historical records.
arxiv-2501-12223:
The Ring Nebula's glowing shell hides a colder jacket of gas, and a 2025 paper by Joel H. Kastner and co-authors gives the first detailed radio map of it. Using a submillimeter telescope array, the team imaged carbon monoxide emission from the famous nebula, NGC 6720.

The gas forms a thin layer around the hot inner shell, closely matching infrared pictures from the JWST telescope. A simple shape model fits the jacket as a squashed, three-way ellipsoid seen nearly pole-on, with a dynamical age near six thousand years. Features that looked like inner filaments in still images turned out to be fast knots flying toward and away from us. The three-dimensional view reshapes how the nebula's structure is read.
arxiv-2501-12323:
Jiaqi Lv, Stefan Antonowicz, and Shan E Ahmed Raza teach computers to outline blood vessels in cancer slides in this two thousand twenty-five paper. Blood vessels shape a tumor's surroundings and may sway its growth and drug response. Tracing them by hand in stained tissue images is slow and hard, since vessels vary wildly in look. Labeled examples are also scarce, so big models overfit. The authors add guiding maps that steer the model toward vessel-like features.

These maps push standard segmentation models to learn what makes a vessel distinct. Both measured scores and visual checks show cleaner outlines. The team next plans tests across other tissue types. Computational pathologists who quantify tumor tissue are the audience.
arxiv-2501-12423:
Roberto Gallotta, Antonios Liapis, and Georgios Yannakakis present FREYR in 2025, a framework that lets language models use tools in clean steps. A tool-using model can run code or call services to answer better, but the usual ways to wire this up are brittle. They tie the model to one tool set, or demand heavy retraining.

FREYR splits the job into separate stages: read the request, pick the tool, run it, and answer. Because the stages are modular, new tools can be added without retraining the model. The team tested it on real tasks in video game design. It beat the standard tool mode of a popular local model service. The authors offer it as a flexible base for tool-using agents.
arxiv-2501-12523:
Kevin Ta, Patrick Foley, Mattson Thieme, Abhishek Pandey, and Prashant Shah train a molecule-generating diffusion model across separated data silos with the OpenFL federated framework. Their paper from twenty twenty-five faces a drug discovery bind: the training data exist, but locked inside proprietary vaults. Their model works on discrete structures, denoising molecule graphs step by step. Federated rounds let each site learn without surrendering its compounds.

Judged on uniqueness and validity of generated molecules, the federated model matches one trained on pooled central data. Parity matters: it means privacy-preserving collaboration loses nothing measurable here. The team offers the run as proof that federated learning belongs in real drug design pipelines, where secrecy is the default.
arxiv-2501-12623:
Daqing Wan and Dingxin Zhang work on a pure math problem about shapes defined by polynomial equations. Their 2025 paper sets new upper bounds for Betti numbers, which count holes and gaps in such shapes. The proof uses basic facts about a tool called perverse sheaves.

From the new bounds, the authors derive bounds for two kinds of number functions tied to these shapes. One set covers zeta functions, and the other covers sums over finite fields. The results improve older bounds by Bombieri, Katz, and others. For a key special case, the new bound is as tight as the size allows.
arxiv-2501-13123:
Somenath Pal wrote a doctoral thesis, submitted to the University of Calcutta in two thousand twenty-five, on strongly interacting matter under extreme conditions. The subject is the hadronic phase of matter, where quarks are bound inside particles such as protons. A family of models called hadron resonance gas models describes that phase.

Pal improves the base model step by step. One version lets particles repel each other by reserving volume, another allows particles of unequal sizes, and a third adds the shrinking of fast particles. A further version adds a mean-field pull. He studies how each change shifts heat properties and charge fluctuations across collision energies.
arxiv-2501-13423:
Yahya Alnashri proves the first general error bounds for numerical solutions of systems of reaction-diffusion equations, in a 2025 paper. Such systems model chemicals that spread and react, and they appear across biology and engineering. Earlier error results leaned on special features of each problem. Alnashri works inside the gradient discretisation method, a single frame that covers many conforming and non-conforming schemes at once.

Under mild smoothness assumptions on the true solution, he shows the approximate solutions exist, are unique, and sit within a stated distance of the truth. The analysis does not depend on the particular reaction terms chosen. A finite volume test case puts the theory to work. The author offers the result as a base guarantee for a whole family of solvers.
arxiv-2501-13623:
Dhruv Mittal and co-authors ask where a policymaker should aim incentives to tip a whole population's behavior, in a 2025 paper. Norms lock in the status quo on climate and health, yet the same social machinery can flip fast once tipping starts. Their game-theoretic model holds varied agents linked in local influence networks. Targeting rules use what is known about each person's preferences and network position.

A trade-off emerges: holding the targeted firm against backsliding versus sparking change among the untargeted. Where the change starts, and which way it spreads, decides success as much as budget size. The authors compute cost-optimal strategies under different levels of resistance, preference spread, and like-seeking-like clustering. The results are meant to be testable in experiments and usable by real campaigns, from vaccination drives to energy habits.
arxiv-2501-13823:
Joe Meagher and Nial Friel model how debate cascades grow on online boards, in a 2025 paper. Each post sparks a tree of replies, and most trees stay tiny while a few explode. That pattern recalls superspreading in disease outbreaks.

Their model builds on a branching process that lets each comment trigger more. They fit it to threads from an Irish forum on Reddit. Debate followed a daily rhythm, with morning posts drawing expected threads of about four replies and late posts fewer. Most posts, near six in ten, drew no replies at all. The authors also give the computing tools needed to fit such models well.
arxiv-2501-13923:
Kenta Kasai cuts stubborn error floors in quantum error correction, in work from 2025. The method uses sparse check codes built on non-binary symbols. At low error rates, decoding can stall in loops where the guessed noise gets trapped. Kasai sorts those loop shapes in the check grid into three types.

For the first type, a tweak makes the guessed and true noise count as the same. The second type proves beyond repair and is flagged as such. For the third, a quirk of non-binary codes lets the true noise be read out. Tests showed far better decoding and much lower floors.
arxiv-2501-14023:
Kaushik probes the non-perturbative side of a two-dimensional string theory, where instanton effects escape the usual step-by-step approximations. The theory, a c=1 string wrapped on a circle of self-dual size, has several mirror descriptions: a zero-dimensional matrix model and a one-dimensional quantum matrix system of free fermions.

Working from the worldsheet picture with string field theory tools, his 2025 paper computes how strongly instantons of the ZZ type weigh in, plus two correlation functions on disk and ring shapes. Each result is then matched against the matrix model predictions. Side results cover stacks of instantons and a general family of them, at both the special radius and generic ones. The matches support the claimed dualities.
arxiv-2501-14323:
Taha Emre, Teresa Araujo, Marzieh Oghbaie, and co-authors build deep learning tools for an eye disease in a 2025 paper. The disease, a wet form of macular degeneration, drives vision loss in older adults. Spotting change in activity early guides timely drug doses and better outcomes.

One model pairs scans from two visits in a twin network to call if severity changed. The other model forecasts change three months out, a first for this task. Its loss treats the severity grades as ordered steps, using a distance built for ranked classes. Both models ranked high on the board of a public contest held in 2024. The team sees clear use in planning care for this disease.
arxiv-2501-14423:
Nuno Paulino and seven co-authors show how a smart wall panel can help Wi-Fi sense hand moves without cameras or worn sensors. Their study appeared in twenty twenty-five. The panel can steer radio waves in a set area, which sharpens what the waves pick up from a hand. The team built the panel to work at a high Wi-Fi band used by Wi-Fi 6E.

First the team checked that the panel steers waves as planned. Next they taped a data set for three hand signs and shared it in full. Two neural nets learned to sort the signs, one from mixed panel settings and one from tuned settings. Both scored above ninety percent right.
arxiv-2501-14523:
Chih-Hao Fu, Pierre Vanhove, and Yihong Wang derive building blocks for heavy mass effective theory from string theory in a 2025 paper. The quantities they want, called numerators, organize how heavy particles exchange gluons. Their route starts from a kinematic algebra built out of string vertex operators. The numerators emerge as nested commutators of gluon operators, evaluated between massive string states.

The resulting expressions are products of the algebra's structure constants, which keeps them gauge invariant. Computing the nested commutators naturally organizes the work into rooted trees. An ordering on the trees helps enumerate every contribution. The authors show this string picture explains the fusion rules used in earlier field theory constructions of the same numerators. The paper links two languages for the same physics.
arxiv-2501-14723:
Ryan Ehrlich and co-authors build a system that spends more compute to fix real code bugs in a 2025 paper. Their system, CodeMonkeys, lets a model edit a codebase again and again while writing and running its own test script. Many such edit paths are sampled for each issue, giving a pool of candidate fixes.

Spending is scaled two ways: more rounds per path, and more paths per problem. A shared first pass over all files spreads its cost across the samples. Final choice mixes votes from model-made tests with a special selection round. The system solved over half the issues in a verified public benchmark. Mixing in fixes from other top systems lifted the score further.
arxiv-2501-14923:
Cuesta and co-authors compare two ways to average solar particle intensities across energy bins, in a 2025 space physics paper. Spacecraft report energetic ions and electrons in narrow energy slices, and analysts merge slices to beat noise. Re-binning integrates the intensity directly and lands at an effective energy that drifts with the spectrum. Spectral binning integrates in log space and lands at a fixed central energy.

Using proton data from the Parker Solar Probe across two solar events, the team show re-binned values run consistently higher, up to five times the spectral ones. Neither method is wrong, they stress, but mixing them invites false comparisons. The paper gives criteria for picking the right average for each scientific question.
arxiv-2501-15223:
Masoud Ataei and Xiaogang Wang design a clearer neural network in a 2025 paper. Most networks are black boxes: they score well but hide their reasons. Their network uses a new activation rule based on the Lehmer mean, a weighted average that can favor large or small inputs.

The rule adapts which features pass at each unit, and it extends to complex numbers, so phase in signals can be used rather than dropped. Math properties of both the real and complex forms are worked out. On standard test sets, the network matched strong rivals on accuracy while staying easier to read, a trade many fields would welcome.
arxiv-2501-15423:
Liang Shang and co-authors improve the automatic outlining of stroke damage in brain MRI scans. Drawing these outlines by hand is slow and needs scarce specialists, yet vague boxes are not enough to study how lesions cause later thinking problems. Their method adds a multi-stage, cross-scale attention block to the U-Net family of segmentation networks. The block links brain structure features to lesions of very different sizes.

On a standard stroke data set, the method beat all rivals on small lesions, where outlines are hardest, and stayed competitive on the full set. An ensemble using the block scored best overall. The authors release their code. Better small-lesion maps could sharpen studies of how stroke location shapes recovery and dementia risk.
arxiv-2501-15523:
Shili Yan and a large team build a one-way gate for electric flow in a superconductor in a 2025 paper. The gate is a Josephson junction cut from indium arsenide sheets with aluminum caps. A flat magnetic field makes the switch point differ by flow sense. That gap is the diode effect: flow runs free one way, not the next. Field aim rules the gap size.

Field across the flow gave the peak gap; field along it gave near none. An electric gate dial could tune the gap and kill it at set marks. The team trace the effect to spin twist in the sheets. Such gates may serve fast cold circuits. They may also flag odd states of superconductivity in new stuff.
arxiv-2501-15623:
Alexander Kaganovich studies the electroweak Standard Model inside two-measure theory, a framework that adds a second volume measure to gravity and particle physics, in 2025. He follows the averaged Higgs field through the history of an expanding universe.

A ratio of the two measures changes as the universe evolves, from near zero during inflation to one near the vacuum. Because it enters every equation, all coupling constants become slowly running quantities. The Higgs self-coupling grows from a tiny value that fits cosmic microwave background data to its normal size, and the Higgs mass term flips sign, giving standard symmetry breaking. The fermion mass hierarchy then appears quite naturally.
arxiv-2501-15723:
Enze Chen and Timofey Frolov reported in 2025 new ground-state structures for grain boundaries in refractory metals such as tungsten and molybdenum. A grain boundary is the seam between two crystal grains, and its atomic pattern controls material behavior. One famous boundary type was thought to be settled, built from kite-shaped units.

A rigorous search that also optimizes the number of atoms in the boundary core found a new split-kite phase with a nearly aperiodic pattern. Quantum calculations confirm it. Atoms in the new phase also diffuse in a distinct collective way. Simulated microscope images of the split kites match experiments better than the old structure, offering a fresh reading of past observations.
arxiv-2501-16023:
Xin Li and co-authors present TransPathNet, a deep learning system that predicts how radio signals weaken as they cross indoor spaces, in a 2025 paper. Indoor maps of signal strength guide the placement of wireless gear, but walls and materials make the physics messy to model by hand. Their system works in two stages, pairing a transformer that reads the layout with a decoder that sharpens details at several scales.

The system won top marks in a 2025 indoor prediction challenge, with low error on both the full test set and a public leaderboard set. It also carried well across new room shapes, frequencies, and antenna types. Code and a project page are shared for others to build on.
arxiv-2501-16123:
Layla Bouzoubaa and co-authors mapped drug talk on TikTok in 2025, tracing 2,333 substance hashtags into sixteen communities. The platform shapes what millions of teenagers see about drugs, and fears of open promotion run high.

The hashtag web proved tightly knit, with recovery tags like addiction, recovery, and sober acting as bridges between communities. Coding 351 sample videos, the team found recovery advocacy the largest class at about a third, then satire at over a quarter. Outright drug display appeared in about a quarter of videos, and actual use in under seven percent. The surfaced conversation leans toward help and humor, they conclude, grown from communities rather than evasion games.
arxiv-2501-16323:
Job Feldbrugge and Joshua Jones make the Feynman path integral computable in real time in a 2025 paper. The path integral sums a quantum system's history over every possible path, a picture that reshaped physics. In real time the sum oscillates fiercely, so direct computation is costly and numerically fragile even for simple systems.

Their method evaluates the world-line path integral efficiently, taming the oscillations that defeat naive sampling. Real-time paths govern how quantum systems actually evolve, from chemical reactions to particle collisions, where imaginary-time tricks cannot go. A reliable evaluator opens those dynamics to direct study and gives approximation schemes a benchmark to answer to. The work is a tool paper other theorists will build on.
arxiv-2501-17023:
Benoit Gay and Sebastien Galtier wrote a 2025 paper on turbulence among gravitational waves, studied through a simplified diffusion equation. When the system is pushed at a middle scale, energy and wave action flow in opposite senses, a dual cascade. Steady runs recover the classic predicted spectra.

In decaying runs, a surprise appears. The wave action spectrum pushes past the starting scale with a steady negative flux, filling one single range. Energy's front advances with a cube root time law while wave action fades at the matching pace. Simple arguments explain both patterns. The work sharpens theory for wave turbulence in strong gravity settings.
arxiv-2501-17123:
Tejal Joshi and co-authors build a detector for cache side channel attacks, a quiet way to steal secrets from shared processors. Attackers who share a chip's last-level cache can watch access patterns and infer keys or user activity, all without touching the victim's device. Their 2025 paper focuses on fingerprinting attacks between co-located processes.

A threat model first maps how the spying works. The defense is a hybrid deep learning model trained to spot the attack's traces. The study compares the hybrid against other detectors on the same task. Because these attacks ride normal hardware sharing, they slip past many classic defenses. Security engineers get a learning-based tripwire for a leak that leaves no footprints in the victim's own logs.
arxiv-2501-17223:
Gregory Korchemsky and Alessandro Testa study correlation functions in quiver theories in a 2025 arXiv paper. Their setting is a family of four-dimensional superconformal theories arranged in a long circular quiver. They compute two- and three-point functions of protected operators.

Supersymmetric localization turns these functions into matrix integrals. In the planar limit, the integrals become determinants of semi-infinite matrices. At strong coupling, the usual expansion breaks down in the long quiver limit. Adding correction terms in two kinds yields a strikingly simple result. The functions decay with node distance and fit a five-dimensional picture, whose excitation masses come from zeros of Bessel functions.
arxiv-2501-17523:
Yongjian Wang and Qi Zhou prove two new exact mobility edges in two realistic quantum models, in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. A mobility edge is the energy line where electron states change their spread kind. Classic edges split free-roaming states from trapped ones.

One new edge splits in-between critical states from trapped states. The second splits those critical states from free-roaming ones. Both edges are exact, not guessed from number runs. The proof rests on spectral study of a singular Jacobi operator on a strip. Readers in quantum matter get new sharp lines in a field of fuzzy ones.
arxiv-2501-17623:
Marco Uguccioni and Luca Dell'Anna compute currents through a quantum dot wired to superconductors in a 2025 paper. Such junctions are testbeds for quantum transport and thermoelectric effects. The Keldysh field theory they use is powerful but often heavy going.

The paper shows the method cleanly recovers known results for plain and mixed junctions. Its main yield is a full formula for the heat-driven current between two superconducting leads at any temperature gap. Beyond the usual Josephson current, a weak extra term appears when electron-hole symmetry breaks. The derivation gives theorists a ready tool for designing superconducting devices that turn heat into signal.
arxiv-2501-17723:
Paul Bittorf and co-authors report in 2025 a new light catcher for electron microscopes, built on an optical fiber tipped with printed micro optics. When an electron beam strikes matter, the glow it provokes, cathodoluminescence, betrays local photonic behavior in minerals, semiconductors, and nanoparticles. A scanning microscope's beam probes that glow spot by spot with fine spatial detail.

Their detector pipes the glow down a fiber whose end carries optics printed in three dimensions at microscopic scale. First measurements prove the fiber can raster scan the emission like a camera. The team resolved the glow's far field pattern across space, took its spectrum, and timed single photons one by one. One flexible probe thus covers the spectral, spatial, and timing views that used to need separate rigs. The authors aim it at nanostructures and atom thin materials whose light is hard to catch.
arxiv-2501-18023:
Vittorio Aita and co-authors show in 2025 how a forest of tiny metal rods can twist the polarization of swirling light beams. Such beams carry a vortex pattern, and steering their polarization serves optical tweezers, communications, and quantum tools. Their material is a metamaterial whose response nearly vanishes along one axis, which boosts spin-orbit coupling.

By tuning how elliptical the incoming polarization is, the team reshaped the outgoing pattern into meron forms, half-skyrmion textures of the light field. The control is flexible and works through the material's strong direction dependence. The work adds a compact dial for complex light.
arxiv-2501-18123:
Aybars Yunusoglu and co-authors use a transformer-based framework to estimate battery health, in a 2025 paper. Electric vehicles depend on knowing how much life a battery has left. Two measures matter most: state of health and remaining useful life. The study focuses on lithium titanate cells, a durable battery chemistry.

Eight cells were cycled under varied conditions for hundreds of cycles. The model learned from both full cycle records and single discharge snapshots. Voltage analysis tracked how capacity faded across voltage ranges. Charge duration shaped the energy storage trends they saw. The framework reached low error in its health estimates. Fleet operators could use such tools to plan battery replacement. Safer, cheaper electric transport is the wider goal.
arxiv-2501-18223:
Mollon and four co-authors test big protein language models on small, specialized tasks in this two thousand twenty-five paper. These models, trained on millions of protein sequences, promise to predict how mutations change a protein's fitness, but most benchmarks use large and varied datasets.

The FLIP benchmark instead stresses constrained settings where only a little task-specific data exists, closer to many real lab problems. The team evaluated leading models including ESM-2 and SaProt across FLIP's tasks. Their findings show how much the recent jumps in model scale actually help when data is scarce. That answer matters for biologists deciding whether a giant general model can stand in for experiments in niche protein projects.
arxiv-2501-18323:
Anusha Bhattacharya and Soma Maity show that graph approximations can recover the vibration tones of curved surfaces, in a paper from twenty twenty-five. The tones are eigenvalues of a classic operator that blends shape and heat flow. The surfaces in view have bounded bending, a floor on how close they come to self-touching, and a cap on size.

A weighted graph built to hug the surface stands in for it. As the graph's mesh gets finer in the right balance, each graph tone settles to the matching surface tone. The convergence holds evenly across the class of surfaces. The proof adapts tools from earlier work on such graph approximations, tying discrete and smooth worlds closer.
arxiv-2501-18423:
Tom Dooney and six colleagues present DeepExtractor, a deep learning tool for cleaning gravitational wave data, in a two thousand twenty-five paper. Detectors such as LIGO, Virgo, and KAGRA hear faint signals from distant cosmic events. Their sensitivity also picks up glitches, brief noise bursts that can imitate or hide real signals.

DeepExtractor learns the detectors' noise distribution, treated as Gaussian and steady over short stretches. It predicts the noise inside a data segment and subtracts it. What remains is a clean reconstruction of the signal or glitch present. The team validated the method on simulated glitches injected into simulated noise. They also compared it against leading state-of-the-art techniques for reconstructing transient signals.
arxiv-2501-18723:
Konstantinos Mitsides, Maxence Faldor, and Antoine Cully scale a diversity-seeking optimizer by letting gradient-trained variants flood modern parallel hardware. Quality-diversity methods build a whole collection of solutions that are both strong and different from each other, like MAP-Elites. Classic versions mutate at random, which stalls in high dimensions. Gradient-based variants learn better moves but train slowly or resist massive parallel runs. Their 2025 paper scales policy gradient quality-diversity through behavioral variations, differences in what a solution does, exploited across many parallel workers.

A diverse archive is insurance: when conditions change, some member already fits. Robotics uses such archives for damage recovery. The authors attack the speed wall that kept gradient versions small. Their scaling recipe aims at neuroevolution on big controllers. The work treats variety as an engineering resource worth computing at scale.
arxiv-2501-18823:
Gonçalo Paulo, Stepan Shabalin, and Nora Belrose wrote this 2025 paper on reading the inner features of neural networks. Two tools compete for the job. Sparse autoencoders rewrite the activity of a network as a sparse set of named features, then rebuild the activity from them. Transcoders instead learn to predict the output of a component from its input, through a similar sparse bottleneck.

Trained on the same model and data, transcoder features proved clearly easier for humans to interpret. The team also add skip transcoders, which carry a direct affine shortcut around the bottleneck. Those rebuilt the activity with lower error while keeping the features just as readable. The results nudge interpretability work toward the transcoder design.
arxiv-2501-19023:
Sepide Mohamadi and Jahanfar Abouie present a 2025 arXiv paper on a quantum chain where topology meets non-Fermi liquid behavior. Fermi liquid theory fails in strongly interacting systems, and the team modifies a classic two-band chain model with long-range interactions of the Hatsugai-Kohmoto kind. They map the ground states that result.

The phase map holds two non-Fermi liquid phases, told apart by a many-body Zak phase of either a full turn or zero. The full-turn phase is topological and shows electric polarization like the plain chain. Exact computer solutions show spectral traits far from standard particle behavior. The authors link the findings to correlated electron systems.
arxiv-2502-00023:
Keon Ju Lee and Philippe Pasquier present two AI systems that make music with human players. Their 2025 paper works in co-creative performance, where the machine is a partner rather than a tool. MACAT leads its own performances, synthesizing sound live while listening to itself.

Its sibling, MACataRT, backs human improvisation through sound mosaicing and sequence learning. Both train on small personal datasets rather than giant scraped libraries. The authors frame that choice as an ethical stance toward artists' work. The systems aim to widen what a performer can try on stage. Live, shared control is the design centre.
arxiv-2502-00323:
Ilya Esterlis and Alex Levchenko derived the magnetism of tiny charged bit crystals pinned in moiré patterns in a 2025 paper. When tiny charged bits in two stacked, twisted semiconductor layers slow to a near halt, Coulomb repulsion arranges them into a Wigner crystal. Neighboring spins interact through ring exchanges where several tiny charged bits rotate places at once. The authors work out those multiparticle couplings semiclassically for triangular crystals held by triangular or honeycomb outer potentials.

Strengthening the possible flips the crystal from ferromagnet to a spiral antiferromagnet in both geometries. The triangular case flips under a weak possible, while the honeycomb case needs one nearly a hundred times stronger. The results map onto broad Wigner phases seen at special fillings of real moiré devices.
arxiv-2502-00523:
Shuyi Liang and co-authors test whether two rates match when data come in linked pairs in a 2025 paper. Eye studies and other trials often measure both sides of a body, and the two sides move together. Ignoring that link can bias the verdict.

Older models force one of three fixed link shapes, which limits fit and meaning. The team instead uses a flexible copula model to capture the link. They assess three test statistics inside that setting through simulations. Error rates stayed controlled and power stayed sound. Two real data sets show the method at work, giving a base for wider use.
arxiv-2502-00623:
Shin-ichi Matsumura and Chenghao Qing prove in 2025 a structure result for a class of compact Kähler manifolds, shapes that carry both complex and metric structure. The class is marked by a tangent bundle with a mild positivity trait. Such shapes arise in the study of how complex spaces can be sorted.

The proof shows each such shape fibers over a flat torus-like base. The fibers are rationally connected, a strong link trait, and the base is a finite cover quotient of a complex torus. With a stronger curve trait, the fibration turns locally constant. The result extends a known theorem from projective spaces to the wider Kähler world, which broadens its reach in complex geometry.
arxiv-2502-00823:
The easy kind of quantum state should be easier to learn, and Maxime Meyer, Soumik Adhikary, Naixu Guo, and Patrick Rebentrost prove that online, it is not, in a 2025 paper. Their setting is online learning, where states arrive one at a time and the learner pays for each mistake as it goes.

Pure states and mixed states, they show, share nearly the same sequential fat-shattering dimension, the quantity that fixes how regret grows. So the regret scaling for learning the simplest states matches the hardest. The paper also extends full tomography results to partially observed states under smoothed analysis, and to a setting where the target is only approximately learnable. The surprise is structural: whatever makes pure states easy in the laboratory's batch setting evaporates when the data must be handled in a stream.
arxiv-2502-01223:
Kalberla maps the cold neutral gas in filaments high above the galaxy's plane in a 2025 paper. Hydrogen gas there stretches into threads that track dust glow and the local magnetic field. Fresh absorption reads from an Australian pathfinder telescope sharpened the known physics of the cold phase, and the author ties those reads to the thread map.

More than half of the absorption spots sat on known dust and gas threads with coherent speeds. The rest matched pure gas threads kin to the dust ones, so all spots rode a thread of some kind. Speed spreads showed mild local turbulence, near two and a half to four kilometers per second. The cold gas runs supersonic at a mean Mach near three point four. The paper frames threads as the cold phase's home.
arxiv-2502-01423:
Vrinda Mehta and co-authors test how quantum annealing performs on hard 2-SAT problems that have several correct answers. Logic problems with multiple solutions stress samplers in special ways. Both simulated and physical annealers were put to work.

The team built a set of especially hard instances. Standard and reverse annealing protocols were tried on each. Ideal theory explains sampling through energy gap behavior. Time to solution depends on the smallest gap along the path. Real D-Wave hardware broke from that ideal picture. Its timing matched equilibrium probability predictions instead. The mismatch reveals noise effects in current machines. Results guide expectations for near-term quantum devices. It is a hard test for both routes.
arxiv-2502-01923:
April Clarke, Tanja Mitrović, and Fabian Gilson ask which communication patterns predict success in student software teams. Their 2025 paper starts from a familiar classroom failure: student groups talk badly, deliverables suffer, and projects sink. Rather than grading talk in the abstract, the authors test two network analysis tools as predictors of actual performance across a two-semester project.
