One tool, triad census, counts connection patterns among every trio of teammates. The other, socio-technical congruence, checks whether people who must coordinate technically actually talk. Triad patterns in each sprint forecast the share of story points the team passed, a close proxy for success. The congruence measure alone predicted poorly. The findings suggest coaches should watch trio structure, not just overall chatter.
arxiv-2502-02523:
Mercer, Spillard, and Martin analyse the DeepSeek R1 reasoning model and its wider meaning in twenty twenty-five. The model was released in late January twenty twenty-five by a Chinese lab. It was built at a fraction of the usual cost yet rivals top models from OpenAI. That happened despite United States export limits on advanced chips.

The report places R1 among other recent Chinese models with like traits. Mixture of experts design, reinforcement learning, and clever engineering appear central to their gains. The piece was written fast as an introduction for general readers. It covers the technical advances and the model's place in the ecosystem. Several directions for further research are identified at the end.
arxiv-2502-03023:
Hao Zeng and co-authors wrote this 2025 statistics paper on a quiet rule-breaking habit in conformal prediction. That method builds prediction sets with guaranteed coverage, and its math assumes the tuning data and calibration data stay separate. In practice, people often tune on the same data they calibrate with.

The authors measure the harm, a coverage gap they call tuning bias. Empirically, the gap stays tiny for simple tuning in many standard methods. A pattern emerges: the bias grows with the size of the tuning space and shrinks as the calibration set grows. The paper proves that scaling law with an upper bound on the bias. It closes with theory-guided ways to keep the bias small.
arxiv-2502-03223:
Alan Lam and Masaru Shibata release a new simulation code for colliding stars in a 2025 paper. Neutron star mergers and collapsing giants obey Einstein's gravity married to fluid motion, a union only supercomputers can follow. Their code, SACRA-2D, assumes symmetry around one axis to keep the price payable.

The code marries a sharp shock-capturing fluid solver to a proven scheme for evolving spacetime itself, and it runs across many processors. Bench tests match rival codes closely. Trial runs ram black holes together head-on, topple neutron stars into collapse, and drop a spinning supermassive star into a black hole with a disk. The tool is built for survey work on cosmic collisions.
arxiv-2502-03323:
Momin Abbas and co-authors present a 2025 trick for spotting inputs that fall outside a classifier's training world. Such out of distribution cases can wreck a deployed model, yet real examples of them are hard to gather. The team's fix has a large language model write fake stand ins for the odd cases.

No outside odd case data is needed at all. Tests spanned nine in and out data pairs, from toxicity and sentiment checks to reward model training and spotting off track model output. False alarm rates fell hard, to zero in some pairs, while in world accuracy held. The method beat bench rivals by a wide edge across model sizes.
arxiv-2502-03423:
Pierre-Louis Taillat and Hadrien Kurkjian compute exact transport coefficients for a cold Fermi gas, in work from 2025. Shear viscosity, heat conductivity and spin diffusivity are worked out in the normal Fermi liquid regime, between the Fermi temperature and the superfluid threshold. Cold atom experiments have grown precise enough to need theory beyond the usual shortcuts.

The collision term is treated exactly over the whole Fermi surface, past the forward-scattering limit of earlier equations. Results run to second order in interaction strength, with tidy formulas set by the scattering length and Fermi wavenumber. Corrections differ in sign across the three coefficients, a detail approximate methods miss.
arxiv-2502-04223:
Ilia Karmanov and co-authors introduced this 2025 document reader called Eclair. Standard text scanners pull words off a page but lose the page's structure. Tables, formulas, footnotes, and multi-column order all matter for search, question answering, and training data. Eclair aims to extract formatted text in true reading order, with boxes and labels for each element's role.

The team also built a human-labeled benchmark spanning many document kinds to grade such tools. Eclair topped rival methods across the key measures on that benchmark. Tools of this kind feed the data pipelines that modern language models depend on, so cleaner extraction lifts everything built on top.
arxiv-2502-04623:
Mengting Ma and four co-authors present a 2025 paper on HetSSNet, a method for sharpening satellite images. Pansharpening merges a sharp gray-scale image with a blurry color one to yield sharp color images. Standard grid-based networks struggle with the irregular shapes of real ground objects. Graphs offer a flexible alternative, but building the right graph and learning from it are both hard. The team builds a mixed-type graph made for this task.

Their network first extracts many relationship patterns from the graph. A second module then merges those patterns into one representation, weighing local and global cues. Wide experiments showed the method beating rivals and generalizing well to new scenes. The authors present graph learning as a strong fit for remote sensing fusion. The work targets clearer earth imagery for mapping and monitoring.
arxiv-2502-04923:
Image generators accept small add-on modules, called LoRAs, each teaching a character or style. Stacking several at once often muddies the picture. Xiandong Zou and co-authors study why, looking at the denoising process through frequency glasses. Some modules boost edges and textures, others shape broad structure and smooth color.

Clashing frequency roles create what they call semantic conflicts. Their remedy orders the modules by frequency behavior during generation, then caches pieces of the process to save compute. The framework needs no retraining. In tests it beat rival fusion methods on image-text match scores and human-style win rates. The 2025 paper makes multi-concept generation cleaner and faster.
arxiv-2502-05223:
Buyun Liang and co-authors build KDA, a model trained to write prompts that jailbreak large language models, bypassing their safety rules. Strong jailbreaks usually need hand-crafted system prompts and many queries for a single success, which makes large-scale safety testing costly. Their idea is to distill what an ensemble of leading attackers knows into one open model.

The distilled attacker writes coherent, varied attack prompts on its own, with no careful prompt engineering. Against a range of open and commercial models, it reached higher attack success than existing methods at lower cost in time and queries. A diversity analysis credits varied, ensemble-style attacks for the gain. The work is aimed at red-teaming defenses.
arxiv-2502-05323:
Orii and nine co-authors supported contraceptive choices in Kenyan pharmacies in this paper from twenty twenty-five. Pharmacies are a main source of contraception for young women in Kenya. The team built a tablet app that teaches options and guides decisions. Workshops with young women and pharmacy staff shaped the design.

In practice, a pharmacist and client used the app together, not the client alone. Those intermediated sessions, where staff enable the technology, proved central to the model. The authors draw lessons for health tech in low-resource settings. Intermediation can extend reach but also strains busy counters. The paper weighs those chances and frictions carefully.
arxiv-2502-05423:
Estimating a person's age from a face is harder than it looks, because aging signs hide in subtle relations between facial features. Yiping Zhang and co-authors build a graph neural network that treats facial key points as nodes and hunts for the links that threshold-based graphs miss. A random walk over an initial key-point graph reveals global structure to guide the search.

Multi-attention layers then assemble fully connected graphs rich in aging information. Deep residual blocks, mixing fixed and dynamic residuals, keep the deep features from washing out. A progressive reinforcement learning stage tunes the final ensemble, and the system beats prior methods on standard age benchmarks.
arxiv-2502-05723:
Edith Cohen, Mihir Singhal, and Uri Stemmer build counting sketches that withstand adaptive attacks. Their paper appeared in 2025. A sketch is a tiny summary that estimates how many distinct items a data stream holds. Recent work showed sketches break after roughly the square of their size in adaptive queries, where each query is chosen from past answers. The team breaks that barrier.

Their estimators survive an exponential number of adaptive queries, as long as each single item appears in only about quadratically many queries. The limit thus moves from total queries to queries per item, a far weaker demand in practice. The authors say the ideas reach beyond counting, offering new tools for designing algorithms that stay sound when the questions react to the answers.
arxiv-2502-05923:
Yaswanth M and four co-authors built a loop that grows rules and fake data for text sorting. Their paper, from twenty twenty-five, calls the frame ARISE. It joins two feeds of supervision. Fake data gives more samples; rules drawn from syntax chunks give a clear, human read signal. A bootstrap loop filters both, round by round, so weak rules and bad fakes drop out.

Rules alone lifted scores in both prompt based and tuned setups. Fake data alone beat more complex contrast based ways. Tests spanned full data, few shot, and many tongue sets. Readers who sort text with thin labels get a self feeding way to gain proof.
arxiv-2502-06023:
Amir Saeidi and co-authors improve how image generators learn from human preferences. In preference training, people pick the better of two images for a prompt, and the model learns the taste. The catch is that the prompt often fits both images about equally, so the lesson is muddy. Their method, DCPO, gives each image its own caption, so the winner and loser are described differently and the contrast sharpens.

They built a doubled-caption version of a standard preference dataset, trying three ways to write the second caption: fresh captioning, small edits, and a mix. Trained this way, the base model beat four rivals on image quality and prompt matching across five scoring systems.
arxiv-2502-06423:
Frederic Jouhet and David Wahiche work in combinatorics, the math of counting structured sets, in a twenty twenty-five paper. The sets are partitions, ways to write a whole number as a sum of parts. Each part has a hook length, a count read off its diagram, and the paper asks how often set hook lengths occur.

Recent work proved matching rules, called congruences, for hooks of even length in a special class of partitions. Jouhet and Wahiche show those rules drop straight out of an older addition theorem, and they widen them. They also prove a new addition rule for a broader class, which recovers known rules for two named classes as special cases.
arxiv-2502-06523:
Robots that act under uncertainty plan with POMDPs, models where the true state is only partly visible. Solving them means weighing countless possible beliefs about the state, so solvers lean on value bounds to prune the search. Merlijn Krale and co-authors derive in 2025 new upper bounds that are provably tighter than the fast informed bound in common use.

Tighter bounds cost more to compute, yet the trade paid off: across a wide range of benchmarks, leading solvers ran faster with the new bounds guiding them. The result is a practical upgrade for planning under uncertainty, from warehouse robots to assistive machines that must act without full knowledge.
arxiv-2502-06823:
Xingye Chen and co-authors wrote this 2025 paper on making ad images that people actually click. Most tools that dress up product photos aim for beauty, which does not always sell. The team instead trains large multimodal models to aim at the click-through rate, the share of viewers who tap the ad. A large e-commerce data set gives the models their first lessons in the task.

A reward model then grades new images by likely clicks, and training by reward sharpens the generator. A product-first tuning step keeps the made backgrounds true to the item on sale. In online and offline tests, the method beat prior state of the art, and the team shares code and models.
arxiv-2502-07123:
Irina-Beatrice Haas and Michael Giles propose a nested multilevel Monte Carlo framework for cheap simulation on field-programmable gate arrays. Their paper aims to cut the cost and power use of option pricing.

The method already lowers cost by joining rough answers of stochastic equations at several levels of detail. It adds rough calculations on flexible hardware. Rough random values and fixed-point steps with tuned bit widths make most paths cheaply. A rounding error model sets the bit width of each value on every level. The result is higher savings than earlier mixed designs for the same accuracy.
arxiv-2502-07223:
Elias Lumer and co-authors teach AI agents to fetch whole toolchains, not single tools, in a 2025 paper. Agents that call outside services must first pick the right ones from thousands. Plain search finds the headline tool but misses its prerequisites: the stock price call is useless without the ticker call feeding it.

Their method lays the tool catalog out as a graph and, after a first search pass, walks the links to gather every dependency, however nested. On a new benchmark of 573 invented tools with tangled dependencies, retrieval accuracy leapt by over seventy points in one measure. The plug-in approach needs no retraining of the agent itself.
arxiv-2502-07423:
Erik Lintunen and co-authors translate a core idea from motivational psychology into the language of artificial intelligence, in a 2025 paper. Self-Determination Theory names competence as a basic human need, but its texts use the word in several senses: having an effect, using a skill, performing well, and growing in capacity. The authors match each sense to an existing formalism from computational intrinsic motivation.

The exercise exposes hidden preconditions the psychology leaves unstated, sharpening both sides. Formal models gain a richer target, while the theory gains testable definitions. The authors propose a cycle: better theory inspires better models, whose results feed back to refine the psychology of motivation.
arxiv-2502-07523:
Daniel Palenicek and co-authors scale up a sample-frugal learning method for robot control. Their 2025 paper starts from CrossQ, a method that learns well from few tries but was run with one update per data batch. More updates per batch promise faster learning, yet training wobbles grow at that pace.

Adding weight normalization steadies the learner, the team reports. The fix holds the true step size steady and guards against loss of flexibility, with no drastic resets needed. Across twenty-five hard control tasks, from dog-like to humanoid bodies, the scaled method stayed in the top tier. The recipe offers a plain path to sharper sample use.
arxiv-2502-08023:
Hao Lin, Mustafa Kishk, and Mohamed-Slim Alouini ask, in 2025 work, how sharing cell net builds changes wide, unbroken cover. Sharing cuts the cost of fifth-wave nets, a boon for poor lands. Firms can share plain ground and towers, or the live gear too. The ask is when cover knits into one vast web.

Spread math gives the frame. The team finds when a signal graph knits, and a mean cover span to stand in for it at low tower counts. Edge tower counts for each share mode are then set side by side, with knit odds. Broader cover for less cash is the frame's gift.
arxiv-2502-08723:
Sebastian Monnet bounded a key group for K3 surfaces in a 2025 math paper. A K3 surface is a smooth shape of a rich, much-studied kind, defined here over a number field. The group at issue can block a hoped-for path from local facts about the surface to a global point on it.

Monnet works with surfaces whose symmetry field is a special CM field. He builds on past work that tied the group to the number traits of that field. From those traits he derives a clear bound on the group's size, stated in terms of the two fields. Such a bound is a step toward testing the block in real cases.
arxiv-2502-08823:
Sebastian Horvat asks which events can be said to occur in quantum phenomena, in work from 2025. The essay moves in two steps. First it tightens a class called statistical phenomena and tests how well chance-based event models describe them. That class, Horvat holds, is where quantum phenomena also belong.

The second step probes chance models of plain quantum cases and what answers they suggest. Odd traits stand out against the classic case. The essay ends in a puzzle state, with no firm answer in hand. Horvat notes that such a standstill is the usual end when ontology meets the quantum world.
arxiv-2502-09223:
Warren offers a short 2025 paper on a small Prolog program with an odd charm. The program reads logic rules and works out their meaning from the bottom up. It turns the rules into meta-rules, then uses them to build the full model step by step. The result works like the classic semi-naive method used in database logic.

Warren calls the piece a programming pearl, a small program worth study for its craft. He singles out its use of one Prolog feature that adds facts as it runs. In most programs he finds that feature murky, but here he calls it the clearest and best way to write the method. The paper is brief and written for logic programmers.
arxiv-2502-09423:
Ziyi Chen and co-authors present a generative model that predicts and creates crystal structures, in a research paper from 2025. A crystal's structure fixes much of a material's behavior, so forecasting stable structures speeds materials design. Generative models are a fresh route, but crystals demand care for their repeating patterns and symmetry.

Their model, TransVAE-CSP, pairs a variational autoencoder with a transformer that respects the geometry of the task. A distance expansion trick and symmetry-aware features help it learn what stable materials look like. It can both rebuild known structures and generate new ones. On three benchmark sets covering carbon, perovskites, and mixed materials, it beat rival methods on standard scores.
arxiv-2502-09523:
A young star in the Rosette Nebula, faint for years, flared up fast in late 2024. Adolfo Carvalho and Lynne A. Hillenbrand report the event in this 2025 paper, based on alerts from the Gaia space mission. The star, named V557 Mon, grew at least 3.3 magnitudes brighter than its usual level, and the rise was still going on.

The pair took a spectrum of the star in near infrared light and found bright lines and extra glow that point to gas falling onto the star at a fast rate. They compare the look to a known erupting star, EX Lup. If the flare keeps growing, the lines may flip from bright to dark, which would mark it as the more extreme FU Ori kind of outburst.
arxiv-2502-09623:
A 3D scene can be stored inside the weights of a neural network, a format called a Neural Radiance Field. Francesco Ballerini and co-authors ask in 2025 whether those weights can be read as data in their own right. Past tools for the task only worked when every network shared one fixed design. Real projects use many designs, so a more flexible reader is needed.

Their framework trains a graph-based meta-network to handle networks of many shapes. It learned from thirteen designs in three families, among them hash tables for the first time. Tests covered sorting, search, and language tasks, even on designs never seen in training. Results matched or beat tools built for one design only. Code and data were shared in public.
arxiv-2502-09823:
Bernhard Beckermann and co-authors explain why a large class of structured matrices can be squeezed into far smaller form, in a 2025 paper. Toeplitz matrices, whose diagonals repeat, fill signal and control work, and fast solvers lean on the fact that their off diagonal blocks have low rank. That fact was used more than understood.

The team traces the compression to the matrices' displacement structure, a kind of hidden simplicity. They give explicit rank bounds for the blocks that arise in hierarchical solvers. The bounds yield lean, adaptive compression schemes and point toward superfast solvers that build themselves as they go.
arxiv-2502-10123:
Izaskun Jiménez-Serra and co-authors model how methanol ice forms in a dark cloud in a 2025 astronomy paper. The James Webb Space Telescope measured the ices coating dust toward two dim stars in the Chamaeleon I cloud, and the pattern hints methanol formed in water-rich ice.

Lab work suggests two grain-surface routes could make methanol there, but no one had tested them in full models. The team ran the cloud's chemistry through five different astrochemical codes, from MAGICKAL to Nautilus, to see whether the answer depends on the code. Comparing the codes shows which formation routes hold up across methods. The result guides how scientists read the icy record Webb keeps sending home.
arxiv-2502-10323:
Cipriano Junior Cioffo, Fabio Gadducci, and Davide Trotta wrote a mathematics paper in two thousand twenty-five that maps out a family of abstract structures. The structures are categories that capture how relations work, such as links between sets. Work on them has grown over many years and now spans many related ideas and names.

The authors give a modern account of these categories, including a richer version that carries extra structure. They show how the categories arise from a construction based on monads, a standard tool in category theory. Their goal is a clear taxonomy that orders the many concepts in the literature and shows how they fit together.
arxiv-2502-10923:
Mohammad Siavashi, Gianni Antichi, and co-authors present Phoenix, a system tool that joins thread and memory placement on large shared machines, in a 2025 paper. On such machines, memory far from a core is slower to reach. Past tools set threads and page tables apart, which left much speed on the table.

Phoenix links the scheduler and the memory manager in one Linux module. It copies page tables on demand and guards shared bandwidth to keep service fair. On real hardware, it cut core cycles by more than half versus top past tools. Page walk cycles also fell by a wide margin.
arxiv-2502-11423:
Yonghyun Jun and Hwanhee Lee studied in 2025 how the mood of a user persona steers chatbot conversation. Personalized dialogue systems feed a user profile into a language model, but the profile's emotional tilt had gone unexamined. The team generated dialogues across a range of polarized profiles. Strongly negative personas made the model lean too hard on profile traits, crowding the exchange.

Positive profiles produced smoother chats that used persona details selectively. Weak or neutral personas gave the weakest dialogues of all. The authors answer with a generation method that plans for polarity: it builds replies turn by turn, orders profile facts deliberately, and prompts with sentiment in mind. Their analysis gives designers a new dial to watch. Persona sentiment, they show, is not decoration; it shapes quality.
arxiv-2502-11723:
Alireza Nik, Michael Riegler, and Pål Halvorsen measured the energy cost of text generation choices in 2025. When a language model writes, a decoding rule decides how it picks each next word. Rules range from always picking the top choice to sampling with more randomness, and settings tune the balance between safe and varied text.

The team benchmarked many rules and settings across translation, math, coding, and open writing, tracking both quality and graphics card energy use. The decoding choice changed energy use a lot, even when quality barely moved. No single rule won everywhere, so each task needs its own balance. Picking well can cut power bills with little loss in output.
arxiv-2502-11823:
Rodrigo Tenorio and Davide Gerosa speed up gravitational wave analysis in a 2025 paper. Next-generation detectors will hear colliding neutron stars and giant black holes for hours or days at a stretch. The core math, matching a candidate signal against the data, becomes a crushing cost at those lengths.

Their approach chops the data into short pieces and works in the frequency domain piece by piece. Gaps, drifting noise, and detector motion are handled naturally by that split. The payoff is large: the key calculation runs thousands to hundreds of thousands of times faster than a naive version, and it parallelizes cleanly. A pilot use case is early warning, alerting telescopes before a merger peaks. The team released public tools, including a fast reimplementation of a standard waveform. Faster plumbing here means more signals analyzed, and alerts sooner.
arxiv-2502-12323:
Luke Sanford and co-authors published this methods study in 2025. Social scientists increasingly use machine learning predictions as stand-ins for hard-to-measure outcomes, then run regressions on those predictions. The catch is that prediction errors can bend the regression results. This paper shows how that bias arises and offers a diagnostic test for detecting it. The settings covered are any where a model's predictions serve as the outcome variable.

Their fix uses adversarial training. A second model component pushes the predictor to make errors that carry no systematic tilt. Simulations and a real exercise with satellite measures of African forest cover demonstrate the approach. Naive model predictions produced biased estimates of the true effects. Predictions from the adversarial model recovered the true coefficients instead. The authors present the test and the debiasing method as practical tools for the growing field of prediction-based research.
arxiv-2502-12523:
Song Kim and co-authors present a 2025 indexing method for finding tight knit groups inside hypergraphs. A hypergraph links more than two items at once, which suits modern networks with group ties. Finding dense, cohesive subgroups inside one reveals how the network is built. The snag is choosing the right settings for the search, an open problem. The team wanted retrieval that is fast and does not crawl the whole graph each time.

Their index is driven by locality, the idea that nearby structure predicts what a query needs. It lets users pull out cohesive subgroups on demand, within a fair time budget. Tests on real world networks showed the method beating the alternatives they compared it with. The authors say fast, informed retrieval of this kind can support decisions in many fields that rest on network data.
arxiv-2502-12723:
Five authors release myEye2Wheeler, a dataset of where motorcycle and scooter riders actually look while driving in Indian traffic. Nearly all gaze datasets come from car drivers on orderly roads, which misses the chaos of mixed traffic. The team's recordings capture the eye movements of two-wheeler riders as they weave through real streets, giving a direct view of how they scan for hazards and make choices.

The test of existing tools was blunt. A leading saliency model, TASED-Net, predicted rider attention far worse here than on a European car dataset. That gap, the authors argue, proves attention models must be fit to local traffic rather than imported. The dataset aims to support safer road design and lane planning for the riders who form the backbone of Indian transport.
arxiv-2502-13023:
Counting palms from the air reads a tropical forest's health and its value to local economies, but wild crowns overlap in messy light. Kangning Cui and co-authors built PRISM, a pipeline that finds and maps palms in giant stitched aerial images. Their dataset spans twenty-one sites in western Ecuador, with nearly nine thousand boxed crowns and five thousand marked palm centres, gathered by drone.

The pipeline races several modern detectors, leans on a zero-shot segmentation model for outlines, then calibrates confidence against overlap so scores mean what they say. Saliency maps expose what the detectors look at. Though tuned for palms, the system adapts to other natural objects, and the authors eye transfer to coarser satellite imagery next.
arxiv-2502-13123:
Lauren Foster and co-authors test whether galaxies falling into clusters form stars in a lopsided burst before they shut down. Their 2025 study starts from gas stripping, where cluster gas sweeps a galaxy's own gas away. Extreme cases with long tails do show boosted star birth.

The team used a sample of more than five thousand satellite galaxies and a larger field comparison set. Blue light served as the star birth tracer, with several measures of lopsided form. No clear gaps appeared between the two samples. Even galaxies picked as most likely to face strong stripping showed no firm boost. The authors conclude any boost must be small, rare, or brief in most falling galaxies.
arxiv-2502-13523:
Omri Dalin, Alexander Ovseevich, and Michael Margaliot link a classic problem to optimal control in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. They study time-optimal controls for a linear system with a single scalar control over a long interval. When the system matrix has real eigenvalues, optimal controls switch only a bounded number of times.

The authors take up the case of purely imaginary eigenvalues instead. They show that, in the generic case, the number of switching points grows at least in line with the interval length. Their proof ties the switching function to the mean motion problem, posed by Lagrange and solved by Hermann Weyl. The result marks a sharp split between the two eigenvalue cases.
arxiv-2502-13723:
Zhang and co-authors introduce in 2025 a training method that sharpens step by step reasoning in language models by grading each step's worth. Standard tuning leans on human likes and dislikes, which are costly and coarse. Their method instead sets a target value for every reasoning step and trains the model toward those targets with a squared error loss.

Targets come from tree search rollouts or a learned outcome scorer. On math and commonsense tasks, the method beat offline preference rivals while using fewer training passes. The authors argue fine grained value signals, not verdicts, are the lever for better reasoning.
arxiv-2502-14023:
Orestis Konstantaropoulos, Theodoris Mallios, and Maria Papadopouli build an energy-saving team of spiking networks in a paper from 2025. Big AI models use too much power for small devices. Spiking networks, inspired by the brain, fire only when needed and suit special low-power chips.

A large teacher model guides a set of small student spiking networks. Each student masters a distinct slice of the teacher's knowledge. All students see the same input at once. The core trick is dynamic activation: only some students wake for each input. That cuts energy while keeping the team's skill. The design narrows the gap between spiking and standard networks.
arxiv-2502-14123:
Xuheng Li and Quanquan Gu prove, in a 2025 paper, why a training trick steadies learning. The trick, exponential moving average, keeps a running blend of a model's recent states. It is now standard in training image generators, yet its theory lagged its practice. The authors study it in the cleanest setting that still resembles a neural network: high-dimensional linear regression trained by online stochastic gradient descent. There the model's guesses update example by example.

Two results stand out. The averaged method's variance error, the noise in its final answer, is always smaller than plain training's. Its bias error, the systematic pull away from truth, fades exponentially fast along every direction of the data's geometry when the average starts later. That is a sharper decay than starting the average from the first step. The proof tools, the authors note, extend to other averaging schemes.
arxiv-2502-14523:
Austin Barr, Robert Rozman, and Eddie Guo pit a large language model against a classic adversarial generator at faking tabular data. Their paper appeared in 2025. Fake data with real statistics lets teams share and test without exposing records. Prompting GPT-4o in plain language, with no fine-tuning and no real data shown, they generated synthetic versions of three public data sets and compared them with a standard conditional GAN's output.

The language model's tables kept averages, spread, and pairwise links closer to the real ones, and protected privacy better, even at large sample sizes. Its weakness was the fine shape of distributions. The authors say zero-shot language models are already a practical synthetic data tool, with polish still needed.
arxiv-2502-14723:
Ognyan Christov, Sevdzhan Hakkaev, Seungly Oh, and Atanas Stefanov analyze a wave system in a 2025 arXiv paper. The Drinfeld-Sokolov-Wilson system mixes a dispersive wave equation with a conservation law. The team studies whether its solutions exist, persist, and stay stable.

They prove well-posedness for rough starting data on a periodic domain, then extend solutions to all time using a conserved quantity. A normal form method gives persistence for smoother, larger data. They also build an explicit family of periodic traveling waves. All of those waves prove spectrally unstable, with a single growing mode.
arxiv-2502-15123:
Some equations of physics and finance involve jumps rather than smooth change, driven by processes with heavy-tailed steps. Jiaying Feng, Changtao Sheng, and Chenglong Xu present a numerical method in 2025 for linear equations of that kind, covering both steady and time-changing cases. Their spectral Monte Carlo method blends random sampling with smooth basis functions shaped for the problem.

Control tricks cut the sampling noise, and a walk-on-sphere device handles the geometry. The team proves the error shrinks exponentially fast with each iteration round, for both the steady equation and the time-based one under one unified method. Tests confirm the speed and accuracy in practice. The work extends a method first built for the smoother case of ordinary diffusion.
arxiv-2502-15423:
Ariel Salort sets floor values for the eigenvalues of a fractional operator in this 2025 paper. The operator is a fractional A-Laplacian, a nonlocal cousin of a classic diffusion operator, where A is a Young function that sets how growth is measured. Eigenvalues of such operators govern vibration, stability, and spread in the systems they model.

Salort derives precise lower bounds for those eigenvalues and for related critical values. The bounds are written in terms of the shape of the domain and the growth traits of the function A. Notably, the proof does not assume the handy doubling condition that earlier work often required of A or its partner function. Removing that assumption widens the family of operators the bounds cover.
arxiv-2502-15723:
Prakhar Gurawa and Anjali Dharmik study in 2025 how much context an AI should read before turning a question into a database query. Their systems pair a language model with a search step that fetches table layouts and notes. More context can help the model pick the right tables, but it also adds noise.

The pair map the trade-off between the size of the fetched material and the quality of the queries produced. They find tipping points where extra bulk starts to hurt, raising made-up details and lowering accuracy. From those points they draw practical rules for trimming and ordering the fetched content, aimed at real-world database tools.
arxiv-2502-15823:
Wenyue Hua and co-authors test in a 2025 paper if large language models can learn rules from data alone. Most tests stress the reverse skill, where rules are given and the model applies them to solve tasks. Learning rules from cases sits at the heart of science, yet it gets far less study.

The team built InductionBench to grade this skill in a clear, staged way. Even the strongest models on hand failed to master the most simple class of rules in the test. That gap held across the models tried, from strong to weak. The result marks a clear limit in how these models think, and the test code and data are free online.
arxiv-2502-15923:
Aleksandra Rybalko and Alexander Fradkov wrote this 2025 paper on estimating the hidden parameters of a network of model neurons. The neurons follow the FitzHugh-Nagumo model, a classic pair of equations for a firing cell. The network can hold any number of them, joined by diffusive couplings.

Only one quantity per neuron can be measured: its membrane potential. The second state variable and all rates of change stay hidden, and the readings may carry sensor error. The authors first reshape the network into a linear regression form. A filter-differentiator turns the measured signals into the needed regressors. They then apply the speed-gradient method to build an identification algorithm. The paper gives conditions under which the estimates close in on the true values over time.
arxiv-2502-16323:
Kamgar and three co-authors ask how much a three-body force among nuclear parts adds to the grip that holds light atomic cores. Most sums use pair forces alone, tuned from how dense nuclear stuff acts. The team add a known three-body form and work out the grip for four light cores: helium, lithium, carbon, and nitrogen. Four pair-force sets were tried in turn.

They also found each core's size and set it next to lab reads. Shape and magnet marks were used to weigh the share of each spin path. The grip with the three-body force sat close to lab values, which the team call fair. The three-body clump share of the grip proved small. For helium with one force set it came to less than a tenth of a unit.
arxiv-2502-16423:
Duo Peng and four co-authors build, in 2025 work, a frame for testing how well text-to-image models resist trick prompts. Such models can be pushed to make harmful images, and their guards sit on both the words fed in and the image that comes out. Past attacks hit one guard or the other, and leaned on slow trial and error.

Their frame joins both attacks and tunes prompts by slope-based steps, which is faster. A probe method keeps tuning alive even when the model blocks all output, so no image comes back to learn from. Two more parts keep the trick prompt close to the aim and hard for a human eye to spot. A transfer part also cuts the number of tries, which are easy to flag. Wide tests back the frame.
arxiv-2502-16523:
Yulong Wu, Viktor Schlegel, and Riza Batista-Navarro test reading models against natural text edits in 2025. Machine reading systems now rival humans on clean benchmarks, but real text is messy. Synthetic typos may not reflect how real writing actually changes.

Their frame swaps benchmark passages for their real edited versions drawn from Wikipedia history. Across question sets and model types, natural edits clearly degraded scores. Even top chat models inherited the same errors. Training on perturbed examples, natural or synthetic, recovered part of the loss. A gap to clean-text scores remained, marking robustness as unfinished work.
arxiv-2502-16623:
Ke-Jian He and co-authors compute what a soliton boson star would look like through a telescope. Boson stars are balls of exotic scalar field, with no hard surface. Lit by a sky of stars or by a thin disk of hot gas, such an object bends light in telling ways.

Ray tracing through the star's gravity gives the screen images. Under weak coupling, the pictures show mostly direct and lensed views, their size set by the field's starting value and coupling strength. Under strong coupling, a nested ring appears inside the Einstein ring, and disk photons can loop the equator many times. Tilt shifts the pattern from redshift dimming to Doppler lopsidedness.
arxiv-2502-16823:
Dexter Le, Baran Arig, Murat Isik, Can Dikmen, and Teoman Karadag review memory options for brain-inspired chips built on FPGAs, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Neuromorphic systems promise efficient AI, but their speed lives or dies on how fast weights and spikes move in and out of memory, the classic memory wall. The review weighs the main contenders.

Standard SRAM and DRAM, high-bandwidth stacked memory, and newer non-volatile types such as resistive and phase-change memory are scored on delay, throughput, power, density, and scaling. Case studies show how each behaves in working systems. The authors aim the survey at builders choosing memory for FPGA neuromorphic platforms, where the right pick can decide whether the design flies or stalls.
arxiv-2502-17123:
Laura Selicato and co-authors automate a tuning headache in a 2025 signal processing paper. Splitting a mixed signal into clean parts with nonnegative factorization works well for sound spectra, but penalty settings steer the balance between fit and sparsity, and hand tuning is fiddly. Their algorithm tunes those settings by itself.

A two-level scheme treats the penalties as row-wise values learned in an outer loop while the factorization runs inside. The method shines on sparse, repeating signals buried in noise. A standout use is spotting bearing faults from vibration data, where faint high tones hide under broad noise. Tests beat prior approaches on synthetic and real data.
arxiv-2502-17223:
Erik Learned-Miller and a colleague present a 2025 arXiv paper on honest lower bounds for the average of a discrete distribution known only through samples. Think of a multinomial die with known faces: how low can its mean safely be claimed to sit? The authors characterize the full set of admissible bound rules, those no rival rule beats everywhere.

Each admissible bound comes from solving one simple optimization problem, and some published bounds pass the test. One negative result stands out: for support sizes and sample sizes above one, no single best bound exists. The paper maps the whole frontier of fair choices.
arxiv-2502-17423:
Eric Frankel and five co-authors teach a solver to solve the solver, in a 2025 paper. Diffusion models build images and other samples by slowly undoing noise, step by step. Each step costs a full pass through a big network, so steps are precious. In the very-few-steps range, classic solvers cannot track the true path, the team shows, no matter how clever the math.

Their method, S4S, learns a custom solver for a given model by copying a strong teacher solver's output. It needs no training data and no change to the model itself, and it drops onto any step plan. Across six models, for both guided and unguided sampling, sample quality rose over classic solvers. A twin version tunes the step plan too, setting top scores on two image benchmarks at just five steps.
arxiv-2502-17623:
Hui-Ru Ho, Nitigya Kargeti, Ziqi Liu, and Bilge Mutlu design tools that let parents steer a robot tutor for young children. AI learning robots are entering homes, and parents worry about content while welcoming help they lack time or skill to give. Their 2025 work builds SET, a card kit that lays out scenarios with different levels of parent involvement. A companion interface, PAiREd, lets parents review and revise the robot's AI-made lessons before delivery. Twenty families with children aged three to five tried the system at home.

Parents could dial their role up or down, choosing what the robot handles alone. The field study shows how families actually negotiate that control. The authors offer a design pattern for family AI: oversight by design, not by warning label. Their cards make an abstract choice concrete.
arxiv-2502-17723:
Alex Jiang and Abel Rodriguez model financial order flow with flexible Hawkes processes in a 2025 paper. Orders in fast markets excite more orders, the hallmark of Hawkes dynamics. Classic models force a fixed shape on that excitement. Order data break those shapes, the team show.

Their semiparametric model builds excitement curves from mixtures of dependent Dirichlet processes. The curves can bend, dip, and share strength across order types. Two fitting engines are offered: a sampling method and a faster variational one. Simulations show lower error than benchmark tools. On real order flow, the model catches non-monotone excitement that fixed forms cannot. Price formation studies gain a sharper lens.
arxiv-2502-17823:
Asking a language model to forget private or copyrighted text is harder than it sounds: the usual fine-tuning tricks erase the target but dull the model overall. Jie Ren led a team that first asks what the two main trick families share. Both, it turns out, work by spotting the target data and damping what the model says about it.

Their framework, GRUN, builds on that insight with two parts. A soft gate learns to tell target data from the rest. A second part then adjusts the model's inner representations, not its weights, to quiet the target. Tests showed stronger forgetting with less damage to normal skill. The method is fast, works with either trick family, and suits repeated rounds of forgetting.
arxiv-2502-18023:
Zhuo Chen and co-authors teach vision-language models in 2025 to know what they do not know. These models falter on questions needing fresh or deep facts. Fetching outside help works but costs too much when done for every question. Their method fine-tunes a model on an automatically built set to flag when a question sits beyond its knowledge.

Tests on several visual question sets showed the boundary drawn well. Using it, the team cut needless fetching while keeping or raising accuracy. One model's boundary even served as a stand-in for others. Smarter fetching decisions could make such systems cheaper and faster in daily use.
arxiv-2502-18323:
Mohamed Ahmed and co-authors speed up AI training on low power edge devices in 2025 without breaking their power caps. Small devices at the network edge are weak in power and memory, and the usual fix, slowing the graphics chip, stretches training time badly. Their idea is to tune the system and the task together instead of one at a time.

The method pairs the chip speed with the training batch size, picking both jointly under a fixed power limit. Predictions of how batch size pays off are combined with measured profiles of the device itself. On real hardware, training ran more than twice as fast as standard baselines and landed near the best possible result, while total energy use also fell by a large share. Model quality after training held steady. The gain matters for learning on site where data cannot leave the device.
arxiv-2502-18423:
Fengshuo Bai, Yu Li, Jie Chu, and a wider team wrote this research paper, published in 2025. It teaches a robot arm with a many-fingered hand to fish a target object out of clutter, digging through the pile itself instead of clearing it piece by piece.

Objects buried under others are slow to retrieve because items rest on one another in tangled ways. Older systems either reason about supports and grasp items one by one, or nudge the pile first as a separate step. RetrDex learns in massive parallel simulation across varied piles. Its spatial encoding captures how the target, hand, and clutter occlude and support each other. From that, the hand learns to push, stir, and poke as part of one smooth skill. Tests on sixteen household objects, seen and new, went well, and the skill transferred to a real robot hand with no extra training.
arxiv-2502-18623:
Ayana Moshruba, Shay Snyder, Hamed Poursiami, and Maryam Parsa test how well spiking networks keep their training set hidden. A spy attack can guess whether a case trained a model, which leaks private facts. Spike networks fire in rare bursts and lack smooth steps, which past work says blurs such leaks. Their 2025 study adds two twists: cut precision grades of the weights of the network, and the choice of stand-in gradient for training.

Cut precision helped both spike and plain networks hide, at small cost to accuracy. Full-precision spike networks still hid best of all, past cut plain networks. Of five stand-in gradients, one gave the best hide-and-accuracy mix, while a curved form made leaks worse. Precision grain and gradient choice both steer the hiding, they say, not just the spike form.
arxiv-2502-19023:
Anastasios Nentidis and co-authors survey how to reason over knowledge graphs that contain clashes, in a 2025 paper. A knowledge graph stores facts as linked items under a set schema, and reasoning over it powers search and question answering. Facts are often pulled from text by machine or merged from unlike sources, so clashes creep in.

The survey sorts fixes into three paths: find the parts that cause the clash, repair the graph until it agrees with itself, or reason in ways that tolerate clashes. Work from logic, databases, and the web is drawn in. The authors end with open problems and where the field may go next.
arxiv-2502-19123:
Behnaz Elhaminia and co-authors review methods for aligning whole slide images of tissue, a key step in cancer microscopy. Their 2025 review spans classic image methods through deep learning. Alignment matters because one tissue slice is stained and scanned in several versions, and matching them lets analysts stack cells into three-dimensional views of the tumor's neighborhood.

The task is far harder than aligning medical scans. The images are gigantic, stains change how tissue looks, and cuts warp shape from slice to slice. The authors sort the methods by approach and weigh their strengths on these challenges. Their map is meant to guide labs picking or building registration tools.
arxiv-2502-19223: Ivan Panin and Anastasia Stavrova wrote a 2025 math paper that extends a classic theorem of Harder from 1967. The topic is bundles, a way to track twisted geometric objects over a base ring. The authors prove that for a wide class of groups over a Dedekind domain, any bundle that looks trivial in each local patch is in fact trivial as a whole. The result covers simply connected isotropic reductive groups and builds on Harder's earlier case.
arxiv-2502-19923:
Anton Varonka and Kazuki Watanabe study, in 2025, when a computer can decide if one state can reach another under repeated maps. The maps here are Bellman operators, which come from decision problems where each step picks the best or worst next value. For general maps of this piecewise kind, the question is known to be undecidable even in two dimensions.

For these special operators, the answer is more hopeful. The team proves the question can be decided in any dimension when the target is not a fixed point, or when start and target are ordered. In two dimensions, it can always be decided. The contrast with the general case is sharp.
arxiv-2502-20023:
Suyeon Son, Minjin Kim, and Luis C Ho read the temperature layout of accretion disks from the way their light flickers. Their 2025 paper studies bright active galactic nuclei, where gas spirals into a giant black hole and glows in ultraviolet light.

Using repeated spectra from a large sky survey, the team built flicker curves across many objects and wavelengths. They fit how the flicker timescale grows with brightness and wavelength. The brightness scaling matched the standard disk model, but the wavelength scaling came out well below it. That gap means the disk's heat falls off with radius in a steeper pattern than the standard model says. The authors offer the numbers as a test for future disk models.
arxiv-2502-20223:
Mingqiang Han and Chunlin Yi build a vision system that sorts palm fruit into five ripeness levels from photos. Their 2025 study starts from a grower's problem: palm oil yield and quality peak when fruit is picked at just the right stage. Judging that stage by eye, across huge plantations, is slow and inconsistent.

The team trained deep convolutional networks on a public set of more than 8,000 fruit images. A small custom network set the baseline, while two large pretrained models were fine-tuned for the task. Test accuracy passed eighty-five percent. The authors argue such systems can sharpen harvest timing and lift production efficiency.
arxiv-2502-20323:
Xuangeng Chu and co-authors present ARTalk, a 2025 model that animates a 3D head from speech in real time. Talking avatars need lip motion locked to sound, plus natural head poses and blinks. Diffusion models make fine motion but run too slowly for live use.

ARTalk learns a multi-scale codebook of motion and reads speech step by step, as an autoregressive model does with words. That design yields fast, well-synced lips with lifelike pose and blink. The model can also adopt speaking styles it never saw in training, giving avatars fresh personal manners. In tests and user studies, it beat prior methods on lip sync accuracy and perceived quality. Live virtual hosts and game characters are natural outlets.
arxiv-2502-20723:
Wei and four colleagues cast transformer networks as trial states for open quantum systems in twenty twenty-five. Open systems leak energy and settle into mixed steady states that are hard to compute. Their ansatz doubles the space so the density operator reads like a pure state. Attention blocks then encode both size and phase of its parts.

The design keeps shift symmetry while catching long range links. Tests on dissipative Ising and Heisenberg chains hit excellent accuracy. Mixed steady states came out right across the board. The work imports a language model trick into many body physics with care.
arxiv-2502-20923:
Christoph Adam and co-authors compute spinning boson stars under a broader field model than the one most often used, published in 2025. Boson stars are hypothetical dense objects made from a self-gravitating complex scalar field. The team swaps the usual kinetic term for one drawn from a nonlinear sigma model.

They find spinning solutions for a family of models set by how curved the target space is, and for several self-interaction choices. They then report mass, compactness, and higher shape traits as those inputs change. Nonzero curvature can shift mass and compactness a good deal. Yet the links between shape traits stayed in line with the standard case, so those universal relations extend to curved target spaces.
arxiv-2502-21123:
Ruta Binkyte and co-authors argue that causality is the key to balancing trust goals in machine learning in a 2025 position paper. Fairness, privacy, robustness, accuracy, and explainability all matter in high-stakes systems, yet teams chase them one by one and end up trading them off badly.

Causal methods already reconcile some pairs, like fairness with accuracy and privacy with robustness, in working applications. The authors map how causal thinking can enter both ordinary models and foundation models in practice. Gains include reliability and interpretability that correlation alone cannot certify. Challenges and limits are aired honestly, with an eye to more accountable AI.
arxiv-2502-21223:
A future electron-positron collider, the FCC-ee, needs a detector matched to its clean collisions and rich physics program. The IDEA Study Group presents its concept, named IDEA, built for exactly those conditions. The paper first sets out how the machine will run and which measurements drive the design. It then walks through each layer of the detector in detail.

At the core sits a very light tracking system, with a fine vertex detector inside a large drift chamber wrapped in silicon. Beyond it, a crystal calorimeter using dual readout promises sharp energy measures, followed by a fiber calorimeter of the same style. A superconducting magnet built with high-temperature materials powers the system, and muon chambers line its return frame. Simulated performance examples round out the concept.
arxiv-2503-00023:
Johann Rafelski and Berndt Müller wrote a 2025 physics paper on fusion reactions inside beryllium. Fusion joins light nuclei and frees energy. The rate and path of such joins at low energy can shift when the nuclei sit in a molecule-like setting, with wide gaps between partners.

The authors argue that some beryllium fusion acts are long distance molecule style events. Those events matter for low energy nuclear reaction studies, a field with open puzzles. For them, the pair builds a new reaction model that fits the wide spacing. They also note a chain of reactions that can arise on its own in a beryllium target hit by protons out of balance. The paper is short and makes a focused theory claim.
arxiv-2503-00123: Thomas Massoni surveys three-dimensional Anosov flows through the lens of contact and symplectic geometry in a 2025 paper. Anosov flows are a classic kind of chaotic motion on shapes, long studied in dynamics. The survey follows work by Mitsumatsu, by Eliashberg and Thurston, by Hozoori, and by Massoni himself. It adds a few new results of his own. It closes with open questions and conjectures for the field, mapping where the geometry of these flows may go next.
arxiv-2503-00223:
Pengcheng Jiang and co-authors train language models to rewrite search queries by trial and error in a paper from 2025. Search engines live or die by the query they receive. Past model-based rewriters needed costly labeled data or a teacher model to copy.

DeepRetrieval uses reinforcement learning with retrieval scores as the reward. No reference queries are needed at all. The model learns phrasing that real search engines reward. On literature search, recall hit about sixty-five percent for papers, far above the prior best near twenty-five. Trial search recall also doubled the old mark. Learning from the engine's own feedback may beat learning from human examples.
arxiv-2503-00523:
Shammi Malhotra, Sarika Goyal, and K. Sreenadh study a class of equations that blend local and far-reaching effects, built around the p-Laplace operator used to model uneven diffusion. Their version adds a Hardy term, a weight that grows strong near a single point. The authors ask which special values, called eigenvalues, such an operator can take, and how solutions behave at those values.

They first prove a Hardy-type bound suited to this mixed setting. With it, they show the eigenvalues exist and pin down their main traits. They then map a two-value spectrum named after Fučík, proving its first curved branch exists and describing its shape. Later sections cover how the shape of the domain affects the lowest eigenvalues, how smooth the solutions are, and a classic bound that links the first eigenvalue to the domain's size.
arxiv-2503-00623:
Lucas Henrique Almeida presents a 2025 method for keeping robot arms safe while they work near moving people and objects. A robot arm must stay smooth and gentle when it touches things, yet it must also swerve fast when a crash looms. The paper joins those two needs in one control plan.

The plan builds safety rules from the shape of the paths that would lead to a crash. A math solver then tweaks the planned motion as little as it can while still obeying the rules. Tests in computer scenes show the arm stays safe across varied moving setups. The method suits factories and labs where arms and people share tight, changing space.
arxiv-2503-00723:
Liu and a large team present a study from twenty twenty-five on tuning multimodal models by editing their internal representations. Full fine-tuning of huge multimodal models costs too many parameters. Lightweight tuning methods lag behind in performance and stay hard to steer. Their method edits meaning-rich representations directly instead of weights. It needs a tiny fraction of tunable parameters. Scores beat leading baselines by wide margins in their tests. Editing special tokens inside the representations steers behavior simply.

The approach gives intuitive control over model conduct. Fewer moving parts make the tuning easier to read. The authors frame representation editing as a fresh tuning path. Gains hold across their multimodal benchmarks.
arxiv-2503-01123: Yuki Minowa, writing alone, studies a motion-planning measure through the lens of rational homotopy theory, in a 2025 mathematics paper. The measure, sequential parametrized topological complexity, counts how hard it is to plan a robot's path in stages while outside constraints ride along. Minowa generalizes known results on the simpler, non-parametrized version and gives an explicit algebraic upper bound for the measure when the underlying fibration splits in a certain way.
arxiv-2503-01623:
David Hartmann and co-authors audit five commercial content moderation services for bias in policing hate speech. Such services promise scale, but they can silence fair speech and miss coded hate at the same time. The team sent five million test queries drawn from four datasets.

All five services leaned hard on group identity words when flagging hate. OpenAI and Amazon did slightly better than the rest. Every service under-flagged implied hate, above all against LGBTQIA+ people. Every one also over-flagged counter-speech and reclaimed slurs from the targeted groups. The authors urge clearer guidance and candor about limits from the providers.
arxiv-2503-01723:
Nakis and co-authors find the true hidden dimension of complex networks in this 2025 paper. Machine learning on graphs leans on low-dimensional embeddings of nodes. Recent work found exact embeddings, but how low the dimension can go stayed unknown.

The authors prove that metric embeddings, which respect distances directly, can go lower than the usual vector method. They give a fast logarithmic search that pins down the exact dimension. Metric structure also lets the search scale to huge graphs with near-linear cost. Tests recover far smaller representations than reported before, even reconstructing graphs of a million nodes exactly. Networks, it turns out, are intrinsically simpler than their embeddings suggested.
arxiv-2503-01923:
Xuying Li, Zhuo Li, Yuji Kosuga, and Victor Bian study how answer length affects the safety of a reasoning model when it is forced to think step by step. Longer replies can help a model correct itself, but attackers may also use long outputs to slip past guards. The team tested the model DeepSeek-R1 against varied hostile prompts.

They find length cuts both ways: more room helps self-correction in some cases, while certain attacks gain from extended replies. The authors suggest that length should be controlled in a flexible way rather than fixed. They propose training tweaks and adaptive limits on output size to keep reasoning strong while improving safety.
arxiv-2503-02123:
Emmanuel Olowe and Danial Chitnis grade language models on the unforgiving dialect of electronic test equipment, in a 2025 paper. Test and measurement work demands exact commands and accurate readings, and labs are adopting generative AI fast. Their benchmark, TMIQ, scores models on matching SCPI instrument commands, ranking candidate answers, chain-of-thought reasoning, and tolerance of output format demands.

Exact command matches ranged from about fifty-six to seventy-three percent across models. The best model's first-ranked answer was right only a third of the time. The study also weighs token use, cost, and response speed, mapping the trade between accuracy and running expense. A companion command-line tool lets any lab regenerate the test with its own scenarios. The authors offer TMIQ as a production-grade yardstick for choosing models in measurement work.
arxiv-2503-02823:
Matteo Spanio, Massimiliano Zampini, Antonio Rodà, and Franco Pierucci published this paper in 2025. It explores turning taste into music with generative AI. Psychology has long linked the senses: high notes taste sweet to listeners, low ones bitter, and composers exploit such crossings.

The team fine-tuned a generative music model on pieces paired with detailed taste descriptions, then asked 111 listeners to judge the outputs. Music from the tuned model matched its taste brief clearly better than music from the untuned model. Listeners could hear sweetness, sourness, or bitterness in the generated clips at rates beyond chance agreement. The authors release their data set, code, and model openly. They frame the work as a step toward embodied AI that treats the senses as one system. Possible futures range from dining experiences scored to a menu to tools for people with sensory impairments.
arxiv-2503-03223:
A team of astronomers relates black hole spin to galaxy growth in a paper from 2025. Spin is thought to power the jets that feed back on host galaxies. The team studied forty-eight nearby supermassive black holes. Multi-band fitting gave each host galaxy's star formation rate and stellar mass. The catalog creator field carries stray symbols and a different author order than the head byline, so the work is described with team framing here.

Smaller black holes spun faster as mass grew, pointing to orderly gas feeding. The largest ones spun slower with mass, pointing to mergers and chaotic feeding. Spin also rose then fell across star formation rates. The authors say spin can hint at how a host galaxy is forming stars.
arxiv-2503-04023:
Zhaoxia Heng and co-authors used the latest Higgs boson data to squeeze a supersymmetric theory's room for light extra Higgs particles. The framework extends the Standard Model with a general singlet sector. It allows the familiar 125 GeV Higgs to decay into pairs of much lighter scalar or pseudoscalar particles, a signature colliders could easily have missed. The team scanned the theory's parameter space with a nested sampling algorithm.

Three constraint tools were applied, covering measured Higgs properties, direct search limits, and dedicated ATLAS hunts. Direct searches bit hardest. In the scenario where the observed Higgs is the second-lightest state, the surviving Higgs must be at least ninety-three percent Standard-Model-like, with limited singlet mixing. Dark matter candidates also survived in specific flavors, dominated by one superpartner type or another depending on the scenario. The authors map exactly which corners of the theory remain open.
arxiv-2503-04223:
Yi Xiao and co-authors sharpen satellite photos with spiking neural networks. Their 2025 paper deals with super-resolution for remote sensing, where spiking nets promise low energy yet lag in power. Spikes swing wildly across textures, a sign of active learning the team exploits. Their spiking attention block tunes membrane charge by inferred attention weights, which steers spike traffic for richer features.

The block joins time and channel cues and reads global self-similarity in wide scenes as a prior. The full net, SpikeSR, topped rivals on three benchmarks while staying lean in compute. Code is promised public.
arxiv-2503-04323:
Eduardo Abi Jaber and four co-authors solved a trading task with lasting price impact through a Fredholm frame. Their paper, from twenty twenty-five, deals with propagator models of market impact. A trade moves price, and that move fades in a set curve, here with power law tails. The trader holds a signal on where price will go and must time buys and sells. The best plan meets a nonlinear stochastic Fredholm equation with terms that look both ways in time.

They prove a sole best plan exists under a monotone term that marks the impact's bend. Past that term, a best plan still exists on a countable chance space. A loop scheme homes in on the plan, with a code run to show it.
arxiv-2503-04723:
Large language models have grown strong at reading long texts, yet their skill at writing long texts lags far behind. Yuhao Wu and co-authors make the case in a 2025 piece that the field should turn its gaze from input to output. Long form work, such as novels, long plans, and deep proofs, needs more than a long read.

Such work asks a model to hold a long thread, keep its facts straight, and stay on plan for page after page. The team maps where today's models fall short on those asks. They call for base models built and graded with long output in mind. The prize, they say, is wide real world use that short form tools can not reach.
arxiv-2503-04923:
Eugene Gorsky, Soyeon Kim, Tonie Scroggin, and José Simental study a family of geometric spaces built from pairs of Young diagrams, in a 2025 mathematics paper. These spaces, skew shaped positroids, live inside the Grassmannian, the space of all planes of a fixed size. Each is fixed by two diagrams, one inside the other, inside a set rectangle. The authors cut into each space with an explicit open patch for every column position.

Each patch turns out to be a product of two smaller spaces of the same kind. The patches also carry a natural cluster structure, and the product map respects it in a precise sense. The proof views the spaces as braid varieties, extending earlier work on the simplest cells of the Grassmannian.
arxiv-2503-05123:
Werner, Adams, and Cary show that smoothing can calm a common plasma simulation method, in a 2025 paper. Particle-in-cell simulations track charged particles on a grid to model plasmas. When the grid poorly resolves a key length scale, the method heats itself falsely and grows unstable, and particle noise swells.

The team proves the fix in theory and in one-dimensional test runs. Smoothing small-scale charge ripples blocks the false heating, provided the smoothing radius grows with the under-resolution. Smoothing also quiets particle noise sharply. The authors map how noise, particle spread, and stray energy flows depend on grid choices. Test particles, they warn, can mislead when noise is high. Since smoothing trades away fine detail, the best grid can be far coarser than the strict scale demands, saving heavy computing time.
arxiv-2503-05223:
Yifan Liu, Yu Fang, and Zhouhan Lin build a system that turns silent video of a talking face into speech. Lip-reading machines must rebuild both the words and the speaker's own voice from sight alone, with no sound hints at all. Earlier systems leaned on acoustic clues during training or traded clarity against voice likeness. This model, DiVISe, predicts the sound picture directly from video frames in one pass.

Despite getting no audio input, the system keeps each speaker's vocal character while staying understandable. On two standard lip-reading datasets, it beat earlier models on both measured and human-judged quality. It also improved faster as data and model size grew, a sign the design has room to scale. The authors post their code and trained weights for others to build on.
arxiv-2503-05423:
Run He and co-authors help a learning system take on new classes without forgetting the old, and without keeping old examples, in a 2025 paper. The trap has two jaws. First, old classes drift in the model's inner map as new lessons land, a semantic shift. Second, the judge at the top leans toward the new, since only new data feeds its training.

Their method, DPCR, reads the drift two ways at once: a learned warp catches task-level moves, and a row-space projection catches class-level ones. The judge is then rebuilt by ridge regression, fed with the old class profiles shifted back into place. Across standard datasets the approach held the old-new balance better than the leading rivals. Code is public. The authors pitch the twin projection as the key: drift is not one motion but two, and each needs its own gauge.
arxiv-2503-05623:
Sakcak, Shell, and O'Kane probe the limits of what a robot can be asked to do in a 2025 paper. Formal methods now describe rich, time-extended robot tasks. But whether a task can even be stated depends on what the statement refers to. It might refer to the robot's states, its actions and observations, its knowledge, or something else entirely.

Earlier work touched on these grounding choices case by case. This paper treats grounding as a first-class question, introducing notation that covers a large class of problems. The results show that whole classes of tasks become statable only under certain combinations of groundings. The work maps the boundary of specifiable robot planning, rather than adding one more planning algorithm.
arxiv-2503-06023:
John Clayton models what happens to liver tissue when it is hit hard and fast, in a research paper from 2025. Such impacts can come from blasts or crashes. The model treats the liver as a mix of solid tissue and liquid blood moving together.

The solid part combines soft liver lobules with a network of tougher fibers. The model covers stretch, slow spring-back, heat change, and damage. Clayton tests it against shock-tube data and against drop-weight tests on liver samples. The results match real trends: at high rates the soft matrix tears more than the fibers, and more blood makes the tissue less stiff.
arxiv-2503-06323:
Jack Foxabbott, Rohan Subramani, and Francis Rhys Ward work in 2025 on diagrams that model how agents reason about each other's beliefs. Multi-agent influence diagrams capture strategic play compactly, but in their standard form they cannot handle settings where agents hold different beliefs about the game, and different beliefs about each other's beliefs.

The authors define an extended form of the diagram that covers such incomplete information, in both endless and fixed-depth versions. They prove it matches extensive form games with incomplete information and no shared prior. The extension also keeps the classic solution ideas from game theory, opening richer reasoning problems to the diagram approach.
arxiv-2503-06823:
Suraiya Tairin and co-authors present eMoE, a system that serves mixture-of-experts language models without keeping every expert in GPU memory. Their 2025 paper notes that these models gain capacity from many specialist sub-networks, but storing all of them is expensive. Loading experts from slower memory on demand can stall answers instead.

The system predicts which experts upcoming prompts will need, based on repeating routing patterns. It refreshes those predictions only every few prompts, since reusing recent experts barely hurts quality. It also skips prediction for tasks that tolerate rough routing, and schedules work with deadlines and output lengths in mind. Tests cut memory use by up to four fifths and trimmed latency as well. Longer prompts and larger batches became practical on the same hardware.
arxiv-2503-07023:
Armin Rainer presents a 2025 mathematics paper on spaces of arc-smooth maps. A function is smooth exactly when composing it with every smooth curve gives a smooth result; such functions are called arc-smooth. Earlier work stretched this test to closed sets with rough edges, like sets with Hölder boundary.

This paper upgrades those set-level matches to the natural topologies on the function spaces, showing they are bornological isomorphisms, meaning the bounded sets align too. The results extend to maps taking values in convenient vector spaces, yielding exponential laws for mapping spaces. Parallel results hold for special ultradifferentiable classes of Braun-Meise-Taylor type. The work firms up the foundations of infinite-dimensional calculus on singular domains.
arxiv-2503-07123:
Saranya and Sunoj develop new ways to measure how much a set of outcomes spreads out and how unsure it is. Their measures build on extropy, a quantity tied to entropy. They define dynamic versions of relative extropy for two cases. One covers the life still left in an item that is still in use. The other covers the time that has already passed since an event. The work studies the properties of the new measures and how they link to older ones.

The authors also give a way to estimate relative extropy straight from data, with no fixed shape assumed. They test this estimator in computer simulations. They then apply the measures to real-life data sets to show practical use. The paper adds to the set of tools for comparing spread and doubt between two sets of outcomes over time.
arxiv-2503-07323:
Yubo Zhao, Qi Wu, and colleagues let language models steer moving agents through crowded spaces in a 2025 study. Earlier tests of model spatial reasoning confined agents to four directions in simple, still rooms with a single mover. Real navigation involves many agents, moving obstacles, and floor plans with clutter.

The authors encode real indoor layouts and dynamic agents in a uniform format the model can read. Language model reasoning then plans routes through the changing scene. Gains over earlier limited studies would show that text-trained models hold usable spatial sense. Such reasoners could sit above low-level controllers in service robots and games.
arxiv-2503-07423:
Poon and Hunter sum build rules for mixed-part climb bots on poles and trunks. Their bot joins wheel drive with grip arms in one frame. Grip arms run on cords and bend to pole widths by plan. Links can be added or cut to fit each pole girth. The drive sits on a spin head at the bot's core. Self-lock lets the bot hang by rub with no power draw.

Free grip and spin round the pole round out its skills. Math forms set the terms for self-lock and straight climbs. Bench tests show the bot climbs and locks as the forms said. Those tests back the forms and flag full-bot paths for trade. The work gives a full frame to grade and build such bots. Tall builds in trade stand as the end use case.
arxiv-2503-07523:
Zhangquan Chen, Xufang Luo, and Dongsheng Li teach a vision model to look where the question points in this 2025 paper. People scan scenes with intent, focusing on what matters for their goal. Earlier systems copied that trick only with hand-drawn boxes marking focus regions, which are costly to label and explode in variety.

Their framework, VisRL, drops the labels and learns focus by trial and error, rewarded for final answers. The model treats choosing where to look as an inner decision refined by reinforcement. Across several benchmarks it beat strong rivals and transferred well between base models. The authors argue reward-only training mirrors how humans learn to perceive with purpose.
arxiv-2503-07723:
Connor Basinger and seven co-authors probed the atmosphere in two thousand twenty-five of an ultra-hot Jupiter called TOI-1518 b. Such planets hug their stars and broil, making them natural labs for air chemistry and winds. Using a high-resolution spectrograph on the Large Binocular Telescope, they took transmission spectra as the planet crossed its star.

Neutral and ionized iron showed up strongly. Chromium and nickel appeared more tentatively. Wind speeds for neutral iron, tracked over time, matched the pattern for ionized iron. The planet joins a small club of ultra-hot Jupiters with time-resolved wind measures, a step toward weather maps of alien worlds.
arxiv-2503-07923:
Robert Besuner and co-authors present the case for a next-generation sky survey machine, the Spectroscopic Stage-5 Experiment. The dark universe, dark matter and dark energy together, resists every probe except large astronomical surveys. Their white paper lays out the science goals, instruments, and observing plan for an all-sky spectroscopic facility of unprecedented scale and precision.

The baseline design upgrades two existing four-meter telescopes into six-meter wide-field facilities. Each would carry a highly multiplexed spectrograph able to take spectra of many thousands of objects at once. By mapping the cosmos in three dimensions far beyond current surveys, the experiment aims to measure the dark sector's properties and history tightly enough to test fundamental physics.
arxiv-2503-08023:
Sudarshan Regmi improves the test that tells a vision model it is looking at something it was never trained on, in a 2025 paper.
