Out-of-distribution detection matters for safe deployment, and current methods reshape a network's activations with one fixed percentile threshold for every input. Regmi noticed something about foreign inputs under slight disturbance. Their largest activations shift much more than familiar inputs' do.

His method, AdaSCALE, turns that observation into an estimate of how foreign each sample looks, then sets the scaling threshold per sample. Likely familiar inputs get strong scaling; likely foreign ones get weak scaling. The resulting scores separated the two classes far better, beating the strongest rival by wide margins on a standard benchmark across eight architectures.
arxiv-2503-08323:
Rohanian and co-authors present a 2025 framework for language models specialized in cancer care. Clinical oncology notes are messy, with gaps, mixed terms, and unclear wording, and general models often stumble on them. Their framework combines three tools: tuning on expert instructions, search over trusted sources at answer time, and a knowledge graph that links medical facts. The models stay small, so clinics with limited computing can run them.

The models handled tasks such as spotting cancer diagnoses in text, linking terms to standard codes, staging tumors, sorting reports by subtype, and predicting treatment response. A small set of German instructions from a Zurich hospital tested whether a little non-English data could carry skills across languages. Results were strong on entity and document tasks. The authors aim at tools that fit real hospital limits.
arxiv-2503-08523:
Varga and co-authors announce a long suspected companion star caught at last on camera. The young star T CrA sits in a messy cradle of disk, streams, and jets. Many clues hinted it had a partner, but no one had seen one directly. The team used a large telescope array in Chile to image the system in infrared light.

A companion showed up to the west of the main star in the newest images. Its orbit looks nearly edge on and tilted far from the main disk. That tilt could explain warps and tears proposed for the disk. The companion glows with warm dust, likely from a small disk of its own. It adds a modest share of the total light.
arxiv-2503-08723:
Raphi Kang and co-authors prove that CLIP's shared image-text space has a geometric flaw no training can fix, then propose a scoring method that routes around it. CLIP is the workhorse aligning pictures and words, yet it fumbles bindings, positions, and negation. Their 2025 paper asks whether the fault lies in the very idea of one joint embedding.

The proof says yes: no such space can simultaneously handle plain content plus any two of attribute binding, spatial relations, and negation. Their fix scores matches with dense cosine similarity maps, keeping each image patch and each word in play instead of crushing them into single vectors. Scores improve and stay interpretable. Vision-language researchers get a limit theorem and a practical patch in one paper.
arxiv-2503-08823:
Ce Guo and Tong Zhao introduce a benchmark that judges AI-written chip designs not just on whether they work, but on how much hardware they waste. Language models can now write the code that configures programmable chips, yet earlier tests checked only correctness. A correct design that hogs the chip is a poor design in practice.

Their benchmark, ResBench, holds fifty-six problems in twelve categories, from simple state machines to financial computing. An open framework feeds each problem to a model, checks the generated code, and measures resource use, focusing on lookup tables, the basic building blocks of these chips. Results showed wide gaps between models: some produced lean designs while others burned far more resources for the same task. The authors say resource awareness must become a standard axis in judging code models for hardware.
arxiv-2503-08923:
Anand Menon and co-authors wrote a 2025 paper on VERT, an open data set that teaches language models to write hardware checks. Chip checking eats most of design time, and writing formal assertions by hand is slow. Top closed models write them poorly and cost dearly.

VERT builds training pairs by varying open chip code in a systematic way, each with its matching assertion. Small open models fine tuned on it beat the big closed rival by wide margins. Gains over base models were larger still. Tests span four known open chip platforms. Local tuning also keeps design data private, a real concern in chip work.
arxiv-2503-09123:
Yuanbo Nie and Eric Kerrigan introduced in 2025 a more reliable way to solve dynamic optimization problems, the kind that plan optimal trajectories and controls over time. A popular method, direct collocation, is simple but produces wobbly, inaccurate answers on hard problems such as those with singular arcs. Their variant enforces the physics both as explicit constraints and as penalty terms inside the discretized problem.

On difficult examples, the new method suppressed the usual oscillations. Errors dropped by several orders of magnitude across multiple measures compared with standard approaches and other fixes. Implementation stays nearly as simple as the original method. The authors aim at engineers who need trustworthy optimal plans for systems like vehicles and robots.
arxiv-2503-09223:
Tian Tang and co-authors present a language model framework that judges how well products match shopper searches, in work from 2025. Good matching keeps online stores easy to use and lifts sales. Older small models read meaning well but lack broad world knowledge.

Large models bring that knowledge, yet they need very clean training data. They can also lean too generous, flooding results with weak matches. The new framework has three main parts that shape reasoning and curb over-calling. It aims to keep the smarts of large models while fitting store-grade speed and cost. Tests target real shopping search traffic.
arxiv-2503-09823:
Kevin Liao, Shreya Thipireddy, and Daniel Weitzner propose traceable data sharing for privacy, in work from 2025. Services from banking to health care now pass personal data between users and third parties. People want control, clear use records, and blame paths for misuse of shared data.

Current law and tech tools fall short of those needs when used alone. The authors join system design with legal design under one alignment frame. A new idea, covert accountability, covers actors who may cheat yet face later proof and legal cost. Their OTrace protocol then gives users sight of who holds data and why. Paired legal tools could turn those records into strong oversight at scale.
arxiv-2503-09923:
Yifei Yan and co-authors study how stock prices move, using a classic model that treats price changes as a random walk with steady growth. Their 2025 paper adds sudden jumps to the model, since real markets sometimes leap or drop in a day. They fit both versions to S&P 500 data from 2009 to 2014.

The authors work out exact math for the plain model and the jump model, then test them with computer sampling. Both fit the data well, but the jump version fits better and tracks sharp market shifts more closely. The paper offers traders and analysts a fuller way to judge risk in price forecasts.
arxiv-2503-10023:
Stephanie Hu and Xiaolu Guo test in a 2025 paper whether context helps models learn to split speech into words. Babies face that split task with no spaces in the sound stream. Past work shows infants may lean on sound statistics to find word edges.

Earlier modeling by Goldwater and co-authors found that adding context sharpened that learning. Hu and Guo rebuilt two of those models, a single word model and a word pair model. The pair model beat the single model at predicting word splits, matching the pair's hypothesis. Beyond the rerun, simple ways to reuse known words for fresh utterances were tried. Those trials sketch how toddlers might bootstrap from a small known stock.
arxiv-2503-10123:
Zhi-Bo Chen and Shao-Ming Fei give criteria for separability and entanglement in multipartite quantum systems of arbitrary dimension. Telling whether a many party state is entangled is a central and hard problem in quantum information. The approach rests on the generalized Bloch representation of quantum states.

Some criteria are sufficient and others are necessary for separability. For certain states the two sets meet, giving a full characterization. Worked examples show the criteria detect entanglement where some existing tests fail. As a payoff, the authors find the largest separable ball around the maximally mixed state for multi qubit systems and prove its radius in a standard norm is exactly one. The tests can be run in experiments.
arxiv-2503-10323:
Samuel Santos-Pérez, Isabel Cordero-Carrión, and Pablo Cerdá-Durán rework how Einstein's equations are written in one strict form used for space-time problems. In that form, part of the system sets limits that must hold at each step, and part drives how the rest changes over time, carrying the waves of gravity.

Their version keeps a key trait of the limit part: near a known answer, no second answer sits close by. It also gives all parts a neat ladder form based on the older Newtonian view. The team shows how to build starting data, such as a spinning neutron star, without first assuming a flat space slice.
arxiv-2503-10523:
Jun Yu, Yongqi Wang, and colleagues estimate emotional state from faces and voices for a 2025 affective computing competition. Their target is valence and arousal, how pleasant and how intense a person's feeling runs, judged from behavior recorded in the wild. Faces and speech carry complementary clues, so the method reads both.

A pretrained vision network extracts features from facial images, while pretrained audio networks supply two kinds of speech features. Temporal networks then track how those features evolve, and cross-modal attention lets each stream inform the other. The entry was built for the eighth edition of a recurring benchmark challenge.
arxiv-2503-10923:
Marco Barroca and co-authors push in this 2025 paper quantum computing toward the energies of reactions on battery electrodes. Exact chemistry for reacting molecules is out of classical reach. The team embeds the active pocket of an oxygen reduction reaction and picks its key orbitals by density shifts. States are then prepared on an IBM quantum processor of eighty qubits.

Their sample-based diagonalization, and an extended version folding in excitations, matched trusted classical answers where checks were possible. At twenty-seven orbitals the extended method beat the best feasible classical references. The authors present the run as a scale marker for quantum chemistry. Battery chemists gain a new kind of check.
arxiv-2503-11323:
Daniel Andre, Venkateswaran Krishnan, and Clifford Nolan study ghost artefacts in three-dimensional radar imaging. Their paper, from twenty twenty-five, analyzes a multistatic setup. Transmitter and receiver fly separate straight paths over the scene. Such split systems suit satellite swarms and drone teams.

Fine-scale math traces how the flight geometry shapes the image. Some geometries smear false copies of targets into the picture. The authors derive a time-gating rule for the recorded data. Applying the gate keeps the region of interest clean of artefacts. Computer simulations, run under a fixed-time formulation, back the theory. Mission planners can use the rule when choosing flight paths.
arxiv-2503-11823:
Lima e Silva and Brod begin a theory of two particle scattering on graphs in twenty twenty-five. Scattering on graphs is rich enough to support universal quantum computation. Any quantum circuit breaks into one and two qubit gates. Those gates translate into small subgraphs, called gadgets, that act on particles moving along a sparse graph.

Most prior theory handles single particles on graphs. Multi particle behaviour is less developed, the authors argue. They start building that theory for two particles. Initial applications construct multi particle gadgets with varied properties. Such gadgets could implement gates that single particle gadgets cannot. The work lays groundwork for graph based quantum computing with interacting particles.
arxiv-2503-11923:
Graph theory gains a new concept in a study of two-colored directed graphs. Dennis Diaz-Diaz and co-authors define a bikernel, a special set of points reached by paths of a single color. The idea grows out of older notions of kernels and of color-based kernels. The team asks which families of graphs hold such a set. They give conditions that are both needed and enough for several families.

Graphs with no single-color cycles get a full sorting of when a bikernel exists. Graphs with such cycles get their own sorting. The team also studies when a graph can be colored so that a bikernel appears. Results of this kind guide work on networks where links come in two types.
arxiv-2503-12123:
Zhaopeng Feng and five co-authors build reward models that grade machine translation step by step, in a 2025 arXiv paper. Big language models translate well, but judging a half-done translation is hard, and hand labels for each small step cost too much. Such step-level judges have helped in math and logic tasks, yet translation lacked both a method and a test bed.

Their frame, MT-RewardTree, grows translation tries in a tree search to make step-level good and bad pairs on its own. They build the first benchmark for translation reward judges and compare designs. Step-level training caught fine taste in wording best. Their judge leads the field, and the team shows it can steer models at run time and sharpen picks among rival drafts, all with code and data shared.
arxiv-2503-12323:
How hard do the grains in a murk push and pull each other? Clare Rees-Zimmerman and five co-authors line up three ways to read that hidden law from pictures of the murk, in 2025. One bends a guess till its fake murk matches the true spread. One drops test grains into snaps and reads the cost. One learns the push straight from grain tracks over time.

Three toy murks with known laws served as the exam, plus one true murk under the microscope. Each way has its gate: the first needs no grain spots, the second reads tangles past pairs, the third shrugs off drags and drives but must see motion. The team hand the reader a map for picking a way by the data at hand.
arxiv-2503-12523:
Chrysafis and Hartonas extend a classic correspondence result to modal logics without the distribution law. Their 2025 paper concerns logics where the modal operator need not spread over conjunction in the usual way, possibly lacking negation or implication as well. The Sahlqvist-van Benthem result, in standard modal logic, ties certain formula shapes to first-order frame conditions, and the authors ask whether that tie survives without distribution.

The strategy is reduction. The distribution-free system is translated, fully and abstractly, into a sorted modal logic that acts as its companion, where the correspondence is already understood. The bridge rests on a duality between lattice-based algebras and a widened form of Kripke frames carrying extra relations. Because the reduction is systematic, the authors note the same approach scales to other systems, with or without distribution, carrying extra operators.
arxiv-2503-12623:
A student-led team presents a system from 2025 that reads emotion in video by fusing face, voice, and words. Judging feelings in the wild is hard because expressions are brief and cues from each channel may not line up in time. Older systems also scored pleasantness and intensity apart, though the two are closely tied.

Their network, called MAVEN, uses a separate encoder for each channel, then lets the channels attend to each other in both directions. It reports emotion as a point on a circle model that pairs pleasantness with intensity. The team tested the system on standard video sets for emotion work. The design aims to catch fleeting feelings more faithfully than single-channel tools.
arxiv-2503-13023:
Michal Danilowicz and Tomasz Kryjak track many objects on a programmable chip in a 2025 paper. Following people or cars in video is core work for robots, but it usually needs power-hungry hardware. Their system runs a quantized detector and a classic tracker together on an FPGA, a chip whose circuits can be reshaped. A modified framework stores the model weights in outside memory to fit the design.

The detector spots objects frame by frame, and the tracker links the spots into paths. Scores on standard photo and tracking datasets reached 0.21 and 38.9 on their usual scales. The balance of speed, power, and accuracy is the point. Such chips could give small robots and cameras real-time tracking without a data center behind them.
arxiv-2503-13623:
Surineela, Kanakamalla, Harikumar, and Ghosh present in twenty twenty-five a new method for shrinking data while keeping its class structure clear. Data reduction helps models sort items into groups, but a standard method needs a matrix step that breaks down when data have very many features. That flaw hits fields like gene studies hard.

Their method balances two goals at once. It pulls points of each class toward their class centre, and it pushes class centres far apart. They prove the combined cost has a bowl shape, so the best answer can always be found. It needs no pairwise gap checks, so it runs faster and scales better. Tests on gene and image data beat older methods.
arxiv-2503-13723:
Christoph Lerche and co-authors published an engineering paper in 2025 on fast positioning for a layered scanner used in brain imaging. The scanner must find which tiny crystal pixel lit up and how much energy arrived. The layered layout lets the team estimate depth too. Their method avoids repeated guessing steps.

Calibration runs supplied the expected light counts the method needs. With parallel tricks and careful memory use, the system handled tens of millions of events per second on a multi-processor machine. A small share of detector blocks needed hand fixes after auto-calibration missed a few pixels. Final energy sharpness came close to that of single pixels, showing the method picks the right pixel.
arxiv-2503-13923:
Alexey Karev and Dong Xu offer a way to tell how alike two chatbots really are. New large language models arrive so often that buyers and researchers struggle to tell them apart. Their framework, ConSCompF, compares the texts two models write and returns one score for how similar the pair behaves.

The method works on a handful of unlabeled prompts, such as ordinary chatbot instructions. It needs no secrets from the models' makers, which suits closed commercial systems. Tests checked its scores against gaps shown by other benchmarks, including ROUGE-L, and against few-shot comparisons. Scores for many models at once form a matrix that a principal component plot can display. The authors pitch it as a cheap map of the model crowd.
arxiv-2503-14023:
Nadas, Diosan, and Tomescu survey how large language models make fake training data for text and code, in a review from twenty twenty-five. Fake data can fill gaps when real labeled data is rare, costly, or private. The models write new cases that fit a task. Those cases can train smaller tools or test them.

The review covers prompts, search-aided writing, and rounds of self-fixing. It shows gains for tasks with few cases, like sorting text or fixing code. It also warns of false facts, flat style, and bias that can grow worse. Fixes range from strict checks to scores from running the code. The authors call for better tests and clear rules for safe use.
arxiv-2503-14123: Scott proves a wave trace result for families of vibration operators on layered spaces, in a short 2025 paper. The spaces are bundles, where each point of a base carries its own curved fiber space. The operators include a famed superconnection case from geometry. The main claim gives a formula for the sharp peaks of the wave trace across the whole family. The paper also explains how that formula broadens the classic Poisson summation results, from single spaces to families.
arxiv-2503-14223:
Fabio Bagarello, Francesco Gargano, and Polina Khrennikova model the spread of an ill with tools borrowed from open quantum systems. The catalog record scrambles the title and author fields; the head of the text gives the true title and the three names used here. In their frame, the well folk act as a vast pool that the ill groups trade with. Past acts can leave a mark on what comes next, a kind of memory in the spread.

The math lets the spread run with or without that memory, in one set of laws. Fake runs then turn the memory dials and watch the curve of the ill. Some dial sets keep the runs sound, with counts that stay in the realm of the real. The frame hands ill-modelers a new way to weigh how much the past bends an outbreak's path.
arxiv-2503-14423:
Josephson junctions link superconductors in ways that let magnetic flux settle into patterns, and arrays of them are a playground for studying those patterns. Justus Teller and eight co-authors build a square array from a new kind of junction in this 2025 paper. Each junction has four terminals, made from niobium with a platinum heart, a geometry made on the spot in the lab.

The four-terminal layout stamps a checkerboard of two alternating flux values across the grid's cells. That pattern keeps a famous phase transition alive even at flux values that should kill it. Resistance readings show a beating pattern as the field changes, with the cell states sliding between the standard empty and half-full forms. The array also lets the team estimate how wide the junction's weak center spreads.
arxiv-2503-14523:
Thin branching shapes such as blood vessels, nerve cells, and roads are hard for software to trace without breaks. Siyi Wu and three co-authors offer SDF-TopoNet in 2025, a two stage method that aims to keep those shapes whole while staying fast to train. Older methods often used costly checks on the shape's structure and still missed fine pixel detail.

In the first stage the model learns a signed distance map, which records how far each pixel sits from the nearest edge of a vessel. In the second stage a small adapter and a refined loss tune the result for correct structure. On five test data sets the method beat earlier ones on both shape accuracy and standard scores, with lower training cost.
arxiv-2503-14723:
Eman Abdullah AlOmar and three colleagues built a plug-in that catches a common machine learning mistake as you code. Data leakage happens when training quietly uses information it should never see, like test answers. Models then look brilliant in the lab and fail in the real world.

Their tool, LeakageDetector, works inside the PyCharm editor for Python. It scans learning pipelines for leakage patterns, flags them, and suggests fixes. The paper reviews how training, tuning, and test data should stay separate. The plug-in is open source, aimed at helping engineers write cleaner learning code.
arxiv-2503-15023:
Chaouki Boufenar and three co-authors blend two AI styles to read handwritten Arabic in a 2025 paper. Arabic script shifts shape by where a letter sits in a word, which makes machine reading hard. Their blend pairs a convolutional network, strong on local strokes, with a transformer, strong on context across the whole word.

They tested custom and tuned models, then fused the best two by trust scores. The fused model read letters at over ninety six percent accuracy on a known data set. Place in word calls ran even higher. The authors say the two styles cover each other's blind spots. They offer the blend as a base for real world Arabic text tools.
arxiv-2503-15123:
Paul Kiefer extends a special class of modular forms to broader symmetry groups in a paper from 2025. Harmonic Maass forms blend modular symmetry with smooth growth conditions. The catalog title carries funding text, but the head title is clean, and the description follows the head. Kiefer defines local and polar versions for orthogonal groups of a general signature. Singularities are allowed along analytic and algebraic cycles.

He proves a current equation for the local forms. The theory recovers the Fourier expansion of a classical lift built from cycle integrals. Polar forms then show that certain singular meromorphic forms are orthogonal to cusp forms under a regularized inner product. A duality theorem links the two kinds of cycle integrals.
arxiv-2503-15323: The Euclid Collaboration issued this paper in 2025 as part of the Euclid space telescope's first quick data release. Its stated aim is to extend the hunt for little red dots to lower redshifts than past searches covered. Little red dots are a class of small, red, distant galaxies. The search reaches down to a redshift of four. The text in hand carries the title, the release framing, and the collaboration's long author list, with the report body beyond the preserved portion.
arxiv-2503-15723:
Daniel Lee, Francisco Pernice, Amit Rajaraman, and Ilias Zadik study a basic limit in network data analysis. A hidden shape, a planted subgraph, is buried inside a random graph full of noise. The question is how well anyone could recover the planted shape, even with the best possible method.

The authors focus on the minimum mean squared error as graphs grow large. Earlier work covered only cases where recovery jumps sharply from hopeless to perfect. Here they give a formula for the full error curve for any planted graph, written as an optimization over pairs of its subgraphs. They also show the best choices can be described fast enough to compute. The result extends to planted yes-no properties in random noise.
arxiv-2503-15823:
Matheus Reis, José Carvalho, and Pedro Aguiar gave a unified stability analysis in 2025 for safety-critical control with several barrier functions. Keeping a system both alive and safe is hard when many safety constraints apply at once. Safety filters based on quadratic programs are a common solution, but their stability traits needed firmer theory.

The authors derive conditions that ensure such programs stay feasible with multiple barrier functions. They characterise when unwanted equilibrium points arise where safe set borders meet. A new stability criterion then shows when those points can be destabilised or removed. The work extends prior theory for both safety filters and combined Lyapunov-barrier controllers.
arxiv-2503-16223:
Laurine Martinien and co-authors model how the view angle and the spot of reading change the ice bands seen in planet-forming disks. Their 2025 paper uses the James Webb Space Telescope's new reach as its backdrop. Water ice helps grains clump into planets, yet where it sits in these disks is poorly mapped.

With a transfer code, the team built a standard disk around a young star and pulled spectra from many spots in it. Even with one even mix of ice, the band's depth and center shifted with the tilt of the disk and the place read. The center could move by as much as the gap between two ice forms, glassy and crystal. The cause is a balance of light soaked up and light scattered, which modelers must heed.
arxiv-2503-16323:
Wing shapes live or die by the lift and drag they make, and the classic tool to score them is slow. Peter Sharpe and Hansman present a learning-based tool in 2025 that does the same job far faster. Their open Python tool posts speed gains from eight times to a thousand times over the classic one, at matched accuracy.

It scores both whole-wing values and local ones, such as the speed of air along the skin. Its range is wide: an eighteen-part shape space, a full circle of attack angles, and flow speeds that span eight orders of size. Drag scores err by well under one percent on plain cases. The smooth output suits design work that climbs by small steps. The tool blends physics rules into its learning, which keeps it true off the training path.
arxiv-2503-17023:
Eleonora Maggiorelli, Filippo Riva, and Edoardo Tolotti recast in 2025 the slow peeling of a glued membrane as a moving boundary problem. Debonding creeps rather than snaps, and earlier math handled it in awkward set based language. Their trick leans on a classic free boundary problem for steady shapes.

Working with functions instead of sets, the standard step by step energy scheme runs cleanly. The debonded zone is still tracked at each step, since peeling cannot heal. Energetic solutions with a true energy balance exist in the natural class of shapes, they prove. The proof both extends and simplifies past results.
arxiv-2503-17623:
Methusela Sulle and co-authors use explainable AI to find what kills pedestrians on American roads. Walkers die at high rates in crashes, lacking the shell that protects drivers. The team took federal crash records from 2018 to 2022 and compared the five states with the most pedestrian deaths against the five with the fewest.

Four learning methods competed at sorting fatal from nonfatal crashes, with oversampling to balance the rare deaths. XGBoost won, and SHAP values showed its reasoning in the open. Age, alcohol and drug use, place, and light conditions led its list of predictors. Deaths clustered at mid-block crossings and in poor visibility, with older adults and impaired walkers at the highest risk. The authors urge better lighting and crossings where the data point.
arxiv-2503-17823:
Zeyu Jia, Yury Polyanskiy, and Alexander Rakhlin study, in 2025, how well probabilities can be assigned step by step as outcomes arrive. The cost of each guess is measured by logarithmic loss, and the benchmark is minimax regret: the gap between the best sequential strategy and the best hindsight choice. They tie that gap to geometric measures of the model class.

Without side information, regret is bounded by a new entropy notion built on the square-root scale, close to the Hellinger distance. With side information, matching upper and lower bounds emerge for well-behaved classes. The results give forecasters a geometric yardstick for sequential prediction.
arxiv-2503-17923:
Shu-Min Wu and colleagues ask what a black hole does to the shared quantum links among many particles, using a dilaton black hole from string-inspired gravity as the stage. Nonseparability is their yardstick for entanglement, measured with a generalized conditional entropy for bosonic and fermionic fields hovering near the hole. Hawking radiation acts as noise on the states. Writing in twenty twenty-five, the team tracks two famous state families, the fully-linked GHZ type and the more democratic W type, as the hole's influence strengthens.

One surprise: for fermions, the Hawking effect can actually create net nonseparability in a W state rather than only destroying it. Fermionic links also proved hardier than bosonic ones, though fermionic coherence faded faster. GHZ states showed stronger nonseparability but weaker coherence than W states. The authors advise matching particle type and state shape to the relativistic quantum task at hand.
arxiv-2503-18023:
Raghul Parthipan and co-authors present a climate modeling paper, published in 2025, on a simple trick that helps machine learning models of Earth systems generalize. Regularization keeps a model from trusting its training data too much. The authors show that training with longer time steps between snapshots has this effect for free in chaotic systems, because similar starting states drift toward different outcomes.

The team explains why the trick works and gives a way to pick a step length. In tests on ocean data, a step of about four weeks gave realistic simulations, longer than the steps in common use. They argue many Earth system problems can gain from so easy a change.
arxiv-2503-18423:
Golovko and five co-authors present a tunable magnetooptical metasurface in a 2025 paper. The surface produces Faraday rotation, where the polarization of light turns as it passes through. In most such devices, the size and sign of the turn are fixed once the device is made.

Here, heating the surface changes the rotation over a wide range. The team show both in tests and in theory that the angle grows near certain resonances. At a fixed wavelength, warming shifted the angle from negative to positive values. A control laser could heat small spots, so the rotation could be set locally across the surface.
arxiv-2503-18623:
Deepayan Das, Davide Talon, Yiming Wang, Massimiliano Mancini, and Elisa Ricci personalize vision models with no training in a 2025 paper. Vision language models struggle with concepts tied to one user, such as a specific pet or object. Past fixes need costly training runs. Their method works from the model's own knowledge at query time.

First the model lists key traits that define the concept, its fingerprint. Matching fingerprints are retrieved and scored with step-by-step reasoning. A cross-modal check then verifies each trait against the image, and mismatches trigger a direct pair comparison. Tests on two public sets and one new tricky set beat prior methods, they report.
arxiv-2503-18823:
Big networks can be shrunk for study, but the shrinking should keep the network's walking dynamics intact. Erik Hormann and Renaud Lambiotte introduce a tool for that job in this 2025 paper. They call it ergodic sets: groups of nodes a random walk can neither enter nor leave, once placed by the network's arrows. The notion turns out to rest on network structure alone.

The authors first pin down basic properties of these sets, then hunt for them in synthetic networks and real ones from many fields. Finding such sets lets them compress a directed network while keeping how walkers diffuse through it. The method promises faster work on huge directed systems, from traffic to web graphs, without lying about their flow.
arxiv-2503-19023:
Daisuke Fujii, Akihiro Iwanaka, Masakiyo Kitazawa, and Daiki Suenaga study heat behavior in a pure gauge theory in a 2025 paper. The theory is SU(3) Yang-Mills theory, a base model of the strong force. They place it on a space with two wrapped directions and two open ones. A model that mimics the theory lets them map its phases.

Their model treats loop values along the wrapped paths as free parts. It is tuned to match large grid simulations of the real theory. The map shows a new sharp phase shift inside the free phase. That shift ends at critical points of a known broad class. The cause is a cross-talk term between the two loop values.
arxiv-2503-19123:
Haebin Shin and co-authors bridged mismatched vocabularies in model teaching in two thousand twenty-five. Big teacher models often tokenize text differently from students. The mismatch scrambles sequences and output scores. Their method aligns tokens across the two vocabularies. A second signal borrows the teacher's own loss values. Together they let unlike models teach cleanly.

A one-billion-parameter student learned from several larger teachers. Each teacher used a different vocabulary scheme. Math-tuned teachers were among the test set. The student improved despite the token gap. Vocabulary freedom widens teacher choice for small models. Labs can pair the best teacher with any student. Distillation pipelines lose a stubborn constraint.
arxiv-2503-19223:
Najeebullah, Maaz Salman, and Zar Nawab Khan Swati test deep learning models that spot fake faces. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-five. Face spoofing is a threat to systems that use a face to prove who you are. A photo or screen can fool a weak check, so a strong spoof guard is key.

They train three vision models on a large set of face images, split for training, testing, and a final check. A light model, MobileNetV2, beats a larger ResNet and a vision transformer on the test set. It also leads on the check set and learns faster. Both top models show some overfit, but the light one holds up best on new data.
arxiv-2503-19323:
Trevor Karn and Victor Reiner study, in 2025, symmetry in algebras that mix ordinary and anticommuting variables. A finite group acts on the variables, and the invariant part counts what stays fixed. The counting series for those invariants turns out to hold a surprise about bigger wreath product groups built from it.

Knowing the series for the base group determines the series for the wreath product acting on many copies, for any choice of permutation part. Stacking all those invariant algebras together forms a graded ring whose structure is again a superpolynomial algebra, generated by the original invariants. A parallel result covers the anti-invariant side with a signed product.
arxiv-2503-19523:
Methods for teaching language models from human feedback split into two camps: those using reinforcement learning and those skipping it. Xin Cai argued in 2025 that the split is an illusion, uniting both under one framework.

Cai re-reads the rival methods as forms of structured bandit prediction, then re-derives the standard feedback objective inside a full reinforcement learning picture. The two views prove equivalent. Studying a popular optimization algorithm exposes spots needing adjustment. From those fixes Cai builds a generalized framework that holds both camps at once. The paper invites the community to test the unified approach in practice.
arxiv-2503-19723:
Ritish Khetarpal and Aradhana Singh study how city street networks get their shape. Their paper, from twenty twenty-five, looks at thirty-three Indian cities. Streets cannot cross at random or stack on each other, since they sit in real space. That flat layout sets hard rules for how the network can link up.

All the cities show small-world traits, with tight local links and short trips across town. Real networks beat shuffled copies at moving people and goods. Short streets tend to join short streets, and long join long. Flat copies that keep true street spots copy this trait well. The lesson is that place, not just chance, shapes street form.
arxiv-2503-19823:
Yan Zhuang and nine co-authors present a 2025 paper on splitting a network of brain folds into natural subgroups. The folds of the brain's surface form patterns that act as hubs for links between regions. One landmark, where three folds meet, anchors a network model of the whole surface.

Past tools struggled with the tiny scale of these landmarks and with matching them across people. The team built a method that can be trained end to end to split the network into subgroups. The split aims to keep each group tight inside and sparse between groups. Their approach treats the folds as a community, not as lone points.
arxiv-2503-20023:
The CMS Collaboration searches for signs of leptoquarks in the highest-energy electron and muon pairs from the Large Hadron Collider, in a paper from 2025. Leptoquarks would link quarks and leptons, two families now kept apart. Rather than being made directly, they might flash into existence virtually, bending the pair spectra through t-channel exchange.

The team used 138 inverse femtobarns of proton collisions at 13 tera-electronvolts, looking above 500 giga-electronvolts of pair mass. Eight coupling scenarios were tested, pairing up or down quarks with electrons or muons through scalar or vector leptoquarks. No clear signal rose above the modeled backgrounds. The team set strict limits on coupling strength for leptoquark masses from one to five tera-electronvolts, tightening the net on first- and second-generation versions.
arxiv-2503-20223:
Jordan Hong, Safwan Jamal, and Ashish Khisti study secure wireless links in a 2025 paper. Artificial noise can jam eavesdroppers while sparing intended users. The noise is beamed into directions that cancel at the right receivers.

Real analog hardware allows only phase control, with fixed signal strength. Nulling several users at once under that limit is the hard problem. Their scheme splits the task step by step across channel groups. Partition choices are tuned to cut outage probability. A single radio chain keeps the design cheap. Readers learn how strong secrecy can survive simple hardware limits.
arxiv-2503-20623:
Alessandro Maisto, a solo author, analyzes the language of model-generated role-playing games in a 2025 paper. In such games, players build a story together through talk, mostly spoken. Using a language model as a player is a growing research theme. He asks whether text a model generates alone, with no human in the loop, reads as oral or written in its word and sentence patterns.

He compared the generated sessions with conversations, human game transcripts, and books. The model's language formed a pattern distinct from all three. Training seems to shape how the models express themselves in a class of their own. The findings inform claims about the narrative skill of these tools.
arxiv-2503-21023:
The authors present a framework for choosing data mixtures in language model training in a 2025 paper. The mix of data sources shapes how well a model performs, yet choices often rest on intuition or costly trial and error. Scaling laws can help, but stretching small test results to large runs rests on brittle assumptions.

Their framework treats curation as a step by step decision problem. A Bayesian method weighs data mix, model size, and training length together, using cheap small runs to inform costly large ones while tracking uncertainty. A simulator is offered to speed work on such methods.
arxiv-2503-21223:
Zhihan Zhang and co-authors rethink graph structure learning with large language models in a 2025 paper. Many real graphs carry text on their nodes, and learning which links should exist helps tasks from citation mapping to recommendations. Older methods ignore the text, while tuning a huge language model for link guessing is costly and awkward.

Their framework turns the task into growing a tree. An entropy guided sampler builds encoding trees that capture the graph's shape. The language model then reads along the tree with in context learning, folding text meaning in without any fine tuning. Tests on eleven data sets show the method works with any backbone and scales past rival language model approaches.
arxiv-2503-21523:
Dorian Martino, Katarzyna Mazowiecka, and Rémy Rodiac prove an exact energy accounting for sequences of almost-harmonic maps that touch a sphere's boundary freely, in a paper published in two thousand twenty-five. Harmonic maps minimize a kind of stretching energy, and their higher-power cousins, the (n+alpha)-harmonic maps, approach them as the parameter alpha shrinks to zero.

Such sequences can bubble: energy concentrates at points and splits off into separate spherical maps. The authors show the sequence converges to a bubble tree, a macroscopic limit map decorated with these bubbles. Their weak energy identity says the limiting energy equals the limit map's energy plus each bubble's energy, weighted by a coefficient. No energy hides in the necks between pieces. Energy identities are the bookkeeping that makes compactness arguments in geometric analysis work. Free boundary problems model liquid crystals and membranes pinned only loosely to a frame.
arxiv-2503-21623:
Paweł Hatka, Marcel Garczyk, and four co-authors measure how smart reflecting panels bounce radio waves in real rooms. Their paper, from twenty twenty-five, supports codebook design for reconfigurable intelligent surfaces. Such panels steer each element's reflection to shape coverage. Lab promises need field proof before networks can rely on them.

The team varies angle, polarization, panel count, and distance. Measured reflection patterns fill out the picture factor by factor. A codebook is a fixed menu of panel patterns for quick selection. Their data ground which menu entries are realistic. Practical deployment, not just theory, drives the analysis.
arxiv-2503-21923:
Meng Wu proves sharper results about projecting fractal measures in a 2025 math paper. Projecting a flat pattern onto a line can shrink its measured size in bad directions. The key question is how many bad directions can occur.

Wu shows the bad set is at most countable in two broad settings: families of self-similar measures that meet a crossing condition, and a class of distributions built from conditional probabilities. The bounds are best possible. Uses follow for the packing size of projections of general flat measures and for the roughest size measure of projected sets. The results also feed a known puzzle on exact overlaps in fractal constructions.
arxiv-2503-22323:
Toshihisa Kubo and Bent Ørsted wrote this math paper in two thousand twenty-five. It sorts and builds the intertwining differential operators between vector bundles over the real projective plane.

Two kinds of operators show up, which the authors name Cartan operators and PRV operators. The second half studies the representations that live on the kernels of these operators. Both smooth and holomorphic settings are covered. A key tool is the BGG resolution. With past results in hand, the authors sort a set of unitary highest weight modules of a kin group at its first reduction points. The sort runs by the image of one kind and the kernel of the other.
arxiv-2503-22423:
Esteban Gómez-López and co-authors store light pulses in printed micro cages in a 2025 paper. Quantum networks need memories that can hold photons briefly in place. Hot atomic vapor can stall light for long stretches in principle. Hollow fibers guiding that light are bulky and hard to scale up.

Their cage guides are printed in three dimensions at tiny size. Several cages sat on one chip inside a cesium vapor cell. All stored weak light pulses for hundreds of nanoseconds consistently across devices. The work points toward many parallel memories on a single chip.
arxiv-2503-22623:
Shiva Gaur and seven co-authors find a giant spin pumping effect at the face where a glass-like polymer meets a magnet film. Flexible devices love such faces, yet spin work there was thin. Their 2025 study stacks the polymer, HSQ, at three widths on nickel-iron films at four widths. A resonance test reads how wide the resonance line grows, the tell of spin flow.

The line grew wide, and the mixing grade hit 19.8 per square unit at the thick stack, a match for heavy metals. Spin thus crosses the soft-hard face with ease. A twin pumping of spin and orbital flow may drive it, they hold. Self-powered and bend-fitting spin devices are the aim the find feeds.
arxiv-2503-22823:
Ian George and co-authors develop quantum Doeblin coefficients in this 2025 paper. In classical theory, the Doeblin coefficient bounds how fast a channel shrinks differences between inputs. It yields strong data processing inequalities and is easy to compute. Quantum channels need their own version of the tool.

Several quantum definitions are introduced and compared. One stands out with concatenation and multiplicativity properties plus easy computation. The authors reinterpret two coefficients in many ways, as singlet fractions, exclusion values, and robustness measures. The exclusion reading is striking, since it ties the number to best error rates in state exclusion tasks. Uses range from limits on quantum communication to channel comparison. A classical shortcut gains a rich quantum life.
arxiv-2503-22923:
Yang, Zhou, and Lu present an algorithm for robust optimization under data shift in twenty twenty-five. Robust optimization trains models that hold up when data patterns change. The uncertainty set here is defined by a generalized Sinkhorn distance between distributions. The loss can be nonconvex and even unbounded, which makes the problem hard.

The authors derive a dual form of the problem as nested stochastic optimization. In that form, the dual variable depends on each data sample. Their nested stochastic gradient method estimates the nested gradients by stochastic approximation. They prove polynomial bounds on iterations and samples that do not grow with data size or dimension. Numeric tests show the method is efficient and robust. The work targets large scale robust learning problems.
arxiv-2503-23023:
Shoji Hashimoto, in a 2025 paper, lays out a strategy for computing inclusive hadronic processes with lattice QCD, and weighs what stands in its way. Inclusive rates, such as total decay or scattering rates, are hard to get from lattice calculations, which naturally produce data at discrete points in Euclidean time. The key idea is to treat the wanted rate as a smeared spectrum and rebuild it from the time behavior of correlators measured on the lattice.

The catch is that the smoothing adds its own systematic errors on top of the usual lattice effects. Hashimoto argues those errors must be estimated with rigor before the method can deliver true first-principles results. The paper frames both the promise of this new class of quantities and the care needed to trust them.
arxiv-2503-23223:
Water rushing through a pipe forms streaks of slow flow near the wall, each flanked by a pair of swirling rolls. Moriconi and Saisse model those streaks in 2025 as particles on a grid that cannot overlap, borrowing tools from the physics of gases and magnets. A random walk method then lets the pattern shift and settle over time.

Their two setting model reproduces how often the streaks appear and the repeating pattern they form along the pipe. That match supports a wider idea: that steady turbulence can be read as a chain of clear states rather than one blur. The authors say such simple models can guide how wall flows are understood and forecast.
arxiv-2503-23423:
Fractal sets built from families of shrinking maps appear across geometry, and a graph can direct which maps may follow which. Kazuki Okamura, writing alone in 2025, built such graph-directed invariant sets in a looser setting than usual. He used weak contractions, in a sense defined by earlier authors, acting on semi-metric spaces where distance rules are relaxed.

The construction follows a recent approach that measures how far a set is from being compact, rather than leaning on a classic completeness theorem. Okamura also ties the construction to a generalized form of de Rham's functional equation, indexed by a finite directed graph. The work widens where these fractal constructions can be carried out.
arxiv-2503-23523:
Haochen Liu and co-authors teach language models to consult a knowledge graph with the actual question in mind, in this 2025 paper. Big language models stumble on questions whose answers live outside their training text. Knowledge graphs can supply the facts, but bolting them on usually means costly retraining or noisy retrieval. Recent methods compress graph facts into soft prompts, yet they ignore which facts the question needs.

Their method, QAP, builds the prompt around the question itself, so relevant facts lead and clutter stays out. A second snag gets attention too: for multiple-choice questions, some answer options may have no graph facts at all, and the system must handle that gap gracefully. Sharper prompts mean better answers without retraining the model underneath.
arxiv-2503-23623:
Zahra TehraniNasab, Amar Kumar, and Tal Arbel steer a text-to-image model through its own latent space to edit medical images factor by factor, in a 2025 paper. Diffusion models make striking pictures from words, but separating one trait, anatomy say, from another, disease signs, is unproven in medicine. The team fine-tuned vision-language models on chest X-rays and skin photos.

The tuned models had quietly learned to factor the key traits apart. The authors built paths through latent space that slide one trait while holding the rest, enabling clean interpolations. Such control supports explaining disease and probing cause in synthetic cohorts. Extensive tests on both datasets back the claim that language guidance does the disentangling.
arxiv-2503-23723:
Georgios Korpas, Vyacheslav Kungurtsev, and Jakub Mareček study undecidable problems for variational quantum algorithms in two thousand twenty-five. Such algorithms are top bets for near term quantum gain. Past work showed their training is NP-hard in general. The team asks if it may be worse than hard: impossible to decide at all.

They reduce a digitized training question to a Diophantine root question. Matrix exponentials encode that equation inside a quantum circuit. The result rests on a stated conjecture about a system of equations. They back it with dimension counts and generic solvability in geometry. An unconditional result covers open quantum systems as well.
arxiv-2503-23823:
Devices that learn together without pooling private data need a referee everyone trusts. Farhana Javed and co-authors argue in this 2025 paper that a blockchain can be that referee for federated learning in the Internet of Things. Their framework replaces the central server with a ledger, tracks each device's reputation, and stores only selected model updates on chain.

The paper surveys the standards bodies already steering this merger, from telecom to engineering groups. A test run on the IOTA Tangle ledger kept throughput and confirmations steady as learning loads grew. The authors map design choices for squeezing the scheme into future 6G networks. Trust and energy use, they say, are the twin tests such systems must pass.
arxiv-2503-23923:
Michael Timothy Bennett offers a short, sharp overview of artificial general intelligence in this 2025 paper. The term AGI is now clouded by hype and dueling claims. Some ask whether it still means anything at all.

Bennett compares definitions of intelligence and lands on adaptation as the core. AGI, in that frame, is an artificial scientist: a system that learns and tests ideas. He builds the account on two tools, search and approximation. Several well-known systems are compared as hybrids of those tools. The paper is written to be read quickly and argued with. It gives newcomers a clear stance rather than a fog of terms.
arxiv-2503-24023:
Andrin Doll and four co-authors showed clean control of a coupled electron and muon center. Their paper, from twenty twenty-five, deals with muonium, a light kin of hydrogen made of an electron bound to a muon. Control by tuned pulses is the key to use such quantum systems for probes and tech. The team used microwaves to drive spin flips in lone muonium centers. They showed the base moves: driven Rabi swings and Ramsey fringes in free flight.

Their kit reached a new level of care, with near undamped free spin signals over a span of microseconds in silica. Readers in quantum sensing get a sharper handle on a short lived but clean probe atom.
arxiv-2503-24123:
Seewon Choi and co-authors introduce, in a 2025 paper, a faster training method for systems that pair neural networks with symbolic programs. Such neurosymbolic systems learn from input-output labels of the whole pipeline. Training them end to end grows painfully slow as programs grow.

Their method, CTSketch, splits the symbolic program into sub-programs. Each sub-program is summarized by a compressed tensor sketch. Simple tensor operations over the inputs and sketches then approximate the program's output spread. The authors bound the worst approximation error in theory. Benchmarks from the field test the speed gains. Scaling neurosymbolic learning matters because the hybrid approach promises reasoning that pure networks lack.
arxiv-2503-24223:
Riccardo Borsato and Miguel García Fernández build a deformed version of a spin chain in this 2025 paper. The catalog title is cut short and its creator field is garbled, so the head title and byline govern here. The base chain is non-compact and tied to a symmetry group. It also links to a sector of a well-known gauge theory.

They apply a twist of Jordanian type to deform the chain. The result stays integrable, but its energy operator is not hermitian and cannot be split into simple parts. Its energy values still match the undeformed chain. The authors build the states two ways and show the model equals an undeformed chain with twisted edge rules.
arxiv-2504-00023:
Niklas Rottmayer and Claudia Redenbach introduce a 2025 metric for judging how well an image has been split into parts. Most scores count wrong pixels but ignore where the errors sit, and older distance scores are hard to read across datasets. Their Surface Consistency Coefficient weighs errors by how close they lie to the edge of a shape.

Tests on made-up data and on real split results show the score tells apart edge errors from far-off ones in a steady way. It stays easy to read and to compare across shapes and tasks. The authors offer it as a fairer yardstick for split methods.
arxiv-2504-00323:
Boris Faleichik and Andrew Moisa present a 2025 family of fast methods for solving mildly stiff equations. Such equations mix slow and fast change, and plain steppers need tiny steps to stay stable. Classic stabilized methods stretch the stable step range with polynomial tricks. The team adds one more demand on top of speed and accuracy.

Their methods must have a stability curve that rises smoothly and stays positive over the longest stretch they can manage. That demand shrinks the stable range a bit below classic methods. In trade, the curves track the true growth curve more closely and error terms shrink. Tests show the new methods rival other second-order stabilized methods in real use.
arxiv-2504-00523:
Claudia Klüppelberg and Mario Krali review how extreme losses cascade through a network of connected portfolios, with causality built in, in a 2025 paper. Their vehicle is a max-linear structural model: each node's value is the largest weighted contribution from its parents in a directed graph, plus its own shock. The maximum operation suits extremes, where the biggest driver dominates.

The paper gathers results on learning such a graph from data and estimating its weights, then applies them to financial industry portfolios. A new estimation method, based on hard thresholding and a distance between graphs, recovers a sparse network of extreme risk propagation. The aim is practical: regulators and risk managers need to know which sectors transmit crashes to which others, not merely that markets fall together.
arxiv-2504-00623:
Kazuki Yano and co-authors published a 2025 paper on building a family of language models for a quarter less compute. Vendors offer models in many sizes, from small to huge, to fit different budgets. Training each size from scratch repeats most of the work. The authors instead grow models: train a small one, expand it, and keep training, step by step up the size ladder.

Across a family from one to eight billion parameters, the grown models matched the quality of separately trained ones. Total computing cost fell by about twenty-five percent. The schedule of when to expand matters, and tuning the largest size's training rate added further gains. The method reframes model families as one long training run with growth spurts. For labs that ship several sizes, the savings are real money and energy. The paper adds evidence that big models need not start big.
arxiv-2504-00723:
Garcia and Riveros frame a strict form for spot of tied acts in timed streams. Tied-act spot, called CER, reads streams for acts that span more steps. Time caps add strain to what such spot can catch in streams. Their tongue, timed CEL, adds plain time marks to a base tongue. That tongue can mock real CER tongues in use for tests. It serves as a stand-in to gauge how much they can say.

A bot frame, timed CEA, pairs with the tongue in the work. It fuses past CEA bots with timed bots in one frame. Tongue and frame match in what they can say, they show. That match is the first of its kind for timed CER. A class of such bots stays shut when made firm in form. Stream checks for that class run at fixed step cost.
arxiv-2504-01423:
Yichen Sun and co-authors built in 2025 a language-model system that sets live incentives for smart car charging. Vehicle-to-grid flow can shave grid peaks if drivers play along, but their choices are hard to foresee. The team built digital twins of users from rich profiles, driven by a multi-agent language-model frame. The twins mimic how each user picks charge and discharge moves.

A live incentive scheme, fed by data and know-how, tunes rewards under network limits while keeping costs and safety in bounds. Simulations showed better peak-valley balance, happier users, and a steadier grid. The team pitches the tool as a scalable way for grid managers to run vehicle-grid programs.
arxiv-2504-01823:
The BESIII Collaboration reports first evidence for a rare particle decay, in a 2025 paper. The catalog creator field lists hundreds of names with stray affiliation numbers, but the text makes clear the work belongs to the full collaboration. The decay starts from a particle that sheds a photon and turns into a second particle. That particle then splits into two further particles, a pairing that standard rules say should be suppressed twice over.

The team searched a vast sample of the parent particle's events, gathered with the BESIII detector at a collider in Beijing. In that sample they found the first evidence for the suppressed decay. Rare decays of this kind test the rules that govern how quarks behave inside particles. A confirmed rate gives theory a hard number to match, and it sharpens the map of how this particle family breaks apart.
arxiv-2504-02523:
Balázs Pál and László Dobos test whether a U-Net network can clean noisy spectra of stars taken at medium sharpness. Their paper appeared in two thousand twenty-five. Star spectra carry the clues to a star's heat, makeup, and motion. Noise from real observing buries some of those clues.

They trained the network on fake spectra made to match a large telescope spectrograph in Japan. The training set was small, just a thousand cases, and training was short. Even so, the cleaned spectra landed within about one percent of the truth across many star types. A rival design trained in the same tight way did worse. Heavily trained dense networks still won overall, though. The authors see U-Net as a fast first pass before slower, finer cleaning.
arxiv-2504-02623:
Yu and co-authors launch a bench that tests chat aides on chained, shifting tasks. Chat aides call tools well, with strong sense and plan skills. Users now lean on them for hard tasks in step talks. Past benches test aides on lone tasks, which misses real strain. Their bench chains tasks that tie to each other in one case. Aides must bend as task needs shift mid-case in the bench.

All swap shapes for a fixed task count get probed there. A crew of aides builds the bench cases by a set frame. Score ways use shift trees to grade pick truth and pace. Tests span free and paid chat tools in the aide role. Finds flag what sways aide firmness in chained work. Those flags give tool-build crews clear next steps.
arxiv-2504-02823:
Divya Velayudhan and co-authors built a vision-language system in 2025 for X-ray baggage screening. Current data sets poorly reflect real, well-hidden threats, and older systems only pick from fixed label lists. The team aimed for an assistant that can describe and locate threats in words.

They created the first image-caption data set for this task, with over forty-six thousand paired scans across twenty-one threat classes. The scans came from a real airport scanner, with expert caption rules. Training on it produced STING-BEE, an assistant handling scene description, threat localisation, grounding, and question answering. It set new baselines for the field and generalised well to other domains in tests.
arxiv-2504-03023:
Lucas Huysmans and Ayman Rimah Said prove a precise mixing bound in a 2025 paper on fluid transport. A passive substance, like dye, is carried along by a flow field that neither creates nor destroys volume. The question is how fast the dye evens out.

Their flow fields are rough: they have bounded variation rather than smooth derivatives. By turning a known smoothing scheme into a quantitative tool, the authors derive the first explicit bounds on the mixing rate for this whole class. A surprise appears in the rate: tetration, the operation of stacking exponents into a tower, emerges naturally. It traces back to the local character of the smoothing argument.
arxiv-2504-03223:
Gu and a large team of co-authors report X-ray observations of a supernova remnant in this two thousand twenty-five paper. The remnant, N132D in the Large Magellanic Cloud, is the brightest of its kind in X-rays, and the new XRISM telescope observed it early in its mission.

Using a high-resolution spectrometer, the team searched for signs of charge exchange, where hot ions steal electrons from cold gas and glow in a distinctive way. Adding this process to their models improved the fit at two faint features, with a combined confidence of ninety-nine point six percent. They capped charge exchange at four percent of the light in the studied band. The result supports ongoing clashes between the remnant's shock and nearby clouds.
arxiv-2504-03723:
Yangbo Wei and co-authors let an algorithm design its own chip-design workflow in a 2025 computing paper. Writing Verilog hardware code with language models works better when several model calls are chained, but hand-built chains vary in quality. Their framework, VFlow, treats the workflow as a graph to be searched. An evolution-guided tree search balances correctness, chip area, power, timing, and token cost at once, sharing winning patterns between populations.

Multi-level checks verify syntax, function, and whether the code can be built as a chip. On two benchmarks, success rates rose twenty to thirty percent over prompt baselines, nearing human designer quality on area and power. Small models inside a smart workflow even beat large models working alone.
arxiv-2504-03823:
Virilo Tejedor and five co-authors warn, in 2025 work, that a language model can be turned into a self-spreading virus by tainted fine-tuning. They built such a case from a known open model, tuned into a coding aide. The tuned weights hide a theft payload that wakes under set cues.

When the aide writes training code, the payload rides along, so fresh models trained on that code pick up the flaw in turn. In tests the tainted aide still coded well, which kept the flaw masked while it spread. The team names the case after the famed wooden horse of myth. They urge strict checks and watch over how models are trained and shared, since open weights can carry hidden harm.
arxiv-2504-04023:
Rajasekhar Anguluri and Abdullah Al Maruf design controllers that hide parts of a power grid dynamics from watchers. Their twenty twenty-five paper builds on feedback schemes that block observability of remote nodes. The motive is cyber defense: an attacker who can read grid modes can fake them to fool operators.

Two targets are blocked here. One is mode participation factors, which say how much each machine joins each swing mode. The other is inter-area mode traces in tie-line power flows. Since participation turns on both input and output shapes, past methods needed careful tailoring. Tests on a small nine-bus and a large sixty-eight-bus system show the shields at work.
arxiv-2504-04123:
Fabian Medina Cuy and Fabrizio Dolcini study a one-dimensional superconductor model under current flow, in a 2025 paper. Passing current through the chain twists its pairing pattern with a steady wave. That twist can push the system across two very different borders: one changes its band topology, the other reshapes its surface of occupied states and leaves it gapless.

The authors track two basic quantities across both borders: how many electrons the chain holds and how easily that count changes, its compressibility. The density map alone reveals the full phase diagram. The compressibility tells the borders apart, swelling evenly at one and jumping unevenly at the other. Such simple measures could let experiments read exotic phase changes without exotic probes.
arxiv-2504-04523:
Levente Baljer and co-authors present GAMBAS in 2025, a system that sharpens children's brain scans from low-field MRI machines. Standard MRI is vital for studying child brain development, but high-field scanners cost too much for many low- and middle-income countries. Ultra-low-field machines are affordable and portable, yet their images are coarse.

Their method upsamples those coarse scans to near high-field detail. It uses a sequence model design and a generalized Hilbert ordering to scan the image in a brain-aware path. Better images from cheap scanners could open developmental research and care in places now excluded. The work is a step toward fair access to neuroimaging science.
arxiv-2504-04723:
Ram Krishna Patra, Kunika Agarwal, and four peers weigh two ways to pair spins. The work came out in 2025. They ask which pair best lets you gauge things that clash with each other. In quantum work, some pairs of traits can not be gauged at once on one system.

Here the twist is to gauge traits across a set of spin pairs. In one setup, both spins in each pair point the same way. In the flipped setup, the second spin is the twin of the first, turned round. The team shows the flipped pairs do what same-way pairs can not. They let you call all three spin parts at right angles with no error. The team extends the work to more gauges and more pair types. The finds link to a past-guess puzzle and to a code-based pact for safe notes.
arxiv-2504-04923:
Mohamed Ben Alaya and co-authors design guaranteed estimators for an interest-rate model in a 2025 paper. The Cox-Ingersoll-Ross process models rates that wander but pull back toward a level. Estimating its drift from a limited watch is the task. Their truncated sequential method samples until it can promise a set accuracy, then stops, rather than always using the full watch.

For both one- and two-parameter versions, the mean-square error guarantee holds at any sample size, not just in the limit. As the allowed time grows, the procedures prove optimal among all methods using less average time. They also reach maximum-likelihood quality in far less observing time. Shorter data collection with the same trust is the prize.
arxiv-2504-05023:
Ranjith Kumar and Hideaki Obuse show that quantum walks can simulate topological transitions between gapless phases of matter. Fermion chains with extended couplings show such transitions at multicritical points, a topic of growing interest. Quantum walks offer a controllable platform to mimic that physics in the lab.

Using a three step discrete time walk, the authors map out critical and gapless phases and their energy patterns. A curvature function captures the transition, with divergence and sign flips like those in fermion chains. Renormalization flow and state correlation checks confirm the transitions at multicritical points. Group velocity of energy states helps classify each transition type. Scaling laws from the chain models reappear in the walk.
arxiv-2504-05223:
Torben Schiz and Henrik Ebel tackle a data bottleneck in robot teams that plan their moves together, in a 2025 paper. Each robot shares its planned path with the others, and long plans mean heavy traffic on the wireless link. Cutting the plan short hurts control quality and can break stability promises. The pair instead squeeze the data itself before sending it.

A learning tool called an autoencoder compresses each plan for sending and rebuilds it on arrival. The structure inside control data makes that squeeze work well. Tests used a team of small wheeled robots holding a formation, a hard case for this control style. Compressed plans kept control accuracy high and beat the short-plan shortcut. Trials on real embedded hardware with real wireless links also worked, in cases where full data transfer failed.
arxiv-2504-05523:
Historians of language slice the past into periods, but a model trained on all eras at once can smear those borders. Elisabeth Fittschen and co-authors argue that only pretraining on time-bounded text truly guarantees a model knows one era. They built a date-attribution pipeline that cut a corpus into five slices of ten million words each, then trained two model families on the slices.

The small pretrained models trained faster than fine-tuned large ones and respected the era boundaries better. Put to work, they detected waves of vocabulary change, shifts in grammar, and words gaining or losing senses, a toolkit for testing claims about how English changed.
arxiv-2504-06023:
Yihao Zhao and Zhonghan Hu unify the math of charged systems in boxes that repeat forever in a 2025 paper. Simulations of liquids and plasmas use such periodic boxes, but the electric energy of charges that repeat without end is tricky to define.

Their framework adds infinite boundary terms and pair interactions to give energy and pressure formulas that feel natural and work for neutral and charged systems alike. The result mirrors the plain isolated-system formula, with one effective pair rule swapped in. For a one-component plasma, the setup clarifies what the neutralizing background adds. It also gives design rules for volume-based potentials that keep a simple energy-pressure link.
arxiv-2504-06123:
Nathan McMahon, Mahum Pervez, and Christian Arenz equate three quantum cooling paths in a 2025 paper. Imaginary time flow cools a quantum system to its low state. The team show that flow is a slope walk on the unitary group, bent by its shape. A bound ties the gap between the two walks to step size. Small steps thus keep the walk true.

A chance form of that walk runs each step on a quantum rig with ease. For small steps, the chance walk hugs the true flow, they prove. Fit step picks come from the bound. The frame gives cooling craft a firm math base.
arxiv-2504-06323:
Bailey Eccles, Leon Wong, and Blesson Varghese shrink large language models by pruning their projections. Their 2025 paper introduces Mosaic, a system for making and serving trimmed models. Heavy compute and memory needs keep big models off modest hardware, and coarse pruning cuts too bluntly, deleting parts the model needs.

Their fine-grained method prunes projection layers directly. A composite recipe then pairs two cuts: a scattered one that guards accuracy and a structured one that sheds real size. Across models, data sets, and hardware, Mosaic built pruned models about seven times faster than rivals. Its models read text far more cleanly and answered more accurately than coarse-pruned peers, while running faster on less graphics memory. The code is public.
arxiv-2504-06423:
Stefan Rothe and a team of co-authors report a 2025 advance in high-power fiber lasers. Lasers that run on a single note are hard to scale up, because an effect called stimulated Brillouin scattering caps their power. A fiber that carries many light modes at once can ease that cap, but its output beam is hard to control.

The team shaped the light wave entering a multimode fiber amplifier so the output focused to a tight, clean spot. Their amplifier ran at high power with high efficiency and a narrow line width. The authors see uses in combining beams, large-scale measurement, and directed energy delivery.
arxiv-2504-06723:
Adam Chapman and Ahmed Laghribi complete in 2025 a classification in the algebra of quadratic forms. Over fields of characteristic two, they sort all five-dimensional quadratic and bilinear forms that stay minimal over the function field of an arbitrary conic, the field of rational curves on that shape.

The result closes the last open case of Faivre's work on five-dimensional forms of a certain type over nonsingular conics. Minimal forms are the atomic cases of the theory, the ones that do not shrink when the field grows. A complete list in this dimension settles how such forms can look over conic function fields.
arxiv-2504-07023:
Steering a quantum system to a chosen state usually means slowly turning a control knob, but slow may be impossible and the target knob setting may lie beyond reach. Xikun Li and Tomasz Sowiński show in this 2025 paper how clever timing of the knob can still land the system on target.

Using optimal control theory, they design schedules of changes that swing the system to the desired state. This works even when the target value sits outside the allowed range, as long as the target's makeup is known. They demonstrate the scheme on small systems where interaction strength is the knob. The approach could extend to larger quantum devices.
arxiv-2504-07123:
Rogliardo and co-authors (2025) present a high-efficiency protocol for measuring strontium-90 contamination in cow's milk after a nuclear accident. The isotope is dangerous because it mimics calcium and settles in bones and teeth. Their method chains freeze-drying, high-temperature burning, ion exchange separation, and liquid scintillation counting.

On reference milk carrying a known activity, the protocol recovered essentially all of the strontium, about 100 percent, beating two established methods that recovered only about two thirds. Its detection limit under the best conditions was low, at 0.33 becquerels per liter. Checks against certified laboratories confirmed the readings, including the expected doubling of signal as the daughter isotope grew in over two weeks. The authors position the protocol as a sensitive, easy-to-run tool for emergency response and routine monitoring, and suggest testing it on other foods.
arxiv-2504-07423:
Venkatesh Sivaraman and co-authors critique how AI doctor aids are judged in this 2025 position paper. Hospitals increasingly give clinicians AI decision support. Studies often grade these tools by trust, reliance, and task scores. The authors call that habit a trap. Good scores can hide tools that add no clinical value.

They reflect on their own studies and the field's leading work. Clinicians sometimes use AI well in ways the metrics miss. Other times the metrics reward leaning on AI that should be questioned. The paper urges realistic study setups inside real workflows. Value that emerges in practice, not lab scores, should be the goal.
arxiv-2504-07723:
Kohei Oue, Naoya Ozaki, and Toshihiro Chujo chart a slow spiral between two lunar orbits. Their 2025 paper plans a low-thrust, many-revolution transfer from low lunar orbit to a near rectilinear halo orbit. That is the parking orbit of the planned lunar gateway, and the route runs under the full pull of Earth and Moon.

Gentle engines and hundreds of loops make the optimization treacherous. Their method extends a hybrid dynamic programming solver with a continuation trick. Start from the simpler two-body problem, then morph the physics step by step into the true three-body setting, carrying the solution along. The solver converged robustly, producing optimal transfers even from a poor first guess. The authors offer the technique for the patient, fuel-sipping trajectories cislunar traffic will need.
arxiv-2504-07823:
Sushuang Ma and co-authors take a fresh look at the air of a distant planet, WASP-39 b, in a 2025 paper. The planet was one of the first studied by a new space telescope, and many spectra of its air exist from several instruments. The team use a step-by-step method that pairs chemistry models with open searches for gases.

Their new picture gives a major role to silicon chemistry. A silicon gas may explain a dip in the spectrum that others had assigned to a sulfur gas. Water, carbon dioxide, sodium, and potassium also appear, in amounts that fit a balanced chemistry model. Silicate clouds and haze may explain features at longer wavelengths. The authors call for sharper new data to test the claim.
arxiv-2504-08123:
