Natalie Kovacevic and co-authors compared the flicker of two galaxy types in a 2025 paper. Seyfert 1 and Seyfert 2 galaxies host feeding black holes; theory says the second type is the first seen through a dust ring, which should muffle its visible variation. The team gathered light curves from two sky surveys for galaxies in a hard X-ray catalog, and measured excess variance for each.

The two types differed clearly in flicker, with type 2s subdued, and the gap did not depend on brightness, feeding rate, or black hole mass. That supports the geometry-only unification picture. A few changing-look galaxies switched type during the survey window, and their flicker rose and fell with their current type. Flicker timing may help date such transitions, the authors suggest.
arxiv-2504-08223:
Kangkang Deng and co-authors present a computing paper from 2025 on hard optimization problems. Many tasks mix smooth and jagged parts and curve the wrong way for easy math. A splitting method that swaps between subproblems is popular, but chance-based versions were slow or hungry for data.

Their single-loop method adds momentum to the swaps and needs just one sampled gradient per step. It hits the best known rate for this problem class without big batches or restarts. Step sizes and penalties adjust on the fly while the rate holds. A plug-and-play version uses image priors inside the loop, with proof of settling under mild rules. Tests on sorting, scan rebuilding, and phase recovery beat past methods in speed and accuracy.
arxiv-2504-08423:
István Gere, Ovidiu-Florin Botos, and Liviu Ancutescu propose a balanced engine layout in a 2025 paper. Ordinary piston engines shake because their parts move back and forth unevenly, causing vibration, wear, and lost efficiency. Their design links four hypocycloidal straight-line mechanisms, a gear-based way to turn rotation into exact straight motion, in a symmetric arrangement.

Calculations show the symmetry cancels both net force and torque ripple, at least on paper. The team then built a working model from acrylic glass using computer-aided design. Accelerometer readings matched the theory: the prototype ran stably, and imbalance appeared only when piston synchrony was deliberately broken. The authors offer the layout as a vibration-free base for piston engines.
arxiv-2504-08623:
Vineeth Sai Narajala and Idan Habler write a security guide for the Model Context Protocol, the standard that lets AI systems reach outside tools and data in real time. The protocol, introduced by Anthropic, speeds up integration. It also opens fresh attack paths that companies must handle before wide adoption.

The paper builds on earlier work on the protocol's design and weak points. Through threat modeling, it maps attack routes, including tool poisoning, where a rigged tool misleads the model. The authors then turn those worries into concrete controls and design patterns. Their aim is practical: a framework firms can implement for safe rollout and governance of connected AI systems.
arxiv-2504-08823:
Xiaobing Yu and co-authors present a lean way for models to learn task after task in this 2025 paper. A model that learns in sequence tends to forget old tasks, a problem called catastrophic forgetting. Many fixes store more and more extra parts for each task, so size and cost keep growing as tasks pile up.

Their method, called FM-LoRA, picks the size of each update on the fly and uses shared prompts that adapt across tasks. Tasks that are alike share a common low-size space, which guards old knowledge. Tests on several image sets, for both new classes and new domains, show strong scores with far less growth in size.
arxiv-2504-09423:
Yanyan Dong, Yan Fang, and Zhibing Zhang wrote a 2025 math paper on steady solutions of a three dimensional tropical climate model. Liouville type theorems say that under set growth rules, the only steady solution is the trivial zero one. They prove two classes of such results.

One class puts conditions on the flow and heat fields. The other puts them on the heat field's slope instead. An energy method with iteration does the work. Solutions in certain standard spaces, or fading fast enough far away, must vanish. A new frame then sharpens the bounds by a log factor. The frame may serve other coupled fluid systems.
arxiv-2504-09523:
Lokesh Chander and C Singh studied a universe model where vacuum energy decays and makes matter as it goes in a 2025 paper. The dark side of the model links the two dark parts, vacuum and dark matter, through creation driven by gravity. Such a link may ease known tensions in sky measures.

The model was fit to many data sets, from exploding stars and galaxy echoes to background radiation distances and growth rates. It gave a clean shift from slowing to speeding expansion. Its present expansion rate fell between the two rival camps, easing that clash, and its clumping measure matched sky surveys. Heat laws also held. The authors read the model as a sound account of cosmic history.
arxiv-2504-09923:
Yujin Kim and co-authors help small language models reason with hints from big ones in a 2025 paper. Small models are cheap and fast but falter on problems needing long chains of logic. Calling a large model for every step wastes the savings. Their framework, SMART, watches the small model's work and steps in only where it looks shaky.

A scoring pass flags the uncertain steps in a draft solution. Only those steps get corrective reasoning from the large model, like scaffolding placed just where a builder wobbles. The search for a good reasoning path is framed as finding an optimal policy, which steers the chain toward right answers without brute-force sampling. On math reasoning sets, the targeted help lifted scores sharply, opening tasks the small models could not solve alone.
arxiv-2504-10023:
The light twin core of heavy water bears its mass in a spread that light can weigh, by the birth of rare grains at the flash's edge. Xiaoxuan Lin and co-authors weigh that spread in a 2025 study of three such births, on old beam data from four labs. A bend tale for the pull form turns each birth's counts to a span.

The three births tell one tale: a mass span near two strides, with a tenth's doubt. That span holds cross the pull form tales the team tried. The new span is far tight than the past one birth take. It bars core builds that spread the twin's mass too wide or too thin.
arxiv-2504-10323:
Molham Aref and co-authors present Rel, a programming language built for relational data, in two thousand twenty-five. Query languages have long lived as guests inside a host language, which splits an app's logic in two and breeds mismatch bugs. Rel aims to end that split.

Its design goal is programming in the large: whole enterprise apps described in one relational tongue. The language covers classic query work, joins, filters, and grouping, plus features that let code grow and stay tidy at scale. Fifty years of database research, the authors argue, now allow this fresh start from first principles. The paper walks through the main features and the thinking behind them.
arxiv-2504-10523:
Goureesankar Sathyanathan and three co-authors look for a wave effect in lensed radio bursts in this two thousand twenty-five paper. Fast radio bursts are brief flashes from deep space, still poorly understood. Their tiny duration suggests a compact source, ideal for wave optics when gravity lenses them. A lensed burst should arrive as several copies at different times. Often only one copy falls inside the survey's view.

The team studies the combined bending by many stars in the lens galaxy, with wave effects included. Their simulation adds scattering from turbulent gas. The signal's self-similarity shows peaks at telling delays. Finding such peaks would confirm lensing and weigh the stars involved. Radio astronomers are the audience.
arxiv-2504-10623:
Melchert and Demircan present a software paper from two thousand twenty-five about solitons, stable wave packets that keep their shape as they travel. Solitons appear across nonlinear physics, but exact formulas for them are often missing. Their Python package, called SWtools, finds such solutions numerically for a family of Schrödinger-type equations.

The package solves a linked eigenvalue problem by iteration. It offers several methods, including a spectral renormalization method and a relaxation method with a fixed norm. The authors verify the code on a case with a known exact answer. They then show examples from nonlinear optics and from matter-wave solitons in quantum mechanics. The package is open source under a permissive license.
arxiv-2504-10723:
Junior da Silva Bessa and João Vitor da Silva study smoothness of solutions to a hard class of partial differential equations, in a 2025 paper. These equations can degenerate where the solution's slope is flat, which breaks standard tools. The model adds drift and absorption terms that mimic flow and loss. The authors work inside a unit ball and ask how smooth any solution must be.

They prove solutions gain a smooth first derivative inside the domain, with sharp bounds at flat points. They also prove the solution cannot dip below its boundary peak in odd ways, and that it stays away from zero where it should. The framework then settles existence and uniqueness for a related family of models with strong absorption.
arxiv-2504-10823:
Ayoung Lee and co-authors build a test of how language models judge high stakes moral dilemmas from many viewpoints, in a 2025 paper. Their set, CLASH, holds 345 hard cases and 3,795 stated perspectives from the people inside them. It probes mixed feelings, mental discomfort, and how values shift over time.

Fourteen models were benchmarked. Even top closed models scored poorly when a choice was truly ambivalent, one hitting about a quarter and another about half. Models foresaw discomfort fairly well but missed value shifts. Tricks that help in math and games did not carry over; instead, models locked in too early or too hard. Steering toward a value worked unevenly.
arxiv-2504-11423:
Dazhong Shen and co-authors fine-tune image-making models by letting them feel their own output path in a 2025 paper. Such models train in one pass from noisy art, but at use time they clean noise step by step, so small slips pile up and the output drifts from true art. The new scheme runs the full clean path during training and grades the end art with a rival judge.

The judge pairs a frozen trained spine with light fresh parts. A mixed sampling trick smooths the judge's task, and the old loss stays to stop gaming. Tests on three big image models show gains in match and quality.
arxiv-2504-11523:
Phu Nguyen and Vladyslav Kozii study a Fermi liquid tied to a quantum critical boson through a two boson link. Their paper from 2025 covers Ngai coupling, a less standard tie between electrons and a critical field. The base claim under test is that the critical point holds as drawn.

The authors find the point is in general unstable: the system falls into a wavy, space patterned state. Two holds can save it, a sideways polar boson and a wide speed gap between electrons and boson. If the flat state holds, a strong coupling zone opens below a set energy, with a self fit solution in two dimensions. There the boson gains an odd scaling mark of one half.
arxiv-2504-11823:
Thu Hang Khuat and colleagues present MultiRRT, a path-planning method that guides a team of drones to reach several goals at once. Joint planning matters as multi-drone missions grow more complex. The method extends the rapidly exploring random tree method. It builds the drone dynamics limit into the form, next to joint and safety needs.

Two new tools, node reduction and Bezier interpolation, keep the paths made feasible and near-best. The paths are proven to meet the safety and dynamics limits set by obstacles and by the vehicles. Tests by simulation, by comparison, and by experiment gauge the path against top random tree variants. MultiRRT made collision-free paths with better path length and smoothness scores than its rivals. The paths were also flown on real drones.
arxiv-2504-12023:
Genetti, Longobardi, and Iacca pair evolutionary search with reinforcement learning to make supply chain choices that managers can read. Industry 4.0 supply chains resist black-box tools, since leaders distrust what they cannot inspect. Their method produces policies in the form of decision trees. Those trees sit inside a simulation framework built for uncertain, random demand. The team says the pairing is the first of its kind for supply chains.

Two test problems were used, one invented and one drawn from real life. Results were compared with widely used rival methods. Readable policies held their own on performance. The authors argue trust grows when a policy can be printed and debated.
arxiv-2504-12123:
Fardad Vakilipoor and a team of co-authors put forth a living test bed for molecular communication. Their paper, from twenty twenty-five, deals with sending signals by molecules, a path eyed for health tools. Tests in real living settings lag behind lab rigs. The team used the CAM, a blood rich membrane in fertilized chicken eggs. This membrane is well known in bio work, cancer studies, and drug tests.

They claim this is the first such platform that works in three dimensions in a living body. They mapped the traits of the membrane that matter for signal tests. Readers who build molecule based links get a cheap, true to life stage. It bridges toy demos and real use in the body.
arxiv-2504-12523:
Aochong Oliver Li and Tanya Goyal study how language models absorb new knowledge in this 2025 paper. Models store facts from training, but the world changes after training ends. Past update tests mostly swapped one entity for another. Real updates are messier, with chains of linked changes.

Their pipeline, KUP, builds realistic update sets with supporting evidence texts. Tests then probe memory directly and reasoning indirectly over the new facts. Even the best continued training scored under two percent on reasoning probes. Their lighter method adds self generated memory tokens during training. At answer time the model surfaces those memories and reasons over them. Memory scores rose by up to 25.4 percent over prior training methods.
arxiv-2504-12723:
James Hale and co-authors published a research paper in 2025 on a new data set of dispute resolution conversations spanning more than seventy-five countries. Culture shapes how people argue, yet most dialogue data come from one place. Volunteers played out a customer service dispute designed by experts to stir real emotion and conflict.

The corpus holds thousands of paired conversations plus rich measures of traits, process, and outcomes. Early analysis backs the theory that expressed anger feeds escalation spirals. It also surfaces cultural differences in how openly emotion is shown. The team releases both the corpus and the collection setup so others can study negotiation across cultures.
arxiv-2504-12823:
Surbhi Rajput, Ashish Chiplunkar, and Rohit Vaish extend a classic online trading puzzle from one stock to many. Their 2025 paper builds on the trading prophet problem, where an algorithm sees prices one by one and must decide when to buy and sell. The benchmark is a prophet who sees the whole future.

In their version the trader juggles many stocks while holding only a limited number at once. They prove the best possible competitive ratio follows a simple formula based on that holding limit and the stock count. A wider version over matroid constraints, where prices can move together, gets a tight bound tied to the matroid's density. Random-order arrivals nearly match the same bound.
arxiv-2504-13123:
Xinsong Zhang and a team of co-authors present a way to make accurate captions for images at large scale in a 2025 paper. Models that join vision and language need vast sets of image and text pairs, but hand checked pairs are running out. Made up captions often invent details that are not in the image, which harms training.

Their pipeline uses a learning step that cuts such invention sharply in tests. Models trained on their captions beat models trained on the short text that comes with web images, across many vision and language tasks. Their data also helped in the reverse task of making images from text.
arxiv-2504-13223:
Angelos Alexopoulos and co-authors measure a European fund's effects in a 2025 economics paper. The Cohesion Fund sends money to poorer regions, yet its impact is less studied than sister programs. Standard evaluation tricks struggle here, so the team used a newer causal method based on completing a data matrix inside a factor model.

Average effects, they show, hide wide variation and can mislead. The fund's impact peaks within the first seven years after a region joins, then fades. Gains in that first cycle are positive but uneven, with a long tail of strong winners. Poorer regions gain more, and past a threshold, extra money yields less per unit. The paper offers a new frame for judging regional aid over time.
arxiv-2504-13423:
William Cook published a paper in 2025 defining a workable notion of information for the heavy-tailed stable distributions where the classical one breaks. Symmetric alpha-stable laws, used for wild, jumpy data, have infinite classical Fisher information, so statisticians lacked a finite yardstick for comparing two such laws of different scales. Cook builds one from how fast relative entropy melts away as one law is interpolated toward another.

Two natural formulas for the new measure are proven to agree exactly, tying the entropy melt rate to differences in score functions through a clean identity. The measure is never negative and vanishes only when the scales match, and the Cauchy case gets a closed form. Numerical checks confirm the identity, grounding future work on heavy-tailed estimation.
arxiv-2504-14223:
Michael Färber and four co-authors present SimplifyMyText, a web system that rewrites hard text into plain language tuned to each reader. Their paper appeared in two thousand twenty-five. Many people face texts too dense for them at work and in daily life. Simplified versions are scarce, which shuts people out.

The system takes typed text or uploaded files in several forms. Users pick their audience and how simple the output should be. Two large language models power the rewriting under the hood. The team graded outputs with a battery of measures. They argue tailored plain language beats one-size rewrites for inclusion. The tool is live on the web for public use. The work ties text simplification research to the plain-language movement.
arxiv-2504-14323:
Leo Harrington and Peter Gerdes set out a building method from logic in a 2025 paper. The method, called tree pulldown, was used by Harrington to settle a conjecture of McLaughlin's. It builds a computable tree whose paths resist comparison at a set level of complexity, yet mimic generic paths in set ways.

Earlier print covered only one level, tied to the first infinite ordinal. The new paper gives the build for any ordinal notation a user supplies. A twist with a non-standard notation yields a tree whose paths defy comparison at every level below a key limit ordinal. The authors then check off several open problems from a famous list of one hundred and two logic problems.
arxiv-2504-14523:
Gabriela Ben Melech Stan and co-authors present a 2025 method for teaching large multimodal models from their own reasoning failures. Such models work with both images and text, but good paired training data are scarce. Making data in bulk does not fix the exact skills a given model lacks.

Instead, the team first finds where a model reasons badly, then creates synthetic training examples aimed at those gaps. The approach mirrors how a tutor targets a student's weak spots rather than assigning general practice. For model builders, the paper offers a way to spend a training budget where it should help most.
arxiv-2504-14623:
Béatrice Bérard, Benjamin Monmege, Srivathsan, and Arnab Sur revisit how to build asynchronous automata from fair specifications. Their 2025 paper deals with distributed finite state processes that synchronize on shared actions.

A classic result by Zielonka shows how to synthesize such an automaton from a global specification and a split of the alphabet among processes. That translation is complex and lacks a complete tool. The authors restrict attention to fair specifications, in which every process acts in each loop, so none is starved. For this class they give a new construction. Each process ends with a number of local states that grows only linearly.
arxiv-2504-14923:
Yasuji Sawada, Yasukazu Daigaku, and Kenji Toma review, in twenty twenty-five, the birth and evolution of life through a thermodynamics principle. The principle states that systems far from balance tend to maximize entropy production, the rate of disorder creation. The authors argue it is essential for a consistent account of life's origin. They first review work on self-replicating systems before RNA life. A critical polymer concentration is reported above which entropy production grows exponentially.

They then review early evolution studies, on cell counts needed for multicellular organization and on differentiation in model systems. Late evolution, they suggest, is marked by society formation and external entropy production. Examples of life under poor thermodynamic conditions are discussed.
arxiv-2504-15023:
Taketo Yoshida and a large team report dust-obscured galaxies with broken power-law energy distributions, in their 2025 arXiv paper. These infrared-bright galaxies are so dusty that their light patterns split into classes: bump galaxies dominated by star formation, and power-law galaxies dominated by an active galactic nucleus.

Using a deep northern sky survey plus infrared data, they identified several hundred such galaxies over a wide area. Most sorted into the two known classes. About half of the power-law group, though, showed a broken pattern, with a steep red slope from optical to near-infrared light. That break signals heavier dust extinction, marking them as more deeply buried active nuclei than their unbroken cousins.
arxiv-2504-15123:
Thiago Oliveira and co-authors present a quantum physics paper, published in 2025, linking two effects seen in waves trapped in a harmonic well. Matter waves are the wave nature of particles such as atoms, and squeezing means narrowing the spread of one property at the cost of another. The Gouy phase is an extra phase a focused wave picks up as it passes through its narrowest point.

Following a Gaussian wave packet as it evolves, the authors show the Gouy phase grows in steps tied directly to squeezing. Over one full swing the phase adds up in a fixed amount set by the interplay of spreading and squeezing. The link could give quantum sensing and precision measurement a new shared control knob.
arxiv-2504-15323:
Donggyun Kim, Chanwoo Kim, and Seunghoon Hong present HyperFlow in 2025, a method that mimics fine-tuning without computing gradients. Fine-tuning at test time helps few-shot learning, where only a few examples are given, but repeated gradient steps cost too much for real-time or low-resource use.

They treat gradient descent as steps along a differential equation, then train a helper network to predict that drift from the few examples alone. Adapting a model then needs only a few forward passes of the helper, with no gradients and no passes through the target model. On two cross-domain few-shot benchmarks, the method raised out-of-domain scores well above the plain baseline. It used only a small share of the memory and time of standard fine-tuning.
arxiv-2504-15723:
Dasol Jeong, Donggoo Kang, Jiwon Park, Hyebean Lee, and Joonki Paik present a 2025 method for editing images with diffusion models while keeping the frame intact. Editors want text-led or reference-led changes with no retraining and no warped layout. The method inverts the source image into the model's code space, then injects codes in stages. Shape goes in early, surface traits late, so edits land where they belong.

Reference codes join through the model's cross-attention to align meaning. Tests on face swaps of expression, texture shifts, and style pours topped past methods. Stage timing, the work shows, is the trick that keeps a photo itself while its look changes. Consumer edit tools chase exactly this balance.
arxiv-2504-15923:
Five authors, Mohsen Sadatsafavi, Paul Gustafson, Solmaz Setayeshgar, Laure Wynants, and Richard Riley, wrote this 2025 statistics paper on sizing validation studies for risk models. A risk model must be tested on new data before clinics trust it. Standard recipes for the test size ask users to fix the model's expected performance in advance.

That step hides real doubt, since past studies give only a rough sense of true performance. The authors propose a Bayesian frame that carries that doubt into the size choice. For measures such as discrimination and calibration, their rules target either an expected level of precision or a set chance of reaching it. They also treat net benefit, a measure of clinical use, where standard precision logic is shaky. The work aims at validation studies that are neither too small to trust nor larger than needed.
arxiv-2504-16623:
Fiete Sieg, Anne-Marie Toparkus, and Rafael Weißbach worked on a statistics problem in 2025: learning from lifespan data that is cut off at both ends and partly missing. Some subjects are lost to follow-up, and some birth dates are unknown. Their test case is the lifespan of firms in Germany.

The team treats the data as a point process that stays close to a simple random process when the sample is small next to the whole group. Assuming a standard lifespan curve, they build the best-fit method and remove the unknown sample size from the math. They show the key value can be pinned down and that their estimator settles as data grows. Both the estimate and its error can be read from the data at hand.
arxiv-2504-16823:
Han Zhou, Yuan-Nan Young, and Yoichiro Mori build maths and sims for open skin sheets in slow thick flow, in a 2025 paper. Open sheets have a free edge, unlike shut sacs in cells. That edge spawns sharp math spots that plain sims blur or miss in runs.

Three span flow, two span sheet, and one span edge join in one frame. A mixed edge and cell way solves the frame as a one span task. Fine mesh near the edge catches sharp spots and thin coats there. Test runs show rich edge dance and scale mix in the flow. Edge acts drive much of the sheet path.
arxiv-2504-16923:
Jacob Levy and six co-authors present a 2025 framework for off-road self-driving that adapts its dynamics model while it drives. Fast off-road work is hard since ground traits shift fast, and models of how a vehicle meets the terrain often fail on new ground.

Their plan pairs a Kalman filter that adapts online with parameters learned ahead of time by meta-learning. Offline work tunes the basis for change and the rules for how fast to adapt. Online, the model updates in real time for model-based control. Tests in the field and in simulation back the approach.
arxiv-2504-17423:
Sambit Mishra and Soumya Dash wrote this wireless engineering paper in 2025. It studies a radio link helped by a reconfigurable intelligent surface, a wall of tiny elements that bounce signals toward the receiver. The sender uses one-sided amplitude-shift keying, which codes data in the strength of the wave. The receiver skips channel tracking and judges each symbol by a best-guess rule, a scheme called noncoherent detection.

The pair work out the math of symbol errors for the setup, with a fresh way to sum two kinds of random spread. They then shape the signal levels to cut errors under a fixed energy budget. The tuned levels, which bunch unlike the even spacing of old designs, gave fewer errors and stronger diversity gains. The gap grew at high signal strength and with fewer surface elements.
arxiv-2504-18223:
G. Lacedelli, E. Palle, and a large team of colleagues report two planets around a cool dwarf star in a 2025 astronomy study. One planet crosses in front of its star and appears rocky and larger than Earth. The second, a smaller Neptune-like world, does not cross and was found by other signals.

Their work sits inside a project that studies Neptune-sized planets in a uniform way across star types. Such planets are common, but their origin and makeup remain debated. Precise measurements of this system add a well described case to the sample. New telescope observations can then test what the inner rocky world and its companion are made of.
arxiv-2504-18423:
Rajesh Yarra proposes LLMpatronus, a design for hunting software vulnerabilities with large language models. The work appeared in twenty twenty-five. Classic scanners drown teams in false alarms and read code shallowly, while language models hallucinate and forget long files.

The approach pairs two fixes. Retrieval-augmented generation feeds the model relevant code and knowledge on demand, easing the context limit. A mixture-of-agents setup lets several models cross-check findings, damping single-model invention. Earlier machine learning attempts failed on weak features and thin context; Yarra argues this architecture answers both. The paper maps weaknesses honestly and lays out a route toward dependable AI-assisted security review.
arxiv-2504-18523:
Thick fluids bleed energy as they swirl, and one puzzle asks whether that loss survives as the fluid turns nearly ideal. Tarek M Elgindi, Milton C Lopes Filho, and Helena J Nussenzveig Lopes settle the question for flat vortex sheets in a 2025 paper. Their flow lives on a torus and may start from rough swirl data: any spread-out measure plus a milder part. Outside forcing is allowed.

The team proves the extra energy loss vanishes as thickness fades. They also give an explicit bound on the loss at small thickness. The proof rests on a sharpened form of a classic inequality by Nash. The result covers a wide class of starting flows.
arxiv-2504-18623:
Jesús Cruz Rojas, Deog Ki Hong, Sang Hui Im, and Matti Järvinen use holography to study gauge theories hovering just outside their conformal window. Near-conformal dynamics interest model builders hunting light scalar states. In the holographic setup, a scalar field dual to quark degrees of freedom moves in a nearly anti-de Sitter geometry. The picture matches what Dyson-Schwinger analyses expect for vector-like theories.

A solvable toy model and a fuller ultraviolet-complete setup are both analyzed. The team derives when a parametrically light scalar appears, a candidate for the pseudo-Nambu-Goldstone boson of broken approximate scale symmetry. Vacuum structure, correlators, and Ward identities in the near-conformal regime get detailed treatment. Such light dilatons are targets for collider and lattice searches alike. The holographic map lets the authors compute what direct methods struggle to reach.
arxiv-2504-18923:
Chris Connell, McReynolds, and Shi Wang bound the homological size of discrete subgroups inside large symmetry groups, in a paper from 2025. The head title adds the word simple to the catalog title. The team uses a flow method they introduced earlier to probe how such subgroups sit inside the group.

New estimates on a critical index give an upper bound built from the space dimension and the group rank. For subgroups whose limit shapes are regular, the bound tightens further. The results cover groups that are dense in a strong algebraic sense but not lattices. The authors add guesses on which sizes can occur and open questions for the wider family of such groups.
arxiv-2504-19123:
Jannik Olbrich presents a fast, light way to build a key text index from compressed data, in this 2025 paper. The Burrows-Wheeler Transform underlies many search tools for huge sequence collections, such as genome banks. Classic builders need the whole data set in memory, which fails at that scale.

Repetitive data compress well into small grammars, and Olbrich's method works straight from one such grammar built on Lyndon words. It also handles collections of many sequences through an extended form of the transform. Tests show the method builds indexes for very large data faster or with less memory than rivals.
arxiv-2504-19223:
Alexander Baumann and co-authors present a model that works across many kinds of spectral cameras in this 2025 paper. Spectral images record light in many narrow bands, not just three colors, and they help in medicine, city scenes, and earth watching. But cameras differ in band count and in which bands they catch, so models built for one camera often fail on another.

Their model, called CARL, turns any spectral image into a shared form that does not depend on the camera. A new encoder picks out the key spectral facts. Large tests in medical, driving, and satellite images show the model holds up when cameras change, beating rivals on both faked and real camera shifts.
arxiv-2504-19523:
Goswami and co-authors presented a model of the expanding universe in 2025. Their model is a Bianchi type-I cosmos that is not the same in all directions, with a thick fluid as its source. The work tests how well the model fits late-time growth.

The team fit the model to four sets of data, covering Hubble rates, supernovae, and distance measures. They used Bayesian tools and chain sampling to find the best values for each free value in the model. Checks on dark energy suggest the model acts like quintessence at late times. It also moves toward the standard model as time passes.
arxiv-2504-19723:
Syed, Utschick, and Joham tackle a design problem for future wireless networks, in a paper published in 2025: smart surfaces that both reflect and pass radio signals. A plain smart surface only bounces signals to one side, limiting coverage. The dual-mode surface serves users on both sides at once. Prior work tuned such systems by recasting the problem for heavyweight solver software, which runs far too slowly for real networks.

The authors propose a low-complexity method to maximize the total data rate across many users. Their approach avoids the slow generic solvers while keeping performance high. Fast tuning is what makes the surfaces usable outside simulations. Base stations must re-aim these surfaces in near real time as users move. The paper brings the dual-mode surface closer to practical deployment in next-generation networks.
arxiv-2504-20123:
Jerome Samuel, Puneet Kumar Patra, and Md Rushdie Ibne Islam model a heat-shield material in a 2025 paper. Superelastic polyimide springs back under strain and insulates well, traits prized in aerospace. Heat effects begin at the atomic scale, so the team linked an atomistic simulation to a smooth particle model of the bulk material.

Properties and state equations flowed from the atomic runs into the larger model. Benchmark heat problems checked the coupling. A final test wrapped an aluminium plate in the material and simulated its heating. Stress, strain, and temperature in the plate all fell sharply with the insulation in place. The authors present the multiscale route as a sound way to study thermo-mechanical behavior.
arxiv-2504-20223:
Ethan Partington and co-authors watch a galaxy's core flicker in X-rays and ultraviolet light to test how its black hole feeds. The galaxy, NGC 7469, hosts a bright center where gas spirals into the hole. A space X-ray telescope stared daily for most of a year, while a second craft tracked the ultraviolet glow. Their 2025 study times how the two lights rise and fall together.

The X-ray pattern split into a hard beam and a soft extra glow. Both varied in lockstep with no delay. The soft glow fits light bounced off the inner disk, and the hard source looks small and central. The ultraviolet lagged the X-rays by under a day, as if X-ray heat drives the glow.
arxiv-2504-20523:
Vicente Ocqueteau and Marius Tucsnak study the small oscillations of a cylinder floating on water, coupled with the waves it makes. The body is an endless circular cylinder, so the water's free surface can be described in one space dimension. Body motion and fluid motion drive each other, forming a coupled PDE-ODE system.

The authors recast the system as an abstract evolution equation in a Hilbert space. They then prove the initial value problem is well-posed: solutions exist, are unique, and depend sensibly on the start. A key step analyzes a partial Dirichlet-to-Neumann map on an unbounded domain with a rough edge.
arxiv-2504-20623:
Antennas that can slide to the best spot on a device dodge fading dips that plague fixed ones. Tianyu Han and co-authors extend that trick to networks with no cells in this 2025 paper. Earlier work on fluid antenna access covered a single cell only. Here users attach to their nearest base station while all share one channel.

Each base station beams with several fixed antennas. Each user leans on one sliding antenna to sidestep interference from others. The team derived how a typical user's signal strength distributes under both slow and fast fading. Outage probability — the chance the signal fails — follows from that math. Cell-free designs promise even coverage; fluid antennas add a personal escape hatch.
arxiv-2504-20723:
Morteza Pashapour-Ahmadabadi and co-authors use counts of radio sources in sky cells to study the cosmos in two thousand twenty-five. The data come from the second release of a low-frequency radio survey of the northern sky. Counting sources cell by cell is a cheap way to gauge how they cluster.

The team tests three models for how counts spread across cells. Plain random spread is ruled out, most likely because many radio sources have several parts. A clustered process fits better, and above a set brightness the counts follow a negative binomial pattern. The mean number of parts per source matches a checked catalog, and the clustering trend follows the expected power-law shape.
arxiv-2504-20823:
Olga Tsurkan and co-authors build a hybrid quantum recurrent network to forecast how much life a jet engine has left, in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. Such forecasts drive safe, cost-wise maintenance. Their design swaps the linear maps inside memory gates for quantum circuits, then adds classical layers on top.

On a NASA turbofan benchmark, the hybrid beat matched classical memory networks by about five percent on error scores across ten seeds. It also topped forest, convolutional, and plain network baselines. Circuit analyses backed its compactness and trainability. Top joint deep models still won, so the authors pitch quantum parts as components, not replacements.
arxiv-2504-21223:
Katsunori Kubo studies the surface states of a model crystal in a solo twenty twenty-five paper. The model places electrons on a diamond lattice, the structure of diamond and silicon, with hops only to nearest neighbors. He looks at slabs of finite thickness with three surface orientations.

A diamond lattice has two sublattices, so each surface direction allows two distinct surface structures. Kubo shows the surface states are fixed by the bulk math, yet the bulk matrix itself depends on the unit cell chosen, which must match the surface. As a result, the two structures put their surface states in distinct parts of the surface zone. The paper maps which case gives which states.
arxiv-2504-21323:
Qian Ma, Chen Wu, Prasenjit Mitra, and Sencun Zhu show how to backdoor image knowledge distillation, in a research paper from 2025. Distillation trains a small student to match a large teacher. It is often assumed safe when the teacher is clean, since classic backdoors need poisoned labels, and distillation uses teacher outputs instead.

The attack poisons the distillation data set itself. Triggered, manipulated images are chosen so the clean teacher already calls them the target class. The student then learns the trigger as a backdoor, while the teacher stays clean. The attack works even at a ten percent poisoning rate, with clean accuracy held. Data provenance joins the security boundary.
arxiv-2505-00623:
Ralph Romero, Hee Taek Yi, Seongshik Oh, and Nicholas Armitage probe how electrons scatter in an iron-based superconductor, in a 2025 paper. Copper oxide superconductors show a famously unexplained resistance that grows linearly with temperature. Whether that odd behavior ties to the pairing state itself remains a central question.

Using terahertz spectroscopy on two samples of iron telluride selenide, the team separated the current into two parallel channels. One channel is broad and barely changes with temperature. The other is sharp, and its scattering rate tracks the so-called Planckian limit set by temperature alone. When the samples turned superconducting, the condensate drew mainly from that Planckian channel. The finding links the strange scattering directly to the pairing that produces superconductivity, at least in this material family.
arxiv-2505-01123:
Castiglione, Maugeri, and Bella propose using a machine learning detector as the guide for automatic security fuzzing, in this 2025 poster paper. Fuzzing finds bugs by hammering software with odd inputs, but someone must first write the test harness and pick a target function. Those choices are usually made by hand.

Their workflow starts with a learning-based detector that flags a likely weak function. A generator then builds the fuzz driver for that target on its own. Fuzzing either confirms the suspected flaw with a real crash or clears it. The team demonstrates the pipeline on a known flaw in a graphics library. A large-scale evaluation is planned next.
arxiv-2505-01523:
Madhav Kotecha, Vijendra Kumar Vaishya, Smita Gautam, and Suraj Racha pick fine tuning subsets for math domain adaptation by balancing utility and diversity. Full set training is costly, so a smart pick can save time and compute. Their work came out in twenty twenty-five.

Utility scores blend perplexity with chain of thought loss to flag hard, high yield cases. Diversity scores keep the pick spread across math subfields. The aim is near full set skill from a small, well chosen slice. Tests on two model families pit the method against random picks, diversity only picks, and top past subset methods.
arxiv-2505-01723:
Heat can cross a tiny gap by light alone, and below ten nanometers the known theory may break down. Geesmann and co-authors measure that cross-gap flow in a 2025 study. A gold-coated ball nears a gold film while a sharp tip sensor reads the heat flow.

In the near zone, readings matched the standard theory with fine precision. Closer in, the flow jumped to about a hundred times the forecast. Rival labs have split on this point, with some camps matching theory and some far above it. The new data back the high camp in the closest zone. The result presses theory to explain the extra flow.
arxiv-2505-01823:
Nitin Rai and co-authors generate synthetic crop disease images with text-to-image models and benchmark the computing cost, in a paper from 2025. Field photos of sick crops are slow and costly to gather, yet training data must be large. Past synthetic work leaned on image-to-image methods and never priced the hardware burden.

The team trained three versions of a leading diffusion model family with two fine-tuning styles. The medium version won: it made five hundred images from just thirty-six field samples in about ninety minutes. Its memory, power, and energy per image were all measured, a first for this field. The authors recommend that model as the efficient choice for farm image generation.
arxiv-2505-01923:
Lívia Deme and co-authors measure the height of meteors that were caught at once by cameras and by a radio sounding instrument during the 2019 Geminid shower, in a 2025 paper. A meteor's glowing trail reflects radio waves, and pairing that signal with a camera-tracked path can pin down the trail's true height. Two observatories in Hungary recorded the shower's peak together.

From two meteors seen by both systems, the team worked out heights of about 90 and 85 kilometers. The method crosses the planes defined by each camera site and the meteor's path to fix its position. Both heights sit above the radio instrument's detection floor of about 80 kilometers, which fits its known limits. The authors present the pairing as a way to study the fleeting physics of meteor trails.
arxiv-2505-02123:
Xinmeng Hou and six co-authors present a multi-agent framework for self-driving cars, in a paper from twenty twenty-five. The system pairs a large language model with fused data from cameras, laser scanners, satellite positioning, and motion sensors. Separate agents handle separate parts of the reasoning, coordinated by the model.

One agent flags key events in the sensor stream. Vehicle agents judge the car's own state and movement from laser and vision data. Further agents explain the scene and why it is changing. A final agent weighs urgency and proposes maneuvers. The split design aims at clear, readable decisions in messy traffic. Tests on hard driving data sets beat baseline methods on several measures.
arxiv-2505-02223:
Armin Hatefi, Ehsan Hatefi, and Park study finite temperature effects on cosmological parameters in two thousand twenty-five. Heat era quantum gravity shifts may bend the vacuum energy story. They add heat based corrections to the Hubble parameter in a solver. Two new density terms carry those off shell vacuum effects.

Neural networks and stochastic search weigh the terms against sky data. One term lands negative, in line with a known regularization quirk. Both terms improve the fit to Planck data from two thousand eighteen. The Hubble tension survives the tweaks, they note. The model is a first pass, not a full derivation.
arxiv-2505-02323:
Sangli Teng and co-authors plan rigid body paths with Lie group math in a 2025 paper. Robots need paths that obey true dynamics. Stock plan tools twist the math frame and slow or break on turns. Their frame works on the matrix group itself, so turns keep their true shape. A Lie-fit step rule writes the dynamics in that frame. First and twin slope forms come in closed shape.

A line-search inner point solver then runs the plan with broad side rules. Each step costs in line with plan length and free marks. Sims beat stock tools by tenfold on hard tasks, the team claim. No frame twists means no turn traps by build.
arxiv-2505-02723:
Marcus Michelen and Oren Yakir work out the pattern of gaps between roots of a random polynomial as its degree grows, in a paper from 2025. Coefficients are drawn independently from one distribution. Roots crowd in ways that decide how hard the polynomial is to solve and factor.

Scaled by a precise power of the degree, the set of root gaps settles into a scattered point pattern of a known non-uniform kind. The smallest gap inherits a clean limit law from that pattern. A side result aids the proof: a random power series almost surely has no repeated root away from the origin. The work joins probability with classical root geometry.
arxiv-2505-03023:
Soler Poquet and co-authors train in 2025 neural networks to spot small solar flare ups called Ellerman bombs in telescope data, signs of tiny magnetic reconnection events low in the Sun's atmosphere. Automatic spotting would let researchers study how often these events occur and what they do. Models were trained on sharp images from a Swedish solar telescope and on several channels from a space observatory.

For the ground telescope, the models proved skilled. Fine spectral detail alone could suffice, but as detail was degraded, spatial context grew in importance, and models using both did best. For the space data, the models struggled to tell bombs from other bright patches. The wings of one spectral line carried the most useful signal.
arxiv-2505-03123:
Wei Yang and co-authors build a forecasting method for colorectal cancer that has spread to the liver. Their 2025 paper notes that return of disease after surgery is common and hard to predict for any one patient. Older tools read a single snapshot after surgery and miss how the illness moves over time.

Their framework, DyPro, starts from a first portrait of the patient and evolves it step by step. Twelve generated snapshots form a latent trajectory, blending tumor layout, disease dynamics, and clinical data. On a major cancer center data set, the method scored well at ranking who stays disease-free and who survives, with strong one-year accuracy. The authors offer the risk scores as cues for planning added therapy and follow-up visits.
arxiv-2505-03423:
Future teachers must learn to counsel parents well, and AI feedback may sharpen that training. Tobias Hallmen and co-authors tested such feedback in a 2025 study. Their seminar mixed theory, practice, and AI tools that read speech, voice tone, and body signals. Students held mock teacher-parent talks that were recorded. AI feedback and interviews with students followed each round.

Voice and body features tracked strongly with how good the talks were judged to be. Students rated the AI feedback in a positive way overall. The team also trained models to spot talk phases and counseling moves. The authors say machine feedback can give fair, practical tips at scale. Next steps include finer speech labels and a larger data set.
arxiv-2505-03623:
Emanuele Caruso and co-authors present a 2025 method for making fake factory images by computer. Factories need images of defects with exact labels to train vision systems. Real defect photos are costly and slow to gather and mark. The team's method builds both the image and its label map at once.

The method guides an image-making model with marked boxes that carry extra detail. Those boxes help the model place each defect in the right spot with the right shape. The authors add two new scores to judge how well the fake data works. They also train a defect-finding system on real and fake data to test the gain. Their results suggest fake data can close much of the gap to real factory data.
arxiv-2505-03723:
Howard Chen, Paolo De Luca, Assaf Hochman, and Thaddeus Komacek simulate how stellar tantrums batter the climates of tidally locked Earth-like planets, in a paper published in two thousand twenty-five. Flares, coronal mass ejections, and proton storms can rewrite an atmosphere's chemistry and brightness, which matters both for habitability and for what telescopes infer about the planet.

Earlier work mostly covered photochemistry, surface ultraviolet doses, and spectra. This study couples three-dimensional circulation models with interactive photochemistry. The test worlds resemble TRAPPIST-1e, always showing the same face to their star. They are subjected to energetic particle events and periodic ultraviolet surges. Statistical methods tally the climate and chemical responses across space and time. A planet's weather, it turns out, has a space-weather season. Characterizing exoplanets remotely will have to correct for their star's mood swings.
arxiv-2505-03923:
Pedram Pad and co-authors add a one-shot feature picker to neural networks in a 2025 paper. Choosing which inputs matter trims data size and sharpens learning, but top methods demand retraining and fiddly tuning afterward. Their layer works during training itself, with no change to the loss or the network shape.

Each input is blended with noise through a trainable gain, and the gains are held to a fixed total budget. That squeeze drives useful features' gains to full and the rest to zero, selecting exactly the wanted count. Tests on standard and real-world data match or beat far more complex methods, with theory support in the linear case.
arxiv-2505-04023: Alexander Polishchuk proves a result about sheaves on an abelian variety in a paper from 2025. He shows that a bounded complex of sheaves whose Fourier-Mukai transform has support of dimension at most one extends to a perfect complex on the standard thickening of the space. The same holds for the quantized form of any constant Poisson bracket on the space. He also discusses a related guess that would characterize Jacobians in terms of such thickenings.
arxiv-2505-04123:
Keshav Sood and co-authors build, in a 2025 paper, a guard against biometric leaks from immersive headsets. Virtual and mixed reality gear tracks head motion, voice, and face movement to run its displays. Studies have shown that such signals can betray what a user said, without consent. This psychographic data, the authors argue, must not slip off the device.

Their framework aims to block sensitive signals from leaving the headset while the device still works. They test it hard, on six data sets, and report that the shield holds and stays practical. The paper's premise is blunt: a leak of this kind is a privacy breach, not a side effect. The authors offer the design as a starting point for safer immersive gear.
arxiv-2505-04223:
Sanghyeon Park and Soo-Mook Moon present FRAIN, a faster and sturdier way to train shared models across scattered devices in two thousand twenty-five. Federated learning lets phones or sites train one model without pooling raw data. Slow devices stall the joint rounds, while loose timing lets stale updates skew the shared model.

FRAIN's first trick, FastSync, lets late or rare joiners catch up without replaying old versions. Its second merges updates by a curved blend that keeps each model's direction, cutting clash between clashing local runs. In image sorting with a neural net and in text work with a transformer, FRAIN held steadier gains than three rival schemes, above all with skewed data or stale inputs.
arxiv-2505-04423:
Guy Nason and Henry Antonio Palasciano forecast United Kingdom inflation with a new network method in a 2025 paper. Their approach, called RaGNAR, fits models to many random networks and each month keeps the networks that forecast best. The goal is to predict the consumer price index more accurately than standard tools.

RaGNAR beat common benchmark models at every forecast horizon on both error measures used. It also gave clearly better four to six month forecasts than those published by the Bank of England in its policy reports. Averaging several top networks gave the most robust results. By studying which networks won, the authors could also spot which parts of the economy drove inflation in each period.
arxiv-2505-04523:
Miljenko Čemeljić, Włodek Kluźniak, and Sukalpa Kundu test a model for flickering X-ray signals from ultraluminous X-ray sources, in a two thousand twenty-five paper. Some of these bright sources pulse, meaning they host neutron stars. Their slow quasi-periodic oscillations, called QPOs, might reveal the stars' magnetic fields and accretion rates.

The authors apply Dong Lai's magnetic precession model to the pulsating sources. In that picture, a tilted magnetic field makes the inner accretion disk wobble. They predict QPO frequency should scale inversely with the neutron star's spin period. The prediction barely depends on field strength or accretion rate, yet it matches the known data. Flat-top noise sources, they argue, behave differently.
arxiv-2505-04823:
Junhao Xiong and co-authors present ProteinGuide in a 2025 paper on protein design. Software that writes new protein sequences has grown powerful, but steering it toward a wanted trait usually means retraining. Labs need a way to guide a trained model with fresh data on the fly.

ProteinGuide supplies that guidance without extra training of the main model. It works across model types, from masked language models to diffusion systems, under one shared statistical view. Tests first steered designs toward higher stability or activity in simulation. Later tests balanced two traits in tension. A wet lab trial raised the editing power of a base editor in living cells.
arxiv-2505-04923:
Yun-Peng Li, Da-Bin Lin, Guo-Yu Li, Zi-Min Zhou, and En-Wei Liang model the flickering light curves of certain gamma-ray bursts. Two bursts believed to come from compact object mergers show violent variability during their decay phase. Their light curves resemble a jetted tidal disruption event, which hints at a shared mechanism.

Earlier work suggests such fluctuations in tidal disruption events arise from debris falling back onto the compact object. The authors introduce fluctuations in the mass distribution of the disrupted debris and study their effect on jet power. Turbulence from tidal forces and the debris's self-gravity can imprint variability during fallback. They find the resulting light curve preserves those fluctuation characteristics, and that the observed variability is reproduced with a suitable power-law index, around minus one. The model ties burst variability to the physics of disrupted material.
arxiv-2505-05223:
Drivers differ: some prize comfort, others speed or thrift, and a self-driving car that ignores taste will annoy its owner. Hendrik Surmann, Jorge de Heuvel, and Maren Bennewitz train a driving agent that can bend its style on the fly. Their method, multi-objective reinforcement learning, encodes preferences as weights over goals like efficiency, comfort, speed, and aggressiveness.

One single policy handles the whole weight range, so no retraining is needed when tastes change. The agent drives from camera input in mixed traffic inside the CARLA simulator, across varied city scenes. It shifted its behavior as preferences changed while still avoiding collisions and finishing routes. The authors present preference weights as a simple dial for personal driving style.
arxiv-2505-05623:
William Godoy leads a team of eleven authors in 2025 in measuring how much energy graphics chips use when they run big science codes. The team picked two programs built for the largest supercomputers: QMCPACK, which models matter at the quantum level, and AMReXCastro, which models stars and other flows on a mesh.

They ran tests on NVIDIA A100 and H100 chips and on AMD MI250X chips, recording power, heat, and chip use in both full and mixed precision. The results show how energy and speed trade off against each other. Such numbers help labs plan machines that are fast without wasting power.
arxiv-2505-05723:
Eric Neiva and Hervé Turlier present a computational method for simulating fluid flows inside animal cells, in a two thousand twenty-five paper. An animal cell's cortex, a thin layer under its membrane, contracts and drives flows at the surface. Those flows move the cytoplasm inside, shaping division, migration, and polarization.

Modeling this coupling is hard because cells deform greatly over time. The authors combine two techniques on a fixed grid, avoiding remeshing. The trace finite element method handles surface flow, while the aggregated method handles the bulk. Their framework also includes feedback from a transported molecular regulator. Tests show the approach stays accurate and stable through large deformations.
arxiv-2505-06023:
Qian Qi, writing alone in two thousand twenty-five, proves a universal approximation theorem tailored to deep Q-learning. Generic approximation theorems ignore the special structure of the optimal Q-function, which solves a Bellman equation.

Qi designs a network class mimicking value iteration itself: layers act as neural operators approximating one Bellman update each, so depth equals refinement steps. The analysis propagates regularity through the iterates, using backward stochastic differential equation tools for single steps and finite-horizon dynamic programming for uniform Lipschitz control. Error propagation stays controlled across layers. The result ties network architecture directly to the control problem's structure, a more informative foundation than generic theorems.
arxiv-2505-06523:
Xijie Yang, Linning Xu, Lihan Jiang, Dahua Lin, and Bo Dai present a system for drawing huge three dimensional scenes in real time in a 2025 paper. A popular method builds scenes from millions of small Gaussian blobs, which is too slow when scenes grow to crowd scale. Their system groups blobs into clusters arranged in a hierarchy of detail levels.

An offline step builds the clusters so each level looks close to the next. At run time the system picks only clusters a viewer can notice, based on their screen footprint. Tests on synthetic and real scenes, from trees to buildings, show a good balance of speed and image quality.
arxiv-2505-06623:
Four mathematicians study the math of a heat exchanger in a 2025 paper. A heat exchanger passes heat between fluids moving through nested tubes. Predicting the temperature in such a device leads to a pair of linked equations that change over time and place.

The authors work with a weak form of the equations, which fits cases where sharp exact answers may not exist. They prove that one answer exists, that it is the only one, and that it behaves smoothly enough to trust. Their proof builds the answer step by step through a classic approximation method. The setup allows varied material traits and real boundary rules. Engineers gain a firmer base for models used in plant design.
arxiv-2505-07223:
Tim Zolkin and co-authors opened a two-part study in 2025 on near-conserved quantities in symplectic maps, the step-by-step systems that model beams and orbits. A classic theorem ties smooth symmetries to exact constants of motion. Their work draws a parallel: flip symmetries of the map may yield almost-constants instead.

By building trial functions that respect the flip symmetry order by order, they expose hidden near-constants. Averaging settles the freedom in the series and leads to a theory that handles awkward rational rhythms without blowing up. Tests on two classic maps match known results and simulations closely. The method needs only basic algebra and simple integrals. The authors promise extensions to wider maps and stability estimates for accelerators.
arxiv-2505-07923:
Furey showed in twenty twenty-five that the known representations of the lightest Standard Model particles fit together into a single superalgebra. The set covers the gauge bosons and three generations of fermions, leaving out only pieces tied to the top quark. The resulting algebra matches a known structure: sixteen-by-sixteen Hermitian matrices over the complex numbers, in their Jordan algebra form.

The algebra is generated by division algebras, which lets internal and space-time symmetries factor apart cleanly. Its internal symmetries come out as the strong, weak, and hypercharge groups of the Standard Model, plus extra circle factors. The paper closes with research directions: placing the construction in a broader periodic picture, grounding it in a sum of number systems, and reframing it through the sedenions.
arxiv-2505-08023:
Silvia Paparini and Epifanio Virga study twist waves in a special kind of liquid crystal, in a 2025 paper. These crystals, called chromonics, form from stacks of flat molecules in water. Their bend energy follows a fourth-power law, not the square law of standard theory. In a twist wave with no friction, the wave face steepens until it breaks into a shock in finite time.

Real materials have friction, though, and whether shocks still form was open. The pair give a test, based on the starting twist shape, that tells when a shock will form despite the damping. They also bound the time at which the break should hit. Screen runs of wave growth matched the bounds well for a family of kink-shaped starts. The work helps predict how these soft materials carry and lose twist signals.
arxiv-2505-08623:
Antoine Jacquier, Adriano Oliveri Orioles, and Žan Žurič extend a leading rough volatility model by swapping its noise for a greyer kind. The rough Bergomi model prices options by treating volatility as a jagged process driven by fractional Brownian motion, and it fits markets well. Its log-normal core, though, blocks the field's holy grail: matching stock index and volatility index options at once. Their 2025 paper replaces the driver with a generalized grey Brownian motion, which behaves like models with a second layer of volatility randomness. Formulas for both option types follow, in semi-closed and approximate forms.

Numerical tests and calibration show the extension's edge. Finance theory advances by such swaps: keep the roughness, change the distribution. The authors write for researchers who price equity volatility. Their class of models widens the search for the joint fit.
arxiv-2505-09023:
Bała and eight co-authors build a sim tool for paired light bits that scatter twice in this twenty twenty-five paper. Paired bits can hold linked spin states, a deep mark of the quantum world. For high-force pairs no spin gauge exists, so the scatter path must stand in for it.

Inside, their tool can start a pair in any spin state a user picks. It then tracks how the gap in scatter planes shifts with that state. A big bank of true pair reads from a ring rig grades the tool in full. Sim and true bands match well and track the spin mark as claimed. The work gives labs a way to read spin in hard pairs.
arxiv-2505-09123:
Guoying Liang and Su Yang wrote this paper in two thousand twenty-five. It tackles camouflaged object detection, the task of finding things that blend into their backdrop, by using the large Segment Anything Model, known as SAM.

Past work said SAM fails at this task, but the authors show it works when it is prompted well. They build a network that scores candidate points for how likely a hidden object is there, then a method that picks key points to feed SAM as hints, both for and against. Tests on three data sets under six metrics beat prior methods. The study shows a big ready-made model can do this job without a new model built from scratch.
arxiv-2505-09223:
Yi-Fei Lu and co-authors demonstrate a quantum key distribution system that beats a classic limit in a 2025 experiment. Quantum key distribution lets two parties share a secret key with security backed by physics. The mode-pairing variant promises long reach, but it demands that distant lasers match wavelength with great care, a hard ask for off-the-shelf lasers left free-running.

Their system uses an optical frequency comb, a laser that emits a ladder of colors, to lock the two ends into coherence while keys are shared. Over standard telecom fiber, they exchanged finite-size secret keys across three spans, the longest past four hundred kilometers. The rates beat the rate-loss limit, the ceiling for simpler repeater-free setups, by up to two and a half times. The trick makes a finicky protocol workable with commercial parts.
arxiv-2505-09523:
Luca Cocconi, Paolo Malgaretti, and Holger Stark wrote a 2025 paper on a tiny information engine that runs on an active particle and imperfect measurements. Szilard engines extract work from a single heat bath by measuring a particle and feeding back control. Real measurements err, and this engine's particle is self-propelled, adding realism on both fronts.

The engine couples the particle, through direct contact, to an externally steered mechanical element. The authors map how measurement error shifts work and power output, and what operation costs. Non-trivial optima exist, and their location moves with the error levels. A defined information efficiency can even beat the classic Landauer bound for this design. Cycling the engine, harvesting leftover correlations between measurements, improves efficiency further. One-shot operation shows a sharp transition in that efficiency.
arxiv-2505-09723:
Yuxin Jiang and ten co-authors build a world model that dreams robot scenes from planned actions in a 2025 paper. Robot learning needs tests in dynamic settings, which are costly. Their model, EnerVerse-AC, renders future views from the robot's next actions. It serves as both a data source and a judge.

A multi-level action link steers the video generation. Ray maps guide views from several angles at once. Training adds failure paths to widen the model's grasp. The system can stretch human demos into varied datasets. It can also test policies with no real robot present. Broad trials confirm the method works well in practice.
arxiv-2505-09923:
Minjung Shin, Donghyun Kim, and Jeh-Kwang Ryu built a framework in twenty twenty-five for judging what makes a question good. Questioning matters for people and for AI, yet question quality had no comprehensive measure. They define two dimensions: appropriateness, the social and linguistic fit of a question to its context, and effectiveness, how well it serves the asker's goal.

On those foundations they built a rubric scoring system whose criteria flex with dynamic context variables, aiming for structure without rigidity. Validation on the CAUS and SQUARE data sets showed the framework can flag both well-formed and problem questions and adapt across settings. The study is a step toward treating questioning itself as an analyzable skill for education and AI design.
arxiv-2505-10123:
Luca Naponiello and a large team launched a search for hot Neptune worlds and weighed the first two finds, in a paper published in 2025. Neptune-sized worlds are prime targets for atmosphere study, yet few are well known. A sparse zone close to stars, called the Neptune desert, tests theories of atmosphere loss and migration. Their plan selects the best TESS candidates and weighs them with two precise spectrographs.

The first world hugs the lower edge of the desert on a fast, unusually oval orbit, the most stretched ever seen at such speed. It may still be in slow tidal migration toward its star. The second world sits in the richer savanna zone on a calm, round orbit. Both are hot sub-Neptunes of similar bulk. The first world's atmosphere should read well with space telescopes. The team presents the pair as prime laboratories for how such worlds form.
arxiv-2505-10223:
Puru Vaish and co-authors wrote this medical imaging paper in 2025. Models that outline organs in MRI scans often sag when the scan comes from a new site or machine. Extra training tricks called augmentations can harden them, but the usual flips and crops are too tame. The team test two stronger tricks that do not aim at any one known shift: MixUp, which blends scan pairs, and a Fourier-based method that swaps texture traits.

Across heart and prostate MRI tasks, both tricks lifted scores on shifted test sets by a wide margin. The learned features also grew cleaner: alike cases clumped tighter, and unlike ones split apart. Both tricks drop into the standard nnU-Net pipeline with ease. The authors offer them as a cheap path to models that hold up in real clinics.
arxiv-2505-10423:
Ari Karchmer and Eran Malach connect gradient-trained models to random feature models, in a 2025 theory paper. Both are ways of fitting functions, and the link between them was unclear. Their setting assumes learning that works for any data distribution, with no special assumptions.

The main result says that whatever a parametric model can learn this way, a modest-sized blend of random features can also approximate, with high probability. The blend's size grows with the number of training steps and the precision used. This limits what distribution-free gradient learning can achieve and explains why data assumptions matter in practice. A new complexity measure built along the way separates cleanly from older ones.
arxiv-2505-10623:
Matija Tečer, Giuseppe Calajó, and Marco Di Liberto study light particles that interact through a flat energy band in a two-dimensional network, in a 2025 paper. Their setup places quantum emitters on a Lieb lattice, linked by a web of waveguides. The system holds a flat band set apart in energy, which can pin light in place even though the emitters couple over long range.

With two excitations, the picture changes by regime. Under soft limits, bound pairs of photons form and carry motion inside the flat band. Under hard limits, the system forms stable dressed states that mix flat and sloped bands. The work frames a test bed for tightly linked light states.
arxiv-2505-10723:
Zihao Song and three co-authors design controls for networks of rigid bodies that can join and split in a 2025 paper. Such networks, swarms of linked blocks or craft, gain power when parts can dock or leave at will. The catch is keeping the whole mesh stable and each part's controls valid through each change, with no redesign of the full set.

They first solve one big design task with a matrix test that vows mesh stability. Then they split that test into small local tasks each body can solve on its own. A body can thus dock or leave while the rest keep their controls. A custom simulator and a match against a top past method back the claims.
arxiv-2505-10823:
Large pretrained models can turn a chest X-ray into a compact numeric summary. Simple adapters trained on those summaries may classify images well without heavy computing. The authors of a 2025 study test summaries from seven general and medical foundation models. Their test set holds 8,842 radiographs across seven classes. The adapters include nearest-neighbor rules, logistic regression, support vector machines, random forests, and small neural networks.

One medical model's summaries paired with either of two adapters reached the best score, a mean area under the curve of 93.1 percent. Training took minutes on a plain processor. A fairness check on the winning adapter found only small gaps across gender and age groups.
arxiv-2505-11723:
Tomasz Maszczyk builds a mathematical home for quantum sets in a 2025 paper on quantum combinatorics. He constructs a topos, a universe like structure for sets, whose members behave as quantum sets, and shows the classic universe of sets sits inside it. The logic of plain sets, read inside the new universe, yields the classic Birkhoff von Neumann rules for quantum propositions.

The paper extends the truth values beyond the classic yes no algebra, studying quantum versions of those algebras in detail. Expected values of measured quantities appear as a built in map inside the universe. It also treats quantum quivers, graph like objects from recent theory, and derives their Leavitt path algebras from a category level construction.
arxiv-2505-11923:
Elena Kopylova proves a stability result in a 2025 math paper on a charged particle coupled to an electromagnetic field in two dimensions. The particle is not a point but an extended, spinning body, and the equations are the two-dimensional Maxwell-Lorentz system.

The system admits soliton solutions: patterns in which the particle glides at a steady speed while spinning at a steady rate, with its field traveling along unchanged. The paper's main result is that these solitons are asymptotically stable. Small disturbances do not grow or scatter the pattern away; over long times, nearby solutions settle back toward a soliton of this family. Such results anchor the theory of how classical particles and fields hold together.
arxiv-2505-12523:
Josh Millar, Hamed Haddadi, and Anil Madhavapeddy survey how deep learning can save energy on small devices in a 2025 review. Running neural networks on phones and sensors avoids the cloud, yet batteries drain fast, and some devices run only when harvested energy allows. Saving power without losing accuracy is the puzzle.

The review sorts published approaches by method, then weighs what each gains in energy and system efficiency. It also maps the limits: which network types each method supports, which chips it runs on, and which tasks it suits. Gaps appear where methods work only on narrow hardware or toy problems. The authors offer the survey as a base map for future work on frugal computing.
arxiv-2505-12823:
Santhosh Raghul and Nishad Kothari sharpen bounds on a matching property of cubic graphs, in work from 2025. A cubic graph gives every vertex three edges. A vertex is called lambda matchable when a spanning subgraph gives it degree three and every other vertex degree one.

Counts of such vertices and of matchable pairs are the paper's focus. Recent work set first constant lower bounds on both. Using parameters from Lovasz's matching theory, the bounds are improved. All graphs that meet the bounds exactly are also described. The authors close by settling an open problem: they characterize the two connected cubic graphs where every vertex is matchable.
arxiv-2505-12923:
Curvo, writing alone in 2025, stages social deduction games among language model agents. His paper presents The Traitors, a simulation drawn from party games of hidden roles. A minority of agents secretly work as traitors. The rest must sniff them out through talk and reasoning.

The setup rests on game theory, behavioral economics, and social cognition. Metrics track deception success, trust shifts, and group inference quality. Agents carry memory and social dynamics across rounds. Three models played ten runs each in early tests. The strongest model, GPT-4o, lied best yet fell hardest for others' lies. Deception skill, it seems, grows faster than lie detection.
arxiv-2505-13123:
Snehashis Majhi and co-authors present PI-VAD in a 2025 paper on weakly supervised video anomaly detection. Standard methods use only color video features, which can confuse events that look alike, such as shoplifting and normal handling. Real world reliability needs richer cues.

Their framework adds five extra signal types to the video stream. They cover fine motion from pose, three dimensional scene layout, surrounding objects, global motion, and language cues. Two plug in modules create prototype features for each signal and fold them into the main video features. The aim is stronger detection with only weak labels.
arxiv-2505-13723:
Pratik Rathore and co-authors speed up Gaussian process inference with an approximate sketch-and-project solver. Their 2025 paper targets a scaling wall: these probabilistic models give predictions with honest uncertainty, but inference needs solving a linear system that grows fast with data size. Big modern data sets break the standard approach.

Their distributed algorithm sketches the system down, projects, and accelerates the iteration. Theory drawn from random sampling processes shows the estimated average prediction converges quickly to the true one, along the directions that matter most. Tests beat leading solvers on benchmarks and on a large optimization task. The method even handled a data set with hundreds of millions of samples, a scale the authors say is new for this model class.
arxiv-2505-13923:
Chinedu Emmanuel Mbonu and co-authors present a study from two thousand twenty-five on recognizing African foods in photos. Food recognition software works well for Western dishes but has barely been tried on African cuisines. Closing that gap matters for diet apps, health tracking, and cultural coverage in image tools.

The team compared a fine-tuned deep network, ResNet50, with a classic support vector machine classifier. Their dataset held about sixteen hundred images across six African food categories. They scored both systems with a confusion matrix and measures of accuracy, precision, recall, and overall balance. The paper reports where each method wins and where it fails. The authors aim to push food recognition beyond its usual Western menu.
arxiv-2505-14023: Debam Biswas and Yulin Cai work in algebraic geometry in a 2025 paper. They study divisors, an object used across the field, when the divisors carry extra metric data and are extended to a compact setting over an adelic curve. For any such divisor, they build a concave transform, a function that captures its shape in a simpler form.
