They then prove a formula of Hilbert-Samuel type for a well-behaved class of these divisors. The result links the new transform to classic counts in the geometry of varieties.
arxiv-2505-14323:
Robert Allison, Tomasz Maciążek, and Henry Bourne protect trained image models in a paper from 2025. Attackers can sometimes rebuild private training photos from a model's details. A common defense adds noise during training, but it works poorly when each class has few photos. The team shows that weakness with new attacks on models adapted from prior training.

Their fix locks the adapted weights with a form of encryption that still allows computing. Inputs stay plain, but outputs stay locked until a trusted key holder opens them. Attackers then cannot rebuild training data from the outputs. The method avoids the accuracy loss of the noise defense. It also costs less than locking the whole model.
arxiv-2505-14423:
Ona de Gibert and co-authors manufacture training data for the languages machine translation forgot. Low-resource languages lack the parallel sentences translation models eat, but large language models can write plausible ones. Their 2025 paper builds a document-level synthetic corpus from English parliamentary text and pivots it outward to 147 more language pairs.

Human and automatic checks found the synthetic data broadly good. The team then studied how to use it. They asked which training regimes work, how it stacks against an existing web-mined corpus, how much of it is enough, and whether it helps beyond pairs involving English. Even noisy synthetic data, they conclude, substantially improves translation for low-resource languages. The corpus is released publicly as SynOPUS, a standing repository of synthetic parallel text, so the recipe becomes infrastructure other teams can build on rather than a one-off result.
arxiv-2505-14523:
Michael Sullivan argues that language models should read logic, not raw text, and builds one to prove it. A model fed formal logical structures starts with grammar and meaning already encoded, so it may learn from far less data. His 2025 paper introduces GFoLDS, a pretrained model over graph representations of logical forms.

Trained on the same data as a standard transformer, the graph model won downstream tasks by wide margins. The built-in structure lets it pick up complex patterns early instead of spending data on basics. Scaling checks suggest more size and more data would widen the lead. The work is a proof of concept with teeth. NLP researchers get evidence that representation, not just scale, buys efficiency.
arxiv-2505-14723:
Subrata Biswas, Mohammad Nur Hossain Khan, and Bashima Islam present a compact system for understanding spoken commands, in a paper from 2025. Voice tools on small devices must be both accurate and light. Past work shrank models in two separate steps, which left gains on the table.

Their method trains a small model and squeezes its numbers together in stages, tuned for very low precision. It scored well on two standard speech test sets, with only small drops from top models. At the same time it cut computing work and model size by very large factors. Tests under extreme squeezing held up well, which suits phones and home devices.
arxiv-2505-15323:
Grading a language model by its first answer token is fast, but the token can mislead the grade. Silvia Cappelletti and co-authors fix that fragility with a prompt trick in a 2025 paper. Their trick, called prefilling, starts the model's reply with a set phrase like the correct option is. The phrase steers the model to give a clean option token at once. No model weights are changed.

With prefilling, first-token grading gains in accuracy, calibration, and steadiness across many models. It often matches the slower full-answer grading that needs extra sorting tools. Two failure modes are named: tokens aimed at the wrong thing, and answer tokens buried in filler talk. The method began in safety work and is here turned to measurement.
arxiv-2505-15423:
Marcell Kurbucz and co-authors present SplitWise, a way to let plain regression models bend without losing their clarity. Step-by-step regression is easy to read but only fits straight lines unless the analyst reshapes the inputs by hand. SplitWise uses small decision trees to cut a numeric input at learned thresholds and turn it into yes-no features, keeping a cut only when a standard score says the model truly improves.

The method ships as an R package and was tested on both made-up and real data. It repeatedly produced smaller, clearer models that held up better on new data than standard stepwise methods and penalized rivals. The authors pitch it for fields that need flexible fits they can still explain.
arxiv-2505-15523:
Yang-hao Chan, Jonah Haber, Mit Naik, Diana Qiu, and Felipe da Jornada wrote this physics paper, published in 2025. It computes how defects in an atom-thin semiconductor change the way the material absorbs and emits light.

Excitons, bound pairs of electrons and holes, govern the light response of these materials, and defects trap them. Computer simulations usually need unrealistically dense defects to see the effect. The authors instead use a first-principles T-matrix method, which folds defect scattering into an averaged picture of the material. The method captured bound states where excitons stick to defects. Its predicted glow spectra matched experiments well. The team offers the approach as a fast, accurate route to modeling imperfect two-dimensional materials for light-based and quantum devices.
arxiv-2505-15623:
Tiasa Singha Roy and co-authors probed whether language models truly grasp math in a 2025 paper. Models can post high scores on math tests, yet most tests grade only the final answer. A right answer can hide shaky steps, and a wrong one can hide near-right logic, so the score alone misleads.

Their MAPLE score grades the reasoning itself: slips, wasted steps, and whether each step is valid. That fuller read names the pitfalls that plain accuracy masks. It shows where multi-step logic frays as problems grow. Such a grade could steer training toward sound steps, not lucky landings.
arxiv-2505-15723:
Abdur Rehman and Daniel Floryan modeled a bendy foil that swims in a wavy flow. Their paper, from twenty twenty-five, starts from how animals swim and fly in mixed flows with grace. Their foil is set on a spring, heaved by a set move, and left to pitch free. The in flow joins a plain stream with a traveling wave. A linear, no friction model reads the thrust that comes out.

Next to the known resonance peak, the wavy flow brings an anti peak at set wave speeds. There fresh forces fight the lift forces. The flow also cancels with itself, so the foil acts as a low pass sieve. Readers in bio inspired flight get new terms for foil craft in waves.
arxiv-2505-16723:
Thibaud Gloaguen and co-authors hide a language model's fingerprint in the style of its answers, in a 2025 paper. Owners need to prove a model is theirs, but classic fingerprints teach fixed odd replies to fixed questions. Fine-tuning or compression erases them, and filters can spot and strip them. The new scheme ties the mark to a whole topic instead: prompts in French, say, draw subtly watermarked replies.

The watermark spreads statistically through each answer, too diffuse to notice or scrub. Owners probe with any question in the chosen domain to verify the mark. Thorough tests show the fingerprint survives the standard deployment steps that kill older schemes.
arxiv-2505-16823:
Fan Wu and co-authors publish an open dataset for finding position indoors by light. Their system reads the strength of signals from optical wireless sources, cheap and accurate, but public test data for it barely exist. The team recorded in two rooms, one empty and one blocked by a metal column to break the line of sight. A small vehicle drove through at three speeds while the team logged light readings, motion sensors, and true positions.

The haul exceeds 110,000 data points across more than 80 minutes. Benchmarks in the paper show light-based positioning alone, then the gain from blending in the motion data through a Kalman filter. The authors release everything so other groups can test indoor localisation methods on shared, realistic ground instead of each collecting their own room data.
arxiv-2505-16923:
AI models sent into the open world must know when an input lies outside what they were trained on. Yuhui Zhang and three co-authors present TULiP in 2025, a method that scores a model's uncertainty after training is done. It imagines a small nudge to the model's weights just before training ended, and bounds what that nudge would change.

The score is built from a set of sample predictions made under such nudges. On large test sets for spotting out of place images, TULiP reached top level results, above all on samples close to the training data, where spotting errors is hardest. The authors ground the method in theory rather than trial and error. They offer it as a safety tool for image systems.
arxiv-2505-17023:
Chateau-Laurent and co-authors make music with untrained neural networks in a 2025 paper. Big music AI raises worries about power use, copied work, and dulled craft. Their system, ReMi, starts from random wiring with no training data at all. Fed simple inputs, the loops produce arpeggios and slow swells that players can shape.

The point is aid, not replacement: the tool widens what a musician can try while sipping power. Settings steer the patterns in real time, so the system acts like an instrument. The authors contrast their light setup with end-to-end generators trained on huge song stores. A project page hosts sounds and details for players who want to test it.
arxiv-2505-17123:
Xiaoyuan Li and co-authors build a test track for language models that must reason across many turns, in a 2025 paper. Most reasoning exams are one-shot: a question, then an answer. Real problem solving talks back, with environments that respond and push. Their benchmark, MTR-Bench, packs forty tasks in four classes and several thousand test cases, all needing sustained interaction.

Difficulty is graded finely within each task. Both the test items and the grading are fully automatic, so the benchmark scales without human judges. Even the strongest current reasoning models stumbled badly on the multi-turn tasks. The authors mine those failures for lessons. Interactive reasoning, they conclude, is the next frontier for model evaluation.
arxiv-2505-17523:
Fred Diamond and Kassaei study modular forms on special strata inside Hilbert modular varieties. Each stratum is a Goren-Oort locus, a slice cut out by conditions at a prime. They ask which weights can occur for nonzero forms living on such a slice. Those weights form a cone, and the authors pin it down for every stratum.

The cones are not simply spanned by the classic Hasse invariants, as one might guess. The team then defines a smaller minimal cone for each stratum and computes those too. For the main case, any Hecke eigenform on a stratum can be matched by one with the same eigenvalues and weight inside the minimal cone.
arxiv-2505-17623:
Rahimi, Khalaj, and co-authors make outsourced AI answers checkable without rerunning them, in a 2025 paper. Blockchains and shared compute nets farm out heavy neural-net work to strangers. Trusting a stranger's answer is risky, and redoing the work defeats the point. Their frame, Range-Arithmetic, turns each awkward step of a net's math into plain sums and range claims that a proof system can check.

The design skips the usual heavy tools: no bit-by-bit encoding, no giant tables, no steep formulas. Tests show it matches older verifiers on speed while cutting three costs at once: the checker's work, the doer's extra work, and the traffic between them. The authors aim the frame at shared machine learning markets where proof must stay cheap.
arxiv-2505-17723:
Benoît Jeanson and Simon Tindemans add risk thinking to the choice of which power lines to switch off on purpose, in work from 2025. Grid operators sometimes open lines to keep the rest safe. In weaker sub-networks, policy may accept losing part of the grid rather than breaking hard limits.

The paper first sets out that policy plainly. It then extends the standard mixed-integer model of safe switching with grid-loss checks for single line failures. Links that keep the network whole get special care. Tests on a standard fourteen-bus system match what operators do in practice. A known pattern appears: early openings that foreshadow cascades. The model helps planners price risk before acting.
arxiv-2505-17823:
Roa-Dabike and co-authors present a 2025 paper on separating the instruments in small classical music ensembles. Splitting pop songs into parts works well with deep learning, but classical pieces resist. Their sound varies more, ground-truth recordings are scarce, and similar instruments blur together. The Cadenza project tackles the problem to remix music for listeners with hearing loss.

The team built a synthesized woodwind data set to fix gaps in an older one. Separate neural models each pull out one string or woodwind voice. Both live, causal processing and offline modes were tested, since hearing aids need the live kind. Results were graded on two small real-music sets.
arxiv-2505-18123:
Dragan Prekrat clarifies a key step in a geometric reading of a noncommutative field model in this 2025 comment. The model, named for Grosse and Wulkenhaar, adds a harmonic term to tame its quantum behavior. A 2010 paper recast that term as background curvature.

Prekrat shows one section of that work used a simpler stand-in term. The real term mixes ordinary and star products, not star products alone. With the correction made, the main curvature conclusion still stands. The match between model settings and curvature, though, must be revised. The fix also settles a puzzle about vacuum solutions in a special limit. Comments like this keep the literature self-correcting.
arxiv-2505-18223:
Data analysis with language models is rarely a one-shot task, and a 2025 paper by Hanyu Li and co-authors builds a test for that back-and-forth work. Real analysts change course as they learn more about a dataset. Most current tests miss that loop by scoring only single turns.

Their test, drawn from complex public notebooks, gives tasks as a chain of plain-language steps from a simulated user. Scores compare the agent's final numbers with human results. Even the best coding agents passed fewer than half the tasks. The authors say models must balance following steps with thinking ahead. The test gives builders a harder, fairer gauge of agent skill.
arxiv-2505-18323:
Nicolas Küchler, Ivan Petrov, Conrad Grobler, and Ilia Shumailov demonstrated in 2025 a darker species of neural network backdoor, one that lives in the architecture and feeds on batching. Classic backdoors flip a model's answer on a trigger. Architectural versions, planted in the model's design, had recently raised the stakes.

Modern serving groups many users' requests into one batch for speed. The team shows a backdoor can be built to exploit exactly that. Information leaks between requests sharing a batch, and an attacker can steer answers sent to other users in it. The theft is not of one answer but of neighbors' data at scale. Readers, above all model deployers, get a warning with a mechanism: the batch, that innocent efficiency, is an attack surface.
arxiv-2505-18423:
Outlining organs in medical scans fails most at the borders, where small structures blur into their neighbors. Afshin Bozorgpour, Sina Ghorbani Kolahi, Reza Azad, Ilker Hacihaliloglu, and Dorit Merhof present CENet in a 2025 paper. Their network adds two parts: a block that sharpens borders in the skip paths, and an attention module in the decoder. The first helps spot smaller organs with context in mind.

The second keeps spatial detail while cutting repeated features. Tests covered X-ray style scans and skin lesion photos. The network beat leading rivals on multi-organ outlining and border quality. Code was released in public. The authors pitch it for mixed-domain hospital use.
arxiv-2505-18623:
Neural networks can learn to run classic algorithms from examples, but how faithfully do they copy the method, and why do they fail when they fail? Saldyt and Kambhampati attack the question with neural compilation. Instead of training, they write a known algorithm directly into a network's settings, so the network computes it exactly. That gives a perfect yardstick for judging learned versions.

They study graph networks on three search and path algorithms, covering cases where learning works well, works faithfully, and fails. Comparing compiled and learned networks exposes gaps between what a network can express and what training can find. The authors suspect learning succeeds mainly for parallel-style algorithms in a known complexity class. The work frames a basic weakness in how networks pick up step-by-step reasoning from data alone.
arxiv-2505-18923:
Yile Li and Shandian Zhe present a study from twenty twenty-five on learning operators that map one function to the answer of an equation. Past stars in this field need a neat grid of points. Real domains are often bent, with points spread in a wild way. Their frame, GOLA, builds a graph from the loose points and learns on that graph.

Attention in the graph net lets far points share facts. A wave based encoder with learnable tones lifts the input function into a rich code, even from sparse points. Tests span four kinds of two dimensional equations. Gains show most when data is scarce. The frame held up across densities of points.
arxiv-2505-19223:
Fengqi Zhu and ten co-authors improve how diffusion-based language models learn from human preferences, in a 2025 study. Their base model, LLaDA, writes text by unmasking words step by step rather than left to right. Tuning such models with preference data is hard, since the score estimates swing wildly. The team studies that swing, bounds it, and builds fixes that cut it without bias.

The fixes spend sampling effort where it pays most and pair samples to cancel noise. The tuned model, LLaDA 1.5, beat its predecessor on math, code, and chat tests by clear margins. It also held its own against strong models of both major types on math tasks. The authors share a project page with demos. They frame the method as a general recipe for aligning diffusion language models.
arxiv-2505-19623:
Yu Shang and colleagues benchmark language model agents as personal recommenders, in work from 2025. Agent recommenders reason and role play to craft picks that adapt to each user. No shared test ground existed to grade those agents against classic methods fairly.

An interactive text simulator stages classic, shifting taste, and cold start scenarios. Rich user and item records feed the agents inside each test scene. A modular frame lets builders swap agent parts for study and comparison. Ten classic and agent methods faced the same benchmark tasks head on. Agent systems won overall, and part level lessons guide future builds.
arxiv-2505-19923:
Learning from a fixed log of past actions, offline reinforcement learning must beware of trusting values for moves the log never tried. Qin-Wen Luo and three co-authors note that the usual fix, holding the learner back everywhere with one strength, backfires. Too weak lets fantasy values creep in; too strong reduces learning to copying the log.

Their method adapts the restraint state by state, trusting Bellman updates where the data is good and clamping down selectively on strong actions elsewhere. They connect the idea to two mainstream approaches and extend it to both. On the standard D4RL benchmark, the method beat leading rivals in both pure offline tests and offline-to-online fine-tuning. The paper appears in 2025.
arxiv-2505-20023:
Yihan Chen and four co-authors train small open language models to act as agents that reflect on and fix their own errors, in a paper from twenty twenty-five. Most capable agents lean on private models and crafty prompting. Training open models on teacher demonstrations alone stalls and copies mistakes.

Their method builds synthetic practice runs in which errors are marked, reflected on, and corrected. A masking trick stops the student from absorbing the wrong steps during training. On three testbeds covering home tasks, web shopping, and science tasks, trained models improved broadly. One seven-billion-parameter model gained ground while using less training data than methods based on spotless expert runs.
arxiv-2505-20123:
Huijie Zhang and co-authors present a 2025 paper on measuring generalization in diffusion models. The head title frames the work around diffusion distillation. Distillation shrinks big diffusion models into fast, few-step ones. Judging whether the small model generalizes or just memorizes is hard. Theory metrics fail on real high-dimensional data. The team offers a metric called probability flow distance. It compares the noise-to-data maps of two distributions under the model's flow equation.

With that ruler, several behaviors come into view. A scaling path from memorization to generalization is charted. A double descent across training epochs appears as well. Model teams get a practical, theory-backed generalization check. Copyright and privacy audits also need such checks, since memorized outputs carry legal risk. The distillation setting is where speed pressure makes memorization most tempting.
arxiv-2505-20323:
Shahriar Noroozizadeh and co-authors build in 2025 a vast timed set from case tales of lone patients in open med files. Sick folk paths live in tale form, yet large timed sets to learn from were scarce. Their build turns tales to event and time pairs by a large model chain.

The set holds near one hundred twenty five thou sand tales and over five mil lion timed events, plus age, sex, and ill tags. A hand checked gold set scores the build on event match, time rank, and time gap. Prompt and model picks are tried side by side. The set is free for time line and fate work.
arxiv-2505-20423:
Julio de la Torre-Vanegas and co-authors present a vision based emergency landing method for drones in cities in a 2025 paper. Landing safely among crowds, cars, and shifting light is hard, above all in an emergency. Their method uses a neural network that rates risk pixel by pixel in the drone's view. A search step then picks a steady low risk landing zone, even as hazards move.

A control system steers the drone toward that zone, with safety limits that depend on height and checks that the spot stays stable over time. Field tests in varied urban scenes passed ninety percent of landings, even in very hard cases. Risk scores improved as well. Readers see a practical path to safer forced landings.
arxiv-2505-20523:
Priyanka Patel, Francesc Molina, and Albert Guillén i Fàbregas study how much data can be sent when the receiver decodes with a slightly wrong rule. In real systems, the channel is never known exactly, so decoders work from a guess. Their 2025 paper treats channels that sit close to the decoding rule, within a small ball measured by relative entropy. For both letter-like and continuous channels, they derive near-exact formulas for the worst-case data rate and for how fast errors fall.

The formulas show the price of a wrong guess as the ball grows. Examples cover symmetric rules and noise with wrap-around structure. Such results help engineers set margins: how much rate to give up so a system stays safe when the channel drifts. The work is pure theory with direct design use.
arxiv-2505-20823:
Mohammad Aarabi and six co-authors simulate the first instants of a molecule flipping shape under light, and find a clean ringing pattern in the newborn product, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Their model molecule is a small retinal-like cation, the kind of switch behind vision chemistry. The model keeps two electronic states and three vibration modes.

The team first tackles a practical worry: getting quantum dynamics runs for such twisting motion to settle at all. Only with tight convergence does the big-amplitude twist emerge correctly in the simulation. With that settled, the product isomer forms with a coherent back-and-forth oscillation in the early moments. The authors link the two points, arguing that sloppy convergence would smear away exactly this signal.
arxiv-2505-20923: Marius Müller studies a harder version of a classic free-boundary problem in a 2025 paper. The usual energy cost is replaced by a bending energy that also cares about direction, making the problem higher order and anisotropic. He proves that smooth direction-dependence does not spoil the best smoothness expected of the winning shapes. The proof needs a new directional version of a classic estimate for the biharmonic equation, and it opens the door to further higher-order free-boundary work.
arxiv-2505-21223:
Power, Umansky and Soukhanovskii simulate the churning mode in a snowflake divertor, a plasma exhaust design with two nearby magnetic null points. The churning mode is a toroidally symmetric vortex near those nulls. A reduced magnetohydrodynamic model with field-aligned heat flow drives the runs, tuned to conditions like those of the MAST-U tokamak.

When the nulls sit close and plasma pressure is high enough, the mode adds transport across the null points, growing as the gap shrinks. A diffusion model can match total transport, but the mode also warps the flux surfaces themselves. As a result, the share of exhaust power sent to each divertor leg can swing sharply, even flipping legs at small angles.
arxiv-2505-21323:
Martin Škoudlil, Michal Sojka, and Zdeněk Hanzálek present a 2025 study of robot software written in Rust, a modern systems language. Robot builders increasingly code with the ROS 2 platform in Rust, often in its async style. Timing proof tools for ROS 2 cover the older C++ style, not async Rust. The team maps how the async Rust binding runs tasks and clocks them.

They set out a structure for such apps: set thread ranks and pin each callback to a set thread. Tests on a mock app show the structure beats other setups on end-to-end delay. A self-driving case study shows the plan works in a real stack. Bounded response times open the door to formal timing checks for Rust robot code.
arxiv-2505-21723:
Are old-school stats dead now that deep nets can fit near any curve? Skyler Wu, Shihao Yang, and Samuel Kou put the claim to a test in 2025 on back-solving rate equations. Two test worlds served: a spread-of-disease model and a chaos model. A physics-fed net stood for deep learning; a curve method bound to the true paths stood for stats.

The catalog title drags grant thanks into the line, and its author field is garbled; the head gives the clean title and byline. On sparse, noisy data the stats method won on bias and spread, with far fewer knobs to tune. It also called the future better, where the big net strayed with no data to hold it. Small math slips hurt the net more as runs grew long. The team close: lean stats still earn their place.
arxiv-2505-22423:
Jonathan Hill derives max laws of large numbers in two thousand twenty five. High dimensional arrays with weak dependence need new limit theory. The maximum across many coordinates is the statistic of interest. Dimension grows with sample size in his triangular arrays.

Weak and strong max laws come with convergence rates attached. Three dependence settings structure the analysis: independence, tau mixing, physical dependence. Martingale style coordinates improve the allowed dimension growth. Three uses show the payoff of the bounds. Max correlation screening and high dimensional testing both extend. Partialling out nuisance parameters fits the frame as well.
arxiv-2505-22523:
Junwen Chen and colleagues at Microsoft Research Asia release open data for images built in transparent layers. Their paper appeared in two thousand twenty-five. Layered images let editors move or restyle each part alone. Text-to-image models rarely produce them well. The blocker is training data: large, clean sets of layered transparent images did not exist. The team attacks that gap on three fronts.

First, they publish PrismLayers, a dataset of two hundred thousand layered images with accurate alpha mattes. A higher-grade subset holds twenty thousand. Second, a synthesis pipeline makes more such data on demand from stock diffusion models. No training is needed for the pipeline itself. Third, their open model ART+ generates layered images at modern quality. Creative tools gain room to grow.
arxiv-2505-22623:
Seokjin Moon and David Limmer build a theory for chemical reactions whose speed is set by diffusion in systems held away from equilibrium, in a paper from 2025. Standard rate theory quietly assumes calm, balanced conditions. Driven systems, pushed by fields or flows, break those assumptions, and rates can stray far from textbook values.

Using transition path theory, the authors generalize the link between reaction rate and the flow of successful reaction paths. A thermodynamic analysis then shows how injected work bounds how much a rate can be boosted over its equilibrium value. A solvable model, ions pairing under a strong electric field, checks the theory end to end. The results frame how far engineers can push reaction speeds in driven settings.
arxiv-2505-22723:
Max Uetrecht and four co-authors study quantum phase changes in this two thousand twenty-five physics paper. Some two-dimensional materials hold Dirac particles that interact strongly. Near the borders between a semimetal state and two ordered states, odd quantum behavior can appear. The authors model this with field theories that couple Dirac fermions to two order fields. Each field has its own symmetry.

They apply a method called the renormalization group, carried to three-loop order. Two cases matter: orders that clash and orders that can coexist. In the coexisting case, a larger shared symmetry can emerge at the meeting point. Its stability depends on the number of fermion flavors. The work maps when such multicritical points can survive. It guides the study of exotic states in quantum materials.
arxiv-2505-22823:
Wang and Atanasova taught models to fix their own explanations in this paper from twenty twenty-five. Language models explain their answers in words, but the words often stray from the model's real reasons. Their framework, SR-NLE, loops a model through critique and rewrite rounds. No outside labels or extra training are involved.

Feedback comes in two flavors: the model's own comments, and word-importance maps that flag load-bearing inputs. Tests covered three datasets and four leading models. The best setup cut the unfaithfulness rate from about fifty-five percent to about thirty-six percent. The gains held across the models tried. The authors say the right feedback lets models police their own explanations.
arxiv-2505-23323:
Madabushi, Torgbi, and Bonial argue that large language models solve tasks by extrapolating from patterns in their training data, steered by context. Debate often frames model behavior as either parroting or near human reasoning. Their 2025 position paper offers a middle account, called context-directed extrapolation.

Examples in a prompt steer base models toward the right stored patterns, which is how in-context learning works, they say. Instruction tuning lets a prompt do the same steering without examples. The authors supply an evaluation checklist and design patterns to separate memory, basic extrapolation, and true generalization in tests. Adopting this frame, they argue, would calibrate claims about reasoning and improve deployment decisions.
arxiv-2505-23523:
Arjun Devraj and four co-authors sped up a core training synchronization step that slow chips usually stall in a 2025 paper. In distributed learning, all processors must pool their updates together, and the pool waits for the last arrival. Their algorithm puts the waiting time to work.

While stragglers catch up, the ready processors run a partial pooling among themselves. A new finishing routine then completes the job once the last chip lands. Theory promises up to double speed on large clusters, beating a bound that holds for lockstep methods. On an eight-chip server the gain over top rivals was twenty-five percent. The authors exploit a simple truth: chips never arrive exactly together, so the schedule should not pretend they do.
arxiv-2505-23623:
Jiaoda Li and Ryan Cotterell pin down exactly what a simplified transformer language model can and cannot express. Their idealization uses fixed numerical precision, blocks attention to the future, uses soft attention, and drops position markers. Within those rules, the model's power matches a specific fragment of temporal logic that uses only a single operator, one that talks about the past.

That fragment also lines up with known classes from automata theory and algebra, giving one unified map of this model's reach. Experiments agree with the math. Trained transformers generalize across text lengths on languages inside the boundary and consistently fail on languages outside it.
arxiv-2505-23823:
Youngseung Jeon and five co-authors present a 2025 benchmark for question answering on protein-protein interactions in drug discovery. Knowing what a protein pair does in the body guides target choice for new drugs. Language models with retrieval can help, but no test set measured their skill at this task.

Their benchmark, RAGPPI, holds 4,420 question-answer pairs on the biological effects of protein pairs. Experts set the rules for question type and sources. A gold set of 500 pairs was labeled by hand. An ensemble judge model, tuned to expert labels, then built a silver set of 3,720 pairs. The authors pledge to maintain the resource for the research community.
arxiv-2505-23923:
Feiteng Fang and colleagues improved reward modeling for open-ended AI tasks in 2025. Reward models grade model answers so the model can learn from the grades. Grading is easy for math, where answers check out, but hard for role-play and other matters of taste, where two answers may both seem fine and the gap between them is fuzzy.

Their method adjusts that gap on the fly, using knowledge already inside the model to judge how clear-cut each pair is. Two versions do this without extra human labels. On public grading tests and on role-play tasks, the approach scored answers more reliably. Sharper grading of fuzzy tasks could make chat models more pleasing without more annotation cost.
arxiv-2505-24023:
Sangwon Jung and co-authors measure fairness in text-to-image models in a 2025 paper. These models draw pictures from text prompts, but they can understate some groups or lean on stereotypes. Groups defined by combined traits, such as age and gender together, face the sharpest erasure. No standard method existed to measure and fix such harms across many groups at once.

The team defines a score that tracks the worst gap in how often any group appears, compared with its fair share. Users can set the groups and shares to fit their setting. They also give a training method that pushes the score down. In tests, models trained this way drew a more balanced mix of people while keeping image quality high.
arxiv-2505-24223:
Jean-Benoit Delbrouck and co-authors argue that radiology reports should be written to a fixed structure, and build the tools to generate and grade them. Their paper appeared in 2025. Free-text chest X-ray reports vary so much that both learning from them and judging quality are hard. The team used large language models to rewrite public report collections into a strict standard format, creating a training set for the new task.

They also trained a fine-grained disease classifier on fifty-five labels to score generated reports by clinical content, and proposed a matching score built on it. The authors say structure makes reports clearer for doctors and measurable for machines, a double win for automating a heavy clinical chore.
arxiv-2505-24323:
A fresh shock wave ripples through two galaxy clusters about to collide, in a 2025 paper by Yanling Chen and co-authors. The pair, cataloged as 1E2215 and 1E2216, is a major merger caught early, a phase astronomers seldom witness, and axial and equatorial shocks were already known in it.

Deep X-ray images from two telescopes, totaling about three hundred thousand seconds of exposure, sharpened the view of the southern outskirts. A new shock front appears a short distance south of the brighter cluster's peak. Its brightness jump and temperature jump agree across both telescopes, each implying a gentle Mach number near 1.2. The front's age and placement suggest it was born from the same event as the known equatorial shock.
arxiv-2505-24523:
Andrea Pedrotti and co-authors stress-tested detectors of machine-written text in 2025. As language models write ever more human-like prose, spotting their output matters for fighting fakes. Detectors lean on style clues, which may be a soft spot.

The team fine-tuned writer models with preference training to bend their style toward human writing. Few examples were needed: detection scores dropped hard after the shift. Three leading detectors were put through the pipeline. The authors also track which language traits moved and which ones detectors rely on. Their warning is plain: benchmarks must test unseen, in-domain text, and detectors need to harden against style attacks.
arxiv-2505-24723:
Lukas Fuchs and co-authors catch a standing wave inside a turbulent bubble behind a ramp. Their 2025 paper deals with separation bubbles, whose slow breathing motion rides on large swirls. Time-resolved flow films in two planes feed a spectral split of the motion field. A dominant slow mode matches known breathing. The cross-span films, though, expose a fresh pattern: fixed nodes and antinodes across the span, like a plucked string.

A model that stacks left and right running waves between the side walls copies the measured modes well. A stability read traces the root to a centrifugal quirk, with lift-up growth downstream.
arxiv-2506-00023:
Yu Zhang and Bing-Zhao Li build a sampling method for graph signals based on a joint time and vertex fractional Fourier transform. Graph signal methods handle data on networks that change over time. Their work came out in twenty twenty-five.

The team sets the sampling theory by finding when band limited signals in this joint frame can be fully rebuilt. They also give a plan to pick the best sampling set. Local sampling tools are designed to speed work on large time vertex signals. Tests on made and real data show gains in rebuild exactness and computing speed, the authors report.
arxiv-2506-00123:
Large models that read images and text are being asked to drive robots, but seeing, reasoning, and moving are usually trained apart. Gen Luo and co-authors unify the three in 2025 in a system called VeBrain. It turns robot control into text tasks drawn in the image plane, then converts the model's words into motion through a small adapter.

A new data set of six hundred thousand guided examples, mixing skills in single conversations, teaches the blend. Across eighteen test suites the system beat strong general models, and on legged robots and arms it gained about half again on task success. The authors present it as one brain for space aware machines. Flexibility across bodies is their headline claim.
arxiv-2506-00223:
Mohammad Saleh Hasankhani presents LatMixSol, a 2025 method to predict how well molecules dissolve. Solubility forecasts guide early drug hunting. Labeled data are scarce, and molecule descriptors run to many dimensions. LatMixSol first squeezes descriptors into a compact latent space with an autoencoder.

Spectral clustering then groups like molecules together. New training samples are blended inside each cluster, mixup style. The blended points decode back into full descriptor form. On a standard solubility benchmark, gains held steady across runs. More training data without new lab work is the draw. The trick may lift other small-data molecule tasks.
arxiv-2506-00623:
Zdziarski and four co-authors reviewed black hole spins in X-ray binaries in twenty twenty-five and their clash with gravitational wave results. Spin is how fast a black hole rotates, scaled from zero to one. Merging black holes seen by wave detectors spin slowly on average, suggesting black holes are born spinning slowly.

Most published spins for black holes feeding in X-ray binaries are instead near maximal. Binaries with massive companion stars are the sharpest puzzle, since their short lives leave no time to spin up by feeding. The authors argue the measurement methods carry large systematic errors. One relies on splitting X-ray spectra uncertainly; the other uses disk models that predict instability where stability is seen. Corrected models give lower spins, easing the tension.
arxiv-2506-00723:
Some reports claim that large language models can forecast future events as well as skilled humans. Daniel Paleka and co-authors urge care with such claims in a 2025 paper. They argue that testing a model's forecasting skill is much trickier than it looks.

The authors sort the traps into two groups. The first is leakage, where facts from after the forecast date sneak into the test and inflate scores. The second is the gap between test scores and real-world skill, which may not carry over. With examples from past studies, they show how these flaws can prop up weak claims. The paper calls for stricter test designs before anyone trusts a model forecaster.
arxiv-2506-01023:
Lu and co-authors present in 2025 a speech cleaning model built for real time use on a single sound channel. Noise can hide speech in calls and recordings, and good cleaning needs clues from sound spots near the target spot. Their model draws on those nearby spots at both entry and exit of the network.

A sub band part gathers clues from nearby pitches at the start. A deep filter part then refines the target spot and its neighbors, split into time and pitch stages to cut cost. A new block boosts feature picking. In tests, the model beat leading systems while using fewer resources, which suits live speech tools.
arxiv-2506-01323:
Waldo Gálvez and co-authors start the study of computing many different good triangulations of one polygon, in this 2025 paper. A triangulation cuts a polygon into triangles with non-crossing diagonals. Their problem asks for a set of triangulations that are both near-best in quality and as different from each other as possible.

The team gives an efficient approximation method that finds such a set, with variety close to the best possible. They also study triangulations that balance two quality goals at once. Both problems turn out to be hard in the strict sense. For a stricter notion of variety, they give a slower method that still guarantees half the best spread.
arxiv-2506-01523:
Jihun Yun and co-authors rebuild the theory of aligning language models with human taste, in a 2025 paper. The standard recipe, reinforcement learning from human feedback, works in practice yet lacked a firm proof of why its goal is the right one. Rival methods were each analyzed in their own frame, blocking comparison.

The team recasts alignment as learning a distribution from pairwise preferences. Three clean objectives fall out of that view, each with fast, proven convergence. One of them closely mirrors the standard recipe, which at last justifies it. The theory also explains why on policy methods tend to beat offline ones in practice.
arxiv-2506-01623:
Ajsal Palattuparambil, Thommen Karimpanal, and Santu Rana published a computing paper in 2025 on teaching learning agents to reuse skills on like tasks by analogy. People transfer knowledge between tasks with little relearning, while agents usually retrain from scratch. Their framework, MAGIK, maps things in a new task to their matches in a known task through an imagination step. The agent then reuses its old policy without touching the new setting.

Tests on grid and robot control tasks show strong zero-shot transfer from only a few human-labeled examples. Comparisons with related methods highlight the analogy mapping as the key gain. The authors present imagination-based mapping as a fresh route to transfer.
arxiv-2506-01723:
Soyoung Oh and co-authors trace how language models handle idioms, whose figurative meanings clash with their literal ones. Their paper appeared in 2025. The team used causal tracing, switching parts of the model's activity on and off to find what carries each meaning. They located three mechanisms. Early layers fetch the figurative reading and quiet the literal one.

When context comes first, the model uses it from the very first layer and revises its reading if the context clashes. Later, two paths compete: one favors the figurative meaning and a direct route favors the literal one. Both readings stay alive until the end. The authors say this tug-of-war explains both the models' skill with idioms and their occasional literal-minded slips.
arxiv-2506-01923:
Amin Karimi Monsefi and co-authors present TaxaDiffusion in a 2025 paper on making images of animal species. Species that share roots look close, with gaps in fine traits of shape, pattern, and color. Standard image makers treat each species as its own box and miss those links.

Training climbs the tree of life step by step, from broad class down to species. Broad traits shared by kin are learned first, then fine gaps are sharpened at each lower rung. That order lets the model learn from kin when samples for one species are few. Tests on three fine grained animal sets beat past methods on image faithfulness. The project page shows samples and code links for the work.
arxiv-2506-02523:
Robin Geens and Marian Verhelst analyze a memory-saving attention design from the hardware side in this 2025 paper. DeepSeek's latent attention squeezes key and value data into a compact space, shrinking the cache models must keep. How that change plays out on chips was unexamined.

The authors compare two ways to run the design, reusing stored projections or recomputing them, which trade memory traffic against arithmetic. Modeling across platforms shows the design shifts attention work toward the compute-bound side. It uses far less bandwidth than standard attention and stays steadier on bandwidth-poor hardware. Execution can be adapted to each chip's limits. The authors frame the design as a co-design opportunity for future AI accelerators.
arxiv-2506-02923:
Explaining an AI agent's behavior often means guessing its goals and beliefs, then predicting what it will do next. Alexis Bellot, Jonathan Richens, and Tom Everitt ask how far that guessing can possibly go in a 2025 theory paper.

Assuming the agent plans with an inner model of the world, the authors derive hard bounds on prediction in new settings. The bounds mark a ceiling for any method that learns only from watching behavior. No amount of clever inference can beat them in general. The results carry lessons for fairness checks and safety cases, where teams must say how an agent will act in places it was never tested. The paper gives those claims a firm floor and ceiling.
arxiv-2506-03023:
The TDCOSMO collaboration measures cosmological parameters from the time delays of strongly lensed quasars, in a 2025 paper. When a galaxy bends a distant quasar's light into several images, flickers arrive at different times, and those delays encode the universe's expansion rate. The method lives or dies on knowing the lens galaxy's mass in detail.

The new sample holds eight lensed quasars, backed by fresh velocity measurements from the Webb, Keck, and Very Large telescopes. Two extra samples of non-delay lenses sharpen the mass models. The team also improved treatment of matter along the line of sight, lens light profiles, and star orbit shapes. Careful bookkeeping like this decides whether lensing can referee the Hubble tension.
arxiv-2506-03323:
Flor Sanders and five co-authors use learning models on small edge hardware to set the pulses that run a type of quantum gate. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-five.

Such gates act on multi-level units held in microwave spaces. The best pulse sets are found by hard classic methods, on big machines with long lag. That lag bars their use in live runs. The team makes training data with the classic way, trains models, tests design choices, and shrinks the models to fit edge chips. The aim is quick, true-to-target pulse picks that can run at the machine itself. Such speed could make fine quantum control of use in real work.
arxiv-2506-03423:
Mahoney, Grayden and John test in 2025 whether EEG sensors placed under the scalp, but above the skull, can serve brain-computer interfaces meant for long-term use. In sheep experiments, they recorded sensory signals with fine spatial detail. They also classified motor execution from the signals with above-chance accuracy. Features in space, time, and frequency could be identified clearly.

The team says the signal quality approaches that of more invasive methods, such as surface arrays on the brain or stents inside blood vessels. Because sub-scalp placement is less invasive, they argue it suits chronic, everyday interface use.
arxiv-2506-03623:
Gugyum Ha, Junkee Jeon, and Jihoon Ok study in this 2025 paper the math behind an American chooser option, a contract that lets its holder pick call or put at exercise time. Its price solves an obstacle problem, where the price sits above a floor set by the better of two plain American options. That floor has a kink where the two option values cross, which makes the math delicate.

The authors build a solution with truncation, penalization, and comparison tools, and prove it is the only one in its growth class. They show contact with the floor happens only on the smooth branches, and that both contact zones appear at every time. The two free boundaries then get sharp traits, ending in full smoothness.
arxiv-2506-03723:
Chaeyun Jang and four co-authors studied what happens when a language model is trained to state its own confidence, in a paper from twenty twenty-five. Safe use of such models depends on honest confidence scores. Past work on this mostly covered short answers, not the step-by-step reasoning these models now produce.

Training on confidence labels alone, with no examples of checking, still taught the models to check themselves. On questions where confidence was low, answers grew longer and included self-checks. On high-confidence questions, answers stayed short. The authors add a rethinking step that uses the confidence score at test time. Scores and accuracy both improved on math and reasoning tests.
arxiv-2506-03923:
Mohammadamin Shafiei, Hamidreza Saffari, and Nafise Sadat Moosavi built this 2025 benchmark exposing a wording bias in AI reasoning. The same math comparison, phrased with the word more or less, can tilt a model's answer toward that word. Their test set, MathComp, holds 300 comparison scenes, each asked in fourteen phrasings across three model families.

Errors often leaned the way the prompt leaned, even though the numbers never changed. Step-by-step reasoning cut the bias, but rigid formats sometimes kept or revived it. Adding identity terms like a woman or a Black person to a scene made the drift worse, despite identical amounts. The authors argue that fairness checks must include framing, not just final answers.
arxiv-2506-04523:
Cliff Abbott, Mark Elo, and Dmytro Bozhko introduce perturbative gradient training, a way to train networks that contain physical reservoirs, published in 2025. Physical reservoir computing uses real physical systems for computation, with energy efficiency gains in view. Its blocker is that backpropagation cannot run through a black-box physical device.

The new method borrows from perturbation theory in physics: random nudges in the parameter space approximate gradient updates using only forward passes. It was tested on simulated networks, including a dense network and a transformer with a reservoir layer. It was also run on real hardware, a magnonic auto-oscillation ring acting as the reservoir. Performance matched standard backpropagation in cases where that method is impractical or impossible, the authors report.
arxiv-2506-04623:
Li, Yu, and Alahi recast three dimensional scene filling as object detection in twenty twenty-five. Self driving systems must map which cubes of space are filled and by what. Past tools classed each cube alone, which blurs object edges and drops whole items. Their trick turns cube labels into object offset labels for free.

VoxDet then splits the job into offset finding and class naming. A special encoder keeps the two feature streams apart. Offsets to object borders guide how class evidence pools per item. The system topped a public leaderboard on a standard driving set. It runs on camera or laser input alike.
arxiv-2506-04723:
Jiayu Wang and six colleagues wrote a 2025 paper on how reinforcement learning improves math reasoning in language models. Training by reward has raised scores a lot on hard problems. Yet why the training works, step by step, stayed murky.

Their frame, SPARKLE, splits reasoning into three parts for close study. It tracks how a model follows a plan, how it pulls in stored knowledge, and how it chains subproblems. Scores alone hide which of these parts gained most. The authors use the split to find sharp, sometimes surprising effects. One involves what happens when the model is handed extra hints. Such insight can guide the next round of training methods.
arxiv-2506-05023:
Enno Adler, Stefan Böttcher, and Rita Hartel showed HyperCSA in 2025, a squeezing method for hypergraphs. Hypergraphs catch relationships including whole groups at once, co-authorships, social memberships, recommendations, and they grow large enough to strain storage, transmission, and query speed. Earlier squeezing methods either answered queries slowly or stopped scaling.

HyperCSA adapts suffix sorting, a method from text squeezing, to squeeze hypergraphs while still supporting standard queries on the squeezed form. On real-world hypergraphs it shrank files to between roughly a quarter and four fifths of their first size, beating current methods on every large test case. And it handled bigger data sets than its rivals. Neighbor queries, a basic operation, ran many times faster than on both normal data forms and competing squeezed versions.
arxiv-2506-05423:
Wong and Rivers argue that recent cosmic data need no phantom dark energy if the universe's degrees of freedom count as extensive. Phantom energy, which would tear physics oddly, was invoked to fit new baryon acoustic oscillation results. Their setting is Tsallis entropic cosmology with three spatial dimensions. In that frame the expansion history takes a linearized form.

That form matches cosmic chronometer readings and the new survey data out to a redshift a little above two. It also respects the microwave background's acoustic scale, a tight early-universe constraint. The need for phantom behavior simply vanishes. So does the need for a large cold dark matter density, in their account. The paper offers an entropy-first route through a live cosmological tension. Whether the extensive assumption holds is left for further tests.
arxiv-2506-05623:
Tianyi Zhang and co-authors test whether language models can write cloud setup code that truly deploys in a 2025 paper. Such templates are often judged on looks, yet real worth is whether they run. Top models passed that bar on only a fifth to a third of first tries.

A new benchmark grades more than one hundred fifty real scenarios across many services. Their framework, IaCGen, loops through format, syntax, and live deploy checks, fixing errors each round. Within ten rounds most templates became deployable. Direct human hints on deploy errors lifted results further. The work mirrors how DevOps teams ship in practice.
arxiv-2506-05823:
Lohse and co-authors measure a nuclear phase shift with a double slit shrunk to the nanoscale, in a 2025 paper. How much a wave's phase bends at a resonance reveals how light and matter couple, but at X-ray wavelengths such measures are brutally hard. The team built paired X-ray waveguides, a Young-style interferometer, tuned to the 14.4 keV resonance of iron-57 nuclei.

From single-photon interference patterns, sharpened by Bayesian fitting, they read the phase shift near the resonance with fine energy detail. Phase plus absorption together exposed coupling values that brightness alone hides. The device points toward chip-scale X-ray sensors for probing tiny samples.
arxiv-2506-06223:
Raphaël Berthon, Joost-Pieter Katoen, and Zihan Zhou simplify a link between two game types in 2025. Stochastic parity games carry rich winning rules, while simple stochastic games use plain reach goals. Fast solvers exist for the simple kind, so reducing the rich kind to it is valuable.

Earlier reductions passed through several middle models. Their direct reduction runs in polynomial time and uses gadgets to erase the priority rule. The built simple game mimics the parity game's behavior, and correctness is proven formally. Under binary encoding the reduction stays polynomial, matching the known complexity class of parity games.
arxiv-2506-06423:
Gero von Gersdorff and Lucas Modesto prove sharp limits on the Standard Model's Yukawa couplings in this 2025 paper. These couplings set the masses of quarks and how the quark types mix. The authors show the coupling matrices obey a set of plain but strong inequalities. The results hold in any choice of field basis.

Among other things, the bounds tightly restrict how the columns of the up-type and down-type matrices can line up. The same holds for their cofactor matrices. The strength of the bounds traces back to the steep ladder of fermion masses and the small mixing angles. Model builders can use the inequalities as strict tests any flavor theory must pass.
arxiv-2506-06623:
Runtong Pan and five co-authors test neural operators on a classic fluids problem in a 2025 paper. The problem links three curves for a fluid in a tight space: how dense it is, how it correlates, and what outside push it feels. Solving those links by hand is slow, so learned models could speed the work.

The team trained several model types on exact answers for a one dimensional rod fluid. One design, the Fourier neural operator, gave the best free energy values. A second family did best with a special multiscale network inside it. The trained models then solved for density curves under new pushes and matched the known answers well in most cases they tried.
arxiv-2506-06723:
Zihe Zhou, Harsha Honnappa, and Raghu Pasupathy wrote this 2025 paper on tuning systems that evolve under chance. Many problems in operations, learning, and statistics can be framed as picking the drift, the average push, of a random process. The process must also obey path limits set by a smooth regulator. The authors build a workable method for this endless-dimension problem.

Their method replaces the true problem with a sampled average version. Building it takes three cuts: slicing paths, slicing the function space, and sampling by simulation. They derive path-wise slopes to drive the search, then prove the method stays consistent. Cost counts guide how to split computing effort between search steps and the cuts. The result is a recipe others can actually run.
arxiv-2506-06823:
Qi Li and co-authors ask whether visual prompting can inherit the robustness of a hardened source model, in a 2025 paper. Visual prompting adapts a frozen model to new tasks by learning a small input pattern. Past work used ordinary source models, leaving the robust case open.

The authors answer three questions in the affirmative: robustness does transfer, a trade off with generalization does appear, and a tailored fix helps. Their fix, prompt boundary loosening, is a light add on that fits the prompting setup naturally. Across many datasets it preserved the inherited robustness while lifting accuracy on new tasks. The authors call the benefits broad and consistent. The work gives a recipe for safer transfer to new vision tasks.
arxiv-2506-06923:
Xutong Zhao and a large team teach language models to check their own math work as they go, in a paper from twenty twenty-five. Self-correction usually runs as a second pass, steered by extra prompts. That design misses the chance to catch an error the moment it appears.

Their method makes one model play two roles in a single pass: proposer and verifier. Solution steps and checks weave together, and generation stops when a check fails. Training used synthetic examples of this woven style, then online reinforcement learning to sharpen both roles. Gains were large across math benchmarks, for both a small and a large model. The authors frame the trick as a way to spend test-time compute wisely.
arxiv-2506-07423:
Janghyeon Yun and Sang-goo Lee wrote this paper in two thousand twenty-five. It fixes a hidden flaw in text-to-SQL tools: the best test sets hand the model a note of domain facts, as if users were experts.

Real users lack that lore, and even the hand-made notes in the BIRD set miss facts or get them wrong. Their system, SEED, builds such notes on its own from the schema, the file notes, and the stored values. On BIRD and Spider it lifts SQL scores a lot in the no-note case. At times it even beats the runs that got the human notes. The work ties lab scores back to real use.
arxiv-2506-07823:
Lorenzo Amatucci and co-authors speed up motion planning for legged robots by moving the math onto graphics chips. Their 2025 paper presents a controller that looks ahead over a horizon and picks the best moves. The core solve step is rebuilt so work spreads across both time steps and state parts at once. A scan method handles the linked system in far fewer steps than older solvers need.

Trials against two leading solvers show strong gains. Runtime improves by a large share for whole-body planning and by several-fold for a simpler body model as the horizon grows. The solver also scales well with state size. One shared controller can steer many legged robots at once within a tight time budget. Since the code runs in a learning-friendly framework, training can include the controller in the loop.
arxiv-2506-08023:
Qifeng Wu and five co-authors build a search engine that finds proteins by shape and meaning together. Labs increasingly solve protein structures without knowing what the proteins do. The team borrows the recipe of vision-language models: train one network on structures and another on written descriptions, pulling matching pairs together and pushing others apart.

They assembled about two hundred thousand protein-caption pairs with rich functional notes for training. The finished model retrieves look-alike, like-meaning proteins from the main structure database. It also handled a harder test, searching across into an electron microscopy database it was not trained on, without any retraining. The authors argue such multimodal foundation models can speed up the interpretation of new structures from imaging methods like cryo-electron microscopy.
arxiv-2506-08123:
Jacob Dineen and ten co-authors present a 2025 method for aligning large language models with stated values, called QA-LIGN. Alignment training usually leans on a single reward score, which hides which value drives the signal. Their method breaks the reward apart into checks tied to named values such as helpfulness, honesty, and harmlessness.

Models learn through a draft, critique, and revise loop, with clear written feedback on each value check. Applied to an open model, the method cut the success rate of attacks by up to about sixty-nine percent. It kept false refusals near zero, at well under one percent. The team reports that it beat two rival training methods at the same cost and argues that open, split rewards make alignment work better.
arxiv-2506-08323:
Hanyang Wang and Gary Slater study in 2025 how cut DNA fragments spread out inside a narrow channel. Long DNA can be mapped by cutting it with enzymes while it sits in such a channel. Once cut, the pieces drift apart by random motion and by crowding effects, until a device can tell them apart and guess their size.

The team used random sim methods to time that spread for pieces of unlike size, each with its own drift rate. The spread time counts as a first-passage time: the wait till the pieces reach a set final spread. Chance in the drift proved as strong a factor as the size mix itself. They define a randomness score for the order of pieces that tracks the final spread time in a straight line. Spread times follow a known first-passage shape.
arxiv-2506-08923:
Holly Casaletto, Jeff Lefevre, Aldrin Montana, and Peter Alvaro present a database design that does useful extra work during a costly housekeeping step, in a 2025 paper. The storage engines they study keep new writes in logs and later merge them in a process called compaction. That merging is needed, but it eats input and output capacity.

Instead of only fighting that cost, their design embeds data transformations into compaction itself. Their prototype, Mycelium, builds on a popular engine and merges across data groups. It can split column groups, convert formats, and build indexes while merging. Tests with standard workloads showed a twenty percent write cost, far below naive methods that transform data apart from compaction. Read delays improved greatly against the base engine in the best cases.
arxiv-2506-09123:
Skylar Grayson and co-authors compare the hot gas halos around galaxies in the real sky against two leading universe simulations, in a 2025 paper. Galaxies sit inside vast atmospheres of hot gas, the circumgalactic medium, shaped by the energy black holes blast out. That feedback is dialled into simulations by hand and poorly constrained. New X-ray observations from the eROSITA telescope now measure the halos' glow directly.

The team generated fake eROSITA observations from the EAGLE and SIMBA simulations and compared them with real stacked images of galaxies grouped by mass and star formation. SIMBA matched the glow's profile better, but neither simulation agreed across all galaxy types. The differences traced mainly to halo gas density near the centre. The test gives simulation builders a concrete target: get the inner halo's density right.
arxiv-2506-09323:
Sang, Hour, and Han teach a compiler to place quantum operations across linked quantum chips with as little cross-chip traffic as possible. Splitting a quantum computer into modules helps it scale, but moving quantum states between chips adds noise and cost. Their 2025 system, QARMA, learns placement and routing with a deep learning method that pays attention to both the whole circuit and local links.

An extension adds qubit reuse, recycling freed qubits mid-circuit through measurement and reset. Against a strong standard compiler, the reuse version cut cross-chip operations by up to one hundred percent in tests, averaging eighty-six percent. The base version still gained on larger circuits. The authors say such compilers let bigger algorithms run on limited modular hardware.
arxiv-2506-09423:
Koushik Pradhan and co-authors report two new compounds and study one of them in depth in this 2025 paper. Both solids mix calcium with oxygen and two metals in a neat double pattern. A prior machine learning search had flagged both as worth making, and lab work confirmed they form as predicted.

The cobalt and ruthenium compound drew the most interest. Math models suggest ruthenium sits in a rare charge state, and the solid acts like a metal for one spin of its electrons only. That spin split, plus a twist in its bands, should yield a strong sideways voltage in a magnetic field. The team urges lab tests to check these forecasts.
arxiv-2506-10423:
Tony Alex and six co-authors find a cheaper way to feed sound into large language models, in a 2025 paper. Machines that listen must hand what they hear to a model built for text, and the usual handoff is costly.

The standard scheme converts sound into tokens and prepends them to the text stream. The authors' lighter scheme injects the sound only through the model's attention layers, skipping the heavy parts. Their hybrid, PAL, prepends a few summary tokens and streams the rest the light way. Across models and tasks, the light method matched or beat the standard one, with gains up to 30 percent. It used about 60 percent less memory and ran about twice as fast.
arxiv-2506-10623:
Julien Berestycki, David Geldbach, and Michel Pain study a branching random walk in this two thousand twenty-five math paper. Particles wander in the plane and split into offspring as they go. The split rate depends on direction: it peaks straight ahead and falls off at a set power of the angle. The question is how far the cloud's edge reaches over time. Slower breeding off-axis drags the front below its usual speed.

The authors find the exact correction to the front's position. It includes a polynomial slowdown term and a logarithmic one, with constants tied to an operator's first eigenvalue. They also show the front's random wobble stays bounded. The result sharpens theory for spread in direction-dependent environments, from epidemics to invasive species.
arxiv-2506-10823:
Particle detectors at the upgraded Large Hadron Collider will soak up radiation doses that eat their own signal. Marco Bomben, named in full in the head byline, simulates that damage in a solo 2025 paper to predict how planar pixel sensors will cope.

The work validates a combined simulation chain, device physics plus particle tracking, against real irradiated modules. Several models of how radiation traps charge were compared to find which predicts best. The winner then forecasts the charge these sensors will still collect at the collider's expected doses. Reliable forecasts set the operating voltages and tell track-finding software how much signal loss to expect, decisions that must be locked years before the collisions begin.
arxiv-2506-11023:
Tomas Bueno Momcilovic and co-authors turn assurance cases into a queryable web of facts, so safety arguments can be kept live as systems change. Their 2025 paper deals with the structured cases that firms build to trust a product's safety or strength. Hand-kept cases rot fast when the system shifts, and false trust can follow.

Their kit, OntoGSN, rests on an ontology, a formal map of the standard notation for such cases. It mirrors the community standard rule by rule, adds a bridge to a popular case tool, and ships a library of ready queries. Graphs built this way can be filled, checked, and updated by machine. A test interface shows the workflow.
arxiv-2506-11123:
Ziming Mao and co-authors present SAE-BrainMap, a 2025 framework that links vision model features to brain activity. Sparse autoencoders break model signals into clean single features. The team trained such tools on each layer of a vision model. They then matched feature activity to fMRI scans of people seeing the same images.

Matches were strong, with the best links quite high. Each brain voxel got assigned its closest model feature, forming a voxel dictionary. Those features kept the layout of known visual brain regions. A layer-by-layer map tied model depth to the human ventral visual path. The work gives a shared language for minds and machines.
arxiv-2506-11223:
Jasem Hamoud, Alexei Belov-Kanel, and Duaa Abdullah published this mathematics paper in 2025. It works on graph numbers that grade how uneven a network's connections are. In a tree, a network with no loops, each node has a degree: the count of its links.

Two such numbers take center stage. The Albertson index adds up degree gaps across every link, and the Sigma index squares those gaps first. The authors study trees whose degree lists follow the Fibonacci pattern, a famous number sequence. For those trees, they give an exact formula for the Albertson index. They also bound its smallest and largest values across tree shapes, and tie it to two other known indices. Such bounds help chemists who use these numbers to guess molecule traits.
arxiv-2506-11323:
Submanifolds of complex hyperbolic space carry a twisting structure in their normal directions. Santiago Castañeda-Montoya and Carlos E Olmos prove a clean fact about it. The restricted normal holonomy group always acts transitively, as long as a certain nullity index vanishes. The twin setting of complex projective space behaves differently, where a Berger-type restriction holds instead.

Their proof lifts the submanifold into a pseudo-Riemannian space and develops new tools for the degeneracies that arise there, including a notion of weakly polar actions. The authors suggest the machinery will help with submanifold geometry in indefinite-signature spaces more broadly. The paper appears in 2025.
arxiv-2506-11623:
Thomas Faestermann and Roman Gernhäuser review recent claims of spotting a bound cluster of four neutrons, in a 2025 paper. Such a tetraneutron would be a purely neutral nucleus. Experiments used transfer, knockout, fragmentation, and light-driven breakup to make neutron quartets. Facilities and methods differed widely between attempts. Results partly contradict each other across the reports.

The authors propose a reconciling picture. Some groups may have seen a bound ground state. Others may have caught an unbound yet correlated state at higher energy. Both signals could then be real but distinct. Theoretical work on the system is surveyed alongside. Binding four neutrons strains nuclear force models either way. Confirming the state's nature remains an open experimental chase. The review organizes a confusing record for the field.
arxiv-2506-11723:
Ziren Xiao, Ruxin Xiao, Chang Liu, and Xinheng Wang build a light deep learning method to guide many robots that haul materials in smart factories in real time. Multi robot teamwork is now core to such plants, and good planning saves energy and cost. Their work came out in twenty twenty-five.

The task sends many sources to one target point, with routes that must update live. Past methods list near best routes but learn little from past runs, or use only bits of past paths, and they slow down on large maps. The new method trains fast with a target guided reward. A trained model picks the next move in a flash, far faster than past plans.
arxiv-2506-12323:
Janet Wang, Yunbei Zhang, Zhengming Ding, and Jihun Hamm build a system that fakes skin disease photos with expert guidance, in a 2025 paper. Diagnostic software needs many example images, but real patient photos are scarce and private. Image generators can fill the gap, yet they often draw diseases wrong, which then teaches the diagnostic software errors.

Their framework, MAGIC, turns doctors' written criteria into feedback that steers the generator. A large vision-language model acts as a tireless stand-in judge, scoring drafts against the criteria so real dermatologists need not grade thousands of images. The synthetic photos matched expert judgment far better than unguided output. Adding them to training data raised accuracy on a hard twenty-disease test by about nine points, and by about fourteen points when real examples were few.
arxiv-2506-12423:
Kniazev, Istomin, and Beskin test pulsar physics against new sky survey data from two large radio telescope programs, in a paper from 2025. The catalog creator field carries a copyright line and journal marks, but the head byline is clean. The surveys greatly expanded the set of pulsars with detailed polarization profiles.

The data confirm that one wave mode forms clearly wider average profiles than the other. They also support a classic vacuum model of particle creation near the star's poles. A slow drift of the magnetic axis toward a right angle with the spin axis gained further support. The authors say the larger sample firms up each of these long debated points.
arxiv-2506-12523:
Montanari and Aldini wrote in twenty twenty-five about digital proofs that a person took part in an activity. Proof of attendance shows someone was at an event, in person or online. The authors extend that idea to proof of engagement in wider settings. A user may want to prove involvement in many kinds of activities. They compare designs using shared ledgers with designs using central systems. Each design makes different trade-offs for users.

Privacy for the user is a central concern in their survey. Scope in time and place also varies between designs. Some proofs can be transferred to others, and some cannot. Rewards for participation can attach to the proof as incentives. The study maps these choices for builders of engagement systems. It weighs openness against control in each option.
arxiv-2506-12623:
A software tutorial video is only useful if a learner can extract the steps without watching all of it. Yuan Zang and seven co-authors built MS4UI, a benchmark for summarizing user-interface instructional videos into concise text instructions paired with key frames. The dataset holds 2,413 videos spanning more than 167 hours, each annotated by hand for segment boundaries, text summary, and video summary.

Existing benchmarks, the authors argue, summarize generic video content at the level of meaning, which misses the executable, step-by-step character that makes a tutorial work. Running current state-of-the-art multimodal summarization methods on their data, they find those methods struggle with the UI setting. The dataset is offered as both a yardstick and a prompt: instructional summarization needs methods of its own.
arxiv-2506-12723:
Ye Li and co-authors present a 2025 method that speeds up robot brains which see, read, and act. Such vision-language-action models steer arms and cars well but run too slowly for live work. Past speedups reshaped the model and missed waste over time and space. SP-VLA splits acts into thought-out ones and gut ones. The big model handles the first kind, while a light maker fills the gaps, lifting the act rate.

A pruning pass also drops image tokens that carry little place or meaning weight. Jointly timed, the two cuts stack. Robots spend most acts on routine moves, so the split fits the work. Live control on cheap hardware is the end goal of such designs.
arxiv-2506-12923:
Pierrick Verwilghen and a large team of co-authors simulate nearby disc galaxies to find when their gas changes shape. Their paper appeared in two thousand twenty-five. Past runs hinted that galaxies above a set mass grow a small, neat inner disc of gas. Lighter galaxies keep their gas in a messy spread instead.

The team ran a wider set of high-detail runs, matched to real nearby galaxies. They tracked the star-forming gas in both mass ranges and mapped its layout. Heavy discs formed a compact core disc, linked by lanes to the ends of the star bar. Light discs showed no such core. These inner discs may form a bridge that feeds gas down to the central black hole. Real sky surveys back the split the runs predict.
arxiv-2506-13123:
Abdelghani Belgaid and Oumnia Ennaji present a software paper, published in 2025, on a toolkit that makes artificial farm data for Africa. Machine learning for African agriculture stalls because real datasets are scarce, holding back precision farming tools.
