The team measured absorption at actinide edges in thorium dioxide and in uranium oxides of two oxidation states. Several theoretical approaches were used to interpret the spectra.

In thorium dioxide, the 5f states were governed mainly by the crystal field of neighboring atoms. In the uranium oxides, by contrast, strong mixing between uranium 5f and oxygen 2p states dominated, raising the 5f occupancy and setting the compounds' properties. Calculations of photoemission spectra for uranium in doped uranium dioxide reinforced the picture. Distinguishing field effects from covalency matters for predicting how nuclear materials age and react.
arxiv-2507-11023:
Jeremy Mould and Adam Batten test the idea that quasars grew from primordial black holes in this 2025 paper. Primordial black holes may have formed before stars, in the hot early universe. If they grew fast, they could seed the giant black holes that power quasars.

The authors work out what this origin predicts for quasar brightness. The predicted spread of brightness matches what telescopes observe. The model also tracks how quasar density changes over cosmic time. Radio galaxies enter the same frame through shared galaxy collisions. Their lower masses fit longer or shorter active lifetimes. A tidy match would reshape how astronomers explain the first giant black holes.
arxiv-2507-11223:
Francesco Ancilotto, Michele Modugno, and Chiara Fort wrote this 2025 physics paper on a thread of quantum liquid that refuses to break into drops. Mixtures of two Bose gases with strong attraction can form self-bound droplets, held together by quantum effects. Stretched into a long filament, such a liquid should suffer the classic capillary instability that splits a stream into beads.

Recent experiments saw that breakup in droplets held in an optical waveguide. The authors study an endless filament held by sideways harmonic confinement. They solve the Bogoliubov-de Gennes equations in a one-component frame and check the results against full simulations. As confinement grows, the instability fades step by step. Past a critical trap strength, it stops in full. The work shows how a trap can protect a quantum thread from a very old fluid effect.
arxiv-2507-11323:
Xiang Yin and co-authors make weighted argument graphs contestable: a user should be able to push an AI decision toward a wanted outcome. In these graphs, arguments attack and support each other with weighted edges, and strengths settle from the weights. The contest problem asks which weights to change so one chosen argument hits a target strength.

Their explanations score how sensitive the target is to each edge, guiding small fixes. An iterative method then nudges weights step by step. Tests on graphs mimicking recommenders and neural nets show the method reaches the target reliably.
arxiv-2507-11423:
Yanjian Zhang and three co-authors tested if language models can be steered among reasoning plans. Their paper, from twenty twenty-five, starts from a human trait: people swap plans by task. Models, by contrast, lean on one plan of thought for all. That lean can cap their reach on mixed tasks. The team asked if prompts can move a model's plan, and what that move does to logic scores.

No one plan won across tasks in their runs. Gains would come if a model could pick its best plan per task on its own. They give ways to guide that pick. Readers who prompt models get a frame for plan choice as a skill of its own.
arxiv-2507-11823:
Yan Lai, Cullan Howlett, and Tamara Davis ask whether using several tracers of galaxies sharpens a cosmic yardstick, in a 2025 paper. The yardstick is a scale in the clustering of matter. It ties to the size of the horizon when matter and radiation were equal. That makes it a tool to test cosmic models.

Using mock data, they forecast how well surveys below a set distance can pin the scale. Pairing galaxy density with galaxy motions did not help, since survey volume or motion data were too thin. Pairing two planned surveys did help, by about 30 percent. A three-survey mix also showed promise. The work guides how future surveys might combine their data.
arxiv-2507-12123:
Sergey Linok and Gleb Naumov present a method for finding named objects inside buildings in this 2025 paper. Their system, OVIGo-3DHSG, builds a layered scene graph from depth camera streams. The graph links floors, rooms, spots, and objects, with their spatial ties spelled out.

Open-word vision models feed the graph, so users can name objects in plain words. A large language model reasons across the layers to answer queries that point at one object through another. Tests on multi-floor indoor scans check both meaning and geometry accuracy. The authors report strong scene grasp and object grounding versus rival methods.
arxiv-2507-12723:
Minyoung Kim and co-authors hide a rescue copy of real audio inside faked videos, in this 2025 paper. Voice cloning plus lip-sync tools now forge audiovisual clips where a target person seems to say anything. Detectors can flag or locate the tampering, but they cannot restore the words actually spoken. That gap leaves victims with proof of fakery yet no truth to publish.

The team defines two new tasks: recovering authentic audio and pinpointing where the audio was tampered with. Their cross-modal watermark embeds recovery data across the media itself, so the original sound can be rebuilt from the forged file. Watermarks that survive editing would give platforms and courts a way to answer a fake with the genuine recording.
arxiv-2507-13023:
Fei Wu, Danning Sui, Thomas Thiery, and Mallesh Pai measure the hidden toll booth between centralized and decentralized crypto exchanges in this 2025 paper. Arbitrageurs skim price gaps between the two worlds, a corner of the maximal extractable value economy long left unmeasured because the centralized half happens off-chain.

Refined detectors found over 7.2 million such arbitrages across nineteen months. Nineteen big searchers extracted an estimated 234 million dollars. The field is concentrating fast: three searchers took three quarters of the volume and the value. Profits tracked how deeply a searcher was fused with the block builders who order transactions, including exclusive pairings. The authors also correct the record on integrated builders' earnings, which earlier work understated. They frame the trade as a live threat to the chain's decentralization.
arxiv-2507-13423:
Edward Henderson and four co-authors built an interpretable graph neural network in twenty twenty-five that estimates air traffic controllers' upcoming workload. Crowded skies strain controllers, and simple aircraft counts miss what actually makes a scenario hard. Their model reads a static traffic scene as a graph and predicts the number of clearances — instructions to aircraft — the controller will soon issue.

Interpretability comes from ablation: remove one aircraft at a time and watch the prediction change, yielding a per-aircraft task demand score. The framework beat a controller-inspired heuristic and proved a more reliable complexity estimator than standard baselines. Attributing demand to specific aircraft could inform controller training and airspace redesign, showing which traffic patterns truly drive workload.
arxiv-2507-13523:
Rading and colleagues with the WAVE Collaboration tested fiber-optic sensing as a stand-in for seismometers in twenty twenty-five. Gravitational wave detectors are limited at low frequencies by Newtonian noise, tiny gravity tugs from moving ground. Canceling it needs dense ground-motion monitoring, but seismometers are costly and sparse.

Distributed acoustic sensing turns a fiber-optic cable into thousands of vibration sensors along its length. Comparing its data with colocated seismometers during natural and controlled events, the team found strong agreement in the three to twenty hertz band that matters for the noise problem. Fiber data predicted geophone signals well and matched geophones at canceling noise in a seismometer, leaving the same small residual. The authors conclude the technique is a scalable alternative for environmental monitoring at observatories.
arxiv-2507-13623:
Rahul Gulia proposes a leaner wireless system in this 2025 study. Modern wireless links join two methods to carry many streams at once, which gives speed and toughness. The catch is high power peaks and heavy drain from many active radio chains, a poor fit for cheap sensors and wide-area low-power networks.

His variant, called MD-OFDM, turns on just one transmit antenna for each slice of the signal band. He works out the math for error rates, energy use, and power peaks under this choice. In simulations, the variant made fewer errors and far lower power peaks than a standard multi-antenna setup. Its peak energy saving was lower, since it gives up some parallel streams. The trade suits battery-run devices, the author argues.
arxiv-2507-13923:
Guillaume Rivière proposes a formal way to record what user studies observe about interaction itself, rather than about one interface. Findings in human computer interaction research often stay tied to one device, design, or task, which blocks replication. His 2025 paper introduces a method he calls interaction loop diffraction to reveal such properties in a calibrated way.

The resulting properties can be checked again across prototypes, technologies, tasks, and user types. Real projects can both use and test these traits while their prototypes improve. Publications from those projects would then feed a shared catalog of properties. Rivière argues this path could grow a cumulative science of interaction for the many interfaces people now meet daily.
arxiv-2507-14423:
Mootez Saad, Hao Li, Tushar Sharma, and Ahmed Hassan study token merging for code models in two thousand twenty-five. Code models split input into tokens, then learn rich codes for them. Token counts run longer than in compilers, which adds compute cost. The team asks what merging subtoken codes does to cost and skill.

They merge codes of subtokens that form one unit, like a name. One route takes the mean, the other learns the merge. Tests span six code models and three tasks. Compute fell by a small to fair share. Skill shifts were small and mixed by task. One task lost a bit, one gained in its score.
arxiv-2507-14523:
Jinyuan Shang and Haiping Hu study how waves settle in uneven grids where travel differs by direction, in a 2025 paper. In a classic effect, disorder traps waves in place. When flow is one-way biased, new odd wave forms appear. The pair focus on a two-dimensional model of this kind. They find mixed modes that cling to an edge along one axis while staying trapped by disorder along the other.

Using a transfer method and size scaling, they map where each kind of mode gives way to another. The map shows a re-entrant pattern, where trapped modes return as settings shift. Their account then extends to any number of dimensions. They also prove the same shifts occur on an endless branching grid, using a forward-scatter method. The work gives a fuller map of how one-way flow and disorder jointly shape waves.
arxiv-2507-14823:
Dong Shu and co-authors benchmark vision-language models on financial charts in a 2025 paper. Charts in finance mix dense time patterns with specialist terms, a blend general chart tests skip. Their FinChart-Bench is the first set built from real financial charts.

Twelve hundred charts from 2015 to 2024 carry over seven thousand questions in true-false, choice, and free-answer forms. Twenty-five leading models were graded. Open models nearly caught closed ones, yet some upgraded versions slipped behind their elders. Many models fumbled instructions, and spatial reasoning stayed weak across the board. The authors warn that current models cannot yet judge such charts reliably either.
arxiv-2507-14923:
Mengyang Cui and co-authors model stray current in silicon infrared detectors in a 2025 paper. These blocked impurity band detectors sense faint heat signals, but dark current, signal with no light at all, limits how well they work. At low voltages the dark current follows a puzzling curved pattern.

The authors propose that sound-like vibrations with a handedness, called chiral phonons, help drive a spin current at the device interfaces. That mechanism, they argue, explains the curved rise at low bias. For the full voltage range they apply a theory of charge transport confined in space. Together the two ideas aim to account for dark current from the lowest working voltages to the highest.
arxiv-2507-15123: Halbeisen, Horvath, and Ozalp prove a consistency result about special ultrafilters in a 2025 set theory paper. A Q-point is a rare kind of ultrafilter with strong selection power. The authors ask how many distinct types set theory can allow at once. Extending an earlier result, they show it is consistent that exactly n Q-points exist, up to sameness of structure, for any finite n. For the case of two, they give a second proof by a long forcing iteration.
arxiv-2507-15323:
Jakob Holstein and co-authors show that cooling boosts the sensitivity of a terahertz detector array. The head of their paper from 2025 frames the work as improving an eight by eight array in a compact low noise cooler. The detectors are transistors with antennas, made in a standard chip process.

Sensitivity kept rising as heat fell, down to twenty degrees above absolute zero in the tests. Projected noise levels at deep cold rival a class of superconducting sensors that need still colder work. The built system uses liquid nitrogen cooling and was tuned for a band near three terahertz. Tests with a laser source showed a wide signal range with no saturation and a fast readout, far past thermal detectors.
arxiv-2507-15723:
Yuqi Zhao proves Sidorenko type inequalities over finite abelian groups in two thousand twenty five. Sidorenko's conjecture bounds homomorphism densities in bipartite graphs. Quasirandom graphs should minimize the density at fixed edge share. The full conjecture stays open despite decades of work.

Szegedy showed Cayley graph hosts suffice to test the claim. Zhao settles it for all even subdivisions of arbitrary graphs. Each edge becomes a path of even length in those graphs. The host is any Cayley graph over an abelian group. Fourier tools turn counts into averages over linear system solutions.
arxiv-2507-15823:
Anton Abilov, Ke Zhang, and Hemank Lamba share lessons on deploying AI for humanitarian groups in a 2025 paper. Most work in this space stops at model building. The messy steps of launch, partner teamwork, and upkeep decide whether a tool helps anyone at all.

The authors describe close work with a network that links aid organizations to each other. Their model had to run in a setting with scarce compute and patchy support. The paper covers how the system is kept updated as conditions change. Practical takeaways address budgets, partner trust, and long-term maintenance. The account aims to help other teams move from promising demos to tools that survive in the field.
arxiv-2507-16323:
Amit Ben-Artzy and Roy Schwartz let word models spell their outs one glyph at a time through twin heads. The work dates to 2025. Wide word sets cut text length but swell the out layer in step, a hard cap on growth. Small tongues pay most for that cap.

Their form splits in and out word sets. A set of small heads each call one glyph at once, so the out space grows vast with lean parts. A self-teach path turns a stock model to the new form. Four stock models kept task grade in the new form and ran a shade fast. The path may cut costs and widen tongue reach.
arxiv-2507-16423:
Planetary boundaries mark the safe operating space for Earth, but no gauge connects a single election, war, or law to those dials. Orfeu Bertolami and Ricardo Elisio propose one in a 2025 paper: an interacting matrix that couples sociopolitical events to the boundary variables.

With boundaries following logistic growth, the model shows how an exponentially intensifying event can drive a runaway in the coupled system. That runaway is the anatomy of a crisis. Stacked crises become a policrisis, and the authors propose a way to describe, classify, and compare whole syndromes of them. The paper is a framework proposal rather than a forecast. It offers a language in which feedback between politics and the Earth system can be written down and compared across cases.
arxiv-2507-16523:
Umberto Borla, Ayush De, and Snir Gazit map the phase diagram of an odd toric code in a 2025 paper. The model adds a fixed background of electric and magnetic charges to a lattice gauge system. Large tensor network and exact calculations chart its phases under a tilted field.

Alongside a deconfined phase and a plain paramagnet, confinement and Higgs routes each produce valence bond solids with patterned order. On the self dual line sits an unusual multicritical point where confinement, Higgs condensation, pattern order, and duality breaking all switch on together. The change looks continuous, with both charge types softening at finite momentum. Wider unit cell solids hint at frustration driven order beyond simple patterns.
arxiv-2507-16623:
Frederic Jonske and co-authors present a system that writes clinical reports with help from fine-grained image maps. Their 2025 method extends a known vision-language model used for medical report drafting. Safe use needs both strong overall skill and a way to ground each claim in the image.

The system fuses mid-level image features and detailed segmentation maps from specialist models into the main model. Only a small set of new parameters is added. Scores rise with features alone and rise more when maps are added too. Gains over two rival map-based methods are larger still. Any number of maps can be fed in, so report lines can be traced back to image regions.
arxiv-2507-16723:
Philippe Brax, writing alone in 2025, revisits a classic claim about dark energy and what it rules out. He studies models where a light field called the dilaton acts as dark energy. The field comes from broken scale symmetry, a deep idea about size in physics.

Brax shows that quantum effects from gravity screen the field near Earth, so local tests see no odd force. He then tracks how the field's push on cosmic growth changes over time. In these models, the push can cross a key line that plain models cannot cross. That crossing stays small at late times unless the field has a tiny mass near the Hubble rate. The limit holds for a broad class of screened models, which narrows what dark energy can do.
arxiv-2507-16823:
Michael Young reports that the card game Collapsi is strongly solved. The 2025 arXiv paper analyzes play on a toroidal board. Sixteen shuffled cards form the board for two pawns. Players move by the value of the card they sit on. A player with no legal move loses the game.

Symmetry cuts the deal count low enough for exhaustive search. The solver finds an optimal move in about twenty milliseconds. The first player can force a win in most deals. The second player wins all remaining deals. Some losing positions can stretch the game to fourteen plies. No forced win arrives in fewer than seven plies. The result closes the game's theory completely.
arxiv-2507-17323:
Yang and a team including Zhu present EndoFinder in twenty twenty-five, a tool to help doctors judge growths in the colon. Such growths, called polyps, can turn into cancer if missed or misjudged. AI tools can help, but they often act as black boxes and need huge labeled data sets. Doctors also want to see the past cases behind a call.

EndoFinder learns the look of a polyp from many views and sums them into one code. That code lets it fetch like cases from a store of past polyps in real time. The fetched cases show why the tool made its call. Tests on public and new data beat older methods on accuracy.
arxiv-2507-17523:
Abhishek Kumar and co-authors report in 2025 the first year of a solar wind sensor aboard India's Aditya-L1 solar mission. The craft sits at a stable point between Sun and Earth and watches the solar wind near full time. Ion spectra feed values for density, speed, and heat of the wind.

Checks against two other missions show the sensor reads in line with peers. A case study tracks a solar mass burst from August twenty twenty four in close detail. Early data came even before the craft settled into its halo orbit. The team maps science the sensor can serve in coming years.
arxiv-2507-17923:
Zachary Nathan, Daniel DiPietro, and Olivia Chu wrote this 2025 study on selfless behavior and energy flow in beehives. Bees live in castes of workers, drones, and a queen. In their breeding system, unfertilized eggs become males and fertilized eggs become females, which creates odd patterns of kinship. Workers often act for the hive at cost to themselves, and the team asked how that selflessness links to the breeding pattern.

The authors built a model that tracks hive numbers over time and varied how selfless workers and the queen were. Hive success needed strong worker selflessness, at levels matching the task split seen in real social species. A modest level of queen selflessness also proved vital for the hive to survive. The authors read the results as a sign of how giving, breeding, and social life grew up together in these insects.
arxiv-2507-18223:
Nenad Petrovic and five co-authors describe a generative AI pipeline that carries car software from written requirements to code running on vehicle hardware, in this 2025 paper. The target is driver assistance and self driving features, where safety rules make development slow. Their workflow asks large language models to do much of the drafting at each stage.

The models first turn requirements into formal model files, with consistency checks borrowed from model driven engineering. They then generate test scenarios, helped by a retrieval step that pulls in driving regulations. Simulation code in Python and target code in C++ follow from the same chain. The authors aim at shorter compliance cycles and less rework when requirements change. The paper frames language models as tireless junior engineers inside a guarded process.
arxiv-2507-18623:
Xuhui Kang and co-authors built a benchmark in 2025 for the kind of teamwork where two partners carry something heavy. Most human-AI joint work tests live in software, but actual joint work adds steady motion, forces. And hard constraints: a couch must be kept level, a table turned through a doorway in one coordinated motion. Their benchmark, Moving Out, simulates a household move with two built tasks spanning a range of joint work modes shaped by weight and geometry.

The authors collected human-human contact data on the tasks, giving them a reference for how people adapt to a partner's actions and to objects with unseen actual traits. To meet the benchmark's challenges they propose BASS, a method joining actions augmentation, model. And selection to widen an agent's repertoire of plans and deepen its grasp of what its actions will do. And they test how far current models get.
arxiv-2507-18723: Vishakh Begari shares a 2025 data set of guitar tablature files built for teaching computers to write and learn guitar phrases. The files come in a common guitar software format and were adapted from two large piano data sets. Rhythm guitar tracks were drawn from the note data, then dressed with bends, slides, vibrato, and palm muting so the phrases play like real guitar work rather than flat keyboard lines.
arxiv-2507-18923:
Zhentao Huang and three co-authors rebuild accurate surfaces from 3D Gaussian splats. Their 2025 paper presents GSSR, a reconstruction method. Gaussian splatting renders new views well but places its blobs loosely. Uneven blobs blur the true surface and fight later editing.

The method tunes each Gaussian's place on its own. Normal agreement is enforced at pixel and blob levels, across one view and many. A fading penalty prunes needless blobs. Periodic resets, guided by depth and normals, tidy the spread. Rebuilt scenes showed far sharper placement precision. Clean surfaces also make scenes easier to edit and reuse.
arxiv-2507-19023:
Ben Andrews and Sophie Chen extend a smoothness yardstick method to non-local heat equations. Their twenty twenty-five paper uses the modulus of continuity, a measure of how much a solution can vary over distance. The two-point method has proven strong results for classic parabolic equations.

For non-local flow on the whole space, an initial yardstick is preserved if its odd twin solves a related one-dimensional problem. The result covers smooth and singular kernels, including the fractional Laplacian. Trouble starts on bounded domains: a smooth counterexample kills the plain version in one dimension and beyond. A spectral twist there ties to a classic eigenvalue question, and the paper maps that too.
arxiv-2507-19223:
Jack Davey and three co-authors test in 2025 whether lopsided error bars on exoplanet spectra distort what scientists infer about planet atmospheres. Retrieval codes usually assume equal upper and lower errors. Fresh telescope data are sharp enough that the shortcut deserves a check.

Two likelihood forms face off: a symmetric Gaussian and an asymmetric split normal. At the asymmetry seen in one well-studied planet, about seventy-seven percent at most, inferred values barely move. At stronger average asymmetry near eighty percent, the choice turns critical. Fitting the shape of lopsided errors from three summary numbers proves tricky. A wrong shape yields wrong parameters, so care in error modeling matters as data sharpen.
arxiv-2507-19323:
Ruojing Peng, Lachlan P Lindoy, and Joonho Lee analyze a discretization step in a method for modeling quantum dynamics that remember their past, published in 2025. The transfer tensor method is a discrete-time form of a classic quantum master equation. A recent paper raised doubts about its consistency, pointing to an extra term at the initial time.

The authors trace where that initial-time term comes from in the discrete scheme. They set up a consistent link between the discrete memory kernel and its continuous-time counterpart. Tests on the spin-boson model confirm the link, with kernels and dynamics converging as the time step shrinks. They note that other schemes are also viable, and that comparing schemes fairly is work still to do.
arxiv-2507-19623:
Prabrisha Rakshit, Xu Shi, and Eric Tchetgen Tchetgen rescue causal estimates when some stand-in variables lie. Hidden confounding blocks many treatment studies, so researchers use proxies, observed variables tied to the hidden ones. Valid proxies must obey strict exclusion rules. With many proxies in play, some surely break the rules and bias the answer.

The team derives exact conditions for identification when an unknown subset of proxies is invalid. In a standard linear model, a penalized median estimator picks the valid proxies while estimating the effect. A flaw in that selector's consistency prompts an adaptive version with uneven penalties. The adaptive estimator converges at the standard rate and yields valid intervals when a sound outcome proxy exists. Extensions cover invalid outcome proxies too. Simulations and a real application support the theory.
arxiv-2507-19823:
Dongquan Yang and co-authors present a way to shrink the memory cache that large language models keep while they read long texts, in a 2025 paper. That cache grows huge with long inputs, and past shrinking methods lose much accuracy once memory falls by more than 85 percent. Their method mixes three moves: it packs the keys, moves the values off the graphics chip, and drops stale entries on the fly.

On a long-text benchmark, the method kept full-model accuracy while cutting the cache to a quarter of its size. It stayed competitive at an eighth of the cache. The authors also ran a model on four million tokens using a single graphics card.
arxiv-2507-19923:
Ohkubo and Hirabayashi report that a long-missing fourth broad hump exists in the scattering pattern of two carbon nuclei. Their 2025 paper deals with rainbows in nuclear physics, where a beam bends much like light in a rain shower. The humps, nicknamed Airy elephants, are split by dips and reveal the force between the two nuclei.

A puzzle had stood for years: one key dip crossed a right angle at a far lower energy for carbon on carbon than for kindred systems. A second rainbow, found later, held the clue. The team shows that the second rainbow's dip crosses the right angle near the expected energy, which proves a fourth hump sits between the two dips and closes the old question.
arxiv-2507-20023:
Vikas Tokala and five co-authors present, in a 2025 paper, a speech-cleaning network for two-ear devices, from hearing aids to virtual reality headsets. Such tools must lift speech out of noise while keeping the sense of where sounds come from, which one-ear cleaning destroys. Their network works end to end on the complex sound signal.

The design stacks a convolutional encoder and decoder around a memory block that handles complex values. It outputs a mask for each ear in the time-frequency plane. A new loss rule grades not only clarity and noise cut but also how well the spatial cues survive. Against baseline methods, the system raised estimated intelligibility and cut noise in scenes with one target speaker and several kinds of diffuse background noise.
arxiv-2507-20123:
Yudai Hamada and Tatsuhiro Misumi simulate a reduced gauge theory in a 2025 paper. The Eguchi-Kawai idea shrinks space-time to a single point. A twist in the setup keeps the physics faithful to the full theory.

Two flavors of heavy adjoint fermions join the simulation here. Monte Carlo runs use a large matrix size of 121. The fermions stabilize the symmetric vacuum at minimal twist. Without them, that symmetry breaks and the model fails. Wider parameter ranges now match the full gauge theory. Readers see model reduction survive with less fine-tuning than feared.
arxiv-2507-20423:
Sungwoo Han and four co-authors present in 2025 CodeNER, a method that prompts language models with code to improve named entity recognition. Tagging names of people, places, and groups in text is a core language task. Past span-based methods lean on context alone and can miss fine labeling rules.

Code prompts embed the BIO labeling scheme as structured instructions the model can follow like a program. Long-range scope handling, a strength of models on code, transfers to the tagging task. Tests span ten benchmarks in five languages, from English to Arabic and Finnish. Code prompts beat text prompts across the board. Adding chain-of-thought steps lifts scores further, which backs explicit structure as a general prompt design rule.
arxiv-2507-20823:
Adamu Issifu, Andreas Konstantinou, Prashant Thakur, and Tobias Frederico model neutron stars mixed with mirror dark matter in 2025. Mirror dark matter would copy the known matter sector, touching normal matter only through gravity. Neutron stars, born hot and lepton-rich, cool over time into dense cold remnants.

A two-fluid model tracks both matters as the star spins at each life stage. Spin swells the star, while dark matter squeezes it tighter and deepens its gravity well. That squeeze also lowers the spin speed at which the star destabilizes. Dark stars run hotter at the center and show stronger light redshift at the surface.
arxiv-2507-21323:
Zhou, Eltareb, Lopez, and Giovambattista tested in twenty twenty-five whether a classic glass rule holds for quantum liquids, not just plain ones. As a liquid nears glass, its flow slows by huge steps in a tight heat range. Light atoms blur by quantum rules, which may bend that slow-down.

Path sims of a two-kind mix that obeys quantum rules fed the test. A shape-count of low lands in its energy map can be set as in the plain case. The old rule, which ties spread speed to that count, held for the quantum mix. One frame thus spans both worlds, they show.
arxiv-2507-22023:
K Neumannová, L Kueß, E Paunzen, and K Bernhard chart how young stars in the Chamaeleon I group brighten and fade. Chamaeleon I is a star-forming cloud still rich in gas and dust, which makes it a good place to study very young stars. Their 2025 paper combines records from two sky surveys, Gaia and NEOWISE.

From positions and motions, the team found 92 stars in the field, 73 of them true members of the group. They gathered light records for dozens of stars and sorted 28 into known change types, mostly young T Tauri and Orion variables. Most members are cool M-type stars. One member may be a rare star with odd surface chemistry.
arxiv-2507-22223:
Kiana Kiashemshaki, Mohammad Jalili Torkamani, and Negin Mahmoudi wrote this 2025 arXiv review on writing web software that resists attack. Secure coding is preached widely but practiced unevenly, blocked by organizational habits, training gaps, and technical friction. The authors survey practices across major frameworks and across web development, DevSecOps pipelines, and cloud setups.

They organize threats around the OWASP Top 10, the standard catalog of web risks, and compare frameworks in a structured way. A second thread examines large language models as security assistants: a reproducible case study tests them on four major vulnerability types, judging whether their advice and evaluations hold up. The authors close with practical guidance for developers, researchers, and teachers on weaving security into daily work rather than auditing it in afterward, a shift they argue the field badly needs.
arxiv-2507-22423:
Kei-Sing Ng proposes a single test for intelligence that works for minds, animals, and machines alike, in this 2025 paper. Anyone building artificial general intelligence first needs to say what intelligence is, in a form that can be measured. Ng's candidate is entity fidelity: given examples of a concept, can the system generate new entities that genuinely belong to the same concept?

The idea is made precise as epsilon-concept intelligence. A system earns the label, for a given concept and tolerance, if no allowed judge can tell its creations from genuine examples beyond that tolerance. The framing swallows many paradigms at once: reinforcement learning, generative models, classification, analogy, and goal-directed choice all become fidelity tasks. Ng lays out the formal framework, sketches how to test systems empirically, and discusses what the definition means for evaluation, safety, and generalization.
arxiv-2507-22623:
Gurgurov and a team including Trinley, Vykopal, and van Genabith map the lean of large language models across tongues in this twenty twenty-five study. Past work checked few models and few tongues, so the broad shape of model lean stayed unclear. The team also asks if that lean can be moved on purpose.

Inside, seven open models took a known views test in fourteen tongues, with each claim reworded eleven ways to keep the check fair. Large models leaned more toward one end of the scale, and the lean shifted by tongue and by model family. A simple tweak to the inner states moved replies toward a new stance in a way that held across tongues.
arxiv-2507-22823:
Alocco and seven co-authors present a study from twenty twenty-five on making microwave cluster states for quantum computing. Cluster states let computation proceed by measurements alone. Their device is a programmable Josephson traveling-wave amplifier. A shaped set of pump tones is fed into it. The tones set custom couplings between many frequency modes. Detectors verify the entanglement pattern matches the target graph. Retuning the pump spectrum rewires the state on demand.

Wide bandwidth and even quality aid scaling. The platform fits superconducting circuit systems well. Measurement-based processing in the microwave range is the goal. The authors stress programmability as the advance.
arxiv-2507-23123:
A large crowd of tiny particles, each nudged by chance and by the weak pull of all the rest, can be tracked as if each moved on its own. Armand Bernou and Mitia Duerinckx prove sharper bounds for that swap in 2025. Two facts were known apart: the swap's error shrinks as the crowd grows, and the crowd settles to a known balance at a steady rate.

The pair show the two effects blend, so the joint gap falls as the product of both gains at once. For crowds that look the same in every place, the swap to the simple view thus gets faster over time. Their route works through a chain of linked equations for group links, and it covers cases with and without momentum. New bounds on the settling rate come with it.
arxiv-2507-23323:
Ulderico Munari and sixteen colleagues present a 2025 astronomy study of T CrB, a binary star overdue for a nova explosion. The system pairs a massive white dwarf with a red giant that completely fills its Roche lobe, spilling matter onto its partner. Eruptions followed bright pre-outburst phases in the past, and astronomers have watched for the next one since a similar phase ended in 2023, so far in vain.

Two decades of photometry and spectroscopy, plus ultraviolet satellite data, pin the orbit at about two hundred twenty-eight days. The masses come out at one point three five and zero point nine three suns. The giant spins far slower than co-rotation. The authors trace how the accretion disk collapsed inward during the bright phase, raising the flow twenty-eight-fold, and how the flow has lately revived.
arxiv-2507-23423:
Ellen Fukuda, Satoru Iwata, and Itsuki Nakagawa wrote this math paper in two thousand twenty-five. It joins two fields that had not met. One is optimization with two goals. The other is discrete convex analysis.

The team shows the full Pareto value set, the set of best trade-offs, can be found in polynomial time. That holds when one goal is a discrete convex function of M type and the other is linear with binary weights. A faster method serves the case where the convex part is of the stricter M-convex kind. A third polynomial method pairs such a function with lexicographic optimization, where goals are ranked in strict order. The work opens discrete convexity to multi-goal choice.
arxiv-2507-23623: Peter Allen, Simona Boyadzhiyska, and Matías Pavez-Signé settle open cases of a hypergraph conjecture, in a 2025 paper. Ramsey numbers measure how large a structure must be before a pattern is forced under two-coloring. The Burr-Erdős conjecture concerned such numbers for sparse hypergraphs. A few cases for three-part hypergraphs had stayed open. The team builds a sparse example whose Ramsey number is large.
arxiv-2508-00023:
Quantum physics has a tool called weak measurement, which takes a very gentle reading of a system and can give odd, oversized values. Mirco Mannucci, writing alone in a 2025 paper, recasts those weak values as a kind of lens that warps the space where quantum states live. From that warped view, he derives a strange wave effect called superoscillations.

Superoscillations are waves that swing faster in places than any of their parts should allow. Mannucci argues they arise on their own from the geometry behind weak values, with no extra device needed. He links the lens idea to known math tools for comparing quantum states. The paper offers a fresh way to see two odd quantum effects as two sides of one rule.
arxiv-2508-00423:
José Manuel Montes-Armenteros and Javier Olmedo study entanglement born in an expanding cavity in a 2025 paper. One wall of a one-dimensional cavity accelerates as prescribed, mimicking Hawking radiation from black holes. The team measured quantum links between one chosen mode and the rest of the field. A partner-mode reconstruction formula gave the same answers at lower cost.

Partner modes do not commute, so pairwise thinking cannot capture the whole web. The cavity acts like a squeezing device, and Hawking pairs behave much like two-mode squeezed states. Purification turned out to be a low-energy affair; high-energy particles barely joined partner modes. Entanglement faded toward the ultraviolet in both gentle and fierce acceleration. Starting from squeezed or warm states, the team tested whether entanglement could be boosted, and how it survives noise. Lab prospects close the paper.
arxiv-2508-00723:
Rebecca Yu, Valerie Chen, Ameet Talwalkar, and Hoda Heidari ask why decision makers do or do not reach for AI tools, in a 2025 study. Adoption, in their sense, is the voluntary choice to consult a system at all. The team interviewed experts in medicine, law, journalism, and the public sector about how AI is used and viewed in their fields.

Four forces shaped adoption: the decision maker's own background, how the tool is perceived, what using it means for the user personally, and what it implies for others affected. The authors turn these into an adoption worksheet and test it on cross-domain cases. Their aim is advice for deploying AI that respects the user's seat.
arxiv-2508-01123:
Aiichi Iwazaki writes alone in a 2025 paper proposing a new dark matter hunt. Axions, hoped for particles of dark matter, may convert to light inside a tuned cavity. Iwazaki adds a quantum Hall sample to that cavity. When the cavity hits resonance, two dimensional electrons in the sample soak up the boosted radiation and warm.

Watching that tiny warming would betray the axion and point to its mass. The paper works through a gallium based sample at very low temperature, with a strong magnet in place. Heat capacity and expected signal power are weighed in numbers. The scheme offers a fresh detection route beside the standing cavity searches, using a well known electron effect as the sensor.
arxiv-2508-01323:
Faruk Alpay and co-authors model how work splits between people and AI in this 2025 paper. They frame task delegation as a map applied again and again. Under broad assumptions, the split settles at a stable point where each task sits with its best-suited agent.

Fixed-point math from lattice theory proves at least one such balance exists. Mild conditions make it the only one. In a simple model, the long-run automated share depends on the pace of automation versus the birth of new human tasks. A simulation to 2045 lifts automation from about ten percent to about sixty-five. The rest becomes a conductor role for humans.
arxiv-2508-01623:
Tadisetty Sai Yashwanth and Dhatri C stage a tournament of game-playing chatbots in a 2025 paper. Their Pokémon League pits large language models against each other as trainers in turn-based battles.

The single-elimination bracket records far more than wins. Logs capture why each model built its team as it did, which moves it chose, and when it swapped fighters. That trail lets the authors compare reasoning style, adaptability, and tactical depth across models. Type matchups and rule limits keep the contest fair and legible. The authors offer the league as a fresh benchmark for strategic reasoning under uncertainty, a skill that standard question tests barely touch.
arxiv-2508-01723:
Danyang Li and six co-authors present OpenMap in a 2025 paper, a zero-shot open-vocabulary visual-language map for grounding instructions. Embodied agents in open worlds must tie plain language commands to what they see, and past maps built from vision-language models often miss the exact scene item a command names.

OpenMap adds a structural-semantic consensus rule. It weighs the global shape of a scene and vision-language match at the same time, to cut drift across views. The map aims for true grounding in navigation tasks, with no task-specific training on the words in use.
arxiv-2508-02723: Haitz Saez de Ocariz Borde and Michael Bronstein review the math behind learning on shapes and nets, in a paper from 2025. Their field studies data that does not sit on a plain grid. Examples include graphs, meshes, and sets of points. Models here need rules that respect shape and order. With only a short summary in the evidence, the review is best described by its aim. It gathers the key math ideas a reader needs to study these models, as a starting point before more narrow work.
arxiv-2508-02923:
Deblurring a photo when the blur itself is unknown is a blind guessing game that often works in practice without a proof of why. Minh-Hai Nguyen, Edouard Pauwels, and Pierre Weiss supply part of that proof in 2025, analyzing the standard maximum-posterior approach under a Morse-Bott model of image priors.

In their model, natural images lie along a flat valley of the prior: moving along the image manifold costs nothing, while stepping off it is punished steeply. They check that modern learned priors really bend that way, valley floor and walls, by probing the landscape and its curvature. Near the true image and blur, they then prove local steady solutions exist that gradient methods find reliably and that shift smoothly with the data. A companion message warns the global best answer can fail.
arxiv-2508-03123:
Jingyi Chen, Ju Seung Byun, Micha Elsner and colleagues speed up text-to-speech diffusion models with human feedback in 2025. Diffusion synthesis sounds natural but needs many denoising steps, which blocks real-time use, and rhythm and intonation can drift.

Their method, DLPO, folds the model's own training loss into the reward used for reinforcement learning from naturalness scores. That keeps the generator's strengths while trimming waste. On the WaveGrad 2 system, objective quality scores rose and listeners preferred the tuned audio 67 percent of the time. The authors present the recipe as a path to fast, high-quality speech on modest hardware.
arxiv-2508-03223: Ming Li and Ao-Li Zhu estimate coefficients for a class of q-starlike functions in complex analysis, in work from 2025. Starlike functions are analytic maps with a geometric shape property. The q-version replaces the derivative with a q-difference operator. Using a classic theorem on positive functions, the authors obtain precise upper bounds for the first few Taylor coefficients when q is real. They also bound Hankel and Toeplitz determinants built from the coefficients.
arxiv-2508-03323:
Zhenpeng Chen and co-authors ask if fairness fixes are a zero sum game in a 2025 software study. Machine learning tools must treat groups fairly, and many bias fixing methods exist. Past work in image and text tasks found a leveling down effect: fairness came by lowering scores for all groups, with no gain for the worst off group.

Whether that effect hits table data tasks was unknown. Eight fixing methods were tested on 44 tasks drawn from five real datasets and four common model types. Table data carries much real world weight, from loans to health. The answer shapes whether teams should trust current fixes or demand better ones.
arxiv-2508-03423:
Isabella da Silva and co-authors design a lawful monitoring system for wireless networks in a 2025 paper. The setting is cell-free massive MIMO, where many antennas spread across an area serve users jointly. Authorities may need to watch an untrusted sender without being noticed. Some monitor nodes can listen in, while others jam the untrusted receiver to hide the watch.

The team first shows how monitors can learn the channels by piggybacking on the signals the untrusted pair already sends. They derive formulas for data rates on both the watched link and the monitoring system. A Bayesian search then assigns each node its role and sets jamming power to raise the odds of a clean intercept. Simulations favor the cell-free design over older setups.
arxiv-2508-03523:
Lester James Miranda and co-authors build a benchmark to test language models in Filipino in a 2025 paper. Models shine on English tasks, but their skill in Filipino, Tagalog, and Cebuano was largely unmeasured. Their benchmark, FilBench, gathers tasks that reflect research priorities in the Philippines, including cultural knowledge, classic language tasks, reading, and generation.

They tested twenty-seven leading models on the suite. Even the best model scored only about seventy-two percent, leaving much headroom. Several models were weak at reading comprehension and translation. Models trained for Southeast Asian languages did not lead; their best entry scored about sixty-one percent. The authors argue that language-specific benchmarks like theirs are needed to drive progress and inclusion for Philippine languages.
arxiv-2508-03923:
Linxin Song and co-authors present CoAct-1, a computer-using agent system that can write and run code as one of its actions, in a 2025 paper. Agents that only click through screens are slow and brittle on long tasks. CoAct-1 adds an orchestrator that hands each subtask either to a screen operator or to a programmer agent that writes Python or Bash scripts.

File chores and data work go to code, while visual steps stay on screen. On the OSWorld benchmark the system reached a 60.76 percent success rate, a new best, and finished tasks in about ten steps on average versus fifteen for leading screen-only agents. The authors argue mixing code with clicking is the practical path for computer agents.
arxiv-2508-04023:
Miguel Rodrigues and Aric Wheeler develop a stability theory for two dimensional periodic waves in this 2025 mathematics paper. The waves travel through parabolic systems that may include conservation laws, the setting of many reaction and flow models. The authors state a diffusive spectral stability condition. They prove that this condition alone implies stability against a wide class of disturbances, including ones that are not localized at all. The proof extends known one dimensional results to two dimensional patterns and to systems with conservation laws.

Two obstacles had blocked that step. Multidimensional spectra can carry cone like singularities at low frequency. Conservation laws add block like singularities of their own. The method handles both. The authors present the result as a general tool for judging when a periodic pattern in a physical system will persist under real world noise.
arxiv-2508-04523:
Prosper Mama Assandje, Joseph Dongho, and Thomas Bouetou Bouetou present a 2025 math paper on a statistical manifold. The manifold collects bivariate beta distributions, a family with three parameters. A gradient system flows across that space. The team proves the flow is fully integrable, a rare and strong trait. Its vector field is Hamiltonian and admits a Lax pair form. Both facts certify the integrability.

The potential behind the system yields a metric matching the Fisher information metric. A classic approximation for gamma functions gives a usable explicit form. In dual flat coordinates the flow becomes linear. Information geometers get a worked bridge between statistics, geometry, and dynamics. Such bridges let tools from one field solve problems in another. The beta family is a workhorse for rates and proportions, so its geometry has practical echoes.
arxiv-2508-04623:
Chirag Seth and Utkarsh Singh test small language models that turn plain asks into database code in a 2025 paper. The task lets non-experts query stored data in their own words, a boon for schools and firms. Three compact models were run on a known bench set in a low-resource frame.

A shared pipe shapes the data schema to fit each model's build, then trains and grades all three the same way. The best small model hit the top score for sound form, ahead of its two peers. The authors read this as a win for pair-built models in schema-aware code tasks.
arxiv-2508-05123:
Finding the object a sentence refers to in a photo is harder than it sounds, because one phrase captures only part of what the eye sees. The authors argue that a single text input leaves out visual details, which leads models to pick the wrong, similar-looking object. Their framework creates several latent expressions from the one given phrase, enriching them with visual information the text never stated. Two new modules do this work: one fixes the shared subject, and one injects distinct visual attributes into the latent forms.

A contrastive learning scheme with a positive margin then aligns all the latent expressions with the original text while keeping their small differences. The method is tested on referring image segmentation and expression comprehension benchmarks, where it beats the best earlier approaches. It also performs strongly on the generalized benchmark, which allows phrases that match several objects or none.
arxiv-2508-05323:
Frank Ruis, Gertjan Burghouts, and Hugo Kuijf adapt a trick from image generation to teach object detectors new things without making them forget. Modern detectors trained on huge image-text data can find objects named in plain words, even ones they were never taught. Still, fine-tuning for a special task usually costs them that open skill.

Their method learns a few new word tokens from as few as three examples. Those tokens teach the detector a new or finer object type, while the original model weights stay untouched. Because nothing else changes, the detector keeps its old language and zero-shot skills. The approach offers cheap, safe upgrades for detectors used in security, industry, and science.
arxiv-2508-05823:
Emily Garrity and three co-authors hunt for better semiconductors in twenty twenty-five. High-frequency and power electronics need devices that switch faster at higher power in smaller packages. Gallium nitride, the current champion, cannot meet every demand. Ultra-wide band gap materials such as diamond and aluminum nitride are candidates, but wafers, doping, and heat all pose problems.

The team screens materials computationally at high throughput. They compute Johnson and Baliga figures of merit for high-frequency performance, combined with thermal conductivity. The search shows many alternative materials worth exploring beyond the known few. Dopability and synthesis challenges are discussed for the promising directions. Readers in materials science get a ranked landscape for the next generation of radio-frequency and power devices.
arxiv-2508-06123:
Lingzhong Zeng addresses a famous open problem in differential geometry in this two thousand twenty-five paper. The question, posed by Yau, concerns the first non-zero eigenvalue of the Laplace-Beltrami operator on embedded minimal hypersurfaces inside the unit sphere. Zeng claims the eigenvalue equals the dimension of the hypersurface. The argument constructs a minimizing sequence inside a suitable Sobolev space and applies the variational principle.

If correct, the result settles Yau's conjecture, which had resisted proof for an extended period. The paper also derives several rigidity theorems from the eigenvalue characterization. Such rigidity results pin down when a hypersurface with given spectral properties must take a specific shape. The work is labeled part one, signaling a continuing series on the eigenvalue problem.
arxiv-2508-06223:
Yichen Zhang and co-authors design a lens to pour light from a quantum dot pillar into a fibre. Their 2025 paper tackles a weak link in single-photon sources. The pillar emits into a wide cone, so most photons miss the narrow fibre core.

A shaped silica microlens placed on the pillar bends the output toward the fibre mode. Losses from poor matching fall from over 80 percent to under a tenth of a percent in the design. End-to-end efficiency reaches about 96 percent. The authors say the fix removes a main block to scaling photonic quantum hardware. The design is offered as a proposal backed by simulation of the full source and fibre system together.
arxiv-2508-06423:
Shifan Zhao studies rare near-one zeros of triple product L-functions, a deep topic in number theory, in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. Such an exceptional zero, if it existed, would skew many results about prime patterns. The functions here blend two smaller building blocks with a third, on two- or three-dimensional groups.

For triples of the general type, Zhao proves a standard zone near one that is free of zeros, with no exceptional zero lurking. For triples outside that type, the paper gives exact conditions for when such a zero could occur. The result firms up a key input for many counting results.
arxiv-2508-06723:
Chen, Leveillee, Van de Walle, and Giustino hunt for strain recipes that make holes move faster in gallium nitride, a semiconductor whose weak hole flow blocks whole device families. Prior strain work was piecemeal. Their 2025 study introduces a piezomobility tensor, a compact map from every strain pattern to the resulting hole speed, computed from first-principles physics with refined energy corrections.

Three strain patterns stand out: two simple squeezes and one shear. A two percent squeeze along one axis promises room-temperature hole mobility up to 164 units, with shear close behind at 148. Both far exceed the material's usual sluggish pace. The authors offer the tensor method as a general strain design tool for semiconductors.
arxiv-2508-07323:
Adeetya Uppal and co-authors describe a way to steer a robot arm so it reaches its goal without hitting obstacles. Their 2025 paper builds on the artificial potential field method, which treats the goal as a pull and obstacles as a push. Older versions can stall in local minima or shake near obstacles, so the team adds energy terms that depend on both position and speed.

The method is paired with a planner that cuts jerk and run time while respecting speed and acceleration limits. Tests in simulation use a seven-joint Kinova Gen3 arm working among obstacles. The arm moves smoothly, on time, and without collisions. The authors see the work as a base for later tests on real hardware.
arxiv-2508-07423:
Giasemis speeds particle track finding with learning models on graphics chips in a 2025 thesis. Colliders pour out data at up to forty million events a second, and only a smart first filter can keep the keepers before storage.

The thesis builds a graph network pipeline that rebuilds charged particle tracks inside one experiment's first trigger stage, running wholly on graphics processors. Its speed, energy draw, and sorting quality are weighed against the classical tracker now in service. The work shows learning models can live inside the harshest real time filter in physics.
arxiv-2508-07623:
Zhun Gou and co-authors model in 2025 market games where endless firms compete under density limits. Demand shifts follow controlled equations, while firms inside one market may clash or cooperate. Two balance types frame the study: a fully rival one and a mixed one.

Both balance hunts reduce to finite projection equation systems under symmetry terms. Those same terms also secure that each balance is the only one. Iterative solvers then compute the balances in practice. Market simulations close the work by testing the frame on sample scenes. Symmetry terms carry the weight of the proof across both game forms.
arxiv-2508-08023: Francesco Dell'Accio, Filomena Di Tommaso, Elisa Francomano, and Clara Lorenzi price traded contracts with a mesh-free method, in a 2025 study. The pricing task rests on the Black-Scholes equation in two space variables. Their method fills space with a multinode Shepard tool, which builds values from scattered points, and steps time with a backward difference rule. Tests are reported to show the pairing is accurate and works well for the equation.
arxiv-2508-08323: Ji-Young Ham and Joongul Lee settle a question about stretching maps on one-sided surfaces in a 2025 math paper. Pseudo-Anosov maps stretch one set of curves and shrink another by a fixed factor, called the dilatation. For nonorientable surfaces of even genus from four upward, they prove a known polynomial gives the largest such factor. The proof shows the polynomial cannot be factored.
arxiv-2508-08423:
Wade and a team of co-authors speed up the calibration of the LIGO detectors in a 2025 paper. Calibration turns the machines' raw output into trustworthy strain data, the numbers behind a decade of gravitational-wave finds. Speed and reliability have both improved across observing runs.

The paper reviews that history and presents new tools for the fourth observing run. The low-latency pipeline grew more robust and accurate. A fresh monitoring tool watches calibration in real time, spotting drift as it happens. Faster, cleaner strain data means sky alerts and source papers can move sooner. The authors frame the work as infrastructure for the next decade of discoveries.
arxiv-2508-08623:
Talal AlRefae and Michael Calkins published a paper in 2025 on how heat escapes a layer of electrically conducting fluid stirred by its own warmth under a vertical magnetic field. Such magnetoconvection models planetary cores and industrial crystal growth. Using direct simulations plus asymptotic theory for strong fields, the authors focus on the thin boundary layers hugging the plates.

Thermal and magnetic boundary layers persist with the same thickness scaling, tied to the width of the convection cells themselves. Because the thermal layer governs the heat flow, the overall transport keeps depending on the field strength rather than settling to a field-free law. The magnetic layers also rewrite the force balance near the walls and boost the induced horizontal field there. Textbook pictures of the regime need the correction.
arxiv-2508-08823:
Christopher Battarbee, Arman Darbinyan, and Delaram Kahrobaei show how to build groups where the discrete logarithm problem is exactly as hard as any chosen task, in work from 2025. The discrete log problem asks for the power that maps one group element to another, and its hardness underlies many codes.

Given any whole-number function, they build a finitely generated group where solving discrete log matches computing that function in difficulty. That yields groups where the problem is arbitrarily hard. One family has easy word problems yet a log problem of the hardest class they target. The frame also seeds a general scheme for cryptographic protocols, which they sketch.
arxiv-2508-09023:
Dongjie Xu and co-authors teach language models to rewrite SQL queries in a 2025 paper. Rewriting a database query into an equal but faster form is skilled work. Fixed rule sets miss novel patterns, while raw language models often return broken or non-equal queries.

Their E3-Rewrite framework targets three goals at once: the rewrite must run, must match the original's meaning, and must be faster. Execution feedback and semantic checks steer generation. Strategies like reordering evaluation and restructuring subqueries emerge from the model rather than a rulebook. Database teams could gain an assistant that drafts optimizations an expert then approves.
arxiv-2508-09223:
Sameer Ambekar and co-authors propose Hi-Vec, a way to make trained vision models adapt at test time when new data drift away from what they were trained on. Most current methods adapt through one flat layer, which copes poorly when the shift is complex or the batch is noisy.

Hi-Vec splits the model's inner representation into layers of growing size and picks, for each test batch, the layer that fits the shift best. It then shares what that layer learned with the rest, and a gating step blocks updates from batches too noisy to trust. Across hard test settings, the method lifts the accuracy and steadiness of the methods it wraps.
arxiv-2508-09423:
Badi Li and co-authors teach a robot to dream up unseen rooms in a 2025 paper. In object goal tasks, a robot must find a named thing in a new home. It must guess what lies past the walls it can see.

Past tools fill maps with one fixed guess, which misses how homes vary. Their GOAL frame uses a flow model fed with chat model smarts on home layouts. Priors are spread as soft fields on the full scene map in training. Tests on three home sets beat past best and held up on a fresh set. Good dreams of unseen rooms guide real search.
arxiv-2508-10023:
Samet Ünsal compares three leading candidates for cryptography that can survive quantum computers. Future quantum machines threaten today's encryption, so key-exchange methods built on hard math problems are being readied. The review weighs Kyber, sntrup761, and FrodoKEM on security, speed, and practical use.

Each design rests on a different flavor of lattice problem, giving different trade-offs in key size, computation cost, and confidence in the underlying hardness. Ünsal surveys their strengths and weaknesses and the hurdles of migrating real systems from classical to post-quantum schemes. Industry impacts, from banking to infrastructure, are discussed as well. The paper serves as an entry point to the current state of the field and its open research directions.
arxiv-2508-10223:
Nabil Kahouadji compares three ways to give a range for a share of a population, in work from twenty twenty-five. Textbooks still teach the Wald interval as the standard choice. That range can miss the true share too often, above all with small samples. It also fails when the true share sits near zero or one. Two Wilson forms are known to do better, but full maps of their skill were lacking.

Kahouadji uses colour pixel plots to show skill across all sample sizes and shares. The sweep runs to a thousand samples and covers three common trust levels. Adding a few fake cases lifts the Wilson form above both rivals. The best count of fake cases shifts with the trust level in use. Three fake cases suit the lowest level, and more suit the higher levels. Teachers and analysts get a clear visual guide for a better default.
arxiv-2508-11023:
Gustavo Amaral and a large team share quantum entanglement across a campus network in a 2025 paper. Entanglement is a core resource for quantum communication and computing beyond classical limits. Linking quantum processors needs it sent over real networks. The team builds a three-node network that mixes fiber and free-space light links.

All parts are off-the-shelf products from partners in the Dutch quantum ecosystem. Pairs of entangled photons cross the full network with success, they report. The result marks a step in the maturity of quantum links, and a path toward early networks on Earth and in space, the authors say.
arxiv-2508-11223:
Austin Hoover and co-authors test whether a working proton accelerator can squeeze its bunches far shorter in a 2025 paper. A future muon collider needs its proton driver to compress bunches to an extreme degree, something no running facility has tried. The Spallation Neutron Source holds record-intense proton bunches, making it the natural test bed.

The team compares the neutron source's running settings with the collider's design needs. They survey the radio-frequency system that would perform the squeeze and the diagnostics available in the storage ring. Early simulations and beam experiments gauge whether the scheme can be studied there at all. The paper lays the groundwork for a hands-on feasibility program.
arxiv-2508-11523:
Ferdinand Ihringer and Robin Simoens show in 2025 that a classic combinatorial object, the balanced incomplete block design, can mint new ways to build look alike graphs. Two graphs are cospectral when their matrices share the same spectrum, a sameness that fools many graph tests. Switching methods shuffle a graph's edges in set patterns to produce such twins without changing the spectrum.

Their result is a bridge: each design of the named type yields a whole class of switching methods. With that bridge, scattered recipes in the literature turn out to be one idea in many clothes. The authors use it to explain two named methods, Godsil-McKay switching and Wang-Qiu-Hu switching, as instances of the general pattern. A single design principle thus organizes a corner of spectral graph theory that had grown method by method.
arxiv-2508-11823: Krishna Marturi and Heba Elwazzan described in 2025 their entry to a shared task on false content in simplified science texts. Making science easier to read can add claims the source never made. Their system mixes a classifier, a likeness measure, a logic model, and a large language model, then combines their scores. For cleanup, a language model revises the simplified text against the source text.
arxiv-2508-11923:
Yan Wu and co-authors propose, in twenty twenty-five, a model for long-term forecasting of traffic emissions. Such forecasts help cities manage air pollution. Past graph models mine time and space links in traffic data to predict emissions. But emissions tangle many scales in time and space. That tangle can amplify errors step by step in long forecasts. Their framework, SDSTM, splits features by scale and fuses them, while keeping the scales independent yet complementary.

A dual-stream split uses a Koopman operator, which lifts a nonlinear system into a linear space, plus wavelet decomposition to mark predictability limits. A fusion step with a cross-term loss refines both streams and cuts interference. Tests are reported as extensive.
arxiv-2508-12023:
Measuring the heart's main chamber on ultrasound must follow strict rules: at the base, across the chamber, at a set height. Durgesh Kumar Singh and co-authors automate that measurement without losing the rules. Their framework, WiseLVAM, first finds the chamber's outline in the ordinary moving image using a weakly supervised detector.

From the outline it draws the official measuring line the way a clinician would, along the chamber's long axis at the valve tips. It then switches to a motion-mode view along that line and places the landmarks there. Clinicians can still adjust the line by hand if they wish. The authors argue that respecting the guideline geometry makes the automatic numbers trustworthy enough for routine care. Code is public.
arxiv-2508-12223:
Amir Shee wrote a solo physics paper in two thousand twenty-five on steering tiny swimmers that move in circles. Many active particles, from bacteria to synthetic swimmers, trace curved paths. That circling biases their motion and wastes transport, which matters for delivery, sensing, and search tasks.

Shee adds random resetting: at random moments, a particle is returned to a set position and orientation. Resetting interrupts the circling and makes the motion tunable. The study maps three regimes, from activity-led circling to reset-led motion with or without rotation. Particles without the circular trait show only one reset-led regime, so chirality enriches the options.
arxiv-2508-12723:
Yang, Wei, Xu, Wu, and Feng design cooperative beam tracking for sensing base stations in twenty twenty-five. Several base stations serve one moving device while also sensing it. Each station works on its own frequency band to avoid interference. Echo signals let the stations track the device together.

Each station first estimates the target locally from its echoes. A Kalman filter then fuses those estimates to predict future positions. Beam choices aim to maximize data rate in the next time slot. A sensing accuracy bound must still be met. The team derives an exact relaxed solution for the design problem. They also give a cheaper penalty based method with good quality. The scheme keeps beams aligned with fast moving users.
arxiv-2508-12923:
Kirill Tuchin studies light produced by chiral matter in a 2025 theoretical physics study. Chiral media treat left-handed and right-handed components unequally, tracked by a chemical potential that can change with time. The question is whether photons born in such a medium carry polarization, a handedness of their own.

Treating the chiral anomaly as a small effect first gives equal rates for right and left photons, so no net polarization. A fuller calculation that sums all orders changes the picture. For a solvable time profile, the spectrum shows strong circular polarization whose direction follows model details. The result matters for chiral semimetals and hot matter in heavy-ion collisions.
arxiv-2508-13123:
Beilina, Gainova, and Bocharov reconstruct how the immune system fights back during acute HIV infection by fitting a mathematical model to real patient data, in a paper published in two thousand twenty-five. The immune response enters the model as an unknown function of time, and recovering it from clinical measurements is the paper's central problem.

The model extends the classic three-equation HIV system with the response term built into the third equation. Data come from four untreated patients. The authors set the task up as parameter identification, tamed by Tikhonov regularization. A Lagrangian approach yields the optimality conditions and the forward and adjoint problems to solve. Three error estimates, computed after the fact, drive a time-adaptive optimization algorithm that refines effort where it matters. Numerical experiments show the adaptive scheme reconstructing the response effectively.
arxiv-2508-13323:
Abdeldjalil Latrach, Lily Jackson, and Minou Rabiei published this carbon storage study in 2025. Burying carbon dioxide underground depends on how much of it dissolves into salty formation water. Dissolution depends on pressure, heat, and brine chemistry, and getting it wrong distorts storage design. The paper makes three contributions. It first reviews the experimental and modeling literature on this solubility across wide conditions.

Second, the team refits the temperature-dependent interaction parameters of a standard brine model. Their values cut average error against measurements by up to seventy-six percent in a common simulation program. Third, they build a machine learning model guided by physical principles rather than data alone. It beats the best existing predictor by fourteen percent overall. At high salinities, where storage brines often sit, the gain reaches forty percent. The authors present the package as a more trustworthy basis for planning carbon capture and storage projects.
arxiv-2508-13423:
Qixin Wang and co-authors present a chat-based job guide in 2025 that aims to be both smart and fast. Job search tools have grown from plain lists into chat helpers that can reason and fix their own slips. The catch is delay: deep thought takes time users will not wait for.

Their system, AdaptJobRec, first judges how hard each query is. Easy asks go straight to the right tool for a quick answer. Hard asks pass through a memory step that filters past chat for what matters, then use stronger tools. Staff lists and personal records shape the picks. The design tries to keep the gains of agent-style help while cutting the wait that makes chat tools feel slow.
arxiv-2508-13623:
Sheng Yu, Di-Hua Zhai, and Yuanqing Xia estimate object pose from color images alone in a 2025 paper. Knowing a category-level object's position and orientation usually leans on depth cameras, which many scenes lack. Their network, RCGNet, must infer geometry from flat pictures.

A transformer predicts and fuses the object's geometric features. A guidance algorithm keeps those features faithful to real shape, strengthening the network's spatial sense. A classic robust fitting routine then computes the final pose, handling the scale swings between object instances. On benchmark data the method runs efficiently and beats earlier color-only approaches. Depth-free pose estimation gains a fresh option.
arxiv-2508-13923:
Gravity Spy volunteers hunt for fresh kinds of noise in LIGO data in a 2025 community science paper. The gravitational-wave detectors pick up many glitches, short non-Gaussian noise bursts that can mask real signals. Glitches spring from instruments or the environment, and new types appear whenever the detectors change.

On the Zooniverse platform, non-expert volunteers sort glitch shapes and propose new classes the known list misses. The paper studies those proposals, tracing links between new shapes and detector states. Fresh classes also strain machine learning classifiers trained on the old set, since the models must learn shapes they were never shown. The authors credit the project with real discoveries by the public. They also stress steady data quality watch as detectors evolve, with people and models working as a pair.
arxiv-2508-14023:
George Karakostas gives a sharp condition for the behavior of solutions to a delay differential equation. His 2025 paper studies an equation where the rate of change now depends on past values through a causal operator with an odd-like shape. Such equations model systems whose response lags behind the present state.

Karakostas shows that any non-trivial solution must either oscillate or fall steadily toward zero. No third path, such as settling at a nonzero value, is left open under his condition. The proof runs through a method based on a sequence of iterated maps, called hyper4-iterations. That sequence converges to Lambert's function, a classic special function that anchors the argument.
arxiv-2508-14123:
Ankita Sharma, Yuqi Fu, and a large team present PhIDO in a 2025 paper, a team of AI agents that design photonic chips from plain language requests. The framework turns a natural language description into a layout mask file ready for fabrication. Seven reasoning language models were compared on a test bench of over a hundred design descriptions. Requests ranged from single devices to circuits with more than a hundred components.

For single devices, success reached above nine in ten tries. For mid sized designs, the best models finished end to end a bit over half the time within five attempts, with one model cheapest in tokens and cost. The authors list next steps: standard knowledge formats, bigger data sets, deeper verification, and robotic automation. The goal is autonomous photonic circuit development.
arxiv-2508-14523:
Riehl, El-Baklish, Kouvelas, and Makridis present Great GATsBi, a system that forecasts where bicycles will move next. Most past work focused on walkers and motor vehicles, yet bike riders account for many road deaths. Their 2025 framework blends physics based and social based views of bike motion.

Physics models capture how a bike moves like a small vehicle, and they do well over short horizons. A graph based network models social links with nearby road users, including guesses about their near future paths, and does well over longer horizons. Blending both beat prior top methods in their tests. A group cycling experiment further checked the system in a live setting.
arxiv-2508-14723:
Guangzhan Wang, Hongyu Zhang, Beijun Shen, and Xiaodong Gu propose a new way to multiply training text for AI models. Standard tricks mostly rephrase words, yielding copies with the same meaning and shape. Their 2025 method, LMTransplant, aims for richer variety while keeping the original's core traits.

The seed text is first planted into a wider context written by a large language model. The model then regenerates a fresh variant grown from that expanded setting. Because the new text grows out of new surroundings, it varies in content, not just wording. Tests across several text tasks beat older augmentation methods. Gains also held as the volume of added data grew, which suits large training runs.
arxiv-2508-14823:
Sean Savage and N Sanjay Rebello present a 2025 study on using a large language model to grade students' written answers to conceptual physics questions. Big classes force teachers toward multiple-choice tests, which show whether an answer is right but hide how a student is thinking. Written answers reveal more, yet grading them at scale is slow.

The team had the model judge explanations on three survey questions as correct or not, a task where it matched human graders within a few percent.
