It then sorted wrong answers into groups that emerged from the writing itself. Those groups differed from the preset wrong choices, giving teachers a deeper view of student ideas.
arxiv-2508-14923:
Andrew Kiruluta proposes a reasoning design built fully on graph signal processing, where logic and neural steps both run in the graph spectrum. Most hybrid models treat spectral graph tools as side parts. The work came out in twenty twenty-five.

In this design, facts and links are coded as signals on a graph. Learned spectral filters steer how those signals spread at many scales, then map them to logic claims for rule based steps. The frame spells out the math, from graph Fourier forms to band choice focus and rule grounding. Tests on five known reasoning sets show gains in logic match, clarity, and speed over top hybrid rivals, the author reports.
arxiv-2508-15423:
Ruiqi Wang and co-authors run a broad test of knowledge distillation for teaching small code models from big ones, in a 2025 study. Big pretrained models read and write code well but are slow and costly to run at scale. Distillation trains a compact student to copy a teacher, yet the method had barely been tried on code tasks.

The team compared two families of distillation, one copying the teacher's answer scores and one copying its inner features. They ran eight student models against two teachers, one general and one code-specific, across three code tasks. Distillation beat plain fine-tuning for students of every size. The code-specific teacher taught best. The newest feature-copying methods let students keep up to 98 percent of teacher skill with only 5 percent of the parameters. Oddly, students shaped like their teacher did not always win.
arxiv-2508-15523:
Salman Habib and co-authors privatize model training by noising a smoothed loss instead of its gradients in a 2025 paper. Standard private training injects noise step by step into gradients, which costs time and steadiness. Their SPOF method first flattens the loss into a polynomial portrait, then adds calibrated noise to its coefficients.

Every users data is shielded at once under local privacy rules. The approach also shrugs off noisy sensor channels during training. Tested on a body-sensor network against private gradient descent, it reconstructed signals more accurately and trained far faster. Privacy, here, gets cheaper and calmer.
arxiv-2508-16223:
Mayank Kumar Jain, Dinesh Gopalani, Yogesh Kumar Meena, and Nishant Jain split fake news detection into pieces in a 2025 paper. False stories spread faster than human fact-checkers can move, so automated detection must be quick. Their model, DaCFake, combines what an article says with how it is written.

Over eighty linguistic features are extracted from each article and merged with word-embedding representations. A divide-and-conquer design lets parts of the problem be handled separately before the verdict. On three public data sets the model scored between 96 and 98 percent accuracy, and ten-fold cross-checking backed its stability. The authors offer it as early-warning machinery against misinformation.
arxiv-2508-16323:
Ferit Öztürk studies curves on surfaces with set crossing numbers in a 2025 math paper. The question is simple to state: given a list of integers, can a set of closed curves on a donut-shaped surface cross each other exactly those numbers of times? The crossings here are algebraic, counting direction as well as contact.

Öztürk gives conditions that are both needed and enough for such a curve set to exist on a torus. He also gives partial answers for surfaces of the smallest possible genus. Results of this kind tidy a corner of topology, the study of shape. They may help others who build curves with planned contacts.
arxiv-2508-16623:
Weilin Ruan and co-authors present RAST in 2025, a traffic forecasting framework that borrows a trick from AI search. City traffic follows space and time patterns that standard graph models can miss at fine scales. RAST adds a memory store of past fine-grained patterns that the model can look up as it predicts.

The framework first splits space and time features, then builds a query from both. It retrieves matching stored patterns and feeds them to the predictor, which can be a big pre-trained model or a light one. Tests on six real traffic networks, some very large, showed top accuracy with modest computing cost. The authors offer RAST as a plug-in upgrade for traffic tools.
arxiv-2508-16723:
Chris Hull, Ulf Lindström, and Maxwell Velásquez Cotini Hutt build conserved currents for gravity from special tensors in a 2025 paper. Certain spacetimes admit tensors called conformal Killing-Yano tensors, which encode hidden symmetries. From them, the authors construct currents of higher form that stay conserved.

They find relations among the currents that let a charge, computed over a region, be rewritten as an integral over the region's boundary. Earlier versions of that boundary form were often not fully covariant, a flaw the new work fixes. For one class, conservation holds without using field equations, giving charges that are topological in nature. The results extend the toolkit for defining mass and other charges in gravity.
arxiv-2508-16823:
Christopher Liaw and Wennan Zhu examined in 2025 when automated ad auctions can still tempt advertisers to lie. Advertisers now delegate bidding to algorithms governed by high-level constraints, a setup called auto-bidding. Incentive compatibility asks whether telling the truth about those constraints is the best strategy. The problem is subtle because one report can lead to many possible auction outcomes, so an advertiser judges a gamble, not a fixed result.

Earlier work defined a strict standard requiring truth-telling to win even in the worst case against any deviation's best case, and showed major auction formats fail it. This paper studies softer attitudes toward uncertainty: risk-averse advertisers who fear bad outcomes, and optimistic ones who hope for good ones. Different risk postures can restore or destroy truthful incentives. Auction designers ignore that psychology at their peril.
arxiv-2508-16923:
Eder Kikianty, Luan Naude, Mark Roelands, and Christopher Schwanke carry classic results from calculus into a more abstract setting, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Their setting is a class of algebras where a special kind of function, one that preserves bands locally, plays the lead role. The concept came from earlier work by Ercan and Wickstead.

The authors first show that a broad class of very smooth functions in this setting always has the band-preserving property. They then prove versions of three classic theorems: the Intermediate Value Theorem, the Extreme Value Theorem, and the Mean Value Theorem. They also show these results can fail for functions without the property. A version of the Mean Value Theorem for complex values points toward a fuller theory of complex calculus in this setting.
arxiv-2508-17023:
Two astronomers in Taiwan model the flickering shape of the famous jet of the galaxy M87, in a 2025 paper. Radio images show the jet's edges glowing brighter than its center, and the brighter side keeps swapping at small scales. The team uses a force-free jet model tied to the galaxy's central black hole. They ask what happens when clumps of plasma enter the jet unevenly, rather than in the steady, even flow usually assumed.

Near the base, the jet's speed runs mostly along its length, which stamps a distinct pattern on the clumps' paths. Uneven, sheared injections reshape the simulated images in ways that match telescope views at high radio frequencies. The model explains both the changing brightness pattern and the shifting speeds seen in the real jet. The authors offer uneven loading as the missing piece in the standard picture of this jet.
arxiv-2508-17323:
Qijia Zhai asks whether neural networks always learn low frequencies first in a paper from 2025. This tendency, called the frequency principle, is widely cited for flat data. Zhai studies shallow networks on a sphere instead, where curvature changes the picture. Spherical harmonic analysis shows an inborn low-frequency preference for fixed neuron directions. Coefficients decay fast enough to favor slow patterns.

Trainable directions add a rotation term but keep the decay. Still, special starting points or error patterns break the principle in both setups. Simulations show trainable directions can speed up high-frequency learning instead. Zhai concludes the principle is a tendency, not a law, on curved domains.
arxiv-2508-18023:
Si-Yi Chen, Angela Sara Cacciapuoti, and Marcello Caleffi wrote this 2025 paper on routing in quantum networks. Such networks must link far-apart nodes with entanglement, a fragile quantum connection. Current methods copy classical routing and hunt for the best path, which grows costly in complex networks.

The authors propose a route that skips path hunting altogether. Their approach creates entanglement directly between remote nodes, using a graph complement strategy. In a graph complement, linked pairs become unlinked and the reverse, which opens new ways to pair nodes up. The team argues this gives quantum networks more flexibility and better efficiency. The paper makes the case for rethinking a basic design habit carried over from classical networks.
arxiv-2508-18123:
Yanjun Yang and co-authors introduce Views in 2025, a graph database model built to store meaning in a way that suits custom hardware. Knowledge graphs can hold links about links, notes on context, and nested descriptions, and plain graph forms handle those awkwardly. Views folds such graphs into chains of link nodes inside one uniform graph form.

Vertices and edges can themselves carry labels in a recursive way, and other common graph styles can be mapped into the model. The authors map the store onto a chip design built for associative search, then test storage size and multi hop traversal on a benchmark social network graph at three scales. Results show storage depends strongly on layout choices, while traversal return counts and delays grow with hop depth on their hardware build.
arxiv-2508-18223: Goswami and Verma build groups in which a free subgroup sits in a hugely stretched way in twenty twenty-five. Distortion measures how much longer a word is spelled inside the small group than in the big one. Their groups are virtually special, a class with a tidy cube based structure. For any set heights, they build one whose stretch grows like a tower of exponentials of that height. They build groups whose stretch beats any tower. The results mark how wild stretching can be in this class.
arxiv-2508-18523:
Steven Diamond proposes in this 2025 paper a simpler mathematics for the chemical networks that run living cells. Cells hold thousands of metabolites steady far from equilibrium, but mass-action equations are nonlinear and hard to steer. Diamond's model watches each reaction's quotient, its distance from equilibrium, and lets that distance decay exponentially on a log scale.

The trick linearizes the whole system in log space. Closed-form solutions then exist for any network shape, energy rules satisfy themselves through the tie to Gibbs free energy, and conservation laws split cleanly away. Outside energy feeds in linearly too, giving one frame for many control tricks biology uses. Control engineers gain equations they can solve.
arxiv-2508-19723:
Yongjiang Wu and three co-authors settle two open problems about families of sets, in a 2025 math paper. A family here is a group of subsets drawn from a fixed set. One measure, called sturdiness, looks at the smallest count left after fixing two points in a set pattern. Past work bounded the size of families that meet two rules.

One rule says any two sets in the family must overlap. The other says no two sets may cover the whole base set. The authors prove a sharp cap on sturdiness for such families, settling a recent guess. They also bound the joint size of split families that share many points. That bound gives counterexamples to a second open problem.
arxiv-2508-19823:
Yong Song, Jiaqi Fu, and Yiting Cen bound the size of stable photon spheres around black holes in a 2025 paper. Light can orbit a black hole on a photon sphere, and stable versions shape lensing and shadow images. When such spheres can exist outside the horizon was an open question.

The authors prove stable spheres exist when surrounding matter meets set conditions. Under one added assumption about how mass thins with radius, they cap any stable sphere below six times the black hole mass in radius. The cap holds across many setups, including hairy black holes. Results bear on accretion disk effects and shadow observations.
arxiv-2508-20023:
Max Newman and twelve co-authors published a paper in 2025 testing a second, independent route to the cosmic distance ladder. Type Ia supernovae measure the universe's expansion, but recent calibrations have favored supernovae in young, star-forming galaxies, skipping quiet elliptical hosts. The authors ask whether the skipped galaxies can carry their own ladder, calibrated by the tip of the red giant branch, a sharp stellar brightness cutoff.

They measured that cutoff in four galaxies with space telescopes and combined them with literature values for a five-galaxy calibrator set, then standardized against 124 matched supernovae from a sky survey. The scatter in the results came out unusually tight, under a tenth of a magnitude. A parallel ladder, independent of the usual one, looks feasible.
arxiv-2508-20223:
Andrei Albu and co-authors build a bridge between two simulation worlds that modern car engineering needs at once. SystemC transaction-level models describe hardware and software interacting, while the Functional Mock-up Interface lets models from many engineering domains run together in one co-simulation. The two standards barely spoke to each other. Their 2025 paper wraps SystemC components as standard FMI 3.0 units, using only open-source tools.

The team supplies a lightweight toolchain and works through the hard joints of the marriage: synchronizing time between the two simulators and exchanging data without distortion. Case studies show the wrapped components running inside mixed-domain simulations as intended. The authors pitch the method at cyber-physical design, above all automotive work, where a chip model must perform beside thermal, mechanical, and control models long before any part is built.
arxiv-2508-20523:
Francesco Bozzola and Edoardo Mainini write a mathematics paper from 2025 on models where mass spreads out while also clumping together. Such models describe crowds, cells, and other swarms. Their version uses a spreading law of porous-medium type and a pull described by a nonlinear Riesz potential, a choice that sets this work apart.

They study still states that are round in shape and show how those states link to best shapes in classic inequality problems. When spreading wins over clumping, the still states also give the lowest free energy. A final part tracks what happens as one key parameter shrinks toward zero.  The results also cover cases where clumping stays weak enough for energy methods to apply.
arxiv-2508-20723:
Michał Bujak and Rafał Kucharski study personal fares for ride-pooling services, in a paper from 2025. In ride-pooling, strangers share a car to cut cost. Each traveler values time in their own way, so each has a top price they will accept, which the operator cannot see.

The authors show that an operator can learn those limits from daily choices. In their model, the learned prices were right for pooled travelers with high accuracy within ten days. Each day the operator shapes an offer that comes closer to what travelers expect, drawing more demand. Both sides gain: travelers get better value and the operator earns more. The operator can also drop pooled rides that waste resources and focus on the best matches.
arxiv-2508-21123:
Ruizhe Shen, Zichang Hao, and Ching Hua Lee test two quantum methods on a finance task in a 2025 study. The task is picking a stock mix with the best trade-off of gain and risk, framed as a ground-state search. Noise on real quantum gear can bend results, so the team ran both methods on true machines and on desk simulators with set error rates.

With no noise, one method hit the best picks with great care. Under noise, the rival method held steadier, though it cost far more desk time. The first method scaled better and stayed sound if noise was curbed. Readers get a fair map of both.
arxiv-2508-21423:
Lining up vectors with plus and minus signs so that every running total stays short is a classic puzzle with a famous non-constructive answer. Kunal Dutta improves the recipe in a 2025 paper: his randomized method actually finds the signs in reasonable time. Earlier builders left totals growing with an extra log factor over the ideal.

His totals match the celebrated bound whenever the dimension is at least the square of that log term. The trick adds fresh sideways constraints while the random walk is steered, plus a new concentration bound for chained random sums. The same gain carries over to the related Steinitz problem about ordering vectors.
arxiv-2508-21523:
Jie Li, Gary Green, and Jian Zhang present a 2025 paper on classifying brain injury from full signal distributions. Mild traumatic brain injury is hard to spot, and standard methods boil brain signals down to summary numbers, which loses shape details like spread and skew. Their method keeps whole probability curves as the data.

They use quantile functions inside a Wasserstein-Fréchet regression, a frame built on a distance between distributions. Age and sex join the model as covariates. Class calls rest on the distance between a subject's curve and the curves for healthy and injured groups. On unseen data from a company set, test accuracy reached up to 98 percent. The authors offer a principled statistical path to sharper diagnosis.
arxiv-2508-21623:
Maxime Allemand and seven co-authors measured the full statistics of an order parameter across a phase change in a 2025 paper. Textbook theory of continuous transitions focuses on averages and exponents. The shape of the fluctuations themselves, expected to stray from a bell curve near the change, stayed largely unexplored. Using single-atom detection, the team recorded the full spread of values in a lattice Bose gas.

From that spread they rebuilt an effective potential. It showed a clear minimum in the ordered, superfluid phase, which vanished at the transition. Finer measures of the spread were nonzero near the transition and flipped sign sharply. Computer models showed those flips follow critical scaling. A quantum model matched the data where classical ones failed. The shape of the fluctuations is itself a sharp probe of what stays universal, they conclude.
arxiv-2508-21723:
Yuta Matsumoto, Xiao-Fei Liu, Arne Ludwig, and five co-authors show control of an electron spin in this two thousand twenty-five quantum physics paper. Semiconductor spin qubits need fast handling and long coherence at once, but the two tend to trade off. Fixes rest on spin-orbit coupling or magnetic field gradients, and both cap how far the way can scale. The team's way tunes the energy levels between dots in a gallium arsenide triple quantum dot, setting the spin-orbit coupling.

In a charge state with tunnel coupling, they drove spin turns past one hundred megahertz. Level tuning kept coherence. Machine learning feedback put the qubit frequency from reads and marked low-frequency noise with overhead. Randomized benchmarking read a half-pi gate fidelity of ninety-nine point seven percent in four nanoseconds, which stands out for gallium arsenide, where nuclear spins tend to spoil coherence.
arxiv-2508-21823:
Guglielmo Grimaldi and co-authors recast the rules that holographic entropy must obey. In holography, entropy of a region is read from a surface area in a twin gravity world. Those entropies obey endless linear rules, forming a cone of allowed values. Whether the moving, covariant version of the rule gives the same cone was open.

The team builds a test from special quantum states called Markov states. Passing the test turns on a tidy ordering trait of the rule in question. Known static rules pass, and, strikingly, only they pass. That both backs the match of the two cones and gives the cone a fresh, simple identity.
arxiv-2509-00123:
Oleksandr Cherednichenko, Josephine Solowiej-Wedderburn, Laura M. Carroll, and Eric Libby present Friend or Foe in 2025, a vast data set on whether bacteria compete or cooperate. Telling those two modes apart across settings is a core puzzle in microbial ecology. Genome-scale metabolic models now let teams simulate thousands of bacterial pairs in thousands of settings, far past lab reach.

The set holds sixty-four tabular data sets with more than twenty-six million shared settings. Pairs exceed ten thousand, drawn from two of the largest metabolic model collections. The data are curated for supervised, unsupervised, and generative machine learning tasks. With it, models can hunt the mechanisms that flip a pair from rivals to partners.
arxiv-2509-00923:
Zakaria El Jaafari presented a robust deep version of a leading poker-solving algorithm in 2025. Counterfactual regret minimization solves extensive-form games, games with hidden information and long decision trees, by repeatedly reducing regret. Adding deep neural networks scales it up but introduces fresh theoretical risks.

Those risks include shifting training targets, collapse of action coverage, exploding variance, and bias from warm starts. El Jaafari shows they manifest differently in small and large games, so one fix does not fit all. His framework adds delayed target networks, uniform exploration mixing, variance-aware training goals, and diagnostic monitoring. Ablation tests on two poker variants showed the best mix differed by game size. Careful selective use beat the classical method clearly on both, and beat blanket mitigation on the larger game.
arxiv-2509-01123:
Opinions on social media rarely settle at one view; groups hold several stances at once, with real doubt mixed in. Yijun Chen, with seven co-authors, models that process with Gaussian mixtures, blends of bell-shaped curves that can hold many opinion clusters. Each person is described by a spread of beliefs, not a single point.

In the model, outside signals such as news update beliefs in a Bayesian way, while chats between users mix views by other rules. Early results let the team study stubborn users who act as influencers. From this they define a kind of centrality based on how easily one person can disrupt the flow of information across a network, a fresh angle on influence.
arxiv-2509-01523:
Mixtures of active and passive fluids can sort themselves, with one part gathering at the walls of its container. Saraswat Bhattacharyya and Julia M. Yeomans use a two-fluid model for a confined mix of an active nematic fluid, made of aligned, self-driven units, and a passive isotropic fluid. They vary how the nematic aligns at the boundary, flat or upright.

An extensile active fluid, one that pushes outward along its axis, piles up at a boundary with flat anchoring, but thins there under upright anchoring. A contractile fluid shows the reverse pattern. The authors trace the sorting to gradients in nematic order, and show it can be driven by imposed anchoring or by anchoring that active flows create on their own. Tests could use microtubule and motor protein networks, and the effect may matter in cell colonies.
arxiv-2509-01823:
Sarbari Mitra and Soumya Bhoumik study graph labelings that use Fibonacci numbers under a balance rule. In such a labeling, each point of a graph gets a distinct Fibonacci number, the famed sequence where each term sums the prior two. Each edge then takes the parity, even or odd status, of the sum of its end labels. The labeling is cordial when edges split almost evenly between the two parities.

The pair probe which structured graph families admit such labelings. Families include generalized Petersen graphs, helm graphs in open and closed forms, joint sum graphs, and small circulant graphs. New results and concrete examples fill out each family. The work adds to a growing line of labeling studies tied to number sequences.
arxiv-2509-01923:
Md Mohibbul Haque Chowdhury, Nafisa Anjum, and Md Rokonuzzaman Mim predict stress from heart signals gathered during daily activities. Stress drives heart disease, depression, and other long term illness, so reliable monitoring matters. Their signals are electrocardiograms, traces of heart electric activity, recorded while sitting, walking, and jogging. Frequency features from power spectral analysis capture nerve system balance.

Those features feed five classic learning models, while two deep models read raw signals directly. Ensemble methods, which blend many models, lead the classic group with high accuracy. A memory based deep network that tracks time order tops all models at higher accuracy still. Balanced scores across error types back its strength. The mix points toward real time stress monitoring tools.
arxiv-2509-02123:
Wang Chen leads seven co-authors with CMRAG, a retrieval framework that fuses text and images for document question answering. Retrieval augmented generation grounds model answers in fetched documents. Layout based pipelines use only extracted text and miss images, while page image pipelines waste text semantics. Their co-modality design uses both channels at once for retrieval and generation.

A unified encoder projects queries, parsed text, and images into one shared space through triplet training. A retrieval step then normalizes similarity scores statistically to fuse cross modal signals. A large triplet dataset is released to support the direction. Across several visual document benchmarks, the fused system beats single modality rivals consistently. Unified co-modality handling proves effective for complex document questions.
arxiv-2509-02423:
Justyna Jaworska, Bartłomiej Kielak, Tomáš Masařík, and Jana Masaříková present a 2025 graph theory paper narrowing an open gap for the four-colouring problem on restricted graph classes. Colouring asks whether graph vertices can take four colours so neighbours always differ.

The classes here ban triangles and long induced paths as subgraphs. Four-colouring was known to be easy when paths stop at length six, and hard when they reach length twenty-two. The authors prove hardness for path lengths nineteen through twenty-one, shrinking the unknown range. Their reduction builds graphs that provably avoid the shorter banned path, with a computer search confirming that property. Results like this map exactly where a classic problem flips from tractable to intractable.
arxiv-2509-02923:
Kunal Kumar and 3 co-authors reviewed research in 2025 on software that helps clinicians choose offloading footwear for diabetes-related foot ulcers. Offloading shoes lower pressure on the sole, which helps sores heal and new ones stay away. In practice, advice on choosing them is scattered and uneven.

The review covered a set of guidelines, rule-based systems, and machine learning studies. Rule-based tools often use pressure sensors and track whether patients actually wear the shoes. Learning-based tools predict well on paper but rarely explain themselves or face long clinical testing. The authors propose a five-part framework, joining shared data, explainable models, and checks tied to patient outcomes. Their aim is footwear advice that clinics can trust and scale.
arxiv-2509-03223:
Mátyás Domokos opened a combinatorial study of cones of classical groups in a 2025 mathematics note. For a classical group, such as the rotations preserving a geometric form, its cone is a related space carrying a doubled group action. The coordinate ring of that cone is a graded algebra, organized by degree like a polynomial ring.

Domokos first determines how the doubled group acts on each degree piece of that ring. With that structure in hand, he computes the Hilbert series for small cases. That series is a generating count of dimensions per degree. The cases are two orthogonal groups, the special orthogonal group in four dimensions, and the four-dimensional symplectic group. One outcome is that the smallest orthogonal case's ring is not Koszul, a regularity property many nice algebras enjoy. Its defining ideal therefore admits no quadratic Gröbner basis.
arxiv-2509-03423:
Fabienne Adam and 58 co-authors, reporting for the ECHo collaboration, improved the limit on the effective electron neutrino mass in 2025. That mass can be read from the endpoint of the electron capture spectrum of holmium-163, provided the spectrum is measured with fine energy resolution and huge statistics. The ECHo-1k experiment uses calorimetric detectors for exactly that purpose.

The analyzed spectrum is described as the most precise currently available, built from about two hundred million events. An extremely low background rate allowed a reliable study of the endpoint region. The derived endpoint energy agrees excellently with an independent Penning-trap mass measurement. The new upper limit on the neutrino mass is almost twice as strict as the lowest previous value, a stated gain for neutrino physics.
arxiv-2509-03623:
Aviad Levis and five co-authors' 2025 research paper is about imaging fine structure inside protoplanetary disks, the gas and dust disks where planets form. Modern ALMA telescope data are sharp enough that older modelling methods miss real features. Recovering a disk's three-dimensional shape is central to understanding how it evolves.

Their framework joins physics-constrained neural fields, flexible learned maps that obey physical rules, with rendering that can be differentiated for optimisation. A new solver, RadJAX, computes how light travels through the disk on graphics hardware up to ten thousand times faster than conventional ray tracers. Applied to carbon monoxide observations of the disk HD 163296, the method recovers the vertical shape of the gas layer. Beyond a certain distance the emission surface narrows and flattens noticeably, a feature earlier approaches missed entirely.
arxiv-2509-03723:
Hassan Mehmood considers how Hawking radiation changes when gravitational collapse never forms a singularity in a 2025 research paper. Recent quantum gravity studies suggest a collapsing body can bounce instead of crushing into a central point, then exit its own Schwarzschild radius, all within one outside region. Particle creation during that bounce is the paper's subject.

Mehmood computes the probability of spontaneous particle emission for this non-singular collapse. The result differs from the classic Hawking radiation probability known from ordinary black hole formation. That difference is argued to imply a deviation from thermality, meaning the radiation would not carry the perfect thermal spectrum Hawking predicted. Arguments are also offered about how Hawking-style emission in such dust collapse might remove shell crossing singularities. Those are places where layers of falling matter cross and densities misbehave. The work connects quantum collapse models with observable differences in principle.
arxiv-2509-04123:
Ayan Banerjee and three co-authors build a system that turns written tales into picture stories in a 2025 research paper. Keeping several characters looking the same across frames is hard for image generators. Dialogue often lands in the wrong place too, breaking the story flow. Their system, TaleDiffusion, works frame by frame in repeated passes. A large language model first drafts each frame's scene, character details, and spoken lines.

Masked attention limits how characters blend into each other while images form. A consistency step keeps faces and outfits stable, and another step places objects carefully. Speech bubbles are drawn afterward and matched to the right character using an image-text tool. Tests beat earlier methods on consistency and dialogue placement.
arxiv-2509-04623:
Uncertainty estimates for neural operators, models that predict whole functions rather than single numbers, are the focus of a 2025 paper by David Millard, lead author with two co-authors. Split conformal prediction gives coverage guarantees in finite settings, but it does not extend directly to function-valued outputs.

Millard and his co-authors first prove finite-sample coverage after discretising the output, then lift the result as the grid is refined. They split the conformal radius into parts from discretisation, calibration, and misspecification, and add a correction for changing resolution. Two diagnostic scores track forecast decay in step-by-step prediction.
arxiv-2509-04723:
The shape of the supernova remnant RCW 89 points to jets, according to Noam Soker in a solo-authored 2025 astrophysics paper. Examining recent radio observations, Soker identifies a point-symmetric shape with two main symmetry axes. He attributes that shape to the jittering jets explosion mechanism, where changing pairs of jets explode the star.

Soker argues a nearby nebula and RCW 89 are two separate interacting core-collapse remnants within one larger nebula. He also suggests energetic jet pairs can feed back on accreted gas and last longer. The study adds RCW 89 to a growing list of point-symmetric remnants.
arxiv-2509-04823:
Staying locked onto a narrow slice of content is a pattern social media may encourage. Yujie Wang, lead author with five co-authors, propose a framework for measuring that cognitive-behavioural fixation in a 2025 paper. Psychology has studied such fixation widely, but detecting it from user behaviour by computer remains underexplored.

Their framework combines a multimodal topic extraction module with a fixation scoring module. The aim is to score that fixation from what users view.. Together they give adaptive, layered, and interpretable assessments from viewing patterns across content types. Tests on existing benchmarks and a new mixed-type dataset show the approach works. The authors release their code for research use.
arxiv-2509-04923:
Characterising a large quantum system is hard because its state space grows exponentially with size. Yuxuan Du, lead author with ten co-authors, review how artificial intelligence can help in a 2025 paper. The review spans theory and experiment, from quantum simulators to very large quantum computers.

The authors organise the field into machine learning, deep learning, and language model approaches. Each is assessed on two core tasks: predicting quantum properties and building surrogate models of quantum states. Applications include certification, benchmarking, better quantum algorithms, and understanding strongly correlated matter. Remaining challenges and future directions close the survey.
arxiv-2509-05023:
Avatars that merely stand still still need to breathe, shift, and look around convincingly. Eneko Atxa Landa, lead author with four co-authors, study how users judge such idle animations in a 2025 paper. Recording genuine idle movement is hard because actors who know they are recorded stop moving naturally.

Their user study reaches two conclusions. Acted and genuine idle animations are both perceived as real, and users cannot reliably tell them apart. Handmade and recorded animations are perceived differently, though. The authors argue recording datasets should become easier, and they publish a three-dimensional idle animation dataset with acted and genuine material.
arxiv-2509-05123: Quantum signals can share one few-mode fibre across several spatial channels. Mario Zitelli demonstrates efficient quantum space-division multiplexing with time-bin and phase encoding in a solo-authored 2025 paper. The system reaches a stated rate of encoded quantum units per second over eight kilometres of few-mode fibre. Detector dead time, usually a bottleneck in quantum transmission, is used here to remove modal cross-talk between channels.
arxiv-2509-05323:
Attention maps inside video generators become both evidence and art material for Adam Cole and Mick Grierson in a 2025 paper. Their work follows early video artists who bent analogue signals into new looks, here applied to the cross-attention of diffusion transformers, which link words to moving image regions.

Built on the open Wan model, their tool extracts and displays those maps during text-to-video generation. Through probes and an artistic case study, they examine how attention moves across space and time. The project belongs to explainable AI for the arts, a field asking how artists can inspect machine internals. It invites creators to treat model workings as a medium, not a black box.
arxiv-2509-05623:
Eruptions on the Sun are cut out and tracked by neural networks trained on masks from an older algorithm, in a 2025 solar physics paper by Oleg Stepanyuk and Kamen Kozarev. Coronal mass ejections, shock waves, flares, and filament eruptions unfold together. Decades of data now demand automated handling.

The earlier Wavetrack method, built on wavelet splitting and brightness ranking, had already described eruptive features across several data types. Here deep networks learn segmentation from Wavetrack's masks, easing the training set logjam that limited data-driven tracking. Pre-trained models are shown on eruption events from a space imaging instrument. The authors present the step as a natural next step for their pipeline.
arxiv-2509-05823:
When can an empirical Bayes rule come from a real prior belief? Jyotishka Datta and Nicholas G. Polson examine that question in a 2025 paper growing out of Tweedie's formula, a classic shortcut that estimates effects from observed data alone. Empirical Bayes methods often model the marginal density of the data directly, skipping the prior.

Their main result draws a sharp line. If the logarithm of the marginal density is a polynomial of degree three or more, no valid prior in exponential family models could have produced it. Degree two is the lone exception, matching Gaussian priors exactly. They also tie genuine Gaussian smoothing to a heat-equation condition. The upshot is a diagnostic: some useful decision rules, however handy, are not Bayes procedures under any prior.
arxiv-2509-06123:
When are the Fourier coefficients of powers of the Dedekind eta function never zero? Bernhard Heim and Markus Neuhauser attack that question in a 2025 paper through the D'Arcais polynomials, whose values encode those coefficients. Non-vanishing results here touch deep patterns in partition-like counting.

The authors generalize and improve earlier results by Heim, Luca, and Neuhauser, and by Żmija. Their methods come from algebraic number theory rather than direct computation. The paper strengthens what is known about where these coefficients can and cannot vanish, tying a classical modular form to modern number-theoretic tools.
arxiv-2509-06223:
Fitting the Matérn covariance, the workhorse model of spatial randomness, to data on a finite grid gets a careful maximum-likelihood treatment in a 2025 paper led by Frederik J. Simons with five co-authors. Variance, smoothness, and range govern the field, but discretization and edge effects distort naive estimates. Their spectral procedure uses a debiased Whittle likelihood that treats those effects explicitly.

A specification test accompanies the estimates, because even the best fit may deserve rejection. Worked examples on real geophysical fields show the workflow, aimed at interpolation, kriging, machine learning, and feature detection in geological data. The authors stress honest uncertainty quantification for sampled fields.
arxiv-2509-06423:
Coefficients of modular polynomials are far more divisible than they look, notes Florian Breuer in a 2025 paper. The modular polynomial for a level N vanishes exactly at pairs of j-invariants of elliptic curves joined by a cyclic isogeny of that degree. Breuer studies its coefficients after shifting both variables by an algebraic number J, especially zero and other singular moduli.

Those coefficients turn out to be highly divisible by small primes at which J has supersingular reduction, a special arithmetic behavior of the matching curve. The note links the polynomial's arithmetic to the reduction of the shift point, in a few exact statements.
arxiv-2509-06623:
Approximating a classic physics model across its whole safe region is achieved by Shuai Shao and one co-author in a 2025 theoretical computer science paper. The ferromagnetic Ising model describes interacting spins, and its Lee-Yang zero-free region is where its partition function stays away from zero. Fast approximation there usually needs a mixing property that may not hold.

Their algorithm follows Weitz's approach: the partition function becomes a product of ratios, each approximated using a self-avoiding walk tree cut at logarithmic depth. Instead of the usual spin probabilities, they approximate a specially designed edge-deletion ratio, which avoids needing strong spatial mixing. A new local dependence property for coefficients does the heavy lifting, proven through a divisibility relation that turns out to hold widely. The framework yields fresh mixing results for several other models, including the random cluster and Potts models.
arxiv-2509-07523:
Jad Yehya and 5 co-authors present RoseCDL in 2025, an algorithm for spotting rare events and anomalies in long signals. Many detection problems split into learning common local patterns and flagging deviations from them, in fields from astronomy to biomedicine. Convolutional dictionary learning models local patterns well, but it is computationally heavy and sensitive to outliers, which has limited its use for anomaly hunting.

RoseCDL trains efficiently with stochastic windowing, sampling small chunks of the signal, and detects outliers inline during training to stay robust. Anomalies are then flagged in an unsupervised way from local reconstruction loss: patterns the dictionary cannot rebuild look suspicious. Experiments on real-world datasets show better detection accuracy and computational efficiency than earlier approaches. The authors aim to make dictionary learning practical for large-scale signal analysis.
arxiv-2509-07623:
Fangqi Cheng returns with 2 co-authors in 2025 on a self-supervised method for diagnosing neurodegenerative disease from MRI. Deep learning diagnosis usually needs large labeled datasets and yields features doctors cannot interpret. The proposed cross-encoder framework instead uses the temporal continuity of longitudinal MRI scans, repeated scans of the same patient, as its supervision signal, so no labels are needed for pre-training.

The learned representation splits in two: a static part, shaped by contrastive learning, captures stable anatomy, while a dynamic part, guided by input-gradient regularization, tracks temporal change and fine-tunes well for classification. On the ADNI Alzheimer's dataset, accuracy and interpretability both improve over baselines. The representations also transfer zero-shot to the OASIS dataset and across tasks to the PPMI Parkinson's dataset, suggesting broadly useful brain features.
arxiv-2509-07923:
Tooth segmentation from dental scans improves with a new pretraining method from Moo Hyun Son and 6 co-authors, described in a 2025 paper on digital dentistry. Accurate digital models of a patient's teeth come from cone-beam CT scans and intraoral scans. Older segmentation methods often lack solid validation and perform weakly in clinical use.

Their framework, ToothMCL, pretrains with contrastive learning across both scan types at once, so the model learns shared structure before tackling segmentation itself. Learning from two views of the same teeth should make the final outlines more reliable. Precise tooth models underpin planning for implants, braces, and restorations, so gains here carry straight into everyday dental treatment.
arxiv-2509-09023:
Austen J. Nelson and 1 co-author characterize near-null error components in composite adaptive AMG solvers in a 2025 paper. Algebraic multigrid, or AMG, solves large sparse linear systems by working at several scales. Adaptive composite solvers stack several AMG cycles in sequence.

Each new component targets error parts the current solver cannot damp well. Aggregates are built with a modularity matrix borrowed from graph community detection, using both the matrix and the stubborn error vector. Theory justifies that construction. Performance is shown on sparse matrices from differential equations and from more general sources. The approach aims at solvers that adapt to their own weaknesses.
arxiv-2509-09323:
Benjamin Hollering and 1 co-author describe the Parke-Taylor variety in a 2025 paper. Parke-Taylor functions are rational functions that encode MHV amplitudes, a basic class of particle clash outcomes. There is one such function for each ordering of the particles.

All nonlinear polynomial relations among these functions are given in a simple combinatorial form. The variety they parametrize is shown to match, by a linear isomorphism, a known embedding of the moduli space of marked curves. Its overlap with the algebraic torus gives back the open moduli space. An explicit form of the isomorphism is written out. The new embedding respects mark symmetry and is built in one step.
arxiv-2509-09423:
Alexandre C. Orthey and 3 co-authors set hard limits in 2025 on a quantum task called conclusive entanglement concentration. The task turns imperfect pairs of qubits into a perfect Bell state, and success is not guaranteed on each try. Universal versions must work without advance knowledge of the incoming state, which makes firm bounds on their odds hard to pin down.

Working from two copies when the Schmidt basis is known, and four when it is not, the team derives the best achievable success chance. A known protocol reaches those bounds exactly, so it cannot be beaten. Averaged broadly, though, universality keeps success rare, a cost the authors make precise.
arxiv-2509-10323:
Hélène Hivert and Tino Laidin build a numerical scheme for a kinetic equation in its rare-event regime in this 2025 applied mathematics paper. After a Hopf-Cole change of variables, the equation's small-parameter limit is governed by an unusual nonlocal Hamilton-Jacobi equation, identified in earlier work by Bouin and collaborators.

Their scheme is asymptotic-preserving: its cost stays steady however small the parameter gets, and it borrows conservation properties of the original model to survive the stiffness. It obeys a discrete maximum principle, keeps equilibria intact, and recovers the correct limiting solution. Because the limit problem is non-standard, textbook convergence proofs do not apply, so the authors craft new tools from a discrete representation formula. Numerical tests back the theory.
arxiv-2509-10523:
Kush Gupta and three co-authors pair deep learning with explainable AI to support autism diagnosis in this 2025 medical imaging paper. Autism spectrum disorder involves atypical brain development, and machine learning research on it has barely used transfer learning, where a model trained elsewhere is adapted to a small dataset.

Their framework has two modules. The first fine-tunes a deep network through cross-domain transfer learning to classify cases despite scarce data. The second explains the decisions three ways: saliency maps, gradient-weighted class activation maps, and SHAP values. Together these techniques point to the brain regions driving each diagnosis. Those regions align well with established neurobiological evidence, which the authors read as support for the framework's clinical relevance, not just its accuracy.
arxiv-2509-10623:
Stefan Ivanov, Alexander Petkov, and Luis Ugarte study instantons on manifolds with special geometry in this 2025 paper. Instantons are connections whose curvature obeys a self-duality condition. The manifolds here carry G2 or Spin(7) structures, the exceptional geometries of seven and eight dimensions. Each has a characteristic connection with torsion, a twist in how vectors are moved along it.

On an integrable G2 manifold whose Lee form is parallel under that connection, it is an instanton exactly when its torsion three-form is parallel. On a compact Spin(7) manifold with closed torsion, the torsion connection is an instanton precisely when the torsion is parallel under it. In plain terms, a hard test collapses to one check. Is the torsion steady, or is it not? The results give clean criteria in a corner of geometry tied to string theory.
arxiv-2509-10723:
Deceptive interface tricks now face a new victim: software agents. Jingyu Tang and thirteen co-authors run a two-phase study of dark patterns in this 2025 paper. The agents are powered by large language models. They operate graphical interfaces from high-level intents. The study compares agents, human participants, and human-AI teams. Sixteen kinds of manipulative design are tested.

In phase one, agents often failed to notice dark patterns at all. Even when aware, they pressed on with the task. Protecting the user came second. Humans failed differently. They succumbed to mental shortcuts and habitual compliance. Agents faltered from procedural blind spots. Phase two added human oversight. Avoidance improved, but at a price. Attention narrowed, and mental load rose. Neither side is reliably resilient. Teaming them creates fresh weaknesses. The design needs point toward transparency and adjustable autonomy.
arxiv-2509-10823:
Yury Yanovich and 8 co-authors build a security audit checklist for smart contracts on the TON blockchain in this 2025 paper. TON executes contracts asynchronously, which scales well but creates failure modes that Ethereum-era audit practice does not cover. The authors set out to close that gap with evidence rather than opinion.

They mined 34 professional audit reports covering 233 real vulnerabilities, and turned the patterns into a checklist aimed at TON-specific traps such as asynchronous message handling. Case studies walk through notable flaws and their lessons. A small survey of practitioners confirmed the checklist's value alongside automated tools. The authors argue such checklists can help a young ecosystem borrow maturity from an older one.
arxiv-2509-10923:
Fine grains sifting down through a bed of bigger ones is everyday physics with surprising structure. Dhairya R. Vyas and three co-authors simulate it in this 2025 paper, using discrete element simulations. They vary how bouncy the grains are, how much friction they feel, and the size ratio between fine and coarse particles. The regime is free-sifting, where fines fall almost unimpeded.

Bouncier grains fluctuate more yet percolate slower. Friction's effect flips sign depending on how agitated the grains are. Bigger size ratios speed everything up modestly. An inverse relation between percolation speed and fluctuation strength persists across static, shaken, and sheared beds. It fits a Drude-style model, where scattering throttles motion, until agitation gets weak. There the authors introduce a staircase-inspired model for gravity-dominated creep. The work speaks to filtration, segregation, and powder handling.
arxiv-2509-11123:
Aditya Kulkarni, Tamal Das, and Vivek Balachandran propose ODoQ in this 2025 networking paper. The Domain Name System turns website names into numeric addresses, and newer private versions of it tend to protect either the user's identity or the lookup speed, rarely both at once.

ODoQ runs the lookup over the modern QUIC transport while routing it through a middleman proxy. The proxy hides who is asking from the resolver that answers, so privacy protections from oblivious DNS designs are combined with the low delay of DNS-over-QUIC. The paper sets out the protocol as a single design that aims to keep lookups both private and fast.
arxiv-2509-11223:
D. H. Minh Nguyen and two co-authors use interference imaging in this 2025 condensed matter paper. They read the wave functions of electrons in twisted bilayer graphene. Two graphene sheets are stacked with a slight twist. The overlap between electron states shapes the material's quantum geometry. That overlap is called the form factor.

Quasiparticle interference patterns display this overlap directly. Scanning probes record the patterns. The authors simulated them with a tight-binding model. An efficient polynomial method did the heavy lifting. They separated interference inside each layer from interference between layers. The between-layer signal has a handedness. It flips between layers and between electron and hole bands. A continuum model explains every feature through the single-layer form factor.
arxiv-2509-11423: Nicholas Cecil and Benjamin Cooper give a new proof of a duality in higher category theory. This short 2025 mathematics paper shows the opposite of Joyal's disk category is Berger's wreath product category. That category comes from iterating a wreath construction on the simplex category. The argument also works with a swap of roles: Connes' cyclic category can stand where the simplex category stood, and so can some other crossed simplicial groups.
arxiv-2509-11523:
Ziliang Wang and four co-authors built a team of AI agents to hunt security flaws in whole software projects, in this 2025 cybersecurity paper. Project-level vulnerability detection is hard because a system must both find the security-sensitive spots in the code and reason correctly about the surrounding context.

Their framework, VulAgent, copies how human auditors work. Specialized agents, each tuned to a viewpoint such as memory use or authorization, first surface and localize suspicious code. For every candidate flaw the system then drafts a hypothesis with a trigger path, and a language model verifies it against the relevant context and defensive checks, which cuts false alarms. Across two datasets VulAgent raised overall accuracy, multiplied the rate of correctly pairing vulnerable code with its fixed version several-fold, and cut false positives by about a third against strong baselines.
arxiv-2509-11623:
Brian A. Davey, Tomasz Kowalski, and Christopher J. Taylor study splittings in lattices that organize logical systems. This 2025 mathematical logic paper asks which logic-related varieties admit them. A splitting would divide a family of logics cleanly.

Their engine is a general Non-Splitting Lemma. Variety-specific constructions pair with it. The results are mostly negative. The variety of commutative integral residuated lattices holds no splitting algebras at all. Three other varieties are treated: double Heyting algebras, their dually pseudocomplemented kin, and regular double p-algebras. In each, the only splitting algebras are the chains with two elements and with three. The paper maps where clean dividing lines in these landscapes can exist.
arxiv-2509-11923:
Small GPS errors can quietly wreck wireless ray-tracing studies. A shift of a few meters puts a signal's bounce points on the wrong walls. Mingjun Ying and three co-authors propose a fix in 2025. Their target is the mismatch between measured and simulated power delay profiles. Those profiles show when copies of a signal reach a receiver.

If sender and receiver spots are off, later tuning of material traits just bakes the error in. So the method corrects the spots in stages. It pairs a grid search with the Powell method. It stops when measured and simulated profiles line up. Tests used urban data at two frequencies from NYU WIRELESS. The fix repaired errors up to seven meters. Loss fell sharply. Peak power estimates improved by about a decibel on average.
arxiv-2509-12123:
Counting how fast states pile up in a class of supersymmetric gauge theories is the aim of Souradeep Purkayastha and two co-authors in 2025. Their tool is the superconformal index of toric quiver theories, a counting function tied to giant gravitons in the dual gravity picture.

Working from the graph structure of the quiver, they build a cycle expansion for the index at large rank, driven by a charge-weighted adjacency matrix. Saddle-point methods then yield Hardy-Ramanujan style growth laws for several named families, with square-root growth in some cases and slower polynomial growth in others. A final section extends a known giant graviton expansion to multi-matrix models.
arxiv-2509-12223:
Idle laptops and phones could, in principle, add up to a giant shared computer for artificial intelligence. Andrei Damian and five co-authors propose Ratio1 in 2025, a decentralized system that rents out that spare capacity for training and running models, coordinated through blockchain records instead of a central owner.

The design bundles several named parts: a login layer, an in-memory state store, a distributed file system, encrypted federated learning, container scheduling, and an oracle network. A token economy pays node operators under two proofs, one for being available and one for doing verified work. The authors argue the whole package lowers cost and widens access.
arxiv-2509-12423:
Danielle Cohen and 7 co-authors show how small models can extract user intent from screen interactions in a 2025 paper. Understanding what a user meant to do from a sequence of interface actions is important for intelligent agents. Large multimodal models handle such sequences well but need data centers, raising cost, delay, and privacy concerns.

Their decomposed approach first summarizes each interaction in a structured way, capturing key information from every action. A fine-tuned small model then extracts intent from those combined summaries. The method improved intent understanding in resource-constrained models that can run on a device. In their tests, it even surpassed the base performance of large multimodal models, suggesting that breaking a hard task into steps can beat raw scale.
arxiv-2509-12823:
Ido Grayevsky and Gabriel Pallier bound how much solvable Lie groups can warp in 2025. Warp is tracked by Dehn counts, which gauge how hard loops are to fill. New bounds come from a near-straight pullback map and two known theorems.

A second result shows a five-size solvable group and its lattices keep their shape under rough maps. A key aid is a full list that the pair builds. The list gives Dehn counts and cone sizes for all such fast-growth groups up to size five. It draws on work by Cornulier and Tessera and a theorem of Peng.
arxiv-2509-12923:
Magnus Wiik Eckhoff and 6 co-authors propose a graph-based approach to security alert context in a 2025 paper. Security operations centres receive a massive volume of alerts. Analysts must quickly distinguish genuine threats from benign activity and prioritize what needs deeper analysis, a task called contextualisation.

Their method aggregates alerts into graph-based groups, where nodes represent alerts and edges denote relationships within defined time windows. Grouping related alerts enables analysis at a higher level, capturing steps of an attack more effectively than individual alerts. To show the format suits downstream machine learning, they employ graph matching networks to correlate incoming alert groups with historical incidents. That correlation provides analysts with additional insight for triage.
arxiv-2509-13023:
Stefan-Claudiu Susan, Andrei Arusoaie and Dorel Lucanu chain tools in 2025 to prove real flaws in Solidity smart contracts. Static tools and chat models raise many false alarms. Users need proof that a flagged flaw is real.

Their pipe joins custom Slither checks, chat models, Kontrol, and Forge. Seven grave flaw types are in scope. Three hard cases are shown in depth: re-entry, complex fallback, and faulty access rules. Run-based proof sorts true flaws from false ones. That cuts hand checks by much. Chat model drift and cost remain open limits.
arxiv-2509-13123:
Kees Wapenaar, Matteo Ravasi and Claudio Bagaini recast in 2025 how to strip surface echoes from ocean-bottom seismic data with down-down methods. Up-down methods handle sideways change in full. Some down-down rivals assume flat layers, a weak base.

Reciprocity lifts that flat guess. New forms serve receiver-side and source-side down-down work. Receiver-side work uses only down waves, which sample shallow ground best, but is not fully data driven. Source-side work uses the better sampled source spread. With sparse receivers it must solve an under-set system. Trade-offs are made plain for field use.
arxiv-2509-13223:
Veronika Chronholm and Tristan Pryer build in 2025 numeric schemes for noisy proton transport that keep shape invariants. Transport couples energy loss, range spread, and angular drift. Schemes must stay positive and hit rate targets while tracking dose with care.

A log Milstein step guards positivity and hits first-order strength for energy. A Lie-group step handles angles. The pair keeps natural invariants of the system. Dose as a smoothed path function yields a pathwise sensitivity gauge. Tests confirm rates and stable dose sensitivities. Therapy planning gains checked tools for dose design and for safe margins near organs.
arxiv-2509-13523:
AERIS, presented in 2025 by Väinö Hatanpää and fourteen co-authors at Argonne and partner groups, is a very large diffusion model built for weather and climate forecasting. Diffusion models generate forecasts by refining random noise into plausible weather patterns. Earlier versions were hard to scale to sharp, detailed maps without becoming unstable.

AERIS uses a pixel-level Swin diffusion transformer with sizes from just over one billion to eighty billion parameters. A companion method called SWiPe splits the model across many machines without extra communication cost. Run on the Aurora supercomputer, AERIS beat a leading operational ensemble system and stayed stable on forecasts out to ninety days.
arxiv-2509-13823:
Alberto Fanizza studies what fractional perimeters become in a limiting case in a solo 2025 analysis paper. A fractional perimeter measures a region's boundary while counting long-range interactions. A parameter s controls how long-range the measurement is. As s approaches one, that quantity should collapse back to a standard perimeter.

Fanizza proves this convergence in the gamma-convergence sense. That is the right notion for limits of this kind. He covers versions where the measurement also depends on direction. General kernels carry that direction dependence. The result assumes only that the kernels converge point by point. It holds on the whole space and on bounded domains with Lipschitz boundaries. The rescaled quantities converge to a matching direction-dependent perimeter.
arxiv-2509-14023:
Sami Ul Haq, Sheila Castilho, and Yvette Graham ask whether translation quality should be judged by ear in a 2025 paper. Machine translation is increasingly spoken aloud by apps, yet human evaluation still means experts reading and comparing texts. Listening is the more natural test for output that users will hear, not read.

The team crowdsourced judgments on Amazon Mechanical Turk for ten systems from the WMT general translation task, collecting ratings from audio alongside text-only ratings for the same material. System rankings were largely consistent across the two modes, but the audio condition exposed some significant differences between systems that text hid. Statistical testing and self-replication checks supported the approach's reliability. They propose speech-based assessment join future evaluation frameworks.
arxiv-2509-14123:
Lorenzo Liverani and Enrique Zuazua introduce HYCO in a 2025 paper. It is a hybrid-cooperative way to model systems governed by partial differential equations from data. Instead of forcing one neural network to satisfy the equation as a penalty, HYCO trains two separate partners. One is a classical physics-based solver with adjustable parameters. The other is a flexible learned model. Updates alternate between them.

Each partner fits the information it can see. Each checks the other through enforced agreement of their predictions. The design swallows sparse, mixed, or disjoint datasets. It never pushes derivatives through equation residuals. The authors show the alternation forms an exact potential game, with balance points in a relaxed convex version. On reaction-diffusion, Helmholtz, and traffic-flow inverse problems, HYCO beat uncoupled, physics-informed, and classical inversion baselines. It recovered solutions and parameters from sparse data.
arxiv-2509-14423:
Meir E. Schochet and four co-authors release a large catalogue in 2025 of stellar variability periods found with deep learning. Stars pulse or dim with periods set by mass, age and life stage. Space telescopes measure such periods well, but ground surveys are messier.

Ground data from the All-Sky Automated Survey for Supernovae have uneven sampling, larger errors and long gaps. A convolutional neural network trained for the task recovered over two hundred thousand periods between one and thirty days. About three fifths were new detections. Recovered classes include active binary systems and odd subgiant stars. Long ground baselines can thus rival space data for time domain astronomy when learning handles the noise.
arxiv-2509-14523:
Mario Hernandez and four co-authors build a radio test bed in 2025 for sharing LiDAR point clouds between vehicles. Cars that pool sensor views can see around corners and occlusions together. Testing vehicle to vehicle links needs hardware between simulation and road deployment.

Their platform uses software defined radios running the vehicular WiFi standard, built on low cost Pluto devices. Any computer running the container, Matlab and a radio over USB can act as a node. LiDAR clouds are shared and fused into a collective perception view in the demonstration. The team also models decentralised storage options and studies channel quality. A cheap modular test bed lets more labs debug cooperative sensing before road trials.
arxiv-2509-14723:
Sosuke Hosokawa and four co-authors apply circuit analysis in 2025 to single cell foundation models, large models trained on transcriptome data for tasks such as cell type labelling. Such models beat older methods, yet their decision process is opaque beside classic differential expression analysis. Clinicians and biologists need reasons.

Transcoders, a tool from language model interpretability, extract readable decision circuits from a model. The team trains a transcoder on the cell2sentence foundation model. Extracted circuits highlight which gene patterns drive a model call, in forms researchers can inspect. Interpretable single cell models could earn trust in perturbation prediction and annotation pipelines where a wrong silent call misleads downstream experiments.
arxiv-2509-15123:
Fang Li, Hao Zhang, and Narendra Ahuja estimate camera parameters from ordinary video of moving scenes using only color images, in a 2025 computer vision paper. The standard tool, COLMAP, assumes static scenes, runs slowly, and needs ground-truth motion masks for dynamic footage. Extra supervision used by newer methods, such as true focal lengths or depth maps, is rarely available for casual video.

Their ROS-Cam method builds patch-wise tracking filters that create sparse, sturdy links across frames. Joint optimization then down-weights moving outliers automatically, with no motion priors needed. A two-stage scheme combines coarse and refined calibration for accuracy and speed together. Supervision comes from the single RGB video alone, which matches how real footage is actually captured and broadens where precise camera recovery is practical.
arxiv-2509-15323:
Miles Lucas and a large team of co-authors track twelve years of motion inside the planet-forming disk HD 169142 in a 2025 astronomy paper. High-contrast polarimetric images record starlight scattered by the disk's dust, in visible to near-infrared light, from four instruments across the period. Persistent lopsided structures appear in both the inner and outer rings.

Transforming images into a frame rotating at the local Keplerian speed, and cross-correlating phases between epochs, tests whether features orbit with the disk material. Brightness variations in the inner ring do follow local Keplerian motion, marking them as intrinsic disk features rather than planet-driven spirals or shadows. The outer ring's motion is only weakly detected, and comparison with millimeter continuum emission rounds out a dynamical portrait of a disk mid-assembly.
arxiv-2509-15423:
Christopher Oeltjen leads a team that watches for tire slip in self driving race cars. Grip between tire and road sets how fast a car can safely go. That grip cannot be sensed directly with standard gear. Older ways to gauge it need detailed car models or large training data. The team wanted a light method that works live.

Their method uses only motion and laser sensors plus the car's own commands. It spots slip by comparing the motion ordered with the motion seen. When there is no slip, it reads grip straight from the car's speedup. Tests with a small race car at varied grip levels matched ground truth well. The method is cheap to run and easy to deploy.
arxiv-2509-15523:
Xinyi Chen leads a team that teaches sound classifiers new sounds without erasing old ones. Sorting sounds from the world around us helps tasks like spotting rare wild animals. As the world changes, the model must learn new classes over time. The hard part is forgetting: new lessons can wipe out old skills. Saving old samples helps, but privacy can forbid that.

Their method, AFT, keeps no old samples. Instead it shifts the stored traits of old classes into the new model's space, in a squeezed form. Tests on two sound data sets show steady gains over base models. Accuracy rose by a bit under four points. The work suits settings where old data cannot be kept.
arxiv-2509-15723:
Nannan Huang, Haytham Fayek, and Xiuzhen Zhang make opinion summaries fairer with a prompt trick. A fair summary should cover the range of views people hold. Past fixes tuned model settings or fed the true view spread into the prompt. Real users seldom change settings, and the true spread is often unknown.

Their trick frames facts as frequencies, a form that helps humans reason with less bias. Mind science shows counts make reference groups plain and ease the load. The team test whether the same framing helps language models. It does: fairness rises when opinions are summed up this way. The gain grows in larger models and with stronger reasoning prompts.
arxiv-2509-15823:
V. Champain leads a large team that finds a spot where a silicon qubit shrugs off heat. Spin qubits in silicon are a leading path to quantum processors. Microwave pulses used to steer and read them heat their surroundings. That heat shifts each qubit's base frequency, which lowers the accuracy of every operation.

The team trace the shifts to an electric cause: as temperature rises, stuck electric dipoles thaw and change the local field. Careful modeling of the qubit's electric setting pins down those dipoles. Turning the magnetic field changes the heat sensitivity, and at one angle it cancels out. That sweet spot renders the hole spin immune to heat. The find guides tougher chip design.
arxiv-2509-16023:
Lip shapes, called visemes, help machines read speech when sound alone is unclear. Aristeidis Papadopoulos and Naomi Harte probe how a leading audio-visual speech model stores these lip shapes inside its learned features. They map the features into flat plots and run small tests to see what each layer has learned.

The plots show clear clusters driven by what the camera sees, with sound sharpening the groups. Sound helps most for lip shapes that look alike or appear rarely in training. These results explain how sight and sound share the work. They also hint at ways to use visual cues better in future speech tools.
arxiv-2509-16123:
Coloring a map so that no linked points share a color is fairer when each color is used about as often as the others. Daniel W. Cranston and Reem Mahmoud ask when this balanced coloring is sure to exist for flat and outer-flat graphs. A clear necessary condition says each point must sit in a large enough set of unlinked points.

For trees the condition was known to suffice for three or more colors. The pair show it fails for outer-flat graphs with three colors, but holds with six or more. They also prove a twin result for flat graphs, with cases in between left open.
arxiv-2509-16223:
Radar helps cars sense objects in bad weather, but the models that read radar must stay small enough for cheap car hardware. Huaiyu Chen and three co-authors design mRadNet, a compact radar detector built with that limit in mind. Its network mixes local detail tools with global attention blocks in a U-shaped layout, plus lean ways to merge features.

On a standard radar data set, the small model beat prior best results while using the fewest settings and the least compute. That balance of size and skill suits live driver aid systems. The work fills a gap that earlier radar studies largely ignored.
arxiv-2509-16423:
Photo-based 3D reconstructions often botch flat, blank walls, leaving them bumpy or ghostly, while pure surface methods sacrifice looks. Maria Taktasheva and five co-authors mix two kinds of building blocks: flat two-dimensional patches locked to planes for smooth areas, and free three-dimensional blobs for the rest. The system finds and refines the flat zones on its own during training.

On indoor scan benchmarks, the hybrid set new best marks for depth accuracy and shone at mesh extraction. It did so without leaning on one camera model. The split approach keeps both visual fidelity and clean geometry for digital twins of rooms.
arxiv-2509-16523:
How small can a set of polynomials be while still generating a whole ideal? Andrei Mandelshtam takes up that counting question in a 2025 paper on polynomial rings. He studies ideals whose generators all stay below a fixed degree. His goal is tight bounds on how many generators are truly needed.

Mandelshtam finds sharp limits that hold for most fields. He also builds explicit examples that reach those limits in key cases. The one-variable case is solved in full. For several variables, he proposes how the counts should grow for finite fields. Readers get a clear map of best and worst cases.
arxiv-2509-17023:
Barkha Khattar, Anzar Ali, Masahiko Isobe, and Yogesh Singh grow and test a new magnetic crystal in a 2025 physics paper. The compound holds ytterbium ions on a perfect triangular lattice. Such lattices frustrate magnetism, since neighbors cannot all align as they wish. Frustrated systems are hunting grounds for a quantum spin liquid, a state with no frozen order.

The team made both powders and single crystals of the selenide. Measures on crystals show only weak magnetic direction preference. Those traits make the compound a promising spin liquid candidate. It also gives physicists a fresh platform for exotic magnetic ground states.
arxiv-2509-17423:
Andrea Vaiuso, Gabriele Immordino, Ludovica Onofri, Giuliano Coppotelli, and Marcello Righi compare ways to tune drone controllers on their own. Their 2025 arXiv paper targets quadrotor UAVs, whose standard PID controllers are touchy about gain choices. Hand tuning tends to land on poor trade-offs among stable flight, energy use, and noise.

The team built one simulation that joins an aerodynamic model, a fast neural stand-in, rigid-body dynamics, turbulence, and an acoustic model that predicts noise at ground receivers. Into that test bed they drop three families of gradient-free optimizers: metaheuristics, Bayesian optimization, and deep reinforcement learning. A composite cost scores noise footprint and power use together. Metaheuristics improved results throughout, with Grey Wolf Optimization best overall. Bayesian methods used few samples but cost more per step.
arxiv-2509-17823:
Jakub Szymanski links how fast integer matrices spread vectors over three number systems. His 2025 paper works with real numbers, whole numbers, and whole numbers modulo a prime. Such spread, or expansion, helps build high-dim expanders, graphs that stay well linked.

Szymanski sets a new kernel test, called integral spanning, on the matrix. When the test holds, real and whole-number spread match. He also bounds spread over finite fields by the whole-number case for a class of matrices. One use bounds the spread of a key map over the mod-two field in low degrees.
arxiv-2509-17923:
Pablo Ochoa and Ariel Salort study a weighted equation in a broad class of function spaces. Their 2025 maths paper deals with the Henon problem, set on the unit ball. The weight grows with distance from the centre, and the spaces used are Orlicz-Sobolev spaces, which fit growth that is not a plain power.

The pair show the weight lets round, radial answers exist even past the usual growth cap. Those answers are also proved to stay bounded. A classic energy identity is set out in the new spaces. With it, they mark a weight range where no bounded answer exists at all.
arxiv-2509-18023:
Lorenzo Gotta sets out a theory of rare steady states in open quantum systems. His 2025 paper deals with systems that leak to their surroundings, ruled by the Lindblad equation. Most such systems settle into a bland, hot state, but strong symmetries can carve out odd ones.

Gotta calls those odd steady states open-system quantum many-body scars. A frame based on symmetry algebras shows when they must exist. Tests check the set of steady states and how a system reaches them over time. A second class of scars fades at last, but with a far slower clock than normal states.
arxiv-2509-18323:
Spinning fluids behave in odd ways: small swirls can merge into flows as wide as their container. Sébastien Gomé and Anna Frishman study that dance in rotating turbulence in this 2025 paper. Three-dimensional waves and flat, wide flows grow side by side in such systems. The puzzle is why the flat flows survive when only 3D waves are fed energy.

The pair built a wave-kinetic theory, a math frame for how waves trade energy. They show that near-resonant wave hits force a new rule: waves keep a trait called helicity split by sign. That rule pushes wave energy into the wide flat flows and holds them steady. Their formulas predict the energy flow from spin rate, turbulence strength, and box shape. Computer runs of the flow equations matched the theory well. As spin rises, the transfer fades and the flow flips to wave-led turbulence.
arxiv-2509-18423:
When oscillators interact, they can fall into step, a behavior called synchronization. Jiarui Liu and four co-authors report the first lab case of it between two quantum oscillators. Their 2025 paper uses trapped ions as a quantum simulator. Each oscillator is a quantum van der Pol type, a self-sustained cycle with a quantum twist.

The team engineered loss in a mixed-isotope ion setup to couple the pair. The synced state hides in the phase gap between the two, which no single-side reading can reveal. Only a joint readout of both oscillators shows the lock. That split from the classic case is stark: classic sync shows up in each part alone. The phase gap could also be set with precision. The pair could even sync to an outside field. The authors see a path to larger synced quantum systems for sensing.
arxiv-2509-18823:
Judging machine-made audio needs scores that track human ears, and compression codecs may supply them. Arijit Biswas and Lars Villemoes test that idea in this 2025 paper.
