Balachandra Devarangadi Sunil, Rakshith Venkatesh, and Shantanu Todmal adapt a crowd density estimation method from still images to video monitoring. Counting crowds matters for public safety and event management, but video adds temporal complexity and heavy computation. Their system generates crowd density maps with a diffusion-based denoising model.

Narrow Gaussian kernels sharpen the maps. A regression branch plus a similarity-based consolidation step combine multiple map outputs into one robust result. An event-driven sampler driven by optical flow keeps only frames with significant crowd movement, cutting computation and storage. Evaluations with overlay plots and mean absolute error show the method capturing crowd dynamics. It works in dense and sparse settings alike, aiming at real-time monitoring.
arxiv-2511-10023:
Farzan Saeedi, Sanaz Keshvari, and Nasser Shoeibi work on automated diagnosis of retinopathy of prematurity, an eye disease of premature infants where timely screening matters. Their study applies deep learning, centering on custom convolutional neural networks built for this task rather than borrowed pre-trained models. They examine data set curation, preprocessing, and design together, weighing accuracy against computing cost and running time.

The tailored networks beat pre-trained counterparts on accuracy and F1 scores, and a voting system over models improved results further. The custom design also eased the computing burden that deep networks usually impose. The authors show deployment in dedicated software and hardware setups, arguing the system can serve as a practical diagnostic aid in clinical settings.
arxiv-2511-10223:
David F. Anderson, Aidan S. Howells, and Diego Rojas La Luz analyze stochastic reaction networks whose reactions happen inside compartments that can split apart. Cells and their internal units make real chemistry non-homogeneous, so models need units with their own dynamics. Here the split rate of a unit depends on how much of a chosen species it contains, following a general approach proposed in 2020.

Earlier work handled content-independent unit dynamics and characterized when the process explodes, meaning infinitely many events in finite time. The authors show that characterization fails once contents matter. Under the assumption that the reaction network admits a linear Lyapunov function, they prove fresh sufficient conditions for non-explosivity and positive recurrence, extending the theory toward cell division and intracellular transport models.
arxiv-2511-10323:
Dávid Kószó, Tamás Aladics, Rudolf Ferenc, and Péter Hegedűs attack alert fatigue in static code analysis by building the dataset the field is missing. Analysis tools flood developers with warnings, many not worth acting on, until real bugs get ignored. Training filters needs large labeled collections, which barely exist, especially for Java. The authors present a methodology that collects warnings and categorizes them as actionable or not.

Applying it produced NASCAR, a dataset of over one million Java static analysis reports, released publicly together with the generation tools. The scale and the actionable labels are the contribution: machine learning researchers can now train and benchmark warning filters on realistic data. The authors frame the release as infrastructure for making static analysis usable again.
arxiv-2511-10423:
Jiayang Meng and four co-authors show that a common privacy defense in federated learning leaks more than expected. In federated learning, devices share model gradients rather than raw data, yet those gradients can hide the training images inside them. Adding noise to gradients is a standard defense, and older attacks lose most of their power against it.

Their attack guides a conditional diffusion model with the leaked gradient itself, using the model's natural denoising strength to undo the added noise. It needs no prior knowledge of the target data distribution. They also prove error bounds and study how noise size and model shape affect reconstruction quality. Experiments confirm reconstructions stay strong under Gaussian noise, beating earlier attacks.
arxiv-2511-10523:
Egor Pakhomov, Erik Nijkamp, and Caiming Xiong introduce Convomem, a benchmark for judging how well artificial intelligence systems remember conversations. It holds 75,336 question-answer pairs covering user facts, recall of what the assistant said, preferences, changes over time, knowing when to abstain, and implicit connections between messages.

Their experiments compare simple full-context approaches, which feed the whole conversation history to the model, against retrieval-based memory systems such as Mem0. On histories shorter than 150 conversations, full context reached 70 to 82 percent accuracy while the retrieval systems managed only 30 to 45 percent. Long context works best for roughly the first 30 conversations and stays viable to about 150, beyond which hybrid or retrieval methods become necessary as cost and delay grow.
arxiv-2511-10723:
Katya Leidig and five co-authors ask how reliably the faint outer glow of a brightest cluster galaxy can weigh its dark matter halo. The diffuse stellar halo records the galaxy's assembly history, and deep Hyper Suprime-Cam imaging has shown the stellar mass in wide annuli tracks halo mass, but the best radial definition remained unclear.

The team built a mock observing pipeline that mimics the survey on IllustrisTNG simulations, reproducing observed profiles across six orders of magnitude in surface density. Simple circular apertures scatter much more than projected ellipsoidal annuli. They identify an optimal annulus range and present Sérsic-based fitting functions that predict the profiles from halo mass, with a median error that improves when the central galaxy's stellar mass is added. The functions are meant for future wide-field surveys.
arxiv-2511-10823:
Tim Randolph and Karol Węgrzycki break a classic algorithmic barrier for subset balancing problems, a family that generalizes subset sum, partition, and equal subset sum. Given an integer vector and a small fixed set of allowed coefficients, the task is to find a nonzero coefficient assignment whose weighted sum is exactly zero.

The textbook meet-in-the-middle method sets a running-time barrier that earlier work had beaten only on average inputs. Randolph and Węgrzycki beat it in the worst case for several coefficient sets. They improve the best exact algorithm for equal subset sum by an exponential margin, answering an open question. Their machinery carries the representation technique of Howgrave-Graham and Joux from average-case to worst-case inputs. It uses new ideas for mixing, flexible representations, and recovering genuine solutions from near misses.
arxiv-2511-11623:
Yushan Jiang and seven co-authors work on predicting graft-versus-host disease after liver transplantation, a rare complication that is often fatal. Catching it early could allow treatment in time, but the disease is so uncommon that ordinary prediction models drown in data from patients who never develop it.

Records from twenty-one hundred transplant patients treated at Mayo Clinic between 1992 and 2025 include only forty-two cases of the disease. A multi-modal deep learning framework combines demographics, lab tests, diagnoses, and medications from before surgery into one risk estimate. Handling four data types at once, under heavy imbalance, is the technical core of an effort aimed at earlier warning.
arxiv-2511-12023:
N. T. Dung and N. T. Hang study stochastic Volterra equations with small noise, a class of models where the present state depends on the whole past path. They focus on how the random solution moves around its deterministic limit when the noise is small. The work gives a precise picture of that fluctuation.

Using tools from Malliavin calculus, the authors show the fluctuation follows a central limit theorem, so its spread takes a normal form in the limit. They also give an optimal estimate for how fast that limit is reached. An example with a fractional Brownian motion kernel shows how the general theory applies.
arxiv-2511-12123:
Zejiao Liu and six co-authors aim to improve how teams of learning agents explore together. In cooperative multi-agent reinforcement learning, agents often explore on their own, with no coordination. That limits both what the joint policy can express and how well the team searches for better behavior.

Their framework adds a conductor that shapes the joint policy and coordinates exploration. A hierarchical method, HCPO, updates the conductor and the agents in directions tied to better joint performance, with a proof that performance moves in a steady, improving way. Local conductors keep training gains without needing messages at run time. Tests on three hard benchmarks beat strong baselines in efficiency and stability.
arxiv-2511-12523:
Adam Dziwoki and Rostislav Horcik examine what happens when the oracle inside equilibrium-finding algorithms answers with slightly wrong utilities. Double Oracle and Fictitious Play are standard methods that build toward a Nash equilibrium in zero-sum games by repeatedly adding best responses. The authors assume the best response is computed after the payoffs are perturbed.

Counter to first intuition, they show such perturbations cut the number of iterations for both algorithms. In some cases a well-chosen perturbation makes the expected iteration count logarithmic. perturbing is costly if every pure strategy must be scanned, but when strategies carry inner structure the perturbation can be done efficiently, keeping the gain practical.
arxiv-2511-12623:
Antonin Barbe, Benjamin De Bruyne and Romain Allez study how the eigenvectors of a large random matrix change when the matrix grows by a few rows and columns. They compare a Wigner matrix with its principal minor, the smaller matrix inside it, in both real symmetric and complex Hermitian cases, while the added size stays fixed as the whole grows.

Two results emerge. In the bulk of the spectrum, an eigenvector of the larger matrix projects mainly onto eigenvectors of the smaller one at the same spectral level, a stability they call local projection. At the spectral edge, the change of basis between leading eigenspaces is governed by a small random antisymmetric perturbation. Both laws are expressed with classic Airy and sine kernels, and extended to sample covariance matrices.
arxiv-2511-12723:
Gennaro Vessio proposes LAYA, a new output head for neural networks that listens to every layer, not just the last one. Standard networks base their final answer on the deepest representation alone, discarding the low-level and mid-level patterns computed earlier. LAYA instead learns attention weights over the features from all layers, tuned to each input, and blends them into the prediction that the network finally reports.

Those same weights double as an explanation: they state how much each layer contributed to a given decision, with no extra explanation tool needed. On image classification tests, LAYA matched standard performance while its layer scores tracked the true contribution of each layer in follow-up checks. The patterns it found were structured and task-dependent, showing which depths a task actually uses. The design fits many architectures, offering interpretability that comes from inside the model rather than after it.
arxiv-2511-12823:
Sajed Jalil, Shuvo Saha, and Hossain Mohammad Seym aim to open up code generation help for Bengali speakers. Bengali has hundreds of millions of native speakers, yet language models are rarely trained or tested for it, and fine-tuning tools demand expertise and money that users in emerging markets may lack. Their approach needs no fine-tuning at all. It combines test-driven development, where tests are written before code, with a code interpreter that runs and checks the generated code, using open-weight models.

With Bengali prompts, the method lifted code generation accuracy to eighty-five percent overall. Even the smallest model in a family reached nearly the accuracy of the largest when wrapped in this loop. All results are shared publicly for checking and reuse. Careful prompting workflows, rather than bigger models, can carry coding tools into low-resource language communities.
arxiv-2511-12923:
Prashasti Tiwari, Dylan Lewis, and Sougato Bose find a fast way to prepare quantum ground states. Ground states of many-body systems are valuable starting points for sensing, hardware benchmarks, and simulations, but preparing them slowly, by adiabatic change, wastes time and invites decoherence. The authors instead evolve a simple starting state for a short, fixed time under a second Hamiltonian whose couplings they tune classically to minimize energy. The question is how to scale that trick from a few qubits to many.

In studies up to fourteen qubits, the winning strategy was a warm start: take the ground state already prepared for one fewer qubit, then add the new qubit's couplings step by step. That incremental route scaled best among those tried, and it offers a concrete recipe for near-term devices.
arxiv-2511-13023:
Jiacheng Wang and five co-authors benchmark whether the compression tricks built for large language models work on small ones. Small language models are meant for phones and edge devices, but how quantization, shrinking their numbers to fewer bits, behaves at that scale was largely unexamined. SLMQuant runs multi-track evaluations of state-of-the-art quantization methods across architectures and tasks, asking where the bottlenecks sit for small models specifically.

The headline finding is that small models are not just little large models. Their quantization sensitivity differs fundamentally, and methods optimized for large models transfer suboptimally because of small models' distinct architectures and training dynamics. The authors extract the factors that govern effective small-model quantization and turn them into design principles for compression tailored to this class. For engineers, the benchmark replaces guesswork with measurements.
arxiv-2511-13223:
Yuxiang Zhang and 7 co-authors present TokenSqueeze, a way to shorten the long reasoning traces of large language models. Models such as DeepSeek-R1 gain strength from long chains of thought, but those chains cost time and memory. Earlier shortening methods often lost accuracy, so balance is the central problem here.

TokenSqueeze trains only on text the model made itself, picking samples whose depth fits each problem's difficulty. A second step rewrites the wording to be clearer and shorter without changing the logic. In tests, a seven-billion-parameter model cut token use by about half on a math benchmark while keeping its score.
arxiv-2511-13323:
Marianne Bessemoulin-Chatard, Tino Laidin, and Thomas Rey prove long-time convergence for a finite volume scheme for a nonlinear kinetic model with two interacting species. Earlier results needed data close to equilibrium and used weighted estimates in a narrow setting. The new work widens the class of starting data that still settle down over time.

Their proof leans on Boltzmann entropy and on bounds that the scheme keeps from the start thanks to its monotone design. Those bounds let them control nonlinear terms without assuming closeness to equilibrium. They also show the scheme's own time-step dissipation helps stabilize the whole argument.
arxiv-2511-13423:
Jorge Lamas studies emergent geometry in the Coherence-Curvature Model, a system of linked graphs shaped by energy rules. The model's energy couples how well a graph stays connected, its Ollivier-Ricci curvature, and a penalty on edge density. Simulated annealing at low temperature then grows the low-energy shapes whose geometry he measures.

He tracks spectral dimension, Hausdorff dimension, and average distance as the graphs grow. Spectral dimension rose clearly with size while Hausdorff dimension rose more gently, and the largest graphs fit values near four and three for each. Typical distances grew as a slow power law, so the model yields finite, fractal-like spaces in a controlled lab.
arxiv-2511-13523:
Nikita Neveditsin and 4 co-authors test compact multimodal language models as a private alternative to optical character recognition for noisy clinic reports. Hospital digitization often starts from phone photos blurred by shadow and shake, where classic OCR tuned for clean scans fails. On-site models could read such pages without sending patient data outside.

Using obstetric ultrasound reports in regionally inflected Indian medical English, they compare eight systems on accuracy, noise response, number accuracy, and cost. Compact multimodal models beat both classic and neural OCR pipelines on transcription throughout. Higher compute cost is the trade-off, but robustness and language flexibility make them viable for local healthcare digitization.
arxiv-2511-13723:
Abhishek Arora and Caglar Oskay extend the variational multiscale enrichment method to the dynamic response of rubber-like materials at large deformation. Wave motion in such materials mixes scales, and nonlinear effects can steepen or flatten waves as they travel. A single-scale simulation either misses fine detail or costs too much.

Splitting displacement into coarse and fine parts yields paired governing equations that include micro-inertial effects naturally. Each unit cell is meshed with a patch of coarse elements to catch short waves, and an operator-split loop solves the two scales in turn. Tests show dissipative multiscale schemes suppress false oscillations and reveal how stiffness contrast and nonlinearity shape dispersion and attenuation.
arxiv-2511-13823:
Dimitri A. Gadotti tests how reliably galaxy images can be split into their stellar parts, with a warning about false classical bulges. Two-dimensional decomposition extracts the traits of discs, bars, and bulges, but common fitting tools can trap in local minima or lean on subjective choices. Distant samples also report far more classical bulges than nearby ones, against the merger-driven picture of galaxy growth.

Using sixteen nearby TIMER galaxies known to lack classical bulges, Gadotti refits original and artificially redshifted images with several methods. A differential evolution optimizer recovered the true structures, including nuclear discs, with little hand guidance. At poor physical resolution, though, bulge profiles inflated systematically, faking classical bulges even in data from top facilities.
arxiv-2511-14023:
Chiharu Hagiwara, Naoki Nonaka, Yuhta Hashimoto, and two co-authors generate synthetic triage cases for testing AI in mass casualty care. Triage under the START method sorts victims into green, yellow, red, and black groups to save the most lives, but real incidents are rare and records scarce. Their framework, Syn-STARTS, uses language models to write training-style scenarios.

Judges could not tell the synthetic cases apart from a curated open data set built from training materials. When language models were scored on hundreds of cases per category, their accuracy stayed highly stable. The authors argue synthetic data like this can support building and evaluating AI for rare, high-stakes medical decisions.
arxiv-2511-14323:
Thibault Ghesquière-Diérickx, Jean-François Molinari, and Guillaume Anciaux find why some crash models of fast breaks gain fake energy. Models that join a cohesive-zone law with penalty contact in fast time steps often show runaway energy growth and fake cracks. In a flat test case the team pinned down three causes, one by one.

First, the starting stiffness of the glue law can grow without bound and squeezes the safe time step. Next, stiffness jumps where glue meets contact add small errors. Last, the softening of the glue adds its own break. Each pass through the switch piles the errors up. A fix ties the contact stiffness to the glue stiffness; the jump then goes away and energy is kept.
arxiv-2511-14423:
Xin Yi, Yue Li, Dongsheng Shi, and three co-authors defend educational language models against two attack routes at once. Jailbreak prompts and malicious fine-tuning can both strip a model's safety training, and education has its own safety demands that general benchmarks ignore. The team built EduHarm, a benchmark of safe-unsafe instruction pairs across five educational scenarios.

Their three-stage shield first realigns attention toward the tokens that signal harm, restoring the feature that separates unsafe from safe inputs. A layer-wise judgment then aggregates safety cues across the network, and dual routing sends benign queries through normally while guarding harmful ones. Tests across eight jailbreak strategies show the combined defense holds up.
arxiv-2511-14823:
Akbar Anbar Jafari, Cagri Ozcinar, and Gholamreza Anbarjafari propose machine learning systems that rebuild their own learning structure as they go. Today's models, even large language models, are stuck with fixed layouts and fixed update rhythms, so they adapt poorly when the world keeps changing. An earlier nested learning idea split a model into levels that update at set rates.

Dynamic nested hierarchies go further: the model can add or drop levels, rearrange how they nest, and change update rates during training or use. The design borrows from brain plasticity to fight the forgetting that blocks lifelong learning. The authors present the scheme as the next step toward systems that keep learning for good.
arxiv-2511-14923:
Tom Dodd, Javier Martínez-Cifuentes, and three co-authors show that a modest classical computer can now mimic a flagship quantum sampling experiment. Gaussian boson sampling sends photons through an optical network and records the patterns, a task long used to claim quantum advantage. Matching the sampling rate of the hundred-mode experiments was thought to need supercomputers.

Their emulator beats those experiments on standard benchmark tests while running on a single processor or graphics card. The method parallelizes cleanly, so a handful of machines match rates that once took more than a hundred graphics cards. Results like this keep raising the bar that quantum hardware must clear to claim a real edge.
arxiv-2511-15123:
Paul Goldsmith-Pinkham and Tianshu Lyu show that the workhorse method of financial event studies can misstate cause and effect. Event studies measure how news moves a stock beyond what a factor model predicts, and abnormal returns are read as the event's impact. When the factor model is wrong, as it almost always is in practice, the authors prove the estimates become inconsistent.

The bias grows in volatile periods, over long windows, and when event timing lines up with market swings. The authors give exact conditions for valid identification and formulas for the bias. They then offer synthetic control portfolios, built from unaffected securities, as a safer route, and revisit four published applications to show some findings may be model artifacts.
arxiv-2511-15323:
Yuyang Zou, Youwei Xiao, and two co-authors present SkyEgg, a hardware synthesis system that keeps every design option open until the evidence is in. Synthesis turns high-level programs into accelerator circuits on FPGAs, whose modern resources vary in function and timing in fine detail. Older tools commit early: they fix the program's form, then its schedule, then its mapping, each step discarding options the later steps needed.

SkyEgg instead uses equality saturation, a technique that keeps many equivalent forms of the design alive at once. Implementation choice, scheduling, and mapping are explored together, with chaining and fusion of operations preserved. The heterogeneity-aware search aims at end-to-end speed that staged pipelines leave on the table.
arxiv-2511-16023:
Nadim A. Mottu studies how much advance notice a real-time scheduler needs to guarantee good throughput. Jobs arrive with release times, deadlines, and processing times. The scheduler must decide on the spot which to run. Its aim is to maximize the total processing time of jobs that finish before their deadlines. Jobs may be announced before release, and Mottu measures that lead time against processing length.

A family of persistent algorithms, set by a patience value, achieves a competitive ratio that rests on that value for inputs with a given notice. Separate bounds cover small and large notice cases. Once notice is at least half the processing time, a fixed competitiveness is reached. Upper bounds limit any method that relies on such notice.
arxiv-2511-16123:
Linyi Han, Shidong Pan, and six co-authors build a method that merges inconsistent vulnerability descriptions from security repositories. Text descriptions help analysts grasp software flaws, but key aspects clash across sources, blocking a full picture. Past fixes aligned text to external knowledge bases. They often dropped valued detail and failed to synthesize a full account.

Their domain-constrained synthesis, based on a language model, runs in three stages. Rule-guided extraction captures key details. Self-evaluation with domain anchor words gauges semantic spread across sources. Fusion by information entropy then reconciles clashes and ranks detail by relevance. Synthesis scores rose, grasp and speed rose by over thirty percent, and a Digest Labels tool shows the merged text.
arxiv-2511-16223:
Vincenzo Pomponi and six co-authors present DynaMimicGen, a framework that builds robot training data from just a few human demonstrations, including for tasks where the scene keeps moving. Collecting large demonstration sets by hand is slow and costly, and older generation methods assume a static world.

DynaMimicGen splits each demonstration into sub-tasks, then uses Dynamic Movement Primitives to adapt the motions to new object poses, layouts, and robot setups, producing smooth paths that adjust in real time. Robots trained on the generated data did well on long, contact-rich jobs such as stacking cubes and putting mugs in drawers. The approach points toward robot learning that needs far less human demonstration time.
arxiv-2511-16723:
Melissa van Beekveld and five co-authors introduce Lund-Tree Shapes, a new family of observables for dissecting jets at colliders. Built from the declustering trees of the Lund jet plane, which pictures how radiation branches inside a jet, these shapes probe the geometry and hierarchy of the radiation pattern in multi-jet events.

At the differential level the shapes act as continuous global variables, akin to classic event shapes; integrated, they define jet rates that characterize final states by multiplicity. They apply to any number of resolved jets and to groomed jets, and they avoid non-global logarithmic corrections. That makes them clean tools for testing shower algorithms and matching calculations. The authors compute high-accuracy predictions for two-leg processes at electron and proton colliders, including matched results for the LHC.
arxiv-2511-17323:
Callie C. Liao, Duoduo Liao, and Ellie L. Zhang present MusicAIR, a music generation framework whose core is algorithmic rather than learned from a large song dataset. Neural music models trained on huge corpora carry copyright risks and heavy computing costs. MusicAIR instead derives a melodic score directly from lyrics, using algorithms that link lyrical and rhythmic information and follow established principles of music theory and song structure. The framework accepts lyrics, plain text, or images as starting points.

A web tool built on the framework, GenAIM, offers lyric-to-song, text-to-music, and image-to-music generation. In evaluations using standard music metrics and comparisons with original works, the system's scores showed an average key confidence above that of human composers in the study. They also aligned closely with music theory standards. The authors position the tool as a composition co-pilot and teaching aid.
arxiv-2511-17423:
Yi Guo and 13 co-authors report superconductivity living on the surface of thick rhombohedral graphene, stacks of carbon sheets in an ABC arrangement. Thin stacks of this material have recently shown a zoo of magnetic, topological, and superconducting states. Theory says even infinitely thick stacks carry flat-band states on their surfaces, and this team detects them directly with layer-resolved capacitance measurements in devices of about thirteen layers.

Transport and local magnetometry reveal several ferromagnetic phases in those surface states, including valley-imbalanced quarter metals and broad spin-polarized regimes. Multiple superconducting states sit localized in a single surface state, on the unpolarized side of the spin transitions, and their strength against magnetic fields points to spin-triplet pairing. Unlike earlier work, superconductivity persists at zero displacement field, suggesting two independent surface superconductors coupled through the graphite bulk between them.
arxiv-2511-17623:
Haoran Li, Zhe Cheng, Muhao Guo, Yang Weng, Yannan Sun, Victor Tran, and John Chainaranont tackle probabilistic forecasting of electricity load for very large customer groups. Forecasts that state uncertainty guide planning and risk calls in power systems, and deep models have lifted accuracy. Scale creates a dilemma, though: one model per customer is too costly to keep, while a single shared model ignores how customer types, places, and phases differ.

Their system extends a known probabilistic forecaster with a global-to-local design, sharing strength across the whole feeder while still adapting to local groups. The aim is to serve thousands or even hundreds of thousands of loads without losing the differences that matter. The paper speaks to utilities facing modern feeders crowded with varied demand.
arxiv-2511-17723:
Moriah Elkin works in pure mathematics on spaces tied to quivers, which are diagrams of points and arrows used to encode maps between vector spaces. Within one such space she defines open quiver loci by placing strict rank demands on those maps.

Elkin gives three formulas for a refined class attached to these loci, one based on geometry and two based on counting patterns. The last uses chained pipe dreams, a picture method adapted from earlier work. The classes refine older quiver polynomials, so the formulas add finer detail to a known algebraic story.
arxiv-2511-17823:
Naitik Gada proposes a new version of k-means clustering, a widely used method that groups data points around a set of centers. Classic k-means judges only how tight each group is, which can leave points, especially outliers, in the wrong group.

The new version also uses distance between groups, and it picks the number of groups with a standard quality criterion. On synthetic data and on public benchmark sets, points settle into their true groups more accurately than with the classic method, including outliers. Gada also notes open questions raised by the approach for future clustering research.
arxiv-2511-18123:
Dachuan Zhao, Weiyue Li, Zhenda Shen, Yushu Qiu, Bowen Xu, Haoyu Chen, and Yongchao Chen rethink how bias sits inside vision-language models. These models can absorb demographic bias into their internal representations, skewing later predictions. A common fix edits the few coordinates most tied to a trait, swapping in neutral values. But the team finds three faults in that approach: features are entangled, gains do not travel across data sets, and removal stays incomplete.

Their analysis shows bias is spread across a few linear subspaces, not pinned to single coordinates. They therefore propose subspace projection debiasing, which finds those subspaces and projects them out. The geometric view, they argue, removes bias more fully and more portably than coordinate edits, a claim they support with systematic tests.
arxiv-2511-18223:
H. Zhang and three co-authors test a weak spot in guard systems that learn by trial and error. Such a system watches network traffic and learns to flag attacks. A single fixed noise pattern, fed to all inputs, can fool it into missing real threats.

The team craft such a pattern under strict rules drawn from how network data must look. Feature links and math ties in the data bound what a real attack input can be. A tuned loss term then makes the noise work better while it stays in those bounds. To their claim, no past work built this kind of attack for this guard type. The study warns builders to test for fixed noise tricks before field use.
arxiv-2511-18423:
B. Y. Yan, Chaofan Li, Hongjin Qian, Shuqi Lu, and Zheng Liu rethink how an AI agent should keep memory. Most agents store a ready made summary in advance, which drops much of the past. Their frame, GAM, works more like a just in time compiler: it keeps a light note of key facts and stores the full past in a page store.

Two parts share the work. A Memorizer marks key past facts in light form while the full record stays saved. A Researcher then digs in the store at request time and builds a rich context for the live task. Tests show the split keeps more of value than a fixed store. The design suits long tasks where the needed fact is hard to guess ahead of time.
arxiv-2511-18923:
Marco Cirant and Nicolò De Bernardi study the long time pull of mean field games toward their steady states. In such games a crowd of agents each optimize against the crowd's spread. The turnpike property says paths spend most of a long horizon near a stationary balance, like a highway between two towns.

Past proofs lean on a monotone coupling claim. The pair swap it for a weaker local claim at the balance, drawn from a strict second order positivity check, plus a symmetry of the system. Near balance paths then home in at an exponential rate, on a flat torus or on full space. A fixed point step shows such stable paths exist on finite and endless horizons, in the periodic case.
arxiv-2511-19023:
Yuting Gao, Weihao Chen, Lan Wang, Ruihan Xu, and Qingpei Guo align a multimodal mixture of experts model with no human preference data at all. Preference training steers models toward better replies, but human labels cost time and money. In a mixture of experts model, a router sends each token to chosen experts and scores that choice.

The team note those routing scores carry a hidden quality ranking: high scored experts tend to yield better output. OrdMoE groups experts into ranked tiers by their routing scores and runs each tier alone to make a ladder of replies. That internal ladder then serves as preference data. Alignment from the model's own signals is the pitch.
arxiv-2511-19623:
Steven Ramnichal, Junkai Zhang, Stijn Wuyts, and Cheng Li present SE3D, a framework for fitting resolved galaxy observations across all wavelengths at once. It models a galaxy's full energy output together with how its size, light profile, and shape change with wavelength. That joint view ties stars and dust into one consistent picture.

A machine learning emulator, a Bayesian neural network, stands in for costly three-dimensional dust radiation calculations. Trained on toy galaxies seen from many angles, it reproduces outputs to within about five hundredths of a dex. Sensitivity checks show the emulator has learned the real links between physical traits and what telescopes observe.
arxiv-2511-19823:
Maria Pia Gualdani, Nataša Pavlović, Justin Toyota, and Dominic Wynter derive a key operator of quantum kinetic theory from another. They show that the quantum Landau operator arises as the weak-coupling limit of the quantum Boltzmann operator. The work covers both Fermi-Dirac and Bose-Einstein statistics, the two counting rules for quantum particles.

Their route follows work by Benedetto and Pulvirenti, who derived the classical Landau operator from the quantum Boltzmann operator. To capture an extra three-part term in the Landau operator, the authors use a new scaling with two parameters that keeps quantum effects in the limit. They also give an explicit rate of convergence that depends on how smooth the interaction potential is.
arxiv-2511-20623:
Szczecina, Gaffori, and Li build a tool letting creators check if AI trained on their work. Their 2025 paper tackles copyright detection in large language models. Models train on web scrapes that swallow copyrighted text silently. Existing detectors like DE-COP are costly and hard to use. Independent creators are effectively locked out of checking.

The open-source platform simplifies the whole verification flow. Similarity detection improves over prior methods in their design. Dataset validation steps were streamlined for scale. Efficient API use cut computing overhead by ten to thirty percent. An intuitive interface hides the technical machinery from users. Models past one hundred billion parameters memorize more, they note. Lawsuits like the New York Times case raise the stakes. Future work targets selective unlearning of flagged content. Standard corpora like C4 and the Pile are named candidates. Transparency and accountability in AI development are the goals.
arxiv-2511-20923:
Rocio Kiman and colleagues pin down in 2025 the age and mass of COCONUTS-2b, a cold brown dwarf orbiting far from an M3 star. Such T9 objects are stand-ins for cold giant exoplanets, but their mass and age are usually entangled. Using the system's motion through space, the team finds a 99 percent probability that it belongs to the Corona of Ursa Major moving group. That group membership fixes the age at 414 million years, give or take 23 million years either way.

JWST supplied the data: NIRSpec spectra from 2.87 to 5.13 micrometres plus MIRI photometry in three bands. Combining luminosity with the age yields a mass of 7.5 Jupiter masses, within 0.4 either way, squarely planetary, though likely formed like a star. A comparison Y0.5 dwarf in the same group weighs only 3.7 Jupiter masses and shows spectral signs of stronger vertical mixing in its atmosphere.
arxiv-2511-21223:
Jasraj Singh, Shelvia Wongso, Jeremie Houssineau, and Badr-Eddine Chérief-Abdellatif rebuild a workhorse of machine learning inside a different theory of uncertainty in 2025. The workhorse is variational inference, a method that approximates hard probability calculations with easier ones. The different theory is possibility theory, which grades events by plausibility instead of probability and drops the rule that chances must add to one, suiting sparse or imprecise knowledge.

Singh and his coauthors derive a maxitive version of the Donsker-Varadhan formula, the identity that links divergence, a measure of mismatch, to a search for the best fit. From it they build a full possibilistic version of the method, with new forms of entropy and divergence that respect possibility rules. Worked through for a standard family of functions, the framework mirrors the classical one while exposing structures, like fully uninformative states, that probability cannot express cleanly.
arxiv-2511-21823:
Bhandari and colleagues work out how the Gaia telescope could spot exotic dark objects, hypothetical dark matter clumps called Q-balls and boson stars, via stellar wobbles. When such an object passes in front of a star, its gravity bends the starlight and shifts the star's apparent position, an effect called astrometric microlensing. Unlike a point-like black hole, an extended object can produce caustics that make the star's image centroid jump.

Those jumps are the smoking gun, and boson stars produce larger caustics than Q-balls, so the two could be told apart. Using Gaia's catalogue of stars, they forecast up to about 6,000 detectable events over a ten year mission for objects of roughly one to ten solar masses. Even with no detections, Gaia could limit such objects to a thousandth of dark matter in the best region, far stronger than existing surveys there.
arxiv-2511-22123:
Waterman and Guay, control engineers, plan flight paths through moving air by marrying two tools that are each too slow alone. Model predictive control repeatedly optimizes a trajectory while respecting limits, but running it against the full Navier-Stokes equations of fluid flow is prohibitive in real time. Proper orthogonal decomposition compresses simulated wind fields into a handful of dominant flow patterns. A Galerkin projection turns those into a small dynamical model cheap enough to optimize against at every control step.

The agent is treated as a lightly actuated particle riding the predicted wind, and the planner deliberately exploits vertical wind shear for station keeping and target tracking. Simulations using ERA5 reanalysis wind data produced physically consistent, computationally efficient paths in realistic wind environments. The authors plan to add detailed vehicle dynamics and connect the framework with learning-based balloon-navigation environments as a physics-informed hybrid.
arxiv-2511-22223:
Lee, Jang, and Dey, statisticians, model longitudinal medical counts that pile up at zero. Following lupus patients over time, most record zero hospitalizations while a few record many. Standard zero-inflated models split effects across two sub-models describing conditional pieces, not the overall average effect clinicians ask about. Their marginalized models restructure the analysis so covariates act directly on the population's overall mean, while random effects carry personal tendencies.

Two versions are developed, a marginalized zero-inflated Poisson model and a negative binomial sibling for overdispersed counts. Both letting the random-effects covariance itself vary with patient covariates, a flexibility earlier models lacked. Simulations show negligible bias and expose how wrongly assuming homogeneous covariance distorts estimates. Applied to lupus hospitalization data, they give directly interpretable marginal effects. Estimation uses a quasi-Newton algorithm chosen for stability with the two-part random-effects structure.
arxiv-2511-22523:
Ricciardi, Bardin, Chareton, and Valiron tackle a verification problem created by quantum compilers. Compilers rewrite quantum circuits constantly, and each rewrite must preserve the circuit's behaviour, so equivalence checking is essential. Most automated checkers handle only purely unitary circuits, but real quantum programs are hybrid: they mix gates with measurements, resets, and classical control, and the few hybrid checkers cover only narrow cases.

Their approach lifts existing unitary checkers to hybrid circuits through the deferred measurement principle, which rewrites measurements so they can be postponed to the end of the circuit. That lifting alone significantly outperformed prior hybrid methods in their tests. Adding two unitary-level techniques they call separation and projection widened the tractable class much further. They evaluated the tool on standard transformations including teleportation, one-way measurement, and the IBM Qiskit compiler's output, where they also found and reported several unexpected compiler behaviours.
arxiv-2511-22623:
Yamauchi asks how much flat-space scattering survives in an expanding universe. In flat space, the S-matrix's structure yields non-perturbative constraints on low-energy theories, the basis of Swampland arguments about which theories quantum gravity allows. De Sitter space, the expanding geometry of inflation and dark energy, frustrates this machinery: expansion breaks time-translation symmetry and blurs incoming and outgoing states.

Yamauchi defines the Hubble flat-space limit: energy and Hubble rate to zero at fixed ratio. In that limit, the de Sitter S-matrix becomes an integral transform of the flat-space amplitude, proven for tree-level amplitudes exchanging a massive scalar with any local derivative interactions. Unlike the energy-conservation limit, recovering only the massless high-energy corner, this one recovers the amplitude, including mass dependence. It also fits effective field theory better, since total-energy dependence trivialises and the Mandelstam variable is the scale.
arxiv-2511-22723:
Bayati and Mallory teach a neural network to see the invisible surface flows propelling microscopic swimmers. Active colloids move because spatial variations in surface chemistry create interfacial stresses and slip flow at their surface. These quantities are almost impossible to measure directly, especially since near-particle flow data are noisy or missing. Their physics-informed neural network combines sparse fluid velocity measurements with the Stokes equations and boundary constraints, reconstructing the near-surface slip plus the full velocity and pressure fields.

Validated against analytical solutions and boundary element calculations for canonical models, squirmers and Janus particles, in open fluid and near walls, the reconstructions agree quantitatively. Crucially, the framework recovers surface slip even when no measurements exist near the particle, proving bulk data encode the interfacial stresses driving motion. The authors present physics-informed inference as a general strategy for inverse problems in complex fluids, wherever boundary conditions are hidden.
arxiv-2511-23423:
Generet resolves a long-standing nuisance in collider physics, the fact that the standard way of labeling a jet's flavour. By the quarks it contains, stops being infrared-collinear safe at next-to-next-to-leading order in QCD calculations. Earlier fixes redefined the flavour assignment, forcing experiments to change their analyses. But Generet argues the safety violation is merely an artefact of the calculation and can be removed perturbatively without touching any definition in this paper.

The remedy correctly reintroduces the flavoured quark's mass at leading power. And after analyzing every source of mass dependence the required changes shrink to simple modifications of subtraction schemes plus one extra contribution whose numerical integration converges unusually fast. Because neither the jet definition, its flavour, nor the cross section changes, predictions compare directly with measurements using the standard anti-kT clustering algorithm, with essentially no extra computational cost.
arxiv-2512-00023:
Hetvi Shastri, Akanksha Atrey, Andre Beck, and Nirupama Ravi survey threats in peer-run wireless networks. In these networks, individuals own and operate equipment, offering access without sign-ups for pay. Older providers earned trust over decades through scale, practice, and rules.

New owners lack that foundation, so some may be tempted to exploit the service. The survey catalogs the threats that follow from misaligned motives and weak checks. Knowing the threat list is the first step to designing networks users can trust. Monetary compensation for owners is the network's engine, and also the source of its exploitation motives.
arxiv-2512-00123:
When one curve rolls along another without slipping, a fixed point on it traces a new curve called a roulette. Osvaldo Santos-Pereira writes about these curves in a 2025 article, using two classic puzzles as motivation. They are the coin paradox and Aristotle's wheel paradox.

The article derives parametric equations for epicycloids and hypocycloids, the curves traced when circles roll outside or inside other circles. Python code produces concrete visualizations and animations of the results. The piece serves teachers and students who want geometric intuition for curves that formulas alone can make feel abstract. Epicycloids appear in gear design, which gives the old puzzles a practical afterlife.
arxiv-2512-00223:
Kagome lattices, named after a woven basket pattern, host magnetic behavior that frustrates simple ordering. Gabriel Capelo and Eric Andrade study a magnetization plateau in such a lattice in 2025. Recent observations found a plateau at one third of full magnetization in kagome-based magnets.

The authors investigate a Heisenberg model with two exchange couplings under an external magnetic field. Although the classical ground state at zero field depends on the sign of one coupling, they find the one-third plateau is robust in both cases. Robust plateaus interest physicists hunting for materials with unusual, controllable magnetic states. Magnetization plateaus are prized because they stay stable across a range of fields.
arxiv-2512-00523:
Glasses of self-propelled particles flow in sudden avalanches, much like passive materials under stress. Roland Wiese, Ezequiel Ferrero, and Demian Levis investigate avalanche statistics in active glasses with finite persistence in 2025, with and without applied shear. Persistence measures how long each particle keeps its direction.

Departing from the infinite-persistence limit, the authors explore the interplay of internal activity and external driving. They uncover when active and passive systems share avalanche statistics and where the analogy fails. The findings matter for understanding living tissues, bacterial colonies, and other active matter that yields in bursts. Finite persistence is the realistic case, since real active particles do change direction. For folks who study such stuff, the gain is a clear map. It shows when crowds of small bits surge as one, and when they do not.
arxiv-2512-00823:
Arpit Kottur, Meet Mehta, and Raka Dabhade compare age and dark matter across spiral galaxies in a 2025 astronomy paper. Dark matter is the unseen mass that holds galaxies together and shapes how they spin. The team asks whether a galaxy's age tracks how much dark matter it holds.

They study sixteen nearby spiral galaxies with well-resolved rotation curves. Each galaxy's mass is split into a central bulge, an exponential disk, and a dark matter halo. Monte Carlo fits find the mix that matches the spin data. Their results test simple stories about how galaxies grow old and gather dark matter.
arxiv-2512-01023:
Orestis Kaparounakis, Yunqi Zhang, and Phillip Stanley-Marbell improve particle filtering in a 2025 paper. Particle filters track hidden states from noisy observations and power tools in self-driving cars, drones, warehouse robots, target tracking, and patient monitoring. They keep many candidate states, called particles, and weight them by how well each matches new data.

Their weakness is representing that match, the likelihood, which can cause particles to degenerate into a few survivors. The authors approximate hard likelihood densities with deterministic arithmetic for optimal filtering. Better likelihood handling matters most for fast, resource-limited systems where filters must run in real time.
arxiv-2512-01123:
Xiaoting Kuang and Boken Lin build a hybrid system for options trading decisions in a 2025 paper. Large language models read context and qualitative nuance well. They struggle, though, with the rigorous, transparent reasoning that high-stakes quantitative domains like financial trading demand.

Their model-first architecture targets the options wheel strategy, a cycle of selling options to collect income. It combines the language model with a Bayesian network, which reasons with explicit probabilities. The language model helps generate the network, and the network keeps the reasoning auditable. Transparent decisions matter when real money rides on each trade.
arxiv-2512-01323:
Sanjay Mishra gives a full base treatment of simplicial complexes. These are shapes built from points, edges, faces, and higher kin. They are core tools in geometry and data study. Mishra stresses worked sums, clear cases, and ways to check each claim.

The path starts with finite point sets in Euclidean space. It shows when points are geometrically free of each other. That trait is proved from how their gap vectors line up. Matrix rank tests make the checks concrete. A firm base like this helps new scholars use complexes with care.
arxiv-2512-01423:
Qi Kuang, Bowen Gang, and Yin Xia offer a way to test many claims on a tight budget. Big tests often need exact p-values or e-values for each claim. Those exact scores can cost a lot to compute. Funds and time are short in genome and AI work.

Their frame uses cheap proxy scores to guide where to spend. Costly exact work goes to the claims that need it most. A shared budget is split with care across all claims. Smart splits keep error rates in check while saving compute for large scans like genome-wide studies.
arxiv-2512-01723:
Saba Kublashvili builds HistoricalML for learning from sparse historical data. Historical sets are tiny, noisy, and mixed in type. Counterfactuals are missing by nature. Answers must also be readable by human scholars. Standard machine learning fits none of those needs well.

The frame blends Bayesian inference with neuro-symbolic methods. Probability handles doubt and scarcity. Symbols keep outputs interpretable. Joint use lets the model state both a claim and its grounds. That fit serves history, where each data point is precious and each claim is debated. Interpretable outputs let historians contest a claim's grounds, which keeps the tool inside scholarly debate rather than above it.
arxiv-2512-02323:
Boltzmann machines are strong models that learn by weights and energy. But training them in the right way has long been too slow. In practice, folks settled for small, cut-down forms. Kentaro Kubo and Hayato Goto take on both blocks in 2025: fast sampling that runs in parallel, and a quick gauge of the model's heat scale.

True learning needs samples drawn by long random walks through the model's states. For rich, fully linked machines, those walks resist being run side by side. A sampler that can run in parallel, plus fast heat gauging, could reopen the full class of models. That class was set aside when a shortcut called contrastive divergence took over.
arxiv-2512-02423:
Software agents that click through real applications must learn navigation across many screens, but real apps are proprietary and complex, starving training of good environments. Haolong Yan and a large team present the GUI Exploration Lab in 2025, with multi-turn reinforcement learning to teach agents screen navigation.

The focus has shifted from single-screen tasks to long navigation challenges across PC software and mobile apps. A lab environment supplies the comprehensive information needed for training and evaluation that real products withhold. Agents that can explore interfaces patiently would automate the multi-step chores that current assistants abandon halfway.
arxiv-2512-02523:
Xueyan Li and six co-authors work on judging songs made by singing voice synthesis systems. Modern systems can now hold pitch and keep a steady style across a song. As output quality rises, fair and useful scoring of that output becomes more pressing.

Common reward systems give a single number, which misses traits like phrasing and expressiveness. Human labels for those traits cost a lot to collect. The team's generative multimodal feedback gives richer, multi angle comments instead. Better feedback could help builders improve synthetic singers and help listeners trust quality claims. Rich notes beat a lone score when a coach must say what to fix next in a take.
arxiv-2512-02723:
Palash Saha and Michał Zegrodnik study a stacked pair of atom thin crystals, molybdenum ditelluride over tungsten diselenide. At two holes per moiré cell, electron interactions and spin orbit coupling compete strongly. Such moiré bilayers are known hunting grounds for new topological phases of matter.

Their analysis finds a robust quantum valley Hall insulating phase. Long range interactions alone can drive tunneling between layers, creating topologically nontrivial bands even without single particle hopping. Interaction driven topology widens the menu of phases that layered materials might host for future electronics. A phase born of sheer push and pull, with no hop to seed it, was not on most lists till now.
arxiv-2512-02923:
Augusto E. Lassen and a large team separate two forces that can stretch a galaxy into similar shapes. In dense environments, ram pressure strips gas as a galaxy plows through hot surroundings. Gravitational interactions with neighbors can mimic those same morphological features closely.

The Size-Shape Difference method compares stellar properties to tell the two causes apart. Applying it to real galaxies tests whether the method survives messy data. Knowing the true cause tells astronomers how galaxies are quenched and reshaped inside clusters over cosmic time. Real sky data is the stern test. Clean mocks can hide the flaws that real noise and real dust will find in no time at all.
arxiv-2512-03423:
Atoms linked to light guides can be steered with care. Weijun Cheng, Da-Wei Wang, Yang Xue, Zhihai Wang, and Liantuan Xiao study such a system in this 2025 work. They use one-dimensional coupled-resonator waveguides with long-range hoppings.

By engineering each order of hopping between resonators, they build linear dispersion relations with a chiral character. Dispersion shapes how light and atoms interact over time. Precise control could help quantum networks and simulators. It also opens routes to study exotic light-matter effects in the lab. Chiral dispersion could steer single photons and atoms in future quantum links.
arxiv-2512-03523:
A young, active star flared through a week-long campaign. Isaiah Tristan and co-authors report the quiet-phase radio data in this 2025 work, the fourth in a series. The star is AU Mic, an M-dwarf known for strong flares.

The campaign ran in October 2018 across many wavelengths. This paper analyzes radio data between flares, at frequencies from twelve to twenty-five gigahertz. Quiet emission reveals the star's steady magnetic activity. Understanding it helps judge the space weather faced by AU Mic's young planets. Quiet radio emission sets the baseline against which flare bursts are judged.
arxiv-2512-03623:
Britain's Shipping Forecast is an iconic weather text. Edward Steele and a large team test whether vision language models can write it in this 2025 work. Application of multimodal foundation models to weather products is still nascent.

The team explores generating the forecast text directly from video-encoded gridded weather data. A model that reads maps and writes clear forecasts could speed up services. It could also tailor forecasts to new audiences. Careful checks remain vital, since mariners rely on these words for safety. Video encoding lets the model see weather evolve, not just a single static chart, which matches how forecasters read moving systems.
arxiv-2512-03823:
Simulating vast numbers of gravitating bodies forces approximations, and small shortcuts can quietly break the rules of classical dynamics. Søren Toxvaerd tests those shortcuts on the simplest possible stage in a 2025 preprint on gravity and astrophysics: three bodies pulling on each other. He compares a particle-mesh shortcut, the MOND modification, and an alternative gravity scheme called MOGA.

In his simulations, the particle-mesh approximation and MOND both destabilised the three-body system. Neither preserves momentum and angular momentum exactly, and the mesh method also violates Newton's third law. Though the errors look tiny, they accumulate until regular motion falls apart. MOGA behaved oppositely: replacing the inverse-square pull with a gentler law for distant interactions made the system more stable. Toxvaerd's message is that the three-body problem is a cheap, sharp test any proposed shortcut should pass first.
arxiv-2512-04123:
Language model agents already work inside real companies, but nobody had systematically asked their builders what works. Melissa Z. Pan and a large team do exactly that in a 2025 preprint, calling the study Measuring Agents in Production. They ran twenty case studies and surveyed practitioners behind eighty-six deployed systems across twenty-six domains.

The picture is more conservative than the hype suggests. Most production agents take at most ten steps before a human intervenes, rely on prompting off-the-shelf models rather than retraining them, and are judged mainly by human evaluation. Reliability, meaning consistent correct behaviour over time, stands out as the top development challenge. Practitioners buy that reliability with systems-level design: guardrails, fallbacks, and supervision around the model. The authors offer the study as a reality check and a map of underexplored problems.
arxiv-2512-04223:
Transport models need made-up people: full daily activity schedules for thousands of simulated people, conditioned on who they are. Fred Shone and Tim Hillel present ActVAE in a 2025 machine learning preprint, a deep conditional generative model of daily routines. The challenge is capturing behaviour that is both complex and genuinely diverse.

ActVAE conditions each schedule on who the person is: household details, age, income, and access to public transit among them. It then generates new ones rapidly, and the authors describe them as precise, realistic, and diverse. Evaluation uses a joint-density estimation framework, comparing the model against baselines across its capabilities. The work is more than a novel alternative to existing scheduling approaches. The authors argue it shows the value of modelling the randomness of how people act, explicitly, rather than averaging it away.
arxiv-2512-04523:
Feng-Yi Liao, Thomas Madden, and Yang Zheng present the first accelerated version of the proximal bundle method, a workhorse for minimizing rough convex functions. Bundle methods build a simple model of a hard function from past cuts, then step toward its low point. For smooth functions, their best known speed lagged behind the optimum, and whether they could be sped up stayed open. Their 2025 arXiv paper closes that question.

The new method reaches the best possible rate for smooth convex problems. It differs from the classic bundle method by a single line, a tweak akin to Nesterov's famous acceleration trick. All key traits of the classic method survive, including its light assumptions and its standard bundle test. Computer runs confirm the faster rate the theory predicts. Practitioners in control, energy, and machine learning gain a faster tool that keeps the bundle method's famed stability.
arxiv-2512-04623:
Krzysztof Pachucki, Vojtěch Patkóš, and Vladimir Yerokhin sharpen a tiny correction to the light given off by helium atoms. Atomic spectra shift slightly between isotopes, and those shifts reveal the size of the nucleus. To read nuclear size from helium's lines, theory must match experiment to extreme precision. Quantum electrodynamics supplies corrections term by term. Their 2025 arXiv paper handles the leading recoil correction, where the nucleus itself moves as electrons orbit.

Earlier work treated the electron-to-nucleus mass ratio only to first order. The team derives formulas good to second order in that small ratio. They then compute the correction for the shift between helium-3 and helium-4. The improved value tightens the inferred difference in nuclear charge radius between the two isotopes. Such precision tests both quantum theory and nuclear models, and it feeds the broader effort to settle proton-size puzzles.
arxiv-2512-04823:
Brian Block and Stephanie Stockar bring constrained control theory to variable speed limits on highways, using a partial differential equation model of traffic. The Lighthill-Whitham-Richards model treats traffic as a flowing density that can jam. Posted speed limits, varied along the road, act as the control input. Their 2025 arXiv paper extends Lyapunov control design from ordinary equations to this spatial setting, where states and limits vary by place and time.

A stabilizing control law aims density at a target profile. Spatial control barrier functions then guard a safety rule: density must stay below set caps everywhere. The unified design adjusts the stabilizing input only slightly while keeping the caps. Simulations show density held inside the safe set across the road. Such methods could let traffic managers smooth flow and prevent shockwave jams without risking over-dense stretches.
arxiv-2512-05023:
Jose Castro-Moreno, Enric Florit, and Nuno Freitas classify the inertial types of elliptic curves over p-adic fields. An elliptic curve's inertial type is a compact label, built from Weil-Deligne data. It records how the curve behaves under the symmetries of the local field. Number theorists need that information when they study curves one prime at a time. Earlier work had not covered every finite extension of the p-adic rationals at once.

The authors complete that classification and turn it into a fully explicit description of every type that occurs. They also implement an algorithm that, given a specific extension field, lists all inertial types arising from curves defined over it. As a demonstration, they work out every type for extensions of small degree. The result gives researchers a ready reference and a computational tool for a basic invariant of elliptic curves.
arxiv-2512-05323:
Adam Lizerbram and four co-authors stress-test an artificial intelligence weather model on a real hurricane. The model, NVIDIA's FourCastNetv2, forecasts by learning from data rather than solving physics equations. Its reliability under messy inputs is an open question — especially for extreme events, where bad forecasts cost most. The team asks how the model responds when its starting picture of the atmosphere is corrupted.

They replay Hurricane Florence from reanalysis data, injecting Gaussian noise of growing strength into the initial conditions and tracking the predicted path and intensity. At low and moderate noise the model preserves the storm well; at high noise the trajectory and structure survive, though position accuracy fades, and the model underplays intensity and persistence. Fed random inputs, it soon settles into smooth, coherent forecasts — a revealing tilt toward stable, smoothed outputs. The simple test protocol transfers readily to other data-driven forecast models.
arxiv-2512-05523:
Kei Irie surveys strong closing lemmas in Hamiltonian dynamics — theorems saying that a nearly periodic motion can be perturbed slightly into a truly periodic one. Closing lemmas are bridges between dynamics and topology: they force the existence of periodic orbits, the atoms of long-term behaviour. The strong versions surveyed here are proved with spectral invariants, quantities extracted from symplectic geometry that act as selectors of action values.

The survey concentrates on the low-dimensional cases where the theory is richest: area-preserving maps on symplectic surfaces and Reeb flows on contact three-manifolds. It outlines the key ideas behind the proofs rather than merely citing them. It then turns to what is known in higher dimensions and to analogous results for minimal hypersurfaces, a parallel world in geometric analysis. For dynamicists, the article maps a technique that has quietly become one of symplectic geometry's sharpest exports.
arxiv-2512-05823:
Kai Zhu, Darong Huang, Luis Costero, and David Atienza release version four of 3D-ICE, a tool that maps heat inside stacked computer chips. Modern designs pile chiplets densely, and heat paths twist through unlike materials. Older compact models fail to keep up. The new release was built specifically for heterogeneous chiplet systems.

Three upgrades stand out. Material differences and direction dependent conduction are preserved straight from industrial layout files, and parallel solvers keep the math fast. Vertical layers are split adaptively, so heat flow between floors is captured faithfully. And the grid is refined only where temperatures demand it. Across benchmarks, the tool ran roughly four to six times faster than leading rivals, on grids simpler by more than a fifth. Against the commercial package COMSOL it matched both sideways and vertical heat flow. For architects, such maps decide what can be built.
arxiv-2512-05923:
Junhan Liu and Alexander Mitov present an algorithm that sorts out the integration by parts equations of particle physics. When people compute scattering processes with loops, thousands of loop sums appear, tied together by these rules. Solving that system reduces all of it to a few master integrals, the choke point of the field. Diagonalizing the system is the key step for hard integrals and closed answers.

The procedure comes with a by-product. The same steps recast the system into triangular form, the shape computers solve fastest, one unknown at a time. A prime application is the Mellin form of loop amplitudes, where recurrences in several variables appear. Extensions to other recurrence relations are treated. Several hard topologies have been computed with it. As colliders demand sharper predictions, such algorithms are core tools.
arxiv-2512-06023:
Jasem Hamoud and Duaa Abdullah bound a measure of how lopsided a tree network is, given only the list of its node degrees. The Albertson index scores irregularity by comparing degrees across every edge. Trees, graphs without cycles, are the test case, and the degree sequence, how many edges meet at each vertex, is the given data. The authors derive sharp bounds, the true minimum and maximum the index can take for trees with that sequence.

For caterpillar trees, a spine with legs, they give an exact formula. The bounds expose how degree patterns force irregularity. Extremal results like these are the graph theorist's surveying work. Knowing the reachable range tells analysts which fingerprints are possible. Earlier bounds are improved.
arxiv-2512-06323: Grigor Sargsyan and Nam Trang work in set theory. Their topic is a claim called Tower Sealing. It concerns how towers of models behave when the set theoretic world is enlarged by forcing. The setting is an enlarged version of special inner models called hod mice. The world holds a strong cardinal and many Woodin cardinals. There, full Tower Sealing fails in general. A weakened form, Partial Tower Sealing, does hold. It still implies Sealing. Its strength sits below a Woodin limit of Woodin cardinals.
arxiv-2512-06723:
Daiki Mizuno and Ken Shirakawa settle a basic question about a model of how grain boundaries move inside a material. The KWC system describes the shifting borders between crystal grains, which govern how metals harden, crack, and age. A solution theory must show the model is well posed: that solutions exist, are unique, and behave sanely. That had not been shown when the mobility of the boundary depends on the unknown state itself, the realistic case.

Earlier work on a close cousin of the system hinted that control of the solution's time derivative is the key to uniqueness. The authors use that cousin as an approximating system and prove stronger regularity for solutions of the true parabolic system. With that regularity in hand, the well posedness theory follows. The result puts simulations of grain boundary motion on firmer mathematical ground.
arxiv-2512-07023:
Melisa Ozen and co-authors measure how a block of plastic scintillator, a material that flashes when radiation hits it, responds to a specific gamma ray. The gamma rays come from a standard neutron source, where carbon nuclei emit them at a well-known energy. Inside the plastic, some gamma rays convert into an electron and its antimatter twin. When both escape, they leave behind a telltale deposit known as the double-escape peak.

To isolate that peak from the heavy neutron background, the team tags the annihilation flashes that escaping twins produce in two dense companion detectors. Their measurement extracts the small peak cleanly and maps the shape of the detector's response around it. The paper also explores the features and practical difficulties of the tagging technique with their apparatus.
arxiv-2512-07123:
Yang Liu and co-authors accelerate deep packet inspection, the security scan that reads network traffic against thousands of pattern rules. Rules are compiled into a deterministic automaton, a machine that steps through states as bytes arrive, but with today's bandwidths and rule sets that machine has become the bottleneck. Their model, Hyperflex, uses the processor's parallel lanes, which apply one instruction to many data items at once, to fire state transitions in batches.

A region detection pass first finds the stretches of the automaton graph where parallel stepping pays, across the whole graph rather than in pockets. A hybrid transition scheme then moves traffic between accelerated and ordinary regions without seams. Built on a commodity processor and tested on real traffic with production rule sets, Hyperflex more than doubled the throughput of the default engine inside the well-known Hyperscan library.
arxiv-2512-07223:
Xuchen Lin and co-authors confront a flagship galaxy simulation with real telescope data on the faint outskirts of galaxies. The new FEASTS survey maps atomic hydrogen around Milky Way-like galaxies down to a wisp of a column density, where the gas is thin and easily disturbed. The team picks hundreds of simulated galaxies from the TNG50 run, matched in stars and hydrogen to a few dozen observed ones. And mock-observes them at the telescope's own resolution and depth, at matching angles and distances.

The comparison stings: more than a third of the simulated galaxies show abnormally ragged, stretched hydrogen shapes that the real ones lack, especially the massive, hydrogen-poor systems. The property that tracks the mismatch best is stellar feedback, the energy stars return to their surroundings, while black hole feedback plays a smaller role than expected.
arxiv-2512-07723:
Yonggeon Lee, Jibin Hwang, Alfred Malengo Kondoro, Juhyun Song, and Youngtae Noh wrote this 2025 engineering paper. Electric car batteries age faster when they sit full for long stretches. Delaying the final charge until just before departure slows that wear.

The delay only works if departure times can be predicted well. The authors build a transformer model for that prediction task. Each day becomes a sequence of time-to-event tokens on a fixed grid. Older methods leaned on historical patterns in a driver's routine. This one also reads streaming context as the day unfolds. The team tests it on passive smartphone data from real users. Irregular departures inside personal routines are the hard cases. The model captures those quirks better than the baseline methods. Delayed-full charging thus becomes practical rather than theoretical. The authors present the system as a step toward longer-lived electric fleets.
arxiv-2512-07823:
Xiaosheng Huang and fifteen co-authors wrote this 2025 astronomy paper on gravitational lenses. A massive galaxy can bend light from a farther source into arcs and rings. Six such galaxy-scale lenses, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope, are modeled here.

The systems come from the DESI Strong Lens Foundry series, this being its fifth paper. Machine learning found the candidates in DESI survey images. Telescopes on the ground confirmed them with spectroscopy afterward. Their modeling tool, GIGA-Lens, fits lens and source together in one inference. Every parameter is sampled at once, a first for an HST lens sample. The authors validate convergence explicitly for each system, with two statistical checks. All six pass those checks with robust margins. Sound modeling is hard for complex lenses. It now looks ready to scale to far larger samples. Euclid, Webb, and Roman will supply those samples in coming years.
arxiv-2512-08023:
Ethan Decker, Christopher Watson, Junyu Zhou, and colleagues, researchers in quantum computing, posted a study on arXiv in December 2025. Their system, called F2, tackles a practical bottleneck in quantum computing. Compiling short and accurate circuits for Hamiltonian simulation is hard, and the usual hand built heuristics cannot learn the structure of each new problem.

F2 uses offline reinforcement learning built around free fermionic subroutines, a class of quantum operations that classical computers can simulate. The framework adds design biases that steady long horizon learning, plus a reversible way to generate training data that is guaranteed to succeed. Across tests from lattice models to protein fragments and crystals, F2 cut gate counts and circuit depth sharply against strong baselines. Errors stayed very small, suggesting learning based compilation can scale with the structure of quantum dynamics.
arxiv-2512-08723:
Chloe Touzet and coauthors argue that risk modeling should sit at the center of managing risks from advanced artificial intelligence. Such systems bring new and uncertain risks, some potentially severe. The authors define risk modeling as joining two tasks: building causal scenarios from hazards to harms, and estimating how likely and how severe each path may be.

They review classic tools from safety engineering, such as fault trees, event trees, and Bayesian networks, and show how each can adapt to advanced AI. A survey of current efforts finds useful pieces but a fragmented whole. Lessons from nuclear, aviation, cyber, finance, and submarine fields point the same way. Those fields pair firm guarantees against unacceptable events with broader probabilistic study. The authors propose a similar dual path for AI governance, with shared tolerance thresholds.
arxiv-2512-08823:
Elena Kulinskaya and David Hoaglin study how to estimate the point where the ordering between two distributions changes. For group comparisons, the standardized mean difference is the usual scale free effect measure. Its use assumes the two group variances are equal, an assumption that data often contradict.

The authors instead base the approach on stochastic ordering of the treatment and control distributions, which accounts for both means and variances. Their development yields a key quantity, the outcome value at which the direction of ordering flips between the groups. Through an extensive simulation, they study the bias of point estimators for that changepoint. They also examine the coverage and width of bootstrap confidence intervals for it. The work offers an alternative effect framework for cases where equal variance cannot be trusted, grounded in the full shape of the two distributions rather than means alone.
arxiv-2512-08923:
Angela van Sprang and coauthors introduce benchmarks to test whether multimodal language models give consistent answers when the same content arrives in different forms. Such models are trained to place vision and language in a shared space, yet they often cannot perform the same task across modalities. The new tests present identical semantic information as image, as text, and as a mix of both.

Across fifteen leading models, inconsistency varies widely, even after accounting for errors in reading text from images. Rendering text as an image, or an image as text, does not fix the problem. Visual traits such as text color and resolution affect performance, as does the number of vision tokens, while font matters less. The consistency score also tracks the measured gap between text and image representations. That link offers a mechanistic clue for why cross modal reasoning remains unreliable in current systems.
arxiv-2512-09223:
Pengfei Zhang, Zhongxiang Wang, and Shunhao Ji report on the aftermath of supernova 2022jli, a star explosion of type Ic discovered in May 2022. Light from the explosion showed extra emissions that rose and fell on a regular cycle of about twelve and a half days. Matching shifts in the light's spectrum suggested a compact object, such as a neutron star, orbiting inside the debris.

The team analyzed a faint gamma-ray source found at the same position.
