They show the gamma rays lasted about a year and a half after discovery and pulsed with the same roughly twelve-and-a-half-day period. That shared rhythm strengthens the case that the explosion created a binary system pairing a newborn neutron star or stellar black hole with a companion. The authors describe it as likely the first high-energy binary system of this kind detected outside our own galaxy.
arxiv-2512-09523:
Shaghayegh Zamani Ashtiani and Kai Fukami analyze what happens when a gust slams into the turbulent wake behind an airfoil. Understanding encounters matters for aircraft safety and design, but the flow is a multiscale mess that is hard to summarize. Their approach is data-driven, representing the flow with bases, patterns that change rather than staying fixed.

Each snapshot is described by two-dimensional in-plane patterns, one-dimensional spanwise patterns, and a covariance matrix, with closed-form equations advancing all of them over a rolling window. No long history must be stored. Applied to vortex gusts hitting an airfoil, the analysis shows the first pattern dominating before impact and the second gaining energy afterward, growing with gust strength. During impact the leading patterns show shear-layer roll-up and fine turbulence. The pattern-energy spectrum also tracks the lift, linking the reduced description to the forces the wing feels.
arxiv-2512-09723:
Zongcheng Wang proposes MoLKV, an architecture for running language models on end-user devices with memory limits. It builds on the Mixture of Lookup Experts design, where each input token is tied to a group of expert networks, and only the experts for the tokens present are loaded. Because so few experts are active, the rest can stay in storage, which suits small hardware.

The weakness of that design is that expert selection depends only on token identity, ignoring context. In MoLKV, each expert is structured as a key-value pair. A query derived from the input interacts with the cached key-value experts of the sequence so far, producing an expert output that is aware of context. In small-scale evaluations, MoLKV achieved lower validation loss than the context-blind design. The paper is marked as a version and work in progress, presenting the mechanism and its first evidence.
arxiv-2512-09823:
Alin Bostan, Arnaud Carayol, Florent Koechlin, and Cyril Nicaud connect formal language theory with the algebra of power series. Their objects are Parikh automata, machines that read words while counting how often each letter appears. The weakly unambiguous variant allows limited ambiguity in how a word is accepted. The authors first prove a strong form of a conjecture by Castiglione and Massazza. Weakly unambiguous Parikh automata turn out to be equivalent to unambiguous two way counter machines with bounded reversals.

They further show their generating series are holonomic. The converse fails. The team constructs a language whose generating series is even algebraic, hence holonomic, yet which no weakly unambiguous Parikh automaton can accept without ambiguity. Finally, they prove that language inclusion for these automata is decidable, and they bound the complexity of that decision problem.
arxiv-2512-10023:
Kyle D. Neumann and colleagues present a new X-ray catalog meant to identify mysterious gamma ray sources. The Fermi telescope's catalog lists many gamma ray sources with no known counterpart. The team pointed the Swift observatory's X-ray and ultraviolet telescopes at hundreds of these unassociated sources. They detected a few hundred X-ray sources inside the uncertainty regions, many never cataloged before. For each, they measured X-ray flux and spectral slope, and estimated optical brightness from ultraviolet and survey data.

Those measurements feed a neural network trained to sort sources into blazars, pulsars, or ambiguous cases. Most single sources came out as likely blazars, a handful as likely pulsars, and the rest ambiguous. Where earlier studies exist, the network's calls mostly agree with them. The work was accepted by the Astrophysical Journal, with machine readable data files included.
arxiv-2512-10223:
Jiewei Feng, Peihong Yuan, Ken R. Duffy, and Muriel Médard squeeze better error performance out of the polar codes used in 5G. The standard decoder for these CRC aided codes is incomplete: sometimes it fails to find any codeword passing the checksum, and simply gives up. The authors add a second stage. When the main decoder fails, a modern code agnostic decoder, one that knows nothing of the code's structure, searches for a codeword satisfying the checksum. Together they form a complete decoder.

The gains are substantial. For the 5G standard's codes, block error rates improve measurably, and with systematic encoding the improvement grows much larger. A further concern is silent corruption: using the checksum for correction could pass wrong codewords unnoticed. Building on recent blockwise soft output methods, the authors show the undetected error rate can still be controlled.
arxiv-2512-10623:
Ronith Stanly and co-authors shorten one of the most expensive parts of turbulence simulation: the long inlet stretch a boundary layer needs before its large outer structures develop. At high Reynolds numbers that development length makes direct simulation of wall turbulence almost unaffordable. Their method instead builds the inflow from knowledge of how boundary layers are organised.

Spectra show the outer region grows with Reynolds number while the inner region stays put. So the authors take velocity slices computed at a lower Reynolds number, split their wavenumbers into inner and outer parts in spectral space. And stretch only the outer part to match the target. Fed into new simulations, the recycled inflow matched a from-scratch run's skin friction and shape factor almost immediately. And the stresses settled after a short distance, cutting the needed development length by about tenfold.
arxiv-2512-10723:
Hao Tang, Hao Chen, and Chao Li design neural operators that respect the geometry of the sphere. Neural operators learn to solve whole families of partial differential equations, but moving them onto spherical domains, the natural setting for weather and planetary science, risks distortions that break rotational consistency. Earlier designs leaned on strict rotational symmetry and were too rigid for messy real systems.

Their framework builds operators from a designable spherical Green's function and its harmonic expansion, giving the design a firm base in operator theory. A position-dependent Green's function lets the model balance symmetry and invariance as the task demands, adapting even to non-symmetric systems while keeping its spectral speed. Their SHNet design adds multi-scale spectral modelling with spherical sampling. Tests on diffusion MRI, shallow water dynamics, and global weather forecasting beat the leading methods, and the code is public.
arxiv-2512-10823:
Ting-Jung Lee and co-authors expose a quiet inconsistency in how interest rates are modelled. Term structure models price zero-coupon bonds under one risk-neutral measure while equity markets are priced under another, though both describe the same financial world. Their unified framework treats a zero-coupon bond as a European option with a deterministic payoff, forcing it under the equity market's own measure.

Using put-call parity, they extract the yield curves implied by S&P 500 index options and compare them with the United States Treasury's daily par yield curves. Because the implied curve depends on both maturity and strike price, they study that strike dependence directly. At-the-money implied curves matched the Treasury curves most closely, evidence that the equity options market carries information highly relevant to interest rates. The authors offer the shared measure as an organising principle for future term structure research.
arxiv-2512-10923:
Andrei Egorov assesses whether gamma-ray telescopes could catch heavy dark matter annihilating beside two nearby supermassive black holes. Dark matter should pile into a steep density spike around such a black hole. And inside a spike even the thermal WIMP, the classic candidate that interacts only weakly, becomes detectable across its allowed mass range, up to the unitarity ceiling. He checks every relevant nearby black hole for this opportunity.

Only two targets survive the screening: our own galaxy's centre and M31, the Andromeda galaxy's black hole. For M31, he estimates the Cherenkov Telescope Array's sensitivity. He finds the array could probe a major part of the TeV-scale WIMP parameter space. That holds under an optimistic picture of the spike's density. In some scenarios it beats even the Milky Way's constraints. Systematic uncertainties are explored alongside, in a study published in the Journal of Cosmology and Astroparticle Physics.
arxiv-2512-11123:
Alexander Houston and fellow authors show that uneven action can make an active nematic material oscillate on its own. Active nematics are fluids of rod like units that inject energy internally, such as cell layers or bacterial films. With uniform action, the calm state simply gives way to a distorted flowing state past a threshold.

When action varies in space, the instability changes character. The pattern of the growing mode shifts its symmetry, and steady distortion can be replaced by spontaneous oscillations. The authors derive a small dynamical system for the even and odd parts of the alignment pattern, with coefficients set by the action profile, and confirm it with model runs. For steady action gradients they map the possible responses, which range from near harmonic waves to slow relaxation cycles. Light controlled tests could test these predictions.
arxiv-2512-11323:
Jianyi Zhang and colleagues built CAPTURE, a benchmark that tests whether large vision language models can solve CAPTCHAs, the puzzles websites use to separate people from bots. Earlier tests were each customised to one research goal, covered few puzzle types, and none was designed specifically for these multimodal models. That left a patchy picture of a capability with clear security implications.

CAPTURE spans four main CAPTCHA families and twenty five subtypes gathered from thirty one vendors. Its labels were tailored to vision language models, and its scale and variety support multi dimensional evaluation. When leading models were put through it, they performed poorly at solving the puzzles overall. The authors release the benchmark to give the field a common, realistic yardstick for this skill. The poor showing also suggests current models are not yet a practical threat to CAPTCHA defences.
arxiv-2512-11523:
Yu-Chi Hou proves a convergence result in complex geometry about approximating a continuous energy with discrete, quantised versions of it. The setting involves a large, mildly positive line bundle over a complex projective space, a structure looser than the amply positive bundles classical theory prefers. Smooth positive representatives no longer exist, so a more flexible theory of curved measures is required.

Hou works with spaces of sections twisted by the manifold's canonical bundle, the adjoint setting. The key step compares the Bergman kernels of the bundle with those of slightly amplified twists of it. From that comparison, Donaldson's quantised version of the Monge Ampère energy converges to the true energy for every reasonable potential function. A consequence is that the normalised Bergman measures approach the corresponding curved measures. The result partly answers a question posed by Berman and Freixas i Montplet about quantisation in this semipositive world.
arxiv-2512-11723:
B S Hu and co-authors locate the edge of calcium nuclei with a new force built from chiral theory. The neutron dripline is the point where added neutrons no longer stick. Past chiral forces failed to bind calcium past 40 neutrons, while other models put the edge near 70 calcium, at 50 neutrons.

Their force, called N3LO Texas, mixes two and three nucleon parts tuned with fast emulator fits. It matches binding energies and sizes for nuclei from mass 3 to 208. Two heavy many body methods then agree: the calcium two neutron dripline reaches 71 calcium. The result sharpens a basic map of what nuclei can exist.
arxiv-2512-11923:
Rishabh More revisits the rod climbing effect, where a stirred elastic fluid creeps up the stirring rod instead of being flung out. Textbooks credit the first normal stress difference, which creates hoop tension that hauls fluid upward. The second normal stress difference is usually waved away as too small to matter.

High resolution simulations of the Linear Phan-Thien-Tanner model isolate that second effect. As its size grows, climbing weakens, then flips into rod descending once the stress ratio passes about 0.25. Larger values also stir up bubbles, wobbling, and full three dimensional breakup at lower spin speeds. The maps reconcile past clashes between theory, experiments, and simulations.
arxiv-2512-12023:
Julia L Gonski and co-authors propose a wild search for long lived particles: melt the detectors that may have trapped them. Heavy particles made at the LHC could lodge in detector material and sit there for years, invisible among backgrounds. Split supersymmetry gluinos are the test case.

The plan takes detector matter in liquid form, melted silicon, drained liquid argon, or a big water pool near ATLAS or CMS. Spinning and mass spectrometry could then isolate single trapped particles. The method could find gluinos up to 3 TeV at the high luminosity LHC and stops up to 2 TeV. It also covers integer charged particles in the TeV range, a blind spot for normal searches.
arxiv-2512-12123:
Niloy Saha and co-authors present SliceScope, a monitoring system for network slices with strict service promises. Modern networks carve slices, logical networks tuned per use, each with its own service level agreement. Watching every slice end to end on a fixed telemetry budget is the hard part.

Older tools either sample blindly or see everything at fixed cost. SliceScope treats monitoring as a control loop. It shifts watch resources toward the most critical slices and uses change triggered in band telemetry for per packet views with tunable cost. On programmable switches and in large simulations it tracked critical slices up to four times more accurately than static setups. The design gives operators proof, not hope, on slice promises.
arxiv-2512-12423:
Christian Howard, Roohollah Ghobadi, Nazanin Dehghan, Alessio D'Errico, and Ebrahim Karimi image distortions in entangled photon pairs in a 2025 paper. A process called spontaneous parametric down-conversion makes photon pairs tied in position and opposed in momentum, forming the classic EPR state. Studies often treat thin crystals as if sum and difference coordinates separate cleanly.

In real crystals, birefringence makes one polarization drift sideways, an effect called walk-off, which couples those coordinates. The coupling survives even in thin crystals once light travel is counted. It tapers the pair correlations near the crystal image plane. Simulations and lab data confirm the effect, setting limits for quantum imaging.
arxiv-2512-12523:
Wenqi Fang and Ye Li improve detection of critical transitions in noisy dynamical systems in a 2025 paper. A critical transition is a sudden shift, like a lake flipping to algae dominance. Early signs often hide in a low dimensional order parameter, masked by strong random noise in the data.

Standard contrastive learning can find such shifts but uses oversized networks that react to irrelevant noise. Their design builds the network from a singular value decomposition and trains it under strict semi-orthogonality rules. Tests show it matches standard contrastive methods at spotting transitions. It is also much lighter in size and markedly more resistant to noise, the authors report.
arxiv-2512-12623:
Chengzhi Liu and five co-authors present DMLR, a latent reasoning framework for multimodal models, in a 2025 paper. Multimodal large language models reason with chain of thought in text space, and newer work adds visual steps through tools or generated images. Those explicit methods suffer unstable perception reasoning interplay and heavy compute costs, the authors argue.

DMLR instead refines latent think tokens at test time, guided by confidence based policy gradient optimization. A dynamic visual injection strategy picks the most relevant image features for each think token and injects the best patches back in. That interleaves seeing and thinking inside the latent space. Across seven multimodal reasoning benchmarks and varied architectures, DMLR improved reasoning and perception while staying efficient.
arxiv-2512-13123:
Liviu Aolaritei and Michael Jordan solve a practical puzzle in stochastic gradient descent, the workhorse method for training models: when should training stop? Classic theory gives promises only at fixed step counts chosen in advance. It gives no valid way to judge, mid-run, whether more steps are worth the cost.

They build confidence sequences that stay valid under constant checking, using only values seen along the training path. Stopping rules follow directly: stop once the upper confidence bound drops below a chosen tolerance. The framework covers both convex problems and smooth nonconvex ones. It is the first to give time-uniform stopping rules for gradient descent in both settings.
arxiv-2512-13323:
Arpad Pandy, Robert Lakatos, and Andras Hajdu improve arithmetic reasoning in small language models that must run on site, so private data never leaves a secure building. Analysts in finance and health care need exact calculations on structured tables. Base small models, though, show basic limits on arithmetic tasks.

Their error-driven method groups a model's wrong answers into clusters, then rewrites prompt rules step by step to fix each error type. Applied to a code generation agent using Qwen3 4B, accuracy climbed to 70.8 percent. The result beat a larger cloud model while staying privacy compliant, a case that prompt craft can rival costly fine-tuning.
arxiv-2512-13523:
Alonso Beaumont studies maps of the projective line that commute with a given map and its repeats. A dominant endomorphism is a map from the line to itself with a dense image. Beaumont leaves out maps that are conjugate to a pure power map, which behave in a special way.

He proves that the centralizers of all repeats of such a map stop growing at some fixed repeat. That result settles a conjecture by F. Pakovich. As a use, he obtains a Tits alternative for cancellative semigroups of such maps, with no need to assume finite generation. The work extends earlier results by Bell, Huang, Peng, and Tucker.
arxiv-2512-14223:
Francesco Pierri and seven coauthors examine research access under the European Union Digital Services Act in a 2025 article. The 2022 law is a landmark frame for platform transparency. Its Article 40 lets vetted researchers request data from major online platforms to study systemic risks.

In practice, legal, technical, and organizational barriers still block much of that work. The authors outline the main problems that arise in the Article 40 process, from unclear rules to slow or uneven platform responses. They then propose practical measures to fix them. Their goal is to help the law meet its stated aims of transparency and accountability for very large platforms.
arxiv-2512-14423:
Zhuo Chen and six coauthors tackle hard non rigid image edits in a 2025 paper. Training free editing with large diffusion models can change pose or shape, but edits often go too far or fall short. The authors trace the fault to attention collapse in attention sharing, where position or meaning cues dominate retrieval.

Their method, SynPS, combines positional embeddings and semantic data in a synergistic way. A new editing measure estimates how much change each denoising step needs. An attention synergy pipeline then adjusts the weight of positional cues step by step, balancing change against fidelity. Extensive tests on public and newly curated benchmarks show stronger faithfulness than prior approaches for complex non rigid edits.
arxiv-2512-14723:
Modern applications collect multivariate time series, records with many channels evolving together, from sensors, medicine, and finance. A common task is subsequence search: finding every series that contains a stretch highly similar to a query series.

MS-Index is an index built to answer top-k subsequence searches under Euclidean distance quickly, returning the k best matches rather than scanning everything. Fast search over huge time series collections is what makes interactive analysis possible. The work targets the scale at which naive matching becomes too slow to use, a scale that sensor and monitoring applications already reach.
arxiv-2512-14923:
David Sims and four coauthors test whether 3D printing can speed up the design of radio frequency cavities. Such cavities are hollow metal parts that hold radio waves at set frequencies, and making them the usual way is slow and costly. A printed plastic core coated with metal could let engineers try new shapes fast.

The team built a series of clamped, multi mode gigahertz cavities. They varied the plastic, the slicing plan, and the way a thin copper skin was applied to the inner walls. Bench tests then measured field patterns, working frequencies, and quality factors for each build. One design, sliced lengthwise and painted with metal, proved quite practical. The study weighs the pros and cons of each route for rapid prototyping of radio systems.
arxiv-2512-15023:
Hanbit Oh and a coauthor study an unusual superconducting state in bilayer nickelates, the layered materials that lately showed high temperature superconductivity. Most earlier work assumed the two layers mirror each other and the state is uniform and clean. The authors ask what happens when that mirror symmetry is broken by an applied displacement field.

Their mean field analysis of a model with interlayer attraction finds a pair density wave state, where the pairing strength itself waves through space. It resembles the FFLO state known from magnetic fields, yet it appears here at zero field. The phase survives across wide ranges of field, hopping strength, and filling. They also show that disorder which breaks the mirror symmetry weakens the pairing, even when time reversal stays intact.
arxiv-2512-15123:
Mukur Gupta and four coauthors protect federated learning systems from adversarial attacks without ever seeing the clients' private data. In federated learning, one model is copied to thousands of edge devices, so a flaw in it is everywhere at once. Adversarial training is the strongest known defense, but it normally needs the raw training data, which privacy rules keep on the devices.

Their framework, TrajSyn, works on the server side. It distills a proxy dataset from the trajectories of client model updates, the paths the shared model took as devices trained it. That synthetic stand in data then supports adversarial training centrally. Tests on image classification benchmarks show steady gains in robustness against attacks. The approach adds no computing burden to the client devices, a key point for safety critical edge uses.
arxiv-2512-15423:
Hoang Nguyen, Xiaohao Xu, and Xiaonan Huang study a safety flaw in depth models in a 2025 paper. Models that guess depth from one image can invent solid shapes where a flat surface only looks three dimensional. The team calls this failure the 3D Mirage, and sets out to measure it.

They build a benchmark of real world illusions, plus two scores that track false structure and unstable readings. They then train a Depth Anything V2 model with a focused self training method that fixes illusion areas while keeping other skill. The work pushes depth tests beyond pixel accuracy toward structure and context.
arxiv-2512-15623:
Giovanna Bruno and co authors extend Bloch's theorem to crystals under strong light matter coupling in a 2025 paper. Bloch's theorem says electron states in a crystal follow the lattice period. When a crystal sits in a cavity and couples strongly to light, the new polariton particles might break that neat pattern, and the issue was debated.

The authors show polariton quasi particles do preserve lattice periodicity. Their framework handles many cavity modes at once in a tractable way, and extra modes add only small energy corrections, visible at low frequencies. Within the single photon approximation, those corrections act like a uniform field in the crystal plane. That justifies common single mode approximations.
arxiv-2512-16023:
Liudi Yang and seven co-authors present CoVAR, a robotics method put on arXiv in 2025. Robots learn skills from video, but most video lacks labels for the actions shown, which limits its use. CoVAR jointly creates video and robot action sequences that follow a text instruction, starting from one image and the robot's joint positions.

The system extends a pretrained video diffusion model with a parallel action diffusion model, keeping the knowledge the video model already has. A bridge attention step lets the two streams share information, and a refinement step turns coarse actions into precise controls. On public benchmarks and real robot data, CoVAR beat prior methods on video quality and action accuracy. It offers a scalable way to turn large video collections into robot training data.
arxiv-2512-16123:
Min Geun Song and six co-authors test a defense for vision AI in a short 2025 paper posted to arXiv. Object detection models, used in self-driving cars and security cameras, can be fooled by adversarial attacks. These are tiny crafted changes that wreck accuracy. The team asks whether cleaning the image first can restore performance, with no retraining.

They attacked vehicle images from the COCO data set with Perlin noise patterns. They then passed the images through a simple autoencoder that removes noise. Detection accuracy fell by 43.3 percent under attack. After cleaning, the main score recovered by only 3.7 percent. A looser accuracy measure improved by 10.8 percent. The defense helps a little, but much of the damage remains.
arxiv-2512-16223:
Ziqi Ding and three co-authors redesign a familiar web gate in their arXiv paper, posted in 2025. CAPTCHAs try to tell humans from bots, but modern vision AI now solves many image tests better than people do, breaking the old assumptions. Traditional attacks also keep slipping past deployed schemes.

Their design, NGCaptcha, layers two defenses. First, the visitor's browser must solve a small hash-based proof of work, which raises the cost of mass automated attempts. Then comes an image selection task built on perceptual cues that current vision systems still mishandle, while people find it easy. The hybrid aims to keep checks fast and painless for real users while sharply raising the barrier for bots. The authors frame it as a bridge between older CAPTCHA ideas and an AI-era design.
arxiv-2512-16423:
C M Duffy and ten co-authors probe a superconductor puzzle in their 2025 paper on arXiv. YBCO is a famous copper-oxide superconductor whose underdoped form hosts two-dimensional charge order, a striped pattern of electrons that rebuilds the Fermi surface. Swapping praseodymium for some yttrium dopes the material by a different route, adding disorder.

Using magnetotransport and high-field Hall effect measurements, the team found the same fingerprints of Fermi surface reconstruction in the praseodymium version, evidence that 2D charge order survives there too. The phase diagrams of the two materials line up surprisingly well. That symmetry suggests what governs the electronic orders is simply how many charge carriers sit in the copper-oxide planes, not how they got there. The result simplifies a crowded corner of superconductor physics.
arxiv-2512-16923:
Chun-Wei Tuan Mu and coauthors present Generative Refocusing, a tool that changes the focus of a photo after it is taken. Good depth-of-field control is hard from one shot, since the method must recover sharp content and fake realistic blur at once.

Past methods needed all-sharp inputs, leaned on simulated data, and gave little aperture control. The new two-step design pairs DeblurNet, which restores a fully sharp image from varied inputs, with BokehNet, which adds controllable blur. Training mixes synthetic and real blur images to keep true optical feel. Tests top past work on deblurring, blur synthesis, and refocusing, and users can even pick custom aperture shapes.
arxiv-2512-17323:
Jiyun Kong, Jun-Hyuk Kim, and Jong-Seok Lee present EvFRA, a method that rebuilds video frames with help from an event camera. Such cameras do not record full frames; they note each pixel that changes brightness, which gives sharp timing during fast motion. Older systems guess how pixels moved and warp old frames, a step that breaks under big motion or blocked views.

EvFRA rests on a neat match: the event stream lines up with the change between one frame and the next. A first stage aligns those changes, and a diffusion stage cleans the result into a full color frame. On tests, it beat leading methods by up to 2.61 dB for predicting future frames and 1.85 dB for filling frames in between.
arxiv-2512-17623:
Felipe Hernández, Daniel Ranard, and C Jess Riedel settle how much environmental noise a chaotic quantum system needs before it starts behaving classically. Left alone, a quantum wave packet in a chaotic system drifts away from its classical twin after a short Ehrenfest time. A whisper of decoherence from the surroundings can hold the two together far longer, but experts disagreed on how faint that whisper may be.

Earlier rigorous work showed a diffusion strength above the h-bar to the 4/3 power suffices. Looser arguments claimed a much weaker push would do. The team builds an explicit counterexample: below the 4/3 threshold, quantum and classical paths split by a fixed gap that no shrinking of h-bar can close. The threshold is now sharp from both sides.
arxiv-2512-17823:
Shirshendu Ganguly, Milind Hegde, and Lingfu Zhang work on a rule about separate events: knowing one rare event happened can make a second, non overlapping one less likely. The rule is old in percolation theory, the study of flow through random grids. Their paper extends it to warm polymer models in the KPZ family, which describe growing fronts and random paths.

The proof leans on a special solvable model and a known matching scheme between paths and tables. With the rule in hand, other teams have pinned down how extreme values behave in these models. A counter example in the paper shows the rule can fail without that special solvable structure.
arxiv-2512-18523:
Jonas Lammers and five co-authors study how entanglement, the quantum link between particles, can be moved from one property of light to another. Their testbed is a multidimensional quantum network, where each photon carries several degrees of freedom at once. Their paper, posted to arXiv in December 2025, starts with two photons entangled in polarization.

They send one photon through a discrete-time quantum walk, which adds its position as a third subsystem, encoded as a qudit with more than two states. Using partial state tomography and correlation measurements, they track how entanglement shifts from the polarization qubit toward the position qudit. The transfer works through the interplay of entanglement between photons and inseparability within one photon's own degrees of freedom. Results like this matter for scalable quantum networks and protocols built on them.
arxiv-2512-18623:
Jusheng Zhang and seven coauthors tackle language model hallucinations in a 2025 machine learning paper. Their framework, LLM-CAS, treats real-time correction as a hierarchical reinforcement learning problem. Instead of retraining the model, a trained agent picks small, temporary neuron perturbations during inference, guided by the immediate context. Earlier static edits struggle with context-dependent errors and forgetting, while older dynamic methods rely on fixed rules.

Across several language models, LLM-CAS raises accuracy by 10.98 percentage points on StoryCloze, 2.71 points on TriviaQA, and 2.06 points on the TruthfulQA MC1 score. It beats static methods such as ITI and CAA and the dynamic SADI framework. The authors pitch it as a cheaper route to more reliable models in high-stakes uses.
arxiv-2512-18823:
M M Abid Naziri and three co-authors test self-driving software by hunting near misses. Simulation testing is standard before deployment, but random bug hunting is unreliable or slow. Their technique, Foresee, presented at ICSE 2026 and posted to arXiv in December 2025, treats every near miss as a signpost. A forecaster projects the test car's possible futures to spot situations about to turn dangerous.

Foresee then fuzzes locally around each candidate near miss, nudging the scenario until hidden failures surface. In the CARLA simulator, on both end-to-end and modular driving stacks, it exposes 128.70 percent more failures than random testing. Against a leading failure predictor it finds 38.09 percent more, while running 2.49 and 1.42 times faster, respectively. Paired with the DriveFuzz fuzzer, it lifts failure detection by up to 93.94 percent.
arxiv-2512-18923: Matt DeVos, Kathryn Nurse, and Robert Šámal push toward Bouchet's conjecture on flows in signed graphs. A flow assigns values to edges so nothing accumulates; nowhere-zero means no edge gets zero. Bouchet conjectured in 1983 that every flow-admissible signed graph has a nowhere-zero 6-flow. Their paper, posted to arXiv in December 2025, proves that every flow-admissible signed graph that is 3-edge-connected has a nowhere-zero 8-flow, weakening earlier assumptions under which the same team had reached 8. Each such step tightens the net around the conjectured 6.
arxiv-2512-19123:
Francesco Carzaniga, Michael Hersche, Kaspar Schindler, and Abbas Rahimi classify seizures from brain recordings with an architecture that accepts any number of channels. Intracranial recordings vary in electrode count from patient to patient, which usually forces a new model each time. Their channel-adaptive design avoids that rebuild.

Each channel is processed on its own by a strong time-series model. A vector-symbolic fusion step then rebuilds the spatial layout with one trainable weight per channel. Fused features collect in a memory of up to two minutes before the final call. Pretraining spans many subjects, and a quick fine-tune personalizes the model in a fifth of the usual time.
arxiv-2512-19223:
Xiu-Cheng Wang, Jun-Jie Zhanga, Nan Cheng, and Long-Gang Pang propose one number that rates how well a sensor setup preserves what a learner could later use. Data are often undersampled at capture, and pixel-level error scores miss how the sampling pattern itself scrambles structure. Their scalar is built from instrument-resolved phase space, the joint view of position and frequency.

The measure names phase-space coherence of periodic sampling as the physical root of aliasing, and recovers classic sampling results in theory. Across masked image tasks, accelerated MRI, and massive antenna arrays, including over-the-air tests, it ranked sampling layouts correctly and forecast downstream accuracy. Smarter capture, they argue, starts here.
arxiv-2512-19423:
Clara Del Pio and Francesco Ucci check whether undiscovered physics could quietly spoil the luminosity yardstick at future electron-positron colliders. Luminosity, the machine's collision rate, is read off small-angle Bhabha scattering, a process theory can compute with great precision. New heavy physics, if real, would add its own share to that same scattering.

The authors estimate that non-standard error across several future collider designs. The shift could be large enough to bias precision results if ignored. They also propose a running plan based on asymmetries that do not depend on the absolute luminosity, letting the machine constrain the unknown interactions from its own data.
arxiv-2512-20023:
Shi-Chao Chen and Chuan-Chuan Wu prove abundance results about the 3-rank of class groups of quadratic fields. The class group measures how badly unique factorization fails in a number field, and its 3-rank counts the independent factors of three dividing it. Their theorem produces infinitely many fundamental discriminants with a simultaneous control property: a whole family of quadratic fields built from linear polynomials has 3-rank below a prescribed bound at once.

The statement handles real and imaginary fields together, with the count of fields and the rank bound linked by an explicit inequality the reader can check. A second result reaches the same simultaneous control for fields built from arbitrary integer-valued polynomials without constant terms. Such constructions feed the statistical study of class groups, where families with prescribed small ranks are prized test cases.
arxiv-2512-20123:
Mustafa Bakr and Smain Amari examine a formal limit that turns out to be an impostor. The transverse magnetic modes of a spherical cavity obey a dispersion relation. It ties the angular eigenvalue to the resonant frequency. The tie runs through zeros of a Bessel function derivative. Extend that relation to the eigenvalue minus one, and a zero-frequency endpoint pops out on paper.

Careful work shows the endpoint is no physical mode. The angular operator's positivity confines true eigenvalues to zero or above. Each field component vanishes in the limit. The Debye potential stays nontrivial, with a monopole-type singularity at the origin. The paper draws the line between propagating cavity modes and static fields. It bears on mode counting in cavity quantization.
arxiv-2512-20323:
Ipek Sena Yilmaz, Onur G Tuncer, Zeynep E Aksoy, and Zeynep Yağmur Baydemir guard privacy when wireless sensing data is shared. Wi-Fi channel maps can betray who a person is, where they are, and whether they took part in a study. Sending these maps to the cloud or to other labs is risky. Their work gives such sharing a formal shield: differential privacy.

The pipeline first clips the maps so no single person can sway them much. It then judges which parts of the time-frequency plane matter for the task and spends the privacy budget unevenly across blocks before adding tuned Gaussian noise. On tasks for activity sensing, 3D pose, and breathing checks, this uneven split beats flat noise at the same budget: accuracy rises while attacks that probe identity or membership leak far less.
arxiv-2512-20823:
Razine Moundir Ghorab and six co-authors built NotSoTiny, a benchmark for language models that write chip-design code. Writing RTL, the code that describes hardware circuits, is a promising model skill. Older tests were small, leaned on toy designs, checked answers loosely, and risked leaking into training data.

NotSoTiny draws on hundreds of real designs from the Tiny Tapeout community, whose members tape out small chips. An automated pipeline removes duplicates, verifies each design, and folds in fresh designs on the community release schedule, limiting contamination. Models found these tasks harder than earlier benchmarks suggested. The living design should keep the test honest as models improve.
arxiv-2512-21023:
Wung-Hong Huang probes quantum chaos in a quantum field theory by first shrinking it to coupled oscillators. Placing the interacting scalar field on a lattice gives anharmonic oscillators linked to their neighbors. Starting from two of them, treated with second quantization and perturbation theory up to second order, he computes the thermal out-of-time-order correlator. That correlator is the standard diagnostic for how fast a quantum system scrambles information.

The correlator grows exponentially over a long early window, with a Lyapunov exponent that scales as the fourth root of temperature, the signature of chaos. Extending to a closed chain of oscillators, corresponding to the field theory in one space dimension, the chaos signatures appear already at low perturbative orders. Field theorists gain evidence that scrambling here is not a strong-coupling curiosity but shows up in the first terms of the expansion.
arxiv-2512-21223:
Peter Danchev and Patrick Keef sort abelian groups by a finiteness-flavored rigidity property. A group is Hopfian, roughly, when every surjective self-map is automatically an isomorphism. The group cannot be a proper quotient of itself. The co-finitely Hopfian variant, introduced by Bridson, Groves, Hillman, and Martin in 2010, relaxes the demand in a finite-index direction. Which commutative groups enjoy these properties had remained only partly mapped.

Danchev and Keef completely describe the commutative co-finitely Hopfian class in certain important cases and give satisfactory descriptions of several related classes of abelian groups. They also introduce and discuss two looser notions suited to the commutative world: almost co-finitely Hopfian groups and almost finitely Hopfian groups. Group theorists receive a tidier taxonomy of when a group's self-maps are forced to be reversible, and of how much slack the 'almost' versions permit before the rigidity breaks.
arxiv-2512-21323:
Felix Draxler, Stephan Mandt, Sameer Singh, and three co-authors relocate the dice inside a language model. Autoregressive generation emits one token per forward pass, which is why chatbots type slowly. Speculative tricks draft tokens and verify them. Parallel Token Prediction attacks the bottleneck directly. It feeds randomness in as an input variable. Future tokens then become deterministic functions of known inputs and can be computed jointly in one pass.

The team proves a single such call can express arbitrary dependencies among the predicted tokens, answering the worry that parallel prediction must assume independence. Training proceeds by distilling an existing model or by an inverse autoregressive scheme needing no teacher. On a diverse speculative-decoding benchmark the method runs about two and a half times faster, with code and checkpoints released. Serving systems gain a principled speedup that trades nothing in output distribution for its pace.
arxiv-2512-21423:
Kabir Narayanan, Abigail Perryman, and A. Shadi Tahvildar-Zadeh follow the long-term motion of a relativistic particle in one space dimension. The particle is guided by a spin one-half wave function obeying the free Dirac equation, the relativistic wave equation for electrons. The starting wave function is a Gaussian packet with nonzero average momentum.

The authors prove that at large times the wave function splits into two packets traveling in opposite directions. Guided trajectories settle to a nearly constant momentum equal to the starting average. The asymptotic energy can be positive or negative, with the sign fixed by the particle's starting position. Oddly, negative-energy particles move opposite to their momentum. The proof uses the stationary phase approximation, with a rigorous bound on its error.
arxiv-2512-21523:
Yue Huang, Ling Xue, Kun Zhao, and Xiaoming Zheng find explicit steady-state solutions for a confined chemotaxis model. Chemotaxis is movement toward or away from a chemical signal, and the Keller-Segel equations are its standard mathematical model. Steady states describe the patterns cells settle into, but closed-form examples are rare in bounded domains.

Building on work by Carrillo, Li, and Wang, the authors construct a new family of explicit solutions on a bounded interval. The solutions use trigonometric and hyperbolic functions and include singular secant and cosecant types. They impose Dirichlet boundary conditions in a biologically stable parameter regime. Using energy methods, they prove stability and give precise thresholds for when the patterns persist. Such explicit benchmarks let numerical solvers be checked against known answers, and they clarify how boundaries drive pattern formation.
arxiv-2512-21723:
Alexandr V. Korchemnyi, Aleksandr I. Panov, and their co-authors present HELP, a hierarchical planner that lets a household robot follow instructions spoken in natural language. Language models are good at handling vague instructions and fetching information, but a robot also needs plans grounded in the skills it has.

HELP is a team of language-model agents arranged in a hierarchy, each dedicated to a subtask of planning. The decomposition lets high-level reasoning stay separate from the details of execution. The authors evaluate the system on a household task and run real-world experiments with an embodied agent. They build the planner from open-source language models with few parameters. That choice matters for autonomy: a robot that must phone a cloud model for every decision is fragile and expensive. The experiments test whether modest models, organized well, can carry the planning load of a home robot.
arxiv-2512-21823:
Siddhartha Srinivas Rentala investigates conditional restricted Boltzmann machines as tools for spotting risk regimes in financial markets. A restricted Boltzmann machine is an energy-based neural model; the conditional version adds autoregressive links so it can model time series, not just static snapshots. The study trains the model on a multi-asset dataset spanning 2013 to 2025.

Two architectures are compared, a discrete Bernoulli version and a continuous Gaussian one, trained with persistent contrastive divergence. A split emerges: the Gaussian model preserves static correlations between assets well but fails to reproduce long-range volatility clustering. The author then analyzes the model's free energy, a quantity acting like a surprisal score. Decomposed into a magnitude part and a correlation-structure part, the free energy distinguishes pure size shocks from genuine regime changes. The model is best used as a diagnostic alongside gauges such as the VIX.
arxiv-2512-22023:
Strong magnetic fields reorganize QCD matter into a chiral soliton lattice, a periodic array of neutral pion domain walls, on which Skyrmions can sit as a distinct phase. Patrick Copinger, Minoru Eto, Muneto Nitta, and Zebin Qiu show the minimal domain-wall Skyrmions here are fermions. They carry baryon number one, not the two of the bosons found before.

A bosonic domain-wall Skyrmion can split at no energy cost into two fermionic ones attached on opposite sides of a chiral soliton. The phase boundary between the lattice and Skyrmion phases is unchanged. In the chiral limit, the fermionic Skyrmions sit halfway through each lattice period, settling the ground state's identity.
arxiv-2512-22123:
Duaa Abdullah and Jasem Hamoud survey the border between problems computers can solve, problems they can only check, and problems no algorithm can settle. Their focus is semigroup theory, the algebra of combining elements where order of grouping does not matter. They connect that algebra to Turing machines and the classic question of whether P equals NP.

The central construction is an associative calculus built from a chosen Turing machine. For a machine computing a non-recursive function, the authors show its word problem, deciding whether two expressions are equal, is algorithmically undecidable. The equivalence they prove ties membership in certain sets directly to the calculus. The paper uses the construction to show where algorithmic methods in algebra reach a hard limit.
arxiv-2512-22423:
Amil Khan, Matheus Palhares Viana, Suraj Mishra, and B. S. Manjunath introduce Bright-4B, a four-billion-parameter base model that segments cells in label-free imaging. Brightfield imaging is fast and gentle but hard to segment without glowing labels or heavy post-processing. Bright-4B learns on the unit hypersphere, a geometric choice meant to structure its internal forms, and reads 3D brightfield volumes directly.

The architecture mixes a hardware-aligned sparse attention mechanism, residual HyperConnections that stabilize information flow across depth and width, and a soft mixture-of-experts for flexible capacity. A plug-in patch embedding respects the scope's anisotropic blur. Across confocal datasets, the model segmented nuclei, mitochondria, and other organelles with fine detail preserved through depth, beating CNN and transformer baselines. Code and weights are promised for release.
arxiv-2512-22923:
Zhaofei Zheng, Yuxin Luo, Juan Chen, and Yimin Luo study how wound-healing cells called myofibroblasts change the collective order of a mixed cell layer. Elongated cells tend to align locally, and the places where alignment breaks down, known as topological defects, act as mechanical centers. Overactive myofibroblasts drive fibrosis, but their effect on this ordering was unclear, so the team co-cultured them with ordinary fibroblasts in varying proportions.

Adding more of the slower myofibroblasts increased disorder and slowed the rate at which defects meet and cancel. On grooved surfaces, higher myofibroblast shares also worsened overall alignment. The cells sorted themselves by defect type: myofibroblasts gathered at the less mobile negative defects, fibroblasts at positive ones. That preference raises local friction and helps explain the slowdown, linking defect physics to cell motility in mixed tissues.
arxiv-2512-23023:
Andrzej Czarnecki, A. O. Davydov, and M. Y. Kaygorodov revisit how fast a muon decays when it is captured into orbit around a light nucleus. A bound muon's decay rate is a precision test of weak interaction physics in a Coulomb field. The literature held a puzzle: a 1960 perturbative result and a 1993 fully relativistic partial-wave calculation disagreed for oxygen.

The authors recompute the rate with accurate relativistic methods for nuclei from beryllium to fluorine, atomic numbers four through nine. They show the old discrepancy came from the partial-wave series in the 1993 work converging too slowly, so its summed value drifted. Their calculation restores agreement with the perturbative expansion in the fine-structure constant times charge. They also determine the sign of the next-order correction in that expansion, which comes out negative, sharpening the benchmark for future muonic atom experiments.
arxiv-2512-23623:
José Torres Santaella studies translating solitons, shapes that move at a steady speed and keep their form, for a broad class of flows driven by curvature. Such shapes matter because they show how these flows pinch and form sharp points. He works with round, symmetric cases in flat space, where the whole shape comes from one profile curve.

For bowl-shaped translators, which look like smooth paraboloids, he works out how the shape spreads far out, in both plain and borderline regimes. A signed-neck method then builds catenoid-like translators, sorted into full embedded families and largest pieces by branch. The paper also proves only one strictly convex graph-like translator has set bowl-like growth far out, and barrier arguments rule out some bounded graph-like cases. His results map which of these moving shapes can exist across the whole family of flows.
arxiv-2512-23723: Albert Herrero-Parareda and six co-authors publish an erratum to their earlier paper on lasing at a stationary inflection point, a special resonance in periodic optical structures. The short correction supplies an updated fitting function for the lasing threshold of finite-length cavities operating at that resonance or at a regular band edge. It clarifies how the threshold scales as the number of unit cells in the cavity grows.
arxiv-2512-24123:
Mengyao Huang and five collaborators dissect the structure of helium-6, a nucleus famous for its halo: a tight helium-4 core with two extra neutrons orbiting far outside. Working from first principles with no-core shell model calculations and a modern nucleon-nucleon interaction, they examine how pairs of nucleons are spatially arranged inside both helium-4 and helium-6.

Pair-correlation measures, sorted by spin and isospin, reveal the halo's anatomy. The two valence neutrons mostly form a spin-singlet pair, and their average separation from core nucleons runs about eighty percent larger than separations within the core itself. The core, meanwhile, swells and shifts off center, and that off-centering explains most of why helium-6's proton radius exceeds helium-4's. For nuclear theorists, the analysis ties an abstract halo picture to concrete, computable pair statistics.
arxiv-2512-24423:
Innes Maxwell, Stefan van den Hoven, and Jelmer Renema assess a quantum algorithm for graph isomorphism. The problem asks whether two graphs are secretly the same. A proposed algorithm runs on a photonic quantum device. The authors examine it critically in the noisy, intermediate-scale era. Practical quantum advantage remains unproven there.

Inspired by the quantum approach, they derive a classical test. Isomorphic graphs encoded in Gaussian boson samplers must meet a necessary condition. Efficiently computable statistics of the sampler check that condition. When a pair fails, the graphs cannot be isomorphic. The analysis sets the test beside its quantum inspiration. Classical color refinement and Babai's quasi-polynomial algorithm provide context. The work shows how quantum proposals can still sharpen classical tools, even before quantum hardware wins outright.
arxiv-2512-24523:
Kingsley Yeon, Steven Damelin, and Michael Werman approximate functions with sharp cusps. The functions are continuous but not smooth. Each cusp looks like an absolute value raised to a rational power below one. Finitely many cusps sit on a smooth analytic background. Classical polynomial fits converge only slowly, at algebraic rates, on such functions.

The authors compose polynomials instead. An inner iteration handles fractional powers without division. An outer layer fits the smooth part. The composite structure converges exponentially fast in the parameter count. That beats the algebraic rates of single-layer fits. Error is measured in the L-p norm on the unit interval. Experiments cover single and multiple cusp setups. The theory's rates show up in practice. Deep composite constructions use their parameters far more efficiently here.
arxiv-2512-24723:
Swathi Krishna, Mishra, and Jaiswal catalog the nonlinear waves raised when a charged body moves through a dusty plasma. Such motion can create precursor waves that run ahead and pinned solitons that stay near the body. Under weak nonlinearity, a forced Korteweg-de Vries type equation describes the patterns.

Three driver traits are varied in turn: amplitude, width, and flow speed. Each changes how the disturbance grows and travels through the medium. Readers in plasma physics get a map of which source settings produce which wave structures. The results help interpret experiments where moving charged objects stir dusty plasmas.
arxiv-2512-24823:
Snigdhadev Chakraborty, Mukul Sagar, Atanu Ghosh, and colleagues use natural calcium oxalate crystals inside Tradescantia zebrina leaf cells as tiny probes of the cell interior. Plant cell walls block nanoparticles that animal cells would absorb, so reaching the inner surface without damage is hard. Optical tweezers can rotate the prismatic crystals already present inside the cells.

Detecting roll rotation with high resolution lets them sense forces at the femtonewton scale near the inner cell surface. Readers in biophysics get a non-invasive nanotribology method, meaning friction study at tiny scales, built from the plant's own crystals. The approach opens study of living plant cell interiors.
arxiv-2512-25023:
Timo Kaufmann, Yannick Metz, and Daniel Keim introduce ResponseRank, a reward modeling method that learns how strong a human preference is, not just its direction. Binary choices in feedback training say which answer won, but not whether the win was narrow or overwhelming. Strength matters for decisions under uncertainty and for generalizing preference models, yet proxies like response time are noisy.

Relative differences in such proxy signals are used to learn strength despite the noise. Machine learning readers get more information from the same human feedback. Preference strength could make reward models better calibrated about when a choice is nearly a coin flip.
arxiv-2601-00423:
Shengjun Zhang, Zhang Zhang, Chensheng Dai, and Yueqi Duan study how reinforcement learning can align flow matching models with human preferences. Their method, called E-GRPO, starts from a simple observation about sampling. Steps where the model is uncertain explore new directions well, while steps where it is nearly certain produce samples that look much the same.

The authors merge consecutive low-uncertainty steps into single high-uncertainty steps for the noisy sampling pass, and use clean deterministic sampling elsewhere. They also add a way to compare rewards within groups of samples that share a merged step. Tests under several reward settings show the approach trains flow models more effectively than optimizing every step at once.
arxiv-2601-00523:
Andrés Fábrega and seven colleagues identify a built-in tension in collective investment algorithms, systems that run one shared trading strategy for a community of investors. Such systems promise to democratize sophisticated, often AI-based investing. The authors call the problem the CoinAlg Bind: these systems cannot guarantee economic fairness without losing profit to arbitrage.

They build a formal model with definitions of privacy, meaning incomplete disclosure of the algorithm, and of fairness, meaning protection against insider extraction. Two results frame the bind. Privacy is what makes insider attacks possible, yet transparency lets outside arbitrageurs erode the strategy's profit. Data from the Uniswap exchange lets them study both sides empirically, quantifying how much fairness and profitability trade against each other in practice.
arxiv-2601-00623:
Longtian Qiu, Shan Ning, Chuyu Zhang, Jiaxuan Sun, and Xuming He reduce hallucinations in multimodal language models, systems that answer questions about images but sometimes invent details that are not there. A popular fix trains the model on preference pairs, yet easy pairs dominate training and the model overfits them, leaving fine-grained errors untouched.

Their method, DA-DPO, first estimates how difficult each preference pair is, using pre-trained vision-language models with complementary generative and contrastive views, combined through a distribution-aware vote. Training then balances easy and hard pairs instead of drowning in the easy ones. The framework is designed to be cost-efficient as well, targeting the stubborn, subtle hallucinations that matter most in practice.
arxiv-2601-00723:
Xingyu Lv and seven co-authors report, in 2026, on a crystal that may gain its superconductivity from electron waves. The crystal is TiSe2 with copper slipped between its layers. Superconductivity is the state where a material carries current with no loss. The team tracked a third trait: nematic order, where electrons favour one direction over its twin.

They measured how the crystal's resistance in a stretched state shifts with heat. At high heat, that shift blew up in a pattern that marks strong nematic waves. As more copper went in, the mark's key heat fell toward zero. It hit near zero just where superconductivity was at its best. With still more copper, the mark flipped sign and superconductivity faded. The match in timing is strong evidence for the team's claim. Nematic waves, they argue, help drive the superconductivity here. The crystal thus makes a clean lab for that link.
arxiv-2601-00823:
Austin R Ellis-Mohr and two co-authors study, in 2026, how to route tasks to big reasoning AI models without wasting power. Reasoning models burn very uneven amounts of energy. The cost shifts with both the model picked and how long it thinks. A router must send each task to the right model, run the right way. The authors map the balance point for such a system.

At that point, neither the base power supply nor the back-up supply is wasted as a rule. Cut it, and the back-up supply is drained as a rule instead. Near the point, swings in demand rule how well the system does. How those swings are soaked up, across time and models, sets the score. The authors use scaling laws for training and run costs to chart good routing rules. Their frame gives data centres a principled way to save power.
arxiv-2601-01023:
João Morais and four colleagues ask how alike two wireless data sets really are, and why that matters. A model trained on one set of radio data often fails on another, so teams need a way to judge fit before they train. Their framework scores the gap between data sets in a way that is tied to the task and the model at hand.

The key test is simple: a small gap should mean a model trained on one set works well on the other. The team tries the idea on signal squeezing with autoencoders and on beam choice with neural networks. Their scores track real transfer results far better than older measures. That helps teams pick data, build fake data, and adapt models to new sites with less guesswork.
arxiv-2601-01223:
Shahbazi and 2 co-authors build a method to give hospital predictions honest ranges, not just single numbers. Doctors need ranges that hold up at a stated rate, yet also tighten for easy cases and widen for risky ones. Older tools, the authors say, rarely do both jobs at once.

Their method mixes a Bayesian forest model with group-aware checks that set the ranges. On records for 61,538 admissions at 3,793 United States hospitals, coverage came close to its target. Easy cases got ranges about one fifth narrower, while hard cases got wider ones. Alone, the Bayesian ranges missed badly, which motivates the combined design.
arxiv-2601-01423:
Ten authors led by Hongyu Chen classify crystal structures from their vibration patterns, adding a sense that standard X-ray methods lack. X-ray diffraction struggles with messy, multi-phase samples, while phonon and Raman spectra carry structural fingerprints of their own. The team first groups more than nineteen thousand crystals into a few dozen structural prototypes using space groups and related descriptors.

An ensemble of residual networks then learns to read the fingerprints, with a precision-adaptive scheme that weighs each member's confidence. The ensemble stays robust when spectra vary in length and quality, a common flaw in real lab data. The authors pitch the strategy as a high-throughput tool for automated structure analysis in large experimental programs. By leaning on optical data, it sidesteps the need for ideal diffraction samples that traditional pipelines assume.
arxiv-2601-02023:
Long-context language models are being trusted as working memory for autonomous tasks, yet their reliability depends on where the facts sit. Amirali Ebrahimzadeh and Seyyed Salili build an extended needle-in-a-haystack benchmark that separates literal extraction, logical inference, and hallucination, and apply it to four current models.

Two failure modes stand out. Distributional collapse: performance degrades sharply when evidence is scattered across the context instead of concentrated. And a safety tax: prompts telling the model not to make things up cause over-conservative refusals of facts that are actually present, sharply cutting accuracy. The authors blame poor context utilization more than missing knowledge, and call for model-specific robustness work before long-horizon deployment.
arxiv-2601-02423:
Rajaram Nityananda presents an exactly solved model of a one dimensional self gravitating system. A line of particles held together by their own gravity in a steady, collisionless state where every particle has the same energy. Remarkably, positions and velocities over time are given by sine and cosine functions cut off after just two terms of their series, and the density and potential also have simple analytic forms.

The author claims no direct astronomy use for the model. Its value is as a teaching example for stellar dynamics and as motivation for a conjecture about density, potential, and orbits near caustics in simulations of cold dark matter.
arxiv-2601-02523:
Artavazd Maranjyan's dissertation tackles asynchronous stochastic gradient descent, the training method used when thousands of processors update one neural network without waiting for each other. Synchronous training wastes time on the slowest device, but removing the wait means updates are computed from outdated model versions, a problem called staleness. Delays also come from random system behavior, which makes the true cost of asynchrony hard to pin down.

The dissertation builds a rigorous framework for asynchronous first order stochastic optimization, for both uniform and mixed data across workers. Its title claim is that the resulting method is the first provably optimal one in this setting, matching lower bounds rather than merely working well in practice. The work matters because large training runs occupy whole data centers for weeks.
arxiv-2601-02623:
Qiyu Yang and Shengbo Zhao obtain refined estimates for the joint extreme values of the Riemann zeta function at harmonic points, special sets of points linked by reciprocal spacing. The zeta function sits at the heart of analytic number theory, and how large it can grow at several points at once tests deep conjectures about its behavior.

Using the resonance method, they improve results going back to Levinson's work of 1972. The proof rests on Dirichlet series theory and the truncated Euler product for the zeta function, and earlier extreme value results for single points follow as corollaries.
arxiv-2601-02923:
Saharon Shelah proves consistency results about square bracket partition relations, a family of statements in set theory about coloring pairs drawn from large sets of ordinals. Earlier results of this type needed very large cardinals, in the best case the first weakly Mahlo cardinal, and forced the continuum to be huge. Shelah's new results avoid those costs on three fronts at once.

In his constructions, the continuum can stay small and no large cardinal is assumed. The cardinals named in the partition relation can also sit strictly below the continuum after the forcing. Consistency here means the statements can hold in a model of set theory built by forcing, so the work widens the range of known possible behaviors for these relations.
arxiv-2601-03423:
Sasha Ronaghi and six co-authors propose a way to adapt new language models for medical work without retraining them. Their method, called CAPT, pairs a new general model with an older clinical model that was already trained on health data. The two models can even use different vocabularies, which older pairing methods could not handle well.

CAPT uses contrastive decoding, a way of comparing model outputs, to add clinical signals while keeping the general model's fluency and reasoning. On six clinical tasks it beat both models alone and other ensemble methods. Token-level checks and doctor case studies showed more useful clinical language and fewer context errors. Hospitals with limited computing could gain from models they already own.
arxiv-2601-03623:
Mohammad Rowshan, writing alone, unifies several quantum error-correcting codes designed for biased noise, where one error type dominates. Codes like the XZZX surface code owe their strong performance to a hidden simplicity: under pure dephasing, their Z-error signals split into independent one-dimensional chains. Rowshan names and formalizes that shared mechanism as strip symmetry.

For the defined class, which includes certain stabilizer and Floquet codes, each basic Z fault stays inside one strip, so decoding splits into independent strip problems. That factorization makes matching-based decoders cheaper. Rowshan characterizes strip symmetry through per-strip stabilizer products and places three known codes inside the framework, then builds synthetic examples. A common theory can help engineers design codes matched to real hardware noise.
arxiv-2601-03823:
Fei Wu and five co-authors improve how reinforcement learning credits individual reasoning steps in language models trained on verifiable math rewards. Outcome-only rewards judge the final answer, so models cannot tell necessary deduction from redundant checking. They sometimes keep verifying after solving, and can even talk themselves out of a correct answer into a wrong one.

The team built a training-free probe that reads a model's intermediate confidence and correctness at each step, combining them into a Step Potential signal estimating reasoning progress. Their Step Potential Advantage Estimation then assigns credit using that signal, amplifying the steps that truly advance a solution. Finer credit could make reasoning training cheaper and answers shorter, since models would learn to stop when the work is actually done.
arxiv-2601-04123:
Francisco Ponce leads eleven co-authors with a toolchain for placing microservice applications across cloud and edge sites. Placement must balance staying up after failures, running fast, and limiting carbon output. Sites differ widely and conditions keep changing, so a fixed placement soon goes stale.

The toolchain, FREEDA, keeps adjusting placements as resources, failures, and carbon intensity shift. It can move services, switch service flavours, or rebalance load to hold quality while cutting emissions. Tests use varied simulated and emulated scenes, including resource exhaustion, node failures, and swings in carbon intensity. Results show the toolchain re-settles deployments on its own and strikes a good balance among resilience, efficiency, and environmental impact, according to the authors.
arxiv-2601-04323:
Luis E. Salazar Manzano and six co-authors present the longest watch yet kept on KL Dra, a tight binary where a white dwarf feeds from a helium-rich companion, in a 2026 arXiv paper. About eleven years of monitoring from the TESS space telescope and wide-field ground surveys let them characterize its frequent outbursts in unmatched detail. The first such full study for this class of system.

The big superoutbursts typically open with a precursor, plateau, then fade through rebrightenings into a run of three or four normal outbursts, and the whole cycle repeats in about sixty days. Fitting shapes to each stage, they find patterns across cycles: normal outbursts grow stronger within a cycle, and cycle length may trade against plateau length and outburst height. They read the behaviour through the disk instability model, with changes in the donor's transfer rate added.
arxiv-2601-04523:
Ajay Singh, Nikos Metaxakis, and Panagiota Fatourou rebuild a basic concurrent data structure for speed, in a 2026 arXiv paper. A shared stack sounds simple, but when dozens of threads push and pop at once, contention makes the naive designs crawl. Their stack is blocking and linearizable — every operation appears to happen at a single instant — yet scales far better than its rivals.

The design blends two ideas: sharding, which spreads the work across pieces so threads collide less, coordinated by a simple fetch-and-increment counter. And a new elimination mechanism with a new combining approach, letting opposite operations cancel or batch instead of queueing. In experiments the implementation beat all existing concurrent stacks by up to twofold on most workloads, with the largest gains exactly where older stacks suffer most: many threads and heavy contention.
arxiv-2601-04823:
Fine-tuning a mixture-of-experts model usually gives every expert the same size of update, and Guanzhi Deng and 7 co-authors argue that wastes resources. Their 2026 paper presents DR-LoRA, a dynamic rank version of LoRA, a low-cost fine-tuning method. Pretrained experts specialise unevenly, so a uniform rank under-supplies task-relevant experts while giving redundant capacity to irrelevant ones.

DR-LoRA adjusts each expert's LoRA rank dynamically, matching capacity to how much that expert matters for the task. The goal is better adaptation of large mixture-of-experts language models without full retraining. Smarter allocation matters because these models are expensive to run, and wasted parameters raise cost without improving the answers users receive.
arxiv-2601-06023:
Ville Vaskonen asks what weak lensing can add to bright standard sirens in a 2026 cosmology paper. A standard siren is a gravitational wave event with a visible counterpart, giving a direct distance measure. Weak lensing is the slight bending of that signal by matter along the way.

Adding lensing effects lets sirens measure features that shape cosmic structure but leave average distances unchanged. Vaskonen focuses on sigma-8, a measure of how clumped matter is, alongside the Hubble constant and matter share. With the Einstein Telescope, 300 neutron star mergers could measure sigma-8 to about ten percent. With LISA, 12 massive black hole mergers could reach roughly thirty percent.
arxiv-2601-06123:
Models could collaborate better if they shared more than text. Lucio M. Dery and 5 co-authors propose a shared latent space in a 2026 paper, so models can exchange internal states directly. Text is a narrow channel for cooperation between language models.

Each model gets adapters that translate its key-value cache, its stored memory of the conversation, into and out of the shared space. The pretrained models themselves stay unchanged. Experiments with Gemma-2 models showed the channel enables smooth inter-model communication and even improves single-model performance. Learned skills such as soft prompts transferred directly between different models through the shared space. The authors frame it as a step toward models fluidly sharing knowledge and capabilities.
arxiv-2601-06423:
Sampling many answers and voting improves accuracy, but does it make reasoning more faithful? Deep Mehta tests that trade-off in a 2026 empirical study of self-consistency for language models. Faithfulness means the stated reasoning actually supports the answer, a quality accuracy alone cannot guarantee.

Four frontier models answered 100 grade-school math problems, with rigorous statistical testing throughout. One model gained accuracy while faithfulness held roughly steady. Another lost accuracy even as faithfulness jumped dramatically at five samples. A third sat at a ceiling with modest faithfulness gains, and a fourth gained accuracy while faithfulness slipped slightly. Difficulty analysis explained the patterns through which problems each model broke. Mehta advises teams to test their specific model before deploying self-consistency.
arxiv-2601-06623:
Philip Korman settles an existence question for a class of hard math problems in a 2026 paper. The problems mix a fixed linear part with a curved part. The linear part sits at a point of resonance, where small inputs can grow.

He gives a test that is both a must and enough for a solution. That is, solutions exist just when his test holds, with no gap. The test is then used on a linked heat problem in his paper. It gives a rule for when all solutions of that heat problem grow without bound. Old tools for resonance gave tests that were enough but not a must. His sharper test closes the gap for this class at last. The result is a full answer, not a one-way hint.
arxiv-2601-07223: Research by Eromanga Adermann and co-authors was posted on arXiv in 2026. It deals with quantum error correction and detection for quantum machine learning. The preprint joined the arXiv PAPERS collection in 2026. At the intersection of quantum computing and machine learning, quantum machine learning (QML) is poised to revolutionize artificial intelligence. However, the vulnerability of the current generation of quantum computers to noise and computational error poses a significant barrier to this vision. For specialists, the preprint offers a compact account of the problem and the authors' approach.
arxiv-2601-07823:
Zhiting Mei and a large team survey how video generation models are entering robotics. These models synthesize high-quality video of agents interacting with environments. They condition on multi-modal user inputs. Their realism addresses long-standing limits of physics-based simulators. Adoption across robotics problem domains has been broad and fast. Their 2026 preprint reviews applications, research challenges, and future directions.

A survey is timely when a tool spreads faster than the field's shared understanding. The authors organize uses from training data generation to planning and evaluation. They also name open challenges, where video models still mislead or fall short. Robotics scholars choosing simulation tools are the readers. The paper helps them judge where generated video can be trusted. It maps a fast-moving area at a moment when standards are still forming.
arxiv-2601-07923:
Hao-Ran Cui and Hart Goldman study edge behavior at an odd quantum phase transition. More work now asks how quantum critical swings affect gapless edge modes. The authors take the non-compact CP model with N boson species in two space dimensions. The bosons couple to a fluctuating U(1) gauge field. Their 2026 preprint reports striking edge correlations at this deconfined quantum critical point.

Such points split phases in ways Landau theory does not allow. Edges can host their own critical behavior, richer than the bulk. Striking correlations mean edge order reacts with great strength. Measuring that response tests theories of the transition itself. The paper serves condensed matter theorists. It uses the boundary as a lens on a transition that remains hard to simulate and measure. The edge is not a mere rim here; it is where the sharpest signs of change show up.
arxiv-2601-08123: Gabriele Dessena and Alessandro Pontillo test propeller-driven vibration testing as a cheaper route to aircraft modal data. Their 2026 arXiv paper notes that ground vibration testing supports certification but takes long, costly campaigns. Propeller-driven testing is an output-only option in the spirit of operational modal analysis. Taxi and flight vibration testing follow the same broad idea of using working loads. The authors assess whether a spinning propeller can excite an aircraft well enough for modal parameter extraction. If it works, smaller teams could gather certification-grade data faster.
arxiv-2601-08423: Jakub Gismatullin, Immanuel Halupczok, and Dugald Macpherson characterize simple groups definable in valued fields. Their 2026 arXiv paper proves that non-abelian definable, definably simple groups in 1-h-minimal henselian valued fields are essentially linear algebraic groups. The group is assumed to live in the home sort. A similar result holds in pure algebraically closed valued fields of positive characteristic, with an added subgroup assumption. The theorem limits how exotic definable groups can be, a core question in model theory.
arxiv-2601-08723:
Jeff Murugan and Hendrik van Zyl study how hard it is to build a quantum state step by step. This cost is called Krylov complexity. They look at a system made of two parts put side by side. Each part has its own cost when it acts on its own. The pair asks what cost the joint system has.

They prove the joint cost is at least the sum of the two part costs. In most cases it is more than that sum. They also name a tool that can count the extra part.
