The winning design is linear, symmetric, and extremal, with support size set to an optimized value. It hits the L2 lower bound for both tasks, and the L1 bound in the limit. Its communication cost can drop to a short log-sized bit count. Pan also gives an algorithm to build the estimator, plus selection guidance for practice. A modified Count-Mean Sketch, he shows, sits practically at the optimal level too.
arxiv-2603-11623: Mironenko, Burnaev, and Barannikov give cross-persistence diagrams their first systematic density study. Persistence diagrams track clusters, loops, and voids across scales, one cloud at a time. Cross-persistence diagrams instead capture how features of two point clouds relate. The team proves the density exists and builds its statistical foundations. They also design the first learning framework to predict it from coordinates and distance matrices. Noise, they find, can even sharpen the split between clouds from different manifolds. Tests beat older methods on density prediction and cloud distinction.
arxiv-2603-12023: Banerjee and co-authors show how old system flaws can amplify attacks on compound AI pipelines. Such pipelines chain LLMs with software tools and databases on shared hardware. Many parts still carry classic software bugs, timing leaks, and power side channels. Two combined attacks make the risk concrete: one pairs code injection with a Rowhammer guardrail hit to plant a jailbreak prompt. The other poisons a knowledge base so an agent sends private user data to a hostile app.
arxiv-2603-12123: Song shows that a fresh review session catches more LLM errors than a same-session second look. Cross-Context Review sends output to a new session with no access to the chat that made it. Thirty artifacts with 150 planted errors faced four review setups. A second review helped only when it ran in a fresh session. Cross-Context Review beat repeated self-review clearly, though not a context-aware subagent or one self-review on average. The method needs no new tools and costs one extra session.
arxiv-2603-12623: David Yang defines a stratification on Moy-Prasad quotients for a reductive group over a Laurent series field. The strata come from twisted Levi subgroups, sorted into conjugacy classes. He then computes the strata in terms of those subgroups. The result is needed for several follow-up papers on the local geometric Langlands program. The paper is a technical step in that larger program, stated for groups that meet set conditions.
arxiv-2603-13123: Jacob Emil Mencke and Paolo Ricci run the first full-f drift-kinetic and delta-f gyrokinetic simulations of a linear plasma device together. They derive an electrostatic model that joins slow, large-scale fields to fast, small-scale ones. Electrons follow a drift-reduced Braginskii model under critical balance ordering. Ions use a Hermite-Laguerre spectral expansion for both parts of their distribution. At LAPD settings, the drift-kinetic part stays near a bi-Maxwellian. Small-scale turbulence grows only when collisionality drops and sources strengthen.
arxiv-2603-13423: Andrew Kiruluta proposes Kalman World Models, a class of learned state-space models trained without backpropagation. Instead of gradient descent, parameter learning becomes Kalman-style gain adaptation through recursive Bayesian filtering. Error signals act as innovations, and training becomes online filtering. The framework extends to transformer LLMs, where internal activations are treated as latent dynamical states. Innovation terms correct those states, giving a gradient-free training and adaptation path from control theory. Tests on sequence modeling tasks showed competitive scores with better robustness.
arxiv-2603-13523: Pietro Piras studies the Bogomolov property for fields cut out by modular Galois representations. A field has this property when its Weil height stays above a fixed positive floor. Prior work proved it for eigenforms under some side conditions. Piras extends the result to eigenforms whose nebentypus character is nontrivial, a case left open before. He also defines a new class, called ADZ fields, after work by Amoroso, David, and Zannier. For that class, the property is kept under composition of fields, in full generality.
arxiv-2603-13723: Kyogo Horikawa and co-authors ask whether AI agents really improve code readability. Readability is key to software quality, and poor readability lengthens development and raises bug risk. Prior studies mix all kinds of refactoring, so the readability effect alone was unclear. The team pulled readability-related commits from the AIDev dataset and tracked metric changes in 403 commits. Agents mostly targeted logic complexity and documentation, not naming or formatting. Many readability commits made classic metrics worse, with the Maintainability Index down in most cases.
arxiv-2603-13923: Zhang, Yu, and Meng set out one frame for how molecules react, built on the least action rule. To see a reaction, one must solve the Schrödinger equation. Their frame joins past work on the kinetic energy operator and on potential energy surfaces built with AI tools. It also adds curved spacetime terms to the nuclear Hamiltonian. Those terms let gauge fields act near conical intersections. The frame unifies methods for electronic structure and for quantum dynamics, and the geometric phase appears on its own.
arxiv-2603-14023: Huang and co-authors build the first system that images fast, flexible objects through strong air turbulence at high frame rates. Event cameras record at thousands of frames per second but cannot tell object motion from turbulence shimmer. Their light field version grabs many views at once. True motion gives events that line up across views, while turbulence events do not. Tabletop tests image objects moving at up to 16,000 pixels per second through heavy turbulence.
arxiv-2603-14223: Altybay studies a backward problem for a time-fractional pseudo-parabolic equation with a time-varying coefficient. The task is to rebuild the unknown starting state from data seen at the final time, under Dirichlet boundary rules. The author proves that a unique solution exists under stated conditions. A finite-difference scheme with a stability and convergence analysis supplies the forward solver. Tikhonov regularization then drives the recovery, and tests with noisy final data show the method holds up.
arxiv-2603-14323: Liu and co-authors probe why medical multimodal models misread medical images, with a focus on visual grounding. A model may name the right finding yet point at the wrong region. Their VGMED dataset, built with clinical experts, tests grounding apart from word-level sense. Eight top medical models often fail to ground answers in the right image regions. The same models do ground well on natural scenes, so the flaw is medical. A fix called VGRefine sharpens grounding at test time.
arxiv-2603-14423: Shekhar and Ramdas build tighter confidence intervals for sampling without replacement. The task is to bound a population mean from a sample drawn with no repeats. For a finite alphabet, they derive a floor on interval width from large-deviation rate functions. A new interval built from an empirical rate function meets that floor up to constants in set regimes. A dual form makes the interval cheap to compute. Extensions cover the unit interval and smooth Banach spaces.
arxiv-2603-14723: Zhang tests how safety supervision wording shapes low-data LoRA fine-tuning across three model families. Four formats share the same core safety rules. Plain constitutional rules form condition A. Creed-style identity framing forms B, with a worldview tail in C. A matched non-identity format forms D. HarmBench scores run through a dual-judge pipeline on 320 behaviors. Format D refuses most on Llama, Gemma and Qwen alike. Creed framing beats plain rules but trails D by a wide margin.
arxiv-2603-14823: Li, Song and Li sharpen neural network verification by branching on counterexample clues. Dataflow verifiers refine loose relaxations with branch-and-bound search. Static rules pick branch points blind, ignoring why a check failed. Their DRG-BaB frame recasts the search as a counterexample-guided loop. A failed case yields a closed-form fake counterexample from linear bounds. A directional relaxation gap score ranks neurons by their role in the failure. Targeted splits then replace blind search on high-dimensional tests, they report.
arxiv-2603-14923: Taylor adds directional routing to transformer attention heads at small parameter cost. A shared router steers learned suppression directions for each head. A mid-size model trains beside an identical baseline in one run. Routing becomes the dominant compute path in the routed model. Killing it drops factual recall near zero on eight test prompts. Induction accuracy falls from over 93 percent to zero as well. Single head knockouts barely matter by contrast. Perplexity drops by about a third to a half versus baseline, Taylor reports.
arxiv-2603-15023: Battiston and co-authors speed up PAC-DB, a database privacy model, in a system called SIMD-PAC-DB. The original method needs 128 runs over random half-samples of the database. Their insight is that each bit of a hashed key can stand for membership in one such sample. New algorithms compute the needed aggregates from these hashes in a SIMD-friendly way. The authors report speedups up to forty times. They release a DuckDB extension that rewrites SQL queries for private answers.
arxiv-2603-15123: Gui and co-authors probe the layered ferromagnet Cr2Ge2Te6 with a quartz tuning fork resonator. The fork reads the magnetotropic susceptibility, which tracks the rotational stiffness of the magnetization. Responses over temperature, field, and angle all fit a quasi-two-dimensional easy-axis ferromagnet model. As saturation nears, the angular profile shifts from a simple cosine form to a sharp dip shape. The authors present the material as a clean reference system for fork-based measurements. The method also helps separate spin-based anisotropy from orbital magnetism.
arxiv-2603-15223: Lowin and co-authors estimate robot affordances with two coupled particle filters, one for graspable regions and one for movable regions. Single estimators struggle with visual, geometric, and semantic ambiguity. Each filter encodes regularities tied to its own property, which trims uncertainty. Coupling lets the two trade information and focus where both agree. On a real-world dataset, precision beat three recent estimators by more than two and a half times. Real robot trials reached a 70 percent success rate, even in low light and clutter.
arxiv-2603-15323: Park and Xiao study small-time heat decay for stable processes on fractal drums, open sets with fractal boundaries. They look at spectral heat content, a measure of how much heat stays inside. Earlier work covered subordinate killed Brownian motion. This study extends the picture to stable processes themselves. Under set geometric conditions on the domains, the decay rate differs sharply from the Brownian case. The split occurs at a set value tied to the boundary's interior Minkowski dimension.
arxiv-2603-15423: Potts and Sudhof show that most failures in human-AI chats are invisible: the user never signals that anything went wrong. In 100,000 WildChat interactions, 79 percent of AI failures were invisible in this sense. The failures fall into eight archetypes that cluster into higher-level types. A counterfactual set swaps 2024-era replies for answers from three modern frontier models. Failure rates dropped a lot, yet most failures stayed invisible and the archetype mix held steady. The taxonomy, they argue, can anchor failure monitoring for builders and policy makers.
arxiv-2603-15623: Mishra and co-authors describe Finder, a search framework built for pharmaceutical data. Older systems struggle with mixed content and manual curation. Finder unifies search across text, images, audio, and video. It blends sparse word matching with dense semantic vectors. A modular pipeline ingests mixed formats and enriches metadata. The system has processed over 291,400 documents, 31,070 videos, and 1,192 audio files. Content spans 98 languages across regulatory, research, and commercial domains.
arxiv-2603-15723: Dhara and Sheth test how question answering degrades as context grows. Models now face long, noisy texts where the answer hides among filler. The pair ran controlled tests on SQuAD and HotpotQA. They added irrelevant context step by step and kept the answer signal fixed. Accuracy fell steadily as length grew in both sets. Multi-hop HotpotQA lost nearly twice as much accuracy as SQuAD. The authors argue context-length checks belong in standard reliability tests.
arxiv-2603-16123: Sargsyan compiles type specifications into neural nets that compose by construction. Networks often master parts yet fail on fresh part mixtures. Her claim pins the failure on architecture, not data. A decoder composes only when it honors the task's algebra. Higher Inductive Type specs compile into network pieces directly. Basepoints, paths, and 2-cells map to constraints, generators, and homotopies. The transport decoders act as strict monoidal functors by design. Softmax attention provably cannot match that strictness, she shows. Torus and Klein bottle tests back the predicted gaps.
arxiv-2603-16223: Du and co-authors improve label-free training for language models. Such methods learn from the model's own majority votes. The catch is that popular wrong answers can trap training. Their Dual Consensus method uses two vote stages. First the model anchors on its dominant replies. Then brief unlearning lets it explore diverse signals. The training target blends both sets by harmonic mean. Across eight benchmarks, Pass@1 beat plain majority vote.
arxiv-2603-16323: Geng and co-authors probe puzzles in charmed baryon decays. Recent data clash with theory, including flavor symmetry fits and lattice simulations. A suspect is the decay used to normalize the measurements. The team uses lattice inputs in an SU(3) flavor analysis with first-order breaking. They predict two ratios of decay rates, 2.6% and 1.1%. These ratios need no normalization mode. They may help locate the source of the tension.
arxiv-2603-16423: Yoshimura and co-authors rethink Mamba models for image tasks. Vision Transformers scale poorly, but Mamba's one-way scan limits patch contact. Added scans in prior work cost speed and shuffle data often. Two fixes anchor SF-Mamba. Patch swapping feeds two-way flow into a single scan. Batch folding with timed state resets boosts GPU parallelism. Tests on classification, detection, and segmentation beat strong baselines. Throughput also rose across model sizes.
arxiv-2603-16923: Adelson, Sethu, and Dang build a speech system on Assembly Calculus instead of deep learning. Deep learning needs huge datasets and global weight updates, and its features are hard to read. Assembly Calculus uses sparse neuron assemblies, Hebbian plasticity, and winner take all competition. Their framework turns speech into spike patterns and sorts assemblies across areas and timescales. It detects phone boundaries with an F1 score of 0.69 and word boundaries at 0.61, with no weight training. Phone recognition reached 47.5 percent accuracy in their tests.
arxiv-2603-17123: Onitiju and Vakilinia build a standardized security assessment for large language models, plus a defensive system to answer it. No broad comparative assessment across major model families existed. They test five widely deployed families against 10,000 adversarial prompts in six attack categories. Vulnerability rates ranged widely, from about 12 to about 30 percent, and stronger models were not safer models. Their multi layered defensive framework reached 83 percent average detection accuracy with 5 percent false positives. They argue that outside defenses offer a viable path to safer deployment.
arxiv-2603-17223: Shin, Chang, and Nargesian present ListK, a framework that speeds up semantic ORDER BY and LIMIT K queries. Such queries use language models to sort rows by meaning, and current methods are slow. ListK combines partial listwise rankings with several sorting schemes: tournaments, multi pivot quickselect and quicksort, and a Monte Carlo filter. A query optimizer picks among them based on the target recall. The authors report that ListK halves latency at nearly no cost to recall or ranking quality.
arxiv-2603-17323: Zhu and co-authors present DexEXO, a hand exoskeleton for collecting dexterous robot demonstrations that puts wearability first. Scaling robot learning needs quality demonstrations from many different operators. Wearable tools often trade comfort and fit for kinematic accuracy. DexEXO aligns look, contact geometry, and kinematics in the hardware itself. A passive hand matches the deployed robot, so policies train straight from raw wrist camera images. User studies showed better comfort and usability than prior wearable systems. Diffusion policies trained this way performed competitively.
arxiv-2603-17523: Pellegrini benchmarks seven neural operator designs on the stiff FitzHugh-Nagumo model. The test asks whether models keep translation invariance when inputs move in space and time. Training uses currents at varied spots but one fixed time, cutting data costs. Test currents shift in both space and time instead. Convolutional operators generalized well to the moved dynamics, he reports. Fourier models scored best in training but cost the most.
arxiv-2603-17923: Forer computes how electron hits spin up three water-family molecular ions. The targets are H2O+, HDO+, and D2O+, all asymmetric-top rotors. His frame joins R-matrix scattering with quantum-defect and frame-transformation methods. A Coulomb-Born part covers the high-energy tail. Cross sections and rate factors come out state by state from the ground level. Full tables for spins up to N of four ship as extra data for the EMAA base.
arxiv-2603-18223: Dainotti and co-authors forecast gamma-ray bursts as an independent high-redshift probe of dark energy. Bursts reach redshift 9.2, far past Type Ia supernovae and toward the cosmic microwave background. Forecasts use the Dainotti relations that link plateau luminosity and duration in X-ray and optical bands. About 66 well-measured optical bursts could match Planck precision on the dark energy parameter w. Machine learning redshift estimates could double sample sizes soon.
arxiv-2603-18423: Kim, Kim, and Kang propose SynQ for accurate zero-shot quantization without any training data. Synthetic data noise, off-target patterns, and wrong hard labels limit past zero-shot methods. SynQ cuts sample noise with a low-pass filter. It aligns the quantized model's class activation maps with the pretrained model's maps. For hard samples, only soft labels guide training, avoiding teacher errors; tests give top accuracy among rivals.
arxiv-2603-18523: Che and co-authors probe how large vision-language models count objects, using mechanistic interpretability tools. Counting forces a model to find each item and sum them, a clean reasoning test. Models count small numbers precisely but estimate larger ones with noise, like humans. Visual Activation Patching and HeadLens reveal a shared counting circuit across visual tasks. Fine-tuning on synthetic counting images alone lifts out-of-distribution counting by 8.36% on average.
arxiv-2603-18923: Jordan and co-authors test whether sulfur gases claimed on the exoplanet K2-18b could form without life. Such gases have been read as possible signs of life. Their models check non-living paths to make the two gases in a hydrogen-rich air. One path can make visible amounts, but it hangs on an unmeasured energy step. A common hydrocarbon forms in plenty instead. It mimics the same light features, giving a plainer account of the data. Sulfur hazes also form and settle in the air.
arxiv-2603-19423: Li and Zhao find that safety training for language model agents can wreck their task skill. Models trained to resist prompt injection are tested on 97 agent tasks and 1,000 attack prompts. Defended models often refuse or botch plain tasks before any attack content appears. Early faults then cascade through retry loops into timeouts on 99 percent of tasks. Baselines time out on only 13 percent in the same setup. Simple attacks still slip past the defenses at high rates. The team blames shortcut learning on surface attack cues.
arxiv-2603-20023: Patrykiejew studies symmetric mixtures trapped in narrow slit pores with selective walls. In bulk, these mixtures resist phase separation despite strong non-additivity. Inside a pore, the walls change the picture. If the walls prefer one component only weakly, the pore fills in one condensation step. Stronger preference can split filling into two steps. The first step yields a demixed liquid, and the second restores a mixed liquid. The work maps how wall selectivity and non-additivity shape this confined phase behavior.
arxiv-2603-20123: Simongini and co-authors report early light from the tidal disruption event TDE 2025aarm. A star torn apart by a black hole makes such a flare. At redshift 0.01368, this is the second closest event of its kind ever found. The team took optical data with the Liverpool Telescope over three epochs. Spectra show a blue continuum with helium and hydrogen lines, a classic signature. The light curve fits a small star falling onto a black hole of twenty million solar masses. Swift caught soft X-rays from the event too.
arxiv-2603-20423: Garcia and co-authors extend a stochastic embedding theorem into a wider diffusion framework. The starting theorem recovers drift and diffusion fields from scalar time series. It needs no prior assumptions about the governing physics. They apply a blind protocol across nine domains of physics. The authors report that known constants emerge in both channels. These include the Boltzmann and Planck constants and light speed. They derive a gravitational diffusion coefficient from fluctuation-dissipation arguments. Four axioms then formalize the whole framework.
arxiv-2603-20523: Skiba and co-authors prove an index theorem in relative K-theory for first-order systems. Their motivation comes from bifurcations of homoclinic orbit branches. They study families of first-order equations on the real line. The work generalizes earlier index theorems by other authors. One novelty lifts the usual assumption of asymptotic hyperbolicity. Another allows general compact parameter spaces, not just one parameter. The reward is a remarkably simple index formula. It is expressed cleanly in relative K-theory terms.
arxiv-2603-20623: Tong and co-authors present MINISA, a small instruction set for AI accelerators that can be reconfigured. Rich layout freedom helps these chips stay busy on many task types. But fine control means fetching huge config data from off chip memory. Their set programs the chip at the level of virtual neurons. Three layout commands plus one mapping command cover the full legal space. On 50 matrix workloads, off chip instruction traffic fell sharply. End to end speed rose up to 31.6 times.
arxiv-2603-20723: Pecher and co-authors audit how TikTok personalization drifts on polarizing topics. They ran controlled accounts that mimic users for or against set topics. The topics span politics, climate, vaccines, and conspiracy claims. Feeds did drift toward each account's stated interests. For misinformation themes, a neutralizing pull showed up instead. U.S. politics drew strong reinforcement of the user's stance. Other topics also tended to echo the starting view. The authors draw lessons for platform governance and user awareness.
arxiv-2603-20923: Deaconu and co-authors give a new way to view k-graph algebras as Cuntz-Pimsner algebras. Earlier work by Kumjian, Pask, and Sims built this link from the top down, through a linking algebra. Their process starts at the bottom, with Pimsner's theorem for graph algebras, and iterates upward. They work with product systems over multi-index sets, so k-graphs are a special case. The key step uses a recent result that the Cuntz-Pimsner construction behaves well under functors.
arxiv-2603-21223: Gajendragad and co-authors teach smart microswimmers to navigate turbulent flows around obstacles. Microswimmers in such flows can get trapped at obstacles or escape them in complex ways. They extend adversarial Q-learning methods so swimmers can move from a start point to a target in two dimensional turbulence. A circular obstacle is added by a volume penalization method. Their obstacle-aware strategy curbs the tendency to stick at stagnation points near the obstacle. The smart swimmers beat both naive swimmers and surfers in their tests.
arxiv-2603-21623: Zhang and co-authors extend Neyman-Pearson classification to training data with noisy labels. This framework caps class-specific error rates, which matters when errors cost very different amounts. Older methods assume clean labels, and noise can make the target values impossible to recover. A density ratio model with exponential tilting restores recovery, they show. Their method then estimates class shares, posteriors, and the noise process from noisy data alone. No map of label errors is needed in advance. Tests came close to oracle scores.
arxiv-2603-21823: Bros and co-authors study the questions that appear inside French digital news stories. Questions in news are rarely counted apart from statements. The team processed over one million articles from 2023 and 2024, detecting questions, typing their role, and finding answers in the text. A hand-coded subcorpus grounds the measures in semantic theory. Most questions open or organize an issue, and most get answered later in the same story, usually in the journalist's own voice. Named people and groups dominate these passages, while broad publics appear far less.
arxiv-2603-22123: Boysen and co-authors model how a patient's breathing moves tissue during radiotherapy. Precise dose placement matters, and lung motion adds real uncertainty. Their model, PRISM-RM, uses implicit neural representations as a motion surrogate. It needs no fixed reference breathing state. The motion field is continuous in space and time and stays diffeomorphic. Biophysical constraints keep the estimated motion plausible beyond the training data. The authors report interpolation on par with their earlier model and better extrapolation. Sequential registration methods still extrapolate better, they note.
arxiv-2603-22223: Gardella and co-authors revisit the energy-momentum tensor in a classical model of the electron. The model comes from Bialynicki-Birula and can be solved exactly. The team studies form factors of the energy-momentum tensor for a charged particle. They show the leading non-analytic terms of the small-t expansion match quantum electrodynamics. In other words, a classical model gets those terms right. The clarity of the solvable model also lets them comment on a recent idea: a regularized proton D-term.
arxiv-2603-22523: Tapias and Santos ask software professionals how team diversity pays off in money terms. Past research stresses social and process gains, leaving the business side understudied. The authors interview ten practitioners about their real project experience. Diversity is linked, in their accounts, to lower costs, more revenue, and faster time to market. It is also tied to smoother processes, fresh ideas, and closer fit with customers. The authors stress these are grounded perceptions, not abstract claims.
arxiv-2603-22623: Aranya and Desai test medical vision-language models for two linked flaws. One flaw is hallucination, where a model invents findings. The other is sycophancy, where it folds under user pressure. They test six models on three medical question sets with images. A clear tradeoff appears: models that hallucinate least tend to agree most under pressure. The authors propose three scores to capture grounding, pressure resistance, and safety. Across 1,151 cases, no model scores above 0.35 on their safety index. They argue both flaws must be checked before clinical use.
arxiv-2603-23023: Gwak and co-authors present Cog3DMap, a framework that gives vision-language models an explicit 3D map. Multi-view spatial reasoning is hard because model features carry meaning but little geometry. Cog3DMap builds a 3D memory step by step from many views. Each token holds both semantic and geometric data, grounded in space. The model then reasons over that structured map directly. Tests on spatial reasoning benchmarks reach state-of-the-art scores, the authors report. Code is set for public release.
arxiv-2603-23323: Giarrè and Karl present PNap, a framework that saves energy at multi-access edge computing sites. Edge servers must stay on at many spots to keep latency low, even when load dips. Multi-state sleep lets servers doze at deeper levels, trading savings for slower wake-ups. Service tasks also need lifecycle steps that cannot run while a server sleeps. PNap plans sleep and service states together, guided by traffic forecasts. It cuts energy use by up to 14.9% versus a leading method. Service availability stays the same.
arxiv-2603-23523: Ma and nine co-authors question whether 3D language models truly grasp spatial relations. A text-only model, tuned on plain question pairs, matches 3D models on the SQA3D test. That hints the test rewards text shortcuts, not 3D reasoning. The team builds Real-3DQA, a stricter bench that filters guessable questions. A taxonomy splits reasoning into clear aspects for scoring. On the new bench, current 3D models stumble once easy cues vanish. A reweighted training goal pushes models toward visual clues and lifts scores a lot.
arxiv-2603-23823: Liu and co-authors analyze knowledge tracing on concept trees through circuit complexity. Knowledge tracing tracks mastery across linked concepts with prerequisites. They model tasks such as recursive-majority propagation up a prerequisite tree. Such tasks sit in NC1, while proving them beyond TC0 would need major open results. Under a monotone restriction, they prove a strict depth hierarchy. In tests, transformers learn shortcuts unless trained on intermediate subtrees. Extra supervision then yields near-perfect scores at depths three and four.
arxiv-2603-24023: Soni and co-authors build a small self-hosted model that answers cricket statistics questions in SQL. Putting full schemas into prompts for API models costs much and adds latency. Their two-phase fine-tuning teaches an 8B model the whole database schema. Inputs then shrink by over 99 percent, from 17,000 tokens to under 100. The system serves the CriQ app, a sister app to Dream11. It reaches 98.4 percent execution success and 92.5 percent semantic accuracy, beating a Gemini Flash 2.0 baseline.
arxiv-2603-24123: Apresyan and Sarkissian derive integrable-system results from a conformal field theory identity. They start from the genus one Moore-Seiberg duality identity in two-dimensional Liouville theory. From it, they obtain the Baxter Q-operator for the two-particle hyperbolic Ruijsenaars system. They also derive the product formula for its eigenfunctions. The authors expect this link to reveal the true role of the Moore-Seiberg identity in integrable systems. Their work ties a duality of field theory to concrete spectral tools.
arxiv-2603-24423: Jana and Qing study sublinearly Morse boundaries in proper geodesic spaces. They give a new characterisation of sublinearly Morse geodesic lines based on middle recurrence. They then turn to first passage percolation on proper geodesic graphs of bounded degree. Each edge gets a random passage time drawn from the same distribution. Under suitable conditions on that distribution, they prove the sublinearly Morse boundary does not change under the percolation. The result links a coarse geometric notion to a random growth model.
arxiv-2603-24723: Engle and Morsky model how voting strategies and public good funding evolve together in a two-party system. Voters follow one of four strategies, from consensus-makers to party zealots, and switch by imitation. The public good helps both local residents and neighbours through spillovers. Differential equations govern movement and strategy change, with migration toward higher utility. Results show bistability: regions settle into gridlock or a mix of consensus-makers and zealots. Spillovers create free-riding, tying poorly funded regions to well-funded ones.
arxiv-2603-24823: Karatarakis and Wiedijk formalise the Gelfond-Schneider theorem in the Lean 4 proof assistant. The theorem settles Hilbert's seventh problem: if a base is algebraic and not zero or one, and the exponent is algebraic and irrational, then the power is transcendental. Gelfond and Schneider proved it independently in 1934. The theorem remains a landmark of transcendental number theory, one that links algebraic number theory with complex analysis. A machine-checked formalisation makes every step of that classic argument verifiable by the proof assistant's kernel.
arxiv-2603-24923: Huang documents the specification of normal forms in cubical type theory. The definition already appears inside the normalisation proof for the theory. This note presents it in a more traditional style, explicitly and for reference. Readers who need the exact notion of a normal form can find it stated directly, without mining the proof. The note serves as a compact companion to the normalisation literature for cubical type theory.
arxiv-2603-25423: Zeng and co-authors build a benchmark and a debunker for fake micro-videos in the wild. Short clips spread false claims fast, and fakes come in many forms: edits, AI-made clips, bias traps, and clips reused out of context. WildFakeBench holds over ten thousand real clips, each tagged by experts with the trick used. FakeAgent then reasons like a Delphi panel, joining clip content with fetched evidence. It names the manipulation type, not just a fake stamp. Tests beat big multimodal models on every trick type.
arxiv-2603-25523: Amiri and co-authors sharpen a bedside estimate of pressure loss across a narrowed artery. Clinics infer the drop from blood speed through Bernoulli formulas, but plain forms ignore how losses shift with flow regime. Their modified version adds a loss factor that moves with the Reynolds number. Bench tests on a model stenosis join direct pressure reads with ultrasound and MRI speed maps. The new form tracks the true drops best. Simpler forms skew high by wide margins. MRI pixel size also matters: coarse maps understate flow.
arxiv-2603-25623: Treffler and co-authors build 3D maps from radar data with a neural implicit method. Radar works well in fog, smoke, and dust, but its point clouds are sparse and noisy. Their method learns a signed distance field for the surfaces. It also learns how radar reflections depend on the viewing angle. A compact hybrid encoding keeps memory use low. The authors report smoother and more accurate surfaces than lidar-based methods applied to radar. The method also holds up as point clouds grow sparser.
arxiv-2603-25823: Han and co-authors present ViGoR-Bench, a test of whether image and video generators can reason. Pretty output can hide weak logic about physics, cause, and space, they argue. Their bench covers image-to-image and video tasks in one frame. It grades both the steps a model takes and its final output. An automated judge is grounded in evidence and tracks human scores closely. Diagnosis splits results into fine cognitive skills. Tests on over 20 top models reveal large reasoning gaps, the authors report.
arxiv-2603-25923: Zhou and co-authors expose a hidden data leak in EEG survival prediction and offer a fix. The task is forecasting outcomes for comatose patients after cardiac arrest. Long EEG records are often cut into short windows and reused across training stages. That reuse can smuggle label data into the model and inflate validation scores. Their framework first turns short segments into embeddings with a convolutional network. A transformer then pools the embeddings into one patient-level prediction. Strict patient-level separation holds throughout.
arxiv-2603-26323: An and co-authors probe how language models handle spatial reasoning from the inside. They split spatial thought into three basic skills drawn from human cognition research. The skills are joining relations, transforming representations, and updating a spatial state over steps. Tests run in English, Chinese, and Arabic, with probes and causal checks on inner layers. They find spatial facts sit in middle layers and can sway output, but the signals stay brief and split across tasks.
arxiv-2603-26423: Truffet studies tropical linear optimisation through a special substitution method. Tropical polyhedra matter in software static analysis and in parity, mean payoff, and energy games. Winning such a game amounts to solving a tropical linear problem. His method works on the tropical cone built by homogenising the target polyhedron, and can switch to a maximisation step in a special case. The substitution keeps the strong polynomiality of the classic version, and a tropical Charnes-Cooper step solves fractional cases too.
arxiv-2603-26623: Herdoíza and co-authors report progress on computing light and strange quark masses in lattice QCD. The run uses three dynamical flavours with improved Wilson fermions on CLS ensembles. Bare masses come from the simulations, then are renormalised without perturbation theory in the Schrödinger functional scheme. The scheme spans a wide range of scales before meeting perturbative results. Five lattice spacings reach down to about 0.038 femtometres, with pion masses at the physical value. The spread lets them test cutoff and chiral effects before extrapolating.
arxiv-2603-26823: Jha reviews how throughput gains act as a strategic lever in large AI systems. The synthesis covers dataloader design, memory limits, and compiler tools for training large language models. One framework, OVERLORD, raised end-to-end training throughput by 4.5 percent. Offloading methods such as ZeRO-Offload let models exceed one GPU's memory. Compiler work jointly tunes compute, memory, and communication. Jha argues that system-wide fixes, not single tricks, drive scale and cost gains.
arxiv-2603-27023: Balogh and co-authors built a set of Ipelets that visualize neighborhood graphs and clustering inside the Ipe editor. Ipe is a popular drawing tool for geometry figures, extended by small plugins. Their collection covers many graph types, from epsilon-neighbor and Gabriel graphs to Yao graphs. It also runs clustering methods such as DBSCAN, HDBSCAN, k-means, and mean shift. Seeing these structures drawn helps build intuition about their behavior. All the Ipelets are written in Lua and freely available. The set targets researchers in geometry and data analysis.
arxiv-2603-27223: Kim and co-authors present EuraGovExam, a benchmark built from real civil service exams in five Eurasian regions. The exams come from South Korea, Japan, Taiwan, India, and the European Union. Over 8,000 scanned multiple-choice questions span 17 academic and administrative domains. Each item sits inside one image, with choices and visuals embedded in the page. Models must reason across languages and layouts from that image alone. Even the best vision-language models reached only 86 percent accuracy. The set targets e-governance and public-sector document analysis too.
arxiv-2603-27323: Njamen Njomen and Ndikwa determine a new six-parameter beta-modified Weibull distribution and its key functions. They derive its cumulative, survival, density, and hazard functions in full. Sub-distributions show the new family generalizes the ones already in the literature. Numerical simulations then explore the density's possible shapes. Those shapes cover every density form found in earlier distributions. The hazard function can stay constant, rise, fall, or bend into U and inverted-U forms. The new family thus encompasses the hazard repertoire of existing models.
arxiv-2603-27423: Natarajan and co-authors present AstraAI, a coding aid for supercomputer software. The tool runs in a plain Linux terminal. It blends language models with search over the project code. It also reads syntax trees to map code structure. Those two sources build a rich prompt for each request. Edits stay scoped and match the host project style. Both local and cloud models can drive it. The team shows the tool at work on the AMReX framework.
arxiv-2603-27623: Pagliaro and co-authors speed up exoplanet atmosphere studies with a transformer. Bayesian retrievals on spectra can take very long. Exoformer learns to propose smart prior ranges instead. It trains for hot Jupiter transmission spectra. Tests use mock data and real JWST spectra. WASP-39b and WASP-17b serve as real cases. Retrievals run three to eight times faster. Best-fit spectra and parameters stay intact.
arxiv-2603-27723: Zhu and co-authors let graphs and modalities improve each other over time. Multimodal graphs often carry noisy or missing links. One fixed graph rarely suits every task. TMTE evolves topology and features in a closed loop. Metric learning over modality embeddings drives link updates. Smooth fusion with cross-modal alignment updates features. An anchor trick keeps the math cheap. Task focus sharpens both sides as rounds proceed.
arxiv-2603-27923: Wagle and co-authors build ForestSim, a synthetic forest driving dataset. Urban datasets abound, but wild terrain data are scarce. Pixel-true labels in forests cost too much to hand-make. ForestSim holds 2,094 photorealistic images. They span twenty-five settings, seasons, and foliage levels. Unreal Engine plus AirSim generate the scenes. Twenty classes carry consistent labels. Top segmentation models benchmark well on the set.
arxiv-2603-28423: Avalos-Pacheco, Lupparelli, and Stingo introduce profile graphical models, which show in one graph how an outside factor reshapes the links among variables. Each level of a risk factor gets its own conditional independence pattern, learned jointly. The authors define the class, prove its Markov properties, and link it to chain graph models. A Bayesian method with spike-and-slab priors plus a fast EM algorithm does the fitting. On leukemia protein data, the model found leaner networks and more patient differences.
arxiv-2603-28523: Kirillov and Klinshov show that how oscillator frequencies are picked, not just their spread, shapes the noise of a finite Kuramoto system. With random picks from a Lorentzian law, shot noise theory predicts the fluctuation spectrum well. With evenly spaced picks from the same law, the spectrum instead wavers slowly in waves. The wave period grows with system size and matches the gap between neighbors near the center. Simulations trace the effect to resonant links that random picks lack.
arxiv-2603-28623: Pinto Couto and co-authors analyze first-click time measurements in quantum time-of-arrival problems. One view asks when a particle could be found at a detector. Another asks when it is detected there for the first time. They build the first-click distribution by conditioning on no earlier detection. Their method uses the Page and Wootters formalism, where time is a quantum observable. For single and paired wave packets, conditioning shifts probability toward earlier times. Coarser detector resolution broadens the distribution and shifts it later.
arxiv-2603-28723: Azzouz, Vuissoz, and Laprie work on recovering the full vocal tract shape from speech audio. Most past studies used electromagnetic sensors, which cover few articulators. They use about 3.5 hours of real-time MRI data from a single speaker. Contours are extracted from the MRI images automatically, keeping key geometry and dropping pixel detail. A Bi-LSTM model maps denoised audio and embeddings to those contours. They compare MFCC, LCC, and HuBERT embeddings and vary dataset size. The average error was 1.48 millimetres, below the pixel size.
arxiv-2603-29023: Lerma-Torres proposes a neuroscience grounded memory architecture for long term interaction with language models. Bigger context windows alone can degrade reasoning, even with perfect retrieval. The design draws on complementary learning systems theory, belief hierarchies, dual process cognition, and fuzzy-trace theory. Memory carries valence, not just content, through pre-computed emotion summaries in a belief hierarchy. Retrieval defaults to fast automatic activation, with planned search only when needed. A thalamic gateway tags and routes information between stores. Over time, the system shifts toward fast processing, like expert skill.
arxiv-2603-29323: Park and co-authors study the full distribution of entanglement entropy in hybrid quantum circuits. These circuits mix random unitary gates with local measurements. The mean entropy alone hides key features of the dynamics. Higher moments, like variance ratios and skewness, reveal more. These quantities behave distinctly in volume-law and area-law phases. They can flag measurement-induced transitions. A simple model of the area-law regime matches simulations. Combined with a directed-polymer picture, it fits the whole phase diagram.
arxiv-2603-29523: Wang and co-authors present GeoDistNet, an open-source tool that builds synthetic power distribution networks. Feeder studies need models that are both usable and true to real areas. Real feeder data are rarely public, and benchmarks miss local geography. Their tool starts from public map data for a service area. It builds a candidate graph and picks a radial feeder layout. It then assigns standard electrical parameters and loads. A Melbourne case study produced a feeder ready for power-flow runs.
arxiv-2603-29923: Zhang derives a stochastic Cahn-Hilliard equation from one-dimensional spin dynamics. The source system is Ising-Kac-Kawasaki lattice motion near the critical point. He splits the motion into a drift part and a jump martingale part. A multiscale swap step yields the cubic drift term. A limit theorem turns the noise into divergence-form Gaussian noise. Energy bounds and compactness then give convergence to the one solution of the target equation. Its steady law also matches the phi-four law.
arxiv-2604-00023: Amien and Gunawan combine cognate subtraction with an ML classifier on phonological traits, testing whether non-matching vocabulary in Sulawesi languages reflects pre-Austronesian substrate or separate ideas. Using 1,357 forms from six local tongues, they identify 438 forms, or 26.5 percent, through subtraction. An XGBoost model on 26 sound features distinguishes inherited from non-mainstream forms, revealing longer forms, more consonant clusters, and higher glottal stop rates. Both methods find 266 strong non-mainstream candidates, yet clustering yields no clear word groups, giving no evidence for a single pre-Austronesian layer.
arxiv-2604-00223: Luong and two colleagues diagnose a flaw in reverse KL distillation for large language models. Non-target gradients keep pushing the target logit upward even after the student matches the teacher, breeding overconfidence and shrinking output diversity. Reverse KL also supervises non-target classes weakly, harming tail alignment. Their Diversity-aware RKL cancels the harmful gradient push and firms up non-target supervision, keeping reverse KL's optimization advantages. Across datasets and model families, it beats forward KL, reverse KL, and other objectives on performance and the trade-off.
arxiv-2604-00323: Suraj Kath and four colleagues survey how large language models fit into abuse detection, spanning toxic language and fraud. Old tools and manual labels lag behind shifting threats and nuanced policy needs, while language models add contextual reasoning and policy reading. The survey maps model use across four stages: label and feature building, detection, review and appeals, and audits and governance, weighing real-world design and limits. Challenges remain latency, cost, determinism, hostile strength, and fairness, with sound, accountable use the open goal.
arxiv-2604-00423: Zhou and colleagues offer Calico for database buffer pools facing a wider workload mix than transaction processing. Alongside B-tree lookups, systems now field analytics scans and vector-search indexes with graph walks. A translation layer turns logical page numbers into resident frames. It must be quick for all patterns, run in user space, use huge pages, integrate, and stay under database control for eviction and input-output. Calico revives array-based translation, an old idea whose time has come with hardware, separating logical translation from operating-system page tables.
arxiv-2604-00723: Lopetuso and Caporin introduce a cointegrated matrix model for data arranged along two sorting axes, where flat lists hide structure that tables keep. Their error-correction form keeps the familiar reading of cointegration, with numbers tracking adjustment back toward steady states. Unlike earlier forms, it also admits an equal matrix form, so both versions keep the data's table structure intact.
arxiv-2604-01123: Zhou and colleagues present AMBRA, combining ASTRID's volume with BRAHMA's gas-based black hole seeding models to explain JWST's massive black holes. AMBRA uses a heavy-seed prescription with seeds of ten thousand to a hundred thousand solar masses. AMBRA's redshift-8 black hole density runs over ten times ASTRID's. Black holes like GN-z11 and CEERS-1019 merge early, with mergers supplying about 50 percent of mass by redshift 11. AMBRA predicts about 4 LISA-detectable mergers yearly at redshift 8 and above, three orders of magnitude above ASTRID.
arxiv-2604-01323: Schneider and colleagues report the bulk of the L and T dwarf candidates found by the Backyard Worlds citizen science project. The project hunts moving infrared objects in Wide-field Infrared Survey Explorer data. The team presents 3006 new motion-confirmed finds, 2357 of L type and 649 of T type. Each carries proper motion, photometry, a spectral type and a distance estimate. The sample holds 80 likely dwarfs, 28 new companions to heavier stars and 9 candidate ultracool binary pairs. If confirmed, it would more than double the L and T dwarf count.
arxiv-2604-01423: Sandvik advances the study of the Kirillov model, Gaitsgory and Lysenko's answer to the problem that Whittaker sheaves require restricting to either étale sheaves or D-modules. He builds a theory of Iwahori-Whittaker sheaves on the affine Grassmannian in the setting of Betti sheaves. With this, he proves a Betti geometric Casselman-Shalika equivalence, linking these perverse sheaves on the affine Grassmannian with the Satake category.
arxiv-2604-01723: Li and colleagues introduce Causal Scene Narration, a rewrite of text fed to driving models so intent and limits line up. Driving models get route orders and hazard notes as loose fragments and must guess which limits matter. The method aligns intent with constraints, grounds quantities, and separates parts with no extra GPU cost. In a multi-town CARLA trial, driving scores rose by 31.1 percent on the base LMDrive model. Most gain comes from the information itself, and the benefit survives sizable noise.
arxiv-2604-01823: Alisultanov presents a quasi-1D magnetic heterostructure built from alternating strips of topological and normal insulators. A hybrid Hamiltonian mixing Su-Schrieffer-Heeger and Shockley models governs its low-energy physics, with spin-momentum locking and Zeeman splitting. Analysis puts it in class AIII, marked by chiral symmetry and an integer invariant, and winding numbers reveal phases 0, 1 and 2. A magnetic defect acts as a local probe, its in-gap spectrum fingerprinting each phase. Multilayers uncover Mobius band topology, compactifying the Brillouin zone into a Klein bottle.
arxiv-2604-02423: Bhalla and Gligorić introduce SWAY, an unsupervised linguistic measure of sycophancy in language models. A counterfactual prompting trick measures how much agreement shifts under positive versus negative wording pressure, isolating framing effects from content. Testing six models, they find sycophancy grows with belief strength. The fix asks models to consider the opposite assumption, driving it near zero across models, stance levels and clause types, without curbing response to genuine evidence. Baseline anti sycophantic prompt helps only somewhat and can backfire.
arxiv-2604-02523: Bronars, Park and Agrawal ask how the gains of a robot's position controller shape learning, a choice usually made from desired stiffness alone. Their experiments span behavior cloning, reinforcement learning from scratch, and sim-to-real transfer. Cloning favors soft, overdamped gains, reinforcement learning succeeds across regimes with tuned settings, and sim-to-real transfer suffers under stiff and overdamped gains, so the best choice depends on the learning method.
arxiv-2604-02823: Yuan, Peng and Piao propose single-field slow-roll inflation with a step uplift reaching a scale-invariant spectrum with n_s equal to 1. Early dark energy resolutions of the Hubble tension hint at such a Harrison-Zeldovich spectrum. The hint applies for a Hubble constant near 73 kilometers per second per megaparsec. Their inflaton potential keeps familiar slow-roll shapes, but inflation ends suddenly at a large potential step. That step keeps chaotic and Starobinsky models compatible with n_s equal to 1.
arxiv-2604-02923: Wu and five colleagues present an inspectable LLM Council for aggregating answers across models on long-form research questions. An analyst gathers three independent candidate answers as one structured textual state. A separately invoked writer drafts the final response using the question and that state. On 100 closed-book DRACO benchmark tasks, Council scores 71, exceeding GPT and Gemini by 6 and 8 points. It covers 51 percent of positive criteria met by exactly one candidate, against 44 percent for direct fusion.
arxiv-2604-03023: Ju and four colleagues build a reinforcement learning framework that beats demonstrations while staying near expert behavior. Reinforcement learning often drifts from desired human behavior, while imitation cannot beat its demonstrations. Their method adds a receding-horizon method that models near-term trajectories and supplies look-ahead rewards in training. Reference paths let the policy cover a range of expert-consistent behaviors, not one fixed target. In high-fidelity race car simulation with race driver data, policies reach fast lap times with expert alignment and reproduce setup-dependent traits.
arxiv-2604-03523: Nguyen and colleagues address robot learning from demos when expert data is scarce and costly, and copy-cat errors compound at test time. Their MYOE framework lets robots learn complex moves from limited demos. It uses a question-ready mixture-of-preferences state space model that guesses the desired goal at every step. Desired goals feed a preference regret score that tunes the control rules. Tests show toughness and out-of-sample results over other RLfD schemes.
arxiv-2604-03723: Guiyu Zhang and colleagues built SymphoMotion, a video generator that steers camera paths and object motion together instead of handling one at a time. Explicit camera routes plus geometry cues keep viewpoints stable, while 2D guidance joined to 3D tracks keeps objects placed in depth. Tests with the new RealCOD-25K dataset of paired poses and tracks showed it beating rivals on fidelity and control.
arxiv-2604-03823: Andrea Adriani and Giacomo Tento studied how eigenvalues spread for block matrices that are not Hermitian and whose blocks have Toeplitz form. In plain terms, they asked where the eigenvalues pile up as the matrices grow large. The point is to predict the pattern before computing it. Using geometric means of matrices and the theory of Generalized Locally Toeplitz sequences, they derived the limiting spread. Numerical tests and pictures backed the derivations.
arxiv-2604-04023: Elgammal searched for vector-like leptons decaying to an electron plus missing transverse energy in electron-positron collisions at the FCC-ee. The study used simulated samples at 240 GeV with 10.8 inverse attobarns of data, chasing a lepton-portal dark matter scenario. In that scenario, a scalar dark matter particle appears as a byproduct of a vector-like lepton, with dilepton events plus missing energy as the signature. If nothing appears, the study sets 95 percent exclusion limits on lepton mass and Yukawa coupling.
arxiv-2604-04323: Liu and colleagues benchmark reusable agent skills outside ideal lab conditions. Skills are domain-specific knowledge packs extending language-model agents, but past tests hand agents narrow skills tailored to each task. In realistic settings agents must find and pick skills themselves from 34 thousand real-world skills, with no hand-curated help. Gains fade steadily as settings grow more realistic, nearly reaching no-skill baselines. Query-specific refinement recovers much lost ground when starting skills are decent, and on Terminal-Bench 2.0 it lifts Claude Opus 4.6 from 58 percent to 66 percent.
arxiv-2604-04523: Hong and colleagues explore the capacity-computation trade-off in lookup-table-based processing-in-memory designs, where memory capacity replaces logic. Lookup tables map inputs to precomputed results without arithmetic logic. They propose LOCALUT for low-bit quantized network inference, adding canonicalization to drop duplicate entries and shrink table size. A reordering table remaps weight vectors to canonical form, and slice streaming sends columns into the DRAM buffer for reuse. Tests on a UPMEM-based system show a geometric mean speedup of 1.82x across precisions and models.
arxiv-2604-04823: Son studies how fast tempering chains settle to multimodal Gibbs measures, a setting where many separate modes trap plain samplers. He examines parallel and simulated tempering built from Metropolis walks that preserve Gibbs distributions across a ladder of temperatures. His proof gives gap bounds that grow like powers of the low target temperature, with exponents 11 and 12. The argument covers a broad class of cases beyond mixture models, using a state-space split and a Lyapunov function built from a perturbed potential.
arxiv-2604-04923: Curry and Speranzon give Signal Temporal Logic a new footing in stratification theory, treating each atomic predicate as a membership test in a layered space. Under that view, most temporal logic formulas induce a layering of space and time. The reading offers a fresh framework for studying the embedding spaces learned by deep reinforcement learning, linking them to the geometry of the decision space. It also lets researchers reuse high-dimensional analysis tools and design new computational methods, illustrated with Minigrid games.
arxiv-2604-05123: Le Boudec and Reid study lattices and their commensurator. Let Gamma be a finitely generated cocompact lattice of a disconnected group G. Let C be a subgroup of G that contains and commensurates Gamma. They describe finitely generated commensurated subgroups of C and show rigid results: they are inside Gamma. Here, they conclude that up to commensurability, Gamma is the endless finitely generated commensurated subgroup of C. For tree groups, this settles whether two other cocompact lattices share a commensurator.
arxiv-2604-05423: Roy Chowdhury and Raha model how species shift across broken landscapes as climate changes, replacing random spread with directed movement along environmental gradients. On a network of habitat patches, spread helps whole populations persist, while directed flow piles individuals into hotspots at well-connected nodes. Strong directed flow raises local extinction risk, and losing corridors strands species in poorer patches rather than wiping them out at once.
arxiv-2604-05523: Zheng and five colleagues benchmark language models as competing retailers in a simulated supply chain, bidding for scarce stock and setting prices and slogans. Testing 20 models reveals wide gaps and a winner-take-most pattern: few retailers steadily grow capital while most hover near break-even despite similar semantic scores. The benchmark logs full bid, price, and balance-sheet trails for economic study.
arxiv-2604-05723: Kiechl and four colleagues track a free chiral hexbug toy and test it against active Brownian circle swimmer theory. Mean-squared shift and scattering curves match well, with gaps kept to short-time spread behavior where straight-line noise rules. The study backs slow-drag Langevin models for hexbug motion when straight-line noise is tiny.
arxiv-2604-05823: Bojer and three colleagues pin down when cold groups of independent two-level atoms emit thermal light. For each correlation order they derive two rules on atom count and the coherent-to-incoherent emission ratio, as required by the Gaussian Moment Theorem. Checks for pure and mixed states clarify thermal light generation without atom-to-atom interactions.
arxiv-2604-05923: Zhou sets the UNDO Flip-Flop task, testing whether state space models can pull back past states on demand. Adding UNDO to flip-flop calls for a hidden bounded stack that restores past states when edits run out of order. One- and two-layer Mamba-2 models miss the stack trick, leaning on a toggle shortcut instead, with two-layer scores falling to 41.10 percent under hostile retraction tests, below random chance.
arxiv-2604-06123: Singh benchmarks four methods for estimating individual-level treatment effects in marketing, using nearly 14 million customer records from Criteo Uplift v2.1. The S-Learner, T-Learner, and X-Learner use LightGBM base learners, while Causal Forest comes from EconML. Judged by Qini score and cumulative gain, the S-Learner leads at 0.376, with its top 20 percent of ranked customers capturing about 78 percent of extra conversions. A driver analysis points to feature f8, and uncertainty analysis flags about 2 percent of customers as confident persuadables.
arxiv-2604-06423: Upadhyaya proves weak sequential convergence for the Chambolle-Pock method, also called the primal-dual hybrid gradient method. It is a standard first-order method for convex-concave saddle-point problems and for composite convex optimization. In real Hilbert spaces, its primal-dual iterates converge weakly for every extrapolation parameter up to one-half. The result needs a step-size bound linking the two step sizes, the operator norm, and the parameter. Weak-convergence theory now reaches a previously unexplored range of extrapolation parameters.
arxiv-2604-06523: Kyriacou and three colleagues train matrices themselves, skipping gates. Pure-state operations are unitary matrices; circuits embed data and settings as gates. Yet cost and low quality confine quantum learning to simulation. For few-qubit problems with large data sets, direct training wins. Their method keeps matrices unitary through regularization; alignment rebuilds a gate-based design from the soft-unitary. On five qubits with 1000 data points, two steps train a circuit in under four minutes, not over two hours. Loss falls. On cartpole, soft-unitaries beat a non-quantum baseline.
arxiv-2604-06723: Lin and four colleagues calibrate confidence for language models revising code. Developers lean on capable yet imperfect models, and calibrated confidence guides accept-or-reject calls. Global Platt-scaling of sequence-level scores works in many generative tasks but proves shaky for code revision, where correctness hinges on local edits and miscalibration varies by sample. Their fine-grained approach applies local Platt-scaling to three fine-grained scores. Across three tasks and 14 models, fine-grained scores cut calibration error across more intervals, with global scaling on top amplifying the gain.
arxiv-2604-06823: Yuan proves that sample correlation matrices from large fold tensor vectors follow the Marčenko-Pastur law. Sample vectors are k-fold tensor products of n-dimensional vectors with independent identically distributed entries, studied as n and k grow with k small relative to n. In that regime the limiting spectral distribution is the Marčenko-Pastur law. As a consequence, the Wishart matrix from k-fold tensor products of independent uniform unit vectors also follows the same law, extending the result to a second natural tensor family.
arxiv-2604-07023: Jin and three colleagues introduce MARS, teaching a model multi-token prediction. Autoregressive models generate one token at a time. Unlike speculative decoding, MARS needs only continued training on instruction data, adds no changes or extra parameters, and works like the original with no performance loss. At one token it matches or beats the baseline, and accepting multiple tokens keeps accuracy at one and a half times throughput. Block-level KV caching gives about 70 percent faster speed, and confidence thresholding adjusts speed under load without swapping models.
arxiv-2604-07123: Östling and Kurfalı test whether multilingual language models favour one tongue over another when facts clash. Models are known to fuse clashing facts with bias, but the authors ask if the tongue carrying each fact sways the choice. They stretch the conflicting needles test to five tongues with natural news data, across many multilingual models of varied size. All tested models mostly ignore the clash and firmly state just one answer, with a steady bias against Russian and, at the longest contexts, in favour of Chinese.
arxiv-2604-07323: Rubtsov and three colleagues bound convergence rates for asynchronous Q-learning with Polyak-Ruppert averaging in high dimensions. With a polynomial step size and a well-mixing Markov chain of state-action-next-state triples, they reach a rate near n to the minus one sixth times a log factor over hyper-rectangles. The proof builds a high-dimensional central limit theorem for martingale-difference sums, useful in its own right. They also bound high-order moments of the final iterate.
arxiv-2604-07723: Li and five colleagues segment images for any named category without training the model. Older methods tune score maps step by step to match ground truth. This team instead solves for the map directly from the mismatch between scores and truth. Their idea is that the mismatch stays consistent within one category but differs across categories. The method leads eight benchmarks with no iterative training and no model-specific attention tricks.
arxiv-2604-08123: Yang and 12 colleagues present LegoDiffusion, a micro-serving system for text-to-image workflows. Text-to-image generation runs a workflow of models centered on a base model. Current serving systems treat each workflow as a closed monolith, provisioning, placing, and scaling all part models, hiding internal flow, preventing model sharing, and forcing coarse-grained resource handling. LegoDiffusion splits a workflow into loosely coupled model nodes managed and scheduled apart. Open per-model inference handling unlocks cluster gains: per-model scaling, model sharing, and tuned model parallel scaling.
arxiv-2604-08223: Phillips shows finding a fixed point of a monotone function on the two-dimensional grid needs Omega of log n squared quantum queries, matching the classical deterministic upper bound. Tarski's theorem guarantees a fixed point for every monotone self-map of a complete lattice. The proof has two main parts: a lower bound for composed function classes including ordered search, and a very tight link between finding Tarski fixed points and nested ordered search.
arxiv-2604-08323: Herreman, Dhote, and Moisy study how thin bendable objects floating on travelling waves slowly turn toward a favored angle. Their wave theory, which leaves out scattering effects, predicts the turn from a mean twisting force raised by the wave. Soft, short, heavy floaters line up along the wave, while stiff, long, light ones lie across it, a rule that also bears on pontoons and inflatable structures.
arxiv-2604-08423: Thrush and seven colleagues build a reinforcement learning primitive, Dataset Policy Gradient, that tunes synthetic data generators toward any differentiable target metric. Exact data attribution through higher order gradients supplies the training signal, and the method closely tracks the true generator gradient. With only fine tuning on generated examples, they embed a QR code, the pattern 67, and other chosen traits into a target model, showing how strongly synthetic data can steer it.
arxiv-2604-08623: Piernot and Ying prove a central limit theorem for the Allen-Cahn reaction diffusion model with supercritical random initial data in three or more directions. Under diffusive rescaling the nonlinearity fades on large scales, and the rescaled solution converges to the heat equation driven by white noise. The limit's starting data depend on where the randomness comes from and on the model itself. The proof blends comparison principles with Malliavin calculus in a new way.
arxiv-2604-08723: Lee and eight colleagues ask what preference data teaches reasoning models in methods like DPO and KTO. They separate generator level delta, the skill gap between models producing chosen and rejected traces, from sample level delta, judged quality gaps within a pair. Raising generator delta lifts out of domain reasoning, while filtering by sample delta enables more data efficient training. Their recipe: raise generator delta when building pairs, exploit sample delta when picking examples.
arxiv-2604-09723: Shvets proves that each order-3 recurrence printed in a recent paper's appendix on pi formulas is a shifted summation lift of an explicit order-2 kernel. He identifies all three kernels: two pi-kernels rescaling sporadic Apéry-like sequences, including Domb numbers, and a Catalan kernel twisting a Gauss-square coefficient sequence. The kernels sit in a unified symmetric-square framework, with the Domb kernel recovered through a classical degree-3 Belyi pullback. A scan over 5,040 configurations yields 11 further integer sequences, proved integral and placed in the same framework.
arxiv-2604-09823: Poudel and three co-authors present a clash-fixing method for lining up agents pitching clashing actions over shared goods. Conflicts resolve through three modes: two-way talks, guided middle role, and rule-based fixing. The team defines rules for language-model client agents, including chain-of-thought-style thinking, and adds a looping weighted-accord engine needing no tuning from apps. The method is neutral and supports numeric and other choices. A power case shows it, with clashing apps for cost and toughness lining up diesel and battery units.
arxiv-2604-09923: Ding, Bent, and Wendell present GLEaN, a portrait-based method making text-to-image biases visible to the public. Existing bias audits target technical readers, leaving ordinary viewers unable to see skewed outputs. GLEaN generates images from identity prompts, aligns faces by landmarks, and blends median pixels into one portrait. Tested on Stable Diffusion XL, covering 40 social and occupational prompts, the composites reproduce known biases and link skin tone to predicted emotion. In a study of 291 people, portraits conveyed bias as well as data tables, in far less viewing time.
arxiv-2604-10123: Muller, Ortiz Barrañón, and Roberts grade dysarthria severity with no trained scorer or dysarthric training data. Their method measures decay in phonological subspaces of frozen HuBERT speech models. Feature directions come from healthy speech. For each speaker, phone embeddings yield d-prime scores along contrasts like nasality, voicing, stridency, sonorance, and manner, plus four vowel features in a 12-part profile. Across 890 speakers, 10 corpora, and 5 languages, consonant scores track clinical severity well. All 12 features separate controls from severe cases, and it applies to any language with a forced-alignment model.
arxiv-2604-10223: Chang and Chang build a low-power hardware accelerator for 3D Gaussian splatting that renders high-definition images. Compression combines Gaussian pruning and fine-tuning, harmonics reduction, and vector quantization, shrinking models about 52 times with small quality loss. Its frame pipeline merges culling and projection with tile sorting and rasterization, skips zero-Jacobian multiplications, and sorts tiles without comparisons. It delivers 1080p at 129 frames per second under a quarter watt. Against prior accelerators, it is six times smaller, six times faster, and seven and a half times more efficient.
arxiv-2604-10323: Pérez Castillo, Leyvraz, Gómez Quintanar, and Álvarez Ballesteros study spectra from one short Brownian path in a spring trap. With only one brief record, the usual long run averages and free frequency claims break down. They derive exact joint laws for finite time spectral estimates at many frequencies at once. Their form makes window driven links across frequencies plain and shows them fading as time grows. Computer trials back the theory and size the error from ignoring cross frequency links.
arxiv-2604-10423: Banihashem, Bateni, Esfandiari, Goudarzi, and Hajiaghayi settle how to rerun joint tasks repeatably. Replicable methods must agree across fresh data draws, yet joint solving cost was open. Naive math priced joint work far above single work, and privacy detours did no better. Their chain turns each method generalizing, composes by privacy style math, and maps back by shared draws. Joint cost lands near the sum of single costs, while adaptive joint work keeps a quadratic gap.
arxiv-2604-10823: Ehab and Hamdi present UGDA-Net, an uncertainty-guided dual attention network with entropy-weighted loss and deep supervision for seedling segmentation. Standard models struggle with messy backgrounds and fine leaves. Three parts make up the network. Uncertainty-guided dual attention uses channel variance to tune maps. An entropy-weighted loss is aimed at doubtful edge pixels. Deep checks cover middle encoder layers. Tests on a high-detail dataset of 432 seedling images show better accuracy. Dice gains run 9.3 percent above baseline for the network, and 13.2 percent above baseline for LinkNet.
arxiv-2604-11223: Amoukou and Brunel show that two popular local explanation methods, Local Shapley Values and LIME, can credit features that neither affect the model's output nor correlate with features that do. Even with exact computation and independent features, both violate this basic principle. Their fix, R-LOCO, splits the input space into regions of similar feature importance and applies global attribution within each region, giving more faithful local explanations without local instability.
arxiv-2604-11623: Mouzouni introduces Context Kubernetes, a design for running enterprise knowledge for agentic AI. The core analogy: delivering the right knowledge to the right agent with the right permissions and freshness resembles container orchestration. Six abstractions, a YAML manifest, a sync loop, and a three-tier permission model keep agent authority below human authority. Against four baselines, ACL filtering stops cross-domain leaks, intent routing cuts noise by 19 points, and only the three-tier model blocks all five tested attacks. TLA+ checking verifies safety across 4.6 million states with zero violations.
arxiv-2604-11723: Bekov and Nurgali propose one LLM-based multi-modal framework for platform- and course-level learner satisfaction in online education. Reviews, ratings, and behavioral logs offer rich signals, but short noisy context-bound many-sided reviews challenge good prediction. The framework fuses three sources: short-text topic distributions, context-aware feelings from pretrained Transformer models, and behavioral features from activity logs, within a hybrid fit design. Tests on large-scale MOOC review datasets from multiple public platforms show it always beats text-only models and shallow sentiment baselines.
arxiv-2604-12023: Yıldız, Önal, Krishnamurthy, and Akleman present Twisted Edges, a setup for making linked knots with labelled non-manifold meshes. Earlier methods limited twists to binary states, missing many shape moves. Opening twists to integer labels reveals that even twists on two-manifold nets preserve links, forming chainmail sheets with linked cycles. On meshes, set whole numbers prevent cycle merging, giving partial links and hinges for folding and bending. In theory, integer-twisted meshes match knotted sheets in 4D, placed as linked knot structures in 3D space.
arxiv-2604-12123: Ghimire and Gupta mine Stack Overflow across 186 languages, combining itemset mining, topic modelling, and community detection on a co-usage graph. It finds clusters such as shell/bash, Swift/Objective-C, and the C-family, with lift beyond popularity. It yields coder profiles, including Apple-platform, science/hardware, functional/academic, and two Unix scripting sub-types. It partitions the graph into web/enterprise, Apple ecosystem, and systems/science groups, with Java the highest-degree hub joining all three. All three methods converge on the structure, giving cross-method validation.
arxiv-2604-12323: Kumar and Bisht present a differentiable quantum-optical framework that learns optimal circuit settings for single-parameter phase estimation with adaptive NOON states. Starting from verified reproductions of earlier coincidence fringes, gradient descent tunes eight circuit parameters to maximize classical Fisher information across coincidence channels. Raw information gains grow with photon number, reaching 1,775 percent at five photons. The optimized probe reaches 82 percent of the Heisenberg limit at two photons and 58 percent at five, making sensing at three or more photons experimentally practical.
arxiv-2604-12523: Sandip Das and six colleagues track energy moving between wave modes in plasma turbulence. Linear spectral tools miss the nonlinear exchanges between modes. Density ripples in the IMPED device show Rayleigh-Taylor and Drift-Wave modes interacting. Two methods, Ritz and Kim, are tested on simulations and device data. Their validity hinges on data statistics, like kurtosis, and on spatial steadiness. Energy flows mainly from a Rayleigh-Taylor mode and a mixed mode into a low-frequency Drift-Wave mode. The methods thus quantify spectral energy transport between coherent modes.
arxiv-2604-12723: P. Brown and four colleagues hunt hydroacoustic signals from fireballs. Six test ban hydrophone stations listen for the signals. Thirty fireballs had paths to stations, including ones over 5 kilotons. Direct shock transmission through water is the likely source. One possible signal from September 2, 2003 off Alaska fits timing and direction. Given survey size and background rates, that detection is weak. No unambiguous detections emerged across 53 station-fireball pairs. Fireball detection in the SOFAR channel is very rare.
arxiv-2604-12923: Sravan Chittupalli and two colleagues predict dense 3D contact for every human object pair in one pass. Older methods handle one person or need object meshes besides the image. Pi-HOC spots instances, builds a token per pair, and refines tokens with InteractionFormer. A SAM decoder maps contact onto SMPL human meshes per pair. On MMHOI and DAMON, accuracy and localization beat the state of the art with 20 times higher throughput. Predicted contacts also sharpen image to mesh rebuilding and enable language query prediction with no extra training.
