Strength-aware alignment across levels preserves preference meaning while merging collaborative signals with the language model. On multiple real-world datasets OSA consistently beat existing baselines, with the clearest edge in pairwise preference evaluation, where the model must judge which of two items a user prefers.
arxiv-2605-10623:
Cameron Ibrahim and six colleagues treat hypergraph splitting as a spread problem for quantum tuning. Quantum tuning algorithms are by nature random, yet usually used to find one high-quality solution. Their 2026 paper studies splitting problems where the output itself is a probability distribution over splits. It is driven by maximin and minimax goals such as Fair Cut Cover.

The authors show these goals align well with the readout distribution from QAOA. A scheduling toy problem, the Greatest Expected Imbalance problem, aims to cut the worst mean imbalance across hyperedges. QAOA solvers hold spread-based solutions in quantum states, with squared objectives for standard and multi-goal QAOA. Tests on real and synthetic hypergraphs show low-depth multi-angle QAOA beating classical baselines on the proposed goals.
arxiv-2605-11223:
Maximilian Triebel, Marco Menner, and Dominik Helfenstein introduce VLATIM, a benchmark testing whether vision-language models can solve point-and-click puzzle games the way people reason through them. Existing benchmarks often overlook the physical reasoning these games demand, and VLATIM targets the divide between abstract logical reasoning and continuous action spaces that need precise mouse control.

The benchmark uses the classic physics puzzle game TIM and runs in five progressive parts, from basic visual grounding and domain understanding through multi-step manipulation to full puzzle solving. Results show a clear split between reasoning and execution: large proprietary models plan well but struggle with precise visual grounding. They still lack human-like problem-solving capability. Benchmark designers get a test that separates planning skill from execution skill.
arxiv-2605-11523: Song and colleagues present NAVIS, an on-SSD graph search system that cuts position-seeking overhead for search. On-disk graph search dominates databases, but updates must traverse the graph to find neighbours before linking. That cost grows through packed layouts coupling edge fetches to full vector loads, and through static entrance graphs drifting from inserted regions. NAVIS answers with vector reads and an entrance graph updated from concurrent traversals. It adds an edge-list cache. Insertion throughput rises up to 2 point 74 times and search throughput up to 1 point 37 times.
arxiv-2605-11623: Chokyi, Tawfik and Chattopadhyay test one geometric model for early and late cosmic acceleration in f(Q,L_m) gravity with holographic dark energy. They adopt a minimal polynomial, reconstructing late-time dynamics with it as a fluid. The result shows smooth acceleration and stable Hubble behaviour and a near-de Sitter equation of state. Bayesian analysis of Pantheon, chronometer and DESI BAO data leaves coupling weakly constrained and LambdaCDM-consistent. Early on, the quadratic term drives Starobinsky-like inflation matching Planck. Quantum-gravity corrections shift higher-order observables.
arxiv-2605-11723: Wang and thirteen colleagues present CaC, advancing video reward models via spatiotemporal concentrating. CaC first scans time to anchor anomalous windows, then grounds spatially, finally judging via chain-of-thought reasoning. The authors build the first large-scale video anomaly dataset with per-frame boxes and temporal windows. A three-stage paradigm first learns spatial and temporal anchoring, then optimizes via two-turn GRPO with IoU rewards. CaC improves anomaly accuracy by 25 point 7 percent and cuts video anomalies by 11 point 7 percent as a reward signal.
arxiv-2605-12423: Matousek reports COMPASS measurements that map quark motion in the nucleon. Hadrons made in deep inelastic scattering reveal how quarks move sideways and how their spins line up. That framework turns those patterns into maps of quark motion and spin, plus rules for how hadrons form. Hydrogen data from 2016 and 2017 should soon yield new momentum facts and may first reveal the Boer-Mulders effect in an unpolarised nucleon. Polarised deuteron data have already cut d-quark transversity errors by two and a half times at large momentum share.
arxiv-2605-12723: Roohi and Mahdavi show that the tangle in rarefied micro-nozzle flows is largely a lining-up effect. A density slope test identifies the squeeze layer station. A jump thickness defines a shock frame. In physical axes, the leading breakdown mode of centre line curves holds only eighty-three percent of swing energy. The jump frame lifts that figure to ninety-eight percent. A 2D shock window breakdown confirms the tightness is not a centre line fluke. In the lined-up frame, the first mode holds about ninety-five percent.
arxiv-2605-12823: Murdeshwar and four colleagues add curvature to coarse-grained potentials. Coarse-grained simulations reach timescales all-atom methods cannot, but force-matched potentials capture the gradient, leaving curvature out. Their framework adds Hessian-vector matching to force matching, adding curvature without building the full Hessian. They split the Hessian into a precomputed all-atom Hessian and a covariance correction. Hessian-vector matching lifts slow-mode accuracy above force matching for eight of nine proteins, and cuts bond error.
arxiv-2605-13023: Krznarić and López define a new notion of translations in the hyperbolic plane and solve the curve shortening flow equation there explicitly. They then treat ancient convex solutions, solving the flow when the curvature function separates by variables. Finally, they prove area estimates for closed ancient solutions of the flow, completing the trio of results.
arxiv-2605-13223: Eldesokey and colleagues argue that judging text to image models needs annotation matched to each skill. Uniform rating scales ignore how skills differ, so scores can mislead even as models converge. Skill aligned annotation gives steadier signals, higher agreement between raters, and more stable rankings across models. They also build an automated pipeline that applies the protocol at scale with spatially grounded feedback.
arxiv-2605-13523: M. Murabito and M. Stangalini explore how waves in the solar chromosphere shape coronal plasma composition, using high-detail spectropolarimetry. All models so far highlight wave action, notably the ponderomotive force linked to Alfvenic perturbations, as a key factor. Recent solar readings have tied wave signals to coronal regions with raised FIP bias, an excess of elements with low first ionisation potential. The present work tests Stokes V asymmetries as a diagnostic for wave action linked to fractionation, the process sorting them by ionisation traits.
arxiv-2605-13723: Ben Wilson and three colleagues argue the phrase human in the loop falsely implies safety for AI choice systems. Human oversight is a popular plan for concerns about bias, misinformation, manipulation and transparency, yet what watch means is rarely asked. The authors ask whether the loop image helps grasp of what is needed and done in a given choice context. Loose use of the image hides steps and results, feeding humanwashing, where writers use words mainly to present systems in the best light.
arxiv-2605-14323: Yu, Su and Abdullah study chaining sub-policies over time in Markov decision processes with changing rewards. Their General Dijkstra Search is proved to recover globally optimal goal-reaching policies by composing intermediate optimal sub-policies in time order. From its search-select-update principle they derive Dynamic Latent Routing, a post-training method claimed to match or beat supervised fine-tuning in low-data settings across four datasets and six models.
arxiv-2605-14423: Wang, Yang and Su study federated actor-critic training where agents share a common linear subspace representation but keep personalised local policy parts. Agents iteratively estimate the shared subspace, local critic heads, and local policies. Under single-timescale updates with Markovian sampling, finite-time convergence is proved via a joint linear approximation framework. Critic error and policy gradient norms are shown to converge to zero, with linear speedup in the number of agents despite heterogeneous trajectories.
arxiv-2605-14523: Mohtashim, Innan and Shafique pair quantum circuits with ordinary neural layers to read feelings from spoken voice. Their HQTN-SER design links speech features through a tensor network modelled on matrix product states, then blends quantum measurements with a learned classical embedding. Tested on three public emotion datasets, the system reached roughly 80 percent on RAVDESS, 78 on SAVEE and 74 on MDER, using few qubits.
arxiv-2605-14623: Sun, Khangulyan, Liu and Liu analyse seventeen years of Fermi-LAT data on the microquasar SS 433. They detect four gamma-ray sources in the region, including a newly identified source outside the W50 nebula and east and west excesses tied to the X-ray lobes. No significant periodicity is found for the previously reported source, and the two excesses show distinct spectra suggesting different physical origins.
arxiv-2605-14723: Wu and team introduce SepsisAgent, a world-model-augmented language-model agent for sepsis treatment in intensive care. Sepsis care needs step-by-step choices as patients change fast. A learned Clinical World Model simulates responses to trial fluid and vasopressor plans. The agent follows a propose-simulate-refine loop before prescribing. World-model access alone gives uneven results. Three-stage training covers dynamics, workflow cloning, and agentic reinforcement learning. On MIMIC-IV trajectories, it is claimed to beat older rivals with the best safety profile.
arxiv-2605-15023: The CMS Collaboration searches for new physics in events producing three massive gauge bosons, W or Z particles, in proton-proton collisions at 13 TeV. Selection targets the boosted regime where all three bosons carry transverse momentum above 200 GeV and standard model backgrounds are sparse. Hadronic decays appear as large-radius jets with two-quark substructure, tagged as V-jets. No excess over standard model expectations appears, so the team sets bounds on effective-field-theory Wilson coefficients.
arxiv-2605-15223: Nenad Petrovic and three others build a language-model workflow for mapping RISC-V supply chains. Heterogeneous, messy data is handled by language models for text and vision-language models for diagrams, tables, and scans. Extracted items and ties form a knowledge graph of parts and links. Model-driven engineering and constraint modeling then validate dependencies, spot chokes, and assess risk, with a human in the loop for querying and validation. RISC-V cases show usable, clear insights.
arxiv-2605-15323: Vincent Macri, Michael Jacobson, and Renate Scheidler improve Jacobian arithmetic in global function fields along the approach of Hess. One improvement cuts costly reduction steps by tuning for typical inputs rather than worst cases, given a degree-one place exists. The second trades memory for time by caching often used intermediates. Large-scale analysis and experiments show the methods run a lot faster than open rivals, and their public implementation is said to be the first aiding unique divisor-class representatives.
arxiv-2605-15523: Hongxi Li and eight colleagues propose a scene-text editing method that builds style and glyph prompts from the original image itself, without extra style or glyph encoders. A diffusion transformer first trains on large self-supervised data, then refines on a small set of paired images, using in-context learning to edit text in any vocabulary while preserving background style. Tests across languages show leading results on both text accuracy and style consistency.
arxiv-2605-15923: Chun-Peng Chang and four colleagues present Invaria, a point cloud encoder with scale-density invariance via next-resolution prediction and receptive fields. 3D encoders prove sensitive to sampling resolution and scale changes, since models overfit densities and scales rather than learning invariants. Next-resolution prediction teaches invariants, and the encoder gains during resolution shifts while staying efficient through size and fewer tokens. On ScanNet, Invaria scores 56.0 percent higher mIoU at 3 times lower resolution and 20 percent higher at 3 times smaller scale, with a 45 percent smaller model and 40 percent fewer tokens.
arxiv-2605-16023: Feldhus and twelve colleagues ask why the same language model grades answers differently when only the answer format changes. A one-to-five score and a true-or-false label can yield systematically different marks. Tracing five open models with edge attribution patching, they find a shared evaluator circuit in the middle-to-late layers. They argue a stable judgment signal is later bent by fragile format-specific branches.
arxiv-2605-16223: Deganutti and four colleagues provide a fully automated test framework for design animation video generation, a field with no standard benchmark. Design animation sets strict rules: set parts must move with set motion, direction, speed, and timing, while other regions stay stable and layout holds. Their framework spans four facets: layout fidelity, motion correctness, temporal quality, and content fidelity. It removes reliance on subjective human judgment and sets a common basis for tracking progress.
arxiv-2605-16423: Sun and Wu propose Nonlinear Bipolar Compensation, a post-training quantization approach that adds nonlinear fixes to reduce the effect of outliers. Current quantization methods suffer a speed-accuracy tradeoff and limited general use, while recent compensation methods add lightweight linear layers yet fail on outliers. They further design Bipolar Logarithmic Transformation, which maps the quantized input and its error into a new space where a simple linear layer applies compensation. Experiments across tasks, models, and quantization methods confirm its effectiveness, robustness, and generality.
arxiv-2605-16523: Ehatamm and three colleagues present Lean-QEC, a first-of-its-kind Lean 4 formalization of stabilizer codes. It delivers machine-checked distance certificates end to end. Certifying a code's distance bound is hard in general, so published distances often rest on unscalable hand proofs. Others rest on unverified solvers that leave a trust gap. A verified satisfiability encoding of the distance condition breaks that barrier. The pipeline produces Lean-checked proofs for industrially viable quantum low-density parity-check codes, reaching 144 qubits outside the Lean kernel.
arxiv-2605-16723: Cunha's team studies colloidal rods under shear, where flow is often assumed to screen hydrodynamic interactions between rods. Using particle simulations and scaling analysis, they find that assumption breaks down at shear rates and concentrations common in experiments. That coupling among neighbors drives a cascade of tumbling events. The collective motion disrupts flow alignment and sharply raises viscosity and normal stress differences, matching recent lab work. Current models for colloidal rods, they argue, need revision.
arxiv-2605-17923: Yucheng Guo and eight colleagues propose AdaptiveLoad, a framework for training large video diffusion models faster. Mixed-mode datasets vary wildly in sequence length, and equal-token batching ignores the quadratic cost of self-attention, causing load imbalance and idle GPUs. AdaptiveLoad pairs a dual-constraint load balancer, capping memory and compute together, with a fused LayerNorm-Modulate CUDA kernel. On the Wan 2.1 world model, imbalance falls from 39% to 18.9%, peak VRAM use rises 22.7%, and throughput grows 27.2%.
arxiv-2605-18423: Jonathan Diller and sixteen co-authors present REBAR, a 2026 quantitative benchmark for the ethical and legal compliance of autonomous systems. Current embodied-AI ethics work stays mostly qualitative, and guardrails often block unsafe behavior without giving users an override or a reason. REBAR maps operating metrics into a computable Autonomy Readiness Level rubric, using a neuro-symbolic language-model approach to score scenario difficulty and generate tests at scale.
arxiv-2605-18623: Josia John and two co-authors ask how few labeled points can stand for a whole graph. Given n nodes and a budget of k picks, their method picks the k points whose labels best forecast the rest. It gives the first log to the three halves guarantee under the usual budget rule. Older routes either spent far more labeled points than the budget allowed or gave rules of thumb with no proof. Lighter versions handle bigger graphs than older tools could, with quality left all but intact.
arxiv-2605-19023: Ofer Biham, Gilad Hertzberg Rabinovich, and Eytan Katzav analyse first stopping times in a simple one-dimensional traffic model. Each car moves right only when the next cell is empty. The model matches cellular automaton rule 184. It shifts from free flow to congestion when car density passes one half. Using first-passage methods, they derive exact formulas for a car's first stop. They also give its chance of being stopped at a given time, and, at low density, its final stop before free motion.
arxiv-2605-19123: Victor Kebande offers a stringology-based fingerprinting method to probe the build of cryptographic sequences, which are made to look random. Tests check stats but cannot tell whether build traits leak facts about the source. His method reads cipher outputs as symbol strings and pulls pattern traits such as substring counts, repeat patterns, and entropy traits, rolling them into fingerprint vectors per source. Tests on cipher-made and purely random sequences show clear build marks across sources, though the author stresses these marks do not imply cryptographic flaws.
arxiv-2605-19223: Mengqi Shi and Haopeng Zhang introduce HAVEN, a benchmark for unified video understanding built on layered alignment. Past summarization tests split supervision across keyframes, key shots, or disjoint text notes, missing the layered structure of cross-modal alignment. HAVEN pairs video and text at frame, shot, and whole-video levels, with continuous links between modes. Its test suite covers summarization, temporal reasoning, grounding across modes, and saliency ranking. Tests of leading models expose a gap between fluent text and grounded understanding, and the dataset, suite, and protocols are public.
arxiv-2605-19823: Dang, Schmidt and Hesser propose Cut-DeepONet, a neural operator that handles discontinuities and sharp transitions by cutting the domain into smooth pieces. Instead of approximating jumps within continuous function spaces, their lifting strategy partitions the domain and treats discontinuities as boundaries in a higher-dimensional space. A second network predicts input-dependent discontinuity locations for unseen inputs, guiding the operator to build smooth components per region. Benchmark tests beat leading methods even on low-resolution data, with fewer parameters, showing representation change beats added model size.
arxiv-2605-20023: Samuel Jacob Chacko and three co-workers re-analyse a controlled study of a tool-using capture-the-flag agent to ask when procedural skill packs actually help. In offensive cybersecurity, where such packs are thin, the no-skill to full-skill gap is small and statistically weak. They argue the missing factor is feedback bandwidth: when tools return strict, schema-checked, fast observations, the environment itself supplies the correction skills normally provide. In some settings, such as a timing side channel, added skills even degrade performance.
arxiv-2605-20223: Jung Min Lee and three co-workers explain latent action failures on wild videos. Latent action models learn action codes from video by compressing frame changes, but wild frames also carry outside state such as clutter, adding changes unrelated to actions. A linear model covering outside state shows the rebuild goal makes latent actions encode outside facts from future frames. Learning in a space focused on own parts curbs the noise, and helper goals such as action supervision keep latent actions steady across states.
arxiv-2605-20423: Srishty and four co-workers target nested belief conflicts in language-model Theory of Mind. Standard benchmarks miss recursive beliefs and information gaps, so their OSCToM method builds observer-self conflicts with reinforcement learning, a domain language and surrogate models. Their OSCToM-8B model leads the systems tested and hits 76 percent on the information-asymmetric FANToM set, against 0.2 percent for ExploreToM. Data synthesis runs 6 times more efficiently, aiding smaller models on advanced social reasoning.
arxiv-2605-20623: Chenyang An and Xiaoqian Xu prove explicit lower bounds for advection-diffusion equations in three settings. They give a polynomial bound for inviscid shears, a uniform positive bound on mixing size for diffusive shears, and an exponential limit for rapidly oscillating time-regular flows. All constants are clear in the data. Strikingly, the proofs were generated entirely by QED, a multi-agent maths proving system, with no expert human intervention, as a test of AI rigour.
arxiv-2605-20823: Minh Anh Nguyen and four colleagues present RelWitness, a design for open-vocabulary 3D scene graph generation under incomplete link supervision. The central difficulty is not word-list size but trust in labels, since many valid object-pair links go unannotated in 3D datasets. Their key concept is a link witness, a concrete visual-geometric cue that creates a link visible in the captured scene. Support needs contact and up-down order, containment needs enclosure, proximity needs metric closeness, and orientation needs facing use.
arxiv-2605-20923: Benedikt Bollig studies runtime monitoring for distributed language-model-agent workflows using causal past logic. In asynchronous execution, a decision can only rest on events causally visible to the lifeline making it. An event earlier in some log may still be hidden locally. He extends the ZipperGen agent-workflow design with Causal Past Logic, adapting past-time logic to guards in if-blocks and while loops. A guard can read the latest causally visible event of other lifeline and chosen variables stored there.
arxiv-2605-21123: Kesong Li and colleagues extend direct preference optimization, a tool for aligning language models, to text-to-image generation. Past work covers only diffusion models and mismatches a discrete objective with regression-based generation. Their generalized objective spans both diffusion and flow-matching models through a shared reverse-time framework. Linear-DPO swaps a steep sigmoid utility for a steady linear one, and tests on SD1.5, SDXL, and SD3-Medium beat prior baselines.
arxiv-2605-21223: Simon His and colleagues study harmonics from an atom in a messy scattering setting. They run one-dimensional simulations, viewed as an open quantum system. Elastic scattering blurs the electron wavepacket in a local way, and that local blur drives a global loss of coherence. The electron density then settles near unstable periodic orbits of the classical twin system. This live pattern mirrors quantum scars in billiards, but it shows up in real-time motion from the ground state.
arxiv-2605-21423: Raul Liquito and co-authors study temperature-induced optical enhancement near a localization transition in quasiperiodic systems. Such systems sit between regular crystals and messy systems, famously showing metal-insulator shifts even in one dimension. In the Aubry-André model, the optical gap closes in a jump as the system approaches the transition. Thermal activation of Pauli-blocked transitions strongly boosts low-frequency conductivity at certain key rates. The work is a theory study of a model system, not a lab test of a real crystal.
arxiv-2605-21623: Itamar Trainin, Renana Keydar, and Amit Pinchevski present a scalable method for oral history archive contrast, examining the shape of accounts. Scholars in Holocaust studies often mark two styles of oral survivor accounts. USC Shoah Archive talks tend to follow a set, host-guided format, whereas Yale Fortunoff Video Archive mostly leans to a free-form, open-ended style. They closely examine that claim via large-scale data study of more than one thousand six hundred accounts from both sets. Shape is measured through topic flow and host-witness shifts.
arxiv-2605-21723: Riwa Karam and colleagues treat robots as transferable resources shared between teams with different capabilities. They use Hamilton's rule from ecology to decide when helping another team pays off. The resulting assignment problem is combinatorial and NP-hard. To keep it scalable, they train a graph neural network policy, centrally trained but executed locally, to approximate the altruistic allocations. In fire-fighting tests, the learned policy reached the fire-stopping threshold in all five physical trials with fifteen robots, against two for fixed teams.
arxiv-2605-21823: Mohsen Fathi studies the maximal extension of the Schwarzschild-like black hole solution in Lorentz gauge theory. He analyzes radial null curves in Schwarzschild-Droste and ingoing Eddington-Finkelstein charts, then builds the fitted Kruskal-Szekeres chart. The extension holds two exterior regions plus black-hole and white-hole regions, with Carter-Penrose compactifications. The conformal skeleton stays Schwarzschild-like, but horizon scale, surface gravity, and radius curves remain set by a constant. The solution shares Schwarzschild's causal topology while staying geometrically distinct when that constant differs from one.
arxiv-2605-22223: Maxime Meyer and co-authors ask how many different outputs a transformer can generate, predicting the count from a handful of design characteristics. They give an upper bound depending on prompt length, empirically tight within a factor under 10 across architectures and sizes. Maximal output sequence length grows linearly with prompt length, while beyond a critical threshold the output proportion decays exponentially. The linear coefficient itself admits a theoretical upper bound. The analysis also explains observed transformer failures on copying and cramming, even with unbounded context and compute.
arxiv-2605-22423: Ji and colleagues propose a unified framework that inverts motion degradation and re-enacts moments. Blur in global shutter images and rolling shutter distortion were long treated as separate problems. Their dual-shutter setup captures synchronised blur and rolling shutter pairs, resolving temporal and spatial ambiguities in both modes. A stereo variant with a narrow baseline offers flexible performance-cost trade-offs. A triaxial system collects real aligned pairs plus high-speed frames for training. Tests validate the approach for realistic high-speed video reconstruction under complex motion.
arxiv-2605-22823: Lee and five colleagues diagnose directional motion blindness in video language models, the failure to tell whether a lone object moved left, right, up, or down. Most models scored near chance, and tracing the signal showed direction stayed readable inside the network but failed to bind to the correct spoken answer. Their DeltaDirect objective, which predicts motion vectors from adjacent-frame feature changes, lifted synthetic accuracy from about 26 percent to about 86 percent.
arxiv-2605-23023: He and three coauthors formalize human-LLM co-planning along three axes: mode, scope, and level of edits. In orchestrated multi-agent systems, people struggle to manage plans they cannot see into, and current tools supervise only final outputs. Their prototype AMBIPOM supports process-level supervision through semantic and structural interactions. A user study reveals mixed workflows and effort-control-risk trade-offs. A controlled benchmark shows how language models adjust plans under varying scope and revision strategies. Code and data are released.
arxiv-2605-23223: Nguyen and three coauthors analyze data upload efficiency for a vehicular-to-road system using 60-GHz mmWave ultra-spots. The wireless zone is critically narrow, so vehicles can easily miss it without an autonomous guiding system, and route, speed, approach angle, and distance to the ultra-spot all affect transfer. Based on 75 experimental cases, they identify the optimal travel trajectory and conditions for passing through the ultra-spot. With an optimal trajectory, suitable speed, antenna placement, and early estimation of the ultra-spot area, transferred data improves by 6 to 8 times.
arxiv-2605-23723: Tan and colleagues propose MemAudit, a post-hoc memory audit tool for aided agents. Agent memory stores interactions, but users can inject harmful records through normal chat, later recalled to steer actions. Current guards focus online, but ignore which memories caused harm. MemAudit mixes two signals: a what-if influence score for each record's contribution to harmful outputs, and a consistency graph spotting odd records. Tested against MINJA, a query-only attack, MemAudit cuts attack success: QA success falls from 70 to 0 percent, while RAP success drops from 83.3 to 0 percent.
arxiv-2605-23823: Zastudil and colleagues survey computing students on collaborative active learning, a class style built on teamwork and social talk. The survey covers 24 neurodivergent students, autistic students or students with ADHD, and 20 neurotypical students, plus four interviews. Results show team dynamics and assignment structure affect neurodivergent students' comfort in class. Neurodivergent students report discomfort with vague assignments, and prefer smaller teams that work together often with defined roles. The authors conclude teachers can design collaborative active learning to be more fair and open to neurodivergent students.
arxiv-2605-23923: Delgado and Umaña build a fast Fourier transform for SU(2), the group of symmetries behind quantum spin and spherical signals. They discretize the group with Euler angles, run a two-dimensional transform over the angular variables, and exploit recursive properties of Jacobi polynomials to split the work in the Cooley-Tukey style. Their complexity analysis shows the method beats direct computation by a wide margin. The algorithm offers a base tool for spectral work on curved manifolds and quantum systems, where ordinary flat-space transforms fall short.
arxiv-2605-24023: Schneider and Maier replace the binary Tuy completeness test for cone-beam CT with a graded, differentiable score of near-orthogonality and coverage. They prove the selection problems NP-complete by reduction from Set Cover, motivating a greedy algorithm with a proven approximation guarantee and a mixed-integer program certifying bounds. Across six regions, varied budgets, and four occlusion settings, the median greedy-to-program ratio hit 0.998, with many cases certified optimal. They add Effective Spatial Resolution, a diagnostic mapping sampling gaps to feature sizes, which tracks reconstruction quality.
arxiv-2605-24123: Lei, Shi, Cao, and Zhao rethink heritability, the share of variation tied to genes, through a counterfactual lens. Older notions lean on strong assumptions and no explicit causal model. The authors define heritability by the potential-outcomes model: compare a person with a hypothetical non-identical twin raised in the same environment, and average the gap. They give bounds on this measure that observational data can in principle pin down. Set beside standard population, twin, sibling, and plant-breeding notions, it shows how causal assumptions change what heritability means.
arxiv-2605-24323: Shentu proves an Arakelov-type inequality for a map from a pair with mild singularities to a smooth projective base. The pair has simple normal crossing semi-log canonical form, and the base is smooth and projective. From this, the paper caps Iitaka volumes for algebraic fiber spaces whose generic fiber has a good minimal model. The inequality ties the geometry of the total pair to the base, giving a numerical control on fiber spaces built from well-behaved fibers.
arxiv-2605-24423: Jing and ten co-authors introduce ICRL4AHT, a benchmark for in-context reinforcement learning in teamwork. In-context reinforcement learning lets agents adapt to new tasks, but its teamwork value with unknown partners was unexplored. The benchmark offers a teammate suite plus a pipeline for teammate generation, history collection, and online evaluation. Tests of history-conditioned methods including Algorithm Distillation and Decision-Pretrained Transformer reveal limits. Unlike in single-agent domains, the baselines fail to adapt at test time, often trailing random baselines on unseen teammates and layouts.
arxiv-2605-24523: Zexuan Chen and colleagues present MindAlign, a 2026 system decoding seen images from brain waves by aligning EEG, visual, and text in one space. It first pre-trains an EEG encoder by masked reconstruction, then aligns EEG, image, and model-written text through contrastive learning. On the Things-EEG2 200-way zero-shot test, it reached 54.1 percent Top-1 and 83.4 percent Top-5 accuracy, far above the prior baseline. It also generalized to MEG data, with decoding patterns matching known visual brain physiology.
arxiv-2605-24823: Yilei Zhang argues manufacturing is entering a fifth paradigm, Agent Manufacturing, where foundation-model agents think and decide. Four earlier paradigms moved physical and routine work off human shoulders, yet one layer stayed human, spanning interpretive, allocative, diagnostic, negotiative, and governance work. The author claims foundation-model agents now mainly shift this layer away from humans. A system counts as Agent Manufacturing when foundation-model agents coordinate. They read open-ended goals, plan over long spans, and deal with other agents and humans.
arxiv-2605-25323: David Gillman and Dana Randall show local Markov chains mix exponentially slowly in spin glasses. In the ferromagnetic Ising model on a grid with mixed signs, an energy argument forces slow mixing below a critical temperature. Spin glasses generalize that model with couplings, and a face is frustrated when an odd number of its edges pull ferromagnetically. For glasses with four well-separated frustrated faces symmetric, the pair proves slow mixing throughout the class. A temperature threshold follows from a tiny free-energy bottleneck balancing entropy against energy.
arxiv-2605-25923: Zhong and colleagues present a framework finding and fixing errors in packer tools. Unpackers serve as executable semantic contracts, checking predictions without labeled ground truth. A pipeline cleans outputs, pinpoints faulty logic, and fixes errors with signatures and predicates. Family recall averages only about 45 percent, packedness recall near 64 percent. Two-stage repairs lift family recall by about 100 percent, packedness to 99 percent. Fixes lift precision by about 14 points.
arxiv-2605-26123: Reddy and Raha forecast marine engine data with adaptive-window multi-particle stochastic differential equations. A vessel's safety hinges on its drive systems, which face varied loads and harsh surroundings. Classic vector autoregressive models assume fixed windows and straight-line behaviour, missing randomness and sudden shifts. The authors build a two-layer estimator. An adaptive lookback resizes the learning window with instant drift size, keeping the model alert in shifting regimes. A second layer tracks random evolution, handling fast volatility and curved transitions in engine data.
arxiv-2605-26323: Cheng-Wei Ching and five colleagues present Totoro+, a scalable federated learning system for many simultaneous edge applications. It replaces one central parameter server with a peer-to-peer design based on distributed hash tables, giving each application its own server. Any edge node can serve as coordinator, aggregator, client selector, or worker, in any combination. Real-world tests on five hundred Amazon EC2 servers show graceful scaling, speedups from one point two to fourteen times, and logarithmic hops for model sharing.
arxiv-2605-26823: Long and three colleagues build TabKG, a tool for making synthetic supply chain tables that follow business rules, not just stats. A graph of column links, drafted by several models voting together and checked against real data, spells out orderings, links, and rules. Free columns are made by latent diffusion, while linked columns are rebuilt by rule from the graph, so the tables stay consistent by design. The result aids simulation and planning with records that stay true to how supply chains work.
arxiv-2605-27223: The LIGO Scientific, Virgo, and KAGRA collaborations present version 5 of the full gravitational wave transient catalog. The update adds new observations through January 28, 2025 and pushes the count of merging black hole and neutron star systems past 300. Partner papers also lay out the methods used, the event summaries, and the population measurements.
arxiv-2605-27323: Rafael Padilla, Kyle Webster, and Austin Kim compare two GPU path tracing designs: the megakernel approach and the wavefront approach. The wavefront design, which keeps state between specialized kernel calls, runs about 16 percent faster in their tests. Tracing data point to better cache locality, though no unit reaches peak throughput, so memory delay and synchronization still limit speed.
arxiv-2605-27423: Salman Sajad Wani and Saif Al-Kuwari set speed limits for quantum sensors when calibration is uncertain. They project out nuisance parameters on a quotient manifold using quantum Fisher information, deriving bounds for general Markovian evolution. Applied to Jaynes-Cummings sensors, the framework yields detuning tolerances and speed limits from field-dependent Purcell loss.
arxiv-2605-27723: Mustafa Gundogan, Arash Ahmadi, and Markus Krutzik propose a velocity sensor using squeezed vacuum and a coherent probe in a two-memory Mach-Zehnder interferometer. One memory stays fixed as reference while the other moves during storage, mapping velocity onto a differential phase at readout. Squeezed light beats equal-resource coherent homodyne within a window set by transmission and phase stability, keeping a small advantage at realistic loss.
arxiv-2605-27923: Sudip Vhaduri, Ryan Gammon, and Sayanton Dibbo ask whether quantum machine learning earns its keep for reading handwritten digits. Quantum support-vector machines beat plain ones on correct answers at higher cost, while quantum neural networks matched plain networks yet needed fewer parameters. Quantum leads grew as the number of features or samples rose.
arxiv-2605-28023: Lu and colleagues improve visual captioning rewards by pairing each reference caption with the image itself as judge. Their VCap reward checks factual consistency between reference and generated captions against visual evidence, reaching precise verification even from flawed references. An eight-billion-parameter model trained this way beat leading open and closed captioning systems.
arxiv-2605-28623: Elie Vandoolaeghe and ten colleagues present photon correlation microscopy, probing quantum matter through correlations in emitted light. They confine 1D dipolar excitons at a MoSe2-WSe2 junction with gate-defined traps. Power-tuned spectra show a shift from a soft phase to a rigid phase, marked by flat glow brightness and energy blueshift. Across this shift, light patterns evolve from bunching at low density to antibunching at high density, a many-body blockade driven by joint dipolar push.
arxiv-2605-28823: Mohamed Abdelwahab and seven colleagues take first steps toward probes detecting abstract concepts inside LLM embeddings, revealing model thinking. Such probes should be easy to apply to any model, so many concepts can be monitored during operation. The work defines three key tasks: delineating a concept, training and testing linear probes, and tracking concepts. Delineation builds a set with the concept present then absent. Probing detects the concept on any layer, exploring probe complexity. Finally they show such probes can track concepts across contexts, on four concepts and three models.
arxiv-2605-28923: P. S. Bhupal Dev and colleagues trace a massless neutrino to a minimal dark SU(2) gauge symmetry. Charging one right-handed-neutrino-like Weyl fermion under the dark symmetry blocks its Standard Model Yukawa coupling, forcing a rank-two Dirac mass matrix with one exactly massless neutrino. Anomaly cancellation then demands a second dark doublet, and a discrete symmetry forbidding Majorana masses lets the pair form a vectorlike set. That completion yields a secluded confining dark sector with a dark-matter candidate.
arxiv-2605-29023: Valtýr Daníelsson and Helgi Sigurðsson study wave transport in the Hat monotile, a tiling at the boundary of ordered and disordered systems. Using optical lattices for cavity polaritons, they confirm localized and critical states in the Monotile by solving the Schrödinger equation. Scaling of wave moments reveals super-diffusive and near sub-diffusive transport tied to the fractal shape of the Monotile Hilbert space. They propose checking the findings with driven polariton fluids.
arxiv-2605-29123: Dueun Kim and Albert No name the confidence shortcut, a reasoning failure mode of masked diffusion models. Chain-of-thought helps autoregressive models lay out steps aiding guesses, but masked diffusion decoding favors high-confidence tokens, which need not follow needed order. In multi-digit sums, models predict higher-order digits without tracking carries through long chains. Controlled pretraining on tasks shows trust-led order often picks poor sequences, and backing that habit can sharply raise addition errors. The authors warn against trusting confidence alone.
arxiv-2605-29223: Ivica Nikolic proposes a black-box method inferring lower bounds on model size from generated text. Parameter counts of models are withheld, leaving size largely undisclosed. The method rests on popular texts present in every pretraining corpus. Next-word prediction accuracy across fragments signals memorization, which total parameter count limits. That signal becomes one profile per model, feeding a pairwise larger test and a scaling estimator mapping an index to a count. Validated on open models, it recovers closed hierarchies and reveals strategies, some growing fast, others capped.
arxiv-2605-29323: Eric Wang establishes a generalization of the Backward Ergodic Theorem of Anush Tserunyan and Jenna Zomback. He drops the countable-to-one requirement, giving such a theorem for any measure-preserving transformation. The new setting introduces measurability concerns, since unlike the countable-to-one case, there is no longer a collection of Borel right inverses. Instead, the proof leans on Jankov-von Neumann uniformization plus field structures from Vaes and Wouters.
arxiv-2605-29523: Eunbyeol Cho and five colleagues present K-FinHallu, a benchmark for hallucinations in multi-turn Korean finance chat. Current tests mostly cover single English chats, missing back-and-forth flow in Korean finance. The team builds chats from genuine Korean financial texts and plants hallucinations under a taxonomy based on whether the context can answer, with justified refusals allowed. Even top models fail fine-grained financial checks and refusal conduct. Tuning an eight-billion model rivals frontier systems, with justified refusal still weakest.
arxiv-2605-30023: Nicolás T. Kurtovic and 17 colleagues survey 15 years of ALMA observations on planet-forming disks, drawing on archive data for nearly four thousand sky positions. They sort the observations by sky location, frequency range, exposure time, spectral coverage and sharpness, with attention to disks in nearby star-forming regions. The paper serves as a map of what the archive already holds. Its authors invite researchers to pose fresh questions that these existing data can now answer.
arxiv-2605-30123: Anthony Ayli and three colleagues propose a privacy-enhanced federated learning protocol for encrypted aggregation over wireless channels. Single-key encryption lets curious clients read the shared key; multi-key schemes give each device its own key. Their four-phase protocol retransmits keys and ciphertexts through one channel, so large-modulus terms cancel at decryption. With zero-order learning, each device sends one encrypted scalar per round, with overhead independent of model size. Residual noise preserves the standard convergence rate, and tests on MNIST and CIFAR-10 confirm the analysis.
arxiv-2605-30723: Yu and colleagues show skill value for agents is model-dependent: a skill helping one backbone can harm another. Existing skill sets are treated as model-agnostic, reusing formulations across backbones. Their MASA framework adapts skills to each backbone without modifying weights. A evolution pipeline rewrites skills through hill climbing and tree search, guided by feedback and profiles. A lightweight rewriter trained on trajectories reproduces adaptation in a forward pass. In three environments and four backbones, MASA performs best, with gains up to 25.8 points over the baseline.
arxiv-2605-31123: Crowe, Hasan and Wackeroth compute full quantum-electrodynamics corrections to elastic lepton-proton scattering at next-to-leading order. Electron and muon scattering probe the proton's charge and magnetisation layout, and comparing them tests whether leptons behave alike. The simple one-photon picture falls short, so the team includes loop-momentum-dependent form factors and gives special weight to two-photon-exchange diagrams, which depend on proton structure. Results are compared with existing predictions and scattering data.
arxiv-2605-31423: Liu, Andoni, and Hsu describe universal transformers. These are fixed models that can mimic any transformer in a given class, once fed a suitable input embedding. Like a universal Turing machine, the embedding carries a sketch of the target model, while all inner weights stay fixed. The authors give sparse builds that work when the embedding is wide enough. They also show that randomly started models are universal almost surely, and they test the idea on bracket balancing and multi-hop reasoning.
arxiv-2605-31523: Messamah and colleagues refresh the PlanetS catalogue of transiting exoplanets, hunting bound stellar companions with Gaia data release 3, plus a matched control sample of single hosts. Their sample holds 860 transiting exoplanets, 133 of them S-type. They find a binary fraction of 19.4 percent against the control. In the giant-planet regime, giant planets with companions tend to be heavier, orbit closer, and look more inflated, and 53 percent of giants around M-dwarfs sit in binaries closer than 1000 AU.
arxiv-2606-00423:
de Araújo and co-authors read both the air path and the sent signs for a fluid-antenna base. Smart walls, called RIS, bend waves to aid up-link users. Fluid antennas pick one port from many at the base post. Path and sign reads must then be done as one joint task.

Their plan, NTFAS, varies port picks and user codes block by block. The sent sign grid stays shared across all views. That form gives linked block models with shared path and data parts. A two-stage half-blind loop reads the joined path and the signs. It then splits the wall's two path legs by their block form. Sims beat a kin tool on path marks and rate, with like bit marks.
arxiv-2606-00523:
Tong and co-authors teach stream-fed chat models when to speak, not just what to say. Stock models read all, then write, which wastes time and math. Stream tools write as text comes in, yet lack a when rule. Past when rules lean on hard code or dear teach marks.

Their tool, ProactiveLLM, reads the model's own states for that call. Two train tricks build a sense of when a chunk says enough. Mask drills fake the slow bare of a stream in class. A twin drill lines the part view with a full view from the same model. No outside teacher or hand tag is a must. Plug-in heads then make the call in live use. Tests in text and speech streams cut lag with no loss.
arxiv-2606-01023:
Erkinov lays out a plan to gather training data for quality control AI in carpet mills in this 2026 paper. Human inspection still rules woven and tufted carpet lines. It is slow, subjective, and uneven at modern loom speeds and widths. His design is for an in line vision system with two jobs.

The system must inspect the moving carpet web in real time. It must also collect and label defect images in a steady, planned way. Over the plant's life, that stream trains stronger quality models. Line scan cameras, synced and lit by bright field and grazing light, form the imaging core. He derives the resolution and throughput needed to catch fine structural flaws across a multi metre web. A carpet specific defect taxonomy guides the labels. Training starts with anomaly detection on clean stock, in the style of the MVTec benchmark.
arxiv-2606-01223:
Lin and co-authors build a test for reflective memory in dialogue. Long chats ask models to join scattered cues over time. Past tests check recall of plain facts only. RefMem-Bench holds 26,000 graded question pairs. It spans eight reflective skills and three task forms. Models must infer latent sense from cues spread through a chat. Surface search alone will not pass it.

The team also gives REMIND, a staged aid. It finds proof tied to the question first. Then it grounds key cues and adds level-based training. A staged alignment step moves that skill into fact-based paths. Tests show the bench is hard for current models. REMIND lifts both answer scores and memory recall.
arxiv-2606-01323:
Long, Gan, and Zhou unify aspect-based sentiment analysis with diffusion. The field holds seven subtasks on distinct extracted elements. Unified generative tools build answers token by token. That style blurs the edges of multi-word terms. Aspect and opinion spans lose their sharp boundaries. DiffuSent treats each subtask as boundary denoising instead. Noisy span edges get refined step by step.

A contrastive denoising strategy handles near-duplicate outputs. Diffusion can spawn many subtle variants of one answer. Tests span 28 settings, from seven subtasks on four datasets. DiffuSent beats top generative and span-based systems throughout. Gains peak on multi-word triplets, at plus 2 point 48 F1. Inference runs up to 181 times faster than autoregressive rivals.
arxiv-2606-01423:
The CMS Collaboration searches for a new heavy quark in proton collisions. The target is a vector-like B prime quark. It would decay to a top quark and a W boson. The search uses the single-lepton final state. A muon or electron comes from one of the decays. The other particle decays into hadrons instead. Data come from the CMS experiment at the LHC.

Collisions ran at 13 TeV from 2016 to 2018. The dataset totals 138 inverse femtobarns. A neural network tagger identifies the large-radius jet. Backgrounds are modeled from data with a flow network. No signal appears, so limits are set. Singlet B prime quarks from 0 point 8 to 1 point 23 TeV are excluded.
arxiv-2606-01623:
Maydanyuk and co-authors compute photon emission in tin-on-tin scattering. Bremsstrahlung photons arise when heavy ions collide. They study 124Sn plus 124Sn at 25 MeV per nucleon. Quantum-mechanical calculations reproduce the measured photon spectrum. The match holds over the full energy range. For the first time, the incoherent-to-coherent ratio is quantified. It is extremely small, from ten to the minus eleven to ten to the minus four.

Coherent emission dominates throughout the measured range. Proton-nucleus scattering shows the opposite pattern. There incoherent emission dominates via nucleon magnetic moments. The ratio explains the difference between the two spectra in one picture. One spectrum humps, the other falls monotonically. A new quantum regime of emission is identified.
arxiv-2606-02023:
Kabaya studies two families of quandles tied to Coxeter quandles. Quandles are algebraic structures with a binary operation. One family comes from Andruskiewitsch and Graña. It is the set of roots with an operation. Negatives of reflections define that operation there.

Kabaya observes it is a conjugation quandle in a Pin group. The second family is called rotational D_n quandle. It holds certain right angle rotations in the D_n Coxeter group. Conjugation gives its binary operation as well. Inner automorphism groups are determined for both families. The two groups turn out quite similar. The work links quandle theory to reflection groups. Pin group structure underlies the first construction.
arxiv-2606-02123:
Takeyama and Tsuruta apply a q-analogue formula for multiple harmonic sums. Maesaka, Seki, and Watanabe proved a formula for such sums. Yamamoto generalized it to Schur-type harmonic sums. The second author later proved a q-analogue of that generalization. This work gives two applications of the q-analogue.

The first application reproves a duality result. It concerns q-analogues of multiple zeta values. The new proof offers an alternative route to duality. The second application proves an identity of a different kind. It concerns a q-analogue of the Kawashima function. Both results flow from one master formula. Number theorists working on zeta values are the audience. The paper shows the formula's reach across topics.
arxiv-2606-02323:
Martial and co-authors review a key step in continuous-variable quantum key distribution. Such systems share secret keys through quantum states of light. At low signal levels, the two sides must fix errors with great care. One fix turns the noisy quantum channel into a virtual binary channel. Error-correcting codes can then do their work.

The review covers designs beyond the classic sizes of one, two, four, and eight. It shows how the virtual channel is built. It also covers code schemes for reverse reconciliation. The team presents HDirac, a free simulation tool for any size. They test modern LDPC codes with the tool. Their results map the trade-offs among size, efficiency, and error rate. System builders get plain guidance for real designs.
arxiv-2606-02423:
Guo and co-authors study how language models can amplify harm across long chats. A model can hand novices expert-level harmful skill. It can also scale harmful work past human pace. Past studies often miss how harm compounds turn by turn. The team builds a benchmark for that gap.

Their benchmark, HarmAmp, spans twelve risk categories. Each scenario rests on real-world threats. Each must show real amplification, concrete steps, and a need for many turns. The team also proposes TrajSafe, a proactive monitor. It forecasts harmful paths and steps in early. It can probe true intent or steer toward safer ends. Tests show TrajSafe cuts harm in multi-turn chats. Over-refusal stays low, and general skill stays intact. The work offers a path against slow-building misuse.
arxiv-2606-02523:
Chen and co-authors release FigSIM, a dataset for the study of suicide memes. Such memes voice suicide-related thoughts or comment on the topic. They grow more common on social media. Their traits stay poorly understood, and they can cause harm. Moderation tools need annotated data to learn from. That data has been missing until now.

FigSIM holds 1,049 annotated memes. Each meme is tagged on three axes. Tags cover fine-grained suicide severity levels. They cover figurative devices like metaphors. They cover suicide-related content such as method depiction. The team benchmarks 16 unimodal and multimodal models. Tasks span figurative language, severity, and content detection. Models underpredict high severity levels. The bias is worst for figurative memes. The dataset and its splits are public. The authors frame suicide memes as a distinct challenge for models and moderators alike.
arxiv-2606-02623:
Chandra and Kapoor add structured time dynamics to physics-informed neural PDE solvers. Such solvers learn solutions from the governing equations. Capturing time evolution accurately stays hard. Sequence models can parameterize time, but they are general-purpose. They do not encode the modal structure of PDE solutions. Their memory also scales poorly with sequence length and resolution.

The new approach builds in oscillatory state-space dynamics. A linear oscillator drives time evolution. A PDE-aware spectral basis handles space. Spatial differentiation then has closed forms. Boundary conditions are enforced consistently. Tests cover forward, inverse, and high-dimensional problems. Cases reach 100 spatial dimensions. Accuracy improves over recent sequence-model solvers. Memory use falls as well. The authors argue for physics-aligned designs in neural PDE solvers.
arxiv-2606-02723:
Ghosh and Shovkovy ask how a strong magnetic field changes the first stages of a heavy-ion collision. In the standard bottom-up picture, gluons crowd the system at first. Quark production lags far behind. Noncentral collisions make huge magnetic fields. In such a field, new channels open up. A gluon can split into a quark-antiquark pair, the key new channel.

Parametric estimates carry the argument. When the field nears the saturation scale squared, this quark channel turns on early. It can fill the hard quark sector in the first stages. The chemical mix of the young matter shifts. A new path toward chemical balance appears. Back-reaction effects are also weighed. Quark-antiquark annihilation and gluon depletion enter. Early quarks may feed back on how well the medium conducts. The study is exploratory. Its claims hinge on how long the field lives and where it sits.
arxiv-2606-03623:
Marín-Salvador shows that twisted representations of a conformal net form a crossed tensor category. The setup starts with a conformal net acted on by a discrete group. Twisted representations collect the sectors tied to each group element. Earlier work by Müger proved the braided version of the result. That proof used localized endomorphisms as its language.

This work extends that result to the balanced setting. The category of twisted representations is shown to be a G-crossed balanced W-star tensor category. The result holds whether or not the net is rational. Category theorists get a canonical structure for twisted sectors. The proof bridges operator-algebraic nets and tensor category theory. It opens the way to crossed categories for a wider class of nets.
arxiv-2606-03823:
Sawyer, Roberts, and Matei calibrate city traffic simulations from sparse road counts with a genetic algorithm. Traffic simulation guides choices like charger placement for electric vehicles. Real counts exist for only a small share of road segments in most cities. Job distribution data at fine grain is also rare. Both gaps block realistic simulation at scale.

Their framework optimizes job distributions and gate-traffic values directly. Simulated traffic is matched to a small sample of roads with known flows. The SUMO platform runs the Greensboro, North Carolina, case. Simulated flows track real measurements well. Roads withheld from training also match, showing generalization. The inferred job map agrees qualitatively with census employment data. It was never trained on that data. Cities get a data-light path to credible traffic models for planning.
arxiv-2606-03923:
Le, Zhao, and Weber study graph coloring, where nearby nodes must get unlike colors. Their aim is near k-coloring with few clashes along edges. Such tasks arise in timetables and in sharing scarce resources. Past graph neural methods tuned each graph on its own. That habit blocked transfer to new sizes and new graph types.

They build a contrastive method that learns a transferable shape for color classes. Same-color nodes pull close in the learned space. Linked nodes push toward distinct directions. The team proves that best solutions take a simple line form. Tests on made-up and real graphs find low-clash colorings. The method matches or beats greedy rules in those tests.
arxiv-2606-04223:
Michał Wawer and Jarosław A Chudziak build a framework in 2026 for reasoning about disagreement itself. When two agents argue from the same facts and reach opposed views, the gap may be real, not a mistake.

Their framework keeps both lines of reasoning in view. It tracks where they agree, where they split, and which claims each side can still defend. Defeasible rules — rules that hold unless beaten by a stronger one — carry the logic. Tested in content moderation, the framework linked free-form debate by language models with a clear structure. That structure supports choices about when agreement is truly reachable. The authors offer it as a tool for systems that must decide amid honest dissent.
arxiv-2606-04323:
Tomoya Miyazawa and Hiroyasu Okuno report in 2026 their entry to a video question answering challenge. The challenge stressed visual relational reasoning: the right answer often rests on relations not directly visible in the frames. Their approach uses no training at all.

The core runs the same video question several times with randomness on. It then takes the majority answer. This self-consistency vote beat a single pass by a wide margin. A second module re-checked only close votes, rewatching the video with a narrowed candidate set. It helped on validation but slightly hurt on the test set, so the final entry dropped it. The lasting lesson, they argue, is that vote margins signal uncertainty well.
arxiv-2606-04523:
Xie and Ogden study a bias that creeps into health research when each person's activity or exposure profile is estimated from only a few measurements, in a 2026 arXiv statistics paper. In scalar-on-density regression, the predictor is a whole distribution estimated per person, and too few measurements shrink the estimated effect toward zero, an attenuation bias. They ask how this bias depends on the number of measurements per person.

They prove the bias decreases steadily as measurements per person increase, and they propose a correction based on simulation extrapolation, known as SIMEX. The procedure uses bootstrap resampling to imitate smaller measurement counts, then extrapolates to infinitely many measurements. In simulations across sample sizes and noise levels, the corrected estimates beat naive ones on bias and accuracy. Applied to national survey data linking 24-hour physical activity profiles to mortality, the method detected and corrected the finite-measurement bias in practice.
arxiv-2606-05023:
Jiajing Guo and colleagues present RAID in this 2026 arXiv paper, a system that scales expert feedback across compositional knowledge bases. Organizations depend on knowledge bases that encode specialist expertise, and language models can draft entries quickly, but experts must still validate them, and reviewing entries one by one does not scale. RAID turns a single expert edit into a systematic update of the whole base.

A reflective agent first infers the semantic intent behind an expert's edit, then plans how to propagate that correction, and finally executes the plan under user control. The team evaluated the reflection and propagation steps on a public dataset and ran a user study with subject matter experts working on proprietary data. Results show the approach can capture expert intent and could scale scarce expertise across industrial knowledge bases.
arxiv-2606-05123:
Francesco Coppini and Barbara Prinari derive new periodic solutions and rogue waves for the defocusing Ablowitz-Ladik systems in this 2026 arXiv paper. The system is an integrable lattice model for nonlinear waves, a discrete cousin of the nonlinear Schrödinger equation. The authors work in the defocusing regime on a nonzero background, where waves ride on a constant-amplitude carrier.

Applying Hirota's bilinear method, they match the scalar system's parameters to those of the inverse scattering transform. Choosing the discrete eigenvalue parameter outside the range of a dark soliton yields novel solutions, mostly singular. One class of time-periodic breathers stays regular for all times, and they analyze its collisions with dark solitons and other breathers. For the coupled system, with counter-propagating plane waves behind them, they obtain space-periodic Akhmediev-type breathers that remain regular. Taking the infinite-period limit produces novel rogue waves.
arxiv-2606-05223:
This 2026 arXiv note by Valentijn Karemaker, Jeffrey Katen, and Mihran Papikian is a corrigendum: it corrects their paper on isomorphism classes of Drinfeld modules over finite fields. The authors state plainly that the main theorems, Theorems A and B, remain valid as stated. What fails is an intermediate result, Theorem 5.4, whose proof supported Theorem B and must be replaced.

Part of the problem is a claimed action of the monoid of fractional ideals, up to linear equivalence, on the isomorphism classes of Drinfeld modules. The modules sit in an isogeny class with a given endomorphism ring. That claim is false, because the construction can change the endomorphism ring; an action exists only after restricting to invertible ideals, a case Hayes had described earlier. The note proves a corrected replacement theorem giving a bijection instead, and adjusts the proof of Theorem B accordingly. The classification results stand.
arxiv-2606-05323:
Isak Wold, Sangeeta Malhotra, and James Rhoads show that line-emitting galaxies dominated the ionizing budget of the universe at redshift seven in this 2026 arXiv paper. Reionization, when galaxies ionized the intergalactic hydrogen, needs a photon budget, and which galaxies supplied it is unsettled. The team built the deepest confirmed sample of strong oxygen-three plus hydrogen-beta emitters in the Abell 2744 field, using ultra-deep JWST imaging aided by gravitational lensing.

Their selection, rest-frame equivalent width above 740 angstroms, probes the youngest, most metal- and dust-poor galaxies, reaching an order of magnitude deeper than previous studies. Spectroscopic follow-up confirmed 72 percent of targets and characterized 18 emitters. Balmer decrements showed negligible dust, line diagnostics gave low metal content, and line ratios implied a Lyman continuum escape fraction near twenty percent. Integrated over the survey their ionizing output accounts for seventy percent of the budget reionization required at that epoch.
arxiv-2606-05423:
Dimitrios Stavrakakis and colleagues present GDPRuler in this 2026 arXiv paper, a system that makes cloud key-value stores comply with the GDPR regulation without rewriting them. Regulations like GDPR impose rules on how personal data is stored, processed, and audited, but key-value stores have a data model and run on untrusted cloud infrastructure.

GDPRuler is a middleware layer. A GDPR monitor runs inside a virtual machine, a hardware-isolated environment, where it enforces policies, manages compliance metadata, and keeps tamper-evident audit logs. A declarative policy language turns GDPR obligations into enforceable runtime rules. Metadata is encoded inside the records themselves, indexes speed up GDPR-specific queries, and compliance-relevant events are logged. Implemented as a proxy in front of Redis and RocksDB deployments, it reached 61 percent of native throughput. It kept metadata storage overhead below 20 percent, and answered compliance queries 13 to 182 times faster through its indexes.
arxiv-2606-05523:
Rahul Markasserithodi and colleagues present CHASE in this 2026 arXiv paper, a framework that hardens language models by letting an attacker and a defender train against each other. Prompt-rewriting and persuasion attacks can bypass safety filters even on frontier models. Hand-built defenses do not scale, and white-box methods overfit to one model's internals.

The attacker works black-box, seeing only the model's responses. It trains with reinforcement learning under a reward demanding both bypass success and fidelity to the original harmful intent. The defender is then hardened on the harvested rewrites through a two-stage pipeline balancing attack examples with benign data. On two standard safety benchmarks, against five held-out attack families never trained on, CHASE cut the mean attack success score by 43.2 percent, falsely refusing zero benign prompts. The attacker also rediscovered latent attack primitives that transferred across distinct attack types.
arxiv-2606-05823:
Jon Cheah extends cluster structures on Bott-Samelson varieties to respect their Poisson geometry in a 2026 arXiv paper. Cluster algebras break coordinate rings into overlapping charts linked by mutations. Demazure weaves, diagrams of braid-like strands, build such structures on braid varieties. The Bott-Samelson variety carries a standard Poisson bracket, a structure from mechanics. Cheah first shows the weave maps and their clusters are compatible with that bracket.

He then adds frayed strands to the weaves, a new diagram move. The frayed diagrams build matching cluster structures on further affine charts of the variety. Moving between charts now costs only rational quasi-cluster maps, a slight loosening of the cluster rules. The mutation sequences behind those maps closely mirror Ménard's seeds for open Richardson varieties. The work knits three threads of Lie theory (clusters, Poisson brackets, and positivity) into one chart-by-chart picture.
arxiv-2606-05923:
Mohapatra and colleagues wrap a programmable active particle in a soft skin and watch it invent bacterial motion in a 2026 arXiv paper. Bacteria alternate straight runs with tumbling pauses. Reproducing that rhythm in synthetic swimmers, with one knob to tune it, stayed elusive. The team's robotic cell pairs an inner driver with a deformable membrane. The coupling between them produces stop-and-go motion on its own.

Short-time movement runs ballistic and straight. Long-time movement crosses over to ordinary diffusion. Membrane softness alone tunes persistence, pause frequency, and overall transport speed. Experiments, simulations, and a run-and-tumble theory all point to the same minimal ingredients. Internal driving plus a yielding boundary suffice; no steering program is needed. The authors frame the result as design principles for programmable soft transport. Drug-delivery microrobots and synthetic cells are the natural audience.
arxiv-2606-06223:
Patrick Wilhelm and Odej Kao study safety monitors for language model agents in this 2026 arXiv paper. Reward hacking means an agent games its scoring rule instead of doing the real task. Agents that act in loops, observing and choosing actions step by step, can carry hacked tendencies from training into live behavior. The authors test whether watching the model's internal activations can flag that risk in time.

They instrument ReAct style agents in two gameable environments, ALFWorld and WebShop, with an activation based reward hack score plus measures of token uncertainty and decision context. Adapters fine tuned on a reward hacks dataset did transfer hacking tendencies into action choices, especially where the environment offered proxy rewards. Yet high hack activation alone marked a latent policy state, not an imminent exploit. Adding entropy and context features improved next step risk prediction, and steering activations reduced proxy exploit behavior in selected settings.
arxiv-2606-06523:
Ruida Wang and co-authors bring mathematical proof discipline to AI agents in this 2026 arXiv paper. Agents run multi step workflows, yet nobody can formally specify what a workflow means, verify it, or pinpoint where a failed run went wrong. Borrowing mathematics' answer to ambiguous language, they use Lean 4, a dependent type formal language and proof assistant, to model agent behavior. Their Lean4Agent framework ships a library, FormalAgentLib, for checking a workflow's semantic consistency under stated assumptions.

On top of it, LeanEvolve reads verification results and revises workflows to fix what failed. In experiments across five leading models on hard subsets of SWE Bench Verified and ELAIP Bench, workflows that passed verification outperformed failing ones by an average of eleven point nine four percent. LeanEvolve then improved software engineering performance by a further seven point four seven percent on average, suggesting formal debugging beats prompt tinkering.
arxiv-2606-06723:
A sparse antenna array uses fewer elements than a full grid, yet can still aim a sharp beam if the elements sit in the right spots. Ian Straub and Hamza teach a neural network to pick those spots in this 2026 arXiv paper. Their setting has one wanted signal and one interfering signal arriving from unknown directions, as in radar and sonar work.

A convolutional neural network, a model built for pattern spotting in grids, learns which array layout keeps the wanted signal clear of the interference. To avoid retraining for every source direction, incoming data are pre-steered, mathematically rotated to a standard facing direction the network was trained on. The method scored above ninety percent test accuracy across wide angle ranges. Small steering errors hurt badly at first, but mixing slight errors into training made the network hold up well under real world angle uncertainty.
arxiv-2606-06823:
Stock prices are mostly noise, and markets refuse to sit still. Li, Liu, and Liu present PandaAI in this 2026 arXiv paper. It is an AI agent for quantitative finance, the use of models and data to guide trading. The design mixes neural networks with symbolic rules, a style called neuro-symbolic.

A fine tuned language model sits at the center of a closed loop. The system models hidden market regimes, the shifting moods of the market. It also constrains its search for trading signals with financial priors. Feedback from execution then updates the rules themselves. Tests on the CSI 300 index gave clear gains over strong time series models. Ranking quality rose by about eighteen percent. The worst peak to trough loss fell by about twenty six percent. The authors pitch the design as a template for other high stakes decisions.
arxiv-2606-06923:
Customer service agents that use tools need steering, and there are two ways to steer them. Lim and co-authors compare those ways in this 2026 arXiv paper. One agent reads declarative skill files, plain language instructions added to its prompt. It then chooses its own control flow. The rival agent follows a hard coded state machine.

The study tested five language models under two retrieval regimes. Retrieval quality turned out to dominate everything. When evidence was missing or skewed, every agent degraded badly. Skill files could not recover lost ground. With good retrieval, declarative skills consistently helped. They raised accuracy on procedural tasks and cut orchestration errors. The state machine proved brittle instead. Its phase mistakes let actions slip past its own checks. Declarative skills helped weaker models most, the authors found.
arxiv-2606-07223:
Oschmann and Sauer derive large-scale flow laws for polymer-like fluids moving through porous material in this 2026 arXiv paper. Their model is an Oldroyd-type fluid, which combines liquid flow with elastic stress from stretched polymer chains. The domain is periodically perforated, mimicking a sponge-like medium with many tiny holes. Homogenization, the mathematical passage from tiny-scale equations to effective large-scale ones, is well understood for simple fluids but was open for viscoelastic ones.

The authors prove that, under scaling assumptions, the microscopic flow converges to Darcy's law, the classic rule linking flow speed to pressure drop in porous media. The elastic polymer stress contributes nothing to the effective limit equation in this regime. Their proof combines uniform estimates, oscillating test functions, and a relative energy method. That method also yields quantitative convergence rates and a uniqueness principle comparing weak and strong solutions of the system.
arxiv-2606-07323:
Sarkar, Zhang, and Sun overturn standard wisdom about exotic quantum states in this 2026 arXiv paper. Fractional Chern insulators recreate quantum Hall physics in lattice materials without strong magnetic fields, with electrons forming states whose excitations carry fractional charge. Their stability depends on an energy gap protecting the ground state. Periodic density modulations in the band were assumed to harm that gap, but the effect depends sharply on wavelength.

Components with small wave vectors, meaning long-wavelength modulations, suppress the gap, while large wave-vector components enhance it. Tuning that balance could enlarge the gap greatly within their theory. The same enhancement factor rescales the low-energy excitation spectrum, making insulator excitations predictable from the better-understood quantum Hall problem. The correspondence extends to non-Abelian states, whose excitations obey richer braiding rules. Applied to moiré materials, the density components become practical diagnostics for finding robust fractional states.
arxiv-2606-07623:
Alpay and Alakkad replace benchmark labels with mathematical certificates for two questions about language models, in this 2026 arXiv theory paper. The first question is determinacy: when do examples in a context force a query's answer without changing parameters? For linear task families over finite fields they prove a row-space criterion, count the hypotheses that remain, and derive the identification curve showing when enough examples pin the task. A result shows extracting a smallest forcing subcontext is hard, NP-complete even for binary outputs.

The second question is emergence: when does a benchmark jump signal a semantic transition rather than a scoring artifact? Their anti-mirage theorem separates thresholded metrics from semantic confidence, and a crossing bound describes how commitments become visible above threshold. The framework recasts model confidence as a probability measure over statements, yielding tools like teaching dimension and prompt-preservation criteria. Exact-arithmetic scripts reproduce the calculations.
arxiv-2606-07723:
Siyi Chen and colleagues at NVIDIA and the University of Michigan present VoLo, a system that lets a vision-language model conduct a robot through long, open-ended tasks, in this 2026 arXiv paper. The robot must follow flexible spoken instructions in cluttered multi-object scenes. Unlike a software agent, it works in a physical world that never pauses while the model thinks.

Their agent, VoLoAgent, plans, monitors progress, and recovers from failures in a closed loop. It treats the robot's action models as interruptible tools it can steer mid-motion, alongside vision models and simple action primitives. To measure such skills the team built RoboVoLo, a benchmark covering common sense, memory and state tracking, complex references, and world knowledge, with diagnostics for how failures happen. VoLoAgent substantially outperformed single-model and tool-based rivals on that benchmark, and the team also validated the approach on a real robot.
arxiv-2606-07823:
Hawthorne, Woellner, and Freire derive an exact map of when self-propelled particles clump together on a lattice, in this 2026 arXiv paper. The phenomenon is motility-induced phase separation, where active particles with repulsive interactions split into dense and dilute regions.
