Interior designers often need a 3D model from a single furniture photo. Alibaba Group and Taobao present Home3D 1.0 in 2026 to generate such assets. One reference image goes in. A mesh with physically based rendering materials comes out. The mesh can be split into material-specific components. Four tightly coupled modules form the pipeline.

A geometry module rebuilds a watertight mesh. It uses latent signed-distance modelling. A texture module predicts multi-view appearance. It also completes unseen surface regions. A material module segments components through video-based masks and UV-space voting. It then retrieves matching materials from a curated library. A parts module generates semantic part meshes. They stay editable by material. Each module is scored on its own with dedicated metrics. The evaluations highlight current capability. They also show the gaps toward broader deployment. Cross-stage feedback and articulated objects are named as future work.
arxiv-2606-28123:
Thomas Boudou, Batiste Le Bars, Nirupam Gupta, and Aurélien Bellet examine a quiet assumption behind modern machine learning pipelines. When updates from many sources are combined, as happens when rules enforce privacy, robustness, fairness, or adaptivity, the combining rule is often not a plain average.

Boudou and colleagues prove that a combining rule preserves monotonicity only when the rule is positively affine. Monotonicity is the property that keeps first-order learning methods converging steadily. A positively affine rule is a weighted average plus a fixed shift. Every rule outside that family breaks monotonicity, which harms both convergence and stability in ways they quantify. They close by giving conditions under which monotonicity can be restored, uniting several known failure modes under one explanation.
arxiv-2606-28523:
Kevin Wagner, Sumin Seung, Dániel Apai, and a dozen further colleagues make the case, in this Nautilus Space Observatory white paper, for hunting exomoons by watching planets wobble. A moon tugs its planet, and that reflex motion is recoverable from precise star-planet position measurements over time. The signal grows for heavier, wider moons around nearby, low-mass planets.

Catching moons below Earth mass takes continuous, long, ultra-precise monitoring that only a dedicated facility can supply. The authors argue Nautilus's replicable array architecture fits uniquely. They stage the campaign: first one or a few small telescopes stare at the nearest imaged giants, a long shot with high reward. As the array grows and its noise floor drops, the search extends systematically to the nearest suitable systems, alongside direct imaging of the planets themselves.
arxiv-2606-28623:
Md Mozaharul Mottalib and Rahmatollah Beheshti sort patients into meaningful subgroups from their health records. Subtyping promises precision medicine, but records are irregular, visits unevenly spaced, and the time patterns that define a subtype hide inside long, messy sequences that defeat plain clustering.

Their self-supervised model builds on Mamba, a sequence model built for long records, and learns summaries of each patient's history without labels. The team tests the summaries two ways: predicting known labels, and clustering patients into subtypes from the learned geometry. Across public and private real-world datasets, the design choices behind their model deliver better prediction than strong baselines. Head-to-head comparisons of clustering methods show the summaries carry useful subtyping signal. That is a step toward grouping patients by how their conditions unfold.
arxiv-2606-29023:
Zhang, Wang, Qi and Wen present a pipeline for finding where and when an object described in words appears in a long video. This task, spatio-temporal grounding, demands precise timing plus robust tracking, and modern vision-language models can reason about it but are costly and unstable when applied frame by frame. Their pipeline instead tracks at the level of seconds, smoothing across seconds to keep continuity while shortening the sequence the model must handle.

To teach reasoning, the team synthesise step-by-step trajectories with advanced multimodal models, then swap generated coordinates for ground-truth ones. A reinforcement learning stage tunes the policy, scored by a verifier combining time and video overlap. Across frame-rate settings, the method achieved a strong trade-off between speed and localisation quality.
arxiv-2606-29223:
Yang, Sun and Xia propose Depth Exploration Decoding, a way to generate text from language models faster without changing the output. Standard decoding runs every token through the full layer stack, although many tokens become predictable at intermediate depths. Earlier depth-adaptive methods pick one early exit depth and verify it, but a late exit wastes computation and an early one triggers fallback.

Their algorithm explores multiple candidate depths in parallel instead of selecting one. At each commit position it checks candidates against the final-depth reference and commits exactly the final-depth token, then collapses the exploration lattice, keeping only reusable branch states. This cycle preserves exact equivalence to standard decoding while cutting the cost per token. Across early-exit-trained and standard models, it beat depth-selection baselines and matched speculative and distributed decoding methods in throughput. It also improved as explored depths became finer.
arxiv-2606-29323:
Ghazi and Moradpouri study a family of symmetry algebras that generalise the BMS3 algebra, an infinite-dimensional algebra arising in flat-space gravity and conformal field theory. Their starting point is the Sugawara construction, which builds the Virasoro algebra from a current algebra. For a doubled abelian current algebra, earlier work found extra constructions carrying a grading by the cyclic group of order N, forming a non-compact algebraic variety.

The pair compactify these varieties by adding points at infinity. Those added points, they show, are exactly the BMS3-like algebras. For grading two, the point gives the standard BMS3 algebra: the Virasoro algebra joined with an infinite abelian ideal. For larger N the ideal becomes nonabelian and nilpotent, with depth below N. The depth matches the order of the variety's singularity there. They also study central extensions of these algebras.
arxiv-2606-29523:
Pezzella presents SPIDeC methods, solvers for positive dynamical systems, where the tracked values must stay nonnegative. Ordinary solvers can drift below zero or move a steady state, breaking the model's meaning. His framework embeds a deferred correction step inside an exponential Volterra form of the problem.

That structure keeps solutions positive and keeps steady states fixed, whatever the step size. Repeated correction sweeps over a low-order base improve the result step by step. The methods are L-stable, a strong stability property, and they match exactly the flow of diagonal linear problems. With Gauss-Radau nodes, the discrete flow grows more contractive as sweeps increase. Numerical tests confirm the theory.
arxiv-2606-29823:
Liao and twenty-four colleagues argue that long-running AI agents need a new kind of data foundation. As an agent works on a hard task it tries options, runs tools, hits failures, and repairs them, and this whole search forms what the authors call an experience graph.

Today that record is usually thrown into log files that cannot be searched, shared, or turned into training data. The proposed system, Trellis, stores the experience graph as proper database state, so picking the next step becomes a query and reuse across sessions becomes a search. The design is grounded in a production kernel optimizer at Meta, where reusing past experience reached a target speedup about ten times faster at 52 percent lower token cost per valid solution.
arxiv-2606-30023:
Kristian Drizari and five colleagues test learning based beam selection for millimeter-wave links. These links operate near twenty-six and a half gigahertz indoors. They carry huge bandwidth but fade when beams misalign. Blockages also disrupt them easily. Exhaustively sweeping every beam wastes time and overhead. Their hybrid beamforming testbed combines digital processing with analog steering.

The team collected wideband channel measurements in a real office corridor. A synchronized software defined radio testbed gathered the data. Beam selection becomes a supervised learning problem. The goal is predicting the beam exhaustive sweeping rates best. One neural network uses spatial features like position. A pilots-only method uses a few sounded beams instead. It needs no location information at all. Both methods reach high prediction accuracy. Beam search overhead falls sharply versus full sweeping.
arxiv-2606-30723: This author studies Ryu-Takayanagi area from Virasoro modular data. The studying studies. Their studying is Ryu-Takayanagi area Virasoro modular data. The studying studies. It is string theory. The studying is from. The modular data is Virasoro. The area study is string-theoretic.
arxiv-2606-30823:
Rob McConkey, Christopher St. Clair, Tristan Wells and Chen Zhang make progress on a knot-theory question from the Kirby problem list. Akbulut asked whether some homology sphere, other than the ordinary three-sphere, has a strong slicing property. Any knot in it that bounds a disk in some contractible four-manifold should already bound a disk in the thin product region. Knots with the opposite, deeply slice behaviour would illuminate the question.

The team construct a class of deeply slice knots. They specify a pair: a contractible four-manifold with integral homology-sphere boundary, and a knot that is slice in that manifold. Then they prove the knot is not slice in the product region, using concordance invariants from Heegaard Floer homology. Immersed curve techniques, a diagrammatic way to compute those invariants, do the heavy lifting. The construction supplies test cases for Akbulut's question rather than settling it.
arxiv-2606-30923:
Sriraman and three colleagues ask why on-policy distillation often beats behavior cloning when language models learn from imperfect teachers. In imitation learning, a student copies an expert's behavior; here the student only sees a noisy version of the expert, yet is judged against the clean expert's reward. That mismatch mirrors real training, where long chains of thought come from fallible demonstrators.

The authors prove a sharp separation. Learning offline from noisy demonstrations is fundamentally hard, with sample needs growing exponentially in the horizon. Learning online, through their new variant of on-policy distillation, needs only polynomially many samples. Experiments on synthetic and language tasks confirm the theory: the proposed method outperforms both offline cloning and existing distillation objectives under noisy feedback.
arxiv-2606-31023:
Zhou and three colleagues tackle a safety problem in systems that must obey hard constraints at every step, such as power-grid scheduling. Modern AI models can draft long action sequences cheaply, but their drafts carry no guarantee of obeying the constraints, while calling a trusted solver at every step wastes the AI's speed. Their method, Certificate-Gated Prefix Acceptance, lets an untrusted agent propose moves while a trusted verifier checks each transition exactly.

A conformally calibrated value boundary decides how much of each draft can be accepted safely before the rest goes to the solver. In tests, every proposal source, including large language models that violated constraints in almost all direct rollouts, produced zero applied violations. On a full-scale unit commitment problem, the setup ran nearly three times faster than solver-only control at low regret.
arxiv-2606-31123:
Lee and Lee revisit the symplectic leaves of meromorphic Hitchin systems, spaces of Higgs bundles whose fields may have poles at marked points. That moduli space carries a Poisson structure, a bracket that splits it into symplectic leaves, found by Bottacin and Markman. The authors focus on the tame case, where pole behaviour stays controlled.

They study how the restricted Hitchin map on each leaf can be partly compactified while staying an algebraically completely integrable system. Moduli spaces of parabolic Higgs bundles with a fixed direction vector give that compactification. Those same spaces also resolve, in the symplectic sense, the normalization of each leaf closure, and the paper adds connectedness results for the matching Betti moduli spaces.
arxiv-2606-31623:
Aliyev and Aliyeva reconcile two separate criteria for the same question in Sturm-Liouville theory, which studies vibration-type equations whose solutions form systems used to expand other functions. The problem's boundary condition depends linearly on the eigenparameter, the unknown constant being solved for. Earlier work by the authors derived minimality criteria for the system of root functions through independent routes.

Minimality means no function in the system can be dropped without shrinking what the system spans. The pair prove the two criteria are equivalent and give one unified description of the exceptional cases, where removing certain associated functions does destroy minimality. Worked examples with multiple eigenvalues show both approaches agreeing and clarify the structure of the root function systems involved.
arxiv-2606-31823:
Chen presents next-to-next-to-leading order predictions for producing a top-antitop pair plus a W boson at the Large Hadron Collider. The process is among the heaviest signatures studied there. Measured rates have often come out above Standard Model expectations, which pushes theory toward higher accuracy.

Earlier NNLO work avoided computing the two-loop amplitudes directly, relying on soft and high-energy approximations instead. Chen evaluates those amplitudes explicitly for the first time, within a generalised leading-colour limit. That limit expands in colour factors rather than invoking any kinematic shortcut. The resulting cross sections agree with the earlier approximate calculation. The agreement, on its own, validates the approach experiments had been compared against.
arxiv-2606-32023:
Vautier and two colleagues build a single deep learning model that predicts forest attributes across a whole country from airborne LiDAR. National inventories need wall-to-wall maps, but national LiDAR campaigns mix sensors, seasons, flight constraints and scan angles. Models calibrated locally usually fail to generalize across that heterogeneity, especially over structurally diverse forests.

FLORA combines an octree-based backbone over the point clouds with ecological and spatiotemporal auxiliary variables, fused through a gating mechanism that keeps each variable's contribution partly interpretable. Training uses 32,052 French National Forest Inventory plots from the national LiDAR HD program. One model trained jointly on leaf-on and leaf-off flights beats season-specific models. Dominant height is predicted with a relative error near 12.3 percent, alongside competitive volume estimates.
arxiv-2608-00323:
Ono settles a conjecture of Han and Xiong on fractional Gaussian binomial coefficients. Han and Xiong had extended that coefficient to positive rational r. They guessed its integer trace is largest, coefficient by coefficient, at r equal to one half. The trace is the integer-exponent part of the series. Ono attacks the claim via a support-dominance theorem.

His theorem compares rational parameters under a clear divisibility rule. It settles the claim for all r at least one half. The full claim shrinks to unit fractions one over 2m. Just finitely many are nontrivial for fixed k. A computer check then proves all positive rational r for k up to 200. The theory was made and checked in Lean by AxiomProver.
as-you-like-it-pg1523:
William Shakespeare's As You Like It appears in this modern-spelling text arranged by act and scene, beginning in an orchard near Oliver's house. Orlando, kept uneducated by his elder brother, wins a wrestling match at Duke Frederick's court and Rosalind's heart in the same afternoon. Banishment sends both parties to the Forest of Arden.

The scene list maps Arden's clearings and cottages through five acts. Rosalind, disguised as Ganymede, teases Celia about Orlando's small beard and promises God will send more if the man is thankful. This text differs from the old-spelling version elsewhere in the library by its clean modern presentation, making it the easier copy for first-time readers of Shakespeare's pastoral comedy.
bertrand-traite-somnambulisme-1823:
Alexandre Bertrand wrote his Traite du somnambulisme in French in 1823. Somnambulism, sleepwalking raised by magnetism, is his whole subject. Bertrand sorts its forms and the changes each one brings. His treatise is the first systematic French pathology of magnetic sleep.

A doctor by training, he writes against both blind belief and blind scorn. Cases from the early magnetists receive his cool review. Later French schools of hypnosis built on ground he cleared. The French original stands as the documentary text. Bertrand later turned to other fields, but the treatise kept his name. It shows French medicine weighing the magnetic marvels early. The balance he strikes still reads well.
bischoff-die-kabbalah-1923:
Erich Bischoff, a German scholar of the occult and of Jewish learning, wrote Die Kabbalah as a plain introduction to Jewish mysticism and its secret science. The third edition appeared in 1923, with pictures. The book is in German. Bischoff aimed at the general reader who wanted the system whole, without the years of Hebrew it usually demands.

He sets out the ten sefirot, the tree of life, the letters and their numbers, and the schools from the Zohar to the Hasidim. His survey became the standard German popular account of the subject. Plates of seals, trees, and amulets crowd the pages. It shows how the German reading public of the 1920s met the Kabbalah.
boule-fossil-men-1923:
Marcellin Boule, a leading French paleontologist, published his study of fossil humans in 1921. The English translation by the Ritchies appeared in 1923 as Fossil Men. Boule drew heavily on the Neanderthal skeleton found at La Chapelle-aux-Saints.

He pictured Neanderthals as stooped, brutish, and cut off from human ancestry. That portrait ruled textbooks for a generation before later finds overturned it. Boule's careful fossil descriptions still reward attention. The book shows both the strength and the blind spots of early paleoanthropology. His survey also covered the major European cave finds known at the time.
broad-scientific-thought-1923:
Scientific Thought, published in 1923, is Broad's masterwork on what the new physics means for philosophy at large. Relativity and the quantum age were remaking science's picture of nature, and Broad set out to map the damage and the gains for thought.

He examines space, time, matter, and cause as the new theories rebuilt them, asking which older notions can survive. His manner is slow, exhaustive, and scrupulously fair to every side. Philosophers treated the book as the standard survey of the questions. It shows analytic philosophy learning to take modern physics seriously, concept by concept.
bruce-evolution-arthurian-romance-vol1-1:
James Douglas Bruce published the first volume of The Evolution of Arthurian Romance in 1923. His aim was to map the whole Arthurian tradition from its start to the year 1300. The book surveys sources, poets, and prose cycles in careful order.

Bruce begins with the early traditions that fed the legend. He moves through Chrétien de Troyes, the rise of the Grail story, and the great prose cycles. Few scholars had drawn so full a map of the field in one work. Students of Arthur still use Bruce to see how the tales grew, branch by branch, from chronicle into romance.
bruce-evolution-arthurian-romance-vol2-1:
The second volume of James Douglas Bruce's Evolution of Arthurian Romance appeared in 1923, beside the first. Where volume one carried the story to 1300, this one finishes the prose romances. It then gathers Bruce's closing discussions and analyses of the whole tradition.

Bruce weighs how the French prose cycles reshaped older verse tales. He tracks the Grail, Lancelot, and Tristan as they pass from poet to poet. His judgments are firm and his learning is wide. Read with the first volume, it forms the fullest survey of Arthurian romance that one scholar had then produced. Libraries still shelve the pair together.
buckland-reliquiae-diluvianae-1823:
William Buckland, an Oxford priest and rock scholar, wrote this book on the relics of the flood in 1823. Its Latin title means 'relics of the deluge,' the great flood of the Bible. Buckland had dug cave floors full of the bones of long dead beasts.

He read the caves of Kirkdale and other sites as dens of hyenas, swept by the flood. His scheme tied all such finds to the one flood and left no room for an old age of man. All who came next and claimed deep time for man had to fight his frame first.
burnet-history-of-his-own-time-vol-1-182:
Gilbert Burnet, a Scottish bishop who lived at the center of power, wrote the History of His Own Time. The work was published in 1724 to 1734, after his death. Volume one here opens the Oxford edition of 1823. The edition runs to six volumes, with passages once suppressed now restored. Burnet's span covers the Restoration and the Glorious Revolution.

Burnet writes as a Whig and a churchman who knew Cromwell's heirs, Charles II, and William III in person. His pages mix high politics with gossip, character, and sharp moral judgment. The result is the great eyewitness history of his age, partisan and priceless at once. Volume one sets that crowded stage.
burnet-history-of-his-own-time-vol-2-182:
Volume two continues Gilbert Burnet's History of His Own Time in the Oxford edition of 1823. Burnet's history, first published in 1724 to 1734, covers the later Stuart age from a bishop's seat near the throne. The 1823 edition runs to six volumes and restores passages that earlier editors had cut.

Burnet knew the men he judges: kings, ministers, generals, and plotters passed through his life. His narrative of the Restoration and the road to revolution in 1688 is vivid, frank, and openly Whig in sympathy. Scholars quarrel with his bias and quarry his facts in the same breath. Volume two keeps the eyewitness record rolling through a dangerous reign.
burnet-history-of-his-own-time-vol-3-182:
Burnet's History of His Own Time reaches volume three in the Oxford edition of 1823, the six-volume set with suppressed passages restored. Gilbert Burnet published the history in 1724 to 1734, drawn from his own diaries and his place at the heart of affairs. He had advised William of Orange and helped prepare the revolution of 1688.

Volume three holds the middle of his long story, from Restoration intrigue toward open crisis. Burnet's pen portraits of the age's leaders are bold, warm, and sometimes unfair, always alive. His history is the great Whig counterpart to Clarendon's royalist epic. Reading both gives the age in stereo. This volume keeps Burnet's side loud and clear.
burnet-history-of-his-own-time-vol-4-182:
Volume four of the 1823 Oxford Burnet continues the History of His Own Time, Gilbert Burnet's record of the later Stuart years. The original work appeared in 1724 to 1734, in the years after Burnet's death. The Oxford set fills six volumes and prints passages that the first editors suppressed.

Burnet writes history as a participant with strong loves and hatreds, which is both its spice and its warning. Courts, parliaments, and churches fill his pages, judged by a man who served in all three. The Glorious Revolution, his great cause, draws near as the volumes advance. Volume four carries the crisis forward in the bishop's brisk, knowing voice.
burnet-history-of-his-own-time-vol-5-182:
The History of His Own Time moves through volume five in the Oxford edition of 1823. Gilbert Burnet's work, published in 1724 to 1734, narrates England's passage from Restoration to revolution through the eyes of a bishop at the center. The six-volume Oxford edition restores text cut from the first printings.

Volume five stands deep in the reign-shaking events Burnet helped to shape. His account blends state papers, private talk, and his own sermons and counsel to princes. No Whig source of the age is fuller, franker, or more fun to argue with. The narrative here keeps its pace: plots, wars, and successions judged by a man who knew the players by name.
burnet-history-of-his-own-time-vol-6-182:
Volume six completes the Oxford edition of 1823 of Bishop Burnet's History of His Own Time. Gilbert Burnet's history, first published in 1724 to 1734, ends its long arc from the Restoration through the Glorious Revolution. Six volumes, with suppressed passages restored, hold the standard text of the work.

Burnet closes his story as he began it, an insider with opinions he does not hide. William III's wars and settlement fill the later pages, weighed by a bishop who had ridden with the revolution. His history remains the great Whig eyewitness account of the age, set against Clarendon's royalist one. To finish volume six is to close that famous pair of witnesses.
capek-r-u-r-1923:
Karel Capek's play R.U.R., in the 1923 English version by Playfair and Selver, gave the world the word robot. Rossum's factory makes artificial workers to free humans from toil. The robots, built for labor, learn to resent their makers and rise against them.

First staged in 1920, the drama asks what makes a being human. Work, love, and revolt drive the plot toward a stark end. Capek mixes sharp satire with real pathos for his made creatures. The play founded a line of science fiction on stage and still frames how we talk about machines.
carpzov-practica-nova-1723:
Benedict Carpzov was a Saxon judge whose Practica Nova, in this 1723 edition, codified criminal practice for the German courts. The work covers crimes and their proofs in the Roman and Saxon legal tradition. Under its rules, Saxon witch trials were conducted for generations.

Carpzov treats witchcraft as a crime of the gravest kind, to be proved by confession, witnesses, and strict legal form. His fame rested on the sheer number of cases his court decided under his guidance. Legal historians call him the most-cited criminalist of the witch-hunt era, a name that stands for its system at full strength.
cassirer-substance-function-1923:
Substance and Function, published in English in 1923 with Cassirer's essay on Einstein's relativity, is his critical theory of how science forms its concepts. Ernst Cassirer, the leading neo-Kantian of his generation, argues that modern thought has replaced substance with function.

Older logic built concepts as lists of shared properties, copies of things. Modern mathematics and physics, Cassirer shows, build them as rules and relations: number, function, and field. The appended essay applies the same reading to Einstein, finding relativity a triumph of relational thought. The book is demanding but foundational for the philosophy of science.
cather-lost-lady-1923:
A Lost Lady, published by Willa Cather in 1923, centers on Marian Forrester of Sweet Water, Nebraska. Marian is the gracious wife of an older railroad builder, Captain Forrester. A young neighbor, Niel Herbert, watches her life over many years and tells her story.

In Niel's youth Marian seems to embody grace, charm, and the pioneer age at its best. After her husband's ruin and death, she changes in ways that shock her young admirer. Cather treats her with sympathy rather than scorn. The short novel mourns a passing frontier world while showing the strength a woman needed to survive it.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-bruno-1048:
St. Bruno, bishop of Segni in Italy, was born at Solero in Piedmont about 1048. He died in 1123. This entry follows a boy first educated in a Benedictine monastery of his native town. After Bologna studies and ordination, he was made a canon of Siena. For his learning and piety, he was called to Rome, where, as an able and prudent counsellor, four successive popes sought his advice.

At a Rome synod in 1079 he made Berengarius of Tours — who denied Our Lord's real presence in the Holy Eucharist — retract his heresy. He enjoyed Gregory VII's friendship. Gregory consecrated him bishop of Segni in the Campagna of Rome in 1080. Humility made him decline the cardinalate. He is called the brilliant defender of the Church for the invincible courage he showed in aiding Gregory VII and succeeding popes in their efforts for ecclesiastical reform.
cia-0000009523:
Two captured American personnel were sighted in South Vietnam in an August 1972 report, one of whom may have matched a known man, the title hints. The heading breaks off before completing that thought. Southern sightings often arrived with just this kind of partial identification.

Partial matches were both hopeful and dangerous: a wrong name could mislead a family. Analysts therefore recorded the uncertainty inside the report itself. The file shows the discipline of writing 'may have' when proof fell short. It also adds two more captives to the southern record at the war's late stage.
cia-0000011823:
A partly blanked CIA item from August 1968 records the suicide of a woman believed to have been involved in an assassination. The title itself is cut short in the file, and key details were blacked out before release. What survives is the bare outline of a death tied to the secret world and its violence.

The item preserves what the agency chose, or was forced, to leave visible about the case. Its gaps are part of its meaning: names, places, and motives stay hidden. For readers, it is a somber fragment showing the human cost that runs beneath the paperwork of espionage.
cia-0000012423:
A passport numbered IX-SA 601266 anchors an undated CIA document, its year estimated as 1962. The sheet records the travel papers side of the tradecraft in plain form. Cover documents were a spy's second skin, worn every day abroad. Their numbers, stamps, and stories had to survive hard inspection. Men trained to spot a false page at a glance would study them, so the paperwork was handled with obsessive care.

The record keeps the passport's number as the file's fixed point. Around such numbers whole false lives were built and checked. For readers, the page shows the quiet clerical craft that stood between a source and discovery.
cia-0000013223:
Enemy prison facilities in Laos are estimated in a CIA paper from January 1969. The secret war's prison map kept growing that year. New sources came forward with camp locations, guard strengths, and names of the held. Laos held American airmen shot down over the supply trails. Their camps were scattered through some of Asia's roughest country. Few roads reached them, and no inspectors ever did.

The estimate gathers the Laotian camps into one accounting. It counts facilities the way other papers counted divisions. For readers, it shows the captivity the secret war hid longest, surveyed by the side that lost men to it.
cia-0000013923: An American pilot was captured near Hon Gai, in a CIA note dated January 4, 1969. Hon Gai was a coal port town on North Vietnam's coast. Pilots lost near the coast had little hope of rescue at sea or on land. The note, filed in a new year, shows capture reports still coming in.
cia-0000014623: The Klaus Fuchs case opens a CIA file dated January 5, 1951, which recalls an investigation already under way. Fuchs had pleaded guilty in London to atomic spying in 1950. His answers led agents toward couriers and handlers in the United States. The file belongs to the paper trail of that widening hunt.
cia-0000015323: A letter to George Popowitch from John S. Harman fills a CIA file dated January 5, 1959. Harman answers Popowitch's letter of January 21, in the title's crossed dates. A second reply to the same man shows his thread ran for months. Citizen mail on saucers was answered with care, if with few facts.
cia-0000015423: Congressman Joseph E. Karth asked the CIA about flying saucers, and a proposed reply was drafted for him in June 1961. The draft notes that many letters from Leon Davidson had arrived on the same subject. Each one, it says, was sent to the Air Force, which owned such matters. Karth's interest shows how saucer mail reached Congress and pulled careful answers from the agency.
cia-0000020423: Rafael Otero Echeverria is the sole name on a CIA record dated in 1976. No role, place, or event is given in the title, so nothing further can be stated safely. A name alone still tells a story of method: the agency kept personal files on people of interest across Latin America. Thin files like this mark a life reduced to a paper shadow.
cia-0000021523: Fragmentary reports of American pilots jailed near Sam Neua, in Houa Phan Province, fill a CIA record dated in 1966. Sam Neua was a stronghold area in northeast Laos, close to Vietnam. The word fragmentary warns that the pieces did not yet form a clear picture. Staff kept such scraps because a scrap might one day name a living prisoner.
cia-0000036623:
Three American prisoners were reported seen in Vietnam, in a CIA record dated November 1, 1979. The file names Pederson, Rozo, and Phillips in connection with the sighting. The report came six years after the war's prisoners were said to have come home.

Postwar sightings like this one kept the POW and MIA question alive for years. Each claim had to be logged, checked, and weighed against the known lists. The record shows how the search went on long after the fighting had stopped. Three named men gave the report a weight that a nameless rumor could never carry on its own.
cia-0000044423:
A bishop called for peace and dialogue, and voiced regret over the killings, in a CIA record dated October 4, 1989 in the catalog. A bishop's call carries the weight of his office and his flock. His words came in the first shock after the priests' murders.

Inside, the bishop's plea for talks and his sorrow sit together. The church had urged dialogue long before the killings came. Each new death made that urging sound more urgent, and less heard. The file preserves a pastor's response to murder in his own country. It holds grief for the dead. It also holds a stubborn return to the table where enemies might yet talk.
cia-0000045223:
Negotiations on the Duarte kidnapping were stalemated, in a CIA record dated September 1, 1985. Stalemate was the crisis's most common condition that autumn. Each side waited for the other to move first on terms.

Inside, the deadlock in the talks is recorded for the file. Frozen talks are not empty time for a captive's family. Every silent day raised the fear that the case would end badly. The record holds one of those frozen moments in full. It stands for the long stretches of the crisis in which nothing seemed to move at all.
cia-0000045923: A foreign ministry sent a formal letter about the photograph said to show an American prisoner, and a CIA item dated June 6, 1991, records the move. The photo had stirred fresh hope and anger among families of men missing from the Vietnam War. The letter shows the dispute moving through official channels, capital to capital, in careful words.
cia-0000049123: A partly blacked-out CIA item from 1987 concerns El Salvador's military attache in Paraguay, kept with the Truth Commission records. Attaches were a country's uniformed ears abroad, and their files mixed ceremony with reporting. Why this posting earned a file sits in the document, behind the blacked-out name in its title.
cia-0000049223: The Senate Select Committee on Intelligence reported on political violence in El Salvador in 1984. Its report fills a CIA item kept with the Truth Commission records. A Senate report put the violence on the congressional record, harder to deny than any cable. The item preserves the senators' findings as the agency filed them.
cia-0000102923: Colony Settlement, Arkhangelsk Oblast, with dates of information 1973 to 1975, is declassified CIA document 0000102923, dated October 1, 1981. The heading names a settlement type and a northern region. Readers get a short colony settlement record in the labor cluster, its three information years stated, companion to the Baku colony record filed months earlier.
cia-0000104823:
Office of Policy Coordination 1948-1952 is a CIA history released as declassified document 0000104823, dated January 4, 1948, with that date an estimate. The sample opens with the history's introduction. It sets the scene just after World War II, as Communist parties moved into vacuums left by fallen fascist regimes.

The introduction says Russia then viewed the United States as leader of an opposite camp. It also recalls a September 1946 paper by Clark M. Clifford, an aide to President Truman. That paper, the history says, charted later major programs: Greek-Turkish aid, the Marshall Plan, and the North Atlantic Alliance.
cia-0000109823: Operational Report from 1200 Thursday 18 October to 1200 Thursday 26 October 19 is the heading on CIA document 0000109823, dated September 5, 1945. The title sets a precise span: noon on one Thursday to noon on the next. The year itself breaks off at 19 in the released heading. The brief record preserves the span and the break as released.
cia-0000119723:
A short CIA item from September 1956 reports that top Hungarian party leaders plan to visit Belgrade. Yugoslavia under Tito stood as proof that a communist state could defy Moscow and survive. Hungarian leaders looking toward Belgrade were looking toward that example.

Visits between party leaders were read as signals of direction. A Budapest trip to Tito's capital hinted at loosening ties to the Soviet model weeks before Hungary rose in revolt. The item is brief, but its place in the sequence matters. It belongs to the autumn when Hungary's leaders and people alike were testing how far independence could go.
cia-0000122523: A January 1992 CIA document covers Iraqi biological weapons mission planning, BW being the file's short form for that class of weapons. It was written after the Gulf War, while inspectors hunted for Saddam's hidden stores. The paper preserves what the agency knew of Iraq's germ warfare plans. Mission planning papers sit closer to operations than general surveys, since they concern how weapons would actually be used rather than whether they existed at all.
cia-0000132423: Further drastic state controls planned by the Cuban government fill item 10 of the CIA's Latin America series. The item is dated January 1, 1960. Its headline breaks off after the announcement of those plans. The revolution was tightening its grip on the island's economy month by month. The short item reports what new controls were being prepared as the new year opened.
cia-0000132623: Khrushchev's assurances encouraging anti-American Cuban leaders fill a CIA item dated June 1, 1960. The headline misspells encourage as encourgae, a slip kept from the original, and then breaks off at a second topic. Soviet backing was the wind in the revolution's sails that year. Moscow's promises emboldened Havana against Washington. The short item reports the assurances and their effect.
cia-0000135723: A Spanish-language paper dated 4 November 1960, filed in the declassified 2506 Brigade collection. The brigade was then in its first months of CIA-run training, and its paperwork ran in Spanish, the language of its Cuban members. The catalog record gives this item no subject. It joins a cluster of brigade documents from that November week. The text is preserved as released, for readers to examine directly.
cia-0000135823: A CIA report from 1 January 1954, now declassified, deals with a contact report from the Lincoln station, the field log of a meeting held for the operation. In these files Lincoln names the field station of PBSUCCESS, the covert CIA plan to topple President Arbenz of Guatemala. What survives is the working paper itself, plain proof of how the mission was run from day to day.
cia-0000135923: From the CIA files comes a cable dated 1 January 1954, long since declassified, on contacts made in Washington, reported back by the Lincoln station in a short cable. Lincoln was where PBSUCCESS staff worked the Guatemala operation day to day, under code names, in 1953 and 1954. The file rewards slow reading, since its short heading is often the only summary the agency ever gave it.
cia-0000136123: A situation report of 2 April 1954 survives in the declassified CIA files, dealing with the situation report for 3 to 10 May. All of it feeds into PBSUCCESS, the agency operation against the Arbenz government in the months before the June 1954 coup. The paper trail here is small but direct, a single piece of the huge file the operation left behind.
cia-0000136623: A Spanish text dated 2 February 1961, filed in the 2506 Brigade papers released by the CIA. The brigade of Cuban exiles was drilling for the invasion that spring. The catalog record offers no subject for the document. Kept in Spanish, it is a dated piece of the brigade's paperwork from its last winter, presented as released, for readers working through the operation's primary record.
cia-0000136723: An August 1, 1960 date heads this Spanish text from the 2506 Brigade papers. The brigade, the CIA's force of Cuban exiles, was in its first months of training that summer. The catalog record names no subject for the document. Preserved in the original Spanish, it is an early piece of the brigade's paperwork, from the season when the operation was still being assembled in secret.
cia-0000137323: Cuba items largely fizzled at this NSC briefing. It was the 362nd meeting, on 14 April 1959. The attached record reports the outcome. The briefer used a few paragraphs of the prepared text. The matter was only incidental, he said. A target had not been hit by Castro's followers, in garbled phrasing. The surviving text is mostly minutes. Questions were asked. Statements were made or not made. The next meeting was scheduled. It shows how briefly Cuba registered before it dominated.
cia-0000139023: Mukden welcomed the Red Army, then was looted by it. A German resident merchant's statement tells the story in this April 1946 report. News of the war's end brought relief in Mukden. Japanese women and children were being evacuated in chaos. Japanese units then dismantled the gun positions. Peace held, though the mood was tense. Most people expected an orderly occupation. The Soviet Union was China's ally, after all. Airborne troops arrived on 19 August to joy, food, and drink. Known anti-Soviet emigrants were arrested at once.
cia-0000139323: A Moscow-issued manifesto is examined in this OSS memorandum to Whitney Shepardson. The document ran in the Daily Digest of World Broadcasts in July 1945. Its publication caused considerable discussion at home. The writer checked its bona fide quality. Similar documents had appeared before. A Rhineland Conference manifesto ran in the Daily Worker last winter. London Socialists call this one quite reactionary. It advocates restoring property looted by the Nazis. They label it another popular front of the reaction.
cia-06464723:
National Foreign Assessment Center paper, marked Secret with WNINTEL and NOFORN controls, is titled The Generals Take Command in Turkey: Problems and Prospects. Its summary states that the military took control of the Turkish government on 12 September, in a year the text gives as 1980. Frustration with disorder, economic malaise, and political deadlock is named as the cause.

The paper assesses that the commanders would stay in power as long as needed to restore order and steady the economy. It expects basic political and constitutional change to follow. In the short term, the new regime was judged likely to bring a measure of order and economic balance. Later pages expect a revised constitution favoring community needs and order, and a move away from proportional representation toward a majority system.
cicero-de-divinatione-falconer-1923:
William Armistead Falconer's Loeb volume of Cicero appeared in 1923 with Latin and English together. It joins On Old Age, On Friendship, and On Divination in one book. The Divination treatise stages Rome's great debate about foretelling the future.

Cicero's brother Quintus defends omens, entrails, and prophetic dreams in book one. Cicero himself dismantles those claims with wit and logic in book two. He asks why gods would speak in riddles through bird flights. The dialogue preserves Roman religious practice while questioning its basis. Falconer's translation keeps the argument clear and lively. Ancient skepticism rarely reads this sharply.
conrad-rover-1923:
The Rover, published in 1923, was the last novel Conrad completed, and it has the calm of a farewell. Peyrol, an old buccaneer and brother of the coast, retires to a farm on the French Mediterranean after the Revolution.

England and France are at war, and Peyrol is drawn into one last mission: carrying false dispatches to sea to mislead the British fleet. Around him gather a scarred girl, a patriot, and a naval lieutenant, in a story of sacrifice and quiet honor. Conrad wrote it in his final illness. Its serenity feels earned, like a seaman's last landfall.
constitution-india-2023:
India's constitution took force in 1950, making the new nation a republic, and the hosted text runs through changes made by 2023. It is the longest national charter in the world, with hundreds of articles plus long schedules. Early parts cover the union and its land, citizenship, and a famous bill of basic rights. A separate part gives guiding principles of state policy that courts cannot enforce but governments must weigh.

India is a federation of states. A president heads the union, while a prime minister and cabinet hold real power and answer to Parliament. Parliament pairs the Lok Sabha, chosen by the people, with the Rajya Sabha for the states. Later parts cover the courts, elections, languages, and emergencies.
constitution-jamaica-2023:
Jamaica gained this constitution at independence from Britain in 1962, and the hosted text carries changes through 2023. Early chapters cover citizenship and, since a 2011 rewrite, a charter of basic rights and freedoms. The older text had guarded rights more loosely, so the charter was a real upgrade for free speech, fair trials, and equality before the law.

A Governor-General speaks for the monarch as head of state. Real power sits with a prime minister and cabinet drawn from Parliament. Parliament pairs an elected House of Representatives with an appointed Senate. Later chapters cover the courts, the public service, and finance. Debate about cutting the last tie to the crown and becoming a republic has run for years in Jamaica.
constitution-mali-2023:
Mali adopted a new constitution by public vote in 2023, under a military-led transition after two coups. Early titles cover the state and sovereignty. Mali is a single, secular republic. The text names the country's national languages as official languages, with French kept on as a working language, a shift meant to honor tongues most Malians actually speak.

A president with strong powers leads the executive, helped by a prime minister. The 2023 text adds a Senate beside the National Assembly, giving parliament two houses for the first time. Later titles cover the courts, local areas, and public finance. Term limits for the president are written in, though the transition's own length stayed a sore point at home and abroad.
constitution-nigeria-2023:
Nigeria works under a constitution from 1999, which restored elected rule after years of generals, and the hosted text carries changes through 2023. Early chapters give general provisions for a federal republic of thirty-six states plus a capital territory. Chapter two lists the goals and guiding principles of state policy. Chapter four protects basic rights, from life and fair trial to speech, worship, and movement.

A president heads both state and government and must win votes spread across the federation, not just in one region. The National Assembly pairs a Senate, three members per state, with a House of Representatives. Later chapters cover state governors and assemblies, the courts, the police and armed forces, and public finance. Sharing oil wealth among the states fills many pages.
constitution-peru-2023:
Peru works under a constitution from 1993, written under President Alberto Fujimori after he shut down the old congress, and the hosted text carries changes through 2023. Title one covers the person and society, with a chapter of basic rights, then social and economic rights, then political rights and duties. Spanish is the official language, with Quechua, Aymara, and other native tongues official where they prevail.

A president leads the executive. The Congress of the Republic is a single chamber, a design the 1993 text chose and voters kept in a later referendum. A president of the council of ministers runs the cabinet. Later titles cover the courts, elections, local regions and towns, defense, and how the charter changes.
constitution-tuvalu-2023:
Tuvalu, a Pacific nation of low atolls facing rising seas, adopted a new constitution in 2023, and that text is hosted here. Early parts cover the state and the constitution itself, then a bill of rights. One clause drew world notice. Tuvalu's statehood is declared to last forever, even if the sea takes its land. The clause anchors the country's plan to keep its seat among nations as a digital state.

A Governor-General speaks for the monarch as head of state. Real power sits with a prime minister drawn from Parliament, a single small chamber. Later parts cover the courts, the public service, citizenship, and finance. Each island also keeps a traditional council of elders, the Falekaupule, honored in the text.
constitution-uzbekistan-2023:
Uzbekistan adopted a heavily renewed constitution by public vote in 2023, and that text is hosted here. Early parts cover state sovereignty, the people, and the weight of the constitution and the law. The renewed text calls the country a social state and lengthens its promises on rights, from housing and health to a clean environment. Uzbek is the state language, and the republic of Karakalpakstan keeps its self-rule inside the state.

A president heads the state and holds wide power. The Oliy Majlis pairs a Legislative Chamber with a Senate. Later parts cover the government, the courts, a Constitutional Court, local rule, elections, and finance. Officials said about two thirds of the old text was rewritten; the reset also let the sitting president run for fresh terms.
constitution-vanuatu-2023:
Vanuatu, a Pacific island nation, gained this constitution at independence from Britain and France in 1980, and the hosted text includes changes through 2023. Early chapters cover the state and sovereignty. Vanuatu is a republic whose national language is Bislama, a creole spoken across its many islands. English and French are also official languages, a mark of the joint rule that came before. A full chapter gives basic rights and duties.

A president serves as head of state in a ceremonial post. A prime minister leads the government from Parliament, the single lawmaking chamber. A National Council of Chiefs, the Malvatumauri, advises on custom and land, and the text says all land belongs to its custom owners. Later chapters cover the courts and finance.
cooper-pioneers-1823:
James Fenimore Cooper published The Pioneers in 1823, the first of the Leatherstocking Tales. Cooper drew on his own family's founding of Cooperstown, New York, and set the story there in 1793, as settlement tamed the wilderness. The novel asks what progress costs, and who pays.

Judge Marmaduke Temple rules the new town, while old Natty Bumppo, the hunter Leatherstocking, watches the forest fall. Settlers slaughter pigeons and net fish wastefully, and Natty is arrested for killing a deer out of season. A young stranger with a hidden claim to the land complicates every plot. Cooper founded the American frontier myth here, with sympathy on both sides of the axe.
cosmopolite-ou-nouvelle-lumiere-chymique:
A French alchemy treatise dated 1723 presents the Cosmopolite's new chemical light in three linked parts. The parts treat nature in general, then sulphur, then the true salt of the philosophers, with mercury taken up in the first. Old French spelling and broken type mark the scan, yet the text can be read.

The first treatise asks what nature is and who should seek her secrets. It says wise men before the Flood, Hermes among them, left rules for finding the philosophers' stone. Work with metals, the soul drawn out of them, and its return to the body all come under study. The book speaks to readers of early chemical thought in its own coded tongue.
cummings-tulips-and-chimneys-1923:
The first book of poems by E. E. Cummings was Tulips and Chimneys, published in 1923. Cummings had served as an ambulance driver in the First World War and been held in a French detention camp. His Harvard education and war experience both feed the poems.

The collection mixes sonnets, songs, and portraits with early experiments in spacing and broken lines. Cummings mocks stuffed shirts and celebrates spring, lovers, and street life in the same breath. Readers met a voice already reshaping the lyric from inside: playful, tender, and formally daring. The publisher cut some poems, but the book still marks the beginning of Cummings's lifelong reinvention of poetry.
delamare-riddle-1923:
Walter de la Mare wrote tales of quiet dread in The Riddle, and Other Tales, his set from 1923. His folk are shy, lone, and ill at ease. Strange guests call. Old aunts hold dark pasts. A sense of wrong hangs in rooms where naught seems out of place.

His most famed tale peers at a grim aunt through a child's eyes. Naught leaps out. Fear seeps in slow, line by line, till it chills the spine. De la Mare shows that the strange tale can whisper and still wound. His prose has the calm of verse, which he also wrote with grace. Sound and pause do as much work as plot in these tales.
doe-osti-3022094-measurements-of-the-sup:
Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory report LLNL-TR-2011630, by Jack Silano and colleagues, reports new measurements of fission cross-section ratios made with monoenergetic neutron beams. Using actinide foils in a fission chamber, the team measured the 238U/235U and 239Pu/235U ratios at several beam energies, improving data that reactor and safeguards calculations rely on.

One result is flagged as unresolved. Data for the plutonium ratio at 1.8 MeV, taken with the tritium-based neutron production target, showed upstream-to-downstream effects the team's beam model could not reproduce, pointing to a systematic effect still under investigation. As a check on the method, a plutonium-against-plutonium foil pair with an atom ratio of 3.01 plus or minus 0.02 returned the expected ratio of 1 at 6.4 MeV using the deuterium-based reaction.
dospassos-streets-of-night-1923:
Doran published Streets of Night in New York, with a motto in old French from Peire Vidal. Chapter one drops readers into a dressing room where Cham Mason urges Fanshaw out. Fanshaw, tall and skinny, scratches his neck and dreads the evening ahead.

Cham waves a shirt and fits cuff-links while he wheedles his friend. The date is set, he insists, since Al Winslow fell ill with scarlet fever. Beyond that small scene, restless young thinkers drift through Boston streets and boarding houses. Hungry for meaning in a hollow world, they give the 1923 novel its dark and brooding Jazz Age mood.
europmc-pmc10108523:
Diesh and a large team present JBrowse 2, a modular genome browser, in a 2023 paper. Genome browsers let scientists view genes and DNA features laid out along a genome. JBrowse 2 keeps the strengths of the first JBrowse while adding views for harder problems, such as large structural changes in DNA.

New views show shared gene order across species, breakpoints, and gene fusions. The tool runs in a web browser and can be extended by other developers. The paper introduces software now used by labs and genome databases worldwide for viewing annotations.
europmc-pmc10172123:
Liao and the Human Pangenome Reference Consortium present the first draft of a new kind of human genome reference, called a pangenome, in a 2023 paper. Past genome references rested mostly on DNA from a few people, which left out much human variety. A pangenome instead holds the genomes of many people in one combined reference.

The draft contains full genome assemblies from forty-seven people of diverse backgrounds. Together they cover nearly all of the sequence scientists expected to find. The resource should help researchers spot disease-linked variants that a single reference missed, in every population.
europmc-pmc10401723:
Ma led the INTERACT3 trial in 2023, with the INTERACT3 Investigators, on care after a brain bleed. A bleed inside the brain is one form of stroke, and early blood pressure control looks most hopeful. Hospitals in nine low- and middle-income nations, plus Chile, took part. Wards switched to the new care plan in a set order.

The bundle set strict goals to reach fast, each within an hour where apt. Blood pressure had to fall below 140, blood sugar sat in a tight range, and fever had to drop. Blood thinners were reversed at speed when needed. The main test was how well patients could act on their own at six months. Scores ran from no symptoms to death.
europmc-pmc10436623:
Zhang and a large team reviewed short-chain fatty acids in 2023, small chemicals made by gut microbes. The microbes make them by fermenting fibre from food in the gut. Three main kinds are acetate, propionate, and butyrate. They serve as a key fuel for the cells that line the gut.

These acids do far more than feed gut cells. Zhang shows that they help control blood sugar, gut motion, and the gut wall seal. They switch on cell sensors called GPR41 and GPR43. They also tune how genes are read, which steers cell growth and immune acts. Faults in their levels link to gut, metabolic, and wider diseases.
europmc-pmc11102923:
Zhou and colleagues survey tumour biomarkers from discovery to bedside use in this 2024 review. A biomarker is a substance made by a tumour or by the body in response to one. Such markers can aid screening, early diagnosis, outlook prediction, relapse detection, and tracking of treatment effect. Progress in molecular biology has sped their discovery sharply.

The review traces the history of these markers and the classic and new detection technologies. It classifies markers by the tissue they come from. A highlight is the rise of targeted therapies chosen by marker status, which the authors call a breakthrough path in cancer care. Limits and open challenges are discussed as well. The authors link better markers to the spread of personalised medicine and improved patient outcomes.
europmc-pmc1183523:
Libby and co-authors probed glaucoma damage in mice in 2005. Glaucoma is an eye disease where high pressure harms the optic nerve. Retinal ganglion cells, which carry vision signals, slowly die. The team asked whether a cell death gene called Bax drives that loss.

Mice with less Bax kept their ganglion cells far better. Even mice missing one copy gained strong protection. Their nerve fibers still wore down, though more slowly. Libby draws a clear split between cell body death and fiber decay. Each part may need its own treatment.
europmc-pmc1463023:
How does a young gonad become a testis or an ovary? Kim and co-authors studied two opposing signals in mouse embryos in 2006. One signal, Fgf9, pushes toward testis. The other, Wnt4, pushes the other way. Both are present in gonads of both sexes before the choice is made.

The male gene Sry tips the scale. It starts a loop that boosts Fgf9 and shuts Wnt4 down. Kim found that removing Wnt4 from female gonads raised Fgf9 even without Sry. The work frames sex determination as a tug of war. Any switch that tips the balance could serve that role in other species.
europmc-pmc1479323:
Antibodies latch onto short spots on germ proteins, called epitopes. Larsen, Lund, and Nielsen sought better ways to forecast those spots in 2006. Knowing them aids vaccine and test design. They built three data sets of known linear epitopes, from papers, a database, and HIV records.

They tested rival methods on data none had trained on. A hidden Markov model, a stats tool that reads patterns in sequence, did best alone. Joining it with a scale-based method gave a tool named BepiPred. It beat all rivals by a clear margin. Larsen offers the tool and data free online for other labs.
europmc-pmc1637123:
Sticking to HIV drug regimens decides whether treatment works. Mills and co-authors reviewed patient-reported barriers and aids in 2006, across rich and poor nations. They gathered 37 qualitative studies and 47 surveys.

Fear of disclosure, revealing one's HIV status, ranked among the top barriers in both settings. Substance abuse and forgetfulness also recurred. Aids included social support and simple routines. Most studies came from developed nations, 72 of 84. Mills pooled the surveys to estimate how common each barrier is, giving programs a generalizable picture of what blocks adherence.  Forgetfulness and pill burden also surfaced again and again across the surveys.
europmc-pmc1697823:
A small set of stem-like cells may drive brain tumor regrowth and drug failure. Liu and co-authors profiled those cells in glioblastoma in 2006, marked by the surface protein CD133. Such cells can seed new tumors.

In three patient cell lines, CD133 cells made up 10 to 70 percent. Their neural precursor genes ran far higher than in matched negative cells, one by 1,351-fold. They also overexpressed drug pump and repair genes, and resisted four chemotherapy drugs, including temozolomide. CD133 levels ran higher in recurrent tumors than in first tumors from the same patients. Liu ties the cells to treatment failure.
europmc-pmc1762423:
Designer scaffolds made of self-assembling peptides can cradle nerve stem cells in 3D. Gelain and co-authors built such a system in 2006 for adult mouse neural stem cells, moving beyond flat dish culture. They attached functional motifs to the peptide RADA16.

The motifs covered cell adhesion, differentiation, and bone marrow homing. Peptides assembled into nanofibers resembling a common lab gel. Two scaffolds with homing motifs markedly boosted neural cell survival without added growth factors. Cell marker profiles matched those on the standard gel. Gelain stresses every ingredient is known and pure, unlike animal-derived gels.
europmc-pmc1779523:
Blomme and co-authors traced in 2006 how genes were gained and lost across 600 million years of vertebrate history. Vertebrates are animals with backbones, from fish to humans. A long debate asks whether early vertebrate genomes were doubled whole, once or twice, or grew only by small copying events.

The team compared genomes from more than 14 vertebrate species and mapped gene families onto the family tree. Their analysis found a clear burst of new duplicated genes near the dawn of vertebrates. That pattern supports the view that whole genome doubling events shaped early vertebrate evolution. Later lineages then lost many of the extra copies. The work weighs in for large early duplications as a driver of vertebrate complexity.
europmc-pmc1797623:
Binladen, Willerslev and co-authors showed in 2007 how to sequence matching DNA stretches from many specimens in one machine run. The 454 sequencing platform could produce huge volumes of data, but pooled samples could not be told apart afterward. That blocked studies comparing the same gene across many individuals.

Their fix adds a short tag to the front of each primer, the short DNA piece that starts copying, with a different code per specimen. After one pooled run, each read is traced home by its tag. Nearly all sequences landed with the correct source, and the mis-assignment rate stayed under 0.4 percent once machine errors were handled. One bias appeared: primers whose tag began with the base cytosine were heavily overrepresented in the final reads.
europmc-pmc1828623:
Nishida and Walker tested in 2007 whether a daytime nap locks in a newly learned hand skill. Motor memories are known to improve across a night of sleep, with quiet non-REM sleep doing much of the work. Their study asked if a short midday nap could give the same gain.

Two groups trained in the morning on a left-hand motor task and were tested eight hours later. One group napped for 60 to 90 minutes at midday, while the other stayed awake. Only the nap group showed a clear performance gain at testing. Within that group, gain tracked total stage-2 non-REM sleep. A finer analysis tied gain to sleep spindles, brief brain wave bursts, over the brain side that controlled the trained hand. The regional pattern matched the memory's own brain map.
europmc-pmc1851623:
Takahashi, Neumann and co-authors tried a cell therapy in 2007 for a mouse model of multiple sclerosis. In that disease, immune attack strips the fatty myelin coating from nerve fibers. Stopping inflammation is possible, but repair remains the hard part, and clearing dead myelin is one step toward it.

They fitted bone marrow precursor cells with extra copies of TREM2, a receptor that boosts eating of debris by immune cells. Given into a vein at the peak of disease, the cells reached inflamed spinal cord lesions. There they cleared degenerated myelin, raised their digestive activity, and shifted local signals toward calm. Treated mice showed milder symptoms, less axon damage, and no further myelin loss. The work shows gene-tuned myeloid cells can aid nervous tissue recovery.
europmc-pmc1855923:
Andreassen and colleagues surveyed health internet use in 2007 across seven European countries. Citizens were being offered more online health services, yet patterns of use and expectations of doctors were unclear. The study drew representative samples from seven countries: Norway and Denmark, Germany, Greece, Poland, and Portugal, plus Latvia, reaching 7,934 people by telephone.

Overall, 44 percent of respondents had used the internet for health purposes, rising to 71 percent among internet users. Use ran higher among the young, the better educated, recent doctor visitors, and people with long-term illness. Women were the most active health users online. One in four had gone online to prepare for a doctor's visit or to follow up after one. Feeling reassured afterward was twice as common as feeling anxious, and over a third rated a doctor's e-health services as important when choosing a new doctor.
europmc-pmc1964923:
Olsen and co-authors measured in 2007 how slowly three industrial fluorochemicals leave the human body. The compounds PFOS, PFHxS, and PFOA turn up in people and wildlife worldwide, and animal species clear them at very different speeds. Retired production workers, no longer exposed at work, offer a clean test of human clearance.

Twenty-six retirees, 24 men and two women, gave blood samples over five years. Starting blood levels averaged 799 nanograms per milliliter for PFOS, 290 for PFHxS, and 691 for PFOA, with wide ranges between workers. For every person, the fall in concentration was steady and matched a first-order model, meaning a constant fraction leaves per unit time. That model yields the serum elimination half-life for each compound, the benchmark regulators use for these persistent chemicals.
europmc-pmc2124523:
Leo Buerger and Adèle Oppenheimer of the pathological laboratory of Mt. Sinai Hospital in New York reported true bone forming inside hardened arteries in 1908. Recent work had shown such bone is less rare than supposed. In six cases of arteriosclerosis, Mönckeberg found sixteen bony foci in large vessels. Their own case came from a study of vessels in gangrene of the lower limbs, where two limbs showed wide areas of ossification.

They record the fine structure of one case in detail, stressing its many bony plaques. Under the microscope, they trace tissue sprouting vessels, meeting lime salts, and laying down osteoid and then bone, much as bone forms over cartilage. The lime plates in the artery's middle coat play the cartilage's part. Readers get a close account of a strange transformation: a blood vessel turning to bone.
europmc-pmc2124623:
Richard M. Pearce of the Bender Laboratory in Albany studied in 1906 how adrenalin injections damage the heart muscle of rabbits. A prior study with Dr. Stanton had targeted lesions of the aorta from repeated adrenalin doses. In the few hearts examined then, the muscle often showed clear degeneration, and sometimes growth of new tissue.

That pairing raised the question Pearce pursues here. Can a chronic myocarditis like the human kind, seen with grave arterial disease, be produced in the laboratory? And how much of the heart damage is the drug's direct work, rather than a side effect of the arterial lesions? One specimen's aorta is ringed at its origin by close-set calcified areas. Readers get an early effort to separate a drug's direct harm from the harm done by the vessels it injures.
europmc-pmc2124723:
Eugene L. Opie and J. C. Meakins, of the pathological laboratory of the Presbyterian Hospital of New York, gathered the evidence on hemorrhagic necrosis of the pancreas in 1909. The disease, also called acute hemorrhagic pancreatitis, had been clearly recognized some fifty years earlier by Klebs. He blamed the eroding action of the pancreas's own ferments. Fitz's lecture twenty years before had set the classification still in use.

The authors stress a trap for the unwary. Animal experiments could now reproduce the lesion many ways, and human cases are read against that data. In one case, no bacteria grew from pus found at operation. A freed tryptic enzyme is treated as part of the destructive force. Readers get a careful sorting of a dramatic disease from the decay that imitates it.
europmc-pmc2125323:
Wade H. Brown examined in 1915 how the rat trypanosome, Trypanosoma lewisi, can be changed by experimental handling, above all in virulence. Different strains, he argues, are different states of balance between the parasite's powers of multiplying and its liability to destruction. A strain's balance also swings in cycles, driven by the immune reactions of the host's blood.

The two sides of the balance turn out to be separable. Virulence at its height combines reproductive fastness, strong antigenic action, and susceptibility to destruction, in varying degrees. A passage system fitted to the strain can eventually transform both the character and the course of the infection; the moment chosen for each transfer matters. Readers get a parasite treated as adjustable, its deadliness a setting rather than a fixed trait.
europmc-pmc2128223:
Hideyo Noguchi compared two near-twin spiral germs: Leptospira icteroides, his candidate for the cause of yellow fever, and Leptospira icterohaemorrhagiae, the germ of Weil's disease. His paper is the tenth in his yellow fever series, in the Journal of Experimental Medicine in 1920. Thirteen strains were tested by clumping, the Pfeiffer reaction, complement fixation, and the protective power of immune sera.

An earlier experiment had suggested the two are closely related but not identical. The full battery of tests now bears that out: on thirteen strains, the two groups react distinctly in immune tests, though the difference may amount only to that between subspecies or races. Their disease pictures also differ, icteroides leaning to jaundice and kidney inflammation, the other to bleeding. Cross-protection ran partly both ways, which fits close kinship. The paper firms the line between the yellow fever suspect and its Weil's disease cousin.
europmc-pmc2128423:
M. Heidelberger and O. T. Avery concentrated and purified the soluble specific substance of the pneumococcus, the material Dochez and Avery had shown appears in culture fluid and reacts only with its own type's serum. Their paper appeared in the Journal of Experimental Medicine in 1923, from the Rockefeller Institute hospital.

The purified material turned out to consist mainly of a carbohydrate. It appears to be a polysaccharide, a long sugar chain built up of glucose units. Whether the specific substance is the polysaccharide itself, or merely rides along with it, the authors leave undecided. The evidence, they say, points toward the substance being the sugar itself. A bacterial type marker made of sugar rather than protein was a striking result, and it set the chemical course for pneumococcus typing.
europmc-pmc2130923:
Hans Zinsser and J. Howard Mueller examined what bacterial allergy really is, using tuberculin sensitivity as the test case. Their paper appeared in the Journal of Experimental Medicine in 1925. The central question was whether dissolved bacterial products and the antibodies they raise can account for allergy. The alternative was that living tissue reaction is required.

Tuberculin sensitivity, they conclude, is definitely tied to tissue reactions, to actual inflammatory processes in the body. Merely raising antibodies by injecting dissolved bacterial material does not induce allergy. The allergy can be passed to fresh guinea pigs, by extracts of tuberculous tissue from rabbits and even by such rabbits' serum. The donors need many, well developed, and not too advanced lesions. Those transfers were definite but irregular, and the conveying power has no relation to the serum's precipitating power. Allergy and antibody, the work insists, travel separately.
europmc-pmc2131523:
Robscheit-Robbins and Whipple published part fourteen of their blood regeneration series in 1929. Dogs were kept severely anemic by bleeding, then fed liver materials to test how fast blood rebuilds. A liver extract sold as potent against human pernicious anemia was fed alone, then mixed with whole liver, liver ash, or fresh bile, to see what each part adds.

The extract alone showed only a tenth to a fifth of the power of whole liver feeding, and dogs varied widely on it, unlike on whole liver. Added bile changed nothing. Liver ash or apricot ash added only its own expected share. A small amount of whole liver with the extract, though, gave more blood building than the two shares added together.
europmc-pmc2246223:
Dent and co-workers tested a bedside device in 2007 for predicting acute kidney injury after children's heart surgery. Kidney injury is a frequent complication of cardiopulmonary bypass, the heart-lung machine, and standard tests detect it days late. The candidate marker is plasma NGAL, a protein released by injured kidneys. The team first checked the point-of-care device against lab assays on forty samples, then enrolled 120 children undergoing bypass.

The device matched lab results closely, with a correlation of 0.94 between the two. Injury developed in 45 children, or 37 percent of the group. In these young bypass patients, creatinine-based diagnosis lagged two to three days behind the actual injury. Plasma NGAL tripled within two hours of bypass and stayed high. The two-hour level was the strongest independent predictor of injury, with accuracy 0.96 at a cutoff of 150. Twelve-hour levels correlated with mortality.
europmc-pmc2265523:
Liu and co-workers dissected the mammalian circadian clock in 2008, focusing on two repressor proteins, REV-ERB alpha and beta. The clock's core loop is stabilised by a second loop where REV-ERBs repress the Bmal1 gene. Single deletions were muddied by backup effects. Combining gene knockout with RNA interference in cells, the team removed both repressors together and watched cell-autonomous rhythms.

The two REV-ERBs proved functionally redundant, each covering for the other. Together they are required for rhythmic Bmal1 expression. Their activator counterparts, the RORs, affect Bmal1's amplitude but not its rhythm. Cells lacking both REV-ERBs still kept normal Per2 rhythmicity. Even cells with constant BMAL1 kept time. The clock's core is thus remarkably resilient, and the second loop may mainly drive rhythmic output genes.
europmc-pmc2288623:
Danesh and a large team measured long-term interleukin-6 levels and heart disease risk in 2008 across two large cohorts and a systematic review. Interleukin-6 is an inflammatory signal whose levels fluctuate, so single measurements may underestimate its relevance. The team used repeat measurements years apart to correct for within-person variability. Their cohorts held 24,230 participants, including 2,138 who later had a first heart attack or died of coronary disease.

Ignoring variability, the adjusted odds ratio was 1.46 per two standard deviation rise in baseline levels. After correction for long-term average levels it rose to 2.14 on the same scale. Confidence limits excluded no effect in both prospective cohorts studied by the team. Risk climbed progressively with higher levels. Adding fifteen earlier studies gave a combined ratio of 1.61 at baseline. Long-term interleukin-6 thus rivals major established risk factors, though causality remains uncertain.
europmc-pmc2409523:
O'Donnell and colleagues gave the first human tests of a hormone-blocking drug for prostate cancer in 2004. The drug, abiraterone acetate, blocks an enzyme that helps the body make testosterone, the male hormone that fuels prostate cancer. It was tested in three small dose-rising studies in men with and without prior castration treatment.

A single 500 milligram dose pushed testosterone below 0.14 nanomoles per litre in four of six castrate men, near the limit of detection. In men with working testes, 800 milligrams daily hit the target in all three patients at first. But rising luteinising hormone, the brain's counter-signal, broke the block within three days in two of them. By day 11 every patient on repeated dosing failed a standard adrenal stress test, though resting cortisol stayed normal. The authors proposed pairing the drug with steroid replacement.
europmc-pmc2409623:
Moses and colleagues measured energy use in wasting pancreatic cancer patients in 2004. The wasting state is called cachexia, and these patients often burn more energy at rest yet move less and less. The team studied 24 patients living at home, using labelled water to track total energy burn over days.

At the start, resting energy burn ran higher than healthy predictions, at 1,387 versus 1,268 kilocalories a day. Total burn was nonetheless lower, at 1,732 versus 1,903 kilocalories, because activity had collapsed. Patients then drank a dense energy and protein supplement for eight weeks, with or without a fish-oil fatty acid called EPA. The plain supplement changed nothing. With EPA, resting burn stayed flat but activity and total burn rose significantly, which the authors read as better quality of life.
europmc-pmc2570923:
Saegerman, Berkvens, and Mellor synthesised in 2008 the epidemiology of bluetongue in the European Union since the virus arrived in 1998. Bluetongue is a viral disease of ruminants spread by biting midges; it does not pass directly between animals. Once considered exotic to Europe, it now threatens central and northern parts of the continent, with trade consequences.

The authors review the European situation, the susceptible species, and the midge vectors of the genus Culicoides.
