The virus has 24 serotypes and a genome of ten segments that can shuffle when strains meet, so virulence varies even within a serotype. They discuss how the virus enters new areas and how it amplifies once established. Before 1998 Europe saw only sporadic incursions, such as Spain and Portugal in the late 1950s.
europmc-pmc2581623:
Snelders and colleagues documented in 2008 the emergence of drug resistance in Aspergillus fumigatus, a mould that infects vulnerable patients, in the Netherlands and beyond. Triazole drugs are the main treatment, and resistant cases had begun appearing. The team screened 1,912 clinical isolates collected from 1,219 patients at their medical centre between 1994 and 2007.

Resistant isolates appeared in 32 patients, all after 1999, reaching an annual prevalence between 1.7 and 6 percent in later years. Almost all shared one mechanism: a change called TR/L98H in the cyp51A gene, which also raised resistance to related triazoles. Genetic typing showed distinct but clustered strains. The same mechanism turned up in isolates from nine other Dutch centres and four other countries, suggesting resistant strains are spreading through the environment.
europmc-pmc2602723:
Hershberg and colleagues surveyed DNA diversity in 2008 across a global collection of Mycobacterium tuberculosis complex strains and found far more variety than the field assumed. Human-adapted members of the complex were traditionally treated as essentially identical. The team compared seven million DNA letters of sequence data and linked the patterns to human history.

The diversity they found tracks human demographic and migratory events, echoing our species' movements out of Africa and beyond. Surprisingly, these bacteria sit under extremely weak purifying selection, the force that normally purges harmful changes. As a result, genetic drift runs strong and much of the diversity likely changes what the proteins do. The authors warn that population growth, urbanisation, and global travel could help drug-resistant tuberculosis emerge and spread.
europmc-pmc2646323:
Blanco and the multicentre Grupo de Estudios y Análisis en Cuidados Intensivos group counted cases of severe sepsis in Spanish intensive care units in a study published in 2008. Sepsis is a whole-body reaction to infection that can shut down organs. The group gathered data over two three-month periods in 2002 to measure how common and how deadly it was.

Of 2,619 patients studied, 311 had at least one bout of severe sepsis, about 12 percent. That worked out to roughly 25 cases per 100,000 people each year. Most patients had two or more failing organs when the illness was found, and pneumonia was the most common source. More than half of the sepsis patients died in hospital. Early death was tied to blood and liver failure at diagnosis, and to catching the infection before reaching intensive care.
europmc-pmc2648723:
Nachev and colleagues reported in 2007 on a patient whose rare brain injury revealed how people stop a movement they have already planned. The damage sat in the pre-supplementary motor area, a region at the front of the brain's movement system. Brain scans in healthy people had lit up this area during action tasks, but its exact job was unclear.

The patient could start movements at normal speed. What failed was braking: he struggled to cancel a planned movement, while the matching area on the other side stayed unharmed. The weakness grew sharper when two responses competed for control. Other patients without this damage did not show the same pattern. The team concludes this small area plays a key part in holding back actions when choices clash, a control skill used many times a day.
europmc-pmc2679223:
Mitchell and colleagues worked out in 2009 how the HIV protein Vpu clears a cell defense called BST-2, or tetherin, from the cell surface. Tetherin tethers new virus particles to the cell, stopping their release. Vpu defeats it, but the steps were unknown.

The team showed Vpu recruits a cell protein, beta-TrCP, part of a tagging machine that marks proteins for disposal. Mutations breaking the handshake in Vpu blocked both tetherin removal and virus release, and even poisoned normal Vpu. A second cell adaptor, AP-2, was also needed, though it did not speed tetherin's intake. Instead, Vpu reroutes tetherin after intake toward the cell's acid-filled disposal sacs, where some is destroyed. Blocking acid in those sacs halted the loss. With tetherin gone from the surface, virus buds no longer sat trapped beside it.
europmc-pmc2690823:
Dubrulle and co-authors measured in 2009 how fast two mosquito species pass on a chikungunya variant. This fever virus swept the Indian Ocean islands in 2005 and 2006 in a new form. The variant carries one change in a surface protein that suits it to the Asian tiger mosquito, Aedes albopictus, which is displacing its cousin Aedes aegypti in many regions.

Both species were fed the variant through the mouth in the lab. The virus copied fast in each and reached the salivary glands within two days. From day two onward, both spat infectious virus in their saliva, peaking around days six and seven. The tiger mosquito delivered slightly more virus and counts as a touch more efficient a carrier. The practical warning is stark: once a case appears, local mosquitoes can become dangerous almost at once, so control cannot wait.
europmc-pmc2724423:
Menze and co-authors tested in 2009 a two-step method to classify spectral data, patterns of light or chemical signals with thousands of features. Standard regularized methods handle such data well but cannot drop useless features outright. Random forests, an ensemble of decision trees, can rank feature importance through its Gini score, but its splits fit spectral shapes poorly.

They used Gini importance to select features first, then classified the reduced set with regularized methods. On data sets from medical diagnosis, food science, and other fields, that pairing matched or beat filtering by standard statistical tests. It also beat random forests alone and regularized methods on the full feature set. Feature choice first, then a linear classifier, gave the best of both.
europmc-pmc2799523:
Liao and colleagues scanned resting brains in 2010 to see how epilepsy of the inner temporal lobe rewires whole-brain networks. The condition, called mesial temporal lobe epilepsy, is the most common hard-to-treat epilepsy in adults. They compared eighteen patients with twenty-seven healthy controls using scans that track linked activity across ninety brain regions.

Patients showed stronger links inside the temporal lobes but weaker links within and between the frontal and parietal lobes. Many areas of the resting default network, active when the mind wanders, lost connections to the rest of the brain. Network measures of clustering and path length also shifted, a pattern the authors suggest could serve as a marker for the disease.
europmc-pmc2805623:
Montazeri reviewed twenty-six years of studies in 2009 to ask whether cancer patients' own quality-of-life ratings can predict how long they will live. Clinicians already track tumor facts, but patients' reports of pain, tiredness, and daily function may carry added signal.

From four hundred fifty-one candidate papers, one hundred four met the strict rules for closer reading. With few exceptions, quality-of-life scores predicted survival on their own, even after known clinical factors were counted. Overall quality of life and scores for appetite loss, fatigue, and pain were the strongest signs. Ratings taken before treatment gave the most reliable forecasts, and the author urges better methods in future studies.
europmc-pmc2806523:
Slaidina, Delanoue, Gronke, Partridge, and Léopold found in 2009 that fruit flies keep growing even when they stop eating. Fly growth is driven by insulin-like signals called Dilps, most made in the brain while larvae feed. During the pupal stage, feeding halts for days, so the growth signal must come from elsewhere.

A sixth family member, Dilp6, switches on in the fat body, a storage organ, during that nonfeeding stage. Its release is driven by a steroid hormone and by a stress-linked factor called FoxO. Starvation in larvae also turns Dilp6 on. The work reveals a stress-triggered signal class that sustains growth when food is gone.
europmc-pmc2820523:
Platt and a large team charted the global population structure in 2010 of Arabidopsis thaliana, the small weed that serves as plant biology's main test species. They genotyped five thousand seven hundred seven plants collected worldwide at about one hundred forty-nine marker spots.

The species fertilizes itself about ninety-seven percent of the time, yet local groups varied in how often they crossed. In its home range across Eurasia, genetic difference grew smoothly with distance at every scale, with no sharp borders between populations. North American plants, where the weed is a newcomer, showed little structure across the continent but clear local distance patterns. The authors warn that standard models assuming neat separate clusters fit such species poorly.
europmc-pmc2830923:
Conow, Fielder, Ovadia, and Libeskind-Hadas built Jane in 2010, a software tool for untangling the shared history of hosts and their parasites. When a parasite's family tree is laid over its host's tree, the mismatch pattern tells how the pair evolved together. Events behind the pattern include splitting together, jumping hosts, or vanishing from a host line.

Jane finds low-cost histories that explain both trees with those events. It pairs a fast step-by-step algorithm with a genetic algorithm, a search that breeds good answers toward better ones, and it finds near-best solutions even for large tree pairs. Users can feed in timing data, cap how far a parasite may jump, and test edits by hand in a graphical screen.
europmc-pmc2918523:
Nikander and co-authors pooled in 2010 the randomized trials of long-term supervised exercise aimed at strengthening bone against osteoporosis, across the whole lifespan. Whole bone strength, not just density, was their outcome, drawn from imaging estimates in ten trials of at least six months. Regimens varied hugely in type, dose, and quality, which the analysis graded carefully.

Pooling showed a small overall benefit of training on bone strength, with effects differing between childhood, adolescence, and younger and older adulthood. Growing bones and aging bones appear to answer training on different schedules and magnitudes, so one prescription cannot fit all ages. Short, small trials and scattered weekly doses limited certainty. The review sets the agenda: longer, well-dosed trials targeted at the ages where bone answers best.
europmc-pmc2966423:
Daneman and colleagues built a catalogue of genes active in the mouse blood-brain barrier in a 2010 study. The barrier guards brain chemistry by sealing its blood vessels, yet the molecules that build and run it were little known.

They devised ways to purify vessel lining cells from brain, liver, and lung, then compared their gene activity. Brain lining cells stood out for fresh junction proteins, transporters, metabolic enzymes, and signalling parts, plus many unknown transcripts. One signalling cascade stood out as barrier-specific, offering a handle for study. The dataset serves as a reference for barrier development and drug delivery work.
europmc-pmc2978323:
Higgins, White, and Anzures-Cabrera worked on a pooling problem in a 2008 methods study. The task is combining trial results when outcomes are skewed. Some papers report raw values, while others report logarithms. Leaving studies out wastes evidence, so a common scale is needed.

They review and extend ways to convert between the two reporting styles for two-group studies, including pooled ratios of geometric means. Simulations and a worked example favour a method assuming log-normal raw data, which held up across varied true shapes, with fresh formulas for its uncertainty. Assuming equal spread in both groups helps only when that guess is right.
europmc-pmc2996323:
Davydov and colleagues released GERP++, a tool that finds genome regions held steady by evolution, in a 2010 article. Spots that change little across species usually do something important, so mapping them helps annotate the human genome.

The tool scores each aligned position by its estimated change rate, then uses a fresh search strategy to carve out constrained segments and rank them by significance. It found well over a million such elements covering a larger genome share than earlier estimates, partly by spotting longer elements. Those longer calls also matched known functional sequences more neatly, one to one.
europmc-pmc3022523:
Black led a large team that in 2011 took stock of what digital tools have actually done for health care quality and safety. Their work is an overview of earlier systematic reviews, covering studies from the late nineteen nineties through 2010. The tools in view include electronic health records, picture archiving systems, and computer systems that guide prescribing and clinical choices.

Instead of testing one program, the authors gathered and judged the review literature as a whole. They set out where the gains looked strongest, where proof stayed thin, and where large costly rollouts ran ahead of the evidence. Health leaders can use the overview to set priorities. It points to the areas with the best chance of real benefit for patients.
europmc-pmc3057423:
Yang, Rendas-Baum, Varon, and Kosinski checked in 2011 whether a short questionnaire on headache impact works equally well for occasional and for chronic migraine. The six question survey, called HIT-6 in short, asks how headaches limit work, home life, and mood. The team drew on two large survey datasets covering more than two thousand people with migraine or other headaches.

Scores were consistent when the survey was repeated, and they lined up with disability scores, pain severity, and monthly headache days as expected. People with chronic migraine, defined by very frequent headache days, scored highest, those with episodic migraine scored close behind, and those with non migraine headaches scored much lower. The gaps between groups were large and clear. The authors conclude the short survey is a reliable, valid way to compare headache burden across the migraine spectrum in clinics and research.
europmc-pmc3080923:
Tamerius and colleagues reviewed in 2011 the still unsolved puzzle of why influenza sweeps the globe in seasons. In temperate zones flu peaks in winter, which long suggested cold, dry air was required. Newer reports showed strong flu activity and clear seasons in the tropics too, where warmth and humidity persist all year, breaking the old theory.

The review weighs the rival explanations, from virus survival in air and indoor crowding to sunlight, school terms, and host immunity cycles. Population studies, lab experiments, and computer models each support parts of different stories, and the mechanisms likely interact. The tropics remain the least understood region and the authors' top priority for new work. Settling the question matters for predicting how climate change will shift flu timing region by region.
europmc-pmc3091323:
Wu and coauthors described in 2009 BioGPS, a website that gathers what is known about any gene from dozens of separate databases into one customizable page. Genome wide experiments hand researchers long lists of unfamiliar genes, and checking each one across many specialist sites is slow. BioGPS was built as a community platform where the layout itself can be tailored to a lab's needs.

A gene page can combine sequence and position, known functions, and activity across tissues. It can add mouse knockout results, drug and interaction data, and more, all drawn live from the source databases. Users can add new sources as plug ins and share their layouts with others. The authors argue no single database can ever hold everything about a gene. A flexible portal that federates the rest is the practical answer, and BioGPS had already become a heavily used hub.
europmc-pmc3095423:
Kleinnijenhuis, Oosting, Joosten, Netea, and Van Crevel reviewed in 2011 how the body's first line defenses recognize the tuberculosis bacterium. Tuberculosis still brings about ten million new cases a year, and the opening encounter between bacterium and innate immune cells sets the course of infection. Several families of sensor proteins detect the bacterium's distinctive parts and raise the alarm.

One sensor family does most of the work, with three members sharing the lead role, helped by a common adapter protein. Sugar sensing and internal sensors add further detection layers. Human studies show that inherited differences in these sensors and their signaling partners change a person's risk of disease and its severity. The authors argue that mapping recognition in detail, paired with patient genetics, can guide new immune based therapies and better vaccines for a disease that badly needs them.
europmc-pmc3140523:
Andrea Bonetto and colleagues traced cancer weight loss to a single gene switch in muscle in a 2011 paper in PLoS ONE. Patients with wasting lose muscle despite eating, and the loss tracks with high blood levels of an immune signal and of emergency proteins. The team studied mice with tumours causing moderate and severe wasting.

Wasted muscle switched on one master control pathway strongly in both stages, and its target genes rose sharply. Surprisingly, muscle itself was making large amounts of the emergency proteins normally blamed on the liver, fed by amino acids freed as muscle broke down. Adding the immune signal to cultured muscle cells reproduced the effect. The pathway thus links the immune alarm, the blood protein surge, and muscle loss in one chain.
europmc-pmc3145623:
Weihua Fei and colleagues found why some yeast cells grow giant fat droplets in a 2011 paper in PLoS Genetics. Fat droplets store energy in cells, and their size affects fat burning and cell growth, but size control was a mystery. A genome-wide screen for oversized droplets, some fifty times normal volume, turned up ten mutant genes.

The mutants span fat chemistry, a known droplet protein relative, a signalling enzyme, and two genes of unknown job. All share one trait: raised levels of a particular membrane fat building block. Tests in living cells and in tubes showed this compound helps touching droplets merge into one big drop. The study names the chemical trigger behind supersized droplets and fresh genes in fat management.
europmc-pmc3169623:
Lucie Zinger and colleagues produced the first global map of ocean bacteria in a 2011 paper in PLoS ONE. Marine microbes drive nutrient cycles and much of Earth's biomass, yet their geography was unknown for most waters. The team pooled nearly ten million short gene reads from more than five hundred samples, spanning sunlit surface water to the deep seafloor.

Communities living in open water and in seabed mud differed profoundly, sharing fewer than a tenth of their bacterial types. Depth, distance from shore, and oxygen levels each sorted the communities into distinct sets. Both realms tracked surface productivity, since sinking particles feed the deep. Seabed communities also diverged faster with distance than water ones. The synthesis sketches true bacterial biomes for the oceans.
europmc-pmc3202623:
Julie Adam and colleagues used a mouse model in this 2011 study to ask how loss of the enzyme fumarate hydratase causes kidney cysts. In people, losing this Krebs cycle enzyme is linked to skin growths, kidney cysts, and tumors. A leading theory blamed activation of the hypoxia-response pathway, driven by the buildup of fumarate.

The mouse experiments showed cyst formation did not depend on that hypoxia pathway at all. Instead, accumulated fumarate chemically modified KEAP1, a protein that normally holds back the antioxidant regulator Nrf2. With KEAP1 disabled, antioxidant defenses switched on strongly, a pattern also seen in gene-expression profiles. The authors propose that this disturbed Nrf2 signaling helps drive the cysts and tumors.
europmc-pmc3248123:
Desmond Powe and colleagues reported that breast cancer patients taking beta-blockers fared strikingly better, in this 2010 study in Oncotarget. Laboratory work had shown the beta-blocker propranolol can stop a stress hormone from driving breast cancer cells to migrate. The team checked medical records of more than four hundred women with operable breast cancer followed for over ten years.

Women already taking beta-blockers for blood pressure before diagnosis developed fewer metastases and recurrences and stayed disease-free longer than both other blood-pressure patients and women without hypertension. Their risk of metastasis was cut by well over half, and their risk of dying of breast cancer over ten years fell by about seventy percent. The authors call this proof of principle and ask for larger studies leading to randomized trials, in breast and other cancers.
europmc-pmc3250423:
Christian Krupke and colleagues traced the many ways honey bees encounter farm pesticides near maize fields, in this 2012 study in PLoS ONE. Bee populations had been declining, and neonicotinoid insecticides, highly toxic to bees, were prime suspects, but the exposure routes were undefined. The team chemically analyzed bees, hive pollen, and materials around plantings of treated seed.

During spring planting, the exhaust dust from planters carried extremely high levels of two neonicotinoids. The chemicals appeared in the soil of every field sampled, even unplanted ones, and in dandelion flowers nearby, showing deposition or uptake through roots. Dead bees at hive entrances contained one of the insecticides, stored hive pollen contained it too, and bees readily collected pollen from treated maize at flowering. Exposure, the authors show, lasts all season by several routes.
europmc-pmc3267123:
Sebastien Gagneux reviewed the long coevolution of tuberculosis and its human host in this 2012 paper in Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society B. Tuberculosis is an ancient disease that still kills more adults than any other single infection. Genetic studies have overturned the old idea that it jumped from animals. Its bacterial complex first appeared as a human disease in Africa. It then traveled the world with the first modern human migrations.

Newer bacterial lineages later expanded with population growth and rode waves of exploration, trade, and conquest. Evidence suggests lineages adapted to particular human populations, and the globally successful modern ones provoke less inflammation in immune cells, possibly reflecting greater virulence and shorter latency. Human gene variants are in turn associated with particular lineages. Gagneux argues the disease's biology and spread were shaped by this long association.
europmc-pmc3270023:
Julia Salzman and colleagues reported that circular RNAs are common products of human genes, in this 2012 paper in PLoS ONE. Textbook splicing joins a gene's exons in their genomic order to make a straight molecule. Deep sequencing of RNA from normal and cancerous human cells kept turning up transcripts whose exons appeared shuffled.

Statistical estimates and biochemical tests gave strong evidence that a substantial share of the spliced output from hundreds of genes is circular, with the RNA's ends joined into a loop. In many cases the circular form was the predominant version of the transcript. The authors conclude this unusual splicing is not an oddity. It is a general feature of how human genes are expressed. That opens questions about what these stable circles do in the cell.
europmc-pmc3326523:
Filippakopoulos and a large team mapped the human family of bromodomains, proteins that read one kind of chemical mark on chromosomes, reporting in 2012. These modules latch onto acetyl tags placed on lysine building blocks, a key step in interpreting the cell's epigenetic code. Humans carry sixty one of them, sorted into eight families by shape and sequence.

The team solved twenty nine detailed crystal structures, covering every family, and compared them to find shared and family specific features. Testing representative bromodomains against arrays of chromosome protein pieces revealed new binding partners and showed that nearby marks, such as phosphate tags, strongly sway binding. One family member could grip two acetyl tags at once through a newly revealed mechanism. The maps lay groundwork for designing drugs against this rising target family.
europmc-pmc3347323:
Heald-Sargent and Gallagher reviewed how coronavirus spike proteins get armed to fuse into human cells, in a 2012 article. The spike, studding the virus surface, must grab a cell receptor and then fold dramatically to merge the viral and cell membranes. That folding is not automatic; the spike has to be primed first, like a trap being set.

Three triggers do the priming: docking onto a receptor, being snipped by host cutting enzymes, and the acidity inside the cell compartments the virus passes through. The review gives special attention to a family of surface cutting enzymes known to activate several viral fusion proteins, likely sitting beside receptors ready to split spikes as viruses arrive. The authors close by showing how this entry choreography points to places where antiviral drugs could jam the process.
europmc-pmc3415623:
Sjögren and colleagues showed in 2012 that gut bacteria help set bone mass in mice. Germ-free mice, raised with no microbes at all, grew denser bones than ordinary mice. Their bones held fewer osteoclasts, the cells that dissolve bone, per unit of surface.

Giving germ-free mice a normal gut community brought bone mass back to normal. The sterile mice also had fewer helper T cells and fewer osteoclast precursors in their marrow, plus quieter inflammatory signals in bone. Colonization corrected those immune features too. The chain, the authors argue, runs from gut microbes through immune tone to bone-eating cells. They float the gut as a fresh target for osteoporosis treatment.
europmc-pmc3471323:
Masella and colleagues presented PANDAseq, a program that joins paired DNA reads into single sequences, in BMC Bioinformatics in 2012. Studies of microbe communities rely on reading a marker gene from both ends, then stitching the two reads where they overlap. Simple stitching throws away many reads over small errors, wasting hard-won data.

PANDAseq uses the quality scores attached to each base to fix mismatches and blanks in the overlap. In tests on simulated and real samples, it joined reads faster than rival tools and kept more of them, with few added errors. Gains in usable sequences ranged widely across test libraries. Masella's team notes the program scales to billions of read pairs on ordinary hardware.
europmc-pmc3494723:
Adults who lost hearing after learning speech vary widely with cochlear implants, and Diane S. Lazard leads a very large author group hunting the reasons in 2012. Their retrospective study pools 2,251 patients implanted since 2003 at 15 international centres, converting speech scores into percentile ranks so centres can be compared.

Fifteen factors from before, during, and after surgery are tested. Significant ones include the better ear's hearing threshold, device brand, share of active electrodes, and hearing-aid use, alongside known factors like duration of profound deafness and age. Gender and education show no influence. The team builds a predictive model of implant performance over time for counseling future patients.
europmc-pmc3636323:
A phone app for weight loss went head to head with a website and a paper diary in a 2013 pilot trial in the Journal of Medical Internet Research. Michelle Clare Carter, Victoria Jane Burley, Camilla Nykjaer and Janet Elizabeth Cade ran the trial with 128 adults who were overweight. The app, called My Meal Mate, set goals, tracked food and activity, and sent weekly text feedback.

Weight change, measured as body mass index, fell most in the phone group, by 1.6 points, against 1.0 with the diary and 0.5 with the website. Body fat fell most in the phone group too, by 1.3 percent against 0.9 and 0.5 in the other groups. The team judged the app workable and liked by users, and called for a full trial to test it at scale.
europmc-pmc3638323:
An enzyme shortfall in the brain's black region sits at the heart of a 2012 Annals of Neurology study by Gegg and six colleagues. The enzyme, called GCase, breaks down a fatty substance in cells, and faults in its gene cause Gaucher disease and raise the risk of Parkinson disease. The team checked enzyme levels in brains of people with Parkinson disease, with and without the gene fault.

GCase activity fell in nearly all brain areas checked in the gene-fault group, with the steepest drop, 58 percent, in the black region. Brains with no known gene fault showed smaller drops in the same region and in the cerebellum. Protein levels of the enzyme fell too, while signs of cell stress rose. Checks in grown cells showed that changes tied to Parkinson disease can push down normal GCase.
europmc-pmc3664023:
Sourer seas hit sea life hard, but not all kinds alike, Kroeker and seven colleagues find in a 2013 Global Change Biology meta-analysis. Ocean acidification, the fall in sea pH as water takes up carbon dioxide, threatens species worldwide. The team pooled 228 studies of biological responses to sourer water, the widest sweep yet. Outcomes covered survival, shell building, growth, development and abundance across many sea groups.

Pooled across all, each outcome fell under acidification. The size of the fall varied by group in ways that partly follow traits, giving forecasters some grip. Mollusc larvae stood out as extra sensitive, though early life stages were not the most tender in every group. Multi-species tests swung wider than single-species lab tests. Warming water made acidification bite harder. The authors urge care in scaling lab results up to real seas.
europmc-pmc3680423:
Mobile tools in the hands of community health workers show promise, Braun, Catalani, Wimbush and Israelski find in a 2013 systematic review in PLoS One. In low-resource settings these workers carry much of front-line care. The team searched health, social science and engineering data banks under standard review rules and found 25 full-text research reports on mobile tools used by such workers around the world.

Most work centred on maternal and child health, HIV care and sexual health. Workers used the tools chiefly to collect field data, get alerts and reminders, run health teaching and talk person to person. Reports credit the tools with better rule-following, wider community teaching and stronger program oversight. Most studies were small pilots, though designs are growing more rigorous.
europmc-pmc3689523:
Evans and Murshudov tackle a question every crystallographer faces: how good are the data, and at what resolution should they be cut off? Their paper describes AIMLESS. The program scales X-ray diffraction measurements together. It also reports statistics meant to judge data quality more honestly than older rules of thumb.

They test how refinement behaves when data are cut at different resolutions. The results argue for newer correlation-based measures. Traditional cutoffs can throw away usable signal or keep noise. The paper is both a software description and a plea to let the data, properly measured, decide their own limits.
europmc-pmc3718823:
Andrew Westbrook, Daria Kester, and Todd Braver reported a study in PLoS ONE in 2013 on the felt cost of mental effort. People tend to treat thinking hard as costly, but how costly varies from person to person. The team used a money-choice method, adapted from studies of delayed rewards, to measure how much mental effort makes a cash reward lose value.

Their measures reacted to the load of the task and to the size of the reward. They also differed between people, tracking age and a trait measure of how much a person likes mental challenge. The authors checked their tool against standard delay measures and argue that such choice-based tools can help separate mental ability from mental motivation in research.
europmc-pmc3749523:
Adriaan de Wilde and a large group of co-authors reported a laboratory study in the Journal of General Virology in 2013 on MERS coronavirus. The virus emerged in 2012 and had caused 49 known human cases at the time, 23 of them fatal. The team studied how it grows and damages human and monkey cells.

Under the electron microscope, infected cells showed sweeping membrane changes, including double-membrane vesicles tied to virus copying. Viral RNA and new virus rose fast, followed by heavy cell damage. The team built a screening assay from these traits and found that cyclosporin A blocked the virus in culture. MERS virus was also 50 to 100 times more sensitive to interferon-alpha than the SARS virus, a gap the authors say may matter for treatment.
europmc-pmc3765323:
Run Zhang and seven co-authors reported a rat study in the Journal of Neuroinflammation in 2013 on mesenchymal stem cells after traumatic brain injury. Stem cell transplants had shown benefit in brain injury, but their effect on the immune response inside the brain was little studied. The team gave the cells by vein two hours after injury in rats.

Treated rats had fewer activated microglia and macrophages and fewer invading white blood cells at the injury site. Inflammatory cytokines fell while calming cytokines rose. A factor called TSG-6 rose as well, and may work by damping the NF-kB signaling path. Brain function scores were also tracked. The authors present immune calming as a core part of how the transplant helps recovery.
europmc-pmc3772323:
Grace Mwai and five co-authors published a systematic review in the Journal of the International AIDS Society in 2013 on community health workers in HIV care in sub-Saharan Africa. HIV services there face weak health systems and a drain of trained staff. Community health workers, local people with basic training, are one proposed answer.

The team searched studies up to December 2012 and kept 21. The workers' tasks ranged from counselling, home-based care, and adherence support to screening, referral, and clinic organization. Their presence widened the reach and quality of HIV services, improved patients' dignity, quality of life, and retention in care, and cut clinic waiting times. Clinical outcomes matched facility-based care. But the workers lacked recognition, pay, and a voice in decisions, which the authors say must change for the gains to last.
europmc-pmc3775123:
Marco Sandri wrote a solo review in The International Journal of Biochemistry and Cell Biology in 2013 on protein breakdown in muscle wasting. Muscle mass reflects a balance: when protein breakdown outruns protein building, muscle shrinks. Two disposal systems do most of the breaking down, the ubiquitin-proteasome system and the autophagy-lysosome system.

Both systems switch on during muscle atrophy, sharing the work in proportions that vary by cause. A gene program controls them, tuning the rate-limiting enzymes of each path. The transcription factors FoxO, held back by insulin signaling, and NF-kB, switched on by inflammatory signals, were the first found to be critical. The review covers recent progress on both systems and the growing list of paths and factors that regulate wasting.
europmc-pmc3799423:
Yang and colleagues reported in Nucleic Acids Research a way to edit the genome of human induced pluripotent stem cells without leaving scars. Their method uses re-coded transcription activator-like effectors, called reTALEs, which can be built quickly and aimed at chosen DNA sites.

At the CCR5 gene, they compared a Cas9 guide RNA system with fifteen reTALEN pairs, each paired with a short single-stranded DNA donor. The Cas9 route cut DNA more often, with unwanted joining in about 3 percent of alleles against 0.4 percent, and donor-based repair in 1.0 percent against 0.6 percent. Even so, the team obtained cleanly corrected stem cells within three weeks, showing the approach can fix a target gene while leaving the rest of the genome unchanged.
europmc-pmc3899523:
Kenji Miura and Yasuomi Tada review a plant hormone in Frontiers in Plant Science, with the record dated 2014. Salicylic acid is a natural plant compound best known for steering defense against germs. It also helps plants weather drought, salt, and cold, which gives it farm promise.

Dose decides the effect. Low doses ease stress strain, while high doses stir oxidative harm and cut tolerance. The review centers on water stress and on the leaf pores whose closing saves water, where the hormone runs a feedback loop with reactive oxygen. How the compound is applied and the plant's state matter as much as dose. The authors sort the proof so growers can judge where the hormone truly helps crops.
europmc-pmc3904523:
Douglas E. V. Pires, David B. Ascher, and Tom L. Blundell present a mutation predictor in Bioinformatics, with the record dated 2014. A single swapped building block can steady or wreck a protein, or break its grip on a partner. Forecasting that impact helps read disease mutations in genes such as the tumor suppressor p53.

Their method, mCSM, turns the atomic layout around a spot into a graph signature, a pattern of distances between atoms. Learned models read that signature to call the effect on stability and on binding to other proteins or DNA. On test sets it matched or beat the widely used rival tools. The signature idea proved portable across tasks, which suggests local atomic geometry holds much of a mutation's fate.
europmc-pmc3948723:
Alexandria N. Ardissone and colleagues look for bacteria in newborns' first stool in PLoS ONE in 2014, testing the old dogma that the womb is sterile. Preterm birth is the second leading cause of death in children under five, and many cases have no clear cause. The team reasoned that meconium, the stool a fetus builds before birth, mirrors the microbes swallowed in womb fluid. They sequenced bacterial genes in meconium from 52 infants born between 23 and 41 weeks.

Bacterial DNA turned up more often in babies born before 33 weeks, and about 61 percent of the reads belonged to genera previously reported in amniotic fluid. Five genera tied to inflammation, including Enterococcus and Lactobacillus, grew commoner the earlier the birth. The authors present this as first evidence that fetal gut microbes may help trigger preterm birth.
europmc-pmc4013623:
Un Ju Jung and Myung-Sook Choi review how fat tissue signals drive the health harms of obesity, in the International Journal of Molecular Sciences in 2014. Obesity comes from taking in more energy than the body burns, and excess fat builds up. Fat is not a passive store: it acts as a hormone organ in its own right.

Swollen fat tissue releases a set of signal compounds called adipokines. In excess, their output goes off balance and feeds steady, low-grade inflammation. That state links to insulin resistance, type 2 diabetes, skewed blood fats, and fatty liver disease. The review works through the main adipokines, what each does, and how their shifts may push each harm. Some newer adipokines are still poorly understood. The authors present the field as a source of clues for care, with much left to map.
europmc-pmc4179323:
Anantha Harijith, David L. Ebenezer, and Viswanathan Natarajan reviewed the link between reactive oxygen species and inflammasomes in Frontiers in Physiology in 2014. Inflammasomes are protein machines inside cells that switch on inflammation. Reactive oxygen species are harsh by-products of cell chemistry that can act as alarm signals.

Their review explains how these oxygen by-products help trip inflammasomes through signal routes involving MAPK and ERK proteins. Once on, the machines activate caspase enzymes and release interleukin-1 beta and interleukin-18, which drive fever and swelling, and they can kill the cell in a fiery way called pyroptosis. The same pathway shows up in gout, silicosis, diabetes, and some virus infections. Antioxidant defences can damp the signal, which points to possible drug targets.
europmc-pmc4231123:
Julian H. Elliott and eleven co-authors tested a latency-waking drug in HIV in PLoS Pathogens in 2014. Antiretroviral therapy suppresses HIV but cannot clear infected cells that hide the virus in a silent state. Vorinostat, a drug that loosens packed DNA, was a candidate to wake the virus so it can be targeted.

Twenty patients on suppressive therapy took vorinostat daily for 14 days. The drug was well tolerated, with no dose changes or dropouts. HIV RNA inside blood CD4 cells rose in 18 of the 20 patients, by a median of over sevenfold at peak, and stayed raised 70 days after the last dose. Yet blood virus levels, total HIV DNA, and the pool of cells able to release virus did not budge. Waking the virus, the study shows, is not the same as clearing it.
europmc-pmc4238323:
Eva Mracsko and Roland Veltkamp reviewed inflammation after brain bleeding in Frontiers in Cellular Neuroscience in 2014. Intracerebral hemorrhage, bleeding straight into the brain, is among the deadliest strokes, and no specific treatment exists. The blood itself triggers a wave of inflammation that adds damage over the following days.

Resident microglia switch on first, then blood immune cells stream in, releasing cytokines, chemokines, cutting enzymes, and reactive oxygen species. Older work blamed the innate arm; newer studies give adaptive immune cells a part too. How the cell types influence each other in the bleed zone is still sketchy. The review weighs early attempts to calm the response with immune-modulating drugs, and it calls for better mapping of inflammation in patients, since animal models of the bleed are imperfect.
europmc-pmc4273623:
Francesca Calabrese and co-authors review how inflammation may harm the brain's ability to adapt, with one growth factor at the center. Their review appeared in Frontiers in Cellular Neuroscience in 2014. The factor, BDNF, supports nerve cell growth and the strengthening of connections, and immune signals can disturb its levels.

The authors trace how pro-inflammatory cytokines, raised during illness or stress, can damage nerve structure and blunt plasticity, the brain's capacity to adjust. They discuss BDNF as the link between the immune system and these brain effects. The review frames testable ideas for why inflammation and mood or memory disorders so often appear together.
europmc-pmc4294323:
George M Sheldrick describes the new features added to SHELXL, his long running program for refining crystal structures. The paper appeared in Acta Crystallographica Section C in 2015, and Sheldrick writes as sole author. Refinement adjusts an atomic model against X-ray or neutron data until the two agree, and SHELXL has served that step for decades.

The update gathers changes made since 2008, explained one by one for working crystallographers. Among the tools covered is SHREDCIF, which pulls refinement details out of the standard CIF files that archives require. The paper doubles as a changelog and a short manual for a program most small molecule labs rely on daily.
europmc-pmc4307623:
Caroline Bähler, Carola A Huber, Beat Brüngger, and Oliver Reich measured how living with several chronic diseases at once drives health care use and cost in older Swiss adults. Their study appeared in BMC Health Services Research in 2015. Multimorbidity is a rising strain on health systems, yet hard numbers on its burden were scarce.

Insurance claims covered nearly two hundred and thirty thousand people aged sixty five and over. Multimorbidity meant two or more of twenty two chronic conditions read from drug based cost groups. People with many conditions saw more doctors, used more kinds of care, and cost far more than peers with one or none. The study gives planners a solid scale for a central problem of aging societies.
europmc-pmc4378923:
Andreas Voss, Rico Schroeder, Andreas Heitmann, Annette Peters, and Siegfried Perz studied how sex and age shape short-term heart rate patterns, in PLoS ONE in 2015. Heart rate variability, the change in time between beats, reflects the autonomic nervous system, which runs the body's automatic controls. Short recordings give results fast but need reference patterns. The team analyzed five-minute recordings from 1,906 healthy people in a German cohort, 782 women and 1,124 men, using many linear and nonlinear measures.

Clear gender differences appeared, above all in frequency-based measures, within both younger and older age bands. The team also tracked how the measures change across five age decades, from 25 to 74, separately for women and men. Patterns that look odd in a patient may be normal for their age and sex. Such reference data help doctors read short recordings with care.
europmc-pmc4384023:
Yoshinobu Igarashi and co-authors opened a large Japanese toxicogenomics database to the public, described in Nucleic Acids Research in 2015. Toxicogenomics judges chemical safety by gene expression patterns. The Japanese Toxicogenomics Project spent ten years profiling 170 compounds, mostly drugs, in rats and in rat and human liver cells, at several doses and time points. Open TG-GATEs makes that archive, with its pathology and chemistry data, freely available.

Gene signatures from large databases should predict safety better than small ones, by tying a compound's harm to its mechanism in target organs. The paper gives a full overview of the data and of the experimental conditions that produced it, so outsiders can reuse it soundly. Expression data sit beside blood chemistry, blood counts, and tissue findings for the same animals. Few public resources pair the layers at this scale.
europmc-pmc4386023:
Alexandra Obregon-Tito and co-authors compared gut microbes across ways of life, in Nature Communications in 2015. Earlier work hinted that city dwellers carry gut communities unlike those of traditional peoples. The team sampled feces from hunter-gatherers and traditional farmers in Peru, and from an urban group in the United States. They read both the species present and the functions the microbes' genes could perform.

Urban and traditional communities differed clearly, and hunter-gatherers formed a distinct subgroup even among traditional peoples. A bacterial genus, Treponema, marked the traditional guts. Rebuilt genomes showed these bacteria are diverse and harmless, close to a pig gut species that digests plant sugars. They occur in non-human primates and in all traditional groups studied so far. They may be old partners lost in city life.
europmc-pmc4393523:
Bo Hu, Jinpu Jin, An-Yuan Guo, He Zhang, Jingchu Luo, and Ge Gao released version 2.0 of a gene drawing server, in Bioinformatics in 2015. Pictures of gene structure, showing exons, introns, and annotated features, help biologists grasp function and evolution and make publication figures. Their Gene Structure Display Server had drawn such figures since 2007 for more than 60,000 users. The upgrade was rebuilt around a new interface and wider inputs.

Version 2.0 accepts more annotation feature types and file formats than before. A built-in visual editor lets users adjust the generated figure directly, instead of regenerating it from scratch. A user-supplied family tree can be drawn beside the genes to support evolutionary comparison. The web server and full source code are free. Small as it sounds, reliable gene diagrams are a daily need in genomics papers.
europmc-pmc4428123:
Lucia Li, Kazumasa Uehara, and Takashi Hanakawa reviewed in Frontiers in Cellular Neuroscience in 2015 why brain stimulation results vary so much between people. The method they discuss, transcranial direct current stimulation, passes a weak current through the scalp. Reports claim gains from stroke recovery to memory, yet effect sizes swing widely and some studies contradict each other.

Person-level factors may explain much of that spread. The starting state of brain cells, head and brain anatomy, age, and the damage left by injury all shape the response, the authors argue. Variability also enters through the magnetic pulse tests used to measure motor effects. Their review urges researchers to plan for these differences rather than treat mixed results as simple failure or success.
europmc-pmc4475523:
F Semeraro, A Cancarini, R dell'Omo, S Rezzola, M R Romano, and C Costagliola reviewed diabetic retinopathy in the Journal of Diabetes Research in 2015. The condition, in which diabetes damages the retina at the back of the eye, is the leading cause of vision loss in working-age adults in the Western world. Its development mixes vessel damage, inflammation, and nerve injury in ways still not fully mapped.

Low oxygen in retinal tissue and a disturbed immune response in diabetes raise levels of signaling molecules in the vitreous, the gel filling the eye. Sampling that gel in patients has revealed cytokines, chemokines, and growth factors that drive leaky vessels and new, fragile growth. The review highlights the main factors found there and how they interact, arguing that inflammation is not a side show but a core driver that future treatments should target.
europmc-pmc4489223:
Mateusz Kurcinski, Michal Jamroz, Maciej Blaszczyk, Andrzej Kolinski, and Sebastian Kmiecik built CABS-dock, a web server for fitting peptides to proteins, in Nucleic Acids Research in 2015. Peptides binding to proteins control many cell functions, and modeling those embraces matters for drug discovery. Most docking tools need to be told where on the protein the peptide binds, information that is often exactly what is missing.

CABS-dock starts the peptide in a random pose and searches the whole protein surface by simulation, letting the peptide bend fully while the protein backbone flexes slightly. On the largest test set of its kind, covering cases with and without a known bound structure, it produced models of high or medium accuracy in most cases. Users can ban regions of the surface from the search or loosen chosen parts of the protein. The free server makes flexible docking available without local software.
europmc-pmc4503723:
Christina S. Nødvig, Jakob B. Nielsen, Martin E. Kogle, and Uffe H. Mortensen published a methods paper in PLoS ONE in 2015 on gene editing in thread-like fungi. Many fungal genomes have been read, yet most of these fungi still lack good tools for changing their genes. The group built a CRISPR-Cas9 system shaped for such fungi, so one plasmid can guide cuts at a chosen gene.

Tests ran in six fungal species, one of which had never been changed by gene editing before. The kit holds four vectors with markers used across many fungi, plus a script that finds guide sites shared by gene copies in more than one species. In a wild strain of Aspergillus aculeatus, the system also set up a marker that lets gene targeting be repeated step by step.
europmc-pmc4557123:
Kuti Baruch leads a ten-author team testing an immune reset for Alzheimer's disease in mice, in Nature Communications in 2015. Alzheimer's involves chronic brain inflammation, yet immune-suppressing drugs have repeatedly failed as treatments. The team flipped the logic: regulatory T cells, which hold the immune system back, might be blocking helpful immune entry into the brain.

In the 5XFAD mouse model, briefly depleting those regulatory cells, or drugging their activity down, cleared amyloid plaques, calmed brain inflammation, and reversed memory decline. The effect ran through the choroid plexus, the brain's gateway for immune traffic, which then admitted repair-minded cells to plaque sites. The authors propose easing systemic immune suppression as a treatment strategy.
europmc-pmc4626023:
In 2015, Emma L. Anderson and colleagues published a systematic review and meta-analysis on fatty liver disease in children and teenagers. Non-alcoholic fatty liver disease, or NAFLD, was often quoted at widely varying rates in young people. No pooled estimate existed. The team gathered studies of one to nineteen year olds using any diagnosis method. The work appeared in PLOS ONE.

Across general population studies, the pooled rate was 7.6 percent. In obesity clinic studies it reached 34.2 percent. Rates were higher in boys and rose with body mass index. Diagnosis method mattered greatly: blood enzyme tests gave far lower rates than scans or biopsies. Studies differed hugely from each other, which the authors flag as a problem for planning screening and care for affected children.
europmc-pmc4745323:
Costa, Garrick, Roquè, and Pellacani review the evidence that quercetin, a plant polyphenol common in apples, onions, and berries, protects the nervous system. Studies in cells, animals, and humans suggest it counters neurotoxic chemicals and helps in models of neuronal injury and degenerative disease, though the mechanism is unsettled.

A direct antioxidant action may be only part of the story. Quercetin also switches on the cell's own defences through the Nrf2 pathway and the enzyme paraoxonase 2. It activates sirtuins, induces autophagy, and mimics oestrogen. The authors weigh each proposed route and mark what remains unproven before dietary claims can harden.
europmc-pmc4752823:
Gillian A. Matthews heads a large author team in Cell in 2016 with a mouse study of how the brain registers being alone. One cell group sits in the dorsal raphe nucleus and uses dopamine, a signal chemical also tied to reward. The group asked whether these cells track social contact itself.

After a spell alone, the cells changed their wiring and fired more when contact resumed. Switching the cells on made mice seek company yet shun the place where the switch happened. Blocking the cells erased the rebound drive to socialize after isolation. Their pull also tracked each mouse's rank in its group. The work ties these cells to a loneliness-like state that pushes animals back toward others.
europmc-pmc4776623:
Richard M. Dodds and five colleagues pool world data on grip strength in Age and Ageing in 2016. Grip strength flags weak muscle in old age, and it predicts disability and death. The team had built British reference curves for what grip is normal at each age, and they asked whether the cut points for weakness travel to other regions.

They gathered 60 papers with age- and sex-split data covering over 96,000 measures. Rich regions matched the British curves closely, landing slightly above them. Developing regions scored far below, by nearly a full step on the scale. The authors endorse the British cut points for rich regions but warn that developing regions need their own, or weakness will be over-called there.
europmc-pmc4786923:
Morgan L. Maeder and Charles A. Gersbach review genome editing for therapy in Molecular Therapy in 2016. Gene therapy once meant adding a fresh gene and hoping it landed well. Editing tools changed the aim: now the genome itself can be cut and rewritten at a chosen spot, to fix a fault, park a helpful gene safely, or delete a harmful stretch.

The review explains the four cutter families, zinc finger nucleases, TALENs, meganucleases, and the CRISPR/Cas9 system, and how each finds its target. It then tours the uses under study: disarming viruses, arming immune cells against cancer, and repairing single-gene diseases. Delivery, off-target cuts, and control of the edit remain the hard problems, and the authors weigh where the field can go next.
europmc-pmc4802023:
Antonio Mancini leads seven authors in Mediators of Inflammation in 2016 on thyroid hormones, oxidative stress, and a debated illness pattern. Both overactive and underactive thyroids upset the body's balance between damaging oxygen forms and its defenses. In many serious illnesses, blood tests also show a drop in the active thyroid hormone T3, a pattern called nonthyroidal illness syndrome.

Doctors argue whether that drop is a helpful adaptation or a true tissue-level hormone shortage. The review walks through the enzymes that convert the storage hormone T4 into active T3, in health and in illness. Stress markers stay raised in the syndrome, which the authors read as evidence for real hormone shortage in tissues. They close by weighing what that reading means for whether patients should receive hormone treatment.
europmc-pmc4846023:
Fengjuan Wang and co-authors boosted rice blast resistance with CRISPR/Cas9 gene editing in 2016. Rice blast is among the most damaging rice diseases worldwide, and resistant plants are the cheapest defense. The group aimed the editing tool at one rice gene, OsERF922, in 50 young transgenic plants. About two in five plants carried edits at the target site.

The edits passed to later generations, and plants keeping the edit but not the added DNA were bred by the second generation. Six stable mutant lines were then tested against the blast fungus and resisted it better. The work shows targeted editing can build in disease resistance without keeping foreign DNA in the final plant.
europmc-pmc4854923:
Yi Zhu and co-authors identified navitoclax in 2016 as a drug that kills aged, worn-out cells called senescent cells. Clearing such cells extends healthy life in mice. Senescent cells resist death through survival paths, and two earlier drugs that block those paths were already known. The team tested navitoclax, a blocker of the Bcl-2 survival protein family.

Navitoclax killed senescent cells of several types, among them vein lining cells and lung and mouse embryo fibroblasts, but spared fat precursor cells. A rival blocker, TW-37, did little. Which cells die depends on which survival proteins they lean on. The find widens the toolkit for clearing harmful aged cells.
europmc-pmc4899423:
David A. Parfitt and co-authors modeled inherited blindness in lab-grown optic cups in 2016 and corrected its cause. Leber congenital amaurosis blinds children, and its commonest trigger is a deep intron fault in the cilia gene CEP290, which garbles the message and cuts the protein short. Why the retina suffers most was unclear. The team grew eye tissue from patient stem cells.

Stem cells formed pigment layers and optic cups normally, yet the optic cups showed the worst garbling and cilia faults, matching the eye-only disease. A short antisense strand blocked the garbling, restored full protein, and fixed cilia traffic. Patient tissue in a dish thus tests gene-targeted cures directly.
europmc-pmc4915023:
Manoshi S. Datta and co-authors tracked microbe successions on model ocean particles in Nature Communications in 2016. Sinking organic bits in the sea host bacterial crowds that digest and recycle nutrients. The team watched which kinds attach, in which order, on lab-made particles, and which traits win each round.

Fast, swimming degraders that secrete enzymes took the early rounds. Later, secondary feeders that cannot use the particle itself moved in and lived off the first wave's work, relaxing the early pressure. The whole succession replayed alike across repeats, driven by interactions, not chance. Ocean carbon flow runs through such micro-scale relays, and the study gives them a timetable.
europmc-pmc4973823:
Damien R. Farine and Hal Whitehead write a practical guide to animal social network analysis. Their guide appeared in The Journal of Animal Ecology in 2015. Network analysis turns sightings of animals together into maps of social structure. Those maps can test hypotheses across behavior, ecology, and evolution. Done carelessly, though, they bake in bias, since observers miss ties and sampling shapes the map. The guide walks through each stage with that risk in mind.

Early chapters cover defining individuals and ties, plus designing data collection. Later ones cover building networks, measuring node and network traits, and testing hypotheses about structure and process. A final section treats power and accuracy, asking how much sampling a sound network needs. The authors supply appendices with common programming routines. They urge pairing observation with simulation to test rival explanations of social structure.
europmc-pmc5075023:
Caroline Turcotte, Marie-Renée Blanchet, Michel Laviolette, and Nicolas Flamand review the CB2 receptor in Cellular and Molecular Life Sciences in 2016. CB2 is the body's second receptor for cannabis-like compounds, and unlike its brain-based sibling it sits mainly in immune tissues. That placement hints that the body's own cannabinoid system helps tune inflammation. The review covers the receptor's drug profile, where it appears, and the signals it sends when switched on.

Evidence from human cells, cell lines, and animal models points the same way. Mice lacking CB2 show stronger inflammation, while switching the receptor on usually calms immune cells down. Drugs that activate CB2 slowed several inflammatory diseases in animals. Open questions remain, including whether the receptor acts in brain cells and how the body's own cannabinoids move human white blood cells. The authors judge CB2 a promising drug target, provided those gaps close.
europmc-pmc5095923:
M. Madan Babu wrote a solo review in Biochemical Society Transactions in 2016 on disordered regions in proteins. Classic theory holds that a protein's chain folds into one fixed shape that sets its job. Disordered regions never settle into a single shape, yet they are common and do real work in cells.

Babu surveys how floppy regions help proteins bind partners, get switched on and off, and be broken down when spent. He explains how gene splicing and the placement of RNA messages inside cells can vary these regions and widen what one protein can do. The review closes with how changes in disordered regions feed human disease and how they may have helped cells grow more complex over evolution.
europmc-pmc5105823:
Catharine R. Gale, Cyrus Cooper, and Avan Aihie Sayer studied falls in older adults in Age and Ageing in 2016, using the English Longitudinal Study of Ageing. Falls are a leading cause of disability and death in later life, and women fall more than men. The team asked whether the risk factors behind falls differ by sex.

They drew on 4,301 people aged 60 and over surveyed in 2012-13, who reported falls in the prior two years along with health and function measures. Severe pain and having a chronic disease raised fall risk in both sexes. Incontinence and frailty stood out for women, while older age, depressive symptoms, and failing a standing balance test stood out for men. Prevention plans, they argue, should be shaped with sex in mind.
europmc-pmc5127123:
Manuel T. Velasquez, Ali Ramezani, Alotaibi Manal, and Dominic S. Raj reviewed a gut-derived compound in Toxins in 2016, with Raymond Vanholder also named in the text's byline. Trimethylamine N-oxide, or TMAO, is made when gut microbes process nutrients such as choline, then the liver finishes the job. Sea animals stockpile it to protect their proteins.

In people, higher blood TMAO tracks with more heart attacks, strokes, and deaths, and it rises as kidney function falls. Proposed harms run through cholesterol handling, inflammation, and foam cell formation in artery walls. Yet whether TMAO causes disease or merely marks it is unsettled. The review weighs attempts to lower it, from antibiotics to engineered gut bacteria, and calls for cell-level studies.
europmc-pmc5131823:
Daehwan Kim, Li Song, Florian P. Breitwieser, and Steven L. Salzberg presented a fast microbe classifier in Genome Research in 2016. Metagenomics reads DNA from whole communities at once, and naming the species in millions of fragments quickly is a computing bottleneck.

Their program, Centrifuge, uses a compact indexing scheme built for this task. Its index for more than four thousand bacterial and archaeal genomes takes only 4.2 gigabytes, and it can label a typical sequencing run within minutes on a desktop computer. The same approach squeezes a national database of 109 billion DNA letters into a 69-gigabyte index, far below older methods. Speed plus a small footprint, the authors argue, makes timely analysis of huge community data sets practical outside big computing centers.
europmc-pmc5149523:
Kankana Bardhan, Theodora Anagnostou, and Vassiliki A. Boussiotis reviewed the PD-1 pathway in Frontiers in Immunology in 2016. PD-1 is a brake receptor on T cells, and its partners PD-L1 and PD-L2 sit on other cells; together they help keep the immune system from attacking the body's own tissues.

The same brake also shields viruses and tumors by damping T cell attack, which is why blocking it has become a major cancer therapy strategy. The review covers the pathway's parts, the signals PD-1 sends inside the T cell, and what those signals do to T cell growth and function. It frames the arc from the pathway's discovery in basic tolerance research to its present clinical use.
europmc-pmc5183723:
Aedín Cassidy and Anne-Marie Minihane reviewed how the body handles dietary flavonoids in The American Journal of Clinical Nutrition, with the hosted text dated 2017. Flavonoids, plant compounds in fruit, vegetables, grains, and drinks, show population-level links to better health, yet individuals respond very unevenly to eating more of them.

The reason, they argue, lies in absorption and metabolism. Liver and gut enzymes transform flavonoids, and gut microbes transform them further. Age, sex, genes, food makeup, and the source plant all shift the result. They cover the main families, including anthocyanins, flavonols, flavan-3-ols, and flavanones, and sort what governs each one's fate. Pinpointing those factors is needed before firm dietary guidance on flavonoids can be written.
europmc-pmc5266623:
G. David Batty, Tom C. Russ, Emmanuel Stamatakis, and Mika Kivimäki pooled sixteen prospective cohort studies to test whether psychological distress predicts death from specific cancers, in The BMJ in 2017. The data came from nationally representative health surveys in England and Scotland begun between 1994 and 2008. Together they held 163,363 adults who were cancer-free at entry and gave distress scores on a standard questionnaire.

Over an average of nine and a half years, 16,267 participants died, 4,353 of them from cancer. After accounting for age, sex, education, social position, body mass, smoking, and drinking, the most distressed group died of cancer overall at clearly higher rates than the least distressed. The excess was sharpest for leukaemia and for cancers of the pancreas, oesophagus, prostate, and colorectum, and it also held for cancers unrelated to smoking. Graded rises with distress appeared for colorectal and prostate cancer.
europmc-pmc5320023:
Heinz Fehrenbach, Christina Wagner, and Michael Wegmann reviewed airway remodeling in asthma in Cell and Tissue Research in 2017. Remodeling means lasting change in the size, make-up, and layout of the airway wall. Some change is normal, as lungs grow or heal after injury. Harmful change builds up under long injury and swelling, and leaves the wall altered for good.

The review asks four hard questions. How can remodeling be measured well and counted fairly? Can it start before any swelling begins? What is known when it follows swelling instead? And what do animal models, from simple creatures to primates, each teach? The authors call for studies matched to asthma subtypes, in both animals and patients. Fresh imaging tools, they hope, will let doctors watch remodeling in the living lung.
europmc-pmc5357723:
Ji Li led a team that built a T cell guiding antibody for a bone marrow cancer, in Cancer Cell in 2017. The antibody has two arms: one grabs FcRH5, a mark on B-lineage cells that crowd myeloma tumors, and the other grabs CD3 on killer T cells. Brought face to face, the T cell should wake and kill. The team asked what makes the handshake work well.

The antibody made target cells clump and pushed a brake enzyme out of the contact zone, which let the T cell signal fire. The size of the target and the spot the arm grips proved key: a grip near the cell surface built the best contact. The drug killed patient myeloma cells at very low doses and cleared B cells and marrow plasma cells in monkeys. Work on this design may guide kin drugs.
europmc-pmc5439023:
The GBD 2015 Tobacco Collaborators track smoking and its death toll across the world. Their systematic analysis appeared in The Lancet. It covers 195 countries and territories. The span runs from 1990 to 2015. Tobacco control has spread in that period. Smoking still ranks among the top risks for early death. The team pooled 2,818 data sources. Models filled gaps by place, age, sex, and year.

Daily smoking fell to 25 percent of men worldwide. For women it fell to 5.4 percent. Those are drops of about 28 and 34 percent since 1990. Progress slowed after 2005 in many places. Four countries saw rates rise. Smoking still caused 6.4 million deaths in 2015. That was 11.5 percent of all deaths. Over half fell in China, India, the United States, and Russia. Population growth and aging push the total toll up. The authors urge faster prevention and quitting support.
europmc-pmc5444023:
Schmaal and co-authors run the largest brain scan study yet of major depression. Their meta-analysis appeared in Molecular Psychiatry. It comes from the ENIGMA Major Depressive Disorder Working Group. Past scan studies were small and clashed. This team pooled scans from 20 cohorts worldwide. All sites used harmonized methods. The sample held 2,148 patients and 7,957 healthy controls.

Adults with depression had thinner cortex in several zones. The orbitofrontal cortex, cingulate, insula, and temporal lobes all showed thinning. Effect sizes were small, near a tenth of a standard unit. First-episode and adult-onset cases showed the clearest gaps. Teens told a different story. They had lower total surface area, not thinner cortex. Frontal and sensory zones shrank most. Recurrent teen cases showed the strongest effects. The authors read this as a moving target. Depression seems to mark the brain in stage-specific ways.
europmc-pmc5445723:
Andersson and co-authors fix a hidden flaw in brain scan correction: movement during a single volume. Their methods article appeared in NeuroImage. Diffusion MRI builds each volume from stacked slices. Standard tools assume the head stays still during those seconds. Movement is treated as jumps between volumes. Real heads drift slice by slice.

The new method models movement as a smooth function over time. It works inside their existing eddy framework. That framework already handles distortion and signal dropout together. Tests on lifelike simulated data came first. The method recovered true movement with high accuracy. Measures such as fractional anisotropy came out cleaner. Gaps between still and moving scans shrank. A volunteer who moved on purpose confirmed the gain. Scans of elderly subjects lost their telltale movement signs. The work should sharpen studies of groups who move most.
europmc-pmc5460023:
Ponnuswamy and co-authors shield tiny DNA structures with a simple coat so they can survive in the body. Their study appeared in Nature Communications. DNA can be folded into precise shapes for drugs and tests. But body fluids break those shapes down. The salt level in blood is too low to hold them. Enzymes that chew DNA attack them as well.

The coat is made of short lysine chains. At the best mix, the shapes stayed stable in low salt. One key enzyme digested them ten times more slowly. Too much coat made the shapes clump. Adding a PEG partner chain solved that flaw. Coated shapes then resisted blood enzymes up to a thousand times better. They survived being taken into cells. In mice, more of them stayed in the blood. The method is cheap and works for any shape.
europmc-pmc5510723:
Yavorska and Burgess present a software paper in the International Journal of Epidemiology. It introduces an R package for Mendelian randomization studies. Such studies use gene variants as stand-ins to test cause and effect. They often run on published summary numbers rather than raw data. Code for the main methods was scattered across paper appendices.

The package gathers those methods in one place. It covers the inverse-variance weighted, MR-Egger, and weighted median approaches. Options include robust fits and penalties for odd variants. Interactive plots help users compare the methods side by side. Data can also flow in from the PhenoScanner database. The authors stress that sound biology must back any causal claim.
europmc-pmc5554123:
Elshaghabee and co-authors present a review in Frontiers in Microbiology. Their subject is Bacillus bacteria as possible probiotics. These spore-forming microbes survive harsh gut conditions well. They also stay stable during food processing and storage.

Bacillus strains make enzymes, vitamins, and compounds that fight other microbes. Such traits suit them for functional foods and health products. Yet the genus also includes harmful strains, which confuses buyers. The authors argue that safety must be judged strain by strain. Only strains that match well-tested safe ones should be used. Readers get a clear view of both the promise and the caution this field needs.
europmc-pmc5618223:
Tasoulis and Isbister gather a decade of snake venom composition studies in Toxins. New gene and protein tools made venom recipes fast to read. Over 100 studies had piled up without a shared view. Their review collates them into one database.

Studies covered 132 snake species across the front-fanged families. About 90 percent of each venom came from few protein families. Four families dominate overall, led by phospholipase A2s. Three-finger toxins and phospholipase A2s rule elapid venoms. Vipers lean on metalloproteases and serine proteases as well. Sixty-three families appeared in total. More than half turned up in under five percent of species, always in small amounts. Their roles stay unknown. Readers get evolutionary and medical bearings from one chart.
europmc-pmc5651823:
Aran and co-authors study tissue that looks normal but sits next to a tumor. This tissue is called normal adjacent to tumor, or NAT. Cancer studies often use it as a healthy control. The team combined data from two large projects to test that practice. They compared healthy, NAT, and tumor samples across eight tissue types.

The analysis covered 6,506 samples in total. NAT proved to be a distinct state between healthy tissue and tumor. The team found 18 genes switched on only in NATs. Shared changes pointed to inflammation signals from the tumor. Those signals seem to stir a response in nearby blood vessel tissue.
europmc-pmc5663723:
Sheth and co-authors review how the cancer drug cisplatin damages hearing. Their review appeared in Frontiers in Cellular Neuroscience. Hearing loss appeared early in cisplatin use. Excess reactive oxygen species harm cochlear cells. Later work added inflammation to the picture. The review traces each mechanism.

Several protection strategies follow from the biology. Antioxidants can scavenge the harmful species. Certain receptors reduce inflammation in animal tests. Blocking the TRPV1 channel also protected hearing. Transporter inhibitors can keep cisplatin out. DNA damage and cell death pathways offer targets too. The authors gather recent drug approaches. Each approach grows from a known mechanism.
europmc-pmc5670723:
Leeman and co-authors present a framework paper in Implementation Science. It argues against lumping all strategies under one term. Implementation research studies how proven interventions enter real settings. Scholars now label every tactic an implementation strategy. The authors say that habit breeds confusion. It also blocks clean synthesis across studies.

Their system classifies strategies by actor and target. Actors sit in delivery, support, or synthesis systems. Targets span five levels, from intervention to process. Sorting by these traits yields five distinct classes. They are dissemination, implementation process, and integration. Capacity-building and scale-up complete the set. A colorectal screening case shows each class at work. The scheme should sharpen reporting and expose listing gaps.
europmc-pmc5679623:
Wu and co-authors present a systematic review in PLoS ONE. It links activity habits with quality of life in young people. Prior reviews focused on children with chronic disease. This one covers the general healthy population instead. Ages ranged from three to eighteen years. The team searched four databases plus reference lists. Work spanned 1946 to January 2017.

In total, 31 studies met the entry criteria. Most used a cross-sectional design, with six longitudinal studies. Three were school-based activity interventions. Higher activity levels tracked with better quality of life. More sedentary time tracked with lower quality of life. Several studies showed a dose-response pattern. The authors back school programs that promote active lifestyles.
europmc-pmc5763123:
Sanchez-Trincado, Gomez-Perosanz, and Reche review methods for predicting epitopes, the parts of antigens that immune cells spot. T and B cells build memory by knowing these small targets. Finding epitopes in the lab is slow and costly. Computer prediction can shrink the list worth testing.

The review first covers how T and B cells know their targets. That base shapes what good prediction needs. It then surveys the main tools for B cell and T cell epitopes. Each method's roots and workings get close review. The guide serves vaccine and diagnosis design work.
europmc-pmc5771023:
Hartman and co-authors test how farm practice shapes microbes in soil and wheat roots. Their field experiment crossed two management styles, conventional and organic. Each style ran at different tillage levels. The team read bacterial and fungal communities in both settings.

Richness barely moved, but community makeup shifted in clear patterns, they report. Tillage structured soil bacteria most, while management shaped soil fungi and root bacteria. Root fungi answered mainly to tillage. About a tenth of the variation traced to the tested practices. Sensitive microbes included common, well connected members. The authors frame the work as a base for smart microbiota farming.
europmc-pmc5789323:
Ježek, Cooper, and Strich review the two way link between reactive oxygen species and mitochondrial shape. Mitochondria constantly split and merge, keeping a fine balance. Their energy chain also leaks reactive oxygen as a side product. Too much of it injures cells, while small amounts carry signals.

Fresh work shows shape and reactive oxygen feed each other, the authors note. Warped shapes can raise output, which then harms the organelles further. That loop can spiral into lasting oxidative stress. The review focuses on what this cycle means for cancer growth and spread.
europmc-pmc5821623:
Steiner and co-authors argue that migraine is a neglected public emergency. Their editorial draws on the Eurolight survey of over 8,000 Europeans. It also cites a world survey run with the WHO. Both show headache care failing on a grand scale.

Migraine now ranks as the top cause of disability in under 50s. Tension and medication-overuse headaches add to the toll. Yet services stay thin in rich and poor nations alike. The authors call this neglect a forgotten epidemic. They press health politicians to fund real headache care. Readers get a blunt brief on a vast, under-treated burden.
europmc-pmc5828423:
