Evolution is the stepwise growth of all living things from one low form, and the entry sets the theory beside Judaism. The names tied to it are Darwin and Spencer, with Haeckel and Huxley as defenders. Darwin's engine was the struggle to survive, passing on traits that help. Spencer stretched the idea to society, religion, language, and art.

The entry holds that Judaism need not oppose the theory. Evolution does not rule out creation, it argues, but requires it. Purpose stays in the process, though not as a machine-like design. Gaps remain at life's start, at awareness, and at conscience, where the theory fails to explain. A later section traces religion itself growing from fetish worship toward ethical monotheism, and weighs that view against revelation.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-felix-elisa-rac:
Elisa Rachel Felix, known simply as Rachel, was a French actress born March 24, 1821, at an inn in the Swiss canton of Aargau. She died at Cannet, near Toulon, on January 3, 1858. Her father peddled goods at Lyons and Paris, where his daughters sang in the streets. Rachel was overheard and given free lessons, then sent to a drama teacher.

Her debut at the Gymnase in 1837 brought only mild success. A year later, as Camille at the Comedie Francaise, she caused a sensation. She made Racine and Corneille pay better than new plays and saved the house from ruin. A hostile clique froze her Roxane one night in 1838; the next night brought a storm of praise. London welcomed her in 1841, and her Phedre ran two full years.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-finta-6123: Finta is a Spanish word for a tax paid to a government. Spanish and Portuguese congregations in London still used the term, the entry says. There it named part of their income, set by assessors called fintadores. Every two years the elders fixed the whole sum to be raised. The assessors then split that sum among the members. The highest finta could not pass £40, and the lowest could not fall below £1. Set rules also governed the tax and the choice of assessors.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-fontainebleau-6:
Fontainebleau is a French town in the department of Seine-et-Marne. Its Jewish community took shape about 1787. The oldest paper about it is dated March 31, 1799. At first devout families met in a member's house. In 1819 the community bought part of a house for 1,200 francs. That soon proved too small. A site for a synagogue was bought in 1853, at the entry to the palace gardens.

The land cost 5,700 francs and the building 15,000. The emperor gave 1,000 francs himself, and state and town gave 3,200 more. The foundation stone was laid in May 1856. The opening rite took place on Aug. 23, 1857, led by the chief rabbi of France. The community counts twenty-nine families, of merchants, day-laborers, and small fund-holders. It often aids poor Jews passing through on their way to America.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-franklin-fabian:
Fabian Franklin was an American mathematician, editor, and author. He was born at Eger, Hungary, on January 18, 1853. He took his first degree at Columbian University in Washington in 1869. Until 1877 he worked in civil engineering and surveying. That year Johns Hopkins University made him a fellow by invitation. He took his doctor's degree there in 1880. He rose step by step to a full chair of mathematics, which he held until 1895.

He had always cared much for economic and public questions. In 1895 he left his chair to take charge of the Baltimore News as editor. He wrote for math journals and for leading American reviews. He was an associate fellow of the American Academy of Arts and Sciences.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-fulvia-6423: Fulvia was a Roman lady of high rank who turned to Judaism through a Jew who had fled to Rome to escape punishment. That man and three others talked her into giving purple and gold for the Temple at Jerusalem. They kept the gifts for themselves. Her husband Saturninus told his friend the emperor Tiberius. The fraud led to the banishment of the Jews from Rome in 19 of the common era.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-gershon-ben-sol: Gershon ben Solomon of Arles, a Provencal thinker of the late thirteenth century, is said to be the father of Gersonides. He wrote Shaar ha-Shamayim, a kind of survey of knowledge in three parts. The first treats nature, metals, plants, animals, and man. The second treats astronomy, drawn from Alfergani and the Almagest. The third treats higher thought, drawn from Maimonides Guide. The book printed at Venice in 1547.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-gotha-6823:
Gotha was the capital of the duchy of Saxe-Coburg-Gotha. A Cologne Jew of the thirteenth century is called a Gotha native. In 1303 a ritual-murder charge brought persecution to Gotha's Jews. The Nuremberg Memorbuch lists the victims. The Black Death wiped out the community. A later community faded again in 1459-60.

Before 1848 no Jews could live in the duchy, though they could trade there under limits. After 1848 they settled freely. A capital community of ten to twelve families grew up. It gained officials in the 1870s and a synagogue in 1903. Teachers, not a rabbi, ran its affairs. In 1903 Gotha held 29,134 people, about 350 of them Jews.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-hagarenes-hagar: The Hagarenes, or Hagarites, were a nomadic people who lived east of Palestine. In Saul's time the tribe of Reuben beat them in war, seized their tents, and took their land across the east of Gilead. The spoil taken from them was large. Psalms lxxxiii names them among the foes banded against Israel. One Hagarite, Jaziz, served as chief overseer of David's flocks. The entry sends readers elsewhere for the question of where the Hagarites came from.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-hannah-7223: Hannah was one of the two wives of Elkanah and the mother of the prophet Samuel. I Samuel i and half of ii are almost wholly hers. The rabbis counted her among the seven prophetesses. Jonathan b. Uzziel read her song as prophecy. It foretold her son, Heman singing in the Temple, and the falls of Sennacherib and Nebuchadnezzar. Her silent prayer is the model for all prayer. She first called God "Zebaoth." Remembered by God on New-Year's Day, her chapter is read as the haftarah then.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-hassler-simon-7: Simon Hassler, born in Bavaria on July 25, 1832, was an American musician. His father, also a musician, brought the family to the United States in 1842. Simon first played in public as a violinist in 1852. He joined his father's Philadelphia orchestra and later led it. For years he directed theater orchestras in that city. In 1876 he led the orchestra at the Centennial Exposition in Philadelphia. He wrote music for Shakespeare plays, marches, and other orchestral pieces. He died on Jan. 25, 1901.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-held-anna-7523: Anna Held, born in Paris on Sept. 19, 1880, was a French comedienne. She was educated at Fontainebleau. Her debut came in "Miss Helyett" in Paris on Sept. 19, 1895, her fifteenth birthday. Her best parts included Mlle. Mars in a play by Jean Richepin. She also starred as the Little Duchess in a comedy of that name. With that play she toured the United States in 1903. In 1902 she married Florenz Ziegfeld, Jr., of Chicago. The entry notes that another source gives different dates.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-herz-elise-von-: Elise von Lamel Herz, born at Prague on Dec. 20, 1788, was an Austrian philanthropist whose Prague home was an intellectual center. After her husband died in 1850, she moved to Vienna. There she became an honorary member of the Jewish community. She founded the Children's Asylum at Jerusalem and charged Ludwig August Frankl with organizing it. The asylum was meant chiefly for Jewish children. A limited number of Christian and Mohammedan children were also received. She died at Vienna on July 25, 1868.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-hezekiah-ben-ma: Hezekiah ben Manoah was a French exegete of the thirteenth century. About 1240 he wrote a cabalistic comment on the Pentateuch, in memory of his father. His father had lost his right hand through firmness in the faith, the entry says. The work rests mainly on Rashi but also uses about twenty other comments. Only four sources are named by him. Printed at Venice in 1524, it saw later editions at Cremona, Amsterdam, and Lemberg. He is usually cited by his book's title.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-hirsch-albert-7: Albert Hirsch, born in Vienna on June 29, 1841, was an Austrian playwright. He first taught in public school, then acted on stage, including in a Josefstadt variety theater. He soon left acting for folk songs and plays, where he gained wide notice. He wrote more than 200 popular plays, mostly of Jewish life. His own company performed them at home and abroad with much success. He also composed music for his works, building most of it on Jewish melodies, the entry says.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-huldah-7923:
Huldah was a prophetess, wife of Shallum, keeper of the wardrobe in King Josiah's time. She lived in the second quarter of Jerusalem. When Hilkiah found the scroll of the Law, he and four companions took it to her. She foretold evil for Jerusalem and its people.

The king himself, she said, would die in peace before those days came. Rabbinic notes add color. Huldah and Deborah were the only professed prophetesses, and both bore unlovely names, weasel and bee. Huldah spoke bluntly to the king's men. She was kin to Jeremiah, and both descended from Rahab. She taught women while Jeremiah taught men, and she taught in public in the school.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-insanity-8123:
Insanity among Jews, this entry reports, was observed at rates far above their neighbors. Buschan concluded Jews were four to six times more liable to mental disease. In Italy in 1870 there was one insane person among 1,775 Catholics but one among 384 Jews. Prussian, Danish and Russian figures point the same way; among troops at Kiev, Jews showed 2.19 per cent insane against 0.91 for Russians.

The entry also notes what Jews largely escaped: alcoholic insanity. At Vienna's clinic, of 205 alcoholic patients not one was a Jew, and syphilitic cases among New York's Jewish insane ran only 4.18 per cent. It closes with the law of the insane wife and the strict proof demanded before her husband may remarry.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-isaac-b-todros-: Isaac ben Todros was a French doctor at Avignon in the late fourteenth century. In 1373 he studied under Immanuel ben Jacob of Tarascon, who wrote on the stars. When plague swept the south of France, the Jews struck first, he wrote in 1377 a short work, "Be'er Lehai," on where plagues come from and how to fight them. He had watched John of Tornamira, doctor to Pope Gregory XI., at work, and speaks well of him. He cites Hippocrates, Galen, Ibn Sina and Razi.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-isaac-ben-samue:
Isaac ben Samuel of Acre was a Palestinian cabalist of the thirteenth and fourteenth centuries, said by Azulai to have been a pupil of Nahmanides. He was at Acre when the town fell, and he was jailed with many other Jews there. He escaped the massacre and in 1305 went to Spain.

Much of the entry turns on his doubts about the Zohar. Isaac had not heard of the book in the Holy Land, so he asked Nahmanides' pupils about it and got no clear answer. Moses of Leon swore he owned Simeon b. Yohai's own copy at Avila, but he died before Isaac could see it. At Avila, Isaac heard a report that Moses had written the book himself; the entry notes that Grätz took the tale as history while Landauer showed it to be untrue. Isaac's own cabalistic works include "Me'irat Enayim" on Nahmanides' Pentateuch commentary.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-israelitische-v: The Israelitische Volkslehrer was a monthly published at Frankfort-on-the-Main. Founded in 1851, it continued to 1862. Leopold Stein edited it; in its last years S. Süsskind, publisher of a family journal, joined him in the work. The Volkslehrer was popular in tone, the entry says. It published sermons, rabbinical decisions, and discussions of religious matters. The notice gives no circulation figures and no account of why the journal ended in 1862.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-jarno-josef-jos: Josef Jarno, born Josef Cohen, was an Austrian actor born at Budapest on Aug. 24, 1866. Trained for trade, he went on stage at nineteen and made his start at Ischl in 1885, returning there in summer seasons. From 1887 to 1890 he played at Laibach, then spent nine years at Berlin theaters. Since 1899 he had belonged to the Josefstädter Theater company at Vienna. The entry also credits him with several plays of his own, among them Der Rabenvater and Die Wahrsagerin.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-johanan-b-torta: Johanan ben Torta was a scholar of the first and second centuries, a fellow of Akiba. When Akiba hailed Bar Kokba as the Messiah, Johanan answered dryly that grass would grow from Akiba's jaws before the Son of David came. His odd surname, son of a cow, is tied by legend to a cow that would not work on the Sabbath and so brought its pagan owner to the faith. No legal rulings bear his name. One teaching survives: hatred of others, he said, weighs like idolatry and bloodshed.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-joseph-ben-gori:
Joseph ben Gorion is the name attached to the Sefer Yosippon, a Hebrew history of the Jews. The book runs from the fall of Babylon in 539 before the common era to the fall of the Jewish state in 70 of the common era. It also tells of Babylonia, Greece, and Rome. In the text the writer claims to be Flavius Josephus, the old Greek historian.

Scholars cited in the entry hold that a Jew in southern Italy wrote the work. Its date is disputed, with views placing it in the ninth century or near 940. For centuries it was read as the Hebrew, or smaller, Josephus. The entry traces its sources, its later additions, and its many printed editions, the first at Mantua in 1476-79.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-joshua-b-perahy: Joshua b. Perahyah was president of the Sanhedrin in the latter half of the second century before the common era. With Nittai of Arbela he formed the second of the five pairs who passed on the tradition. When John Hyrcanus turned on the Pharisees, Joshua lost his post and fled to Alexandria. He was called back when the Pharisees won again. Only one legal ruling of his survives. His known saying runs: get yourself a teacher, win yourself a friend, and judge others toward innocence.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-judah-siciliano: Judah Siciliano, also called al-Shaari, was an Italian poet of the fourteenth century. He made his living by teaching poetry and writing poems for set occasions. None of those poems has survived. He did leave a rhyming dictionary, kept in manuscript at Oxford and Rome. Judah met Immanuel ben Solomon of Rome by sending him a poem. Immanuel praised Judah's skill with many meters in his own book, the Mehabberot. The entry rests on Zunz and on a history of the Jews in Rome.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-karman-moritz-o:
Moritz Kármán, born Kleinmann, was a Hungarian educator. He was born on Dec. 25, 1843, at Szegedin. He grew up under the sway of Leopold Löw. At the University of Budapest he studied philosophy and philology. He took his doctorate in 1866. Teaching methods soon became his chief concern.

In 1869 the minister of education sent Kármán to Leipsic on a grant. His task was to study how teachers for secondary schools are trained. Back in Hungary in 1872, he taught at the University of Budapest. He also led a practice gymnasium for new teachers. Through his many pupils his views shaped schooling across the country. The entry lists his Hungarian versions of works on logic, psychology, and the history of teaching.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-kinanah-9323: Kinanah was an opponent of Mohammed at Medina. He was a son of the poet Al-Rabi' ibn Abu al-Ḥuḳaiḳ. His brothers Al-Rabi' and Sallam were also declared enemies of the Prophet. Kinanah belonged to the tribe of the Banu al-Naḍir. After that tribe's expulsion he retired to Khaibar. His family held a castle there called Ḳamus. When Mohammed conquered the strongholds of Khaibar, Kinanah was taken prisoner. He was accused of hiding the Banu al-Naḍir's treasure. He died under torture.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-kohn-pap-david-: David Kohn, who in 1896 changed his name to Pap, was a Hungarian political economist born on Dec. 2, 1868, at Csecse. He studied law in Budapest. An 1890 essay on buying grain on margin won a prize from the Hungarian Academy of Sciences and brought him wide notice. In 1893 he joined the academy's commission on political economy. His later books, several also crowned by the academy, cover the Italian currency, tax reform, settlement, and the Hungarian agrarian movement, with titles dated from 1893 to 1897.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-krochmal-menahe: Menahem Mendel ben Abraham Krochmal, a Moravian rabbi born at Cracow about 1600, died at Nikolsburg on Jan. 2, 1661. His teacher was Joel Sirkes. Krochmal soon opened his own yeshibah with his master's leave. Its pupils included men who later led in their own right. Cracow made him a dayyan. About 1636 he moved to Moravia as rabbi of Kremsir. Posts at Prossnitz and then Nikolsburg followed, the last from 1650. His son later printed his responsa as Ẓemaḥ Ẓedeḳ at Amsterdam in 1775.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-landsberg-meyer: Meyer Landsberg, a German rabbi born at Meseritz in Prussia on May 1, 1810, died at Hildesheim on May 20, 1870. He followed his teacher to Hildesheim in 1826 and lived in his house until 1830. Berlin study ran from 1834 to 1838, where he grew close to Leopold Zunz. With Zunz he set up a teachers' seminary in 1840. In 1846 he became district rabbi of Hildesheim for life. Strict in his own practice, he still brought an organ, mixed choir, and German prayers into a new synagogue.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-lehren-9723:
Lehren was a Dutch family whose name came from Lehrensteinfeld, a village in Württemberg. The entry profiles three brothers of Amsterdam. Hirsch, born in 1784, was a rich merchant. Akiba, born in 1795, and Jacob Meïr, born in 1793, were bankers and communal workers.

From 1810 Hirsch helped forward funds sent each year to Jews in Palestine, the system called the Halukkah. His strict rules for the money sparked a bitter public quarrel in 1843 and 1844. He also aided the Jews of Damascus in 1840. Meïr led the Amsterdam congregation for over thirty years. Akiba and Meïr both owned rich Hebrew book collections.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-leon-8423:
Leon was an old Spanish kingdom bounded by Old Castile, Portugal, and Galicia. Saracens ruled there until Spaniards drove them out and set up their own kingdom. In 1218 that kingdom was joined to Castile. Jews lived in Leon by the end of the tenth century, working at vine growing and trades.

Hebrew sale deeds from the early eleventh century survive there, many for vineyards. The Cortes of 1020 and the Fuero of 1090 gave Jews rights equal to Christians, though they paid special taxes. The entry follows their taxes, their losses in the plague years 1348 and 1349, the attacks of 1391, and the synagogues of towns across the kingdom.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-levi-leone-9823:
Leone Levi, an English political economist, was born in Ancona, Italy, in 1821. He died in London on May 7, 1888. He came to England young, converted to Christianity, and joined the English bar in 1859. He gave much time to setting up chambers of commerce across the country.

In 1850 Levi published his "Commercial Law of the World." In 1852 he took the chair of commercial law at King's College, London. He wrote often for the Royal Statistical Society on the work people did. His push for one shared trade code helped pass the acts of 1858 that unified much of British trade law. His books treat taxation and the history of British commerce.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-lewinsohn-joshu: Joshua Lewinsohn, a Russian teacher and writer, was born in 1833 at Vyeshiuti, in the Kovno government. He had his Talmud schooling at Zhagory, in his uncle's house. He graduated from the Mitau gymnasium in 1865 and stayed at Mitau until 1874. He then became inspector of the Jewish school at Tukum, in Courland. His Hebrew articles began in "Ha-Maggid" in 1857. His books include a geography of Russia from 1868, lives of about fifty Jewish authors, and a history of Jewish commerce.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-lisker-abraham-: Abraham ben Hayyim Lisker was a Russian rabbi of the seventeenth century, a native of Brest-Litovsk. He studied at the schools of Lublin and Cracow and was called to serve as rabbi of Rossiena, in the government of Kovno. He wrote Be'er Abraham, a commentary on the six orders of the Mishnah. It built on earlier commentaries and added his own notes. Only the parts on the first three orders were printed, at Frankfort-on-the-Oder in 1665 and 1683.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-lots-10123:
Lots were a means of settling chances and finding hidden guilt. Early peoples cast lots for omens, and the sailors with Jonah cast lots in a storm to find who had angered God. Haman used a lot when he planned to destroy the Jews.

In ancient Israel the lot shared out land west of the Jordan among the tribes. Its Hebrew word also came to mean a share and then fate itself. Lots helped choose men for tasks, divide war spoils, and settle disputes. Jewish tradition taught that the land division was guided by the Holy Spirit, with the lot as its visible sign. Talmud notes describe small stones or sticks shaken in the lap.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ma-arabi-al-mag:
Israel ben Samuel ha-Dayyan, called Ma'arabi, is profiled in the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia as a Karaite scholar of Cairo. He lived in the thirteenth and fourteenth centuries. Among his pupils was the Karaite physician and writer Japhet ibn Zaghir. His own main work, written in Arabic, dealt with the precepts of Karaite law.

The article explains how little of that work survives. Only the sections on slaughtering animals and on the calendar remain, in manuscripts held from London to St. Petersburg. The slaughter laws were printed in Hebrew at Vienna in 1830. Ma'arabi also wrote on the six articles of belief and gave a commentary on the Ten Commandments. In his legal work he attacked rival views on marriage law and backed reform. The entry traces a scholar known mostly through fragments in distant libraries.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-malachi-b-jacob:
Malachi ben Jacob ha-Kohen, an Italian Talmudist, is profiled in the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. He served as a judge at Leghorn in the eighteenth century. The entry calls him the last of Italy's great rabbinical authorities. A decision of his from 1732 survives inside another rabbi's responsa. He died before 1790.

The article centers on his famous handbook, Yad Mal'aki. Printed at Leghorn in 1767, it teaches the method of Talmud study in three parts. The first lists the Talmud's rules and technical terms in alphabetical order. The second covers rules for the codifiers. The third explains principles behind legal decisions and responsa. The book was reprinted at Berlin and Przemysl, a sign of lasting use. Malachi also wrote prayers for a Leghorn fast day. In the Eybeschutz-Emden dispute he sided with Eybeschutz. The entry preserves the methodologist Italian rabbis trusted last.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-marks-b-s-10423:
B. S. Marks, an English portrait painter, is profiled in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Born at Cardiff in 1827, he trained there and painted portraits in Wales. As a Welshman he became a Royal Cambrian Academician. In 1867 he removed to London, where he worked for more than thirty years.

The article lists sitters worthy of a court painter. They include the Prince of Wales, Lord Rothschild, and Chief Rabbi N. M. Adler. Lord Shaftesbury, Lord Aberdare, and Field-Marshal Sir John Burgoyne also sat for him. Marks gave time to Jewish schools, serving on the Jews' Free School committee. For a long period he taught art without pay to pupils and teachers alike. He also backed the free-library movement and helped found libraries at Cardiff and Ealing. The entry closes with his children: an architect son, a mathematical editor daughter, and two daughters who paint.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-menahem-eliezer:
Menahem Eliezer ben Levi, a Lithuanian Talmudist who headed the yeshivah at Minsk, is profiled in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906 by Herman Rosenthal and M. Seligsohn. Born at Wilna and trained under Solomon of Vilkomir, he won his reputation young with the "Ya'ir Kinno," a commentary on Kinnim, the most intractable of the Mishnah's tractates. Elijah of Wilna, the Gaon himself, praised it in words the entry quotes: heaven had aided him to find the meaning of a treatise in which so many commentators had failed.

After the Gaon's death his pupils commissioned Menahem Eliezer to comment on their master's notes to the Shulhan Aruk, a work he began but did not finish. His own writings on the Pentateuch and Mishnah, his novellae, and his responsa all remained unpublished when he died at Minsk on December 23, 1816.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-meshwi-al-ukbar:
Meshwi al-'Ukbari was the founder of the Jewish sect called Al-'Ukbariyyah, or the Okbarites, named for the city of 'Ukbara near Bagdad where he is said to have lived. Isidore Singer and Isaac Broydé wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. The Karaite writer Ḳirḳisani is a main source for what is known of him.

His real name was Moses, the article says, until opponents twisted it into Meshwi, meaning one whose ideas are confused. He broke with both Karaites and Rabbinites, ruling that the Day of Atonement must always fall on a Sabbath and that prayer should face west, not toward the Temple. He also barred Sabbath sacrifices in the Temple and reportedly allowed his followers to eat fat.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-mihaileni-10823:
Mihaileni, a small town in the Rumanian district of Dorogoi, was founded by Jews in 1792 under a written bargain with the land's proprietor. Richard Gottheil and E. Schwarzfeld tell its story in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Prince Alexander Moruzi confirmed the deal, which gave the founders free ground for a synagogue, a bath, and a cemetery.

In 1835 Prince Michel Sturza made the town his district capital and turned on its people, beating a leading Jew and jailing his son while trying to rewrite the old agreement. Relief came through law: new artisans won five rent-free years, and an 1838 settlement, negotiated with seven Jewish representatives at the table, freed the synagogues and bath from rent for good.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-moise-10923:
Moïse is a Charleston family with a dramatic arrival. Cyrus Adler, L. C. Harby, and L. Hühner trace it in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Abraham Moïse, born in Alsace, made a fortune in the West Indies. He married into a Jewish family of St. Eustace. The slave insurrection of 1791 drove the family out. They landed in South Carolina with four sons.

The generations that follow are bankers, lawyers, and editors. One Aaron Moïse was cashier of the Bank of the State of South Carolina. Another Aaron, born at Charleston in 1820, clerked in the United States Treasury. He ended as a Richmond editor. His son Welborne was a page in the House of Representatives. Then he became a Confederate soldier promoted for bravery. It is a thoroughly American family record.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-morpurgo-samson:
Samson ben Joshua Moses Morpurgo was an Italian rabbi, physician, and liturgist who lived from 1681 to 1740. Wilhelm Bacher and M. Seligsohn wrote his Jewish Encyclopedia entry in 1906. Born at Gradiska in Austria, he studied medicine at the University of Padua and took his degree there.

Morpurgo settled at Ancona, where he became sole rabbi in 1721 and held the post until his death. During an influenza outbreak in 1730 his medical work won him a testimonial from the archbishop of Ancona. His responsa on the Shulhan Aruk were printed after his death as Shemesh Zedakah. The entry also notes his early commentary Ez ha-Da'at and the trouble it caused him with Padua's rabbis.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-munster-sebasti:
Sebastian Münster was a German Hebraist and cosmographer born at Ingelheim in 1489. Crawford Howell Toy and Joseph Jacobs wrote his Jewish Encyclopedia entry. Taught by Elijah Levita, he became professor of Hebrew at Basel in 1529. He edited Levita's grammar works and Reuchlin's Hebrew rudiments.

In 1536 Münster published the first complete Hebrew Bible edited by a Christian, with a German translation. He wrote Chaldaic and rabbinical grammars, a Jewish calendar, and an edition of the Yosippon. He was also the first to render part of the New Testament into Hebrew, the Gospel of Matthew, in 1537. He died at Basel in 1552.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-narbonne-hebr-o:
Narbonne, a city of southern France, had Jews as early as the fifth century. Isidore Singer and S. Kahn wrote the Jewish Encyclopedia article on the community. Legend says Charlemagne gave its Jews a third of the city for help in a siege. From Baghdad, at the emperor's request, came Machir, whose descendants ruled the community as princes.

In the twelfth century some two thousand Jews made Narbonne a chief center of Jewish science. Benjamin of Tudela called it a place from which the Law spread through all the region. Decline followed war and riot, and in 1306 Philip the Fair expelled the Jews and seized their property. The article maps their two Jewries and their self-governing consuls before that end.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-nehemiah-book-o:
The Book of Nehemiah bears its hero's name as author. Emil G. Hirsch and David Samuel Margoliouth wrote its entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Some canons list it as Esdras II or III. It rode on the same scroll as Ezra's book. So readers long treated it as Ezra's appendix.

The core is Nehemiah's own memoir, finished late in life. First-person chapters tell of walls, plots, and reforms. Prayers for reward and curses on foes mark his style. Sanballat and Tobiah appear as foes in both parts. Other chapters shift into the third person about him. Lists are worked in: wall builders, returned exiles, covenant signers. One list names those who drew lots to live in Jerusalem.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-nunes-henrique-:
Henrique Nunes was a Portuguese convert turned informer. Gotthard Deutsch and Meyer Kayserling wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was born at Borba, in Portugal. Baptism in Castile put him in Lucero's service. That inquisitor employed his zeal against his old faith.

His hatred of his former brethren was notorious. King John III summoned him from the Canary Islands. Portugal wanted his counsel on planting the Inquisition. He posed as a Jew among New Christian families. Lisbon and Santarem unsuspecting, he harvested their secrets. Even his own brother stood on his list. Maranos learned the truth and plotted his end. Two, disguised as monks, stabbed him in 1524. The name Firme Fé clung to him after death.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-oppenheim-11723:
Oppenheim is a German town in the Rhine land of Hesse. Joseph Jacobs and Schulim Ochser wrote its entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. The first texts on Jews there date from the twelve hundreds. Jews there fared far better than in most German towns. They stood under the guard of the castle lords.

To those lords alone the Jews of Oppenheim paid tax. The lords kept them safe in riots of 1280 and 1298. In 1352 the town was pawned to the see of Mainz. Then a dread slaughter of the Jews took place. That same year the town won its freedom back. The lot of the Jews then grew less harsh. In 1400 Emperor Rupert backed their old rights once more.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ovary-leopold-1:
Leopold Óváry was a Hungarian keeper of the state records. Isidore Singer and Ludwig Venetianer wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was born at Veszprim on December 31, 1833. He took part in the Hungarian fight for freedom. That fight broke out in the year 1848.

In 1860 Leopold fought in the Italian war for freedom. When calm came, he gave his life to the study of the past. He soon won a name in that field of work. In 1876 he was made a keeper of the state records. In 1904 he rose to chief keeper of those records. In 1892 he joined the Hungarian Academy of Sciences. His books had great sway in the rule of his land. They struck at Rumanian claims made against Hungary in Italy.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-partnership-119:
Partnership law in Jewish sources is the subject of this long article. It was written by Lewis N. Dembitz with the Executive Committee of the Editorial Board. It appeared in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. The article traces the topic from the Mishnah to the later codes.

The Mishnah used the word shotefin mostly for joint owners of land. Later ages applied it to trading partners. The article explains how a partnership forms through a formal act of acquisition. It weighs strict rulings by Maimonides and Joseph Caro against looser views. It then covers equal sharing of profit and loss. It also covers a partner's duty of care and his power to bind the firm.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-peretz-abraham-:
Abraham Peretz was a Russian Jewish financier of great reach. Herman Rosenthal and J. G. Lipman wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He came from Galicia and married into the Zeitlin family. Under Czar Paul he won a state salt contract.

The contract covered the salt of Crimea for the crown. Peretz later settled in St. Petersburg without legal right. Great statesmen like Speranski filled his house. When a royal commission studied the Jewish question in 1802, he helped it. His influence shaped the laws that followed for Russian Jews.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-poetry-12223:
Poetry in the Hebrew Bible is the subject of a long article written by Emil G. Hirsch, Eduard König, Joseph Jacobs, H. Brody, and Israel Davidson for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. The writers ask which parts of Hebrew writing count as poetry. They start from the songs and chants named in the Bible itself.

The article sets out the marks of old Hebrew verse. It notes that Hebrew poems have no rhyme. Short likeness of sound comes only now and then. The writers then work through form, rhythm, and the kinds of poems found in the Bible. Readers get a clear guide to how Hebrew poetry differs from prose.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-poznanski-samue:
Samuel Poznanski was a scholar of Arabic and Hebrew books, born near Warsaw in 1864. Herman Rosenthal and Alexander Kisch wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He served as rabbi and preacher at the Polish synagogue in Warsaw. He knew modern Karaism as few men did. His schooling took him from Warsaw to Berlin.

At Berlin Poznanski studied at the university and the Hochschule. He grew close to his teacher Moritz Steinschneider. For that man's eightieth birthday in 1896 he made a festal book. His own works deal with Hebrew grammar of old times. They deal with Karaite faith and books as well. The entry lists his books and his many essays.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-pseudo-phocylid:
Pseudo-Phocylides is the false name of a Jewish-Hellenic poet. Crawford Howell Toy and Samuel Krauss wrote the article for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He wrote a teaching poem in epic style. It runs to some two hundred fifty verses. He took the name of Phocylides of Miletus. That bard was famed of old for wise short sayings.

Learned men long took the poem for a true Greek classic. Its teaching is of the highest moral kind. It fits both Christian and Jewish faith in one God. Schools used it as a prized book of verse. It held that place into the sixteenth century. Later study of Greek laid bare its true, Jewish source.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ptolemy-iv-surn:
Ptolemy the Fourth, surnamed Philopator, was king of Egypt. Richard Gottheil and Samuel Krauss wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He reigned from 222 to 205 B.C. He is the hero of a passage in Daniel. That passage tells of his wars with Antiochus the Great. Their clash came to a head at Raphia in 217.

At Raphia Ptolemy won a bright and full victory. The win shows him abler than men have thought. Two tales of that fight stand in Third Maccabees. One tells of a plot to kill the king. A Jew named Dositheus led the plotter into the royal tent. The article sifts fact and tale in the fight's fame.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-reddinge-robert:
Robert de Reddinge was an English Dominican friar who converted to Judaism. Joseph Jacobs wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. His conversion took place about 1275. Study of Hebrew seems to have drawn him to Judaism.

The article says he married a Jewish woman. He was circumcised and took the name Hagin. King Edward I brought the case before the Archbishop of Canterbury. Some said this case fed a royal push for expulsion. The Jews of England were later expelled under Edward. A single source from Grätz supports the entry.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-rezin-12723:
Rezin was the last king of the Damascene dynasty. Emil G. Hirsch and Schulim Ochser wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. He was slain in 732 B.C. With Pekah of Israel he planned war against Ahaz of Judah.

The article says both kings feared Assyria's Tiglath-pileser. They first tried to pull Ahaz into their coalition. When he refused, they tried to force him in. Ahaz appealed to Assyria with rich presents instead. Tiglath-pileser marched at once to help him. He captured Damascus and seized sixteen districts. Rezin himself was killed in that fall. The article then lists the whole Damascus dynasty. It runs from Razon, about 950, down to Rezin.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-root-12823:
A root is the fundamental part of a word. Crawford Howell Toy and Eduard König wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. Talmud teachers used no Hebrew term for it in grammar. They did dispute the makeup of single words, though.

The article says they split the word shahat into two elements. They also played on the word ikker in Genesis. A clear idea of root as a base form came later. Menahem ben Saruk spoke of letters in the fundamental form. Hayyuj argued against Menahem on verb structure. He held that no Hebrew verb has fewer than three letters. That three letter form was called root until modern times. Later study questioned whether three letters were original. The entry traces a basic grammar idea taking shape.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-rubinstein-jose:
Josef Rubinstein was a Russian pianist and composer born at Staro-Constantinov on February 8, 1847. Herman Rosenthal and Frank Cramer wrote his entry for the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. He studied under Hellmesberger, Dachs, and Liszt in his youth.

Rubinstein became a friend and ardent admirer of Richard Wagner. From Wagner's Ring des Nibelungen he made fine piano transcriptions for solo players. In 1869 the Grand Duchess Helena named him her chamber pianist in Russia. He joined Wagner at Bayreuth for the Ring's piano rehearsals there. His biting attacks on Schumann and Brahms won him an unenviable notoriety.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-salem-asher-ben: Asher ben Immanuel Salem was a Turkish scholar of the eighteenth century. The Executive Committee of the Editorial Board and Isaac Broydé wrote his entry for the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. His Matteh Asher, printed at Salonica in 1748, contains responsa and novellae on parts of Maimonides' Yad ha-Hazakah. It also gives laws for slaughtering animals after Jacob Weil's method, and a set of sermons.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-samuel-ha-kohen:
Herman Rosenthal and A. S. Waldstein wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia entry, published in 1906, on Samuel ha-Kohen. He was a rabbi of the sixteenth century. The entry is short, and it centers on the three books he wrote. No details of his life are given. His name marks him as a kohen, a member of the priestly line.

His first book, Derek Ḥayyim, deals with the 613 commandments. It was printed at Constantinople, with no date recorded. His Ner Miẓwah came out at Venice in 1598. It holds seventeen sermons on the thirteen articles of faith. His Torah Or appeared at Venice in 1605. That book gives sermons on the Pentateuch, the first five books of the Bible.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-satyr-13223:
Joseph Jacobs and I. M. Casanowicz wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906, on the satyr. English versions use that word for the Hebrew se'irim. The term appears in Isaiah and in Leviticus. Older versions render it as demon or false god. The Revised Version often prefers he-goat. No ordinary animal is meant in these passages.

In Isaiah the se'irim dance and call to each other among ruins. They keep company with Lilith and desert beasts. Elsewhere they appear as objects of worship. The old versions suggest hairy, perhaps goat-shaped beings. Belief in such creatures haunted desert folklore in Arabia and Syria. The Arabian jinn also take hairy, monstrous forms. The Talmud compares the Ishmaelites to se'irim of unclean places. It names other half-human beings as well.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-schuler-gelauf-:
Joseph Jacobs and Julius Gottlieb wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906, on the Schüler Gelauf. The German phrase names organized attacks on Jews by Christian schoolboys. Pupils of Poland's many Jesuit schools led these riots. They beat Jews in the streets. They also formed bands to invade and loot Jewish quarters. Towns with large Jewish populations suffered most.

Brest-Litovsk, Cracow, Posen, and Wilna all saw such riots. In 1663 Jesuit students stormed Cracow's Jewish quarter. They claimed Jews had blasphemed the Christian faith. They killed or wounded many people. They wrecked 120 houses and stole over 4,000 florins. They even forced their victims to promise no prosecution. Authorities tolerated and even encouraged the attacks. To buy safety, Jews paid the Jesuit schools every year.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-senior-abraham-:
Abraham Senior was court rabbi of Castile and its chief royal tax farmer. Joseph Jacobs and Meyer Kayserling wrote the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia entry on him. Born at Segovia early in the fifteenth century, he won favor through wealth and polish. Castilian nobles trusted his judgment in great affairs.

In 1469 Senior helped arrange the marriage of Isabella to Ferdinand of Aragon. Four years later he made peace between Isabella and her brother Henry IV. Isabella thanked him with a large life pension, later confirmed. He also held royal posts despite lacking a rabbi's usual training. The entry shows a Jewish courtier near the center of Spain's royal story.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-shusslowitz-jud: Judah Löb Shusslowitz was a Russian scholar who lived at Shklov in the nineteenth century. Herman Rosenthal and Isaac Broydé wrote the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia entry on him. He wrote Ozar ha-Shemot, a concordance of proper names in the Bible. It supplemented the general Bible concordance printed at Wilna in 1878. His second book, Massoret ha-Keriah, came out at Warsaw in 1888. It is a Masoretic and grammar manual for the public reader of the Law.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-simeon-ben-yoha:
Simeon ben Yohai was a second-century tanna, famed as the supposed author of the Zohar. Kaufmann Kohler and M. Seligsohn wrote the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia entry on him. He was born in Galilee, in northern Palestine. Tradition says he died at Meron on Lag be-Omer.

In the Mishnah he is quoted simply as Rabbi Simeon. He was a principal pupil of the great Akiba. Under Akiba he studied thirteen years at Bene-Berak. Earlier he may have studied at Jabneh under Gamaliel. A quarrel between chiefs there was blamed on him. One scholar doubts that early story on timing grounds. Simeon's sharpness was tested when he first reached Akiba. Akiba recognized the boy's gifts at once, tradition says. The entry begins the vast lore around Judaism's great mystic.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-societe-des-etu:
The Société des Études Juives is a society for Jewish history and literature. Isidore Singer and Israel Lévi wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. Its headquarters are in Paris, France. It was founded in 1880 by several leading figures. Chief Rabbi Zadoc Kahn played a leading part in its founding.

The society publishes the quarterly Revue des Études Juives. It also issues books on Jewish subjects and funds others. It organizes public lectures for a wider audience as well. Members pay set fees, with life members paying once. Official recognition came by decree in December 1896. That status lets it accept legacies and donations from supporters.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-sonneschein-sol:
Solomon H Sonneschein was an American rabbi born in Hungary in 1839. Cyrus Adler and Frederick T Haneman wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. He was born at Szent Marton Turocz on June 24. He was educated at Boskowitz in Moravia for the rabbinate. He took his rabbinical diploma there in 1863.

He later studied at Hamburg and at the University of Jena. He took his doctor's degree at Jena in 1864. He served as rabbi at Warasdin, Prague, and New York. He then served at St Louis, in Missouri, for years. By 1905 he officiated at Temple B'nai Yeshurun in Des Moines. He wrote for German and English journals for forty years.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-stern-abraham-1:
Abraham Stern was a Polish inventor and educator born at Hrubieszow in 1769. Herman Rosenthal and J. G. Lipman wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article about him in 1906. Stern grew up poor and loved Hebrew books as a boy. A local minister spotted his talent for mathematics. Stern died at Warsaw on February 3, 1842.

Stern perfected a computing machine in 1817 that could extract square roots. The invention won him election to a Warsaw science society. Emperor Alexander the First granted him a yearly pension. He also built a wagon for measuring level ground. His improved threshing and harvesting machines aided farmers. Stern served as inspector of Jewish schools and as censor. Warsaw's rabbinical school followed a plan he proposed.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-tamarisk-14223:
The tamarisk is a tree found in and around Palestine. Isidore Singer and M. Seligsohn wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article in 1906. Its Hebrew name in scripture is doubtful. One word occurring three times is read as tamarisk. The Revised Version renders it so in each place.

Abraham planted a tamarisk at Beer-sheba, says Genesis. Saul sat under a tamarisk at Ramah in Samuel. The bones of Saul and his sons rested under one at Jabesh. A parallel passage in Chronicles uses another word. Both English versions render that word as oak there. The margin offers terebinth as a further option. Several tamarisk species grow in the region today. The short entry shows translators weighing one tree's name.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-te-omim-jonah-h:
Jonah Hayyim Te'omim was a rabbi in three Polish and German towns. The Executive Committee of the Editorial Board and Isaac Broydé wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article in 1906. He served at Przemysl, Zülz, and Breslau in turn. He lived across the 1600s and 1700s. Marriage tied him to two great rabbinic houses.

Te'omim wed into the family of David Oppenheim of Prague. Later he married a daughter of Berlin's Rabbi Hirsch. His book Aleh de-Yonah holds novellae on Hoshen Mishpat. It also prints parts of his Maimonides commentary. A separate tract treats certain ritual laws in detail. It appeared at Jesnitz in 1723. Novellae on the Shebu'ot tractate followed in 1724. The short entry lists a traveling rabbi's learned output.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-tockels-mordeca:
Mordecai ben Abraham Tockels was a German Talmudist who died at Berlin in 1743. A. Peiginsky wrote this article with the Executive Committee of the Editorial Board for the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. Born at Lissa, he came to Berlin as a poor young man. A Frau Tockels adopted him there. He took her name in gratitude for her kindness.

Berlin named him dayyan, or judge, in 1723. Three years later he rose to assistant rabbi. In 1729 he took charge of the burial society. He held that office until his death. His book Torat Hayyim we-Ahabat Hesed appeared after he died. His brother-in-law edited it for print. His marriages linked him to leading Jewish families.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-triwosch-joseph:
Joseph Elijah Triwosch was a Russian Hebrew writer and poet born at Wilna in 1856. Herman Rosenthal and M. Seligsohn wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. He settled at Grodno as a teacher of Hebrew and Russian. His first articles appeared in Ha-Lebanon in 1873. He later wrote for most Hebrew literary periodicals.

His one book, Dor Tahapukot, appeared at Warsaw in 1881. It describes the work of Russian Social-Democrats. His novels instead picture Jewish life in Russia. They ran as serials in journals like Ha-Shahar and Ha-Asif. Titles include Tohelet Nikzabah and Ha-Lito'i. His poems also filled the Hebrew periodicals of the day. The entry maps a busy career in the Hebrew press.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-uzziel-14623:
Six men named Uzziel appear in the Bible, and all are listed here. Emil G. Hirsch and Schulim Ochser wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. The first Uzziel was Kohath's son and Amram's brother. His sons Mishael and Elzaphan served in the Tabernacle. At Moses' word they carried out Nadab and Abihu's bodies.

Elzaphan later led the Kohathite family in the wilderness. Another Uzziel was a Simeonite chief under Hezekiah. His band crossed the Jordan and destroyed Amalekite remnants. A Benjaminite hero bore the name among Bela's sons. One Uzziel sang in David's Temple by lot. Another helped resanctify the Temple under Hezekiah. The last was a goldsmith repairing Jerusalem's walls. Nehemiah records that work in his memoir.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-vogel-sir-juliu:
Sir Julius Vogel led the colony of New Zealand as its premier. Joseph Jacobs and Goodman Lipkind wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia entry, published in 1906. Vogel was born in London on February 25, 1835. Left an orphan, he emigrated to Australia in 1852. Gold digging failed him, so he turned to newspapers.

In New Zealand he started the Otago Daily Times. It was the colony's first daily paper. He rose through the provincial council to head its government. In 1873 he became premier of the whole colony. Later he served as agent general in London. The entry follows a swift climb from poverty to power.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-weil-gustav-148:
Gustav Weil was a German Orientalist and historian. He was born at Sulzburg, in Baden, on April 25, 1808. Isidore Singer and E. O. Adelbert Marx wrote this entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He died at Freiburg on August 29, 1889. Raised for the rabbinate, he learned Hebrew early. Talmud study at Metz did not hold him.

In 1828 Weil entered Heidelberg to study language and history. He studied Arabic in Paris under De Sacy. He followed a French army into Algiers as a reporter. In Cairo he taught French at a medical school. There he mastered Arabic, Persian, and Turkish. He returned to Europe by way of Constantinople in 1835.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-worms-rene-1502:
Rene Worms (born 1869) was a French state officer and teacher of law, the son of Emile Worms. Isidore Singer and Jacques Kahn wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Born at Rennes, he schooled at Paris and took three degrees. He won high honors from the French Institute as well.

In 1891 he began work as a court pleader in Paris. Three years later he joined the council of state staff. He sat on boards for trade schools and farm counts. In 1895 he began to teach state wealth at Paris. That post was in the law school of the city. He served as a clerk for sea and colony meets too. The entry shows a young man of law with a wide brief. His posts touch courts, schools, farms, and the sea.
journal-of-discourses-vol-23:
Volume Twenty-Three, also from 1883, finds the crusade at its cruelest. Leaders sit in prison, families scatter, and church funds face seizure. The Saints' suffering peaks in the sermons gathered in this book.

Preachers frame the pain as fire that refines, not breaks, the faithful. Discourses console the jailed men's wives and fatherless homes directly. A people drinks its Gethsemane, in their own stark biblical phrase. Endurance becomes the chief virtue preached from every stand in Utah. The record of those who bore the cup fills this grim, moving volume. Consolation, not complaint, is the note its preachers strike most often.
julian-works-wright-vol3-1923:
Wilmer Cave Wright's third Loeb volume of Julian's works came out in 1923, ten years after the first two. It holds the emperor's letters and the fragments of works that survive only in pieces. Julian wrote these texts in the brief reign when he tried to turn the empire back to its old gods.

The chief piece is Against the Galilaeans, his case against the Christians, kept in quotes by Cyril, the church writer who answered it. Julian mocks the claims of the Bible and defends Greek religion and learning. The letters beside it show his rule in daily detail. The volume completes Wright's English Julian.
jung-psychological-types-baynes-1923:
C. G. Jung published Psychological Types in German in 1921. The English text here is H. G. Baynes's translation of 1923. Jung sorts people by two attitudes: introversion, turned inward, and extraversion, turned outward. He adds four functions: thinking, feeling, sensation, and intuition. Combinations of these form his famous types.

Jung draws examples from history, literature, and his patients. The book became the source of all later personality typology, including popular tests used today. Jung warns that types are tools, not boxes for souls. His aim was to explain why thinkers see the same facts so differently. The work remains a classic of personality theory.
keynes-tract-monetary-reform-1923:
Keynes's Tract on Monetary Reform, published in 1923, tackles the money chaos that followed the First World War. Prices in Europe had swung wildly, and several nations saw their currency collapse. Keynes asks how a state should manage money in such a world.

He applies the quantity theory of money to wartime and postwar inflation in plain, forceful terms. He faults the gold standard, which ties a nation's money to a fixed stock of gold. His call for managed money pointed toward the policies he would urge for the rest of his life. He writes for citizens as much as for bankers, in brisk, quotable prose.
kierkegaard-selections-hollander-1923:
Soren Kierkegaard's selected writings appear here in L. M. Hollander's translation of 1923, the first broad English gateway to his work. Kierkegaard was a Danish thinker of the 1800s who wrote under many pen names. The selections cover dread, faith, and the stages of life. Aesthetic, ethical, and religious ways of living stand in sharp contrast.

Kierkegaard defends the leap of faith against cold systems of thought. He insists truth for faith is personal and inward. Later thinkers named him a founder of existentialism. Hollander's volume let English readers meet him at length for the first time. It remains a useful door into a demanding author.
lawrence-birds-beasts-flowers-1923:
D. H. Lawrence wrote most of Birds, Beasts and Flowers during his travels in Italy, New Mexico, and Australia. The collection appeared in 1923, after he had left England for good. Lawrence arranged the poems by their subjects, as the title announces.

The poems watch plants and animals with fierce attention. A snake drinking at a trough in Sicily shames the poet's fearful education. Figs, bats, kangaroos, and dark Bavarian gentians all appear, each treated as a living otherness to respect. Lawrence rejected smooth traditional forms for free, breathing rhythms. Many readers call this his finest book of poems.
lawrence-kangaroo-1923:
Lawrence and Frieda spent months in Australia in 1922, and Kangaroo grew directly out of that stay. Published in 1923, it follows Richard Somers, a writer much like Lawrence, settling near Sydney with his wife Harriet.

Somers is courted by 'Kangaroo', a charismatic lawyer building a paramilitary movement of returned soldiers, and by socialists who want him too. He refuses both, and the novel becomes a reckoning with politics, loyalty, and Australia itself. Long passages simply watch the sea and bush with fierce attention. It is the antipodean chapter of Lawrence's search for a new life and a new faith.
lawrence-ladybird-1923:
The Ladybird, published in 1923, gathers three long stories from Lawrence's post-war years: 'The Ladybird', 'The Fox', and 'The Captain's Doll'. Each turns on power and surrender between men and women in a Europe broken by war.

In the title story, a wounded German count draws an English lady toward a dark, chthonic faith. 'The Fox' sets two women farming alone against a young soldier and the fox that haunts them, toward a shocking end. 'The Captain's Doll' plays the same tensions as comedy. These are among Lawrence's most perfectly made tales, written at the height of his powers.
lawrence-studies-classic-american-1923:
Lawrence's 1923 criticism took on the classic American writers and read them against the grain. His essays on Franklin, Cooper, Poe, Hawthorne, Melville, and Whitman became the most famous single book of American literary criticism by an outsider.

Lawrence claims that American literature hides a dark secret: a continent won by violence, and a soul split between innocence and blood. He distrusts what these writers say they mean and hunts what their tales confess. The style is wild, funny, and prophetic. Scholars have argued with his readings ever since, and few have matched their force. The book remade how America read itself.
leonora-pg13723:
Arnold Bennett published his novel Leonora in 1903. Its contents open at the household at Hillport, in Bursley. Bennett sets the tale in his familiar Five Towns country.

Meshach and Hannah appear in the second chapter. A call, an intimacy, and a chance follow in turn. Comic opera, a dance, and a death in the family widen the plot. Leonora herself must refuse something in a late chapter. The story closes in a garden and in London. Edgeworth's father helped shape her early writing career. Leonora's letters debate whether feeling should rule marriage.
li-bai-the-works-of-li-po-the-chinese-po:
Li Bai, called Li Po in this 1923 English version by Shigeyoshi Obata, was China's most loved poet. He sang of wine, moonlight, high mountains, and friends far away. His Tang dynasty lyrics date from the eighth century, China's golden age of verse.

Obata chose and Englished the poems with a scholar's care and a poet's ear. Parting, longing, and drunken joy recur like notes in music. Li Bai's ease hides deep craft, and his freedom still startles readers. This selection carried his genius to the West and helped fix his name among the supreme lyric poets of the world.
library-of-the-world-s-best-literature-a:
Edited by Charles Dudley Warner, Volume Six extends his anthology of world literature. Mabie, Runkle, and George Henry Warner served as associate editors. The advisory council mixed professors from eastern universities and California. Together they chose writings they considered the best of every age.

The volume offers passages and pieces spanning ancient authors to modern ones. Arranged for the home reader, it favors famous, durable works over novelties. Short selections let readers compare styles, subjects, and centuries side by side. It stands as both a reading collection and a record of period taste. Willard Fiske's Cornell post covered Germanic and Scandinavian languages and literatures. Edward Holden directed California's Lick Observatory while advising the editors.
life-and-death-of-john-of-barneveld-comp:
Motley's complete Barneveld history, dated 1880, spans 1609 to 1623. Project Gutenberg issued it as Volume 99 of his Netherlands history. John of Barneveld, Advocate of Holland, directs the Dutch Republic throughout. The work links his fate to the coming Thirty Years' War.

Its preface calls both wars one tragedy lasting eighty years. The Twelve Years' Truce was only a pause in the struggle. Persons and scenes change, yet motives and events form one succession. Readers can follow the whole arc in a single complete text. Designs reaching back to Charles V open his long historical view. Generations of actors succeed one another across the eighty years.
lizerand-dossier-affaire-templiers-1923:
Georges Lizerand, a French scholar, built Le Dossier de l'Affaire des Templiers in 1923 as a working file of the case. The Knights Templar fell in 1307, when the French king's men seized them across the realm. Lizerand prints the core papers of that fall in one volume.

Readers get the arrest order, the long interrogations of the brothers, and the acts that ended the order in 1312. Grand Master Jacques de Molay's own words sit among the records. The dossier lets the case be read from its papers, not from legend. Students of the Templar trial still start with this file.
llull-lover-beloved-peers-1923:
Ramon Llull was the Catalan mystic of the 1200s. His Book of the Lover and the Beloved is a string of 366 short prose poems, one for each day of the year. E. Allison Peers translated the work into English in 1923, with an essay on the life of Llull and his famous Art. The poems stand inside his great romance Blanquerna.

The Lover seeks the Beloved, who is God, through forests of signs, questions, and joy. Each piece is a spark: a dialogue, a sigh, a small parable of longing and praise. Llull drew on the Sufi poets he had read in Mallorca. The book is the sweetest fruit of Catalan mysticism, still read day by day.
machen-christianity-and-liberalism-1923:
Machen's Christianity and Liberalism, published in 1923, is the fundamentalist manifesto of the American church fights of the 1920s. Its claim is blunt: liberalism is not a kind of Christianity but a different religion entirely. Machen wrote it while Princeton Seminary slid toward the split he would soon lead.

He compares the two faiths on God, man, the Bible, Christ, salvation, and the church, finding them opposed at every point. Liberalism, he says, rests on naturalism, the denial that God acts in history in supernatural ways. The book still anchors conservative arguments about the boundaries of the faith.
millay-harp-weaver-1923:
Edna St. Vincent Millay published The Harp-Weaver and Other Poems in 1923, and it won the Pulitzer Prize for poetry. Millay was the first woman to win that prize. The book catches her in her prime, when her sonnets were being memorized across America.

The title ballad tells of a poor mother who weaves fine clothes for her son on a magic harp as she dies. Behind its fairy-tale shape sits real poverty Millay knew from her own childhood. The volume also holds a celebrated sonnet sequence on love and loss. Ballads, lyrics, and sonnets together make this the fullest single display of Millay's gifts.
monroe-doctrine-1823:
President James Monroe laid out his doctrine in a message on December 2, 1823. The Seventh Annual Message to Congress holds the famed passage. Europe's monarchs are warned to keep hands off the Americas.

The Western Hemisphere, Monroe declares, is closed to fresh colonization. Any bid to crush the new Latin republics will count as hostile. The young republic thus claims a sphere of its own age. The statement became the base stone of foreign policy for a century. Later presidents stretched its reach far past Monroe's first intent in 1823. The doctrine's few lines grew into a creed of hemispheric power.
muir-life-mohammad-weir-1923:
William Muir built The Life of Mohammad from Arabic sources, first in 1861 and revised by T. H. Weir in the 1923 edition. Muir read Ibn Ishaq, Ibn Hisham, Waqidi, and Tabari at first hand, a rare feat for a Victorian writer. His critical biography follows the Prophet from Mecca to Medina to the conquest of Arabia.

Muir admired his subject's power while judging the faith by his own Christian lights, and readers have argued with him ever since. The book long served English readers as their fullest life of Mohammad from the sources. It also stands as the public-domain stand-in for the early Sira in English.
openalex-w1595049023:
Cristian Koepfli, Ivo Mueller, and co-authors studied malaria spread. Their paper appeared in PLoS ONE in May 2015. Gametocytes are the parasite forms that infect mosquitoes. Knowing what drives their carriage aids malaria control, they note. The team surveyed people in Papua New Guinea.

More than two thousand samples were gathered in the survey. Tests used both light microscopy and molecular methods. Two malaria species were tracked in blood samples. The title reports that parasite load and age matter most. Both factors shaped gametocyte levels for each species. The findings help target the human reservoir of infection.
openalex-w1985667523:
Rajwant Kaur and co-authors studied an invasive tree's impacts. Their paper is dated 2012 in the catalog record. Prosopis juliflora is a tree that invades dry lands. It forms a complex with its relative Prosopis pallida. Communities feel its spread in varied, debated ways.

The team coordinated comparisons across the tree's ranges. They compared impacts in native and non-native regions. A comparison with a close relative added control. Such grounded designs separate plant effects from place effects. Findings can guide where to clear or use the tree. Dryland policy needs that local, tested evidence base.
openalex-w2040593023:
Harald Schunck, Gaute Lavik, Dhwani Desai and colleagues studied a huge toxic plume in the ocean off Peru. Their paper appeared in PLoS ONE in 2013. The waters hold a zone with very little oxygen. Sometimes hydrogen sulfide builds up there. That gas is toxic to most larger marine life.

A research cruise in 2009 found a giant sulfide plume. It covered a vast area of shelf water. It was the largest such plume ever reported. The team sampled the microbes living inside it. Many were bacteria that oxidise sulfur compounds. Rate tests showed active carbon fixation in the dark water. Microbes there live by chemical energy, not sunlight. The plume offers a rare look at that way of life.
openalex-w2068794323:
Tomas Duffy, Margarita Bisio, Jaime Altcheh and colleagues built a precise PCR method to track Chagas parasites in blood. Their paper appeared in PLoS Neglected Tropical Diseases in 2009. Parasite load guides care for Chagas patients. Existing tests could not count parasites reliably. A standard counting method was needed.

Their test targets a repeated DNA stretch in the parasite. It detects extremely low parasite levels in blood. Accuracy held across a very wide range. A commercial kit step reduced test interference from blood. An added control corrected each sample's processing losses. The method expressed parasite loads in exact terms. It gave clinics a tool to monitor treatment response.
openalex-w2073840323:
Tania Kelnert and Claudete Silva reviewed a bestselling American book on reforming government. Their review appeared in a Brazilian administration journal in 1993. The book, by David Osborne and Ted Gaebler, argued for entrepreneurial government. It had become one of the most discussed books in the United States.

Osborne was a journalist and government consultant. Gaebler had managed American cities. Their proposal urged government to act more like a business. President Clinton used the same reform language publicly. He promised to cut federal bureaucracy. The reviewers explain the book's ideas for Brazilian readers. They place it within public administration debates of the time.
openalex-w2092288223:
Steven Stoddard, Amy Morrison, Gonzalo Vazquez-Prokopec and colleagues examined how human travel spreads mosquito-borne disease. Their paper appeared in PLoS Neglected Tropical Diseases in 2009. Movement shapes who meets biting insects. It works across many time and place scales. The authors built a model to weigh its role.

They focused on dengue and its day-biting mosquito. Daily routines carry people through many small places. Mosquito biting habits interact with those movements. Short trips can matter as much as long ones. Exposure varies strongly between individuals. Standard models often ignore such fine movement. The paper shows when movement details change predictions. Control plans should account for daily travel patterns.
openalex-w2119721623:
Martin Kulldorff, Richard Heffernan, Jessica Hartman, and colleagues published this study in PLoS Medicine in 2005. They asked how officials can spot a disease outbreak early. Their problem was simple: case counts often come with no good population data. Daily records from emergency rooms, ambulances, and pharmacies often lack that base.

The authors propose a scan method that uses case numbers alone. It makes few guesses about when or where an outbreak starts. They tested it on daily emergency room visits in New York City. Four of the five strongest signals looked like early local signs of wider outbreaks. Those outbreaks were rotavirus, norovirus, and flu, and false alarms were few.
openalex-w2316628323:
Jessica Lleixà, Valentina Martín, María Portillo, and colleagues published this study in Frontiers in Microbiology in 2016. They compare fermentations and wines made by inoculating two different yeasts. The standard wine yeast does the job reliably, but winemakers increasingly try wild yeasts to add complexity and character.

Grape must ferments when yeasts turn its sugars into alcohol and carbon dioxide. Wild yeasts riding in on grape skins once meant unpredictable, sometimes spoiled fermentations. Yet many carry enzymes the standard yeast lacks, including ones that free aroma compounds locked in grape sugars. The study sets the two species side by side through fermentation and into the finished wines. Such comparisons tell winemakers what each yeast brings, and what it risks.
openalex-w2742149023:
Ayelén Dichdji wrote this 2017 article in the journal Luna Azul, in Spanish with an English summary. It stages a dialogue between two fields: environmental history and anthropology. Both study how people relate to nature, a topic gaining urgency as socio-environmental conflicts grow more visible. The article reviews what anthropology has contributed to historical studies of environmental questions.

Dichdji tours the central authors who tried to define environmental history as a field. She then turns to anthropologists who approached the nature-culture divide from different angles. Environmental history, she notes, is hard to pin down because it welcomes many approaches. That openness makes it a multidisciplinary field that folds nature into human history. The essay helps readers see how the two disciplines sharpen each other. It suits students entering either field in Latin America and beyond.
openalex-w2898493623:
The MiniBooNE Collaboration reported a neutrino anomaly in Physical Review Letters in 2018, with A. A. Aguilar-Arevalo heading the author list. The experiment at Fermilab watches a muon neutrino beam for electron neutrinos appearing. Standard physics with three neutrino types predicts very little appearance at this distance. An earlier experiment, LSND, had seen an unexplained excess decades before.

With doubled data, MiniBooNE saw an excess of about three hundred eighty electronlike events, at 4.5 standard deviations. Adding its antineutrino running brought the combined excess to about four hundred sixty events. An oscillation explanation would need at least a fourth, sterile neutrino type. The result matches LSND's excess in size and energy. Together the two experiments reach six standard deviations. Either a discovery or a stubborn systematic error, the anomaly refuses to fade.
openalex-w2949716623:
M. A. Acero, P. Adamson, L. Aliaga, and colleagues of the NOvA collaboration published this paper in Physical Review Letters in 2019. It reports the first measurement of neutrino oscillation parameters made with both neutrinos and antineutrinos. Neutrinos are ghostly particles that shift between types as they travel.

Oscillation is the name for that shifting, and its exact rates test the basic rules of particle physics. NOvA is a long-distance experiment built to watch neutrino beams over hundreds of kilometers. By comparing how neutrinos and their antimatter partners changed along the way, the team measured the governing parameters in a new way. The result sharpens tests of whether matter and antimatter behave alike.
openalex-w3004109123:
Savitha DeBritto, Tanzeembanu Gajbar, Praveen Satapute, and colleagues published this study in Scientific Reports in 2020. It isolates pyocyanin, a blue-green pigment made by a common soil germ, and tests its uses. The pigment has valued uses in medicine, farming, and green technology.

The team found a strong pigment-making strain in farm soil and confirmed its name by gene checks. Feeding the cultures unlike foods changed output, with a soybean-enriched broth giving the best yield. They cleaned the pigment and proved its makeup with lab tools. The pure pigment then did well as a dye and in farm chemical tests, the authors report. Such finds may add new uses for a germ best known as a cause of infection.
openalex-w3006366423:
Members of the Malaria Genomic Epidemiology Network published this study in Nature Communications in 2019. It hunts for human gene variants that change a person's risk of severe malaria. The network gathered genome data on about seventeen thousand cases and controls from eleven countries across Africa, Asia, and Oceania.

The team also sequenced family trios and typed candidate spots in fifteen thousand further samples. They found five sturdy links between gene regions and severe malaria, including a newly implicated variant on chromosome six. Together the variants explain about one tenth of the inherited share of risk. The new chromosome six signal tied most strongly to cerebral malaria, the deadliest form of the disease.
openalex-w3172681723:
Michela Antonelli, Annika Reinke, Spyridon Bakas, and colleagues introduce the Medical Segmentation Decathlon in Nature Communications in 2022. Segmentation means outlining structures, such as tumours, in medical scans so computers can measure them. Thousands of algorithms do this task, yet picking a starting design for a new problem stays hard.

The Decathlon is a contest where one algorithm must handle many imaging tasks and scan types. Its data sets were built to include common hardships: few images, uneven labels, data from many hospitals, and tiny targets. A final mystery round tested whether entries could solve unseen tasks without any changes. The contest gives the field a fair test of general-purpose tools.
openalex-w4308769923: Josef Smolen, Robert Landewé, J. W. J. Bijlsma, and colleagues present the EULAR recommendations for managing rheumatoid arthritis with disease-modifying drugs. The catalogue record lists an earlier update. The preserved sample, though, is the publisher's page for the 2022 update in the Annals of the Rheumatic Diseases. That page gives only citation details and the author list. It has no readable recommendation text, so the guidance itself cannot be summarised from it here.
openalex-w4360603423:
Anna Gilmore, Alice Fabbri, Fran Baum, and colleagues define the commercial determinants of health in The Lancet in 2023. The phrase names how business products and practices shape health, for good or ill. The largest global corporations, they argue, drive much avoidable illness, planetary damage, and inequality. Just four industry sectors already account for at least a third of deaths worldwide.

The paper describes a system in which powerful firms can cause harm while others pay the costs. As company wealth and power grow, governments and citizens grow weaker in response. Known policies then stall, unenforced, while health systems strain under rising disease. The authors insist governments can and must act, for the sake of future generations.
openalex-w4366091323:
Shams Forruque Ahmed, Md. Sakib Bin Alam, Maruf Hassan, and colleagues review deep learning modelling in Artificial Intelligence Review in 2023. Deep learning teaches computers to find patterns by passing data through many layers of transformation. It has produced striking results in health care, education, security, and industry. Yet surveys covering the whole field's designs remain surprisingly few, the authors note.

Their review compares the main model families, how each is trained, and where each works best. Many models excel only in narrow domains, they find. Training can be slow and costly and demands huge datasets for accuracy. Models can also be fooled, misclassify, or settle into poor solutions. The authors map these strengths and weaknesses to guide builders toward sturdier designs.
openalex-w7128498023:
Marvelous Popoola, Sharmeen Malik, Kaushalendra Mani Tripathi, and colleagues study bleeding severity and quality of life in immune thrombocytopenia. Their study appeared in the Juntendo Medical Journal in 2026. The disease destroys platelets, the cells that stop bleeding. Bleeding ranges from bruises to dangerous brain haemorrhage.

Patients also live with fatigue and constant fear of bleeding. The team ran a cross-sectional study at hospital haematology clinics. They set out to measure how bleeding severity tracks quality of life. Most past work comes from wealthier countries, not South Asian practice. A clear link would push clinicians to treat the condition's daily burden, not only its platelet counts.
openalex-w7204939723:
Marlisson Jose de Sousa Silva led a Portuguese-language article, published in Brazil in 2026, on drone technology in the service of the Military Police of Pará, in the Brazilian Amazon. Digital technologies have transformed public security, and remotely piloted aircraft are now part of police operations. The theoretical and documentary study analyzes the force's acquisition of drones and the technical training of its personnel, and the resulting use of the technology against crime.

Using new technologies modernizes the force's equipment and operational actions, the authors report. Investment in state-of-the-art technology expresses an attempt to raise policing effectiveness and, above all, to preserve life in high-stakes police actions. In a state of vast distances and rivers, an eye in the sky changes what a patrol can do.
openalex-w7206151423:
Daiane de Lourdes Alves Velho and five colleagues weigh smart tools in schools that take all kids. Their 2026 Brazil study reads past work and state rules. To take all kids, they stress, is more than a seat in a room. Walls must come down in how staff teach, talk, and use tech, so each child can join in.

Smart tutors, tools that adapt, and mixed forms of text can widen the door to lore and help staff shape plans to each child. But the team sets firm terms. Staff must guide the use. The tools must be fit for all kids. Child data must stay safe. Rules must fight the gaps in who has tech at home, and bias baked into the code. Used with clear aims and care for each child's worth, the tools can back the school of all.
openalex-w7212194923:
Julia Gomes da Silva, Mariana Fernandes Ramos dos Santos, and Renato Marcelo Resgala Junior review a thin shelf of work: how grown children fare when their parents split. Most past work tracks young kids and teens when a marriage ends. These three ask what the same break does to sons and daughters who are past age eighteen. The review is broad and reads work in three tongues across six databases.
