In disseminated intravascular coagulation, clots form throughout small vessels while clotting factors run out, driving organ failure. Whether the clotting state predicts kidney injury in septic shock had never been charted.

The team followed consecutive septic shock patients admitted to intensive care in Strasbourg, all on blood-pressure drugs for infection. They tracked who developed the clotting disorder and whose kidneys failed, how badly, and whether they recovered. The association proved strong, which makes the clotting score a warning sign worth watching at the bedside.
pmc-10693623:
Giorgio Piazza, Marina Kalashnikova, and Clara Martin test whether the way people naturally talk to language learners actually helps them learn, in a study published in 2023. Speakers adjust their pronunciation when addressing non-natives, a register called non-native directed speech. Fifty Spanish speakers learned made-up English words, some heard in that adjusted register and some in ordinary native-directed speech.

The adjusted-speech group recognized the new words faster, learned them better, and pronounced a tricky vowel contrast more distinctly. The words contained English vowel pairs that sit close to, or far from, Spanish categories. Interestingly, a separate test of vowel discrimination showed no improvement in either group, so the benefit lies in learning support rather than sharper ears. The study validates a common teaching instinct with controlled evidence.
pmc-10694123:
Kei Yamamoto and co-authors retune an enzyme to spot citrulline, a disease marker amino acid, in a 2023 study. Citrulline reads today need pricey machines or fussy color tests, and no enzyme locks onto it specifically.

Starting from an arginine oxidase that barely notices citrulline, the team first exploited a side activity that already favored it. One targeted swap at a key residue then tripled its citrulline pace and flipped its preference fully. The tuned enzyme gives straight line reads across a useful range, opening a simple dipstick style citrulline test.
pmc-10694923:
Tilda Herrgårdh and co-authors stitch two body models into a digital twin that follows insulin resistance from a single meal to years of weight change, in a 2023 study. Insulin resistance grows on two clocks: meal responses shift within hours, while diabetes brews over years, and it spans gut, organs, and cell signaling. The team joined their short-term glucose and signaling model to existing long-term weight regulation models, fitting the combined system to human data.

The twin then predicted, without refitting, the results of a weight-gain study: body weight, fasting insulin and glucose, and even signaling inside cells. It also matched a weight-loss study using the drug topiramate, and it can report variables no one measured. The authors see a teaching and motivation tool in the making, and eventually a clinical aid against insulin resistance.
pmc-10695023:
Suad Dukhaykh examines how conflict between work and family life affects how tied women feel to their jobs, in a 2023 study. The study surveyed women who work in the private sector in Saudi Arabia. Spillover runs both ways: work can disrupt family life, and family demands can disrupt work. Both forms were expected to drain women emotionally and weaken their job ties.

Survey answers from more than two hundred sixty women were tested with standard statistical models. Emotional exhaustion fully carried the effect of both kinds of conflict on job ties. Women worn out by clashing demands felt less bound to their jobs. Dukhaykh urges firms to give staff more control over work time and place, and to set clear rules for flexible and part-time work.
pmc-10695623:
Hua-Ying Chuang and co-authors map the most-cited research on remote rehabilitation after joint replacement, in a bibliometric study from 2023. Remote rehab can add to or stand in for in-person therapy after surgery. The field has grown fast, but its leading papers had not been charted as a set.

The team searched a major citation database and pulled the top 100 cited papers from 712 candidates. Output rose steadily and peaked in 2022, with the United States as the top source. One university in Canada led among institutions, and one Canadian author led among writers. Four themes ran through the set, with replacement named in 89 percent of papers. Papers whose keywords stood out drew more citations, a link the authors flag for writers.
pmc-10695923:
David Frantz and a large team of co-authors published this 2023 study weighing the built environment of the United States. Buildings and infrastructure now outweigh all living biomass on Earth, and the team wanted the pattern at fine scale. They mapped the mass of fourteen stock-building materials across eight building types and nine kinds of mobility infrastructure.

The maps show built structures 2.6 times heavier than all plant biomass in the country, with most inhabited areas dominated by construction mass. Dense settlements use far less material per person, while sparse regions carry the highest intensities because roads and networks run everywhere. Depopulation worsens the rural figure, since people leave but structures stay. The authors offer the atlas as groundwork for leaner settlements and a circular economy.
pmc-10697723:
Matthew Tan and colleagues show vessel cells steer breast cancer invasion through metabolism. Their study from twenty twenty-three uses a microfluidic platform. Cancer spreads when tumour cells cross tissue to reach blood vessels. Metabolic flexibility is known to power that invasion step.

The device grows tumour cells near an artificial microvessel channel. Vessel lining cells released factors that pulled invasion toward them. Invading cells burned more glucose and oxygen than resting ones. Imaging and chemical profiling confirmed broad metabolic rewiring. Limiting glucose sharply reduced vessel-directed invasion. Blood vessels are active partners in spread, not passive escape routes. Cutting their metabolic signals may slow metastasis.
pmc-10698723:
Saenz-Garcia, Figuerola, Turnes Palomino, Leal, and Palomino Cabello report a water cleaning device in a 2023 paper. Heavy metals in drinking water pose a clear health risk, and traps that grab them must work in real taps, wells, and lakes. Their trap builds on an iron based sponge like crystal with huge inner surface.

Sulfur groups grafted onto the crystal grip mercury far better than the plain form, pulling out 96% against 78%. The powder was set into a printed plastic support that stirs and soaks at once. The device pulled mercury well, could be reused, and also trapped lead and arsenic. Tests on tap, well, and lake water back its use for both cleaning and sensing.
pmc-10698923:
Baolin Wu and co-authors mapped the gene network behind sterile wheat pollen in two thousand twenty-three. Male-sterile lines power hybrid wheat seed production. One type borrows cytoplasm from a wild grass relative. Its pollen aborts partway through development. Microscopy pinpointed when the failure strikes. The pollen nucleus fails to split as it should.

Starch never fills the dying grains. Gene activity was compared with a fertile twin line. A core network of genes emerged from the contrast. The abortion window spans two pollen stages. Breeders maintain and restore such lines by design. Knowing the network sharpens that control. Hybrid wheat yields could climb in consequence.
pmc-10699023:
Sébastien Leruste and co-authors interviewed in 2023 family doctors on Réunion about spotting alcohol harm in pregnancy and its effects on children. The island has the highest rate of fetal alcohol syndrome among French regions. Doctors sit at the front line of detection. Interviews followed a grounded theory approach until no new themes emerged, with four researchers checking the analysis.

Doctors described real barriers: social taboos, mixed public messages, patchy knowledge, and symptoms that vary widely. Diagnosis needs a specialist team and long consultations. The doctors felt confident spotting developmental problems generally, but worried about long waits for specialist care. They asked for better promotion, training, and coordination so affected children get identified and helped sooner.
pmc-10700323:
Yajing Zhang and co-authors present a 2023 study of how people act after wins and losses in games. Standard feedback marks losses as bad, which can hurt later play. The authors argue that players can reset what counts as success when the goal of the task changes.

Players took part in game tasks where they tried at times to do as well as they could. At other times they tried to do as poorly as they could. Acts after wins stayed more steady when the goal was to win. Acts after losses stayed more steady when the goal was to lose. The split shows that feedback helps or harms based on the goal at hand. The authors urge a fresh look at losing.
pmc-10700623:
Floressy Juhim and eight colleagues blast tellurite glass with gamma rays to see if it can serve as a radiation shield that survives its own job. The glass carried titanium and aluminium oxide nanoparticles, hoped to harden it against damage. Samples took fifty and one hundred kilogray doses.

After exposure the glass changed color and grew more broken oxygen links inside. Surfaces roughened and let less light through, yet the glass stayed transparent. Aluminium oxide lowered density while the best mix kept strong photon blocking, judged by its mass attenuation values. One recipe stood out as a shielding candidate for hot zones.
pmc-10702023:
Chuang Wang leads a team that compares dog and pig clot models. Their study from twenty twenty-three deals with chronic deep vein thrombosis. The models help test devices for vessel treatment.

Clots were formed in the left iliac vein of both species. Thrombin and fibrinogen made a solid clot at a narrow spot. Vessel imaging and tissue stains tracked clot progress. Clots formed in all the animals in the study. Dogs all survived to the ninety day mark. Pigs fared worse, with deaths at varied days. Dogs suit the model better, they conclude.
pmc-10702123:
Ahmed A Abu-hassan measures a hyperactivity drug at nano levels with a light scattering trick in a 2023 paper. The drug steadies a brain messenger tied to behavior control, and dose checks in pills and blood call for cheap, keen assays.

Mixed with a pink dye in acid, the drug forms clumps whose scattered light swells in step with drug amount across a wide range, read at one wavelength. Detection sinks to about thirteen billionths of a gram per milliliter. Checks passed world validation rules, and pill samples read cleanly. The one pot method stays green and simple.
pmc-10703223:
Malin Ekelund and Magnus Bergquist tested whether hotels can nudge guests greener by giving first, in a 2023 paper. Two large preregistered experiments, with over two and four and a half thousand people, varied the appeals. In the first, hearing the hotel itself conserved resources lowered guests' irritation, a reciprocity effect, though towel reuse plans did not move, perhaps because baseline intentions already ran high.

The second study targeted meat eating. All three reciprocity appeals raised feelings of obligation and goodwill against a standard appeal. One variant, where the hotel had donated to an environmental cause, truly cut meat intentions. Reciprocity, refined, shows early promise for greening travel choices.
pmc-10703923:
Gabriella Leighton and co-authors show that caracals around Cape Town are feeding lower on the food chain as the city grows, in a 2023 study. Urban growth reshapes what wild animals can eat. Top predators vanish, and human food waste floods the system. Mid-sized hunters like the caracal then face a predation paradox. Their wild prey may shrink while easy scraps abound.

Fur samples carry chemical traces of long-term diet. Stable isotope analysis read the cats' trophic position and diet breadth. Urban and wildland cats were compared across the region. Diets shifted toward lower trophic levels near the city. Niche overlap between groups also changed. Conservationists gain evidence that ecological roles erode quietly in cities.
pmc-10704623:
Joseph Tonna and co-authors run a clinical trial from 2023 testing a fluid taken from around unborn babies as a treatment for COVID-19. The fluid is known to fight germs and calm swelling, and an early check had shown it could be given safely to very ill patients. The team wanted to know if it also lowered signs of body-wide swelling.

The trial was held at one center and assigned patients by chance to get the fluid or a dummy treatment, with neither side told which was which. All patients were adults in hospital with breathing symptoms from the infection. The study was an early-phase trial, so safety and swelling markers came first. Results would guide whether larger trials are worth doing.
pmc-10707123:
Wen Zhou and co-authors test whether a plant saponin, and the forms it takes after the body processes it, can calm inflammation. Their 2023 study starts from a traditional herb whose root is prized for anti-inflammatory effect. The compound, ardisiacrispin B, makes up over sixteen percent of the extract, yet its fame so far was anti-tumor, and as a large molecule it likely acts partly through metabolites.

Network pharmacology first predicted the targets of the parent compound and its breakdown products. Cell tests then checked the predictions in vitro. Including metabolites matters: judging only the swallowed form can miss the agents that actually do the work.
pmc-10707523:
Filippo Familiari and nine co-authors pool trials comparing two ways of sizing the thigh component in knee replacement. Their meta-analysis was published in twenty twenty-three. Referencing from the front or the back of the bone changes fit and joint line.

Four databases were searched under standard review rules. Scores for knee function, pain questionnaires, bend range, and bone offset measures were extracted. Study quality and bias were scored with standard tools. Five comparative studies met the bar for pooling. The synthesis weighs whether the front-referencing habit protects the kneecap joint at any cost to the back of the knee. Surgeons get one balanced readout instead of single-center claims.
pmc-10707923:
A team of chemists reviews electrochemical sensors for new kinds of water contaminants in a paper from 2023. These contaminants of emerging concern include drug residues, personal care chemicals, and new pesticides. Even tiny amounts can harm health and build up in living tissue. Sensors that read electrical signals offer a fast, sensitive way to detect them. The review sorts the literature by contaminant class.

For each class it covers sources, pathways, and health effects. It then surveys sensor designs reported for the major members. The authors praise the platform's selectivity, stability, and low detection limits. They frame the review as a guide for building safer monitoring systems.
pmc-10708623:
Hilda Bax and three co-authors study starch building enzymes from a hot spring microbe in a 2023 paper. Glycogen is a branched sugar store found across life. Branching enzymes add the side chains that make it compact. Two unrelated enzyme families share that job.

The microbe Petrotoga mobilis carries one enzyme from each family. The team tried them alone and together on a straight sugar chain. Together, the pair packed far more branches into the product. One enzyme grew long branches from the chain. The other trimmed those branches shorter and denser. Used alone, each enzyme did less than the pair achieved. The result hints at bakery and materials uses for denser starch.
pmc-10708723:
Chen and co-authors design a car insurance claims system built on blockchain and distributed file storage, in this 2023 paper. Today's claims process suffers fraud, lost records, slow steps, and pricey data storage. A tamper-proof ledger could answer several of those problems at once.

Claim data are signed and encrypted with an elliptic curve method before storage. The heavy files live in the InterPlanetary File System, while the chain keeps the fingerprints that prove nothing changed. Every step stays traceable for later audit. The design also adds an arbitration path for disputed claims. The authors aim for cheaper, safer, and more open claims handling.
pmc-10708823:
Qihang Yang and co-authors tested ways to clean weather noise out of satellite radar maps in this 2023 study. The radar method, InSAR, measures ground movement from orbit, but shifting air moisture bends the signal and blurs the result. Their test ground sits where high plateau meets monsoon rains in southwest China.

Four districts with sharp terrain and seasonal swings were studied. Three fixes were compared: a simple straight-line model, an online weather correction service, and a global weather data set. All three cut the air delay, judging by steadier phase readings and checks against ground GPS. Which fix won depended on place and season. The study helps surveyors pick a method that fits local skies.
pmc-10709323:
Yixiao Zhu and co-authors study a long non-coding RNA in stomach cancer in a 2023 paper. Stomach cancer comes in many forms, and one fast-spreading form shifts cells to a mobile state. Long RNA strands that make no protein can still steer such shifts.

The team name one strand, MIR200CHG, as a master switch for that shift in this cancer form. The strand is silenced in tumors by extra chemical marks, and low levels track poor outlook. Restoring it flipped cells back and slowed spread in animals. It also shields a small partner RNA from targeted decay. The work maps a subtype-tied control web in this cancer.
pmc-10710823: Wei-Lin Jin highlights a newly found route by which cells shred short-lived nuclear proteins, in a 2023 commentary. The pathway centers on midnolin, which hands its catches straight to the proteasome, skipping the usual ubiquitin tagging. The underlying study mapped how this route disposes of fast-turnover proteins, many of them products of immediate-early genes whose overactivity tracks with cancer growth. Jin argues blocking the pathway could become a cancer strategy, since tumor cells lean on rapid protein turnover.
pmc-10712123:
Ayumi Takakura and co-authors report a case where adding an anemia drug seems to have driven blood sugar too low in an older patient, in work from 2023. The patient, a man aged seventy-two, had diabetes and chronic kidney disease. He had taken two sugar drugs at steady doses for three years.

The new drug treats anemia from kidney disease. Twenty-three days after it began, his blood sugar fell to a low reading. Mean sugar levels across the day ran lower in the first weeks on the new drug than just before it. The team suspects the new drug changed how one sugar drug acts in the body. They urge care and close sugar checks when this mix is used.
pmc-10713423:
Meng, Zhou, Chen, and Chen study a gene called CBX2 in liver cancer in a 2023 paper. The gene had been linked to several cancers but little studied in this one. Data came from many cohorts and many kinds of molecular measurement.

CBX2 levels were high in liver tumors, tied to copy changes, chemical marks, and open DNA regions. High CBX2 tracked with a stem cell-like state in tumor cells, with faster growth, spread, and resistance to radiation. Cutting the gene slowed the cell cycle in tests. CBX2 also switched on partner genes by binding their start regions. Patients with high levels answered immune therapy better, a surprise the authors flag for treatment design.
pmc-10716723:
The European Food Safety Authority assessed a farm insecticide's residue limits in this 2023 opinion. The chemical is flupyradifurone, and its breakdown product is a small acid called DFA. The maker, Bayer, asked Dutch authorities to adjust limits and set import tolerances for several crops.

The panel found the data sound for avocados, mangoes, papayas, asparagus, and several seeds and roots. Lab methods can police both chemicals in those foods at very low levels. Eating the residues, over one meal or a lifetime, is unlikely to harm health under the stated farm practices. The opinion gives the proposed limits a scientific basis for regulators to adopt.
pmc-10717323:
Anna-Clara Ivarsson and five co-authors compare two rapid molecular test kits for malaria head-to-head in Sweden, in a two thousand twenty-three diagnostics paper. Loop-mediated isothermal amplification, or LAMP, detects parasite DNA in about an hour with modest laboratory needs.

One hundred thirty-three stored blood samples from suspected malaria cases were tested against highly sensitive PCR, which found forty-one positives. The HumaTurb Loopamp kit matched PCR exactly, with perfect sensitivity and specificity. The Alethia Illumigene kit reached about ninety percent sensitivity and ninety-six percent specificity. In a non-endemic setting where missing low-level infections matters, the authors judge the first kit the stronger performer.
pmc-10717523:
Mario Kossmann and co-authors analyzed brain damage caused by radiation treatment itself in a 2023 study. After radiation for brain tumors, new harm can appear on scans that looks much like tumor regrowth. The damage ranges from early swelling that fades to dead tissue that does not heal and can cause severe symptoms.

Tissue diagnosis is the gold standard, but few studies have checked scan calls against actual tissue samples. The team gathered cases where tissue proof existed and charted dose details plus where and when damage arose. Their aim was to learn which brain areas are most at risk. Such maps help doctors read follow-up scans with more confidence and plan doses that spare tender regions.
pmc-10717623:
Lei-lei Lv and co-authors identify in this 2023 study a distinctive killer T cell gathering in the chest fluid of lung cancer patients. Malignant pleural effusion bathes tumors in immune signals, and gene mutations shape that mix. Cells wearing the CD39 marker turned up selectively in fluid from adenocarcinoma patients whose tumors kept the normal EGFR gene, and more so after targeted drugs stopped working.

These cells looked exhausted yet kept their killing tools, and their receptor patterns were unusually clonal, a hint they react to the tumor itself. The authors propose the subset as a window into how drug resistance reshapes local immunity. Drug trials can sort patients by this mark.
pmc-10717723:
Shenglin Xu and co-authors lay out a 2023 trial plan to compare dry and wet suction in needle biopsy of solid growths in the pancreas. Past work on a related sampling method favored wet suction, but results for biopsy needles stay mixed.

Two hundred patients at four hospitals in China will be split at random into dry or wet suction groups. All biopsies use the same fine Franseen needle type. The main check is how often each method gives a correct diagnosis. The plan also seeks the best number of needle passes. Trial teams get a clear, fair design for settling the question.
pmc-10719923:
Ayaz, Üzer, Dilgin, and Apak build a light-based sensor for blood sugar in a 2023 paper. The sensor pins a sugar-splitting enzyme onto tiny magnetic beads coated with a gel. When glucose meets the enzyme, a partner molecule changes form. That new form then turns a copper mix into a yellow-orange dye.

A magnet pulls the beads out, and the dye shade tells how much glucose was present. The sensor read sugar across a wide range, from very low levels up, with a tiny detection floor. Common other substances did not spoil the reading. Tests on real samples matched well. The authors present the device as a cheap, selective tool for sugar checks.
pmc-10720023:
Lithium for batteries is locked inside clay minerals mixed with aluminum, and pulling the two apart cleanly is a key step. The authors test a membrane solvent extraction process built around an organic extractant held inside a porous membrane. First, lithium is captured from clay leachate into a solid lithium aluminum compound. That solid is dissolved in dilute acid to make the feed. The membrane unit then strips aluminum out of the feed continuously, leaving lithium behind.

At the best settings found, feed acidity, strip acid strength, and extractant share all matter. The process recovers about 92 percent of the lithium at a purity of at least 94 percent. Because the extractant stays immobilized in the membrane, the method saves both time and energy compared with classic solvent extraction. The authors present it as a route to high-purity lithium for batteries and other clean energy uses.
pmc-10720223:
Chung-Yen Lu and co-authors study which obesity measures best predict death among people with diabetes in Taiwan. Their 2023 cohort study follows thirty-four thousand six hundred eighty-six adults who took part in a health screening program between 1996 and 2017. Death records were traced to early 2022.

Five body measures were compared: body mass index, waist size, waist-hip ratio, body fat share, and a body shape index. Over a median of fifteen years, more than eight thousand deaths occurred, about one fifth from heart and vessel disease. One shape index showed a steady dose-response link with all-cause death after adjustments. The study helps clinics pick which simple measures carry the most warning for diabetic patients.
pmc-10720423:
Shaohua Liu and co-workers test whether a chest CT slice at the first lumbar vertebra can stand in for the standard muscle measure, in a 2023 paper. Muscle mass guides the diagnosis of sarcopenia, but the standard slice sits in the abdomen, not the chest. Routine chest scans are far more common.

In more than eight hundred adults from a health check center, muscle measures at the two levels correlated strongly in both sexes. Men carried far more muscle than women at the upper level. Age tracked with lower muscle in men, while body size tracked with higher values. The authors derive cut-offs for low muscle mass and conclude the chest-level slice is a feasible substitute.
pmc-10726123:
Wenchao Gao and nine co-authors map a pig virus across China in a 2023 study. Pseudorabies virus can infect many animals, and the wild type still circulates despite vaccine use. The team drew blood from pigs in sixteen provinces through 2022 and tested for signs of past infection with the wild strain, setting aside vaccine traces.

Out of nearly 162,000 samples from 556 farms, about twelve percent of pigs tested positive, but nearly half the farms had at least one case. Farm place and season shaped the odds. Five hot spots of high rates stood out on the map, and rates peaked from April to June. The authors offer the maps as a base for tighter control plans against the virus.
pmc-10727123:
Baker and co-authors find germ shed blocks rust of iron in plain air tests. Iron is a rife earth part and a must for near all life. Yet it rusts fast in air and sinks in its rust form. That makes it a scarce food in air-rich, mid-sour seas. Some germs burn raw iron to gain force for growth. Those germs need raw iron and air at one time to live. Stock thought penned them to low-air zones for that cause.

Yet some such germs live where air runs high in the sea. The team guessed the germs bend their zone to slow plain rust. Shed juice from a deep-sea germ was mixed with raw iron and air. That germ burns iron and a light gas for its force. The shed mix is called the exometabolome in the text.
pmc-10734023:
Zhizeng Xia, Xuewu Wang, and Weiwei Ren model a better way to draw gas from hydrate deposits. Their 2023 paper studies class-III hydrate reservoirs, where pressure release alone yields little gas. Hydrates are ice-like solids that trap methane under the sea floor. The team tests a combined method in computer models of a South China Sea site.

The method pairs cracking the rock open with repeated shots of nitrogen gas. In the models it lifted methane output to about two point eight five times the plain pressure method. Wide cracks, rich gas flow paths, and strong nitrogen doses helped most. The approach freed the most hydrate of all methods tried. Its drawback is heavy cooling of the reservoir, which future work could offset with added heat.
pmc-10734423:
Juliana Bragazzi Cunha and a large team published a virology study in twenty twenty-three with a surprising twist on interferon, the body's antiviral alarm. In severe COVID-19 the lung lining is injured and regenerates poorly. A CRISPR screen hunting genes that change infected lung cells' survival put the interferon pathway on top.

Four of the five top genes were parts of the type I interferon signaling chain. Knocking the pathway out made infected cultures fitter, not weaker. Follow-up work showed interferon did not push cells to die; it stopped survivors from multiplying after the virus peaked. The delayed brake on regrowth may explain slow lung recovery, complicating the simple story of interferon as pure protection.
pmc-10735123:
Yusuf Başkiran and co-authors study how pelvic organ sag affects vaginal birth for mother and baby, in a study from two thousand twenty-three. Over six hundred women who had given birth before were grouped by sag type: bladder sag, bowel sag, both, or none. Birth stages and complications were tracked at one large center.

Women with both sag types had longer first and second labor stages. Tears and womb infection after birth were also more common in that group. Bleeding risk trended up but not clearly. Newborn outcomes did not differ across groups. The authors urge closer watch for such mothers.
pmc-10735423:
Lauren Cerino and co-authors explore longevity planning for older adults who care for adult children, in work from 2023. More than two million adults in the United States provide unpaid care to an adult child, a role with unique strains.

Interviews at the MIT AgeLab found three key transition points: learning the child has special needs, the child reaching legal adulthood, and the caregiver growing older. The last stage brings hard choices about balancing two sets of care needs and arranging care after the caregiver dies. The session names support that caregivers want at each stage.
pmc-10735523:
Education is one of the strongest known shields against dementia. Pamela Herd frames a research panel on why that shield works. Among people over eighty, the risk of dementia is about three times lower for college graduates than for those without a high school diploma. The gaps run even larger across ethnic groups. Yet the reasons are poorly understood, and medicine still lacks treatments that truly slow the disease. Unpacking the education link may be the best route to delaying it.

The panel's papers trace the pathways in between: genetic risk, childhood conditions such as early thinking skills and school quality, and midlife factors. They ask which of these carry education's effect and which change its strength. The papers also watch for differences by gender and ethnicity. Herd presents the collection as an agenda for turning a strong statistical link into usable knowledge.
pmc-10735623:
I-Fen Lin, Emily Wiemers, Janecca Chin, and Anna Wiersma Strauss study help that adult children gave older parents during the COVID-19 pandemic. Their 2023 paper uses a United States aging survey from before and during the pandemic. Many elders live apart from their children but have one nearby, and that help supports daily life.

The help in focus is time: shopping, errands, rides, and chores. Parents who had trouble buying food were more likely to get such help from children who lived elsewhere. Nearby children were far more responsive to pandemic needs than those who lived far away. Parents with a child nearby received much more time help overall. The team also weighed how parents' thinking ability shaped the pattern.
pmc-10735923:
Yi Wang, Man Guo, Jinyu Liu, Yifan Lou, and Kara Carter published this study in 2023. It asks how neighborhood conditions feed depression among older Chinese immigrants in the greater Chicago area. Crowded, disordered, or fraying blocks may erode mental health, but the pathways for this group were unstudied.

Data from 2,801 participants fed a path model linking block stress to coping resources to its symptoms. Blocks with more social disintegration predicted more depression, partly because people there felt less mastery and engaged less. Physical disorder worked mainly through hope and mastery: worse blocks, weaker coping, more symptoms, a fully mediated path. The authors read coping as the mechanism that turns environment into mood. They recommend steps that rebuild mastery, hope, and social ties in immigrant areas, alongside repairs. Community groups, they suggest, are natural points for such support.
pmc-10736023:
Trudy Gaillard and six colleagues describe a 2023 project on how to bring more diverse older adults into aging research. Their team drew scholars from four research institutions tied to three participant registries on aging across Florida. The registries aim to enroll people who often get missed, including Black, Caribbean, and Hispanic adults over 55, rural residents, and cancer survivors.

The team used both surveys and interviews to describe who is registered and to share outreach plans. Their main lesson is that recruitment works better when it is shaped by culture and built on long-term trust. They also sketch a statewide model that could help registries coordinate their efforts.
pmc-10736123:
Pandemic rules split dementia caregivers into two worlds: those at home suddenly doing everything, and those locked out of care facilities. Inga Antonsdottir surveyed 133 family care partners in 2023, eighty-nine tied to assisted living and forty-four in the community. Their burdens were mirror images.

Nearly four in five facility partners could not visit their loved one at all. Two thirds were fully separated from them. Community partners, meanwhile, mostly reported a large jump in hands-on care time, seventy percent against thirteen percent. Routine disruption hit both groups at similar rates. The author argues policy should be tailored to each setting rather than treating caregivers as one group.
pmc-10736523:
Laura Keyes, Sowmya Balachandran, and Simon Andrew published this study in 2023. It describes a San Antonio project to coordinate rides for older adults and people with disabilities. The plan centers on a one-call, one-click system joining many providers. Mapping tools chart where riders live, where services run, and where the gaps fall. Interviews with transit, non-transit, and health agencies add the coordination picture.

Surveys and focus groups with riders round out the needs side. The maps can flag hot zones of high demand and low capacity. They also show where joined-up booking could cut the patchwork feel of current service. The authors present the mapping as a way for any community to gauge its readiness. From that gauge, a staged build-out plan with timelines can follow.
pmc-10736623:
Ronna Robbins and four co-authors study food insecurity among United States veterans, in a 2023 paper drawn from national health surveys. The team pooled three survey rounds from 2011 to 2016. Veterans were matched with non-veterans of like age, race, sex, and schooling. The question was whether veteran status itself tracks with steady access to food.

Raw shares of high food security were near equal, at about four fifths in each group. After health and social factors were weighed, veterans leaned less likely to have high food security. The gap was clear for non-Hispanic veterans and for those with some college. The authors point to race and schooling as key drivers to watch.
pmc-10736823:
Peeples, MacDonald, and Matthews evaluated a veterans' care model in this paper from twenty twenty-three. Behavioral Recovery Outreach teams help aging veterans with tangled behavior, memory, and medical problems. Each core team joins a social worker, a nurse, and a psychologist. They plan care inside veterans' facilities, then support veterans after discharge home.

The authors interviewed ten members from seven teams in late twenty twenty-one. Staffing levels, ties between departments, and clarity of the model shaped how well teams worked. Members said families learned to understand dementia better through the program. Veterans got help finding their way through the VA system. The study names what helps or hinders the model as it spreads.
pmc-10736923:
Natalie Galucia and Nancy Morrow-Howell present a 2023 journal article on age in campus diversity work. Universities are expanding diversity, equity, and inclusion programs while the population ages, yet age rarely figures in those plans. The team ran six focus groups with 42 diversity staff from 36 colleges and universities, then coded the themes.

Staff said age gets little attention and that other identities, above all race and gender, take priority under tight resources. The authors tie the neglect to wider ageism and to age-segregated campus life. They list interventions and advocacy steps that could raise the standing of age in such programs.
pmc-10737023:
Jennifer Klinedinst and co-authors describe a traveling wellness clinic for older adults in low-income housing. Their 2023 report covers an interdisciplinary program that visited four senior housing communities fifteen times, offering care on site rather than asking residents to travel.

One hundred ninety residents, averaging seventy-seven years old, used the clinics, most of them women. Services ran from blood pressure checks and shots to medication reviews, hearing checks with earwax removal, foot care, and yearly wellness visits. Staff also completed life-sustaining treatment orders and made emergency home visits to judge whether a resident needed hospital care or a call to their own doctor. The authors present the model as a way to bring full care to frail seniors.
pmc-10737123:
Yixuan Sun, Thomas Kwan, Douglas Bowlby, and Matthew Lee study a swap that can follow recovery. Some people who stop heavy drinking start using other drugs instead. Their paper, from twenty twenty-three, calls this addiction substitution. Past work links the swap to relapse and worse recovery.

The team uses two waves of a large United States survey on drinking and health. They test if people who got past alcohol problems began new drug use by the next wave. They also test if health problems change that link. Their early result points to a lower, not higher, chance of new opioid use after recovery in this sample.
pmc-10737323:
Elder abuse harms health and dignity, and anxiety often follows for victims who live in the community. Sukyung Yoon studies how abuse, anxiety, and social support interact in older adults in a solo 2023 paper, asking whether gender changes the picture.

About one in nine older adults in the United States reports abuse each year, and the true rate is likely higher. Past work has dwelt on risk factors more than on what protects victims. Yoon sets out to test how abuse relates to anxiety, and whether support from others softens that link. Comparing men and women matters because their support networks and abuse patterns differ. Findings of this kind can guide nurses and social workers toward sharper, fairer intervention.
pmc-10737423:
Penny Lewis and co-authors studied talking with hearing-loss patients in community pharmacies, in a 2023 paper. Pharmacists guard safe medicine use through conversation. Age-related hearing loss breaks that channel for many older customers. The team interviewed patients, older adults, and pharmacists online.

Sixteen people with hearing loss joined, plus eight pharmacists. Barriers and helpers were sorted with a framework method. Noise, masks, and rushed counters hurt understanding. Clear speech habits and quiet spaces helped. The study points pharmacies toward changes that keep older customers safe. Simple fixes at the counter could change daily visits for many older people.
pmc-10737623:
A twenty twenty-three study reports how senior meal programs reopened after the pandemic shutdowns. Group dining under the Older Americans Act had to halt in person. Programs kept serving through inventive delivery during closures. Surveys, focus groups, and interviews gather program experiences nationwide. Over five hundred programs complete the full survey. Most say they kept pandemic-era service changes for good. Grab-and-go meals drew new participants during the crisis.

Pairing meals with extras like entertainment helps retain people. Medically tailored and culturally fitting meals also spread. All adults over sixty qualify, yet attendance lags eligibility. The authors share practices that could strengthen programs nationally.
pmc-10737723:
Susanny Beltran and co-authors gather nursing home leaders' views on a standard way to move residents with dementia into hospice care, in this 2023 paper. Most dementia patients die in nursing homes, where hospice referral often comes late. A rule that demands a prognosis under six months fits dementia's uneven course poorly.

The team interviewed eleven leaders, among them nursing directors and social workers. A proposed process used a death-risk index to flag residents ready for hospice. Staff also took a survey about their homes and experience. Early analysis shows providers see value in the index-guided process, meant to make referrals timelier.
pmc-10738023:
Hye Won Chai and co-authors link why midlife spouses have sex to how depressed they feel in this 2023 study. Self-chosen sexual motives predict mental health, but most evidence came from young straight couples. The team analyzed paired data from 124 gay, 171 lesbian, and 124 straight married couples.

Across all couple types, people whose sexual motives felt self-chosen reported happier marriages, and happier marriages meant fewer depressive symptoms. Partner effects appeared too: in same-sex couples, a spouse's motives reached the other partner through marital quality. Straight couples showed gendered detours in whose marital happiness carried the effect. The authors name marital quality a practical lever for midlife mental health.
pmc-10738223:
Magdalena Tolea, Lilah Besser, and James Galvin study muscle loss as an early sign of dementia risk in a 2023 paper. Sarcopenia, the age-related loss of muscle mass and strength, affects up to thirty percent of older adults and tracks with thinking decline. The team asked whether it separates high-risk from low-risk people before dementia sets in.

They studied 141 community-dwelling older adults, classed as healthy low risk, healthy high risk, or mildly impaired by a brain health platform that weighs resilience, vulnerability, and cognition. Sarcopenia grew more common across those groups, from about twelve to thirty-nine percent. Flexibility and a timed stand-and-walk test also worsened with risk and separated impaired participants well. Mobility checks may help flag hidden risk.
pmc-10738423:
Alex Yue Feng Zhu and Kee Lee Chou tested personal pension forecasts for working adults in Hong Kong, in a study from twenty twenty-three. Four hundred middle-aged workers took part in a trial with three arms. One group got a forecast of their own future pension. A second group also got help naming doable plans to reach the retirement life they wanted.

The forecast alone raised how well people prepared their money for retirement, both at once and weeks later. The added planning step made both gains stronger. The forecast worked in part by cutting how steeply people discounted future needs. The authors suggest ways policy makers can spread the tool more widely.
pmc-10738523:
Arne van den Bosch, Radboud Marijnissen, Denise Hanssen, and Richard Oude Voshaar ask how skill to choose is judged in Dutch cases of aid in dying with loss of mind. The Netherlands lets aid in dying go on for such folk. Such cases rose to 288 in 2022. The team read sixty case notes put out by the Dutch check boards from 2012 to 2021.

Twenty sick folk had set down their wish in the past and could not choose well when death came. Forty could still choose well at that time. The four set tests for thought proved shades of gray, not clear cut lines. Six back up points shaped each call. They were speech skill, traits of the self, past writ wishes, and the bond with the doctor. The team calls for steady gains in care and for set time to think in day to day care.
pmc-10738623:
Cleopatra Kum and co-authors ask what wears down the health of people caring for a stroke survivor at home. Most survivors are looked after by family, and caregivers often report depression and upended lives, yet their own physical health gets less study. Guided by a stress and coping theory, the team analyzed intake data from 254 caregivers in a large trial.

Caregivers, mostly women and mostly spouses or adult children, reported nine unhealthy days in the past month on average. Harder care tasks, a darker view of threats, depressive symptoms, and negative life changes all tracked with more unhealthy days, while optimism tracked with fewer. Together the factors explained about thirty-eight percent of the differences. Depressive symptoms stood out as the strongest single predictor, though the factors shared much of their weight.
pmc-10738723:
Heather McNeil, Courtney Genge, Shannon Freeman, and Patricia Debergue distill five messages for policy makers on tech that helps elders stay home, in a 2023 paper. Gadgets for aging in place flood the market, from fall sensors to pill reminders. The authors warn that buying tech for its own sake can tangle care instead of easing it. Their first rule: the tool must solve a real problem in a real life.

Second, elders differ widely and change over time, so tools must bend as needs shift. Third, tech should back human care, not swap it out, since visits carry both warmth and health clues. Fourth, builders should design with elders and carers as true partners. The fifth message rounds out a plea for care in how such tools are rolled out and kept up. The paper speaks to any system betting on home tech.
pmc-10738823:
Verena Kleissner, Tim Kuball, and Georg Jahn test in 2023 whether a course on the psychology of aging softens prejudice against older people among psychology students. Ageism, from sour attitudes to unfair treatment, harms the health of older adults and the care they get. Training is known to help, so the team checked one semester of specialist coursework.

Fifty students who chose the aging course were compared with twenty-six who chose other topics, before and after the term. The aging students gained clear self-rated knowledge about aging and older adults. Yet scores for attitudes, stereotypes, and unfair behavior did not reliably improve in one semester. Knowledge alone, the authors note, does not melt prejudice. Their discussion weighs stronger ways to reach well educated students, and how to measure deep-set bias in such groups.
pmc-10738923:
Fang Yu, Dereck Salisbury, and Feng Lin report a feasibility study in 2023 on fitness testing in older adults with memory loss. The group had amnestic mild cognitive impairment. Fitness may be one way exercise slows Alzheimer disease, but peak fitness is hard to measure in this group. Data came from the ACT Trial.

The test used a lab cycle ergometer with rising effort until symptoms limited the rider. Among 146 enrolled adults, 145 completed the test. About half reached a true max effort by standard criteria. The rest stopped at near max or below max levels. A shortcut based on work rate greatly overestimated peak oxygen use. The authors conclude the full test works for only about half of such patients.
pmc-10739023:
Lauren Roe and co-authors examine in 2023 how the mix of a full day's activities relates to repeated falls in older men. Activity, sitting, and sleep each link to falls on their own, but studying one alone misses the rest. Using a method for compositional data, the team analyzed 2,705 men in a long running study of bone health, with movement measured by a device worn on the body.

About thirty eight percent of the men had repeated falls over four years. More active time relative to sitting and sleep meant lower odds of falls, while more sitting relative to the others meant higher odds. The links weakened a lot after health and body factors were added. Readers see the value of treating the day as a whole.
pmc-10739123:
Esther Kane and co-authors report what caregivers of people with frontotemporal degeneration live through. The term covers young-onset brain diseases that strike the front and side lobes, changing speech, conduct, and character. Their 2023 survey drew more than twelve hundred past and current caregivers. It asked about the ill person's awareness, the hardest changes, and the load of care.

Most caregivers gave more than eighty hours of care a week, and one in ten cared for more than one ill person. Most patients were diagnosed in their fifties or sixties. Only about a third of patients grasped their own symptoms. Changes in speech, character, mood, and conduct hurt caregivers most. The authors urge wraparound support for these families.
pmc-10739323:
Kristine Margaryan and co-authors survey wild grapes in Armenia in a 2023 paper. Wild vines are a storehouse of genetic variety that breeders can use, yet the Armenian pool had barely been studied. The team explored five regions with a long history of grape growing and collected samples from the wild population.

In all, they gathered well over a hundred unique wild types, plus seed-grown plants from an earlier collection. DNA markers showed a rich pool, with many distinct gene variants at each marker. The plants sorted into eight genetic groups. Tests at a resistance-linked site found many vines carrying gene variants tied to defense against powdery mildew, a major vine disease. The authors urge ongoing survey and care of this resource as vineyard challenges grow.
pmc-10739423:
Falsetta opens a study set in twenty twenty-three on vulvodynia, a lasting vulvar pain with no clear visible cause. Patients feel burning or stabbing pain, wait months or years for a diagnosis, and climb a ladder of treatments that may end in surgery. The condition drags down quality of life and is often met with stigma or dismissal, she notes.

The set she introduces focuses on early immune sensing, microbes, and inflammation as drivers of the pain. New rodent and cell models built over the past decade now let labs probe mechanisms and screen therapies. Falsetta frames the set as a step toward better screening, faster diagnosis, and kinder, better-funded care.
pmc-10740623:
Angelo Michele Inchingolo and co-workers reviewed how well clear trays can push molars back in the mouth. To push teeth back with loose trays is in vogue since the trays are near clear to the eye. The 2023 review searched three data banks for ten years of work. Of 146 works found, 19 met the bar. The point was if trays on their own can give this back shift in a sound way.

Trays could push teeth back, but grip on front teeth was apt to slip. Bone grip tools and shave of thin bits of tooth coat stayed the scores firm. The mixed way, trays plus short term bone grip tools, showed the best gains. The review gives tooth staff a true map of what trays can and can not vow for this shift.
pmc-10741023:
Ted Joanen and co-authors show that the right menu can make captive alligators breed like wild ones, in a 2023 study. Farms and conservation programs have long struggled to reproduce American alligators in enclosures. At a Louisiana ranch, the team fed breeders a newly formulated commercial diet plus crawfish waste as a supplement, from 2016 to 2022, and counted the results nest by nest.

Captive nests averaged about sixteen hatchlings, essentially matching wild nests incubated in the same chambers, and far ahead of a famous refuge program from decades earlier. Egg production, fertility, and hatch rates all improved together. The lesson reaches beyond one ranch: closing the diet gap may be the cheapest lever in alligator husbandry, with value for both the leather trade and restocking wild wetlands.
pmc-10741223:
Roshni Lalwani and co-authors reviewed in 2023 the role of osteopontin, an inflammatory protein, in the immune responses of Alzheimer disease. The disease builds up amyloid plaques and tau tangles that spread through the brain and trigger inflammation in support cells, which drives nerve damage. Inflammation also spills into the blood, where it can harm or help.

Osteopontin sits in that web as a signaling protein made during inflammation. The review sets its actions in context: where it is made, which cells it moves, and how it may feed or brake the toxic cycle between protein clumps and immune cells. The head byline is shorter than the catalog list, so the work is framed as a team review. Readers get a careful placement of one molecule in a crowded field of Alzheimer targets.
pmc-10741523:
Lab researchers in Serbia and Croatia gave rats a sleep drug for five days to see how it changed brain proteins. The drug, zaleplon, helps people fall asleep and acts on a brain signal system tied to calm and sleep. That system uses GABA, while a second system uses glutamate and drives alert states. Both systems help set sleep and wake, yet past work on this drug mostly tracked behaviour, not proteins.

After the drug course, the team checked protein levels in the hippocampus, a brain area tied to memory. Proteins of the calm system rose, as the team expected from the drug action. Proteins of the alert system rose too, which was a surprise. A drop in a third signal, adenosine, may explain that rise. The authors note that more work is needed on long-term effects.
pmc-10741623: Francisco Nieto-Escamez and co-authors survey the non-motor side of Parkinson's disease in this 2023 paper. The disease is known for shaking and stiff movement, yet its reach is wider. Thinking problems and mood and psychiatric troubles are part of the picture, along with body-system faults such as blood pressure and gut issues. Sleep troubles add to the load. Together these hidden disorders shape daily life as much as the motor signs, the authors argue, calling for care that treats the whole condition rather than movement alone.
pmc-10741923:
Poornima and five co-authors modeled heat flow from a wet wavy fin with a genetically tuned neural network, in a study published in 2023. Fins shed heat from hot equipment, and waves plus wet air bend the mathematics hard. Breeding-style mathematics, which mixes and mutates trial answers, tuned the parameters of the network. The base law was cast in a scale-free form first.

Heat radiation and convection were both in the model, as wet fin work needs. Across the runs, fin heat fell as the wet and flow parameters rose. The tuned network matched the direct mathematical answer with high care and fast settling. The authors present breeding-tuned networks as a quick stand-in for fin mathematics in design work.
pmc-10742023:
Kathrin Maitz and co-authors study a receptor in lung cancer in mice in a 2023 paper. DDR1 is a tyrosine kinase receptor linked to poor prognosis in non-small cell lung cancer, but its role in tumor growth was unclear. The team blocks it with a drug and knocks it out in a mouse model driven by KRAS and p53 changes.

Both moves raise tumor burden, they find. Knockout tumors hold fewer killer T cells and more helper and regulatory T cells. Human data agree: tumors with low DDR1 show higher levels of a regulatory T cell marker. Blocking DDR1 may backfire, the authors warn.
pmc-10742123:
Arianna Piccirillo and co-authors present a 2023 review of nutrition as a risk factor for delirium in intensive care patients. Delirium, a sudden confused state, is common and harmful in the unit. Poor nutrition, muscle burning, and metabolic shifts are known risks, though the chain is not fully mapped.

Bad nutrition can unbalance salts, weaken immunity, and alter how drugs are handled, all feeding delirium. A bedside impedance test can size up body composition and water. The authors argue for full metabolic checks and tailored feeding to cut risk. They call for research on the mechanisms so care can be fitted to each patient, improving life after the unit.
pmc-10742723:
Constantin Ehrengut and co-authors weigh X-ray exposure during a liver cancer treatment that places radioactive beads in liver arteries, in a 2023 study. Hard anatomy can stretch scan time, raise radiation dose, and drive more contrast dye use. The team asked how bead type and doctor experience shape those costs. Records covered more than one hundred sixty treatments and checks.

Resin beads went with longer scan time and more dye than glass beads, at like dose. Seasoned doctors cut dose and scan time much, most in the check step. When the same doctor did both the check and the treatment, dose fell by more than two fifths. Training and steady staffing are the authors' main advice.
pmc-10742923:
Seven authors test whether used rapid antigen tests can feed virus surveillance in this 2023 study. During COVID-19, home antigen tests replaced lab swabs for many people, which threatened the genome sequencing programs that track new variants.

The team extracted viral RNA from the leftover buffer in the swab tubes of positive rapid tests, confirmed positivity by PCR, and sequenced the virus genomes. Sequence quality was good enough to identify the lineages and sub-lineages in circulation at a time when molecular swabs had fallen sharply. The study shows surveillance can ride on tests people already take at home, keeping variant tracking alive at low cost.
pmc-10743123:
Fatih Tarlak and co-authors review in 2023 how math models forecast how long food stays safe to eat. Germs grow and spoil food over time, and producers need sound ways to predict that clock. The field, called predictive microbiology in the paper, builds models of how microbes grow, survive, and behave in foods and other settings.

The review compares three modeling styles. Older routes chain a growth model with an environment model, in one or two steps. A newer route lets machine learning read the patterns directly, with no fixed growth model. The authors weigh strengths and limits of each, aiming to help producers and regulators make sharper, safer shelf-life calls.
pmc-10743423:
Sena Zeynep Usta and co-authors offer a 2023 review of immunotherapy for oral malignant melanoma, a rare cancer of the mouth lining with a poor outlook. Checkpoint inhibitor drugs have opened a new era in melanoma care and serve in first-line, added, and pre-surgery roles. No full review had covered their use in the oral form.

The review gathers clinical studies on these drugs in oral mucosal melanoma. It maps how tumors resist the drugs, a web of mechanisms that blunts immune attack. The authors argue that naming those routes is the step toward better therapies. They also chart future prospects for the field. The piece aims to guide care for a patient group with few options.
pmc-10743523:
A large team led by Malgorzata Zielinska reviews wound care in a 2023 paper. Healing moves through set stages, from clotting to growth of new tissue. Small living germs in the wound can help or harm each stage. The review sets out what is known about that balance. Age, body-wide illness, and local wound state all shape the outcome.

Some normal skin germs help skin cells grow and help new blood vessels form. Other germs settle in the wound and slow healing down. The authors trace how germs stir the defense system and change each healing stage. Care teams can use the review to think past clean dressings alone. A wound plan may need to guide the germ mix, not just kill germs. The paper pulls past work together rather than reporting a new trial.
pmc-10743823:
Yong Sun Choi, Samuel Ryan Sorkhi, Hyuk Jin Cho, and their co-authors compare two operations for large stones stuck high in the ureter, the tube from kidney to bladder. One route threads a flexible scope up from below and breaks the stone with a laser. The other reaches through the kidney from the back, in a modern variant that leaves no drainage tube.

Reviewing about sixty cases of each, they found the two routes cleared the stones at nearly the same high rate by three months. Hospital stays and complication rates also matched. The scope route took longer in the operating room but left patients with less pain afterward. The authors judge both approaches sound choices for these large stones.
pmc-10744223:
Krzysztof Kurek and co-authors present a systematic review, published in 2023, on a blood marker used after cardiac arrest. When the heart restarts, doctors must judge the chance of survival and brain recovery, and no single test settles that question. The marker, neuron-specific enolase, is released when nerve cells are damaged, and the review pools what is known about its predictive power.

Eighty-six studies with more than ten thousand patients met the criteria. Higher marker levels tracked both death and poor brain outcomes, at admission and at later time points after arrest. The authors support using the marker as one part of a combined judgment, never alone, when families and teams face hard decisions about care.
pmc-10744423:
Guleid Hussein and co-authors review plasma exchange treatment in intensive care in this 2023 paper. The therapy removes a patient's plasma outside the body and replaces it, carrying away harmful molecules. Units use it for many disease states, sometimes as first-line care and sometimes as a last resort.

The review covers the basic principles of how the treatment works and where it fits in critical care today. It walks through the main conditions treated in the unit and the evidence behind each use. The authors also look ahead to possible future directions for the technique. The paper serves as a brief guide for clinicians weighing this option at the bedside.
pmc-10744823:
Volodymyr Hutsaylyuk and co-authors test weld metal from power plant steam pipes in a 2023 study of long wear and hydrogen harm. Samples came from heat-resistant steel joints, both fresh and after twenty-three years of service.

Long service hurt weld metal more than base metal, with lower hardness, strength, and squeeze at break, yet oddly higher stretch. Used joints also held far more hydrogen than fresh ones. Added hydrogen cut strength and stretch further, most in the used welds. The authors suggest short tests on charged weld metal can gauge service damage. Plant engineers get a way to judge aging pipes before failure.
pmc-10745123:
Takanobu Takata and co-authors develop a lab method for finding proteins in Japanese herbal medicines in a 2023 paper. Kampo, Japan's adaptation of traditional Chinese medicine, blends crude plant and other drugs whose full makeup is unknown. Their proteins are scarce and wash out in watery solvents, which makes them hard to identify and count. Yet dose and safety work needs those numbers.

Their method rests on membrane chromatography with a plastic PVDF membrane that grabs proteins. A slot blot format built on the same idea has a further perk: the sample volume is not capped, so dilute proteins can be loaded until they register. The paper weighs the method's potential for naming and measuring proteins in Kampo formulas. Better protein data could tighten quality control of these widely used medicines.
pmc-10745523:
Joseph Boachie and co-authors show why metformin stops trimming liver fat when vitamin B12 runs low, and how adiponectin restores it. Long metformin use drains B12, and low B12 itself tracks fatty, disordered blood lipids. The team grows human liver cells in media with graded B12 levels to isolate the effect.

Their 2023 study finds low B12 piling triglycerides into the cells, switching fat-building genes on, and dimming fat burning and mitochondrial work. The energy sensor AMPK and its upstream hormone signal both sag. Metformin alone cannot fix the fat load in the low B12 state. Adding adiponectin reawakens the AMPK axis and clears the block, pointing to a paired fix for a common drug side effect.
pmc-10745623:
Helen Hoi Yin Chan and colleagues offer a two thousand twenty-three study of a multi-strain probiotic for mood and sleep in Hong Kong Chinese adults. Gut microbes talk to the brain through well-mapped routes. A new three-strain formula was tested over eight weeks.

Sixty-eight participants with sleep and mood complaints gave gut samples before and after. Sleep quality scores improved clearly by the final week. Depression and anxiety scores also fell. Gut community structure shifted alongside the symptom gains. The open results support controlled trials of gut-targeted support for everyday mental health complaints.
pmc-10747123:
Salmonella in food sickens people worldwide, and the lab tests that find it are slow and laborious. Gabrielle Silva and co-authors review a faster option in this 2023 paper: lateral flow assays, the strip tests that give a reading in minutes. The review explains how the strips work and the main formats used for catching this pathogen in food.

New nanomaterials have sharpened the strips' accuracy over the years, letting them pick out different Salmonella types at low levels. The authors weigh portability, ease of use, speed, and cost against lab methods. They close with open problems and future directions for the tests. Quick, cheap detection could stop tainted food earlier in the supply chain.
pmc-10747523:
Errol Hassan and co-authors test plant essential oil mixtures against the silverleaf whitefly and its tiny wasp parasitoid, published in 2023. The whitefly is a diverse, destructive crop pest worldwide. Chemical sprays control it but pollute, breed resistance, and harm natural enemies and pollinators, so safer options are wanted.

Three new mixtures, built from mustard oil with different soaps as spreaders, were tested on the pest's life stages and on the wasp that attacks it. The mixtures worked well on eggs and young stages: the best mixture killed most eggs, another most nymphs. Adults were much harder to kill, with mortality under forty percent for all mixtures. The study weighs this pest control benefit against safety for the helpful parasitoid, a balance any field use must strike.
pmc-10747723:
Xiaohan Wang and seven co-authors map the genetic diversity of adzuki beans, an early domesticated crop of East Asia. Their study came out in 2023. The team sequenced hundreds of traditional varieties from Korea, China, and Japan.

The beans fell into three groups matching their home regions, each with its own domestication path. The Korean group had the heaviest seeds, the Japanese the most grains per pod, and the Chinese the most pods per plant. Gene scans tied yield traits to regions rich in stress-resistance genes. Signs of balancing selection, where stress favors hardy types over high-yield ones, appeared in each group. The authors argue that local stresses shaped these beans as much as breeders did. That history matters for breeding better varieties today.
pmc-10748023: Benedikt Ley and Lucio Luzzatto open a 2023 piece on Plasmodium vivax malaria and G6PD testing. The visible text is only the start of the article: it notes that early malaria investigators were right to place the falciparum and vivax species in the same genus, Plasmodium. The title promises a discussion of testing for G6PD deficiency, which matters because some malaria drugs can harm patients who lack that enzyme. The hosted head breaks off before the argument begins, so the piece is cataloged here in short form.
pmc-10748123:
Alexander Litov and co-authors catalog the viruses carried by horseflies in Russia, in a 2023 study. Biting flies spread many pathogens, yet their own virus communities were barely explored compared with mosquitoes and ticks. The team sequenced flies from four genera gathered in two far-apart regions, the Primorye Territory and the Ryazan Region, and assembled the viral genomes they found.

Fourteen complete and four partial genomes of new viruses turned up, plus fragments of perhaps a dozen more. Sixteen of the viruses grew in at least one lab cell line, though most faded over time rather than thriving. The survey gives tabanid virology its first broad map.
pmc-10751923:
Yi-Wei Wang and five co-authors wrote a case report in 2023 on a teen whose sick liver held two diseases at once. The boy was 19, with multiple congenital abnormalities and an intellectual disability. For more than five years he had itch and abnormal liver enzymes. Tests ruled out germs and the most common gene based causes of blocked bile flow.

A liver biopsy gave the clear result. The boy had stage four primary biliary cholangitis, a disease of adults that is rare in teens. The biopsy showed traits of autoimmune hepatitis as well. A gene-array test found a loss of close to four million DNA letters on chromosome 14, at 14q24.1q24.2. The loss helps explain the birth defects. A drug called ursodeoxycholic acid, plus steroids, calmed the liver. The team warns that this pair can show up in teens with chromosome faults too.
pmc-10753523:
Runsheng Zheng and co-authors set up a high sensitivity liquid flow system in 2023 for proteomics on tiny samples, even single cells. Protein studies on such small inputs need both sharp detection and fast turnaround.

A narrow column run at a very low flow rate was tuned to balance the two, handling from twenty four to seventy two samples a day. Three data gathering strategies were compared for how many proteins they could name. The widest window method named more than three thousand protein groups from a tiny standard sample in a ten minute run. A trap and elute tweak pushed the pace to one hundred samples a day. Single cell tests named over seventeen hundred groups.
pmc-10753723:
Gan and co-authors review self-inducing reactors and their place in bioengineering, in this 2023 analysis. These vessels pull gas into liquid on their own, without separate sparging gear. Their simple build, strong mixing, and low energy use make them attractive for growing cells and microbes.

The review compares them with packed towers, stirred tanks, airlift designs, and gas-inducing cousins. Five measures guide the comparison: the critical speed for gas intake, the suction rate, how fast gas transfers into liquid, power draw, and how much gas the liquid holds. Progress on each measure is surveyed in turn. The authors close by weighing the open challenges and chances ahead. Their map should help engineers pick and tune reactors.
pmc-10753823:
Gholampour wrote an editorial in twenty twenty-three introducing a set of seven papers on modeling disorders of cerebrospinal fluid. That fluid surrounds the brain and spinal cord, and its disorders can be hard to tell apart on scans. Computer models offer a safe, non-invasive way to study them.

The editorial explains why models matter and where they can go wrong. Key choices include which settings to use, how much to simplify, and how to set edge conditions. The papers in the set cover fluid flow analysis and brain simulations, aiming at cheaper and more exact methods. The goal is better tools for diagnosis, outlook, and care planning.
pmc-10754423:
Ehiremen Adesua Azugbene, Llewellyn J Cornelius, and Crista E Johnson-Agbakwu report a study from 2023 on the birth care of African immigrant women in Clarkston, Georgia. The team asked how these women use health services and what shapes their care during pregnancy and birth, a topic with little past research.

Fourteen women took part in long interviews, and the team sorted their answers into eleven themes. The themes cover trust in care, health beliefs, language limits, cost, long waits, lack of rides, and fear of drugs and birth procedures. The authors urge better health teaching and care shaped to each woman's needs, so more women seek care early and have safer births.
pmc-10759723:
Knee ligament tears are rising among young athletes as youth sports grow more competitive. Khushi Khurana and Gajanan Pisulkar reviewed in 2023 how children with torn anterior cruciate ligaments should be rehabilitated. Their review weighs surgery timing, graft choices, and exercise-based recovery for a group whose bones are still growing.

They argue for early surgical repair to get children back to sport and to protect cartilage and the meniscus from lasting harm. Techniques that spare the growth plates, often using hamstring grafts, gave the best outcomes with the least growth disturbance. The authors offer the review as a practical guide for clinicians and families facing these injuries, and as a base for further study.
pmc-10763523:
Takuro Nishimura and thirteen co-authors map dangerous heart rhythms from inside the coronary arteries, in a study published in 2023. Scar-related ventricular tachycardia is a fast, life-threatening rhythm born in damaged heart muscle. Some of its circuitry hides within the wall or on the outer surface, beyond the reach of standard mapping from inside the chamber.

Ten patients with non-ischemic heart disease underwent mapping with a slim multi-electrode catheter threaded into coronary arteries. Combined maps merged thousands of points from chamber and vessels. Abnormal signals inside arteries, near the inner scar, appeared in seven patients. In some, the rhythm's critical corridor ran through the vessel itself. The authors judge the technique safe and useful for finding circuits that chamber mapping alone would miss.
pmc-10764223:
Rosehip seed oil, a by-product of food processing, already soothes skin disorders. Van-Long Truong and Woo-Sik Jeong ask whether it can also regrow hair. They treated the shaved backs of laboratory mice with the oil for twenty-one days. The mice were at the resting stage of the hair cycle. Treated skin pushed follicles into the growth phase early.

Under the microscope, treated mice showed denser follicles, bigger hair bulbs, and thicker skin. Genes tied to hair growth switched on more strongly, including signals from the beta-catenin and hedgehog pathways. Growth factors rose as well. The findings point to a waste-stream oil with a second life in cosmetics. The authors suggest it may help prevent or treat hair loss, pending human studies.
pmc-10768523:
Sonia Díaz, Ruth Palma, Edna Gamboa, and Álvaro Idrovo published a cross-sectional study in 2023 on diet and mercury exposure among Afro-Colombian communities. Mercury exposure is common near gold mining and harms health. Selenium, found in Colombian geology, can bind mercury in the body, so the team looked for local selenium-rich foods people already eat.

The researchers surveyed several hundred people in five municipalities in Chocó about how often they ate selenium-rich foods and compared answers with mercury measured in hair. Guava, whole wheat flour, strawberries, cow liver, spinach, and yeast extract were among the foods eaten most. Statistical analysis pointed to walnuts, whole wheat flour, and yeast extract for future programs, and the authors propose familiar local dishes as the delivery route.
pmc-10771823:
Mahima Kuruvila and co-authors track gender trends among lead authors in one disease's literature in a paper from two thousand twenty-three. The disease, antiphospholipid syndrome, drives blood clots and pregnancy losses through misdirected antibodies. The team asked whether women lead more of its research over time.

They reviewed nearly twelve hundred PubMed papers from two thousand eighteen to two thousand twenty-two with the disease name in the title. Gender was read from names and countries by a name tool. Female lead authors peaked in two thousand twenty-two. A forecast sees rough parity by two thousand twenty-seven. The highest female-to-male ratios were in Russia, Poland, and Greece. The authors conclude parity has not clearly improved and gaps need work.
pmc-10774623:
Abdullah Alyoussef reviews a laser treatment for psoriasis, a long-term skin disease marked by scaly red patches. The 2023 review covers about one hundred million patients worldwide who live with the condition. Light therapy is a standard care option, alone or with other drugs.

The focused light source is a 308 nanometer excimer laser, long used in skin clinics. The review walks through how the laser is applied, the treatment plan, and its side effects. Choice of light source must fit the type of psoriasis each patient has. Close watch during sessions helps avoid harm. The author presents the laser as a precise tool that treats patches while sparing healthy skin.
pmc-10782423:
Kevin Tang and four co-authors review how long patients should take two blood-thinning drugs after a heart stent is placed. Their 2023 review notes that stents have improved fast, yet the right length of dual therapy stayed debated. The pair of drugs guards against clots in the stent, but it also raises the risk of bleeding.

Older guidance favored twelve months of dual therapy, and longer for some patients. Newer trials and safer drug-coated stents have shifted the field toward shorter courses. Cutting months of therapy lowers major bleeding while modern stents keep clot risk in check. The authors walk through current guidelines, the fresh proof behind them, and the gaps that remain. Heart teams can use the review to tailor duration to each patient's clot and bleed risks.
pmc-10784823:
Zhi-Peng Lin and co-authors compare two treatments for mid to late liver cancer, in a 2023 study. The standard path threads a tube to the tumor and blocks its blood supply while dosing it with drugs. Heat ablation through the skin can kill more tumor cells, and the pair may beat either alone.

One hundred fifty patients at one hospital split into a standard group and a combined group. The combined group had more full and partial responses. Blood tumor markers fell further in that group after four weeks. The team also tracked one year survival and the traits that shaped outlook. Their results back the combined path for this hard stage of disease.
pmc-10792723:
Sujata Maharjan and co-authors report a rare case of two pregnancies at once in different sites in a 2023 paper. In this condition, one pregnancy sits in the womb and another sits outside it, often in a tube. It is dangerous and rare after natural conception, and its mixed signs make it hard to spot in time.

A woman aged twenty eight was found by ultrasound at eight weeks to have such a paired pregnancy. Doctors removed the tube pregnancy with keyhole surgery, while the womb pregnancy stayed safe. It went on to full term with no problems. The case shows that fast action can save both mother and baby.
pmc-10800423:
Miyoung Yoo and co-authors describe a sharper way to measure two trans fatty acids in food, in a study published in 2023. Vaccenic acid occurs in natural fats and may aid health. Elaidic acid forms in hardened plant oils and is linked to heart disease risk. Telling the two apart matters, but other fats get in the way.

The team used a silver ion cartridge to strip out most cis fatty acids first. They then ran samples through a two-stage gas method with mass detection. The cleanup let them measure the ratio of the two acids more precisely. That ratio also split natural trans fats from industrial ones more clearly. Food testers gain a tool for fairer product checks.
pmc-10803423:
Chongdie Wu and co-authors trace microbes that pass from parent cotton seeds to new plants. The head dates the work to 2023, though the catalog lists 2024. Microbes inside plant tissue can aid growth and help the plant adapt, and seeds are one route they travel.
