The team sampled soil, root, stem, leaf, and seed across three cotton types. Diversity fell as they moved from roots toward seeds, and the local setting shaped the mix more than plant type did. They found 29 core variants shared in seeds. The work shows how seed microbes are passed on and what roles they may play.
pmc-10806123:
Victoria Nakibuuka and co-authors tell how the first human milk bank in Uganda took shape at one hub. The study appeared in 2023. Gift milk is the backed pick for small babes when mum's milk lacks. Most banks sit in rich lands, though.

Steps ran from a fit check of the hub to guard rules, staff teach, and state talks. A world tool kit for such banks set the path. Since the bank opened in late 2021, near one hundred seventy gift mums were screened. Most whose milk was took are in their mid-twenties. Over one hundred babes drank the milk, most born too soon.
pmc-10807423:
Giacomo Basini and eight co-authors track how foot surgery eases walking pain and reshapes the foot in people with an inherited nerve disease, one month after the operation. Their study was published in two thousand twenty-three. Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease weakens muscles and twists foot posture, making walking hurt. Functional surgery aims to restore the foot's alignment and load path.

Ten patients were checked before and after surgery plus rehabilitation. Walking pain fell, most sharply in those who started with the worst pain. Ankle bend recovered toward a useful range, and pressure rolled through the foot far better. Walking speed and balance, though, had not yet budged. More than half the patients felt improved or much improved. The authors call the surgery a good short-term fix that lets patients wear shoes again.
pmc-10808723:
Sung Won Lee and three co-authors review how CD1d and invariant natural killer T cells shape gut inflammation, in work from 2024. These unusual T cells sense glycolipid antigens shown by CD1d and help steer many immune responses. In the gut they interact with epithelial cells, hormone-linked gut cells and several immune cell types.

Through those contacts the cells help hold immune balance in the intestine. The review weighs cell and molecular factors that tune their activity in Crohn's disease and ulcerative colitis. Both protective and harmful roles are covered, since the same cells can calm or drive inflammation. The authors map open questions for therapy aimed at this pathway.
pmc-10823023:
Roberta Ferrante and co-authors present a meta-analysis from two thousand twenty-three on helpful soil bacteria and drought response in plants. Certain root bacteria, called PGPR, can switch on plant genes that help crops endure dry spells. Many small studies report such effects, but their gene-level claims needed a pooled check.

Following standard review guidelines, the team screened thousands of reports and kept forty-one. Only four of the nine target genes had enough studies for full analysis. Pooled results showed no significant rise for three genes, while one drought gene responded in both treated and untreated plants. Differences between studies were large, and tests hinted at publication bias. The authors urge caution and better standard studies in this field.
pmc-10832023:
Guoyan Lu, Xing Li, Jie Tang, and four colleagues ask whether a germ makes Kawasaki disease worse in this two thousand twenty-three study. Mycoplasma infection is a key added factor in Kawasaki disease, a childhood illness that can damage heart arteries. The team reviewed two hundred forty-seven patients seen between mid two thousand seventeen and the end of two thousand twenty-two at a Sichuan University hospital. Thirty-eight had mycoplasma infection; two hundred nine did not.

The infected group had a harder course: longer hospital stays, more cases lacking full signs, and more added health problems. Infection also tracked with severe blood disorders, poor clotting, and heart muscle injury. Swelling lasted longer after treatment in the infected group. First heart checks looked much the same in both groups, but infection made artery bulges worse. The authors conclude the infection adds to the heart harm.
pmc-10860423:
Vishnu Pannipulath Venugopal, Lakshmi Babu Saheer, and Mahdi Maktabdar Oghaz published a computing study, with the head dated 2023, on reading COVID-19 rapid test photos with deep learning. Automated reading could speed mass testing. No public dataset of test images existed, so the team crowdsourced nine hundred real photos of positive and negative results. A generative model added simulated images to fix gaps and class imbalance.

Their best network hit ninety-three percent accuracy in validation. Accuracy reached eighty-eight percent on simulated tests and eighty-two percent on real ones. Adding simulated images to training helped simulated tests but not real ones. The authors stress dataset limits as the key challenge for such tools.
pmc-10864623:
Foster Kangben and co-authors analyze branch angle genes in cotton in a paper published in 2023. Branch angle shapes how plants capture light, and tighter angles raise yields in dense plantings of cereal crops. A gene family known from rice and corn also controls branching in broadleaf plants, making cotton a target.

The team mapped the gene family across cotton and other flowering plants. Duplication produced three copies in diploid ancestors and six in the modern tetraploid crop. Expression differed by tissue. Gene editing silenced the most active stem copies, and mutant plants were checked for changed branch angles.
pmc-10875123:
June Corry and co-authors review the quality checks on radiotherapy inside a head and neck cancer trial. Published in 2023, their report covers the TROG 12.01 randomized trial and asks what good quality assurance for such treatment should include, since no shared standard exists. All sites first passed a credentialing test with a sample case.

Live checks before treatment covered each doctor's first patient and one in five after that. Plans that broke the rules on tumor outlines or dose counted as major violations. The team then reviewed every case where the cancer came back nearby, hunting for quality links. Their data feed a proposed minimum standard for future trials.
pmc-10876023:
Pier Luigi Lopalco and co-authors argue, in a 2024 paper, that medicine needs a new name for a new kind of antibody drug. The term monoclonal antibody now covers too much: cancer drugs, immune therapies, and long-lasting shots that shield babies from RSV, a common lung virus. A panel of RSV experts, a linguist who studies doctor-patient talk, and communications specialists met, convened by Sanofi, to find clearer language.

Their proposal is 'direct long-acting antibody' for the subclass used to prevent RSV disease in infants. The name stresses that the protection is given directly and lasts, unlike a vaccine that trains the body to make its own. Clearer terms, they argue, help parents and clinicians grasp what the product does, and keep unlike products from being confused with one another.
pmc-10903323:
Elif Köse and co-authors map three decades of research on leisure constraints in a 2023 study. Leisure constraints are the barriers that keep people from taking part in free-time activities. Less leisure harms body, mind, and mood, so knowing the barriers matters for policy. The team used bibliometric methods on three hundred six articles from a major database, spanning 1991 to 2019.

Output in the field grew steadily across five-year periods. Authors from the United States, Australia, and Canada led production. Recent hot topics sat inside the intrapersonal family of constraints: self-efficacy, segmentation, mental health, and fear. The authors urge broader, more complete studies of constraints. They also back health policies that raise participation, as aging populations and screen-bound modern life deepen inactivity's harms.
pmc-10994623:
ALS robs patients of movement as nerve cells die, and approved drugs slow it only slightly. Alfredo Firstenfeld and co-authors tested an add-on drug in this 2023 trial report. The drug, Cerebrolysin, is thought to protect nerve cells and help them regrow. It was layered on top of the standard drug riluzole.

Twenty outpatients with a firm ALS diagnosis joined the single-center study. Half received the add-on by daily vein infusions on weekdays; half received a placebo. Neither patients nor doctors knew the assignments. The title reports the outcome: symptoms improved in the add-on group. Small trials cannot settle a drug's worth, but the signal supports larger tests. Families facing ALS have few options, so each lead counts.
pmc-11075023:
Satvika Sharma, Avneet Saini, and Dhawan review how fat metabolism goes wrong in brain diseases, centering the androgen receptor. Their 2023 review covers Alzheimer's, Parkinson's, multiple sclerosis, and Huntington's disease, all marked by steady loss of nerve cells. Lipid balance keeps cell walls and signals working, and its failure is now tied to each of these illnesses.

The receptor, best known for answering male hormones, also helps run the cell's fat economy through ties with mitochondria and peroxisomes. When the cascade it anchors is disturbed, lipids and cholesterol pile up in the wrong places. The review gathers proof that turning the receptor up or down shifts those levels. The authors frame the receptor as a lever for future therapies aimed at the metabolic side of brain decline.
pmc-11078223:
Pooya Derakhshan and co-authors study airway checks before surgery in a paper whose text is dated 2023. Placing a breathing tube is routine in anesthesia, but a hard airway can turn it risky. Two scoring tools help: LEMON, a bedside check of the mouth, teeth, jaw, blockage, and neck movement, and a scale that grades how hard the tube placement proved.

The study covered 105 patients aged 19 to 60 who were set for planned surgery. Expert anesthesiologists scored each airway with LEMON first, then graded the actual placement. Comparing the two scores showed a clear link between the bedside check and real difficulty. The findings support using the check to plan safer airway care.
pmc-11080423:
Four authors, led by Yuchun Yang, survey in 2023 Chinese nurses working in Japanese hospitals about what keeps them engaged in their jobs. Engagement, a state of vigor and absorption, shapes the quality of care. Nurses who cross borders face unlike practice habits and stalled career paths, both of which may dull that engagement.

One hundred forty nine nurses answered paper or online surveys sent through fifty eight hospitals and a chat group. Measures covered the practice setting, career stage, and engagement itself. The team mapped how the three move together. Findings are meant to help hospitals keep migrant nurses committed.
pmc-11532323:
Xuan Zhao, Zhenjiang Liu, Haifeng Qin, Yarong Liu, and Yi Zhang report a cervical cancer case treated with the patient's own tumor-fighting T cells. Standard chemotherapy answers only about 13% of advanced cases, so cell therapy draws interest. Their patient had recurrent cancer with wide spread and received autologous tumor-infiltrating lymphocytes, grown from a metastatic groin lymph node, plus IL-2 after a modified lymphodepleting regimen.

The patient reached a partial response with limited, tolerable immune side effects. Blood sequencing afterward showed strong expansion of dominant T cell clones from the infused product. Those clones persisted in the body long term, which supports the staying power of the approach.
pmc-11532623:
Hongbin Jin, Yang Han, and Jennifer Zenker review in a 2024 paper how one egg can yield twins of one germ set. Such twins were long said to come from a split of the early clump of cells. Lab-made births have thrown fresh light on when and how that split runs.

Cases where one lab ball of cells gave twins with two sacs clash with the old tale, which put that split far earlier. The team sifts lab cases and beast tests for the cell steps of each split kind. Their sweep reworks the classic split chart. Birth teams gain a finer tale of a split they meet in the lab.
pmc-11534823:
Jorge Sancho-Muriel and co-authors compare, in a 2024 study, outcomes of severe gut pouch infection in patients with weak immune systems versus those with normal immunity. The infection, a complicated form of diverticulitis, can often be handled without surgery at first. Whether that holds for immune-weak patients was the core question, along with the need for later planned surgery.

The study covered 290 first-episode patients over six years, fifty of them immune-weak. Emergency surgery was twice as common in the weak group, and it brought more complications and far higher deaths. The results caution against assuming the standard no-surgery path is equally safe when immunity is low.
pmc-11535223:
Yu Zhang and co-authors probe brain rhythms with a portable scanner in a 2024 paper. Alpha waves in the front of the brain matter for mental health care, since stimulation treatments aim at a person's own alpha pace. Forty volunteers were recorded with eyes open and eyes closed, repeatedly over up to nine months.

Alpha strength in the two states tracked together within each person, mostly through the rhythmic part of the signal. Yet the fine structure differed: the closed-eye rhythm split into sub-parts unlike the open-eye one. Readers get a guide for picking a stable personal alpha frequency for stimulation therapy.
pmc-11535523:
Tanner Simpson and co-authors present a way to make clean terahertz pulses in a 2024 paper. A laser pulse with two colors drives a current in ionized gas, which emits broad terahertz waves. As the pulse travels, the two colors drift out of step. That drift slows energy build-up and smears the pulse.

Their setup fixes the drift with optics that pre-set the phase across the beam. A lens flaw, spherical aberration, is used on purpose to shape the phase map. Paired with a flying focus, simulations form a half-cycle pulse. The pulse has a set emission angle and far less spread than standard setups give.
pmc-11536623:
Ludovic Le Renard and three co-authors describe a fossil fungus from Jurassic Yorkshire in a 2024 paper. Fungi that live on leaves have a rich record from the age of mammals, but their earlier history is sketchy. The new find grew on the leaf of an ancient cycad-like plant about 170 million years ago.

The authors name it a new genus and species. Its dark, spreading fruiting mats match a major living group of filamentous fungi. To place it, they rechecked other leaf fossils of the era against family trees built from DNA. Features like spore-release pores and entry pads first show up in this middle era of Earth history. Two younger fossils mark the oldest clear members of other major groups. Warm, wet forests of broad-leaved gymnosperms may have been the first home of these leaf fungi.
pmc-11536823:
Evans Paul Kwame Ameade and co-authors report a survey study, published in 2024, on what medical students in Ghana know and think about animal-assisted therapy. Such therapy uses trained animals to support treatment, and it is common in wealthy countries but rare in Ghana. Future doctors who never meet the idea are unlikely to recommend it to patients who might gain from it.

Two hundred and six senior medical students at a university in Tamale answered a structured questionnaire. Knowledge scores were very poor, and almost no student had met the therapy at school or at home. Attitudes, though, leaned mildly positive. The authors argue that adding the topic to training could open a low cost support option for Ghanaian patients.
pmc-11536923:
Ferdinando Bonfiglio and co-authors set out best practices for reading inherited DNA variation in a 2024 review. Modern sequencing comes in second and third generation forms, each with its own error habits. Clinics lean on the results for diagnosis, so each pipeline step must be handled with care.

The review walks from raw alignment and cleanup through quality control, variant calling, and artifact removal. It stresses close inspection of doubtful variants, a step that guards accuracy where results guide patient care. Sections cover annotation, structural variants, copy number changes, and methyl marks on DNA. Hard spots get their own advice, from the immune gene region to runs of sameness and the mitochondrial genome. Tool choices are compared throughout, aiming at precision a clinic can trust.
pmc-11538223:
Angela Farley and co-authors compare the hearts of elite horse jockeys in Australia with those of the general public in a 2024 study. Racing makes hard demands on the body, with high heart rates and heavy oxygen use. What years of that work do to the heart was not known for this group.

Forty-six jockeys and thirty-three adults from the public had ultrasound scans of the heart. The groups matched in age, but jockeys were shorter and much lighter. One heart chamber held more blood in jockeys than in controls. The gap grew larger once body size was factored in. The study gives a first clear picture of how racing shapes the jockey heart.
pmc-11539823:
Xiankun Liu and co-authors review layer by layer coatings for bone repair in a 2024 paper. Bone implants fail through weak bonding, infection, stress damage, and immune pushback. Layer by layer assembly stacks charged films one skin at a time on a base, a cheap and flexible way to load healing goods.

The review covers the method base, its growth, and the chemistry used to dress bone implants. Stacked films can meter drug release on a set clock, coax bone bonding, grow new vessels, and fight germs and oxidation at once. Recent orthopedic uses fill the survey.
pmc-11539923:
Daniel Butler and three co-authors listen to family doctors who work in Northern Ireland’s poorest neighborhoods, in a 2024 interview study. People in deprived areas die younger and live sicker, and their doctors carry heavier, more complex caseloads than colleagues in wealthy areas. The Deep End network links practices serving the most deprived patients.

Nine such doctors described why they stay, what wears them down, and what would help. Their accounts, analyzed for lived experience, mix strain with real reward: deep ties to patients and a sense of mission against the odds. The study carries their suggestions upward, from consultation length to staffing, for planners who rarely hear frontline voices from the Deep End.
pmc-11545623:
Young adults in China face new work and life pressures, and how fair they find society may shape how well they feel. Liyun Wu and Gang Wang study that tie in a 2024 paper. They use a national survey from 2021 with 1,726 adults aged 18 to 34 across 19 provinces.

Well-being split into five strands, from health to a sense of purpose and growth. Body and mind health formed the base of the whole set. Those in poor health saw society as less fair and people as less worthy of trust. A bright view of the future tracked with high fairness and trust. The authors say well-being is a group trait as well as a private one.
pmc-11545923:
Geyner Gaona and co-authors review how wearables can map the full set of influences on heart health in a 2024 paper. That full set, the cardiovascular exposome, covers external and internal factors across a lifetime. Tracking it well could improve prevention, diagnosis, and treatment of heart disease.

Wearable and digital tools now record heart rate, rhythm, activity, and sleep in real time over long periods. The review covers sensor advances and methods for collecting and analyzing the data. It also sets out the allure and the gaps of turning daily life into a continuous heart health record.
pmc-11547923:
Ruiji Li and co-authors wrote a 2024 review of light switch molecules that work with visible light alone. These compounds flip shape when lit, which suits them for light driven movers, circuits, and data storage. One prized family holds both shapes well and resists wear, but it has long needed ultraviolet light to flip.

Ultraviolet light harms living tissue and passes poorly through many media. That need has capped the family's use in medicine and materials. The review gathers design plans that shift the flip into visible light. It sorts the plans so chemists can pick a route for a target use. The authors say all-visible switches could widen the field a lot. Work now spreads across labs that build such molecules.
pmc-11562123:
Trine Toft-Bertelsen and co-authors compare in 2024 the fat profile of spinal fluid in patients with a treatable cause of dementia like symptoms against healthy controls. The condition, marked by fluid buildup in the brain with walking, bladder, and thinking problems, is often missed and can be hard to tell from other brain diseases. Fluid from nineteen patients and twenty one controls was run through a broad scanning platform.

The scan found 244 fats across seventeen classes. Several fat classes and single fats ran low in patients, while one storage fat class ran high. Yet patients who improved after a shunt operation showed no distinct profile from those who did not. The authors say the profile may aid diagnosis, but cannot yet predict who will benefit from surgery.
pmc-11570823:
Man Nguyen and Mario Vazdar simulate cell-penetrating peptides at a membrane in a 2024 paper. Their test peptide is a short chain of one amino acid type, known for crossing cell membranes. Simulations varied peptide amount and salt levels in the water around a model membrane. The peptides clumped on the membrane surface, and salt made the clumping worse, an odd salting-out effect for such charged chains.

Bigger clumps formed and lasted longer as salt and peptide rose, while fewer lone peptides stuck to the membrane. Charge pairing quirks of this amino acid explain the effect. The authors link clumping to how these peptides slip across membranes.
pmc-11572123:
Ji Ma and co-authors report a 2024 study of testosterone and bone density in men over 60. Aging shifts hormone levels, and testosterone is thought to weigh on bone health in older men. The team used a national United States health survey from 2013 to 2014 to test that link.

The analysis held 621 older men. After weights and adjustments, the link took an inverted U shape: bone density at the hip neck rose with testosterone up to a point, then fell. The turn point sat near 406 nanograms per deciliter. In the middle band of hormone levels the link was positive, while the lowest and highest bands showed a negative tilt.
pmc-11572523:
Veronica Apetorgbor and co-authors test whether group antenatal care improves newborn outcomes in Ghana, in a 2024 trial. Mothers who can spot newborn danger signs seek care faster. That knowledge is low in many settings. Standard one-on-one antenatal visits may not teach it well. Group care replaces some visits with shared sessions.

Clinics were randomized to group or usual care in the Eastern Region. The study measured danger sign knowledge and newborn care practices. Postnatal visit use was tracked as well. Group sessions let mothers learn from each other's questions. Midwives gain a model that may teach more per hour. Results inform how antenatal care is reorganized across Ghana. Newborn survival is the bottom-line stake.
pmc-11573323:
Siri Urquhart and co-authors review five patients whose mouth and face swelling syndrome, orofacial granulomatosis, appeared alongside Crohn's disease, in a 2024 case series. The condition is rare, and records at their center were searched for both diagnoses to see how cases were treated and how they fared.

Most patients had Crohn's affecting both small and large bowel without strictures or penetrating complications. Steroid injections into the lesions helped three of four patients partly, and infliximab featured in several regimens, yet flare-ups after treatment were common. No patient achieved a complete response to any therapy. The authors conclude the syndrome often needs long-term treatment and that better options are worth investigating.
pmc-11573423:
Martina Weiss and co-authors read the genes of two water isopods living in a once-polluted German river system, in a study published in 2024. The Emscher catchment was heavily degraded and has since been largely restored. The isopods are pollution-tolerant detritus feeders, and their population patterns can reveal whether restored streams are truly reconnected.

Sampling across the catchment, the team combined a mitochondrial gene with genome-wide markers. Both species split into many isolated populations only a few kilometers apart, yet kept high genetic diversity. Related species complexes raised the worry of hidden cryptic species, but the genome-wide data showed each set of lineages is a single species locally. Restoration alone has not restored gene flow, and fine-scale markers are needed to see that.
pmc-11574023:
Jeevitha Kannan and co-authors extended a math tool for choices under vagueness in a 2024 paper. Fuzzy sets let each option carry grades of truth rather than a hard yes or no. Their richer form, with more parts per grade, suits hard calls in medicine and engineering where facts blur.

The team built new ways to weigh such sets: how alike two sets are, how much doubt one holds, and how far apart two sets sit. They proved theorems on how the measures play off each other. Worked cases in medical and engineering fields show the tools in action. The aim is choices that stay sound when inputs are soft.
pmc-11574123:
Yanfei Shao and co-authors profiled sugar-coated proteins tied to colorectal cancer spread, in a 2024 study. When this cancer reaches lymph nodes, outlook worsens sharply. A sugar coating change called sialylation is a known event in that spread, but its protein map was unclear. The team labeled and measured coated proteins in spread-prone tumors with mass tools.

They found over eleven hundred coated proteins in the relevant samples. Blending biology data with machine learning narrowed the field to twenty-five genes that forecast outcomes. Those genes split patients into groups with distinct survival, immune makeups, and drug responses. A nine-gene risk score stood on its own as a risk factor. The authors also name candidate drugs matched to each risk group, aiming at more personal treatment.
pmc-11574523:
Jia Zhao and co-authors review how gut microbes talk to the brain in depression and bipolar disorder, in a 2024 paper. The two illnesses are hard to tell apart during a depressive episode, and blood or scan tests cannot yet help. The gut-brain axis, meanwhile, carries signals both ways, and patient microbiomes look altered.

The review compares the microbial changes reported in each disorder and tracks how treatments, from standard drugs to probiotics and even stool transplants, shift the gut community. The authors hope microbe signatures could one day sharpen the differential diagnosis and open gentler therapies. They frame the axis as a two-way street clinicians can no longer ignore.
pmc-11574623:
Arpit Raturi and co-authors compare photosynthesis genes across crops in a 2024 study. Some crops use a more efficient path for capturing carbon, which lifts yield and saves water and nitrogen. Past work showed that even crops on the plain path carry and use all the genes for the richer path.

Genes for five key enzymes of the pathway were found and compared in five crops. The set spans rice on the plain path, three rich path crops such as maize and foxtail millet, and pineapple on a third path. Rich path crops held the most copies of these genes. The history traced here may guide efforts to boost plain path crops.
pmc-11575023:
Vincenzi and colleagues present in 2024 a semi-automatic pipeline that aligns microscope sections of lung tissue with matching slices from micro-CT scans in a mouse model of lung fibrosis. The two views complement each other: scans follow disease over time, while histology shows fine damage. The tool rotates the scan volume, finds the coronal slice matching each section, and extracts density measures from it.

Matching succeeded in most cases and cut alignment time from forty minutes to five. Scan and tissue scores correlated well. The authors say the link gives drug studies a fuller, faster read on fibrosis.
pmc-11575323:
Patients are the true experts on their own conditions, yet medical training often treats them as cases, not teachers. Clare Kennedy and co-authors set out a protocol for mapping how patients take part in teaching obstetrics and gynaecology. The specialty raises the stakes: its exams and topics are intimate, and involvement must be handled with care. The team wants to know what forms that involvement takes worldwide.

Their scoping review will search eleven databases for literature from 1960 onward. It follows an established framework for mapping broad topics. The goal is twofold: chart what exists, and expose the gaps. Challenges unique to this field, from consent to comfort, get special attention. The finished map should guide schools designing patient involvement that respects everyone in the room.
pmc-11576923:
Asma Khalid and co-authors offer a 2024 math study of porphyrazine, a ring-shaped molecule prized for stability. Such rings interest drug and materials designers. Number-based fingerprints of its bonding pattern can predict how it acts.

New index formulas captured how atoms connect across the structure. An entropy measure built on those indices gauged disorder and stability. Logarithmic regression tied the indices to the entropy values. Strong links would let chemists estimate traits from structure alone. The work adds a compact tool that predicts traits for a compound family with wide promise.
pmc-11577723:
Rongzhou Wang and co-authors report a lipid paradox: the 'good' cholesterol tracks with weaker bone and muscle in older adults. Osteosarcopenia, the pairing of low bone mass and low muscle mass, was read from chest CT scans in 1,995 adults over fifty. It appeared in 141 people, about 7.7 percent.

Those affected actually carried higher HDL cholesterol than their peers. Adjusted models gave an odds ratio of 2.72 for the condition per unit rise, and the top HDL quarters tripled the odds against the bottom quarter. The link held in men and, at the top quarter, in women. The authors caution this is association, not cause, but it complicates the good-cholesterol story.
pmc-11579323:
Mohammad Souri and co-authors use a math model in 2024 to test a mixed plan for treating tumors that are rich in blood vessels. Drugs placed right into a tumor can work well, but blood flow washes them out fast in such tumors. That wash out caps how much good the drugs can do.

The plan pairs two tricks. Drugs that curb new blood vessel growth thin out the vessel web, which helps keep the treatment in place. Tiny drug loaded particles with a negative charge spread through the tumor tissue more fully. The model tracks drug flow and spread in the tumor under this mix. It shows how the two tricks work as a pair to push more drug deep into the tumor. The study is a model, not a patient trial, so it guides later lab and clinic tests.
pmc-11579723:
Five geotechnical researchers test how clay changes the strength of sediments that hold natural gas hydrates. Such clay-rich deposits are candidate gas reserves, and their safety under extraction depends on how they deform and fail. The team ran squeezing shear tests on lab sediments holding hydrates, comparing two clay minerals, illite and montmorillonite, at several clay contents.

The montmorillonite samples hardened more under strain and changed volume more, and both trends grew with clay content. The illite samples were stiffer and failed at higher strength. Failure strength rose with clay content and with the pressure confining the sample, while grip and friction measures each varied in straight-line fashion with clay share. The team folds clay content into the standard Mohr-Coulomb failure rule, giving engineers a way to predict shear strength in clay-rich hydrate reservoirs before mining them.
pmc-11582023:
Pan Jiang and co-authors report a materials study, published in 2024, using a plant polymer to steady an ultra thin ceramic material. MXenes are sheets only atoms thick with promising electrical traits, but they clump and degrade in air and water. Lignin, a woody plant polymer, turned out to coat these sheets and slip between their layers.

The coated sheets stayed spread out and resisted oxidation in water and in several organic solvents. The spacing between layers could be tuned finely over a wide range by a shifting bond between lignin and the sheets. Conductivity, heat glow, and shielding against electromagnetic noise could also be adjusted, pointing toward uses in electronics and photonics.
pmc-11584123:
Bisrat Teketelew and seven co-authors pool data on anemia in refugee children in a review from two thousand twenty-four. Anemia hits displaced children hard, driven mainly by poor nutrition and iron deficiency. The team searched major databases and gray sources for studies from two thousand nine to two thousand twenty-three.

Fourteen studies met their quality checks and entered the meta-analysis. The pooled rate of anemia among refugee children worldwide was about thirty-seven percent. Rates were highest in Africa, at about fifty-six percent, and lowest in North America. Children under five showed the highest rate of all. The authors call anemia a moderate public health problem in this group and urge focused prevention in lower-income host settings.
pmc-11585523:
Liu, Wei, and Ding studied a stem-cell gene's role in cervical cancer, in a paper published in 2024, with an eye to predicting patient outcomes. The gene helps cells stay flexible and stem-like. It also seems to sway a form of cell death driven by iron. Death of that kind can kill cancer cells that resist other treatments. The team profiled the gene's activity across tumor data using computing tools and lab profiling.

They traced how the gene's level relates to the death pathway and to survival. On that basis they built a prediction model centered on the gene. Such a model could sort patients by risk and hint at who might benefit from death-inducing drugs. The authors frame it as a step toward personal treatment choices in cervical cancer. Validation in patients remains ahead.
pmc-11585623:
RNA marks that shape the immune mix in prostate tumors are mapped by Fajing Jia, Shaoze Jing, and Jianjin Guo in work dated 2024. Prostate gland cancer is the most common non-skin cancer in men. A mark called m6A is the most common tag on RNA, steered by a set of writer and reader proteins. How that mark web drives tumor growth and outlook was not clear.

The team ties the mark web to gene faults and to the immune cells that enter the tumor zone. They split tumors into subtypes by a mark score. Each subtype shows its own immune mix. The split may guide care picks and sharpen outlook calls.
pmc-11586423:
Chen and co-authors test a simple blood-sugar ratio as a warning sign for intensive care patients with coronary heart disease. The stress hyperglycemia ratio compares a patient's admission glucose with the level expected from their longer-term blood sugar control. Using the MIMIC-IV database, the team followed 2,059 such patients in intensive care.

Patients were split into four groups by ratio level, and death rates were compared across them. A higher ratio went with a higher risk of dying in hospital or in intensive care. The link was not a straight line: risk rose in a J-shaped pattern, and patients with high ratios stayed longer. The authors present the ratio as a cheap, practical marker that could help flag the heart patients most at risk in intensive care.
pmc-11587123:
Tsalta-Mladenov, Dimitrova, and Andonova report a rare case of painful legs and moving toes syndrome in a 2024 paper. The disorder pairs burning leg pain with toes that move on their own. It is little known among clinicians.

Their patient, a man in his late fifties, had back and leg pain with toe movements worsened by touch on the thigh. Imaging showed multilevel disc disease in the neck and lower back, with cord involvement. A daily nerve pain drug eased both pain and movements, and the benefit held over three months of follow-up. The paper reviews other options, from injections to stimulation, for stubborn cases. Early use of the drug is recommended.
pmc-11587723:
Seddon and co-authors review inflammation and DNA methylation in Alzheimer's disease in a 2024 article. Alzheimer's brings memory loss, confusion, and behavior change, with plaques and tangles building up in the brain. No cure is known. Causes are many, and inflammation, oxidative stress, genes, and blood vessel problems all play a part.

The review asks how oxidants from immune cells that enter the brain might rewrite DNA methylation patterns. Those patterns help control gene activity and change with age. The authors gather current work on that link. Understanding it may show new paths to slow the disease, they suggest.
pmc-11588423:
Hawraa Ali-Jerman and co-authors compared two ways of making gene-delivery particles for brain tumor cells, in a 2024 study. The particles, called dendriplexes, wrap DNA in a branched polymer that shields it and carries it into cells. Hand mixing is the lab standard but varies from batch to batch; microfluidic chips promise uniform, scalable production. The team made the same particles both ways and tested them on glioma cells in dishes.

Microfluidic particles bound DNA more completely over time, reaching ninety-seven percent condensation at a day. Both kinds came out positively charged and stable. Surprisingly, the hand-mixed particles were smaller and entered cells better, producing significantly stronger gene expression. The authors acknowledge the manual win on performance while arguing microfluidics wins on the standardization and scale-up that real therapies need. The study maps the trade-off for groups developing dendrimer-based gene delivery.
pmc-11589023:
Sayan Banerjee, Dibakar Nayak, and Anindya Sinha study how a tea-garden community in Assam lives beside wild elephants in a paper from two thousand twenty-four. Barriers and other technical fixes for human-elephant conflict have often failed over time. The authors argue such fixes ignore the history that shaped today's encounters.

Fieldwork in Udalguri district gathered life stories and daily accounts from the Adivasi, or Tea Tribe, community. People read elephant moves, diets, and calls closely, and their tales link elephant hardship to their own losses of land and food. Empathy runs through these accounts. The authors suggest that living as uneasy neighbors, rather than apart, could guide conservation policy.
pmc-11590523:
A team led by Erlie Jiang ran a phase two trial of cord-blood stem cells for a severe reaction after bone marrow transplant, where donor cells attack the patient. Steroid drugs fail many of these patients, and stem cells are a hopeful second line that lacked firm trials. Seventy-eight patients at seven centers got stem cells or a dummy infusion, each with standard second drugs.

By day twenty-eight, sixty percent of the stem cell group had responded, against half of the control group, a gap too small to prove. Later chronic disease rates leaned lower with stem cells. Response came at a median of two weeks. The authors call for larger trials.
pmc-11590823:
Michihiro Iwaki and co-authors present a 2024 protocol for a trial of a drug for fatty liver disease paired with high blood fats. The liver condition, tied to metabolic problems, is rising worldwide. No agreed drug treatment exists for it or for its inflamed form.

The drug, pemafibrate, targets a switch that controls fat burning and is known to lower blood fats. The trial will run at many centers, with patients assigned by chance to drug or control, and the design is open label, so all know who gets what. The protocol sets out who can join, what doses are used, and which liver and fat measures count as success.
pmc-11591523:
Huan Liu leads a team on verb cues and pronoun inference in second language use. Their study from twenty twenty-four uses Chinese learners of English. Eye moves were tracked as they read test sentences.

Some verbs hint who caused an act in a sentence. Learners used those hints to guess pronoun links early. Strong learners made those guesses faster than weak learners. The hints were used before the clear clue showed in text. That backs a focusing account of how reading works. Skill level shapes the speed of this process.
pmc-11591823:
Shan Gao and Yunpeng Ma build a framework to tune boiler burning in this 2024 paper. The boiler type they study is a circulating fluidized bed unit. Tuning must raise heat efficiency and cut nitrogen oxide emissions at once. Those two aims pull against each other, which makes the task hard.

Their framework pairs a readable boosting model with a tweaked slime mould search method. The model predicts efficiency and emissions, and a tool shows which inputs drive each output. The search then adjusts working settings for a large 330 MW unit. Tests showed a small efficiency gain, a large emissions cut, and fast run times. Extra benchmark tests backed the method's edge over rivals.
pmc-11593123:
Desi ter Woerds and co-authors test a way to find the first draining lymph nodes in early lung cancer in this 2024 study. Those sentinel nodes are the most likely place for cancer to spread, so finding them without surgery could shape future care. The team added tracer injections to a standard camera-guided airway exam.

Thirty-one patients received injections of a radioactive tracer and a contrast dye into or near the tumor, guided by ultrasound. The special catheter placed the dose safely in every case. Later scans found a sentinel node in about a third of patients. Tracking the dye first helped aim the needle. The authors call the injection step feasible, though node detection stayed uneven.
pmc-11595223:
Jawwad Hassan Mirza and co-authors published this 2024 taxonomic revision of Bryobia, a genus of plant-feeding spider mites. Sorting its many species has long been tangled, so the authors re-examine the subgeneric divisions using stable body characters, above all the paired bristles on the hind legs.

Three subgenera survive the review: Bryobia, Allobia, and Lyobia, told apart by which rear legs carry the paired bristles or none. Inside each, the authors propose three species groups keyed to the position of one back bristle pair, nine groups in all, to speed identification. DNA barcode data from public databases, they note honestly, could not confirm the family tree behind the scheme. Notes on eight species described by one earlier worker round out the revision.
pmc-11595523:
The authors present a 2024 study building a machine learning model that forecasts late fetal growth restriction. When a fetus stops growing well late in pregnancy, risks climb sharply, and early warning lets doctors watch the right mothers. Data came from seven hospitals over eleven years, covering more than thirty-two thousand pregnancies.

Two models were built, one from first-trimester data and one adding information up to twenty-eight weeks. The later model discriminated better in both training and test sets. A simplified version, using only the features an importance ranking picked, performed about as well. Prediction was modest rather than sharp, with precision-recall scores staying low. Still, the authors say a lean model could help flag individual risk by the early third trimester.
pmc-11595623:
Julia Grass and Anja Strobel study how the drive to think, called need for cognition, links with well-being in adults, in a 2024 paper. This drive reflects how much people enjoy effortful thinking. It was first treated as general, unlike related traits that are seen as domain-specific.

Across three samples totaling 1,074 participants, including students and professionals, they test general and domain-specific forms of the drive. Both forms linked positively with positive affect, life satisfaction, and work or study satisfaction. In part, the domain form tied more strongly to satisfaction in the same domain. The findings support measuring the drive by life area, not only overall.
pmc-11596223:
Wenming Zhang and co-authors seed fertilizers with built microbe teams to rescue tired potato soil, in this 2024 study. Fields cropped with potatoes year after year lose vigor, partly because root leftovers feed the wrong microbes. The team assembled bacterial and fungal communities that can break those leftovers down.

The teams were loaded into sheep manure fertilizer, alone and combined, and tested in pots of soil from a four-year potato field. Tracking showed bacteria settled weakly near roots, at about one percent of the local total. Fungi settled far more strongly, reaching up to eighteen percent in open soil. Combined teams boosted fungal settlement in both zones.
pmc-11597823:
Felix Niebisch, Ullrich Scherf, and co-authors grow a chiral plastic film straight on an electrode. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-four. Conducting polymers serve in solar cells, sensors, and electronics. A built-in twist, chirality, could add chiral sensors and light tools to that list.

Their new polymer is built from a ring-shaped triad with a dye-like core, fused by benzene rings. Charge-driven growth lays it on the electrode in one step. The pure-twist films bend left and right light to unlike degrees, and tests show the signal is true chirality, not a layout artefact. The twist is part of the chain itself, not an add-on.
pmc-11598323:
Horim Lee, writing alone in 2024, reviews how plants balance growth against stress through G protein signaling. Plants cannot flee bad conditions, so they must adapt in place. That forces a constant trade: energy for growth or for defense. A family of signaling proteins, the heterotrimeric G proteins, helps run that trade. The review lays out what those proteins are and how they signal. It then traces their role in plant immunity.

Heat-driven shape change, called thermomorphogenesis, is the second case study. In both, the proteins tune how much the plant spends on each side. The balance shifts with the stresses the plant faces. Understanding the switch could help breed crops that yield under stress. The review pulls scattered findings into one account. It is aimed at plant scientists and breeders.
pmc-11599423:
Matthias Gröger and co-authors hunt blood markers that foretell whether a leaky tricuspid valve will settle after its mitral neighbor is clipped. Published in 2024, the study follows 242 patients through catheter based mitral repair. Right heart failure and tricuspid leakage ride along often in these patients and darken the outlook, yet the leak frequently improves after the mitral fix, for reasons little understood.

Patients with worse leaks were sicker on standard scores and carried many raised markers. One, the binding protein IGFBP-2, rose about 1.4 fold in severe leakage. In the ninety-nine patients rechecked at three months, marker patterns predicted right heart reverse remodeling. The authors offer the protein as a planning signal before the procedure.
pmc-11600823:
Ozan Baytas and three co-authors trace what breaks at brain nerve ends without the enzyme GPT2. It sits in mitochondria, the cell parts that burn fuel. Their 2024 study starts from genes in man. Kids born with broken copies of this gene develop intellectual disability. The enzyme moves glutamate, the main signal that stirs brain cells to fire, linking fuel use to cell talk.

In mouse brain, the enzyme packs into nerve ends. With no GPT2, those ends changed how they held glutamate and glutamine, and let less glutamate go when probed. Tests in hippocampus slices found weak excitatory currents, while the calm-side currents stayed the same. Fuel-cycle parts fell, and a back-up enzyme worked harder. Adding alpha-ketoglutarate, one lost fuel piece, brought release back and calmed the fuel shifts. The rescue marks a lead for help in man.
pmc-11600923:
Dexian Zhang, Xinxin Xu, Zhibin Ye, Zhenxing Zhang, and Jing Xiao built a prediction tool for high uric acid in older adults in this 2024 study. Uric acid builds up when the body breaks down purines, and high levels can lead to gout and kidney harm. A simple chart that flags risk a year ahead could help clinics act early.

The team followed a cohort of 2,788 older adults at Huadong Hospital for at least a year. They screened for traits that predict a rise in uric acid, then built a logistic regression model drawn as a nomogram. The model sorted people well in its home cohort and in an outside check group. Its calls also matched the real outcomes closely. Men proved more prone to high levels than women. The tool gives doctors a quick, visual way to spot elders who need watching.
pmc-11602023:
Andrew McCormack and co-authors present in 2024 a grainy gel that can hold soft printed structures while they set. Building tissue-like constructs in three dimensions is a standing challenge in medicine. A new trick prints watery inks inside a support bath that flows around the print head, then holds firm. Their bath is made of gellan gum, sheared while it gels so it breaks into grains.

The grains give the bath a paste-like behavior across a wide heat range, from fridge cold to body warmth. Its resistance to flow is very low, which allowed print speeds up to sixty millimeters per second. The team printed droplets carrying live cells and kept them for seven days. They also built features inside a version of the bath that can itself set firm. Easy making, speed, and that setting option make it a strong candidate, they argue.
pmc-11603323:
Kun Pan and co-authors stabilize a coal mine roadway that must survive next to a mined-out void, in work from 2024. Gob-side entry retaining reuses a tunnel beside the worked panel, but layered roofs of mixed rock fracture unpredictably and pressure relief often fails.

Studying one panel at Longtan Coal Mine, the team modeled how roof stability depends on where the hard rock layer sits and how much load it can bear. They sorted roofs into four grades, from stable to extremely unstable. Each grade gets its own relief cuts, support strength, and slope reinforcement, built on strong support, reinforced sides, and precise roof cracking. Field use kept the roadway's surrounding rock stable and the entry serviceable.
pmc-11603423:
Yi Mu and a very large team measure how much health care people with long COVID use over two years in Britain. Their 2024 study links national health records for more than a quarter million adults with the condition. Four matched comparison groups frame the counts. They include people who had COVID without the long form, people from before the pandemic, and the same patients before their own illness. Visits, tests, and costs are tallied by month and year.

Care use per person runs higher for the long COVID group across primary and hospital care. The gap holds against each comparison group in turn. Costs are adjusted for price rises so years can be compared fairly. The sheer group sizes make the pattern hard to dismiss as noise. Planners gain a firm count of the lasting load this condition places on clinics and hospitals.
pmc-11603623:
Hyeonjeong Go, Masae Kuboniwa, and Youn-Hee Choi published a long-term study in two thousand twenty-four on dental check-ups in Korea's national screening programme. Regular oral exams aim to catch disease early, and scaling prevents gum disease. Whether attending exams leads to more preventive care over time was the question.

The team followed over four point six million adults for nineteen years using insurance records. People who attended exams more often later received far more scaling sessions. Their odds of periodontal treatment were also higher. The gradient rose steadily with exam frequency. The authors argue that pushing exam attendance lifts population oral health. They suggest widening preventive coverage tied to the exams.
pmc-11603723:
Shen and Zhao survey what hives patients know and do about their medication. Urticaria causes itchy welts, and steady drug use shapes how well it is controlled. Gaps in knowledge or poor habits can weaken care, so the team measured all three areas.

The cross-sectional survey ran in the dermatology department of a Kunming hospital from June 2023 to March 2024. Patients answered questions on what they know about urticaria drugs, how they view them, and how they take them. Scores show where teaching may help most. Staff can then target advice to real gaps.
pmc-11603923:
Charuai Suwanbamrung and co-authors present a 2024 journal article evaluating a school-based dengue control model in southern Thailand. Dengue keeps rising in Southeast Asia while lasting control tools lag. The participatory project built its plan with students, community leaders, health educators, officials, and volunteers, then trained high schoolers in dengue facts and mosquito larva surveillance.

Nearly all 248 students joined the before and after rounds. Knowledge scores rose after training, and trained students taught their own circles, spreading a sense of shared duty. Girls and better-educated students grasped the material most. The authors present schools as engines for community-wide mosquito control.
pmc-11604123:
Georgina Cole and co-authors measure how capture and tagging stress the critically endangered flapper skate. Catch-and-release fishing underpins both sport and research tagging programs. Sixty-one skates were angled in Scotland and checked twice before release. Blood chemistry, heart rate, and breathing rate were logged through handling and tag surgery.

Most skates showed mild metabolic acidosis, with blood acidity up and lactate raised. A milder breathing-based acidosis rode alongside it. Warmer water and longer fights deepened the strain, and deck time made it worse. Prior angling injuries showed in about ten percent of the fish. Shorter fights and cooler, shaded handling are the practical fixes.
pmc-11604823:
Katja Jung and four co-authors test, in 2024 work, whether a video can teach young adults to floss well, and whether hands-on help adds more. Clean gaps between teeth guard gum health, yet most people floss badly. Close to one hundred young adults were filmed flossing before any teaching.

Half saw a teaching video alone, half saw it plus hands-on coaching. A week later, both groups reached more gaps, used a steadier order, and handled the floss better. Two weeks on, gains grew again, and many flossed the whole mouth right. The hands-on half gained no edge at any point. Flossing felt less hard after teaching, though people said it took longer. The team backs video teaching as a fast, cheap tool.
pmc-11604923:
Hao Xu and co-authors count cells where cartilage meets bone in the knee, in a 2024 study. That border zone holds two cell types in tiny pockets: cartilage cells above and bone cells below, and the two talk to each other. Counting them in 3D helps track joint wear and disease, but the pockets are hard to pick out by hand.

The team used a bright X-ray imaging method that reaches very fine detail, far sharper than a normal scan. They paired a classic region-growing method with a deep learning network to outline each pocket. The network made the outlines cleaner and more complete on samples from human knees. Better cell maps can sharpen study of how joints age and fail.
pmc-11605123:
Senne Heeren and fifteen co-authors mapped the genome of a tropical parasite across the Americas, in a study from twenty twenty-four. The parasite causes skin sores that can progress to disfiguring wounds of the nose and mouth. It spreads through sand fly bites in Latin America's forests.

Hundreds of cultivated samples covered most of the parasite's range. Two big groups emerged: one tied to the Amazon and one to the Atlantic Forest. The Amazon group was genetically mixed and varied, as if mating often. The Atlantic group was more uniform and clone-like, with tight linkage between genes. Small isolated groups added further variety. The authors tie the split to deep ecological differences between the two forest worlds.
pmc-11605623:
Nayuta Higa and co-authors report on joint gene testing for glioma across many centers, in work from 2024. Their team built a custom DNA and RNA panel tuned to this brain tumor in 2018 and has run it on hundreds of cases. A wider study with the fused-gene version began in late 2023 with twenty-one sites.

The panel reads fifty-one DNA genes and thirty-seven RNA genes from stored tissue samples. Among two hundred ten tumors, about one in six held a fused gene. About one in eleven held a gene that drugs can target. Rates of key gene changes in the harshest tumor type are also given. The authors back the panel as a screen for gene-guided care.
pmc-11605823:
Yibeltal Addis Melese and colleagues measured late malaria care in northwest Ethiopia in 2024. Late treatment raises the risk of severe disease. The team surveyed patients at six health centers in one district. Just over four hundred patients took part. A tested questionnaire captured care timing and personal factors. Statistical models sorted which factors tracked with delay. Most patients were young adults on average.

More than three quarters sought treatment late. Several factors stood out in the final model. Not knowing what causes malaria raised the odds of delay. Not knowing its signs also raised the odds. Living far from care raised the odds most sharply. Fear of treatment cost added a further push. The authors call community teaching the key response. People must learn the cause, the signs, and the value of speed. Cost fears also need direct attention, they say.
pmc-11606023:
Tiantongfei Jiang and seven co-authors build a data atlas for heart research in a 2024 paper. Single cell studies read gene activity cell by cell in heart tissue. Such data sets were scattered across many papers and labs. No shared home existed for heart data of this kind.

Their resource, CardioAtlas, gathers millions of cells from human and mouse studies. Human sets hold near two million cells across many heart conditions. Mouse sets add over a million more. The atlas sorts cells into dozens of types for each species. Five tool modules let users label cells, find marker genes, and trace cell talk. Users can also upload their own data for a custom run. The team offers the atlas as a free web resource.
pmc-11606123:
Lei Zhuang and co-authors trace 70 years of wheat breeding gains in China in a 2024 study. Knowing which traits improved, and where, helps plan the next steps for the world's most eaten grain in that country.

They grew 481 wheat lines, both old landraces and modern cultivars, at many sites over many years. Modern lines split cleanly from landraces in gene profile. Over the decades, grain number per ear and grain weight rose in a steady line, while plant height fell. Heading and flowering dates moved earlier. Some trait pairs that once traded off began to improve together, which the authors credit to modern selection.
pmc-11606223:
Beyond the chromosomes, cells carry small circles of loose DNA. Such extrachromosomal circular DNA is well studied in tumors, but almost unknown in heart failure. Zhenhao Lin and co-authors mapped these circles in 2024 in heart tissue from patients with dilated cardiomyopathy and from healthy controls. That disease stretches and weakens the heart muscle. The team paired a circle-hunting method with gene-activity profiling.

The circles came from every chromosome, most under a thousand bases long, about half carrying genes or gene fragments. Gene-rich chromosomes 17 and 19 were especially enriched. Lab checks confirmed the circular shape, and some large circles were actively transcribed even in non-dividing heart cells, hinting they help run gene expression. Small synthetic circles also provoked a stronger immune signal than the same DNA in linear form. The authors offer the map as groundwork for studying circles in heart disease.
pmc-11606523:
Marcos Aurélio Barboza de Oliveira and co-authors take stock of a Brazilian heart surgery journal and where it heads next, in an editorial from two thousand twenty-four. The journal has run without break since nineteen eighty-six and leads its field in Latin America. The piece lists its editors, its reviewer pool, and its recent intake of work.

Since early two thousand twenty-three the journal had received close to nine hundred papers from fifty countries. Its impact score rose from just under one in two thousand eighteen to above one in two thousand twenty-two. Most papers sent in were full original studies, with reviews and how-to pieces next. Readers see a regional journal with a growing world reach.
pmc-11607223:
Esra Akçiçek and six co-authors catalog lung nodule causes that are not cancer spread in a review from two thousand twenty-four. Many nodules together usually raise fear of metastasis, above all in patients with a known cancer. Yet infections, inflammation, and rare benign diseases can look the same.

The article walks through the impostors, from common diseases in rare form to rare tumors that mimic spread. Size, density, borders, and inner structure on scans all carry clues. Growth on follow-up scans and findings elsewhere in the body add more. Matched against symptoms and lab results, these features guide the call. The authors stress that careful reading can spare patients wrong cancer labels and late treatment.
pmc-11607323:
Matthias Sipiczki and Kinga Czentye studied a yeast that switches a pigment tool on and off by chance, in a 2024 paper. The yeast makes pulcherriminic acid, an iron-grabbing compound that forms a maroon-red pigment. A tight gene cluster, called PUL, controls its making. The trait marks a whole yeast group used against plant pests.

The team followed eighteen generations of single-cell clones from one stock strain. Pigment making flipped on and off as cells spread. The pattern looks like epigenetic silencing near quiet chromosome zones in other yeasts. The strain also carried two unlike copies of a key gene. Knowing this switch matters for using the yeast as a biocontrol agent.
pmc-11607423:
Gizachew Kassahun Bizuneh and ten co-authors measure alcohol use disorder and its impact on antiretroviral adherence in adults with HIV in Gondar, Ethiopia. Alcohol problems are common in this population and linked to lower treatment adherence, yet local data were scarce. The hospital based study runs at a university clinic from late 2023 to early 2024.

A standard screening tool finds alcohol use disorder in 38.8 percent of participants. Hazardous use accounts for 24.6 percent, harmful use 6.1 percent, and dependence 8.1 percent. About 67.8 percent of participants report medication adherence above the study threshold. Regression analysis probes which factors travel with alcohol problems, informing support for patients whose drinking threatens their HIV treatment.
pmc-11607823:
Claudia Alteri and co-workers tell of a ward germ that beat a last chance drug in patients who had not had that drug at all. Cefiderocol is kept for Acinetobacter baumannii strains that beat carbapenem drugs. Drug strength loss most often grows while on the drug. In one Milan ward from March to July 2024, staff saw 33 such cases. Gene scans ran on 29 samples.

Most samples sat in one line, but four sat in a next line. Just those four could not be curbed by cefiderocol. They shared an early stop and a lost chunk in the PirA protein. Since the patients had not had the drug, the strength must have come in by spread, not grown on site. The 2024 report warns ward teams to watch for drug strength brought in from the world past the ward.
pmc-11607923:
Mingfang Tang and co-authors model how a Chinese bay district could shape its land use to store more carbon in a 2024 study. Many nations now aim for carbon neutrality, and city plans that count carbon can lift a region's efficiency. Prior work shows the pattern and quality of land use steer how much carbon a region holds in buildings, plants, soil, and water.

The team studied the core area of Taihu Bay with precise three-dimensional city data. They counted all four carbon pools, then used two models in turn: one that sets patch-level goals by weighing many aims, and one that grows land patches in a realistic way. They compared scenes that push carbon storage highest against scenes that balance growth needs. The work gives planners a way to weigh climate goals in land choices.
pmc-11608023:
Nicole Mejia and co-authors test whether swallowed plastic harms wedge-tailed shearwaters in a 2024 paper. Plastic fills the oceans and seabirds, as top hunters, often eat it. The team worked on Maui, Hawaii, checking adult birds from three colonies for plastic in the stomach and for signs of strain in blood, genes, and body condition.

Plastic turned up in twelve of twenty-eight birds. Yet no clear links tied the plastic load to body condition, gene activity, or blood values. Lighter birds did show a pattern: certain blood measures rose together, and genes for metabolism, inflammation, and protein building ran hotter. The authors read that as dehydration and higher energy demand in stressed birds. They urge repeat sampling across the breeding season and multi-signal studies of plastic's quieter harms.
pmc-11608223:
Gizaw Sisay Belay and Tsion Mulat Tebeje wrote this 2024 study mapping births attended by unskilled helpers across Ethiopia. Such attendants may lack the skill to handle childbirth emergencies, so health planners need to know where the practice clusters. The authors drew on a national survey of more than seven thousand women who had given birth in the prior five years.

The map showed strong clustering, with hotspots in the Somali region, parts of Amhara and Oromia, and other pockets. Statistical modeling tied unskilled attendance to being younger, less schooled, poorer, and rural. Women with antenatal visits, media exposure, and health insurance used skilled care more. The authors urge that skilled staff and facilities be steered first to the hotspot regions and to mothers with no schooling, no insurance, and no checkups.
pmc-11608323:
Robin Karpstein and five co-authors published a 2024 study of whether new air vehicles could speed up organ transport in Austria and Germany. A donated organ must reach its recipient fast, because time outside the body, called cold ischemia time, strongly affects success. Advanced air mobility, using small electric aircraft, promises shorter trips than road transport.

The team simulated past transplant journeys using European registry data. They found 48 percent of German transports and 80 percent of Austrian ones were under 150 kilometres, within reach of today’s air vehicles. Time savings of up to 30 minutes are possible on such trips. Better routing of the whole transport process could cut organ waiting time further.
pmc-11609123:
Ami Feder, Yair Graithzer, and Michal Pinhas probe, in a 2024 study, how adults actually picture infinity when it wears a symbol. In theory, infinity outranks every finite number. The team asked people to compare the infinity word and the infinity symbol against ordinary numbers, written as digits or as words, and timed their answers.

Comparisons against the infinity word were fast, faster than number-against-number trials. The symbol alone, matched against digits, lost that edge. Stranger still, both forms of infinity behaved as if they sat on the number line itself. They sat closer to big numbers than to small ones, the classic distance pattern of an ordinary large quantity. The authors conclude that adults quietly misconceive infinity as a very large natural number, and that the notation chosen can hide or expose the error. The work speaks to mathematics teaching as much as to psychology.
pmc-11609423:
Mohammed Abdelrahem and co-authors grow two fungi together to unlock chemicals neither makes alone, then test the brew against the fungus that rots onion bulbs in storage. Basal rot is a leading limit on onion yields, and growers need alternatives to chemical fungicides. The paired culture's extract was tested in dishes and in a greenhouse.

The extract strongly halted the rot fungus at low concentration and showed antioxidant power too. It was richest in phenolic compounds, and chemical profiling confirmed the pairing changed what the fungi produced. In the greenhouse, treated infected onions grew better on every measure and built up more pigments, sugars, and proteins. The authors present fungal partnerships as a source of new crop protectants.
pmc-11609723:
Rohat Cankaya and co-authors report, in a 2024 letter-style case series, rare complete remissions of Sezary syndrome under a light-based blood treatment. This skin lymphoma with blood involvement usually carries a poor outlook, and full remission had been seen almost only after donor stem cell transplant.

Patients from Berlin and Mannheim centers who reached complete remission on extracorporeal photopheresis were gathered. In the treatment, blood is drawn, exposed to light-activated drug, and returned. Some received it alone, others in combination. Skin and blood responses were scored by standard criteria, with time to response and relapse-free spans tracked. The series argues the gentler therapy can, in selected patients, clear the disease durably.
pmc-11610123:
Five authors, led by Yong Yi Tan, gather in 2024 what reviews say about wearable sugar sensors for type 2 diabetes care. The sensors track sugar all day and are growing popular, yet past reviews used unlike methods and reached mixed points. The team ran a review of reviews to build one clear picture.

They searched eight data banks and kept thirty one reviews that pitted the sensors against finger prick checks or usual care. Patients on and off insulin both counted. The team summed effects on long term sugar control and on time spent in a safe range. Overlap between the reviews was also scored.
pmc-11610623:
Kaori Yamoto and co-authors report a rare genetic case in this 2024 paper. A child had growth delay and several birth anomalies. Tests used a chromosome scan, full gene reading, and RNA reading from cells grown from the child's urine, to find the cause.

They found a tiny deletion, present in two copies, that removed the first part of two genes at once. Both copies of one chromosome had come from the father only, which made the deletion double. The two genes are tied to two syndromes, one affecting aging-like traits and one affecting cell energy. The child showed a blend of both syndromes, with a severe course. RNA tests confirmed both genes were under-expressed.
pmc-11612023:
Soft corals of the genus Alcyonium live in the cold waters between South America and the West Antarctic Peninsula, two coasts once joined and now split by a fierce current. The authors read three genetic markers in these corals to reconstruct their history and map their diversity. Family trees, species delimitation, and divergence dating all draw on the same sequences. The aim is to learn how the group spread and split as the southern ocean changed.

The genes show a sharp break between the South American and Antarctic populations, and the analysis points to four likely species. The group's diversification begins about 41 million years ago, close to the opening of the Drake Passage and the birth of the Antarctic Circumpolar Current. That timing suggests the corals have survived in place through long swings of climate. The authors argue that this deep history should inform forecasts of warming impacts.
pmc-11612423:
Liquan Xiong and co-authors bent and loaded replaceable steel links in 2024, the sacrificial pieces designed to take an earthquake's damage so the rest of a frame survives. After a quake, crews swap the ruined links and the building reopens fast.

Four links of differing shortness were cycled back and forth until they failed. All showed fat, stable load loops and strong sideways resistance, with large bending before giving way. Damage came in two families: weld tears and buckling of the web or the flanges, depending on the failure mode. Computer models of the tests matched the measured curves and stress maps closely. The authors back short links as dependable fuses.
pmc-11614223:
Danica Goulet and co-authors evaluated remote specialist advice in prisons in two thousand twenty-four. People in federal custody often wait long for specialists. Ontario's eConsult service lets doctors ask specialists online. Correctional doctors began using it for their patients. The team reviewed four years of those consultations. Volume, topics, and response times were analyzed.

Over nine hundred consultations were completed in the window. Twenty-one correctional doctors submitted them. Heart questions led the specialty list by far. Skin and hormone questions followed behind. Specialists answered in about a day, typically. Each answer took roughly a quarter hour to write. Advice often averted transfers out of facilities. The service improves access behind bars measurably.
pmc-11615123:
Roses resist genetic engineering, partly because the bacterium used to deliver genes transforms some varieties far better than others. Philipp Rüter, Thomas Debener, and Traud Winkelmann hunted the genes behind that difference in 2024. They treated one hundred four rose varieties with a bacterium that induces hairy roots, scoring callus and root growth on leaves and stems.

A genome-wide scan tied root formation to regions on two chromosomes. Five key regions explained between twelve and twenty-seven percent of the trait differences. Some regions matched known spots for ordinary root formation, and the two traits correlated modestly. Ten candidate genes emerged, tied to bacterial response, hormones, and stress. The authors say the map can raise transformation success in ornamental breeding.
pmc-11615323:
Johanna Maria Hölken and co-authors build, in a 2024 study, lab-grown human skin that carries stand-ins for immune cells. Tests of dendritic cell response have long relied on animals, but human cell types differ in key ways. The team grew full-thickness skin and seeded it with cells that mimic the two dendritic cell types found in skin, grown from human cell lines.

Known skin sensitizers, nickel sulfate and a strong chemical allergen, were placed on the skin models. With only one cell type aboard, the stand-in cells moved into the deep layer after a day, a sign of activation. With both types aboard, a response showed within eight hours. The model lets labs spot sensitizers and test drugs in human-like tissue, in line with efforts to cut animal testing.
pmc-11615723:
Khan and Becker review strategies for recognizing and managing post-COVID conditions, in a review from twenty twenty-four. Lingering symptoms fluctuate or persist without established diagnostic tests. Up to twenty to thirty percent of recovering adults may develop them. That implies tens of millions affected in the United States alone.

Related chronic diseases include lung scarring and heart and vessel damage. Screening is recommended especially for high-risk individuals. Early detection improves quality of life and psychosocial health. Patient-centered approaches and standard screening tools are urged. Programs like RECOVER support better understanding and treatment.
pmc-11616123:
Erik Thorvaldsen Sandbakken and seven co-authors examine biofilm on orthopedic implants in a rat model of chronic infection, in a two thousand twenty-four microbe paper. Doctors and nurses use ultrasound sonication of removed implants to help diagnose infections, but how much bacteria it in fact shakes loose was unclear.

Seven rats carried bone graft implants seeded with about five hundred Staphylococcus epidermidis cells. After twenty days, heavy infection surrounded the implants, yet microscopy found only sparse colonies on the steel plates. Sonicate cultures and DNA counts were very low, and sonication's bacterial removal was modest but steady. The authors conclude sonication adds to, but cannot replace, tissue biopsy cultures.
pmc-11616323:
Melanie Lloyd and co-authors price a short-stay pathway for hip and knee replacements in this 2024 study. Demand for joint replacement keeps rising, and long hospital stays strain budgets. Enhanced recovery pathways aim to send suitable patients home sooner, safely.

The team modeled the budget effect of a national roll-out in Australia from 2023 to 2030. Their model drew on projected surgery counts, published costs, and insurer data. Both public and private hospitals were covered. The question was not whether the pathway works, but what it costs or saves at scale. The answer helps health systems plan the shift.
pmc-11616423:
Xiaoxia Chen and co-authors report two dialysis patients who developed chorea, the twisting, involuntary movements that can wreck daily life. Chorea is rare among people on maintenance dialysis, and reports are few. Both patients' limb movements grew steadily worse, and sedatives alone did not help either of them.

Careful work-up split the pair: one had diabetic striatopathy, treated by tight blood sugar control. The other had uremic metabolic encephalopathy, treated with dialysis plus hemoperfusion to clear the blood. Both improved markedly once the true cause was treated. The lesson is that similar movements can hide very different causes.
pmc-11617123:
Chinedu Okoli, Brianna Philbrick, and Syed Quadri report a rare lung cancer case from 2024, with a short review. The cancer, choriocarcinoma, normally grows in the placenta or reproductive organs and makes a hormone that is easy to track in blood. Finding it first in the lung, already spread to lymph nodes, is extremely rare.

Their patient was a woman of thirty-two. Surgeons removed the tumor, and she then received three rounds of a drug regimen built from several cancer medicines. Scans after treatment showed no sign of disease, and her hormone level stayed at its lowest point. She remains on monthly hormone checks and is doing well. The authors share the case to show that surgery plus drug therapy can succeed even in this rare form.
pmc-11618523:
Mohamed Abdeen, Mahmoud El-Dabah, and Ahmed Agwa propose a controller pairing to calm dangerous power oscillations in wind farms in this 2024 paper. The wobble, called sub-synchronous oscillation, arises when compensated lines interact with turbine generators, threatening grid stability. A gate-controlled capacitor is a standard damping device.

Earlier designs paired one standard controller with an added damper. The authors cascade a resonant controller with an integral one instead. Simulations on a benchmark grid model covered varied wind speeds, line compensation levels, and control cross-talk. The new pairing beat recent damping methods overall, especially at low wind and high compensation. The authors present it as a stronger shield for wind farms tied to compensated lines.
pmc-11618623:
Virus shape data for SARS-CoV-2 variants is shared by Tobias Hoffmann and co-authors in work dated 2024. Thin-cut microscopy can track how a virus's body shifts as it evolves. The team shot near nine hundred images of four variants, Alpha through Omicron BA.2. Two early isolates join the set for a straight compare. All grew in like cell cultures for fair shots.

Size and spike counts were measured by a past shared method. The image and count sets are open for reuse. They can feed shape-change reads on new variants. Auto image tools can also train on them.
pmc-11618923:
