Marisa Brizzi and five colleagues ask whether clever new drug mechanisms suffice for the hardest-to-treat HIV patients, in a review published in two thousand twenty-four. Heavily treatment-experienced patients have two or fewer fully active drug classes left. Integrase resistance is rising worldwide, shrinking options further.

The review covers identifying such patients, novel resistance mechanisms, and management in rich and poor settings alike. New antiretrovirals with fresh mechanisms and combination strategies are assessed. These patients face elevated risks of AIDS-defining events, so management errors are costly. The authors press the distinction between having new drugs and having enough fully active combinations. Protecting this small population also protects the wider epidemic response from resistant virus spread.
pmc-11620023:
Fadila Kouhen and co-authors report a rare breast lymphoma case in a 2024 paper. A forty-eight-year-old woman found a painless, fast-growing breast mass. Lymphoma starting in the breast is uncommon and easily mistaken.

Ultrasound and mammography showed extensive involvement of the breast. Tissue analysis revealed large, abnormal lymphoid cells in the sample. Standard combination chemotherapy began once the diagnosis was firm. Four cycles brought complete remission for the patient. The authors stress keeping lymphoma on the list for breast masses. Readers see a cancer that hides inside a common presentation.
pmc-11620723:
Jose Rafael Garcia, Felicitas Allende, Monica Kogan, and Jorge Chahla wrote a 2024 guide for surgeons on what to do when an operation goes wrong. Complications are an unavoidable part of surgery, and the response spans medicine, ethics, and law. The guide stresses fast, honest disclosure to the patient, close work with risk management, and careful records. It was written for orthopaedic surgeons, who lacked a roadmap for these events.

The guide also covers the toll on surgeons themselves, whose distress can spiral into poor coping and worse care. Support programs and a culture that favors learning over blame can blunt that harm. Readers get a step-by-step path for the hours and weeks after an adverse event, plus ways to care for the team as well as the patient.
pmc-11620823:
Adam Wright and co-workers present a data-driven method to segment pulsing brain vessels in functional MRI, in a 2024 paper. Functional scans hold rich fluid and vessel information, but vessel maps from other scan types misalign with them due to distortion. Their method works directly in functional scan space.

Large arteries and the brain's main venous sinus pulse with the heartbeat, giving them a distinct signal pattern the method exploits. Validation against hand-made ground truth in a local dataset went well. On a large ageing dataset with hundreds of participants and repeated scans, the segmentations were highly reproducible. The authors say the tool enables reliable fluid dynamics studies in these vessels.
pmc-11621123:
Xiangliang Tian and co-authors study how ceiling beams change the way fire smoke spreads through a tunnel. Beams along tunnel roofs are common in real projects, and hot smoke rising under them behaves in ways flat-ceiling models miss. Their 2024 paper varies beam height and spacing to see how the smoke's heat fades as it travels.

The team ran scale experiments alongside computer simulations of tunnel fires. Ceiling temperature rise and fall followed exponential patterns. Taller beams set closer together raised the peak ceiling temperature and made the heat fade faster along the tunnel. From the runs they built two forecast models, one for peak rise and one for the fade, and both matched experiments within about fifteen percent. The tools can guide smoke control and exhaust design in beamed tunnels.
pmc-11621223:
Liver cancer is often found late, and the standard blood marker misses many early cases. Zhao and co-authors review the search for better blood tests, spanning protein markers, DNA mutations, chemical marks on DNA, and several kinds of RNA. Much of the review focuses on cell-free DNA analysis, the technology for reading tumor traces in a blood draw.

They weigh why so many promising markers stall before clinic use: methods differ between labs, tumors vary between patients, and signals are faint early on. The authors map the technical and biological hurdles that, if cleared, would sharpen early detection and follow-up care for this deadly cancer.
pmc-11621323:
Sharon Berkowicz and co-authors study supercooled droplets of water mixed with a little glycerol, in work published in 2024. Water is thought to hide a transition between two liquid forms in its supercooled state. How that hidden behaviour affects water-based solutions was an open question with practical stakes for freezing biological samples.

The team cooled tiny droplets by fast evaporation and probed them with femtosecond X-ray pulses, reaching far below freezing without ice forming. Density fluctuations in the solution grew as it cooled. Computer simulations matched the trend and showed glycerol shifts the temperature of peak fluctuation downward compared with pure water. The findings clarify how pure water's odd behaviour carries into real solutions used in cryopreservation.
pmc-11621523:
Jiao Wang and Dandan Wang review mitophagy in cancers of the female reproductive system in this 2024 paper. Mitophagy is the cell's cleanup of worn-out mitochondria, the power plants inside cells. Done right, it keeps the cell healthy; done wrong, it feeds disease.

Faulty cleanup has been tied to brain disorders, heart disease, metabolic illness, and cancer. In gynecological cancers, the process shapes how tumors grow and how they resist drugs. The review sorts the signals that trigger mitophagy and the paths it takes. It then walks through recent findings in ovarian, cervical, and related cancers. The authors close on therapy: tuning this cleanup process might open new treatment routes, or rescue drugs that tumors have learned to resist. The paper maps a young field for researchers entering it.
pmc-11621623:
Jukka-Pekka Verta and co-authors wrote a 2024 paper on how one gene sets the timing of adulthood in Atlantic salmon. Some salmon mature early and others late, and a gene called vgll3 explains much of that split. Yet a single gene must act through many paths to change the whole body, and those paths were unclear.

The team read genes, proteins, and other molecules in salmon testes from both types. Fish with the early form of the gene switched on a wide set of signals tied to puberty. So a simple genetic difference fans out into a complex chain of effects. Work of this kind connects a DNA letter to a whole life path, a link that evolution studies and fish farming both care about.
pmc-11624123:
Lili Wu and a team of co-authors trace how uneven blood flow helps clog arteries. Their study is from two thousand twenty-four. Where flow is disturbed, the cells lining the vessel wall change, and plaque can build up. A force sensor in those cells, called Piezo1, sits near the start of the chain they found.

When flow disturbed the cells, a protein called KDM5B rose in them. Piezo1 switched on two signals that raised KDM5B in turn. KDM5B then stripped marks that keep genes active. Silencing KDM5B or Piezo1 blocked these steps in lab cells. In mice bred to have high cholesterol, removing KDM5B from vessel cells cut plaque build-up. The chain offers new targets to prevent clogged arteries.
pmc-11624223:
Raymond Nicks and co-authors measure brain cell loss in a brain disease tied to repeated head hits, in work from twenty twenty-four. The disease, chronic traumatic encephalopathy, shows a key protein clump deep in the folds of the brain. Hard numbers on cell loss by brain region had not been reported.

The team studied brain tissue from contact sport athletes and from non athlete controls. Cortex was thinner and nerve cells were fewer deep in the folds in the disease group. Years of play linked strongly to both thinning and cell loss in that zone. Part of the cell loss ran through the protein clumps, while thinning mostly did not. The work pins the worst damage to the fold depths.
pmc-11624823:
Elizabeth McLellan and four colleagues audited melatonin prescribing for children in the North East of England, in a 2024 paper. Melatonin helps many children sleep, yet the best dose and timing remain unclear and products vary widely. The team reviewed national and regional data plus one year of prescriptions at a large children's hospital.

The audit covered 220 patients under eighteen who received the drug for poor sleep. Local guidance asks for behavior-based help first, fixed timing, licensed products, and follow-up review. No standard was fully met. Only nine percent had tried a behavioral approach first, and other sleep disorders were rarely considered. Off-license liquid forms drove much of the cost. The findings led to a hospital-wide sleep education program. The authors also call for better access to behavioral sleep help.
pmc-11625123:
Francesca Arfuso and co-authors track blood protein patterns in newborn lambs and goat kids across their first month, in work from 2024. Protein shares in blood shift fast after birth, above all once the first milk is taken in. Those shifts mirror the young animal's immune state.

Ten lambs and ten kids were sampled from minutes after birth, then after first milk and weekly for four weeks. Total protein, the main protein, and three globulin groups all moved with time in both species. Two globulin groups ran higher in kids than lambs at several points. The authors read the patterns as signs of normal immune build-up, useful as baselines for spotting sick newborn stock.
pmc-11625223:
Elahe Alivaisi and co-authors clash, in a 2024 study, a drug and two drill forms on a muscle RNA mark in diabetic rats. The mark, miR-133a, tracks with muscle insulin fight. Sick rats held more of it than sound ones. Hard burst drills and fair pace drills each cut the mark, alone or with the drug metformin. The pair of hard drills plus drug cut it most of all, past each part alone. A learn tool, CatBoost, then built a call model for the mark from body traits: weight, blood sugar, insulin, and fat marks.

The call model hit its marks in a tight way. The team casts the drug-plus-drill pair as a care path, with the RNA as a guide mark for tuned care.
pmc-11625823:
Haifeng Jiao and seven co-authors show that blood guard cells pack alarm signals into tiny parcels that home to sore spots, in a 2024 journal article. The signals, called cytokines, must pile up where harm is, yet blood flow spreads them thin. How a local heap forms was unclear.

When guard cells met a germ toxin, they shed many parcels called migrasomes, stuffed with two lead alarm signals. The signals ride carrier pods into the parcels and are freed at once or when a parcel breaks off. The team fished such parcels from the blood of dosed mice and found a large share of the total signal rode in them. In the body the parcels pile fast at sore sites. The authors name a new route for signal delivery.
pmc-11626723:
William Schnapp and co-authors follow patients treated with nerve burning for lasting low back pain, in work from 2024. The nerve serves the caps of the spine bones, and in patients with a certain wear pattern it can carry pain signals. Burning it is a small procedure meant to cut that signal.

Thirty-five patients were treated at one clinic, and thirty-one finished all surveys through twelve months. Scores for disability, pain, and body and mind health all improved in ways that count in daily life. About two thirds beat the key disability gain mark, and over three quarters beat the pain gain mark. The authors note there was no control group, and results match prior trials.
pmc-11626823:
Luhui Zhang and a large team of co-authors sequence and model the salt-loving bacterium Halomonas bluephagenesis to supercharge its plastic production, in a two thousand twenty-four systems biology paper. The microbe is a candidate industrial workhorse for bioplastics.

The team produced a complete annotated genome, built a genome-scale metabolic network matching experimental phenotype data at about eighty-six percent, and made it browsable interactively. Network analysis showed biomass, plastic, and several byproducts compete for the same resources. A new analysis framework predicted nutrient effects, guiding staged feeding strategies. Fermentation reached a cell dry weight of one hundred point four grams per liter with seventy percent plastic content, surpassing previous benchmarks.
pmc-11627223:
So Jin Lee and Jung Yoon Kim mine text in 2024 to learn how South Korean media and online groups portray male hormone levels and prostate health. Public views on these topics shape how men seek care.

Three years of news and community posts from three major platforms were gathered with a keyword search on male hormone levels. News first drew attention with celebrity and event angles. Talk of prostate enlargement, by contrast, leaned on treatments and medical facts. Community threads then reworked news topics through personal stories and opinions. Those threads leaned more toward sexual problems than prostate issues, which shows the two spaces shape views in different ways.
pmc-11628523:
Yu and nine co-authors present a case report from twenty twenty-four on a cervical cancer that vanished on a dual immune drug. Spread cervical cancer has poor survival, at ten to twenty percent over five years. The patient had stage four disease with markers for two drug targets. She received a bispecific drug that blocks two immune brakes at once. Scans showed a complete response that held for ten months. Even a spread site lacking one marker cleared fully.

When care later switched to a single-brake drug, the disease surged back fast. The contrast hints that dual blockade hits harder than single blockade. The authors back the dual drug as a promising option for spread cases. They also flag the second marker as a possible guide for its use.
pmc-11628723:
A difficult airway can turn routine anesthesia dangerous, and the usual bedside checks predict it poorly. Claudia Rodiera and co-authors tested whether the voice itself carries warning signs. In a multicenter study they enrolled 438 surgical patients and kept 313 after exclusions. Each person recorded the vowels A, E, I, O, and U in normal, flexed, and extended neck positions. They combined the voice recordings with clinical features and standard airway tests, then trained machine learning models against the Cormack grade seen at intubation.

The best models used clear-cut cases, easy grade I versus hard grade IV airways. One model, mixing demographics with the vowel A and voice harmonics, reached an AUC of 0.91. A second, using the vowel O plus shimmer and jitter, reached 0.90. Models that tried to separate all four grades did worse. The authors present voice analysis as a promising preoperative screen.
pmc-11629023:
Five researchers test two pump blockers against drug-resistant Pseudomonas in a paper from 2024. The bacterium resists aminoglycoside antibiotics by pumping them out. One hundred hospital isolates were profiled for drug response and pump gene activity. Forty-five percent overproduced the pump gene mexY. Two blockers, a synthetic compound and curcumin from turmeric, were then paired with the antibiotics.

Both pairings lowered the drug levels needed to stop growth. Curcumin helped against every resistant isolate for several drugs. The strongest combined effect appeared with one antibiotic, the weakest with another. The authors back curcumin as a helper that could revive old antibiotics. Clinical use would need safety and dosing studies first.
pmc-11629523:
Lanxiang Tian and six co-authors warn of a quiet risk for crews bound for the Moon and Mars: the near loss of Earth's magnetic field. Deep space and both worlds offer fields far weaker than home. Their 2024 review gathers animal and human clues on what such weak fields do to bodies.

Lab work links weak fields to harm in breeding, growth, body clocks, hearts, and brains. Young born under weak fields died more in some species, and offspring grew with flaws in others. Clock genes dimmed, and heart rates shifted. Direct human data are thin, the authors grant. Still, they urge planners to count weak fields beside radiation and low gravity. Shield ideas and more studies are their call.
pmc-11630723:
Qi Zheng and co-authors test whether gut and skin microbes causally affect scabies, the itchy mite infestation, in a 2024 genetics study. Earlier work hinted that body flora shapes who gets scabies, but correlation alone cannot prove direction. The team used Mendelian randomization, which leans on inherited variants as natural experiments, with flora data from two large studies and scabies data from the FinnGen database.

Five analysis methods plus sensitivity checks backed the findings. Thirteen gut microbes and seven skin microbes showed causal effects on scabies risk, matching what observational studies had suggested. The authors say the results support developing probiotic approaches to prevent or treat the infestation.
pmc-11630923:
Mingyang Li, Ling Ding, Qilong Nie, and Zeping Jiang report in 2024 the case of a 22-year-old man with a rare benign growth in the lining of his knee. The condition, lipoma arborescens, grows fatty fronds inside a joint and usually strikes middle-aged people, most often in the knee. In a young adult it is unusual and can mislead doctors.

The man came in with sudden knee swelling and pain after a minor sprain, and the signs grew worse over days. A first check gave no clear answer. Magnetic scans hinted at a torn cushion inside the knee plus the fatty growth, with fluid in the joint. Surgery through a small scope confirmed the growth and trimmed both it and the torn tissue. Tissue tests backed the diagnosis. Follow-up scans showed no regrowth, and knee function improved a lot.
pmc-11631023:
Vehbi Sirikci, Cem Onur Kirac, and Huseyin Avni Findikli track blood sugar control in diabetes patients across the COVID-19 lockdown years, in a 2024 paper. Whether lockdown harmed control was unclear, and older patients faced special risks. The team followed more than twelve hundred patients with measures in each of three one-year periods.

Results split by age. In patients over sixty-five, the long-term sugar marker rose during lockdown, most sharply in the seventy-five to eighty-five group. In younger patients it fell instead. Patients over eighty-five showed no change. The authors urge close monitoring of elderly patients during lockdowns, with home care, remote visits, and structured diet and exercise support.
pmc-11631123:
Nobukazu Fujimoto and co-authors track real-world safety of an immune drug in a rare chest cancer in a 2024 study. The drug, nivolumab, treats malignant pleural mesothelioma after first chemo fails. Regulators in Japan required a post-marketing watch on everyday patients.

The watch enrolled 124 patients at forty-eight sites from 2018 to 2021, with six months of follow-up. About forty percent had treatment-related side effects, and about thirteen percent had severe ones. Lung inflammation was the most common severe effect. The pattern matched the earlier phase two trial, with no new safety signals. Side effects ran higher in inpatients and in patients with autoimmune disease or higher body weight. About a third of patients stayed on therapy at six months.
pmc-11631223:
Alexandra Johns and seven co-authors explored whether blocking a certain cell receptor can protect motor neurons, using human stem-cell-grown neurons, in this 2024 study. The receptor, P2X7, responds to ATP, a molecule that floods out of injured tissue. Its role on motor neurons themselves, rather than on immune cells, had not been a focus.

The team showed the receptor sits on human motor neurons and works there. Bathing the neurons in ATP killed them through this receptor, in step with the dose. A specific blocker shielded the neurons from that death. The authors argue the receptor is a fresh drug target for diseases where motor neurons die, separate from its known part in inflammation.
pmc-11631423:
Mélibée Morel and co-authors compare how young and adult gulls forage at their first migratory stopover. Leaving the nest is the deadliest stretch of a young bird's life. Twenty juvenile lesser black-backed gulls wore GPS trackers for twenty days. Thirty-eight seasoned adults supply the comparison set.

Juveniles roamed less and spent more time feeding than adults. Both age groups kept steady personal spaces across days. Adults shrank their ranges and cut flight time as days passed. Their travel distances fell while feeding time grew, a clear learning curve. Juveniles showed no such spatial learning in the window watched.
pmc-11631523:
Faris Rustom and co-authors train neural networks to spot brain tumors in a study from 2024. The networks, called CNNs, learn from images and mimic some traits of the visual brain. A handy trait is transfer learning: skills from one task can seed another.

The team added an odd step: first, the network learned to find camouflaged animals. Then it trained on MRI scans of glioma tumors and healthy brains. Both contrast-enhanced and plain scan types were used. The camouflage step improved tumor classification in their tests. The trick hints that hunting hidden shapes in nature preps a network for hidden shapes in scans. Public scan data made the study possible.
pmc-11631823:
Jorge Curiel-Esparza and four co-authors present a decision method from 2024 for restoring wetlands. Their test case is the Tablas de Daimiel National Park in central Spain, where dry wetlands need a new water supply. Picking a source means weighing social, green, and cost concerns at the same time.

The method scores each option against a long list of drivers, from energy use and land cost to public support. Experts rank the drivers step by step, and the scores combine into one clear index. In the test, water moved from another river basin ranked first, with well pumping and treated wastewater close behind. The authors offer the method as a clear, traceable tool for policy choices.
pmc-11632423:
Herlihy and co-authors report how three independent labs fared when adopting a fast genetic test panel for lung cancer, in a 2024 evaluation. Many patients miss targeted drugs because biomarker testing is slow, costly, or starved of tissue. The ASPYRE-Lung panel reads DNA and RNA together and checks 114 actionable variants across 11 genes from small samples. Seventy-seven patient samples were run across the three sites and compared with standard methods.

Results agreed across sites, operators, and sample types, including scant cytology specimens. The authors argue the panel's speed and low input needs can close testing gaps that keep patients from matched therapies.
pmc-11632523:
Zhen-Tao Fei and co-authors measure how often tuberculous meningitis damages the eye nerves, in a 2024 study. The infection inflames the brain lining and can crush or starve the optic nerve. Records covered 250 patients treated in Shanghai from 2013 to 2022.

Seventeen patients, just under seven percent, developed optic nerve palsy. Those patients showed higher pressure inside the skull, more protein in spinal fluid, and more tumour-like lumps on scans. Pressure, one immune cell share, and lumps each predicted the complication. One antibiotic aided recovery from the palsy. The authors urge close eye checks for high-risk patients and further study of that drug's promise in this setting.
pmc-11632923:
Nadin Hannoon, Basel El-Khodary, and Zhongming Zhang study how war-worn pasts shape a mind ill of fixed rites in the Gaza Strip. Their study, from two thousand twenty-four, splits the tie three ways.

Past work hints the rite ill ties to hurt pasts, in depth of signs and in twin ills. Gaza, a land of long strife, lacks such reads. Just past one hundred patients with the ill took part, all grown folk. Talks and self-scores were used. The team parts three grades: those once bared to hurt; those who hold their ill as hurt-born; and those whose ill began in the half year past a hurt. Each grade is weighed for its stamp on the ill.
pmc-11634623:
Utpal Dhar and four co-authors published a biomechanics study in twenty twenty-four comparing three ways to fix a severely slipped lower spine vertebra. High-grade spondylolisthesis at the L5-S1 junction is usually fused, but how the hardware is arranged affects stiffness and stress. Clinical data comparing options are thin, so the team modeled them.

A finite element spine built from a patient's CT scan was modified to create the slip. An interbody cage was then paired with an anterior plate, bilateral pedicle screws, or transdiscal screws in turn. The simulations measured motion, stress on implants and neighboring discs, and resistance to further slipping. The comparison gives surgeons mechanical evidence for a choice usually made by habit.
pmc-11635023:
Sylvie Hermouet and co-authors study smoldering multiple myeloma in a 2024 paper. The illness sits between a mild blood state and full myeloma, a cancer of plasma cells. These cells make one copied antibody in large amounts. In kindred illnesses, that antibody often aims at a germ or at a body fat, which hints at what first woke the cells up.

The team checked what the antibody targets in 182 people found by a screening study in Iceland between 2016 and 2022. They compared patient traits by target type. They also looked at whether care that cuts the target, such as treating a stomach germ, can help. The work links first triggers to how each case may act.
pmc-11635423:
Ruishu Jiang and Youlian Lai test two blood proteins as warning signs after stroke in this 2025 paper. The proteins, neuron-specific enolase and S100-beta, leak from injured brain cells. The team followed 286 patients with blocked-artery strokes. Blood was drawn on arrival and again at one and two days.

Patients whose condition worsened early carried higher levels of both proteins. So did patients with poor recovery at three months. The first protein, measured on arrival, predicted early worsening on its own. Both markers helped predict the three-month outcome. The authors suggest that watching these levels could flag patients who need closer care in the first days after a stroke.
pmc-11635523:
Martina Petráková and a team of co-authors test new coatings for iron implants that the body slowly absorbs, in a study published in twenty twenty-four. Iron is strong, but it breaks down too slowly inside the body and does little to help tissue. The team added layers that speed decay and can also fight germs.

One layer was a calcium phosphate coat, with the antibiotic gentamicin mixed into some samples. A soft plastic-like coat went on top of some pieces, making a two-layer cover. In soak and electric tests, the two-layer coat sped up decay, while the ceramic coat alone slowed it. The drug-bearing coats decayed a bit faster than plain ones. Early cell tests looked promising for safety.
pmc-11638323:
Nicole Warrington, Geng Wang, and Tom Bond wrote a 2024 commentary disputing a claim that low birthweight itself causes later heart disease. The claim came from a genetic study suggesting babies born lighter face higher coronary risk as adults. The trio argue the link more likely reflects shared genes that sway both traits at once.

Birthweight, they say, is a rough marker of how development went in the womb, not a lever on future health. If it were a true cause, nearly every factor that lowers birthweight would raise heart risk, which does not hold. The piece is a caution on reading cause into genetic correlations.
pmc-11639823:
Tadele Kabeta and seven colleagues survey Ethiopian poultry farmers about three intertwined health threats, in a study published in two thousand twenty-four. Salmonella, feed mycotoxins, and weak biosecurity reinforce each other on small farms. Farmer awareness is the first line of defense.

Thirty-eight farmers around Jimma answered questionnaires and received biosecurity scoring. Over two-thirds did not know salmonellosis harms both birds and people. Nearly four-fifths had limited grasp of its production and economic damage. Practical hygiene knowledge was similarly thin. Poultry underpin food security and income in Ethiopia, so awareness gaps translate directly into losses and human illness. The findings argue for farmer education built around the connections between risks.
pmc-11639923:
Luisa Amato and co-authors test a new drug pairing against lung cancers that resist targeted therapy. Their study appeared in 2024. The cancers carry changes in one of two genes, EGFR or KRAS, and are treated with drugs aimed at those genes. Over time, resistant cells that no longer depend on the gene take over. The team instead attacked support systems the tumor needs, a tactic called non-oncogene addiction.

They paired a drug that blocks DNA damage repair with one that blocks cell energy use. Cell lines included both drug-sensitive and drug-resistant forms. The pairing was tested alongside the standard targeted drugs. The aim is to hit the tumor's backup systems so resistant clones cannot grow out. The authors present the pairing as a fresh route for cancers that have run out of targeted options.
pmc-11640223:
Nunzia Colonna Romano and co-authors study brain development in fruit flies that lack a working clock gene. Their 2024 study uses a null mutant of the period gene, a core part of the daily clock. The clock's role in the adult brain is well mapped, but its role while the brain grows was less clear.

In larvae, absence of the gene raised DNA damage in the central nervous system. Dividing precursor cells showed broken strands and chromosome flaws. Reactive oxygen proved to drive the damage, and restoring the gene in support cells alone blocked it. Loss of the gene also left DNA packing looser, which added to the harm. The authors link clock function to genome guard duty in youth.
pmc-11640323:
Sara D'Arcangelo and co-authors test in 2024 whether almond hulls, a farm waste product, can fight harmful bacteria. Food waste piles up worldwide, and finding value in it cuts both waste and the need for new chemicals. The hulls are rich in plant compounds, above all polyphenols. The team extracted them with an ultrasound method tuned to be gentle on the environment.

The extract was checked against two bacteria that trouble food safety, in both free-floating and biofilm forms. It slowed and killed the free cells of both strains. It also blocked the bacteria from sticking to surfaces and helped strip away mature biofilms, the slimy layers that shield germs. Tests on normal human skin cells showed no toxicity. The authors present the extract as a sustainable antimicrobial drawn from waste, with promise for food protection.
pmc-11640423:
Suyeon Kim and co-authors look for warning signs of liver failure after surgery for Klatskin tumors, cancers at the junction of the liver's bile ducts. Removing half the liver is the main treatment, but the remnant sometimes fails, with grim consequences. The team reviewed thirty-four patients operated on at two Korean hospitals and tested demographic, laboratory, and volumetric measures as predictors.

Three signals stood out. High blood sugar before surgery raised the risk, as did a low ratio of future liver remnant volume to spleen volume. A high bilirubin level on the first day after surgery also flagged coming failure. Each of the three discriminated reasonably well on its own, with accuracy measures near 0.78. The authors recommend tightening glucose control before surgery, checking the remnant-to-spleen ratio during planning, and watching day-one bilirubin closely afterward.
pmc-11640523:
Fabiano Flauto and a large team review mitotane, a targeted therapy for adrenocortical carcinoma, in work from 2024. These adrenal cortex cancers are rare, aggressive and poorly understood, with a poor outlook. Mitotane is the sole approved drug for advanced disease and is used more often after surgery as well.

The drug attacks the adrenal cortex and disrupts steroid production. It also affects cytochrome P450 enzymes, depolarizes mitochondrial membranes and lets free cholesterol build up until cells die. Many patients still progress over time, so the review covers predictors of response and routes to primary and acquired resistance. Readers get a full account of how the drug works and fails.
pmc-11640623:
Martina Cotena and ten co-authors test an AI tool for aortic dissection detection on chest CT scans, in a multi-reader study from 2024. Fast detection of this life-threatening tear can save lives. Three expert readers each read the same scans twice, once unaided and once with AI help after a one-month gap, while two other experts set the truth.

With AI, the time from scan to assessment for true cases fell by about two thirds. Reading time per case also fell in a clear way. The tool works by flagging and ranking urgent cases ahead of the standard first-in, first-out queue. The authors present AI support as a way to speed radiology work without changing who makes the call.
pmc-11640723:
Charlotte Klein and co-authors test what happens when skin cells lose parts of their inner scaffold, in a 2024 study. The scaffold, built from filament proteins, holds cell shape and supports daily tissue balance. Its flaws are poorly grasped at the cell level. The team quieted three scaffold genes in mouth skin cells at unlike stages of change, some pre-treated with alcohol.

Loss of any of the three slowed growth shifts and altered the packing of genetic material. A nuclear guard protein and a skin maturity marker also fell. Quieting that marker in turn cut scaffold levels, hinting at a two-way link. The authors say targeted scaffold loss is a sharp tool for probing tissue health.
pmc-11640823:
Kitaru Suzuki and co-authors test whether crystal orientation in a bone like ceramic changes bone cell growth, in a 2024 paper. The ceramic, hydroxyapatite, matches the main mineral in bone and tooth enamel and is used in artificial bone. The team made ceramics with a preferred crystal face exposed by a templated growth method.

Bone forming cells grown on the oriented ceramic showed higher early bone marker activity than cells on standard ceramic. Protein patterns also differed between the two surfaces. The results suggest the exposed crystal face aids early bone differentiation. Tuning crystal structure could thus yield stronger artificial bone materials.
pmc-11641323:
Marija Petrovic and co-authors build tiny drug pairs to wake the immune system inside a harsh brain cancer. The cancer seeds the zone with white cells stuck in a tame mode that shields the tumor. Tumor sacs carry a small gene script that blocks an alarm path in those cells. Their 2024 study pairs a blocker of that script with an alarm trigger, each packed in small spheres.

Packed pairs shrink and hold steady across acid and heat ranges found in the body. Lab tests show a tight grip on a blood protein that ferries iron, a hint the pairs may cross into the brain. The alarm trigger flips white cells from tame mode to attack mode. Used as a pair, the two lift attack marks more than each alone, the team reports.
pmc-11641623:
Ben Singh and three co-authors review how long it takes for a healthy habit to form. Their review appeared in twenty twenty-four. Lasting change in diet, movement, or daily care depends on habits becoming automatic, yet the time that takes was poorly pinned down.

The team searched six databases for trials that tracked habit scores or time to automatic action. Twenty studies with about twenty-six hundred people qualified. The habits ranged from exercise and healthy eating to flossing and drinking water. Four studies gave times: half of people formed a habit in about two months, while averages ran past three months. Times varied widely between people. Habit scores did rise from start to end across the trials.
pmc-11641823:
Ebony Hargrove-Wiley and co-authors compare, in a 2024 study, breast tumors in male and female mice to expose sex-specific immune patterns. Breast cancer is seen as a women's disease, yet men who get it die at higher rates, and the immune surroundings of a tumor help decide its course.

Using single-cell gene reading, tissue staining, and cell counting in a transgenic model, the team found male tumors carried more estrogen receptor and fewer invading white cells overall. Yet the male immune mix was more attack-ready, in both the main tumor and lung spread sites. Despite that friendlier profile, males carried more spread, a paradox the authors probe.
pmc-11641923:
Bogdan Cylwik and co-authors tested whether a blood protein can flag how severe a COVID-19 case will get, in a 2024 study. The protein, hyaluronic acid, builds tissue scaffolding and rises when tissue is inflamed or harmed. The team measured it in eighty-seven patients and forty-five healthy controls. They then tracked how levels lined up with illness severity, oxygen needs, and survival.

Levels ran far higher in patients than in controls, and higher still in critical cases than in moderate ones. Patients on ventilators, those given steroids or immune therapy, and those hit by a cytokine storm all showed higher levels. Non-survivors carried more of the protein than survivors. As a test, it sorted critical illness and death risk with excellent accuracy. The authors propose it as an early warning marker for COVID-19 care.
pmc-11642123:
Reshef and co-authors test whether a few seconds of heart rhythm data can predict how heart attack patients will fare. The study covers 183 patients admitted with a non-ST-elevation heart attack at one Israeli hospital in 2014. From their electrocardiograms, the team computed ultra-short heart rate variability measures, which reflect how flexibly the heart adjusts beat to beat. They then checked which factors predicted complications in hospital and death over two years.

Nineteen percent of patients died within two years, and lower variability was clearly tied to that higher risk. The same measures showed weaker links to death at 90 days and one year. In a surprise twist, higher variability was tied to a greater risk of dangerous ventricular rhythms in hospital. The authors back the standard reading — low variability warns of danger — and call for larger prospective work to firm up both signals.
pmc-11642223:
Kishen Mitra and co-authors survey, in twenty twenty-four, user opinions of compression products for two conditions that cause fainting and dizziness on standing. In one, heart rate spikes on standing. In the other, blood pressure falls due to nerve damage. Compression garments squeeze the legs or belly to reduce blood pooling and raise cardiac output. The team surveyed people diagnosed with either condition. Most respondents were women, with a mean age near thirty-eight. Nearly all had tried at least one garment since diagnosis.

Leg compression was the most used type, ahead of shapewear and belly compression. Two thirds had tried multiple product types. Participants rated their most used garment on comfort, looks, ease of use, durability, cost value, effect, and consistency.
pmc-11642323:
Ewa Maria Kratz and co-authors hunt for a blood mark that separates two look-alike joint diseases. Psoriatic arthritis and rheumatoid arthritis can be hard to tell apart, and both are autoimmune. The team measured levels of one protein, clusterin, and charted its sugar coatings in 37 patients with the first disease, 34 with the second, and 21 healthy controls.

Clusterin ran higher in the psoriatic group. One sugar form — sialic acid attached in the 2,6 position — was raised in both diseases over controls, most visibly in the psoriatic group. Two fucose coatings thinned as clusterin rose. The authors propose the combined pattern as a panel that tells the diseases apart.
pmc-11642423:
Augusta Ivaškė and co-authors test whether bacteria inside self-healing concrete survive cold climates in a 2024 study. The concrete repairs its own cracks when embedded bacteria wake and deposit mineral. Freezing and thawing can burst bacterial cells, which threatens the whole idea in northern regions.

Bacterial spores were packed inside expanded clay grains within the concrete. Cold snaps and freeze-thaw cycles killed about half the viable spores, yet enough survived to matter. Curing under water backfired, since it woke spores early and cut counts nearly tenfold. Crack healing also depended on the conditions during incubation. The authors conclude the material can work in cold areas if curing and spore protection are handled with care.
pmc-11642823:
Aina Manzano-Torra and co-authors use virtual reality to preview the psychological shock of losing a leg. Many amputees develop anxiety, depression, or post-traumatic stress, but studying that reaction before it happens is impossible in real life. Their 2024 study embodies healthy participants in a virtual body with a right lower-limb amputation, and compares the experience with a whole-body avatar.

Participants first rated how much they appreciate their own bodies, then wore each avatar in turn, rating anxiety after each. Anxiety ran significantly higher in the amputated body. Across both bodies, lower body appreciation went with higher anxiety, suggesting that people who already feel worse about their bodies suffer a sharper jolt from the virtual loss. The authors propose such simulations as a safe way to study, and perhaps one day soften, the mental blow of amputation.
pmc-11643423:
Kinga Kostrakiewicz-Gieralt surveys patents for plant-based meat in this 2024 paper. Fake meats answer worries about farm harm, animal pain, and health, and inventors have rushed to patent new recipes. The survey covers grants from a recent decade across three patent banks.

Close to two hundred patents were found, with a surge in the early years of this decade. Most came from United States teams, and one large food firm led the filers. Inventors named close to two hundred plant types as sources of protein, fat, fiber, and more. Many named plants are edible and rich yet little used. The author urges work on those neglected sources.
pmc-11643623:
Paweł Pieśko, Jarosław Korpysa, and Magdalena Zawada-Michałowska test deep cold cures for fast-cut steel in a 2024 study. The cure cools a part in steps to deep cold, holds it, then warms it back in steps. Its aim is to turn a soft left phase in the steel into a hard phase.

Less of that soft phase should mean more hardness, shock strength, and wear life. The team set cured and plain steel side by side on those three traits. Cut tests with drills add a shop-floor check of the gains.
pmc-11643823:
Lei Cao and co-authors model how slabs made of a tough cement mix and strong steel-strand mesh bend under load. Their 2024 study pairs computer simulation with a theory model. The aim is to learn how these paired materials behave under bending stress.

The simulation tracks damage in tension and compression, plus slip where steel meets cement. The theory model predicts load capacity from mesh share, slab size, and material traits. More mesh sharply raises stiffness and load capacity while cutting sag. Simulation, theory, and lab tests line up closely. The authors offer the models as a guide for slabs that must bend well without failing.
pmc-11643923:
Ilma Nugrahani and colleagues made a new salt form of piperine in 2024. Piperine is a natural compound from pepper plants. It fights inflammation but dissolves poorly in water. Poor dissolving limits its use as a medicine. Past work improved it through paired crystal forms. Salt forms had drawn far less study. The team reacted piperine with an organic acid. Heat, light, and X-ray tools checked the new solid. A single crystal study revealed its final structure. Wet grinding could reproduce the salt reliably.

Tests confirmed a true salt with ordered crystal packing. The salt dissolved better than plain piperine. Its stability also improved in storage tests. Animal tests showed stronger anti-inflammatory effects. The authors see development promise in the new form. Better dissolving could raise the compound's usefulness. The work extends salt design to plant compounds. Later studies can tune dose and safety, they imply.
pmc-11644223:
Teresina Laragione, Carolyn Harris, and Pércio Gulko test whether extra magnesium in the diet changes gene activity in mice with arthritis. Their earlier work had shown that the mineral eased joint damage in this mouse model of rheumatoid arthritis. Here they fed one group a high-magnesium diet and another a normal diet, then read out gene activity in spleen and joint tissue after fifteen days of induced arthritis.

Many genes differed between the two groups. The changed genes clustered in pathways tied to cell stress, cell aging, and the wear that drives joint disease. A few genes stood out for how strongly their activity rose or fell with the mineral. Spleen tissue showed changes in pathways for vitamin handling and protein folding help. The authors say the results back magnesium as a possible add-on therapy for arthritis and like diseases.
pmc-11644323:
Maja Mikulic-Petkovsek, Eva Ravnjak, and Denis Rusjan study health-linked compounds in two invasive plants, in a 2024 paper. Staghorn sumac and Himalayan balsam spread fast and harm local nature. The team ask how the choice of solvent and the length of soaking change how many phenolic compounds can be pulled from each plant.

Alcohol pulled far more of most compound groups from balsam than water did, and one pigment group appeared only in alcohol. For sumac, water beat alcohol for several groups. Time mattered too: sumac gains rose more than threefold over eighty-four hours, while balsam gains fell. Both extracts cut ryegrass seed sprouting and slowed root and shoot growth. The authors suggest using such invasive plants for their chemicals could help control their spread and cut management costs.
pmc-11644423:
Xiaowei Zhuang and co-authors turned bamboo waste into a light, porous molding material in a 2024 study, then tested how drying choices shape the result. Bamboo grows fast and leaves heaps of residue. Their method grinds the fibers in hot water, waking the plant's own glues so no added binder is needed.

Pressing out water and then drying in two steps kept costs low. Freeze-drying gave the lightest foam, while oven drying gave the strongest blocks, with solid crush and pull strength. The team explains the self-gluing through fiber grip, chemical linking, and heat and water softening. The material is a rebuild of the bamboo cell wall and can be recycled again. They point to uses in building, packing, and furnishings.
pmc-11644523:
Jingjing Geng and co-authors test whether two small organic acids can help persimmon rootstock cuttings grow roots, published in 2024. Organic acids occur naturally in plants and aid development. The team asked whether malic acid and tartaric acid could boost adventitious root formation in cuttings of Diospyros lotus, used as a rootstock.

After treatment at a set dose, both the rooting rate and the survival rate rose notably. Cuttings also grew more side roots. Tissue study showed the acids enhanced the formation of root primordia, the early root structures. Sugar and starch stores fell early on, while a key growth hormone peaked higher than in controls. A second hormone moved the other way. The authors present the acids as an alternative rooting aid.
pmc-11644623:
Hee-Yeon Kwon and co-authors test a fermented noni fruit extract in testis cells in a 2024 study. Aging men often lose testosterone, a state that harms body, mood, and sexual health. Hormone therapy has side effects, so natural options draw interest.

Two cell lines stand in for the testis cells that make testosterone and support sperm. Hydrogen peroxide first damaged the cells, cutting viability and hormone output. The extract then restored testosterone output and the proteins that build it. It also lowered enzymes that break testosterone down. In the support cells, it revived hormone receptors. The authors see promise, while noting cell results are an early step.
pmc-11644723:
Basil Mohammed Al-Hadithi and co-authors published a study in 2024 on the overcurrent capabilities of insulated gate bipolar transistors in resonant circuits. These transistors are the power switches widely used in electric vehicles and photovoltaic systems. Correct switching keeps the transistors within safe limits; beyond them, they can be destroyed.

The team built a double resonant transformer that produces very high currents. A full bridge of resonant transistors then switched those currents, with feedback control from two current sensors. The aim was to demonstrate that the transistors can exceed their maximum permissible peak current inside a resonant system. In the tests, currents exceeded the transistor's peak rating by a large margin, about 170 percent, without problems. That means resonant circuits can be designed with transistors rated below the circuit's own peak current. The authors note that this reduces both circuit cost and switching losses, bringing the losses close to zero.
pmc-11644923:
Big roundabouts tangle traffic in complex ways, and testing fixes on real roads is slow and risky. Xiao Liang and co-authors build a three-stage computer model of roundabout driving in this 2024 paper, splitting each trip into entering, following, and exiting, based on watching real drivers.

Simulations showed delays and risky encounters clustered at middling traffic levels. Of four fix ideas tested, letting drivers pick paths by how full each road looked worked best, lifting flow and cutting delays and risky events. Space-based fixes helped local spots. The findings can pair with in-car sensors that warn drivers in real time.
pmc-11645023:
Ze-Yu Wang, Ji Young Cho, and Yi-Kyung Hong study how indoor design affects focus and creativity in a 2024 paper. Brain wave recordings can reveal responses that surveys miss, yet few studies have used them on classroom design. The team tested many design elements at once, rather than one at a time.

Twenty people viewed nineteen images that combined room shape, furniture layout, ceiling height, and color, plus special scenes such as a window wall facing nature. Eight channels of brain data gave a concentration index and a creativity linked measure. Participants also picked the scenes where they felt most focused or creative. Brain responses were stronger in the back regions of the head than in the front. The results compare measured and self reported responses.
pmc-11645723:
Xiaoyu Tu and five co-authors compare residency training results by degree level in China, in a 2024 cohort study. The study follows graduates of a standard residency program in women's and birth medicine. Graduates held one of three degrees: a bachelor's, a master's, or a doctorate in medicine. The team compared exam scores, yearly marks, and pass rates across the three groups. A total of three hundred ninety-seven graduates were included.

Doctorate holders were older and trained for less time than the other groups. Their final results were much the same overall, though bachelor's holders scored lowest on the written test. No trait the team tracked predicted who passed the final exam. Extra checks on doctorate holders with short training showed no gaps. The authors say training quality was good across groups, with extra written support wise for bachelor's holders.
pmc-11646123:
Aishwarya G Jacob and seven co-authors show how one splicing protein pushes lab-grown blood vessel muscle toward its grown-up, contractile self, in this 2024 study. Vessel smooth muscle cells earn their keep by squeezing, and that identity is written partly in which gene versions they splice. A protein called RBPMS drives the mature splicing pattern in rat cells; its role in human cells was the open question.

Their platform was smooth muscle grown from human embryonic stem cells, stuck young with low RBPMS. Forcing RBPMS up flipped the splicing of contractile genes to the adult pattern. Evidence says it works by binding RNA directly and by teaming with a second splicing factor, RBFOX2, on many shared targets. Treated cells also behaved older: their movement and division shifted toward the settled contractile style. Splicing, it seems, is a lever on cell identity.
pmc-11646923:
Myotonic dystrophy type 1 is the most common form of muscular dystrophy in adults, caused by a repeated stretch of DNA in one gene. Gianluca Pagnoni and co-authors present a case from 2024 in which the disease came paired with metabolic syndrome, the cluster of insulin resistance and blood fat problems. Muscle weakness leads to a sedentary life, which makes that pairing more likely.

The patient could not tolerate the standard statin drugs, so the team turned to a newer mix: PCSK9 inhibitors, ezetimibe, and bempedoic acid. The case shows how that mix can manage blood fats when first-line drugs fail. The authors stress that care for such patients must be tailored, since no set guidance exists for this exact pairing of diseases.
pmc-11647923:
Toshiki Abe and thirteen co-authors track how people returned to Fukushima's evacuation zones after the nuclear accident, in a 2024 study. Planners need true headcounts to rebuild clinics and services. Phone based estimates give crowd sizes by hour of day.

The team studied two cities, seven towns, and three villages over four years. From 2019 to 2022, eight areas gained people and four lost them. The areas fell into five patterns of change. Each pattern shows a different stage of recovery. The method can guide health and social planning after future disasters too.
pmc-11648123:
ALS kills motor neurons while its wiring diagram of gene control stays hidden in plain blood samples. Xena Pappalardo and nine co-authors rebuild that diagram in 2024 from nearly eight hundred expression profiles of patients and healthy controls, using a reverse engineering algorithm. They slice the data by sex, by where the disease began, and by survival time.

The rebuilt networks exposed candidate driver genes and a signature tied to radiation damage responses in women and in bulbar onset cases. Four hub genes linked into pathways governed by the cell's damage sentinel, suggesting vessels and inflammation conspire in the disease. The authors offer the maps as diagnostic leads for an incurable illness. Blood, they show, remembers what the nerves cannot say.
pmc-11648223:
Kumaresan and Rammohan study how air temperature changes the energy use of electric two-wheelers, in a research paper from 2024. Riders and makers need to know how heat and cold affect range and battery health. The team ran a bench setup with drive cycle, speed and motor controls, and a battery pack.

Tests spanned 15 to 40 degrees Celsius, with sensors logging speed, current, voltage, charge, and range. The best zone sat between 20 and 30 degrees, where range peaked. At 15 degrees, range fell about two percent, while at 40 degrees it rose slightly. Extreme heat or cold still cut usable battery capacity and power.
pmc-11648923:
Coraline Rinn Iordan and co-authors show that new visual categories can be carved straight into the human brain, without lessons or practice. They fed brain scan signals back to people in real time and shaped activity in the sight areas to match the patterns that learning would make.

After the shaping, people showed biases in sight and in brain response for the taught categories, but not for control ones. They did not know the shaping had been done. The method gives a clean way to test how brain patterns cause behavior. The authors see uses past sight, in thought, memory, and movement.
pmc-11649323:
People who pass through prisons die of drug overdoses at rates far above the public's, and Canada's toxic opioid supply has made the gap deadlier. Benedikt Fischer, Elnaz Moghimi, and John Weekes survey that burden in this 2024 commentary. Prison populations carry heavy loads of chronic illness, addiction, and mental disorder into cells where drugs circulate anyway.

Deaths inside custody are rising, and the danger peaks for the corrections-exposed after release as well. The authors tie their survey to a cost-benefit study in the same journal issue on expanding needle exchanges across federal prisons. Their prescription is plain: take up, widen, and properly run the harm-reduction measures that already exist, since the tools to cut these deaths are known and merely underused. Commentary, here, is a call to implement.
pmc-11649723: Sonsoles Hernandez Barbosa published a journal correction in 2024. The notice corrects an article on the senses in culture. The original study discussed fin de siecle debates. Scholars argued whether senses diversify or unify experience. The correction adds missing funding information to the record. The funding came from a Spanish research project. That project studied art in its historical context. A second fix corrects the author name display. Online tagging had shortened the name incorrectly.
pmc-11651523:
Zuzana Drotarova and co-authors report two cases of mouth white lesions that turned harmful, in this 2024 paper. Such lesions can become cancer, and early markers of that shift are needed. The team measured small RNAs and defense enzymes in the two patients.

One patient had a warty lesion type and the other had mouth cancer. Both showed the same RNA pattern versus healthy people: two small RNAs rose and one fell. In the cancer patient's blood, enzymes tied to a key defense compound ran higher. A deep look at past studies backed the link between these shifts and harmful change. The authors propose both measures as candidate markers.
pmc-11653723:
Juliette Lagreula, Vincent Lorant, and Olivia Dalleur built a questionnaire to measure psychiatrists' professional social capital in a 2024 paper. In psychiatry, new clinical ideas spread through clinicians' networks, so the reach of those networks shapes care. No tool had been made to measure that resource for psychiatrists in particular.

Their Resource Generator asks which useful contacts and resources a psychiatrist can actually reach, in eleven items. An online survey sent by email supplied data to develop and validate the scale. A validated tool lets researchers link network strength to how fast good practice spreads. It also lets services spot isolated clinicians who may miss new methods and support.
pmc-11653823:
Wei Kang and Haoyi Guo test a scale for town well-being in big-city China. The study appeared in 2024. Fast growth packed folks into dense towns, yet pay gains did not plain yield more cheer. The team asked what shapes how well a town feels to live in.

Close to five thousand adults from three zones of China filled the scale. Four trait groups came out: fit to live, reach, ties, and cheer. Scores held firm in split tests across sex, age, and home-rights class. Towns with old-age and child care scored high next to towns with none. Reach, ties, and cheer rose with age, but fit to live did not.
pmc-11654023:
Yi Yang and a large team of co-authors review deep brain stimulation for disorders of consciousness, in a 2024 paper. Some patients stay unresponsive after grave brain harm. Stimulating deep brain hubs with placed wires offers one hopeful route. The review traces the method from early trials to finer network-based plans.

A network model holds that these disorders stem from breaks in a key loop of brain hubs. That model guides where wires should go. The team weighs bedside scales, brain wave tests, and scans for judging patients. Tools such as single-cell records and field signals now sharpen targeting. Open snags include patient choice, exact targets, and best settings.
pmc-11654123:
Ayla Eren Ozdemir, writing alone in 2024, tests whether melatonin guards eye cells in diabetic rats. The study targets the retinal pigment epithelium, a support layer at the back of the eye. Diabetes can scar this layer and cloud vision. Telomere length, a marker of cell aging, had never been measured in these cells under diabetes.

Forty male rats were split into four groups: healthy, diabetic, diabetic with melatonin, and healthy with melatonin. Diabetes was triggered by a standard drug, and melatonin shots ran for eight weeks. The team then measured telomere length in the eye layer by a gene-copy method. Comparing the groups shows how diabetes and the hormone each move the aging marker.
pmc-11654323:
Banan Al-Natour and colleagues survey dental students about online learning in their curriculum. Their cross-sectional study from twenty twenty-four comes from a Jordanian university. Lockdowns forced dental teaching online almost overnight. Hands-on subjects adapt awkwardly to screens, making student views vital.

Nearly one thousand students answered the web survey. All study years were eligible and represented. Students weighed benefits and drawbacks of online teaching. Factors that improved the online experience were also rated. Responses were anonymous and gathered over one month. Statistical tests compared views across student groups. Dental schools can blend online and in-person teaching more wisely from such feedback.
pmc-11654423:
Alparslan Demiray and four co-authors report kidney injury after use of a common edible plant in a 2024 case paper. Lambsquarters is eaten as food and used in folk medicine, where it enjoys a gentle reputation. Rising herbal use without expert guidance can still bring poisoning, though.

A sixty-eight-year-old woman arrived with nausea, vomiting, and flank pain after using the plant. Tests showed her kidneys failing, and a biopsy named inflammation of the kidney tissue as the cause. Steroid treatment and dialysis brought a positive response. The authors urge clinicians to ask about herbal products when kidneys fail without a clear cause. Natural origin, they stress, does not guarantee safety.
pmc-11654923:
Brianne Palmer and seven colleagues rot water lily leaves in aquariums to watch how fossils begin, in a study from two thousand twenty-four. Leaf preservation rests on the sediment under the leaf. It also rests on the microbes that colonize the tissue as it decays.

For three months, leaves decayed in pond water in the tanks. They sat over three sterile substrates: kaolinite clay, fine sand, and natural pond mud. A water-only control was run at the same time. Gene sequencing named the bacterial and fungal biofilm communities on the leaves. The mud gave rise to a biofilm composition that stood out from the rest. So the type of sediment steers the microbial crews that drive decay. Paleobotanists can read such work in reverse. They can infer the state of past ponds from fossil leaf assemblages.
pmc-11655023:
An interview profile introduces Mireia Sueca-Comes, a researcher who studied mesenchymal cells in bile duct cancer. The piece belongs to a journal series spotlighting first authors. It pairs her career story with the paper she led.

Sueca-Comes did the work as a doctoral student in Nottingham. Family experience with cancer sparked her path into science. Curiosity about how cancer grows kept her in the field. She now designs study proposals for firms and universities. Her industry role sits at a science services company. The interview traces her shift from bench work to client work. It offers early researchers a view of varied careers after a doctorate.
pmc-11655323:
Michelle Shiller, Melissa Johnson, Robert Auber and Sandip Patel discuss testing for STK11 and KEAP1 mutations in advanced lung cancer, in work from 2024. Standard first care for metastatic non-small cell lung cancer often uses immune checkpoint inhibitors, alone or with platinum chemotherapy. Yet a large share of patients gain little from those regimens from the start.

Mutations in these two tumor suppressor genes are linked to aggressive disease and resistance to checkpoint therapy. The article gives new prevalence data from a large clinical group, covers practical testing choices, and shares the authors' experience with such hard-to-treat patients. Its aim is to help clinicians spot a group that needs distinct treatment paths.
pmc-11655523:
Yangyang Shen and colleagues built a multi-omics buffalo database in 2024. Water buffalo support many rural Asian livelihoods. Milk and meat value is high. Two Yangtze valley buffalo types were compared. They show the diversity of the species. Both types are local mountain and lake populations.

Data covered genes, blood, and rumen fluid. Gene activity and metabolites were profiled. Whole genomes were sequenced as well. The two types differed clearly across layers. Seven and ten male animals were sampled respectively. The database now supports diversity research. It may reveal causal gene variants. Regulatory mechanisms can also be studied.
pmc-11655823:
Amirhossein Aghajani, Amin Zand, and five co-authors report a worm found under the surface of a man's eye. Their case report, from twenty twenty-four, concerns a healthy twenty-year-old man. He had recent contact with wildlife in a rural village. A swollen mass sat on the white of his left eye.

Surgery removed the mass, and lab checks named a young roundworm of a dog heartworm kind. He then took an anti-worm drug by mouth for two weeks. Two months later the spot had near cleared. No return showed in six months of checks. The authors stress full removal and lab study for such rare eye cases.
pmc-11655923:
Yi Pei and eleven co-authors published this study in 2024. It explores how aging-related genes behave inside head and neck cancers, the world's sixth most common malignancy. Half of patients still die within five years, largely because the disease is caught late.

Using large public data sets plus single-cell and spatial gene-reading methods, the team mapped which cells carry which aging genes. Tumors held more monocytes and macrophages, and fewer B cells, than healthy tissue. One gene, APOE, stood out in monocytes and tracked patient outcomes closely. A risk model built from one protective gene and the patient's age predicted recurrence. Communication maps between cell types suggested how the tumor's neighborhood is rewired. The authors say aging genes could guide prognosis and personalized treatment choices. They frame the work as a map for follow-up experiments rather than a clinical tool in itself.
pmc-11656723:
Shilpa Thandla and co-authors compare student research papers with AI-written ones in a 2024 study. The setting is a graduate course in global health at Case Western Reserve University. Students wrote a required research paper, then generated a second paper with ChatGPT-4o from the same assignment prompt. They then graded both papers section by section, and judged the references the model had cited.

Twenty-eight of fifty-four students joined the comparison. On a five-point scale, their overall satisfaction with the AI paper averaged well below the midpoint, rating it inferior or about equal to their own work. Most section scores told the same story. The reference check was sharper: of over seven hundred citations the model produced, close to half did not exist. Real ones formed only a small share of the sound references, the authors report.
pmc-11656823:
Larson and colleagues asked what medical specialists learn when they lead group peer telementoring. Their 2024 qualitative study focuses on Project ECHO. In that program, specialists and community clinicians learn from each other in online groups. Past work showed gains for community clinicians. Less was known about what the specialists themselves take away.

Interviews with 53 specialists yielded 129 accounts of learning. Specialists learned about care in community settings and about patient needs there. They deepened their knowledge of patient care and took a broader team view. They also learned about learning itself, including power gaps and humility. The authors say leading such groups can aid the growth of specialists.
pmc-11656923:
Zhongning Jiang, Wei Huang, Raymond Lam, and Wei Zhang present a tool that maps cell types in tissue in a 2024 paper. Spatial transcriptomics reads gene activity while keeping place in tissue. The task is to infer which cell types sit at each spot. Past tools trade off smooth maps against cell-level detail.

Their network, Spall, joins single-cell data with spatial data for the task. A graph attention module learns links between spots in the tissue. Skip links guard the fine traits of rare cell types. On many test sets Spall beat the best prior tools. It mapped tumor variety in pancreas cancer samples with care. It also traced layered patterns in mouse brain tissue.
pmc-11657423:
For advanced ovarian cancer, chemotherapy before surgery is common, but doctors lack a firm way to predict who will resist the platinum drugs used. Chuying Huo and co-authors build such a predictor in this 2024 study, combining two measures from patient records and tissue samples.

One measure scores how much the tumor tissue changed after treatment, and the other is a blood ratio that reflects inflammation. Together in their index, the pair predicted drug resistance better than either measure alone. Patients with low index scores also lived longer without the cancer returning. The index could help sort patients into better-matched treatment plans and trials.
pmc-11657623:
Gyumyoung Kim, Minkyung Yim, Hayoung Bae, and Ji-Won Hur test short forms of an emotion scale in Korean adults in a study from 2024. The Difficulties in Emotion Regulation Scale measures how hard people find it to manage feelings. Short versions save time, but each must still measure well.

Two community samples, of about eight hundred and twelve hundred people, filled out online surveys. Three short forms were tested: DERS-SF, DERS-18, and DERS-16. Factor models checked the hidden structure of each form. Two forms fit best when one subscale, Awareness, was set aside. Reliability and links to other measures were also checked. Clinics in Korea can pick a short form with known strengths.
pmc-11657823:
Jingfang Lin and co-authors test whether a stress sugar ratio predicts heart harm around surgery. The ratio joins blood sugar at admission with a long-term sugar mark. It aims to catch sugar spikes driven by surgical stress alone. Records covered 5,609 patients who had non-heart surgery between 2011 and 2020.

Heart events and heart deaths rose step by step with the ratio. Curve checks showed J-shaped links, with risk turning up past set points. Adding the ratio to old risk models sharpened their sorts in firm tests. A cut at the turn point lifted the sorting score by a clear margin. Machine learning models built on screened traits are also reported. The authors back the ratio as a cheap risk sign.
pmc-11658323:
Breast cancer can carry shame in the eyes of others, and that shame may feed low mood. ChunYing Cui and Lie Wang test one path for that link in a 2024 study of Chinese patients. They ask whether feeling blocked from sharing worries sits between shame and sad symptoms.

Of 256 women who took part, 222 finished the full set of forms. About one in five showed sad symptoms. Shame raised the sense of being blocked, and that block raised sad symptoms in turn. Shame also kept a direct tie to mood when the block was held fixed. The authors urge care that cuts shame and opens talk.
pmc-11659123:
Wenyu Li, Zhijie Xu, and Wenjie Tang compare men's and women's health reports in a 2024 study of older Chinese workers. They drew on a national survey of people aged 45 and up, run in 2020. The focus fell on adults still in paid work. Models weighed income, habits, care access, and other factors to see what shapes how each sex rates its own health.

Older men smoked and drank more, and earned less on the whole. Women showed healthier habits, helped by care access and lifestyle changes. For men, steady income and moderate drinking lined up with better self ratings. For women, health coverage and healthy routines mattered most. The authors urge health programs shaped by sex, since the levers that lift well being clearly differ for each group.
pmc-11659223:
Yong-qi Lian and co-authors review how a standard transplant injury and the gut's microbes shape each other in a 2024 paper. When a donor organ is cut off from blood and then reconnected, the restart itself damages tissue. This ischemia-reperfusion injury haunts transplantation, worsening survival and inviting infection and rejection. Meanwhile the gut hosts a dense microbial ecosystem that talks to the immune system.

The review traces the two-way street. The injury disturbs the gut balance, and the disturbed gut then feeds back into transplant complications. Studies show shifts in microbes after injury line up with infection and graft rejection. The authors gather treatment ideas that work through the gut, from diet to microbial therapy. Protecting the gut may be a back door to protecting the graft.
pmc-11660723:
Green and co-authors probe how care hands for mind-loss hosts sit in ward files. Kin and free hands bear a chief load for such hosts. Yet health webs fail to spot and log them in a set way. Codes and drug lists in the file flagged hosts with the ill. Chart reads then mapped how hand facts got logged per host. Reads also checked if hands held shared reach to the host gate.

Hands of fit hosts were called by post and phone for talks. Half-set talks ran with hands, docs, and ward staff in the work. Talks sought how best to spot, draw in, and back hands. File reach is the path such backs would use in the web. The work pairs chart facts with talk themes for that aim.
pmc-11661023:
Beata Pszczółkowska and Sylwiusz Retowski survey burnout among Polish dentists, in a 2024 study. Two hundred one dentists filled in scales for burnout, sensory sensitivity, and emotional intelligence. Sensitivity here means a trait of noticing and feeling stimuli strongly. The team asked whether that trait predicts burnout, and whether emotional skill shields against it.

Sensitive dentists reported more exhaustion and more detachment from work. Emotional skill predicted less of both, across the group. Its shield, though, shrank as sensitivity rose, and it vanished for detachment among the most sensitive dentists. The authors say sensitivity checks can flag dentists at risk early. Training in emotional skill helps most dentists, they add, but the highly sensitive need extra kinds of support.
pmc-11662323:
Adam Whitelock and co-authors set reference ranges for a vein-to-artery ratio in healthy cats in a 2024 study. The ratio may one day help judge fluid needs in sick cats. First, normal values and the most reliable scan site had to be pinned down.

Two operators scanned forty-two healthy awake cats twice each at four body sites. All sites gave usable ratios with low spread around their means. Still, readings varied within and between operators at every site. Two sites, near the kidney and at the pelvis split, were easiest to see clearly. The authors give ranges for both and call for tests in sick cats.
pmc-11666223:
Yongzheng Yao and co-authors study what predicts poor healing and long-lasting pain when rib fractures are treated without surgery, in a 2024 study. Rib fractures are a common result of blunt chest injury. They can bring complications such as air or blood in the chest and lung infections, and they harm breathing. Knowing who heals badly helps doctors choose and plan care.

The team look back at 342 patients treated with conservative care from January 2023 to May 2024. They gather background, clinical, and follow-up data for each patient. They then compare the poor healing group with the good healing group. They also compare patients whose pain lasted long with those whose pain was short. The contrasts point to the risk factors that matter.
pmc-11666423:
Gracious Ross, Sanja Vodanovic-Jankovic, and Ivor Benjamin study the part a lipid molecule plays in fibroblast activation in a 2024 paper. Fibrosis, excess matrix buildup, drives organ failure and much death worldwide. Fibroblasts turn into contractile myofibroblasts during fibrosis, gaining marker proteins including a collagen specific chaperone. The team posited that a molecule needed for protein prenylation, a lipid tagging process, is key to that switch.

Blocking the making of the molecule sharply cut the switch driven by a growth factor, and adding it back revived it. Blocking either of two tagging enzymes also lowered key markers. A surprise finding was a steep drop in the collagen chaperone, a sign of a narrow role downstream. Readers learn lipid tagging gates a core fibrosis program.
pmc-11666523:
Xiaoxia Zeng and co-authors search for a gene that can predict outcomes in head and neck cancer and reflect the immune cells around the tumor. Their 2024 study starts from a large public cancer database, scores each sample for immune and support cells, and then uses four machine learning tools to pick key genes. One gene, ITM2A, stood out for deeper checks.

ITM2A levels were low in this cancer and low levels tracked with poor survival. The gene links to many immune paths and shows up in several immune cell types. Raising its levels in lab cells slowed tumor growth. The authors propose ITM2A as a fresh marker that could guide care for these patients.
pmc-11667523:
Yanfei Lang and co-authors weigh neutrophil types and lymphoid structures for outlook in liver cancer in a 2024 study. Tumor neutrophils can fight tumors in an N1 form or aid them in an N2 form, and lymphoid clusters also shape immunity.

Tissue from close to eighty resected patients was stained to map both features in tumor and nearby tissue. In tumor tissue, more N1 cells tied to better outlook, while nearby patterns flipped. Mature lymphoid structures nearby also favored survival. Most neutrophils sat outside the lymphoid clusters. Combined patterns sharpened prognosis beyond single marks. The work guides immune-based risk grading after liver cancer surgery.
pmc-11667723:
Tao Yu and co-authors build a prized three-ring scaffold, six, eight, and six members fused, in a single reaction step. Their study appeared in 2024. Eight-membered rings sit inside many natural products and drugs, but the classic routes take many steps and give poor yields. Starting from a diazo compound carrying an alkyne and a nitrogen ring, a rhodium catalyst runs a cascade: carbene exchange, a hydrogen shift, an internal attack, then two selective carbon-hydrogen insertions.

A spiral charged intermediate steers the nitrogen ring's migration and closes the eight-membered ring. One insertion unexpectedly chose the bond near oxygen over the one near nitrogen. The authors call the route mild, atom-efficient, and ready to supply drug-like scaffolds.
pmc-11669523:
Huaidong Peng and co-authors test whether watching blood levels of a powerful antibiotic saves lives in sepsis, and whether age changes the answer. Their 2024 study mines a large intensive care database for over fourteen thousand sepsis patients treated with vancomycin. About half had their drug levels monitored during the stay.

After matching patients on other characteristics, the monitored group died within thirty days at a clearly lower rate, about twenty-three percent against twenty-eight. Adjusted models agreed, cutting the death risk by roughly a third. The benefit appeared across age groups, with spline analysis probing how risk bends with age.
