Monitoring also guards kidneys by preventing overdosing, a second channel of benefit. Observational data cannot prove cause, and the authors lean on matching and sensitivity checks. Still, the scale and consistency make a practical case for routine level checks.
pmc-11669723:
Bian and a large team of co-authors built a goat pangenome in this study from twenty twenty-four. A pangenome gathers the full DNA of many breeds into one graph-shaped reference. The team assembled genomes for eight goat breeds from long-read data. The graph revealed over one hundred megabases of sequence missing from older references.

They catalogued well over one hundred thousand structural variants, the large insertions and deletions that single-letter studies miss. Genotypes from that catalogue were then read in over one thousand goats worldwide. One duplicated immune gene grew steadily more common from ancient times to today. Other variants tied to cashmere output and high-altitude life. The resource opens complex variation to goat breeding and evolution studies.
pmc-11670723:
Zengliang Jin surveyed in 2024 how new tools and fresh theories are moving the study of brain and mental disorders forward. These disorders touch a large share of the world's people, have tangled causes, and still lack widely effective cures. Jin points to single-cell gene methods as one bright path, since they reveal how brain traits are regulated cell by cell.

Paired with machine learning, such methods build predictive models for conditions from schizophrenia to Alzheimer's disease. The piece introduces a themed set of papers on the topic. Its message is hopeful but measured: progress will come from tools and theory advancing together.
pmc-11671023:
Odette Verdejo-Torres and co-authors identify a copper-handling protein as a quiet director of muscle building. Copper is vital in small amounts and harmful out of balance. Scanning mouse muscle-forming cells with X-ray methods, the team found the protein CRIP2 loaded with copper in both the cell's nucleus and its body, gripping two to four copper ions tightly.

Deleting the protein's gene stalled muscle formation and let copper pile up inside the cells. The protein was also found sitting on gene switches, including the master muscle switch and genes that mop up metals. The authors present CRIP2 as a copper-responsive regulator linking metal balance to how muscle matures.
pmc-11671223:
Pallavi Sarma and co-authors screened rural women in Assam, India, for cervical cancer risk in a study published in 2024. Two tests were used: one for the virus that drives most such cancers, and a smear test for abnormal cells.

The study enrolled 480 women aged twenty to seventy in Kamrup District and took two samples from each. About three in a hundred tested positive for the high risk virus, and about eight in a hundred had an abnormal smear. Tobacco chewing and alcohol use were tied to both positive results. Irregular periods, genital infection, and having more than three children were also tied to a positive virus test.
pmc-11671923:
Markus Friedrich Neurath, Bruce Eric Sands, and Florian Rieder reviewed a new class of treatments for inflammatory bowel diseases: therapies built from living immune cells or designed to remove harmful ones. Despite modern biologics and small-molecule drugs, many patients still cannot control gut inflammation. The review covers engineered CAR-T cells, two kinds of calming regulatory T cells, and antibodies such as rosnilimab that deplete selected immune cells.

These approaches aim to hit several disease pathways at once and to switch on the body's own inflammation-resolving routes, offering a chance at lasting remission. Cell therapies could reset a misdirected immune system rather than merely suppress it. The authors weigh early evidence and safety questions, asking whether this strategy could become the field's next major advance.
pmc-11672423:
David Waters and co-authors build a frailty score for very old Rottweiler dogs and test whether it forecasts death, in work from 2024. These dogs live about thirty percent longer than the breed norm, much like human centenarians. Frailty means a raised risk of bad outcomes as body reserves fade with age.

The score counts thirty-four health deficits, drawn from owner phone interviews with ninety-three dog owners. The deficits span thinking, senses, heart, glands, and movement. The team then checked whether higher scores tracked shorter survival after the survey. A sound score would give vets and owners a shared gauge of risk. The study also tests how well dog aging mirrors human aging.
pmc-11672623:
Nari Kim and co-authors read the spring diet of Siberian musk deer from droppings in a 2024 study. The deer is a shy forest kind at risk in South Korea, and past diet work lacked fine detail on which plants it eats. Gene reading of dung can name those plants far more sharply.

Sixteen April samples from Gangwon Province held 213 plant kinds. Three tree and shrub groups made up most of the diet, and near half the plant groups were new to the deer's menu. Plants of wood kinds made up 98.8 percent of the feed. One find hints the deer may climb to reach a mistletoe-like shrub.
pmc-11672723:
Shayan Boozarjomehri Amnieh and co-authors study a gene called ACOX1 in horses kept in Iran, in a 2024 paper. The gene helps the body burn fatty acids. One variant of it is linked to higher enzyme activity and to how horses handle hard exercise and stress. The team asked how this variant is spread across six horse breeds.

The team tested DNA from 324 horses. Three gene forms appeared. One form dominated in Kurdish and Arabian horses. Another form was most common in Turkmen and Thoroughbred horses. The spread differed clearly by breed, but not by sex. The authors suggest the gene may be shaped by selection for breed traits. They propose it as a possible marker for performance and hardiness in breeding plans.
pmc-11672923:
Dongying Lv and ten co-authors test whether melatonin protects white fat metabolism against the combined hit of aging and a high fat diet in mice. Obesity threatens health and worsens with age, yet most studies treat the two factors apart. Melatonin, a circadian hormone with antioxidant properties, also plays in fat metabolism.

Aged mice on the diet show more lipid deposition, more inflammation, and lower protective glutathione than younger mice. Lipid and gene profiling finds raised triglycerides, diglycerides, ceramides, and cholesterol in belly fat, with lower sphingomyelin and fatty acids. A battery of tissue, molecular, and imaging tests tracks the damage. Melatonin treatment is then evaluated for how far it restores healthy fat function.
pmc-11673023:
Minkyeong Kim and co-authors survey body image and life quality among teens in Japan born with physical disabilities, in a 2024 study. How teens see their own bodies can shape mood, health habits, and social life. The team gave a set of forms to 107 teens and scored both body image and life quality by area.

Body image scored near the middle of the scale, with health views on top and looks views at the base. Life quality also scored mid-range, led by social ties. Scores split by sex, school level, type of disability, and daily self-care skill. Most body image areas rose and fell with life quality. School level and self-care skill stood out.
pmc-11673123:
Ruwen Liang and Karla Van Leeuwen study young children in rural China whose mothers migrated to cities for work. Their 2024 paper follows children aged three to six who live with grandparents. The question is how the mother-child bond before separation shapes later adjustment, through phone-based parenting and the current bond.

Data came from triads of grandparents, migrant mothers, and preschool teachers, each rating part of the picture. The bond before separation related to the bond after it and to warmer distant mothering. No chained pathway held, but two single links did: the current bond carried effects toward friendly behavior, and positive distant mothering toward acting-out problems. The work shows remote parenting quality still matters after families split across distance.
pmc-11673223:
Xuewei Qin and co-authors use brain scans to study disorders of consciousness in a 2024 paper. Such disorders follow severe brain harm and are hard to assess. The team tested whether a scan measure of slow brain waves could sort patients and predict who would improve after a spine-based therapy.

They scanned fifty-three patients before therapy and checked awareness three months later. Patients with injury-based harm showed distinct wave patterns from those with other causes, in areas tied to awareness and sight. Those who later improved showed their own pattern in key areas. Readers learn that the scan measure may help forecast recovery and guide care choices for these patients.
pmc-11673423:
Jin-Long Shen and Szu-I Yeh published an aerodynamics study in twenty twenty-four borrowing fish scales to fix an efficiency leak in compressors. Where a blade meets the casing, the flow separates into a messy corner stall that wastes pressure. A scale-like surface texture, known for low drag, was applied to the blade's suction side in simulations.

Flow analysis showed the texture shrank the pool of sluggish, low-energy air by about eighteen percent. Total pressure loss at the outlet fell by three and a half percent. A velocity-density visualization proved good at pinpointing the loss regions. The authors present the biomimetic surface as a practical, passive upgrade for compressor blades.
pmc-11674023:
Inflammation may cause, not just mark, two common womb ills, and Simon Alesi and co-authors used gene tools to test the arrow's direction, in work from twenty twenty-four. Finnish cohort data supplied both ills: a cystic ovary syndrome and tissue growth outside the womb. Gene variants stood in for blood inflammation marks.

One draw signal showed a clear causal push toward the ovary syndrome. A second signal, an interleukin, pushed toward the tissue ill. Both held under the main method and passed quality checks. The pair are named as leads for work on how these ills start, and where drugs might cut in.
pmc-11674723:
Cuthbert Mario Mahenge and co-authors link body makeup to tumor proteins in endometrial cancer, in this 2024 study. This cancer of the womb lining is strongly tied to obesity, and its tumors often carry changes in known growth pathways. Whether a patient's muscle and fat amounts track with the proteins her tumor makes was unclear. The authors call their work hypothesis-generating, a first look meant to raise sharper questions.

They studied one hundred thirteen patients from two large cancer data programs, with matching belly scans. For forty-five of them, tumor protein data were on hand, covering one hundred thirty-three proteins. Muscle and fat measured from the scans were set against those protein levels. Any firm links could one day fold body makeup into how targeted drugs are chosen.
pmc-11675023:
Brain maps that divide the cortex into regions usually pick one scale, yet the brain organizes itself at many scales at once. Adrian Allen, Zhengwu Zhang, and Andrew Nobel build a whole family of maps in a 2024 paper. Their CoCoNest parcellations grow from structural connectivity data, the wiring diagram of white matter, rather than from activity.

Bottom-up clustering merges the smallest units step by step, while pruning balances the complexity of each map against how faithfully it preserves fine-grained connectivity. Tested on a battery of internal and external measures, the family matched or beat the standard atlases in wide use. Because the maps nest inside one another, researchers can zoom between resolutions. The authors offer the family as an exploratory tool for the multiresolution brain.
pmc-11675323:
Shared kitchens let food startups rent professional space cheaply, but many cooks sharing one kitchen makes hygiene a moving target. Taeyeoun Roh and co-authors build a predictive model for food quality in these spaces, using Escherichia coli counts as the measurable stand-in for general contamination. They first map the stakeholders and quality factors unique to shared kitchens, then quantify bacterial growth with a classic growth curve and a transfer-rate equation for cross-contamination.

The integrated model lets managers watch quality drift with numbers rather than inspections alone. The authors argue continuous expert oversight, the old model of food safety, cannot fit a volatile multi-tenant kitchen. Their system aims to give the new business model a safety backbone it can actually run.
pmc-11675423:
Junhu Shao and a team of co-authors study a radio method for links that bounce off a layer of air, in two thousand twenty-four. Such scatter links can reach beyond the horizon, but their signals are weak and fade hard. A swept tone method can lower the level a receiver needs to read a signal.

The team first derived a formula for error rates over a fading channel. They then computed how errors shift with the method's settings. A seven-path fading model stood in for the deep fades of a real scatter link. With the best settings, the system gained a clear edge over un-tuned setups at low error rates.
pmc-11675823:
Qinhao Liu and six co-authors study, in a 2024 paper, a sugar chain drawn from abalone gonads and its power to slow blood clotting. The extract is a polysaccharide joined to protein, and few studies have asked what the protein part does for its effects. The team varied how the extract was made to find out.

All extracts lengthened two standard clotting times. Extracts from females made at two set heat levels worked best, and the most active part sat in a mid-size range. Cutting the protein with an enzyme quickly weakened the effect, while the fraction richest in protein worked strongest. The results say the joined protein is a real part of why the extract slows clotting.
pmc-11676123:
Adam Płoński and co-authors describe fixing a burst branch in an aortic stent graft in a case study from 2024. Branched stent grafts now treat aneurysms spanning chest and belly. The Zenith t-Branch system leads that field, with high success rates. Rare failures include leaks, kinks, and the graft's own branches rupturing.

Their patient, an eighty-two-year-old man, carried such a graft for four years. One branch then split open on its own. The team repaired the damage from inside the vessel, without open surgery. The paper reviews how such ruptures are managed across the literature. Long-term graft watching matters: a quiet implant can fail late, and endovascular rescue must be ready.
pmc-11676723:
Xiaoqing Hu and co-authors study how surface molecules shape a dangerous milk-borne bacterium in a 2024 paper. Cronobacter sakazakii can cause severe meningitis and blood infection in newborns. Its outer coat of lipopolysaccharide, or LPS, forms a barrier, and the team disabled two genes that build that coat to see how the bacterium changed.

One mutant resisted acid, alkali, oxidative, and salt stress worse than the normal strain, while the other dried out faster yet handled salt better. Lipid profiling showed both mutants shifted their fat makeup sharply, with many more unsaturated lipids and big changes across eleven lipid classes. The study is the first to tie this bacterium's coat structure to its lipid profile.
pmc-11676823:
Fuchun Jia and co-authors present a 2024 study of a power diode built from gallium nitride on silicon. Such diodes serve in chargers and power gear, where low loss and high voltage strength both matter. The team paired a slanted sidewall with a fluorine plasma wash. They then probed how the diode blocks current in reverse, the trait that sets its voltage limit.

The treated diodes held off 790 volts before breaking down, with low leak current. On-state loss stayed low as well, giving a strong combined score. Tests across diode sizes showed the sidewall is the main leak path. Computer models of the field inside the device credit the fluorine step for most of the gain. The work supports cheap silicon-based builds for high-power uses.
pmc-11677023: Ramón Cacabelos surveys a quarter century of gains in drug science and the hard parts still ahead, in a review from 2024. The head of the hosted text gives only the start of the piece, so this note stays at the level that start supports. Twenty-five years brought finds that changed how care is done, lifted how well patients fare, and made disease workings clearer. The piece is one author's broad look at the field, its wins, and the tests to come.
pmc-11677223:
Ivana Milošević and colleagues weigh addiction history against hepatitis C cure rates, in work from 2024. People who inject drugs carry high hepatitis C loads due to needle sharing and poor care access. Direct drugs cure most cases, but follow through gaps may split outcomes by group.

More than four hundred patients at one Serbian centre took direct acting drugs. Cure by plan start ran lower in the injecting group than in controls. Among those who finished care as planned, cure rates matched between groups closely. Deep liver scarring predicted failure to finish in the injecting group data. Mood and alcohol issues linked with stops before the planned end date.
pmc-11677323:
Frederick Koh and co-authors report interim results from the HEROS study of pre-surgery conditioning for frail, muscle-wasted patients. Programs that combine exercise, nutrition, and medical tune-ups aim to get sarcopenic patients through major gut surgery in better shape. The optimal recipe is unknown, and a supplement ingredient called HMB may protect muscle, though its effect on muscle quality was untested.

Patients scheduled for major elective gut surgery joined a two-to-four-week program of resistance exercise, vitamins, comorbidity care, and smoking cessation. They drank three high-protein supplements with HMB daily before surgery. The main outcome is change in fat inside the muscle, a stand-in for muscle quality, measured with help from an AI-aided ultrasound method. Functional outcomes are tracked as well in this interim analysis.
pmc-11677523:
Rika Iwawaki and seven co-authors test strong fluoride varnishes on early tooth decay, in a research paper from 2024. Early decay eats into enamel below the surface before any hole appears. The team used cow enamel as a model of this early lesion.

They compared two high-strength varnishes with a fluoride mouthwash and with no treatment. Neither a single varnish coat nor short mouthwash use rebuilt minerals in the damaged layer. But treated enamel resisted acid better afterward, so later acid attacks caused less mineral loss. The authors say the main benefit of these products, at least in this model, is protection rather than repair.
pmc-11677623:
Paolo Piterà and nine co-authors report a cold therapy case in a 2024 paper. Their patient was a woman of fifty five with cerebral palsy. Stiff leg muscles shaped her walking and limited her life. Standard spasticity drugs often help little and carry side effects.

She joined a ten day rehab program with five whole body cold sessions. Each session held her at deep sub zero cold for two minutes. Walking speed and step length rose right after the cycle. A reflex test pointed to better nerve muscle efficiency. Pain scores dropped sharply, and quality of life rose. Sleep and mood questionnaires rounded out the gains. The authors call for controlled trials to test the single case hints.
pmc-11677723:
Lee and colleagues present a study from twenty twenty-four on a nanotube sensor that detects a stomach germ's DNA. The germ, Helicobacter pylori, is classed as a stomach cancer cause. Yet only a small share of infected people develop that cancer. Early, exact detection still matters for care. Their sensor uses carbon nanotubes with a fluorine coating on an electrode. Handheld circuits tune the voltage readings for best response. Under tuned settings, the sensor reads the germ across a wide range.

Detection reaches down to very low germ counts in their tests. Precision stays high across the working range. The team apply the method to stomach tissue from healthy people and patients. They present it as a tool for early infection diagnosis.
pmc-11677823:
Friedemann Schad and co-authors study mistletoe therapy added to immune treatment for lung cancer in a 2024 registry study. Three hundred patients with advanced non small cell lung cancer received either immune checkpoint drugs alone or the drugs plus a mistletoe extract. Registry data from an accredited network allowed a real world comparison.

Patients on the combined plan lived a median of about thirteen point eight months versus six point eight on drugs alone. Among patients whose tumors carried a key marker and who got first line treatment, the added therapy cut the adjusted death risk sharply. The authors suggest immune calming and less resistance as possible routes. They frame the extract as a support worth further controlled testing.
pmc-11677923:
Larisa Titire and co-authors sim in 2024 how stacked fiber cloth stands up to shot hits in body shields. Law crews wear such cloth on the chest. Which break ways rule, and how layer count and shot speed sway the stand, are the asks.

Two shot kinds for one guard grade form the test pair. The cloth is built yarn by yarn, since thread grade sims cost too much to run. Just the thick est stack at the low speed meets the grade bar. Thin stacks or fast shots fail: stress waves race, cloth warps hard, and the shot breaks through.
pmc-11678223:
Israel Martínez-Espinosa and co-authors review tiny RNA markers for lung cancer in a 2024 paper. The markers ride inside exosomes, small sacs shed by cells into body fluids. Their stable shell makes them fit for blood tests that skip surgery.

Studies show lung cancer patients carry distinct sets of these markers next to healthy people. The sets may aid first diagnosis, outlook calls, and checks on how care works. The review covers the last five years of work on blood, chest fluid, and lung wash samples. It weighs where the field stands and what proof is still needed before clinic use.
pmc-11678323:
Leonardo Barbosa and co-authors hunt for fungus allies in a 2024 plant study from Brazil's dry northeast. Sisal, a fiber crop, suffers a bole rot caused by a mold, its main disease problem in the region. The team tested Trichoderma fungi, found in local soils, inside local plants, and from other hosts, as living shields against the mold.

Several strains slowed the mold's growth by up to seventy percent and nearly stopped its spore making and sprouting. In plant tests, disease occurrence fell by up to ninety-three percent and severity by near all. Some strains attacked the mold directly, while treated plant tissue thickened its walls, a sign of switched-on defense. The authors name the best strains as candidates for field biocontrol.
pmc-11678523:
Mariko Takada and co-authors wrote this 2024 study on a skin lotion for sun spots, the flat brown marks that sun leaves on the face with age. The lotion carries a paired compound built from a vitamin C form and an amino acid. Proof that whitening agents help these spots, rather than general skin tone, was thin.

Twenty-seven Japanese women took part in a blinded half-face trial for twenty-four weeks, with the test lotion on one side and a plain lotion on the other. By the end, spot scores on the test side had fallen clearly against both the start and the plain side. Lightness rose and the melanin index fell at twelve and twenty-four weeks. No lightening of normal skin or other skin trouble appeared. The authors judge the compound plainly effective on these spots.
pmc-11678923:
Christoph Angermann and co-authors teach a generative adversarial network to synthesize three dimensional bone images. Published in 2024, the work answers a data problem in medical imaging: scans are scarce and privacy bound, which slows model building. Synthetic volumes can stand in for new patients with chosen traits, at far larger scale.

The network learned to produce high resolution volumes with fine voxel level bone structure. The team also carried GAN inversion into three dimensions, opening tools like image morphing, attribute editing, and style mixing for study of the model itself. Validation ran on a database of high resolution scans of the wrist bone's inner architecture. The authors present the pipeline as both a data source and a lens on the model.
pmc-11679023:
Wei Lu and co-authors propose a construction method for steel structures in a 2024 engineering paper. Design work often assumes one uniform temperature across a whole frame. Real building sites heat unevenly, so stress in temporary supports shifts in ways a uniform model misses.

Their force feedback method uses temperature measured in stages during construction. The build sequence and the measured heat both feed into the stress calculation. That lets crews track how the frame and its temporary system respond as work proceeds. The aim is a truer match between the model and the molded structure. Safer staging and fewer surprises on large steel jobs are the practical gains.
pmc-11679123:
Arne Sørensen and three co-authors test if eleven extra soccer drills lift skill course marks in youth players. Their chance study appeared in twenty twenty-four. Ninety kids aged nine to twelve were split to a drill pack and a plain pack, with course tests pre and post. Drills stressed ball craft and picks in one-on-one and small games.

Both packs cut course times by the end, the drill pack by more in raw span but not past the true bar. Track time, cone touch, and pass flaws tied too. Short spans and low course likeness may tell the flat split.
pmc-11679223:
Oily sludge from oilfields must be cleaned before disposal, and the sand mixed into it decides how well the oil lets go. Shuhui Wu and co-authors studied that link in 2024, floating sludge made with sand of one size or of three sizes mixed. They varied temperature, time, stirring speed, and the water-to-sludge ratio to find the best settings.

Coarser sand released oil more readily, and mixed sizes did better still, since unlike grains help each other separate. Microscopy and infrared scans backed the pattern. A standard kinetic model fit the process well, and stirring speed proved the main control. Tuning it cut the leftover oil in mixed sludge to under three percent.
pmc-11679523:
Iosif Tammas, Konstantina Bitchava, and Athanasios I Gelasakis review vaccine boosters used in farmed fish and their effects on welfare. Their 2024 review explains that adjuvants strengthen vaccine responses and are widely used to prevent disease in aquaculture. The same ingredients can harm the fish they protect, a tension the field increasingly weighs.

Traditional boosters include oil emulsions and aluminum compounds. The authors describe how each works and what side effects follow. Nanoparticle formulas emerge as a promising alternative, aiming for strong immunity with gentler impact. The review weighs immune benefit against welfare cost species by species. Its goal is a practical frame for choosing boosters that protect both fish health and farm output.
pmc-11679723:
Straka, Pitel, and Corny assess surface quality after precision electrical discharge machining of hard steel. Wire EDM cuts conductive materials with electric sparks, leaving a surface whose integrity is a top quality sign. Engineers watch micro and macro geometry to judge if a cut part will perform and last.

The test material was high-speed steel EN HS6-5-2C, used for cutting tools. The team measured surface crack density under varied main machine settings. Their goal was a setting mix that keeps cracks low while holding precision. Results help shops tune wire EDM for tool steels where surface flaws can start failure.
pmc-11679823:
Sara Al-Dahir led a large team studying COVID-19 testing and vaccination in Louisiana in a 2024 paper. Vaccine hesitancy, fed by misinformation and distrust, slowed uptake. Whether other health-seeking habits, like getting tested, predict vaccination was little explored. Their cohort followed several hundred adults seeking routine care at pharmacies and clinics across a year, with records checked where possible.

Three quarters of unvaccinated participants and nearly nine in ten vaccinated ones had been tested. Tested people were much more likely to be vaccinated, and testing stayed linked to uptake after other factors were counted. Past refusal pointed the other way. The authors say testing behavior can guide future health messaging.
pmc-11680423:
Carlotta Lambertini and co-authors compare two drug mixes for putting horses under in surgery in a 2024 study. Both mixes pair a main sleep drug with a calm drug. The team pulled records for 138 horses that had planned surgery from 2021 to 2023 at their clinic.

Sixty horses got the first mix and 72 got the second, after the same starter drugs. Sleep came a bit slower with the second mix, at a median of 60 seconds against 50. Waking also took longer with the second mix. Heart and breath rates stayed in line across the groups. The team reads the second mix as a sound stand-in, while calling for deeper drug studies.
pmc-11683223:
Yujun Liu, Xin Zou, Henry Tong, Yuan Ji, Lianjiang Tan, and Jie Hao present a protocol in this two thousand twenty-four paper. The goal is predicting which cancer patients will respond to immunotherapy from their starting state. The protocol uses scCURE, a method built on single-cell RNA sequencing. It spots which cells stay unchanged during immunotherapy, in cell and molecular function, amid the cells that change.

The protocol first shows scCURE applied to single-cell datasets to pick out those unchanged cells. It then shows how to build prediction models from single-cell or bulk RNA data, built on the unchanged-cell signature. The unchanged group acts as a stable reference against which treatment effects become readable. For full steps the authors point to the first scCURE study. Such protocol papers aim to make a niche method reusable by other labs.
pmc-11684023:
Hartmut Maennel, Oliver Unke and Klaus-Robert Müller wrote a 2024 paper on learning molecule traits with machine learning. A good model should respect how molecules turn in space. Low-order features that do this are known to be incomplete. The team set out to prove what higher-order features can do.

They prove broad claims about when such feature sets are complete. For a molecule with a set number of atoms, they give a count of features that is enough. They also swap a common step for plain matrix work, which cuts the cost a lot. The method fits quantum chemistry, and any task with points in space.
pmc-11685023:
Ning Wang (2024) measured how the rare earth element neodymium damages DNA in mouse liver. Workers and communities near rare earth mining face growing exposure, and the element was already known to be genotoxic. Mice received neodymium nitrate by stomach tube for 28 days. The team measured the metal stored in liver tissue. They gauged DNA breaks with the comet assay and tracked damage markers and stress genes.

The metal built up in the liver. Treated mice showed more broken DNA strands in liver cells, plus higher levels of reactive oxygen and two damage markers. A whole defense pathway switched on: genes around the guardian protein p53 rose, including its sensors and brakes. Wang used benchmark dose methods to put numbers on the harm. The study links the damage to oxidative stress and the cell's alarm system, and argues exposure limits deserve closer study.
pmc-11685123:
Ralph Brinks and Annika Hoyer examine, in a 2024 paper, when the classic simple epidemic model can stand in for a richer one that tracks how long each person has been infected. During the COVID pandemic the effective reproduction number guided policy, yet its behavior inside detailed models is rarely studied.

The pair prove, with exact analysis, how and under what conditions the plain susceptible-infected-removed model approximates the infection-age version, where the reproduction number hides implicitly. A simulated intervention during a COVID-like outbreak illustrates the math. So does real data from a 1918-1919 influenza outbreak in Prussian army camps near Arnsberg, Germany.
pmc-11685223:
Tao Meng and co-authors published a research paper in 2024 on a simple blood ratio that predicts death in a severe tick-borne fever illness. The illness kills a large share of its sickest patients, and doctors need early warnings. The ratio divides one enzyme that leaks from damaged tissue by albumin, a blood protein that falls in severe illness.

Among 209 patients, fifty-seven died. Age, one liver enzyme, and the new ratio each predicted death on their own. The ratio scored best on accuracy tests, and patients above a set cutoff died at much higher rates. The authors say the cheap, routine measure can flag high-risk patients on arrival.
pmc-11685523:
Andrea Spinelli and co-authors follow root canal outcomes over three years in 2024. The study tests a simple filling method that uses one fitted cone per canal. A premixed ceramic based sealer completes the fill. Patients were treated by postgraduate dentists under a set protocol.

X rays were taken before care, right after filling, and at yearly visits. A standard index scored healing of the area around the root tip. Crowns were added when the tooth lacked firm structure. Three year results show whether a simpler fill can match older, more complex methods in lasting success.
pmc-11686523:
A teenager's infected fingernail led to a rare spine infection in a case report by Dan Zhang and co-authors, published in 2024. Infections of the neck spine are uncommon and hard to spot early, since fever and neck pain have many causes. Late treatment risks damage to the spinal cord.

The fifteen-year-old patient had a bloodstream infection from Staphylococcus aureus, seeded by a long-standing nail infection with an abscess. Antibiotics calmed the fever, but weakness in the limbs grew worse. Surgeons cleaned the infected neck bones and fused them with a bone graft and plate. Three years later the neck was stable, with no pain or limb problems. The authors stress early scans and lab markers.
pmc-11687123:
Kevin A Henry and co-authors open a 2024 journal editorial introducing the second volume of a research collection on single-domain antibodies. These small binding proteins, first found in camelids and sharks, have moved from curiosity to clinic since the first volume in 2017. The editors survey that rise and frame the new set of papers.

An approved drug for a rare clotting disorder, strong antiviral results during the COVID-19 pandemic, and cell therapies built on these binders mark the field's growth. The volume holds twelve research articles and two reviews. Imaging and diagnostic uses stand out, often aimed at the pandemic virus, alongside work on basic binder properties.
pmc-11687223:
Junxiao Zhang and co-authors recycle wastewater phosphorus onto peanut fields in a 2024 study. Phosphorus fertilizer grows scarce while waste streams leak the same element into water. Iron-coated biochar can catch that phosphorus and carry it back to crops.

Batch tests set the best catching conditions and the binding mechanism. The loaded char then joined a blocked field trial on peanuts. Plots mixed char and standard fertilizer in varied doses for comparison. Yield and nutrient use show whether recovered phosphorus can replace fresh stock. Closing the phosphorus loop helps farms and rivers at the same time.
pmc-11687923:
Alexander Rakowski and co-authors let neural nets mine brain scans for gene links in a 2024 paper. Classic gene hunts test one trait at a time, which misses fresh patterns in rich scans. TransferGWAS codes each scan into a short feature list with nets trained on other image sets, then tests those codes.

Over 36,000 UK Biobank brain scans fed the hunt. It found 289 apart gene spots, tied to bone density, brain, and heart traits, plus 11 spots with no past report. Scores built from the deep codes sharpened trait forecasts. Gene ties also linked diffusion scan traits to type 2 diabetes.
pmc-11688023:
Ou Gao, Yinghua Chen, and Honglang Xie describe a blood disorder triggered by COVID-19 in a patient already living with lupus, in this 2024 case report. Thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura is a rare emergency where tiny clots form body-wide. In a lupus patient with kidney involvement, telling a flare from this complication is genuinely hard.

The 43-year-old arrived with high fever, cough, and tea-colored urine. A swab confirmed COVID-19, and testing showed the protective enzyme ADAMTS-13 completely absent, the hallmark of the purpura. Plasma exchange came first, then biologic and immune-suppressing drugs. One year on, the patient had fully recovered from both infection and purpura, and the lupus kidney disease sat in remission with zero activity score. The authors conclude the virus, layered on longstanding autoimmunity, lit the fuse, and they walk through the reasoning.
pmc-11688923:
Jason Johanning recounts in 2024 how the Surgical Pause program was born, tested, and spread through veterans' hospitals. Frailty flags surgical patients at high risk of dying within six months, and half of older veterans seeking major surgery qualify as frail or prefrail. An Omaha program screened for that risk with a simple index before operating.

The survival gain seen in Omaha was replicated across five Pittsburgh hospitals, where one-year deaths after surgery fell from 20 to 16 percent. Even three weeks of exercise before surgery improved endurance and breathing strength. The pause has since rolled out to more than 50 VA centers. The account argues that a short screening pause can change surgical outcomes at national scale.
pmc-11689023:
Christopher Kaufmann, Soomi Lee, and Katie Stone summarize a symposium on sleep and well-being in older adults, in a 2024 article. Sleep problems and broken body clocks affect health widely. They touch mobility, mood, and daily function. The symposium gathered four studies on aging groups. The first used national survey data on sleep and frailty. It also checked for gender differences in that link. The second tied broken rest rhythms to metabolic syndrome.

Wrist sensors measured the rhythms in a long-running aging study. The third study looked at family caregivers' sleep. It asked whether resilience softens the cost of caregiving. The fourth used retirement study data on sleep apnea treatment. It sought which health conditions predict quitting the airway pressure therapy. Together the talks argue sleep is a lever for healthy aging. The article maps the session for readers who missed it.
pmc-11689323:
Hong Mi and Peter Lichtenberg present a 2024 symposium of five papers on money fraud against older adults in mainland China and the United States. Four papers map risk factors for falling victim, and one tests an intervention. The set aims to show how risk shifts with culture and place.

One study built a machine learning risk model from a 2015 survey of older Chinese, tying risk to low education, high age, and loneliness. A second traced how body function, family ties, and personal means feed fraud through weak points in mind and wealth. A third profiled postal scam victims in the US. A fourth studied elders in forest areas of northeast China, where money skill and internet use stood out.
pmc-11689423:
Frail patients face rougher recoveries from surgery, so screening before the operation should steer them to strengthening services. Mehraneh Khalighi and co-authors report rolling out a frailty index program for veterans over sixty-five awaiting joint replacement. Providers scored patients and referred them by score; patients also mailed in their own scores.

Screening reached only forty-eight percent of eligible patients until nurse champions began reminding providers. Referrals were least accurate for the middling frail group. Patient and provider scores correlated moderately, but patients reclassified twenty-nine percent of cases upward, with memory and weight loss the shakiest items. The 2024 report shows the tool works, if the workflow carries it.
pmc-11689823:
Sheryl Zimmerman presents a 2024 session paper on a national center that joins research, practice, and policy. Research should inform care and rules, yet the three sides often work apart. The center in focus works on assisted living, the largest form of residential long-term care in the United States. It ran for twenty years as a joint body of national groups.

In 2023, the center joined a university in North Carolina to grow its reach. New cores for consumers, practice, policy, and research are being built. The session covers the center's history, its planning process, and its push to speak with one voice. Lessons may apply to topics well beyond assisted living, Zimmerman argues.
pmc-11689923:
Barbara Nicklas, Denise Houston, and John Batsis survey, in a 2024 paper, new approaches to treating obesity in older adults. Obesity among Americans over 65 has nearly doubled in three decades. About forty percent of older adults now live with it.

Modest diet-based weight loss, around five to ten percent, already improves blood pressure, blood sugar, and fitness. New approved drugs push losses to fifteen or twenty percent. Yet few older adults joined the drug trials, the authors warn. Weight loss by any route also costs muscle and bone, a real danger at older ages. The paper weighs these gains and risks to guide safer treatment choices for seniors.
pmc-11690023:
Jodi Waterhouse describes how a large medical campus checked whether it truly welcomes older visitors. The University of Colorado Anschutz Medical Campus won an age-friendly designation in 2021. It sits inside a bigger community with a health system, a children's hospital, and a VA center that lack the designation. More than 30,000 people pass through daily, and visitors can easily get lost in partner buildings.

Two tools framed the review: an age-friendly inventory and a campus climate survey. Representatives walked the campus to feel the hurdles themselves and gathered built-environment assessments. The process surfaced problems with parking, payment kiosks, signs, and maps, both printed and online. Recommendations went to campus leadership and won support. The account shows how a designated campus can hunt down the everyday obstacles that older guests face, and it offers a model for other large sites.
pmc-11690123:
Elinor Schoenfeld and co-authors describe a college seminar that teaches young students how technology can aid aging at home. Faculty from engineering, medicine, nursing, and social welfare built the ten-week course together. Freshmen and sophomores met topics from home sensors and data privacy to loneliness and social drivers of health. Each week they also spoke with family or neighbors about growing old at home.

Students built persona stories of older adults and pitched tech fixes for a chosen challenge. At the end they presented their personas and graded each other's work. The 2024 report shares lessons from the first run. A graduate version of the course is now in development.
pmc-11690323:
Shannon Freeman, Keone Gourley, Emma Rossnagel, and Mark Groulx assessed neighbourhood walkability for people with dementia in a 2024 analysis. Outdoor activity supports health and ageing in place, but people with dementia face extra barriers such as confusing street patterns. Their project asked what cities must change.

A geographic analysis, joined with interviews of people with dementia and family caregivers, mapped current barriers and supports. The study city lacked much of what safe walking needs, from missing sidewalks to disorienting layouts. The authors present the findings as a guide for municipal protocols, so that dementia-inclusive design shapes infrastructure decisions and helps residents keep social ties and independence.
pmc-11690423:
Evan Plys and seven co-authors design an online program for people with advanced dementia and their care partners, in a 2024 paper. Programs that engage both partners at once are growing in favor, but advanced disease makes shared tasks hard to pitch right. Their program blends story work, digital art, and calm sounds and images. The goals are good mood, closer ties, and a better sense of well-being for both partners.

Clinicians, couples, and care partners all fed into the first draft through group talks. Ten couples then tried the draft in eight rounds of workshops, and the team revised fast after each round. Testers pushed for calm content that would not stir distress, strong visual clarity, and room to tailor each session. The paper lays out the safety and ease-of-use lessons for anyone building such shared tools.
pmc-11690523:
Manka Nkimbeng, Truphosa Aswani, and Joseph Gaugler ask what words African immigrant communities use for dementia and for caregivers. Their 2024 study notes that the experiences of African immigrants with dementia are poorly understood. Without shared terms, outreach and research falter before they start, so the team went to the community to listen.

They drew on ten interviews with community leaders and three group conversations with thirty participants. A clear pattern emerged: many languages spoken in the community have no accepted word for dementia at all. Where translations exist, they often rest on symptoms, insults, or myths. The role of caregiver is likewise unnamed, even by people doing the work. The authors argue that naming these ideas plainly is a first step toward fair access to care, in communities hit hard by the disease.
pmc-11690623:
Patrice Fuller and co-authors adapt a walking and reminiscence program for dementia caregivers in a 2024 study. The original program pairs one mile walks with image prompts that spark memory talk, aiming to support brain health. This version assigns family caregivers, their care partners with mild impairment or early dementia, and a support person as walking triads.

Seven triads walked routes three times a week for sixteen weeks with a walking app, or first spent sixteen weeks in observation. Weekly health updates were shared, and most triads also opted into watch and sleep sensor tracking. Caregivers logged more daily steps than care partners, while sleep hours were similar. Recruiting proved a practical hurdle worth reporting.
pmc-11690923: Judith Howe presents two award talks for a society of aging scholars, in a short notice from 2024. One talk marks the Kent Award, given for strong leadership in aging study through teaching and service. The other marks the Kleemeier Award, given for fine research in the field. The 2023 Kent talk was given by Kathleen Wilber of the University of Southern California. The 2023 Kleemeier talk was given by David Almeida of Pennsylvania State University. Both awards come from the Gerontological Society of America.
pmc-11691023:
Chandra Reynolds and five co-authors study how leisure activity, social capital, and rurality shape IQ near midlife in this 2024 paper. The sample holds about twelve hundred adults from a Colorado twin and adoption study, averaging thirty-three years old. The team asked whether thinking activity and county resources predict cognitive scores.

As expected, people who did more demanding leisure activities scored higher, wherever they lived. The surprise lay in social capital: city residents scored higher only where social capital was high, and worse than rural peers where it was low. Rural scores barely moved with social capital levels. The authors say lifestyle and place interact in shaping cognition. They frame the findings as relevant to keeping minds sharp decades before old-age decline.
pmc-11691123:
Lauren Stratton and Sam Fazio introduce a set of studies on help for people who care for family members with dementia, in a 2024 symposium summary. Most dementia care at home comes from family and friends, yet few proven programs reach them online or by phone. The symposium gathers checks of two programs and a round-the-clock helpline run by the Alzheimer's Association. The aim is to show the full effect such services can have.

One study reports strong early results for a new course called The Empowered Caregiver. A second weighs an online and virtual program that guides carers through money matters. A third reviews three rounds of checks on the helpline, which offers phone support and care advice at any hour. Fazio closes by naming gaps in the field and the next steps for building proven, easy-to-reach support.
pmc-11691223:
Yeonsoo Shin and Giyeon Kim traced quality of life paths among frail older adults in Korea in a 2024 study. Frailty marks a state of low reserve where small setbacks can trigger decline. Social networks may buffer that decline, but their role across time needed testing.

The team used six waves of a national aging study, from 2006 to 2016, covering more than three thousand adults aged sixty-five and over at the start. They charted quality-of-life trajectories for the whole group and for frail and non-frail subgroups. They then tested how network size and contact shaped those paths. The findings can guide community programs that protect frail elders by strengthening their social ties.
pmc-11691423:
A day holds a fixed budget of hours, and how older adults split it among activity, sitting, and sleep may shape muscle health. Lauren Roe and co-authors analyzed wrist-sensor data from 714 adults in their mid-seventies, treating the twenty-four-hour mix as one composition. They related shares of moderate-to-vigorous activity, light activity, sedentary time, and sleep to leg power, stair-climb power, and strength.

A higher share of brisk activity went with stronger leg and stair power in both men and women, while a higher share of light activity went with lower power. Strength showed no clear links. Modeling time swaps suggested that trading sitting or light activity for brisk movement is the most promising way to protect muscle power in later life.
pmc-11691523:
Azza Alharrasi and Marie Boltz scope the research in 2024 on nurse led care for adults whose thinking suffers after stroke. Stroke is a top cause of death and lasting limits, and muddled thought after stroke raises costs and care needs.

Searches across three databases found twelve studies of nurse led help aimed at thought skills. The studies showed gains in overall thought, daily living skills, movement, and life quality. Gains were clearest soon after stroke, which backs early screening and rehab. Long term gains stay unclear, and the pair call for larger, tougher trials across many centers.
pmc-11691623:
Anni Wang studies resilience and distress as a two-person system, pairing homebound disabled elders in China with the family members who care for them. Each person's strength plainly leaks into the other's mood, but studies usually score them separately. Her 2024 survey covers two hundred forty-six elder-caregiver pairs across five provinces.

Both members complete a resilience scale and a distress thermometer. An actor-partner model then splits the effects: how one's own resilience guards one's own distress, and how it crosses over to guard the partner's. Both directions show the crossover. A tougher elder calms the caregiver; a tougher caregiver calms the elder. Family care programs get statistical permission to treat the pair, not the patient, as the unit of support.
pmc-11691723:
Jianhong Xu and three co-authors published a study in 2024 on blood proteins linked to physical frailty, the state of becoming weak and slow with age. The biological roots of frailty are still not well understood. The researchers searched for protein patterns that mark who develops frailty and who fares worst afterward.

The study drew on the UK Biobank, with close to forty-four thousand adults. The researchers measured close to three thousand proteins in blood samples. Hundreds of proteins were associated with being frail or prefrail at the start. Other sets of proteins were associated with death among those who began prefrail or frail. Models built from small sets of proteins sorted people by risk well. Two proteins stood out as the strongest markers in both groups.
pmc-11691823:
Bove and six co-authors study social factors in rehabilitation use after hip replacement in a 2024 paper. Recovery care at home or in clinics is a key part of regaining function. Past work shows social gaps in surgery rates, but rehab use was less clear.

Five years of data from a large health system covered home and outpatient rehab. Women used more rehab on most measures. People in more deprived areas had more home visits, but not longer care overall. Rural residents got fewer home visits and shorter outpatient care. Race showed no clear link with any outcome. The authors call the pattern mixed, with rural access a concern.
pmc-11692023:
Matthew Schurr, Emily Post, Teresa Walker, and Brenna Renn report a pilot rollout of the Engage psychotherapy in a geriatric mental health service in this 2024 paper. Engage is a brief, structured behavioral therapy for depression in older adults, proven in trials but rarely used in daily care. Its simple protocol suits delivery by nonspecialists. Twenty-two care managers, drawn from occupational therapy, social work, and nursing, were trained and coached to deliver it.

After the pilot, providers joined a focus group, and their comments were coded against an implementation framework. Thirteen themes emerged. The group judged Engage workable for providers, patients, and the wider system. Barriers included heavy symptom burden, complex patients, and provider doubts about their own skill. The authors urge services to gather such feedback whenever they adopt a new therapy, and to adapt the rollout to match.
pmc-11692223:
Lina Ma, writing alone in 2024, builds and validates a short scale for measuring physical resilience in older adults, the capacity to bounce back from stressors. Few instruments existed for the concept, so her team drafted one through expert consultation. Two Delphi rounds settled three main dimensions: intrinsic capacity, adapting to change, and external support.

After early testing on 172 older adults trimmed two weak items, the final scale holds fourteen secondary items. It was then validated on 1,982 community-dwelling and 362 hospitalized older Chinese adults. Reliability scores landed in the good range, completion ran near 91 percent, and factor analysis recovered the three intended dimensions, explaining 57 percent of variance. Ma presents CHEES as a practical tool for hospital and community screening alike.
pmc-11692323:
Marja Jylha examines how social class shapes trust in Finland, a famously high-trust Nordic welfare state, in a 2024 study. The project surveyed 3,085 people aged sixty-five to eighty-four nationwide. Trust in institutions and in health and elder care services was measured against education, income, and occupational class.

Schools earned the most trust of five institutions; business life the least. Every institution's trust score rose in a straight line with each class measure, a gradient inside an egalitarian showcase. Acute and chronic health care kept majority trust in all classes. Home care and long-term elder care did not: only a quarter trusted long-term care, and that distrust crossed all classes evenly. Jylha concludes that institutional trust tracks social position even in Finland, while failing elder care has become a shared national grievance.
pmc-11692423:
Bethany Leach and four co-authors published a study in 2024 on racial and ethnic differences in end-of-life care among people in Texas who died of colorectal cancer. Disparities in advance care planning, palliative care, and hospice enrollment are documented. The researchers asked whether disparities appear in this group during the last thirty days of life.

The study linked the Texas Cancer Registry with Medicare claims for 5,757 decedents aged sixty-six or older. All had died between six months and five years after diagnosis, during 2010 to 2018. Rates of advance care planning were low in every group, at about two percent or fewer. Non-Hispanic Black patients were most likely to receive a palliative care consultation, yet least likely to enroll in hospice. After adjustment for characteristics, odds of hospice enrollment remained lower than those of white patients. The authors call for earlier planning conversations for everyone.
pmc-11692523:
Christina Miyawaki, Angela McClellan, David Russell, and Erin Bouldin published a study in 2024 comparing dementia caregivers in rural and urban areas of the United States. Rural caregivers are well known to lack services, but urban caregivers had been studied less. The researchers asked what services each group lacks and what shapes their use of home and community-based services.

The team interviewed twenty caregivers in rural western North Carolina and eighteen in Houston, Texas. Rural caregivers wished for more information and caregiver support. They also expressed guilt about using services, because services were limited and felt zero-sum. Urban caregivers searched for information until they found satisfactory answers and shared leads with peers. They asked for services tailored to their own language and culture. Rural caregivers' needs were tied more closely to place. The authors support more online groups that can reach both populations.
pmc-11692723:
Dawon Baik wrote this 2024 study of a digital activity program for older people who care for a partner with heart failure. Older family care partners face more social isolation and worse mental and physical health than younger carers. Loneliness in this group raises the risk of poor health and low well-being.

The team used scenario-based design to learn what these carers need and prefer. Fifteen care partners were recruited at a university hospital in late 2022 and took part in interviews. Their mean age was about 66, most were women, and most cared for a spouse. The planned program joins one-on-one activity coaching, a fitness tracker, and motivational text messages. Participants felt the program could support their social connectedness. Their input shapes a tool meant to fight isolation, not just to count steps.
pmc-11692823:
Eight authors led by Cynthia Felix sort older adults with sound minds by brain scan marks of Alzheimer disease. Early care works best, so spotting who will slip matters a great deal. A quick clinic poll, the MoCA, is the usual first screen, yet its worth before symptoms show was unclear. The team split 147 sound-minded elders by two scan marks: amyloid and tau, the twin protein signs of the disease.

Poll scores split the groups in a clear way. Elders with both marks scored lower than those with none, on both tau scan types. Those with amyloid alone sat between the two on total and recall scores. One tau tracer proved the keener tool of the pair. The cheap poll may thus flag scan-proved risk far before symptoms, a gain for trial picks.
pmc-11692923:
Dominique Como presents a 2024 study of how minoritized older adults live through post-acute care, the rehab phase after a hospital stay. Over 40 percent of Medicare patients use such care each year, and gaps in access and outcomes track race and social strain. Yet patient voices on the stay itself are rare in the record. Eight Black and Latino patients in Southern California care sites gave long talks across mid-2024.

Four themes rose from the talks. Patients prized a say in their own care and the will to speak up. Staff skill and warmth shaped trust. The flow and feel of daily care left marks as well. The findings name where small fixes could close real gaps. Care that hears patients first is the study's core plea.
pmc-11693023:
Zvinka Zlatar and co-authors present a 2024 study of how to adapt a physical activity program for Latino adults. This group faces higher risk of Alzheimer disease and related dementias, yet few prevention programs are built for their culture and language. The team used community voice at each step of the design.

A small pilot gave older adults a fitness tracker and two coaching calls from a bilingual coach over three weeks. Focus groups and a community board then shaped the full program. Users liked the tracker and felt more drive and more time for self care. Blocks named were duties, old habits, bad weather, and health strains. Users asked for group events and face to face contact.
pmc-11693223:
Sarada Lakshmanan and co-authors test follow through in a 2024 aging study. People high in conscientiousness tend to enjoy better health, thanks to self control and steady habits. The question was whether that trait predicts sticking with a demanding home program.

Forty four adults aged 57 to 95 took on a self guided digital fall prevention course. It packed eleven lessons and sixty short classes, plus avatar led leg and balance work drawn from a known exercise program. Personality was scored with a standard five trait test. Lesson completion and exercise days were tracked against the scores. Diligent starters, the design bets, would prove diligent finishers.
pmc-11693323:
Lane-Nelson reports a 2024 interview study with members of one African Methodist Episcopal church. Seventeen members spoke at length about their lives from childhood to the present. The study uses life course theory, which tracks how early events, hard periods, and built-up strain shape later health. Questions followed those themes closely.

Members named early money hardship, family strain, and racism as lasting forces on their health. Many said food was short and home life felt tight in childhood. They also named strong supports, such as love, safety, and lessons from parents. Shared stories stressed unfair treatment based on race across the whole life span. The work ties church life to the long arc of health.
pmc-11698223:
Nicholas Brown and John Dundon report a rare break in a hip implant in a 2024 case study. A 73-year-old woman had her right hip replaced with a ceramic ball on a plastic socket, and the surgery went smoothly. Three days later, with no fall or blow, the ceramic ball cracked.

Scans showed the break after the woman felt a clunk and her leg seemed short. A second surgery swapped the ball and liner and swept out all ceramic bits. She healed well with no more trouble. The case warns that even new, tougher ceramic heads can crack, from flaws or poor fit.
pmc-11698923:
Xiyun Gong and co-authors study why shoppers impulsively buy blind boxes, the sealed packages that hide which toy is inside, in a paper published in 2024. Curiosity is the engine of the trend, and the team modeled how store settings and product traits feed it, using a stimulus-organism-response framework.

An online survey of 306 Chinese consumers showed that atmosphere, surprise, and novelty all raised curiosity, and curiosity in turn drove impulse buying. Price awareness pushed the other way, weakening the pull. Curiosity also carried the effect of the store and product factors into the purchase itself. The authors suggest ways sellers can present blind boxes responsibly and ways buyers and regulators can curb the habit of buying on impulse.
pmc-11700023:
Sofia Leandro and co-authors report a rare surgical emergency in a 2024 case paper. A 67-year-old woman with a slipped womb and bowel wall lifted a heavy load. She felt sudden pelvic pain, and a loop of her small bowel had pushed out through a tear in the wall of the birth canal.

Such cases most often strike older women who have had pelvic surgery or harm. Here the woman stayed stable, so doctors eased the bowel back and gave fluids by vein. Surgery then found a full tear with about 40 centimeters of live bowel outside. The tear was sewn shut, and she went home on day five.
pmc-11700523:
Akiko Kudo, Akihiro Fukuda, Koro Gotoh, and Hirotaka Shibata investigate in 2024 a possible link between a waste toxin and hormone signaling in chronic kidney disease. The toxin, indoxyl sulfate, builds up when kidneys fail and is known to push the disease forward, but its effect on the mineralocorticoid receptor was unclear.

The team combined animal work, using a model where most of one kidney is removed, with lab experiments on cells. They tracked clinical measures and stained tissues to see where the toxin and the receptor appear. The study asks whether the toxin switches the receptor on, which would help explain worsening kidney damage.
pmc-11703623:
Qiaoqiao Li and colleagues priced a rural blood pressure program in two thousand twenty-four. The Chinese program uses non-physician community workers. It clearly improved pressure control in its trial. Heart events also fell under the program. Whether benefits justify costs was unknown. A simulation model forecast twenty years ahead.

The intensive program cost less per person overall. It also delivered more healthy years of life. Usual care cost more and achieved less. Prevented heart events likely drove the savings. The analysis used healthcare system perspective. Rural scale-up looks economically justified by these numbers. Policymakers gain a strong value argument here.
pmc-11704623:
Yuanxin Wang and co-authors present CellTran, a statistical method that spots cells caught mid-transition in single-cell RNA data, in a 2024 paper. Most tools chart how gene activity changes along a cell's path but miss shifts in how genes are regulated together. CellTran instead watches paired-gene correlations, which flag cells whose control wiring is being rebuilt, without needing to map the full regulatory network.

Tests covered tissue regeneration, embryo development, early lesions, and immune responses after vaccination. In each setting the method found transition cells with distinctive expression profiles. The authors argue that catching cells at the switch point reveals mechanisms that drive change and may expose drug targets.
pmc-11705623:
Somyata Somendra, Saurabh Mehrotra, Parag Barwad, Himanshu Gupta, and Ajay Bahl measure a rare infection risk in this two thousand twenty-four cohort study. Infective endocarditis may threaten patients with hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, but incidence data were sparse. The authors followed five hundred twenty-nine patients in a tertiary cohort, entered between two thousand three and twenty twenty-two, totaling thirty-two hundred patient-years.

Only three patients, zero point five seven percent, developed endocarditis, an incidence of zero point nine two per thousand patient-years. Two had outflow tract obstruction, where incidence ran higher at one point three nine, against zero point five five in non-obstructive disease; nobody with mid-cavity gradients was affected. Two infections sat on the mitral valve and one on the aortic, and both mitral cases left severe leakage and heart failure. Rare, the authors conclude, but devastating when it strikes.
pmc-11708423:
Zhu Jiang, Giulia Sorrentino, and their co-authors examined heart tissue from people who died of a heart attack, looking at the small blood vessels inside the heart wall. Their 2024 study asked whether scarring around those vessels helps explain how a heart attack develops. Tissue came from deaths in the first hours, deaths days later, and people without a heart attack.

Stains and microscope work showed more scar tissue around the vessels in both heart attack groups than in controls. Cells that line or wrap the vessels also showed signs of turning into scar forming cells. The border zone next to the dead tissue showed the most scarring of all. The results point to vessel scarring as part of the damage a heart attack leaves behind.
pmc-11708823:
Lin and co-authors study in 2024 how emus rise from rest and move off, a task little studied outside humans. Standing up needs wide joint swings and strong muscle work, which may push leg design to its limits. The team paired live measures with computer models of the emu leg.

Models suggest some leg muscles work near half their full length change in both rise and rise to walk moves. Key straightening muscles fired hard early in each move. Moving off at once needed larger joint forces and side motions than a plain rise. The work sets a base for study of how tendons may ease muscle load in large birds.
pmc-11709023:
Menstrual cups are a reusable, low-waste option, yet very few women in India use them, held back by low knowledge and poor attitudes. Lakshmi Prasanna and co-authors tested a simple fix in 2024: a thirty-minute teaching video. Their study ran in selected colleges in Patna with one hundred women aged eighteen to forty-five.

Each woman answered the same survey before and after the video. Knowledge scores rose with clear significance, and attitude scores moved in a positive direction as well. Many participants said a government scheme would help spread use of the cups. The authors conclude that short video teaching is a cheap, workable way to promote this greener form of menstrual care.
pmc-11709423:
Roberto Cruz and Oscar Gutierrez Trevino present a rare nerve case in a 2024 report. A 22-year-old pregnant woman came in with migraine and a drooping, weak left eye movement. Scans showed nothing clear. Doctors first suspected a muscle disease and tried its standard drug, without success.

Steroids slowly improved the eye. Months later her double vision worsened, and new palsies appeared in other eye nerves on both sides, all within weeks. A blood panel for autoimmune brain disease came back positive for an antibody called anti-GAD65. The doctors wanted antibody-filtering infusions, but insurance approved a different immune drug instead. That drug, plus steroids, eased the palsies. The case is unusual because eye weakness alone opened the illness. The authors say such immune syndromes deserve a place on the checklist for shifting eye palsies.
pmc-11709523:
Elizabeth Boots and co-authors pilot in 2025 a self-run thinking test for people with progressive supranuclear palsy, a rare brain disease that stiffens movement and clouds thought. Self-run tests can flag decline in Alzheimer disease, but their fit for this condition was untested. Their platform, Mayo Test Drive, runs on many devices.

Eleven patients, average age near seventy, took the platform's two tasks in clinic and filled feedback forms. Scores were compared with standard paper-and-pencil style testing. The study checks whether patients can use the tool on their own and whether its scores track the established measures, a first step toward home testing.
pmc-11709623:
Marie Emilie Tuil and thirteen co-authors map immune cell activity in the Alzheimer's brain in 2025. Microglia, the brain's resident immune cells, react as the disease advances, but whether their response helps or harms may depend on stage and region. Past drugs that simply suppressed immunity disappointed.

Forty-eight people, healthy controls and patients with mild impairment or Alzheimer's, received brain scans tracing microglial activity plus memory tests. The Alzheimer's group showed stronger activity across many regions, including memory areas. Samples of donated brain tissue added markers of calming and inflaming cell states. The pattern supports a two-phase response, informing when immune treatments might help rather than hurt.
pmc-11709823:
Byron Creese, writing alone in twenty twenty-five, tracks how mild changes in mood and conduct shift over five years in older adults. The focus is on people who feel their thinking has slipped, even though tests may still look normal. The study asks if these felt slips warn of worse mood and conduct problems ahead.

Data came from more than three thousand adults over age fifty, checked each year. Those who felt a slip began with higher scores for mood and conduct problems. Their scores then rose fast, while scores for the rest rose only a bit. Creese reads felt slips as a risk sign for both thought and mood decline.
pmc-11709923:
Ling-Qiang Zhu studies how a salty diet feeds the tau tangles of dementia through a brain adenosine receptor. His 2025 paper starts from two facts. Heavy salt intake is an independent risk factor for cognitive decline. And the A1 adenosine receptor, dense in memory regions, shapes synaptic signaling and sleep. His group had already tied this receptor to Alzheimer's cross-talk between neurons and glia.

Using protein and gene readouts and a water maze for learning, the work tests a chain. The receptor, acting by suppressing a lipid-making enzyme, may carry the salt signal into tau pathology and odd behavior. The chain, if confirmed, names a druggable link between diet and dementia.
pmc-11710023:
Adejoke Olukayode Obajuluwa and five co-authors test red light therapy on rats kept under harsh LED light in a 2025 study. Round-the-clock LED glow can wreck sleep and strain the brain, and it has been tied to Alzheimer-like harm. Red light, in contrast, is said to calm anxiety and aid sleep, but its inner workings are murky.

Male rats lived under four light plans for 60 days, with behavior checks every two weeks. Some got scheduled red light on top of the harsh glow. The team read two clock genes in a deep brain zone and tracked anxiety-like acts. Red light softened the harm the glow caused.
pmc-11710123:
Tau protein tangles track memory loss in Alzheimer's, but the chain between them may run through shrinking tissue. Anika Wuestefeld and eight co-authors test that chain in this 2025 study of three hundred and twenty-five amyloid-positive adults across the disease spectrum, all inside a national imaging initiative. Tau scans, brain volume measures, and a battery of memory tasks were collected for each.

Higher tau and thinner tissue each meant worse scores on every task. The mediation question is sharper: does tissue loss in the memory hub, the medial temporal lobe, carry tau's effect mainly for the later stages of remembering, while other regions serve other skills? Splitting tau into hub and cortex measures, and adjusting each memory score to isolate its stage, the authors probe that division of labor. The answer shapes where anti-tau drugs must act.
pmc-11710323:
Brain organoids grown from stem cells can model Alzheimer's disease, but they form on their own and so vary from batch to batch. Stefano Sorrentino and co-authors built a more controlled model in 2025 by 3D bioprinting, laying down living cells and materials in a wood-pile pattern that mimics the cortex. Their ink carried precursor cells that can become neurons and support cells.

The printed cells stayed alive, grew, and matured into working cortical neurons and astrocytes. When a synthetic amyloid protein was added, immune cells grown from the same stem cell source moved into the structure and ate the deposits. The authors say the model could reveal the earliest steps of the disease and serve as a test bed for drugs, without animal models.
pmc-11710423:
Ashley Carey and Silvia Fossati present a 2025 mouse study of two heart and vessel risks in Alzheimer type disease. High levels of a blood compound and high blood pressure can each harm brain vessels. The team asked if mice exposed to both would show worse vessel harm and disease signs.

Disease model mice and normal mice got a diet, a drug in water, or both from midlife. Brains were checked months later for cell death, barrier leaks, new vessel growth, and amyloid load. Mice with the risks showed more vessel cell death and worse barrier and growth harm. Amyloid signs also trended higher. The authors say the mix adds harm through shared paths.
pmc-11710523:
Hulya Ulugut reports a 2025 study of emotion reading tests for sorting forms of frontotemporal dementia. Exact sorting helps predict the disease type and plan care. One newer form is marked in part by weak emotion reading, so the test used can change the result.

Ulugut compared a short video based test with two older tests in early stage patients and healthy adults. Video based tests beat still face tests at telling the newer form from the behavior form. The short video test also beat its rival at telling it from the speech form. Brain scans tied scores to right side areas for meaning and focus. The author urges care in test choice for exact sorting.
pmc-11710623:
Warnakulasuriya Fernando and co-authors test whether butyrate, a fatty acid made by gut bacteria, can slow Alzheimer's disease. Their 2025 paper sums up the group's work across several models. The disease builds up sticky amyloid beta protein in the brain, harming memory and learning, and few treatments change its course.

In mice bred to model the disease, butyrate cut brain amyloid by 40 percent and improved fear-based learning. In cell models, it shielded cells from amyloid harm and changed cell firmness. Work on support cells and stem cells also looked promising. The team calls butyrate a new candidate amyloid blocker, with dose studies next. The authors frame the work as a first step toward human studies.
pmc-11710723:
Grace Rocco and co-authors study a protein called Sorbs2 in a 2025 mouse report on memory. Sorbs2 helps hold the cell skeleton in place and is found in hippocampus neurons, the cells of a key memory area. Its exact job there was not known, so the team bred mice that lack it.

Female mice without Sorbs2 froze less in fear tests and explored a moved object less, signs of weaker memory. Brain tissue showed the neuronal form of the protein was fully gone in whole-body knockouts. The inner scaffolding tubes of cells, called microtubules, also grew less stable without the protein. The authors plan tests of whether this loss interacts with Alzheimer's-like changes in mice.
pmc-11710823:
Yixiang Jiang reports a 2025 mouse study of a small antibody tool against alpha-synuclein, the protein that clumps in Parkinson's-like diseases. Full antibodies are too large to enter the brain well. Single-domain antibodies are ten times smaller and reach the brain far better. Jiang's team had built such a tool, called 2D8, that binds the protein.

The team linked 2D8 to a drug tag, making a version that sends the protein to the cell's shredder. In cell tests the new version cleared the protein and blocked its toxic effect. In mice, three doses cut the brain signal of the protein by about four fifths, far more than the plain tool. Lab checks confirmed deep clearance with no clear harm.
pmc-11711823:
Mohamed S Dabour and co-authors write a 2024 editorial on diabetes drugs that may protect the heart during cancer care. The drugs, called SGLT2 inhibitors, are now core treatment for diabetes, heart failure, and kidney disease. Some cancer drugs damage the heart, and only one approved protector exists, so new options are wanted.

Early animal work and five patient record studies hint that these drugs blunt heart damage from cancer therapy. The editorial discusses a large new study of over ninety-five thousand patients with cancer and diabetes. After matching, users of the drugs faced lower rates of heart damage than non-users. The authors present the class as a strong candidate for heart protection in cancer care.
pmc-11712123:
Sai Spandana Chintapalli and co-authors split Alzheimer's disease into subtypes by translating patient brains into healthy-looking ones, in a 2025 paper. No two Alzheimer's brains shrink in the same pattern. That variety confuses diagnosis and treatment planning. Normative modeling measures how far each person strays from a healthy reference. A generative network can draw the healthy version of a patient's scan.
