Their method adapts an image-to-image GAN for that translation. The gap between real and translated scans quantifies personal abnormality. Patterns in that gap can then cluster patients into subgroups. Subtypes may respond differently to the same drug. Trial designers gain a tool for cleaner enrollment. The work joins a shift toward precision neurology.
pmc-11712223:
Maria Bunyan and co-authors test a phone app that coaches older adults toward habits that may cut dementia risk, in a study from 2025. About four in ten cases of dementia link to habits that can be changed, but face to face coaching is costly and hard to scale. The app pairs a risk check with daily coaching on sleep, food, exercise, mood, and brain use.

The trial ran for twelve weeks with 154 adults aged fifty to sixty nine. One group used coaching alone, one added short video calls with a clinician, and one had no app. App users improved their habit scores more than the group with no app. Extra calls added no clear gain. Users stayed active at a high rate, so the team calls the app a workable first step.
pmc-11712323:
Saif Ahmad Khan and co-authors pack two Alzheimer drugs into fat-based carriers for brain cells in this 2025 paper. The pair, an enzyme blocker called RV and a kinase blocker called KI, may work better together. The team loaded each alone and both together into nanostructured lipid carriers. A lab cell line modeled nerve cells.

Drug doses from low to high were tested for cell survival. At one low dose, each single-drug carrier beat its plain drug suspension by roughly a quarter to a third. The pair-loaded carrier scored highest of all at the top dose. The authors argue the carriers deliver more drug to cells, with the pair ahead, and call for deeper Alzheimer testing.
pmc-11712423:
Jayden Lee and co-authors ask why some people with dementia are easy prey for money scams. Older adults lose vast sums to fraud each year, and weak social and emotional skills may raise the risk for people with Alzheimer's disease or a second form of dementia.

The study covered twenty-five patients with one disease and thirty-nine with the other. Patients played a game that tests how they react to unfair offers. People who knew them well rated their risk of being conned. The team also checked how far patients misjudged their own social faults, and they scanned brains for areas that had shrunk.
pmc-11712623:
Max McLachlan and co-authors compared in 2025 two ways of scaling brain amyloid scans in adults with Down syndrome. Amyloid PET studies divide brain signal by a quiet reference region to get comparable numbers. The cerebellum is the usual choice, but its signal can drift over time, a worry made worse by cerebellar shrinkage in this population. White matter is the candidate replacement.

Participants came from a long-running Down syndrome brain study and received one of two tracers. The team computed yearly change using each reference in turn. The eroded white matter mask was built to keep the reference clean of gray matter spillover. The abstract presents the comparison setup and early rate displays. The aim is steadier longitudinal numbers for tracking Alzheimer's change in this high-risk group. Trial designers depend on exactly that steadiness.
pmc-11712723:
Catherine Still and five co-authors ask, in a 2025 study, how hospital space shapes the place of family carers in dementia care. People who care for a hospitalized person with dementia can feel invisible on the ward. Hospitals promote dementia-friendly spaces, yet little is known about how the physical setting itself helps or blocks carers from taking part.

The team watched four units of a large teaching hospital for twenty-seven hours and interviewed fifteen carers and twenty-three clinicians. They found spaces set aside for families and tools such as education boards and patient whiteboards often went unused. Their findings point to simple design changes that could bring carers into the care team more fully.
pmc-11712823:
Crawford and four co-authors study how older adults judge their own memory, in this 2025 paper. The skill, called metamemory, fades with age and fades more in Alzheimer's disease. Changes in it may warn of disease before symptoms show. The team asked whether mood and a disease-linked brain protein shape this self-judgment.

Forty-eight older adults with normal thinking took memory tests, filled in surveys on memory and mood, and had brain scans for the tau protein. Worse mood scores, not worse memory scores, tracked with poorer self-judgment. Tau in one deep brain region, the amygdala, sharpened that link: people with both high tau and low mood rated their memory worst. The authors argue that mood deserves a place in studies of early disease signs.
pmc-11712923:
Manvi Punukollu and Archana Venkatesan grade how hard Alzheimer web pages are to read. Sick people and kin turn to the web for facts, yet dense prose can lock them out. Their 2025 study picks top health sites by search rank for the plain term, then strips the text clean for tests. A code kit runs seven read scores on each page, from ease marks to grade marks.

Set health guides urge prose at a sixth-grade mark. Scores for the picked pages sit well past that mark in the part of the sums shown. The gap spans each score type, not just one. Plain rewrites of key pages could open facts to more minds. The study gives site hosts a clear bar to aim at.
pmc-11713123:
Justine Sefcik and co-authors ask what shapes how often older Americans living at home get outdoors. Their 2025 study uses a national ageing survey of Medicare members aged sixty-five and up. Going outside supports activity and health, yet little work has asked what drives the habit itself. The team weighs thinking skills, neighborhood traits, and physical function together.

Rates of going out were mapped across personal, health, and neighborhood traits, and odds were estimated for each factor. The design is a snapshot, so it shows links rather than causes. Results can help towns and care programs spot which supports, from safer streets to stronger bodies, might keep older adults engaged with the world beyond their doors.
pmc-11713323:
Eric Li reflects on dementia cafés in rural Canada in a 2025 paper. The café model, begun in 1997, gives people with dementia, carers, and professionals a relaxed place to meet and share.

Rural and remote areas were little studied, so a six month participatory project ran cafés in three interior British Columbia communities. Three themes emerged. First, listening and inclusive space mattered greatly, since isolation runs deep and patients and carers wanted room to speak openly. Second, money and volunteer shortages threatened the cafés' survival, and government programs left gaps. Third, creativity and generations meeting each other added value. The paper draws lessons for keeping such spaces alive where resources are thin.
pmc-11713523:
Veronica Yank and co-authors report a national trial of an online workshop for rural dementia caregivers, in this 2025 paper. Rural family caregivers in the United States are often isolated and poorly served. The workshop, Building Better Caregivers, aims to build self-care and care skills.

Caregivers joined a six-week online course led by peers, working at their own pace from home. They also chatted with each other on discussion boards. The trial compared the course with a control group that got phone calls and a handbook. Outcomes covered low mood, stress, and loneliness at six weeks and six months, testing whether remote support can reach families far from clinics.
pmc-11713723:
Margarida Vaz and four co-authors use infrared light to watch Alzheimer's-related peptide reshape proteins in cell vesicles, in a 2025 study. Amyloid-beta, the peptide behind the disease's plaques, travels between cells inside extracellular vesicles and may seed further aggregation. The team treated mouse neuroblastoma cells with a short amyloid fragment for two days. Vesicles released into the medium were collected by ultracentrifugation and characterized.

Infrared spectroscopy then read the fold patterns of the proteins those vesicles carried. If the peptide changes its carriers' cargo, vesicles become part of the disease mechanism, not just messengers. That possibility matters for blood-based Alzheimer's tests, many of which already read vesicle contents for diagnostic signals.
pmc-11713823:
Arnaud Charil and five co-authors report how a drug for early Alzheimer's disease affects tau, a protein that builds up in the sick brain. The drug, lecanemab, is an antibody that binds loose clumps of a second protein, amyloid. Their 2025 report draws on brain scans from a large trial of the drug.

Scans showed that tau built up more slowly in treated patients than in those on placebo, most of all in side regions of the brain. A math model of the disease was built to trace how tau grows over time. The model matched thirty months of trial data and suggested the drug can halt tau growth in a key memory region. The authors back longer treatment.
pmc-11713923:
Pamela Ferreira and co-authors test a blood tau measure for Alzheimer's drug trials in a 2025 conference paper. They ask whether it can serve as a stand-in outcome. The measure, plasma p-tau217, tracks amyloid, tau tangles, and thinking loss. Blood tests are cheap and simple next to brain scans or spinal taps.

The team used 189 people from two cohorts, one in the United States and one in South Korea. Each person had blood tests two years apart and a brain amyloid scan at the start. They checked how change in the blood measure matched thinking change. They also worked out how many patients a trial would need. The goal was to spot a drug cutting the measure by a quarter. The authors argue the test could serve as a second outcome across the full span of the disease.
pmc-11714023:
Lloyd Tran, Zung Vu Tran, and Fern Vu lay out a Phase 3 trial plan in a 2025 conference paper. The plan pairs a test drug with an approved antibody in early Alzheimer's disease. The approved drug, lecanemab, clears amyloid but slows decline only a bit. The test drug, NA-831, passed early safety and effect checks.

The plan enrolls 600 adults, ages fifty to ninety, for an eighteen month core phase. People are split at random into groups: the test drug alone, the pair of drugs, or a dummy pill. No one knows who gets what while the core runs. An open phase follows where all can take the pair. The team will weigh thinking change and side effects, with a hope that the pair can use lower doses.
pmc-11714123:
Raj Amin and co-authors tested a new brain receptor drug in Alzheimer's mice in two thousand twenty-five. Cholesterol handling in brain goes wrong in the disease. A nuclear receptor steers that handling. Older drugs for it harmed liver and blood counts. Their molecule was designed on a computer first. It favors the safer receptor subtype strongly.

Partial activity at partner receptors adds balance. Treated mice behaved better in memory tasks. Synaptic plasticity, the learning substrate, improved too. The design aims to dodge past side effects. Human safety remains to be proven, of course. The study nominates a cleaner drug candidate. Cholesterol pathways stay in Alzheimer's crosshairs.
pmc-11714323:
Anna Dreyer and eleven co-authors ask whether living in a poor area shortens life and free living for people with Parkinson's disease or frontotemporal illnesses, in a 2025 conference paper. Past work found that lack hurt survival in Alzheimer's disease, but these other brain illnesses were less studied. The team used three long term groups of patients in the United Kingdom.

Each person's home area was scored for lack of jobs, income, and services at the time of diagnosis. The groups held 283 people with frontotemporal linked illnesses and more than four hundred with Parkinson's disease. Staff tracked entry into care homes and deaths through health records. The study weighs whether area lack joins known factors such as age and genes in shaping how long people live and cope on their own.
pmc-11714423:
Arne Stinchcombe and Douglas William Hanes wrote this study, published in two thousand twenty-five, on childhood ADHD and thinking skills in later life. ADHD is a condition marked by poor focus and easy distraction, and it often starts in childhood.

The pair used a long-running United States survey of adults aged fifty-one and older. Of more than ten thousand people in the sample, ninety-nine said they had an ADHD diagnosis as a child. That small group scored lower on thinking tests at the start and at each later check. The gap stayed after the authors weighed age, sex, wealth, schooling, and race. Both groups lost ground at the same rate over time, though. The authors read this as a lasting mark of childhood ADHD, not a faster slide.
pmc-11714523:
Weiyi Xia, Anum Zafar, Olga Jarrín Montaner, and Haiqun Lin wrote this 2025 methods paper on linking aging paths to the traits of older people without fooling oneself. Studies often sort people into aging trajectory groups by a latent class model, then relate group membership to health and social traits. The snag: class assignment errs, and naive follow-ups inherit that bias.

The team studies a three-step fix that reweights each person by their assignment odds, correcting the error. Computer trials test the fix against the naive path. Then the method is turned on Medicare data, tying aging paths to social and clinical traits. The authors set out when the correction changes the answer and when the naive path will do.
pmc-11714623:
Valentina Garbarino, Hanzhou Wang, and Chih-Ko Yeh pilot a spit test protein as a stress marker tied to Alzheimer's disease, in work from 2025. Millions of Americans live with the disease, and millions more give unpaid care to family members. Over sixty percent of those caregivers report high stress, which itself raises disease risk.

The protein, lactoferrin, helps immune defense in saliva and other fluids. Its levels fall under stress in animals and are lower in Alzheimer's patients than in healthy peers. The pilot probes how well the marker tracks stress in people. A simple spit measure could one day flag caregivers who need help early.
pmc-11714823:
Blanca Zufiria-Gerboles, Daniel Vereb, and Joana B. Pereira report a 2025 scan study of a small but key brain hub with age. The hub sends a chemical signal across much of the brain and helps with alertness and memory. The team used brain scans from six hundred and eighteen adults aged eighteen to eighty-eight. They traced the paths that link this hub to the rest of the brain.

Those links grew weaker with age in many areas, including parts linked to memory and choice. People who said they had memory problems showed a stronger link to one mood-related area. People with high blood pressure or diabetes had weaker links to some of the same core areas. Low mood and poor sleep were also tied to weaker links. The results suggest the hub's paths fade both with age and with common health problems.
pmc-11714923:
Guilherme Balbim and colleagues link daily movement mix with brain size in memory loss, in work from 2025. People with mild cognitive impairment face higher Alzheimer's risk than peers. Sleep, sitting, and activity fill one full day cycle and shape brain health jointly, not alone.

One hundred ten older adults with mild impairment wore motion watches for a week. Brain scans gave grey matter volume for each person in the study group. A higher share of hard activity tied with larger volume in one temporal zone. A higher share of light activity tied with smaller volume in that same zone. Swapping half an hour of sitting for hard activity gave gains.
pmc-11715123:
Dhillon and co-authors review whether long-term outdoor air pollution raises Alzheimer's disease risk, using brain scan proof. Air pollution is a world health threat, and scans now show its harm to the brain. The review followed PRISMA rules and was logged in PROSPERO.

Four databases, MEDLINE, Embase, Scopus, and CINAHL, were searched with set terms. People of all ages and nations counted, with no place limits. Study quality was scored with the Newcastle Ottawa Scale. Findings were summed in narrative form, not pooled numbers. The focus stayed on months-to-years exposure and how scans track disease change.
pmc-11715323:
Han Tong and co-authors connect diabetes, fraying brain wiring, and the speed of late-life memory loss. Diabetes is tied both to damaged white matter, the brain's cabling, and to dementia risk, but whether the wiring damage is the bridge between them was unproven. The team used a long-running Chicago aging cohort with annual cognitive testing.

Six hundred seventy-four older adults, about one in seven with diabetes, received brain scans measuring white matter microstructure. Diabetes-related disruption of that wiring tracked with faster decline across global cognition and specific domains. The result nominates white matter integrity as a measurable waypoint on the road from blood sugar to dementia, and a target for prevention trials.
pmc-11715423:
Ke'alohilani Worthington Antonio, writing solo, lays out a hula-based plan to cut dementia risk in Native Hawaiian elders. Rates of the disease run high in Hawai'i, and Native Hawaiians face early onset more often than most groups. High pressure, weight, diabetes, and blood fats run high as well. Hula, the group's own dance form, joins motion, song, social time, and language in one act.

The plan grows out of two past trials in the same group. Classes mix dance with lifestyle lessons and craft and culture teaching. Group members and hula experts shaped the course, and each site bends it to its own means. Dance thus works on many risk points at once, in a form elders know and trust. The team aims to slow mild thought loss before it hardens into disease.
pmc-11715523:
James Doecke and co-authors compare two blood tests that promise to replace brain scans for detecting Alzheimer's amyloid. Their 2025 study draws 197 participants from an Australian aging cohort, spanning healthy, mildly impaired, and Alzheimer's groups with scan results. Two assay platforms each measured the amyloid ratio and the phosphorylated tau marker pTau217 in plasma.

Both markers separated amyloid-positive from negative participants clearly. The tau marker performed best, with stepwise increases tracking the brain's amyloid load, while the amyloid ratio flattened after the positivity threshold. Accuracy for predicting scan status was highest for pTau217 in the sample and dipped in the healthy-only group. A cheap, accurate blood triage would reshape dementia diagnosis, reserving expensive scans for uncertain cases. The authors position pTau217 as the front-runner, with the amyloid ratio still informative. Platform differences were modest, which matters for adoption.
pmc-11715723:
Heidi Jacobs and co-authors estimate when a small brainstem hub starts to fail in aging, in work from 2025. The locus coeruleus helps wakefulness and memory and may falter early in Alzheimer disease. Timing its decline could open a window for prevention trials.

Data came from 101 adults in a Harvard aging study with repeated brain scans. A modeling method dated each person's onset of low hub integrity. Those dates were set against the onset of raised tau in a memory cortex. Thinking scores over time were tracked as well. Most participants also had amyloid scans at entry. Linked timing would place the hub early in the disease cascade.
pmc-11715823:
Sebastian Palmqvist and co-authors test a blood test for Alzheimer disease in a 2025 study. Nine hundred forty people with early memory complaints gave blood in primary and specialist care. A combined score from two blood markers was judged against spinal fluid results, using cutoffs fixed in advance.

The score sorted patients with high accuracy in both settings, near ninety percent correct calls on either side. It beat primary care doctors, who were right fifty-eight percent of the time, and dementia experts at seventy-four percent. Repeat testing in fresh batches held up. Readers get strong evidence that blood tests can streamline memory clinic work.
pmc-11715923:
Antoine Garnier-Crussard and Gael Chetelat challenge the usual view of white matter hyperintensities, bright spots seen on brain scans. Their 2025 paper notes that these spots are common in aging and Alzheimer disease. They are most often blamed on blood vessel damage and small vessel disease in the brain.

The authors pull together four lines of proof for a second path tied to Alzheimer disease itself. Brain tissue studies, early timing, scan patterns, and gene and marker data all point that way. They propose that tau and amyloid build-up, plus inflammation, can wear down fibers and create some spots. Vessel harm still matters, but it may not explain the whole picture.
pmc-11716023:
Julia Wittrock and Björn Schmitz-Luhn examine what happens when tests can predict a person's risk of Alzheimer's disease years ahead, focusing on insurance, in this 2025 paper. Simple blood or urine tests may soon flag risk for the general public. Insurers may want those results when setting prices for life or health cover, which could deter people from testing at all.

The authors review laws and court rulings across several countries. Rules that do exist mostly cover genetic tests and only partly balance the two sides. Non-genetic prediction is growing fast while legal protection stays thin, leaving patients and insurers unsure of their rights. The paper weighs ways to keep premiums fair without exposing sensitive test results, and argues that clearer rules are now overdue.
pmc-11716123:
Jordan Palms and co-authors ask how feeling in control connects to brain health through mood and body in a 2025 study. Belief in ones own influence splits into mastery, the inner sense of capability, and constraints, the outer sense of barriers. A Michigan aging project gave brain scans and surveys to one hundred twenty adults past fifty-five.

Mastery and constraints were tested against brain measures separately. Earlier work hinted that stronger feelings of constraint track with thinner cortex. Activity and metabolic health have carried the control-to-memory link before. The team probes which health paths carry each half of control into the brain. The split itself is the point.
pmc-11716223:
Grzegorz Walkiewicz and co-authors test whether harmful tau protein can spread from the eye into the brain, in a 2025 mouse study. The retina is part of the central nervous system and can gather the same proteins seen in Alzheimer's disease. A distinct form of tau buildup in the retina might act as an early warning sign. What stayed unclear was whether that buildup could seed damage deeper in the brain.

The team used mice bred to make a mutant human tau protein. Extracts from human brains with tau disease were injected under the retina of young mice. Retinal tau grew with age in the mice and came with loss of nerve cells. Extracts from Alzheimer's brains sped up retinal changes and seeded tau in a visual relay area of the brain, showing spread from eye to brain.
pmc-11716323:
Yiying Gong and co-authors compare eating patterns and brain aging in a large 2025 survey study. Diet shapes how the mind ages, yet few studies had weighed major diets against both Alzheimer deaths and mild cognitive loss. The team used a national health survey with many thousands of adults. Five diet scores were built from daily food recalls.

The scores covered healthy eating, Mediterranean style diets, a blood-pressure diet, and a plant-based index. Death records tracked Alzheimer mortality over years of follow-up. A smaller group took cognitive tests scored against age and schooling norms. Readers can see how each diet pattern lines up with death and test outcomes side by side. That direct comparison is the study's main value.
pmc-11716423:
Younghoon Seo and Hwamee Oh guess brain protein loads in older adults in a 2025 study. The two loads, of sticky amyloid and tangled tau, mark Alzheimer's disease, but the scans that read them are dear and rare. Cheap, plain measures that flag the loads could cut trial screen fails and speed drug tests.

The team built tree-based learning teams on two data sets from a large shared bank. One set held more than a thousand adults for amyloid, the other about four hundred for tau. All members had sound minds or mild loss. The models sort who bears each load from plain tests.
pmc-11716523:
Debora Guerini de Souza and co-authors study, in a 2025 paper, how brain energy use links to anxiety in people with long COVID. Long COVID is still poorly mapped, though it affects many people after the infection clears. Lasting nerve and mind symptoms, such as anxiety, are a common part of it.

The team worked with a group that is often left out of such research. They set out to gauge the true burden of these after effects on the brain. Brain metabolism measures how actively brain tissue uses fuel, and can shift with illness. By linking those measures to anxiety levels, the study tests whether a brain based pattern tracks the symptom. Such a pattern could help define long COVID more firmly, or show it is not a risk factor of its own. Either answer would sharpen care.
pmc-11716623: Igor Levy, writing alone in a conference abstract from two thousand twenty-five, studies patients with mild memory loss and dementia at a general nerve clinic. The work compares two kinds of tests. One records the brain's electric responses to stimuli. The other measures amyloid and tau proteins in spinal fluid, which are signs of Alzheimer's disease in the brain.
pmc-11716723:
Eduardo Garcia Chacon, Annalise Woodring, and Monica Crane compare amyloid scan rates across racial groups in one Southeast practice. Groups outside the majority show more dementia signs yet more often get a label with no biomarker proof. The team reads scans ordered for patients with mild impairment or dementia.

Their 2025 study matches patients across groups and weighs the share with a positive scan, the mark of Alzheimer-type change. About half the whole group scanned positive. In the tight matched read, White patients showed a higher positive share, though the gap fell short of firm proof. The authors press the point: access to the confirming scan itself is part of fair diagnosis.
pmc-11716823:
Craig Ritchie and co-authors set out the design of a large cohort study in 2025. The study follows adults aged fifty and over in Scotland who face some risk of brain decline. New tests and treatments for Alzheimer disease need checks in real world groups, not just tight trials. The cohort gathers deep data on each person who joins.

Records cover risk factors, thinking tests, disease markers, and genes. Early data from the first members show the plan works at scale. Such a rich group can test whether new tools hold up in daily care. It may also speed the search for care matched to each person.
pmc-11716923:
Uyen Vu and co-authors explored in 2025 the trauma histories of older Vietnamese Americans in a cognitive aging study in Northern California. The cohort follows 548 adults aged 65 and over. Short interviews at the first visit asked about life in Vietnam and immigration to the United States. The team analyzed 35 recorded interviews from participants reporting the heaviest trauma exposure.

Six themes emerged, including imprisonment, hardship after release, and escaping Vietnam. Witnessing trauma and rebuilding life in a new country also featured. Most participants were men in their early seventies. The authors frame the stories as testimony of both damage and strength. Understanding this history, they argue, is essential context for studying brain health in this community.
pmc-11718523:
Bastian Schulz and co-authors measure ear dimensions on CT scans across age and sex in a 2024 study. The outer ear helps forensic work such as facial reconstruction and identification of remains, and its shape also interests medicine and industry. Ear size is even tied in folk belief to health and long life, while surgeons rebuild ears for birth defects and looks.

Head scans from hundreds of women and men aged eighteen to ninety seven were measured in three dimensional renderings. Several lengths, widths, and outlines were taken on both sides, plus the area in front of the ear. The paper reports how those measures vary with age and sex, giving reference values for clinical and forensic use.
pmc-11719623:
Textbooks long taught that most cardiac arrests begin with a malignant ventricular rhythm; newer series, counting what medics actually find, claimed still, pulseless rhythms had taken over. Philippe Maury, Nathan Marimpouy, and Maxime Beneyto push back. Their short paper challenges the revisionist reading and defends the older dogma: ventricular arrhythmias remain the main direct trigger of sudden cardiac death.

The stakes are practical, since the first rhythm found decides what treatment can work and how survival statistics are read. The authors marshal the diverging data and argue the discrepancy says more about when rhythms are recorded than about what started the collapse.
pmc-11726923:
The authors review homocystinuria, a state where a sulfur amino acid builds up in the body, and its links to heart and kidney harm, in a 2024 paper. Heart attacks often strike in the morning, when blood pressure fails to dip in sleep as it should. The review ties that lost dip to the body clock and to gene marks that switch genes on and off.

The authors trace how diet, a fat-rich one in their account, may tilt the gene mark system and raise uric acid. Blocking one mark-writing enzyme eased heart and kidney strain in the work they cite. They also propose that hydrogen sulfide, a gas the body makes from the built-up acid, could one day serve as a treatment.
pmc-11727023:
Yi Yu and seven co-authors showed that switching on a longevity enzyme protects the cornea's inner lining in a 2024 paper. After injury, corneal endothelial cells can morph into scar-like mesenchymal cells, clouding the window they should keep clear. The switch is driven by the TGF-beta pathway, and the enzyme SIRT1 is one of its brakes.

In injured rats and in human cells in dishes, activating SIRT1 with resveratrol restored transparency faster, cut scar markers, and preserved the cells' proper identity markers. Blocking SIRT1 reversed every benefit. The enzyme also engaged directly with the pathway's Smad messengers. The authors propose SIRT1 activation as a way to keep corneal cells themselves after damage.
pmc-11727223:
Chia-Cheng Chang and co-authors present a case report and literature review from 2024 about a rare cause of high red blood cell counts in a teenager. The girl had epilepsy, rising hemoglobin levels, and low levels of a hormone that normally drives red cell growth. Tests ruled out the usual bone marrow disorders.

Imaging then showed severe swelling of one kidney, caused by a narrow joint between the kidney and its drainage tube. After surgeons removed the affected kidney and tube, her hemoglobin slowly returned to normal. The authors review past cases and argue that kidney problems belong on the list of causes doctors check in young patients, even when hormone levels are low.
pmc-11728223:
Samantha Montandon and co-authors report a giant skin melanoma removed from an older woman's forehead, in work from twenty twenty-four. Melanoma is a fast spreading skin cancer, and giant forms over five to ten centimetres are rare with poor outlook. The patient was eighty-two and came to care with confusion and urine problems.

A large growth had grown on her forehead for a year and blocked the bridge of her nose. She had first skipped checks for fear of catching COVID. A biopsy proved giant nodular melanoma, the largest face case in the literature per the authors. Surgeons cut it out fully and grafted skin. Two years later she stayed well with no spread and no need for drug or radiation care.
pmc-11728423:
Kota Kakeshita and co-authors watch urine chemistry shift when a herbal formula joins a modern diuretic in heart failure, in a 2024 study. Even on today's best therapy, including the water-channel drug tolvaptan, congestion lingers in many patients. The Kampo formula goreisan is gaining attention as an add-on, but its effect on urine salts was unmeasured.

Twenty-one patients already on tolvaptan-based care received goreisan, and their urine was tracked for the first day. Urine concentration fell significantly, potassium and glucose dropped, and volume tended to rise, while sodium excretion held steady. The team also hunted baseline traits predicting a sodium response. The pattern suggests goreisan moves water more than salt, a nuance for dosing.
pmc-11728623:
Golia and co-authors review a decade of work on cleaning metal-polluted farm soils with useful plants, in a 2024 meta-analysis. Energy crops, aromatic plants, and medicinal plants are attractive because their products can still earn money, but metals might taint them. The review tracks nine toxic elements through plant parts across many studies.

Aromatic plants took up the most metal, and mixtures of metals could raise uptake further, even of cadmium. Energy plants showed interference between copper and cadmium that cut their heating value. Most species parked metals in their roots, keeping harvestable parts fairly clean. The authors frame plant cleanup as a fit for the circular economy.
pmc-11728823:
Ioana Dejeu and co-authors present a 2024 review of new ways to improve liposomes, tiny fat bubbles that ferry drugs in the body. Liposomes can aim drugs at set sites, release them slowly, and cut side effects against plain dosing. The review walks through how they are made and measured.

Fresh tricks in design aim to sharpen targeting and stability. The stakes are wide: cancer care above all, where hitting the tumour and sparing the rest is the whole game. The authors survey where the field's interest is moving and what must improve before these carriers fill their promise in clinics.
pmc-11729723:
Yoshitsugu Nakamura and co-authors test a leaner heart lung machine setup in valve surgery, in a paper whose head dates it to 2024. The operation swaps the aortic valve through a small cut on the right side of the chest. Blood runs through an outside circuit during the work, and a mini version of that circuit aims to spare blood.

Of 242 patients, 166 had the mini circuit and 76 the standard one; matched pairs of 71 were then compared. The mini group diluted the blood less and needed transfusions at under half the standard rate. No deaths or strokes occurred in either group, and silent brain injury rates were the same.
pmc-11732323:
A twist at the top of the spine, where skull meets neck, can lock the head awry after a crash. Omoba and co-authors report a gentler fix in 2024: set the joint by open surgery, with no rods and no fusion. Their patient is a woman of forty-eight, hurt in a high-speed crash.

Tongs and hand traction came first, the standard pulls, but scans showed the twist held. In theatre, the joint was eased back into place by hand and left unfixed. The usual route fuses the joint, trading motion for safety. A set that holds without fusion would spare that trade. The report gives the steps, for a rare injury most surgeons meet seldom.
pmc-11735123:
Kamran Saeed and seven colleagues report outcomes for 278 pituitary tumor patients treated with CyberKnife robotic radiosurgery at one center between 2013 and 2021. The tumors were split into hormone-secreting and non-secreting types. Clinical, visual, hormonal, and imaging results were tracked after treatment delivered in three or five sessions.

Vision improved in about eighty percent of assessable patients, and tumors shrank in about seventy-nine percent. New hormone deficiencies appeared in twenty-six patients across both groups. No significant differences emerged between tumor types for vision or hormone outcomes. Median follow-up was only twelve months, so the authors call the technique effective and safe so far, while urging longer follow-up for late toxicity.
pmc-11736823:
Roslyn Alfred-Demas and four co-authors present a case of liver disease in pregnancy, from 2024. The disease was autoimmune hepatitis, in which the immune system attacks the liver. It is rare, its diagnosis is often unclear, and it raises risks for both mother and unborn child.

Their patient's course was eventful, and the usual proof was shaky: a liver biopsy did not settle the diagnosis. Lab results and the clinical picture still pointed to the autoimmune cause, and the patient responded well to steroid treatment. The authors share the lessons they drew, including the value of a biopsy. They also stress frequent pregnancy testing in women with the disease, and the gains from a team of specialists guiding care together.
pmc-11748423:
Building a transcriptome from raw gene reads is a fiddly chain of tools, and a paper by Miles D Woodcock-Girard and co-authors, published in 2024, wraps that chain into one program. Semblans automates the assembly and processing of RNA sequencing data from short reads to annotated coding sequences.

The flood of public sequence data has spawned many assembly tools, yet running them end to end still demands expertise and hand-tuning between steps. Semblans handles the quality checks, error fixing, trimming, and chimera removal in a fixed, tested order. Compared against earlier published assemblies, it produced the better assembly in nearly every case tried. The authors pitch it as a way to make high-quality transcriptomes routine rather than artisanal.
pmc-11773623:
Jessica Root and twelve co-authors test a rescue plan for brains that lack a key protein, in a 2024 paper. Missing progranulin raises the risk of several brain diseases, among them a form of dementia. The protein is cut inside cell recycling bins into small pieces called granulins. What each piece does on its own has been unclear, with claims pulling both ways.

The team used a virus to add single pieces, or the full protein, into the brains of mice bred to lack it. Each single piece broadly fixed the disease signs. Swollen recycling bins, stray fats and proteins, immune flare-ups, and waste buildup all eased. The pieces homed to the bins in both mouse brain and dish-grown cells. The authors argue the pieces share one helpful job, which makes them candidate drugs.
pmc-11782023:
Wang and coauthors report a lung cancer case with late immune side effects. The patient had spread lung cancer with a HER2 gene change. First immune care failed to hold the cancer back. A drug that links an antibody to a toxin was tried next.

The patient responded well to that linked drug. Five months after immune care stopped, adrenal failure arose. That late effect links to the prior immune care, not the new drug. The team reviews how linked drugs kill cancer cells. They also weigh how such drugs may shift the tumor milieu. The case guides care for like patients.
pmc-11795823:
Jake Cumber and co-authors published a 2025 study that uses scan data and machine learning to find soft tissue markers of a dog skull malformation and its related spinal cord illness. The malformation crowds the brain and the upper spinal cord. It brings pain and, at times, a fluid-filled cavity in the cord. Small flat-faced toy dogs bear it most often. A scan is the standard test, but the diagnosis is hard.

The team trained tools on scans to separate dogs with pain from dogs without, and dogs with the cavity from dogs without. Four regions of the scan separated the pain dogs with strong scores: over eight in ten hits, three in four correct clear calls. A set of shape features came with the regions. Four regions separated the cavity dogs too, at similar scores. The team says the markers could make diagnosis more certain and objective.
pmc-11805123:
Chitra Kamble, Aakash More, and Sudhanshu Dakre report a case where diet supplements and careful sperm choice helped a couple conceive. Their case report was published in twenty twenty-four. The man's sperm moved poorly and carried a high rate of DNA damage, while the woman's womb lining was slightly thin.

For three months the man took two forms of carnitine, a nutrient tied to cell energy. His sperm motion improved and DNA damage dropped by more than half. Doctors then used a high-magnification method to pick the best-shaped sperm for fertilization. The woman got estrogen and her own platelet-rich plasma, which thickened her womb lining. A frozen embryo was placed a month later. A blood test two weeks on showed pregnancy. The case backs combined care for both partners.
pmc-11821423:
Dryland soils lose fertilizer fast, which wastes money and water. Girijaveni V and co-authors tested a natural mineral, identified as mordenite zeolite, as a soil helper in India. Lab tests measured how much nitrogen, phosphorus, and potassium the mineral can hold. Column tests then tracked how much nutrient washed through treated soil. The mineral came from a local market and was checked with X-ray and microscope methods.

The mineral held nitrogen best of the three nutrients. In columns, treated soil lost about fifteen percent less nitrogen than untreated soil at one dose. A pot trial extended the checks to growing plants. The study, published in twenty twenty-four, supports zeolite as a low-cost aid for dryland farms.
pmc-11821923:
Fan Wang and co-authors defend hearing neurons from a chemotherapy drug in a 2025 ear biology study. Cisplatin saves lives but poisons the spiral ganglion neurons that carry sound from the inner ear, and the self-cleaning process called ER-phagy may be part of the story.

The receptor FAM134B, which feeds worn endoplasmic reticulum to the cell's recycling machinery, sits in these neurons. In cultured mouse cochlea tissue, cisplatin stressed the cells, and the team tracked the receptor, oxidative damage, and cell death together. Boosting or silencing the pathway shifted survival, marking ER-phagy as a lever for protecting hearing during cancer treatment.
pmc-11827423:
Mahsa Ghamari and co-authors study a hardy germ in very ill COVID-19 patients in Tehran, in a paper whose head is dated 2024. The germ, Acinetobacter baumannii, thrives in hospitals and shrugs off many drugs. Heavy drug use during the pandemic fed its rise.

The team set out to count cases in critical care and map drug resistance in the samples found. They also read the gene traits of the samples to see how strains relate. Such maps show which drugs still work and how the germ spreads in wards. The work supports tighter drug use and infection control in intensive care units.
pmc-11830923:
Seyedeh Narjes Roudbaraki and co-authors compare mental health in men who cannot father children with men who can in two thousand twenty-four. The study ran at a fertility center in Mashhad, Iran, with sixty men in each group. All men filled in a standard scale for low mood, worry, and stress by phone.

Severe or very severe low mood showed up in about two thirds of the infertile group, far above the fertile group. High worry and stress showed the same gap, again by wide margins. The team also looked at how age, schooling, job, and length of marriage or of infertility shaped these scores. The results argue for mental health care as part of fertility care for men.
pmc-11841423:
Ashish Gupta and three co-authors compare brain states during music videos in a paper whose text is dated 2024. Brain activity flickers through brief stable patterns called microstates. Happy and sad music should tilt that flicker differently. Electrode recordings were split into microstate classes and mapped to brain sources.

Happy videos boosted the class tied to attention in all participants. The class tied to mind wandering faded at the same time. Sad videos flipped the pattern exactly. Source imaging showed stronger activity in central parietal regions when happy. Women showed reduced connectivity in one hub during happy viewing. Women also produced microstates more often overall. The authors link the classes to attentiveness versus drifting thought. Music mood, in short, retunes the brain's idle rhythms.
pmc-11888623:
Lakshmikumari and co-authors compare four simple actions for restoring mouth acidity balance after an acid surge in young children. Saliva pH shapes how cavities form and grow. Many hygiene steps exist, but few studies rank them after acid hits. Forty-three children aged four to five took part. Options were rinsing with water, brushing with water, and brushing with two kinds of toothpaste. Saliva was collected and read with color strips.

Brushing with fluoridated paste raised pH the most clearly. Other steps helped to lesser degrees. Statistical tests compared the changes across methods. The study gives dentists a ranked set of first responses for acid attacks in preschool children.
pmc-11936323:
Laura Ruiz-Gaona and seven co-authors evaluated a digital platform for informal medicine sellers in Lagos, Nigeria, in a 2024 study. Such sellers are many Nigerians' first source of care. The platform offered online ordering, business training, and peer exchange. Sellers from an earlier program round were compared with similar sellers nearby. Statistical weighting balanced baseline differences between groups.

Overall, the platform showed few gains. Business practice scores, genuine medicine counts, and regular client numbers barely moved. Client views of quality dipped slightly. Use of the platform was low across the board. Frequent users kept better records, yet reported lower daily profits. Hardship may have pushed struggling sellers to engage more. The pandemic's turmoil also overlapped the program window. The authors name engagement the platform's central challenge.
pmc-11959123:
Sanal Fernandes and co-authors report outcomes for an ultra-rare slow soft tissue cancer at a large center in North India, in a study from two thousand twenty-four. The cancer spreads widely despite its slow growth. Charts covered thirty-four patients treated from two thousand sixteen to two thousand twenty-three, most with disease that had already spread.

Legs and arms were the most common start sites, and lungs were the most common spread site. Most spread cases got a targeted kinase drug first, with about a year before growth resumed. A small group got immune drugs, and a few stayed free of growth for long spans. Brain spread marked a poor outlook. Readers gain rare real-world detail for this cancer.
pmc-11960323:
Chen and a large team track side effects of valproic acid in children with epilepsy in real clinic records in twenty twenty-four. The drug is a first line treatment, but fears include liver harm and hormone effects. Their hospital in Shenzhen followed close to two thousand children for at least two years. Checks covered blood, liver, and, for teen girls, reproductive scans.

Rates of liver harm and clotting issues stayed flat across short and long use. Blood platelet counts did dip at set points in the first two years. Two children stopped the drug for side effects and recovered after stopping. Teen girls showed no rise in reproductive harm. The authors call first use of the drug broadly safe, with set checks for the youngest.
pmc-11967523:
Sang Gyun Kim wrote a 2023 Korean-language editorial asking whether a staged drug course can replace the standard triple therapy for clearing Helicobacter pylori, a stomach bacterium tied to ulcers and cancer. In Korea, the standard three-drug course was long the only covered first option, yet cure rates have slipped below eighty percent. The staged course gives one antibiotic for five days, then two others for five more, aiming to weaken the bacterial wall first.

Korean trial data put the staged course ahead of the standard one, and the study under discussion reached a higher cure rate still. Side effects ran slightly higher, though rarely enough to stop treatment. Second-line therapy worked less well after staged failure, hinting at resistance. Kim calls for trials of tailored therapy based on resistance testing.
pmc-11971823:
Namenge Philip Tendet and co-authors survey in 2024 what blocks steady home food in a fast growth part of Nairobi, Kenya. City growth has pushed staple food costs up, which leaves many homes short. The study zone is a sub county in the north of the city.

Forms and expert guides drew data from three hundred twenty eight farm folk. Most were men, and most earned in a low band per month. A third farmed in the city, for food, cash, or both. Flood stood out in the block list, with land and cost woes in the mix the team logs.
pmc-11975523:
Jingyue Su and co-authors review how RNA-binding proteins drive osteoarthritis by mishandling RNA, in a 2024 article whose title is printed in Chinese. Osteoarthritis, the wearing disease of joints, still lacks treatments that change its course, partly because its mechanisms are murky. The proteins in question grab specific RNA molecules and govern their lives.

Across a message's lifetime, splicing, editing, stabilizing, and translating, these proteins sit at every checkpoint. When they misbehave, cartilage cells receive wrong instructions and the joint degrades. The review assembles what is known about their roles in healthy and diseased joints, and weighs the challenges of drugging them. Targeting the managers of RNA, rather than single gene products, offers a fresh angle on an old disease.
pmc-11978423:
Maria Caputo and Benedikt Schoser revisit a gene linked muscle illness family in a 2024 review, adding two new patients. Changes in the gene can cause six named illnesses that hit skeletal and heart muscle in distinct mixes.

Shared signs run through the family: weak shoulder and calf muscles, a stiff spine, heart strain, and odd bodies inside muscle fibers. The two new patients share one gene change tied to a posture muscle form. Course ranges from fatal in infancy to mild late in life. Once the main rival gene is ruled out, the authors urge screening this gene in males with high muscle enzyme counts.
pmc-12008323:
A thirteen-author team runs a small randomized trial on whether the choice of anesthesia changes anti-tumor immunity in oral cancer surgery. Ninety adults were split into three groups: standard opioid anesthesia, a lignocaine infusion approach, and a dexmedetomidine infusion approach. Blood drawn before surgery and again 24 hours later was tested for a growth factor tied to tumor spread, helper T cell profiles, and inflammation markers such as IL-6 and IL-10.

The groups looked alike at the start. After surgery, none of the immune measures differed in a statistically firm way among the three techniques. One practical difference did appear: the dexmedetomidine group used markedly less opioid overall, with no major side effects noted. The authors present the trial as a pilot that frames larger studies of anesthesia and cancer immunity.
pmc-12038123:
Francesca Dakin, Tanvi Rai, Sara Paparini, and Trisha Greenhalgh wrote a 2023 paper on support staff in general practice during crises. Support staff include reception, secretarial, and office workers who keep daily practice running. Their workload and health have drawn far less study than those of doctors and nurses.

The years from 2020 to 2023 piled new burdens on these workers, yet pandemic studies of health staff left them out. The authors set out the distinct work support staff do and the strain it adds. They then give practice leaders practical advice: build a workplace based on strong daily relations, notice hidden work, and back staff before a crisis peaks, not only after.
pmc-12068023:
Rayala Naveen Kumar and co-authors report hypervalent iodine chemistry that builds steroidal spiroiminals in a 2024 paper. Steroid amines are reshaped into ring systems with a shared spiro center, a motif prized in drug design.

With excess iodine reagent and iodine in acetonitrile at ice temperature, steroid amines cyclized smoothly. The product mix held both spiroiminals and spiroaminals with twin five-membered rings. The route is the first case of spiroiminal forming through carbon-hydrogen activation. The authors propose a radical-driven ring closure, then oxidation from amine to imine. Chemists get a new way to build complex steroid shapes in one pot.
pmc-12199923:
Krum Vladov and co-authors reported this 2024 case of two linked tumors found at once in a postmenopausal woman. Granulosa cell tumors of the ovary release estrogen, which can drive the womb lining to overgrow and turn cancerous. Bleeding after menopause is the alarm bell that can signal trouble in both organs at once.

Their patient, aged sixty-seven, bled and underwent removal of the womb, both ovaries, pelvic lymph nodes, and part of the abdominal lining fat. Tissue study showed an adult-type granulosa tumor in the ovary and a cancerous polyp in the womb lining, itself overgrown. Staining confirmed hormone receptors and a growth marker in the polyp. The case shows why one hormone-making tumor should trigger a hard look at the whole tract.
pmc-12216523:
Thomas Cudjoe and Ashwin Kotwal ask in a 2024 paper whether machine learning can help explain social connection and its effects on health. Social ties shape health across the whole lifespan, and interest in the topic has grown worldwide. A 2020 national report urged health systems to address loneliness and isolation among older adults.

The pandemic then made isolation common, and later advisories called for joint action across sectors. Care that fits each person must account for fine differences in social life that standard measures miss. The authors weigh what large data sets and learning methods can add, and where they fall short. Clinicians and researchers get a sober map of promise and limits.
pmc-12400323:
Jovan Liau and Vishal Shelat trace how the Declaration of Helsinki changed across sixty years, in a 2025 essay. The declaration guides ethics for research on human subjects worldwide. Each revision answered gaps, harms, or shifts in values since the last.

At its core sits a tension: doctors must do no harm, yet treatments prove themselves only by testing on people. Early versions stressed the lone patient's consent and safety. Later ones added weight to fair sharing of benefits and burdens across society. The authors note standing complaints, such as consent rules that strain in emergencies, even as protections grew steadily stronger.
pmc-12640123:
Sobia Ramzan and co-authors wrote a study, dated 2024 in its text, on hunting useful bacteria in tainted soil in the Layyah district. Soil near waste can hold bacteria that make strong enzymes for factory use. One prized enzyme, named amylase, breaks down starch. No such survey had been done in the district. The team took soil from four waste sources, among them factory, home, and poultry waste.

Soil from animal waste held the most bacteria and the most starch-breaking action. Home waste soil held the widest range of such bacteria. One strain stood out, making the most enzyme under mild heat and neutral water. It kept working in heat, salt, and a wide span of acidity that would stop many kin. Gene tests named the strain. The team says district waste soils are a rich source of hardy factory bacteria.
pmc-12661523:
Dunc Williams, Ganisher Davlyatov, John R Bowblis, and Robert Tyler Braun ask in a 2025 paper what would happen if Medicare stopped repaying hospitals for unpaid patient bills. The program now returns part of those bad debts, worth 1.7 billion dollars in 2022, though the sum is a sliver of hospital revenue.

Using Medicare cost reports, they recalculated every short-term hospital's margin for 2022 without the payments. Small critical access hospitals and rural hospitals stood out as most exposed, with effects varying by state and region. A recent law kept the payments, but the analysis shows which hospitals a future cut would endanger.
pmc-12661723:
Bone forming in soft tissue after injury is traced to immune signals by Jian Wang, Jiangwei Fan, and Xiaohui Yang in this 2025 study. The condition, heterotopic ossification, turns muscle and other soft tissue partly to bone. Which cells drive the change, and what signals they send, was unclear.

The team sequenced single cells from injured mice developing the condition. They found varied states among both progenitor cells and macrophages, the immune cells that clean up injury sites. A signal sent by macrophages, called Osm, tracked with progenitors turning down a wrong, cartilage-like path. A gene named Spi1 switched macrophages on early after injury. Blocking that signal path may lower the risk of unwanted bone.
pmc-12661823:
Qi Zhang studies in 2025 how rural doctors in China bent their practice under money pressure during the COVID-19 pandemic. Township hospitals there work under a capped global budget for insured patients, which rewards thrift. Records show how doctors answered when the pandemic squeezed funds.

Prescribing of traditional herbal decoction pieces rose, driven by doctors who already favored them rather than new converts. Doctors also trimmed drug counts and service volume for patients whose insurance shared costs, cutting average payments per visit by about five percent. Self-paying patients saw no such shift. The paper weighs how pay design steers doctor choices.
pmc-12662923:
Jingxiong Chen and five co-authors asked whether removing the main tumor helps colon neuroendocrine cancer patients whose disease reached the liver, in a 2025 study. A national registry supplied four hundred forty-nine cases from twenty ten to twenty twenty-one. Right-sided tumors made up most of the set. Matched comparisons balanced the groups before judging surgery.

Right-sided cases lived slightly longer than left-sided ones. Resection of the primary tumor extended survival on both sides. Gains were clear after matching as well. The team built a scoring chart from age, tumor size, and surgery status. The chart predicted six, twelve, and twenty-four month survival with fair accuracy. Checks confirmed its clinical usefulness. The authors offer it for counseling in this high-risk group. Surgery deserves consideration even with liver spread, they argue.
pmc-12663123:
Yuan Tian and co-authors trace how health beliefs ease treatment choice conflict in slipped disc patients in a 2025 study. Back pain disables millions of people worldwide, and herniated discs offer many care paths, leaving patients torn between surgery and gentler care.

A survey of 737 patients linked three scales: beliefs, expectations, and decision conflict. Stronger beliefs came with far less conflict, and rosier expectations also calmed choices. Expectations carried about a fifth of the belief effect, a partial bridge in the model. The path suggests that shaping what patients expect can soften hard treatment choices.
pmc-12663223:
Kee Kee Chng and co-authors improve how mosquito control programs sort male from female mosquitoes. Their paper appeared in 2025. Programs that release sterile or incompatible males must not release females, which bite and can spread disease. The team added a salt bath, a 15 percent sodium chloride treatment, to an automated sorting system.

The salt step cut female contamination among released males about thirtyfold. The study also reports how salt water affects mosquito larvae and pupae, which matters for mass rearing. Sorting sits at the heart of both control methods named in the title. Cleaner sorting means safer, cheaper releases. The authors present the tweak as a practical upgrade for large programs fighting dengue and other mosquito-borne diseases.
pmc-12664223:
Matthias Burkard Aulbach and co-authors test a phone-based training that nudges people to approach healthy food and avoid the rest. Approach-avoidance training has shown promise with alcohol, and food is a natural next target. Users push the phone away from bad picks and pull it toward good ones.

Their 2025 trial gave the training six times over two weeks, with personal lists of foods to cut and foods to add. A placebo group did a balanced version of the same task. Craving and intake were logged daily, before, during, and after training, with a check one month on. Active training lowered the strength of cravings for cut foods, though not how often cravings struck.
pmc-12664323:
Vyshnavi Sathish reviews the role of suction in kidney stone surgery in a narrative review from two thousand twenty-five. Kidney stones affect at least one in ten people, and flexible scopes passed through the urinary tract are a main treatment. The method can leave fragments behind and carries infection risk.

Suction has long been used in a related stone surgery, but its use with flexible scopes is new. The review weighs studies from the past decade on several suction designs. Suction lowered pressure inside the kidney, shortened surgery, and improved the view. Newer sheath designs raised stone-free rates and cut fever after surgery. The author notes added complexity and calls for large randomized trials to set best practice.
pmc-12664823:
Brianna Shepherd and four co-authors present a 2025 field study on beech leaf disease, a fast-spreading illness of American beech trees. The team asked what the disease does to fallen leaves after they drop to the forest floor. Sick leaves break down at a different pace than healthy ones, and that pace shapes how carbon and plant food move through the woods.

In a litterbag trial, the team tracked sick and healthy leaf litter as it decayed in the field. Sick litter broke down faster than healthy litter. The fungi living on the two kinds also differed, with more fungi that feed on dead matter on the sick leaves. The authors warn that wide beech loss could shift how whole forests store carbon.
pmc-12665023:
Melikt Esuyawka and co-authors compared overweight and obesity in bankers and teachers in southern Ethiopia in two thousand twenty-five. Both jobs involve long sitting, little activity, and high mental load. Workplace wellness support in Ethiopia is limited, and local data were scarce.

Their survey in Wolaita Sodo in August two thousand twenty-two covered two hundred twenty-seven bankers and two hundred eighty-seven teachers. Overweight affected about forty-four percent of bankers versus twenty-two percent of teachers, and obesity was also about three times higher in bankers. Low activity, female sex, and marital status mattered in both groups. Snacking, higher income, and alcohol added risk for bankers. The authors urge workplace health programs.
pmc-12667423:
Qian Liu and four co-authors trace how massage eases inflamed muscle at the molecular level in mice. Their study appeared in twenty twenty-five. Massage relieves pain widely, yet its inner workings, and its ties to traditional Chinese medicine, stay murky.

Mice with inflamed leg muscle got daily pressure at two classic acupoints for fourteen days. Their pain thresholds for heat and touch rose clearly. In the nerve clusters serving the leg, one receptor tied to cannabis-like signals rose. Two partners in a touch-sensing pathway fell. The authors read this crosstalk as the mechanism: pressure retunes the sensors and calms inflammation signals inside muscle cells. The work gives massage a testable biological story.
pmc-12670723:
Karl Sallin looks back on resignation syndrome, the illness that struck refugee children in Sweden and then vanished, in this 2025 paper. For over two decades, some asylum-seeking children sank into a state of complete withdrawal. Recovery was thought to require permanent residency, and that belief became part of the treatment.

The author traces how the story changed. The condition respected borders and picked only some migrant groups, and cases of abuse and feigned illness came to light. Policy then flipped: permits became temporary, courts gave the syndrome little weight, and care centered on child protection, sometimes separating child and family. The new strategy worked, and the endemic faded. Sallin argues the syndrome was created, fed, and finally reversed by the society around it, and that other fashionable illnesses deserve the same hard look.
pmc-12672623:
A large international team built an explainable AI tool that helps brain surgeons plan tumor removal, in a 2025 study. Glioblastoma surgery improves survival, but forecasting how much tumor can be safely removed is hard. The team wanted estimates that doctors can inspect, not black-box guesses.

Their model learned from 811 patients who had microsurgery at many centers. It sorted likely outcomes into total, near-total, and subtotal removal. Tests at outside centers confirmed the model travels well. Health scores, age, tumor size, and awkward tumor locations drove the forecasts most. When surgeons and the model worked together, accuracy jumped far above experts working alone. The authors argue that pairing human judgment with a transparent machine gives the best preoperative plans. The study spans model building and outside validation in one report.
pmc-12679123:
A heart attack treated with a stent often leaves anxiety behind, and that anxiety can harm the heart in turn. Xin Tang and two co-authors review in 2025 how often such anxiety disorders follow the procedure, how they show themselves, and what helps. Between a fifth and two fifths of patients are affected, women more than men.

Signs tend to appear within two weeks and mix body symptoms, fearful thoughts, and avoidance of effort. Risk runs higher in younger patients, women, and those with past mental illness or weak support. Left alone, anxiety tracks with more readmissions and repeat events. The authors back screening about a week after the procedure and care that joins talk therapy, medicines, and rehab.
pmc-12681423:
Yuru Zhang, Haiying Fan, Yiman Zhang, and a wider team wrote this research paper, published in 2025. It feeds bitter melon powder to carp on high-starch diets and finds the supplement shields the fish from the metabolic harm that starchy feed usually causes.

Cheap starch in fish feed saves money but overloads carp, piling up fat and disturbing blood sugar. The team added the powder at three doses. Supplemented fish showed lower blood sugar and triglycerides and stronger antioxidant defenses. Damage to the liver-like organ and gut lining eased visibly. Muscle regained two healthy fats that the starchy diet had drained. At the highest dose, stored sugar and fat in tissues fell. Gene activity shifted toward burning sugar rather than storing it. The authors pitch bitter melon as a practical feed additive.
pmc-12683923:
Mattan Arazi and four co-authors review, in a 2025 paper, the eye care system of Israel as a case study in public health. Israel has promised basic care to all residents since a 1994 law, and eye care sits inside that universal frame. The team judge the system with the World Health Organization's building blocks for health systems.

They find strong points: eye care is well joined to general care, specialists are plentiful, and advanced services are widely on offer. Gaps remain for poorer and outlying communities, who face cost and travel barriers to advanced treatment and steady follow-up. The authors urge stronger local and primary eye services, a fairer spread of staff, and better national data, and draw lessons for other countries.
pmc-12691023:
Yuan-Chi Lin and co-authors review in 2025 blood and urine tests based on small molecule profiling as a way to predict serious prostate cancer. The standard blood marker cannot tell cancers that need treatment from harmless ones, which leads to overdiagnosis, while scans are costly and slow. Profiling many small molecules at once offers a sharper tool.

Studies found shifts in how patients handle fats, sugars, and amino acids. A few molecules moved the same way in more than one study. Combined panels beat the standard marker, above all when joined with clinical factors. Two urine tests may outdo most shop bought assays. The authors warn that methods differ so much across studies that direct comparison is risky.
pmc-12692323:
Gehan Abdelsamea and co-authors test a phone app exercise program for new mothers whose abdominal muscles have separated after cesarean birth, in a 2025 randomized trial. Forty first-time mothers were split evenly between the app program and a traditional exercise routine. Each was done at home for half an hour, three times a week, for eight weeks, with weekly clinic check-ins. Ultrasound measured the muscle gap, and strength, girth, and satisfaction were tracked.

Both programs shrank the gap and strengthened the muscles. The app group gained more on the upper gap, strength, girth, and satisfaction scores. The authors present guided app training as a practical upgrade for post-cesarean recovery.
pmc-12693423:
Bikash Isaac and co-authors make in 2025 tiny dots of bismuthene, a sheet form of bismuth, for clean chemical production. The dots, about 2.2 nanometres wide, are peeled from the bulk material by an electric method in a solvent at room temperature. Their small size gives them many active edges.

The dots drive the oxygen reduction reaction, a step in fuel cells and in making hydrogen peroxide. They steer the reaction down the two-electron path that yields peroxide, rather than water. Their speed measures beat standard platinum catalysts, and they held up well over repeated cycles. The work points to a cheap, green catalyst for peroxide making.
pmc-12693923:
Fuchao Li and eight co-authors describe a new current sensor in a 2025 paper. Modern power systems carry currents that range from very weak to very strong. That wide range is hard for one sensor to cover well.

The sensor uses a magnetoelectric composite that pairs a magnetic material with lead zirconate titanate. It works in torque mode. Tests showed strong sensitivity at power frequency and a linear range up to the top value tested. It could also detect very weak alternating currents. The authors say this mix of wide range and fine detection suits power system tasks. Those tasks include load checks and fault finding.
pmc-12694823:
Pérez-Sindín, Wójcik, Chen, and Prishchepov present a study from twenty twenty-five testing night lights as a stand-in for local inequality in Spain. Official income data at town level are rare and slow. The team compute light per person from satellite and population grids. A Gini index per town follows from pixel-level light spread. Over eight thousand towns are covered for twenty fifteen to twenty twenty. Light-based and official income indices link significantly. The link is strongest in small and rural towns.

Tracking over time beats one-off snapshots in their models. Some towns show high light inequality despite low official figures. Informal work may explain those gaps, they suggest. The method offers cheap, global inequality monitoring.
pmc-12696023:
Kyle Rodman and co-authors track drought death risk in dry woodlands of the US Southwest in a 2025 study. Pinyon-juniper woods span 40 million hectares of the dry West. Drought now comes in fast runs. Past drought may prime trees for death in the next, a feedback loop. The team used a long watch net that spans 1998 to 2023. Models weighed tree size, ground facts, and past drought change.

Tree counts and trunk bulk fell through the whole span. Since 2014 death outran new growth, and near half the live trees showed crown dieback. Soil food and root fungi friends did shield lone trees. Yet stand shifts swamped those shields: death risk rose 28.2 percent from 2014 to 2023 for trees that lived. The loop, the team say, is live and self-feeding.
pmc-12696923:
Orazio Palmieri and eleven co-authors offer a 2025 review of precision medicine for inflammatory bowel disease. The review covers ulcerative colitis and Crohn disease, the two main forms. Rates of these chronic, relapsing diseases have risen sharply in recent decades, likely tied to diet, city life, and less early microbe contact.

Genes alone do not explain onset, so gut microbes and their products take center stage. A skewed microbe mix, with fewer helpful species, marks the diseases. The authors weigh how machine learning and connected devices can join multi-omics data from noninvasive tests. Such joins could expose how microbe and metabolite paths drive inflammation. The goal is sharper diagnosis and care matched to each patient.
pmc-12699623:
Husakova and co-authors gauge mental health in Czech patients with joint diseases in a 2025 study. They compared 233 patients with rheumatoid arthritis or spine arthritis against 170 healthy adults. A trained worker ran a standard mind interview, and patients filled mood surveys. Disease activity scores were logged the same day.

About a quarter to a third of patients had at least one mental disorder, far above the healthy group. Depression, long low mood, and suicidal thoughts led the list. Patients with a disorder showed higher disease activity and worse self-rated health. Most of them turned down offered mind care. The authors press clinics to screen minds as part of joint care.
pmc-12699823:
Hao Cheng and co-authors report a case of pain control after major liver surgery, achieved with a new nerve block and a long-acting drug. Open liver removal hurts from both the wound and organs, and standard options carry risks for patients with clotting problems. Before surgery, the team used ultrasound to place a retro-superior costotransverse ligament block at three spine levels in a 38-year-old woman, injecting a mix of standard and slow-release bupivacaine.

The block numbed a band of her chest and back. Her blood pressure and heart rate stayed steady during surgery, and for two days her pain scores, at rest and while coughing, stayed between zero and two out of ten. She needed no rescue painkillers and never touched her pain pump. The authors call the technique a promising, opioid-sparing option for abdominal operations.
pmc-12699923:
Maëlle Scouvemont and seven co-authors reviewed in 2025 whether physical activity is the bridge between living setting and sleep. Homes and neighborhoods shape both how much people move and how well they sleep, but the middle step is rarely tested head-on. The team searched three databases and screened over a thousand studies.

Only five studies tested the full chain, and their quality was moderate. Better access to recreation areas was among the links reported. The thin yield is itself the finding: a plausible and important pathway rests on very little direct proof. The review marks exactly where new studies should aim.
pmc-12700123:
Getachew Kassahun and co-authors traced nine years of malaria at one hospital in western Tigray, Ethiopia, in a study published in 2025. Malaria still ranks among the top causes of hospital admission and death in the country. The team read all confirmed cases in the hospital records from 2011 to 2019, and checked the control measures in use there.

More than 36,000 cases were recorded, with fifty deaths in the hospital. The more severe parasite species made up over six in ten cases. Deaths were highest in the last quarter of the year and among people aged fifteen and older. Case counts rose and fell from year to year in a clear pattern, while death counts held steady. No shift in parasite species appeared. The authors say control efforts have gained ground but malaria remains a heavy burden, and they call for steady monitoring.
pmc-12700923:
Sirarat Ittipuripat and co-authors test a late-start birth control pill plan in a 2025 trial. Starting the pill a week into the cycle could cut the risk of an unplanned pregnancy for women who start late. A newer pill mix with a natural-type hormone had little data for such late starts.

Thirty-six healthy women with steady cycles were split by lot between the new mix and an older one. Both groups began on day seven to nine of the cycle. Staff checked whether egg release was blocked as it should be. The trial asks whether the new mix is no worse than the old at this late start, a fact clinics need.
pmc-12701823:
Preeti Solanki, Mohini Rana, Karnail Singh Choudhary, Vishal Ahuja, Vinay Kumar, and Anuradha Tyagi review bee venom as a candidate treatment for leukemia, in a 2025 paper. Leukemia forces abnormal white cell growth from the marrow. Current care mixes transplants, immune therapy, and chemotherapy. Resistance, side effects, and cost all limit those options. Bee venom offers a natural alternative worth testing. Its main active part, melittin, makes up about half the dry venom.

Lab studies show the venom kills leukemia cells in dishes. It triggers programmed cell death and blocks survival pathways. Effects vary with dose, time, and cell line. Many standard leukemia cell lines have been tested. The review gathers this in vitro evidence in one place. It also weighs the gaps in present studies. Pairing venom with standard drugs may boost effect. Targeted delivery could cut harm to healthy cells. Human trials remain a future step.
pmc-12703023:
Warayoot Luangmaneerote and co-authors report real-world outcomes for a rare brain lymphoma treated where top care is scarce. Their 2025 study covers primary central nervous system lymphoma, newly found in 94 patients from 2011 to 2024. Rich settings favor strong drug rounds plus stem cell transplant.

In this center, high-dose drugs plus whole brain radiation form the local standard. One group of 56 patients got a two-drug round, and a second group got the main drug alone. The team tracks survival with standard models. Separate tests compare thinking skills and life quality in patients in remission against matched lymphoma peers. The data show what the local standard achieves outside trial settings.
pmc-12703823:
A European Food Safety Authority report describes a training project on weighing risks and benefits when diets shift toward climate-friendly foods. The fellow learned risk-benefit assessment, a method that combines nutrition, toxicology, microbiology, and human health data. The test case replaced meat with insects or plant foods such as lentils and red kidney beans.

The work covered Croatia, France, and Greece. The fellow defined the diet options, listed the data needed, and noted what was missing. A multi-criteria tool ranked the options for each scenario. The report also suggests ways to develop these assessment methods further for future dietary shifts.
pmc-12705823:
Reza Moshfeghinia and his four co-authors pool, in a 2025 review, the trial evidence for treating depression with gentle electric stimulation used at home. The technique passes a weak current through the scalp to nudge brain activity. Clinic versions exist; home versions promise reach and convenience. From over 500 studies, five randomized trials with 415 patients met the bar.

Active stimulation beat sham treatment on both standard depression scales, by roughly two to three points, and eased anxiety scores as well. Reported side effects were mild and local: skin redness, tingling or burning, and occasional headaches. The authors judge home treatment effective on current evidence. They call for bigger trials with better adherence tracking and long-term follow-up before it can be recommended broadly.
pmc-12706023:
Saravanan and Nirmala test concrete made almost fully from crushed old concrete, stiffened with steel fibers. Their 2025 study swaps in recycled coarse stone entirely and a tenth of the fine sand, chasing relief for quarries and dumps alike. Few studies replace both sizes at once, and recycled mixes usually lose strength.
