The recycled blend flowed more easily in the wet state, a welcome surprise. Steel fibers then cut that flow by a fifth to a third, as fibers do. Strength tests told the expected harder story: recycled stone alone lowered crush and split strength against a natural mix. The fiber arm of the study checks how far steel thread can claw that loss back. Full numbers fill the paper's test tables.
pmc-12706523:
Grace Blackburn and co-authors run the first test of central place foraging theory in a bird that breeds cooperatively, in a study from 2025. The theory says a parent bird should carry bigger loads when it gathers food farther from the nest. That rule, from Orians and Pearson, keeps the trip worth its cost.

The team fed wild Southern Pied Babblers one, two, or three mealworms at varied distances from active nests. Birds were more apt to return with bigger loads and from nearer spots. But the key link was missing: at far distances, bigger loads did not raise returns. More chicks per adult did raise provisioning, and older birds responded to the largest loads more than younger ones.
pmc-12706923:
Victoria Odemary Lyimo and co-authors test lessons on health cost risk for rural homes in Tanzania in a 2025 study. State health cover grows, but low grasp of ruinous care costs slows sign-up. Over five hundred home heads split by lot into lesson and plain groups.

The lesson group got a month of risk lessons, then two months of watch. Its grasp of risk cover and of health cover rose by a clear gap at the end check. Will to sign up rose with grasp, the team finds, which backs lessons as a sign-up lever.
pmc-12707823:
Sabelo Hadebe and co-authors present a 2025 study on an antibody's role in asthma. Allergic asthma is driven by a type of immune response, with twitchy airways as a key trait. The antibody studied is the first kind the body makes, and its wider role was unclear. The team gave house dust mite extract to normal mice and to mice lacking that antibody, then measured airway response and immune signs.

Mice without the antibody kept the allergic inflammation but lost much of the airway twitchiness. Gene scans of lung tissue pointed to one gene that may carry the effect. Deleting that gene in human airway muscle cells changed how they contracted under some triggers. The authors say the antibody acts on airways apart from allergy itself. That split could guide new asthma drugs.
pmc-12708623:
David Calvo and a large team of co-authors studied 25 patients with persistent atrial fibrillation in a 2025 report. Atrial fibrillation is a common heart rhythm disorder. The team gave patients adenosine, a drug known to accelerate the rotational activity thought to drive the disorder. They mapped electrical activity across the atria from outside the body, twice at baseline and again at the peak effect of a 12 mg dose.

Adenosine changed the distribution of dominant frequencies across the atria in an uneven way. The authors built a new measure, the DF Stability Index, which combines how much a site's frequency rose with how stable that site was. Patients in whom all high-index regions were ablated were more often free of arrhythmia on follow-up. The authors propose the index as a physiological guide for ablation treatment.
pmc-12708823:
Marie Vinches and co-authors run a trial of physical rehabilitation during head and neck cancer treatment in a 2025 study. Radiation-based cures leave many patients weak and tired, and a deconditioning cycle can worsen side effects and quality of life. Their NUTRIMOUV trial tested whether structured exercise plus nutritional care could break that cycle.

Seventy patients were randomized across centers. The exercise group got electrical stimulation of the thigh muscles during treatment, then home bike training three times a week for twelve weeks, while controls got standard care. Success meant a forty percent gain in endurance time or sustaining thirty minutes at three months. The exercise group succeeded at sixty-eight percent versus twenty-seven percent for controls, with endurance rising rather than falling.
pmc-12709023:
Xiongwen Yang and nine colleagues build a blood-test score to predict who benefits from immunotherapy for a rare lung cancer. Pulmonary lymphoepithelioma-like carcinoma is linked to Epstein-Barr virus, and the standard PD-L1 test predicts checkpoint inhibitor response poorly. The team analyzed 254 patients treated across six Chinese centers.

Their composite score combines routine blood indices and serum tumor markers, fitted against progression-free survival. High scores meant much shorter survival in both training and validation groups, and the score outperformed PD-L1, which lost significance in adjusted models. Nomograms using the score discriminated well. The authors pitch the cheap, universally available test as a practical aid for individualized treatment decisions.
pmc-12709723:
Zheng and co-authors pool trials of interval training done with blood flow restriction cuffs, in a 2025 review. The method pairs hard interval work with cuffs that limit blood flow, and earlier work shows gains from gentler pairings, but the interval version was untested as a whole. The team screened six databases and kept twenty-four studies with six hundred seven adults.

The pooled effect was small but real for aerobic capacity and moderate for muscle strength. Peak and mean power, the anaerobic measures, showed no clear gain, though the samples were small. Effects shifted with training intensity, program length, and cuff settings.
pmc-12709823:
Bauci and co-authors compare rates of severe appendicitis during Switzerland's first COVID-19 lockdown in two regions hit very differently by the virus, in a 2025 study. Surgeons in many places reported more burst or gangrenous appendices during lockdowns, fearing patients delayed care. The literature, though, is mixed, so the team tested the claim across two Swiss centers.

They compared March to June 2020 with the same months in 2019, covering 393 patients in all. The share of complicated cases rose from 28 percent before the pandemic to 39 percent during lockdown. In Ticino, the harder-hit region, the share nearly doubled, and patients arrived later than in both the prior year and the other region. Among patients under 20, the complicated share jumped from 12 to 47 percent.
pmc-12710223:
Anna Ratiu and co-authors cost out life-support ECMO hospital stays in Medicare data, in work from twenty twenty-five. Extracorporeal oxygenation saves lives but consumes heavy hospital resources. Medicare inpatient records span the years around the pandemic. Payments, estimated costs, and stay lengths are tallied per case. Cases split by procedure group, code, and ECMO circuit type.

Venovenous support carries the highest median cost and payment. Venoarterial support is the most common type by far. It is also the only type whose median payment beats median cost. Central support sits between the other two on most measures. Rural and teaching hospitals log ECMO cases far more often. Hospitals mostly lose money on this lifesaving care. Payment policy faces the gap these numbers expose.
pmc-12710423:
Julien Cohen, Matthieu Papillard, and Romain Messe report a rare delayed bleeding emergency after a standard lymph node sampling procedure. Their 2025 case report follows a thirty-one-year-old woman with a liver vein disorder. The sampling, done by ultrasound-guided needle through the airway, went smoothly.

Seven days later she coughed up large amounts of blood. Scans and a camera check found two bulges on an artery near the sampled nodes, and vessel imaging confirmed them. Doctors sealed the lesion with tiny coils fed through the vessel. Two months on, no new bleeding had occurred, even after blood thinners resumed. The authors urge pre-checks of nearby vessels and fast imaging when delayed bleeding strikes.
pmc-12710723:
Torous and Cipriani comment on the evolving role of generative artificial intelligence in mental health care, in work from twenty twenty-five. Generative tools are reshaping mental health, but the direction of change is unclear. Earlier waves, smartphone apps and virtual reality, stumbled on weak evidence and poor integration.

The commentary reviews recent evidence and trends. It asks where the tools can add real value while avoiding past pitfalls. Moving from wellness chatbots to clinical psychiatric tools needs a new generation of investigation, integration, and leadership, the authors argue. The piece is a field level agenda, not a trial report.
pmc-12711123:
Adilson dos Santos and co-authors test in a 2025 rat study whether the acid drug pantoprazole harms the heart around a blocked artery event. Hearts were starved of blood for ten minutes, then reperfused for 75 minutes. Rhythm faults, block, and death were scored from tracings across four arms.

Drug dosing split by timing, one arm dosed before the block and one before reperfusion. Ventricular rhythm faults did not differ between any of the groups. Dosing before the block raised block events, deaths, and tissue injury against saline controls. Dosing before reperfusion instead lowered those harms and a blood injury marker. Timing flips the drug from threat to shield in this model.
pmc-12711523:
Farhan M Asrar and six co-authors trace the role of doctors who became astronauts, in twenty twenty-five. Their account spans six decades of space flight. The first doctor in space was Boris Yegorov, who flew in nineteen sixty-four. A year later, NASA first chose doctors as astronauts. The authors write in part from their own first-hand time in this field.

Doctors bring medical skill, a science-based way of thinking, and leadership to crews. Those traits mattered on short early flights and matter still more now. Flights are moving toward deep space and much longer stays away from Earth. Readers see how care for the body and care in flight grew up side by side.
pmc-12711623:
Niklas Amann and co-authors examine how care changed after a German center for inherited breast and ovarian cancer gained formal certification, in this 2025 study. The center, at the University Hospital Erlangen, was certified from 2021 onward. The team compared patient records from 2018 to 2023, split into the years before and after that step.

Genetic testing rose sharply after certification, from nine hundred sixty-two tests to one thousand seven hundred thirty-two, and testing among women with breast cancer doubled. Enrollment in the close-watch surveillance program grew even faster, and doctors advised risk-reducing surgery more often. The share of tests finding harmful variants stayed near one in nine in both periods. The authors credit certification with widening access to counseling and prevention that follow shared standards of care.
pmc-12711923:
Wei and coauthors study a vessel receptor that may drive cervix cancer spread. The receptor sits on vessel cells and pairs with a kin receptor. That pair steers new vessel growth, which tumors need to spread. The role of the first receptor in tumors stayed fuzzy.

The team cut the receptor in cervix cancer cells in the lab. Growth, motion, and invasion tests tracked the effect. Mouse grafts and lung spread models added in vivo proof. Fluid from cut cells was tested on vessel cells too. Receptor loss curbed growth and spread in the tests. Vessel growth from tumor signals also fell sharply.
pmc-12712123:
Kyungwon Min and co-authors compared freeze survival plans in the two flowering plants native to Antarctica in 2025. Both plants face freeze-thaw swings even in the growing season. Survival needs both freeze tolerance and good recovery after thaw, a combined trait that past studies measured in clashing ways.

The team used a standard freeze test and two checks: salt leakage for membrane health and light response for leaf cell health. One species hardened both systems in the cold, and its two injury scores agreed. The other species hardened mainly its leaf cells, so the light check proved the better guide. Sugar shifts backed the split in strategy.
pmc-12712623:
Paul Frandsen and Ralph Holzenthal revisit a famous 1939 drawing of caddisfly family history in this 2025 paper. Caddisflies are insects whose young live in fresh water, and many build cases or shelters. The 1939 figure, by Margery and Lorus Milne, sketched how the group evolved. The new paper redraws that figure in the same style, using fresh gene-based trees.

Their study infers that the first caddisfly larva lived free in flowing water and ate dead plant matter. Before pupating, it spun a cocoon inside a dome-shaped shelter. Later branches gained varied building habits, from cases to nets. Those skills helped caddisflies spread widely and become one of the most varied groups of freshwater animals.
pmc-12713223:
Marek Oleszczyk and co-authors check how far family medicine has come in ten Central and Eastern European lands. Their twenty twenty-five study updates a twenty twelve survey done after health reforms. Those reforms adopted family practice models late in the last century.

A mix of literature review, data sets, and a key informant survey drove the update. Family medicine is now a named specialty in all ten lands, with firm legal bases. How much care it covers still varies, with some systems splitting child care away. The title asks how far on the road each land has traveled, and the answer is: far, but unevenly.
pmc-12713623:
Lata Rani and co-authors review ways to clean PFAS out of water sustainably, in this 2025 Europe PMC review. These synthetic 'forever chemicals' resist breakdown, accumulate in water supplies and are linked to cancer, nervous system and reproductive harm. Human activity is their main source.

The review critically compares the toolbox: chemical oxidation and reduction, adsorption onto materials, electrochemical treatment, biological cleanup and membrane filtration, plus treatment trains that chain methods together. Each approach has strengths and limits against such stubborn molecules. The authors conclude that much more research is needed before PFAS remediation is truly effective and sustainable at scale.
pmc-12714823:
Mohammed Rashed and co-authors compare hip fracture treatments for older patients in 2025. They studied people over 55 with a broken socket in the hip joint. One path fixes the bone with plates, while the other replaces the hip right away with a modular cup.

The review covered 36 patients treated by one senior surgeon over five years. Hip scores at six months were far higher in the replacement groups than in the fixation group. All repeat operations fell in the fixation group, and none were needed after replacement. Scans showed the new cups stayed firmly fixed in every replacement case.
pmc-12715923:
Felix Heinrich and co-authors propose a better score for breeding prediction models in a 2025 paper. Genomic selection ranks animals and plants for breeding by DNA. Standard scores reward overall fit, not picking the best few.

A model can fit well yet choose mediocre parents for the next round. Normalized cumulative gain measures the payoff of the chosen top group. Four datasets from animals and plants tested the idea broadly. Nine common prediction methods were compared under both scoring styles. Rankings of methods shifted when selection gain was the target. Readers learn to judge breeding models by what breeding actually needs.
pmc-12716723:
Musa Adekunle Ayanwale and co-authors survey four hundred Nigerian vocational educators on what makes artificial intelligence enter their classrooms with its ethics intact. Technical and vocational training leans on trust and hands-on norms, so ethical slips carry weight. The team measured guiding ethical principles, compliance with AI guidelines, expected adoption outcomes, and the backing of institutional policy.

Statistical modeling showed teachers' ethical principles driving both their compliance and their hopes for adoption. Compliance in turn carried part of the principles' effect on outcomes, acting as a bridge. Policy support, surprisingly, did not sharpen the principles-to-compliance link. Even where formal AI rules were missing, ethically minded leadership filled the gap. The study urges schools to grow that ethical culture alongside any rulebook.
pmc-12717223:
Yasmin Jolasun and co-authors present a method called SIDISH in a 2025 paper that joins two kinds of gene data to find high risk cells. Single cell data show detail for each cell but come from small groups. Bulk data cover large groups but blur the detail of each cell. The new method aims to gain the strengths of both.

SIDISH learns from both data types at once and links cell patterns to patient outcomes. A test module then mimics drug action in the computer to flag targets that could cut the high risk cells. The method also works on maps of gene activity in tissue. For care teams, it offers a way to find warning signs and rank treatments before lab tests.
pmc-12717323:
Siyuan Yang and co-authors show how chronic stress feeds pancreatic cancer through the immune system. Stress is a known risk factor for this deadly cancer, but the wiring was unclear. Working in mice under chronic stress, the team traced a chain that starts with the stress hormone norepinephrine and ends with immune cells that shield the tumor.

The hormone reached the liver and switched on its complement system, an ancient defense arm. One complement fragment, C5a, then recruited suppressor cells into spleen and tumor, where they raised shields that blunt anti-tumor attack. Blocking the fragment's receptor broke the chain, as did atenolol, a common drug that blocks the hormone's liver receptor. Treated mice grew smaller tumors. The authors propose this stress-to-complement-to-suppressor axis as a treatment target.
pmc-12717423:
Mohsen Alizadeh Noghani, Sebastian Green, and Edgar Bolivar-Nieto share a data set of whole-body movement in healthy adults, released in twenty twenty-five. Balance research and wearable robot control both need accurate tracking of the body center of mass. Many data sets lack full-body markers or complete ground force records, and most cover only repeating motions like walking. Their recordings cover a set of mostly one-off balance tasks drawn largely from a standard clinical balance scale. Motion markers and three-dimensional ground forces were captured together.

Alongside the raw records, the team provides worked results: joint motions, forces, and estimates of center of mass position and speed. Researchers can use the data to study balance in less routine movements, to test estimation methods, or to design controllers for powered prosthetic legs. The data set fills a clear gap for non-repeating whole-body motion.
pmc-12717723:
Wajahat Mirza and co-authors pool randomized trials to test whether a glow-guided blood flow check during bowel surgery lowers leak rates, in a review from 2025. A leak where bowel ends are joined is a feared outcome after colorectal surgery, striking up to one in five patients in some series. A dye that glows under special light lets surgeons see blood flow at the join in real time.

The team searched five databases for trials comparing the glow check with standard white-light judgment. Seven trials were found. Leaks of the severe grades were the main outcome, with repeat surgery, complications, death, and hospital stay also tracked. Study quality was graded with standard tools. The review was registered before data work began.
pmc-12718223:
Riccardo Semproli leads a team in a 2025 paper on turning cheese whey permeate into fully bio-based surfactants. Whey permeate is the main waste stream of the dairy industry, and surfactants are compounds that help oil and water mix, used in soaps and many goods.

One path used an enzyme to build a sugar-based head for the surfactant, with a good yield. A second path fermented the waste with a yeast to make single cell oil. Those fats were then turned, in one pot, into ethyl esters for the tail. The result is a surfactant made from waste on both ends.
pmc-12719623:
Rongxia Guo, Peng Wu, Shuxin Yao, and Fumei Liu identify a blood protein, LRG1, as a driver and marker of acute myeloid leukemia, in a 2025 study. The cancer's variety and poor outcomes keep the hunt for targets alive. The team measured the protein in patient samples against controls, and before and after treatment, then tied levels to mutations and disease subtypes.

Levels ran far higher in patients and dropped after therapy. High levels tracked with a common mutation and with certain subtypes, and they forecast worse outcomes. Silencing the gene in lab models weakened colony growth and pushed cells toward maturity, while single-cell profiling showed where the protein concentrates.
pmc-12719923:
Sumeyye Cakmak and co-authors ask what drives test spending in emergency care in a 2025 study. In a busy tertiary unit, low urgency visits still rack up lab, imaging, and drug costs that vary by doctor. The team pulled one month of records for green triage visits handled by 71 residents.

More than twenty two thousand visits fed the counts. Women residents ordered costlier labs and scans than men on average. Mid level trainees spent most overall, while senior residents spent least once traits were weighed. Night shifts looked pricier in raw counts but that gap shrank after full checks. The study helps units coach fair and lean test use.
pmc-12721223:
Yue Sun and co-authors build an expert-agreed index system for judging health recommender systems. Their twenty twenty-five study uses the health technology assessment frame. These systems give personal health advice and content, yet most past checks graded only the algorithm.

No shared, validated score set existed, so studies could not be compared well. The team ran a two-round Delphi process, where experts rate and re-rate items toward consensus. User-centered measures join accuracy in the final index. Regulators and builders gain a common ruler for tools that now advise millions on diet, exercise, and care, with proof beyond code speed.
pmc-12721723:
Sijia Yan and co-authors report a case of engineered immune cell therapy for blood cancer in a paper published in 2025. The patient, a 48-year-old woman, had multiple myeloma that kept returning. She had already failed seven lines of treatment, including a stem cell transplant and several drug classes, and the cancer had spread outside the bone marrow.

Her doctors used CAR-T cells aimed at a target called GPRC5D on the cancer cells. The outside-marrow lesions vanished, and she stayed in complete remission for up to seventeen months. She carried high-risk gene changes, which makes the result more striking. A review of past reports follows the case. The authors call for larger studies with longer follow-up to confirm the approach.
pmc-12722223:
Amlan Ghosh and Padmaja Mondal assess the health of mangrove forests in the Indian Sundarbans, a vast delta on the Bay of Bengal. Their 2025 study notes that mangroves blunt climate change impacts and shelter rich ecosystems. Yet the forests face stress from natural forces and human activity, and their weak spots need mapping.

The pair used satellite data from 2010 and 2020 to compute six vegetation indices, measures of greenness and chlorophyll drawn from reflected light. A spatial model combined the indices into a health map. Some areas showed more stressed vegetation, tied to waterlogging and spreading fish-farming ponds. The map targets protection where the forest is frailest.
pmc-12722323:
Xu Xiang and colleagues present a printing method that uses plain water evaporation to assemble nanomaterials into large, even films. Turning tiny materials into full-size films is a bottleneck for uses such as water cleanup, energy harvesting, and soft robotics, and most methods work only for materials with special chemical traits. Writing in twenty twenty-five, the team shows that as water evaporates from a porous support, nanomaterials drift toward the drying surface and stack into an ordered film. The process runs continuously in a roll-to-roll setup and can be patterned in space.

The method handled flat nanosheets, nanotubes, and mixes of materials, with no extra additives, and used films could be recycled. As a demonstration, graphene oxide films made this way were applied to desalination. The authors present evaporation printing as a generic, high-throughput route that frees film making from material-specific recipes.
pmc-12722523:
Runbu Lv and eight co-authors hunt the gene behind a cosmetic trait of watermelon seeds in this 2025 study. Some seeds carry dark patches where the seed stalk attached, the hilum, and some do not, a handy marker for breeders sorting varieties. The team crossed patched and unpatched lines and followed the trait through a backcross population, where it split one to one as a single-gene trait should.

Dense DNA mapping placed the controlling region on chromosome 3, among thirty-five candidate genes. A custom marker inside the region tracked the trait perfectly, letting the team narrow the hunt to a forty-kilobyte stretch holding one gene, Cla019481. Sequence differences agreed, and the gene's activity climbed as hilum patches darkened across three stages of seed growth. The authors name Cla019481 as the regulator of the trait and offer the marker for breeding work.
pmc-12722723:
Mi-Kyoung Cho and Yoon Hee Cho review trials of electrical stimulation for women with urinary incontinence, in a 2025 paper. The treatment is non invasive and aims to improve both symptoms and quality of life. Past trials vary widely, so a pooled review can clarify the overall picture.

The review searched six databases for randomized trials from 1995 to 2025 and kept fourteen. A pooled estimate for quality of life was not statistically firm, and results varied greatly across trials. Some subgroups did show gains, including women with urgency type leakage and groups in smaller studies. The authors also compared stimulation types indirectly through a network analysis. They call for care in reading the mixed evidence.
pmc-12722923:
Rasha Tawfiq and co-authors tested two drugs in a 2025 study of liver harm after blood flow returns. When a liver is cut off from blood and then fed again, as in a transplant, the return itself wounds the tissue. Two routes of cell death drive much of that wound, one rust-like and one flame-like.

The team gave rats a drug for each route, alone and as a pair. One drug locks up iron, which feeds the rust-like route, and the other calms the flame-like route. They tracked two gene paths tied to each death route. The paired aim is to shield donor livers and cut post-transplant failure.
pmc-12723823:
Ryota Kanno and five co-authors wrote this 2025 case report on restarting a cancer drug after it nearly killed the patient. A woman in her early eighties with spreading pancreatic cancer received nano-liposomal irinotecan, a second-line therapy wrapped in fatty bubbles. Five minutes into her first infusion she collapsed with breathing distress and convulsions, a severe hypersensitivity reaction.

Emergency drugs revived her. With options few and the patient determined to continue, the team tried again under armor. They used stronger premedication and a three-step infusion that crept from a third of the normal rate to full speed over an hour. No reaction came. She completed eleven cycles on the same careful schedule until the cancer progressed. The authors present the protocol as a first detailed map for continuing a valuable drug past a frightening first reaction.
pmc-12724123:
Paul Van Houtte, Félix Lamarche, and Susanna Every-Palmer review what face masks did to care inside mental health services. Mask rules ran for years during the COVID-19 pandemic, and psychiatry leans hard on facial cues and trust. Their 2025 scoping review gathers the studies that looked past infection control at how masks changed treatment itself.

The team searched five databases in August 2024 and kept 28 studies covering 5,385 people. Twenty-six of them found harm in at least one area. Surveys reported weaker communication, strained trust between patient and clinician, and poorer assessments. Lab tasks showed that patients with mental disorders were hit harder by masks when reading emotions on faces. The review maps a scattered field and names the gaps that future studies and mask policies should address.
pmc-12727623:
Xindong Luo and co-authors compared two ways of guiding lung segment surgery, where only the diseased segment of a lobe is removed. One group of patients received AI-built three-dimensional reconstructions from their chest scans before surgery. The other group had a hook-wire placed into the lung under CT guidance to mark the target. Records covered 257 patients, and matching produced 97 comparable pairs.

The AI group had shorter operations, less bleeding, and quicker chest tube removal and discharge. Two patients in the wire group suffered a collapsed lung and four had bleeding into the chest, while the AI group had none. Six months later the AI group also showed better lung function and quality of life. The authors recommend the reconstruction approach.
pmc-12727723:
Federico Lucchetti and co-authors add a missing layer to brain mapping: chemistry. Network studies chart the brain's wiring and activity, but metabolic links between regions had no map. Using fast three-dimensional spectroscopic imaging, the team measured five key metabolites across gray matter parcels in fifty-one healthy volunteers and correlated their patterns region to region.

The resulting metabolic connectome proved stable and repeatable, even in a small validation group scanned at another site. Its leading pattern ran as a smooth gradient from back to front of the brain. That chemical similarity tracked cell-type architecture and gene co-expression more than it tracked physical wiring. The authors pitch the gradient as a signature of how the brain organizes its biochemistry.
pmc-12727823:
Yusuff Adebisi, Don Lucero-Prisno, and co-authors weigh the felt burden of long term lung disease in Scotland, in a 2025 study. Short survey grades of health and life joy are used in wide health counts. Their power to show real disease burden had rarely been put to a straight test.

Pooled survey waves held more than eighteen thousand adults. Folks with the lung disease had far lower life joy and far worse self grades than peers. Gaps stayed strong when age, smoke, school, and want were weighed in. Short grades thus track true lived burden well and can aid fair health plans.
pmc-12727923:
Bahram Ghafari Goushe and co-authors present a 2025 study on how learning a movement makes it feel easier. Motor learning is thought to trim the physical and mental resources a task needs. Effort is the felt cost of investing those resources, yet nobody had tracked how felt effort changes as a skill takes hold.

Thirty young adults practiced a continuous tracking task across four visits. Some blocks repeated one hidden sequence, while others stayed random. After each block, participants rated how much effort they had spent. The repeated sequence was learned, as a later retention test confirmed. Felt effort fell only for that learned sequence, and the drop tracked the amount of learning. Skill, it seems, literally lightens the felt load.
pmc-12728423:
Jing Lou and co-authors hunt for blood signs of an eye disease that can follow a stem cell transplant in two thousand twenty-five. The disease, eye graft-versus-host disease, often starts with vague signs and is judged mostly by eye exams. The team looks at blood proteins tied to a fiery form of cell death.

The study enrolled transplant patients with and without the eye disease, plus healthy controls. A screen first flagged proteins raised in the disease group, many tied to immune paths. Five proteins linked to that cell death path were then much higher in patients with the eye disease. Levels also tracked with worse dry eye signs. The team built a risk score from these proteins to aid early calls.
pmc-12729323:
Jiali Lv and co-authors built a flexible Pickering emulsion to treat ulcerative colitis, studying how carrier flexibility shapes drug delivery in the gut. They are stable systems with a layered structure that can raise the uptake of the compounds they carry, but how much they bend affects mucus crossing was poorly understood.

The emulsion was held together by tiny chitosan particles and carried epigallocatechin gallate, a plant compound, as its cargo. Once at the gut wall, the droplets deformed to fit what was around them. That flexibility helped them pass through mucus with ease, kept them longer in the gut, and improved absorption. The work links a physical trait of carriers to better oral delivery and offers design clues for gut-targeted drugs.
pmc-12729423:
Jeremie Bauer, Jorge Olmos, and Enric Gisbert present a 2025 review of feeding farmed sea urchins to fatten and colour their roe, the part people eat. Wild urchins from bare rock zones are thin; short feeding can make them marketable while clearing barrens that smother kelp. The review weighs feeds across many studies.

Seaweed feeds grow and colour roe best, but cost and supply bite. Soy protein is cheaper, yet anti nutrient factors cap how much can be used. Fat share in the feed proves critical. The authors map gaps: big scale economics, new additives, and mixed species farming that pairs urchins with their own waste eaters.
pmc-12729623:
Beáta Ružbarská and a team of co-authors studied food, activity, and body makeup in Slovak teens, in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. They used survey data from a school health study done in two thousand twenty-two. Height and body makeup were measured for each teen in the sample.

Eating breakfast more often on school days was linked to lower body mass and less body fat. More daily active play and exercise showed the same kind of link. It was also tied to more lean mass. Strong, hard exercise showed a mixed pattern across the measures. The authors stress breakfast and regular activity as habits tied to a healthier body makeup.
pmc-12729723:
A cancer that looks like a harmless fibroid until it is too late anchors a 2025 case report by Nigat Amsalu Addis and seven co-authors. A 40-year-old Ethiopian woman arrived with a month of belly pain, bleeding, and swelling. Imaging suggested an ordinary intramural fibroid, and she underwent removal of the uterus and ovaries.

Only the microscope told the truth: uterine leiomyosarcoma, a smooth-muscle cancer making up barely 1 to 2 percent of uterine malignancies. Seventy-seven days after surgery the disease was back, a vaginal mass with fever and foul discharge. The authors pair the case with a literature review to stress the trap: in clinics without advanced imaging, this aggressive cancer hides behind the commonest benign diagnosis in gynecology. Their plea is for suspicion, tissue examination, and referral pathways that assume the worst a little earlier.
pmc-12729823:
Bárbara Caffarel-Rodríguez and co-authors link Big Five traits to risky digital habits in 2025. The Big Five model sorts personality into five broad traits. The team reviewed work on phone use, gaming, and social media, then surveyed 492 people on trait scores and heavy internet use.

People high in openness and extraversion used social media and online entertainment most heavily. Those high in neuroticism, agreeableness, or conscientiousness showed lower exposure. The pattern fits earlier work tying traits to brain structure and behavior. The authors suggest trait profiles could flag users at risk of addictive digital habits.
pmc-12730023:
Enrico Ciminello and co-authors track the use of hearing implants across Italy over more than two decades, in a study from 2025. Implants such as cochlear devices can restore hearing for many people with severe loss. Knowing who gets them, and at what ages, helps plan services and spot gaps in access.

The team used hospital discharge records from 2001 to 2023 and split patients into six age bands, from infants to people over eighty. They charted raw counts and rates per million people for each year and age band. Trend tests then showed how use rose or fell over time. The full picture gives health planners a base for judging whether implant care in Italy is keeping pace with need.
pmc-12730223:
Neha Singh-Reilly and co-authors studied language loss in a brain disease in a 2025 paper. Posterior cortical atrophy eats at the back of the brain, and sight fades first for most patients. For some, language trouble stands out as well, yet the exact breaks in the language system were not well known.

The team compared 37 patients with 39 healthy adults of like age. Brain scans read how well the language web's parts, sight, movement, and thought nets among them, talk to each other. The pattern of weak links maps onto the patients' grasp and speech faults. Such maps may help doctors name the disease sooner.
pmc-12730323:
Paolo Gennari, Andrea Willeke, and Atanas Ignatov published a cancer registry study in two thousand twenty-five on surgery for advanced womb cancer. In stage IVB disease the cancer has spread widely, and doctors disagree on whether removing tumour bulk helps. The team used a German regional cancer registry to test the question.

From over six thousand recorded cases, two hundred ninety-four patients had stage IVB disease. Combined treatment with surgery plus other therapy gave the best survival. After statistical weighting to balance the groups, surgery still linked to longer survival and longer time without the disease returning. The benefit was clear in the more recent decade studied. The authors support surgery as part of combined care for selected patients.
pmc-12730623:
Haifa Alhasson and Shuaa Alharbi systematically review, in a 2025 paper, how machine learning and deep learning read images to diagnose diabetic foot ulcers. These ulcers are a serious complication of diabetes, and early, accurate reading can prevent amputations. Image based tools promise faster triage than the eye alone.

The search ran across 14 databases in October 2025, covering work from 2010 to 2025. From 4,653 records, 1,016 got detailed review, and 102 met the criteria. The tools did detection, segmentation, and classification of the ulcers. Reported accuracy ran from 0.88 to 0.97, with sensitivity and specificity in similar high ranges. Classic methods like support vector machines led the machine learning side, while U-Net style networks led the deep side. Newer work also tried thermal infrared imaging. The review maps trends, quality, and open problems in a fast moving field.
pmc-12730823:
Sarah Blake and Michael Gatzoulis argue that digital technology must now reshape care for adults born with heart defects, in a 2025 viewpoint article. This growing group needs lifelong, complex care that health systems struggle to deliver, and gaps in access and specialist oversight are widening. The authors survey what digital tools could offer this field.

AI risk models already predict deaths and events fairly well but need testing in these specific patients. Video visits proved safe and popular during the pandemic, though blended care paths are still missing. Wrist devices track rhythm, oxygen, and activity, yet consumer gadgets are poorly checked against these patients' unusual physiology. The authors set three priorities: prove tools work in this population, roll them out fairly, and govern them with specialist oversight and privacy built in.
pmc-12730923:
Vincenzo Loly and co-authors reviewed computer flow studies of brain aneurysms in two thousand twenty-five. An aneurysm is a bulge in a brain artery that can grow or burst. Flow forces on its wall are thought to drive that risk, and fluid simulations can measure them.

The review covered thirty-five studies of human saccular aneurysms from two thousand nineteen to two thousand twenty-four. Commercial software dominated each step of the work. The most used measures were wall shear stress metrics and shape ratios like aspect and size ratio. A core set of six measures best split risky from stable cases. But methods varied widely, so the authors urge shared standards.
pmc-12731323:
Ke Qin and co-authors screen spit for warning signs of jaw bone death in diabetic rats, in a 2025 study. The bone disease, called BRONJ, can follow treatment with bone drugs and is a special risk for people with diabetes. Spit tests would offer a painless way to watch that risk.

They build a rat model with diabetes, the bone drug, and a pulled tooth, which together produce the jaw damage. The sick rats show shrunken spit glands and make less spit, yet samples could still be drawn from every group. Two spit chemicals, urea nitrogen and total ketone bodies, ran high in the full disease group. Both may serve as early flags for the disease in diabetes, pending checks in people.
pmc-12731423:
Sameh Abd El-Ghany and AA Abd El-Aziz build a multi stage hybrid learning model that sorts prostate cancer in MRI scans by fusing deep and hand made features. This cancer is the second most common and deadly in men, and tissue looks vary widely. The study came out in twenty twenty-five.

Sharp sorting needs both deep meaning features from convolutional networks and hand built texture marks like gradient histograms. The frame joins those two streams across stages. It also tests ways to shrink feature sets and to classify, hunting for a tougher, more telling mix. The aim is better computer aided diagnosis from scans.
pmc-12731723:
Bin Deng wrote a 2025 study on adapting vision-language models to new image tasks when the target classes are partly unknown. Such universal adaptation must sort known classes and flag new ones. Deng tested leading methods built on a big pretrained model. The foundation model lifted plain baselines a lot.

Yet fancy adaptation methods failed to beat that baseline, a surprise. Careful checks pointed to score calibration as the key lever. A simple automatic temperature scaling sharpened detection of out-of-class images. One learned temperature beat older approaches on most benchmark tasks. Deng offers the method and findings as a base for future work.
pmc-12732023:
Retinal vasculitis inflames the blood vessels at the back of the eye, and the standard way to see it, fluorescein angiography, needs an injected dye. Harrigill, Nguyen, and Noori test a dye-free alternative built from swept-source OCT angiography.

Their method stitches five overlapping scans into a wide montage reaching past the central retina into the near periphery, and overlays a thickness map to expose swelling around vessels. In 30 eyes of 16 patients, the montage showed that perivascular thickening both centrally and peripherally, and its findings tracked the dye-based gold standard across repeat visits. The authors present the technique as a noninvasive partner to angiography for diagnosing the disease and following it over time.
pmc-12732323:
Alfred Shumba Hara studies racial microaggressions, the small everyday slights at work, as a source of chronic stress in Malawian workplaces. His 2025 study surveys 384 employees in Asian-owned workplaces, a setting where this topic had barely been studied. Interviews with fifty workers add lived detail to the numbers.

Nearly half the group faced slights three or more times a week. Frequent slights went with higher anxiety, depression, and distress scores on standard scales. Interview themes centered on micro-insults and stereotypes. Workers also reported insomnia, headaches, and stomach trouble, matching chronic stress patterns. No body markers were measured, and Hara frames the stress-hormone pathway as a hypothesis to test. He urges anti-discrimination rules at work.
pmc-12732523:
Lamiae El-Hajjami Nachit and co-authors test a twelve-week CrossFit-adapted program for older adults living in the community, in a 2025 trial. Standard strength training is proven safe for this group, with gradual load increases. Adapted CrossFit raised worries about overexertion and poor technique, in particular for people with joint or heart conditions. Yet scaled, supervised sessions had shown low injury rates and high satisfaction.

Sixty older adults were split at random between the adapted program and a control group. The team measured functional capacity, balance, and strength. The sample size was set in advance with standard power software. The trial asks whether this style of training can match its promise on balance, mobility, and leg power in later life.
pmc-12733223:
Erika de Simone Molina and co-authors describe, in a 2025 study, a rebuilt form of factor VIII, the clotting protein missing in hemophilia A. Treatment with the normal protein has a catch. Close to a third of patients make antibodies that block it. The team built a version with most of one large section removed, hoping it would provoke less of that immune attack while still stopping bleeds.

They gave the new protein, called rhFVIII-H6A, to mice bred to have hemophilia A. The mice made lower levels of blocking antibodies than mice given standard forms of the protein. Yet the new version fixed the bleeding defect just as well in the living animals. If the effect holds in people, this design could lead to safer long-term treatment.
pmc-12733323:
Charissopoulos and co-authors make a new set of thiadiazine compounds and test their antioxidant power. The design joins known active parts to boost two effects at once. Starting points were two chlorinated thiadiazine building blocks.

Each compound was tested for radical scavenging, fat damage blocking, and soybean lipoxygenase blocking. Results ranged from fair to strong on the first two tests. One compound quenched 92 percent of test radicals in sixty minutes and blocked 70 percent of fat damage. Another blocked the enzyme best, with an IC50 of 7.5 micromolar. Docking scores backed that enzyme result.
pmc-12733623:
Hanin Yeslam and co-authors soak dental crown materials in everyday drinks to see what patients' habits do to them, in a 2025 study. Two machined materials were tested: a feldspar glass ceramic and a nano-ceramic hybrid composite. Three hundred samples were steeped in water, coffee, matcha, or protein drink. Hardness and color shift were measured before and after.

Every drink softened both materials compared with dry controls. The glass ceramic stayed far harder than the hybrid overall. Coffee stained both materials the most. Protein drink caused the least color change in the hybrid. Water alone softened the glass ceramic more than matcha or protein did. The results give dentists concrete talking points about diet and crown care.
pmc-12733723:
Blasco-Bonora and six co-authors compare NESA neuromodulation with tibial nerve stimulation for overactive bladder in a pilot trial, in a study from twenty twenty-five. Overactive bladder disrupts quality of life, sleep, and daily function. Twenty-four women aged thirty-eight to eighty-five receive ten sessions of either therapy. Both arms add identical exercises and patient education.

Both groups improve pelvic function, incontinence symptoms, and sleep significantly. No significant differences emerge between groups on any variable measured. Only the NESA group shows compelling quality of life improvement. Follow-up extends two months beyond treatment completion. Larger trials are warranted to confirm the quality of life edge.
pmc-12734323:
Cristina dos Santos and co-authors trial shoulder blade-focused exercise for rotator cuff pain in this 2025 study. Shoulder pain from the rotator cuff is common and stubborn. Physio care for it lacks consistent backing. Sixty patients joined a three-arm trial. One group did the focused exercise program. A second added live muscle-signal feedback to the same program.

The third group got standard control therapy. Pain and function were scored with a standard shoulder questionnaire. Short-term effects were the trial's focus. Feedback tech is the added twist being tested. If it adds nothing, clinics can skip its cost. The trial is randomized, a strong design for the question. Results appear in the full report.
pmc-12735323:
Vuk Radojicic and co-authors review a light-based method for watching stress in green microalgae in this 2025 paper. The method, pulse-amplitude modulated fluorometry, tracks how well the algae turn light into chemical energy. It harms nothing and gives fast readings of culture health. Two gauges matter most: the top efficiency of one photosystem and its working efficiency under light.

The team gathered 38 sources and compared the reported values across species and stressors. Chemicals, heat, and other pressures left different marks, and some species proved far more sensitive than others. Newer pollutants such as ionic liquids and artificial sweeteners remain little studied. The authors call for plain numerical reporting so later work can compare results across labs.
pmc-12735523:
Lavinia Lupa and co-authors published this 2025 study on pulling zinc out of polluted water with engineered plastic beads. Zinc ions in natural water harm health and ecosystems, and they linger. The team built sorbents from a plastic network studded with groups that grip zinc tightly. Both plain and treated beads were tested side by side.

The treated beads soaked up far more zinc, thanks to the gripping groups. The best version held about 101 milligrams of zinc per gram. Uptake peaked after about sixty minutes of contact. The balance data fit a single-layer model, and the speed data fit a chemical binding model. The authors present the beads as strong candidates for cleaning metal-laced water.
pmc-12736123:
Wenjun Zhu and co-authors feed a candidate probiotic bacterium to obese mice and watch their metabolism change. The strain, Clostridium cochlearium 2316, was given daily for sixteen weeks to mice on a high-fat diet. A second high-fat group got no supplement, and a third stayed on low-fat food as a baseline.

Supplemented mice gained about seventeen percent less weight and carried clearly less fat. Their fasting blood sugar fell by over a quarter, fasting insulin by more than half, and cholesterol by about forty percent. Oddly, they absorbed more calories yet burned more energy: metabolic rate, activity, and total expenditure all rose. The authors suggest the bacterium retunes whole-body energy use, and they position it as a candidate aid against metabolic syndrome, pending mechanism work.
pmc-12736323:
Timur Saliev and co-authors wrote a 2025 review of drugs that target worn-out cells in the aging brain. As the brain ages, some cells stop dividing but stay active and spew harmful signals. Those cells are linked to swelling, decline in thinking, and a higher risk of diseases such as Alzheimer disease.

One class of drugs kills those cells, and another calms their harmful output without killing them. In aged animals, such drugs cut brain swelling and improved memory and learning. Early human trials in Alzheimer disease are under way. The review weighs open problems, such as getting drugs into the brain and proving long-term safety.
pmc-12736823:
Qin and five co-authors built a memory transformer in twenty twenty-five to spot odd runs in many-channel time data. Stock nets fix one map per stream, which costs much and bends poor-ly to new streams. Their net codes stream kinds into shared memory slots first.

Those slots then seed a maker model that picks fit priors per stream. A two-way guess step reads the hidden states of each stream. On six data sets the net led one-for-all odd-spot tasks. Shared memory gives the flex that fixed maps lack, they show.
pmc-12737023:
Dake Zeng and co-authors design a login protocol for factory networks that keeps users anonymous. Their 2025 paper addresses the Industrial Internet of Things, where staff pull live sensor data over public channels and intruders must be kept out without exposing who is asking.

The protocol mixes hash functions, chaotic maps, chip fingerprints that cannot be cloned, and fuzzy extractors that verify biometrics from smart card, password, and body traits together. It also handles new device enrollment, password and biometric changes, and card revocation. Formal proofs in a standard security model and attack-by-attack review support its session keys. Benchmarks against rival protocols show it faster and safer at once, the authors report.
pmc-12737123:
Smart city cameras pour out video, and spotting abnormal behavior in that flood is a core surveillance task. Weakly supervised detectors struggle: abnormal clips are scarce, normal and abnormal segments look alike, and time structure is under-modeled. The authors add temporal structural attention, armed with causal masks and decay weights so the model respects time order and never peeks at the future. They also add contrastive learning with positive and negative offsets to pull abnormal segments apart in the latent space.

On several public video anomaly data sets the method beat mainstream models, reaching an AUC of 98.1 percent, accuracy of 96.1 percent, and an F1 score of 94.5 percent. The authors present it as a more reliable anomaly detector for Internet of Things surveillance and public safety.
pmc-12737623:
Maria Eugenia Ariza and co-authors argue, in a 2025 review, that a long-lasting fatigue illness may be driven by several herpesviruses acting together. The illness, known as ME/CFS, disables millions worldwide and often starts after flu-like symptoms. Yet no single virus has been proven to cause it. Herpesviruses live in the body for life, switching between quiet latency and active copying.

The review focuses on a third, messier state: abortive copying, where the virus starts to reactivate but does not finish. The authors suggest this stalled activity could keep the immune system inflamed and drive symptoms. If several herpesviruses can each do this, hunting one culprit would miss the picture. They frame the illness as a possible poly-herpesvirus condition and call for studies designed to test that idea directly.
pmc-12738623:
Moein Borghei and co-authors build a compact feed-through that holds back very high voltage in a vacuum in a 2025 paper. Such parts serve beam machines, X-ray tubes, and fusion rigs, yet shop types stall near one hundred thousand volts. Their build, called Hammerhead, pairs a tube-in-tube layout with a shaped ceramic bridge that resists surface flashes.

Tests took the part to 330 kilovolts, and it ran for six days at 300 with a trickle of stray flow. It packs near twice the hold-off per unit of bulk of prior art. It needs no rare vacuum or mirror polish, and plugs straight into a standard high-voltage cable.
pmc-12738723:
A buzzing form of brain stimulation may ease the pull of negative images, and a 2025 trial by Daisuke Sawamura and co-authors tests it head to head against the standard method. Too strong a focus on the negative feeds several mental disorders, and steady-current stimulation of the left forehead area is known to loosen that grip.

Thirty-two healthy right-handed men each received all three conditions in random order, a week apart: the noise-based stimulation, the steady current, or a sham. An emotional Stroop task measured how much negative words slowed them down. The noise-based method cut the negative bias clearly compared with sham. The study asks whether the newer, gentler signal can match a proven tool.
pmc-12741423:
Subhash Tard and three co-authors report a rare toddler case in a 2025 paper. A two-year-old boy arrived with long fever, cough, and hard breathing. Scans showed repeated collapsed lungs on both sides and many thin-walled cysts in the lungs. A chest scope biopsy gave the diagnosis: a rare cell disorder that often spans several organs.

A whole-body scan then found liver and spleen involvement, confirming the multi-system form. Chemotherapy with steroids brought clear improvement. The authors also review nine similar child cases in the literature. They stress that lung findings like these can be the doorway to spotting the wider disease early.
pmc-12741523:
Didar, Haddad Khodaparast, and Goharjoo make a vegan probiotic ice cream from sesame milk. The mix adds capsules of Lactobacillus casei and hibiscus extract. Fat content matched the plain control at about 2.1 percent. The enriched batch was softer and melted more slowly. Air uptake during churning also rose with enrichment.

Plant pigment and antioxidant levels ran far above the control. Probiotic counts fell over 45 days but stayed near six log units. Some pigments faded by the end of storage. Total phenolics held steady through the full span. Gut-like lab tests checked survival of the bacteria after storage.
pmc-12742123:
Older adults in poor areas gather diseases and drugs faster than their richer peers, but the pace over time was unmapped. Tran Quoc Bao Tran and co-authors track that pace in a 2025 study of Glasgow health records. They follow 414,746 adults aged 51 and up at three points from 2016 to 2021.

By 2021, 26 percent of the poorest group held five or more conditions, against 13.8 percent of the richest. The richest were near forty percent less likely to jump from one condition to five. Counts of diseases and drugs both rose in all groups. The gap did not stem from who lived longer. Early support in poor areas may slow the pile-up.
pmc-12742223:
Gufa Bagus Pamungkas, Eddy Heriyanto Habar, and Maria Tanumihardja test a shell-derived filler for braces glue in a 2025 dental paper. Brackets that pop off teeth slow orthodontic treatment. A nano-sized mineral found in bone and teeth can stiffen glue, and Asian moon scallop shells supply it cheaply. The team mixed two percent of the mineral into a standard bracket adhesive.

Thirty-two pulled human premolars were split evenly between the new glue and the plain one. A testing machine sheared the brackets off and measured the force needed. The leftover glue pattern on each tooth was scored afterward. Stronger bonds with clean removal are the goal; the lab numbers say whether shell waste earns a place in the clinic.
pmc-12742323:
Wang, Tan, Tan, Merchant, and Sevdalis set out in twenty twenty-five a study plan for rolling out a World Health Organization ageing program in Singapore homes. The program screens older people for drops in core abilities and links them to care, but it has mostly run through clinics. How community teams handle it is little studied, so the team will follow the rollout closely.

The mixed study tracks reach, effect, uptake, delivery, and staying power over a year of follow-ups. Surveys, health records, interviews, and group talks feed the picture. The authors aim to name what helps or blocks adoption by staff and older residents. Findings should guide scaling in lean settings and policy for ageing at home.
pmc-12743023:
Matthew Dunn and co-authors asked how much of the metastatic breast cancer burden traces to tumor biology and how much to access to care, in a 2025 study. The team drew on a North Carolina population cohort of nearly three thousand patients diagnosed between 2008 and 2013, followed for twelve years. Tumor data came from records and gene expression; access data came from surveys.

About fifteen percent developed metastatic disease, either at diagnosis or as a later recurrence. Aggressive biology mattered greatly: high grade, a LumB subtype, and high recurrence scores each raised the odds several-fold. So did social position: Black race, poverty, and low education each carried higher risk. Accounting for screening, regular care, treatment delays, and community resources softened the poverty and education links but barely moved the race link. The authors conclude that cutting the burden in Black women requires attacking biology and access together.
pmc-12743223:
Yiming Lu and co-authors reported a flap technique for ankle wounds in a 2025 surgical study. Soft tissue loss around the outer ankle bone is hard to cover, since little spare tissue sits nearby. A flap that rides on the last branch of the peroneal artery can swing in to fill the gap.

From January 2018 to April 2020, seven patients were treated with the flap. Ultrasound found the artery branch first, and the lowest branch near the wound served as the pivot. The team then judged how well the covers healed and held. Their look-back gives other surgeons a map for this tight spot.
pmc-12744223:
Qianqian Song and co-authors set in 2025 two pace train forms side by side for heart patients in heal care. Pulse ease back post work out is a known fate mark in heart ills. Short hard bursts and mid pace sets are both in ward use.

Two hundred nine patients who did twelve sits form the set, split by form. Ease back rose by near the same gain in both arms. Top breath scores rose in step as well. No gap set the forms apart on the core marks. Age and start marks, not the form, drove who gained most in the tuned reads.
pmc-12744823:
Minghua Fan, Yan Li, Haiyan Diao, and Yanhong Wang report five adult cases of a fierce fever-linked seizure syndrome treated with a ketogenic diet, in work from twenty twenty-five. The syndrome, called FIRES, erupts after a feverish illness with seizures that resist drugs. Its cause is unclear, and death and lasting harm run high. Records cover five adults treated at one hospital over five years. All had drug-resistant seizure states after a febrile illness.

Brain wave tests show slowed traces with widespread seizure spikes. Most patients also show abnormal brain scans in the series. All get many seizure drugs, sedation, and immune therapy first. The high-fat diet starts about a month after onset on median. Seizures ease within days once ketosis is reached in most cases. Scores at three months show fair function for all five patients. Side effects are common but settle with standard care.
pmc-12744923:
Hoda Mahdavi and four co-authors checked whether two simple blood ratios predict survival in patients with gut neuroendocrine tumors. These tumors vary widely in outlook, and cheap markers would help doctors plan. The ratios compare neutrophils and platelets with lymphocytes, all from a routine blood count, and both reflect body-wide inflammation. The study reviewed eighty patients treated between 2017 and 2019.

Patients with a low neutrophil ratio had about one third the risk of death of the others, even after accounting for spread and tumor grade. The platelet ratio pointed the same way but not firmly. Higher grade and a higher growth index both meant worse survival and more spread. Two other inflammation markers showed no link. The authors propose the neutrophil ratio as an easy, low-cost aid to prognosis.
pmc-12745223:
Bin Zhao and co-authors review heat shock proteins in osteoarthritis in two thousand twenty-five. These proteins act as chaperones that fold other proteins and guard cells under stress. In worn joints, several family members are out of balance, feeding inflammation, cartilage breakdown, and death of cartilage cells, yet at times protecting them.

That double role makes the proteins both markers of disease activity and candidate drug targets. The review maps how the main family members steer cell death, self-cleaning, and inflammatory signaling in joint tissues. It then surveys ways to tune them: drugs, natural products, nano-medicine, stem cells, physical treatments such as heat and ultrasound, and antibody agents. The authors argue such targeting could slow joint damage and preserve cartilage cell function.
pmc-12745323:
Andrew Penunuri, Eliyahu Greenberg, John Phillips, and Andrew Katims published a 2025 review of B cells and immune cell clusters in bladder cancer. B cells are white blood cells that make antibodies. Sometimes they gather inside tumors into clusters called tertiary lymphoid structures, which can help the body attack the cancer.

In muscle-invasive bladder cancer, certain B cell types and these clusters are linked to better outcomes and better responses to immunotherapy. In earlier-stage disease the picture is less clear: clusters may mark more aggressive cancer, yet also better responses to a bladder-delivered immune treatment. The authors see the clusters as a possible test to guide treatment choices. Researchers are even trying to trigger cluster formation in tumors that lack them.
pmc-12745423:
Zhenqi Wei and colleagues test a structured rehab programme after knee replacement surgery. Their randomised trial from twenty twenty-five uses the information-motivation-skills model. Recovery depends on patients actually doing their exercises. Standard nursing care often leaves compliance weak after discharge.

Ninety patients split evenly between standard care and the new programme. The programme taught, motivated, and coached exercise skills together. Checks ran at discharge and at later follow-up visits. Knee scores, pain, walking distance, and compliance were all tracked. Recovery paths differed clearly between the two groups over time. Early scores started similar, then separated with follow-up. Structured support may help surgical patients stick with rehab longer.
pmc-12746123:
Muhammad Saleem Akhtar and co-authors report a 2025 study of flat nickel and cerium sulfide flakes for supercapacitors. Such devices need electrode stuff that stores much charge and lasts well. The team grew six-sided flakes straight onto nickel foam with a microwave-aided hot water method, with no binder needed.

Lab tools mapped the flakes' shape and makeup. Charge tests in a half cell gave a very high storage score and strong energy marks. A full device built with the flakes was also tested, and the team reads the gains as a fruit of the flat shape and fast charge flow.
pmc-12747923:
Izzet Karakulak and ten co-authors, publishing in 2025, test how evening caffeine at three doses affects rowing performance and the night that follows. Thirteen trained university rowers each completed four 2,000-meter time trials between 7 and 8 in the evening. Each did one trial after a placebo. Each also did one after low, medium, and high caffeine doses in capsules, without knowing which he had taken. Sleep quality and morning sleepiness were scored after each trial.

The medium and high doses made the rowers clearly faster and stronger than the placebo, with the high dose best. The same doses, though, cut sleep quality and left the athletes sleepier the next day, and the high dose brought headaches, sleeplessness, and stomach complaints. The low dose helped a little with almost no sleep cost. The authors advise athletes and coaches to weigh the speed gain against lost recovery.
pmc-12748123:
Natalie Reindl and co-authors followed up on scar quality and satisfaction years after surgery for birth defects of the belly wall, in a 2025 study. Scarring is a lasting worry for patients and parents after repair of omphalocele or gastroschisis, where the organs sit outside the body at birth. The team guessed that parents judge the scars more harshly than their children do.

Patients treated at one German hospital from 2001 to 2011, and their parents, filled in scar scales in 2022 and 2023. Twenty-eight patients took part. Parents did rate scar appearance more negatively than the children, clearly so for omphalocele. Scores for symptoms and satisfaction also split between the generations.
pmc-12749223:
Vahid Adiban, Masood Entezariasl, Pedram Poshtareh, and Khatereh Isazadehfar ran a trial of two drugs to prevent shivering after spinal anesthesia, in a 2025 paper. Shivering often follows spinal blocks for hernia repair and can strain the body. The usual preventive drug carries risks like slowed breathing, so alternatives matter. One hundred fifty patients were split at random among ketamine, dexmedetomidine, and a control group.

Patients, drug givers, and outcome judges were all blind to group assignment. Shivering was scored at set times from the block through recovery discharge. The dexmedetomidine group shivered notably less at several early time points, the abstract reports. The trial's careful blinding and timing give its comparison weight. Full results run beyond the summary, but the design shows how the two rivals were tested head to head.
pmc-12749423:
Chadni Patel, Frank Diglio, Benjamin Durham, and Peter Cole test whether a known Alzheimer's risk gene also worsens chemotherapy-related memory problems in the young. Many childhood cancer survivors develop cognitive impairment, but not all, hinting at genetic vulnerability. Five-week-old rats carrying either the human ApoE3 or ApoE4 gene variant received the chemotherapy drug doxorubicin or saline for four weeks.

The ApoE4 rats on the drug showed worse visual and spatial memory than every other group. Their brains also grew fewer new neurons in the hippocampus, and a blood marker of brain injury rose. The authors link the genotype's effect to impaired neurogenesis and propose it as groundwork for genotype-specific protective strategies.
pmc-12749823:
Davide Zaccagnino and co-authors report a break in the pattern of how fast Earth's plates move. Their 2025 paper analyzes global plate motions in distinct reference frames. A kink appears in the size and frequency pattern of plate speeds. Current models of plate tectonics do not predict it, the authors say. Larger plates move more slowly, in angular terms, than smaller ones.

Faster plates tied to more uniform layers beneath them, judged by wave speed data. A strong negative link was found between speed and latitude. A steady westward drift also persists. Two explanations are offered. Distinct driving forces may rule large and small plates, making a two tier system. Or current reference frames based on hotspots may be biased, missing a net westward rotation of the mantle frame.
pmc-12750823:
Jinyan Shao, Kaiming Liu, and twelve co-authors test a migraine drug for vestibular migraine. Their study, from twenty twenty-five, enrolls thirty-three patients at several centers. This migraine type brings spinning dizziness and is a top cause of episodic vertigo. Good treatments are scarce, so a new option matters.

Patients took rimegepant every other day as prevention for four weeks. Each person served as their own control, comparing before and after. At the start, symptom burden was high across dizziness, mood, and balance scores. After treatment, monthly days with dizziness or headache fell a lot. Balance confidence rose as well. Longer trials can confirm the gain.
pmc-12750923:
Miriam Boot and co-authors published this study in 2025. Surgeons often treat a patient's two knees as natural pairs, using one as the healthy template for the other. The study asked whether that holds when a knee has trochlear dysplasia, a misshaped groove tied to kneecap instability. The team used CT scans from 187 people. Most had no dysplasia, while fifty had low- or high-grade forms.

They built 3D models of the thigh bone, kneecap, and shin bone, then matched left to right point by point. Median gaps were under a millimeter in both groups. Dysplastic knees were a touch less symmetric, yet the gaps stayed too small to matter in care. Only the kneecap gap grew with severity, mostly due to loose bone bits. The pair assumption looks safe.
pmc-12751123:
Lili Xing and co-authors report a hospital study from 2025 on a blood-cleaning treatment for very sick children. The children had a group of inherited disorders in which acids build up in the body. When the balance breaks down, organs can be harmed and life is at risk. The study looked back at cases treated in one intensive care unit over more than a decade.

Forty-six children were split into two groups by the years of their care. One group got the blood-cleaning treatment, and the other got standard care alone. After a day of the added treatment, levels of acid, ammonia, and organ stress marks fell more sharply. Time on a breathing machine and time in the unit were also shorter. The authors conclude the added treatment helps clear toxins and shields organs.
pmc-12751423:
Kubra Taka and co-authors compare two scan methods in a 2025 lab study for finding foreign objects lodged in the face and jaw. Objects left in the body can spark inflammation, so they need to be found and removed fast. Which scan works best depends on what the object is made of, where it sits, and how big it is.

Working outside a living body, the team placed items such as wood, glass, tooth, plastic, and stone, plus dental wires and brackets, in test material. They scanned them with cone beam computed tomography, a focused X-ray method, and with ultrasound. They then compared how well each method spotted the items, how true its size measures were, and how the items behaved in sound images. The results help dentists pick the right scan for each case.
pmc-12751523:
Adel Mutahar, Renu Dayal, and Bharathi Salimath test a drug pair against breast cancer in lab-grown tumor balls in a 2025 study. Ball cultures mimic real tumors better than flat cell layers, including drug resistance. Triple-negative breast cancer is fast-growing and lacks targeted options.

A standard chemo drug alone lost much of its punch in the balls, needing about twenty-five times the flat-culture dose. Adding a new two-domain protein that soaks up a vessel growth signal cut the needed dose roughly tenfold in one cell line. A rival antibody gave only modest help. The pair also shrank balls, slowed spread traits, and cut vessel growth signals. In mixed balls with vessel cells, a key adhesion pathway faded as well.
pmc-12751823:
Rocio Polanco-Fernandez, Patricia Penas, and Ioseba Iraurgi review, in a 2025 paper, how clinicians measure the mental side of facial palsy gained in adult life. A weakened face changes expression, speech, and social ease, yet no agreed tool set exists for the psychological side of the condition.

The scoping review found forty-six instruments in use, many also touching social life and quality of life. Their content grouped into five areas, from symptom load to care experience, and into six broader life domains by importance. Gaps where few tools reach were named as well. The map gives clinics a clearer menu for assessing patients whole, not just facial movement.
pmc-12751923:
Rong Wang and co-authors test whether two simple blood-based scores can warn of bad outcomes after a heart stent procedure, in a 2025 study. The scores combine blood fats and sugar, with one also using body mass index. The team followed patients who had a blocked heart artery opened at a hospital in Chengde, China.

Of 105 patients followed for a year, 23 had a major event such as a heart attack, severe rhythm trouble, or a re-blocked stent. Those patients had higher scores on both measures, along with higher age and blood fat levels. Checks with resampled data suggested the scores predict risk with fair strength. The authors propose them as cheap warning tools next to standard risk checks.
pmc-12752123:
Edgar Luis Waschburger and co-authors study jumping genes in the myrtle family in a 2025 paper. The family holds more than five thousand tree species, with genome sizes that vary more than threefold. Jumping genes, which copy and paste themselves around the genome, are the main driver of that size spread.

The team mapped these elements in eighteen species. One class of retro elements drove most size gaps, and certain lineages flared at set times in family history. Element profiles tracked climate and range, and one element seems to have jumped between tribes, landing near defense genes. Readers get a view of how restless DNA shapes plant adaptation.
pmc-12752823:
Baas and co-authors review markers that could track disease activity in ANCA-associated vasculitis. These rare autoimmune diseases inflame small and medium blood vessels. Drugs can force the disease into remission, yet many patients relapse. Doctors lack reliable tests to spot returning activity early. The review weighs four candidate markers found in urine or blood. They are CD163, CD206, CD25, and MCP-1.

The team searched three databases and screened studies by set rules. Data pulling and quality checks were done by separate reviewers. Twenty studies entered the final pool. A standard tool for diagnostic accuracy studies graded each one. The review asks which markers are ready for clinic use.
pmc-12753323:
Bingyang Wang and co-authors review the immune cells that shield glioblastoma, the deadliest brain tumor, from treatment. The tumor's surroundings are packed with microglia, the brain's own immune cells, and macrophages drawn from the blood. Together they form a major compartment that helps the tumor grow, spread into vessels, and hide from therapy, and the tumor actively recruits and reprograms them.

The review maps where these cells come from, the signals and metabolic switches that keep them tumor-friendly, and the therapies now aimed at them. Strategies include blocking the CSF-1R pathway that sustains them, using nanoparticles to re-educate them, and infecting the tumor with engineered viruses. The authors argue that cracking this myeloid shield is a frontier for immunotherapy in a cancer that has resisted nearly everything else.
pmc-12753423:
Svenja Royeck and co-authors draft the first scale built to measure the stress that chronic itching causes. Their 2025 pilot study notes that stress and itch feed each other in long-lasting skin diseases, yet no tested tool measures that specific strain. The team interviewed 55 patients with three itchy conditions at a German center to shape the items.

Nearly 95 percent of patients reported itch-related stress in the prior two weeks. A trial version of the scale held together tightly, with a reliability score of 0.91. Twelve strong items cover nerves, coping tactics, tiredness, and urges to scratch harder when stressed. A second patient group helped refine the wording. The authors plan a wider test of the full item pool next.
pmc-12753823:
Brinda Balakrishnan and co-authors study how viruses compete inside the mosquito that spreads dengue, Zika, and chikungunya in a 2025 paper. A single mosquito can carry several viruses at once, and their rivalry may decide which reaches humans. The team mined hundreds of public gene datasets from this mosquito species.

Across twenty-one viruses, they found a strong antagonistic pattern: chikungunya rose where flaviviruses fell, and the reverse. Gene activity pointed to a few interaction hubs, including the insect's antiviral silencing system. One gene, DDX5, stood out as a balancer whose response shifts with the relative loads of the two virus families. The work names a possible switch for transmission dominance.
pmc-12753923:
Zhaoyu Kong and co-authors report a 2025 study of helpful germ mixes added to metal-tainted soil where Indian mustard grows. Such mixes can aid plant-led cleanup, but how they mesh with the soil's own germ web was murky. The team compared growth-boosting mixes with plain ones, reading germ types in root soil and open soil alike.

Both kinds of mixes shifted the root germ mix a great deal. Only the growth boosters, though, made the germ web denser and steadier. They also lodged in the root zone and linked up with native helpful strains, which hints why they work better in the field.
pmc-12754623:
Yanfei Du, Daohong Jiang, and Huiquan Liu review how RNA editing works in fungi and why it may help or harm them. Editing changes a letter in an RNA copy after it is made from DNA. One common form swaps one base for another that the cell then reads as a different base, so one gene can make more than one form of a protein.
