The review contrasts the animal system, which uses a family of enzymes, with a fungal system found in recent work. In fungi the editing is tied to sex and growth, and it may aid defense against viruses. The authors weigh that gain against costs to growth and health. Readers get a plain guide to a trade-off that shapes how fungi adapt.
pmc-12754923:
Xianghai Wang and seven colleagues test whether blood lipids carry the heart risk of forever chemicals, in a study published in two thousand twenty-five. PFAS compounds are being phased out in long-chain forms, but their true relationship to cardiovascular disease remains unsettled. Lipids are the suspected middleman.

Over twenty-five thousand American survey participants from twenty fifteen to twenty twenty contributed data. Individual compounds and their mixtures were modeled against disease and lipid measures with several advanced methods, including mixture regressions and causal mediation. Nonlinear dose patterns were checked. Mediation analysis quantifies how much of any PFAS effect travels through cholesterol changes. That decomposition matters for regulation: blocking a mediator differs from banning an exposure.
pmc-12756923:
Xinyue Zhang and Ruyuan Zhang write a letter from 2025 on ultrasound guided vein access in critical care. A reworked trial study compared infection, clot, and harm rates across three vein sites. In the first trial most under collar bone placements used surface landmarks, not live ultrasound.

Live ultrasound hit full success and near zero artery hits in cited early work. Landmark runs had lower success and a clear share of hard complications in that study. A new method shows artery and vein together in one long view for safer aim. That method also hit full success with no chest harms in its own series. The letter asks whether live guidance should lead.
pmc-12757523:
Aleksandra Jaromin and Aleksandra Wardzyńska review off label uses of an allergy drug in a 2025 paper. The drug, omalizumab, traps a key allergy antibody in the blood and calms allergic chains. It has been sold for twenty years with a strong safety record, approved for asthma, hives, and sinus growths in Europe.

Reports in the wider record stretch much further. Doctors have tried it for eye allergy, food allergy, drug reactions, a lung mold illness, and as a helper for allergy shots, among other uses. The review sorts what is known for each use and where proof is thin. The authors see the drug as the most flexible tool of its kind for allergy care.
pmc-12757823:
Jens Nielsen, a solo author, surveys the many roles of yeast in science and industry in this 2025 review. Yeasts have fermented human food and drink for thousands of years. One species, Saccharomyces cerevisiae, also became a favorite laboratory organism and a workhorse for making useful products.

Nielsen traces yeast research from early brewing to its central place in the molecular biology revolution, noting Nobel-winning work on the cell cycle, protein trafficking, transcription, and autophagy that yeast made possible. Many cell pathways in yeast closely match their human counterparts, which adds medical value. Industry favors the species for its easy genetics, safety record, and ability to scale up in fermenters, and engineers have tuned it to make chemicals, fuels, and medicines. New tools, from genome-scale models to directed evolution, keep raising yields, and Nielsen closes on yeast as both a window into cell life and a factory.
pmc-12764023:
Jin Seong Park and co-authors trace the worldwide spread of maize through its chloroplast genomes in this 2025 paper. Maize is the most recently domesticated major cereal and now grows worldwide. Chloroplast DNA passes mainly through the mother line, which makes it a clean tracer of seed movement. The team assembled 286 plastomes in total.

Most plastomes were newly built from landraces around the world. Wild teosinte relatives and mapping founders were added for context. Family trees split the landraces into four main clades. The trees point to one teosinte form as the direct donor of the maize chloroplast. European landraces closely resembled those in China and Korea, suggesting fast, broad dispersal after contact with the Americas.
pmc-12764923:
Ziyang Wang and co-authors plan joint control of virtual power plants in 2025. A virtual power plant links scattered solar, storage, and loads into one fleet. Fleets of fleets must coordinate without a single boss. The setting here is a high altitude region with mixed energy sources.

Their plan pairs a robust tuning model with a bargaining scheme among fleets. An uncertainty set guards against swings in wind and demand. Bargaining based on Nash theory splits gains and cuts interaction costs. Case tests check whether the plan holds up under stress. Fair coordination may unlock more clean power on shared grids.
pmc-12765923:
Hiroki Mizusawa, Kazuki Okura, Masashi Shiraishi, Masaya Noguchi, and Yuji Higashimoto pooled studies on breathing muscle strength and survival in chronic lung disease in twenty twenty-five. Weak breathing muscles are common in COPD, but whether they foretell death beyond airflow measures was unclear. The team searched three databases across three decades and kept six cohort studies.

Only two studies could be pooled for in-breath strength. They showed that weaker in-breath strength went with higher death rates. In severe-case groups, set cut-off values for in- and out-breath strength marked groups where about half died within roughly four to five years. Out-breath strength gave a mixed signal across studies. The authors say in-breath strength carries real survival information and deserves a standard place in assessment.
pmc-12766123:
Shengwei Liang, Lai, and Xu test whether medical residents can actually read the heart tracings they order daily. Across centers, 165 residents in China interpreted eight standard ECGs, each paired with a short clinical vignette, and rated their own confidence. The backdrop is grim worldwide: most doctors judge themselves weak at ECGs, and few students call themselves proficient.

The scores agreed. The median result was 6 of a possible spread where only one resident in ten topped 10 points. A heart-attack pattern was read best, correctly by about fifty-five percent; a long-QT pattern and a left bundle block were read correctly by almost no one. Confidence lagged skill claims further still. The authors call for rebuilt ECG training.
pmc-12766823:
Jinlin Zhang and eight co-authors set out a trial protocol in 2025 for Tuina therapy in knee osteoarthritis. Tuina is a Chinese manual therapy that shows promise for knee pain, but high quality evidence is thin and guidelines do not agree on it. The trial will recruit eighty four patients at a Shanghai hospital.

Patients will be assigned by chance to Tuina plus infrared therapy or infrared therapy alone, twice a week for four weeks. Follow up runs to six months. The main outcome is a standard knee function score, with pain, muscle tone, and pain sensitivity also measured. Assessors will not know group assignments. All patients receive education on knee exercise and protection during the study.
pmc-12767023:
Hala Bawadi and co-authors survey in 2025 what shapes birth mode choice among pregnant women in Jordan. Surgical birth rates climb worldwide, with elective surgery a large part of the rise. Personal, cultural, and system factors all feed the trend.

Near four hundred women in mid or late pregnancy filled a set survey. Doctors and nurses were the top news sources on maternal health. Knowledge averaged above seventy percent, higher for women at university or private care sites. Choice leaned one way in the full data, and the study maps beliefs and who shares in the final call.
pmc-12767423:
Sisay Kirba, Abdulfetah Abdulkedir Abdosh, Ekram Muhammedasrar, and Abraham Fessehaye Sium study pregnancy ultrasound timing in Ethiopia. Their 2025 paper checks how many women get a first scan before 24 weeks, as world guidance urges. Data came from women who gave birth at three public hospitals. A structured survey gathered the facts in advance of analysis.

About two-thirds of the 385 women had a first scan at the best time. One-third did not, even though public sites offer the service. Where a woman first sought care mattered a lot. Private clinics and hospitals, and government hospitals, tied to higher rates than health centers. A past major pregnancy problem also raised the chance of a timely scan. The authors flag the gap for action.
pmc-12768623:
Jose Evangelista and three co-authors report the first income based study of quality of life in families served by a Brazilian aid group. The Dara Institute fights poverty with joined up support. The team used a short wellbeing survey to test how scores relate to income before and after help.

One hundred family members took part, most in the lowest income bands. Scores on standard health surveys were nearly equal across the two income groups. The wellbeing survey showed slightly lower scores for the poorer group, though ranges overlapped a lot. The authors say the tool shows promise for judging wellbeing in at risk groups. Income gaps mattered, but modestly.
pmc-12768723:
Thiago Trindade and colleagues overview evidence on GLP-1 drugs for severe obesity. Their 2025 rapid overview supports health technology assessment planning. These drugs produce nearly twice the weight loss of older options. At least nine such drugs are approved or in late-stage testing. Clinical hopes for the class have risen sharply in recent years.

The team searched for systematic reviews with meta-analysis on severe obesity. Children-only studies and other drug classes were excluded. Reviews had to test GLP-1 agonists or polyagonists as the active treatment. The overview maps clinical outcomes reported across those reviews. Its goal is to help pick topics for a full assessment. Decision makers can see where evidence is thick or thin. The report frames a fast-moving treatment area.
pmc-12768823:
Mariana del Grossi and co-authors grade three tests for a grave gut germ ill next to the flesh proof. The study appeared in 2025. The ill, borne by a sand-fly germ, needs fast true finds to curb its spread. Quick strip tests, code tests, and plate tests all serve in sick lands.

Two dozen works fed the pool cross four base banks. Code tests hit high marks on both true-find shares in sound-guard folks. The strip test ran a shade low yet stays a less harsh pick than bone draws. Grade checks and faith marks ran on each work. The pool gives wards a firm base for test picks.
pmc-12770523:
Satoshi Takatori and co-authors mimic DNA packing with a shaken bead chain in a 2025 paper. A lone DNA strand coils into toroids and coils at the micrometer scale. The team scale the puzzle up: a centimeter bead chain, shaken in a dish with granular spheres. Crowding and shake strength are the knobs.

The chain took forms that mirror DNA shapes: compact toroids, swollen toroids, rods, and loose coils. Monte Carlo simulations of a semiflexible chain matched the core patterns. Tuning shake strength and crowding in the model did the trick. The match suggests shared rules for semiflexible chains across vast size scales. Bench demos could teach polymer physics by eye.
pmc-12770923:
Simmi Tiwari and co-authors run in a 2025 national study a ranking of animal-borne diseases for India, as a first step toward a One Health system joining human, animal, and environmental care. Fifty experts scored forty diseases on five grounds: human severity, economic burden, pandemic potential, control capacity, and the risk of arrival or spread in India.

Zoonotic influenza topped the list, with anthrax among those that followed in the top ten. The workshop followed a United States public health method adapted to Indian needs. A shared priority list, the authors argue, lets scarce resources aim at the spillovers that matter most.
pmc-12771223:
Miao He and co-authors test clear aligners for fixing a common bite problem in teens, in a clinical study from 2025. The problem, Angle Class II Division 1, is an overbite pattern that can harm oral health and facial looks. The study covered teens whose permanent teeth had just come in.

Thirty patients aged 12 to 15 wore clear aligners with elastic traction between the jaws, and none had teeth removed. Care lasted 28.6 months on average. All patients ended with better overjet and overbite and a sound molar fit, and their facial profiles improved. Most X-ray measures of jaw and tooth angles shifted in the right direction. Three jaw angles stayed put, which the authors report as well.
pmc-12771823:
Ray-Chang Tzeng and three co-authors test a known seizure drug in lab cells in a 2025 study of electric currents in cell walls. The drug, topiramate, is used for seizures, nerve pain, and migraine, but its exact effects on cell currents were not fully clear. The team used fine glass tools to clamp onto cells and record the currents directly.

They worked with hormone-making cells grown in the lab. The drug blocked two forms of the sodium current, both the brief pulse and the late tail, more strongly as the dose rose. It also blocked a second current that is switched on when the cell voltage drops. The dual block helps explain how the drug calms overactive cells.
pmc-12772023:
Drugs that block the EGFR pathway should suit liver cancer, where that pathway matters, yet their benefit has been unsure. Zizhong Yang and co-authors hunted for immune markers of resistance in 2025, growing tumors from fourteen patients in mice and testing an EGFR antibody on them. Half the tumors responded.

A class of helper T cells marked by the protein CCR7 clustered in the tumors that resisted, and their share tracked closely with poor response. These cells sat near other immune cells in patterns tied to a suppressed tumor setting, and fewer of them went with better outlooks across datasets. A nine-gene signature based on them strongly predicted survival. The authors built the signature into a chart for judging patient risk.
pmc-12774923:
Clémentine Rivière and co-authors test in 2025 whether older adults with thinking problems still know the rules of the road. Deciding when to stop driving in dementia is hard, and rule knowledge is one part of fitness. Geriatric day hospitals gave a computer-based driving theory test to 144 patients with cognitive complaints, average age near eighty.

Their scores ran firmly below those of 249 young healthy drivers. Knowledge tracked scores on standard cognitive tests, above all a global screen and a symbol-coding task. The findings suggest a theory test can flag shaky rule knowledge, though the authors stop short of equating that with unsafe driving.
pmc-12775023:
Sarah McDowell and co-authors present a 2025 animal study on how radiation therapy affects the bladder. Pelvic radiotherapy often leaves patients with urinary symptoms. Image-guided irradiation in mice lets researchers study the bladder's response under controlled conditions that mimic the clinic.

Female mice received a single 20-gray dose aimed at the bladder under CT guidance. Urination patterns were tracked with void spot tests before and after. Bladder strips were also tested for squeeze strength in the lab. About half the mice showed more void spots and smaller volumes in the weeks after treatment. Nerve-driven contractions weakened at two weeks, then partly recovered over months. The model gives a baseline for testing protective drugs.
pmc-12775323:
Caiping Chen and co-authors study a tumor suppressor protein, PERP, and its role in breast cancer spread, in a 2025 paper. Whether this protein restrains metastasis, the spread of cancer to distant sites, was unclear. The team set out to test its role, its clinical meaning, and the mechanism behind any effect it has. Their title already signals the direction of the answer.

They measure the protein in cancer cell lines, public data sets, and 142 patient samples. Tests that raise or lower the protein in two cell lines track migration and invasion in dishes and spread in animal models. Gene silencing and sequencing trace the pathway through two partner genes. The protein's level was much reduced in tumor tissue, and restoring it curbed spread.
pmc-12775623:
Elizabeth Raulston, Maya Bhutwala, and Kyle Kesler report pressure headaches after spinal fluid leaks in a case paper from 2025. Spine surgery sometimes nicks the sac around the cord, leaking spinal fluid. Even after leaks seal, some patients keep stubborn headaches. Their symptoms point the other way: pressure inside the skull running too high.

Two patients fit that pattern, with ringing ears, vision changes, and dizziness. One man's headache worsened lying down and peaked before dawn. A myelogram confirmed excess pressure in the first case. The drug acetazolamide, which cuts fluid production, eased the picture. The report warns that post-leak headaches are not always low pressure. Treating the wrong direction would fail these patients.
pmc-12776223:
Lin Mi and co-authors study a chemical messenger that reins in tumor-helping macrophages in lung cancer, in a 2025 paper. Macrophages in tumors often take an M2 form that feeds growth and spread. The messenger CXCL9 has been flagged as a brake on that form.

In dish work, M2 macrophages boosted lung cancer cell growth, movement, and invasion. Adding CXCL9 blunted all three boosts and curbed the M2 shift itself. Protein and gene reads tracked how the messenger rewired the cells. Patient sample checks and prognosis data framed the lab results. The study positions CXCL9 as a lever on the tumor's support crew, a route that attacks cancer's helpers rather than the cancer alone.
pmc-12779423:
Prostate cancer is rising among aging men in China, yet screening habits are little studied. Shuxian Tang and co-authors survey 518 middle-aged and older men at one hospital clinic about what they know, feel, and do regarding the disease and early testing. A custom questionnaire scored each area.

Knowledge scored low, averaging about 7.6 of 20 points. Attitudes and practices scored much higher on their scales. Men with more knowledge were slightly more likely to act proactively. Current smokers were also more likely to report proactive practice, while men already screened once showed an odd lower score on the practice scale. Knowledge shaped practice directly rather than through attitudes. The authors see a clear teaching gap: goodwill is present, facts are not.
pmc-12779723:
Pavlos Texakalidis and colleagues wrote a 2025 guide to reading MRI scans of cysts inside nerves. These cysts are benign and filled with mucus-like fluid. They grow inside the sheath of a peripheral nerve. Pressure from the cyst can damage the nerve. Most cases cause weakness or pain in one limb.

The leading theory traces the fluid to a nearby joint. Fluid travels along a small nerve branch into the main nerve. Scan signs can reveal that hidden connection. Finding it changes the surgery completely. Surgeons now treat the joint connection, not just the cyst. The guide organizes scan signs by disease phase.
pmc-12780423:
Sebastian Veliz Padilla writes in 2025 to add marks to a debate on blood tests for heart attacks. A past study showed one small gene bit rises fast in the first hours of an attack and tracks harm depth. Padilla backs a multi-mark plan as the way ahead for sharp heart care.

He cites a scar-linked mark that rises days after an attack and tracks heart reshaping. Paired with a stress mark, it sharpens calls on risk and outcome, he notes. A fast heart protein test may also beat the standard mark on speed, which rounds out his case.
pmc-12781023:
Xinrui Li and six co-authors trace right heart scar in lung press ill, from guard to harm. Their review appeared in twenty twenty-five. Lung press loads the right heart, which first swells and scars as a shield, then scars past use and fails. The tie tween scar and heart work is laid out, with its worth in the ward.

Ways to count the scar, from scans to cuts, are weighed. Cure paths that aim to keep right heart work as scar grows are set out. The team frame scar as both a mark to read and a mark to treat.
pmc-12781723:
Teng Fei Qi and co-authors trace a long noncoding RNA that shields throat cancer from treatment in this 2025 paper. Esophageal squamous cell carcinoma resists DNA-damaging therapy, and its genome often amplifies a stretch of chromosome three. Within that stretch, one long RNA, nicknamed PARylator, stood out as the most boosted.

The RNA binds the repair enzyme PARP1 in the nucleus and boosts its activity. Silencing it let damage pile up, pushed cells toward death, and sensitized them to cisplatin and radiation. Animal tumors shrank more under treatment when the RNA was cut. The authors name the RNA a driver of resistance and a candidate drug target.
pmc-12783123:
Samiran Dey and five co-authors show how AI can fill a missing data gap in cancer care in this two thousand twenty-five paper. Combining tissue images with gene activity data sharpens cancer grading and risk forecasts. But hospitals rarely order gene tests, so the second data type is usually absent. The team instead generates gene expression from the tissue image itself. Their model learns the link from cases where both exist.

They tested the idea on four cancer cohorts from two public collections. Adding the generated gene data clearly improved grading and risk estimates. Scores with faked data came close to those with real gene data. The trick could bring multimodal AI into clinics that only have slides. Pathologists and oncologists stand to gain.
pmc-12783623:
Md Imran Hosen and co-authors design a vision system that parses people in images on weak hardware. Human parsing tags each pixel as a body part or clothing item and ties parts to the right person. Heavy models need helper inputs and big chips, which shuts out cheap devices.

Their end-to-end design folds detection and parsing into one pass. A transformer attention block deepens scene context without a heavy frame. New polygon labels around each person let the model learn detection and parsing at once. The system runs in real time on a Raspberry Pi board and keeps fine detail. Speed without a sharp accuracy loss is the headline gain. Such lean parsing could serve home robots, store cameras, and aid tools in the field.
pmc-12784023:
Gianluca Vadalà and three co-authors wrote a 2025 commentary on a study of back pain tied to worn spinal discs. Low back pain is a top cause of disability in the world. Its roots in disc pain are still poorly grasped, since standard scans show shape, not the chemistry inside the disc.

The study under review used a scan that reads fat signals in the disc, plus lab studies of fats and proteins. Patients whose scans showed a strong fat peak reported worse pain and disability. The signal seems to link changed fat in the disc to inflammation driven by a signal called interleukin-17. The commentary praises the mix of scan, lab, and patient data. It argues that biology, not shape alone, should guide how disc pain is judged.
pmc-12784623:
Joaquim Segalés and co-authors review what remains unknown about porcine circovirus 2, one of the costliest germs in pig farming. Vaccines have sharply cut the severe disease and breeding losses the virus once caused, yet it still circulates in farm and wild pigs worldwide. It mutates fast, swaps genes, and infects many hosts, which keeps control fragile.

Open questions fill the review. Shots prevent sickness but not infection or shedding, so the virus keeps evolving, and nobody knows how that drift affects protection or deadliness. Host immunity, co-infections, and farm conditions are only partly understood. New gene-based tests are sensitive but cannot replace tissue examination outright. The authors map the gaps that research must close.
pmc-12784923:
Kathryn Swaby and co-authors report an early study from two thousand twenty-five on blood markers after brain injury in children. Traumatic brain injury is a leading cause of death and disability in the young. Doctors still lack blood tests that judge severity and forecast recovery with confidence, so the team tested immune signal proteins.

They measured many cytokines and chemokines in blood from twenty-six injured children and twenty-one controls. Several signals were higher after injury, and a few were lower. Two signals at enrollment tracked severe injury very closely. A handful of signals also linked to poor function over the following year. The authors treat the results as exploratory, pointing to candidates for larger confirmatory studies.
pmc-12785123:
Anna Lange-Consiglio and co-authors model how stressed womb cells talk to early cow embryos across a shared membrane. Before implantation, embryos feed on uterine secretions. Infection stress in the mother can alter that fluid.

Cells were stressed with a bacterial toxin fragment. Embryos at the morula stage sat across the barrier. Vesicle traffic and two signal proteins were measured. Embryo growth rates were tracked over several days. Early results showed similar blastocyst rates between groups. Later stages may still reveal subtler effects. The model isolates womb-to-embryo signaling cleanly. It serves cattle fertility research under infection pressure in the herd on farms.
pmc-12785723:
Charlotte Boven and five co-workers wrote a 2025 pilot study on screening older adults for violence in Belgian hospitals. Abuse of older people is a rising health concern. Many will talk about it if asked in the right way. Geriatric wards could spot cases early, but staff need clear guidance.

The team tried a new guide in three hospital departments. Just over a hundred admitted patients past age seventy-five took part. One in five shared experiences of violence, recent or long past. The dozen staff who ran the screen rated the guide well. They asked for clearer wording, more flexibility and more training.
pmc-12785923:
Seyyed Bahram Borgheai and six co-authors review how thinking problems show up in the brain signals of people with ALS, in a 2025 paper. ALS destroys movement control, usually within a few years. It shares roots with a dementia that attacks the front of the brain, and the two are now seen as one disease process striking different systems.

Many patients with mainly motor disease also lose ground in memory, planning, or language. The review gathers what brain-wave and signal studies reveal about those losses. Such signal markers could track illness more sensitively than bedside tests. They might also judge whether new treatments help the mind as well as the body. The authors map where the evidence is firm and where it is thin.
pmc-12786423:
Katarzyna Olechno, Julia Higuchi, and Katarzyna Winnicka review sticky drug forms for oral fungal infection in a 2025 paper. Fungal mouth disease challenges patients with weak immunity most. Cancer therapy and antibiotics also raise the risk. Local treatment beats systemic dosing when it stays in place.

Forms that cling to wet mouth tissue hold drug at the infection site. Longer retention means adequate levels with lower doses. Fewer side effects and better patient compliance follow. Few such products actually reach the market, though. The review explains how mucoadhesion works mechanically and chemically. Polymers that deliver the stickiness are cataloged. Recent development reports and quality tests are surveyed. Conventional forms wash away too fast in the moist mouth. Optimal adhesion is framed as the key design problem. The paper maps a formulation agenda for oral candidiasis.
pmc-12786523:
Antonio Libonati and co-authors compare two core-carrier filling methods for root canals with a bioceramic sealer in a 2025 pilot study. Filling the canal well, with few voids, is key to lasting root canal success.

Eight resin models of upper first molars were filled by GuttaFusion or SoftCore carriers. Slices near the tip and higher up were measured for gutta-percha, sealer, and void shares. One method packed more gutta-percha and less sealer near the tip, with slightly more voids. Higher slices filled better under both methods. The study is small and early, with plain stats only. Dentists get first comparative data for a new sealer pairing.
pmc-12787023:
Ying Wu and co-authors link in 2025 a copper driven form of cell death in ovarian cancer to the cell's power plants and to one guard protein. A copper carrying drug sparks this death by striking fat tagged parts of a core energy cycle. The team treated ovarian cancer cells with the drug and tracked power plant stress, copper handling proteins, and death markers.

Stress signals and a death marker rose, while a protein needed to build the fat tag fell. Several copper movers and parts of the breathing chain's last complex also fell, along with the guard protein. Blocking that guard changed the death course. The authors name it as a key factor and a possible lever for therapy.
pmc-12787423:
Tianxiao Zhu, Ziyu Xu, Rujiang Zhu, Wei Zhang, and Zhonghua Miao plan robot paths that respect slopes in a 2025 engineering paper. On rough ground a shortest path can tip a robot over. Standard planners ignore how terrain tilts the body. Their two-layer algorithm refines elevation maps in a guidance layer, sharpening posture estimates with a smooth interpolation trick, then plans with a Hybrid-A* search in the layer below.

The planner switches cost functions as it goes, adjusts its step size, prunes dead ends, and activates phase windows that refine the route in stretches. Real-time feedback keeps the path honest as the ground changes. Stability-aware planning matters most where no road exists to forgive mistakes.
pmc-12787623:
Mahsima Seifollahi and Mohammad Zaman Kabir studied how long 3D-printed plastic parts last under repeated loads in a 2025 paper. The plastic, called PLA, is printed layer by layer by a common method. Parts often have notches or holes, and those shape breaks can start cracks, yet few studies had tested them under repeated loading.

The authors printed test pieces on edge to cut flaws, then ran still and repeated load tests. They tracked how print direction and notch shape changed strength and the growth of damage. Their results give designers firmer numbers for printed parts that must flex many times, such as brackets and clips, rather than bear a single load once.
pmc-12787723:
Jacksaint Saintila leads a seven-author team linking breakfast and produce habits to life satisfaction in students, in a study published in two thousand twenty-five. Fruit, vegetables, and regular breakfast are established health goods. Why they might raise life satisfaction, psychologically, was less clear.

Five hundred eleven health sciences students completed self-report measures. The team tested whether positive affect, feeling good day to day, mediates the diet-satisfaction link. Mediation models separated direct from indirect associations. The study sits within a Latin American university context. Understanding the pathway matters for designing student wellbeing programs. If mood carries the effect, interventions can target eating routines as a lever on both body and outlook.
pmc-12787923:
Xiaohui Du and co-authors test rubber seals under radiation in a 2025 study. Seals in nuclear plants must hold after long exposure to gamma rays. Four rubbers with distinct molecular builds faced cobalt source doses at three levels, up to 100 kilograys. The team paired strength and leak tests with fine structure measures to link build to damage.

Whether the rubber's main chain is saturated decided how it broke down. Unsaturated chains and saturated chains followed different damage routes, seen in spectra, heat scans, and crosslink counts. The map helps engineers pick seal materials by chemistry rather than habit. It also warns which rubbers age worst where radiation runs high.
pmc-12788223:
Minsoo Kim, Jalel Ben-Othman, Lynda Mokdad, Paolo Bellavista, and Hyunbum Kim propose a layered tracking system for mobile networks watched from satellites. Their study was published in twenty twenty-five. Direct satellite links to fast-moving ground gear suffer delays and heavy data loads.

Their design stacks three layers: low orbit satellites, high-altitude platforms, and low-altitude platforms. Event-based summaries cut needless data sending, and a map service tracks the moving infrastructure in blocks. Tests showed sharper surveillance at low speeds and steady tracking under movement. Processing delay fell compared with the direct satellite-to-ground way. The system targets real-time sensing for nomadic setups such as disaster or military networks. It offers a way to watch wide areas without choking the link.
pmc-12794523:
Supriya Garapati and co-authors chart the genetics of inherited high cholesterol in Telangana, India, in a study from 2025. Familial hypercholesterolemia floods the blood with LDL cholesterol from birth. It drives early heart disease if missed. Indian data on its gene faults are thin.

Suspected patients were flagged by a standard clinical score. Their close relatives were then screened in cascade fashion. Targeted gene sequencing and family tree analysis hunted the faults. Both new and known mutations appeared, some that stop genes cold. LDLR, the classic gene, was hit in a share of families; other genes, from LPL to CETP, also carried faults. Finding a family's fault lets doctors screen children early.
pmc-12796423:
Samuel Mañas-Valero and a large team image spin waves with diamond and boron nitride defect sensors, a step toward magnon spintronics, where spin waves carry information. The catch was that the magnetic fields steering the waves also detuned the sensors, and each sensor type hears only a narrow band. Their fix picks sensor defects whose axes sit square to the film's magnetization, freeing them from the control fields.

Two sensor materials cover matching frequency bands side by side. The team imaged field-steered spin waves at a fixed frequency across a magnetic half-plane. Natural anisotropy at device edges created two-state textures that govern how waves travel there.
pmc-12797523:
Yanqian Xu, Zhongyuan Han, and Qi Lu test whether two blood proteins track scarring in failing hearts, in a 2025 study. Chronic heart failure stiffens the heart as fibrous tissue builds. The proteins, ECM1 and LRP1, both have past links to fibrosis in other organs. The team drew blood from 93 patients with weak hearts and 80 matched controls with steady disease, and read the pair beside known scar markers.

Both proteins ran far higher in the failure group. Their levels tracked with worse pumping and higher scar signals from partner markers like TGF-beta and collagen fragments. Curve tests showed the pair could sort patients from controls with useful accuracy. The authors pitch ECM1 and LRP1 as candidate blood marks of heart remodeling. Such marks could help grade risk and watch change over time, if larger studies confirm them.
pmc-12798423:
Dina Mohamed Elawady and co-authors compare mouth scanning with classic molds for denture patients with flabby gum ridges, in a study from two thousand twenty-five. Flabby ridges move under pressure, so recording them true is hard. Twelve patients with no teeth had both a digital scan and a classic window mold.

The scan beat the mold on trueness and on repeat precision across all measures but one. That one measure, outward drift, tied between the two methods. The authors judge scanning a strong swap for the classic method here. Larger studies with patient outcomes should confirm the gain, they add.
pmc-12799523:
Arash Babaei-Ghazani and seven co-authors weigh the toll of spine-and-brain birth faults in the Middle East and North Africa across three decades. Their study, from two thousand twenty-five, draws on a world health store.

Few past works gauged this toll, and those were thin in span of lands and years. The team took counts of new cases, deaths, and lost sound years, by sex, age, land, and year. Rates were set to a standard age base, so lands can be matched. A wealth-and-school index for each land was joined in. The aim is a full map of how the toll moved, and where it now stands.
pmc-12800023:
Mattiske and a large team identify in twenty twenty-five a long non-coding RNA that helps a key gene answer to hormones during male genital development in mice. The RNA sits beside the gene in the genome and is strikingly conserved across species. When the fetal testis starts making testosterone, the RNA rises and boosts the gene's activity, while estrogen suppresses both.

Deleting the RNA lowered the gene's output and caused a severe birth defect where the urethra opens in the wrong place. In human tissue, the same RNA-gene pair switched on together during penis development. The authors name the RNA a regulator of urethral closure. They flag it as a possible hit point for hormone-disrupting chemicals behind the defect.
pmc-12800523:
Hong Kyung Shin and co-authors flagged a scan sign that marks the most dangerous pelvic injuries, in a 2025 study. Bleeding inside the pelvis can kill, and scans that show dye leaking from vessels sort the worst cases. The team reviewed records for 195 pelvic injury patients treated at their hospital from 2003 to 2013.

Thirty-four patients had vessel injuries and needed far more transfused blood than the rest. Within that group, dye leaking in the later, venous phase of the scan spelled grave danger: far more heart stops and deaths than leaks seen only in the early phase. Patients whose leak was purely venous all died. The authors urge teams to treat that sign as a red flag.
pmc-12802123:
Foster Opoku-Mensah, Albert Ahenkan, Berhanu Temesgen, and Theophilus Maloreh-Nyamekye asked in 2025 what drives green buying in Ghana's health sector. Sustainable procurement is rising in interest, though Ghana lacks a full policy for it. Two of the country's oldest teaching hospitals served as cases.

Interviews with nineteen hospital informants and four from regulators were analysed for themes. Both hospitals named shared drivers: saving resources, obeying the law, avoiding lawsuits, pleasing clients, health concerns, saving cost, and value for money. Each also had its own drivers, from donor pressure and ethics at one to culture, guarding public funds, and durable equipment at the other. Local and global forces mix, the authors conclude.
pmc-12802623:
Prossy Kiddu Namyalo, Robert Setekera, and Primrose Nakazibwe gather patient and provider views on using mobile phones against stroke in rural Uganda, in work from twenty twenty-four. Stroke ranks among Uganda's top killers and hospital burdens. Phones are widespread even where clinics are thin.

District records supplied counts, while interviews with providers, patients, caregivers, and survivors supplied the texture. Every participant backed phone based support. They asked for three content types: warning signs of stroke, its underlying causes, and prevention steps. Expected hurdles are local context, health system strain, and cost. The baseline study frames a phone program as a plausible tool, provided the design tackles those barriers head on.
pmc-12804323:
Jennifer Tuokkola and Kathryn Schwertfeger review, in 2025, how a growth factor signaling system drives breast cancer partly by rewiring its metabolism. The receptors in this system are often amplified, mutated, or fused in breast tumors, pushing growth, spread, and drug resistance. Newer work shows they also reset how cancer cells burn fuel.

The review covers effects on sugar burning and fat handling, and links with metabolic enzymes, gene switches, and nutrient sensors. Different breast cancer subtypes show different metabolic weak points under this signaling. That plasticity helps tumors vary and resist targeted drugs. The authors point to combined metabolic and signaling attacks as a path forward.
pmc-12804723:
Guangyao Ran and six co-authors propose measuring children's eyes a few fractions of a millimeter deeper, and argue myopia care should follow, in this 2025 study. Axial length, cornea to retina, is the yardstick of eye growth and shortsightedness. The trouble: the spongy choroid behind the retina swells and thins, jiggling the conventional measurement. Their real axial length runs instead to the choroid's back surface, captured by swept-source OCT angiography.

The cross-sectional study enrolled 1,833 Chinese children aged five to seventeen with normal uncorrected vision. The new metric averaged 24.04 millimeters against 23.52 for the conventional one, the choroid's thickness made visible as a number. Standard measurements agreed closely between the new device and the clinical standard, an intraclass correlation of 0.956. The team also built age-specific reference values for the new measure, the baseline charts any clinic adopting it would need.
pmc-12805323:
Moses Okumu and a large team link digital health skill to sex health facts and access for displaced youth in Uganda. Their study appeared in twenty twenty-five. Phone health tools can lift fair access for pushed-out groups, but youth skill was thinly known. A tablet survey in five poor town zones of Kampala held near four hundred fifty youth aged sixteen to twenty-four.

Skill fell into four bands, from low to very high. Top-band youth knew more of where to get condom training, condoms, and HIV tests than low-band youth. Sex splits ran through the links, with men and women gaining on distinct goods. Past-three-month access was taped too.
pmc-12805923: Stefano Barbaro and seven colleagues review nerve pain caused by cancer and its treatments. Tumors or therapies harm the body's sensing system, causing burning, shooting, or electric-shock pain that standard painkillers control poorly. The pain can outlast the treatment itself and badly cut quality of life. Care must combine several approaches. Drugs borrowed from epilepsy and depression care serve as added pain relief beside standard therapies. Checks must be ongoing, since response varies and care needs adjusting to protect comfort and function.
pmc-12807923:
Xiaojun Wu and co-authors study how a corn herbicide reshapes soil life in a study published in 2025. Mesotrione lingers in soil and can harm following crops such as tobacco. Its effects on the soil microbes that cycle carbon and nitrogen were unclear. The team ran a two-month greenhouse test at a field dose and a fivefold dose.

Both doses cut soil nitrogen and organic matter within a month. Microbe diversity dipped early, and the community's ability to use varied carbon foods stayed suppressed. Gene profiles shifted in mixed ways: several nitrogen-handling paths were curbed, while nitrogen fixation genes rose. Under the high dose, the microbe network grew denser and more connected, with rare genera forming a busy hub. The authors say such shifts matter for soil health after spraying.
pmc-12808223:
Ali Uromeihy and colleagues reinforced artificial stone with fibers in two thousand twenty-five. Stone waste from marble and quartzite formed the aggregates. Resin bound the pressed slabs together. Best resin shares were chosen for each stone type. Polypropylene and glass fibers were then added. Identical processing allowed a fair comparison.

Quartzite kept its compressive strength with fibers. Its bending strength trended upward nicely. Marble behaved oppositely under the same treatment. Its strengths fell substantially with fiber addition. Porosity in marble rose sharply as well. Finer marble powder made the mix stiffer and less workable. Powder traits explain the split outcome.
pmc-12812623:
Yao Liu and co-authors ease face nerve pain with sound waves in a mouse study whose head gives the year as 2025. The pain is trigeminal neuropathic pain, a burning state after nerve harm. Swelling along the nerve drives much of it. Gentle pulsed ultrasound, called LIPUS, is known to calm swelling in other diseases. The team tied off part of a face nerve in mice to mimic the state.

Tied nerves brought lasting swelling and sharp touch pain. Ultrasound care eased both. A channel called Pannexin 1 rose after the tie and helped drive the swelling. Ultrasound held that channel down in nerve, ganglion, and cord tissue. Silencing the channel with a gene tool also eased the touch pain, which pins its role.
pmc-12812723:
Bo-Min Kim and colleagues identify a gum bacterium as a periodontitis pathogen that worsens gum disease by driving nitric oxide production. Their 2026 study uses a mouse model of ligature-induced gum inflammation.

Applying the bacterium to an upper molar worsened bone loss and tissue damage. Gum tissue showed more bone-eating cells and higher levels of the enzyme making nitric oxide. The bacterium triggered nitric oxide in cultured immune cells, an effect blocked by a compound implicating its surface molecules. Purified surface material raised nitric oxide through two immune receptors. Injecting that material into gum tissue further aggravated disease in the mouse model, confirming a pathogenic role.
pmc-12812923:
Five authors report a hard skin case tied to a sugar drug in a 2025 note. A 68-year-old man in Japan on a DPP-4 drug grew wide tight blisters with mouth sores. Tests named a rare self-harm skin ill that hits a deep skin glue.

Care with strong drugs failed to tame the ill in the case. At day 80, lung ills, kidney fail, and a platelet crash hit at once. The crash was named an immune platelet ill once kin causes were barred. Short gains came, yet the man died.
pmc-12813023:
Jinting Zhu and colleagues built a machine learning model to flag dental staff at risk of workplace exposure accidents. Dental workers face needle sticks and splashes that can carry infection. The team surveyed 367 oral healthcare workers across twenty-seven hospitals in Tianjin, China.

About sixteen percent had suffered an exposure. Work attitudes, resilience, workplace climate, job rank, hospital level, and sex all shaped the risk. A random forest model predicted exposure best among four algorithms tried. Hospitals could use such screening to target training and protection at the staff most likely to need it.
pmc-12815723:
Ken Nakamura and three co-authors report an emergency rescue procedure in a torn aorta, in this case report published in 2025. The patient, a sixty-seven-year-old woman, had an acute type B aortic dissection, a split in the wall of the lower aorta. On day twelve she suddenly lost blood flow to both legs when the split channel swelled and crushed the true channel.

Scans showed a new entry tear feeding the false channel, which had collapsed the true channel at the belly aorta and both hip arteries. The standard repair devices were not on hand, so the team worked through both groins and placed four self-expanding bare-metal stents. The true channel reopened at once, pulses returned, and later scans confirmed the flow. The authors stress the fix saves limbs as a stopgap, not as a cure for the tear itself.
pmc-12815823:
Yanwei Guo and co-authors pool gene-based studies on blood fats and stroke in a paper whose head dates it to 2025. Ischemic stroke follows blocked brain vessels, and which fat particles truly cause it has been debated. Gene-based tests can separate cause from mere correlation.

From over 400 candidate papers they kept ten Mendelian randomization studies. Higher LDL cholesterol, apoB, and VLDL each raised stroke risk in the pooled results. ApoA1 and HDL particles tied to lower risk. The particle Lp(a) showed no clear link here. Combined non-HDL fats also raised risk. The authors weigh uneven study quality across the set.
pmc-12815923:
Mostafizur Rahman and co-authors survey health worry among tannery workers in Bangladesh. Their twenty twenty-five study covers the Savar Tannery Industrial Estate, where toxic chemicals are part of daily work. Safety gear and rules are often thin in this trade.

Four hundred workers answered the cross-sectional survey. Most said they were concerned about health risks, and many were very concerned. Men, married workers, and those with more than ten years on the job showed higher odds of concern. Knowledge, attitudes, and site practice also shaped worry. The results show risk is felt on the ground, a base for stronger safety steps.
pmc-12816223:
Mingyu Han and five co-authors present a review, published in 2025, on drugs that block the FGFR growth signal in gliomas, aggressive brain tumors. Changes in this receptor, from mutations to gene fusions, drive growth, stemness, and metabolic rewiring in a subset of tumors. The review gathers recent advances on how the signal goes wrong and what inhibitors have achieved in patients.

One dedicated inhibitor showed anti-tumor activity in a mid-stage trial for recurrent tumors carrying the changes. A broader drug gave a modest survival gain in glioblastoma. Responses often needed a second drug to block escape routes. The central obstacle is the blood-brain barrier, which keeps drug levels in the brain low. The authors push for better-penetrating compounds, smarter delivery, routine gene screening, and combination plans to make the benefit last.
pmc-12816323:
Moorman and three co-authors built machine learning models to forecast the course of severe COVID-19 in twenty twenty-five. Patients may need mechanical ventilation or ECMO, a heart-lung support machine, but who will need them, and for how long, is hard to predict amid varied disease courses. Better forecasts would aid care and the allocation of scarce machines.

Using records of over ten thousand patients treated at Emory hospitals during twenty twenty to twenty twenty-two, the team trained hierarchical models on demographics, vital signs, and laboratory time series. The models predicted ventilation duration in day bands, ECMO use, and death. Best models reached strong discrimination scores for ECMO and ventilation duration, and moderate scores for mortality. The authors conclude such models show promise for planning intensive care resources in future surges.
pmc-12816623:
Ferris and colleagues published in twenty twenty-five a systematic review and meta-analysis of disease clusters in multimorbidity. People with several chronic diseases often show recurring disease groupings. The team searched major databases for cluster studies up to mid twenty twenty-four. Seventy-nine articles met their criteria for the review. Hierarchical clustering was the most common method used. Latent class and center-based methods followed, with network approaches in a fifth of studies.

Their meta-analysis pooled over twelve hundred clusters from seventy-three studies. Six clusters showed moderate stability across the literature. Those mostly featured heart and metabolic conditions. No cluster reached high stability, and few considered disease timing. Methods and disease definitions varied widely between studies. The authors give suggestions to improve reporting and performance. Consistent clusters still emerge despite the messiness, they note.
pmc-12816723:
Youhui Zhao and co-authors track how blood salt balance changes over time in patients with sepsis who develop delirium. Earlier work linked the level itself to outcomes in very ill patients. This study asks whether the path of change in the first days also matters.

Using a large intensive care database, the team grouped patients by the shape of their early readings. Higher starting levels tied to higher death risk within a month. Groups whose levels rose, or rose and fell, also fared worse than the steady group. The pattern was strongest in older patients, which may help staff watch risk more closely.
pmc-12817723:
Coraline Dubot and co-authors report a 2025 study on long-term quality of life in survivors of rare ovarian cancers. The two forms in view arise from germ cells and from sex cord tissue, and most patients live long after care. Surgery, with or without chemotherapy, can leave late effects that drag on daily life for years.

The team drew 144 survivors who were cancer-free at least two years after care, and matched them with 284 healthy women of like age. All filled standard scales for quality of life, fatigue, mood, sleep, nerve harm, thinking, and sexuality. Overall quality of life, fatigue, mood, and sleep matched the healthy group at a median of six years after care. Survivors did face more early menopause, worse sexual quality of life, and more thinking and nerve complaints.
pmc-12819423:
Ying Wu and co-authors present a 2025 study on a vitamin form that fights gut bacteria. Vitamin B6 comes in six forms, with roles in stress defense and metabolism. One form, made by gut bacteria, killed a wide range of pathogens in lab tests. At high doses it broke bacterial membranes and spilled their DNA.

Two bacterial strains from carp gut made the vitamin together during pathogen exposure. They held back mixed pathogens by at least 63 percent. In infected carp, feed with those strains raised survival by half. Gut microbe variety recovered and body-wide inflammation eased. A rise in the vitamin form in the gut tracked the protection. The authors call it a new probiotic weapon.
pmc-12822023:
Megha Anchan and co-authors tested whether a simple behavior in mice, burrowing, can reveal growing lesions in a model of endometriosis. That disease causes severe pelvic pain and infertility, and progress in treating it is slowed by weak animal models. Existing mouse models do not always produce lesions, and checking for them usually requires killing the animal.

Burrowing is a natural habit that sick mice perform less well. The team used a burrowing test to predict whether lesions had formed in mice given the disease. A behavior test that works without surgery would let drug trials track lesions over time in the same animal. That would cut animal use and make trial results more reliable.
pmc-12822123:
Mehdi Torabi and three colleagues blend classic shock scores with age, consciousness, and oxygen readings to sort trauma patients faster, in a 2025 study. Quick triage decides who gets scarce emergency resources first, and single-number scores often miss the full picture.

Four hundred thirty-seven high-acuity patients at one trauma center were analyzed retrospectively. Composite formulas, such as a reversed shock index multiplied by oxygen and consciousness then divided by age, separated the two triage tiers perfectly in this sample. Other blends predicted death in hospital and the need for transfusion with fair accuracy. The authors argue composites beat their parts and deserve a place in emergency triage.
pmc-12822223:
Lili Xie and co-authors build and test a scale for patient trust in AI follow-up care. The study appeared in 2025. AI follow-up tools give cheap post-stay care, but trust gaps hold back use. Past scales were not built for this trust type.

The work ran in three stages, from item draft to scale build to score checks. Items came from theory, past work, talks, and group chats. Expert rounds and a pilot run honed the draft. A survey of past users then set the scale's shape. The final scale holds items in three groups, from the patient's own lean to trust in the tool and its setting.
pmc-12822323:
Yue Chen and a large team of co-authors followed in 2025 a belly fat score and death risk in older Chinese adults over ten years. The score estimates visceral fat from routine measures. Their group held 1,794 community-dwelling adults with a mean age near seventy-one. Artery stiffness was measured at the start as a possible middle step between fat and death.

Over about ten years, 328 participants died. Those in the top quarter of the fat score faced more than double the death risk of the bottom quarter after adjustments. The link bent rather than running straight. Artery stiffness carried a clear share of the effect, the mediation analysis found. The authors read stiff arteries as one path by which deep belly fat shortens life.
pmc-12824323:
Shermin Lim and a large team study how hearing devices affect work life for adults with hearing loss. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-five, based on a long-term study in Australia. Hearing loss is common in older adults and is tied to tiredness, lower output, and early exit from work.

They compare three groups: hearing aid users, cochlear implant users, and those who use both. Implant and dual users score higher on work output and on work engagement than aid users, even after other factors are held in check. The result points to a need for strong hearing care as workforces age, so older staff can stay active and do well.
pmc-12825223:
Severe malaria caused by the parasite Plasmodium vivax can harm the body in ways that stay poorly mapped. Priyanka Roy and four co-authors focus on the parasite's mitochondria, the small cell parts that make energy and help build key molecules. These parts carry a tiny genome, quite unlike our own, and shift their work as the parasite grows in red blood cells.

The team joins gene activity data with machine learning to read how these cell parts are controlled. They find that a class of long RNA strands, once thought to be mere by-products, acts as strong switches. In severe cases, those switches form clear patterns. The findings open a new view of why some infections turn grave.
pmc-12826123:
Abdulsalam and co-authors present in 2025 a case of an infected dentigerous cyst with an outside skin fistula in a child. Such cysts are the most common developmental jaw cysts, but infection with an external opening is rare in children. A healthy ten year old girl had pain, swelling, and discharge on the left jaw for a month.

Scans showed a clean edged cyst holding an unerupted premolar tooth. Surgery removed the cyst, the retained teeth, and the fistula tract. Culture grew an anaerobic germ that guided antibiotic choice. Tissue study confirmed an inflamed dentigerous cyst. Recovery was smooth and complete, which stresses early imaging in lasting jaw swelling.
pmc-12827323:
Iva Dolečková and co-authors report a 2025 trial of a skin compound taken by mouth, in 150 healthy adults. Past trials of oral hyaluronan for skin were loose in method and narrow in scope. This trial split adults at random into two dose groups and a dummy pill group for twelve weeks, with no one told who got what.

Skin water, water loss, oil, stretch, and wrinkle depth were read monthly on the face. The high dose beat the dummy on most counts and thickened the skin layers, while the low dose helped less. Self-rated skin state was checked each two weeks as well.
pmc-12827623:
Ye Liang, Min Zuo, Chaoyang Wang, and Lei Zhu pooled studies in 2025 on whether two blood fat ratios warn of eye damage in type 2 diabetes. The ratios combine blood fats in ways that reflect vessel risk. Damage to the retina is a common and feared harm of diabetes, so cheap warning signs are valuable.

Searching eight databases, the team gathered observational studies that reported the ratios in patients with and without eye damage. Their pooled analysis weighs how strongly each ratio tracks with the damage and its severity. A clear link would give clinics a low-cost triage tool drawn from tests they already run.
pmc-12828023:
Eline De Borre and co-authors test, in a 2025 study, whether 5G radio fields change how mosquito larvae grow. The mosquito studied spreads dengue and other diseases, making it both a health concern and a useful test species. Insects live bathed in telecom signals, yet dose checked lab evidence on development is rare.

The team built a reverberation chamber to expose larvae at 3.6 gigahertz, a 5G band. Simulations computed the dose the larvae actually absorbed. Larvae were raised on two diets, one weaker, and exposed for five days. At a moderate field level, development slowed, especially in the underfed larvae. At a much higher level, heating from the fields changed development timing and adult size. Separating a true field effect from plain heating is the study's central care, and its design speaks to regulators weighing insect safety.
pmc-12829223:
Settachote Maholarnkij and co-authors piloted this 2025 phone app for feeding malnourished children in hospital. Nutrition care for sick children involves assessment, planning, and monitoring steps that eat staff time, and few apps cover the whole chain. Their iNutri platform bundles all three. Pediatric residents used it inside the normal care routine for sixty malnourished inpatients.

Fourteen children reached their early energy and protein targets during the pilot. The team measured how fast targets were met, how long children stayed, and how the residents rated the app for speed, satisfaction, and comfort on a five-point scale. Early results linked the app with better time efficiency and user experience. The pilot sets up larger trials of app-guided nutrition care.
pmc-12829623:
Pooja Parmar and co-authors evaluate, in a 2025 study, a text-message program that teaches first-time mothers about pregnancy care in South Gujarat, India. Expectant mothers in semi-urban and rural areas often miss key knowledge about nutrition, hygiene, and warning signs. Sixty first-time pregnant women joined the Active Moms program. They received standard text messages in Gujarati, drawn from world health guidance, covering food, rest, supplements, danger signs, and delivery readiness.

Knowledge scores climbed steeply after the messages, and attitudes toward healthy practice rose as well. The two gains moved together: women who learned more also shifted their attitudes more. Schooling level shaped parts of the response. The authors judge simple texting a low-cost way to strengthen antenatal teaching where clinic time is scarce, and they note the design lacked a comparison group.
pmc-12830523:
Koichi Furuhashi profiles abused children sent by Child Guidance Centers in Japan to a child psychiatry unit, and their hospital stay patterns. These centers lead child protection in Japan, yet data on such referrals are thin. The study came out in twenty twenty-five.

Records covered dozens of children across four years. Mental abuse was most common, then physical abuse, neglect, and sexual abuse. Girls had far higher odds of sexual abuse on record and were hospitalized more. Children with brain growth disorders had lower odds of sexual abuse being logged. Hospital stays linked to more abuse types and to sexual abuse, most of all by non caregivers.
pmc-12830623:
Mohammad Hajjar and eleven co-authors trace the directed evolution of a TNA polymerase and find that fidelity and catalysis took separate paths. The enzyme was bred to build threose nucleic acid, an unnatural genetic strand, at near natural speed. The study came out in twenty twenty-five.

Crystal forms of key steps along the breeding path were solved and their chemistry gauged. Against the usual view, exactness did not ride on faster catalysis. The two traits split: ground state checks govern accuracy, while transition state checks govern speed. The result gives a rare look at how new enzyme roles emerge, the authors argue.
pmc-12831323:
Cai-li Li and co-authors hunt ageing linked genes behind obstructive sleep apnea in a 2025 study. In this common disorder, the upper airway closes off in sleep, again and again. Ageing is a strong risk factor, yet the molecular bridge between the two is murky. The team paired gene data mining with machine learning screens.

Gene groups tied to the disorder also tied to ageing and immune activity. One gene, EGR1, survived the screens and was checked in cell data, where it sat at the hub of senescence, immune control, and DNA damage response. The authors name it as a candidate drug target for the disorder.
pmc-12831423:
Li and colleagues published in twenty twenty-five a study of a tumor subgroup in esophageal cancer that may predict immunotherapy response. This cancer is aggressive, and checkpoint drugs help only some patients. The team analyzed single-cell data from twelve patients receiving pre-surgery therapy. They found an epithelial subgroup marked by a receptor called HCAR2. Those cells carried high levels of the drug target PD-L1. Signals from them suppressed killer T cells through known pathways.

Lab and mouse tests confirmed the subgroup drives immune evasion. Patients with more of these cells had worse prognosis overall. Paradoxically, they also responded better to checkpoint therapy before surgery. Wider data sets confirmed the marker predicted favorable drug response. The authors propose HCAR2 as a dual-purpose biomarker. Targeting its pathway might boost immunotherapy for this cancer, they suggest.
pmc-12835523:
Alqaraleh and co-authors test machine learning tools for finding brain tumors, with real hospital use in Jordan in mind. Tumors vary widely, and older reading methods rely on human judgment. The team asks if trained models can sort cases with more speed and steadiness.

They compared seven methods, among them decision trees, random forests, support vector machines, and neural networks. A set of 7,023 cases supplied the data for training and testing. Each method was scored on how well it sorted tumor cases. The study weighs which model suits hospital use in Jordan best.
pmc-12836823:
Xiaoxiang Zhang and co-authors test blood index blends against extra weight in older diabetics in a 2025 study. Type 2 diabetes in later life often travels with overweight, which worsens control. Cheap ratios from routine labs might flag the patients at most risk.

Nearly two hundred inpatients past sixty were split into overweight and normal-weight groups. Four derived indices, mixing glucose, fats, and inflammation cell counts, were computed for each. All four ran clearly higher in the overweight group. Correlation and curve tests weigh how well each index sorts the groups. A lab-based flag could target diet and activity help where it counts most.
pmc-12836923:
He and five co-authors review deranged brain networks in COPD patients with cognitive impairment, in work from 2025. Thinking problems are a common side effect of the lung disease, yet reviews had not tied them to brain network measures. The synthesis runs from symptoms through mechanisms and scan findings to candidate treatments, along a lung-brain axis.

Chronic low oxygen, inflammation and oxidative stress are cast as the main drivers of network damage. Deficits centre on executive function and visuospatial skill, with odd links between the default mode and visual networks. Long-term oxygen, anti-inflammatory care and cognitive rehabilitation each show some benefit, the authors report.
pmc-12837023:
Jun Jing and co-authors published a 2025 study of esketamine, a drug related to a known anesthetic, given around the time of uterus surgery to ease pain and low mood. The surgery, done with laparoscopic keyhole tools, removes the uterus in full. Pain and depressed mood are both common in its wake.

The trial recruited 135 women and randomly split them into three groups. One group received the standard pain drug alone. Two groups received esketamine with it, at a low or a middle dose, during surgery and in the pain pump afterward. Blood markers linked to mood and growth, mood scores, and pain scores were measured at set points. So were pump presses and side effects such as nausea and dizziness. Both esketamine groups kept those mood markers higher than the standard group did, the team reports.
pmc-12837123:
Seven authors present a qualitative study in two thousand twenty-five on hernias that form beside a stoma. A parastomal hernia is common after ostomy surgery, usually cannot be reversed, and hurts quality of life. Prevention and management strategies remain weak, and most research asks patients, not the specialist nurses who manage stomas.

The team interviewed enterostomal therapists from eighteen top hospitals across eleven Chinese provinces in late two thousand twenty-four. Using structured interviews, they mapped what helps and what blocks good prevention and care from the therapists' viewpoint, aiming to improve daily practice.
pmc-12837423:
Daniel Brandhorst and co-authors test a way to keep donor insulin cells alive inside a device. Their 2025 study deals with islets, the pancreas cells that make insulin, sealed in a flat silicone case. Sealed cells are cut off from blood flow at first, so they lack oxygen and food.

The team filled the case with gels, some charged with oxygen, and watched the cells for days. A gel without extra oxygen stopped the islets from breaking apart but did not cut cell death. Oxygen-charged gel raised the yield of living islets and calmed harmful signals. Insulin release stayed slow and weak in all cases. The authors say a longer-lasting oxygen source is needed next.
pmc-12837523:
Six researchers test for a link between a common parasite and low thyroid function in a paper from 2025. The parasite, Toxoplasma gondii, infects many people and can stay quiet in the body for years. Low thyroid function, called hypothyroidism, is also widespread. The team compared patients with the thyroid problem to people without it, using an Iranian registry.

Blood tests looked for signs of past parasite infection in both groups. Past infection was far more common in the thyroid group than in controls. After adjusting for other factors, infected people had more than twice the odds of the thyroid problem. The authors say the link deserves more study before screening is advised.
pmc-12837723:
Xiong Zhang and five colleagues reviewed outcomes for nineteen patients whose splenic artery aneurysms were treated from inside the vessel. These aneurysms can rupture fatally, and catheter treatment avoids open surgery. Cases treated between twenty nineteen and twenty twenty-four were analyzed retrospectively. Fifteen aneurysms were blocked with embolization; four received covered stents. Median patient age was fifty-three.

Technical success reached nearly ninety-five percent. Three patients developed post-embolization syndrome, one suffered an artery dissection, and almost half had partial spleen infarctions, usually tolerable. Over a median three years of follow-up there were no deaths and no repeat procedures. The twenty twenty-five series supports endovascular repair as first choice for these aneurysms, with spleen tissue loss the common but manageable price.
pmc-12840323:
Güntülü Şık and co-authors describe severe flu in children treated in intensive care in Türkiye after the COVID-19 pandemic, in a study from 2025. Flu still sends many children to hospital each year. Pandemic rules left a gap in immunity among children, which may have changed how the illness looks.

The team reviewed eighty-five children admitted to five intensive care units in İstanbul over about a year. Flu A combined with a second virus hit younger infants hardest, with worse breathing trouble. Flu B stood out for brain effects, such as seizures, and a higher risk of sepsis, a dangerous body-wide response. Low oxygen and other signs marked children who needed a breathing machine. Very few of the children had been given a flu vaccine.
pmc-12842123:
Yuhao Nie, Gaopeng Yu, and Hongying Hu present a 2025 study of microbes in a three-level food chain on willow trees. A sawfly makes galls on willow leaves, and tiny wasps attack the sawfly inside. Microbes ride along at each level and shape how the chain works. The team profiled bacteria and fungi across leaf surfaces, gall chambers, host larvae, and wasps.

Fungal variety peaked on the wasps but ran low inside galls and host tissue. Bacterial richness ran the other way, peaking in the gall chamber. Web analysis showed fungi linking as hubs with warm ties, while bacteria hubs tied in a cooler pattern. Each niche favored its own set of microbe jobs, from transport to energy work. The map shows how hidden microbes sort themselves across a small, layered world.
pmc-12842923:
Tingting Fang and co-authors probed how raised carbon dioxide reshapes a medicinal fungus in a 2025 study. High carbon dioxide in cultivation often makes the fungus Ganoderma lucidum grow antler-shaped fruiting bodies instead of normal caps. The molecular response behind that change was unclear.

Gene activity and metabolite profiles were compared across three growth stages under normal and raised gas levels. Hundreds of metabolites shifted at each stage. Amino acid production fell broadly, while certain triterpenoids and steroids built up. At a key stage, genes for cell division and DNA repair were suppressed, which may block normal cap growth. Genes for sensing the gas and remodelling cell walls also changed, sketching the antler pathway.
pmc-12844123:
Meruert Qairat and co-authors gave a full workup of a commercial electron-beam resist called ELP-20 in a 2025 paper. Resists are coatings that record fine patterns when an electron beam writes on them, a key step in making tiny electronics. Users need to know a resist's makeup, film behavior, and response to the beam.

Light-scattering tests showed the resist is a methacrylate much like the standard material PMMA, which allows direct comparison. Films spun from solutions of varied strength followed a clean power law linking thickness to spin speed. The films were also notably even. The study hands chip labs a reference sheet for a resist that had lacked public data.
pmc-12844923:
Yinhua Tan and co-authors hunt for a weak point in lung cancer that has learned to resist targeted drugs, in work from twenty twenty-five. The cancer is lung adenocarcinoma with a growth gene flaw. Drugs that block that gene work at first, but tumors adapt and the drugs fail.

The team bred drug resistant cancer models in the lab by slowly raising drug dose. Gene scans of the models found one gene, MUC16, raised in all of them. Turning that gene off made all models respond to the drugs again. Patient data linked high levels of the gene to worse outcomes. The authors name the gene as a drug target to beat resistance.
pmc-12845023:
Dongyeon Kim, Hyungwon Moon, Sunyoung Han, and Hak Jong Lee built an ultrasound-triggered drug carrier for pancreatic cancer in a 2025 paper. The cancer's dense tissue keeps drugs out, so they loaded the drug exatecan into a liposome, IMP305, that bursts under ultrasound-driven cavitation.

Packaging raised the dose mice could tolerate about fourfold. Ultrasound broke open about 85 percent of carriers and freed a matching share of drug. In mice bearing human pancreatic tumors, the carrier beat free drug. Adding focused ultrasound cut tumor volume by about half at day 48. Eighty percent of mice were alive at day 60. The authors present IMP305 as a way to concentrate treatment inside the tumor while sparing the body.
pmc-12845123:
Vladimir Ponamarev reviews how copy versions of complex animal medicines are developed and judged, in a solo 2025 paper. The focus is medicines built on hemoproteins, above all cytochrome c, a protein used to support liver function and treat metabolic disorders in animals. Such copies, called biosimilars, could widen access to costly biological therapies.

Rules for these copies borrow heavily from European and United States paths for human drugs. Makers must show similarity step by step, with deep checks of structure and function, and must control quality across the whole life of the product. For cytochrome c, key traits include the intact protein chain, its bond with its heme group, and the state of its iron. Swapping one copy for another may be acceptable when similarity is very high. Regional rules differ, but the core science stays the same, Ponamarev argues.
pmc-12845623:
Hongyou Wan and six co-authors build a new material for pulling the weed killer atrazine out of water. Their 2025 paper notes that atrazine lingers in soil and water and resists natural breakdown, while standard adsorbents hold too little or break down too soon. The team turned to sesame hulls, a farm waste, and sepiolite, a natural fibrous mineral with a large surface area.

Mixed, heated, and treated with alkali, the two became a composite the team calls KNPB. Under the best test conditions it removed about eighty-nine percent of the atrazine in the water, and it kept working across repeated uses. Tests on how the uptake proceeds, plus surface analysis, point to three ways the pollutant is held: filling of pores, stacking between flat molecules, and hydrogen bonding. The authors offer the material as a low-cost use for farm waste that also cleans water.
pmc-12846523:
Nika Heidari Gazik, Mark Holodniy, and Vafa Bayat review how highly pathogenic avian influenza H5N1 and H7N9 are widening their host range, and how they can be treated. Their 2025 paper deals with viruses that present major public health concerns.

The dominant H5N1 clade has shown a stronger capacity to adapt to mammals, raising fears of mixing with human seasonal flu. Unlike H7N9, H5N1 infects birds, many mammals, and humans. They note wide infection of dairy cattle in the United States, with virus in milk and human cases mostly from occupational exposure. Pasteurization inactivates the virus in milk. Mammal-to-mammal spread has also been documented.
pmc-12846623:
Calvin Mehl and colleagues measure past exposure to lymphocytic choriomeningitis virus in German forestry workers. Their 2025 seroprevalence study screens blood samples collected in twenty oh eight from ten forestry offices in Brandenburg.

Forestry workers face many rodent-borne pathogens through their jobs, and this virus spreads through infected rodent excreta. Of five hundred sixty-three samples, about one point four percent carried reactive antibodies. Prevalence varied by office, reaching its highest in one location at over six percent. A parallel mouse study nearby also indicated very low prevalence. Rates resembled a nineteen sixties West German study despite occupational risk. The authors call for more screening in humans and wild rodents.
pmc-12847723:
Maryam Sabooni Asre Hazer, Sami Malola, and Hannu Hakkinen simulate heat effects on gold clusters in a 2025 paper. These tiny gold cores wear a coat of sulfur based guards and serve in catalysis, imaging, and medicine. Their still traits are well mapped, but how they move and change with heat is not.

A machine learned force model, trained on exact quantum data, runs motion for up to 0.12 microseconds. Heat from 300 to 550 kelvin wakes the coat layer by layer, the team found. Gold and guard units form chains and rings that can break off at high heat. What is left matches cluster types seen in lab work. Two clusters that meet merge into a core close to known lab forms.
pmc-12847823:
Jiaxin Du and eight co-authors report a new catalyst for making urea from waste gases in this 2025 paper. Their route joins carbon dioxide and nitrate in one electric step. Slow steps and weak contact between the key parts have kept yields low. The team built a catalyst of copper and ruthenium held inside hollow carbon spheres with tiny pores.

Held in these small spaces, the parts meet more often and react by a faster path. The catalyst made urea at a high rate and kept working for 125 hours. Light based tests and computer models showed the pores shift the route away from the slow path. Pore sizes from four to eleven nanometers were tried, and mid sizes worked best. The authors present tight pore design as a broad tool for multi step electric synthesis.
pmc-12849123:
Melahat Nur Akkese and co-authors follow parents who care for adults with anorexia nervosa in a 2025 study. Parents often stay the main carers for years. Past work stressed carer strain and unhelpful responses. The skillful side of caregiving got far less study.
