The team compared fathers and mothers over eighteen months, as patients moved from intensive hospital care back to daily life.

The study drew on data from a larger trial, with fifty two fathers and two hundred twenty four mothers. Skill and distress scores were tracked at four time points. At the start, fathers and mothers scored alike on most skills. Over time, mothers' skills grew in several areas, while fathers' scores stayed flat. Distress, though, moved in the same pattern for both parents. The authors say fathers and mothers may need different kinds of support.
pmc-12849423:
Low mood in teens is common, and many teens stick poorly with talk care or pills. Huimin Gao and co-authors test a virtual reality route in a 2025 study at a Chinese hospital. One hundred teens took ten short VR rests paired with thought and act care over two weeks.

Eighty four teens saw the course through. Mood scores fell by a clear margin, and about a third hit the study's mark for full lift of low mood. Boys in the group hit that mark more than girls. Teens who began with lower mood and fear scores also did better on first checks. In the full test, though, no start trait stood as a firm call on its own. Blood marks of swelling did not split the groups.
pmc-12853623:
Onur Karaaslan and co-authors present a 2025 study of plasma exchange as rescue therapy for severe HELLP syndrome after delivery. The syndrome destroys red cells, injures the liver, and drops platelets in late pregnancy. Birth usually ends it, but some mothers keep worsening afterward, and options run out.

The team reviewed twenty-one such patients treated between 2010 and 2023. Two thirds had the severest class of the syndrome. Exchange took one to three sessions depending on response. Platelet counts rose significantly afterward, while liver enzymes, bilirubin, and clotting times all improved. Even so, grave complications such as sepsis, lung edema, and kidney failure still struck some patients. The authors present the exchange as a promising bridge when delivery alone fails.
pmc-12853723:
Qifei Zhou and Kun Fu pool past studies on surgery for heterotopic pregnancy, in a 2025 meta-analysis. In this rare condition, one embryo grows in the womb and another outside it, which can turn life-threatening. Two operations can treat it: keyhole surgery and open surgery. The team searched six databases for work up to January 2025 and kept twenty-two studies with over a thousand patients.

Live birth, miscarriage, early birth, and full-term birth rates all came out alike for the two operations. Delivery method rates matched as well. A check on high-quality studies alone hinted at more miscarriages with keyhole surgery, but the signal was not firm. All patients in the pooled work were from China. The authors warn that the tie may not hold in other groups and call for wider studies.
pmc-12853823:
Nebiyu Mengistu, Carmen Axisa, and Priya Saravanakumar review alcohol disorder with mental illness in older adults in poorer countries in a 2025 paper. The double burden grows as populations age, while health systems in low and middle income countries lack tailored services for it. Research on the pairing in these settings stays thin, so the team ran a narrative review with a systematic search across six databases plus hand searching.

Rates of drinking and dual diagnosis varied widely across studies, reflecting mixed definitions and tools. Men drank more, while women showed more depression and thinking decline. Low schooling and living alone recurred as linked factors.
pmc-12853923:
Lin and co-authors follow people recovering from a first stroke to see how social alienation, the feeling of being cut off from others, changes over time. Stroke can leave patients dependent, depressed, and stigmatized, and these burdens can push them away from family and community life.

Using repeated follow-up surveys and group-based trajectory modeling, the team found three paths: stable low alienation, high alienation that steadily fell, and stable high alienation. Depression, resilience, daily-living ability, lasting stroke effects, and the wish to return to work or study all shaped which path a patient followed. The authors say nurses should tailor support to each pattern rather than treating alienation as one fixed state.
pmc-12857023:
Zhu, Zhang, and Fu review how mitochondria, the cell's power plants, are kept in good order while a baby's lungs are still forming. Lung growth takes a great deal of energy, and the fetal and newborn periods are sensitive windows. Cells control quality by removing damaged mitochondria, splitting and joining them, and building fresh ones.

The review explains how stress, such as infection or extra oxygen given to premature babies, can push this system out of balance. Damaged mitochondria then pile up, raising cell stress and inflammation and harming lung growth. Early treatments aimed at mitochondria, including stem cells, are presented as a route to better lifelong lung health.
pmc-12859123:
Yiheng Shi and co-authors build a DNA detection method for food-contaminating bacteria in work from 2025. Their tool centers on a heat-loving enzyme called PfAgo that cuts target DNA when guided, but older designs needed ready-made guide DNA.

The new method uses primers with a special base that another enzyme clips to create the guide in place. That makes the system more flexible across targets. The detection limit reached a low DNA level in tests, and the method successfully found bacteria that contaminate food. The authors present it as a general tool for pathogens and viruses.
pmc-12864823:
Qian Xie and co-authors present a 2025 design method for aqueous zinc-ion batteries. These batteries are safe and cheap, but both electrodes cause trouble in use. Zinc metal grows spiky deposits, and the other electrode can dissolve. Swapping both for host materials helps, yet pairing hosts that move ions at matched speeds is hard.

A machine learning model now scores how well host pairs match in ion flow. Two simple measures, tied to layer spacing and zinc spread, guide the pairing. One chosen pair held strong charge over twelve thousand cycles. The idea also extends to soft, stretchable gel batteries that bend in all directions.
pmc-12864923:
Yingzheng Tan and co-authors map lactic acid in lung tumors, in a study published in 2025. Tumors rewire their energy use and spill lactate, a waste acid that can reshape nearby tissue. Where lactate gathers, and which cells it affects, was poorly known. The team combined several spatial methods with machine learning in lung adenocarcinoma.

Tumors rich in lactate held more surface and support cells and fewer immune cells. Maps showed lactate and a related compound sat unevenly across cell types, with vessel cells holding least. Vessel cell groups in high-lactate tumors showed growth and stress programs and linked to poor survival. Several learning models agreed that vessel and support cell programs mark the high-lactate state. The authors name lactate pathways as drug targets.
pmc-12866323:
Dennis Bardoe studies feeding in early infancy across 18 African countries in work published in 2025. He asks how rates of feeding babies only breast milk differ from place to place. National figures alone can hide wide gaps between regions inside the same country.

Bardoe uses modelled data for 2019 and simple gap measures to compare regions. Rates ran from about 14 percent in Comoros to about 66 percent in São Tomé and Príncipe. Only four countries passed the world mean for that year. Nigeria, Tanzania, and Cameroon showed the widest gaps, while a few small states showed very little gap. The findings point health teams toward the places where support is most needed.
pmc-12866523:
Shiyamalee Arunasalam, Rohitha Muthugala, and Faseeha Noordeen track seasonal coronaviruses in respiratory patients in Sri Lanka. Their 2025 study covers samples taken from early 2020 to late 2022 in the Central Province. Seasonal coronaviruses cause common colds, but they are rarely tested for in routine panels there.

The team tested more than a thousand samples for over twenty respiratory pathogens. About half the patients had a pathogen found, and seasonal coronaviruses made up a small share. Three virus types appeared, with fever, cough, and sore throat as the most common signs. The authors note that weak tracking of mild coronaviruses can hinder early spotting of new ones. Their data fills a local gap for pandemic readiness planning.
pmc-12873423:
Meng Fu and co-authors identify a silenced tumor suppressor gene in small cell lung cancer in 2025. Small cell lung cancer is highly lethal and often resists chemotherapy fast. DNA methylation, a chemical off-switch on genes, may drive part of that course, yet its role was unclear.

Genome-wide methylation scans of tumor tissue and blood DNA found a switched-off region in the promoter of a gene called RASA4. Drugs that remove the marks switched the gene back on. Restored RASA4 slowed growth, invasion, and drug resistance in lab tests, while its loss sped all three. Low RASA4 in patient samples tied to poor survival. The gene looks like a marker and drug target.
pmc-12875723:
Hae-song Yoo, Jin-myong Lee, and Min-sun Jeon explore how to build a digital nutrition program for older adults, in work from 2025. Eating well gets harder with age, low income, and living alone. A phone or tablet program could coach daily choices if it fits older users' real lives.

The team ran focus groups in May 2025 with ten adults aged 65 to 83 years. All had used digital devices before, which shaped the talks. Notes were coded by classic content methods until no new themes arose. Three main themes and thirteen subthemes emerged from the talks. Themes cover daily eating habits, barriers to self-care, and what a helpful program should do.
pmc-12875923:
Lu and seven co-authors tracked reproductive hormones across the mouse cycle in twenty twenty-five, with a focus on a peptide called secretoneurin. A surge of luteinizing hormone triggers ovulation. Secretoneurin is known to stimulate that hormone's release. Its periovulatory link to the classic reproductive controller, GnRH, was unclear.

Using a sensitive mass spectrometry method, the team measured two steroids and three peptides. They measured them in brain, pituitary, and ovary tissue. Secretoneurin and GnRH both peaked around proestrus in the hypothalamus and pituitary. Their levels moved together in part. Secretoneurin fibers sat near GnRH neurons. In cultured GnRH cells, the peptide raised the GnRH gene's activity in a dose- and time-dependent way. It switched on growth and calcium signaling pathways. The authors say the link sets up focused tests of cause and effect.
pmc-12878823:
Annalisa Tanzilli and six co-authors look at the inner defenses and social drives tied to grandiose narcissism, in a 2025 study. They asked 478 people to fill out scales on the two sides of narcissism, the wish to be admired and the wish to best rivals. Scales also covered defense style and social views, such as a sense of belonging or a drive to compete.

The rival side looked darker. It went with defenses that worked less well, more self-doubt, and more urge to clash, plus less warmth, less sense of being part of a group, and less play. The admired side linked most to an urge to compete and to sex drive. Defenses shaped how narcissism came out through these drives, and the paths split by gender. The authors say this helps show the drives and defenses that clinicians meet in such patients.
pmc-12881723:
Hossein Ebrahimi and co-authors pit two ways of gluing orthodontic brackets against each other in the lab. Traditional bonding etches enamel with acid before priming, a strong but fussy, time-sensitive craft. Self-etch adhesives merge the steps into one, promising speed if the grip survives.

Sixteen extracted premolars were split into two groups of eight. Metal brackets were bonded with either the classic etch-and-rinse system or a self-etch rival, following each maker's instructions, then soaked and sheared until they popped. Shear bond strength decides whether convenience costs reliability. Orthodontists feel the answer daily: a bracket that fails mid-treatment means an emergency visit and lost progress.
pmc-12883423:
Jiao Cheng and co-authors review the skin damage that radiation therapy itself inflicts, from the first redness to ulcers that will not heal. Radiation-induced skin injury limits how much dose a tumor can receive, and it arises from DNA damage, reactive oxygen, and inflammation gone off-script. Their review, published in 2025, searches three databases for studies from 2020 onward and gathers 122 of them.

The authors compare the grading scales clinics use to score the injury, then weigh treatments. Steroids and moisturizers ease symptoms but do not prevent lasting damage such as fibrosis and thinning. Newer options, including mesenchymal stem cells and antioxidants aimed at mitochondria, show real promise for repair. Patients facing a second course of radiation suffer severe skin reactions more often, and the authors press for tighter limits on the dose skin itself receives.
pmc-12894323:
Seven authors build a training tool in 2025 for spotting fleeting face moves, called microexpressions, as they play over other face states. The old tool taught still moves on a blank face only. Their new tool trains dynamic reads, with a matched test used before and after training.

Trials crossed seven base face states, two heat grades, and six quick moves in a staged design. Training lifted dynamic reads with sound test traits, and skills from the old tool carried over well. No broad sex gap showed in skill, though women gained a bit more from training.
pmc-12907823:
Na Li and eight co-authors study work and family strain among medical staff in this paper, published in 2025. They asked how conflict between work and family life links to being shut out by coworkers, a pattern called workplace ostracism. They also tested whether a sense of coherence, a feeling that life is manageable and meaningful, sits between the two. The survey covered 527 staff at three hospitals, from January 2022 to December 2023.

Work and family conflict tracked strongly with ostracism. Sense of coherence carried part of that link: it acted as a mediator between conflict and ostracism. As coherence rose, the effect of conflict on ostracism grew weaker. The buffer mattered most for staff with low coherence. The authors point to support that builds this inner resource as one way to protect medical staff.
pmc-12917423:
Rafael Martins da Costa and co-authors track weight trends among young people in Porto Velho, Brazil, in this 2025 Europe PMC paper. Overweight and obesity are rising fast in low- and middle-income countries. Porto Velho is the largest capital city in Brazil by land area, in the western Amazon region.

Using repeated surveys from 2006 to 2024, they measured more than twelve thousand schoolchildren aged six to nineteen. About eighteen percent had overweight and nine percent had obesity, with obesity more common in younger children. Obesity rose clearly among girls and among children aged six to ten, while other groups showed no clear trend. The authors call for targeted action.
pmc-12937123:
Twelve authors, led by Tainara Yamanaka, tested stem cell transplants for tooth repair in rats in this 2025 study. Standard root canal care works well, but it leaves the tooth without living pulp. Regrowing the dentin-pulp complex, the tooth's inner tissue and hard layer, is a goal many groups chase.

The team compared stem cells from two sources: the pulp of human baby teeth, and the periosteum, the membrane over bone. Eighteen root canals in the upper first molars of immune-suppressed rats were split into three groups. One got baby tooth pulp cells in a gel, one got periosteal cells in a gel, and one got no cells as a control. Tissue sections then showed how each site responded. The study weighs which cell source better supports new dentin and pulp growth.
pmc-12940023:
Yongqing Liu and co-authors fed probiotics to Simmental bulls and tracked growth and meat quality in 2025. Probiotics are known to aid immunity and gut health, with side gains in tenderness and antioxidant status. Forty bulls were split into four diet groups, from no probiotic up to a top dose per kilo of feed.

Feed intake and carcass traits did not change. Daily weight gain rose in step with dose, and feed conversion improved. Meat grew redder, lost less water in cooking, and sheared more easily as dose rose. Fat inside the muscle and blood-fat markers also climbed. Antioxidant measures strengthened with dose. Fat makeup shifted away from saturated forms toward a healthier profile.
pmc-12957723:
Derek Marsh reads the COVID-19 pandemic as a physics problem in a 2025 paper. Daily case and death reports from Italy, Germany, and England carry a strong weekly rhythm from reporting habits. A seven-day moving average strips that rhythm away, exposing clean stretches of exponential growth and decay. Rate constants from those stretches, paired with serial-interval estimates, give the reproduction numbers that describe spread.

Testing rates are corrected for, and death-to-case ratios estimate how much early infection went uncounted. The same numbers set the vaccine coverage needed for population immunity as variants succeeded each other. One integrated, equation-driven account shows how much of the pandemic's shape was set by simple dynamics.
pmc-12971523:
Pati and co-authors screen maize for drought tolerance in two stages, lab first, field second. Fifty inbred lines grow in water culture under a chemical that mimics dry soil, and their roots are measured for length, tips, forks, and thickness. The promising lines then face real rainfed trials in Hyderabad, India, with water withheld before flowering, in work published in 2025.

Root vigor lines up strongly with yield parts and canopy health in the field, and the lab ranking predicts the field ranking almost exactly. Two introgressed lines lead the pack, with three more close behind. The authors offer the two-tier route as a fast, cheap way to find drought-ready breeding stock.
pmc-12975823:
Jadance Black, Alexandra Moya, Matt Van Sant, and Dana Lee search for adenoviruses in bats of southwestern Texas, in work from 2025. Few studies have checked these viruses in United States bats. The team tested droppings from ninety-four bats across nine species, targeting a piece of a virus gene.

Five samples held virus DNA. Three came from pallid bats and matched each other exactly. Single samples from two other bat species held distinct forms. Family tree checks placed all close to a virus found earlier in an Oklahoma bat species. Each form differed enough from known viruses to suggest they are new kinds. The work adds baseline facts for virus watch in wild bats.
pmc-13037623:
Kananub and co-authors measure disinfectant residues in wastewater from slaughterhouses in western Thailand. The chemical, benzalkonium chloride, is a common sanitizer in meat plants. Samples and surveys came from 20 pig and poultry sites. A precision liquid method detected residue types in the water. Residues turned up at every site, even at the 40% that said they did not use such products.

Four large plants sent wastewater into public waterways, a clear environmental risk. Bigger sites scored better on safety training and gear supply. Spill kit readiness also rose with plant size. The links were strong by standard measures. The study flags gaps between reported and real sanitizer use.
pmc-13040823:
Ahmet Koçyiğit and Uğur Cavlak wrote a 2025 trial report on a game-based tool for teaching physiotherapy students. The course topic was electrotherapy, a technical subject where classic teaching can fall flat. A visual novel engine, Ren'Py, hosted interactive scenarios for the digital arm. Students were split by chance into three groups.

One group got classic teaching, one digital only, and one a mix of both. About eighty second-year students took part, none with the course before. Theory and practical exams followed the teaching block. Scales for mental load, attitude to the field and drive toward the materials were also filled in.
pmc-13081423:
Nesa Kazemifard and co-authors study why gut drugs that calm swelling work well for some patients with bowel disease and poorly for others. Their 2025 study focuses on small gene changes, called SNPs, in people with inflammatory bowel disease. Such changes may alter the proteins that drugs act on, or the spots where tiny RNA strands bind to genes.

The team searched past studies for genes tied to drug response, then checked 41 key genes with computer tools and gene databases. They studied 69 changes in gene coding parts and 27 in tail regions that affect RNA binding. Some changes, in genes named ABCB1 and HFE, were predicted to shift protein shape and stability. Tests with cell data and motion models backed that view. The work points to gene checks that could help match patients to the right drug.
pmc-13084323: Hinpetch Daungsupawong and Viroj Wiwanitkit wrote to a journal editor in 2026 about a study of chatbot answers on chronic pain in children. They praise its time-tracked design and ten set criteria, then raise three worries. One fixed prompt may not reflect real questions from young patients. Scores for usefulness and tone lacked any check that raters agreed. And perfect scores once criteria were spelled out hint at a ceiling that hides real gaps between models.
pmc-13085923:
Shira Fisher and Hanah Margalit study how codon choice shapes small RNA binding in bacteria in this 2026 paper. Small RNAs control bacterial genes by pairing with messenger RNAs. Binding sites were first found before the coding part of messages, but large studies now show many sites inside the coding stretch itself.

Using interaction data, the authors found the key pairing positions inside coding regions. Those positions line up with the reading frame far more than chance allows and tend to be the most common codons. Across related bacterial genomes, the pairing at those spots is well conserved, and where the code's flexibility breaks a pair, other positions often compensate. Codon bias seems to help these encounters form.
pmc-13086623:
Stefano Luminari and co-authors track complete responses to a bispecific antibody in lymphoma in this 2026 study. The trial, called ELM-2, treats follicular lymphoma that returned or resisted care. Full disappearance of disease is a prized goal in this cancer.

Response chances fall with each new line of treatment, and high-risk patients fare worst. The drug joins two targets, one on tumor cells and one on T cells. Earlier results showed deep, lasting responses with manageable safety. This analysis follows only those patients who reached a complete response. It asks how long those responses last and who reaches them. The detail helps doctors set expectations for a hard-to-treat group.
pmc-13086723:
Ferhan Celik and co-authors present a 2026 review of plant-based diets during pregnancy. Such diets skip or nearly skip animal foods and center on vegetables, grains, beans, nuts, and seeds. They are popular for health and environmental reasons, but their safety in pregnancy is less settled, so the team surveyed the evidence on pregnancy disorders.

Studies link well-planned plant-based eating with lower risk of pregnancy diabetes and high blood pressure disorders. A few report more anemia or low birth weight, while others find no difference from mixed diets. Shortfalls in vitamin B12, iron, and omega-3 fats are the main worry when diets are poorly planned. With supplements and care, the authors conclude, plant-based diets can support healthy pregnancies.
pmc-13096823:
Xinyi Li and five co-authors pool trials of pharmacist-led care for chronic lung disease in a review from 2026. Poor medication management drives flare-ups and hospital visits in COPD, a long-term lung disease. The team searched three databases for randomized trials of pharmacist care and merged eleven trials with more than two thousand patients.

Pharmacist-led care cut the risk of flare-up hospital admissions by more than half. Patients also stuck to their medicines better and quit smoking more often. Quality of life gains were reported but varied a lot between trials. Lung function and symptom scores did not change firmly, and many trials were small or flawed.
pmc-13097023:
Arjun and four co-authors report outcomes of a gender-affirming operation in a 2026 study. The operation builds a vaginal canal using a segment of the sigmoid colon, a part of the large intestine. It is an option for transgender women, above all when other tissue is too limited to give enough depth.

Thirty patients were treated at one center between 2023 and 2025 and followed afterward. The new canal reached a good depth during surgery, and all patients kept working sexual tissue. Two serious problems, a bowel injury and a leak where the bowel was rejoined, needed further surgery, and no one died. One in ten patients had narrowing at the opening, fixed by stretching routines. The authors call the method reliable while warning that bowel risks demand careful screening.
pmc-13105623:
In a letter to the editor, Wang Ziyuan and Li Chen comment on a review that pooled 16 trials of transcutaneous electrical acupoint stimulation. That needle-free method sends mild current through acupuncture points. The review, covering 2,300 patients having abdominal surgery, found faster gut recovery, less nausea and pain, and shorter hospital stays when the stimulation joined standard recovery care.

The letter writers praise the synthesis but urge caution. Recovery programs bundle many elements, from early feeding to pain plans. The trials varied in how fully those elements were used, so part of the benefit may reflect the bundle rather than the stimulation alone. They also note the wide spread of points, frequencies, and session plans across trials. They call for a few standard, easy-to-deliver treatment packages so hospitals can adopt the method consistently.
pmc-13113523:
Piotr Baranowski, Katarzyna Grocholewicz, and Aleksandra Gawlikowska-Sroka studied in 2026 the skull of an early medieval dog from Wolin, Poland, with several teeth missing. Such birth defects are well known in clinic dogs but rarely reported from digs. X-rays showed a fully formed upper canine that never erupted. Nearby, the bone where a molar and incisors should sit was smooth, with no socket at all.

The team weighed birth defect against early arrest, loss during life, and damage after burial. The smooth bone and lack of healing marks favored a congenital origin. The dog lived an estimated seven to ten years with no sign the defect hurt chewing. The authors stress that missing sockets in old skulls should not be read as poor health without imaging.
pmc-13116623:
Iva Kutija Fučkar and four co-authors map gene variants tied to inherited hearing loss in Croatian Roma, in a 2026 study. Many cases of deafness from birth trace to one gene, GJB2, which builds a channel protein in the ear. Roma groups often carry their own variant mix due to a distinct history. The team tested five known variants of the gene in this group and compared rates with groups worldwide.

Altered copies turned up at three of the five sites. Rates at those sites differed clearly from other groups and from world averages. One variant, which stops the protein short, stood out most. The authors say clinic tests for hearing loss in Roma patients should weigh this local mix. Such tailoring can sharpen diagnosis, prevention, and family advice.
pmc-13128623:
Khursheed Ul Islam and colleagues present a two thousand twenty-six single-cell study of lung tissue in HIV infection. People living with HIV face many lung diseases. Even on treatment, ongoing immune activation keeps injuring the lungs.

The team sequenced RNA from single cells in lung tissue from infected and uninfected people. Smokers and non-smokers were both included. Tens of thousands of cells were grouped into distinct populations. HIV changed surface cell behaviour and remodelled support cells called fibroblasts. The maps help explain how infection-driven inflammation unsettles the lung's air sacs over time.
pmc-13133223:
Rawya Ramadan and four co-authors made 2026 floor tiles from cement mixed with waste ceramic and waste tires. Their goal was a cheaper tile that also blocks stray radio waves for roof use. Waste iron powder joined the mix in some tiles. The team checked grain size, chemistry, density, water uptake, and strength after a twenty-eight-day cure.

Ceramic and rubber waste made tiles lighter and more porous, raising water uptake. Iron powder worked the other way: it packed the mix tighter and raised both strength and conductivity. Tiles with ten percent iron powder performed best overall. With a metal mesh added, the tiles blocked over ninety-nine percent of incoming waves. The authors say the tiles meet Egyptian and European rules for outdoor use.
pmc-13135223:
Ryan and co-authors report in 2026 that two small RNA molecules regulate protein handling in non small cell lung cancer. Runaway protein building is central to tumor growth, but its regulators are incompletely known. The two RNAs are made together from one gene stretch.

The pair was found to regulate genes across many metabolic and disease pathways, protein handling among them. Adding copies of the pair to lung cancer cell models cut both cell growth and protein synthesis rates. The authors cast the pair as metabolic regulators and possible treatment targets. Such a brake on protein building could be useful if it can be delivered to tumors.
pmc-13135423:
Christopher Thom and co-authors present a 2026 case series on eye ultrasound used by the first doctor a patient meets in a busy emergency department. Triage doctors have minutes, not hours. Three patients arrived with sudden sight loss in one eye.

A quick eye scan at triage nailed the cause in each case. In one, a blocked retinal artery called for stroke team action at once. In the other two, the scan ruled that cause out and spared the same heavy response. The authors argue for picking ultrasound cases where a fast answer changes the next steps, not scanning by habit.
pmc-13135623:
Simran Sandhu, Varchasvi Mudgal, and Priyash Jain poll doctors on India's law that freed suicide bids from crime. Their study appeared in twenty twenty-six. The twenty seventeen act reads a bid as a sign of grave stress in need of care, not blame. Yet what ward doctors know of the law, and their views on it, shape how it lands. One hundred thirty-four non-mind doctors at a hub in central India filled a form.

Three fourths knew bids are no crime now, and most backed the shift as a cut to shame. Yet four fifths wrongly thought bids must still be told to law staff, and just half knew of shield from suits. The team call for law drills and clear ward rules.
pmc-13136223:
Ansarizadeh and co-authors build a lab model of venous malformations, birth defects where veins grow into enlarged, weak-walled channels. Most cases trace to a faulty switch in vessel lining cells, yet drug testing lacked a faithful model. Their 2026 model grows human vessel lining cells carrying that fault together with fat-derived stem cells that support the vessels.

Side-by-side runs with normal and knocked-out versions of the switch show how vital its signaling is for network growth. The faulty version copied the cell traits and gene patterns of real malformations. The setup also worked as a screening bench for candidate drugs. The authors offer the model as a general platform for vessel disease research.
pmc-13136523:
Federica Pulicari and co-authors published a case report in 2026 on a lymphatic malformation of the tongue in a child, following the case from diagnosis to surgery. These benign growths arise from a malformed lymph system and usually appear in the skin of the head and neck; the tongue is the commonest mouth site. They are classed by cyst size into microcystic, macrocystic, and mixed types.

Early diagnosis matters because growth can disturb speech, chewing, and swallowing, and in severe cases the airway. Ultrasound, MRI, and CT map the lesion, while tissue examination confirms it. Treatment mixes surgery, injections that shrink the cysts, laser work, and sometimes drugs. Full removal is tricky because the lesion infiltrates and hugs vital structures.
pmc-13137323:
Hakan Anil and seven co-authors build a score to call who gains from shock wave care in a 2026 study. Their patients bear the blood-flow kind of erectile failure, the most common kind, tied to vessel wall harm. Gentle shock waves to the organ have won ground as a drug-free care, yet who will reply was not well marked.

The team tracked clinic and vessel traits in men set for the care, with no random split. Traits that split gainers from flat cases were folded into a plain score any clinic can use. The score aims care at those most likely to gain.
pmc-13139923:
Dian Karssen and co-authors chart which pneumococcal types sicken German adults in a study from 2026. Pneumococcus bacteria cause a large share of pneumonia cases that land people in hospital. Vaccines cover a fixed set of types, called serotypes. Knowing the local mix guides which vaccine to use.

Seven German hospitals enrolled adults with community-acquired pneumonia from August 2022 onward. Labs typed the pneumococcus strain in each confirmed case. The interim analysis maps how common each serotype is. It then checks what share current vaccines would cover. Such maps can shift as vaccines change the bacterial landscape. Public health teams use them to update vaccine policy with evidence.
pmc-13141523:
Jansåker and co-authors ask whether pneumonia predicts later diabetes and heart disease, in a 2026 Swedish cohort study. Earlier small studies hinted that many pneumonia patients carry undiagnosed diabetes and face higher heart risk afterward. This study uses nationwide registers plus primary care data, where most pneumonia is treated. It follows adults aged 35 to 75 from 2007 to 2018, excluding those who already had the outcomes.

More than 4.5 million people entered each analysis. Pneumonia came before about 30 percent of new diabetes cases and 32 percent of new heart disease cases. After age adjustment, pneumonia was linked to a 12 percent higher diabetes rate and an 18 percent higher heart disease rate. The authors present pneumonia as a warning sign worth follow-up.
pmc-13145023:
Fadoua El Hafa and co-authors build a national score for whether stroke patients are sent to the right next place of care. Their conference abstract from 2026 uses French national health data. The score was built from five guide rule points for referral after stroke. It was checked against a gold standard set from eighteen hospitals in one region. It was also checked for gaps between hospitals and for change over time. The score showed limited strength against the gold standard set. The authors still set out how such a tool could help track care paths at scale.
pmc-13145223:
Fayzullo Mallaev, Gulnora Rakhimbaeva, and Gulchexra Usmanova reported a conference abstract in 2026 on a brain marker after bleeding stroke. The marker, a growth factor made mainly in support cells of the brain, may limit swelling and protect nerve cells. The team asked if its blood levels predict outcome.

They studied eighty-three patients in the acute phase, using standard scales for nerve status and daily function. Marker levels rose sharply within three hours of onset, then fell over the next month. Patients who did poorly showed flat or falling levels, while those who did well rose by day fourteen. Dynamic change may predict outcome, they conclude.
pmc-13145423:
Hua Shen and co-authors pool data from three phase 3 trials to test a cholesterol-lowering antibody in patients who have both blood-vessel disease in the brain and high cholesterol. At twelve weeks, LDL cholesterol had fallen by about sixty-two percent on the drug while rising slightly on placebo. Nearly all treated patients reached the target cholesterol level, versus a small share on placebo. Side effects occurred at similar rates in both groups, with none serious and tied to the drug.
pmc-13145523:
Anissa Ourtani and co-authors present a 2026 conference study on whether body rhythm faults in the first days after stroke foretell deep tiredness at three months. The tiredness is common and crushing, with murky roots. Heart rate swing reads from short heart traces served as the rhythm mark.

Thirty-five patients with mild strokes were traced within three days of arrival. About a third met the tiredness mark at three months. One wave band of the swing ran clearly lower in the tired group. A second band leaned lower as well. The authors read the split as a sign that rhythm imbalance feeds later tiredness, and back larger checks with longer tracing spans.
pmc-13145623:
Junpei Koge and co-authors ask whether a sharper scan after stroke treatment reveals blood flow that standard grading misses. Their 2026 conference study reviews 176 patients whose blocked brain arteries were reopened by thrombectomy. A flat-panel CT taken right after the procedure can show leftover blockages as bright dots or tubes, which the team folds into a revised flow grade.

The revised grade reclassified 16 patients whom operators had scored differently. The authors suggest the extra scan sharpens tissue-level judgment after treatment.
pmc-13145723:
David Devine and co-authors present a 2026 conference audit of lung infection care on one stroke unit. The unit treated more patients for the infection than peer units on average. Before fixing the problem, the team wanted a clear picture of how the illness was found and treated.

Records showed about a quarter of unit patients were treated for lung infection, and over half of those cases were logged as food or fluid entering the lungs. Test results often clashed with the logged call, and most patients never got a virus swab. No treated case met a published strict rule set for stroke-linked lung infection. The team plans staff teaching, more of the right tests, and tighter drug use.
pmc-13145823:
Taraneh Ebrahimi and co-authors present a 2026 conference study on the gap between felt and measured thinking trouble years after stroke. Patients often report thinking complaints, but how they map to test scores long-term was murky. A German group sub-study checked both at three and five years.

Low mood was the one steady driver of complaints, and the authors read the felt trouble as part mood, part mind.
pmc-13146023:
Hamdy A Makhlouf and co-authors report a 2026 conference review on starting clot-preventing drugs within a day of clot-busting care for stroke. Early drugs might stop vessels from closing again and ward off early decline. They could also raise bleeding risk, and past trial results clash.

The authors call the proof unsettled and ask for larger trials.
pmc-13146123:
Rachel Jennings and Fathalla Elnagi present a 2026 conference study on stroke patterns in patients who had eye shots of a growth-blocking drug. Whether the shots sway stroke risk is unclear. The pair read scans of stroke patients with two eye diseases the drug treats.

pmc-13146223:
Stroke care for the oldest patients is the subject of a 2026 conference abstract from a team in Argentina led by Julieta Rosales. pmc-13146323:
Elizabeth Murphy and co-authors present a 2026 conference study on unplanned hospital returns in the eighteen months after stroke discharge at an Irish center. Survivors face returns for falls, lung infections, fits, heart trouble, and drug harms. Two discharge spans fed the work.

Return risk rose with illness load, thinning pill use, many-drug lists, and a past lung infection. Fall returns tied to disability after stroke, sugar disease, and mood drugs. The authors name drug load and past infection as fresh flags to act on.
pmc-13146423:
Hanna Marie Otterholt Bekkeseth and co-authors present a 2026 conference study on ambulance stroke checks in patients whose main symptom is dizziness. Dizziness is hard to sort in the field, since most stroke screens target strokes at the front of the brain. The data come from a Norwegian trial of ambulance stroke care.

Two common check scores both sorted these cases poorly, one missing cases and the other flagging too many. Stroke cases had more blood vessel risk factors, and the authors suggest adding risk signs to field sorting.
pmc-13146623:
Jiyeon Ha and co-authors compare blood thinning drugs after gut surgery in a 2026 study. The patients had atrial fibrillation, a heart rhythm flaw that raises stroke risk. Gut surgery can change how oral drugs are absorbed, so the best drug choice was unclear.

Using a Korean claims data base, the team tracked more than eight thousand such patients. They weighed stroke, clots, and major bleeding for four common drugs. One drug tracked with higher stroke risk than another in the matched tests. The study gives doctors rare hard data for a group that trials tend to leave out.
pmc-13146923:
Simon Trüssel and co-authors report a 2026 conference follow-up study on a drug tested as an aid to stroke rehab. The drug, levodopa, boosts a brain signal tied to reward and motor learning. The ESTREL trial gave the drug or a dummy pill alongside standard rehab for thirty-nine days.

At three months the trial had shown no gain in arm and leg movement scores. This report checks the same scores at twelve months for more than three hundred patients. pmc-13147123:
Anderson Brito and co-authors build a model to predict poor recovery after stroke caused by a block in a medium-sized brain vessel. Recent trials suggest that a tube-based clearing treatment may not help these patients much. The team wanted a way to spot, early, who faces the worst odds.

Older age raised the odds of poor recovery. The clearing treatment seemed to help only patients younger than sixty-nine, a split that could guide who gets picked for care and for future trials.
pmc-13150923:
Chia-Jung Lin, Meng-Jung Lin, and Jihn-Fa Jan study mental illness and crime in Taiwan in this twenty twenty-six paper. They used text-reading software on court rulings to flag cases that mention signs of mental illness. On that base, only a small share of crimes, well under one in a hundred, showed such signs. Maps and models over place and time then linked care resources to crime patterns, giving planners a fuller picture than headlines alone.
pmc-13151523:
Fleur Delva and her eleven co-authors, publishing in 2026, study French retirees who worked around asbestos, asking whether other workplace dusts added to their cancer risk. pmc-13152923:
Tomas Seeman and co-authors collect cases of visible blood in the urine among children with polycystic kidney disease at four European centers, in a study from 2026. At last follow up, high blood pressure was notably more common in the children who had bled than in those who had not. The authors argue the episode should prompt closer blood pressure watch in young patients.
pmc-13153523:
Robert Klamroth and eight co-authors present the final results, published in 2026, of the German AHEAD study on hemophilia A care. In severe disease, preventive dosing cut bleeding compared with treating bleeds as they came. Treatment-related side effects appeared in about one patient in twenty for each product. The authors say the real-world data back the long-term benefit and safety of both products.
pmc-13153723:
Jiaxuan Wu and co-authors build a scoring chart to predict which pre-COPD patients will cross into full disease. Pre-COPD means symptoms and risk without the spirometry reading that defines COPD. Statistical modeling distilled the independent predictors into a nomogram, a paper chart that turns patient traits into a personal risk number, then checked its accuracy. Chest physicians get a triage tool for the stage when prevention still works.
pmc-13155123:
Cyrille Mesue Njume and co-authors test whether complex AI methods really help find disease markers, in a 2026 study. Rich multi-layer data sets promise strong markers for disease. Yet ever more complex tools may not pay off in practice. The team built a broad benchmark to check.

The results argue for care in adding complexity: small, sturdy panels from simpler methods may serve clinics better.
pmc-13155623:
Qin and co-authors present a model, published in 2026, for predicting where valuable minerals lie deep underground. Prospectors read chemical traces in soil and rock to guess where ore hides.
