Drugs helped at first, then the illness flared again.
pmc-13191823: Rahul Atodaria and Randa Abdelmasih report an infertility case tied to a gene deletion in this 2026 paper. The patient was a 32 year old man with no sperm in his semen. Testing found a complete deletion of the AZFb and AZFc regions on the Y chromosome. For deletions of this kind, sperm retrieval surgery is very unlikely to succeed.
pmc-13192323:
Munshi Md Rasel, Daniel Cohan, Daniel Tong, and Lucas Henneman show that cuts at coal power plants could help US counties meet the new fine particle air standard. The tightened national cap has pushed a check of which fixes can bring lagging counties in line. The study came out in twenty twenty-six.

A chemical transport model traced plant shares of fine particles, and a leaner model pinned down single plants. Nine counties could have met the cap if sulfur output ended at a set of plants. Retiring them would also dodge huge tonnages of sulfur, nitrogen oxides, and carbon dioxide, plus many early deaths a year among older people, the authors estimate.
pmc-13192523:
A large Colombian team led by Julian Rojas presents a two thousand twenty-six study of chronic granulomatous disease in thirty-nine patients. The inherited condition cripples a key microbe-killing system in immune cells. Patients suffer repeated infections from early life.

Cases came from thirty-two unrelated families across multiple centers. Genetic testing covered most patients and found faults in several oxidase genes. One gene accounted for most cases by far. Clinical and microbe patterns were catalogued alongside the genetics. The report gives Latin American clinicians a regional picture of a rare immune disorder and its usual culprits.
pmc-13193623:
Mana Sato, Robert Kanaly, and Jiro Mori study two bacterial species sharing polluted soil, in a paper from two thousand twenty-six. Polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons are toxic leftovers of petroleum in the ground. As a rule, they need bacterial teamwork to break down in full. A soil consortium grown on these pollutants held two dominant genera in its ranks.

One isolate, a Sphingobium, degrades the pollutants on its own. The other, an Achromobacter, cannot do that work at all. It seems to live off the breakdown products the first one leaves. Genomic and transcriptomic analysis maps this dependence in molecular detail. Who eats what is one core question in the work. Which genes switch on in partnership is the other one. To grasp such cross-feeding helps engineers build cleanup communities for contaminated land. They can do so in place of a hope that single strains will suffice.
pmc-13193823:
Wei and a large team (2026) asked whether nutrition at hospital admission predicts poor bowel preparation in patients with inflammatory bowel disease. A clean bowel is essential for a good colonoscopy, and malnutrition is common in these patients. The team reviewed 697 patients at one hospital from 2021 to 2025 and scored nutrition three ways, using two index formulas and a screening tool, then tested which scores forecast inadequate preparation.

The three tools disagreed on how common malnutrition was, giving rates from about 6 to 28 percent. All three still independently predicted poor preparation, and for two of them the link curved rather than running straight. The risk index had the best predictive performance of the three. Effects also showed up in particular patient subgroups. The authors conclude that a quick nutrition score at admission could flag patients who need extra preparation support before their procedure.
pmc-13195023:
Suryo Kuncorojakti and eight colleagues compare stem cells taken from fat at two sites in rabbits, in a study dated twenty twenty-six. Fat is a handy source of stem cells for healing therapies, since it is easy to gather. Yet little is known about whether the body site changes the cells. The team took fat from the belly lining and from between the shoulder blades of three young male rabbits.

The cells from both sites looked the same under the microscope. Still, they differed in growth rate, in how well they formed colonies, and in how readily they turned into bone, fat, or cartilage-like cells. Two surface markers also differed between sites. The authors conclude that the source site shapes what these cells can do, which matters when picking cells for therapy.
pmc-13195823:
Grosso, Grosso, and Dias Filho challenge a 2025 surgical guideline that endorses treating simple appendicitis with antibiotics instead of surgery. Writing in 2026, they grade the evidence behind that advice and find it weak. Scans taken at admission, they argue, miss small perforations and cannot rule out hidden tumors of the appendix, found in up to about three percent of cases.

They also cite follow-up data showing that antibiotic-treated patients relapse at a rate above forty percent within three years. The apparent safety of the drug-first route, they say, is skewed by these flaws. Their letter argues that lasting repair and safe surgery should stay the main goals in emergency abdominal care.
pmc-13196423:
Ann Mercier and co-authors test whether a chatbot can handle cancer clinic phone triage, in work from 2026. Patients with gynecologic cancers often call with urgent symptoms after hours. Fellows judge those calls by phone, and AI help could speed safe answers.

Thirty real call scenarios were put to a leading chatbot version. Four doctors rated each reply for accuracy, completeness, clarity, relevance, and fit for use. They also flagged any false content and compared advice with fellow judgment. Agreement with fellows on the core call was measured directly. Patterns of over-triage and under-triage were tallied as well. Results weigh whether AI can draft triage replies under human review.
pmc-13196723:
Nicola Manocchio and seven co-authors weigh a vine plant, Cissus quadrangularis, as an aid in bone loss care. Their tale review appeared in twenty twenty-six. The plant is rich in bone-fit parts and fights rust and flare while it prods bone build cells and curbs bone eat cells. Beast and human proof was summed for breaks and thin bone.

In beasts, the plant sped break heal and bone fill. In folks, small trials showed fast break heal, less pain, and a hold on bone loss marks in thin-bone women past change of life, with no grave harms told. The team call for big, long, set-dose trials.
pmc-13196923:
Shu-Xian Lin and Kuang-Sheng Yeh published a 2026 study of a drug-resistant germ strain in pets. The strain is a type of E. coli, a common gut germ that can infect the bladder. They checked samples from dogs and cats treated for bladder infections in Taiwan.

The team studied 400 germ samples from a teaching animal hospital, gathered over nine years. Gene tests confirmed 26 samples as the ST131 strain, known for resisting many drugs. Those samples carried many harm-linked genes. All resisted two common drugs, but all still responded to one strong reserve drug. Some resistance genes could pass between germs. The spread in pets matters for both animal and human health.
pmc-13197023:
Dan Wang and co-authors report a rare pairing of severe pancreas inflammation with a nerve disorder in a 2026 case report. A thirty-nine-year-old woman with fat-driven pancreatitis and autoimmune disease lay in intensive care on breathing and kidney support machines. When sedation stopped, she showed sudden symmetric weakness in all four limbs.

Electrical nerve studies and spinal fluid tests confirmed Guillain-Barré syndrome, the motor-sensory axonal kind, where the immune system attacks nerves. Treatment with intravenous immunoglobulin brought gradual recovery of strength. The authors warn that this syndrome hides easily in very sick patients, since weakness can be blamed on the illness itself. They urge early nerve testing when weakness after sedation has no clear cause.
pmc-13197223:
Bingchen Wu and co-authors study how a clock gene shapes dopamine signals in the mouse brain, in a research paper from 2026. Daily body rhythms affect mood and body health, and breaks in those rhythms link to brain disorders. The team used mice with a changed Clock gene, called ClockΔ19, and mice with the normal gene.

The team placed fine coated fibers in the brain area called the striatum to sense dopamine levels. Two drugs helped show how the system reacts: one blocks D2 and D3 receptors, and one blocks dopamine reuptake. The mutant mice showed a faster response to the blocking drug, which points to more sensitive receptors. Tests of gene activity also showed more of the enzyme that helps make dopamine, and more D2 and D3 receptors in key brain areas.
pmc-13197323:
Marianne Damholdt Bergin and co-authors track semi-feral cattle and horses at ten Danish rewilding sites to see where each species spends its time. Large grazers shape ecosystems, so their space use matters for planning. GPS data over two years covered ten cattle and seventeen horses, joined with direct watches of behaviour.

Both species used open land, such as dry grassland and heath-dune, more than its share, and dense shrub and forest less. Horses used open wet ground and heath-dune more than cattle did. Horses spent most watched time grazing, while cattle rested and ruminated more. Winter feeding pulled activity to feeding spots, and summer saw more use of wetlands and woods.
pmc-13197423:
Rym Baccouch and colleagues ran a 2026 trial on music paired with exercise for teens with poor vision. Teens born with visual impairment often have lower fitness and less daily independence. Music has boosted drive in other groups, so the team tested it within strength and body-sense training.

Fifty-nine teens split into three groups: training alone, training with music, and no training. After eight weeks, both training groups improved on all fitness tests. The music group scored higher than the plain group on sit-to-stand counts, a wall-sit hold, and one-leg balance. Reach distance did not differ. The control group showed no real change. Music may add gains for daily autonomy.
pmc-13197723:
Xindong Bai and co-authors survey a mastitis-causing bacterium in dairy goats in Shaanxi, China. Their 2026 study also maps the genes of a drug-resistant subset. The bacterium is a major cause of udder infection and a store of drug resistance.

Milk samples from nineteen farms yielded the bacterium in about one sample in ten. Most isolates stayed sensitive to the eighteen drugs tested. A small share resisted many drugs, and a few resisted a key drug class. Gene maps tied those strains to types known in people and pigs, hinting at host spillover. The authors call for joint human-animal watch on such high-risk lines.
pmc-13198123:
A hidden heart-rhythm ill can be treated by burning its source patch. Michael Byers and Dominik Beer report a United States case in a man with no gene found, in work from twenty twenty-six. The man, in his early fifties, had fainting with fever and a rhythm that could be provoked into chaos. He had refused a shock device.

Mapping found abnormal local signals on the outer wall of the heart's outflow zone. A provoking drug deepened both the pattern and the signals. Burning the patch erased the signals and normalized the tracing. The tight match pins the ill on delayed firing, the authors argue.
pmc-13198723:
Modern drug and gene screens produce huge tables of measurements, and grouping samples into clusters is a standard way to spot real patterns. The trouble is that noise and unknown group counts make many clusters shaky. Bao and a fifteen-author team present Untangled, an unsupervised tool for this job. It runs clustering at many levels of fineness and merges the results into a stability-based picture. It then picks the group count and grades each cluster for strength.

The team benchmarked the tool on simulated data, on sets with known true groups, and on real screening data from several fields. Untangled recovered the hidden structure more reliably than rival methods. It also did a better job of flagging clusters with a shared mechanism or response pattern. The authors pitch it as a way to spend follow-up effort on the signals most likely to hold up.
pmc-13200623:
Dariusz Skalski and five co-authors tested computer models that predict race walking results and guide training, in a study published in two thousand twenty-six. Thirty top female race walkers were tracked over four seasons. Tests covered oxygen use, blood lactate, heart rate, stride form, and leg strength. The team compared standard math models with two kinds of neural networks.

Heart rate, step length, peak oxygen use, and top leg strength best predicted race outcomes. A radial basis network beat the other models, while plain regression lagged well behind. Results also swung with the season, so models that track time did better. The authors say heart rate and step length can steer day-to-day training, while fitness and strength tests guide longer plans.
pmc-13200923:
Yangqing Cui and co-authors report a hard case of a tumor found behind the belly in a woman in her forties. Their twenty twenty-six case report weighs two look-alike growths. One is a benign smooth muscle tumor, and the other is a PEComa, which can turn harmful.

Scans found the mass by chance, and surgery removed it in full. Under the microscope the cells looked even, with very low growth, yet one marker clouded the call. The team chose care matched to the risk and then tracked the patient for years. She stayed free of return, a result readers can weigh against the doubt at the start.
pmc-13201323:
Wolves shift where they roam as the seasons change, and a 2026 study led by Nathaniel H Wehr tests whether those shifts track the movements of their prey. The research article follows gray wolves, moose, and white-tailed deer in Minnesota, plus wolves and moose on Isle Royale in Michigan.

The team analyzed GPS collar records gathered from 2008 through 2021 and used cluster analysis to define seasonal patterns of space use. Mainland wolves changed their ranges in step with deer migration, while island wolves and moose kept steadier patterns. The results link predator movement to prey movement and argue for managing several species together.
pmc-13202423:
Amir Rafati and Esmaeil Karami build an imprinted polymer sensor for curcumin, in work from 2026. Curcumin checks in food and drug samples need fast, cheap, and selective tools. A polymer cast around the target molecule keeps shaped pockets after the template washes out.

The film grew straight on a carbon electrode by electric polymerisation with curcumin inside. Washed pockets then rebind curcumin with far stronger signal than a plain film shows. Tuning of acidity and growth settings set the sensor at its best working point. Wide range, low detection floor, and repeat use all scored well in bench tests. Rival substances barely disturbed the curcumin signal in selectivity checks.
pmc-13202523:
Anh-Tuan Pham and co-authors glue graphene oxide sheets into epoxy with molecular bridges for year-stable coatings in a 2026 study. Epoxy guards ships and steel, but nano fillers clump inside it and lose their punch. Sheets made by an electrochemical route carry many oxygen handles for chemistry.

A chosen silane links the sheets covalently into the resin, locking them apart and bonded. The blend stayed evenly mixed for over a year with no visible clumping. Strength and corrosion resistance rose together at the best loading. The recipe answers the shelf-life problem that has dogged nano-epoxy coatings.
pmc-13202823:
Research on blood and tissue markers for lung cancer screening is expanding fast, and a 2026 bibliometric analysis led by Huange Zhu maps the field's shape. The study retrieves publications from the Web of Science Core Collection and visualizes trends, collaboration networks, and emerging topics with several analysis tools.

The analysis covered 3,636 publications and found output growing exponentially since 2014 across the field. Collaboration formed a dual core around China and the United States, with Chinese volume high and American work more cited. Topic modeling grouped the literature into five directions, and burst analysis pointed to DNA methylation, liquid biopsy, and artificial intelligence platforms as future priorities.
pmc-13202923: A short correction notice from Tao Liu and co-authors, published in 2026, amends their 2025 BMC Plant Biology article on cotton PLATZ transcription factors and drought resistance in tomato. The notice states that a paragraph was duplicated by mistake in the introduction and must be removed, and it confirms the error does not affect the article's conclusions. Only the correction notice itself survives here, so the underlying experiments and results are not described.
pmc-13203023:
The gut talks to the skeleton, and a 2026 review by Alba Rodriguez-Bryant surveys that talk for ways to protect bone. The article studies the gut-bone axis in osteoporosis, on how gut microbes and their products influence nutrient uptake, gut leakiness, acidity, and immune control.

Rodriguez-Bryant and co-authors review diet plans meant to steer the microbiome toward bone protection. Options include butyrate and other postbiotics, chosen probiotic strains, prebiotic fibers, synbiotic mixes, and dietary patterns such as Mediterranean and vegetarian diets. The review also maps microbe product pathways and flags gaps that must close before these plans become standard osteoporosis care.
pmc-13203223:
Gabriel Levy-Hara and colleagues present a two thousand twenty-six framework for strengthening antibiotic stewardship in six Latin American countries. Hospital antibiotic overuse feeds resistance and harms patients. Stewardship programs must fit local settings to work.

The shared package began with a snapshot survey of antibiotic use in each hospital. A baseline checklist covered leadership, interventions, training, and monitoring. Online education ran for over a year. Each facility then got meetings with its own strengths-and-gaps analysis and recommendations. The report gives other regions a tested template for building stewardship step by step.
pmc-13203323:
Luisfelipe Carlos Alarco-Jurado and co-authors simulate stress inside large back-tooth fillings in this 2026 study. Big class II restorations fail in complex ways that are hard to predict. A three-dimensional model of a human molar let the team compare core materials under a strong bite force.

Five setups were tested: three fiber or bulk-fill cores, a standard composite, and the intact tooth. A polyethylene fiber core spread stress most kindly, with the lowest peaks in tooth and bonding layer. A short-fiber core showed the highest stress in the remaining tooth. The bulk-fill core peaked inside its surface layer instead. The fiber core also absorbed the most internal stress itself.
pmc-13203423:
Making art may measurably lift mental health, and a 2026 meta-analysis led by Xu Song pools the randomized evidence for painting-based interventions. The study gathers trials of painting activities for outcomes such as depression and anxiety, across age groups and types of art practice.

Forty-five randomized controlled trials met the inclusion criteria and passed a formal risk-of-bias assessment. The pooled effect was significant and large, indicating better scale-measured mental health after painting interventions in the combined data. Effects looked similar across intervention lengths, art forms, and gender mixes, while older adults appeared to benefit the most from taking part.
pmc-13204223:
Jingzhou Li and seven co-authors published a dental cell biology study in twenty twenty-six on the power plants inside cells that build teeth. Dental papilla cells must become odontoblasts, the dentin makers, and the role of mitochondrial reshaping in that change was unclear. Microscopy and gene manipulation traced the sequence.

When differentiation was triggered, mitochondria fragmented early and their contact sites with the endoplasmic reticulum multiplied. A fission protein drove both changes, and an enzyme called malic enzyme 2 recruited it and kept the contact sites organized. Breaking any link in that chain stalled dentin formation in dishes and in animals. The authors name the axis a metabolic switch and a target for regenerating the dentin-pulp complex.
pmc-13205623:
Xuchun Yang and five co-authors study how salts and surfactants team up to push oil from rock in 2026. Single surfactants free only so much trapped oil. Salt ions can tune the oil-water boundary and rock wetting, but the joint mechanics were not well understood.

The team paired two common salts with four surfactants and ran bench tests plus tiny flow devices with dead-end pores. Salt type and dose shaped the boundary strongly. Sodium ions generally beat potassium ions on tension, film strength, and wetting. One pairing, a surfactant with strong sodium salt water, freed the most oil in the tests.
pmc-13207923:
Glowing carbon specks are too small to reach tumors well alone, and a 2026 review led by Xiaowen Xu examines hiding them inside membrane vesicles. The article surveys carbon dots and their hybrid carriers, which range from natural extracellular vesicles to laboratory-made liposomes, for biomedical delivery.

The review first covers how carbon dots are synthesized and why they fluoresce, then details strategies for loading them into vesicles. Hybrid systems are being tried for targeted drug delivery, imaging, tumor therapy, antibacterial work, and wound care in the literature surveyed. Loading efficiency, burst release, and what the dots do to vesicle stability remain open problems for clinical translation.
pmc-13208123:
Severe leg artery disease becomes far deadlier when inflammation and poor nutrition combine, a 2026 study by Paula Luque-Linero and co-authors finds. The condition, chronic limb-threatening ischemia, starves leg tissue of blood. The team tested whether blood markers of inflammation and nutritional state could sort patients by risk.

The study followed 170 patients admitted to one hospital, most of them older men with high heart risk. Within six months, about a third had a major amputation, a major heart event, or had died. Poor nutrition was the strongest single predictor of bad outcomes. Two inflammation markers also held up as independent predictors, and survival curves split clearly by risk level.
pmc-13208923:
Li Yang and six co-authors present a better way to predict how long a drive shaft lasts under repeated heavy loads in a 2026 paper. Shaft failure in special vehicles threatens the whole transmission system. Classic formulas miss two effects: how loads interact with each other, and how the metal's strength fades as damage builds.

The authors add a fading strength term to a standard stress based model and a load ratio to a damage summing model. They then compute stresses at the shaft's critical points with a detailed computer model and run the load record through both improved models. The combined method raises prediction accuracy, they report.
pmc-13209523:
Xiaojing Wang and co-authors reviewed in 2026 how tiny hairs on cells tie into metabolic disease. Each cell bears a lone hair, a primary cilium, that senses the world around it. When those hairs fail, the body can drift toward obesity and diabetes. The review lays out a two-way model. Bad hairs skew appetite, insulin release, and fat storage. In turn, the marks of metabolic disease wear the hairs down.

That loop can spin itself worse over time. The authors say drugs that heal the hairs could break the loop. New work aims to restore hair shape and work in key tissues. The review maps where such care might help most and why the link has been missed.
pmc-13209823:
Meng Ling Moi reviewed in 2026 how tests for antibody driven enhancement of virus infection have grown into full assessment platforms. Antibodies can either block a virus or, through cell docking sites, help it enter cells, and that double nature haunts vaccine work on dengue like viruses.

Over the past decade, these tests moved from niche tools to shared platforms with set virus doses, graded sample dilutions, hard numbers for enhancement, and strict quality checks. Such platforms now support vaccine trials and population surveys across labs. A key lesson is that enhancement reflects a shifting state of a person's immune system, not a fixed danger sign. Reading it in context helps separate brief effects from real risk.
pmc-13210223:
Jens Sobek and co-authors watch a single DNA letter change into a damaged form, one molecule at a time, in a 2026 paper. The letter guanine can oxidize into a product called 8oG, a change linked to mutation. In a short labeled DNA strand pair, the team triggered the change with light and read the glow traces to tell which of two paths each molecule took.

One path, where water adds to a charged form, finished in under 150 milliseconds. The other, through a neutral radical meeting superoxide, ran over a thousand times slower, with a pause lasting minutes. Adding a helper compound raised the yield by favoring the fast path. The method lets chemists watch reaction order and timing that bulk tests blur.
pmc-13210623:
Seranee Srisuk, Thanakorn Sodsai, and Penwisa Pisitsak report a study from two thousand twenty-six on turning banana stem fiber into plant-based leather with low energy. Banana pseudo-stems are farm waste, and dyeing their fibers naturally could yield a sustainable leather substitute. The team tuned dye recipes for two natural colors, lac and indigo.

Lac dyeing worked best with a two-part mordant, a set dye dose, and mildly acidic conditions over six hours. Indigo needed a strong bath with alkali and a reducing agent at low heat. Dyed fibers held up well to sweat staining but faded more in light, as natural dyes tend to do. Laminated and coated with rubber latex, the material reached solid bursting strength and proved naturally waterproof.
pmc-13210723:
Jeferson Grisales and co-authors report a 2026 study of a diatom that may clean clay from mine water. Copper mines reuse process water, but fine kaolinite clay clouds it. The diatom, a Nitzschia species from Paposo in northern Chile, makes sticky polymers outside its cells that can clump clay.

Adding a small amount of glucose raised polymer output the most, well above the plain culture. The polymer dropped cloudiness fast, and the glucose-grown batch cleared near 99 percent of the clay in 15 minutes. Gene maps showed many genes for building such polymers. Tests showed the polymer is made of several sugars whose groups grip clay grains. The authors see a green option for mine water care.
pmc-13210823:
Mariam Murad and five co-authors test whether pollen shells make perfume last longer. Their 2026 study wraps fragrance in sporopollenin exine capsules, tiny husks from spores. The husks already carry drugs for oral delivery. Here they hold scent against the skin instead.

Ten healthy women wore encapsulated scent on one wrist and plain scent on the other. No one knew which wrist held which. Wearers and a blinded reviewer rated strength over eight hours. From two hours on, the wrapped scent smelled stronger by both ratings. Cell tests checked the husks for toxicity. Slow-release scent could stretch how long a perfume stays noticeable.
pmc-13212423:
Janith Galhenage and colleagues report in 2026 on methamphetamine use and mental illness among patients at a large psychiatry clinic in Sri Lanka. Use of the drug is rising across South and Southeast Asia, yet local evidence on who uses it and what harm follows has stayed thin.

The team studied 245 consecutive patients with questionnaires and standard diagnostic criteria. Nearly all were men, most had first been introduced to the drug by friends, and about six in ten met criteria for dependence. Nicotine and heroin use were also common, while psychosis and depression appeared in a minority. Dependence strongly predicted heavier psychiatric symptoms, supporting services that treat addiction and mental illness together.
pmc-13212623:
Muhammad Saleem and co-authors compare catheter treatments for narrowed arteries below the knee in a 2026 network analysis. Options range from plain balloons to drug-coated balloons, stents, plaque shaving, and a newer removable scaffold. Head-to-head trials are scarce, so the team pooled the evidence statistically.

Twenty-five trials with over three thousand patients fed the network. Plaque shaving ranked best for early safety and cut one-year deaths against plain balloons. It also cut repeat procedures, as did drug-coated balloons and drug-eluting stents. No method clearly cut amputations. The removable scaffold landed mid-pack throughout, promising but thinly studied.
pmc-13213223:
Rania Nada and her team report the first known case set of Zika virus in Yemen, in two thousand twenty-six. Zika is spread by a type of mosquito found in many parts of the world. No case had been reported in Yemen before this work.

The team tested one hundred eighty-six patients who came in with a fever. A lab test that copies small bits of the virus found eight of them were positive. That is just over four in a hundred of those tested. The authors say the find is also the first for the wider region. They call for stronger checks for the virus there.
pmc-13213623:
Jinyu Sun and co-authors present a 2026 paper on a two-agent system meant to make language model tools for science more reliable. Single agents often slip when they must plan many steps and call tools in the right order, inventing facts or losing the thread. Their design splits the work between a planner and a doer.

The planner agent breaks a problem into steps and revises the plan as results come in. The doer agent calls a set of thirty tools with care. A self-correction loop lets the system rethink and recover when a step fails. In tests on hard tool-calling tasks, the system beat strong rivals on success rates.
pmc-13214723:
Filip Tkaczyk, writing alone in 2026, presents a nursing case study of a man with diabetes, obesity, and erectile dysfunction. Such sexual problems are a common result of diabetes and excess weight, and they weigh on quality of life. The case uses a standard nursing language, called ICNP, to plan care in a shared, clear format.

The patient was treated in a heart ward in Poland in 2025. Checks showed poor blood sugar control, mild obesity, low testosterone, and reduced quality of life, most of all in social and mental areas. The care plan set diagnoses and steps for sugar control, daily habits, sexual health, and mental support. After the plan ran, the patient's habits, knowledge, and mood all improved.
pmc-13214923:
Felix Narvaez Irizarry and three co-authors study brain tumors in this twenty twenty-six paper. They look at gene activity tied to amyloid, a protein best known from brain diseases of old age, and ask whether it plays a role in two kinds of slow-growing brain tumor. Such a role in tumors is still poorly understood.

The team used gene data from about two hundred tumors of each kind. They scored each tumor for the activity of thirty gene groups tied to amyloid and checked which scores lined up with how long patients lived. The link between amyloid-linked activity and survival differed by tumor type, a clue that the two tumors may need different care.
pmc-13216323:
M. A. Helal and co-authors present a 2026 chemistry study of a new Schiff base ligand and the metal complexes built from it, tested as possible anticancer and antimicrobial agents. Schiff bases grip metal ions at several points, which makes them versatile drug scaffolds.

The ligand, assembled from a pyridine building block and a benzene-diol partner, was combined with copper, cobalt, manganese, nickel, and palladium ions. Spectral evidence showed it binding through two oxygen and two nitrogen atoms, with most complexes taking octahedral shapes and the palladium one square planar. The compounds inhibited the tested fungi more strongly than the bacteria. Cell tests against the MCF-7 breast cancer line showed notable antitumour activity, and docking simulations suggested plausible fits to cancer-related protein targets.
pmc-13217823:
Nilesh Kumar Sinha and co-authors present a 2026 imaging case report of a rare inner ear malformation in a four-year-old boy with delayed speech and severe-to-profound hearing loss in both ears. The defect, incomplete partition type 3, is tied to X-linked deafness and makes implant surgery risky.

High-resolution CT showed the signature picture: a corkscrew-shaped cochlea with its central bony pillar entirely absent and a wide-open connection to an enlarged internal auditory canal. MRI confirmed a normal cochlear nerve and no further labyrinth problems. Naming the anomaly before surgery matters because the open channel can release a gusher of fluid during cochlear implantation. The authors use the case to teach the distinguishing scan features against the other incomplete partition types.
pmc-13218123:
Linhao Hou and colleagues report a 2026 bioadhesive hydrogel sensor that keeps working at temperatures down to minus 30 degrees Celsius. Hydrogel sensors are soft and body-friendly for monitoring wounds, but standard versions freeze in the cold, stick poorly to wet tissue, and do little to shape the wound environment. The team built its gel from polyethylene glycol, a glycerol-water solvent, and carboxylated carbon nanotubes.

Hydrogen bonding in the glycerol-water mixture blocks ice formation, while the nanotube network carries current and strengthens the gel. The sensor adhered to wet tissue and kept its conductivity and strain sensitivity at minus 30 degrees, giving fast, stable readings as it stretched. In diabetic mice with full-thickness skin wounds, readings accompanied much faster healing, with wounds closed by day twelve and new tissue resembling early developmental skin. Tests on pig heart wounds showed the sensor also follows moving tissue in real time.
pmc-13218223:
Afiqah Saffa Suriaslan and three co-authors build error bands for a bent-line form of logistic modeling, in this 2026 study. The model's bent lines let it track curves that a straight model would miss. Error bands tell how much trust to put in each driver's weight. The team test the bands in fake runs, then put them to work on real data.

The real case is the Human Development Index across Indonesia. Clean water access had a small but firm link with the score. A high share of poor folk pulled the score down. Job lack bent in a curve, with bands on both the up and down arms. School sign-up rates bent as well. The model beat a plain yes-no model on the same data, and its bands held up in the fake runs.
pmc-13218723:
Saule Spokaite and colleagues report a 2026 study that uncovers a second, ancient binding site for the RAB5 protein on a sorting machine. The VPS34 complex II builds identity signals that drive endosomal sorting, the eating of particles by cells, and the shutdown of receptors. RAB5 switches it on. Textbooks placed RAB5's grip on one helical insertion of the complex. A sister complex used for autophagy preferred a switch.

A cryo-electron microscopy structure of complex II revealed an extra RAB5 contact on the VPS15 subunit's solenoid region. The team argues this is the original site inherited from eukaryotes. Mutating the classic site in the human complex abolished RAB5 binding. Mutating the matching region in baker's yeast broke cargo sorting and the complex's association with its RAB5 counterpart. The authors suggest evolution added a grip to strengthen membrane binding as cells' transport systems grew more complex.
pmc-13219023:
Lucie Jedličková and co-authors catalog proteins shed by parasite eggs inside host tissue in this 2026 study. The eggs belong to Schistosoma mansoni, a worm that causes schistosomiasis. Egg proteins drive much of the disease and help the parasite spread. Past work studied eggs in dishes, which may not match life inside the body.

The team cut tiny samples from infected mouse liver and gut with a laser. A shared core of 149 egg proteins appeared in all samples. Liver samples from early infection carried a richer mix than later ones. Gut samples stayed steadier over time. The map shows how egg output depends on organ and stage.
pmc-13220823:
Qiang Tan and colleagues read five years of disease surveillance from Chongqing, China, for trends in lung disease in a 2026 study. The Chongqing Chronic Disease Surveillance System captured a million new cases and over 1.2 million cases of COPD, chronic bronchitis, and emphysema among residents aged fifteen and over between 2020 and 2024, plus 239,000 deaths. Age-standardized rates were computed against the 2000 census.

Standardized prevalence doubled for COPD and tripled for emphysema and chronic bronchitis across the period, which the authors attribute to better case finding rather than an explosion of disease. COPD and emphysema stayed male-predominant, while chronic bronchitis flipped to female-predominant after 2023, a divergence they flag for prevention. Rural areas carried the heavier burden. The success story is diagnostic: the share of COPD cases confirmed by spirometry jumped from seven percent in 2022 to twenty-six percent in 2024, and the urban-rural gap in that rate vanished.
pmc-13221123:
Amal Rammah and co-authors follow more than 415,000 London-born children in a 2026 cohort study of air pollution and bronchiolitis admissions. Fine particles and nitrogen dioxide were estimated at home addresses during pregnancy and the first year of life. Evidence on longer exposure windows for this chest illness had been limited.

Overall results were inconclusive, though some windows hinted at raised risk. Signals appeared for pregnancy exposure in the first month after birth, and for exposures late in infancy. Confidence ranges were wide, so no firm claim is made. The authors call for work covering emergency and primary care cases, not only hospital admissions.
pmc-13221623:
Fernanda Muñoz-Sepúlveda and co-authors test phone-based dental support for older adults in Chile, in a trial from two thousand twenty-six. Adults aged sixty and over in two town and two country areas were split by lot into two groups. One group got face-to-face oral health teaching alone, and the other got the same teaching plus short videos sent by WhatsApp for two weeks.

Both groups knew more and felt more sure about mouth care after six weeks. The phone group did better on facts about tooth decay and on general outlook in some checks. Gains in outlook and floss use stood out most in the country phone group. Readers see a cheap tool that helps, though not in every area.
pmc-13222223:
Anne-Mari Mustonen and colleagues profile blood proteins in knee osteoarthritis around the time of joint replacement, in a 2026 proteomics study. Serum came from eight healthy controls and eight patients with end-stage disease, sampled again twelve months after knee surgery. Mass spectrometry catalogued the proteins, and statistical models linked them to pain and function.

Patients showed 151 raised proteins and five lowered ones at baseline, tied to immunity, clotting, inflammation, and tissue remodeling. One protein, complement factor I, stood out as a biomarker candidate. Several proteins predicted cartilage loss, pain sensitivity, and physical function. Changes persisted a year after surgery, suggesting the disease leaves a lasting systemic signature.
pmc-13222523:
Davin Lee and co-authors turn doubt in labeling into a detector of abnormal cells. In single-cell sequencing, software assigns cell types by matching reference atlases, but many cells get shaky labels and are usually thrown away as noise. In perturbation experiments, those odd cells may be exactly the interesting ones.

Their Python tool, AnnQ, extracts signals of doubt such as confidence, confidence gap, and label entropy, then scores how far each cell stands out from the reference group. Applied to genetic perturbation and drug resistance data, the scores flagged odd cell states that clustering and abundance analyses missed. The code and docs are public.
pmc-13222623:
Merrick Harris, Paola Pedraza Cruz, and Shoaib Junejo report a 2026 case of chalky lumps from long overdrive of the parathyroid glands in a kidney patient. The woman, aged forty-six, had the cystic kidney disease that ends in kidney failure. A scan found one overgrown gland, and surgery took it out while the rest looked sound.

Yet hormone levels stayed sky high on top drug care. In the next year she grew deep bone pain, joint aches, broken bones, and chalk lumps by many joints. The case shows how gland overdrive can rage on past surgery.
pmc-13223123:
Seven authors report 2026 screening results for hidden tuberculosis infection among new students in Taishan District. Skin tests were given to 38,863 new students in 2025, with a valid screening rate near 93 percent. A total of 5,395 students met the mark for latent infection, a rate of about 14 percent.

Risk ran higher for female students, for those in degree programs, for students aged 19 and up, and for those with past contact with the disease. School level and no past contact went with lower risk. The authors urge stronger entry screening plus close follow-up and preventive steps for infected students.
pmc-13223923:
Joseph Beljan and colleagues use engineered small RNA to skip harmful pseudoexons and restore full-length dystrophin in Duchenne muscular dystrophy cells. Their 2026 study works with patient-derived cell lines.

Deep intronic mutations cause a small share of Duchenne cases by inserting intron fragments into the gene's message. Such patients retain all normal coding exons, so excluding the pseudoexon restores a full-length transcript. The modified RNA targeted splice signals in those fragments. Treatment produced dose-dependent skipping above ninety percent in all four cell lines. Dystrophin protein sometimes exceeded normal levels. The authors present this as bespoke gene therapy for an orphan mutation class.
pmc-13224023:
Garyfallia Papaioannou and co-authors trace how bone's resident cells convert a squeeze into a chemical whisper. Osteocytes sense mechanical load along their branching arms, and loading briefly quiets focal adhesion kinase, FAK. Phospho-proteomic profiling of osteocyte-like cells went hunting for what FAK touches.

Three cAMP-signaling proteins surfaced as candidate targets, including the phosphodiesterase PDE8A, an enzyme that chews up cAMP. Blocking or deleting FAK raised cAMP levels and downstream signaling; blocking PDE8A copied the effect exactly, and the two proteins were found physically associated inside the cell. The authors propose that load-regulated FAK throttles cAMP through PDE8A, wiring mechanical signals into the hormonal pathway that parathyroid hormone uses.
pmc-13225523:
Chewing well may matter for survival after stroke in ways few expect. Wenshu Zhang and four co-authors use two decades of United States survey data covering 1,708 adults with a history of stroke. They count working tooth pairs as a measure of chewing function and track deaths through 2018. They also test whether body-wide inflammation carries part of any link.

More working tooth pairs went with lower overall death risk, a link that held up in statistical models, while the tie to heart-related death was weaker and less certain. Two inflammation indexes explained a small slice of the association, a few percent each. The authors suggest chewing function could serve as a simple marker for spotting higher-risk stroke survivors. The study appears in 2026.
pmc-13226023:
A. S. Aderibigbe tracks a 2026 poultry research note comparing stress in fast-growing and slow-growing broiler chickens raised on pasture. Feather samples store corticosterone, a stress hormone, giving a noninvasive record over time. Two commercial genotypes, Cornish and Freedom Ranger, were followed for five weeks in the same outdoor system.

Feather hormone levels did not differ significantly between the fast and slow growers at any point. Levels did shift significantly across the five weeks for both types, showing that time and changing conditions registered in the birds even when breed did not. Under these pasture conditions, genotype alone did not explain stress, a result relevant to welfare claims made for slower-growing birds.
pmc-13226123:
Merzu Belete and colleagues build a 2026 prediction tool for head and neck cancer patients receiving immunotherapy, where only a minority benefit and the usual PD-L1 score predicts poorly. Their model fuses three kinds of information: clinical data, gene-activity signatures from the tumour, and features from digital pathology images. Artificial intelligence combined them into a single risk signature.

Immune-related gene patterns, especially those tied to T cells and organised immune clusters called tertiary lymphoid structures, tracked with longer time before the cancer progressed. The combined model beat any single data type in real-world patient groups. Its survival-aware design also highlighted which tissue regions drove each prediction, keeping the output interpretable for clinicians.
pmc-13227223:
Zihan Xue and six co-authors published a review in twenty twenty-six on nanomaterials for chronic pain. Today's mainstays, anti-inflammatory drugs and opioids, bring side effects and tolerance with long use. Nanotechnology offers both smarter delivery of old drugs and materials that are themselves therapeutic.

The review sorts painkillers into traditional drugs and newer biological agents, then assesses the nanoplatforms carrying them. Special attention goes to materials with inherent pain-relieving action and to designs that home to pain sites or release on demand. The authors close with the obstacles between laboratory promise and clinic, including safety testing and manufacturing. Their map aims to guide a field hunting for non-opioid relief.
pmc-13227323:
Tom Chun Wai Tsoi and colleagues set out a 2026 trial protocol for an online coaching programme aimed at Hong Kong family carers of older adults. Carers often develop anxiety and depression, yet most studies of digital coaching stop at those symptoms. This three-arm randomised trial also asks whether self-directed learning can build resilience and overall well-being, especially for carers whose needs are still mild.

Participants will receive either the full module set, a partial set, or control access through an online platform. Modules cover lifestyle habits, family relationships, and emotion regulation. Standard scales measure anxiety and depression as primary outcomes, while quality of life, caregiving burden, self-care confidence, and unmet needs fill out the wider picture.
pmc-13228023:
Yao Ma and co-authors pair two antibodies against different parts of the coronavirus spike to block the virus from evolving around treatment. Antibodies against the spike have been a main therapy for COVID-19, but variants have escaped every approved one so far. Their 2026 study uses a weakened, light-emitting version of the virus to watch resistance grow safely in the lab.

One antibody targets the binding domain that grips human cells, and under its pressure a resistant mutant appeared fast, carrying a single change that also defeated three other antibodies of that class. The second antibody targets the stalk of the spike, and no resistant mutant emerged under it. The pair together also blocked escape. The authors argue the stalk is hard for the virus to change without hurting itself, and that such cocktails are the way forward.
pmc-13231023:
Kritika Agarwal and four co-authors study how hospital psychiatry referral work changed across the COVID-19 years. Their 2026 paper looks at a consultation team at a medical institute in Patna, India, which visits patients admitted for physical care who also need mental health support.

The team compared charts from six months in 2019 with the same span in 2022, covering 285 patients in all. Referrals rose by about two thirds, with more cases sent from emergency and general medicine wards. Delirium became far more common among referred patients, while mood and psychotic disorders made up a smaller share. The authors urge hospital psychiatry teams to stay flexible as referral patterns shift.
pmc-13231423:
Sergio García-Vega, Enrique Pérez-Carreño, Javier Cabeza, and Pablo García-Álvarez stress-test claims that certain heavy tetrylenes shrug off air. Their 2026 paper studies germanium and tin compounds held by a pyridyl alkenol ligand. Earlier work called the twin-ligand versions highly air-stable.

All tested compounds do hydrolyze at room temperature, the team finds, though at wildly different rates. Computer calculations trace how water breaks them down. First coordination tests follow: a germanium chloro compound binds iridium cleanly, while its tin twin gives a messy mix. A gold complex forms from the twin-ligand germanium compound. Some reactions degrade the ligand outright. The authors urge care with air-stability claims for this reactive family.
pmc-13231523:
Tao Sun and co-authors follow heart risk in patients with coronary disease in a 2026 study. The focus is lipoprotein(a), a fatty particle in blood that raises heart risk on its own. A second factor, homocysteine, may sway how strong that risk is. The team tracked 530 patients for 36 months and split them by lipoprotein level.

High lipoprotein levels more than doubled the risk of major heart events in the full group. The risk for acute coronary events was higher still. In patients with mid to high homocysteine, high lipoprotein marked a high-risk set for both event types. In patients with low homocysteine, the same high lipoprotein showed no link to events. The split hints the two factors act together.
pmc-13231623:
Rachel Kawuma and the PrEPVacc trial team published a longitudinal qualitative study in twenty twenty-six on whether trial participants actually understood the unusual HIV prevention trial they had joined. The East and Southern African trial tested vaccines and, in a second randomization, preventive pills at once. One hundred five participants were interviewed three times across a year, and over a hundred more joined focus groups.

Repeated information sessions led by health workers gradually built real understanding of the design. Participants widely recognized the pills as proven protection alongside the experimental vaccines. The study traces what helped comprehension and what influenced joining. For trial designers, it is evidence that complex designs can be made legible to the people inside them.
pmc-13232023:
Erin W Kavanagh and a large team test base editing and tiny carriers as a route to treat cystic fibrosis. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-six. The disease stems from faults in one gene, which thicken mucus in the airways. Some patients gain nothing from the current gene-target drugs, so a lasting fix in airway cells is a key goal.

They fix a common splice fault in airway cells from patients, using base editor RNA. Most cell types then show far more of the gene's message. Tiny polymer carriers send the editors into lab and patient cells and bring the gene's work back to a level that matters for care. The route is non-viral and can scale.
pmc-13232723:
Yael Riahi and colleagues identify in 2026 glucosamine as the missing link between high blood sugar and a growth switch that harms diabetic tissue. Chronic sugar excess keeps the switch, called mTORC1, stuck on in pancreas and kidney, driving stress and cell decline. Tracing labeled glucose in diabetic rodents showed tissue sugar and glucosamine rising in lockstep.

The same tie appeared in human blood data and grew stronger as insulin-making function worsened. Small glucosamine doses switched the pathway on in dish tests through a sugar-tagging step. Dimming the switch genetically in insulin cells, or lowering sugar with a common drug class, eased cell stress and restored function. The pathway offers a fresh target for protecting both pancreas and kidney.
pmc-13232823:
FuGuo Liu and colleagues build in 2026 a structure-aware model that predicts what viral proteins do from messy wastewater samples. Fast viral change makes look-alike proteins drift into new jobs, which breaks tools that read letter sequences alone. Their framework mixes short sequence chunks with meaning tags drawn from a protein database.

Training used more than sixty-six thousand coronavirus samples pulled from wastewater sequencing records. Scores in repeated testing ran high for sorting proteins by function, and a slimmed student model kept nearly all that skill while training much faster. Attention peaks in the model landed on known working parts of the spike protein, which makes its calls easier to trust. Earlier wastewater warnings for new variants are the intended payoff.
pmc-13233323:
Alexander Tyshkovskiy and colleagues published a 2026 study hunting for shared molecular signs of ageing across mammals. The team integrated more than 11,000 gene activity profiles from over 25 tissues in mice, rats, macaques, and humans. From these data they built clear markers that estimate age in years and expected mortality, and that respond to lifespan-changing interventions.

Ageing-related gene changes proved conserved across species and cell types, with genes such as CDKN1A and LGALS3 standing out. Their protein levels also tracked death and multiple illnesses in UK Biobank data. Damage models in cells and animals echoed the same signatures, while reprogramming and other rejuvenation steps reversed them. Separate clocks for pathways like inflammation and mitochondrial function showed that diseases and diets age different systems at different speeds.
pmc-13233723:
Hiryahafira Mohamad Tahir and co-authors review house dust mite allergy in tropical regions, in a 2026 narrative review. This allergy is a leading cause of allergic disease worldwide. The steady warmth and damp air of the tropics are ideal for mites, so people there face allergen exposure all year. Yet the ecology and patterns of the allergy in the tropics are still poorly mapped.

The review sums up what is known about which mite species live where and how people become sensitized to them. It gives close attention to the three main species of the region. It also surveys how the allergy is diagnosed across tropical countries. Tests range from skin prick tests and blood tests to newer molecular methods that resolve single allergen parts.
pmc-13233923:
Sibel Bozgeyik-Bagdatli and colleagues published a 2026 cross-sectional study of symptom burden across the severity grades of knee osteoarthritis. Eighty-two patients were sorted into grades two, three, and four on the Kellgren-Lawrence X-ray scale. They were then compared on pain, sleep, daily function, walking and standing tests, and leg strength. Age and body mass were accounted for.

The most advanced grade carried the heaviest burden. Grade four patients reported worse constant pain than grade two patients. They moved more slowly on the timed up-and-go test. Their thigh muscle was weaker in the sore knee, and they rated knee function lower. Differences between grades two and three, and between three and four, were much narrower. Sleep scores did not differ significantly. The authors say the top grade marks a clear step up in suffering.
pmc-13234023:
Dorsa Manavi and co-workers issued a 2026 mixed-methods study on living with fibromyalgia alongside body-wide autoimmune diseases such as lupus and rheumatoid arthritis. Surveys came from 1,269 adults, backed by talks with 19 patients and 21 doctors. About a quarter of the adults reported fibromyalgia, and over half of those doubted the diagnosis was right.

People with the dual label reported lower wellbeing, less trust in their doctors, less faith in getting help, and a worse view of their care than peers without fibromyalgia. Talks traced the doubt to overlapping symptoms and the lack of a decisive blood test, with uneven doctor habits feeding mistrust. Feeling dismissed or wrongly labeled added stigma and delays. Accepting the label, by itself, changed few outcomes.
pmc-13234323:
Eva Niessen and colleagues introduced in 2026 a new laboratory task for studying whether people notice their own mistakes. Theories of cognitive control hold that behaviour adjusts more strongly after errors that a person has detected. Older tasks produce few undetected errors, which limits comparison between the two kinds. The Speeded Inference Task was built to create many errors of both types at a steady rate.

Two small studies with about twenty adults each tested the task in practice. The first study confirmed the desired error pattern over time. Exploratory results there suggested post-error slowing and accuracy gains were not clearly tied to awareness. Changing one task feature in the second study shifted error detection without changing the overall error rate. Researchers can now use the task to probe brain and behaviour links more cleanly.
pmc-13235523:
Ganglong Duan and colleagues proposed in 2026 a system that detects distress in posts on Weibo, a major Chinese social platform, and responds with supportive content. Their approach first judges the emotional polarity of a post, then classifies negative posts by the cause behind the feeling. Positive content matched to that cause is then recommended to the user. Weakly supervised learning reduces the need for hand-labelled training examples.

Tests on a real Weibo dataset reached high accuracy for recognizing emotional polarity in posts. Sorting negative posts into cause categories proved harder, with accuracy in the low eighties. Recommendation performance was also reported as strong in the experiments described. The authors frame automatic emotional support as a scalable complement to counselling, which faces staff, distance, and stigma limits. Further validation would be needed before any mental health deployment is claimed.
pmc-13236523:
Emmeline Monique T. Ngo and co-authors described in 2026 an autoimmune cause of extreme insulin resistance in a 20-year-old woman. She arrived with diabetic ketoacidosis and blood sugar that stayed dangerously high despite enormous insulin doses. Antibodies in her blood were attacking her own insulin receptors, a rare condition called type B insulin resistance. Testing confirmed the diagnosis alongside other autoimmune markers in her profile.

Supportive diabetes drugs, including a GLP-1 medicine, cut her daily insulin need from thousands of units to a few hundred. Immune-suppressing treatment with rituximab and azathioprine then allowed insulin to stop entirely within a week. As antibody levels fell, the same antibodies began causing low blood sugar episodes during fasting. Steroids and another drug managed that second phase under continuous glucose monitoring. The authors highlight the swing between extremes as a signature of the disease.
pmc-13237323:
Mohammad N Kheshfeh and colleagues ran a randomized trial at the University of Damascus in 2026 comparing two orthodontic wire designs for pulling upper canine teeth backward after premolar removal. Thirty-eight patients aged 18 to 25 with Class II bite problems were split evenly. One group used a bi-dimensional wire, rectangular at the front and round at the back, while the other used a conventional rectangular wire throughout.

Monthly retraction was faster with the bi-dimensional wire, at roughly 1.17 millimeters per month against about 0.82 in the conventional group. The trial also tracked tooth rotation, tilt, anchor-tooth drift, bite depth change, and root shortening on scans and X-rays, with assessors kept blind to group. The authors present the mixed wire as a more efficient sliding system for this common extraction treatment.
pmc-13238223:
Jiahui Mao, Hao Lin, Feng Gu, and Zhaoji Pan review small RNA strands and cancer in a 2026 paper. These strands normally guide chemical marks on the cell's protein-making machinery. New sequencing work shows they go off balance in many diseases, above all in cancer.

The review covers how the strands form, how they are classed, and what they do beyond their classic job. They can shape gene splicing, message stability, and protein contacts. In tumors they sway growth, spread, metabolism, and drug resistance. The authors map their changes across major cancers, including colon, liver, stomach, lung, breast, and ovarian types. The strands may serve as markers or drug targets.
pmc-13239123:
Maximilian Reuber, Christian Coachman, and Daniel Engler-Hamm reported in 2026 a 62-year-old woman whose collapsed bite and obstructive sleep apnea were treated together with an implant-supported jaw advancement. She had lost her occlusal height badly, a situation where ordinary mouthpieces for apnea have nothing to grip. A digital workflow planned six implants across both jaws and a same-day provisional prosthesis that held her lower jaw forward.

The bite was raised by five millimeters, and the provisional went in on the day of surgery. After three months of healing, final telescopic crown prostheses restored function and appearance. She reported that her snoring eased and her sleep improved markedly. The authors present prosthetic-driven implant therapy as an expanding answer where dentistry meets sleep medicine.
pmc-13239223:
Moamen Al Zoubi and colleagues reported in 2026 a 70-year-old man whose spreading brain lesions, first feared to be cancer, proved to be infection by the free-living amoeba Balamuthia mandrillaris. He had recently worked with soil in rural Mexico. Extensive testing for infection, cancer, and autoimmune disease found nothing, and brain biopsy showed dense granulomatous inflammation with no organism visible on ordinary stains.

A gene-amplification test on the brain tissue finally named the amoeba, a diagnosis the national disease control agency confirmed. Treatment with a multidrug regimen including miltefosine and the investigational drug nitroxoline damaged his kidneys and liver, and after brief radiological improvement the disease advanced and he died. The authors stress molecular testing when conventional work-ups fail on rare pathogens.
pmc-13239623:
Qi-Hua Yu and colleagues review recent work on piperine, the pungent compound in black pepper, as a possible cancer drug source in a 2026 article. Interest is high, yet the natural supply is small and the compound dissolves poorly in water, limiting how much reaches tumours in the body.

Covering studies from 2012 to 2025, the review explains the molecule's structure, how chemists build it in the laboratory, and how living systems produce it. Most attention goes to modified versions, especially changes at one end of the molecule that add new chemical groups. Those derivatives often killed cancer cells more strongly while keeping favourable behaviour.
pmc-13240023:
Sirena Gutierrez and a large team ask how much of the thinking gap between Indigenous-speaking and other older Mexicans runs through schooling, in this 2026 study. Indigenous adults face deep educational inequities, which may echo into late-life cognition.

The study covered 1,958 adults aged fifty-five and over from a Mexican aging cohort. Eleven percent spoke an Indigenous language, and they scored lower on memory, language, executive function, and orientation tests. Statistical mediation split the gap: formal education explained roughly a third to three-fifths of it, literacy another eleventh to a quarter, and numeracy a small slice. The authors conclude that high-quality education could narrow these cognitive disparities. They also urge future surveys to measure Indigenous identity beyond language, including self-identification and skin-color bias.
pmc-13240323:
Dante Van Arman and co-authors pilot a plant compound against exercise heat strain in a 2026 paper. Berberine, from several medicinal plants, lowered body temperature and heart rate in animals under passive heat. The team tested it in people: eight young adults took berberine or a placebo for a week, then ran for an hour on a treadmill in a hot, humid room.

On berberine, average body temperature, heart rate, and breathing rate all ran slightly lower. The runners also felt cooler, less uncomfortable, and less exerted. Every measured edge favored the supplement. Yet the gaps were small, and the group tiny. The authors caution that the practical value for work or sport in the heat remains doubtful, and frame the trial as a pilot for bigger studies.
pmc-13240523:
Ngawang Norbu and co-authors report a 2026 survey of white birch forests in the Nyang River Basin on the southeastern Tibetan Plateau. Plots ranged across a wide band of elevation. The study examines how woody plant variety changes with height and soil conditions.

Field teams recorded dozens of woody species across the survey plots and sorted the stands into four plant groupings. Richness and diversity measures fell as elevation rose, while dominance by a few species increased. Statistical analysis pointed to elevation plus soil nitrogen, organic matter, and phosphorus as the main influences on community makeup. The results give managers baseline data for protecting alpine forest under climate change.
pmc-13240923:
Li and colleagues in Luoyang linked the stress hyperglycemia ratio to delirium risk across two thousand ninety-three intensive care patients. The ratio compares acute blood sugar against a patient's usual level. Logistic models, curve fitting, and threshold analysis probed the shape of the link. Subgroup checks tested whether severity scores modified it.

Risk stayed flat until the ratio passed roughly two-thirds, then climbed steeply. Beyond that bend, delirium odds nearly doubled with each step upward. The association strengthened in patients with higher severity scores and inflammation markers. Li proposes the ratio as an early flag for targeted glucose management.
pmc-13241423:
da Silva and colleagues in Rio de Janeiro asked how little enlargement root canal retreatment can get away with. Fourteen extracted lower molars with severely curved canals were filled, then retreated. A paired design tested conservative and conventional protocols inside the same roots. Micro-CT scans gauged leftover filling at three stages.

The conservative protocol cleared more material early, removing ninety-five percent at the first pass. After final shaping, both approaches ended near complete removal. Less than five percent of filling stayed either way. The authors endorse the smaller preparation for sparing root dentin.
pmc-13241523:
Brandy Ndirangu and colleagues publish a 2026 review of breast artery calcification as a clue to heart disease risk in women. Calcium deposits in breast arteries show up often on screening mammograms. Unlike plaque that narrows arteries, this calcification stiffens the artery wall.

Studies link the finding to heart attack, stroke, and heart failure. Standard risk calculators often underestimate danger in women, so an extra marker already visible on routine scans is attractive. New artificial intelligence tools can measure the deposits automatically and at scale. The authors argue that standardized measurement and reporting are the missing steps. Widespread use could flag at-risk women without any extra testing.
pmc-13241923:
Mojdehbakhsh, Spencer, Uczkowski, and Godecker compare uterine cancer research funding with disease rise, in work from twenty twenty-six. Uterine cancer incidence is rising steadily in the United States. Government funding is the second largest source of cancer research money through a defense department program for peer reviewed studies.

The team compiled grants from that peer reviewed cancer program by organ site. Funding was then stratified by incidence of each disease to allow fair comparison. Uterine cancer funding lagged behind its rising incidence compared with other sites, the title states. Funding per case is a fairness lens that can guide future program priorities and advocacy.
pmc-13242023:
Chenchen Li and co-authors report a 2026 study of a protein modification that worsens brain injury when blood flow returns after stroke. The protein, PKCγ, gains a phosphate tag at one specific site following the injury. A small share of the tagged protein moves into mitochondria, the cell energy centers.

Versions of the protein that mimic the tagged state suppressed a protective gene switch, raised harmful oxygen species, and pushed neurons toward death. A version that cannot be tagged did the opposite. Silencing the protein in mice shrank damaged brain areas and improved movement outcomes. The authors propose blocking this single tagging site as a stroke treatment strategy.
pmc-13242323:
Terui-Kohbata's team in Tokyo let five lay reviewers rewrite a survey about children's genomic data before fielding it. Japanese teens re-consent at sixteen for new samples, while earlier data stay usable regardless. Four involvement stages structured the public feedback. Every change was logged under the GRIPP2 standard.

83 percent of first-round comments were adopted, then 87 percent in round two. Wording, opt-out notes, and parent-child framing all sharpened. The five disagreed productively on allowed side uses of data. The report ranks among Japan's first ordered accounts of structured patient input.
pmc-13242423:
Pureum Sun and co-authors asked whether extracts from three traditional herbs could help mice resist Toxoplasma gondii, a widespread parasite. Their paper appeared in Acta Parasitologica in 2026. One extract came from Gypsophila oldhamiana, a plant long used in herbal medicine. Mice received the extracts by mouth before and after infection, and the team tracked parasite loads and immune responses in the spleen.

Only the Gypsophila extract clearly limited the infection, leaving treated mice with far fewer parasites than the other groups. It pushed dendritic cells to mature and release interleukin-12, which in turn expanded killer T cells that produce interferon-gamma. At the same time it raised checkpoint proteins that keep the response from overshooting. The authors present the plant as a preventive candidate worth further study.
pmc-13242623:
Yu Rao wrote a short piece marking the first approval of a PROTAC drug. It appeared in Cancer Innovation in 2026. On May 1, 2026, United States officials approved vepdegestrant, sold as Veppanu, for some advanced breast cancers with ESR1 changes. Arvinas built the drug with Pfizer after more than twenty years of work.

Most drugs block a protein only while they sit on it. A PROTAC instead tags its target so the cell destroys it. Rao argues the approval proves this event-driven idea can pass review and reach the market. It also gives the many degrader drugs now in testing a path to point to. He sets degraders beside antibodies, gene therapies, and RNA drugs as one more small-molecule tool. For Rao, a lab idea has become a real treatment.
pmc-13242823:
Abdukadir Mohamed Hassan and Abdiwali Mohamed Hussein report a 2026 case of a maternal death during transfer in Somalia, framed by conflict-related service collapse. A 22-year-old first-time mother labored at home with a traditional attendant in a remote nomadic community. The nearest district facility had been shut for about six months because of insecurity.

Her labor became obstructed, and her condition worsened before the family attempted the long trip to a regional hospital. She died in transit before arrival. The authors map the failure onto the three delays model of maternal death. They urge protected emergency obstetric care, stronger referral transport and communication, and community teaching on danger signs for remote populations.
pmc-13243123:
Fang Yang and colleagues report a 2026 case of severe side effects from a new lung cancer drug. Their patient was a 72-year-old man with stage IV squamous lung cancer and an EGFR gene change. Soon after his first dose of ivonescimab with chemotherapy, he developed a lasting high fever.

Blood tests showed very high levels of IL-6, a protein that fuels inflammation, and steroid drugs calmed the fever fast. A second dose brought a worse reaction, plus heavy urine output that pointed to a hormone problem near the brain. Care with steroids and other drugs eased his symptoms over time. The team urges early hormone checks and close IL-6 tracking when fever will not settle.
pmc-13243823:
When a birth goes wrong, midwives need support from their managers to cope and keep working. pmc-13244423:
Feiyuan Ding and Kezhou Yang build ultra-clean graphene devices to carry spin signals in 2026 work. pmc-13247023:
Jingxi Hu and a large team wrote a 2026 paper on fast body scans for children with lymphoma. These children face many PET and CT scans, and the CT part adds radiation dose. The team built a tool that starts from very short PET data alone. It aims to screen and sort cases before any CT is done.

pmc-13247423:

pmc-13247923:
Hua Ren and co-authors follow hazy lung spots, called subsolid nodules, in children and teens to see how they behave over time. Care for such spots in the young is unsettled. The team reviewed 105 patients at one large center, holding 141 nodules between them, most of them pure ground-glass type.

pmc-13248323:
Bektas-Dag and colleagues analyzed personal memories written by people with anorexia nervosa, in a 2026 qualitative study. Participants answered cue words linked to disgust toward themselves or moral disgust. pmc-13249423:

pmc-13249923:

pmc-13250323:
Ari Solomon, Laura Roberson, and Karim Jreije describe an unusually large pancreatic tumour in this 2026 case report. The tumour type, acinar cell carcinoma, makes up only about one to two percent of pancreatic cancers, and most are five to ten centimetres wide.

pmc-13250623:

pmc-13250723:
Henrik Åberg and co-authors test a precise way to track broken hip bones in this 2026 study. Flat X-ray pictures can understate how far fragments of a hip fracture have shifted in three dimensions, which matters when judging a repair.

The CT-based motion analysis repeated measurements to within less than a millimetre. It showed the initial shift was large, surgery cut it sharply, and fragments then moved only slightly as they healed, mostly by shortening. The method looks reliable for follow-up checks.
pmc-13250923:
Xiao and co-authors review how an aging immune system may drive idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis, a scarring lung disease of older adults. pmc-13251023:
Kim and a large team are the authors of this 2026 Publisher Correction in Genome Biology, attached to their whole-genome study of lung function and COPD. No data, results, or conclusions are altered by this notice.
pmc-13251223:
Xiaoming Shi and colleagues introduce a special journal issue on climate change and infections in this 2026 article. A warming world is shifting where germs spread and how they pass between people, animals, and food, yet turning that evidence into action has lagged.

Policy makers, researchers, and clinicians must work together, they argue, if the growing disease burden from climate change is to be cut.
pmc-13251823:
Chloe Bird and Hamad Al Ibrahim argue that precision medicine has a blind spot in this 2026 commentary. Care tailored to each person's biology still rests on evidence built mostly from male bodies, a legacy of decades of excluding women from early research.

pmc-13252723:
Amera Al-Amery and co-authors review simulation studies of targeted vaccination in this 2026 paper. Who gets vaccinated first can decide how an outbreak unfolds, and computer models that track contact networks or single agents let planners test targeting before acting.

It compared how network shapes, from household clusters to wide mixing, changed the payoff of targeting strategies. The authors find modelling practice still leans on simplified networks that miss real contact patterns. pmc-13253023:
Le Shang Teo and colleagues review how children's ankle fractures are classified in this 2026 paper. Many competing systems exist for sorting these injuries, and doctors lacked consensus on which are reliable and which actually guide care.

pmc-13253123:

pmc-13253723:
C Meyer and colleagues ask, in a 2026 study, which patients with endometriosis face lower egg supply and embryo quality. Endometriosis is tissue like the womb lining growing outside the womb. pmc-13253923:

In small animals, the agent brightened soft tissues on CT scans and caused no local swelling. The authors call it proof of concept and plan versions that also carry treatments.
pmc-13254323:
Maurício Garcia and co-authors describe a new fossil reptile in a 2026 study from southern Brazil. The fossil comes from Middle Triassic rocks and belongs to the archosauriforms, the wider group that later gave rise to dinosaurs and crocodile kin. They name the new form Silescelida acristata.

pmc-13254823:
Sarah Hardcastle and co-authors explore exercise barriers in pulmonary hypertension in a 2026 interview study. pmc-13255023:

pmc-13255323:

pmc-13257523:

pmc-13257623:

pmc-13257823:

pmc-13258123:

pmc-13258423:

pmc-13259123:

pmc-13259323:

pmc-13259423:

pmc-13259623:

pmc-13260523:

pmc-13262023:

pmc-13262223:

pmc-13262623:

pmc-13262723:

pmc-13263023:

pmc-13263423:

pmc-13264123:
