Claudia A.S. Wyer and a large team profile sperm storage cells in dengue-carrying mosquitoes in a 2026 study. Female Aedes aegypti mate once yet store enough sperm for hundreds of offspring. Secretory cells in the storage organs likely keep sperm alive, but their molecular program was unknown. Single-nucleus sequencing mapped cell types in the organs, confirmed with fluorescent tagging, then compared gene activity after natural mating versus injection of male gland material alone.

Natural mating triggered a much stronger response in the secretory cells after a day, implying sperm arrival itself is the critical activation signal. Gland proteins alone did not reproduce the full program. Knowing storage control points could inspire mosquito control methods that sabotage fertility after mating.
pmc-13264423:
Gabriela Fort and co-authors build an AI tool for exploring real-world side effects of cancer immunotherapy, in a study from 2026. Checkpoint inhibitor drugs changed cancer care, but they can trigger immune attacks on healthy tissue. The US FDA's event database holds the scale needed to study these harms, yet cleaning its fields takes expert skill.

The team built a cancer-only set of 71,175 event cases from reports spanning 2012 to 2025. Their assistant turns plain questions into Python code that filters cohorts, plots data, and runs tests. A retrieval layer grounds answers in clinical guidelines. Benchmarks covered question sorting, table questions, statistics, and plotting. As a check, the tool recovered known patterns, such as apart event profiles by drug class and tumor type.
pmc-13264623:
Julia Jelitzki, Alexandra Reichenbach, and Alexander Windberger wrote a 2026 study on whether brain scan AI models decide for the right reasons. Deep learning can sort schizophrenia from MRI scans, but its choices are hidden. The team used saliency maps, which highlight the scan areas a model leaned on, to judge seven common models.

All seven models scored much alike at sorting the scans. Yet only two based their choices on brain areas that make medical sense. The other five leaned on areas with no clear link to the illness. The team also turned the maps into shared anatomical markers and found regions that match known schizophrenia markers. They argue that explanation tools must sit beside deep learning in medical imaging.
pmc-13264723:
Xianwei Long and colleagues build a prediction model to spare some breast cancer patients full underarm node removal in a 2026 study. When the first draining node contains cancer, surgeons often remove many more nodes, causing arm swelling and pain. Records covered one hundred thirty-three patients treated at a Liuzhou hospital from 2023 to 2025. Clinical and pathology features were analyzed. The team looked for features tied to additional node spread beyond the sentinel nodes already sampled.

Statistical screening selected significant predictors, which were combined into a model checked with discrimination and calibration methods. A reliable score could identify patients whose remaining nodes are almost certainly clear, letting them avoid bigger surgery safely. Wider validation across hospitals is the expected next step before routine adoption.
pmc-13264823:
Angelo Lamadrid and colleagues wrote a 2026 scoping review of how the COVID-19 pandemic changed hepatitis C care. Hepatitis C is a liver virus with a step-by-step care path: testing, linking to care, treatment, and cure. Reports of pandemic harm existed but were scattered, so the team mapped them all.

They kept 28 studies, most from Europe and North America. Declines showed at every step. Diagnosis fell in 15 of 21 studies that checked it, treatment starts or completions fell in 18 of 27, and cure fell in 6 of 13. Linkage to care was the step most often reported as disrupted. The authors urge stronger tracking and tougher services to protect the 2030 goal of ending hepatitis as a public threat.
pmc-13264923:
Azharul Islam, Mahjabeen Haque, and Mohammad Salim Chowdhury examine childhood adversity and partner violence among young adults in Bangladesh, in 2026. About two-thirds of Bangladeshi women report partner violence. Past research summed all childhood hardships into one score. Separate kinds of hardship may push risk in different ways.

The analysis used a 2022 national survey and kept 2,016 partnered adults aged 18 to 35. Threat experiences, such as exposure to violence, more than doubled the odds of perpetrating partner violence. Deprivation, such as missing emotional support, also raised the odds. Women reported lower perpetration than men. The authors urge prevention that fits each kind of adversity.
pmc-13265223:
Chengning Xu and colleagues test blocking an enzyme called EHMT2 in glioblastoma cells, in a 2026 study. EHMT2, also known as G9a, helps control gene activity and is raised in many tumours. Its levels across glioma subtypes were first mapped. A targeted inhibitor, BIX-01294, was then applied to tumour cells.

EHMT2 was highly expressed in glioblastoma, especially in two subtypes. The inhibitor strongly reduced cell growth, invasion, and self-renewal. Proteins tied to invasion and growth also fell. Data analysis linked EHMT2 to the STAT3 signalling pathway. The authors suggest blocking EHMT2 as a promising treatment strategy.
pmc-13266223:
Davide Gatti and colleagues systematically review the natural history of osteogenesis imperfecta, a brittle bone condition, published in 2026. Sixty-six studies were included from major medical databases. Diagnosis, symptoms across ages, and mortality were collated. Studies needed long follow-up or age-based analysis.

Severe forms were usually diagnosed in early childhood, while milder forms varied widely. Fractures peaked in youth yet continued lifelong, mostly in limbs. Some problems progress fast in childhood, while heart, eye, and hearing issues emerge in adulthood. Life expectancy was reduced by several years on average. The authors urge tailored lifelong multidisciplinary care.
pmc-13266623:
Hatice Betigul Meral, Sena Tolu, and Zeynep Noyan report a 2026 study adapting a muscle-loss risk scale for Turkey. Sarcopenia is the slow loss of muscle mass and strength with age. Their scale asks older adults how at risk they feel, an area with no Turkey-specific tool before.

The team translated the scale and tested it on 323 adults aged 60 to 93. Expert review supported the content of the Turkish version. Statistical tests found two parts: how likely people feel they are to get sarcopenia, and how serious they judge it. Scores were steady on repeat testing. The authors say the scale can support screening and health teaching.
pmc-13266723:
Scott Young wrote a 2026 introduction to a special section of The Permanente Journal on access to health care. He argues that being able to get timely, fitting care is basic to health itself. Gaps persist across places, groups, and stages of life despite steady gains in medical treatment.

Young previews themes the collected papers take up. Access matters most at key moments such as early childhood, pregnancy, and mental health care. Culture, language, and trust shape whether people seek care at all. New tools like video visits and AI add reach but also confusion. Coverage alone is not enough when costs and paperwork block use, so systems must be designed for real access.
pmc-13266823:
Xiangyu Du and co-authors compare in 2026 first treatments for advanced non-squamous lung cancer carrying a KRAS mutation, using records from a Beijing hospital over a decade. They followed 180 patients whose cancer was locally advanced or had spread. Groups received immune drugs with chemotherapy, either alone, chemotherapy alone, or a triple mix adding a blood vessel blocker.

Immune drugs plus chemotherapy gave the longest control and survival, with responses in about four in ten patients. Adding the vessel blocker brought no clear extra gain. Immune treatment beat chemotherapy alone on survival, while marker levels did not separate who benefited. The authors name the two-drug immune combination as their preferred first choice.
pmc-13267623:
M Moghadam and co-authors test in 2026 whether strong ultrasound can make blue mussel protein work in low-salt surimi, the gelled seafood product usually dependent on salt. Mussel protein dissolves poorly when salt is low, limiting its use despite mussels being a low-impact protein source. Their experiment varied salt level, ultrasound strength, and treatment time in a full factorial design.

Stronger and longer ultrasound more than doubled protein solubility and cut particle size by nearly three quarters. Sound waves broke large protein clumps into smaller pieces and reshaped their structure. Water holding rose sharply at the highest settings, though too much treatment at high salt weakened gels. Whiter, less viscous gels also appeared, pointing to new low-salt mussel products.
pmc-13267823:
Mengqi Huang and colleagues wrote a 2026 study of hormone therapy and womb growths during the menopause transition. Uterine fibroids are common non-cancer growths that react to hormones. Whether menopausal hormone therapy makes them grow was unclear. The team followed 83 women at a Nanjing hospital who took a standard two-hormone sequence from 2016 onward, with repeat ultrasound scans.

Fibroid area shifted slightly during the first four years, in ways the team judged too small to matter in practice. By year five no difference from the start could be detected. Side effects were mostly brief and faded on their own. Unexpected bleeding affected about 18 percent, breast discomfort about 11 percent, and stomach symptoms about 2 percent. The authors call the therapy a safe option with regular checks.
pmc-13267923:
Jiangchuan Liu and colleagues wrote a 2026 perspective on smoking, vaping, and osteoarthritis. This joint disease was long blamed on wear and tear, but inflammation now looks central to it. Population studies of smoking and joint damage disagree, yet smoke clearly disturbs immune function. The authors map several linked paths by which cigarette and e-cigarette exposure may harm joints.

Smoke may stir immune cells in the joint lining and set off alarm signals from damaged tissue. Those signals switch on inflammation pathways and a protein complex called the inflammasome. Helper and regulator T cells may fall out of balance, and small gene-control molecules may shift. Together these changes could poison the joint's inner setting. The authors flag weak points in the field, including few joint-specific studies.
pmc-13270223:
Yang Wang, Hong Jiang, Bo Xu, and Meng-Qi Han describe in 2026 a new flowering plant species. It clings to the rock walls of an isolated limestone hill near Mang City in western Yunnan, China. The plant belongs to Oreocharis, a genus of mostly cliff-dwelling herbs now holding more than 160 species across East Asia. It was first spotted during an orchid survey in 2019 and revisited in 2025.

No other populations turned up in nearby suitable habitat. The plant grows as a ground rosette with hanging flower clusters, two-lipped tubular blooms, and four stamens whose stalks bend sharply near the tip and pair their anthers. Those traits, checked against herbarium specimens and the literature, set it apart from known relatives. The authors call for survey and protection of such unreserved karst hills.
pmc-13270523:
Shasha Yang and co-authors engineer in 2026 a sturdier way to zap a stubborn groundwater pollutant, 1,4-dioxane, out of drinking water at the point of use. Electric oxidation can destroy the suspected carcinogen, but single reactors demand heavy energy, scale up with minerals, wear out anodes, and breed perchlorate byproducts. Their design stacks several flow-through cells and pulses the current on and off in fifteen-second beats.

In synthetic groundwater, pulsing cut perchlorate formation sharply and suppressed scale. A four-stage pulsed unit ran for twenty days at a realistic trace concentration, removing roughly seventy percent of the pollutant per pass on average, with little voltage creep. Pairing stages with pulsing, the authors argue, fixes the failure modes that kept electric oxidation impractical for home-scale treatment.
pmc-13271123:
Junrui Chen is lead author of a 2026 multicentre study linking a blood fat ratio to osteoarthritis, the wear-related joint disease. The ratio, triglycerides divided by the protective HDL cholesterol, is a combined marker of metabolic problems whose link to joint disease was unclear.

With 6,570 participants, each unit rise in the ratio carried an 11 percent higher odds of osteoarthritis after adjustment. The link was not a straight line: risk rose more steeply at lower levels in women and in people with diabetes. In a machine-learning model the ratio ranked second only to age in importance. The team also built an interactive web tool that shows estimated risk by age, sex, diabetes, and ratio.
pmc-13271423:
Tom Lapidus is lead author of a 2026 pilot study on how the chemotherapy drug irinotecan changes immune checkpoints on neuroblastoma cells. Neuroblastoma is the most common solid tumour outside the brain in children, and only about half of high-risk patients survive, making combined chemo-immunotherapy a central strategy.

Two neuroblastoma cell lines were exposed to low doses of irinotecan and an immune signal. The drug shifted several immune markers, including GD2, CD47, PD-L1, and MHC class I. It reduced eating of cancer cells by immune scavenger cells, but an anti-CD47 antibody reversed that. T cell killing improved after irinotecan treatment, and in mice the drug plus immune cells shrank tumours more than either alone.
pmc-13271723:
Charu Yadav and co-authors study a birth defect where the food pipe fails to form fully and joins the windpipe by an abnormal link. Published in 2026, the study covers 60 patients with the type C form of the defect. During surgery the team measured where the link ended and how long the gap in the food pipe was.

The link most often ended five millimeters below a landmark vein, though its site varied widely. Cases were split by gap length into three groups. The lower the link sat below the vein, the longer the gap tended to be. In the longest gap group, the lower food pipe was more often thin walled and narrow, facts that matter for surgery.
pmc-13272023:
Xiqiong Yi and coauthors survey in 2026 how adults in China feel about smart care devices that can read emotions for home rehab and elder care. Trust in such tools cannot be taken for granted, since they sense feelings, not just steps or heart rate. The study asked both future users and family caregivers what they would accept.

Among 506 people who replied, most were open to the devices but set clear terms. They wanted open rules on private data, tools that work well, and accurate emotion reading. Most liked wearable sensors more than cameras, and they wanted a person in charge rather than a fully automatic reply.
pmc-13272223:
Nian-Shiuan Lai and colleagues built a drug level model in 2026 for Asian heart patients. The drug is rivaroxaban, a blood thinner that prevents stroke. Patients took it for an irregular heart rhythm. Blood levels vary widely between people on the same dose. The team measured levels in a real-world patient cohort. Hundreds of samples came from over two hundred patients. A separate cohort tested the model. Outcomes included clots and major bleeding events.

A simple one-compartment model described the drug well. Kidney function strongly shaped how fast it cleared. Certain interacting drugs also slowed clearance. Lean body weight shaped its spread through the body. Outside tests predicted levels accurately. Low resting levels tended to track with clot events. High resting levels tended to track with bleeding. The authors offer the model as a practical clinic tool. It can flag patients at risk from standard doses.
pmc-13272523:
Walter Ageno and co-authors examine, in a 2026 study, the risks of blood clots and major bleeding in hospital patients with obesity who receive a preventive blood thinner. People with obesity admitted with an acute illness face a higher clot risk. Yet doctors have little guidance on who most needs protection, or who might bleed. The team drew on a large United States health database to study patients given enoxaparin.

More than fifty-eight thousand patients qualified, and about three in ten had the most severe level of obesity. Just over half received a higher dose of the drug, while the rest got the standard dose. Over ninety days of follow-up, clots were uncommon but real, and bleeding was rarer still. Cancer admissions carried the highest clot rates. A past clot or past bleed proved the strongest warning sign for the same event recurring.
pmc-13273023:
Hirut Basha leads a 2026 small field trial of a plant extract that kills snails carrying schistosomiasis, a parasitic disease. The plant, Hagenia abyssinica, grows in Ethiopia, and its female flowers were extracted with alcohol and chloroform. Biomphalaria snails, which host the parasite, were exposed for up to 72 hours, and fish toxicity was also tested.

Both extracts killed snails, with the chloroform form stronger at 24 hours. For fish, the alcohol extract's lethal level was lower than for snails, meaning fish were more sensitive than the target snails. Fingerlings showed no harm up to 16 milligrams per liter. The authors flag this gap as an ecological concern for wider use.
pmc-13273123:
Fangfang Bi, Juning Wang, and Mingquan Su tested a blood protein as a marker for stroke recovery in a 2026 cohort study. Klotho is a protein linked to aging and tissue protection. The team asked whether early Klotho levels predict how well patients function ninety days after an ischemic stroke.

They followed 200 patients at one center and split them by outcome on a standard disability scale. Patients with poor outcomes had much lower early Klotho levels than those who recovered well. Higher levels meant lower risk of a poor outcome even after adjusting for age, stroke severity, and other factors. A model using Klotho alone predicted outcome fairly well, though adding it to standard clinical factors did not clearly improve prediction.
pmc-13273223:
Everson LA Artifon and a large team reported the first clinical use of robotic telesurgery in Brazil's public health system in a 2026 case series. Telesurgery lets a surgeon operate from a remote console, which could widen access in public systems. Most prior proof came from wealthy, tightly controlled settings.

Five patients were treated through the public system. Four operations were finished fully from the remote console, and one was safely converted to a standard approach. Signal delay over the wired hospital network was very low. Staff at the console, bedside, and anesthesia roles all rated the experience well. One moderate complication occurred, with no deaths, reoperations, or readmissions within thirty days. The authors offer the series as early proof of feasibility.
pmc-13273423:
Denise Veltkamp and co-authors pool, in a 2026 review, the long-term heart risks that follow a bout of acute kidney injury. Surviving damaged kidneys was once the whole concern. Evidence now ties the injury to later heart disease as well.

The team searched two major databases for studies tracking patients at least a year. They compared heart attacks, strokes, heart failure, and cardiovascular death between people with and without the injury. Pooling asked whether risk grows with injury severity, duration, or care setting. Clinicians discharging kidney patients need to know whose hearts deserve watching. A pooled estimate sharpens discharge planning beyond the kidney clinic.
pmc-13273523:
Luiz Felipe Azevedo Marques leads a 2026 profile of five patients in Brazil hospitalized with COVID-19 who had one of two rare genetic syndromes. Berardinelli-Seip syndrome involves near absence of body fat and metabolic problems, while Silver-Russell syndrome involves poor growth before birth and other abnormalities. Such features were feared to worsen COVID-19.

Two patients had Berardinelli-Seip syndrome and three had Silver-Russell syndrome. Most had breathing symptoms and low oxygen at admission, two needed intensive care, and two needed noninvasive breathing support. Four were discharged, while one unvaccinated 19-year-old with Berardinelli-Seip syndrome and multiple other conditions died. The authors found no consistent link between these syndromes and severe COVID-19.
pmc-13273623:
Kristine Marie Vege leads a 2026 study of medical problems during rehab for children with brain or spinal cord injury. Children aged 2 to 17 were treated at a tertiary center. Data came from charts and surveys on admission and discharge, for a set list of problems.

Of 64 children, 59 had problems, with 183 instances across 19 types. Sleep problems, pain, constipation, anemia, infections, spasticity, and poor nutrition were most common. No clear link appeared with age, sex, or diagnosis. Most problems, 74 percent, did not affect rehab. But poor nutrition, infections, and spasticity could prolong stays and worsen outlook.
pmc-13273923:
Gangapersad and colleagues track how often lithium is dispensed to young people in the Netherlands. Their 2026 paper uses a national community pharmacy database covering 2011 to 2022. Lithium is the first-choice long-term treatment for bipolar disorder, which often begins in the teens, yet its use has fallen as other psychiatric drugs have risen.

The study included 567 people aged 6 to 25 who received lithium in that period. Yearly prevalence stayed roughly flat, between about 30 and 35 per 100,000 young people, and ran higher in females than males. New starts shifted with age: incidence fell in 13 to 19 year olds but rose in 20 to 25 year olds. About half of patients also received other psychiatric medicines, most often antipsychotics and antidepressants.
pmc-13274423:
Diana Sahonero-Canavesi and co-authors find in 2026 new forms of span lipids in a large germ phylum, which shed light on how kin soil lipids are made. Those soil lipids are wide used as marks to rebuild past heat and acid states. Their germ source and cell role stayed half known.

Fine mass scans bare span lipids built on a branched acid core in the new host group. Forms span full ester, mixed, and vinyl tied types, with open forms in the mix. The finds look like step stones on the path to the soil lipids. That path can now be traced in live germs.
pmc-13275123:
Caroline E Terry wrote a 2026 commentary highlighting a new hormone test for tracking rhino pregnancies. Black and white rhino pregnancies run well over a year with few outward signs, leaving zoo managers guessing. The study she describes, by George Mason University researchers with thirty-seven North American rhino facilities, measured the hormone DHEA in blood.

The team first tuned their extraction method for rhino serum, then took monthly samples from forty black rhinos and seventy-one white rhinos for a year. DHEA rose with age until about fifteen years, matching peak breeding ages. Crucially, it also climbed during pregnancy, especially from the middle onward, compared with non-pregnant animals. One white rhino that miscarried never showed that rise.
pmc-13275523:
Julian Ananyev and Todd M Myers review intramuscular ketamine dosing in humans in a 2026 article. Ketamine has served for decades in anaesthesia and pain relief, and new uses keep emerging. Shots into muscle matter most where staff, equipment, or vein access are limited.

Ten studies covered doses from very low levels up to six milligrams per kilogram of body weight. Peak blood levels rose in a straight line with dose, arriving within ten to thirty minutes. The share of drug reaching the blood varied widely between reports, so that figure stays uncertain. Children absorbed the drug faster than adults, and the authors call for more data at higher doses.
pmc-13275723:
Andrea Benech and a team of soil scientists study alpine tundra soils shaped by lingering snow, published in 2026. How long snow covers the ground sorts plant communities into distinct types. Climate change is shortening snow cover, which may disturb soil carbon, nitrogen, and microbes together.

Three vegetation types were compared, from long-snow snowbeds to short-snow sedge swards. Carbon forms tracked vegetation type, while mineral nitrogen tracked timing within the snow-free season. Microbe communities differed by vegetation, with sedge soils richer in cellulose-breaking groups. Snowbed soils favoured nitrogen-linked groups, so losing snowbeds could remove a distinct microbial habitat.
pmc-13276123:
Shruthi Venkateswaran and co-authors report a dental case in 2026 about fixing a weak tooth after root canal treatment. The tooth had lost much of its inner dentin, the hard layer under enamel, so a standard post would fit poorly.

The team shaped a fiber post to match the canal by lining it with resin, using a putty mold as a guide. They then built up the core and placed a full crown. The snug fit spread stress, kept cement thin, and cut the risk of root fracture. The case argues for posts shaped to each tooth in fragile roots.
pmc-13276223:
Sk Injamamul Islam and co-authors report a 2026 journal article on mining a workhorse bacterium for hidden antibiotic potential. Corynebacterium glutamicum is famous for making amino acids in factories. Whether it also carries genes for natural antimicrobial products had never been checked across the whole species.

The team compared thirty-six complete genomes and catalogued their gene clusters for making secondary compounds. Strains differed in cluster content, and some carried mixed clusters. Alongside known terpene pathways, they found clusters tied to polyketides, a rich drug family, never before reported in this species. Machine learning models then scanned small gene fragments for likely antimicrobial peptides. The best model flagged eighteen strong candidates after duplicates were removed. The authors say these leads need lab testing.
pmc-13276323:
Marco Stracqualursi, Alberto Cereda, Francesca Croce, and Andrea Baldo write a 2026 letter on a heart care puzzle called no-reflow. In this state, blood fails to reach heart tissue well even after a blocked vessel opens. A recent pooled study ranked drugs given into the heart artery for the problem.

The letter praises that work but flags a blind spot in how drugs were given. Routes range from a vein drip to a thin tube placed deep past the block. Trials mixed those routes and rarely reported them in a set way, so route effects blur with drug effects. Local drug dose in the small vessels may shape results as much as the drug picked. The authors urge trials to treat delivery as a factor in its own right.
pmc-13276523:
Amir Naiem and colleagues present a 2026 video case report of pelvic masses that mimicked cancer. The patient was a 31-year-old man with episodes of visible blood at the end of urination. Scans found two masses behind his bladder, a spot where tumours would be a natural first suspicion.

His history mattered: he had lost his spleen in childhood after injury. Tissue from a ruptured spleen can seed itself elsewhere and grow for decades, a benign condition called splenosis. Robot-assisted surgery removed the masses, and tissue tests confirmed splenic tissue rather than cancer. The authors flag this rare location as a diagnostic trap after splenectomy.
pmc-13276723:
Giulia Pollice and co-authors present a 2026 systematic review and meta-analysis on the social exclusion of people with mental disorders. Inclusion means joining social, economic, and cultural life, not just being present. Evidence using proper measuring tools, rather than rough population statistics, had never been pooled.

Ten studies qualified, and six entered the pooled analysis covering about nineteen hundred people. Those with mental disorders scored far lower on inclusion than the general population, a large gap by statistical standards. The review found weaker relationships, less support, and reduced community participation. Disadvantages stacked up in jobs, income, education, and housing, including money hardship and unhappy neighborhoods. Several studies showed people could take part in activities yet still not feel they belonged. The authors note class, gender, and ethnicity deepen the exclusion.
pmc-13277423:
Xu, Rajan, Phoon, Ren, Hussain, and Schlame study how an enzyme recycles lysosome products in twenty twenty-six. Lysosomes break down phospholipids from cell membranes. That breakdown yields fragments that can be degraded or reused. One fragment type carries an unsaturated fatty acid chain.

The enzyme LPLAT7 sits in the endoplasmic reticulum and reacylates those fragments. It acts specifically on the lysosome derived, unsaturated forms. Knocking it out in liver cells blocked reuse of fragments from labelled phospholipids. In mice, knockout raised unsaturated fragment levels and cut key membrane lipids. Membrane regeneration slowed, and fat droplets accumulated instead. The authors say the enzyme shifts lipid flow from droplets toward membranes.
pmc-13277823:
Kara Saiki leads a 2026 survey study of a media campaign in Hawai'i that urged adults at risk for type 2 diabetes to join a prevention program. The state campaign, called Beat Diabetes, ran from July to October 2024, with a focus on Native Hawaiian, Pacific Islander, and Filipino communities, which face high diabetes rates. A survey of 860 at-risk adults followed.

Forty percent of respondents recalled the campaign. Those who had seen it gave higher ratings for how likely they were to join a prevention program. They also scored higher on believing diabetes may be unavoidable, a belief the campaign may need to address. The design is a one-time survey, so it shows links rather than proof that the campaign caused the difference.
pmc-13278023:
Xiaoyi Bai leads a 2026 cohort study of survival factors in the most common type of womb cancer, endometrioid endometrial cancer, in China. The team followed 142 patients diagnosed from 2009 to 2013 for up to ten years. They sorted patients into no recurrence, recurrence with survival, and death groups, and tested which features predicted each path.

Advanced stage and larger tumors predicted shorter survival, and the highest tumor grade also worsened outlook. For recurrence, advanced stage and tumors of three centimeters or more mattered most. Hormone receptor positivity and absence of vessel invasion looked protective in simple analyses but faded in adjusted models. Tumor size and stage remain the core guides for personal risk planning, the authors conclude.
pmc-13278623:
Vicky Bennett leads a 2026 mouse study of a new bacteria-killing compound for skin infections caused by MRSA, a drug-resistant Staphylococcus strain. The compound, epidermicin NI01, is a bacteriocin, a natural antimicrobial made by bacteria, with a novel mode of action. Infected skin on immunosuppressed mice was treated daily with the compound or with standard antibiotic creams.

No adverse effects appeared from infection or treatment. A single-dose group showed no benefit, but repeated three percent dosing cut bacterial counts about as much as the standard creams. The dose needed to kill the test strain stayed unchanged after treatment. Further development is warranted, the authors say, and clinical use could spare standard antibiotics for severe infections.
pmc-13278723:
Nadia Luthfia Adani, Hendry Purnasidha Bagaswoto, and Irsad Andi Arso compare two mortality scores for cardiac intensive care in a 2026 study. The local SCIENCE score uses seven simple measures from the first day of admission. The established Mayo score predicts well but needs specialist lab tests that many units lack.

Records from Sardjito Hospital covered 1,503 eligible patients treated between 2022 and 2024. More than half of the starting group was excluded over missing Mayo score data. Both scores predicted unit and hospital deaths with acceptable accuracy, the Mayo score slightly ahead. Stroke carried notably higher death risk in this cohort. The authors back the simpler score as a practical substitute.
pmc-13279023:
Carmen Bango and co-authors link teen pain to how brain networks talk at rest in work dated two thousand twenty-six. Teen pain is common and costly, yet its brain roots are little charted in large community samples. Resting scans from a big United States youth study offered a wide lens.

Near five thousand youths, about half with pain in the past month, were compared with mixed models. No link split the pain and no-pain groups as wholes. Inside the pain group, though, stronger average pain went with weaker links between the frontoparietal control network and hand, mouth, and hearing sense networks. Hearing and sight networks linked more strongly as pain rose. The pattern hints at how control and sense systems trade off in sore teens.
pmc-13279723:
Xin Lai and colleagues report a 2026 dog study of nerve cutting to aid heart repair after heart attack. A heart attack, or myocardial infarction, scars the heart and warps its left pump chamber. Nerve balance loss makes the warp worse. Heart nerve hubs called ganglionated plexi drive that imbalance. The team cut sensory nerve input with a nerve toxin called resiniferatoxin, shot in a front nerve hub.

Thirty one beagle dogs split in three groups: heart attack alone, heart attack with nerve cut, and sham surgery. After four weeks, the nerve cut group showed lower nerve hub activity and less hub warp. Left pump dilation eased and pump function rose versus the attack alone group. Scar linked tissue change in the pump also eased. Calm nerve tone may guard heart shape after attack.
pmc-13281623:
Eugeni Mas and a large consortium publish the protocol for a school health program delivered through an online platform, in a 2026 paper. Early adolescence is when lasting habits form, yet disadvantaged communities often lack support for healthy ones. The ePro-Schools project aims to close that gap in Central Catalonia, Spain.

Six secondary schools, about a thousand students, will enter a randomized trial. Intervention schools co-created the platform with students and stakeholders through focus groups, then pilot-tested its usability. Trial students in intervention schools get the full interactive platform; controls get an information-only version covering activity, nutrition, and healthy habits. Questionnaires before, after, and six months later track movement, eating, mood, quality of life, and social isolation. The protocol also covers depressive symptoms. The authors argue digital delivery can scale health promotion where resources are thin.
pmc-13281923:
Ying Wang and colleagues hunted brain signs that foretell failed face pain surgery in a 2026 study. The surgery lifts a blood vessel off a pinched face nerve. It is the standard fix when drugs fail, yet up to three in ten patients gain little. The team enrolled sixty such patients and thirty healthy peers. Before surgery all had brain scans of links and wiring. Patients were split by their relief three months after surgery. Pain levels before surgery were alike in both groups.

Those who fared poorly had gentler vessel pressure found in surgery. Their brains showed tighter links between rest and movement networks and deep feeling hubs. Those hubs govern memory, reward, and fear. A learning model fed the top links called the outcome right in most cases. The authors say lasting pain can rewire the brain itself. Such rewiring may cap what surgery can give back.
pmc-13282323:
Freddy H Marin-Dett and co-authors report a 2026 lab study on how a fungus changes a bacterium's effect on mouth cells that may precede cancer. The fungus Candida albicans and the bacterium Staphylococcus aureus often live together in biofilms, slimy microbial layers. The team treated human immune cells with fluid from single-species and mixed biofilms, then exposed precancerous mouth lining cells to the immune cells' output.

Bacterial fluid alone stirred strong inflammation signals in immune cells. Fluid from the mixed biofilm suppressed those signals. pmc-13282423:

Contrast against noise was comparable, and small branch visibility was preserved. Artifacts in a large chest vein fell. pmc-13283323:

pmc-13283523:
Ammar Sawaf questioned in a 2026 review whether worn spinal discs deserve the blame they get for long-term low back pain. pmc-13284023:

Function scores also favored robot cases with no side gap.
pmc-13284123:

pmc-13284323:

pmc-13284423:

The review calls for better use of advanced materials and nanozymes to lift sensitivity, stability, and repeat results before wide clinical use.
pmc-13284523:
Changhong Wang and a large team surveyed in 2026 what obstetric patients in China know and feel about expanded carrier screening. pmc-13284823:
Rei Takeichi and co-authors present a 2026 case report where a small brainstem bleed mimicked Bell palsy. Signs began to ease by day four in hospital, scans showed shrinkage by day seven, and he left after fifteen days. The authors urge selective imaging for atypical cases.
pmc-13285223:
Althea Pabico, Elisa Coo, Elizabeth Tianco, and Zharlah Gulmatico-Flores report a 2026 case of a stubborn inherited blistering skin disease in a fifty-five-year-old Filipino woman. pmc-13285323:
Rudi Campo pens an obituary, published in 2026, for Stephan Gordts, a founder of modern fertility care in Belgium who died on May 22, 2026. Gordts helped deliver the first baby born through in vitro fertilization in Belgium in 1983. A year later he set up the Leuven Institute for Fertility and Embryology, leading its science work until his death.

World fame came from his skill in gentle fertility surgery and from a viewing method through the vagina that first filmed normal egg release. His early microsurgery courses in Leuven drew wide praise, and he taught at many meetings with patience and warmth. The European endoscopy society gave him its top honorary rank in 2024.
pmc-13285423:
People with a slipped lumbar disc must manage their own care daily, and digital skills increasingly gate that work. pmc-13285623:
The Quran is recited in several canonical reading styles that differ in fine points of pronunciation, and machines need examples to learn them. Linda Smail and co-authors release AQQD in this 2026 paper, an open audio collection of recitations labeled by style.

The set holds more than twenty-four thousand short clips from over three hundred reciters, covering seventy chapters, gathered from public sources. A smaller studio set from a single reciter lets researchers compare styles without voice differences getting in the way. File names carry the labels, and the whole set is free to reuse for speech research and teaching tools.
pmc-13286223:
Umanath R Poojary and co-authors tie steel microstructure to machining ease in a 2026 study of AISI 1040 steel. Bars annealed, normalized, or oil-quenched went under the lathe in a planned grid of speeds, feeds, and depths.

Annealed bars, with their soft two-phase grain, gave the longest tool life and the cleanest overall cutting. Quenched bars hardened into a tough phase that wore tools fastest, and normalized bars landed between the two. pmc-13286523:
Jair Camargo Ferreira and colleagues test ozonated sunflower oil as an antibiotic-free womb treatment for fresh cows in a 2026 veterinary study. pmc-13287223:

Before extra shavings were taken, 19 of 196 specimens held positive margins. Surgeon reading found 16 of those, matching the standard pathway on detection while ruling out clear cases more often. Surgeon reading took a median of six minutes against 33 minutes for the standard route. The authors present surgeon-led scan reading as a faster option with similar accuracy.
pmc-13287323:
Feiyun Huang and co-authors compared gut microbes in 2026 in 75 captive forest musk deer kept near 3900 metres and near 1450 metres under the same care routines. Gene sequencing, chemical profiling of droppings, and lab growing of microbes were combined for the endangered species.

High-altitude deer held a tighter, more filtered gut community. Helpful bacteria that make short-chain fatty acids were enriched and sat opposite known pathogens in network maps. Chemical profiles shifted in energy and amino acid routes. Seven microbe strains passed safety checks and fought pathogens in dishes. The authors propose altitude-aware housing, donor choice for gut transplants, and deer-derived probiotics for captive care.
pmc-13287623:

pmc-13287823:
Danladi C Husaini and co-authors surveyed health students in 2026 at the University of Belize about infections picked up during care, a problem hitting about four in ten patients locally. pmc-13288423:

pmc-13288723:
Jinhong Zhao and colleagues sequence a worm genome in full in 2026. The worm is a parasitic roundworm. Its name is Brevimulticaecum sinensis. It is the first of its genus sequenced this way. It came from a captive Chinese alligator. The host had died in China.

pmc-13289223:

pmc-13289323:

pmc-13289423:

pmc-13289823:

Clearing ran higher with bands at two and three months, then evened out by six months in follow-up. Early rebleeding was less common with bands, and time to rebleed ran longer. pmc-13290123:

pmc-13290523:

pmc-13290823:

pmc-13291023:

pmc-13291123:

pmc-13291223:

pmc-13291423:

pmc-13291723:

pmc-13292023:

pmc-13292323:

pmc-13292823:

pmc-13293623:

pmc-13294323:

pmc-13294423:

pmc-13294923:

pmc-13295223:

pmc-13295823:

pmc-13295923:

pmc-13296123:

pmc-13296623:

pmc-13297523:

pmc-13297823:

Growths of immune tissue after transplant are uncommon in the brain but can kill, and their signs mimic infection or drug harm. Fourteen months after her transplant, while on immune-damping drugs, the patient grew confused.

Brain scans, spinal fluid tests, and finally a brain biopsy named an EBV-positive large B-cell lymphoma confined to the brain. Despite joint specialist care, she declined steadily and suffered bleeding inside the brain. New nerve symptoms in any transplant patient should trigger fast imaging, virus testing, and tissue checks, the authors urge.
pmc-13299323:
White blood cells can roll along vessel walls using a sugar-based grip when their usual integrin grip is unavailable, show Marcus Hubbe and Robert H Eibl in a 2026 flow-chamber study. They examined how monocytes interact with cell monolayers through the CD44 receptor binding hyaluronan.

On one monolayer type, adhesion and rolling depended on CD44 and hyaluronan: blocking the receptor, adding free hyaluronan, or digesting the sugar coat all reduced the interaction. On true endothelial layers, integrin blockade mattered instead. Fresh human monocytes behaved the same way. The authors frame the sugar pathway as a backup that surfaces when integrin adhesion is not dominant, noting the model system's limits.
pmc-13299723:
Rie Goryo and co-authors report two cases of a rare, fast thyroid cancer that arose while benign lumps were being watched, in a paper from 2025. The cancer spreads through the gland and into lymph paths and is hard to spot on scans, with a low rate of correct calls before surgery. Most past cases were found late, so its early scan signs were almost unknown.

Both patients had long follow up for lumps first judged benign. In the first case, clusters of tiny bright spots showed on scans of one lobe years before the cancer was proved. Lab checks after surgery confirmed the rare type at the same site. The authors propose that those bright spots may be an early sign worth close watch in such glands.
pmc-13299823:
Y Baek and a team test whether AI reading a standard heart tracing can forecast later atrial fibrillation in monitored patients, in a 2026 multicentre prospective study. Participants received implantable cardiac monitors after stroke of undetermined source at four centres. Baseline tracings taken during normal rhythm were scored by a checked algorithm.

During roughly two and a half years of follow-up, fibrillation including silent episodes appeared in about one patient in nine. Patients the algorithm flagged as high risk developed the rhythm problem clearly more often, and the score on its own predicted detection with stroke history and age. The authors propose the tool for personalised surveillance and treatment planning.
pmc-13301323:
Giorgia Citriniti and co-authors ultrasound the tendon attachments and joints of 152 patients with acute inflammation at the front of the eye, in a 2026 phenotyping study. Such eye attacks often hide undiagnosed spondyloarthritis, a family of joint diseases inflaming exactly those attachment points. The series mixed 103 non granulomatous and forty-nine granulomatous cases, scanned at six attachments plus knees and ankles on both sides, using standard definitions for damage and active inflammation.

The non granulomatous group carried more attachment erosions, more blood flow signal at attachments, and more active attachment inflammation than the other group, with no clear influence from the HLA-B27 marker. Clinical and imaging criteria uncovered hidden spondyloarthritis in twenty-nine patients. Feeding the ultrasound findings into the classification criteria caught thirteen more. The authors present joint and attachment ultrasound as a practical route to sharper disease typing and more personal treatment choices in patients.
pmc-13301723:
Three ways to unblock a tear duct work about equally well, Çağla Hakkani Öznay and colleagues find in a 2026 study. Sixty-nine patients with a blocked tear duct chose, with scans guiding the pick, among three operations: through the skin, through the nose, or by laser through the tear canal. All got silicone tubes and were checked for about seventeen months.

The skin route cleared the block in 92 percent of cases, with the other two close behind near ninety percent. Relief from watering eyes fell in the same tight band, and no gap between the methods reached significance. Life quality scores rose in all groups, tilting a bit toward the nose route, while the skin route hurt most after surgery.
pmc-13301823:
Viruses that eat bacteria could replace antibiotics in sea cucumber ponds, Wan Zhang and colleagues argue in a 2026 review of phage therapy for aquaculture. The survey centers on Apostichopus japonicus farming, where Vibrio infections drive heavy losses and drug resistance keeps climbing. Application routes, treatment results, and the obstacles between laboratory success and pond-side use structure the account.

Feed-delivered phages and multi-phage cocktails gave the strongest survival gains in challenged animals. Narrow host range, bacterial resistance to phages, poor survival of phages in pond conditions, and unclear rules all hold the method back. The authors map the gaps and frame phages as a sustainable disease strategy awaiting field proof.
pmc-13302523:
M Bergonti and co-authors assess, in a 2026 multicentre study, tiny extra electrodes on ablation catheters that read heart signals at very fine scale. Extra heartbeats from the outflow tracts are mapped before burning, and judging whether the source sits on the surface or buried in the wall matters. Microelectrode signals might make that call better.

The review covered 81 patients whose outflow-tract beats were successfully ablated. In surface cases, the micro signal fired earliest in ninety percent, ahead of standard readings. A timing gap over ten milliseconds between standard and micro signals flagged cases needing burns in both outflow tracts. The micro-based target area measured half the size of the automatically marked one, promising tighter ablation.
pmc-13302623:
Six years on, the arteries of rheumatoid arthritis patients keep stiffening even as their joints calm down, Attila Sas and colleagues report in a 2026 follow-up study. Forty-three of sixty patients first examined in 2017 returned in 2023 for labs, carotid ultrasound, transcranial Doppler, and brain MRI. Each person's new results were set against their own baseline.

Disease activity scores fell significantly and vitamin D rose. Yet carotid plaque burden grew on both sides, and brain artery flow velocities dropped while pulsatility and resistance climbed. Cerebrovascular reserve shrank, and MRI signs of small-vessel disease trended worse. The authors recommend routine multi-modal vessel monitoring alongside arthritis care.
pmc-13303723:
Conrad Leitsmann heads a 2026 review of whether every suspected bladder tumor needs immediate surgical resection through the urethra. That operation is the standard way to diagnose and first treat bladder cancer, but it burdens patients and health systems.

Records for 217 patients who had a first resection for suspected cancer at one large center in early 2023 were checked. About one third of removed tissue held no cancer at all. Growth pattern at first scope exam, older age, matching scope judgments, and larger tumor size each predicted true cancer. Fuller checks before surgery could spare some patients an operation they do not need.
pmc-13305523:
Wenwen Chen and Yehai Liu build a tissue-matrix gene score to forecast outcomes in head and neck squamous cell cancer in a 2026 study. The scaffolding around tumors helps drive growth, and its genes may flag patients headed for worse courses.

Gene data from several patient groups fed ten learning methods in over a hundred combinations to pick the best score. Twenty-three matrix genes tied to outlook shaped the final signature, which sorted high and low risk groups with steady accuracy. Immune cell mixes and drug responses differed by group. Lab checks confirmed raised gene activity in tumor tissue beside normal samples.
pmc-13306223:
Elena Enachi opened a 2026 journal set on health compounds from plants and foods. Nine papers make up the set, six with new lab work and three that sum up past work.

Themes span plant phenols for long term illness, new ways to pull compounds out, and tests of germ kill and cell harm. Kidney illness gets close care among the long term ills in the set. Uses span food, drugs and biotech, and the intro frames such compounds as aids for heart, immune and body fuel health in daily life.
pmc-13306523:
Erin Eickholt reported a 2026 case where bee pollen supplement use led to severe allergy and later asthma. A 26-year-old woman arrived at an emergency unit four hours after taking bee pollen with swollen lips and tongue, breath trouble, nausea, belly pain and itching.

Standard allergy emergency drugs settled the attack, and she went home the same visit. One month later, during peak autumn pollen, wheezing returned and tests showed raised total IgE at 189 kU/L plus strong reactions to ragweed, mugwort and cocklebur. Doctors diagnosed allergic asthma linked to the supplement episode.
pmc-13306723:
Eman Marzouk framed carbapenem failure in resistant gut bacteria as loss of drug before it reaches its target in a 2026 review. Resistant Enterobacterales leave few options and kill many patients, even after dose tuning and newer resistance-focused drugs.

The proposed Pre-Target Interception Model tracks active drug lost to enzymes, blocked membranes, pumps and film barriers inside infected tissue. Tiny carriers are judged by how well they shield drug, enter tissue and stay at the site under those pressures. Factory and safety hurdles still block wide clinical use, the authors note.
pmc-13306823:
Chuantao Zhao and colleagues tackle in 2026 a practical problem for plant disease apps: models trained on clean laboratory leaf photos fail in messy field images. Their lightweight method adapts during training using unlabelled field images only to recalibrate internal statistics. Classification then matches new images against class prototypes.

Tested from the PlantVillage collection toward the field-based PlantDoc set, accuracy averaged about forty-three percent with one example per class and about fifty-four percent with five. Those scores beat the standard prototypical network by clear margins. Extra adaptation tricks at test time added nothing consistent, so the simpler training-time step carried the gain. The encoder also ran fully on a phone-class processor with very low estimated delay. Mobile field diagnosis is the intended destination.
pmc-13307023:
Lianghao Huang printed resveratrol tablets with differing internal patterns in a 2026 study. The plant compound dissolves poorly in water, so hot-melt shaping plus fused filament printing turned it into a spread, glassy form inside polymer carriers.

Patterns varied the inner grid while size accuracy, strength, floating and drug release were tracked across builds. Heat, X-ray and light checks confirmed the compound lost its crystal form after processing in reported results. Pattern choice shifted mechanical behaviour and release pace, showing how printed inner geometry can tune a poorly soluble drug tablet.
pmc-13307423:
Seoyoon Heo and colleagues review in 2026 how the cell's recycling system, autophagy, shapes liver disease and ageing. Fatty liver disease tied to metabolism speeds liver cell ageing, which weakens regeneration and pushes tissue toward scarring and cancer. Protein-level studies, the review argues, reveal changes that gene activity alone misses.

Specialised recycling routes for fat droplets, mitochondria, iron stores, and other organelles all falter in ageing, fatty livers. Protein signatures differ by organelle, showing a broad breakdown of quality control. The authors propose that failed selective recycling drives liver cell senescence at the protein level. They call for finer protein mapping, including location-aware methods, to find treatment targets. Transcript data alone, they warn, cannot guide such therapy.
pmc-13307523:
Yunquan Wang and co-authors trace in 2026 how fungal partners of trees shape which neighbours help or hurt young trees in a subtropical forest. They joined census records with fungal type and sprouting strength for multi stemmed species, and they tracked survival at sapling, juvenile, and adult stages.

Neighbours with arbuscular fungi helped survival at every stage, while other fungal groups mattered only at some stages. Ericoid neighbours counted at the sapling stage, and ectomycorrhizal neighbours counted later in life. Help from neighbours also grew with sprouting strength, most of all for saplings. Forest models should thus weigh age and fungal type together, not treat neighbourhood effects as fixed.
pmc-13307623:
Sayan Deb Dutta and co-authors present a 2026 study of a 3D-printed gel that may help bone grow back. Large bone gaps from injury, tumors, or infection often fail to heal with plain grafts. Their gel mixes a gelatin base with a conductive polymer and flakes of MXene, a thin layered material. It can be printed by direct ink writing, sticks to tissue, and breaks down over time.

Printed and cross-linked, the gel turns push and pull into small electric signals, like a tiny generator. It proved strong, kept its conductivity, and was gentle on human bone stem cells. The cells grew well and were pushed toward making bone by the electric cues. A coated version could also sense a key bone enzyme without labels, hinting at a tool that both heals and monitors.
pmc-13307823: Yerbol Bulatov and co-authors issue a 2026 correction to their 2024 study of camelpox virus in western Kazakhstan and the role of local fauna as reservoirs. The item itself is only a brief affiliation notice, so it adds no new data or findings. It records that Sholpan Turyskeldy holds an added post at Al-Farabi Kazakh National University in Almaty, and it states that the results of the study stand unchanged.
pmc-13307923:
Thomas Fotas and co-authors describe in 2026 imported tungiasis, a skin infestation by the flea Tunga penetrans, in Greece, with a rare case passed on at home. Seven men who worked in Tanzania came home with painful foot lumps, and one man who never left Greece caught it at home.

Skin checks and gene tests confirmed the flea, with all samples matching one shared sequence in the lab work. Liver blood tests rose mildly in all eight men and settled within two weeks after care was given. No spread turned up in other housemates or pets. Doctors in low risk lands should still weigh travel linked skin ills and check the home setting.
pmc-13308523:
In 2026, Gillian H Ice and co-authors describe a two way learning exchange on age friendly practice between Athens County in Ohio and partners in Slovenia. A seven member Ohio group visited Slovenia in January 2025, and a six member Slovenian group came to Ohio in May 2025 for tours and talks.

Five themes arose, from fresh ideas sparked by travel to bonds that may seed joint work in years ahead. Seeing a unlike system up close helped each side name what shapes its own choices at home. Gains came more as drive and insight than as ready plans to copy across. Focus time and group thought, the authors argue, turn short trips into lasting equity work.
pmc-13308623:
Margalida Esteva-Socias and co-authors show in 2026 that METTL3, a protein known for tagging RNA, also drives cell secretion in breast cancer by a path that skips that tagging job. In patient tumours the protein sat in the cell body, not the nucleus, where it held up a partner called EXOC7.

Silencing METTL3 slowed packet traffic, dulled the mix of goods the cells shed, and curbed spread traits such as invasion arms in dish tests. Blocking its tagging skill alone did none of that in these checks. The finds recast METTL3 as a hands on traffic aide in cancer, which may open fresh drug angles beyond enzyme blocks.
pmc-13308723:
Lin Li and co-authors compare in 2026 high versus low doses of polymyxin B for lung infections from hard to kill germs, in one hospital from 2020 to 2024. Records held 235 adults who got the drug by vein, split by the dose style their teams chose in routine care.

Death rates at 28 and 42 days differed in a firm way between the dose groups in this data set. Cure response and hospital stay did not differ, and liver, kidney, and blood harms also stayed alike on firm tests. Low dose care, under 1.5 milligrams per kilogram a day with a longer course, tied to lower drug cost. Forward trials must test the dose call before rules change.
pmc-13308823:
Yinfeng Lin and co-authors compare in 2026 ultrasound guided microwave ablation with standard surgery for granulomatous lobular mastitis, a lasting breast swelling that brings pain and shape change. Records from two centres held 233 women, with 102 in the heat group and 131 in the surgery group, tracked for a median 18.5 months.

Cure rates sat near equal, at 97.06 percent for heat care and 96.18 percent for surgery in this set. Return rates also sat close, and blood loss, work time, drainage, and hospital stay all favoured heat care. Scores for breast and scar joy favoured heat care as well, while mind and chest scores matched.
pmc-13309023:
Dominik Witczak and co-authors present in 2026 GrassSV, a hybrid tool that finds all main kinds of large genome changes in short read DNA data in one pass. Most tools excel at one kind or force users to chain many tools, which piles up cost and fuss for each genome.

GrassSV pairs depth of cover counts with shape matching on built contigs to keep both reach and care in one flow. Tests on the Genome in a Bottle human set and on fake yeast data gave high marks across all change types at lower run cost. False hits stayed low as well. One tool may thus swap for whole pipelines in clinic and lab gene work.
pmc-13309523: Jianhua Wen heads the author list on a 2026 correction notice in Scientific Reports for a study comparing two surgical methods to fix a blocked kidney drainage point in children. Corrected here is only authorship credit: Dehong Liu and Pin Li were left out as co-corresponding authors and are now named, with their contact details added. No data, methods, or results change, since the item exists solely to repair that omission.
pmc-13309623:
Yufei Wu, Els Rommes, and Rachel Kronick wrote this research paper, published in 2026. It studies how mothers seeking asylum in Montreal, Canada, hold onto a sense of control over their own lives while they resettle.

Such mothers are often painted as passive and helpless. The team interviewed thirteen of them at length and sorted the talks by theme. The women described real hardship: shortages, bias, and shaky legal and housing status. Even so, they pushed back on the label of dependence. They spoke of clear purpose in raising their children, and of endurance built on the meaning they found in that task. The authors say seeing this strength should steer research, policy, and health services toward backing the women's own drive.
pmc-13310623:
Ezequiel J. Tolosa and co-authors show in 2026 that losing KMT2D, a gene-writing enzyme, accelerates pancreatic cancer driven by the KRAS oncogene. Human tumour data first flagged KMT2D as frequently mutated and turned down in pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma, with low expression tied to shorter survival. Mouse models then tested cause and effect directly.

In two engineered mouse strains carrying mutant Kras, deleting Kmt2d raised tumour incidence and shortened survival. The effect held whether or not the guardian gene Tp53 was present, matching the human pattern where TP53 status did not change outcomes for low-KMT2D patients. Resulting tumours looked poorly differentiated, and gene activity analysis highlighted growth pathways with more dividing cells. Normal pancreas development was unaffected by the loss alone. KMT2D thus behaves as a candidate tumour suppressor whose absence worsens an already lethal cancer.
pmc-13311023:
Sandra Stuhr and colleagues survey dental implant patients on home care and disease awareness in a 2026 early study. Implant life depends on daily cleaning and upkeep, yet patient knowledge and habits are uneven. The team paired a short survey with implant health checks at a Michigan dental school.

Thirty four adults with 71 implants took part, and disease touched most implants despite most patients reporting daily cleaning. Plaque scores and fixation type linked to disease at the implant level. All patients with the deepest disease had past gum disease. Cleaning frequency best foretold health, while near one third got no professional care teaching.
pmc-13311323:
Fabian Méndez-Paz and co-authors argue for a decolonial turn in One Health in a 2026 article drawn from the One Amazon project. One Health joins human, animal, and land health, but its frame was set mostly in the Global North.

Field work ran from 2021 to 2024 in Colombia, Ecuador, and Peru alongside Indigenous, Afro-descendant, and Campesino communities. Mapping, interviews, and surveys done with residents grounded the claims. The authors fault the usual frame for prizing outbreak security over local illness, shallow community input, and sidelining ancestral knowledge. Their results show what health work looks like when communities lead.
pmc-13312023:
Claudia Pommerenke and colleagues report, in a 2026 study, which neuroblastoma cell lines can be turned into neuron-like cells for modeling brain disease in the lab. The SH-SY5Y line is the usual model, but many other lines from this childhood cancer had never been tested for the same trick.

The team profiled 18 cell lines with RNA sequencing and treated them with retinoic acid and a growth factor. Lines fell into adrenergic and mesenchymal types, each with its own pattern of neurotransmitter genes. Three adrenergic lines, CHP-134, LAN-5, and SIMA, grew into neuron-like cells carrying synaptic markers after treatment. The results help researchers pick a line whose biology fits the disease they want to study.
pmc-13312823:
Deling Zeng and colleagues examine, in a 2026 study, whether depression raises the risk of new heart disease in older adults already staged within the cardiovascular-kidney-metabolic syndrome framework. Evidence for this group was scarce, so the team turned to the China Health and Retirement Longitudinal Study for participants at syndrome stages 0 to 3.

Among 4,738 participants, those screening positive for depression carried significantly higher odds of later ischemic heart disease after adjustment, with an odds ratio of 1.62, and even higher odds of progressing to stage 4 disease. The pattern survived six sensitivity analyses, held across subgroups, and rose in a straight line with depression scores. Tests found no sign that body mass, inflammation markers, or white cell counts carried the effect. The authors argue depression deserves a place in heart risk assessment for ageing patients.
pmc-13313223:
Andrew Thake and co-authors review leukotrienes, fat-based signals made through the 5-lipoxygenase path, and their two-sided role in cancer in a paper from 2026. These signals shape inflammation around a tumor and touch vessel growth, immune action, and the spread of cancer to new sites.

The review weighs lab, clinical, and population studies chosen by set rules, with weight on recent work. Signals through this path track with markers such as the CysLT1 receptor, beta-catenin activity, and HIF-1 alpha signals. In lab models, drugs such as montelukast and zileuton and blockers of the FLAP protein slowed tumor growth and restored cell death, while human proof so far rests mostly on observed data. The authors argue for trials that pick patients by markers, so the path can be targeted where it matters most.
pmc-13313423:
Sheilabi Seeburun reviews bispecific antibodies, a newer class of drugs for multiple myeloma, a cancer of plasma cells that still has no cure. These lab-made proteins grab a cancer cell with one arm and an immune cell with the other, pulling the two together so the immune cell can kill its target. Four such drugs have won approval in the United States for patients whose cancer came back after other care. Response rates passed 60 percent, and one drug reached 74 percent even in people who had already had similar therapy.

The review also covers three-armed versions now in early trials, which have shown response rates as high as 75 percent and some complete clearances of the disease. Seeburun weighs how the drugs work, what trials show about benefit and side effects, and how doctors might order or combine them.
pmc-13314123:
Ibraheem Zedan, Layth Alkattan, and co-authors compare two drugs as ways to end life in dogs with as little pain as may be, in a 2025 study. Six adult dogs were split into two groups. All dogs first got a mix to make them sleep deeply.

One drug acted in about one to twelve minutes, with calm signs and no fits. The other acted in about one to four minutes but caused brief harsh fits. Heart tracings showed strain in both groups, more so with the second drug. The team finds the first drug safer and more smooth for this hard task.
pmc-13314323:
Viski Fitri Hendrawan and colleagues test, in a 2026 mouse study, whether oral nanocurcumin can protect the pregnant uterus from noise stress. Chronic noise during pregnancy disturbs the uterus's balance between cell death and calming immune signals, tracked through caspase-3 and interleukin-10. Twenty-five pregnant mice were split into five groups: quiet controls, noise-exposed controls, and three noise-exposed groups receiving nanocurcumin doses by mouth from day six to day eighteen of gestation. Uterine tissue was then stained for both markers.

Noise alone pushed the death marker up and the calming marker down significantly. Nanocurcumin reversed both shifts in step with dose. At the highest dose, caspase-3 expression fell by 20.7 percent while interleukin-10 rose by 41.7 percent against the noise-only group. Regression tied dose to both readouts. The authors frame the supplement as a candidate for protecting pregnancies under stress, and connect the work to maternal health goals.
pmc-13314423:
Juan Chen and co-workers test whether gut signs before brain surgery can warn of lung infection after it, in a study of 2026. Patients with space-taking lesions in the skull often get pneumonia after surgery due to deep wounds, dulled awareness, and long bed rest.

The study enrolled 50 patients and took stool and blood samples before and after surgery. Gene sequencing tracked gut microbes, and mass spectrometry mapped body chemicals at large. Surgery lowered microbe variety in all patients, yet those who later got pneumonia started out with a clear lack of Roseburia, a gut bacterium, before surgery. Their blood also showed a state the authors call metabolic deficiency before the operation. The gut-lung link may give surgeons an early warning tool.
pmc-13314923:
Daniele B. Santana puts forward a bias theory for emotional violence by teachers, in a 2026 paper. Harsh words and shaming by teachers are a grave yet little-studied harm in schools, seen across the world.

Santana argues the root is not a few bad teachers but a built-in tilt in adult-child ties, named adultcentrism, joined with a bleak view of pedagogy. Those shared attitudes, the hypothesis holds, predict which teachers turn emotionally violent. The paper reviews what is known, sets out the two frames, and calls for studies that match teacher beliefs against student reports of victimization. If the bias proves real, training and school rules could target the shared mindset rather than chase lone offenders.
pmc-13315023:
Kanae Fukutsu and co-authors report, in a 2026 real-world study, what happened when Singaporean patients with stubborn diabetic macular edema switched to faricimab. These patients had already spent a median of 1.8 years on other therapies with suboptimal results. Reviewing charts at the national eye centre for switches made between 2022 and 2024, the team measured vision and retinal thickness after a loading course of three or four injections. They compared the two regimens.

The switch paid off quickly. Across 157 eyes from 131 patients, mean vision improved from 57.8 to 62.4 chart letters at roughly seven weeks. The swollen central retina thinned from 431.4 to 334.2 micrometers on average, and both changes were strongly significant. Three loading injections matched four on every outcome, suggesting the shorter course suffices for the initial gain. The authors present faricimab as an effective rescue option for chronic edema in Asian patients, a population underrepresented in the trial literature.
pmc-13315423:
For stomach cancer that returns after first treatment, pairing the antibody ramucirumab with the chemotherapy docetaxel had never been formally tested.
