The pairing was chosen partly to cut nerve damage and hospital visits compared with the standard partner drug.

About a quarter of patients saw their tumors shrink, and nearly three quarters achieved disease control. Typical survival without growth was 3.1 months, and overall survival 11.5 months. Low blood counts and related fever were the main severe side effects, and a protocol change adding preventive growth-factor support stopped the fevers. Nerve symptoms were common but never severe. The authors call the pairing a reasonable second-line option, in 2026.
pmc-13315523:
Julia Moore Vogel and a very large team report in 2026 on lasting limits in heart and lung fitness after COVID-19. Using wearable sensors in a digital substudy of a nationwide recovery cohort, they linked fitness measures with survey reports of long COVID symptoms over a six-month window.

All measures came at least six months after infection, letting the team judge longer-term effects rather than early recovery. They estimated how sensor-based fitness tied to symptom patterns across many participants and sites. Lasting drops in fitness matter for work, daily life, and care planning, and objective wearable data can show limits that self-reports alone may miss.
pmc-13315923:
Xuefei Shi and co-authors identify a tiny peptide that drives lung adenocarcinoma growth, in a 2026 study. The cancer is among the most common lung cancers and survival is poor. The peptide, named SCAPEP, is produced from a circular RNA through an internal entry site, and such RNA-encoded peptides are a new area of cancer biology.

Tumours that were large, spread to lymph nodes, or at an advanced stage carried high levels of the peptide. Raising or lowering its level in experiments changed cell growth, spread, and the cells self-cleaning process, both in dishes and in animals. The peptide acts by driving a kinase to tag a structural protein, which lifts levels of a recycling enzyme. Restoring that enzyme reversed the effect of removing the peptide. The authors present the chain as a new insight into how such peptides feed this cancer.
pmc-13316223:
Yannic Volz and colleagues traced surgical care in 2026 for male stress incontinence in Germany, using the nationwide GRAND inpatient register from 2005 to 2023. Leakage after prostate treatment burdens many men, and care splits between the gold-standard artificial sphincter and sling procedures for chosen patients.

In total, 24,234 men had surgery, with the artificial sphincter making up 63 percent of cases in the reported split. The study charted long-term trends, in-hospital complications, death, and stay length, plus reasons devices were removed or replaced, adjusted for age, other illness, prior radiation, and surgery year.
pmc-13316423:
Rana Salah and co-authors introduce DeepTaxa in a 2026 methods paper, a hybrid deep learning tool that names bacteria from their 16S gene reads down to species level. Older tools lean on exact matching or word-count tricks and suffer when reference lists are incomplete.

DeepTaxa pairs a multi-scale pattern network with a transformer built for DNA text, giving calls at all seven ranks of the classic naming ladder. On a held-out Greengenes2 test set it reached species accuracy of 92.96 percent in the reported runs, ahead of DADA2 and QIIME 2, with near-perfect scores at broad ranks. A short-read version still hit high accuracy. Code, trained models, and data are public for reuse.
pmc-13316623:
Xin Ye and co-authors describe, in 2026, a laboratory test that measures several chicken immune genes at once. Knowing how strongly inflammation genes are switched on helps explain host responses during poultry infections. Older tests often measure one gene at a time or use dyes that limit specificity.

Their probe-based multiplex test quantifies four pro-inflammatory transcripts together, with a ribosomal RNA target measured separately as a reference. Standard curves showed good efficiency and strong linearity in both single and combined formats. In lung tissue from chickens challenged with pathogenic Escherichia coli, two genes rose sharply one day after infection while two others did not change. Follow-up checks supported those readings.
pmc-13317123:
Jue Wang, Fumihiko Ino, and Alia Benkahla present RAM-MSA in a 2026 computing paper, a method for aligning many DNA or protein sequences exactly without blowing up memory. Exact aligners give provably best answers but eat memory as sequences pile up, while fast shortcuts sacrifice accuracy.

Their recursive method bounds memory, returns a first alignment quickly, then keeps improving it until the exact answer lands. Tests cut memory use to 62.51 percent of a leading exact method's footprint in the reported comparison, and the first output scored near heuristic speed with a quality score of 0.96 in the benchmark. It also handles the more realistic affine gap costs that older path methods skip.
pmc-13317323:
Felix Teufel and a large team of co-authors measure how faithfully a health package was delivered in Nepal in a 2026 study. The World Health Organization package guides primary care for long-term diseases such as high blood pressure and diabetes in poorer countries. Nepal rolled it out nationally, but whether clinics followed the steps was unknown beyond pilots.

The team watched care at more than one hundred clinics across all provinces and interviewed providers and patients. Core steps such as checking blood pressure and adjusting medicine were mostly done, while blood sugar checks and risk scoring were mostly skipped. Counseling covered salt and follow-up more than other topics. Overall fidelity scores were low, though trained providers did notably better. The authors urge support that closes the skipped steps.
pmc-13317423: Jun Jiang and co-authors issued a 2026 correction to a 2024 study of targeted exosomes carrying gene-silencing cargo against lung cancer spread to the brain. The notice is a correction only: a Ki67 fluorescence image in Figure 7D was duplicated by mistake during assembly, and the corrected figure is shown. The original article has been updated.
pmc-13318123:
Jianan Wang and a Dutch team report a sobering 2026 gene therapy study on TBX18, a developmental switch once hailed as a way to grow a biological pacemaker in the heart. Early short bursts had produced pacing in animals, raising hopes of replacing hardware devices.

Long-lasting virus-delivered TBX18 scarred mouse hearts badly at full strength. At gentler, safe levels it still rewired cell identity genes but never switched on the pacemaker program or its signature current, and cells beat oddly with stretched recovery. In rats with complete heart block, a rival channel gene, Hcn2, paced robustly with stimulation while TBX18 added nothing. The authors close the case: Hcn2, not TBX18, deserves development money.
pmc-13318723:
Shikhar Kumar and colleagues report a 2026 pair of user studies on robot politeness and mistakes. They asked whether polite behaviour can offset error-prone performance. Two non-humanoid robots were tested: a mobile robot and a manipulator arm. Participants were 59 young adults with engineering backgrounds, aged 24 to 28.

Politeness followed a classic three-rule scheme, present or absent. Correctness was varied by adding deliberate errors or none. Correct and polite robots earned the best ratings overall. Crucially, politeness never made up for errors. A correct but strict robot beat a polite but mistaken one. The polite, error-prone robot could even frustrate users more. The authors stress testing across robot types and tasks.
pmc-13319423:
M. A. van Bree and co-authors report a hands on study from 2026 on fully plant based meals for hospital patients. Hospitals want meals that cut climate harm yet still give sick people enough protein and taste good. Few ready options give a full mix of the building blocks found in animal foods, so a mixed team of staff and food firms built new menus from scratch.

Thirty recipes were shaped into seven day plans giving 90 to 97 grams of protein a day, drawn from soy, lentils, grains, and nuts. Extra pea protein and soy drinks lifted breakfast and lunch without bigger plates. Day costs stayed near ten to twelve euros, though trade offs with taste and cost remain.
pmc-13319723:
Arun K Simon and co-authors review, in 2026, remote dentistry combined with artificial intelligence in India. Oral disease affects billions worldwide, and rural Indians have very limited access to dentists despite widespread mobile connectivity. Remote consultation grew during the pandemic and has since gained clinical validation.

Evidence supports live and store-and-forward remote platforms for cavity screening, triage of mouth lesions and community surveillance. Artificial intelligence tools, from image networks to language models, can raise diagnostic accuracy and support patient education. Barriers remain substantial: professionals lack formal training, rural infrastructure is weak, digital oral health programmes are few and national rules are absent. The authors call for coordinated policy, curriculum reform and equity-focused implementation research.
pmc-13319923:
Linxi Wang and co-authors review cage like nano carriers for cancer immune drugs in a 2026 article on metal organic frameworks. Immune care has changed cancer treatment, yet side harm, tumor escape, and a hostile tumor setting still cap its reach. Tiny cages built from metal joints and carbon links can carry large drug loads and free them in a timed way, which makes them a fresh delivery route.

The review weighs cage strengths for safety, aim, and load, then maps joint delivery of immune drugs with tumor bits that train the immune system. Pairings with heat, light, and chemical attack therapies are also covered. Hurdles for clinic use, such as scale up and long term safety, close the survey with paths for next work.
pmc-13320023:
Paul Scheidegger and co-authors test whether a short video improves consent talks before shoulder replacement in a 2026 trial. Barely three in ten patients grasp standard verbal explanations of this operation. Sixty patients were split evenly: half watched a two-minute explainer first, half heard the talk alone.

On a seven-question knowledge test, the video group averaged 5.7 against 4.67 for controls, a clear gain. Every subgroup improved, with older patients, those with less schooling, and non-native speakers gaining the most. The authors recommend folding brief videos into routine consent for this surgery, an easy change with outsized benefit for vulnerable patients.
pmc-13320423:
Francesca Vedovo wrote a letter in 2026 on a trial of music during prostate biopsy, the VIVALDI trial by Basadonna and co-authors. Music is a cheap, safe, drug free way to ease pain and worry during the through skin biopsy, and the trial found gains worth noting. The letter holds that music, once tested as care, must meet the same reporting rules as any other care step.

In the trial arm, patients picked their own music, played on speakers from the wait room to the end of the biopsy. Free choice aids comfort but makes the dose a moving target, since genre, beat, words, and volume all shift the effect. Set guides for music care ask for full detail on content, chooser, delivery, and checks that the plan was followed.
pmc-13320523:
Huining Gu and a large team report a 2026 study on how the liver regrows after injury. A protein piece called immunoglobulin kappa, made by liver cells, had earlier been tied to cell survival during harm. The team asked how it guides regrowth and whether it could anchor the whole repair process.

Kappa levels rose in liver samples from patients with drug caused liver injury and in mouse injury models. Mice lacking kappa in liver cells regrew poorly, with disordered cell scaffolding and fewer new cells. Lab work showed kappa binds directly to a protein called MYLK that supports cell structure. The results place an unlikely immune protein at the heart of liver repair.
pmc-13321023:
Prashant Sharma, Awanit Kumar, and Harsh Verma comment in a 2026 letter on a review of prediction models for atrial fibrillation after heart bypass surgery. The review, by Eini and others, pooled machine learning and regression models for this common rhythm problem. The writers argue that how the outcome was defined shapes what the pooled scores really mean.

Studies set episode length cut-offs from 30 seconds to over 5 minutes and used anything from constant heart monitoring to spot checks, which miss brief episodes. A pooled specificity of 0.83 may thus reflect monitoring intensity more than model skill. The letter also flags missing calibration and decision curve proof as the bridge to clinic use.
pmc-13321223:
Yi Hao and co-authors warn that plant water saving under rising carbon dioxide may be overstated in a 2026 study. Higher carbon dioxide makes leaf pores narrow, which should cut water loss and ease land drying. The team shows an indirect feedback that works the other way.

As plants change, surface energy balance shifts, making air warmer and drier, which in turn raises water loss from land. That feedback offsets about half of the water saving in northern mid to high latitudes, yet most assessments leave it out. Ignoring it may understate future drought risk for farms and ecosystems that depend on soil moisture.
pmc-13321423:
Madison Aitken and co-authors set out, in a 2026 protocol paper, a trial to test if calm control of ill feelings is how youth therapy works. Youth anxiety, low mood, and rule breaks are common, yet therapy helps just a fair amount. A weak grip on ill feelings cuts across all three ills, but few tests have read it as the path of change. The trial will use MATCH, a known program that mixes parts for anxiety, low mood, trauma, or conduct ills. That mix suits a test of shared paths.

Two sites will run the trial, and youth will be split by chance to therapy or a control. Body and behavior reads of ill-feeling control will track the course. The aim is proof of the path, so care can be tuned to it.
pmc-13321523:
Muhammad Asif and co-authors test what draws Pakistani bank customers to mobile banking apps, in this 2026 study. They extend a classic adoption model with two social and personal factors: how much peers sway a person, and how eager that person is to try new things. Two hundred sixty-eight customers with app experience answered an online survey.

Peer sway shaped both how useful and how easy the apps felt, and those two views in turn drove the intent to use them. Eagerness to innovate strengthened the link between peer sway and ease, but not the other links. The authors advise banks to work through social influence.
pmc-13321723:
Guiling Liao and four colleagues study the mental health needs of people with osteoarthritis, a joint wear disease, in a paper dated twenty twenty-six. Care often focuses on joints and pain while mood needs go unasked. The team surveyed 385 patients at three large hospitals in Changzhou and rated their anxiety, low mood, and stated needs. They then interviewed twenty-eight patients in depth.

More than half screened positive for anxiety or low mood. The top need was plain knowledge about the disease, then pain control. Most patients wanted a bone surgeon to lead the service, face-to-face talks, and pain content. Age and schooling shaped needs. Talk themes covered the mental weight of illness and the base role of self-care.
pmc-13322023:
Mads Aarhus and co-authors review civilian penetrating brain injury care in south-east Norway, in a 2026 paper. Such injuries are rare but often devastating. Guidelines call for vessel imaging, preventive antibiotics and anti-seizure drugs, early surgery with closure of the brain's lining, and pressure-guided care.

The team found all such patients admitted to Oslo University Hospital from 2015 to 2023 in a regional trauma registry. About four in ten patients died within thirty days, yet seventy percent of survivors reached a favorable outcome at six months. Vessel imaging matched guidelines well, but preventive drugs were given far less often than advised. The audit shows where a strong trauma system still falls short of its own rulebook.
pmc-13322723:
Mohsen Rostami and co-authors report a case series on a spine operation that corrects a rigid forward lean at the neck-chest junction. Their 2026 paper covers patients whose deformity often followed earlier neck fusion or an inflammatory spine disease. The standard correction site carries risks to arteries and nerve roots.

The operation they study removes a wedge of bone at the second thoracic vertebra instead. The team reviewed close to twenty patients treated over several years. Alignment measures improved clearly after surgery and largely held at final follow-up. Complications and repeat operations were tracked as well. The authors present this level as offering like correction with a kinder risk profile, a claim their series data are meant to test.
pmc-13322823:
Yifan Luo, Jiarong Wang and Jichun Zhao review the enzyme MMP-12 and its mixed roles in artery disease, in work published in 2026. MMP-12, also called macrophage elastase, sits where inflammation meets breakdown of the tissue that holds artery walls together.

Across diseases such as atherosclerosis and aortic aneurysm, MMP-12 can break down matrix, draw in immune cells, switch on other enzymes, or at times help calm inflammation. Which role dominates depends on the inflammatory setting, the stage of disease and the material present in the wall. That context shapes whether blocking MMP-12 could help, and the authors urge care when moving findings from models to patients.
pmc-13323023:
Shanshan Li and co-authors ask who stays up to date with lung cancer screening in the United States, in a 2026 analysis of the 2024 Behavioral Risk Factor Surveillance System. Their weighted sample held 6,234 adults aged 50 to 79 years who were eligible for screening.

Only about a fifth were up to date with screening in the weighted figures. Fourteen social and health measures were grouped into four components, covering resources, physical health, psychosocial health and work and neighbourhood. Only socioeconomic resources linked clearly to screening after full adjustment. Cluster and SHAP analyses showed differing barriers by subgroup, and the authors argue that outreach should be tailored rather than uniform.
pmc-13323223:
Shengqi Zheng and co-authors evaluate negative-pressure therapy for children whose concealed penis returned after surgery, in a 2026 retrospective study. They reviewed 126 patients who finished a standard 20-session, pressure-titrated course between September 2022 and June 2025.

Visible, flaccid and stretched lengths plus diameter all rose significantly after treatment in their records, and gains held at three months without clear regression. Older age, higher body mass index and smaller starting size each predicted larger gains. No serious side effects appeared. The authors present suction-based treatment as a non-surgical salvage option that uses mechanical stretch to loosen fibrotic restriction, pending stronger controlled evidence in children.
pmc-13323523:
Mario Thevis, Andreas Thomas, and Nana Naumann survey how anti-doping labs try to catch gene doping, the banned use of gene therapy tools to boost athletic performance. Their 2026 review covers detection methods now in development, from PCR tests and high-resolution mass spectrometry to detection built on CRISPR tools. It sets this work against a wide field of gene therapy research, which keeps producing new substances that could be misused in sport.

The authors note that unapproved products aimed at athletes are already sold online, including preparations said to carry follistatin, VEGF, or EPO genes for self-use. No gene doping case has yet been proven, but signs of interest among elite athletes are already visible, and the health risk of uncontrolled use is hard to predict. The review argues that routine lab testing must add new methods fast, before misuse outruns detection.
pmc-13323623:
Kelly Marriott-Statham and colleagues study how care home settings shape shared decisions between older residents and nurses, in a 2026 qualitative study from an Australian residential aged care home. Shared decision-making is widely promoted, yet routine, rigid rules and scarce resources often block it in practice.

Emotional touchpoint interviews with five older people and six nurses, eight practice observations and development methods fed a joint interpretive analysis. Seven components shaped how connected residents and nurses felt and how fully decisions were shared, led by affirming personhood and mutual trust in the reported themes. The authors argue that the wider practice environment, not goodwill alone, decides whether residents hold a real voice.
pmc-13324423:
Abdul-Jabbar and co-authors design a system that joins data security with AI-based compression. Protecting data is a core goal of any information system, above all for financial records. Compression cuts storage needs for the growing volume of stored data, but it must not weaken safety.

The authors argue an integrated design is now necessary. Their approach aims to keep sensitive financial data secure while shrinking its storage footprint. It is meant to work across various domains, not one file type alone. The study lays out the design and tests its balance of safety, size, and speed.
pmc-13324623:
Linmei Dong and co-workers optimize the extraction of medicinal compounds from a rare herb's roots, in a 2026 paper. The plant, a Paris polyphylla variety from Yunnan, is in high demand and its wild supply is running low. Efficient extraction helps use the resource well.

Using a response surface method, the team tuned an enzyme-assisted process for three target compounds called polyphyllins. The best settings combined a moderate temperature, about half an hour of extraction, and a set liquid ratio. The yield matched the model's prediction closely and beat the control by more than a quarter. Statistical checks showed the model fit well. The authors offer the method as a reference.
pmc-13325123:
Wenyi Sun and colleagues read the fluid history locked in calcite veins of the Ordos Basin in a 2026 geology study. The veins sit in the subsalt fourth member of the Ordovician Majiagou Formation, a target for gas search.

Microscopy, isotope ratios, trace elements, and fluid inclusions were combined to date the vein fluids. Most veins grew in a single stage from burial fluids buffered by the host rock. Trapped droplets record three hydrocarbon chapters: light early charging, wide oil charging from the Late Triassic to Early Jurassic, and later cracking of that oil to gas in the Early Cretaceous. The story guides where mature gas may sit today.
pmc-13326323:
Said Mohamed Mohamud and co-authors read lab records in 2026 on drug resistance in a common germ at a large hospital in Mogadishu, Somalia. The germ, Staphylococcus aureus, lives on skin in health yet can drive grave blood and wound infections. Records from 2019 to 2024 held 1,381 samples of the germ from wards and clinics. Standard lab tests named each sample and its drug profile.

Near half of the samples were of the hard type that shrugs off a key drug family. Wound and blood samples were the most common sources. The hard type held out against the oldest pen drug in near all cases and beat two other common drugs in most. The soft type also showed high rates against the pen drug. The team calls for tighter drug use.
pmc-13327323:
Naoki Sakane and three co-authors measure emotional strain tied to type 1 diabetes in Japanese adults, in a study published in twenty twenty-six. Daily life with this disease demands constant care, and the burden can weigh on mood and self-care. How common that strain is in Japan was not well known.

The team surveyed adults using three standard scales, one built for type 1 diabetes, one for diabetes problems in general, and one on fear of low blood sugar. Of those analyzed, about three in ten had moderate strain and about one in six had high strain. Those with high strain scored worse on worry and eating distress, though their blood sugar control was no worse. Feelings of powerlessness scored highest. The authors back the scale as a useful screening tool.
pmc-13327923:
Eva Karaskova and colleagues review heart risk in inflammatory bowel disease in a 2026 article. Crohn's disease and ulcerative colitis are now seen as body-wide illnesses whose vessel risk runs above what standard factors explain, above all in younger patients and during gut flares. The authors gather the shared mechanisms.

Chronic inflammation harms vessel linings, speeds clotting, and feeds plaque growth, aided by a leaky gut barrier, shifted microbes, and troubled belly fat. Lipids mislead in this setting: blood levels can look low while risk stays high, because inflammation warps lipoprotein quality, a pattern dubbed the lipid paradox. Tight control of bowel activity and care with steroids anchor the prevention advice.
pmc-13328323:
Kenan Moral and eleven colleagues track how a diabetes drug class reshapes liver fat and body chemistry, in a 2026 study. The drugs, SGLT2 inhibitors, help fatty liver disease, but the metabolic route of that help was unclear.

Twenty-nine patients with type 2 diabetes and fatty livers were profiled before and after six months of treatment. Liver fat fell from about seventeen to under fourteen percent, and blood sugar control and weight improved. Seventeen small molecules shifted, mostly amino acids, and nearly five hundred fat species remodeled. The authors conclude the drugs' liver benefit runs deeper than glucose control, through amino acid and lipid pathways alike.
pmc-13328423:
Rana Abdelaal and co-authors map skin microbes in Egyptian acne patients in a 2026 study. Acne ties to the bacterium Cutibacterium acnes, yet diversity shifts may matter more than sheer growth, and Middle East data are scarce. Swabs from 45 patients, 37 urban and 8 rural, plus 25 healthy urban controls, underwent gene sequencing.

In city patients, worse acne came with richer, more even microbe mixes rather than more species, and village patients showed their own distinct, diverse patterns with different metabolic leanings. Surprisingly, the namesake bacterium's types thinned as acne worsened in both groups, hinting that only certain strains misbehave. Future treatments might spare friendly strains and target only harmful ones, tuned to local environments.
pmc-13330223:
Nakauchi and co-authors compare two ways of judging hormone status in breast cancer and check patient outcomes. Standard lab tests use staining and gene probes to set ER and HER2 status. RNA-based tests can set the same status, but the two methods often disagree.

The team measured how often results clashed and whether clashes meant worse outcomes. Mismatch rates were 11.8 percent for ER and 19.4 percent for HER2. They used matched comparisons and weighting to adjust for patient traits. The work also sought factors most tied to the mismatch between methods.
pmc-13330523:
Lizhi Liu and colleagues show new uses for a bacterial Argonaute enzyme in handling lab-made RNA in a 2026 study. Argonaute cutters can be guided to chosen sequences without the strict site rules that limit Cas enzymes. The team used a DNA-guided enzyme from Mucilaginibacter paludis that cuts RNA.

Uses shown include polishing the tail end of messenger RNA made in vitro. Paired with mass spectrometry, the cutter helped grade cap quality at the head end and tail length and makeup at the other end. One-pot cutting with many guides aided RNA sequencing, change detection, and fingerprint checks. The authors present the enzyme as a flexible quality tool for RNA production.
pmc-13330623:

Resistance stayed very low in camels, goats, and sheep under nomadic herding, and low in cattle in the reported findings. Intensively raised chickens and pigs carried far more resistance, with high multi-drug shares in both. Horses and dogs also carried high rates. Worryingly, high-threat resistant types appeared only in owned dogs. Close human contact tracked with higher carriage. Joined human and animal action is urgent, the authors argue.
pmc-13332323:
Raffaele Epis and co-authors review treatments targeting the downstream damage pathways of Duchenne muscular dystrophy rather than the missing protein itself. Their 2026 narrative review covers more than one hundred articles, most from the last fifteen years, spanning forty different approaches.

Each approach was judged on whether it promoted regeneration or limited degeneration. Calcium- and mitochondria-targeted interventions overwhelmingly preserved muscle structure and slowed regeneration cycles. Fibre stability approaches split evenly between regeneration and delaying wasting. Cell therapies aimed at the muscle stem cell pool mostly enhanced regeneration, while anti-inflammatory strategies more often slowed degeneration than built new fibres. The authors argue the field is shifting: limiting chronic degeneration and its exhausting repair cycles may preserve muscle better than chasing regeneration alone.
pmc-13333523:
Xingwei Zhao and colleagues propose in 2026 that stray mitochondrial DNA acts as an amplifier inside the inflammation of heart failure with preserved ejection fraction. The condition is increasingly read as a multi-organ inflammatory state, and the puzzle is how stresses, ageing, obesity, diabetes, kidney trouble, fuse into a self-sustaining network.

Their framework gives mitochondrial DNA the messenger's role. Stressed cells oxidize and shed it, free, packaged in vesicles, or caught in neutrophil traps. Sensors such as TLR9 and cGAS-STING read it as danger. They trigger inflammasomes and waves of IL-6, TNF, and interferon signals across endothelium, heart muscle, and organs. The authors are careful with the claim. They position the DNA leak as one amplifier among phenotype-dependent mechanisms, not the cause. They admit evidence cannot prove it drives the disease. Longitudinal and intervention studies, they say, must settle where it sits in the causal chain.
pmc-13333623:
For newborns with a rare heart defect, Shuo Chen and co-authors asked in a 2026 retrospective study whether gestational age at birth predicts short-term recovery after biventricular repair surgery. The defect is pulmonary atresia with intact ventricular septum.

The study covered 97 children treated at one referral center between 1999 and 2024, including 21 born preterm and 76 born at term. Each extra week of gestation cut the risk of a poor outcome by roughly half in adjusted analysis. A threshold appeared near 37.6 weeks, beyond which risk fell sharply compared with earlier births. The findings help surgical teams judge risk and counsel families when a baby with this rare heart defect is born early.
pmc-13333723:
Yongfu Wang, Li Yang, and Qiang Shi compared two ways to treat femur fractures that occur after surgery for developmental dysplasia of the hip in children, in a 2026 study. The options are elastic stable intramedullary nailing and hip spica casting.

From 396 children treated for hip dysplasia between July 2012 and July 2018, the team identified 18 with fractures after proximal femoral osteotomy. Ten received nailing and eight received casting, and the groups differed clearly in age and fracture pattern, which usually drives the choice. Hospital stay, surgery time, and complications were compared between groups. The small head-to-head series helps surgeons weigh an operation against casting for a rare but troublesome complication of dysplasia treatment.
pmc-13333923:
Yoshio Nishida and co-authors report a cohort study from 2026 on hip shape and thigh bone breaks. The team asked whether a hip socket that forms too shallow before birth changes how the neck of the femur breaks. They studied people treated with surgery at nine hospitals during part of 2023.

Scans showed the shallow socket was linked to one break pattern, while a socket turned too far back was linked to a steeper, less stable pattern. The links held after other traits were taken into account. Readers learn that hip shape may help explain why similar falls lead to quite different breaks.
pmc-13334023:
Sri Priyanka Kommula and co-workers test whether learning from data-rich river basins can help find rainwater harvesting sites in basins with little data, in a 2026 paper. Models need training data, which scarce basins lack. The team worked across three Indian catchments with different climates.

They tried direct transfer, transfer with some local data, and training on all basins at once. Direct transfer failed when key features differed too much between basins. Adding a small share of local data lifted scores a lot in each place. Training on all three basins gave the best results. Two tree-based models coped best with change.
pmc-13335023:
Calum Lindsay and co-authors designed a package of interventions for 'missingness' in healthcare in a 2026 study. Missingness means a repeated pattern of not taking up offered care, which tracks with multiple illnesses, precarious lives, and poor outcomes, while services often respond punitively.

The work braided three strands: a realist review of 253 documents, interviews with 61 informants who know missingness personally or professionally, and co-design with affected people. Together these produced a suite of interventions aimed at the specific, tangled causes that keep people from care, rather than at the missed appointments themselves. The authors argue that engaging with causes, instead of penalizing absence, is the only route that will not widen access inequalities for the patients who most need care.
pmc-13335823:
Xiaoke Nan and co-authors report a 2026 study that tracks a Parkinson's drug inside the living brain. Blood tests often fail to show how a drug behaves where it acts, so the team built a sensing method that reads drug levels in brain tissue in real time. They tested it with safinamide, a drug used for Parkinson's disease.

The sensor showed the drug built up more in a deep brain area than blood levels suggested, and it cleared at a different rate. At the same time, the team watched nerve activity in a vision-linked brain area. Firing there dropped when drug levels peaked and recovered as levels fell. The authors say the tool can help scientists study how brain drugs act and whether they are safe.
pmc-13336423:
Guangming Ma and colleagues study 2026 multi-trigger response H-bonded organic framework nano-carts enabling targeted fungicide release and plant immune regulation. H-bonded organic frameworks offer ordered, metal-free porosity and tunable host-guest links to realize this goal.

The authors therefore built a multi-trigger response system using the F-bearing HOF PFC-1-F as a pesticide carrier and label-free in planta fluorescent marker. Pyraclostrobin (PYR) was packed in PFC-1-F with about 30 wt percent load, and the resulting mix was surface-coated with crab-shell polymer salt (HACC). The HACC shell imparts leaf stickiness and bio-surface fit, thereby enabling enzyme/ROS/pH-fired, site-chosen release of the fungicide while curbing leaks near neutral pH. Under germ-mimicking settings, the composite shows stepwise planned, multi-trigger response release with spread-led rates.
pmc-13336523:
Sariya Khan and colleagues study 2026 the share of eating disorders among young adults in the west of Saudi Arabia. Eating disorders are complex mental health conditions, with a higher share among young adults aged 18 to 26. They involve breaks in eating habits, thoughts, and feelings, with big physical and mental effects.

There is now a lack of eating disorder share studies in the west of Saudi Arabia. Such studies help health workers and policy makers spot at-risk groups and weigh the burden of eating disorders in the region. They can build fact-based plans to tackle this public health issue. They can also raise awareness, cut stigma, and improve timely care access for people in need. The study ran 6 months, from September 2023 to February 2024, with 390 young adults aged 18 to 26 in the west of Saudi Arabia. It used an Arabic version of the Eating Disorder Examination Questionnaire.
pmc-13336623:
Xu leads a large team building printed magnetic sensors with machine learning, in work from twenty twenty-six. Next generation electronics demand sensors that are green to make, flexible, clear, and smart at once. Magnetoresistive sensors detect magnetic fields for interactive devices.

Their vertical sensor design is printed from tailored inks, making it transparent and bendable. Machine learning at the system level interprets signals for multimodal interaction. Device, algorithm, and system were designed together rather than apart. The result points toward interactive magnetic electronics that can be printed like circuits on flexible films.
pmc-13336923:
In a 2026 chemistry study, Yuewen Wu and co-workers built a new catalyst for splitting water to release oxygen. The rebuilt surface embeds the ruthenium in a nickel oxyhydroxide layer joined by short ruthenium-oxygen-nickel bridges.

Tests and theory together showed the rebuilt catalyst grabs hydroxide ions well, raising the cover of oxygen radicals on its surface. A shorter gap between ruthenium and nickel also lets two oxygen radicals join more easily, so the reaction shifts to a faster oxide path. The result is a catalyst design that makes oxygen release cheaper in energy and quicker in rate.
pmc-13337123:
Jiaying Zhang leads a large 2026 team trapping an intermediate gas inside catalyst pores to make two-carbon products from carbon dioxide. Composition formed a volcano pattern, peaking at the version with 15 wt.% silver and 40 wt.% copper in the catalyst series. That version reached a top C2 Faradaic efficiency of 75.4% at −1.4 V in half-cell tests and kept 63.5% efficiency at high current in a full membrane device during the reported runs. Spectra and calculations confirmed spillover and confinement raise surface coverage and coupling speed.
pmc-13337423:
Emily Jones and Kiki Cano-Gamez review loose DNA as both driver and marker of lupus in a 2026 article. In systemic lupus, the immune system attacks self-DNA. Dying cells release cell-free DNA, normally cleared by the nuclease DNASE1L3. Its fragment lengths, end patterns, jaggedness, and chemical marks can signal disease activity.

When DNASE1L3 is missing or blocked by cross-reacting autoantibodies, DNA fragments grow more provocative. They fire interferon signaling through plasmacytoid dendritic cells, pushing B cells to make anti-DNA antibodies and worsening inflammation. The review ties these mechanisms to therapies targeting interferon and those dendritic cells, while warning that large-scale validation and standard tests are still needed for precision care.
pmc-13337523:
Wenyan Wang and colleagues profile 30 Chinese children with Gitelman syndrome, a salt-losing kidney tubule disorder, in a 2026 study spanning cases from 2015–2025. Onset came at a mean age of 7.9 years in the cohort, with muscle weakness in 50% of children and limb numbness in 40% of children in the symptom tally. Genetic testing found 55 variants in the SLC12A3 gene, 6 of them novel, led by two frequent changes. Which protein domain a variant hit did not predict symptoms, so the authors urge early screening and long follow-up.
pmc-13337723:
Tanmoy Ghatak replied in 2026 to comments on liver stiffness scans in very sick patients, backing their role as a live, pain free marker. Liver stiffness reflects a mix of vein blockage, swelling, and blood flow problems, and the first viewpoint cast it as a step from raw signal toward bedside use. Critics asked how far the scan can be trusted on its own.

Ghatak agrees it should not stand alone, since long term liver disease, breathing machines, blood pressure drugs, and belly pressure all shift readings. Its worth lies inside broad checks next to vein scans and blood flow data. Used that way, it can help doctors track shifting body states in intensive care rather than give one lone diagnosis.
pmc-13338223:
Yixing Guo and co-authors score in 2026 how inflammatory the everyday diet of adults in Ganzhou, China, looks on paper, and how that score tracks with metabolic trouble. Among men, age and even starting to smoke nudged scores upward. The authors read the web of links as a case for targeted anti-inflammatory eating advice. They propose folding the score into chronic disease prevention systems so dietary guidance can be personalized rather than broadcast.
pmc-13338723: Keda Cao and co-authors issued a 2026 correction. It covers only the funding note of a study on jaw deformity care. The note was wrong as printed. Support had in fact been received. Three named programs in Shaanxi and China gave the grants. The corrected note lists them. The rest of the study stands unchanged.
pmc-13340023:
Ángel Sebastián Rodríguez-Pazmiño and seven co-authors race three commercial PCR kits against classic methods for spotting tuberculosis bacteria in patient samples, in a low-income, high-burden setting. Six tin frames were read with new spin tricks that can catch very wide spreads. Sums from first rules were set next to the reads. The sums matched the core read well but fell short on the spread each time. That miss tells sum makers where their models of the lone pair need work. Truer sums would help design new frames.
pmc-13374123:
Yavuz, Onder, Sen, Sahin, and Yilmaz study body measurements in native goat breeds in twenty twenty-six. Such measurements can help tell breeds apart in the field. The team asked whether that power changes as animals grow. They measured four Turkish breeds at birth, at weaning, and at one year of age.

They took six body measures, such as height at the withers and chest girth. Statistical methods reduced the measures and then sorted goats by breed. Sorting worked best in mature animals, with a correct rate above ninety percent. That rate was much higher than at birth. Chest measures were the most useful traits for sorting. The authors advise using mature age measurements for breed work.
pmc-13374323:
Satimanon and four co-authors tracked how long treated baby molars survive in twenty twenty-six. Pulpectomy, a root canal for primary teeth, is used when infection reaches the tooth's tip. Long-term survival data for infected primary molars were scarce, so the team reviewed records at a Thai university clinic.

Three hundred twenty-six molars from two hundred forty-two children aged three to six were followed. About fourteen percent failed. Survival was perfect at one year and about ninety-five percent at two years, but fell to roughly fifty-two percent by four years. A preoperative sinus tract, a small drainage channel, was the most consistent failure predictor, raising risk about fivefold. Older age and advanced root resorption also raised risk in the main analysis. Treatment details like visit count or filling material did not matter.
pmc-13376423:
Mingye Ding and co-authors build a light-switching material in a 2026 study. The material glows when lit with unseen light, a trick called upconversion, and such glow can encode hidden marks. Switching that glow back and forth in a fixed material, under outside control, has been a hard goal.

Their crystals pair missing oxygen spots with erbium, a rare earth element that emits the glow. Ultraviolet light and water washing take turns, flipping the glow with strong contrast and little wear over many cycles. Tests and theory tie the switching to the interplay of the gaps and the erbium. The team shows colour and brightness displays that change in space and time, aimed at anti-faking marks.
pmc-13376623:
Roshana Sattari, Gholam Reza Khayati, and Esmaeel Darezereshki test a plant-based shield against rust in a study published in 2026. Carbon steel rusts fast in salty water, and plant extracts alone often protect poorly in neutral settings. The team paired lavender extract with zinc ions to form a hybrid inhibitor.

In salty solution tests, the mix cut the corrosion current sharply, reaching about ninety-two percent protection at the best dose. Readings showed a strong protective layer forming on the steel surface. Light and surface tests confirmed the plant compounds bind with zinc at the surface. Computer simulations backed the strong binding. The authors present the mix as a green option to replace harsher rust blockers.
pmc-13376823:
Yajuan Zhao and others review the two-way link between ferroptosis and macrophage polarisation in a 2026 paper. Ferroptosis is iron-driven lipid peroxidation cell death, while macrophage polarisation reflects immune plasticity. Evidence now points to deep bidirectional interplay through iron metabolism, lipid signals, and axes such as RAGE-STAT3. The review surveys routes and their roles in tumours, inflammation, heart, and brain disease.

Pro-inflamed M1 immune cells can trigger ferroptosis through cytokines and reactive oxygen species, while M2 immune cells suppress it by managing iron and protective defences. The review also weighs therapies targeting the ferroptosis-macrophage axis. It gives researchers a framework for precise actions that tune cell death and immune state together, rather than treating either process alone.
pmc-13376923:
Patrícia Brito, Victoria Gil, Ana Pontes, Margarida Silva, Carla Gonçalves, and Paula Gonçalves published a 2026 yeast genetics study on how foreign genes survive after jumping between species. Two yeast genera they study carry far more horizontally transferred genes than any other yeasts, close to six hundred between three species. Where those genes land in the genome turns out to matter.

Most transferred genes were metabolic, bringing new functions or restoring lost ones. Gene activity measures showed foreign genes run quieter than native ones. They cluster in large, terminal chromosome regions with low overall expression, which the team calls End domains. In one species, those domains let foreign proteins diversify faster. Quiet neighborhoods, they argue, shelter new genes while they adapt.
pmc-13378023:
Jacob A Orkwis and co-authors read worm takes on a human fire part in a 2026 study. Gut worms make kin of a human part that fans fire, and they use them as arms in the host. Such arms could be hit to lift worm loads, a wide ill.

The team found a wide set of the kin in worm code banks and checked their shapes. A picked set then faced man-made tests: work acts, grip to the part's own port, and talk through two more ports. The kin kept the core shape yet gave wide acts from small shifts. That spread is the tale of how worms tune man's fire.
pmc-13379523:
Jinyu Chen measured how far early life-span guesses miss the mark in cost analyses of immune checkpoint drugs, in a 2026 study. Quality-adjusted life year estimates lean on trial life data, but immature data force projection past observed follow-up. Checkpoint drugs complicate that step with delayed responses and long life tails.

The team rebuilt patient-level data from published life curves of pivotal trials for drugs approved in China, then compared early guesses with updated follow-up at a shared horizon. A split-survival model using overall and progression-free life spans fed the life-year math. The comparison sizes up projection error, helping payers judge how much trust early cost claims deserve.
pmc-13380423:
Tanun Jitwatcharakomol and colleagues compared single-dose intraoperative radiation with whole-breast radiation in suitable breast cancer patients, in a 2026 retrospective cohort study. Intraoperative electrons had shown higher same-breast recurrence than whole-breast external beam therapy, yet a subset of patients might still suit the shorter option. The team reviewed 204 patients treated from 2011 to 2021, with 74 receiving intraoperative therapy and 130 receiving whole-breast therapy.

Median follow-up reached 5.1 years. Five-year disease-free survival was 95.61 percent with intraoperative therapy versus 98.08 percent with whole-breast therapy, and local control was 98.46 percent versus 100 percent. The gap, though modest, favors whole-breast treatment even in carefully chosen patients and tempers enthusiasm for the single-dose shortcut.
pmc-13380523:
Jose Garcia and co-authors move a chest muscle to aid a weak shoulder in a 2026 paper. A reverse shoulder swap works well when the deltoid muscle is sound. When the deltoid is dead, lift and joint stability both fail, and the swap alone falls short.

Past fixes moved the whole chest muscle, which scars wide and warps looks. Garcia moves just its clavicle head, still on its blood stem. That part keeps strength and reach while the rest of the muscle stays put. Rehab is less odd, since less of the lift path changes. The paper sets out the cut and its grounds.
pmc-13380723:
S Brown, E Best, and A Kirby wrote a 2026 letter on drug-resistant gut bacteria found in waste water inside a hospital building. Resistant bacteria living in patients are linked to hospital drains and sink traps, which can release them back onto wards through blockages or fine sprays. Most earlier work followed outbreaks in intensive care units.

Their study, at a large teaching hospital trust in Leeds in July 2024, looked beyond intensive care. Samples were taken throughout one hospital building to check for bacteria resistant to commonly used antibiotics, not only the most feared types. Finding such bacteria matters because routine prevention may be missing routes by which they reach patients.
pmc-13380823:
Claire C Russell and colleagues describe a 2026 case where a special stain revealed the cause of gut bleeding in a woman with amyloidosis. In this disease, misfolded protein chains deposit in organs and can make gut vessels fragile. Their patient was a 65-year-old woman whose disease already affected her heart and kidneys.

She arrived passing blood from the bowel. An early camera examination found a large clot but no active bleeding. Days later the bleeding returned heavily, and samples taken from an ulcer at the clot site were examined. The title refers to the Congo Red stain used to prove amyloid in tissue. The case shows why this disease belongs on the list of bleeding causes.
pmc-13381523:
Yuyang Xia and co-authors published an engineering paper in 2026 on making fake fabric faults with computer models so real faults are easier to spot. Real fault samples are scarce, and thin scratches are hard to catch yet matter for cloth grading. Older generators chase lifelike images but lose the long, unbroken shape of real faults. The team built a system aimed at detection, not just looks.

Their system, called GAN-PD, uses parts that focus on fault-relevant detail and enforce line flow along the fault. Tests on a benchmark cloth dataset gave sharper thin faults and smoother blending with the weave. Detectors trained with the fake faults found real ones more accurately than with rival generators.
pmc-13381723:
Dan Nakamura and a large team create and test a Japanese version of a questionnaire on odd self-experiences tied to schizophrenia. Their study was published in twenty twenty-six. A disturbed basic sense of self is a core feature of the illness, and the original inventory measures it well, but no Japanese form existed.

The study enrolled one hundred and eighty-two people: eighty-three with schizophrenia and ninety-nine healthy comparisons. All took the new Japanese form, plus standard symptom and mood scales for checking. Every domain and the total score ran higher in the schizophrenia group. Consistency of the form was good. Scores also lined up with symptom scales in the patient group. The team concludes the Japanese version is reliable and valid for clinic and research use.
pmc-13381823:
Peiyue Jiang and eight co-authors test a nanoparticle therapy for preeclampsia in mice. Preeclampsia is a severe pregnancy problem driven by placental dysfunction and oxidative stress, with no targeted therapy yet. Their particles are lipid based, modified with folic acid, and loaded with polydopamine plus a kinase called NUAK1.

In cells under stress, they lower reactive oxygen species and hold back the NLRP3 inflammasome. They also promote protective autophagy and cut cell death. In a drug induced mouse model of the disease, treatment makes placental structure and fetal growth better. This dual action, calming the inflammasome while boosting autophagy, offers a promising path ahead.
pmc-13381923:
Kaixin Tang and co-authors map the many magnetic states of a honeycomb magnet as a field is applied, in a research paper from 2026. The material, Na3Ni2BiO6, has its magnetic atoms on a honeycomb grid with spin one. Strong quantum effects in such grids can produce a rich set of states.

The team measured heat and other bulk traits while raising the field step by step. At one third of full magnetization, the material held at least three distinct states with nearly the same net pull, split by sharp jumps. Past that plateau, the system passed through many more odd phases before all spins aligned. Heat upturns at very low temperatures hint that some of these phases hide ordered ground states.
pmc-13382523:
Vanessa Vento, Luis Cabeza-Osorio, and Erika Esperanza Lozano-Rincon present a 2026 case series, written in Spanish, on infections that follow BCG therapy placed directly into the bladder. That treatment is the standard add-on for bladder cancer that has not invaded muscle. Infections from it are uncommon but can be severe and take many forms.

Four cases treated at their centre between 2019 and 2025 illustrate the range. Diagnosis is hard because standard cultures and DNA tests detect the organism in only a minority of cases. The first case involved a 77-year-old man who developed testicle pain and low fever after his second treatment, with all cultures negative. The series underlines clinical suspicion as key.
pmc-13383223:
Yuzhou Zhang and colleagues hunt blood proteins linked to future cataract in a 2026 UK Biobank cohort study. Nearly 49,581 adults without cataract at the start took part, and 2,920 plasma proteins were tested against later disease. Genetic methods then probed which links might be causal rather than mere markers.

Fifty-eight proteins tied significantly to cataract risk, led by a lens protein, beta-crystallin B2, with the strongest signal. Genetic analyses supported causal roles for four proteins, with the lens protein backed by shared genetic evidence. Pathway results pointed to immune activity, cell fate choices, and tissue remodeling as routes worth targeting for early prevention.
pmc-13383423:
Tang Tang's team reports psoriasis triggered by the heart drug sacubitril/valsartan, in a 2026 case report and literature review. The drug is widely used for high blood pressure and heart failure, with known risks such as swelling, low pressure, and kidney effects, but skin disease had drawn little attention. A middle-aged man grew sharp-edged red and purplish scaly plaques on the drug.

Topical clobetasol and switching to ramipril brought marked improvement, yet plaques returned when the drug was restarted. The patient had also developed the rash on nifedipine before. The positive restart test strengthens the causal case and warns doctors to consider drug-induced skin disease in new rashes.
pmc-13385223:
Jianan Zhao and co-authors turn a standard balance test for older adults into a camera-based game and validate it, in a study from 2026. Falls injure and kill many older people, and clinic balance tests are subjective and hard to access. A skeleton-tracking camera can score the same test at home or in a community hall.

A small first phase checked the digital scores against clinician scores in ten adults. A randomized trial in thirty community-dwelling adults then compared a gamified interface with a plain one. The game layer aimed to lift the user experience without hurting score quality. Participants were recruited from a Shanghai community. The authors present the tool as a scalable path to routine balance checks.
pmc-13385423:
Bao Q. Thai and colleagues trace how WNT signals prepare stem cells to form hormone-responsive gut-layer tissue in 2026 work. Human pluripotent stem cells can supply immune cells for therapy, but only through the right early tissue steps. Early WNT activation pushed cells toward a marked mesoderm type needed for later T cell growth.

Single-cell gene and chromatin maps charted the path, and network models fingered the regulator HDAC2. Removing HDAC2 blocked the key step, adding more of it boosted yields, and blocking it with drugs had the same blocking effect. The findings suggest practical ways to raise lymphocyte output from stem cells.
pmc-13385723:
Ayesha Kafeel and colleagues examine how a desert shrub copes with salt and drought across sites near Sargodha, Pakistan, in 2026 work. Capparis decidua thrives in arid lands, but populations face differing local stress mixes. Samples from Shahpur faced the strongest salinity, while Chak 48 NB offered richer soil organic matter.

Shahpur plants grew tallest with the longest roots, thicker skin layers, and more support tissue for holding water. Their light-protecting pigments ran higher while chlorophyll stayed stable under stress. Grouping analysis split Shahpur cleanly from the other sites, which the authors read as a stress-adapted trait suite worth probing at molecular level.
pmc-13385823:
Julia Kaiser and seven co-authors identify a direct cortex to brainstem circuit for skilled forelimb movement in this 2026 paper. Skilled movement depends on cortical neurons that project downward to the brainstem and cord. The team found a subset that projects only to the brainstem, from the earliest stage of axon growth, and never reaches the cord. During development, these neurons can be picked out by one marker gene, Npy. In adults, they aim mainly at rostral brainstem motor areas.

Silencing the marked neurons in mice impaired the precision and targeting of reaching. The circuit thus carries part of the skill signal, not a redundant copy. The authors read the result as a developmental logic: molecular programs laid down early sort descending neurons into channels. That sorting can now be used to study one channel at a time.
pmc-13386923:
Sin-Wook Park's team reports presumed acute heart muscle damage in a British Shorthair cat with prior hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, in a 2026 case report. Reversible heart thickening can follow acute injury from stress, toxins, or systemic illness, but had not been reported in cats with pre-existing HCM. A 6-year-old castrated male British Shorthair first seen for a heart murmur showed a maximum left ventricular wall thickness of about 8 millimeters and earned an HCM diagnosis.

Three days later the cat returned after eating paracetamol. In hospital it developed congestive heart failure, with pleural effusion and diffuse lung changes on X-ray, wall thickness up to about 11 millimeters, and an enlarged left atrium. Stopping fluids and giving diuretics improved its condition, and six months later thickening persisted near the first measurement. The case urges clinicians to weigh acute damage atop chronic disease when wall thickness jumps in sick cats.
pmc-13387423:
Ankita Shrivastava and a large team map selective protein production under mutant KRAS control in 2026 work. Mutant KRAS drives many cancers, yet how it steers which messages get translated stayed poorly defined. The team charted KRAS-dependent translation programs and how they remodel fast when KRAS is blocked.

A chosen message subset, including messages for the protein-making machinery itself, answered to KRAS in their data. Those messages share short, weakly folded leader regions and low-energy sequence motifs. Ribosomes piled up on the selected messages, which the authors read as a distinct control route apart from known mTOR and initiation factor paths.
pmc-13388423:
Stefania Morelli and colleagues present a careful sequencing workflow in 2026 for naming species from tiny amounts of badly damaged DNA. The method was built for hard cases in ecology, wildlife crime work, museum study, and efforts to protect rare species, where old material often leads to false matches.

The workflow combines very small sampling, special library preparation, removal of duplicate reads, mapping against a chosen set of reference genomes. A final check then separates reads unique to one species from reads shared across close relatives. Tests on collagen-rich material showed correct identification from pieces as small as one square millimetre, even in mixtures. Readers gain a cautious approach that favours accuracy over speed.
pmc-13390023:
Mohannad AbuHaweeleh and co-authors test a bandage laced with juniper oil against drug-resistant germs, in work from 2026. Resistance now blunts many standard antibiotics, above all in hospitals. Plant oils with a long folk history offer one fresh source of leads.

The bandage is spun from fine polymer fibers soaked with the oil. Tests used a tough panel of hospital germs known for resistance, covering both drug-sensitive and drug-resistant strains. Growth curves and killing tests measured direct attack on the germs. Separate tests checked whether the bandage could break the slime shields germs build on surfaces. Positive results would support a low-cost dressing for hard wounds.
pmc-13390223:
Mariana Reyes-Prieto's team weighed energy-use-linked networks across 101 insect inner-guest genomes to see what change over time leaves behind as genomes shrink fast inside host cells. Free-living germs keep spare, robust networks. Inner guests shed genes until their networks are smaller than the supposed minimum for independent life.

Genome size tracked network traits such as clumping, width, and node count, yet the shrunken networks kept a scale-free shape, keeping essential links. Network shape also echoed germ family trees, showing that even the most reduced energy uses carry readable change signals about their hosts and ancestors.
pmc-13390323:
Manjula Manikandan's team surveyed mental health among 330 Irish children with brain palsy aged six to 17, using a standard troubles survey plus check and social gauges. Brain palsy services often focus on body needs, leaving mental health under-mapped.

Mean troubles scores sat in the edge range, twenty-nine percent were at risk for feeling and conduct problems, and twenty-one percent had at least one mental illness on record, most often worry. Learning limits, poor sleep, friendship trouble, bullying, and family strain model worse scores. Girls and less active children faced higher illness odds, showing a need for focused support.
pmc-13391223:
Dave K Garg and Jeffrey Wei report, in 2026, substantial weight loss with a daily diabetes injection in a young man with a rare genetic obesity syndrome. Smith-Magenis syndrome drove excessive hunger and rapid weight gain despite portion control and behaviour support over five years.

With prediabetes, abnormal lipids, and fatty liver emerging, the team started liraglutide, a GLP-1 receptor agonist, and raised it gradually to the maximum dose over five months. The patient tolerated it without severe stomach side effects and, with lifestyle support, lost a large amount of weight over eleven months. Endocrine readers gain a single-case signal that appetite-targeting drugs can work even when obesity has a strong genetic driver.
pmc-13392423:
Dimakopoulou and colleagues test whether virtual reality can soften food avoidance in anorexia nervosa, in 2026 neuroscience research. Women with anorexia, 29 patients, and 31 controls completed sessions: a baseline plus illusion sessions in VR where they embodied avatars slimmer or larger. Each session measured responses to food images in a binocular rivalry task, and approach-avoidance behavior toward high- and low-calorie foods. It measured body-size guesses and questionnaires.

At the start, patients showed salience of, and stronger avoidance toward, high-calorie foods than controls, matching the disorder's pattern. Embodying a larger avatar attenuated that bias in patients, while controls shifted the reverse way under the same trick. The manipulation transiently rewired implicit food biases in opposite directions depending on group. Dimakopoulou suggests body-illusion therapy might loosen the automatic bias that sustains it, a possible adjunct to treatment worth testing.
pmc-13392623:
Mengying Xiao and co-authors describe a 70-year-old woman whose slipped lumbar disc was treated with a hook-shaped needle worked beside the spine under local anaesthetic. She had lived with on-and-off back pain for more than ten years, then developed leg pain and numbness over two weeks. Scans showed herniations at two low levels plus a loose fragment pressing the nerve.

After the needle procedure her pain scores fell sharply, walking returned to normal, and leg strength recovered fully over follow-up. Later imaging showed the loose fragment had vanished, and no relapse appeared within a year. The authors are careful to note that such fragments often shrink on their own, so one case cannot prove the needle caused the change, and controlled trials would be needed.
pmc-13393523:
Hiram H Plata-Huerta and five colleagues watched for patulous Eustachian tube after bariatric surgery. In this ear condition the pressure tube stays open. Rapid weight loss has been blamed for it in earlier reports. Fifty-two patients having bypass or sleeve operations were examined before surgery, just after, and at three months, using Japanese diagnostic criteria plus a standard symptom questionnaire. Average weight loss by three months was substantial.

No patient met the bar for definite disease at any visit. Possible cases crept up from about a tenth before surgery to just under a quarter at three months, a shift that did not reach significance, and symptom scores stayed flat. Weight loss size did not track ear outcomes. The authors suspect earlier high rates reflect loose diagnostic standards, and they recommend symptom-driven checks over routine screening early after surgery.
pmc-13393623:
Qiuzhe Chen and four co-authors report a 2026 study of opioid use for back pain in Australian hospitals. Strong pain drugs are often given to patients admitted with low back pain, yet high daily doses carry real risks. The team asked how much patients actually received, and which patients were most likely to get high doses.

The researchers read records from three public hospitals in Sydney, covering thousands of emergency visits from 2016 to 2021. Nearly all admitted patients received opioids, and about one in six got a high daily dose. High doses were more common for younger patients, men, patients from poorer areas, and those found to have a serious cause for their pain. The authors call for wider use of proven non-drug and non-opioid options to bring these doses down.
pmc-13393723:
Rafael Hortêncio Melo and Chiara Robba argue that transcranial Doppler ultrasound, a bedside probe of blood flow speed inside the brain, can personalise blood pressure targets after acute brain injury. Standard care chases fixed perfusion pressure thresholds, yet the right pressure likely differs by patient and hour as vessel resistance and self-regulation shift. Doppler measures such as diastolic flow velocity and the pulsatility index expose how the brain's circulation answers each pressure change.

Watching those signals while clinicians adjust arterial pressure in controlled steps could reveal the range where an individual's brain perfusion looks healthiest. The authors insist Doppler never be read alone: cardiac output, fluid responsiveness, and the cause of low pressure belong in the same picture, inside multimodal monitoring. They present the piece as a viewpoint mapping rationale, uses, and current limits.
pmc-13394723:
Yi Zhen Bao and colleagues review, in 2026, a young method for testing the lining of brain blood vessels in people. The method watches the neck artery widen when extra carbon dioxide raises brain blood flow. That widening reflects nitric oxide from the vessel lining, much like a known arm test. Early studies have tried the method after exercise, in heat and cold, and across ages and sexes.

Some results match the arm test, while others break away, such as with smoking or long sitting. The review weighs the two ways of raising gas levels and the hitches in each. The authors sketch next steps toward clinic use.
pmc-13395423:
Lisa A. Niemann leads a 2026 account of how bedside nucleic acid tests for HIV were rolled out in Seattle. Such tests catch infection earlier than antibody kits and give virus counts on the spot. The study ran at a hospital clinic and a community centre from 2022 to 2024. People seeking tests or prevention drugs, and people living with HIV, joined different arms.

More than seven hundred people completed study visits. Each got standard care plus a bedside test and lab checks for comparison. Subsets answered surveys and interviews on how the tests felt. Staff also timed clinic flow. The authors lay out the full protocol as a model for wider rollout studies.
pmc-13395823:
Boryeu Mao, a bioinformatician, reworks the E value that BLAST reports when it matches a new sequence against known ones. A low E value marks a strong match, but comparing E values across very different searches can mislead. The mix-up stems from treating one number as both a likeness score and its opposite.

Through a simulated setup, Mao shows that adjusting the E value for self-matching fixes odd comparisons that crop up between searches. The corrected score behaves more like a true distance: it gains the reflexivity and triangle rules that metric spaces demand. In practice, the fix sharpens clustering of sequences and the picking of diverse subsets. The paper aims at cleaner all-against-all comparisons in big databases.
pmc-13396423:
Prateek D. T. and co-authors compared the prices of branded and generic creams for skin fungal infections in India, in a 2026 pharmacoeconomic study. These infections, called superficial mycoses, are common in tropical climates, need long treatment, and often return, so the price of each tube matters to households.

The authors gathered prices for the same antifungal drugs across many brands and measured the spread between the cheapest generic and the costliest branded twin. Wide gaps for identical medicine mean doctors can cut a patient's bill sharply by prescribing choice alone. The study frames antifungal pricing as a resource question for clinics as much as a shopping question for patients.
pmc-13396623:
Junaid Younus is the lead author of a 2023 RSC Advances study on tuning nickel sulphide films with zinc for solar uses. The Royal Society of Chemistry wholly retracted that study in a 2026 notice. The publisher states that concerns over the reliability of the data forced the withdrawal.

Two microscope images in the paper had already appeared elsewhere, described there as a different material. Two pairs of light-absorbance charts also looked strongly alike across figures that should have shown separate results. The authors replied and supplied new data, but the response did not settle the concerns. The original raw data could not be produced, so the retraction covers the whole article.
pmc-13396723:
Yanjiao Liang and co-authors fed a Chinese herbal mixture to chickens infected with H9N2 bird flu and measured whether the blend fights the virus and calms the inflammation it causes. Their 2026 study uses specific pathogen-free chickens, a clean test population for a virus that costs poultry farms heavily and can infect people.

Vaccines lose ground as the virus surface keeps drifting, so alternatives are in demand. Birds given the Siji antiviral mixture carried far less virus in liver, spleen, lung, kidney, brain, and windpipe than untreated infected birds. The mixture also turned down the excessive inflammatory response the infection provokes, a dual action the authors back with tissue-level measurements.
pmc-13396923:
Jiaxin Zheng and co-authors review how labs measure acylcarnitines, a family of molecules that ferry fatty acids into mitochondria, in a 2026 article. Best known from newborn screening for inherited metabolic faults, these markers now show promise in heart disease, diabetes, and drug injury.

Measuring them well is hard: family members span a wide range of water-loving and fat-loving behavior, their levels differ by orders of magnitude, and near-identical isomers hide among them. The review tours sample preparation and detection platforms, with liquid chromatography at the center, and weighs where each method strains. A closing section maps clinical uses that better measurement could unlock.
pmc-13397523:
Jessica Berns, Justin L Anderson and Detlev Erdmann reviewed the portal messages sent to one plastic surgeon at Duke University Hospital. Their 2026 study spans 18 months, from July 2023 through December 2024. Secure messaging helps patients stay in touch, but each note adds work, and plastic surgeons also face pressure from public ratings.

Every message was logged by topic, timing and patient details, then stored in a secure REDCap database for study. Patterns in the inbox show what patients most often ask before and after surgery. Spotting the common themes points to clearer handouts and pre-visit guidance, which could trim message load while keeping patients informed and doctors less strained.
pmc-13397823:
Jianqing Li and a large team scan the protein-coding genome for genes that shape the retina and its diseases. Their 2026 study uses whole-exome data from 356,982 UK Biobank participants. The retina is a reachable outpost of the brain, yet the coding variants behind its structure, its function and its blinding diseases were only sketchily known.

Gene-level tests of rare variants found 22 strong links across 16 genes, 12 of them new, with most backed in a second cohort of 245,388 people. Common variant scans added 243 independent signals in 126 genes. Three genes (CFI, C3 and RIOX1) touched structure, function and disease alike, and a new gene, FYB2, was picked for lab follow-up.
pmc-13399323:
Pattara Kanoksing and colleagues genotyped adults with asthma to see which cytokine gene variants track with the disease's inflammatory patterns, in a 2026 cross-sectional study. Asthma driven by type 2 inflammation depends heavily on interleukin-4, interleukin-5, and interleukin-13. These proteins drive allergy responses and eosinophil production. Inherited changes in their genes influence asthma, but links to specific patterns needed clarifying.

The study enrolled 125 adults and tested seven variants across the IL33, IL4, IL5, and IL13 genes. One IL5 variant, rs2069812, stood out. Each extra copy of its T version raised eosinophil counts in a dose-like pattern and lowered post-bronchodilator lung function. Carriers faced more than double the prevalence of blood eosinophilia in the reported analysis. An IL13 variant, rs1800925, was tied to higher Th2 cell counts and fixed airflow obstruction. The authors propose both variants as markers for sorting asthma patients into precise treatment groups.
pmc-13399523:
Haein Kim, Seungwon Shin, and Kuo-Cherh Huang analyzed a decade of national insurance claims to show how South Korea's long-term care hospitals have quietly become end-of-life settings, in a 2026 study. The team built three views from claims filed between 2014 and 2023: yearly inpatient trends, profiles of newly admitted patients, and the final trajectories of patients who died.

Deaths involving a long-term care hospital stay climbed from 68,357 in 2014 to 112,157 in 2023. New patients typically arrived in their early eighties, at a median age of 81, and 62.1 percent were women in the admission profile. Those who died had spent a median of 79 days as inpatients, and 68.5 percent of them died inside the hospital itself. The authors call for palliative care and advance planning to be built into these hospitals.
pmc-13399923:
Ping-Chen Chen and nine co-authors studied what happens inside stomach cancer cells given healthy mitochondria, in a paper from twenty twenty-six. Mitochondria are the cell's power units, and moving them from healthy stomach cells into cancer cells was already known to make the cancer less aggressive. The team wanted to learn why.

Protein and small-molecule scans showed wide rewiring of the cancer cells. Key growth and stress proteins shifted, and fuel use changed so that a building block called pyruvate piled up inside the cells. That buildup alone slowed the cancer cells' movement. pmc-13400523:

pmc-13400623:

pmc-13400723:

pmc-13400923:

pmc-13401223:
Susanna Williams and co-authors interview speech and language therapists about working with Wernicke's aphasia, in this 2026 study. pmc-13401323:

pmc-13401523:

pmc-13401723:

pmc-13402023:

pmc-13402723:

pmc-13402823:

pmc-13403023:

pmc-13403523:

pmc-13404623:

pmc-13404923:

pmc-13405623:

pmc-13406623:

pmc-13407823:

pmc-13408123:

pmc-13409323:

pmc-13409823:

pmc-13410923:

pmc-13411023:

pmc-13411223:

pmc-13411323:

pmc-13412123:

pmc-13412323:

pmc-13414423:

pmc-13414723:

pmc-13415823:

pmc-13416823:

pmc-13417023:

pmc-13417723:

pmc-13419323:

pmc-13419623:

pmc-13420123:

pmc-13420923:

pmc-13421223:

pmc-13421423:

pmc-13421523:

pmc-13421823:

pmc-13422923:
