pmc-13423623:
Tyler Oliver and co-authors measure in 2026 how men and women weather the Army's Ranger course, a grind of over sixty-one days across harsh ground. Traits like grit, bounce-back, sleep, and strength have been tracked there, but not split by sex since women joined in 2015. Thirty-seven candidates, ten of them women, were tested before and after.

Men showed higher raw strength and jump power at both ends, the team reports. Both sexes lost similar amounts by the end. Sleep soured for all, with quality, length, and daytime function all down. Grit and bounce-back scores started high and held. The shared slide suggests the course taxes bodies the same way, whatever the starting gap.
pmc-13424023:
Muhanned Faisal Towfig and six colleagues systematically review what predicts the return of atrial fibrillation after catheter ablation, a procedure that burns or freezes faulty heart tissue to restore rhythm. Recurrence is common and varies widely between patients, so dependable predictors would sharpen follow-up planning.

Following standard review guidance, the team searched five sources for studies from 2016 to 2026 and screened thousands of records down to 21 studies with multivariable models. Recurring predictors included older age, the persistent form of the rhythm disorder, a larger left atrium, and higher pressure inside it. Because studies differed too much to pool, findings were combined narratively, with bias and certainty graded formally.
pmc-13424123:
Wu and colleagues release a long-run crop calendar in this 2026 dataset paper, mapping when maize passes eight key growth stages across Northeast China, one of the world's great corn belts. Knowing stages from emergence to maturity at field scale guides fertilizer timing, irrigation, pest control, and yield forecasts, but existing products cover few stages.

The dataset spans 2001 to 2024 at 500-meter spatial resolution with daily time steps, built by coupling satellite vegetation data with weather drivers in a gradient-boosted model. Validation against records from 91 agrometeorological stations for 2009 to 2024 gave timing errors under five days on average, with agreement scores above 0.63 for every stage in the reported checks. The maps preserve sensible regional gradients and year-to-year wobbles, offering a benchmark for crop model calibration and climate impact studies.
pmc-13424323:
Qingpeng Han and five colleagues assess nineteen heavily fished species in China's Bohai Sea using five assessment methods designed for data-poor fisheries. The Bohai fleet, like small-scale fleets worldwide, lacks the long catch records that standard models need, so the team leaned on fish length data instead and graded each stock's condition.

Five stocks, 26%, rated sustainable with no risk. Seven more, 37%, were acceptable but need targeted management, while the rest need stronger action: 16% are overfished and 21% face high risk. Advice is matched to status, from effort and quota control to larger minimum landing sizes and wider net mesh. The authors argue such graded management can rebuild stocks, as seen elsewhere.
pmc-13424423:
Naoki Yago, Masami Saito, and Hiroki Yago report a refined flap operation for severe anal stenosis, including the Whitehead deformity, where scarring leaves the opening too narrow. Their method, developed with plastic surgeons, moves nearby skin inward on a deep fat pedicle whose pivot point is shifted toward the midline, letting the flap advance without twisting or tension.

Fifty-two consecutive patients treated between 2021 and 2025, median age sixty-seven, mostly had scarring from earlier surgery or chronic fissure. Of forty-nine who completed six months of follow-up, 48 passed the success test, a dilator of at least 22 millimetres. No flap died. Wound splitting in nine patients healed without surgery within about four weeks.
pmc-13424523:
Lurquin and colleagues examine in 2026 whether ABO blood group changes the risk of microangiopathy, damage to the smallest blood vessels, in type 2 diabetes. Blood group was already known to shift the risk of large-vessel disease.

The single-center study covered 1,006 patients with type 2 diabetes, just over half of whom had some microvascular complication. Patients outside blood group O showed lower insulin sensitivity and weaker beta-cell function, along with higher long-term blood sugar exposure. Overall microvascular damage ran about a quarter higher in non-O patients, and nerve damage showed an even larger gap. After accounting for diabetes duration, blood sugar, smoking, cholesterol remnants, and blood pressure, group A patients still carried clearly higher odds of microvascular damage. The comparison was against group O patients.
pmc-13424623:
Rangxi Jin and seven colleagues test whether training the trunk on unstable surfaces sharpens elite air pistol shooting more than the same training on firm ground. Twenty national-level shooters were randomised for eight weeks. Half used unstable tools such as Swiss balls and balance discs; half trained on stable surfaces. Pressure plates and a laser system measured body sway and gun steadiness in the final second before each shot.

The unstable group improved more on nearly every measure. Sway area shrank by about 11% against about 2%, and scores rose about twice as fast. Steadiness inside the top scoring ring jumped sharply. After strict correction for multiple testing, only the finest stability measure and muzzle control stayed significant, so the authors label the rest exploratory.
pmc-13424723:
Hu and a large team studied two diabetes-linked genes, MYT1 and ST18, that act as gene regulators in human insulin-producing beta cells, asking how they protect those cells from failure. They silenced each gene in donated human islet cells, then measured survival, insulin release, and gene activity in culture and in mice under obesity-related stress.

Silencing MYT1 killed beta cells outright, while silencing ST18 weakened glucose-stimulated insulin secretion by reducing calcium entry into the cells. Under obesity stress in transplanted tissue, ST18 silencing also caused cell death, showing the two regulators back each other up differently. Each gene controlled distinct stress, mitochondria, and ion-channel gene sets in the expression data. Genes regulated by either factor were enriched 2.05-fold for type 2 diabetes risk locations, tying the pair directly to inherited disease susceptibility.
pmc-13425023:
Hörold and colleagues present a protocol for building a survivorship care program. It serves people living with metastatic melanoma, who report unmet needs even as modern treatments extend life. The LeMela project follows the UK Medical Research Council framework and an intervention mapping approach. It builds the program with patients rather than for them.

Phase A combines a scoping review of existing evidence with interviews and focus groups. Those involve survivors, relatives, and health workers. Partners including physicians, psycho-oncologists, nurses, epidemiologists, and health services researchers then merge their knowledge. They use a joint process to shape a theory-based program. Phase B will test whether the program can work, through a pilot study with structure and process review. That will guide whether a full randomized trial is warranted. The project and its short protocol were both pre-registered on the Open Science Framework.
pmc-13426023:
Ross and colleagues bred 55 inbred lines of the dengue mosquito Aedes aegypti in 2026 to test how inbreeding affects fitness and the bacterial community the insects carry. Inbreeding shrinks genetic variety and can sap vigor, which matters for mosquito control programs that rear and release insects. Whether it also reshapes the microbes inside the mosquito was unclear.

Lines were raised from two founding populations and scored for life traits, genetic diversity, and gut bacteria. Fitness costs varied widely: many lines suffered badly, while others held up despite equally low diversity. Bacterial mixes differed a lot between lines but did not track fitness or origin. The authors conclude inbreeding harms fitness unevenly while leaving the microbiome largely to other forces.
pmc-13426123:
Jeongeun Choi and colleagues used a national South Korean survey to study how confidence with digital tools shapes satisfaction with digital change. The survey covered 4,155 adults aged 40 and over, split into middle-aged and older groups.

Older adults reported lower digital confidence, weaker social ties, and less satisfaction than the middle-aged group. Confidence in one's digital skills linked to higher satisfaction in both groups, and the link ran stronger for people with few social ties. Schooling and digital skill also lifted satisfaction, while income mattered only for the middle-aged. Choi urges training that builds digital confidence, above all for older adults with small social networks.
pmc-13427723:
Zhao and colleagues built in 2026 a game-theory model of how attackers and defenders adapt to each other on a network, and how that contest decides whether the network survives disruption. Modern systems are so interlinked that one local failure can cascade, and many failures come from opponents reacting to each other, not from chance. Static defense plans miss that back-and-forth.

In the model, both sides revise their strategies round by round based on past payoffs. The outcome turns on network shape: on uneven networks, where a few hubs hold many links, attackers gain the upper hand, while on even networks defenders prevail. The best attack strategies settled at the network's percolation threshold, the tipping point where it falls apart, across artificial and real networks. The authors argue topology, not just effort, governs resilience.
pmc-13427923:
Tudor-Daniel Huţul, Joshua Grubbs, and three co-authors test a model of problem pornography use in Romanian adults. Their study, from twenty twenty-six, builds the less-studied half of a known model. The model gives two paths to distress: moral conflict and dysregulation. The moral path is well mapped, so this team takes the other.

More than sixteen hundred adults filled out surveys. Items cover rash action, sensation seeking, and trouble steering emotions. Poor emotion control and impulsivity link to distress and to feeling addicted. The measures fit into the dysregulation path as the model predicts. Most of the sample were women in their late twenties on average.
pmc-13428023:
Kgokolo and colleagues reported in 2026 a patient with pemphigus vulgaris, a blistering disease where the immune system attacks the glue between skin cells, whose mouth sores refused standard care. Skin lesions and mouth lesions do not always answer treatment alike. In this case, high-dose steroids cleared the skin, but the mouth disease stayed stubborn.

The turning point was rituximab, an antibody drug that wipes out B cells, the white cells that make the harmful antibodies. After rituximab, the mouth disease finally entered remission. The authors set the case against trial evidence in which most rituximab patients reached full remission off treatment, far more than on steroids alone. They stress tailoring therapy by site, and note a second gain: rituximab spares patients long steroid exposure and its damage to bones, metabolism, and mood.
pmc-13428123:
Barnes and colleagues reviewed in 2026 how giant cell arteritis affects quality of life, how steroid treatment adds to the burden, and how patient-reported measures capture it. The disease inflames large arteries, mostly in women over fifty, and can blind if missed. High-dose steroids control it but add weight, mood, and bone problems of their own.

General health surveys used in trials have shown gains from newer drugs. Symptom scales reveal that about half of patients suffer anxiety and a third depression. Disease-specific and steroid-specific questionnaires have now been validated so patients can describe impact in their own terms, which the authors say improves shared decision making in clinic. Digital versions promise faster triage, but they risk shutting out older patients with low digital access.
pmc-13429023:
Cate V. Cheney and colleagues review, in a 2026 paper, an overlooked link between gut microbes and the most common childhood blood cancer. Acute lymphoblastic leukemia now sees survival above 90 percent in children, yet its harsh treatment leaves lasting harm. Gut bacteria ferment fiber into short-chain fatty acids, small molecules that feed gut lining cells and tune immunity. Evidence in other cancers ties these molecules to treatment response and side effects.

Direct evidence in this leukemia remains sparse, which the authors state plainly. They assemble plausible routes from related fields: the molecules might blunt treatment toxicity, shape immune recovery, and even touch early-life factors tied to leukemia risk. Their aim is to provoke targeted experiments and clinical studies. Supportive care that spares children late effects is the prize motivating the agenda.
pmc-13429123:
Camille Bosc and colleagues compare, in a 2026 study, three artificial lens designs that share the same springy double-loop frame. These toric lenses, implanted at cataract surgery, correct astigmatism, the uneven focusing caused by a misshapen eye front. Sixty-nine eyes received one of three optic designs built on the shared frame, with 23 eyes in each group. Vision, refraction, and lens rotation were checked three months after surgery.

Sharp distance vision was excellent across all three designs, and every lens stayed within ten degrees of its intended angle. One design put every eye within a tight half-diopter of the target refraction. Another gave the finest corrected acuity on average, a small but measured edge. Rotation stayed near one to two degrees in all groups. Surgeons choosing among optic styles on this frame can expect steady positioning either way.
pmc-13429223:
Dilşat Tepe and co-authors review, in a 2026 study, a stubborn breast inflammation and the germ increasingly tied to it. Granulomatous mastitis causes painful breast lumps and abscesses that mimic cancer and resist simple treatment. Records covered 165 women treated at a university hospital between 2018 and 2023. The team compared patients whose samples grew Corynebacterium bacteria with those whose did not.

The germ appeared in about 15 percent of cases, most often the species kroppenstedtii, which hides inside fatty tissue. Positive cases formed more abscesses and needed more procedures. Combined treatment with steroids, antibiotics, and sometimes surgery gave the best outcomes overall. Fat-loving antibiotics paired with steroids looked helpful, though the edge fell short of statistical proof. About 16 percent of patients relapsed, especially those whose symptoms had dragged on before treatment.
pmc-13429323:
Kim Berg Johannessen and co-authors studied why Danish adults stop ADHD medication, in a 2026 paper. The drugs work well, yet registry studies show many quit over time. Past work blamed traits like illness load and income. This study asked patients for their own reasons.

Adults with ADHD reported how they see the condition itself. They weighed the drug gains against its downsides. Choices to live with or without medication were explored by gender too. Self-reports add the inside view that registries miss. Clinics may use the themes to support patients at quit risk.
pmc-13429523:
Doua Elamin and colleagues examine, in a 2026 database study, the rare practice of removing part of the stomach and transplanting a kidney in one operation. Obesity blocks many kidney failure patients from transplant lists, and sleeve gastrectomy can restore eligibility. Doing both at once is tempting but risky. A national bariatric surgery database from 2020 to 2023 held over 580,000 sleeve operations, of which only 22 included a simultaneous kidney transplant.

Those 22 patients were older, more often male, and far sicker at baseline, with more diabetes, high blood pressure, and dialysis dependence. Their operations ran longer and their hospital stays stretched further. Serious complications and readmissions ran higher, and about 9 percent died within thirty days, against about a tenth of a percent for sleeve surgery alone. Adjusted analysis kept the combined operation as the strongest predictor of harm. The authors urge extreme care in selection.
pmc-13429923:
Wenqian Ren, Jing Liang, and Xu Peng warn, in a 2026 study, that China's electric vehicle boom can backfire at the power plant. Electric cars cut street-level emissions, yet charging draws on a grid still dominated by coal. Panel data covered Chinese regions from 2017 to 2022. Statistical methods designed to separate cause from correlation linked vehicle sales growth to power sector emissions.

A 10 percent rise in electric vehicle sales came with about a 0.4 percent rise in power plant carbon emissions. The effect also spilled across plant networks, with plants influencing one another regionally. Scenario modeling showed the picture flips when renewable growth keeps pace with electrified transport. Paired together, clean power and electric driving deliver the deep cuts each promises alone. The authors argue for sequencing the two transitions as one policy, not two.
pmc-13430023:
Qin Wang leads a large team that pins, in a 2026 study, a new inherited brain disorder on faults in a chromatin-shaping gene. Chromatin remodelers open and close DNA to time gene activity, and their failure often disrupts brain development. The gene DMAP1 helps run several of those processes yet had no linked human disease. The team gathered 20 affected people from 16 families, each carrying two damaged copies of the gene.

Fruit flies with the matching gene silenced in the brain died early or showed shrunken learning centers, stunted nerve branches, odd social behavior, and seizures. Adding back the healthy human gene mostly rescued the flies, while patient versions rescued weakly or not at all. Two downstream genes emerged whose boost repaired the damage. A chemical fingerprint on DNA then identified one more patient. Genetic testing panels for developmental disorders gain a new entry.
pmc-13430323:
Chon and colleagues tested whether a liver MRI measure called iron-corrected T1, which reflects liver inflammation and scarring combined, also predicts cancers outside the liver in the general population. They followed 24,003 cancer-free UK Biobank participants with liver imaging and complete data over a median of 4.28 years during the study.

During follow-up, 1,144 participants developed an extrahepatic malignancy, meaning a cancer arising outside the liver itself. Each standard deviation rise in the MRI measure carried a hazard ratio of 1.116 for future cancer after adjustment for demographic, metabolic, and liver factors. People above the 771 millisecond cutoff showed a cumulative incidence of 6.1 percent, versus 4.6 percent below it in the cohort. Older age and male sex also predicted risk, while liver fat fraction pointed the opposite way, leading the authors to suggest the marker captures systemic processes.
pmc-13430523:
Li and colleagues isolated in 2026 three rare sugar-bearing indole compounds from a microbe that lives inside sugarcane. The new finds also corrected the known structure of a relative. The microbe is an actinomycete, a thread-like bacterium prized for new chemistry. Its products carry a cyano group seldom seen in this family.

Two of the compounds, named sugarnitriles A and B, had never been described before. The team worked out their flat structures with mass measurements and magnetic resonance spectra, then pinned down the shape of their sugar parts by comparing signal patterns and light-twisting readings. Those data forced a revision of the structure long assigned to the known relative, SF-2140, in the older literature. Two of the three compounds showed modest to weak power against E. coli in lab tests.
pmc-13430823:
Brice Even and colleagues argue that weight-loss drugs may push big food firms toward poorer countries. GLP-1 medicines such as Ozempic, Wegovy, and Zepbound are spreading fast in rich countries, with clear effects on shopping and eating.

Early United States household data show grocery spending falling about 5 percent within six months of a household member starting a GLP-1 drug. Falls ran bigger for richer households, and bigger still for snacks and energy-dense foods. Firms already sell smaller packs and GLP-1-friendly brands. The paper warns that if rich-world demand for ultra-processed food softens, firms may hedge by marketing harder where regulation is weaker.
pmc-13432523:
Santi Nolasco, Jaime Bernaola, and Parameswaran Nair asked a pointed question in 2026. Could starting targeted biologic drugs early in asthma lift the odds of full calm, or does the hope run ahead of proof? Such drugs aim at key sparks of one asthma type. Calm, by agreed marks, blends quiet symptoms, steady lung tests, and no flare-ups or daily steroid pills.

Across drug kinds, calm stalls at a fifth to two fifths of patients. Wider tests to pick the right drug may push the share higher. Long disease runs cut the odds of calm, since harm and side faults pile up over years. The authors press on weak spots in the early-start case. Calm on the surface may not mean the deep disease has cleared. Mild asthma may never march toward severe forms at all.
pmc-13433823:
McGregor and colleagues build a statistical model for a stubborn problem in microbiome science: samples never catch every species, so diversity counts come out low. Diversity sums up how many species live in a sample and how evenly they share it. Their 2026 paper uses a hierarchical Pitman-Yor process, a flexible probability model. The model can guess the unseen tail of rare species. The team fits it across several populations at once with a sampling algorithm.

Simulations show the fitting method works. Diversity estimates from the fitted model beat naive counts that use only what was seen. The gain is biggest when samples are small, exactly where naive counts fail worst. The team derives a formula for Hill numbers, the family of diversity measures, inside the model. An infant gut dataset shows the method in action. Ecologists gain a way to compare diversity without pretending the sample saw everything.
pmc-13434223:
Jiao Liu and colleagues map in 2026 how a germ builds and exports Psl, a sugar coat that helps it form sticky films on surfaces. The germ is Pseudomonas aeruginosa, a common cause of hard to treat lung illness. The sugar coat moves out through a guarded path that spans the cell wall.

Cryo electron images of two linked proteins show a sealed channel from inside to outside the cell. A third protein likely sits in the channel and links sugar units one by one. Side ports may feed new units in while the chain grows. The model may fit many germs that use the same export route.
pmc-13434423:
Xiaocui Li and a large team settle a puzzle about flaws in perovskite crystals in 2026. These crystals bend at room heat in a way that should need free sliding flaws. Older images showed stuck flaws instead, which clashed with the bendy behavior. A pulsed electron beam let the team view crystals with less beam harm.

With pulses, the true flaws show the free sliding split form that models predict. Steady beams push flaws into the stuck form, and the end shape depends on which atoms line the flaw core. The fix in method matters for any soft crystal study. Device makers gain a truer picture of how these crystals deform.
pmc-13434623:
Hossain and a collaboration report a charge density wave inside a material that should not host one. A charge density wave is a ripple in electron density that repeats. The material, alpha-Bi4Br4, is a band insulator with no Fermi surface. A Fermi surface is the usual breeding ground for such waves. Low-temperature topographic and spectroscopic imaging showed the state in the bulk and at the surface.

The one-way charge pattern appears below 40 kelvin. It breaks the crystal's translational symmetry across regions. It opens an energy gap on top of the compound's existing insulating gap. That deepens the behavior at low temperature. Transport tests showed nonlinear current flow. That sliding behavior is usually tied to incommensurate charge density waves in metals. The authors present this as a charge density wave of a different type. It forces a rethink of where electron states like these can arise.
pmc-13435423:
Büşra Karadağ's team compared eye scans in 2026 among people with early to mid glaucoma, people with high eye pressure but no glaucoma, and healthy controls. Using OCT angiography, they measured macular ganglion cell thickness and small-vessel density near the center of vision in 150 eyes from glaucoma and high-pressure patients plus 50 healthy eyes. Scans were taken at a glaucoma unit in Istanbul over two months in 2022.

High-pressure eyes looked much like healthy eyes on both measures, while glaucoma eyes showed clear drops that grew with disease stage. Vessel loss hit surface layers harder than deep layers, and in early glaucoma, cell layer thinning stood out more than vessel loss. Eye doctors get a staged picture of which retinal change leads, useful for tracking early disease.
pmc-13435523:
André Pereira's team surveyed flea-borne pathogens in Portugal in 2026, screening 1,261 fleas from dogs and cats across the mainland. Fleas plague pets and can carry germs that sicken animals and people, yet nationwide pathogen data were thin. Lab tests targeted Bartonella, Rickettsia, and the tapeworm Dipylidium, with positive samples sequenced and linked to host, flea species, lifestyle, and region.

About a quarter of fleas carried at least one pathogen. Rickettsia appeared in about sixteen percent and Bartonella in about eight percent, the latter more common in fleas from cats, especially strays and shelter animals. Three Bartonella species were named. Vets and public health workers get a national baseline for flea control and for watching spillover risk from pets.
pmc-13435823:
Lonergan and colleagues explore training placements for occupational therapy and physiotherapy students inside research teams, a rarely used setting. Universities struggle to find enough placements as enrolments rise, and research roles could host students if the fit is right. Their 2026 study interviews thirty people: students, therapists who work in research jobs, and university educators, and sorts the transcripts into themes about gains, worries, and barriers.

Views ran positive overall. Placements in research built confidence with evidence, sparked interest in research careers, and still met core skill goals. But some educators doubted every research setting could satisfy accreditation rules, the formal standards a placement must meet. Students feared missing hands on client time, and researchers feared harm to study quality. Seven themes in all were mapped. The authors call for placement models built jointly by universities and research teams, then trialed and judged on real results.
pmc-13436023:
Guanghui Chen, Yang Zou, and Keqian Chen caution that cutoff values for Sporothrix fungi may rest on flawed test heat in 2026. Standard broth tests run at thirty five degrees, which pushes the fungus to shift form mid test. Mixed forms skew the drug levels that set wild type cutoffs.

Yeast form fungi can read eight fold lower drug levels than the thread form. Rejected data sets ran seventeen to thirty percent for one species, the letter notes. A terbinafine cutoff for a second species rests on just thirty eight isolates with a split pattern. The authors urge retesting at thirty degrees before cutoffs harden into clinic rules.
pmc-13436423:
Kei Furui Ebisawa and coauthors test an AI app that reads Gram stains from blood cultures in 2026. Specialists are not always on hand, which delays care. Phone photos from two hospitals cover 126 aerobic and ninety anaerobic samples for the head to head test.

Specialists hit about ninety one percent accuracy on both bottle types. The app reached about seventy five to seventy seven percent, short of parity. Errors clustered on a few tricky germ types, while most common germs read well. Off hours cover is the prize if accuracy climbs. The authors flag the weak germ classes for retraining.
pmc-13436923:
Takashi Wada and co-authors followed surgical patients to learn how often throat growths linked to breathing tubes appear after long operations. Their 2026 study enrolled forty adults at one hospital whose planned surgery was expected to last at least five hours. Most had heart surgery, and the group had a median age of 73 years.

Scope checks of the voice box were done the day after the tube came out, then again at one week, one month, and three months. Growths were found in ten of forty patients at one week, and most cleared on their own within a month. Two grew larger and needed two months of inhaled steroid treatment. Tubes left in for thirteen hours or more raised the risk, as did wider double-lumen tubes. The authors urge care with tube choice and early checks for high-risk patients, though the small single-center group limits firm claims.
pmc-13437323:
Saara Krishnamurthy and colleagues mapped what research says about favorite colours among people with common mental health disorders. Colour has been used as a healing aid for centuries, yet hard evidence stays scarce. Their 2026 scoping review searched four databases for studies that asked diagnosed patients which colour they preferred. Sixteen studies qualified, most using a standard colour test, coloured cards, or screen displays.

Patterns differed by diagnosis. People with depressive disorders leaned toward blue, those with anxiety-related disorders toward grey, and those with schizophrenia toward black. Healthy participants never favored the flat colours black or grey. Healthy groups also varied by region, with Europeans preferring blue and Asian participants red and yellow, while patient groups showed no such geographic pattern. The authors read colour choice as a soft clue tracking diagnosis more than culture among patients, and they stress how thin the research base remains for clinical use.
pmc-13437623:
Anil Kumar Monga and colleagues reviewed real-world records for a paired nasal spray used against allergic rhinitis, the allergy-driven sneezing, blocked, itchy nose. Current guidance backs a steroid plus antihistamine spray as a first choice for moderate to severe cases. Their 2026 study drew on 4,500 patient records from 424 ear, nose, and throat clinics across India, tracking symptom scores and any harms during treatment.

Scores improved quickly and firmly. Nasal symptom totals fell by about two points at day seven and by over three and a half at day fourteen, with eye and other symptoms easing in parallel. No patient was hospitalized, suffered a serious side effect, or stopped treatment. The authors conclude the mometasone and azelastine spray pair relieved symptoms well and was tolerated smoothly in daily practice. They present the work as real-world backing for guideline advice, drawn from routine records rather than a controlled trial.
pmc-13438623:
Tamir Edri and colleagues found the missing link between folic acid and the birth defects it famously prevents. Folic acid supplements cut neural tube defects, failures of the early spine and brain to close, yet nobody could say how, and some cases resist it. Their 2026 study names an enzyme, ALDH1L1, as the bridge. The vitamin works only because this enzyme helps turn vitamin A into retinoic acid, a signal the embryo needs.

Folic acid feeds a pathway whose messenger is retinoic acid; without the bridging enzyme the supplement cannot deliver. That insight reframes old arguments over dose: a pregnancy could take folic acid faithfully and still fall short if vitamin A supply runs low. They present the mechanism as a way to sharpen a prevention that already ranks among public health's clearest wins.
pmc-13439023:
Buşra Tozduman and İrem Zengi report a 2026 choice study on what draws public health specialist doctors to one post over another. Public health specialists shape health promotion policy and support care at every level, yet posts in remote areas often stay hard to fill. The authors asked 183 specialists to weigh job features against each other and to show which trade-offs they would accept.

Five of six job features shaped choices in the survey. Being close to family and friends ranked first, ahead of the working setting, pay, how developed the workplace area was, and holding a manager role. Pay mattered most for manager posts among younger specialists with no past manager experience. Readers learn that fair pay alone will not fix staffing gaps, while posts near home and supportive workplaces may do more.
pmc-13439523:
Abun and co-authors test fermented fish waste as chicken feed in a 2026 feeding trial. Low-protein diets for poultry need cheap local ingredients that birds can still digest well. Waste from pangasius catfish processing, once fermented, may fill that gap for Indonesian super native chickens.

Day-old chicks grew on a starter diet, then moved to six test diets for the grower phase. The team varied how much fermented waste each diet held. Energy use and nutrient digestibility were the key measures for picking a best dose. A waste stream turned into feed cuts costs and landfill at once. Village producers gain most if the dose proves safe and steady.
pmc-13439723:
Skinner and colleagues test whether early liver injury from alcohol feeds back into drinking behavior in this 2026 mouse study. The liver-brain connection is suspected in alcohol use disorder, but the behavioral effects of early liver disease were largely unexplored. Female mice were fed an alcohol liquid diet to induce early fatty liver. They were then allowed to choose freely between alcohol and water. Meanwhile, their memory and anxiety were tested.

The alcohol-fed mice developed fatty, enlarged livers, and then drank significantly more than controls in the choice test, with intake rising in step with the degree of liver fat. Their spatial working memory was impaired, though recognition memory and anxiety-like behavior were unchanged in the tests used. The injured livers later recovered their fat but showed lingering inflammation, and a brain growth factor and its receptor were reduced in the hippocampus.
pmc-13439923:
Yen and co-authors build a gene drive that rewrites mosquito populations from inside a native gene. Their 2026 paper describes nanosd, an integral gene drive inserted into the nanos gene of Anopheles gambiae, the main malaria mosquito. Integral drives use the host gene's own control sequences, shrinking the added machinery compared with earlier designs.

The drive inherited at striking rates, 98.4 percent through females and 99.5 percent through males. Females carrying two copies paid a price, with reduced fertility and underdeveloped ovaries, linked to lowered nanos expression and shifts in other fertility genes. Broader gene activity stayed largely undisturbed, and infected mosquitoes remained as susceptible to malaria parasites and a second virus as wild types. In cages, the drive spread efficiently, kept supplying its cutting enzyme after resistant variants appeared, and mobilised a separate antiparasitic modification.
pmc-13441223:
Xiaohui Kong and co-authors published a research paper in 2026 on a pressed feed made from peanut vines, corn, and urea that helps beef cattle gain weight. Peanut vines are a cheap crop leftover, but cattle digest them poorly raw. Pressing the mix under heat and pressure was meant to unlock more of its value.

Bag tests in the rumen picked a winning recipe at sixty-five parts vine to thirty corn and five urea. Then thirty-six cattle were fed for sixty days, half on the new feed. Those cattle ate more, gained faster each day, and earned slightly more profit per head. Their rumen germ mix shifted toward fiber-cutting kinds.
pmc-13441323:
Mateja Zorko, Tomaž Lunder, and Thomas Peric track contact allergy trends in Slovenian youth in a 2026 study. Data on which substances sensitize children and teens are limited, especially over long spans. The team reviewed patch test records from a single large medical center across three periods, from 2000 to 2024.

The review covered 1,052 children and adolescents tested with the standard allergen series of each era. Nickel sensitivity fell sharply, from about thirteen percent in the first period to four percent in the last. Two newer entries, a textile dye mix and a preservative, emerged as important allergens in the latest period. Children with eczema had higher sensitivity rates than others, while the pattern reversed among adolescents. The authors urge ongoing surveillance.
pmc-13441523:
Fusao Ikawa writes in reply to a colleague's letter, defending curves over straight lines when forecasting brain hemorrhage outcomes. pmc-13441823:
Sanchun Wang and colleagues compare a through-the-mouth plasma ablation surgery against open neck surgery for chosen voice box cancers, reporting in 2026. pmc-13442923:

pmc-13443523:
Fallah and colleagues recounted in 2026 how research was organized across Africa during the mpox outbreaks, and what that effort taught about preparing for the next epidemic. pmc-13443823:
Ackerman and colleagues reviewed procedural sedation and pain relief practice in 2026 at a regional hospital emergency department in KwaZulu-Natal, South Africa. pmc-13444123:

pmc-13444223:
Ze-Mei Chen and colleagues name two new Ophiocordyceps fungi that grow on wasps and kin in Yunnan, China, in a 2026 paper. These fungi parasitize insects of the Hymenoptera order. Shape checks plus five-gene family trees placed the finds in the Hymenostilbe branch of the genus.

pmc-13444323:

Turbulence runs used the patch as a fine-grid fix where old models wander. In neat settings, symbol distillation squeezed the patch into compact formulas that fed back into the old code. pmc-13444623:
Tatsumi Tanaka and colleagues test two small RNA molecules, miR-126-3p and miR-140-5p, as a joint injection for knee osteoarthritis pain in rats, in a 2026 study. In rats with a ligament injury model of joint damage, treated limbs bore more weight over time, and joint swelling eased most when the pair was given together. Cartilage wear did not improve, so the gain reads as pain relief rather than joint repair, and more safety work is still needed.
pmc-13445523:
Hamid Eshaghi and colleagues report a sixteen-month-old boy in Iran whose brain shunt let a skin fungus reach his brain, published in 2026 with a review of past cases. The fungus, Neoscytalidium dimidiatum, usually stays on skin and nails, and brain infection is rare and often fatal. The boy had been healthy before a head injury led to the shunt.

The first drug mix failed, so care shifted to drugs picked by lab sensitivity tests, among them drug delivery straight into the brain fluid spaces. pmc-13445923:

pmc-13447623:
Wendemi Daniel Ouedraogo and colleagues assess a 2026 evaluation of Burkina Faso's national malaria control program from 2020 to 2024, a period of progress shadowed by elimination hurdles. pmc-13447823:

A pile-base case in Southwest China showed fixed layout, calmed mess and self-crossing, and kept nodal traits. Cross-platform rock workflows gain a reliable transfer path.
pmc-13449223:
Dinkar Regmi and co-authors build an integrated Raman spectroscopy platform with embedded artificial intelligence for real-time cancer detection during surgery. Raman scattering reads a tissue's molecular fingerprint, but workflows are fragmented across proprietary tools and ad hoc scripts. The authors stress that the end-to-end audit trail, archiving every intermediate output, is as important as the classifier itself.
pmc-13449323:
Dominik Martinát and colleagues published a 2026 paper turning a membrane database into linked open data. pmc-13449523:
Kazi Md Azman Hossain and colleagues compared two group exercise plans for older adults in a 2026 trial. Activity, function, fall confidence, and quality of life were scored before and after. Both plans raised scores over time, with the sense-and-balance plan showing larger gains in activity. Local centers gain a head-to-head basis for picking between the two plans.
pmc-13449623:

Fuzzy roles between teams risked split care, the authors warn.
pmc-13449923:
Janna Teigeler, Yannik Stegmann, and Matthias Gamer examine in 2026 how the body braces for a threat it can dodge versus one it cannot. pmc-13450123:

pmc-13450523:

pmc-13451223:

pmc-13451423:

pmc-13452123:

pmc-13453023:

pmc-13453723:

pmc-13454623:

pmc-13454823:

pmc-13455223:

pmc-13455423:

pmc-13456823:

pmc-13457023:

pmc-13457123:

pmc-13457223:

pmc-13457523:

pmc-13457623:

pmc-13457723:

pmc-13458523:

pmc-13458823:

pmc-13458923:

pmc-13459023:

pmc-13459223:

pmc-13459323:

pmc-13459623:

pmc-13461823:

pmc-13463823:

pmc-13465323:

pmc-13465423:

pmc-13465923:

pmc-13466123:

pmc-13466323:

pmc-13466623:

pmc-13466823:

pmc-13466923:

pmc-13467023:

pmc-13467123:

pmc-13467823:

pmc-13467923:

pmc-13468223:

pmc-13471723:

pmc-13472923:

pmc-13473023:

pmc-13473423:

pmc-13473523:

pmc-13474623:

pmc-13474823:

pmc-13475823:

Hansen Shi leads an eight-author team reporting a 2026 study of the immune checkpoint CD274, better known as PD-L1, in liver cancer. Its prognostic meaning in hepatocellular carcinoma has been disputed. Mining the TCGA and GTEx databases, the team compared gene activity in tumour and normal tissue, ran survival models, and stained tissue microarrays for the protein. They measured blood levels by ELISA in untreated patients and controls.

Tumour tissue expressed CD274 less than normal liver, yet patients whose tumours expressed more of it lived longer, and models confirmed it as a protective factor for disease-specific survival. The protein staining showed no tumour-versus-normal difference. Blood told the opposite story to tissue: median serum PD-L1 was 349.6 picograms per millilitre in patients against 181.3 in controls on those assays. The authors describe a low-in-tissue, high-in-blood pattern and propose serum testing as a forecasting tool.
pmc-13502923:
Hamad A Alhussain leads a four-author team reporting a 2026 survey of what patients want their doctors to wear at primary healthcare centres in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia. Between April and May 2026, 1,176 adult visitors at centres in the Riyadh Second Health Cluster completed a bilingual questionnaire. It rated male and female physician outfits and eleven statements about trust, respect, and willingness to return. Appearance mattered to 80.8 percent of respondents across every demographic subgroup.

The white coat won decisively for both sexes of physician, chosen by 85.5 percent for men and 78.4 percent for women, while jeans and expensive clothing were rejected. For female doctors, the niqab or veil and the skirt also ranked high, reflecting local modesty norms, and niqab preference shifted significantly with respondent age. Preferred attire travelled with higher perceived respect, satisfaction, intention to follow up, and expected treatment compliance. The authors advise dress codes that take these preferences seriously.
pmc-13503423:
Adeeti Chiplunker and co-authors argue that bowel surgery patients with inflammatory bowel disease should borrow the playbook of short bowel syndrome, even without the full diagnosis. Surgery changes gut function past the cut itself, and many patients absorb and move food poorly afterward. Formal labels lag that reality.

Their 2026 review names the history and anatomy clues that flag short bowel trouble early. Diet tuned to the remaining anatomy forms the base of care. On top sit anti-motility drugs at proper doses and oral rehydration solution as twin foundations in every setting. The authors urge teams to spot the pattern fast and treat it with the structured regimen, rather than waiting for a textbook case to declare itself.
pmc-13503623:
Geraldine Huynh and co-authors build a case-based lesson that teaches trainees to manage bacterial meningitis in children. The infection is a life-threatening emergency for the young. Missed or late treatment still happens far too often.

Their module runs ninety minutes with a guided patient case. Questions are woven through the case for active learning. A facilitator guide, quizzes, and surveys complete the package. Specialists in infection and microbiology shaped the content. A pilot round drew seventy-five learners and thirteen facilitators. Learners rated the session near the top of the scale. Everyone surveyed reported gains from the training. The module offers a ready tool for residency programs.
pmc-13503923:
Zengler argued in 2026 that engineering soil microbes is one of the most promising, and most stubborn, routes to sustainable farming and carbon storage. Soil covers only about a fifth of Earth's surface yet grows about ninety-five percent of the world's food, and land ecosystems soak up a third of carbon emissions. Its microbes drive both crop nutrition and that carbon capture.

New molecular tools now allow targeted work: editing single microbes, dosing soils with helpful microbes or their feed, or breeding plants that recruit the right partners. Zengler traces why field success lags behind lab promise, citing cost and the poor survival of introduced microbes. He weighs modest near-term paths, such as tuning plant-microbe partnerships, as likelier to pay off soon.
pmc-13505023:
Anitha Jeyagurunathan leads a team measuring partner violence among women treated for mental illness in Singapore, in a 2026 study. Partner violence is common worldwide, and women with mental illness face added risk. Local rates and their ties to quality of life were unmapped.

The study enrolled 255 women with psychosis or depression at a tertiary hospital. Half reported partner violence on a world-standard scale, spanning mental, physical, and sexual forms. Women with stronger positive psychotic symptoms faced higher odds of each violence form. Those who faced mental abuse scored lower on social and environmental quality of life, while physical abuse tracked with lower physical quality of life. The authors call for routine screening in psychiatric care.
pmc-13505123:
Hai Wang and colleagues report a single-child case in which two genome-wide methods were combined to explain a rare disorder of sex development. The child, aged about eighteen months, had a male appearance but a 46,XX karyotype, along with an unfused scrotum and hypospadias. Standard tests had not shown how Y-chromosome material came to sit on the X chromosome.

Copy-number sequencing flagged losses on both the X and Y short arms, while optical genome mapping traced the actual structure. Mapping showed a piece of Yp inserted into Xp22.33, with three rejoining events, a deleted stretch, and a local inversion. The kept segment held SRY, the gene that drives male development, which fits the child's condition. The authors argue the two methods add different detail and can sharpen genetic counselling, including growth checks linked to the X deletion.
pmc-13505323:
Yu Lu and co-authors report, in a 2026 study, that tiny calcium hot spots near a nerve cell's membrane drive repair after peripheral nerve injury. Calcium is a puzzle in nerve repair. Cells need it to grow, but a cell wide rise often poisons them instead. The hot spots offer a way out of that paradox, by keeping the signal local.

Imaging at fine scale showed that a channel called TRPC3 creates these hot spots in sensory neurons. The spots act as a signaling module that starts axon regrowth, through calmodulin linked pathways. After a sciatic nerve cut, the channel and spot axis proved essential for both structure and function to return. The authors note the lesson may also protect central neurons, which normally repair far worse.
pmc-13507223:
Florian Schneider and seven co-authors show in 2026 that a common mineral dust can start ice growth on a flawless face, with no special active sites. Dust from the feldspar microcline seeds ice better than most particles, a fact that matters for clouds and climate. Why it wins was a puzzle.

Fine imaging shows ice starts across the main face of microcline itself. A close cousin mineral, by contrast, seeds ice only at step edges, as expected. Computer models point to a snug lattice match with a slanted ice plane. The find explains the mineral's edge at the nanoscale. Climate models may need to weigh such hidden faces when they tally ice birth in clouds.
pmc-13507523:
Makoto Nagasawa and co-authors test whether a wearable robot belt raises exercise confidence in frail older adults, in a 2026 study. Confidence in one's ability to move is a key driver of staying active, and frailty erodes it.

The analysis pooled two earlier studies with ninety-six users of the lumbar assist device. Users practiced sit-to-stand and squats twice a week with the belt reading their muscle signals. Confidence scores rose by about one point on average. The gain concentrated in those whose exercise habits were not yet set, with the least ready group gaining most. Against a waitlist group the edge was favorable but not firm.
pmc-13507823:
Muhammad Mubashar Zafar leads an eleven-author team reviewing how genome editing turns domestication into an engineering task, in a paper from two thousand twenty-six. Climate shifts, genetic erosion, and new pathogens strain farms world-wide. Old ways of breeding are too slow for these pressures. The review asks what new tools can do to close that gap.

CRISPR editing, pangenomics, synthetic biology, and AI-assisted prediction now join into programmable domestication. Wild crop relatives and neglected germplasm become raw stock for redesign. Multiplex editing can put in a range of such traits at once. Pangenome data shows variation that single reference genomes miss. Phenomics guides which changes to make first. The review pulls these advances into one whole, aimed at hardy crops fit for a changed climate. What was once an accident of millennia is now a design task.
pmc-13508323:
Inken Kirschbaum-Lesch and eight colleagues compare, published in 2026, how teens with anorexia, teens with depression, and healthy teens relate to their bodies. Body image trouble is part of anorexia and is gaining notice in depression too. The study ran two lab tasks: a word task and a viewing task that track where attention goes when body words and images appear. Surveys added shape worry, appearance anxiety, checking, and avoidance. Thirty-four inpatients had anorexia, twenty-eight had depression, and thirty-nine were healthy controls.

Both the anorexia group and the healthy group showed a body-focused attention bias. The depressed group did not. Both patient groups judged their bodies more harshly than controls. Checking and avoidance barely set healthy teens apart from the anorexia group. The authors read body dislike as a shared thread across both illnesses. They urge prevention aimed at checking and avoidance habits.
pmc-13508423:
Hasan Nawaz Tahir leads a nine-author review comparing full intravenous anesthesia with gas-based anesthesia for robot-assisted belly surgery, in 2026 work. Robot surgery changes anesthesia needs, and the choice of method may shape pain, sickness, and pressure inside the eye after surgery. The team searched databases for randomized trials from 2017 to mid-2024. Eligible operations included prostate, womb, kidney, gallbladder, and bladder procedures done by robot through the abdomen. Only six trials with 340 patients in total met the rules, a thin base the authors state openly.

Just one trial measured post-surgery pain, and it favored intravenous anesthesia. The eye pressure measure named in the review plan rests on few data as well. With evidence this sparse, the authors avoid firm verdicts and map what is missing. Their message is that robotic surgery has outrun its anesthesia evidence, and larger head-to-head trials are the pressing need.
pmc-13509223:
Zhivkova and colleagues tested whether herbal feed additives can protect rabbits from ochratoxin A, a mold toxin that contaminates animal feed, in 2026 animal research. The trial used 48 New Zealand White rabbits aged 37 days over an 80-day period. Some rabbits received the toxin alone at 2 parts per million in feed. Others also got supplements such as ashwagandha, milk thistle, gotu kola, or silymarin at doses reaching 25,000 parts per million.

Rabbits on the toxin alone lost body weight and showed the worst damage, concentrated in the liver, kidneys, and spleen, with milder injury in the heart, gut, and lungs. Blood markers of organ strain and measures of oxidative stress, meaning damage from reactive molecules, also peaked in that group. Rabbits given herbal additives showed the same pattern in milder form, with protection strongest in the kidneys and liver. Zhivkova concludes the supplements blunted, but did not remove, the toxin's harm.
pmc-13509323:
Bing Song leads a seven-author team examining which immune cells help cause frozen shoulder, a painful condition where the shoulder joint grows stiff, in work published in 2026. The group combined genetic data for 731 immune cell traits with gene readings from shoulder capsule tissue taken from patients and controls. They also tested whether steroid drugs known as glucocorticoids change the same immune patterns.

The genetic analysis flagged seven immune traits that may raise risk and seventeen that may protect against the condition. Tissue readings confirmed five of these traits at higher levels, tied to swelling, scarring, and new blood vessel growth in the capsule. Steroid drugs showed no direct causal link to the disease, yet they lowered one protective immune trait, a trade-off the authors say deserves closer study.
pmc-13511723:
Dimitrios Lytras and co-authors (2026) tested whether magnetic stimulation speeds recovery from shin bone stress injuries in athletes. Such injuries, marked by swollen bone marrow, force long rest and slow returns to sport. Forty athletes with moderate stress injuries were split into two groups of twenty. Both followed a four-week load-based rehabilitation program. The stimulation group also received eight half-hour sessions at 40 hertz. Pain, leg function, and scan findings were tracked at the start, four weeks, and sixteen weeks.

Every measure favored the added stimulation. Pain fell further, function rose higher, and the marrow swelling shrank more than with rehabilitation alone. Scan severity grades also improved faster, especially by four weeks. The authors note a real caveat: with no sham treatment and no blinding, the self-reported gains may carry a placebo share. Still, they present the therapy as a promising add-on for a stubborn injury.
pmc-13512623:
Juan Pablo Carvajal and Fred Gustavo Manrique-Abril tested whether morning cortisol, a stress hormone in blood, matches burnout scores in Colombian health workers. The study covered 69 staff in Boyacá and paired fasting blood samples with a standard burnout survey.

Almost all workers, 96.6 percent, had cortisol in the normal range, and full burnout was rare at about 5 percent. About 68 percent scored as engaged, though 16.9 percent showed high emotional exhaustion, a warning sign worth watching. No link appeared between cortisol levels and any burnout dimension, with all tests far from significance. Carvajal advises watching the exhausted subgroup early and studying stress with several body markers over time.
pmc-13512923:
Kerim Esenboga and co-authors compare heart stent methods in a 2026 study of tricky artery forks. When a blockage sits where a heart artery splits, doctors must prop open both branches, and guidelines favor placing two stents up front for complex cases.

The team reviewed 142 patients treated between 2019 and 2022 with one of three two-stent methods: DK-crush, mini-culotte, or T and TAP. They compared patient traits, procedure details, hospital course, and major heart events over six months. They also hunted for traits that predict bad outcomes on their own. The side-by-side data help heart teams pick a fork strategy with real outcomes in view.
pmc-13514623:
Ziyang Yu, Shuaiwang Huang, and Xiyang Peng compare exercise therapies for regaining movement after acute ischaemic stroke in a 2026 systematic review and network meta-analysis. Stroke survivors often keep lasting weakness, and clinicians face a crowded menu of rehabilitation methods with little guidance on which suits which deficit. Searching four databases through late 2025, the authors pooled sixty-six trials covering 3,675 patients and used Bayesian ranking to compare methods across several recovery domains.

Different winners emerged for different goals. Tilting postural training and one-sided strength work ranked high for balance, robot-assisted Tai Chi and home guidance for daily living, and robot hand training paired with electrical stimulation for standard motor scores. Visual feedback training led for walking endurance. Yu's team stresses that no single method tops every domain, so prescriptions should match the patient's main deficit.
pmc-13514823:
Simon Wagner and eight colleagues report, in a 2026 lab study, a drug pairing that pushes colorectal cancer cells toward death. Colorectal cancer often survives by dodging the cell's built-in suicide programme, often through the protective protein Bcl-2. The team combined dimethyl fumarate, a redox-shifting drug already approved for multiple sclerosis, with venetoclax, which blocks Bcl-2 directly. Experiments centred on a widely used colorectal cancer cell line, HCT-116.

Dimethyl fumarate hobbled the cells' mitochondria, draining their energy currency and triggering recycling responses and cell-cycle arrest. Together, the two drugs deepened that stress, slowed growth, and held cells in a lasting arrest phase while switching off the cyclin proteins that drive division. Cell death rose most clearly when both drugs were given. Wagner's group frames the pairing as attractive because both drugs already exist in clinical use for other diseases.
pmc-13515323:
Junlin Dong and colleagues studied how bacterial communities in reservoir water and mud shift with the seasons in dry northwest China. They sampled eight reservoirs in Guyuan, Ningxia, in April, July, and October 2025 and read bacterial genes.

Mud communities held far more kinds of bacteria than water ones and barely changed across the year. Water communities swung strongly with the seasons, tracking temperature, acidity, and nutrient levels as they changed. Chance-like processes shaped the water communities most, while mud ones followed firmer environmental selection. Links among mud bacteria formed the richest networks, peaking in July, Dong reports, when nutrients ran high.
pmc-13515923:
Ruminal acidosis is a major metabolic disorder of intensively raised ruminants, long defined by a drop in rumen pH. The five authors argue it is better seen as a whole-system failure: microbial ecology destabilizes, metabolic cross-feeding breaks down, the gut barrier leaks, and host inflammation follows. High-concentrate feeding tips the balance among starch eaters, lactate producers, lactate users, and fiber digesters.

Acids, lactate, endotoxin, and histamine then pile up, strain the epithelium, loosen tight junctions, and fire inflammatory signals. The review unifies these threads into a microbiota-metabolism-barrier-inflammation framework. It judges remedies, from diet control and buffers to probiotics, yeast products, postbiotics, and plant compounds, by whether they restore microbial function rather than merely fix pH. The authors also back continuous rumen monitoring joined to precision feeding for earlier, individualized prevention.
pmc-13516423:
Yahia AL-Helih and five colleagues compare how well nurses keep resuscitation skills after training in a 2026 prospective study. CPR skill fades without practice, and ward setting may shape the fade. The team assessed 265 registered nurses right after basic life support training. Each nurse was then retested once, at one, three, or six months, so the design compares groups across time points rather than tracking each nurse throughout.

Knowledge scores sat lower at every later check in both critical care and general care nurses. The slide looked clearer among general care nurses. Hands-on skills told the same story: more nurses needed remediation at later checks, again worst in the general care group. AL-Helih's team backs refresher training aimed at each setting's exposure level. They caution that the design cannot prove why the gap opens.
pmc-13516523:
Irina Kim and co-authors study disease resistance in potatoes in a 2026 paper. Virus infections lower the quality of seed potatoes and cut yields, and no chemical cure works well. Breeding plants that carry resistance genes is the main defense, so knowing which plants hold them matters.

The team screened twenty-nine potato cultivars and thirty-one hybrids from the Russian Far East with gene tests. Several cultivars carried genes against potato virus X and against two nematode pests at once. Two resistance genes sat close together on one chromosome and tended to pass down as a pair. Fourteen hybrids held rich sets of resistance markers. One key gene passed to offspring in a steady, additive way, which supports its use in breeding.
pmc-13516923:
Liu and colleagues improved in 2026 a candidate drug for autism spectrum disorder so it can reach the brain. Their earlier work showed XAV939, a tankyrase blocker, eased social problems in two autism mouse models by damping Wnt and sugar-burning pathways. But the drug crosses the blood-brain barrier poorly and has low bioavailability. The team created ester versions, called prodrugs, and coated the best one in cell membrane for brain targeting.

Of three ester versions, one named XAV939-L1 kept the dual pathway blocking in cells and in neurons from Shank3b-mutant mice. Injected plainly, it improved social behaviour in those mice but caused liver side effects. Coating it in a hybrid neuron-astrocyte membrane greatly increased brain accumulation. The authors present membrane-coated prodrugs as a route to brain delivery for autism drug candidates that otherwise cannot cross.
pmc-13517123:
Uğur Ergün leads a thirty-six-author survey of healthcare workers' history and knowledge of shingles in a 2026 Turkish study. The virus behind chickenpox sleeps in nerves for life and can wake as painful shingles, especially with age or weak immunity. A strong recombinant vaccine exists and was licensed in Türkiye in 2024. Over five thousand health workers, nearly half of them physicians, answered an online questionnaire.

About one in ten reported having had shingles themselves. Nearly nine percent knew nothing of the disease, and only about forty percent knew a vaccine exists. One in five would refuse to pay for it. Being a physician roughly doubled the odds of solid knowledge, and having heard of shingles tripled it. Ergün's team concludes that staff education must come first, since uninformed health workers cannot protect themselves or steer vulnerable patients toward vaccination.
pmc-13518223:
Hélène Martini leads a twenty-nine-author study of how aged cells fuel their own inflammatory chatter in a 2026 paper. Senescent cells stop dividing but broadcast a cocktail of signals, the SASP, that damages tissue over time. Leaked mitochondrial DNA was known to flip the alarm switch. This team found the second half of the circuit: the same powerhouses supply the raw material that lets the alarm be transcribed.

Senescent mitochondria ramp up a pyruvate-to-acetyl-CoA pipeline, and that molecule feeds the chemical tagging that opens SASP genes for reading. Blocking the citrate exporter that feeds the pipeline closed those genes down. In aged mice the same block softened inflammation and improved healthspan measures. Martini's team calls it a metabolic checkpoint: signalling proposes the inflammatory programme, but metabolism decides whether the cell can afford to run it, a distinction drug hunters can target.
pmc-13518523:
Ahmet Emre Eşkazan leads an eighteen-author survey comparing what leukaemia patients and their doctors prioritise in a 2026 Turkish study. Chronic myeloid leukaemia on modern targeted pills now allows near-normal lifespans, so conversation quality steers switching and adherence. One hundred twenty-nine haematologists answered online and one hundred twenty patients by phone through the national society.

Both sides agreed on what must be explained at the start, then ranked it differently: patients wanted disease course, daily-life impact, and whether treatment works; doctors stressed safety and monitoring. On switching, patients again chased effectiveness while doctors chased manageable side effects. A quarter of patients admitted imperfect adherence, mostly forgetfulness, and follow-ups ran about ten minutes every few months. Patients also felt sunnier about daily life with the disease. The team urges shared decision-making to close the gap.
pmc-13518623:
Jawad Fares and seven colleagues report a 2026 case of a brain tumor in a 19-year-old woman who came to care after a first seizure. Imaging showed a small lesion in the right frontal lobe that looked like a low-grade glioma. Tissue study found mixed glial and neuronal elements with low growth activity. Standard tests found no IDH1, IDH2, or BRAF changes, while methylation profiling matched no known tumor class.

RNA sequencing then found a CLIP2::MET fusion as the only harmful change present. Fares and the team argue that the fusion may mark a separate molecular group within glioneuronal tumors. Readers gain a worked example of broad genomic testing, plus a reminder that MET fusions can guide treatment because approved inhibitors already exist for other cancers.
pmc-13518823:
Baqer M. Merzah leads a seven-author team introducing BioPars in 2026, a large language model built for Persian biomedical text. General chatbots remember medical facts well yet stumble on deeper real-world questions, and Persian medical question answering had no dedicated model. The team assembled training material from over 10,000 articles, textbooks, and medical websites.

Their benchmark, BioParsQA, holds 5,231 Persian medical questions and answers. BioPars scored a ROUGE-L of 29.99 on that set, edging GPT-4 by 1.0 point in their reporting, with a BERTScore of 90.87 using one ranking method. MoverScore and BLEURT also topped the three rival models tested. Fine-grained reasoning, the authors note, still needs work.
pmc-13518923:
Madison Caballero and colleagues offered a new way to find autism risk genes whose effects are too modest to stand out alone. Published in 2026, the study drew on 10,795 families from the SPARK collection and looked for gene pairs that raise risk only when inherited together. The idea rests on a threshold view of autism, in which many small genetic and life factors add up until they cross into the condition.

The search found 97 modest genes forming 50 pairs with a strong joint link to autism, though no single gene crossed the line alone. Checks against control groups sharpened the result, and gene-activity patterns in brain tissue backed the biological fit of the pairs. The authors argue that paired genes help explain why autism varies so much from person to person. The work opens fresh paths for research and, in time, for more targeted forms of support.
pmc-13519023:
Jorge Lora, Andrea Torres, José I Hormaza, Javier Rodrigo, and Afif Hedhly read apricot mate-block genes by deep gene scans in a 2026 paper. Most fruit crops bar self-mate by a gene block that halts kin tube growth. One gene spot with two genes runs that block in plum kin, the team notes.

Gene type calls steer breed picks and yard lay for fruit set in the crop. Old lab tests plus part reads can blur or miss types in the spot. Their deep scan way gives a sharp type read from genome sets.
pmc-13519223:
Leena Vuolteenaho and co-authors report a 2026 study of how well health workers in a Finnish hospital rate their own end-of-life care skills. Need for such care is growing, yet past studies show gaps in staff skill. Good care near the end of life can raise quality of life and cut costs.

One hundred staff took part in 2024. They rated their skills on a 30-item tool built for the study. The team used counts and group checks, plus open answers sorted by theme. The aim was to find which skill areas are weakest, so training can target them first.
pmc-13519523:
Lesley Andrew, Michelle Pedlow, and Bev Ewens study how a module on Aboriginal culture and history changes postgraduate nursing students, through the reflections students must write. Australian nursing programs must include this content, yet unsafe care and racism persist. Their 2026 study analyzes critical reflections from fifteen students in a module built to foster culturally safe care.

Three themes emerged. Students first faced gaps in their knowledge and the weight of wider social messages. The learning itself stirred emotion, identification with Aboriginal experiences, and fresh doubts about standard care habits. Finally, students described seeing practice through a new lens and intending to work differently. The authors say planned reflection can transform learning, while warning that student discomfort needs careful handling.
pmc-13520423:
Nilufer Zorlutuna Kaymak and colleagues review in 2026 vitrectomy surgery for eye inflammation from many causes, covering why surgery was chosen and how vision fared afterward. Inflammation inside the eye can detach the retina or cloud diagnosis, and removing the gel can treat both problems.

Records spanned 32 eyes in 30 patients treated from 2019 to 2025 with fine-gauge surgery. Detachment repair and diagnostic sampling were the leading reasons. Retinal reattachment succeeded in nearly all detachment cases, vision gains held at one year, and nearly half the eyes gained at least two chart lines. No severe post-surgery inflammation occurred in the series.
pmc-13520523:
Hoshiko Furusawa and colleagues test in 2026 whether a DNA methylation blocking drug called decitabine can calm spine and joint inflammation in a mouse model of spondyloarthritis. Gene silencing by methylation may fuel immune imbalance in this chronic disease, yet its role was unclear.

Arthritis was triggered in susceptible mice, with weekly drug dosing thereafter. Treated mice showed milder joint disease and better tissue scores, including less lining overgrowth. Immune profiling focused on Th17 responses, a cell type that drives inflammation. Tissue sequencing pointed to raised VIPR1, a receptor gene freed by reduced methylation, as part of the mechanism.
pmc-13520923:
Elias Kassir and co-authors check whether a sound-wave test of womb arteries can help predict a dangerous problem of the placenta in pregnancy. In that problem, the placenta grows too deeply into the wall of the womb and can cause heavy bleeding at birth. Patients at risk were referred to a specialist center for closer checks.

The team measured blood speed and flow patterns in the left and right womb arteries. They adjusted the readings for the stage of pregnancy and compared patients with and without the problem. They also looked at how deeply the placenta had grown and whether the test could warn of heavy bleeding during surgery. A simple scan that flags risk early could help teams plan safer births.
pmc-13521123:
Mirza Nusrat Sweety and co-authors made zinc oxide particles with a plant extract in a 2026 study, then tested what the particles can do. The extract came from the stems of Indigofera tinctoria and stood in for harsh chemicals. The team checked whether the size and order of the crystals shaped the particles' performance.

Tests confirmed a pure hexagonal crystal form, with grains about thirty-six nanometers wide and mostly round in shape. Under sunlight, the particles broke down a blue dye by about ninety-three percent in two hours, and they still worked after five rounds of reuse. They also killed both broad classes of bacteria and showed mild action against cell damage. The authors link the strong light-driven work to the crystal quality.
pmc-13521323:
Sharmin Sultana and colleagues search in 2026 for respiratory germs other than COVID virus among adults with flu-like illness at a Bangladesh teaching hospital during the pandemic. Testing focused heavily on COVID at the time, leaving negative cases unexplained despite ongoing symptoms.

Swabs from 165 adults between July and December 2022 were tested with a broad panel covering viruses and bacteria. At least one germ appeared in about 36 percent of patients, split between viral and bacterial finds. Statistical checks confirmed that germ types were unevenly distributed rather than random. Co-infection patterns were also tested, giving clinicians a fuller local picture for future flu seasons.
pmc-13521523:
Zhikui Wei and colleagues link in 2026 wrist-measured sleep patterns with fat-hormone levels in older adults from a long-running Baltimore ageing study. Sleep and fat hormones both steer metabolic health, yet their interplay late in life was poorly mapped.

Participants numbered 350 people aged sixty or older, averaging about 75 years, with roughly a week of wrist sleep recording plus fasting blood tests. Longer wake bouts inside sleep tracked with lower adiponectin and leptin at baseline. Longer total sleep predicted adiponectin gains over time, while short sleep predicted decline. Links varied by sex and belly fat level in subgroup checks.
pmc-13521923:
Srihari Srinivasan and colleagues adapt in 2026 a large vision transformer for two jobs at once, depth estimation and human segmentation, using tiny trainable plug-in modules instead of full retraining. Full fine-tuning for dense prediction is costly, so cheap adaptation matters for small teams.

Only about 150,000 new parameters were trained inside the decoder of a depth model. Segmentation scores reached competitive levels against leading dedicated models, with strong average precision and overlap scores on filtered public datasets. Depth accuracy of the base model stayed intact. Dual output from one adapted backbone suits robotics and editing tools with tight compute budgets.
pmc-13522123:
Yoshika Tsuji and co-authors present a 2026 exploratory study of smoking's fingerprints in the lungs of people with rheumatoid arthritis. Smoking is a known trigger both for arthritis-related lung disease and for a separate condition marked by IgG4-type immune cells. Whether smokers with arthritis carry more of those cells in lung tissue was unknown.

The team studied twenty-eight arthritis patients with abnormal chest scans who had lung washings and biopsies. They counted IgG4 cells in tissue and profiled immune cells in the washings and blood. An exploratory threshold defined rich infiltration, since almost nobody met the classic cutoff. The work probes how smoke may steer lung immunity in arthritis.
pmc-13522223:
Aleksandra Pieta and co-authors compare gut microbes of pro athletes on paleo and standard diets in this 2026 pilot study. Diet shapes the gut community, and strict diets can thin it out. The paleo pattern is sometimes pitched for sports nutrition despite thin evidence. Ten male professional handball players joined a small controlled trial. For eight weeks, half ate paleo and half a balanced rational diet. Both diets carried the same calories.

Stool samples revealed each group's microbe mix and its functional potential. The study asks whether cutting food groups costs the gut anything. Small pilots like this test feasibility before bigger trials. Athletes chase any edge, so diet claims aimed at them need checks. Results are early and based on very few players. The authors frame the work as groundwork.
pmc-13522523:
Funda Ersoy Atalay and colleagues made clean, intact microcapsules from walnut pollen for future medical delivery. Published in 2026, the study worked with Juglans regia pollen, whose tough outer shells, called sporopollenin exine capsules, suit drug carrying but normally retain allergy-triggering proteins. Sequential chemical washes stripped proteins, while a PEG-4000 step repaired shells that collapsed during acid treatment.

Lab checks found no detectable protein bands and faded protein signals, showing allergen content below detection limits. PEG treatment restored round shape in about five sixths of capsules examined and raised surface area, with roughly one quarter of material recovered as product. The authors present the capsules as sustainable natural carriers. Readers get a verified recipe, still awaiting tests with real drug loads.
pmc-13522623:
Reza Nouri, Erfan Ayubi, Shiva Borzouei, and Sajjad Farashi apply machine learning to predict thyroid cancer recurrence in a 2026 retrospective study. Three hundred fifty-five patients with differentiated thyroid cancer were followed for ten years after thyroid removal and radioactive iodine treatment. Records supplied tumor, treatment, and blood marker data, and six learning algorithms were compared head to head.

One boosted-tree model performed best, reaching accuracy near ninety-eight percent with an almost perfect discrimination score. The strongest predictors were prior recurrence count, a stimulated blood marker level in the first year, spread to neck nodes, and first response to treatment. The authors also propose reserving whole-body scans for high-risk patients, which could spare low-risk patients unnecessary testing while keeping close watch where recurrence is likely.
pmc-13523223:
Ruth Namazzi and colleagues show that a sickle cell drug distorts a bedside kidney test in Ugandan children in a 2026 analysis nested in a clinical trial. Two hundred forty-eight children with sickle cell anemia had creatinine, a kidney marker, measured by a point-of-care device and by a reference laboratory method. About half started hydroxyurea during a year of follow-up as part of routine care.

At enrollment the two methods agreed well. At follow-up, children on hydroxyurea showed device readings notably higher than laboratory values, with some results crossing into the abnormal range, while untreated children showed no such gap. Drug levels in blood explained most of the variation in device readings. The authors warn that the interference can misclassify kidney function and mislead care decisions.
pmc-13523323:
Pramana Adhikari and Mahesh Bhatta explore the hidden social burden of infertility in a 2026 review. Beyond its biology, it interacts with stigma, gendered expectations, and unfair systems. Peer-reviewed studies were read through three lenses: how people cope with stress, how stigma works, and how overlapping disadvantages intersect, producing three linked themes.

It was commonly felt as a threat to identity, relationships, and future plans, producing intense turmoil. Coping differed by gender, with peer support and therapy helping some, while shutting it out and denial harmed others. Stigma eroded gendered self-image, with men linking infertility to lost manhood and women cast as failures, and racial bias in medicine deepened the harm. System-wide gaps worsened every layer. The authors call for mental health support that fits local culture, cheaper treatment, and anti-stigma campaigns.
pmc-13523423:
Elena Campilii leads a team building an automatic engagement meter for children in robot-assisted walking therapy in a 2026 study.
