Twenty children with cerebral palsy were monitored across multiple sessions on a robotic gait system. Heart rate changes, facial heat imaging, and movement data from the robot frame were collected to capture body and behavior signals linked to engagement, which an expert clinician rated in three classes.

Combining all signal types with one ensemble model gave the best result, with a moderate combined score across classes. The system distinguished the clearly disengaged and clearly engaged states best, while most errors confused neighboring classes, especially the neutral middle. Feature analysis supported the value of mixing body and movement inputs. The authors aim at neutral, scalable engagement monitoring for children's recovery care.
pmc-13523523:
Lotte Nijhuis and colleagues investigate, in a 2026 study, whether nicotinamide, a form of vitamin B3, can calm inflammation in juvenile idiopathic arthritis, the most common rheumatic disease of childhood. The disease involves chronic joint inflammation with an imbalance between regulatory T cells, which restrain immunity, and effector T cells. Nicotinamide helps make a molecule central to cell energy and immune control.

In laboratory work, nicotinamide raised the share of regulatory-type T cells in blood and joint fluid cells from patients and increased suppressive capacity in healthy control cells. In a small pilot phase, six patients took high-dose nicotinamide by mouth for three days, and similar levels appeared in blood plasma and joint fluid, showing the vitamin reaches inflamed joints. The authors call for larger studies on dose and long-term place in care.
pmc-13523623:
Grace Ferencz and co-authors reviewed what women believe causes their chronic pelvic pain, in a 2026 paper. How a woman explains her pain can shape care and coping. The team gathered qualitative studies from databases and gray sources up to August 2025. A meta-ethnography blended the findings across studies.

Thirty studies with 1,255 women from many lands met the rules. Only seven fully met a standard quality checklist. Reports often lacked detail on who took part, and most women were white and from Western lands. Four themes emerged from the synthesis, per the review. The authors urge richer, more diverse research. Clinicians may also gain from asking women their own causal views.
pmc-13524023:
Gabriele Panicucci and co-authors show that oxygen gradients steer how a young leaf takes shape, in a 2026 paper. Growing tissues are not evenly aired: plant embryos and shoot tips sit in low-oxygen pockets, and a dedicated sensing pathway reads those levels through the stability of key transcription factors. What oxygen does once a leaf starts forming was unknown.

The team found a moving oxygen gradient across the developing leaf, read by that same sensing machinery. Early low oxygen restrained cell expansion. Then a wave of oxygenation, running from tip to base, cleared a set of response factors, unlocking special cell fates and pacing cell division. Oxygen, they conclude, acts as a positional signal in normal growth.
pmc-13524623:
León and colleagues presented in 2026 a computer method that labels ten tissue types in microscope slides of oral cancer. Pathologists now mark these slides by hand, which is slow, and rare tissue types get few examples to learn from. The method aims to cut that hand work while keeping the labels sharp at tissue borders.

The team grouped nearby pixels into small clusters called superpixels, and used them both to build training labels and to clean up the final maps. They trained on slides from ten patients and tested on slides from two more. Across nine model setups, their best runs reached mean accuracy near 92 percent, with strong overlap scores even for rare tissue classes. The tool plugs into the free QuPath program, so labs can rebuild whole-slide maps with it.
pmc-13525023:
Amir Jahanian Najafabadi and Bernhard Hommel study how age affects the feel of using a cane while blindfolded in 2026. When a tool feels like part of the body, people can act through it. Sight is thought to help that feel, but the link was unclear. Adults young and old used a cane in two tasks with eyes covered.

One task was a search for objects. The other was finding a path. After each task, people rated how much the cane felt like theirs and how much control they felt. Control ratings were higher than ownership ratings at all ages. Shifts in reach judgment tied most to the sense of control. Blind cane use can give control without a strong sense of ownership.
pmc-13525623:
Aisha Krieger-Hussain, Zaineb Ahmad, Lejla Hodzic and Besher Kabak published this 2026 case report of one patient, a 67-year-old man whose high-grade B-cell lymphoma first announced itself through two emergencies at once. They were acute confusion and cardiac tamponade, fluid crushing the heart. He arrived from a group home with altered mental state and breathlessness. A head scan cleared stroke but revealed a large fluid collection around the heart plus fluid around the lungs.

Heart ultrasound confirmed tamponade, and emergency drainage removed 2.2 litres of bloody fluid from the pericardial sac. His course grew complicated, with respiratory failure needing a ventilator and abnormal heart rhythms. Testing of the lung fluid then revealed the lymphoma cells. Surgeons cut a pericardial window for the fluid. He improved, came off the ventilator, and was discharged to begin chemotherapy. The authors urge clinicians to consider hidden blood cancers behind bloody pericardial fluid.
pmc-13526123:
Josef Zahner leads a large team in a 2026 dosimetry analysis asking whether hormone blocking drugs change radiation doses from PSMA-targeted therapy in advanced prostate cancer. Androgen receptor signaling inhibitors improve results and might raise PSMA expression and tumor dose. Patients got one of two lutetium-177 PSMA radioligands.

The retrospective analysis at one center covered fifty men at their first treatment cycle, half also taking abiraterone or enzalutamide and half on radioligand therapy alone. Imaging at three time points after dosing fed dose math for 148 tumor lesions and for kidney, spleen, and liver. Median tumor dose was comparable between combination and control groups for both radioligands, with no significant differences. Organ doses were also comparable in the results noted, which the authors call preliminary.
pmc-13526523:
Kim and colleagues reported in 2026 that a stress protein called GRP78, also known as BiP, helps drive liver cancer growth. Hepatocellular carcinoma is the third leading cause of cancer death worldwide, so new drug targets are badly needed. The team found GRP78 enriched in lab-grown liver cancer spheroids, small balls of tumor cells, and linked high levels in tissue near tumors to worse outcomes after surgery.

Blocking GRP78 slowed cancer cell growth and weakened their response to DNA damage. The protein peaks during cell division and sits in the midbody, the bridge between two new cells at the final step of division. Extra GRP78 held onto another protein, PLK1, and kept it stable in the midbody, so cells failed to finish dividing and ended up with several nuclei. The authors argue that blocking GRP78 could become a new treatment route for liver cancer.
pmc-13526723:
Ananthika Vijayan and others build, in a 2026 study, an antioxidant and anti-inflammatory scaffold from hydroxyapatite taken from bovine bone waste. Hydroxyapatite, the mineral of bone, was mixed with polyethylene glycol, zinc oxide nanoparticles, and ascorbic acid, better known as vitamin C. The goal was a material safe for bone that also calms inflammation and lets zinc out slowly.

Tests confirmed the zinc particles and vitamin C were mixed in and that the polymer changed crystal size and order. Adding ascorbic acid gave stronger antioxidant and anti-inflammatory activity than the version lacking it, while germ-killing action came mainly from zinc oxide. Macrophage cell tests showed the scaffold fit well with cells at low doses, with viability above ninety percent, but marked toxicity at higher concentrations. Dose control is therefore central to any use.
pmc-13527123:
Ruveyda Unal and nine co-authors test a heart drug against sepsis damage in rats in a 2026 study. Sepsis, the body's runaway answer to infection, often bruises the heart through stress chemicals and inflammation. Nebivolol, a gentle beta blocker with antioxidant side talents, had protected other organs in earlier work.

Thirty-two rats were split into healthy, drug-only, septic, and septic-plus-drug groups, with sepsis induced by gut puncture. The drug slowed the racing heart, eased a conduction delay, and softened oxidative and tissue damage in the heart. But blood pressure, swelling, and vessel injury stayed unmoved. The authors call it local protection worth probing further, not a cure.
pmc-13527223:
Lin Faqu and co-authors review why chronic low back pain and depression so often arrive together, in a 2026 article. The pair resist treatment and worsen each other's outlook. The team read eighty-six studies from 2015 to 2025 and built a frame that links brain, immune, hormone, and gut systems.

Pain signals grow stronger through spinal and brain circuit changes the review details. Immune activation in the brain raises key swelling signals several-fold. Stress hormone rhythms flatten, and gut life shifts toward pro-swelling species. For care, one drug eased both pain and mood scores in trials. Closed-loop spinal stimulation beat open-loop versions, though gains faded over a year.
pmc-13527423:
Khan and Sher write a letter about a study of the AlzoSure Predict blood test for Alzheimer's disease, which measures a folded form of the protein p53. They praise the study for testing the assay against spinal fluid markers, but they raise points that qualify what the test can claim. Their letter is a comment and reports no new data.

They note that the study never tested whether spinal fluid tau markers add value on top of the blood markers already known. Nor did it compare the assay head-to-head with the strong plasma tau tests now in use, or run the standard added-value statistics. The comparison also covered only healthy people against those with mild impairment, not the full clinic population. Until such checks are done, they argue, it stays unclear whether the assay adds anything beyond what existing markers already show.
pmc-13527523:
Hai Lin and twelve co-authors ask whether body weight and blood sugar help cause myasthenia gravis, a disease where the immune system weakens muscles, in a 2026 study. Past links between weight, sugar, and autoimmune disease were suggestive but unsettled.

The team used two methods. Genetic analysis, which uses inherited variants as natural experiments, tied higher predicted weight to higher odds of the disease. It also hinted that part of the path runs through glucose, though that hint flipped with the method used. In hospital records, patients weighed more and had lower glucose than matched controls. The authors treat the weight link as real and the glucose path as unproven. The work may guide prevention research.
pmc-13527923:
So Ree Kim and Seong-Mi Park survey heart ultrasound in women, in a review from 2026. The scan is the first tool for heart disease checks: no cuts, no rays, found in most wards, safe to run again and again, even in pregnancy. Yet female hearts are not just small male hearts.

Women start with smaller hearts and a higher pump share, both of which can skew reads. The review walks the scan's part in ills that hit women hard: stiff-heart fail, fine-vessel chest woes, lung pressure, valve ills, and stress-born heart shock. It ends with the heart shifts of pregnancy and the rare fail that can strike near birth. The charge: read each scan with female norms and life stage in mind.
pmc-13528023:
Ristha Kamar and nine colleagues report a 2026 genomic survey of MRSA carried by healthy people in Qatar. MRSA is a drug-resistant staph germ usually studied in hospitals. The team swabbed noses and armpits of 576 residents with no recent hospital care or antibiotics. Lab tests confirmed the germ and its resistance genes. Whole genomes were read for a subset.

Sixty people carried staph, and twenty-one of those strains were MRSA. That gives a carriage rate near four percent. Most carriers were men aged eighteen to forty-five. Resistance to common antibiotics was frequent, and seventy-one percent of MRSA strains resisted several drug classes. Only one strain carried the PVL toxin gene. Genome family trees showed four separate clusters. The authors urge community surveillance and careful antibiotic use.
pmc-13528223:
Gary Doan and four co-authors test a new robot help with no scans for part-knee swaps, set against hand tools, in donor bodies. Their study appeared in twenty twenty-six. Part-knee swaps heal fast but fail and need redo more than full swaps. Robots aim to place parts with more truth to cut redo risk.

Six surgeons each did both legs of forty donor knees, robot on one leg and hand tools on the other. Scans before and after let the team check cut angles and depths against the plan. Robot cuts hit angles with far more truth on most marks. Both ways hit depth and leg line well, but robot work had far fewer wild misses.
pmc-13528323:
Elmer Victor Bernstam, Todd R. Johnson, and Fares Alahdab weigh academia against industry in the AI age in a 2026 review. Industry holds the biggest computers, the largest datasets, and most AI doctorates. Top models now come from firms. Academic medical centers still run research, teaching, and care, the trio note. Their edge lies elsewhere.

Centers steward rich health data, a key fuel for medical AI. That asset only pays off with investment. Data quality, tidy management, and easy reuse all need work. Rules should lower hurdles for sharing while guarding the public interest. The authors cast centers as careful stewards rather than racers. Used well, their data could shape health AI more than raw computing power. Neglect would hand the field to industry by default.
pmc-13528823:
Angela Campbell and three co-authors weigh social sites versus fit phone apps for mind aid in the birth span, in work from 2026. A joint design study with birth span women in far zones set five core needs. Peer cheer, case fit care, and true facts lead that list, with place fit and ease close by.

Site picks should count as a care part, not a mere host choice, the team says. Social sites bring a built crowd and plain reach to the mix. Fit apps bring more hush and rule of posts. A blend may meet all five needs at once.
pmc-13529023:
Sarah H Ooi and co-authors published a research paper in 2026 on how dengue fever spreads through one Thai province, street by street. Four types of the virus circulate at once, so chains of spread overlap and hide the pattern. The team merged twenty-five years of case records with virus gene reads from the same area.

Cases near each other, up to about five kilometers apart, proved more alike than chance would suggest. Inside one small town area, about ten chains of spread ran at any one time. After a busy season, local immunity against that season's type rose in the same spots. The map shows dengue control can be aimed at tight local zones.
pmc-13529923:
Nobuhiro Kanazawa and co-authors report a seventeen-year kidney case in a 2026 paper. Fibronectin glomerulopathy is a rare disorder where fibronectin piles up in kidney filters. It often traces to faults in the FN1 gene. Signs include protein in urine, blood in urine, and high blood pressure.

A 26-year-old woman carried one such variant. Seventeen years after protein was first found, she developed full nephrotic syndrome with swelling. Standard supportive drugs fell short. Steroid and immune-suppressing therapy then brought partial remission. A diabetes drug with kidney benefits was added as doses tapered. The case suggests immune therapy can help late-onset cases hold remission.
pmc-13530023:
Abdishakur Mohamud Hassan Hidigow wrote a 2026 commentary on family needs in intensive care. Admission to an ICU shatters family routine, with fear, strange machines, and deep reliance on staff for news. A study by Regalado and co-authors, covered in the piece, surveyed 140 patient and family pairs in a Portuguese ICU. It matched patient condition scores against family need scores.

Families rated information and a role in care as most pressing. Needs grew stronger when the patient's condition was poorer. The commentary argues that a sicker patient should signal a more vulnerable family, not just a heavier clinical load. It urges nurses to treat family support as a core priority of critical care.
pmc-13530223:
Seonghwan Park, Jaeseong Lee, Jaewoo Park, and Inkyu Moon present an imaging platform that reads both the structure and the chemistry of cells from a single hologram, in a 2026 paper. Microscopes usually need fluorescent dyes, complex optics, and separate channels to get both kinds of information. Their system instead records one low-cost Gabor hologram and lets artificial intelligence do the rest.

A diffusion model trained without paired examples converts the hologram into a quantitative phase image plus virtual fluorescence views. Ground-truth images from a conventional system were used only in training; at run time, one snapshot suffices. Tests across several cancer cell lines and organelle channels support the approach, aimed at cheaper, high-throughput cell analysis.
pmc-13530523:
Aregahegn Dona, Kassech Assefa, and Amelo Bolka published this study in 2026. It looks at harm to mothers after cesarean births at a general hospital in Yirgalem, in Ethiopia's Sidama region. Cesarean delivery saves lives, but it also carries real risks of complications.

The team reviewed the records of 372 mothers who gave birth by cesarean over about two years. Just over a quarter, 27.7 percent, had a bad outcome after the surgery. Three factors stood out: living in a rural area, having no checkups during pregnancy, and having an illness before the birth. Each of these roughly doubled the odds of harm. The authors urge wider rural access to care, fuller pregnancy checkups, and earlier treatment of illness in mothers.
pmc-13531223:
Garcia and eight colleagues hunt for blood signs of fatty liver disease in people with obesity in twenty twenty-six. The disease builds up fat in the liver and is hard to grade without scans or tissue tests. The team looked at tiny sacs that cells shed into the blood. Proteins on the sac walls may show how much fat the liver holds.

They compared sac proteins in three groups: obesity with liver disease, obesity without it, and lean adults. Single proteins split the groups only weakly. Pairs of proteins and small sets of them did much better. The authors call the results early leads that need tests in larger groups before clinic use.
pmc-13531723:
Six authors, led by Mike Lin, wrote this 2026 study of bone drug use after low-trauma fractures in New South Wales, Australia. A fracture from a minor fall signals weak bones, and osteoporosis drugs can cut the risk of the next break. Care after such a break, though, is often slow to start.

The study used linked health records for the whole state. It covered adults aged 50 and over who had a first low-trauma fracture between January 2011 and June 2019. The team tracked who started osteoporosis treatment, and when, over three years. Starts counted as early within 12 months, late within one to three years, or never. A second analysis hunted for traits that predict a start within the first year. The work shows where the treatment gap sits after fracture.
pmc-13531923:
Liwei Liao and co-authors set out a 2026 trial protocol comparing two biopsy routes for unexplained fluid around the lung. A newer ultrasound elasticity-guided biopsy promises high yield with less invasion than camera surgery inside the chest. Five Chinese centers will randomize 420 patients whose fluid tests came back negative.

Half start with the guided biopsy and move to camera surgery only if no diagnosis emerges. The other half go straight to camera surgery. Diagnostic yield leads the outcomes, with a five-point non-inferiority margin. Safety, hospital days, drainage time, avoided surgeries, and costs follow behind.
pmc-13532123:
Hanan Al Hamwi and co-authors build two-metal catalysts for making polyethylene in a 2026 paper. Their complexes pair zirconium and titanium centers in one molecule, bridged by small carbon groups. Such pairs might cooperate in ways single-metal catalysts cannot.

Crystal and spectral analysis caught a surprise: an alkynyl bridge migrated from zirconium to titanium during assembly. Switched on by aluminium-free activators, the paired and single-metal versions polymerized ethylene. The activator's identity decided the chemistry, plucking an electron or a methyl group to wake the catalyst. The working species seems to stay double, growing straight polyethylene chains. One titanium setup in one solvent capped chains with silicon instead.
pmc-13532823:
Mhandu and colleagues reviewed in 2026 how researchers set the loads placed on hearts removed from the body and kept beating in the lab. Such isolated heart setups, including the Langendorff and working-heart models, are a basic tool for studying heart mechanics and energy use. Preload means the stretch on the heart as it fills, and afterload means the resistance it pumps against, and both must be set with care to mimic real life.

Mhandu gathers the physical and software methods used to present, control, and vary these loads, whether by pressure or by flow resistance. The review also covers how models copy the body's blood flow patterns inside a working-heart rig. The authors look ahead to a smart afterload device that adjusts resistance beat by beat, which would copy living conditions more closely and fix limits of current setups.
pmc-13533023:
Egemen Bilgin, Gülçin Tuğcu, and Ahmet Aydın mined drug safety literature in 2026. Some drugs trigger a dangerous heart rhythm called torsades. The trigger is often blockage of one heart channel gene product. Standard pre-market checks focus on the parent drug. The body breaks drugs into metabolites, though. Those breakdown products can change the risk. The team used a text-mining tool built for harm pathways. They examined sixty-four active ingredients with known risk grades.

Evidence showed metabolites shift risk in varied ways. Some metabolites add rhythm danger on their own. Others spare the heart channel entirely. Those safer products could replace riskier parent drugs. The authors call metabolite data essential for honest risk checks. Current checks that ignore metabolites can mislead developers. The study is qualitative, drawn from published text.
pmc-13534223:
Ville Päivärinne and co-authors study whether active free time and active commuting cut later sickness absence, in a 2026 paper. The team used a 2017 health survey of Helsinki city workers aged nineteen to thirty-nine, linked to register records of sick leave through 2020. Free-time activity covered about 3,600 workers and commuting about 3,500, each scored in weekly energy units and split into bands.

Women logged more absence than men overall. Women with moderate-to-vigorous free-time activity had clearly lower rates of total, short, and long absence than inactive women. In men, vigorous free-time activity stayed protective after full adjustment. Commuting results were weaker and less even. The study speaks to employers who weigh wellness perks.
pmc-13534623:
Lei Fan and colleagues test in 2026 how sky view factor, the share of sky visible from a spot, shapes body and brain responses in urban settings. Standard comfort models treat people as passive heat systems and miss brain processing. Volunteers moved from a calm baseline through a stress step to places with varied sky openness.

Brain waves, heart measures, and skin temperature were tracked together. Main effects of sky openness on brain power and heart rate did not reach significance in this modest sample. A trend toward higher calm-linked brain activity in open-sky spots hints that openness may buffer heat stress.
pmc-13534823:
Laura Ben Olivo, Bibiana Verlindo de Araújo, and two co-authors model how an antibiotic reaches tissue in sepsis. Their study, from twenty twenty-six, builds a whole-body model of meropenem. Sepsis changes blood flow and kidney work, so plasma levels may mislead. What matters is the drug level in the fluid around cells, where germs sit.

The model was checked against real plasma and tissue data. Kidney clearing includes a pump protein that pulls the drug out. Sepsis settings tune that pump and tissue leak. Simulations show tissue levels can split sharply from plasma levels. Two common germs are then tested against the tissue levels in a linked effect model.
pmc-13535423:
Suhail Sapkota and co-authors check in a 2026 study how well race is reported in kidney cancer trials. Care guides from a major cancer network rest on these trials, yet the groups hit hardest by the disease may not be in them. Black, Native American, and Alaska Native groups face a higher burden, the authors note.

The team screened 262 sources cited in the network's kidney cancer guide and kept 92 trials. Of those, just 39, or 42.4%, reported the race of the people in the trial. The review also tracked who took part, year, and place, and it compared US trials with those from abroad. The gaps raise doubts about how well the guide fits all patients.
pmc-13536623: A correction notice fixes two figure errors in a study of a dual-targeting liposome drug for early atherosclerosis. In the first figure, an image from a treatment group had been used by mistake as the control image, and a fresh version now shows the right picture. A scale bar in the second figure was also mislabeled, reading 200 micrometers where 200 nanometers was meant. The authors state that neither slip touches the fluorescence analysis, the results, or the conclusions.
pmc-13536723:
Jin Suh Yu and colleagues propose a biology-first approach to cervical cancer screening in a 2026 review. Nearly all cervical cancers follow lasting infection with high-risk human papillomavirus, leaving a long window for prevention. Current options each have trade-offs in accuracy, judgment, and access, especially where clinics and labs are scarce. The review sorts tools by the biological target they measure rather than by device type.

Four target groups are covered, from virus markers and host cell-cycle proteins to small chemical signals and marker-free light-based methods paired with computer reading. Attention goes to bedside-ready tests, sampling without invasive exams, and layered risk sorting that fits large programs. The authors frame the scheme as a path toward screening that is both precise and widely reachable.
pmc-13536823:
Charlotte Leboeuf-Yde and Claire Gudex offer a practical guide to writing the discussion section of clinical and population studies. Their guide is the last of three on structuring a research paper. A good discussion, they argue, stays driven by the study aims and shows clear, critical thought.

They break the section into six common parts, from a summary of findings to a conclusion. For each part they explain what belongs there and what to avoid, such as restating the background. Examples come from their journal. They also treat self critique and future outlooks, and they discuss the use of smart writing tools. The aim is papers that are easier to write and to read.
pmc-13538323:
Monira Alaujan and co-authors test a medicinal plant extract against breast cancer cells, in this 2026 study. Cancers that lean on a survival protein resist standard care. The plant has a folk record and early anti-cancer hints.

The alcohol extract cut the life of two cancer cell types in a dose-linked way while sparing normal breast cells. Treated cells showed the marks of programmed death, with death enzymes active and key genes shifted. Computer docking placed plant compounds inside the survival protein's grip site. Safety screens of the compounds looked clean. The authors propose the extract's parts as leads for new blocker drugs.
pmc-13538823:
Sungho Bea and colleagues weigh severe low blood sugar risk when a heart rhythm drug joins a common diabetes pill in a 2026 Korean claims study. The rhythm drug slows liver breakdown of the diabetes pill, plausibly raising its levels. Among 12,730 adults with type 2 diabetes starting rhythm therapy while on the pill class, starters of the drug in question were weighted against starters of three rival rhythm drugs.

After weighting, starting the drug in question carried nearly double the hazard of severe low blood sugar needing hospital or emergency care versus the rivals. The elevation persisted across sensitivity and subgroup checks. The authors urge caution and close monitoring when the two medicines combine, given how widely the pill class remains used.
pmc-13539023:
Long-term pain and loss of muscle strength often show up together in older adults, but which one drives the other is unclear. Weijie Wang, Qiankun Zhang, and Zhenhua Wu tackle that puzzle in a 2026 study using gene data as a natural experiment. They looked at grip strength, walking pace, and muscle mass as signs of muscle loss.

The team ran the test in both ways, from pain to muscle traits and from muscle traits back to pain. Pain at many body sites was linked to weaker grip and slower walking. Stronger grip, in turn, was linked to a lower risk of widespread pain. The results hint that pain and muscle loss feed each other, so care may need to treat both at once.
pmc-13539823:
Tesfay Gebreslassie Gebrehiwot and nine co-authors survey, in a 2026 study, suicidal thoughts and attempts among young people in Tigray, Ethiopia, after the region's war ended. School pupils and students aged 15 to 24 answered validated questionnaires about mood, trauma, and violence exposure.

Among 599 respondents, about one in five reported suicidal thoughts and roughly one in ten reported an attempt. Depression, anxiety, and post-traumatic stress raised the odds of both outcomes, while sexual abuse and witnessing violence also mattered. Physical activity appeared protective against thoughts of suicide. The authors argue that post-war schools need mental health support built into recovery programs.
pmc-13540123:
Six authors present a case report dated two thousand twenty-six on a hidden gut tumor behind unexplained bleeding. The patient, a man of seventy-two, had two days of dark stools and vague belly discomfort. Standard scopes of the stomach and colon found nothing, a pattern called obscure gastrointestinal bleeding.

A specialized scan spotted a small enhancing lump, about eleven by eight millimeters, in the lower small intestine. Surgery with a scope used inside the bowel pinned down the spot, and a short segment was removed. The lump proved to be a tiny neuroendocrine tumor. The title also records a later heart rhythm problem treated with a pacemaker.
pmc-13540223:
Jennifer Brown and colleagues present a modelling study, published in 2026. It estimates avoidable heart-related deaths in the United States. The comparison is between two pills for chronic lymphocytic leukaemia. Zanubrutinib and ibrutinib are both targeted pills for this blood cancer. Ibrutinib carries a higher cardiac risk. No real-world head-to-head death comparison exists.

The model applied trial-based risk numbers to real prescribing data. Five years of data were used. About eighty-one avoidable cardiac deaths were estimated in later-line treatment. About one hundred forty were estimated in first-line treatment over five years. The numbers rise over a decade of use. The estimates rest on model assumptions and trial populations, the authors caution.
pmc-13540823:
Malgoda Gamage Nimesha Madushani Amarasinghe leads a 2026 survey of job satisfaction among married female nurses at a district general hospital in Sri Lanka's Southern Province. Married nurses juggle ward duties with family demands that may colour how they feel about work.

A random sample of 306 nurses received a questionnaire built around a validated satisfaction scale, and 251 replied. Overall satisfaction scored high. Professional recognition drew the warmest ratings, while recognition tied to pay scored lowest. Age, the ward or unit where a nurse worked, and education level each showed significant links with satisfaction. The authors ask for wider research into the forces behind these patterns.
pmc-13540923:
Lizzy Winstone and colleagues study social media feeds in a 2026 project. They asked how recommendation algorithms shape teen mental health. Most research blames screen time or personal weakness. The commercial machinery that picks the content gets less attention. The team built a grounded theory from teen accounts.

Twenty-seven British teens took part in interviews. Their ages ran from fourteen to nineteen. Each shared screenshots from TikTok and Instagram feeds. The algorithms organised what appeared, and how often. They also set the emotional punch of the feed. Three loops kept exposure going. Teens fought back with savvy tricks, yet those tricks were unevenly shared.
pmc-13542123:
Jorge Jonathan Nué-Martinez and colleagues mapped how a hopeful parasite drug grips parasite DNA. Published in 2026, the study used magnet-based resonance to solve the structure of JNII40 bound to a DNA double strand with four AT repeats. JNII40 kills Leishmania parasites in animals and homes in on AT-rich DNA in their energy hubs.

The drug sank deep into the DNA minor groove, held by direct and water-aided H bonds, among them direct links from drug amidine parts to DNA phosphate oxygens. Two ordered water units bridged drug and DNA, keeping the complex shape true, while drug entry narrowed the groove. These contacts explain the drug's tight grip and AT pickiness seen in heat and magnet tests. The authors offer the structure as a blueprint for designing choosy DNA-targeting drugs against kinetoplastid parasites.
pmc-13542223:
Frederik Schliephake, Isabella Lurje, and Georg Lurje reply to critics in 2026. Their trial tested hypothermic oxygenated machine perfusion. That cold, oxygenated rinse protects donor livers. Their study showed the treatment improving bile chemistry. The letter answers a commentary on that work. Bile duct scarring is the point at issue.

Critics asked why better bile brought no visible drop in strictures. The trial held only twenty-six patients. This donor type rarely develops such strictures at all. Too few events occurred to judge the question. Trials in higher-risk donation showed scarring roughly halved. The authors also discuss glands around the bile ducts. They propose long warm perfusion of discarded livers next.
pmc-13542423:
Nihel Ammous-Boukhris and co-authors report a new gene fault in a Tunisian ovarian cancer case in a 2026 paper. The fault sits in BRCA1, a gene whose damage drives many such cancers. Faults there also open the door to a targeted drug family, the PARP inhibitors.

Their patient was a fifty-year-old woman with severe anemia from heavy bleeding. Scans showed no ovarian mass, but surgery found a belly lining nodule. Gene tests on tumor and blood found a ten-letter deletion in BRCA1, seen only in the tumor. Databases class the new fault as disease-causing. After standard chemotherapy, the drug olaparib kept her disease-free for twenty-three months with good tolerance.
pmc-13542523:
Yansheng Wang and ten co-authors ask whether fluid collecting in the belly signals worse outcomes in a rare, life-threatening overreaction of the immune system. Their study came out in 2026. The syndrome floods the body with inflammatory signals and damages many organs at once.

Records covered just over a hundred adults with the secondary form of the syndrome. About one in five had belly fluid at presentation. Those patients showed lower blood cell counts and a distinct immune profile, with fewer helper T cells and more natural killer cells. Their median survival was far shorter than patients without the fluid. Statistical modeling kept the fluid as an independent predictor of death. The authors urge clinicians to treat its presence as a warning sign demanding early, aggressive care.
pmc-13542923:
Cemal Demirlek and Paulo Lizano wrote a 2026 comment on a bold new theory of schizophrenia. The theory holds that unstable dopamine signals in the retina, the eye's light-sensing layer, start a chain that ends in the illness. It pulls together eye changes, immune pruning of brain links, and growth of new links.

The theory wins praise for joining facts that are usually kept apart and for making claims that tests can prove wrong. Demirlek and Lizano still find the proof thin. They ask for stronger data before the eye is moved to the center of the story. Their reply shows how a field should greet a grand new idea.
pmc-13543323:
Shuai Shao and Gail Heyman ask how children and teenagers judge award systems that give trophies to everyone or only to top finishers. Their study appeared in 2026. They worked with two age groups in the United States: 43 children aged 7 to 9 and 44 teens aged 15 to 18. Each read about a running race and predicted what each award style would do to effort, feelings, and behavior.

Both age groups expected selective awards to raise effort and pride. Even the youngest saw how rewards shape work. Teens went further: they noted that selective awards might tempt cheating or risky acts. Teens who saw themselves as slow runners also liked selective awards less. The study shows self-interest joins moral reasoning as children judge fairness in reward systems.
pmc-13543623:
Satoru Hagiwara and co-authors published a 2026 study of liver cancer returning after hepatitis C was cured with modern direct-acting antivirals. Clearing the virus does not erase cancer risk, especially in patients who already had a tumour. Records of 279 patients who reached sustained viral clearance after 2014 were reviewed for who developed cancer. The twenty-eight recurrences were sorted into spread within the liver, reawakened dormant tumour, or genuinely new cancer.

Thirty-three patients developed cancer after cure, and a prior cancer history was the only independent predictor, multiplying risk about fourteenfold. Recurrences split fairly evenly among the three patterns. Because follow-up was strict, nearly all recurrences were caught at the earliest stages, and curative treatment proved possible in twenty-seven of twenty-eight patients. Whatever form recurrence takes, the authors conclude, vigilant surveillance after viral cure keeps it treatable.
pmc-13543923:
Shazia Sarela and colleagues report a study of mnemonic-based teaching led by near-peers for third-year medical students, testing whether the memory tricks students swap informally actually work when taught on purpose. Over eight months, twenty-three peer-led sessions on commonly examined clinical topics wove mnemonics into every class. Students answered single-best-answer questions and rated their confidence before and after each session, and later rated how useful the mnemonics felt and whether they would use them again.

Scores improved significantly after teaching, especially on questions tied to the taught mnemonics, and confidence rose as well. Students left more likely to use mnemonics in future, and the students whose confidence grew most were the keenest adopters. Formalising a folk study technique, the authors conclude, pays off twice: the peer format and the memory aids each earn their place in the timetable.
pmc-13544223:
Thirteen authors, led by Yiwei Zhang, report a 2026 study of very strong graphene fibers made by a spinning method that copies nature. High-grade fibers that are light yet strong are in wide demand. A common problem is that fibers tend to gain strength or stiffness, but not both at once.

The team took cues from the layered build of natural materials. They spun bundles of graphene gel fibers and fused them across scales into thick fibers. The result pairs a tensile strength of 3.0 gigapascal with bending stiffness far above that of Kevlar fibers of like size. The fusion step also suppresses flaws, so thick fibers keep an even inner order. The fibers conduct heat and electricity well too. The authors see them as a structure-and-function material for robots that work in harsh settings.
pmc-13544423:
Ndlovu and co-authors explored how nursing students at a public college in South Africa felt the caring presence of their lecturers during online learning. Nursing is founded on care, yet the pandemic forced the diploma program out of classrooms and onto screens in 2020. Whether students still felt cared for at a distance was an open question.

In this study, caring presence covers communication, emotional support, being reachable, quick institutional responses, and fair access to devices and data. Students described their experience of each element during the online period. Their answers show where presence survived the move online and where it broke down. Colleges can use the findings to design remote teaching that still feels human.
pmc-13545123:
Mosalam and co-authors map the genes behind cold tolerance in sorghum in a 2026 study. The crop feeds many people but suffers in cool lands. The team grew 394 types across ten settings and three growth stages. They tracked how type and place interacted, then scanned the genome in blocks.

Cold strength proved tied mostly to stage and place, not one master gene set. Types that shared a stage shared more gene control than types across stages. Stacking good gene blocks helped at first, then gains leveled off. Yield traits mostly moved in a good direction, but flowering came later, a cost to weigh. The authors urge breeders to treat cold tolerance as several linked traits.
pmc-13545223:
Ramon Garcia Maset and co-authors report a microbiology study, published in 2026, testing bladder infection treatments inside a model that mimics the human urinary tract. Standard lab tests often fail to predict whether a urinary infection will clear, because real infections unfold in urine, on living tissue, and under flow. The team combined human urine, a three dimensional bladder tissue model, and a flow platform that washes the tissue.

A standard antibiotic looked strongest in simple tests yet failed to wipe out infection in the tissue model. A virus cocktail that infects bacteria attacked hidden bacterial communities and kept tissue alive, while provoking immune signals. Pairing both cleared free bacteria and shrank communities further under still conditions, showing why realistic models matter before trials.
pmc-13545423:
Douglas J Marr and colleagues set out in 2026 to explain how a small switch protein called ARL11 turns on phospholipase D1. That enzyme makes a signaling fat linked to cancer and brain disease. Earlier work knew ARL11 could activate the enzyme, but not how the two fit together. The team combined test-tube activity assays with computer-predicted structures of the pair.

ARL11 stimulated the enzyme only when loaded with GTP, the usual on signal for such switches. Mutations at the predicted contact surface broke the activation, confirming the model's layout. Parts of a loose loop on the enzyme appear to fold into shape against ARL11, giving three neighboring contact zones that together explain the activation.
pmc-13545523:
Silja Bühler and co-authors report an outbreak study, published in 2026, on a bacterial disease striking vulnerable adults in Hamburg, Germany. The germ, Haemophilus influenzae type b, usually threatens young children, but here it caused invasive illness in middle aged people who use drugs or lack housing. Twenty cases were reported in the first year of the outbreak.

Gene sequencing linked most cases into one cluster, and many patients shared time in the open drug scene of the city. Response steps included preventive antibiotics for close contacts, dozens of vaccine doses, and an information campaign through addiction support centers. The authors call it the first such adult outbreak recorded in Europe and urge wider vaccine advice.
pmc-13546423:
Zi Qiang Glen Liau and co-authors (2026) offer surgeons a formula that predicts the size of a knee graft before the first incision. The quadriceps tendon is gaining favor for rebuilding a torn anterior cruciate ligament, but harvesting it can weaken the thigh more than other graft choices, so size planning matters. A graft under ten millimeters risks failure. Until now, prediction from pre-surgery MRI used only rough cutoffs. The authors test a continuous method instead.

Their formula converts the tendon's MRI width into an estimated graft diameter, two times the square root of width over pi. They checked the estimate against the real grafts, within one millimeter counting as accurate, tested the old cutoff approach too, and measured whether two raters using the method agree. A reliable prediction lets the surgical team plan the harvest, or choose a different graft, before the patient is asleep.
pmc-13546523:
Yan Ming and co-authors compared in 2026 the two classic forms of stomach cancer, intestinal and diffuse, once the disease has already spread. Their analysis drew on a large United States cancer registry and included 4,696 patients with metastatic disease. Statistical matching balanced the two groups so that differences in spread patterns and survival could be read more fairly.

Intestinal-type tumors reached the liver more often, while diffuse-type tumors reached bone more often. Diffuse-type disease also carried a worse outlook for both overall and cancer-specific survival, even after matching. Among spread sites, patients whose cancer reached the liver lived relatively longer than those with bone, brain, or multiple sites of spread. The authors say the subtype should inform risk discussions.
pmc-13546723:
Šimon Halás and a large team fed dairy cows humic substances, natural compounds from decomposed organic matter, in 2026 to see whether they ease the difficult weeks around calving. Sixty pregnant Slovak spotted cows were split into groups, with the treated group receiving the additive daily from two months before calving through the first week of lactation. Rumen fluid, blood, milk, and udder health were monitored.

Treated cows showed a friendlier rumen pattern, with higher pH, relatively more acetate, and less ammonia, alongside lower urea in blood and milk. Their milk carried more protein and fewer somatic cells, and fewer udder quarters were infected shortly after calving. Immune measures calmed as well. The authors propose the additive as part of a herd health program.
pmc-13547323:
Safia Abbas leads a team that predicts vehicle carbon dioxide output. Their study from twenty twenty-six deals with tailpipe emissions per vehicle. Exact forecasts aid regulation and greener design.

A public Canadian registry gave data on thousands of vehicles. Data split into training, validation, and test shares. A firefly method picked the input features first. Ant colony tuning set the model settings jointly. Five learner types were tuned and compared head to head. The tuned memory network won on the test set. Its error rates were the lowest of the group.
pmc-13547723:
Prichayudh and co-authors studied a 2026 test problem in children with cyanotic congenital heart disease, where low blood oxygen drives haemoglobin unusually high. That compensation hides iron deficiency, because standard measures look normal even when iron runs out. One hundred and ten patients aged six months to fifteen years were enrolled.

Twenty-eight children, about a quarter, proved iron depleted by ferritin or transferrin measures between September 2022 and September 2023. Haemoglobin and haematocrit matched between depleted and sufficient groups, confirming they cannot separate the two states. Prichayudh found two red cell measures did separate them: wider spread of red cell sizes and lower haemoglobin inside young red cells. Combined, the pair reached about eighty-five percent diagnostic accuracy, a practical option where full iron studies are unavailable.
pmc-13548123:
Severe asthma that is not driven by the usual allergy pathway is the subject of a 2026 review by Hiroki Tashiro and co-authors. New biologic drugs have tamed the classic type 2 form for many patients, but a large share show a different pattern, often with neutrophil-heavy airways and poor response to steroids.

The review sums up the traits, causes, and candidate targets of this non-type 2 form. Obesity, dirty air, smoking, and chest viruses all feed it. At the cell level, signals such as interleukin-17 switch on pathways that steroids barely touch. The authors chart what is known from lab to clinic and where new treatments might break through.
pmc-13548223:
Future health workers should know better than most how antibiotics work, yet self-treatment is common among them. Asma Ben Mabrouk and co-authors survey paramedic students at a health sciences school in Monastir, Tunisia. Of 500 students, 324 took part. The survey covered what they know about antibiotics, how they feel about them, and how they actually use them.

Most students knew antibiotics target bacteria, but 40 percent wrongly thought they also work on viruses. About 62 percent had never taken a course on antibiotics. Still, 60 percent reported treating themselves with antibiotics, most often amoxicillin. Past success with a drug and seeing symptoms as minor were the main reasons. Keeping leftover antibiotics at home strongly raised the odds of self-treating. The authors call for focused teaching and behavior-change work to curb the habit and slow drug resistance.
pmc-13548423:
Karola Diósi and András Vargha asked how teenagers' bonds with their parents line up with the ways they handle stress. They surveyed 1,485 Hungarian secondary school students, aged 16 to 23, using standard questionnaires on parental attachment and coping styles. Instead of treating each trait separately, they grouped students into attachment profiles, letting patterns across the whole person emerge.

The grouping settled on six clusters with clear separation. Cluster membership differed by gender, and each attachment pattern came with its own coping mix. Students with secure attachment blended coping strategies more flexibly when stress hit. The authors argue that support for stressed teenagers should account for these whole-person patterns, and for gender differences, rather than treating coping skills in isolation.
pmc-13548523:
Hafiz Bilal Ahmed Jilani and colleagues pool randomized trials of omega-3 fatty acid supplements for people on hemodialysis, in a 2026 systematic review and meta-analysis. Heart disease kills more dialysis patients than any other cause, and fish-oil fats have shown heart benefits in the wider population. The team searched three databases through November 2025 for trials comparing these supplements against placebo.

Across the pooled trials, supplements did not lower deaths from all causes. Deaths from heart causes fell by nearly half, however, and heart attacks and problems with dialysis access sites also became less common. The authors support omega-3 as an add-on protective treatment, while warning that one large trial supplies most of the data. They call for further big trials before firm guidance can follow.
pmc-13548623:
Mary Ofuru Kama and five co-authors review how far machine learning has come in predicting sickle cell crises and deaths, and how much weather has been let into the models. Sickle cell anemia brings recurring pain crises and early death, heaviest in poorer countries, and heat, humidity, rainfall, pollution, and season all nudge the disease. The review covered thirty-four studies published between 2005 and 2026.

The models ranged from neural networks and random forests to support vector machines and deep learning, and the climate inputs most used were temperature, humidity, rainfall, wind, air quality, and season. Yet most models still fed mainly on clinical and demographic data, barely touched climate, and rarely came from the hardest-hit region, Sub-Saharan Africa. Where weather was included, predictions improved. The authors recommend climate-aware, interdisciplinary models, longer environmental datasets, and far more research where the burden actually sits.
pmc-13548723:
Yi Wang and colleagues trace how pancreatic cancer prepares the liver for invasion using tiny parcels shipped from the tumor, in a 2026 study. The liver is this cancer's favorite distant target, and a fibrotic landing pad forms there before tumor cells arrive. Comparing tumor and normal tissue gene activity, then testing in cells and mice, the team singled out a transcription factor, RUNX1, whose levels tracked with liver spread.

Silencing RUNX1 in mouse tumors cut liver metastasis dramatically. The factor switches on a sticky surface protein, ITGB1, which tumor cells pack into their extracellular vesicles. Liver support cells swallow those parcels and, through an inflammatory pathway, start laying down scar-like matrix and calling in other cells, building the fibrotic niche. Blood vesicle levels of the protein also marked patients with liver spread and poor outlook, suggesting a diagnostic use.
pmc-13549323:
Nawal Al-Malahi and co-authors test tiny metal particles against liver cancer cells in a 2026 lab study. Liver cancer kills many people worldwide and often resists standard drugs. The particles join zinc and iron oxide in one speck about 30 nanometers wide. The team grew human liver cancer cells in dishes and dosed them with rising amounts of the specks.

Cell death grew with dose. The dose that halved cell life in a day was 61 micrograms per milliliter. At high doses, harmful oxygen radicals rose inside the cells. Guard molecules fell, and the cells' power hubs lost their charge. Those shifts mark the start of programmed cell death. The authors frame the particles as a candidate worth more study.
pmc-13549923:
Olivia Hahl and Mika Martikainen review, in 2026, every published case of pancreatitis in people with confirmed mitochondrial disease. The pancreas is often affected in these disorders, usually as diabetes, but inflammation of the gland is poorly mapped. Their search found twenty reports covering twenty-four patients.

The average age at first attack was thirteen, and most cases recurred or became chronic. Belly pain and vomiting were the most common signs, and none of the patients had the usual risk factors like gallstones or alcohol. Two genetic causes dominated. A quarter of patients died soon after admission, underlining that this rare pairing can be deadly.
pmc-13550023:
Dieter Seifert traces how German psychiatry and criminal law renamed intellectual disability across a century, in a 2026 German-language article. Words carry attitudes, and the terms used between lawyers and psychiatrists shape real legal outcomes. The old word Schwachsinn was once a diagnosis, but it hardened into an insult. Yet it survived inside the criminal code's insanity paragraph until the end of 2020. Another outdated phrase, for deep personality deviation, survived with it.

Seifert walks through how diagnostic labels for people with reduced intelligence shifted across classification editions and why each generation renegotiates the line between normal and disordered. He notes stubborn public prejudice, including surveys where many people reject neighbors with schizophrenia. His plea is for careful, current wording in statutes and diagnoses alike, so that law keeps pace with psychiatric knowledge and language stops branding the people it describes.
pmc-13551223:
Walaa Aldairi and colleagues surveyed women eye doctors across Saudi Arabia in a study published in two thousand twenty-six. They asked what helps and what hinders these doctors at work and at home, including discrimination, motherhood challenges, and mental well-being. Interviews used a structured questionnaire over an eight-month period.

Strong family support and understanding spouses stood out as the top helpers. The survey also measured happiness at home and work and how balance linked to family and job factors. Hospital leaders gain a grounded picture of what keeps skilled women doctors in the workforce, and where workplaces still make their jobs harder.
pmc-13551323:
Ahmed Sohaib and seven colleagues test whether dropping the 5-fluorouracil bolus harms patients with metastatic colorectal cancer. The bolus adds worry about blood toxicity in modern multidrug regimens, yet its value is uncertain. Their 2026 retrospective cohort covers 267 patients treated from June 2020 to June 2024 in Egypt. Patients got bolus-free nbFOLFOX or standard mFOLFOX6, with or without targeted therapy.

Bolus omission gave a small but significant progression-free survival gain, with mean 10.029 months versus 9.319 months. Overall survival was similar, at mean 21.7 months versus 20.7 months. pmc-13551423:
Nan Yao and co-authors present a 2026 review on sparing organs after immune therapy for a subtype of colorectal cancer. These tumors lack mismatch repair, and checkpoint drugs given before surgery melt many of them away. The review asks when surgeons can safely skip the operation and watch instead.

For colon tumors, the evidence still rests on what pathologists find after removal, and nonoperative checks are unproven. Rectal tumors are different: response can be rechecked by exam, scope, and MRI over time. In highly chosen patients with a complete clinical response, watch-and-wait may be fair. The authors weigh salvage surgery, surveillance burdens, side effects, and open disputes. They urge caution outside expert centers.
pmc-13551623:
Sudhir Kumar, Koichiro Tamura, and Sudip Sharma review a shortcut for evolutionary tree analysis on big data. Their twenty twenty-six article deals with phylogenomics, which builds trees from whole genomes. Full analyses are slow and memory-hungry, since cost grows with the count of distinct site patterns in the alignment.

Their framework takes small subsamples of sites, stretches them back up by upsampling, and merges the results. Cost falls by orders of magnitude, while the signal is kept. Tests on fake and real data show it can recover support values, pick models, and date branches well. Spread across subsamples also reveals clashes in the signal that the standard bootstrap can hide.
pmc-13551923:

Records covered 1,373 adults at three districts of one hospital. The index, called TyG, blends triglycerides and glucose as a stand-in for insulin resistance. The team related it to death in hospital. Curve methods allowed bent, not just straight, links.

The index stood as an independent risk factor for death in hospital. The link bent in a U-like shape. Both very high and very low values tied to more deaths. Heart size and function measures also shifted across index levels. No subgroup changed the main link. The team proposes the cheap index as a short-term warning sign in myocarditis.
pmc-13552023:
Jinhong Li and co-authors test, in 2026, whether a plant compound can ease early failure of the ovaries in rats. The compound comes from a plant widely used as a food supplement in East Asia. The team caused the condition with a drug, then treated the rats and checked cycles, hormone levels, and ovary tissue.

Treated rats regained regular cycles, better hormone balance, and more stored eggs. A cell-death pathway tied to inflammation was quieter after treatment. In lab cells, the compound also reduced injury, unless the pathway's trigger was forced high. The results suggest a protective effect worth further study, not yet a proven remedy.
pmc-13552223:
Kamol Suwannakarn and co-authors trace an mpox outbreak in Thailand in a 2026 paper. The virus spread world wide from twenty twenty two, in lands where it was once rare. How it took hold in Thailand was not yet clear.

The team read the full genomes of virus samples from sixteen patients. Early cases matched mixed world strains, a sign of many entries. Later cases were near all one lineage that formed its own Thai cluster. Mutations bore marks of a human enzyme at work. The pattern points to steady local spread from mid twenty twenty three.
pmc-13552323:
Onifade and nine co-authors count food ads aimed at kids in Senegal in this twenty twenty-six study. Ads for foods low in good nutrients can push poor diets and weight gain in youth. Rules that limit such ads to kids are still weak in Senegal, the team notes.

Inside, the study mapped ads near forty schools in four zones and logged ads on four TV channels. Close to four in five ads near schools and three in four on TV were for foods that fail health checks. Kids in group talks recalled brands and said they asked for goods they had seen in ads. Parents backed firmer rules to curb such ads.
pmc-13552423:
Sayed Saleh, Riaz Khan, Lotfi Aroua, and Hamdoon Mohammed review how nanotechnology could turn plant flavonoids into real infection fighters. Their 2026 review covers these plant compounds, also found in propolis, with activity against oxidation, inflammation, viruses, and bacteria. With infections rising and drug options strained, the class is clinically attractive. One problem blocks it: the compounds dissolve poorly, absorb weakly, break down fast, and barely reach target tissues.

Nano-scale carriers attack each weakness in turn, improving solubility, absorption, stability, and controlled release at the site of action. The review surveys carrier designs aimed at antimicrobial and antiviral uses, weighing how delivery changes the compounds' activity. The authors frame targeted flavonoid therapy as a plausible answer to resistant infections, pending better trials.
pmc-13552523:
Stefani Maria Ferreira and co-authors describe a 2026 study of a pest drug poured on cattle skin. The drug kills ticks and flies, and its traces in meat matter for food safety. The team tracked how long the drug and its break-down products stay in blood under farm conditions.

Bulls got one skin dose, and blood was checked for near half a year with a fine lab method. The parent drug peaked on day one and was gone by about five weeks. A sulfone product peaked near two weeks and lasted far longer, up to about twenty weeks. A third product, made by sunlight on the skin, showed up now and then at low levels. The authors name the sulfone as the best safety marker.
pmc-13552723:
Yaacov Schul, Yoav Ganzach, and Asya Pazy revisit, in 2026, a debate about how party identity shapes hostility toward political opponents. They propose a different model and apply it to the original data plus a second large dataset. The effect of identity strength on animosity differed between Democratic and Republican respondents. That pattern fits an asymmetric view of partisan hostility. The authors close with lessons on method and on how political dislike should be studied within the same person over time.
pmc-13553723:
Jinyan Wu and nine co-authors describe older hospital patients eligible for a dementia care payment in Japan, in a study from 2026. The add-on payment began in 2016 to reward hospital dementia care, yet who receives it nationwide was unclear. The team used a national inpatient database.

They covered more than one million stays from 2016 to 2019 for patients aged sixty-five and older with moderate to severe dementia. Patients averaged over eighty-five years old, and most needed full help with daily tasks. Billing for both payment levels rose sharply over the period. Stay length and hospital death fell slightly, as did risky drug use at discharge.
pmc-13554023:
Mengwei Zhang and co-authors build a prediction tool for a harsh liver cancer subtype in a 2026 study. The macrotrabecular-massive form of liver cancer tends to return early and end poorly, so spotting it before surgery helps.

The team studied over six hundred patients who had early stage cancer removed at many centers. Scan traits, blood tests, and deep learning scores from tumor zones were joined in one chart tool. The tool sorted patients well in training and test sets. Scores also split patients by how long they stayed free of return. Key drivers were scan habitat scores, deep scores, and two blood marks. Surgeons get a clear aid for risk talks.
pmc-13554123:
Immunotherapy under the tongue can tame dust mite allergy, but doctors lack a blood test that says who is improving. Ghada Mokhtar and eleven co-authors measured two candidate markers in 2026 in fifty-four patients with moderate-to-severe mite-driven rhinitis, against fifty-four healthy controls.

Both markers, a decoy receptor called sST2 and a small RNA, miR-223, ran significantly higher in patients. The receptor tracked with mite-specific antibody levels and white cell counts. After six months of therapy it fell, and it fell furthest in patients whose nose scores improved by at least thirty percent. The authors propose the pair as activity and response gauges for a slow treatment.
pmc-13554223:
Juan Pablo Cisneros-Barba leads a five-author team field-testing a cheap printed sensor that reads soil acidity nonstop in a 2026 study. Soil acidity steers crop health, yet dense readings are hard to gather with pricey lab gear. Their printed carbon strip uses a dye whose electrical signal shifts with acidity. Tests spanned wet and dry soils, loose and packed ground, and several soil types.

Readings stayed steady across all those changes, with no fresh calibration needed. Mounted on a small board with a low-power reader, the sensors logged data alone for months outdoors. Weatherproofing kept the setup running through field conditions. The authors see cheap, dense acidity maps guiding fertilizer choices field by field, rather than by rough averages.
pmc-13554523:
Yen Nguyen Thi Ngoc and co-authors describe dengue cases with warning signs among hospitalized children in northern Vietnam. Published in 2026, the cross-sectional study covers 319 children with confirmed dengue at a tertiary children's hospital, in records from late 2022 plus prospective enrollment into 2023. Dengue is a major mosquito borne infection and a common cause of child admission in endemic areas.

About forty percent of the children met the criteria for dengue with warning signs. Older age, urban residence, low platelet count, and a raised liver enzyme each raised the odds on their own. Belly pain was the most common warning sign, followed by repeated vomiting and mucosal bleeding. The authors say the four factors can flag children who need closer watch.
pmc-13554923:
A blood gene variant tied to marrow overgrowth may also touch movement, and Elena Ardila Jurado and co-authors describe five patients where the two meet, in work from twenty twenty-six. The variant drives thick-blood ills known for clots and inflammation. Shaking palsy in that setting had barely been charted.

The five split across kinds: two classic cases, one atypical, one with motor nerve disease, and one who moved from chorea to parkinsonism across two years. Brain scans, where done, ran abnormal. Drug response varied. Coincidence is possible, the authors grant, but vessel, immune, and treatment paths give real cause to look closer.
pmc-13555223:
Yoonha Lee and colleagues report long-term outcomes for Korean children with lipoid congenital adrenal hyperplasia, a rare steroid-making disorder, publishing the multicentre study in 2026. Faults in the STAR protein block cholesterol transport inside hormone-making cells, crippling cortisol, aldosterone, and sex-hormone production. The team followed 31 patients from ten centres, nearly all with the classic form diagnosed in infancy.

Salt wasting affected about six in ten patients, and darkened skin was the most common feature, seen in over seven in ten. Most classic patients carried the same East Asian founder variant, and those reaching adulthood attained near-average height on hormone replacement. The authors call for continued follow-up of puberty and fertility, since ovarian cysts and varied pubertal timing appeared in the cohort.
pmc-13556023:
Jiahui Qi and ten colleagues tested in 2026 whether simple combined blood indices can flag people at high risk of heart and metabolic disease. They built two scores from routine glucose and lipid measures. One score uses six factors and the other uses seven. Both were checked against disease records in a large United States survey and a Chinese ageing cohort. Machine learning models measured how well each score predicted illness.

A short panel of routine tests may thus serve long-term risk monitoring.
pmc-13556423:
Y-H Lee and eight co-authors test a new drug target for ADHD-like behavior in young mice, in a conference abstract from 2026. ADHD has been linked to faulty circuits in the cerebellum, a brain area at the back of the skull. A receptor found mostly in that area's granule cells helps set how active those cells are.

A drug that disrupts a key brain receptor was used to trigger hyperactivity, impulsivity, and poor attention in the mice. A compound that boosts the cerebellum receptor reversed all three behaviors. The effect vanished in mice bred without the receptor gene. The authors call this a proof of concept for a new ADHD treatment route.
pmc-13556523:

pmc-13556723:
Pan and Yeh compare brain wiring in children with two overlapping behavior disorders in a 2026 conference abstract. One disorder brings lasting irritability and fierce reactions to frustration. It often comes with attention deficit hyperactivity disorder, which clouds what is unique to each.

pmc-13556823:

pmc-13558323:

pmc-13558623:

pmc-13558723:

pmc-13559223:
Xingguo Fu and co-authors hunt for key genes behind recurring mouth ulcers, in a 2026 study. These painful sores return again and again, and their cause is poorly understood. Five of them looked protective, while two raised risk. The seven cluster around cell movement, immune response, and metabolism control. The authors say these genes could seed new markers and drug ideas for a common, nagging condition.
pmc-13559323:
Ji-Yoon Jung and Tae-Yun Sung comment on a new chest tube that also delivers pain relief, in this 2026 piece. Chest tubes after lung surgery are a stubborn source of pain that slows walking, breathing, and recovery. The device they discuss joins drainage and drug delivery in one tube, sending local anesthetic into the chest through small side holes.

In the trial under review, patients with the new tube reported less pain at rest and when coughing, and felt better recovered. Total drug use and hospital stay did not change. The authors value the shift in thinking: the tube becomes a treatment tool, not just a drain.
pmc-13559523:
Phillip Hogan, Ralph Edward DeWalt, and Scott Grubbs compile a checklist of stoneflies across the American Midwest in this 2026 paper. pmc-13559923:
Neil Philip Hobbs and co-authors published a modelling study in 2026 on drug resistance in worm control for farm livestock. The work deals with gut worms in animals such as cattle and sheep. Drugs used to treat these worms are losing effect as the worms adapt. The authors ask how resistance can be measured well and how treatment can slow its spread.

pmc-13560123:
A large Benin team led by Serge Akpodji weighs how much malaria germ load the bite glands of mosquitoes carry by farm zone. Bite worth of a mosquito turns in part on that germ count in its glands. Crews caught the Anopheles kind by hand-on-skin at twelve spots in seven farm zones. Kind sorts, germ checks, and load counts ran on near three thousand caught bugs.

One kin kind made near two thirds of the sorted pool in the run. Germ rates and loads split by zone and by kind in the maths. Such splits can aim spray and net work where loads run hot. Zone maps join kind maps as watch tools for the land.
pmc-13560723:
Pisut Pongchaikul and colleagues review infection inside the womb, a leading cause of early birth and harm to mother and baby. Their survey covers naming, diagnosis, treatment, and the lab tools used to find the germs involved.

Standard culture tests are slow and miss germs that are hard to grow in the lab. Newer DNA tests can name single species or read a broad bacterial gene, catching organisms that culture misses. Whole-genome and sweep-all sequencing go further, spotting bacteria, viruses, and fungi at once, plus resistance and attack genes. pmc-13560923:
Dezhi Lu and five co-authors present a review from twenty twenty-six on care that goes on at home for kids after surgery for Hirschsprung's disease. In this birth defect, a stretch of gut lacks nerve cells. Surgery is the main fix, but risks run on: gut inflammation, bowel habit flaws, and mood or behavior issues. Steady nursing at home links hospital care to full recovery.

Smart tech care and team based care get close looks. Gaps named are thin standards and short follow up. Parent schooling sways home care quality a lot.
pmc-13561023:
Hannah Edwards and co-authors check whether a brain-protecting drug reaches mothers fairly in England, in this 2026 study. Magnesium sulphate given before very early birth guards the baby's brain. The team studied mothers of babies born between twenty-four and thirty weeks from 2014 to 2024, across a national quality drive that began in 2018.

Before the drive, mothers in the North and in poorer areas were less likely to get the drug than mothers in the South and in richer areas. After the drive, both gaps faded to nothing. A small gap by ethnic group stayed flat. Age showed no link with treatment.
pmc-13561523:
Matthias Weigl and co-authors follow doctors and nurses through a switch to electronic health records. Most past studies look back after the fact. Their 2026 study instead tracks staff before and after the switch, five months apart. In all, 163 physicians and nurses from several hospital units took part. Surveys gauged workflow breaks, multitasking, information load, and burnout.

The rollout itself differed by job. Nurses got a structured, on-site launch with set training. Physicians got a looser, self-led path with fewer shared resources. Stakeholder interviews filled in how each launch felt on the ground. The team compares the two professions' paths over time. The design shows how the same software can land very differently by role.
pmc-13561723:
Steffen Rausch and co-authors wrote a study from 2026 on drug targets in bladder cancer. New drugs for this cancer latch onto marks on the tumor cell, so doctors need to know which marks a given tumor bears. The team asked whether those marks change as the disease moves from its first site to nearby nodes. They tested four marks on tissue from healthy lining, first tumors, and spread found in lymph nodes.

pmc-13561923:
Dodangeh and co-authors report an unusual surgical case: a man's appendix found inflamed inside a groin hernia, in a 2026 case report. The fifty-five-year-old arrived with groin pain, vomiting, and signs of blocked bowel from a recurrent hernia. Scans suggested the hernia was trapped.

Surgery confirmed an Amyand's hernia, the rare finding of the appendix inside the hernia sac, with acute appendicitis. The surgeons removed the appendix and repaired the hernia. Lab examination also found a benign serrated growth in the appendix, with no cancer. A follow-up colonoscopy three months later was clear. The authors stress checking removed tissue and the colon afterward.
pmc-13562223:
Nikolaos Kapouleas and David Wiygul build in 2026 new smooth surfaces inside a round three-sphere that merge three torus shapes. The three tori cross each other at right angles along six great circles. The new surfaces smooth out those crossings while staying closed and smooth.

Each surface comes from one small disc with six sides, copied around by a set of symmetries. The authors prove that such a disc is unique for its type. That proof also shows that some surfaces built in past work by gluing are the same as these. For low counts, the surfaces here are new results.
pmc-13562323:
Mercè Sitjà-Rabert and colleagues studied why frail older adults in Barcelona stick with, or drop out of, a community program meant to prevent disability. The + AGIL Barcelona program mixes exercise, nutrition, medication review, and social support for people showing early frailty. In this 2026 qualitative study, researchers ran focus groups with 22 participants averaging 82 years old and 18 primary care professionals.

Warm, personal communication, exercise plans tailored to each person, and a sense of group belonging kept people going, the interviews showed. Caregiving duties, tight budgets, and scarce local resources pulled the other way. Lasting success, the authors conclude, depends less on the program's contents than on steady staffing and close links between clinics and community services.
pmc-13562623:
Sergio Barbero and two colleagues explain an optical puzzle: why the starburst spikes around a night light come in countable patterns. When a bright point is viewed in dim light, faults in the eye's optics fold light into caustic patterns on the retina, and those patterns often show rotational symmetry. Counting special fold points in that surface, called cusps of Gauss, predicts how many peaks appear and how they arrange. A round aberration mixed with a three-lobed one yields a three-peak starburst. Swapping in a four-lobed term yields four-fold patterns with four or eight peaks. The authors add that the link runs backward too: a measured starburst could betray facts about a person's eye aberrations.
pmc-13562723:

Eleven randomised trials with 568 adults covered exercise started after successful weight loss, during the maintenance phase when regain usually strikes. pmc-13563223:
Amanda Pádua and co-authors compare two kinds of daily movement and thinking skills in a large Brazil adult health study, in a paper from two thousand twenty-six. Travel activity showed the reverse pattern at first, but the link faded once job type was taken into account. The split held for both men and women in the leisure results. pmc-13563723:
Nigatu Admasu Desta and three colleagues investigate a sharp malaria outbreak that hit Meinit Goldia District in southwest Ethiopia in 2025. pmc-13563923:

pmc-13564123:
Zhang leads a team proposing an Asian registry of wrongful convictions in a 2026 paper. Wrongful convictions are poorly documented across Asian legal systems. Records are scattered and hard to compare between countries, which blocks shared learning.

pmc-13565423:

pmc-13565523:

pmc-13565723:

pmc-13566823:

pmc-13567323:

pmc-13567623:

pmc-13567723:

pmc-13567823:

pmc-13568023:

pmc-13568323:

pmc-13568423:

pmc-13568523:

pmc-13569523:

pmc-13570423:

pmc-13570623:

A gene pair showed a joint effect, while one gene, ABCB1, dominated alone. The authors aim to sharpen risk sorting for such families.
pmc-13570823:

pmc-13570923:

pmc-13571123:

pmc-13571423:

pmc-13571523:

pmc-13571623:

pmc-13571723:

pmc-13572023:
