pmc-13584123:
Ali Zakiei and co-authors sort 1,187 adults in western Iran into lifestyle types based on sleep and activity, then compare their well-being. Healthy habits are praised one at a time. This study asks how the pair combines. A cluster analysis grouped residents aged 16 and up across five provinces.

One cluster stood clearly on top. Its members posted the best quality of life, self-rated health and happiness scores. The gaps between clusters were large for the first two outcomes. The design is a snapshot, so cause cannot be claimed. Still, the pattern tells planners which mixes of rest and movement travel with a good life, and where tailored programs might help most.
pmc-13584823: A 2026 notice corrects a study of a leaf extract that protected the heart during chemotherapy. The original paper reported that extract of Apocynum venetum leaves eased the heart damage caused by the cancer drug doxorubicin in experiments, apparently by reshaping how gut microbes process organic acids. The correction points readers to the article it amends and keeps the scholarly record accurate. Notices of this kind carry no new findings of their own.
pmc-13584923:
Kimberly Vidmar and co-authors report a rare infant case that does not fit the classic mold of its condition. The condition, complete androgen insensitivity, leaves a child with male gene makeup unable to respond to male hormones. Such children most often show female outer traits, inner testes, and no womb. Scans of the baby in the 2026 report show a womb, which is not the norm.

Gene tests find a fault in the hormone receptor gene, plus two unclear changes in other genes. The authors note those extra changes may hint at why womb tissue stayed. Care rests on a broad team, with talks on sex assignment, watch over the gonads, and what to expect at puberty. The case adds a data point to a thin record on odd forms of the condition.
pmc-13585223:
Li Zhu and co-authors build a system to compare single Chinese handwritten characters, rather than whole lines or a whole signature. Work like this helps banks, firms, and exam boards spot forged writing, yet whole-text checks can be thrown off by noise and spacing.

Their model sends each of two character images through its own channel, with layers that focus on key parts of the strokes. It then gives a score for how alike the pair is. In tests the best form cut false accepts and false rejects by a large share next to an older method, and it lifted overall accuracy as well.
pmc-13585323:
Bibek Saha and co-authors report a rare chest pain case in a 2026 paper. A young man came in with sharp chest pain that was blamed, more than once, on heart, lung, muscle, or throat causes. The true source sat higher than expected.

Scans found a large fluid sac from the pancreas pushed into the chest, pressing on his food pipe. Such sacs form weeks after pancreas swelling and most fade on their own. Drainage is due when they press on nearby organs, as here. A scope-guided drain into the stomach cleared his pain. The case warns teams to widen the search when chest pain defies first reads.
pmc-13585623:
Chanli Wu and co-authors build in 2026 a prediction tool for a common problem after spine surgery: a swollen, distended belly. The team studied 1,234 patients who had spine surgery under general anesthesia at one center. They used seventeen routine measures from around the time of surgery to train four kinds of machine learning models.

About eleven percent of patients developed the problem. On held-out test data, a random forest model scored best at telling who was at risk, though all four models were only moderate. A method that explains each prediction ranked pain pump use, drainage tube placement, and surgery length as the top drivers. Pain pump use and drains pushed risk up, while better daily function scores pushed it down. The authors aim the tool at early nursing checks for high-risk patients.
pmc-13585823:
Jason Liu and co-authors study why cancer patients skip outcome surveys in a 2026 paper on radiation oncology care. Clinics now collect patient-reported outcome measures as routine care, but missing replies can skew what the data seem to say. The team focused on a short global health survey sent through the patient portal.

They covered 12,214 patients, 71 providers, and five clinics over one year. Only about 35 percent of patients ever completed the survey, and rates ranged nearly fivefold across clinics. Recent surgery raised the odds of nonresponse, while more time since diagnosis lowered them. Clinic habits, such as how early the program launched and past collection rates, mattered more than patient traits once all levels were modeled.
pmc-13586023:
Daniela Ilie and co-authors study heat stress in Romanian Holstein cows in a 2026 gene study. Heat stress cuts milk output, health, and fertility in dairy cattle across the world. The team asked which genes switch on or off when cows face real heat.

Blood samples from the same cows were sequenced in hot and in neutral conditions. Hundreds of genes changed activity under heat, and most of them turned down. Many sit in immune and body-response pathways, so heat reshapes defense as well as comfort. The gene list gives breeders and vets clear targets. Herds in warming climates need cows that can hold health through hot spells.
pmc-13586323:
Confidence Dordoe and colleagues review growth factors as a possible repair therapy after ischemic stroke. Such a stroke blocks blood flow to part of the brain, and the only approved drug must be given within hours, which many patients miss. Fibroblast growth factors, a family of signaling proteins, have shown in lab models that they can protect nerve cells, calm inflammation, guard the blood-brain barrier, and grow new vessels.

The 2026 review weighs that promise against a hard record in human trials, where dosing and side effects have tripped up progress. Timing and context seem to matter: the same factor may help early and hinder late. The authors also note that growth factor readings in blood might help pick who could benefit. Their prescription is better delivery systems, clearer treatment windows, and smarter trial design before these proteins can earn a place in stroke care.
pmc-13586523:
Ho-Chang Lee and co-authors search for tissue markers that predict relapse in a common breast cancer type after chemotherapy, in a 2026 study. Luminal-type breast cancer often responds less sharply to pre-surgery chemotherapy. The usual burden score predicts outcomes weakly in this subtype. Extra markers could sharpen that forecast.

The team stained surgical samples from fifty-five patients for several proteins. Two markers drew focus: Ki-67, a growth index, and galectin-3. Scores were compared with disease-free survival over follow-up. Other clinical traits entered the analysis as well. Markers that flag high relapse risk could guide added therapy. Pathologists gain candidates for routine panels. Larger studies must confirm the signal before clinical use.
pmc-13586823:
Emeka Elosiuba and co-authors report a deep vein clot found by bedside ultrasound in a teen, in a 2026 case. Deep vein thrombosis is uncommon in children and its signs can mimic a muscle injury. Adult decision tools fit children poorly, which makes early diagnosis hard in the emergency department.

A boy aged fifteen came in with growing pain and swelling in the right leg. The first read was a muscle injury, but a bedside scan showed the main thigh vein would not compress and held clot material. A formal scan confirmed a blocking clot that ran into the pelvis vein. Fast bedside imaging sped up expert care for a clot that had no clear trigger.
pmc-13587523:
Mingcong Chen, Qingshan Ma, and Qiqi Sun study whether clean home heating sharpens the minds of older rural adults, in a paper from 2026. Northern China ran a policy that swapped coal stoves for clean heat in winter. The team used that rollout as a natural experiment. They drew on five waves of a national aging survey from 2011 to 2020.

On average, the policy raised thinking scores of rural elders by a small but clear share. The gain ran through two paths: more homes used clean fuel, and local air grew cleaner. Women with less schooling gained the most, as did elders who live with their children. The authors say energy policy can shape human capital, not just air quality. Their proof may guide clean heating plans in other poor regions.
pmc-13587723:
Mabel Kyei Kwofie and Valerie Orsat test ultrasound treatment of cranberry juice in a 2026 study. Heat pasteurization kills microbes but can harm the plant compounds that give cranberry juice its value. Strong ultrasound offers a non-heat option. Past work often lumped all phenolic measures together, missing which compound types rise or fall.

Juice is treated for one to seven minutes with a high power probe. Mid-length treatment raises total flavonoid and phenolic content by large shares. Carotenoids climb through the longest run. Anthocyanins and two antioxidant scores fall, though. The team also checks minerals, microbes, and basic juice traits.
pmc-13588423:
Da-Young Kim and five co-authors test how temperature shapes the survival of African swine fever virus in blood, swabs, and tissues. The virus kills pigs at high rates and lasts long in the wild, which drives spread through dead animals and soiled goods. The study came out in twenty twenty-six.

Samples sat at four set heats, from deep freeze to warm room, for set spans. Gene copy tests and virus growth assays tracked both genome and live virus over time. Type, heat, and time all swayed survival, with lower heat keeping virus longer. Whole blood lasted longest, held for months in the cold, while live virus fell fast at high heat.
pmc-13588923:
Veronica Romero and co-authors release a free toolkit in a 2026 paper for the study of how people act as one. Human talk runs on more than one lane at once: words, pose, face, and tone. That wealth makes it hard to study with care, and each lab had built its own rig.

Their kit takes plain video and draws three lanes of time data from it. Pose tools read body moves, a speech tool writes the words, and face marks can ride the same clock. One box thus serves a whole field. Talk scholars gain a shared bench where once each bench was home-made.
pmc-13589123:
W.Y. Son and eight colleagues test two kitchen-chemistry tricks for upgrading chicken breast protein into a better food ingredient. Plain chicken protein dissolves poorly and forms weak emulsions, limiting its use in powders and processed foods. Their 2026 study compared four versions: untouched protein, protein linked to a tea polyphenol called EGCG, enzyme-chopped protein, and protein given both treatments in sequence.

Chopping loosened the protein and exposed reactive groups; EGCG bonding then consumed some of those and clouded the mixes further. Both treatments raised water holding, oil absorption, and emulsifying power, and together they produced the strongest defense against oxidation. Chopping alone weakened emulsion stability, which EGCG then restored. Digestion in a test system improved with chopping and held up when EGCG followed. The authors recommend the sequence for functional protein ingredients.
pmc-13589523:
Haifeng Wang and Ang Liu comment on a study linking pain relief to mood after weight-loss surgery, in this 2026 letter. The study reanalyzed a trial of sleeve gastrectomy, a stomach-reducing operation. Patients who received numbing injections into the abdominal wall, on top of general anaesthesia, showed larger drops in anxiety and depression scores. The original authors suggested that easing gut pain may have lifted mood.

Wang and Liu raise three cautions. First, the trial registry named pain, emotion, and memory as outcomes but did not fix the scales, timings, or analysis plan in advance. Second, the registry planned 150 participants while the parent trial enrolled 225, a gap needing explanation. When plans shift quietly, reported links can look stronger than they are. The letter asks for fuller reporting before the pain-mood link guides care.
pmc-13590123:
Neha Chivukula Venkata and co-authors explore how gene activity is organized around nuclear speckles, small bodies inside the cell nucleus. Genes sitting next to speckles often boost their output, yet across the genome greater distance from speckles can also track with higher expression. That paradox drove the study.

The team found two dynamic protein patterns spreading outward from speckles. Active chromosome regions weakly tied to speckles instead hugged these outer patterns closely. When speckles were removed, genes near speckles fell quiet while genes near the outer patterns grew louder. The authors propose that the space around speckles splits into niches that tune gene output in opposite ways.
pmc-13590223:
Wen Xu and Guotao Peng review how two-dimensional materials affect gut microbes in a 2026 paper. Atom-thin sheets, from graphene types to newer carbides, are used more in health and industry, raising gut safety questions after swallowing.

Animal studies, mostly in mice and zebrafish, show these materials can upset gut microbe balance. Host gut and body responses often follow. Lab studies add how sheet size, surface traits, and change over time drive contact with bacteria. The authors call for models that mimic real gut groups and for work on how microbes change the materials. Safety teams get a map of known risks and gaps.
pmc-13590823:
Prabha Adhikari and co-authors explore in 2026 how African bermudagrass tolerates salt, using genomics and molecular profiling together. The grass is a parent of hybrid turf used in lawns and sports fields. Salt stress grows as non-drinking water is used more for irrigation in dry areas.

Offspring of one genotype were tested for leaf firing and green cover under salt in two years. Fifteen genome regions linked to salt response, four of them stable across years. Salt raised activity of more than a thousand genes, plus many metabolites and lipids. Candidate genes touch stress hormones and transport pathways.
pmc-13590923:
Yu Xu, Lian Xia, and their co-authors studied a classic herbal formula's antidepressant like effects in stressed mice. Their 2026 paper examines Chaihu Shugan San, a traditional Chinese formula long used for depression, with a focus on glutamate balance in the hippocampus. A chemical scan first identified the formula's contents, finding flavonoids as the main group.

Computer based network methods then predicted targets and paths, pointing at one signaling route and several flavonoid compounds with likely binding. Mice under chronic restraint stress served as the test model. Behavior tests and molecular checks weighed the formula's effects against the glutamate story. The design pairs prediction with hands on validation, a common pattern in modern herbal research.
pmc-13591023:
Silvia Guil-Luna and co-authors review, in a 2026 paper, how giant cancer cells with many genome copies sleep through treatment and later restart the tumor. These polyploid giant cells were long dismissed as dead-end and senescent. Evidence now shows they bud off fast-growing, drug-resistant daughters without normal division. That makes them a suspect engine of relapse after therapy seems to work.

Surviving dormancy takes special housekeeping. The review traces how the giants rewire their metabolism and lean on autophagy, the cell's self-eating recycling system, to hold energy balance under stress. Blocking those supports might stop the giants from spawning new growth. The authors weigh such attacks as a route to deeper remissions. They frame the sleeping giant as a target the field can no longer afford to ignore.
pmc-13591123:
Hong Jing Wang and colleagues published a 2026 review pooling trial results for rocatinlimab, an injected antibody drug being tested for moderate-to-severe eczema. Eczema of this kind is a chronic, relapsing skin inflammation that often resists standard creams. The authors gathered randomized trials comparing the drug against placebo injections.

Three trials covering more than seventeen hundred patients fed into the combined analysis, which weighed both symptom relief and safety reports. Pooling small trials this way gives doctors and regulators a clearer picture of a new drug's short-term balance of benefit and harm than any single study can provide on its own.
pmc-13591223:
Ting Liu and Yaomin Hu review how skeletal muscle ages, arguing that loss of bulk alone does not explain frailty in later life. Strength and speed often fall faster than mass. Drawing on recent single cell and multi layer studies, they frame aging muscle as a loss of resilience across many parts at once. Fibers, stem cells, immune and vessel cells, and nerve links all change together.

Faults in protein house keeping, cell power stations, and long term low grade swelling sit at the core, the review says. Signals from the liver, fat, gut, and brain add further pressure. Exercise and diet stay the proven base of care. Liu and Hu weigh newer ideas, from power station repair to clearing worn out cells, as still in testing.
pmc-13591423:
A team of metal researchers studies thin films of a nickel, iron, and chromium mix in a 2026 paper. Such films serve in sensors that read magnet fields. How the film's inner build shifts with thickness can make or mar that use, so the team grew films at set thicknesses and probed them.

Their tests ran across a cold-to-room heat range. The thinnest film, at 5 nanometers, showed no crystal form, yet it still held magnet order, as three field effects proved. At 8 nanometers the film formed crystals and a grain slant. Chromium then spread more evenly through the mix, and the long-range magnet order faded.
pmc-13591623:
Jin Yuan Wang and Yu Li report a 2026 case of lung collapse that struck twice in one teen during two chest surgeries. The boy, aged fifteen and healthy before, faced repeat surgery for a recurring burst lung. In both operations, thick mucus plugs blocked airways as the lung was re-filled.

He had shown no breathing signs before either operation. Lab marks, though, hinted at quiet airway swelling from past germ bouts. In the second surgery, live airway viewing let the team wash out mucus as it formed. The pair blame hidden swelling, surgical stress, and one-lung breathing for the mucus surge, and urge pre-checks plus watched airways for teens in chest surgery.
pmc-13591823:
Mallapu Ajay Kumar and six co-authors report a death that arrived an hour after the all-clear, in this 2026 case report. A 72-year-old man with hypertension and diabetes took three to four bee stings on his right shoulder. His reaction stayed local: no anaphylaxis, no systemic signs. After sting removal, antihistamines, and pain relief, he rested twelve hours under monitoring, stable throughout, and went home.

About an hour later he collapsed, unresponsive. Bystanders started CPR; paramedics found his heart in asystole, and hospital resuscitation won back a pulse. The electrocardiogram then showed an inferior heart attack pattern. The team's diagnosis is probable Kounis syndrome, a coronary event triggered by allergic chemistry, here delayed past the observation window. They are candid about the proof gaps: no mast-cell markers, no imaging inside the artery. The lesson stands anyway: a quiet sting reaction does not clear the heart.
pmc-13592323:
Jun Hyeon Lee, Minlang Yang, and Takuma Yasuda grow, in 2026, three pure color light emitters for displays from a single starting platform in one pot. Their emitters belong to a boron based family prized for razor thin color bands in organic screens. Stretching that sharpness into red has long proved hard. Rival reaction paths in the pot yield one, two, or reshaped boron insertions, giving green, yellow, and red emitters side by side.

Each color stayed under a 25 nanometer band width with near perfect light yield in doped films. Test screens hit top efficiency above 35 percent. Lee and the team present the forked one pot route as a unified way to stock a full color set from one precursor.
pmc-13592423:
Yusuf Hared Abdi and two co-authors review the state of drug resistance tracking across Africa under the One Health idea, which joins human, animal, and environmental health. Resistance already carried a heavy toll: about 1.05 million deaths in the African region in 2019 were linked to bacterial resistance, and roughly 250,000 were directly caused by it. The review gathers studies from 2015 to 2026 across four databases.

Human health tracking has grown, with more countries joining global reporting and labs improving. Animal and environmental tracking lag far behind, held back by weak labs, split data systems, thin funding, and poor coordination between sectors. The authors urge joined-up governance, stronger lab networks, shared digital platforms, and steady domestic funding first. Gene sequencing, wastewater checks, and regional teamwork can follow as resources allow. Stronger tracking, they argue, is the base for earlier warnings and wiser drug use.
pmc-13592823:
Julie M. Schallhorn and Alekya Rajanala report, in 2026, on a phase four registry tracking the light adjustable lens in people implanted in both eyes. The lens is unique: after cataract surgery, ultraviolet light can fine tune its power in the clinic, then lock it in place. That promise matters most for eyes with prior corneal refractive surgery, where standard lens math often misses. The registry enrolled people with and without that history across many sites.

Entry required sharp corrected vision after implant and completed light treatments, and one visit one to three months after lock in gathered the outcome data. Records spanned September 2021 to January 2025. Schallhorn and Rajanala frame the registry as a real world check on whether adjustability delivers the targeting that fixed lenses struggle to reach.
pmc-13593323:
Manuel Castro-Menéndez and co-authors compare two operations for carpal tunnel syndrome in a 2026 study. The syndrome arises when a nerve is squeezed at the wrist, and surgery frees it by cutting a tight ligament. One group had open surgery. The other had a through-the-skin release guided by ultrasound imaging, which needs strong technical skill.

Two hundred patients took part, split evenly between the two methods. Both groups improved a lot on a standard symptom and function survey. The guided group improved more, even though it started worse, and grip strength came back faster by three months. Scar tenderness, pillar pain, and lingering tingling were all less common after the guided operation. Problems were few and alike in both groups, and satisfaction topped ninety-seven percent in each. The authors back the guided method in skilled centers.
pmc-13593523:
Xuefeng Fan studies traditional Chinese ethnic sports and anxiety in college students in a paper from two thousand twenty-six, written alone. Anxiety is common in this group, and regular practice of such sports may help. Fan asks whether any benefit runs through easier emotion control and lower felt stress.

Five hundred forty-six students from two universities in Tianjin were surveyed three times. Students who stuck with the sports later reported fewer problems regulating emotions and less stress. Both of those, in turn, predicted lower anxiety later. The indirect paths were real but modest. Fan cautions that the design cannot prove cause, and highlights the quality of adherence as a factor for campus health programs.
pmc-13593823:
Mikayla Castellon, Talia Panadero, Elizabeth Moore, and Sonya Gabrielian ask homeless-experienced veterans how a health portal could work better in a 2026 paper. The portal is My HealtheVet, used by the veterans health system in the United States. Only 36 percent of homeless veterans use it, far below other patients. The team wanted views from users who had faced homelessness.

They spoke with 17 veterans in a housing support scheme in Los Angeles. Users liked secure messages, drug lists, and record access in the portal. Login trouble and lack of devices held many back. Stable housing and help from peers made use much easier. Users asked for simpler screens, training at housing intake, and more staff help.
pmc-13593923: A conference program listing for a session of late-breaking research abstracts, published in 2026. The session belongs to a meeting on women's and children's health research, and its entries give talk times, titles, speakers, and their institutions. The first listed study is a nationwide French project on toxoplasmosis in pregnancy, tracing screening, treatment, and transmission to babies using national health records from 2018 to 2023.
pmc-13594323:
Furlong and co-authors show in 2026 how a brain like vector code can make self driven search far cheaper. Long running robots must learn as they roam, yet standard search tools grow in cost with each new sight. On small gear, that growth ends the run early.

Their code packs parts into one fixed size vector, so time and memory stay flat as data grow. A search method built on the code ran sixty to two hundred times faster than top rivals at the same score. On brain style chips, energy per sample fell thirty to one hundred eighty eight fold.
pmc-13594423:
Xiaowei Ma leads a seventeen-author trial of near-infrared light therapy aimed precisely at the angular gyrus on both sides of the brain in Alzheimer's disease. Earlier work shone the light over the whole head with mixed results. This randomized, sham-controlled study instead treated thirty-six patients with confirmed Alzheimer's biomarkers. Each side received twenty minutes daily over fifteen days.

The targeted group improved in cognition, memory, language, attention, and executive function, and their psychiatric symptoms eased. Brain scans showed stronger connections inside the default mode network, the system active at rest, and better teamwork between that network and attention and emotion systems. A combined stimulation and recording method found richer information flow, especially at the front and back of the brain. The authors present targeted light therapy as a precise, promising way to re-tune large brain networks in Alzheimer's disease.
pmc-13594523:
Zheng Zhou and Ling Kuang hunt shared gene shifts between weight surgery fat and psoriasis skin, in a study from two thousand twenty-six. Public gene sets from fat before and after surgery and from skin patches were mined. Shared changed genes fed path, web, and learning screens.

One signal gene, CXCL9, stood out as the hub across methods. It scored well as a test mark in fresh sets. Its levels tracked with attack-type guards and against calm-type guards in tissue. A swelling path shared by fat and skin frames the link. The authors pitch the gene as the bridge for why surgery calms skin. Readers get a named knot in the fat-skin tie.
pmc-13594723:
Rodolfo Ferreira Marques and co-authors test an mRNA vaccine aimed at a malaria parasite that dominates outside Africa, in work from twenty twenty-six. The parasite, Plasmodium vivax, still has no licensed vaccine. The target is a protein called E140, found at many life stages. It is shared across related parasite species, which aids broad design. The vaccine rides in tiny fat shells, as recent mRNA shots do.

Shots against the mouse and human forms of the target raise strong antibody replies. Germinal centre cells and long-lived plasma cells also rise after the shots. In mice, the mouse-form shot cuts blood parasites and lifts survival after challenge. Antibodies from the human-form shot block the parasite in human cell tests. The block cuts cell entry by more than half in the lab assays. E140 thus looks like a strong pick for next-step vaccines.
pmc-13594923:
Usama and ten co-authors weigh two selenium food forms in quail growth in this twenty twenty-six study. The ore bit guards cells from rust and feeds growth in birds. Its fine dust form may beat the stock salt form in feed.

Inside, four hundred young quails split in five feed bands for weeks. Dust-form bands at the top dose gained most weight in the trial. Ore stocks piled most in the liver of all fed bands. Rust-guard tools rose in all ore bands, top in the dust band. Salt-form birds at top dose bore the most code strand breaks.
pmc-13595123:
Lasse Alajärvi, Outi Lapatto-Reiniluoto, Henna Kyllönen, and Piia Siitonen survey how drugstore buyers throw out used drug patches, and where they learn of it. Their study, from two thousand twenty-six, brackets a state drive.

Right throw-out of drugs is a chief way to cut their harm to the wild world. Patches are a hard case: guides are thin, and the theme was near unread. Buyers of patches were asked twice, a year apart, with a half-year news drive in the gap. Just past mid-hundreds replied each time. The team read their acts, their word paths, and if the drive moved them.
pmc-13595523:
Mingze Chen and co-authors map a childhood brain tumor at single-cell and spatial detail, in a 2026 study. Medulloblastoma is the most common malignant brain tumor in children. Its tumors vary widely, and outcomes differ even within the same risk group. That variety makes treatment planning hard.

The team sequenced single cells from tumors and nearby normal tissue. Samples spanned the main molecular subgroups of the disease. Spatial methods then placed cell types back into the tumor layout. The maps revealed developmental hierarchies among tumor cells. They also flagged a tumor-immune link, named PPIA-BSG, that tracks with prognosis. Such markers could help doctors sort patients by risk. They may also suggest new drug targets.
pmc-13596123:
Aurelio Ciancio and Ugo Picciotti review fungi that eat crop-eating worms, in a 2026 paper. Plant-parasitic nematodes are tiny worms that drain farm yields worldwide. Certain fungi attack, infect, and digest those worms, offering a green control option. The review sorts these fungi by how they hunt.

Groups include trappers that snare worms, parasites that live inside them, and fungi that attack eggs and females. Others release toxins or grip worms with special structures. Soil conditions, helper bacteria, and fungal by-products all sway how well they work. Family trees suggest trapping gear was a turning point in their evolution. The survey frames these fungi as a strategic resource for sustainable farming.
pmc-13596923:
Lisamarie Moore and co-authors studied how excess oxygen affects young mouse brain cells in a 2026 paper. The cells are progenitors that mature into oligodendrocytes, which insulate nerve fibers and support neurons. Mouse progenitors are famously hard to grow in large numbers, unlike rat ones, limiting studies that use mouse disease models.

The team first set out a clean method to prepare large, nearly uniform cultures of these cells. They then raised the cells under high oxygen. Growth slowed, yet the cells matured faster into oligodendrocytes. The split effect matters for understanding oxygen injury in premature infants, whose developing brains face similar exposure in intensive care.
pmc-13597223:
Sukanya and co-authors tune feed, spacing, and harvest timing for barnyard millet fodder at a Bengaluru research farm, in a study from two thousand twenty-six. Fodder land is shrinking while demand grows, so dual food-feed crops matter. Trials crossed three nitrogen doses, two spacings, and two harvest stages over two seasons.

The top nitrogen dose gave the most green and dry fodder. Tight spacing beat wide spacing on bulk yield. Cutting at ear-head stage gave the most green yield and protein, while late cutting gave more dry bulk and fiber. Spacing did not sway quality marks. The authors back tight spacing with high nitrogen, timed to the yield-quality aim.
pmc-13597323:
Yushan Dong, Tingting Liu, Peng Wang, and Songjiang Liu review radiation for early breast cancer. Their review from twenty twenty-six weighs both cure and looks. Breast cancer is common and its rates rise each year.

The team searched four data sets for trials and cohort work. Two reviewers screened and pulled data by a set plan. Quality was judged with two known rating tools. Main check was return of cancer in the same breast. Life span, disease free time, and looks were also checked. Few direct trials exist, so pooled proof helps.
pmc-13597423:
Yue Xiao and co-authors test a small ring-shaped peptide as a shield for skin cells against sunlight damage. Ultraviolet light scrambles the skin's support matrix and ages its fibroblast cells early. The peptide was known to switch on collagen genes, but its wider effects were unmapped.

Human skin fibroblasts were grown in dishes and exposed to ultraviolet light with or without the peptide. Gene and protein readouts, aging stains, and stress markers tracked the damage and rescue. A proteome-wide scan showed which pathways moved. The peptide acted through a known growth signaling route named in the title. Safer sun care may one day borrow such molecules. The work is early cell evidence, not a product claim.
pmc-13597523:
Ying Liu and colleagues read ancient DNA from lake sediments around Siberia and Alaska. They watched Arctic plant communities change across the last twenty-four thousand years. Shrubs and trees advanced into tundra during that span. Nine lake cores preserved the DNA of past vegetation, and statistical null models separated true plant-to-plant interactions from mere shared habitat preferences.

During the ice age, interactions leaned positive, with plants sheltering and helping each other. As the Holocene warmed and woody plants took over, interactions flipped toward competition, and the community grew taller with longer roots on average. The authors propose a feedback: climate enabled the woody advance, the new arrivals intensified competition, and that competition further squeezed native low plants, shrinking their ranges even as diversity between sites rose. They offer the deep-time pattern as an analogy for today's Arctic greening.
pmc-13597723:
Lizhuo Fu, Zipei Ouyang, and Qingtian Wu track trust in AI teaching assistants over a semester in this 2026 study. Such assistants now sit inside many university courses. How trust, fairness judgments, and motivation shape each other over time was unknown, because one-off surveys cannot split stable traits from real change.

The study followed 450 undergraduates in three waves, four weeks apart. A panel model separated each student's steady level from their ups and downs. Trust was split into ability, benevolence, and integrity; fairness into shares, process, and treatment. The design shows which feeling moves first. Course designers gain a timeline, not a snapshot.
pmc-13597823:
Titli Saha, Aniruddha Basu, and ten co-authors ran a first test of brain training in at-risk children in eastern India, in work from twenty twenty-six. The children have close kin with drug or drink problems, or severe mental illness. Such children often show slow growth in the front brain area that guides focus and self-control. The training uses a cap that reads blood flow in that area and feeds it back as a game-like signal.

Eleven children, aged six to twelve, took eight sessions aimed at two spots on the right front of the brain. The study had no control group by design. Its job was to check if the method is safe, workable, and well borne by young children.
pmc-13598523:
HaiCheng He and co-authors report a rare case where a long-standing skin disease turned into cancer, in a 2026 paper. The disease, lichen planus, causes chronic inflammation of skin and moist tissues. Change to cancer is uncommon, and most reports involve mouth or genital sites rather than skin.

In this case, disease on the left lower leg changed into a squamous cell cancer. The cancer had spread to lymph nodes in the groin. A combined scan that tracks sugar use in tissue showed strong signals at both the leg lesion and the nodes. That scan helped the team stage the disease and plan care. The authors warn that long-standing skin lichen planus can, rarely, turn malignant, and they commend the scan for judging how far such disease has spread.
pmc-13598823:
Arkaprava Singharoy, Payel Bose, Tanmay Banerjee, Sagnik Das, and Prerona Bhowmick report a rare fatal case of lung failure caused by chikungunya, in this 2026 case report. The mosquito-borne virus usually brings fever, rash, and severe joint pain. Lung damage strong enough to cause acute respiratory distress syndrome is very uncommon.

The patient was a sixty-two-year-old man with obesity, diabetes, heart disease, and prior lung disease, who arrived with fever and fast-worsening breathlessness after travel in India. Tests confirmed chikungunya and ruled out dengue, malaria, and scrub typhus. Despite a ventilator, prone positioning, and steroids, his lungs and then other organs failed, and he died after forty-one days in hospital. The authors warn doctors to watch for this rare turn in older, sicker patients.
pmc-13599123:
Giovanni Muscolo and Daniele Binosi review smart technology for skier safety in a 2026 paper. Sensors in gear and on slopes, digital twins, and body motion simulation may cut ski injuries. The field is scattered, so the pair map what is proven, what is trial stage, and what is still an idea.

Their search kept 150 sources after screening and citation chasing. Gear that measures or protects is ready now, while live prediction systems face hard barriers. Calibration, error bounds, data standards, and false alarms top that list. They sketch a safety index and a skills based frame as untested proposals, and set a road map led by trials with human data.
pmc-13599223:
Xueqian Wang, Bing Liu, and Lianghai Cao report a rare emergency: a lung malformation that burst during pregnancy and flooded the chest with blood. A pulmonary arteriovenous malformation is an abnormal tangle of vessels, and pregnancy's higher blood flow and hormone shifts raise the chance it ruptures. Their patient was thirty-three, at nearly thirty-two weeks, with sudden chest pain spreading to shoulder and back.

Her condition worsened with falling oxygen levels after arrival. A triple-rule-out CT angiogram, a scan protocol that checks several chest emergencies at once, revealed the ruptured malformation in her left lower lung lobe with blood in the chest cavity. Doctors sealed the vessel from inside using catheter embolization, which stopped the bleeding quickly. She recovered, stayed pregnant, and delivered a healthy baby at thirty-six weeks. The authors urge emergency clinicians to keep this rare but deadly cause in mind.
pmc-13599623:
Patrycja Jaroniek and co-authors review shell derived particles as helpers against the stomach germ Helicobacter pylori in a 2026 paper. The germ survives stomach acid, burrows into mucus, and resists more and more antibiotics. Chitosan, from crustacean shells, sticks to mucus, breaks down safely, and can ferry drugs to the stomach lining.

The review covers particles carrying antibiotics, plant compounds, and microbe killing peptides, plus designs that block the germ's anchors, films, or acid shield enzyme. One concept packs a vaccine strain of bacteria inside the particles. Lab and animal results so far look promising, the authors say.
pmc-13599823:
Isaac Seow-En and co-authors set out the plan for a registry tracking a surgical technique that removes bowel specimens through natural body openings, in a 2026 protocol paper. The method avoids an extra cut in the belly wall during minimally invasive colorectal surgery. Early studies suggest less wound trouble and faster recovery, but most evidence is retrospective and uneven.

The AP-NOSES registry, coordinated from Singapore, will enroll about 800 adults across Asia-Pacific centers having elective bowel resections. Its main comparison pits planned natural-orifice extraction against planned extraction through the abdomen in patients eligible for either. The chief outcome is time to incisional hernia within twenty-four months, alongside recovery and patient-reported outcomes.
pmc-13600623:
Sara Hana Weisz leads a nine-author team testing a simple risk score in patients with infective endocarditis, an infection of the heart's inner lining. Their 2026 study asks whether the ACEF score, built from just age, a kidney blood marker, and the heart's pumping fraction, can flag patients headed for poor outcomes. The team reviewed 143 patients treated at one infectious diseases hospital between January 2023 and February 2025.

Thirty patients died during follow-up. In adjusted analysis, a higher ACEF score tracked with worse survival, alongside diabetes, infection with Staphylococcus aureus, and cases where heart surgery was advised but never done. A score of 1.30 or above marked the higher-risk group in both operated and non-operated patients. The authors suggest ACEF as a quick bedside tool for sorting newly diagnosed patients by risk, since it needs only three routine values and no lengthy calculation.
pmc-13600823:
Cheng-Ta Lai and co-authors test whether a red cell anion channel shapes how a common drug alters breathing. Their 2026 study uses acetazolamide, a drug that blocks carbonic anhydrase, the enzyme speeding carbon dioxide and bicarbonate swaps. The channel, named AE1, gates bicarbonate across the red cell wall and may limit the whole exchange.

A mouse strain with extra AE1 faces drug and high carbon dioxide challenges. The drug pushes breathing the same way excess carbon dioxide does, toward acidosis responses. Extra AE1 blunts both pushes and speeds the breathing response. Sensitivity to the drug drops as AE1 rises. The authors conclude the channel and enzyme work in concert inside red cells to manage the gas exchange that breathing depends on.
pmc-13600923:
Preeti Gupta leads a seven-author team presenting a 2026 deep learning system that reads ventilator waveforms with near-perfect accuracy. Ventilators push air into critically ill lungs, and harm can follow when the machine's rhythm fights the patient's own breathing. Spotting that mismatch requires marking exactly where each breath begins and ends, a job rule-based software often fumbles in noisy recordings.

The team trained a one-dimensional attention-gated U-Net network on 9,719 breaths from 33 patients. It beat published rule-based methods, scoring above 0.99 at detecting breath starts and ends within a tenth of a second. Performance held on mismatched breaths, scoring at least 0.98 there. When used to count patient-ventilator mismatches, the model matched human reference counts, while rule-based methods drifted widely. Visual maps showed which waveform features guided the model. The authors offer it as a fast base for studying ventilator interactions at scale.
pmc-13601523:
Zhenxiang Xiong and nine colleagues present a way to print fine electronic circuits on the inside walls of hollow parts, in a study dated twenty twenty-six. Printing circuits on curved outer surfaces is now common, but inner surfaces of deep cavities stayed out of reach. That leaves much usable space idle in advanced devices. Their idea draws on the old Chinese art of painting inside snuff bottles.

The method steers a fine spray jet to lay down lines as narrow as about twelve micrometers across many materials. It worked inside cavities more than ten times deeper than wide, and built stress sensors inside honeycomb frames. Such inner circuits could serve health checks of structures, wearable gear, and medical tools.
pmc-13602223:
Nikhil Vallabhaneni and co-authors describe a surgical technique from two thousand twenty-six for hip replacement through a front approach. During total hip replacement, surgeons sometimes pass wires around the thigh bone to prevent or fix cracks. The front approach changes which blood vessels and nerves lie near the wire path, so back-approach habits can be risky.

Structures at risk include branches of a key artery and nerve bundles feeding a large thigh muscle. The authors lay out a step-by-step way to pass the wires that lowers the chance of harming those structures. The paper is a practical guide for surgeons who use the direct anterior approach and need wire support for stability or fracture care.
pmc-13602323:
William Carter and co-authors report, in a 2026 case study, a teenage girl whose eye infection after an injury involved a fungus never before tied to this disease. A welding wire accident cut her cornea and damaged the lens. Five weeks later she had a stubborn fungal infection inside the eye. Standard surgery and antifungal drugs failed to control it, and the retina detached within a week.

A second, urgent operation cleared the eye, repaired the detachment, and added stronger drugs. Vision then slowly improved over seven months, from seeing only hand motion to reading large print. Cultures finally grew two fungi: a known Aspergillus species and Tropicoporus texanus, a woodland fungus rarely seen in human infection. The authors warn eye doctors that this genus can drive aggressive, drug-resistant disease after trauma.
pmc-13602823:
Zijing Wen and Jianming Su review gene editing tools and their path toward treating genetic disease, in this 2026 paper. The review frames each choice around the mutation itself: its shape, its effect, and how well a model system proves the damage. Editing styles range from the classic CRISPR cut to base and prime editing and gene dimmers or boosters.

Delivery splits into editing cells outside the body, which is most mature for blood diseases, and editing inside the body, which still faces safety and durability hurdles. The authors urge judging new tools by lasting, safe, and affordable benefit, not by whether an edit is merely possible.
pmc-13602923:
Titanium dioxide is a workhorse for breaking down pollutants with light, but its performance depends on how its surface is built. The five authors made mesoporous titanium dioxide by a sol-gel route using tannic acid, a cheap and renewable plant compound, as the structure guide. By varying the tannic acid dose, they traced how the guide shapes crystal form, surface traits, heat behavior, and light absorption.

The crystal lattice stayed close to standard anatase at every dose, so the guide changed pore and surface layout more than the crystal itself. Oxidation path analysis gave numbers for how feasible hydroxyl radical formation is. Methylene blue broke down with pseudo-first-order kinetics under ultraviolet light. Activity reflected surface access, light capture, and charge behavior together. The paper shows tannic acid can direct a porous catalyst that degrades dye under low-energy UV-LED light.
pmc-13603123:
Buse Akça and co-authors print a custom neck brace in a 2026 pilot study for young adults whose heads tilt forward and whose upper backs curve too much. Each brace was built from a body scan of its wearer with a common printer. Ten volunteers aged eighteen to twenty-five wore the device for six weeks.

With the brace on, head angle rose and back curve fell at every check, a quick effect of wearing it rather than proof of lasting change. Users rated the device and its service near the top of the scale. One person quit over discomfort, and no grave harm was seen.
pmc-13603223:
Xingbo Liu and co-authors fed broiler chickens varied forms of selenium in this 2026 feeding study. Selenium is a trace mineral birds need in tiny amounts. The team tested a nano-sized form at five dose levels, then compared it with a common salt form and two yeast-based forms.

A dose of 0.20 milligrams per kilogram of feed worked best for the nano form. Birds on it grew well, fought cell damage better, and stored more selenium in breast meat. The nano and yeast forms beat the salt form on carcass traits. The authors advise the nano form at that dose for broiler diets, since it matched the yeast forms at lower cost of dose.
pmc-13603423:
Halil Turktemiz, a solo author, studies joy at work among nurses. The study from twenty twenty-six deals with compassion satisfaction. Nurses feel it when their care helps folks in need.

How that feeling shapes joy at work was not well known. The study rests on self drive theory and positive mind science. Joy from helping raised both well being and work joy. Well being fully carried the link to work joy, he found. That means good feelings alone are not quite enough. Bosses are urged to fix loads and offer flex time.
pmc-13603523:
Evaristo Carrillo-Moreno and co-authors (2026) asked whether richer milk before weaning pays off at slaughter for beef-on-dairy calves. Eighty Holstein cross calves were split into two groups. One drank whole milk at eleven percent solids. The other drank milk boosted to fourteen percent solids with replacer. The richer feeding lasted only until weaning, before sixty days of age. The team then followed growth for 49 weeks and graded the carcasses.

The boosted calves gained faster and weaned heavier. Their growth edge shrank slowly but never vanished, leaving them about seventeen kilograms heavier at the end. More of them landed in the top sale lots, and more carcasses graded Choice. The authors estimate about 117 extra dollars of revenue per calf under grading-based payment. They conclude that a short, richer start pays for itself many months later. The results strengthen the case for beef-on-dairy systems.
pmc-13604123:
A blow to the head can raise the risk of Alzheimer's disease years later, and Roxana Kaveh and co-authors review the biology that may connect the two. Their narrative review follows several pathways that switch on after a traumatic brain injury. The brain's immune system fires up fast, and while that response protects at first, it can smolder for years when it fails to switch off.

Injured brains also clear the amyloid-beta protein more slowly while making more of it, so it piles up. The tau protein gets over-tagged by chemical marks and tangles inside cells. Damage to brain blood vessels and a leaky blood-brain barrier let outside immune cells and blood proteins in, feeding the inflammation. The authors argue these pathways interact as one network rather than acting alone.
pmc-13604223:
Jin and seven co-authors review how gas bubbles in the blood drive decompression sickness, the danger divers face when pressure drops too fast. Tiny stable bubbles on vessel walls can grow, break loose, and jam small vessels. The review traces three linked injury routes.

Bubbles trigger clotting where they touch blood, injure vessel linings on contact, and stir immune attack that adds inflammation. The authors also sort the lab models used to study all this. Whole-animal and blood systems make their own bubbles under pressure change, while cell and chip models use ready-made bubbles for tighter control. Knowing which kind a study used, they argue, decides what its results can prove.
pmc-13604823:
Cong Zhao and eight co-authors test an old blood thinner drug for a second life against diabetes enzymes, in a 2026 journal article. The drug, dipyridamole, is known for stopping clots and for fighting cell stress. Two gut enzymes that split starch and sugar are prime targets in type 2 diabetes.

Computer docking showed the drug fits both enzymes through hydrogen bonds and water shy contact. Long simulations showed the pairs hold steady over time. The authors put the drug forth as a lead for new diabetes care, with more tests to come.
pmc-13605023:
Moustafa Kardjadj and co-authors rework a urine infection test panel and check the change in a 2026 study. Version two's agreement with culture and with drug-susceptibility results was measured on 773 samples from a multi-center trial. Shared targets were compared head to head. The work shows how a diagnostic menu can evolve without losing its evidence thread.
pmc-13605223: Rikke Thea and Karsten Buschard wrote a short 2026 comment on a study of type 1 diabetes and myelin, the sheath that wraps nerves. That study linked immune marks in diabetes to a nerve protein and drew a line toward multiple sclerosis. Thea and Buschard add sulfatide, a fat found in the sheath and in the pancreas, to the debate. Their note argues the fat may help explain how the two diseases meet.
pmc-13605923:
Cecília Beatriz Bittencourt Viana Cruz and co-authors review how ultrasound of the heart helps track patients after a heart transplant. A new heart is still the best care for some people with end-stage heart failure, yet rejection and artery disease in the graft can cut life short. Tissue samples and vessel scans remain the truth tests, but they are invasive.

Heart ultrasound is painless and can be repeated often. The review lays out what scans should look like after each type of surgery, and what they show in early graft trouble, rejection, and late failure. Newer tools that track strain add value, but no single measure settles the call on its own.
pmc-13606223:

Groups got plain diets, shop custard, the vegan custard, or the vitamin-boosted version as a tenth of intake. Custard quality, nutrient values, and how much calcium the gut could reach were measured. pmc-13606423:

The reviewers searched several databases for studies across two decades and a half. Eighteen studies covering tens of thousands of people were pooled. About a quarter had never been treated in any round. Quality checks and side analyses probed the uneven results. Program leaders get a scale estimate and leads on why people stay unreached.
pmc-13606723:
Sudharani Banappagoudar and three co-authors survey phone dependence, sleep, and mood control in young adults in a 2026 study. An anonymous web survey spread through social media and snowball sharing gathered adults aged 18 and up. It measured problem phone use, sleep trouble, and trouble steering feelings. The team then tested whether poor sleep sits in the middle, carrying part of the phone's effect on mood control.
pmc-13607323:
Teofana-Otilia Bizerea-Moga and co-authors review links between body weight and early puberty in a 2026 paper. Child obesity tracks with earlier puberty, above all in girls. Whether fatness directly triggers true early puberty, driven by the brain's hormone axis, is less settled.

pmc-13607923:

pmc-13608523:

The authors present the formula as a multi-pronged kidney protector worth further study.
pmc-13608623:
Athanasios Armakolas leads a nine-author team testing titanium scaffolds for bone repair, in a study published in two thousand twenty-six. pmc-13609123:

pmc-13609223:

pmc-13609323:

Bleeding shock is a top killer in intensive care, and testing treatments needs animal models that mirror the long aftermath, not just the first hours. The team withdrew forty percent of the blood volume of each rat, waited an hour, then replaced half the loss with either the own blood of the rat or a salt-and-albumin fluid. Pressure fell and heart rate spiked during the bleed, with body temperature dropping too. Thirty percent of the fluid-rescued rats later died, while every blood-rescued rat lived. Checks ran to day twenty-nine, covering organs, marrow, and blood.
pmc-13609623:
Baskar Selvaraj and co-authors test a set of oxindole compounds in cells in work from 2026. The compounds were checked for their power to switch on a defense path in cells that fights damage from oxygen and swelling.

All nineteen compounds switched on the path, and two stood out for strong effect at low doses. Both raised levels of two defense genes over time in breast cancer cells. In mouse immune cells, they also cut the swelling response. Computer work pointed to the likely site of action. The authors name the two compounds as leads for further study.
pmc-13609823:
Shuaibo Han and co-authors name a new bacterial species from rotting bamboo that can break down lignin, the tough plant polymer, in work from 2026. Alone on lignin, the strain broke down a small share, and added sugar raised that share a lot. It cut the most common lignin bond and nicked side chains and rings. Its genome holds genes for several lignin-attack enzymes and for paths that use the pieces. Paired with a white-rot fungus, the strain broke down more than either alone.
pmc-13610323:

pmc-13610923:

pmc-13611523:
Guowei Liang and colleagues proposed a new indoor positioning method in 2026 for places where satellite signals fail. The model handled step counting, step length, heading fixes, and rebuilding the walked path.

In tests, the method counted steps more accurately and held its own on step length. It also curbed the slow drift in walking direction that ruins indoor tracks, and the rebuilt paths stayed more consistent overall. The authors argue that, with the right background knowledge, language models can reason usefully over raw motion signals. They present the work as a fresh route to smarter indoor navigation without extra building equipment.
pmc-13611623:
Alexandru Munteanu, Cosmin Bonchiș, and Gerardo López Saldaña corrected air quality estimates in 2026. European satellite reanalysis gives pollution estimates. Its grid is too coarse for single stations. The study focused on Lombardy, Italy. Years from twenty eighteen to twenty twenty-one were covered.

Station links were mapped as a graph. Central stations gained extra context weight. Corrections improved some pollutants at stations. Nitrogen oxides and fine particles gained most. Nitrogen dioxide results were mixed. Coarse particles improved over time with kriging. The authors say graph context helps. It cannot replace true dispersion modelling.
pmc-13611723:

Under still weights, both plates slightly under-read the lightest load and sharpened as loads grew. Repeated sessions a day apart agreed within one percent. Ten men then performed two kinds of jumps on both plates. The readings matched closely across the whole force curve, with about a two percent dip at the hardest impacts. The authors say the portable plate is accurate enough for field work.
pmc-13611923:
Qingli Yang and five co-authors review ten years of a dangerous heart inflammation in children at one hospital, in a 2026 study. Gene-based tests, including broad sequencing, identified culprit viruses. Treatments and outcomes were tracked together. The resulting picture can guide faster virus hunting and support decisions in the first critical hours.
pmc-13612023:
Agata Malyszek and Maciej Janeczek revisit an ancient letter to test whether a named healer at Mari was an early veterinarian, in a 2026 history paper. One royal archive letter from Mari mentions Ipiq-Enlil, whom a leading editor once called a kind of veterinarian.

That reading had never been examined in the veterinary literature itself. The authors re-read the letter against its editor’s commentary and compare it with other Near Eastern sources on animal care, including an Egyptian veterinary papyrus. Their verdict weighs how far a specialist animal-healing role truly existed in the Bronze Age, and what the letter can and cannot prove.
pmc-13612323:
Huayang Gui and co-authors review a DNA alarm path in colorectal cancer in a 2026 paper. Immune checkpoint drugs help only a slice of bowel tumors long term. Most bowel tumors stay cold and shrug those drugs off.

Cell context bends the path toward attack or calm. Drug plays that tune the axis are weighed with biomarker hints. Context, not mere switch on, sets the gain.
pmc-13612423:
Xiaoqian Fu leads a four-author team reviewing how mitochondria handle calcium inside eggs and ovaries. It then connects that machinery to reproduction.

Obesity, aging, freezing, heavy metals, and oxidative stress all disturb the balance. The authors are candid about weak spots: blunt drug tools, poorly calibrated sensors, and almost no direct human egg data. They call mitochondrial calcium a promising biomarker candidate, not yet a clinical target.
pmc-13612823:
Tobias Rindfleisch, Emilie Fjeldberg Taule, Markus S Miettinen, and Jarl Underhaug publish a 2026 reference dataset of NMR chemical shifts. pmc-13614123:
Zhong Wei and four co-authors assess the future of polypropylene, one of the world's most used plastics, in this 2026 viewpoint.
