The piece gives a clear-eyed view of a giant industry squeezed by its own success.
pmc-13614423:
Chang-Ho Yun and co-authors test a one-hour group talk for poor sleep in Korea. Their twenty twenty-six study joins scarcity theory with standard insomnia therapy ideas. The aim was to ease false beliefs about sleep that keep people awake.

The session ran once at a Seoul hospital for a large lecture crowd. Of those who joined the study, twenty-nine finished all checks over four weeks. Scales tracked false sleep beliefs and insomnia severity at each point. A drop in beliefs would show that a mass format can reach people therapy cannot. Readers get a frank view of high dropout and modest scope.
pmc-13614923:
Yiping Lu and colleagues report a 2026 study of how a blue-green bacterium grabs phosphate, the nutrient it needs to live, using two different binding proteins. In nutrient-poor water, matching phosphate intake to the cell's needs is vital. Crystal pictures at very fine detail showed both proteins, called PstS1 and SphX, holding a phosphate ion with a web of hydrogen bonds, 14 in one and 15 in the other.

Despite the similar webs, SphX held phosphate 26 times more weakly. The difference came down to one part of the protein: a threonine that takes a proton in place of a special strong bond used by its cousin. Changing single parts of the protein one by one confirmed each piece's role. The work explains how one cell can run a tight, high-grip system and a looser one side by side.
pmc-13615223:
Bente de Roos and co-authors argue that exercise pays off well past weight loss in a 2026 review. In obesity care, training is often judged by kilos shed, yet weight shifts from exercise alone are modest. The authors gather proof on heart, metabolic, and body makeup gains in people with overweight or obesity.

A step wise plan starts with less sitting, then adds aerobic and strength work in layers. Such training can lift heart and metabolic health and reshape body makeup even when weight barely moves. Built into surgery and drug based care paths, it can also guard muscle mass and back gains after treatment ends.
pmc-13615423: Dixon and co-authors review how patient-specific cell therapies could be made at the point of care in the United States. It is a narrative review from 2026. Such therapies use a patient's own immune cells, reshaped to fight disease. Central plants make them slowly and at high cost. The review covers global rule frameworks and cost. It also sets out a plan for a joined facility and digital platform in community settings. That plan spans regulators, manufacturing standards, and cell-tracking data systems.
pmc-13616123:
Nazanin Zargar and co-authors test whether tooth roots can betray a person's age. They use cone-beam CT scans of 1,200 front teeth from 100 Iranian patients. Teeth change slowly across life. Ratios of canal length and widths at several depths were measured for each tooth type.

Several measures tracked with age, each in its own teeth. A width ratio at the neck of the tooth linked to age most often. Canal shape narrowed with age in the central incisors. The best single model, for an upper central incisor, explained about 47 percent of age variance. Sex clues were weak and patchy. The authors see forensic promise, tuned tooth by tooth.
pmc-13616323:
Dimitra Mantzara, Richard Whitfield, Glen R. Jones, Nghia P. Truong, and Athina Anastasaki report the first controlled version of a reaction that unbuilds polymers made by a popular controlled method. In that method, called atom transfer radical polymerisation, chains grow in a managed way because most sit dormant at any moment. Recycling those materials, though, has been all-or-nothing: chains unzip completely with no say over the stopping point.

By raising catalyst levels and lowering the heat, the team tipped the balance toward putting chains back to sleep over letting them run. Molecular weight then fell in a straight, even line, proving the chains shortened uniformly on demand. Controlled unbuilding opens a path to recovering graded feedstock from plastic waste, or to trimming a polymer to a chosen size instead of shredding it to monomer.
pmc-13616523:
Children who cannot understand health information grow into adults who struggle with it, and Jiayue Guo and co-authors build a quick health literacy test for Chinese schoolchildren. Existing tools for the young are patchy and weakly grounded. Their questionnaire covers seven domains — hygiene, nutrition, activity, safety, prevention, mental adaptation, and digital health — organised into knowledge, skills, motivation, and participation.

Four versions match four school stages, from thirty-nine items for the youngest to fifty-eight for junior high. Over seven thousand students across four regions took part in validation, and a formal measurement model showed strong fit and reliable items, though the test ran slightly easy for this sample. The authors offer the tool for monitoring and school health promotion, and they suggest widening its difficulty range and testing it across cultures.
pmc-13616623:
Samyia Safdar and co-authors open a journal research topic on leading multicultural teams in an inclusive way. Workforces now mix cultures through migration, global business, and remote work, which brings fresh ideas but also friction over fairness, trust, and communication. Their 2026 editorial sets out why inclusive leadership, marked by openness and respect for each person's difference, has become a live research theme.

Studies link such leadership to engagement, new ideas, well-being, and firm performance. Yet how it works inside multicultural teams is still patchy, the editors say, above all the settings that shape it and the mental steps that carry its effects. Artificial intelligence in the workplace adds both chances and risks for fairness. The topic gathers work across psychology, leadership theory, technology, and cross-cultural study to close those gaps.
pmc-13616723:
Johanna Wunderl and co-authors compare, in 2026, machine-driven and hand tools for root canal work in the canine teeth of dogs. Dog root canals are large and complex, making the treatment hard. Thirty extracted teeth were split into three groups and treated with two machine systems or with hand files, then checked with fine scans.

Machine tools matched the canal size more closely in one comparison, while overall canal volume change did not differ between groups. A second scan type was also tested for judging the filled canals after treatment. Air pockets and size mismatches were measured for each method. The work helps vets judge tools and imaging for this demanding procedure.
pmc-13617123:
Keyan He and colleagues studied bud banks in long-established perennial pastures. Their 2026 paper asks whether bud loss limits pasture recovery. Underground buds drive regrowth in perennial grasses. They may signal how much regenerative power a pasture keeps. Kentucky bluegrass pastures aged four, seven, and thirteen years were compared.

Nitrogen was added at low and high rates beside a control. Added nitrogen raised total bud density in younger pastures. The strongest response came under low nitrogen at year seven. High nitrogen cut rhizome bud density, while tiller buds stayed stable. Buds, tillers, and biomass all peaked at year seven. All fell sharply by year thirteen. The results tie pasture age to shrinking regrowth reserves.
pmc-13617223:
Amy L. Sweeny and six colleagues report a 2026 analysis of what makes intravenous cannula insertion painful for children in an emergency department. Research staff observed one hundred ninety-eight insertion attempts in one hundred thirty children under sixteen, scoring pain with a faces scale. A secondary analysis of that prospective study then searched for child, clinician, and situational factors tied to high pain scores.

More than two in five children hit the high pain range. Younger age raised the odds, and so did needing three or more attempts, a past bad cannulation experience, a child who fought the procedure, and choosing the inner elbow site first. The authors argue the first attempt matters most: teams should optimize it and use proven pain-reducing strategies, especially for younger children and those already fearful from earlier experiences.
pmc-13617423:
Pernille Tveden-Nyborg and four co-authors set out the rules a pharmacology journal will apply to studies of natural products, in this 2026 guideline paper. Such products, from isolated compounds to traditional Chinese preparations and marine or microbial extracts, remain rich sources of new medicines. Their variability, in source, preparation, and chemistry, too often wrecks reproducibility.

Authors must document the rationale, the organism's identity and origin, lawful and sustainable sourcing, extraction, and chemical makeup. The preparation actually given to subjects is what must be studied, at sensible doses, with controls for solvents and assay interference. Mixtures need not be reduced to one molecule, but claims about parts, synergy, or opposition need experiments. Computer network analyses must be transparent and their key predictions tested at the bench. The editors apply natural products the same standards as any intervention.
pmc-13617523:
Kristina Goryunova and Yunis Gahramanli compare the main ways to make porous geopolymers, a class of cement-like materials built from industrial by-products rather than energy-hungry Portland cement. Pores decide whether these materials insulate buildings, filter water, or carry catalysts, yet earlier reviews treated each foaming method in isolation. The authors line the methods up inside one processing, structure, and properties framework.

Direct foaming emerges as the most practical and scalable route for low-density insulation, while lightweight fillers give the best balance of strength and density. Emulsion templating, replica processing, and sacrificial templates better create the connected pore networks that adsorption, catalysis, and filtration need. Printing offers the finest architectural control but remains slow and costly, and microwave foaming is fast yet hard to scale. The review closes with a selection guide that starts from the pore architecture a job requires.
pmc-13617623:
Somaya Al Kiswani and six colleagues report a rare case of Klippel-Trenaunay syndrome, a vascular malformation condition marked by abnormal capillaries, veins, and lymph vessels plus overgrowth of a limb. Their patient, a thirty-seven-year-old Yemeni man, arrived with blood in his urine with clots, rectal bleeding, and back pain radiating into his leg. Two separate pelvic masses raised fears of cancer.

Careful teamwork across clinical examination, imaging, endoscopy, and pathology showed the masses were vascular malformations involving both the urinary bladder and the rectosigmoid colon, not malignancy. Internal organ involvement is uncommon in this syndrome, and pelvic disease can announce itself through exactly these bleeding symptoms. The syndrome is usually managed conservatively, with lifelong follow-up aimed at bleeding control and complication prevention. The authors stress that a full multidisciplinary workup protects patients from misdiagnosis and unneeded aggressive treatment.
pmc-13618223:
Jiawen Ding and co-authors study a protein called IRP2 in lung cancer in a 2026 paper. The cancer type is non-small cell lung cancer, the top cause of cancer death in the world. Around tumors sit macrophages, immune cells that can help or hinder the fight. The team found that IRP2, a protein that controls iron inside cells, is high in many tumors. They asked what it does in those immune cells.

The results paint IRP2 as a brake on immune attack. With more IRP2, the immune cells shifted to a state that helps tumors grow and spread. The protein also kept PD-L1, a shield tumors use, at high levels on the cells. It did so by slowing the breakdown of a partner protein in cell waste units. Blocking IRP2 in these cells is put forward as a fresh drug aim for this cancer.
pmc-13618723:
Guoping Yang and Weiwei Liao report a delayed lung complication in 2026. A woman in her late sixties came in with chest tightness and breathlessness over many days. Two years before, she had a spine procedure that used bone cement to fix crushed vertebrae. Her heart tests came back normal, which pointed doctors elsewhere.

Scans showed cement traces in her spine and thin dense lines inside her lung arteries. A dye based scan confirmed bone cement blockages in those vessels, with raised pressure as a result. The case warns that cement can travel and cause harm long after spine repair.
pmc-13619123:
Peng Wang and five co-authors fed Simmental cattle a plant-and-probiotic mix in a 2026 trial and tracked the results. Beef producers want faster growth and stronger immunity, and the mix joins herbal additives with helpful microbes. One group of cattle ate a basic diet, while the other got the mix at one percent of dry feed. The trial ran for 120 days.

Cattle on the mix ate more, gained more each day, and digested fat better. Their blood showed stronger immune and antioxidant markers, and key cholesterol measures fell. Meat from the group was lighter in color, held more of several amino acids, and cut with less force. Gut microbe balance in the stomach shifted as well. The authors see the mix as a useful feed addition.
pmc-13619323:
Stefan Sieber led a 2026 study of how cleaner air and more schooling might have cut low birth weight in Spain between 2010 and 2018. Low birth weight, below 2,500 grams at term, carries risks across life, and both pollution and maternal education shape its odds. The team analyzed administrative records for 1,409,084 term births, pairing each with fine-grained estimates of fine particles and nitrogen dioxide exposure. They then modeled what would change under cleaner-air targets or universal higher education.

Each 10-microgram rise in fine particles was tied to about 6 percent higher odds of low birth weight, and nitrogen dioxide to about 1 percent higher odds. Lower maternal education carried much larger odds, at 1.32 times for secondary and 1.76 times for primary education against tertiary education. Meeting stricter particle limits might have prevented roughly two thousand cases, while universal tertiary education might have prevented more than nine thousand.
pmc-13619423:
Daniela Sebastião and co-authors profile stroke patients in Angola in this 2026 multi-center study. Stroke is a top cause of death and disability worldwide. Its burden falls hardest on low and middle income countries. In sub-Saharan Africa, stroke strikes younger people, bleeds more often, and ends worse than elsewhere.

The team followed patients admitted to three large hospitals in Luanda over six months in 2024. Most patients were under sixty, and men were slightly more than half. Blocked-vessel strokes were most common, but bleeding strokes made up nearly half. High blood pressure was by far the leading risk factor. Function was scored at discharge and again over the next ninety days.
pmc-13619523:
Xiong and co-authors build a tiny probe that both images and treats bone cancer with heat. The cancer grows aggressively and often sits deep, where heat therapy is hard to aim. Their 2026 study coats flower shaped iron and gold particles with a branched polymer and glucose, then tests them in mice.

Probes gathered at the tumor, confirmed by fluorescence scans and magnetic resonance imaging. Under laser light, treated tumors heated fast in the first minutes and grew much more slowly than controls. Body weight stayed stable, and major organs showed no clear damage. Blood and tissue measures tracked how the probes spread and cleared, giving context for the heat response.
pmc-13619823:
Suhail Serbaya and co-authors test how well artificial intelligence platforms can spot autism from written case stories, in a 2026 study. Twenty standardised child case reports were used, ten describing autism and ten not. Each platform, general-purpose and health-specialised alike, had to read the narrative and give a diagnosis, and the answers were scored against the clinical truth.

One leading general model reached the best balance of sensitivity and specificity. The rest spread widely, with sensitivity between sixty and ninety percent. General and specialised systems did not differ significantly overall. The stronger large models could reason through tangled diagnostic stories rather than matching surface cues. The authors conclude that advanced general platforms can genuinely support reading complex autism cases. They still insist on layered safety frameworks and standard protocols before any clinic use, and on more testing to fix the precise role of such tools.
pmc-13621623:
Jin-Yang Yu and eleven colleagues profiled the genetics of inherited ataxias across more than two thousand Chinese patients, building the HARMONY cohort from two Yangtze River Delta centers. These coordination disorders come in dozens of flavors, and the local mix shapes how testing should be ordered. The team combined diagnoses with systematic testing and sorted results as definitive, probable, unclear, or undiagnosed.

Nearly eighty-five percent of the 2,096 patients received a molecular answer. One subtype towered over the rest: spinocerebellar ataxia type 3 accounted for about sixty percent, trailed by types 2 and 1 in single digits. Beyond those giants stretched a long tail of rare causes, and five candidate genes turned up empty. The authors convert the landscape into a stepwise testing algorithm tuned for their region, testing the common expansions first. They argue such maps speed diagnosis, sharpen counseling, and point therapy developers to the subtypes that matter most.
pmc-13621823:
David Aini and co-authors report the case of a sixty-six-year-old man whose month of pain in the lower right belly led to a very rare finding. Scans showed an enlarged appendix with no signs of inflammation around it. Surgeons removed the appendix through small incisions, and his symptoms cleared within three weeks.

Under the microscope, the appendix tissue showed lipomatosis, a harmless overgrowth of fat cells inside the organ wall. The authors note that only five earlier cases of this appendix condition had been reported, which makes firm guidance hard to give. The case adds one more documented example, with the patient's history, scan measurements, and tissue results laid out in full. For doctors, the lesson is that fat overgrowth belongs on the list of causes when an appendix looks enlarged without infection.
pmc-13623523:
Mustafa Allouch and seven co-authors argue in this twenty twenty-six review that the human stomach was shaped for hard times. For most of our past, food was scarce, bulky, and low in energy, and people moved a lot. A stomach that could stretch to hold large, fibrous meals helped people survive lean seasons and rare feasts.

That old design now meets a world of rich food at every hour and little daily movement. The authors say this mismatch may help drive weight gain and blood sugar disease, and that stomach size is an overlooked part of the story. The review pulls together what is known and calls for more study of this angle on obesity.
pmc-13623623:
Suren Lai and seven co-authors report real-world results for telitacicept, a B-cell drug, in lupus nephritis, in a study published in two thousand twenty-six. The kidney disease flares when the immune system attacks the kidneys. Three groups were compared at two centers: new patients given the drug plus standard care, new patients on standard care alone, and hard-to-treat patients given the drug as an add-on. Fifty-five patients took part.

New patients on the drug reached full remission a bit sooner than those on standard care alone, though the gap was not firm. Both drug groups showed better kidney blood tests and needed less steroid. New patients answered better than the hard-to-treat group, hinting that early use helps most. Infections were the main side effect and stayed mild to moderate.
pmc-13623723:
Yiru Wang and co-authors build a scoring chart that forecasts breast cancer response to pre-surgery drug therapy, in a 2026 study. Some tumors vanish fully under the drugs, a sign of better odds ahead. Guessing who will respond, before treatment starts, is still hard. Standard scans also miss clues in the tissue ring around a tumor.

The team studied 534 patients at one center and split them into training and test groups. Their chart blends hand-crafted scan traits, deep learning traits, and routine clinical markers. It draws on the tumor and on rings of nearby tissue at three widths. The six-millimeter ring looked best in training. The full chart scored highest on the test set, though gains over a tumor-only model were not firm. The authors call the tool early-stage and ask for wider trials.
pmc-13624023:
Toshiaki Taoka and colleagues published a 2026 review arguing for a new reading of a popular brain scan measure, the DTI-ALPS index. The index uses diffusion MRI, which tracks water movement in tissue, and it was sold as a gauge of the glymphatic system, the brain's waste-washing flow. Years of use have complicated that simple story.

The authors point out that the index samples water movement at one fixed spot and says nothing direct about whole-brain flow. Its value bends with the local white matter itself: fibre direction, crossing fibres, the spaces between cells, and plain ageing all shift it. Two brains can also reach the same low index by opposite internal changes. The review proposes calling it a fixed-point biomarker of the tissue environment instead, bundling fibre structure, vessels, and fluid dynamics. Used that humbler way, they argue, it still serves brain health research well.
pmc-13624123:
Doris Hagan leads a team on HIV drug adherence in Ghanaian teens. Their study from twenty twenty-six is set in the Ashanti Region. Teens with HIV in Africa bear a large share of the epidemic.

They also stick to therapy less well than adults do. Past work counts who fails, not how teens cope day to day. Group talks were held at three hospitals in the region. All teens knew their HIV status in full before joining. A paired survey found high self told adherence overall. Daily tricks teens use are the core focus.
pmc-13624823:
Ramón Eizaga Rebollar, José Manuel Muñoz Quintero, and Rafael Eduardo López Alfaro report a child surgery scare in a 2026 paper. The child bore a neck nerve zap device for drug-proof fits and had belly scope surgery with the device left on. Such devices can spark heart and lung snags in surgery, the team notes.

Mid-surgery, as the belly filled with gas, the child's heart rate crashed to a grave low. Drugs alone righted the rate, with no need to switch the device off. The team tells why they held that line and what the course taught.
pmc-13625023:
Marlene M Meyer, Marina Proft, Jan Engelmann, and Hannes Rakoczy test whether three-year-olds know when they do not know. Older work said clear judgments about one's own knowledge arrive near school age, yet those tests asked children alone. Across four pre-registered studies with 195 children, this team placed three- and five-year-olds in a social task where a partner depended on the child's advice despite partial views of a hidden setup.

Even the three-year-olds spoke up about doubt when they had seen only part of the picture, and they stayed confident when they had seen it all. Two control studies gave mixed clues about why the social setting helped. Knowing may be voiced earlier when a child must guide someone else.
pmc-13625123:
Britanny Stark and colleagues built a 3D-printable, electrically conductive gel for heart and vessel repair. After a heart attack, adult hearts barely regrow muscle and lose electrical signalling, yet drugs replace neither muscle nor conduction. Their 2026 study made a light-cured gel from modified hyaluronic acid linked to a conductive thiophene compound, printable into tissue scaffolds.

The new gel conducted electricity far better than plain modified hyaluronic acid, though it softened somewhat. Heart and vessel cells stayed active in both gels, and stem-cell-derived heart muscle cells kept their cardiac marker and kept beating spontaneously. Stark and colleagues present the gel as a step toward printed heart patches.
pmc-13625523:
Boron signals in NMR scans blur together, hiding which boron site in a molecule is which. Penghui Li and co-authors teach machines to unblur them in a 2026 study. A hand-checked data set, built with language model help, anchors the training.

One molecular trait tracked boron bonding type with surprising strength. A graph transformer fed that trait as prior knowledge. It then forecast each boron's signal at atom level. Sites that lab scans cannot split came apart in the model's read. A free web tool puts the method in chemists' hands. Drug and materials work both lean on boron maps.
pmc-13625623:
William Penberthy and Charles Vorwaller argue that power is the missing ingredient in laser therapy, in a 2026 review. Gentle low-level lasers are approved for shallow problems like mouth sores. Trials on deep tissue often fail, though, because little light arrives and the dose falls short. High-intensity class IV lasers run at roughly a hundred times the power.

Pooling 105 studies with over twenty-seven hundred treated patients, the review finds pain relief in every randomized trial for knee, spine, and shoulder problems, mostly with large effects. No serious side effects were reported. Gains in movement, function, and quality of life were also common, and pain relief held at three months and beyond. The authors credit raw power and depth for the gap.
pmc-13625723:
Tim Hensen and co-authors build personal computer models of whole-body metabolism to test how gut microbes may stir the blood chemistry of Alzheimer's disease. Earlier modeling in healthy older adults had forecast microbe-driven changes, unproven in real patients. The team therefore built models for thirty-four patients with Alzheimer's dementia, fifty-one with mild cognitive trouble tied to the disease, and 298 healthy controls, each tuned to that person's gut microbe mix.

The models foresaw greater capacity to make five blood compounds, including creatine and taurine, in Alzheimer's patients. Two Bacteroides species carried most of the blame for the shift, and the forecasts also tied to variants of the APOE risk gene in healthy people. Computer twins like these may expose testable links between gut and brain.
pmc-13626223:
Hafiz Syed Zaigham Ali Shah and co-authors describe a typhoid emergency that hid behind a birth defect. A 33-year-old man arrived with six days of fever, fierce upper belly pain, vomiting, and septic shock, and X-rays showed free air, so a burst stomach ulcer topped the working diagnosis. Typhoid perforation usually declares itself low on the right side, where the end of the small bowel normally sits.

Surgery told another story. The belly was heavily soiled, and a two-centimeter typhoid hole gaped in the small bowel. The bowel's end sat high in the upper belly, because the gut had never finished its fetal rotation. Surgeons diverted the bowel through the skin, blood tests confirmed typhoid, and he healed well enough to have the diversion reversed. Odd anatomy, the case warns, can scramble classic signs.
pmc-13626623:
Muhammad Iqhrammullah tracks rheumatic heart disease in children across three countries in a study from two thousand twenty-six, written alone. The region covers parts of Indonesia, Malaysia, and Thailand linked as a growth triangle. The study asks whether social and economic development has cut the disease burden since nineteen ninety.

Using global burden data through two thousand twenty-three, the author finds the overall burden fell, driven by fewer deaths, while new case rates showed no steady drop. Higher development scores tracked with lower burden in every age group. Against what its development would predict, Indonesia underperformed, Thailand did better than expected, and Malaysia matched the expected path.
pmc-13626923:
Sinha and co-authors review a form of heart failure in which the heart still squeezes normally but relaxes badly. They argue its roots lie in the mitochondria of several cell types at once. In muscle cells, faulty calcium handling inside mitochondria and redox imbalance starve the cell of energy and stiffen relaxation. In fibroblasts, rewired metabolism feeds scar tissue build-up. In vessel-lining cells, sick mitochondria cut nitric oxide and raise oxidative stress.

The authors weave these strands into one axis of calcium, redox, and energy failure that could explain the syndrome's odd split: a heart that pumps fine yet fills poorly. They also discuss early treatments aimed at mitochondrial pathways. The review is a call for precision thinking about a disease that has resisted one-size drugs. For cardiologists, it reframes scattered cell findings as one connected problem.
pmc-13627323:
César Sampaio and co-authors built hybrid catalysts by loading a porous crystal with a strong acid, then tested them on a reaction run without solvent. The crystal, ZIF-8, is a zinc-based metal-organic framework full of cages. The team tucked a Keggin-type acid inside it by two routes, soaking it in or growing the crystal around it. Both versions were checked with many imaging and chemical tools.

In the test reaction, joining styrene oxide with aniline, both catalysts converted ninety-eight percent of the feed in a day. They favored the amino alcohol product and survived reuse well. Running the reaction with no solvent makes the process cleaner and cheaper to separate. The authors present the pair as a study in preparation method: two ways to build the same partnership, both ending in a sturdy, recyclable catalyst for green chemistry.
pmc-13627423:
Sonjia Kenya, BreAnne Young, and Olveen Carrasquillo describe how HIV community health workers pivoted to COVID-19 in a 2026 paper. In Miami-Dade County, Black residents bore a heavy share of AIDS deaths and higher COVID-19 death rates than White residents. A trusted worker network offered a path into those communities.

Built over a decade with nine community groups, the network added COVID-19 education and vaccine support to its HIV outreach. Work ran for two years in high-risk minority neighborhoods. The approach kept community values at the center while adding new tasks. The account shows how existing trust can be redeployed in a crisis.
pmc-13627723:
Zhihao Jiang and co-authors uncover a molecular handshake that speeds methane making in oxygen free digestion, in a study from 2026. Quinone based materials are known to boost this process by shuttling electrons from bacteria to methane making microbes. Exactly how electrons cross from the material into the microbe at their shared boundary was unknown.

Working in a microbial electrolysis cell with a well known methanogen, the team found a neat fit between two ring shaped structures. The electron rich rings of the reduced quinone stack against the iron bearing rings of heme, a pigment microbes release into their surrounding slime. That stacking may hold the heme in place and ease electron flow across the boundary. The finding explains part of why these materials raise gas output.
pmc-13627823:
Fabio de Paula Domingos and co-authors hunted for what predicts running economy in women recreational runners in 2026. Running economy, the energy cost of a run, decides how far fitness carries a runner. Sixty-one women aged twenty to sixty took a battery of tests.

Energy cost tied most strongly to body fat share: higher fat, higher cost. Flexibility, lean mass, and top aerobic speed also linked to cost, with speed pulling cost down. Age, years in the sport, peak oxygen uptake, and knee strength showed no clear link. In a joint model, fat share and aerobic speed explained about forty-four percent of cost spread. The authors read fat share as the firm lever and speed as a borderline one.
pmc-13628223:
Bhagyashree Pasarad and co-authors turn cauliflower waste into useful dietary fiber in 2026. Processing scraps hold much fiber, but most of it is the insoluble kind with weak food value. Sound waves plus enzymes offer a green way to upgrade it.

Ultrasound raised fiber yield and the share of soluble fiber, while shrinking particle size. The treated fiber held more water and oil and swelled better. Mixed into biscuits, a tenth share gave the best balance of nutrition, texture, and taste. The biscuits stayed sound through ninety days of shelf storage in their tests.
pmc-13628523:
Davide Auricchio and three colleagues examined how drugs designed for one unusual DNA shape behave toward its mirror-image partner. Their 2026 study concerns G-quadruplexes, knots formed in guanine-rich DNA, and i-motifs, folded structures on the matching cytosine-rich strand that may also help switch cancer genes on or off.

The team screened four well-known quadruplex-binding compounds against a small, well-defined i-motif using magnetic resonance and light-based methods. One compound, TMPyP4, bound a specific region of the i-motif and gradually unfolded the structure as it attached. Knowing exactly where such a ligand grips should help chemists design molecules that tune i-motif stability on purpose, a step toward drugs that act on both DNA shapes at once.
pmc-13628623:
Konstanty Zdunek, Tatiana Korona, and Agnieszka Więckowska study what adding platinum does to tiny gold clusters, in a chemistry paper from 2026. Each cluster holds twenty-five metal atoms wrapped in a shell of sulfur-linked chains. Adding one platinum atom is known to shift how the cluster handles charge, but pure samples are hard to make.

The team worked with mixed batches made by a classic method, without harsh cleaning steps that damaged the platinum form. Tests of size, light uptake, charge steps, and shell vibrations all differed from pure gold batches. Computer models matched the trend, showing a more warped core when platinum sits inside.
pmc-13629323:
Federica Bruno and two colleagues give a step-by-step protocol for infecting lab mice with a rodent malaria parasite. The parasite is Plasmodium chabaudi. People in malaria regions are infected again and again across a life. The protocol copies that pattern. Researchers can then study how immunity builds, and what it costs the host.

The method covers a first infection and full natural recovery. No malaria drugs are used. A second infection follows. Each stage is set out in detail. Letting the mice clear the parasite themselves is the point. It mirrors how partial immunity forms in humans. Hidden costs come with it, such as lasting anaemia. The authors frame the method as a shared platform. Labs studying long-term responses to repeated malaria can all use it.
pmc-13630723:
João Matias and Joana Carneiro Pinto ask in 2026 whether support from an employer shields workers from worry about AI at work. Their study draws on a theory that weighs job demands against job resources. It links fear about AI to job safety, skill growth, and long-term career contentment.

The team surveyed 106 workers in Portugal and added open-ended accounts for context. Fear about AI went with lower felt job safety and lower career contentment, but not with skill growth. Support from the firm softened the link with job safety only. Workers also pointed to weak contact from firms and few chances to learn new skills.
pmc-13630823:
Liang-Chen Lin and five colleagues ran a split-face trial of skincare support after laser treatment for sun-aged skin. The study appeared in 2026. Thirty-five Asian patients received three picosecond laser sessions a month apart. One cheek got a standard soothing serum and sunscreen. The other got an added three-product regimen. It included an antioxidant serum and a lipid cream.

pmc-13631323:

pmc-13631423:

pmc-13632123:

pmc-13632923:

pmc-13633323:

pmc-13633523:

pmc-13633623:

pmc-13633923:
Mariam Aamir, Zachary Fitzgerald, and Collin Kitchell (2026) report severe anemia in a 46-year-old woman who ran extreme distances daily. She came in with growing tiredness and hip pain. pmc-13634023:

pmc-13634123:

pmc-13635223:

pmc-13637023:

A simpler method shifted that state too far blue. The pair stayed docked through the full simulation run. Average coupling came out at a modest set value. Thermal spread of the coupling was also tracked.
pmc-13638023:

pmc-13638323:

pmc-13639423:

pmc-13641523:

pmc-13644823:

Average tone balance holds broadly steady across the span. Yet sentiment states last far longer now, with fewer flips and lower swing size. Negative bursts outlast positive ones in the recent data. A slow memory model fits the shift, with weaker short-run correction over time.
pmc-13646723:

pmc-13649423:

pmc-13650123:

pmc-13651623:

pmc-13651823:

pmc-13652123:

pmc-13652423:

pmc-13654123:

pmc-13655423:

pmc-13655823:

pmc-13656823:

pmc-13657823:

pmc-13658623:

pmc-13658723:

pmc-13659123:

pmc-13660523:

pmc-13661223:

pmc-13662523:

pmc-13665623:

pmc-13667923:

pmc-13668023:

pmc-13669023:

pmc-13669123:

pmc-13669223:

pmc-13669323:

pmc-13670323:

Their surveillance scans show no return so far. Under current guidelines, shared decision-making favored keeping the thyroid and watching closely.
pmc-13670723:
Xinyue Chang and co-authors wrote a 2026 review of a joint infection cure that pairs one stage surgery with drugs placed right into the joint. Infection around a man made joint is a grave problem after joint surgery. One stage surgery swaps the joint in a single operation, which cuts the number of procedures.

The team searched four databases for studies of adults treated both ways at once, with at least a year of follow up. Ten studies met the rules. Across them, control of infection looked sound. Drugs were picked for each case, and the review sums up the methods used, the safety record, and the results, to guide teams weighing this joint approach.
pmc-13671123:
Lakkaraja and colleagues report in 2027 two patients transplanted for IL-10 receptor deficiency, an inherited immune defect that causes severe bowel disease in infancy. Standard immune drugs control it poorly, and anakinra can calm it but not cure it. Both patients received blood stem cell transplants prepared with treosulfan-based conditioning. The approach gave full donor engraftment and excellent survival.

The two cases span nearly a decade, showing the method's durability. The report also confirms new disease-causing gene variants. The authors highlight anakinra as an effective bridge that holds the disease until transplant can proceed.
pmc-13672123:
Yinpeng Ma and co-authors designed a hybrid lens system in two thousand twenty-six. Metalenses bend light with tiny surface patterns instead of curved glass. Wide versions that work across colors remain hard to build. Full computer checks of wide lenses also take enormous effort. The team paired a metalens with a standard glass lens.

Their design method links three tools in one loop. Ray tracing handles the glass lens part. Wave spread models handle the patterned part. A mapping step keeps the pattern buildable in a factory. The glass gives most of the focusing power. The metalens then corrects leftover image flaws across colors. The team built and tested a wide prototype to prove the route.
pmc-13672723:
Hospitals use a lot of energy, and imaging departments are among the hungriest parts. Stefania Rizzo and co-authors measured that footprint for one radiology department in a 2026 study. They accounted for the scanners themselves, workstations, lighting, ventilation, cooling, medicines, and outside services such as laundry and computing.

The biggest lever turned out to be the electricity supply. When the hospital switched from coal-based power to hydropower, the department's primary energy use fell by about 64 percent and its greenhouse gas emissions by about 92 percent. Even so, MRI scanners remained the most energy-hungry machines per exam. The authors pair their accounting with strategies for running imaging more sustainably without cutting care.
pmc-13673123:
Mohammed Hashem and co-authors test a stomach bacterium's link to a heart rhythm disorder in a 2026 study of heart attack patients. Chronic Helicobacter pylori infection stokes body-wide inflammation, and some suspect it encourages atrial fibrillation, but the clinical evidence has swung both ways.

Three hundred patients hospitalized with acute heart attacks took a breath test for active infection during their stay. One in five tested positive. Fibrillation was actually less common among the infected group, about seven percent against twelve, and the gap was not statistically significant after adjustments. The authors conclude active infection shows no clear tie to fibrillation here.
pmc-13673223:
Xiao Xue, Yaning Feng, Yu-Ping Lin, Pui-Ching Chan, and Hon-Cheong So published a 2026 genome wide study of severe influenza. Flu sends many people to hospital each year, and genes shape who fares worst. The genetic basis of hospitalization, as apart from catching flu at all, was poorly mapped, as was its overlap with COVID-19 genetics.

One analysis used British biobank data with about a thousand hospitalized cases. A meta analysis with a Finnish study raised the count past eleven thousand cases. A second analysis asked which genes set the age of first hospitalization. The team found four risk regions for severe flu. Follow up work compared these signals with COVID-19, finding both shared and distinct genetic factors.
pmc-13674723:
Espinoza and co-authors test whether removing one enzyme from immune cells protects mice from chronic gut inflammation, in a 2026 study. The enzyme, acid ceramidase, works in fat signaling inside cells and runs high in patients with inflammatory bowel disease. Earlier work showed that losing it in myeloid immune cells blunted short-term colitis. The team bred mice lacking both the enzyme in those cells and the calming signal IL10, a recipe for lasting colitis.

The protected mice developed milder disease with fewer inflammation markers. Their colons held more ceramides and less of an inflammatory fat signal. Immune cell entry into the gut wall dropped, above all for neutrophils and aggressive T cell types. The authors name the enzyme a promising drug target for bowel disease.
pmc-13675123:
Hilde Marie Engjom and co-authors argue, in a 2026 article, that the Nordic countries should track maternal deaths and severe birth harm together, as a routine. Five countries take part: Denmark, Finland, Iceland, Norway, and Sweden. Their joint groups already study causes of death and severe illness around birth.

Several European countries run steady systems that learn from every severe case. The Nordic groups also work inside a wider world network of such survey systems. The authors want that learning made routine and shared across their five systems. Rare tragedies are too few in any one small country to teach clear lessons alone. Pooled, careful review can turn single sad cases into safer care for all.
pmc-13676423:
Boxuan Hu and co-authors keep magnesium from evaporating while cooking a top thermoelectric material, in a study published in 2026. The magnesium-bismuth-antimony family converts heat to electricity well, but magnesium boils off during high-temperature synthesis, wrecking the recipe. Their method parks a sacrificial magnesium reservoir nearby and controls the gas atmosphere, holding the metal in place. That removes the need for costly sealed tantalum capsules and scales to bigger batches.

The resulting magnesium-rich alloy posted a very high power factor and a strong efficiency figure at room temperature, peaking higher still when hot. Adding a touch of barium squeezed heat conduction further and lifted the peak figure again. The trick also worked for two other magnesium compounds. The authors present retention-assisted synthesis as a general platform for magnesium materials.
pmc-13677023:
Kahlman and a large team of co-authors report a study, published in 2026, on low magnesium in a rare inherited syndrome. The syndrome combines a hormone gland fault, hearing loss, and kidney defects. It stems from changes in one gene that helps build several organs. Low blood magnesium had been noted in some patients but was not well charted. The team gathered cases to define how often it occurs and how it shows up.

Their work confirms that low magnesium is part of the syndrome, not a side issue. It can add cramps, weakness, and heart rhythm risk to patients' other burdens. The authors describe which patients are affected and how the problem relates to kidney handling of the mineral. The study tells doctors to check magnesium in these patients as routine care. It also sharpens the picture of what the gene does in the kidney.
pmc-13677223:
Sharma, Sharma, and Asbell argue, in a 2026 article, that studies of proteins in tears need shared rules for handling their data. Tears carry proteins that reflect the health of the eye and the wider body. Taking a tear sample is easy and painless, so labs prize tears for finding markers of disease. Such markers have been reported for dry eye, diabetes damage to the eye, and brain diseases.

The authors say the field has a quiet problem. Each lab adjusts its raw protein data in its own way, or not at all. Without a shared method, results from one lab are hard to check against another's. Promising markers then stall before they can be used in care. The article calls for agreed rules that mix careful lab work and tested computer methods. It sets out why such rules would make tear studies more trustworthy.
pmc-13677423:
Gabriel Moraes Kuniyoshi and co-authors present a 2026 meta-analysis comparing a heart plug procedure with blood thinners for atrial fibrillation. Sealing the left atrial appendage aims to prevent strokes without lifelong anticoagulation. The team pooled four randomized trials with 5,890 patients, nearly all controls on modern direct anticoagulants.

Overall stroke, embolism, major bleeding, brain bleeding, and death did not differ firmly between strategies. Ischemic stroke leaned toward the drug side, nearly significantly. The plug clearly cut non-procedure bleeding by half. The authors read the contest as close, with wide error bars, traded along different risk lines.
pmc-13677723:
Tyler K Fenstermaker, Svetlana Petruk, and Alexander Mazo studied, in a 2026 paper, how fast the genome's 3D shape returns after DNA copying. When a cell copies its DNA, the folding of the genome is torn down and must be rebuilt. Past work tracked proteins alone, not the shape itself.

Working in human cells, the team watched both shape factors and folding right after copying. Two key shape proteins, CTCF and YY1, latched onto fresh DNA at once. Loops from 39 to 425 thousand bases long re-formed within ten minutes of copying. Gene control networks also snapped back fast. The genome's shape, it seems, is only briefly disturbed by copying, which helps daughter cells resume the parent cell's program.
pmc-13678423:
Lia Spencer and co-authors gather everything that can go wrong after elective foot and ankle surgery into one map. Complication studies usually cover a single procedure, leaving surgeons and patients to guess the wider landscape. The review searched three databases for studies from 2020 to mid-2025 on adults having planned, non-emergency operations.

Nine studies covering more than twenty thousand patients met the bar. Infection, wound breakdown, failed bone union, hardware removal, and nerve injury each appeared at rates that swung widely by procedure and by patient risk. The synthesis sorts risk factors and prevention strategies alongside the rates. For consent conversations, one honest complication atlas beats a shelf of single-procedure brochures.
pmc-13680323:
Basma Souayeh and Najib Hdhiri simulate heat flow in a 2026 engineering study. Their setup is a tilted box filled with water carrying two kinds of nanoparticles, heated by flower-shaped fins inside. A magnetic field acts on the fluid, and the team tracks both heat removal and wasted energy, a pairing that matters for cooling electronics and storing energy.

Computer runs swept a wide range of heating strength, field strength, tilt, and particle load. Stronger heating and more particles stirred the fluid and lifted heat transfer. A stronger field damped the flow and cut transfer, though tilting the box softened that penalty. Without a field, the upright box worked best; with one, the tilted box won. Fin layouts also shaped the circulation.
pmc-13680623:
Ana Lopez-Jimenez and co-authors unveil, in a 2026 study, a hidden defense that human cells use against bacteria living inside them. Their new mapping method tags proteins near the host-bacteria boundary during infection, letting them see which defenses gather at the surface of invaders such as Shigella.

The maps showed an enzyme that attaches a small tag called UFM1 to targets at the bacterial surface. Shigella fights back twice: its outer coat hides it from the enzyme, and one of its proteins strips the tag away. Without this defense, bacteria multiplied more in human cells and in zebrafish larvae. The pathway works apart from the cell's usual recycling system.
pmc-13681323:
Johanna Grinat and co-authors identify, in a 2026 study, a signaling helper that the placenta needs to build its exchange surface. The labyrinth layer is where mother and fetus trade nutrients and gases. When it fails, the fetus grows poorly.

The helper, called IRS2, sits in the fused cell layers of the mouse labyrinth. Mice lacking it built a disorganized labyrinth with poor cell fusion and fewer fetal blood vessels. Stem cells engineered to lack the gene confirmed the fusion defect in a dish. The work ties one signaling protein to the placenta's core construction job. It may explain some growth restriction cases that currently lack a cause.
pmc-13681723:
Hiroki Narita and six co-authors untangle a rare artery variant behind a man's returning face pain, in a 2026 case report. Trigeminal neuralgia strikes with electric jolts, and blood vessels pressing the nerve are the usual cause.

Nineteen years after his first decompression surgery, the 79-year-old's pain returned. Imaging found a fetal artery remnant, a persistent primitive trigeminal artery, giving off the very cerebellar artery that squeezed the nerve. An old Teflon pad had also grown into a granuloma hiding the vessel. Three-dimensional reconstructions mapped the tangle before surgery. The team cleared the granuloma and moved the artery aside. Rare vessel families, they warn, draw unusual compression maps.
pmc-13682123:
Jana Rogler and co-authors ask which parts of balance matter for riding a bike outdoors in older age. Their 2026 study uses first-visit data from the BiPerAge trial, held at two centers. Cycling is healthy, but age-related decline can raise the risk of a fall or crash.

The study enrolled 116 adults aged 65 or older who each made at least three errors on a standard outdoor cycling course. Each rider took tests of standing balance, stepping, and trunk control on a special bike rig that tilts without warning. The team then matched test scores to course errors, adjusting for age, sex, and country. Results can point trainers to the balance skills that cycling safety needs most.
pmc-13688123:
Dabin Jeon and Tatsuya Unno compared DNA sequencing platforms in two thousand twenty-six. Gut samples came from cattle, pigs, and humans. Antibiotic resistance genes travel on mobile plasmids. Short reads may miss much of that traffic. Three platforms and seven assembly strategies competed. Long reads assembled far more plasmid sequence in livestock.

Human gut samples behaved differently, though. Dense coverage let short reads perform comparably there. Long reads found more resistance genes on plasmids overall. Hybrid assembly quality depended heavily on algorithm choice. Many unique multi-drug resistance plasmids emerged only from long reads. Method choice clearly shapes resistome conclusions. Surveillance programs should not treat platforms as interchangeable.
pmc-13693323:
Ram Rahim and Puneet Maheshwari write to the editor proposing a simple add-on to a traditional Ayurvedic nasal therapy, in this 2026 letter. The therapy, Marsha Nasya, delivers oils through the nose as part of Panchakarma care. A recent expert consensus set out steps toward standard practice for it, including preparatory warming of the body. The letter writers welcome that framework and its call for practical guidelines that stay flexible in daily clinics.

Their proposal, which they call the THAW protocol, is a traditional body-mechanics adjunct that costs nothing to add. They present it as a way to strengthen the preparatory stage the panel endorsed. The letter also backs people-centered design so access to Ayurvedic care stays fair. Short letters like this one are how practitioners test new practice ideas before formal trials.
pmc-2996323:
Davydov, Goode, Sirota, and co-authors present GERP++, a method for finding parts of the human genome under selective constraint. Parts of DNA that stayed nearly unchanged across species are likely to do important jobs. Computer methods hunt for those conserved regions using comparative sequence data.

GERP++ computes constraint scores position by position, following a bottom-up approach. The team reports that a high fraction of the human genome shows such constraint. Those maps point researchers toward functional elements hidden outside protein-coding genes, including switches that control development and disease.  Conserved stretches also guide the search for harmful variants in patient genomes today.
pmc-3270023:
Salzman, Gawad, Wang, and co-authors report that circular RNAs are the main transcript form from hundreds of human genes. Most human gene transcripts are spliced into linear molecules that keep the genome's exon order. Deep RNA sequencing of normal and malignant human cells told a different story.

The team found transcripts from many genes in which the exons were joined in scrambled order, forming circles. Such circles turned out to be the predominant form for hundreds of genes across diverse cell types. The finding revealed a whole class of RNA whose roles researchers are still unravelling.
pmc-3326523:
Filippakopoulos, Picaud, Mangos, and co-authors analyse the human bromodomain family, a set of protein modules that read epigenetic marks. Bromodomains recognise a specific chemical tag on lysine, a key event in reading marks that control gene activity. The human genome holds dozens of them, grouped into eight families.

The team presents recognition studies and a large-scale structural analysis across the family. Comparing shapes reveals which members might be druggable. Their map guided drug hunters toward bromodomain blockers, a class since explored in cancer and inflammation.  Crystal structures in the paper gave chemists concrete pockets to aim compounds at.
pmc-3471323:
Masella, Bartram, Truszkowski, and co-authors present PANDAseq, a tool for assembling paired-end Illumina reads. Researchers analyse microbial communities with paired-end reads, targeting pieces of the 16S rRNA gene. Public tools were needed to overlap and merge read pairs while fixing errors.

Many mismatches and uncalled bases can be corrected when the two reads overlap, yielding longer, cleaner sequences. PANDAseq performs that assembly efficiently for large datasets. Cleaner merged reads improve every later step in microbiome analysis, from counting species to comparing patient groups.  Error correction in the overlap also raises the accuracy of species counts.
pmc-3689523:
Evans and Murshudov explain how to judge data quality and resolution in crystal work. Their paper sets out the new scaling program AIMLESS, which merges repeated diffraction readings into one dataset. Tests of refinement at different detail levels are checked against analyses from the scaling step itself.

Resolution decides how much detail a crystal structure can honestly claim. Overstating it builds false detail into models; understating it wastes good data. The authors give practical criteria for choosing the cutoff. Their guidance is now standard reading for crystallographers reporting new structures.  Worked examples contrast strong and weak datasets so readers can calibrate judgement.
pmc-4294323:
Sheldrick described crystal structure refinement with SHELXL in a 2015 paper. Refinement is the step where an initial crystal structure model is adjusted to fit the measured data as closely as possible. SHELXL is one of the most used programs for that task worldwide.

Its growth was closely tied to the CIF format, the standard framework for checking and storing crystal structures. Recent changes simplified key steps while keeping the program's power for hard cases. Good refinement is what turns raw diffraction into a structure others can trust and reuse. The paper serves as a guide for crystallographers who rely on the program daily.
pmc-4393523:
Hu, Jin, Guo, and their team upgraded the Gene Structure Display Server in 2014. Drawing a gene's structure and features helps biologists grasp its function and evolution at a glance. The server, known as GSDS, had been used by tens of thousands of people since 2007.

Version two improved how gene features are drawn and compared across genes. Users can show exons, introns, and conserved parts in a clean figure for papers and talks. Good figures make gene comparisons clear to readers in seconds. The upgrade kept a popular free tool in step with the needs of genome research.
pmc-5510723:
Yavorska and Burgess made an R package in 2017 for gene-based causal tests that use summary data. The package is called MendelianRandomization. Such tests had spread fast because public summary data from gene studies are easy to get and free to use.

The package runs the field's main methods in one place. They include the inverse-variance weighted method, MR-Egger, and the weighted median method, all for sets of gene variants. When the methods agree, a causal claim gains strength; when they clash, the user gets a warning. Free shared tools like this raised the standard of work in the field and made results easier to check.
pmc-6245623:
Zachary Munn, Micah Peters, Cindy Stern, and coauthors wrote guidance on choosing between review types in 2018. Scoping reviews map what evidence exists on a topic. Systematic reviews answer a focused question with stricter methods.

At the time, little guidance helped authors pick the right approach. The authors spell out the aims, questions, and steps that set the two apart. Picking wrong wastes effort and can mislead readers about how firm the answer is. Their clear comparison is now cited in methods sections whenever a scoping review needs defending. Worked contrasts in the text show the same topic handled well by each approach.
pmc-6430823:
Parysatis Sachs, Dong Ding, Philipp Bergmaier, and coauthors reported a silencing role for the SMARCAD1 protein in 2019. Endogenous retroviruses are viral relics embedded in our genome. They can help the host, but loose activity threatens genome stability.

Working in embryonic stem cells, the team found SMARCAD1 enriched at these viral relics. When its enzyme activity was lost, the retroviruses woke up and nearby genes were disturbed. The result names a guardian that keeps ancient viral DNA quiet during early development. It adds a layer to how stem cells protect their genomes.
pmc-6651423:
Nathan Kelley, Devon Jeltema, and Yanhui Duan gave an overview of the NLRP3 inflammasome in 2019. This protein machine is a core part of innate immunity. It switches on an enzyme that releases two powerful inflammatory signals.

The review explains the two-step process: a priming signal, then a trigger from infection or cell damage. When control fails, the machine drives diseases from gout to Alzheimer disease. Blockers are in development for several of them. New readers get the activation logic, the regulators, and the disease list in one organized account.
pmc-6769923:
Luca Pinzi and Giulio Rastelli reviewed molecular docking in drug discovery in 2019. Docking predicts how a small molecule fits into a protein's binding pocket. It is a core computer method for finding new drug candidates.

The review traces how docking grew from rigid fitting to flexible, physics-aware scoring. It covers screening huge libraries, refining hits, and reading structure-activity patterns. Limits are plain too, since scores remain rough guides, not proof. Medicinal chemists read it for a balanced view of where the method shines and where experiments must decide. Case examples from real drug projects show where docking scores matched later experiments and where they failed.
price-new-geology-1923:
In 1923 George McCready Price published a geology textbook with a startling claim at its center. Price argued that the earth is young and that Noah's Flood, not slow change over ages, shaped the rock layers. He wrote against the view, then held by most geologists, that the same slow forces still at work today explain the past.

Price lays out his case layer by layer, reading fossils and strata as records left by one great flood. Later writers on creation and the Flood built on his scheme, which is why the book is often called the founding text of flood geology. It also shows the sharp clash between faith and science in its day.
principle-of-relativity-1923:
Methuen issued The Principle of Relativity in 1923, in W. Perrett and G. B. Jeffery's translation. Inside stand the primary papers of relativity by its makers. H. A. Lorentz and Albert Einstein represent the theory's first steps. H. Minkowski contributes Space and Time, his famed address on the new geometry of physics.

H. Weyl's Gravitation and Electricity carries the story into general relativity. Notes by Arnold Sommerfeld help readers through the hard parts. The volume let English readers study the sources, not just summaries. It fixed the canon of early relativity in one binding. Students still use it to meet the founders directly. Few source books match its lineup.
proudhon-general-idea-revolution-robinso:
John Beverley Robinson published his translation of Proudhon's General Idea of the Revolution in the Nineteenth Century in 1923. Proudhon wrote the work in 1851, from a French prison cell, as Louis Napoleon tightened his grip. It is his fullest plan for a free society.

Proudhon proposed ending rule by the state and letting work and trade run by free pact. He called for free credit, shared banks, and loose unions of towns and workshops. Robinson, an American writer, kept the case clear in English. The book links Proudhon's early attack on property to the shared, local plans that later rebels took up across Europe.
radin-the-winnebago-tribe-1923:
Radin's great monograph on the Winnebago, now called Ho-Chunk, appeared in 1923 in the annual report of the Bureau of American Ethnology. It was the fullest statement of his years of fieldwork with the tribe in Wisconsin and Nebraska.

The study centers on the medicine rite, a major ceremony taught in secret and passed down at great cost. Radin also describes the night-spirits society and prints autobiographies of native thinkers in their own words. His method treated Winnebago men as authors, not just informants. The monograph remains a foundation for the study of Native American religion.
rasaprakasasudhakara-1923-1923:
Rasaprakasasudhakara is a Sanskrit treatise on rasa, the mercury science of Indian alchemy. It is shown here in a second edition dated 1923, in the year Samvat 1980. Yadavji, son of Trikramji, edited and published it. Its long introduction, the bhumika, is in Sanskrit, printed in Devanagari script with some numbers garbled in the scan.

The introduction names the work's author as Yasodhara. He was the son of Padmanabha. He was a Gauda brahmin of Junagadh in Saurashtra. The introduction places him in the thirteenth century. It rests on Prafulla Chandra Ray's history of Indian chemistry. It then surveys the book's matter: the processing of mercury, the marks, qualities, cleansing, and killing of metals and minerals, instruments and furnaces, and rasa medicines.
rattray-ashanti-1923:
Robert Sutherland Rattray wrote Ashanti in 1923, the foundational ethnography of the Ashanti people of the Gold Coast. Rattray served as the colonial government's own anthropologist in what is now Ghana, recording law and religion at first hand for years. The Golden Stool, soul of the nation, abusua kinship, gods, shrines, and courts fill his account.

Ashanti priests, queen mothers, and elders speak through his pages, explaining custom in their own terms to the reader. Rattray's respect for his sources and his care with their words made the book a model of its kind. A century on, Ashanti remains a first source for the kingdom's religion, law, and social order.
richet-thirty-years-psychical-research-1:
Charles Richet looks back on a life's hunt in Thirty Years of Psychical Research, his book of 1923. Richet had won the top prize in the science of the body. He gave the field its French name, metapsychics. Here he sums three decades of sittings, tests, and famed seers from his own notes and the work of peers he trusts.

He grants fraud in bulk, yet holds a strange core stands firm. His calm, grave tone gives the claim weight. The book is the field's own tale of its first age. No sum since skips it.
robson-fixed-stars-and-constellations-19:
Vivian Robson was a British astrologer and librarian whose Fixed Stars and Constellations in Astrology appeared in 1923. The book gathers the lore of the fixed stars, the bright stars beyond the planets, into one compendium. It became the standard modern reference for stellar astrology.

Robson lists each star's position, nature, and reputed effects on health, fortune, and character, drawn from Ptolemy and the long tradition after him. He sorts a scattered inheritance of Greek, Arab, and modern claims into usable order. Astrologers still reach for Robson first when a chart raises a question about the fixed stars.
rowlands-mona-antiqua-restaurata-1723:
Henry Rowlands, a priest on the isle of Anglesey in Wales, wrote this study of the isle's old remains, first printed in 1723. The text here is from the 1766 second edition. Anglesey, called Mona in Latin, is rich in stone works from deep time.

Rowlands read the stone rings and tombs of Mona as druid shrines and graves. He built the first druid based view of the isle's past from its own ground. His scheme taught readers to see great stones as temples, a view that held for years. His maps and plates of the sites still have worth today.
saadi-gulistan-ross-1823:
James Ross published his translation of Saadi's Gulistan in 1823, the first English version of the most famous Persian prose classic. This text follows the 1890 Camelot reprint of Ross's work. Saadi wrote the Gulistan, meaning The Rose Garden, in 1258, after years of travel.

Eight chapters of short tales and verses treat kings, dervishes, lovers, and schoolboys with equal wit. A story may end in a laugh, a proverb, or a sudden sting of moral judgment. Persian speakers have memorized its lines for seven centuries, and Ross first opened that garden to English readers. Its humor keeps the moral lessons from ever feeling heavy.
santayana-scepticism-animal-faith-1923:
George Santayana published Scepticism and Animal Faith in 1923, the start of his mature system. Santayana pushes doubt to its limit, questioning even memory and the past. What survives is animal faith: the body's trust that a world exists and can be known in part. Knowledge, he says, is faith mediated by symbols.

He distinguishes essences, the pure characters of things, from matter and truth. The book is a modern classic of epistemology, the study of knowledge. Santayana's wit and calm style carry hard arguments lightly. Later volumes built the full system of The Realms of Being. This first volume can stand alone.
shaker-summary-view-1823:
Calvin Green and Seth Y. Wells wrote A Summary View of the Millennial Church in 1823. The work gives the first official account of Shaker faith. The United Society of Believers speaks here in its own voice.

Mother Ann Lee, the sect's founder, stands at the account's heart. Celibacy, shared goods, and the dance of worship mark Shaker life. The authors write at the height of their society's growth and fame. Their calm self-portrait explains a faith many outsiders found strange. Readers meet American communal religion drawn by its own leading hands. The book also serves historians as the Shakers' own yardstick of belief.
shakespeare-complete-works-1623:
William Shakespeare's plays and poems fill this complete works text, drawn from the First Folio canon of 1623. Fellow actors saved the plays in that folio seven years after his death. Project Gutenberg's standard text makes the whole set easy to search and read.

Inside are the great tragedies, the comedies, the histories, and the late romances. Hamlet, Macbeth, Lear, Falstaff, and Rosalind all speak in these pages. Sonnets and long poems sit beside the plays in one vast store. No single book in English holds so much of the tongue. Teachers reach for it for almost any age of English.
shakespeare-macbeth-1623:
William Shakespeare's Macbeth first reached print in the First Folio of 1623. The short, fierce tragedy tracks ambition and guilt in old Scotland. Three witches hail Macbeth as a future king and plant a dark seed.

Macbeth and his wife murder King Duncan to seize the throne. Guilt dogs them both, in sleepless nights and a spot of imagined blood. More murders follow, and Birnam Wood comes at last to Dunsinane. The play shows how a brave man can rot from one foul choice. Stage and screen return to its witches and daggers on stages yearly, in every land and tongue.
shakespeare-the-tempest-1623:
William Shakespeare's The Tempest first reached print in the First Folio of 1623. Most readers take it as his last solo play. Prospero, a duke turned mage, rules a lone island with his daughter Miranda.

A storm Prospero raises wrecks his old foes' ship on his shore. His sprite Ariel and the wild Caliban serve and chafe under his rule. Young Ferdinand and Miranda fall in love at first sight on the beach. Prospero tests them, forgives his foes, and gives up his magic staff. The play blends wonder, mercy, and a fond farewell to art.
shaw-saint-joan-1923:
George Bernard Shaw wrote Saint Joan in 1923, soon after the Catholic Church made Joan of Arc a saint. Shaw, then in his sixties, treated Joan not as a plaster saint but as a practical, stubborn genius. He called the play a chronicle play in six scenes and an epilogue.

The action follows Joan from Domrémy, where her voices send her to the French court, through her victories and capture. Church and state join to try her for heresy, and she is burned at the stake. An epilogue set years later shows her judges regretting their work. Shaw argues that institutions destroy the very saints they later honor.
sinclair-uncanny-stories-1923:
May Sinclair brought new thought on the mind to the ghost tale in Uncanny Stories, her set from 1923. She knew the work of Freud and his peers well. Her ghosts grow from guilt, grief, and wants long held down in the self.

Lovers parted by death meet in odd ways. A man's past sins take shape and dog him. Sinclair asks if the shade is real or a trick of a hurt mind. She leaves both doors ajar. The set marks a new, sharp turn for the old ghost tale. Sinclair helped found a clinic for mind care in London in her day. That work gave her tales a depth few ghost scribes could match.
spr-proceedings-vol33-1923:
Parts eighty five through eighty eight form volume thirty three, printed in 1923. The Society for Psychical Research spreads four parts across this single year. Telepathy experiments continue, now a tradition with its own classics. Reports on trance sittings take the largest share, as they long had.

Investigators compare new mediums against the great Piper record. Apparition cases, each with its witnesses and documents, keep their place. The society prints criticism from members who doubt the whole enterprise. Volume thirty three shows the archive in its last full decade. The debate of 1882 to 1930 nears its close here. Its files outlasted every verdict offered on them.
state-of-the-union-addresses-pg5023:
James Buchanan gives four yearly addresses, from December 8, 1857, to December 3, 1860, parted by three stars. The first performs the duty the Constitution commands in its own words: to give Congress word of the state of the Union and urge such steps as he judges needful and fit. First and above all, Buchanan says, thanks are due to God for the many gains granted this people.

Since Congress last parted, folk have known a rare degree of health, and the earth has yielded her fruits in plenty. Great staples brought high prices, and making, mining, and craft work shared the broad thriving till late. Yet with all the seeds of wealth in rich store, Buchanan warns, the country's money affairs stand at this hour in a sad state. Plenty in crops and goods has not saved the cash side of the nation from a hard fall.
stevens-harmonium-1923:
Wallace Stevens published Harmonium in 1923, his first book of poems. Stevens was an insurance executive in Hartford who wrote poetry on the side. The poems play with lush language, strange images, and bright wit. Sunday Morning, The Emperor of Ice-Cream, and Thirteen Ways of Looking at a Blackbird are among them.

Stevens pits imagination against plain reality and finds joy on the side of imagination. Florida scenes, music, and food recur in sensuous detail. The book sold poorly at first and Stevens wrote little for years. Later readers raised it to classic status. It remains a dazzling start to a major poetic career.
tales-and-novels-of-j-de-la-fontaine-vol:
Volume 23 of The Tales and Novels of J. de La Fontaine contains The River Scamander, The Confidant Without Knowing It, or The Strategem, and The Clyster. Love laughs at the poet's oaths from the first line of the volume.

He opens disposed to give a pretty tale, confessing that love will prevail over all he has sworn, since men and gods alike show full obedience to the urchin god. In future, he resolves, his expressions will not run so warm, and he would rather let his writing want spirit than plant abuses in it. The Scamander tale takes its name from the river of Troy. A lover's stratagem is played out there. The confidant and the clyster complete the set. The clyster is a doctor's instrument turned to farce. All three tales treat schemes that outwit their makers.
the-box-with-broken-seals-pg9923:
The Box with Broken Seals, by E. Phillips Oppenheim and dated 1919, starts in Chicago at the Hotel Magnificent. James Crawshay rests on a couch in a too-fine room, calm after a long trip. Hobson, the man who rode with him, walks the room and frets. Crawshay finds his collar foul with train coal and wants a bath. Hobson forbids it in sharp words.

The two must stay put till Chief of Police Downs arrives, Hobson says. He smells a crooked game in the call that brought them west, and fears a fake dispatch sent them on a fool's errand. Crawshay cools himself with an iced whisky and soda. Hobson leaves his own glass alone. He is a big, clean-shaven man with a square jaw and deep-set eyes, wholly given to his work. The wait, and the doubt, set the hook of the tale.
the-great-round-world-and-what-is-going-: Dated April 15, 1897, No. 23 of The Great Round World and What Is Going On in It is a weekly newspaper for boys and girls. Only front matter is present here. It gives the masthead and two appeals. One urges teachers to take the special trial subscription rate of $1 a year before the time expires. The other praises the paper itself to parents. Teachers today, it says, must keep pupils up with the questions of the day. Parents should watch the quality of reading placed before their children.

Number 23 of volume 2 of The Great Round World and What Is Going On in It, dated June 9, 1898, is also number 83 of the whole run. The paper is a weekly newspaper for boys and girls. Only front matter is present here. It gives the masthead and a rates notice. The notice repeats the rates of the other volume 2 numbers here. A year costs $1.50; six months, seventy-five cents. Foreign subscriptions cost two dollars and a quarter. It is published every Thursday of the year. Single numbers cost five cents.
the-history-of-don-quixote-volume-2-part:
In Ormsby's translation, Don Quixote by Miguel de Cervantes moves on to Volume 2, Part 23. Chapter nineteen relates the adventure of the enamoured shepherd, with other truly droll incidents. A short way past Don Diego's village, Don Quixote falls in with two priests or students and two peasants, all mounted on beasts of the ass kind.

One student carries a bundle wrapped in green buckram, holding a little linen and ribbed stockings, while the other carries new fencing gear. Meeting on the road turns into talk and company, in Cervantes' usual pattern. A wedding tale and a lovesick shepherd wait along this stretch of the journey.
the-phrenological-journal-and-miscellany: The Phrenological Journal and Miscellany, 1823. The Edinburgh journal. This book preserves that periodical. The historical record keeps it. Such papers rarely see the light of day. The file is now open to the public. The archive guards it with care.
thelma-pg3823:
Marie Corelli's Thelma opens in Book I, titled The Land of the Midnight Sun, under a quotation from Swinburne. Midnight over the Altenfjord brings no darkness and no stars. The sun stands visible like a king on a purple and gold throne.

Light turns the fjord water from bronze to copper, then silver and azure, while hills glow violet and red. A solitary refined man watches from a rug of skins on the shore. Readers get lush Norwegian scenery at the Arctic edge, where summer feels like Italy, before the human story has properly begun.
tob-0123:
William Reed argued in The Phantom of the Poles, published in 1906, that the earth is hollow and open at both poles. Explorers' reports of open water, warm winds, and birds flying north past the ice became his proof. Beyond the rim, he claimed, lies a warm inner world.

Reed answered objections with care and built his case like a lawyer. Later writers on the hollow earth treated his book as their bible. Science has long settled the matter against him: ships and planes have crossed both poles. The book survives as the most argued, and most enjoyable, statement of a lost theory.
tob-10623:
Ancient Egyptian priests carved the Book of Gates on tomb walls in the New Kingdom, the age of Egypt's empire. It maps the night voyage of the sun god Ra through the underworld. Tomb scenes pair its text with rich pictures of gods and beings.

Ra's boat passes twelve gates, one for each hour of night, each guarded by beings he must name and pass. Along the way the dead are judged and foes of order are punished, until the sun rises renewed. Alongside the Book of the Dead, it is a chief source for how Egyptians pictured the afterlife.
tob-10823:
H. P. Blavatsky edited Lucifer, a Theosophical magazine whose provocative title meant light-bringer, not the devil of popular fear. Volume one gathers the movement's monthly output at its combative start. Essays on occult philosophy, Eastern religion, and the hidden side of science fill its pages.
